context: He was Jesse B. Jackson, the United States vice-consul at Aleppo, who funneled relief to survivors and documented the catastrophe. Deir ez-Zor, on the Euphrates, was the terminal point of the death marches; historians estimate roughly 192,000 Armenians perished in that area alone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deir_ez-Zor_camps

question: As news of the Armenian Genocide reached America, ordinary schoolchildren gave their pennies to feed 'the starving Armenians' an ocean away. The relief group Near East Relief saved over a million refugees and raised 132,000 orphans, and a single rallying phrase became tied to its rescue mission. What was the phrase?
answer: They Shall Not Perish
choices: They Shall Not Perish
Lest We Forget Them
Bread For The Nations
Mercy Knows No Border
context: Founded in 1915 at Ambassador Morgenthau's urging, Near East Relief raised more than $116 million and cared for Armenian, Greek, and Assyrian orphans alike — one of the first great humanitarian campaigns in history. Source: https://neareast.org/our-history/

question: The Polish-Jewish lawyer Raphael Lemkin was haunted, as a young law student, by the Ottoman destruction of the Armenians and by the fact that no law on earth existed to punish it. In 1944 he built a brand-new word for the deliberate destruction of an entire people. Which word did he invent?
answer: genocide
choices: genocide
holocaust
pogrom
extermination
context: Lemkin built it from the Greek 'genos' (race or tribe) and the Latin '-cide' (killing). He later said the Armenian case was directly on his mind when he made the word, and he was the first person ever to write the phrase 'Armenian Genocide.' Source: https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/coining-a-word-and-championing-a-cause-the-story-of-raphael-lemkin

question: Aurora (Arshaluys) Mardiganian, a teenage survivor of the Armenian Genocide, was forced to march more than 1,400 miles, watched her family killed, and was sold in Anatolian slave markets before escaping to America. In 1919 a Hollywood silent film told her story — and she did something almost no survivor ever does. What did she do?
answer: She starred in it, playing herself on screen
choices: She starred in it, playing herself on screen
She refused to watch it and walked out
She sued the studio that had made it
She wrote the music score for it
context: The film was 'Ravished Armenia' (also called 'Auction of Souls'). Mardiganian testified she had seen sixteen young Armenian girls crucified, and the film depicted it; her tour helped raise enormous sums for Armenian relief. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora_Mardiganian

question: On a Berlin street in 1921, Soghomon Tehlirian, a young Armenian who had lost dozens of relatives in the genocide, shot the exiled Talaat Pasha dead. It was no lone act of rage: it was one killing in a secret Armenian campaign that had drawn up a hit-list of about 100 genocide organizers, with Talaat at the top. What was that campaign called?
answer: Operation Nemesis
choices: Operation Nemesis
The Dashnak Pact
Operation Ararat
The Zoryan Plan
context: Nemesis was the Greek goddess of retribution. Because the men who ordered the killings were never tried, survivors set out to deliver justice themselves; Tehlirian used a Luger pistol and shot Talaat once in the back of the neck. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soghomon_Tehlirian

question: Komitas, an Armenian priest and composer, had single-handedly rescued and written down thousands of Armenian folk songs — he is called the father of Armenian classical music. Arrested on April 24, 1915, he was freed after powerful friends intervened, but he had already seen the slaughter. What became of the man who saved Armenia's songs?
answer: He broke down and lived his last 20 years silent in an asylum
choices: He broke down and lived his last 20 years silent in an asylum
He fled to Paris and composed there into old age
He led survivors across the Syrian desert to safety
He went home and rebuilt the national choir
context: Among those who intervened to free Komitas was the U.S. ambassador, Henry Morgenthau. Having witnessed the killing, Komitas suffered a complete mental breakdown and spent his final two decades in psychiatric asylums, silent, until his death in 1935. The man who saved his nation's music was broken by watching its people die. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Komitas

question: When the American ambassador Henry Morgenthau begged him to stop the deportations of the Armenians, Talaat Pasha — the chief architect of the killings — gave one short answer and considered the matter closed. What did Talaat say?
answer: There are no more Armenians.
choices: There are no more Armenians.
The matter is out of my hands.
They will be returned after the war.
We did only what Russia forced on us.
context: His full reply, recorded in Vahakn Dadrian's History of the Armenian Genocide, was: 'What on earth do you want? The question is settled. There are no more Armenians.' The flat finality of that line captures the intent behind the killing better than any statistic. Source: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Mehmed_Talat

question: Henry Morgenthau Sr., the U.S. ambassador in the Ottoman capital, watched the deportations of the Armenians with his own eyes and cabled Washington on July 16, 1915. His words named exactly what he believed was happening — and became one of the strongest contemporary records that the killing was deliberate. What phrase did Morgenthau use?
answer: a campaign of race extermination is in progress
choices: a campaign of race extermination is in progress
a tragic famine has gripped the eastern provinces
a wartime disorder threatens the Christian population
a forced migration of doubtful necessity is underway
context: Morgenthau confronted the Ottoman leaders to their faces and later published what he saw in his 1918 book 'Ambassador Morgenthau's Story.' An American diplomat in the capital naming it 'race extermination' as it happened is among the clearest proofs that the killing was intended, not wartime chaos. Source: https://www.armenian-genocide.org/morgenthau.html

question: In May 1915 the Ottoman government gave its killing of the Armenians a legal disguise: a decree presenting the round-ups not as murder but as a routine, lawful wartime measure — the paperwork said one thing while the Syrian desert proved another. What did the decree claim the Armenians were merely undergoing?
answer: a temporary relocation for safety
choices: a temporary relocation for safety
an emergency military draft
a tax on enemy property
a quarantine against disease
context: The decree, passed May 29, 1915, is known as the Tehcir Law, or Temporary Deportation Law. Dressing genocide in the language of an orderly 'resettlement' is the trick later regimes copied: the paperwork said relocation, the desert held the truth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_genocide

question: Soghomon Tehlirian admitted in a Berlin courtroom that he had shot the exiled Talaat Pasha dead. Instead of denying the killing, his lawyers turned the proceedings into a trial of the genocide itself, parading evidence of the massacres before the world. Asked to speak, Tehlirian gave the court one unforgettable sentence. What did he say?
answer: I have killed a man, but I am not a murderer.
choices: I have killed a man, but I am not a murderer.
I only did what your courts refused to do.
Judge me as you judged my whole people.
I acted alone and I regret nothing at all.
context: The twelve-man German jury deliberated barely over an hour and acquitted him; the not-guilty verdict made headlines around the world and is part of what drew Raphael Lemkin to study the case. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soghomon_Tehlirian

question: A week before invading Poland in 1939, Adolf Hitler is reported to have brushed aside his commanders' fear that the world would punish mass murder, pointing to one earlier slaughter the world had already forgotten. Historians dispute the exact wording, so it survives as a contested quote — but as a warning it stuck: a forgotten genocide invites the next one. Which forgotten killing is Hitler reported to have named?
answer: the annihilation of the Armenians
choices: the annihilation of the Armenians
the famine in Soviet Ukraine
the massacres of the American Indians
the slaughter in the Belgian Congo
context: The line comes from a contested transcript, the 'L-3 document' handed to the Nuremberg prosecutors by the journalist Louis Lochner; some historians doubt its precise wording, which is why it is treated as testimony rather than verified record. Reported words: 'Who, after all, speaks today of the annihilation of the Armenians?' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hitler's_reference_to_the_Armenian_genocide  (Legend.)

question: At eleven o'clock in the morning on November 11, 1918, the guns of the Western Front went quiet and the fighting of World War I stopped. Officers loved how easy the date and time were to remember, because the war ended on a moment built entirely from one repeated number. What was that pattern?
answer: The eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month
choices: The eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month
The seventh hour of the seventh day of the seventh month
The ninth hour of the ninth day of the ninth month
The first hour of the first day of the first month
context: 11:00 a.m. on the 11th day of the 11th month, 1918 — three elevens — is why the moment is so easy to remember. November 11 became Armistice Day, first marked in 1919, and is honored today as Veterans Day in the United States and Remembrance Day in the Commonwealth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armistice_of_11_November_1918

question: The papers that ended World War I were signed inside a railway carriage — Marshal Ferdinand Foch's own dining car, parked on a hidden siding in the Compiègne forest in France. Twenty-two years later, in June 1940, that exact same carriage became the scene of a stunning act of revenge. What happened to it?
answer: Adolf Hitler had it hauled out so he could force a beaten France to surrender in it
choices: Adolf Hitler had it hauled out so he could force a beaten France to surrender in it
French soldiers hid it underwater in a flooded tunnel to keep it safe
It was given to the United States and put on display in Washington
It was rebuilt into a moving hospital train for wounded soldiers
context: In June 1940 Hitler had the carriage dragged from its museum back to the same forest clearing and made defeated France surrender inside it — even deliberately sitting in Marshal Foch's old chair before storming out early. The carriage was later taken to Germany and destroyed near the end of WWII in 1945, reportedly burned or blown up by the SS as American troops closed in; an identical sister car stands in its place at Compiègne today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compi%C3%A8gne_Wagon

question: The ceasefire ending World War I was set for exactly 11:00 a.m. on November 11, 1918, and commanders all along the line knew it was coming. An American soldier, Private Henry Gunther, charged a German machine-gun nest in the final moments — and the German gunners, knowing peace was seconds away, stood up waving and shouting for him to stop. He kept charging and fired, so they shot back. When was Gunther killed?
answer: At 10:59 a.m., one minute before the war ended
choices: At 10:59 a.m., one minute before the war ended
Three days after the armistice was already signed
The night before, in a raid that started early
At noon, an hour after the guns had fallen silent
context: Private Henry Gunther is considered the last soldier of any nation killed in World War I, shot at 10:59 a.m. — sixty seconds before the 11:00 ceasefire. He was one of about 2,738 men killed on that final day, even though commanders already knew the armistice had been signed before dawn (between roughly 5:00 and 5:45 a.m.) and had simply set the ceasefire six hours later. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Gunther and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armistice_of_11_November_1918

question: In 1917 the artist Marcel Duchamp bought a plain porcelain urinal from a New York plumbing showroom, laid it on its back, signed it with the fake name "R. Mutt," and submitted it to an art exhibition as a serious sculpture mocking the whole idea of "fine art." What single-word title did he give this urinal?
answer: Fountain
choices: Fountain
Cascade
Monument
Spring
context: Marcel Duchamp signed the urinal "R. Mutt 1917" and titled it Fountain, submitting it to the 1917 Society of Independent Artists exhibition in New York. The Society had promised to show any work by any artist who paid the fee — yet they rejected Fountain an hour before the show opened. Duchamp was secretly on the board himself and resigned in protest over his own anonymous urinal being thrown out. It became the most famous example of Dada "anti-art." Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fountain_(Duchamp)

question: The Spanish Surrealist painter Salvador Dalí filled his 1931 painting The Persistence of Memory with limp pocket-watches drooping and melting over a bare landscape. By Dalí's own account, the soft, melting look of the clocks came from staring at one ordinary thing he had just eaten at dinner. What was it?
answer: a runny Camembert cheese
choices: a runny Camembert cheese
a bowl of warm honey
a melted candle stub
a spoonful of soft butter
context: Dalí said the limp watches in The Persistence of Memory (1931) were inspired by a runny Camembert cheese melting on his plate. He built such dream-images using what he called the "paranoiac-critical method" — deliberately inducing a hypnotic, dream-like state so his hand would paint the irrational logic of dreams rather than the waking world. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/topic/The-Persistence-of-Memory ; https://www.salvadordali.com/melting-clocks-persistence-of-memory/

question: Under the Articles of Confederation, the United States Congress could not tax a single person — it could only ASK each state to chip in money, a plea called a requisition. In its last requisition before the Constitution, Congress asked the states for $3,800,000 to keep the country running. Of that enormous sum, how much did the states actually pay in?
context: Out of $3.8 million requested, the states sent a grand total of $663 — they treated the demands, in a phrase of the era, as 'mere recommendations' and 'pompous petitions for charity.' A government that can beg but not collect cannot pay its soldiers or its debts; this is the central reason the Constitution gave Congress the power to tax directly. Source: Constitution Annotated, Library of Congress (constitution.congress.gov, ALDE_00013388).

question: Under the Articles of Confederation, Congress could not stop states from taxing each other's goods like foreign rivals. New Jersey, lacking a great seaport, got squeezed between New York's port to the north and Philadelphia's port to the south, both draining its trade. Benjamin Franklin mocked poor New Jersey's plight with what homely image?
answer: a barrel tapped at both ends
choices: a barrel tapped at both ends
a sheep penned between two wolves
a coin worn smooth by two hands
a candle burned at both ends
context: Franklin likened New Jersey to a barrel tapped at both ends, its trade drained into New York and Philadelphia at once; the line is preserved in Abram Browning's 1876 Centennial speech. New Jersey struck back by taxing a New York-owned lighthouse on Sandy Hook. Source: libquotes.com (Franklin, via Browning 1876); Project MUSE, 'A Barrel Tapped at Both Ends.'

question: The Rigveda is the oldest collection of sacred hymns in India, and it opens by praising one particular god in its very first hymn. Which god does the Rigveda name in its opening words?
answer: Agni, the god of sacred fire
choices: Agni, the god of sacred fire
Indra, the dragon-slaying warrior
Soma, the sacred pressed potion
Savitr, the shining sun-god
context: The first word of the entire Rigveda is 'Agni' — the fire god. Hymn 1.1 opens by praising him, and roughly 200 of the Rigveda's 1,028 hymns are addressed to Agni, making him the most-invoked god after the warrior Indra. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigveda.

question: The Rigveda's books are called mandalas, and one whole mandala — all 114 of its hymns — is devoted from start to finish to a single deity, sung as his offering was strained and purified for the ritual. Which one of the Rigveda's three chief gods gets an entire book to himself?
answer: Soma
choices: Soma
Agni
Indra
Varuna
context: The 9th mandala — the 'Soma Mandala' — is made up entirely of 114 hymns sung as the soma juice was strained and purified. Soma is one of the Rigveda's three chief gods alongside Indra and Agni. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigveda; wisdomlib.org 'The Ninth Mandala of Rigveda'.

question: The single most famous verse of the Rigveda is a prayer to the sun-god Savitr that Hindus still chant every day, more than three thousand years after it was composed. By what name is this still-living daily prayer known?
answer: The Gayatri Mantra
choices: The Gayatri Mantra
The Soma Mandala
The Nasadiya Sukta
The jata-patha
context: The Gayatri Mantra (Rigveda 3.62.10), a prayer to the sun-god Savitr, is traditionally credited to the sage Vishvamitra and is preceded by the 'great utterance' om bhur bhuvah svah. It is still chanted daily by Hindus today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gayatri_Mantra.

question: For over a thousand years the Rigveda was never written down — it was kept perfectly by memory alone. To catch any slip, reciters even chanted the words backwards as a check, which works for one striking reason about Sanskrit. Why does reversing the words still let reciters verify the text?
answer: Reversing Sanskrit words doesn't change their meaning
choices: Reversing Sanskrit words doesn't change their meaning
The backward version is a separate sacred hymn
Only priests were allowed to hear the forward version
The words rhyme the same forwards and backwards
context: Reciters used elaborate cross-checking patterns: jata-patha 'braids' words forwards-and-backwards, and the hardest, ghana-patha or 'bell' mode, repeats them in bell-shaped back-and-forth sequences. Backward recitation works as an error-check because reversing Sanskrit words doesn't alter their meaning. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedic_chant.

question: In 2008 UNESCO honored Vedic chant as a Masterpiece of humanity's heritage, calling it 'a perfect canon' kept unaltered in word and even in sound. What sweeping claim did UNESCO make about this chanting?
answer: It may be the oldest unbroken oral tradition in existence
choices: It may be the oldest unbroken oral tradition in existence
It is the most widely performed chant on Earth today
It is the longest single hymn ever composed by anyone
It is the only chant memorized by an entire people
context: UNESCO named Vedic chant a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity on Nov 7, 2008, calling it possibly 'the oldest unbroken oral tradition in existence' and 'a perfect canon not just in terms of unaltered word order but also in terms of sound.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedic_chant.

question: The Rigveda's Hymn of Creation (the Nasadiya Sukta) asks how the universe began — but it refuses to give a confident answer. After wondering aloud, it says even the god who watches creation from highest heaven 'knows — or maybe even he does not know.' What did Carl Sagan praise this hymn for showing about ancient India?
answer: A tradition of skeptical questioning
choices: A tradition of skeptical questioning
A hymn of pure praise to the creator
A poem matching later Greek philosophy
The oldest written cosmology on record
context: The Nasadiya Sukta (Rigveda 10.129) opens 'Then even non-existence was not there, nor existence...' and ends not with an answer but a shrug. Carl Sagan praised it as evidence of ancient India's 'tradition of skeptical questioning.' Translation by A.L. Basham, The Wonder That Was India (1954). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasadiya_Sukta.

question: Around 1380 BC a peace treaty was signed in northern Syria between the Hittites and the Mitanni kingdom — far to the west of India. To seal their oaths, the two kings swore by Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatya twins. Why did this treaty astonish later scholars?
answer: Those are the same gods praised in the Rigveda, found far west of India
choices: Those are the same gods praised in the Rigveda, found far west of India
The treaty was written in flawless Sanskrit script
It named gods no other ancient people ever worshipped
It was the first treaty ever signed between two kingdoms
context: The Mitanni-Hittite treaty (c. 1380 BC) swore oaths by Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatya twins — Vedic deities — making it one of the earliest references to these gods anywhere, and turning up in Syria, far west of India. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Mitanni.

question: A Mitanni horse-trainer named Kikkuli wrote a training manual, preserved on Hittite clay tablets, that counts the horses' laps with words like aika, tera, panza, satta and na. Scholars seized on these counting words as hard evidence of one thing about the Mitanni elite. What did the numerals reveal?
answer: They were Indo-Aryan speakers, since the words match Sanskrit numbers
choices: They were Indo-Aryan speakers, since the words match Sanskrit numbers
They were Hurrian speakers who hired Indo-Aryan horsemen
The counting words were really Old Persian, not Sanskrit
The numbers were a secret jargon invented just for trainers
context: Kikkuli's lap-counts — aika (eka, one), tera (tri, three), panza (pancha, five), satta (sapta, seven), na (nava, nine) — are almost identical to Sanskrit numbers, hard evidence of an Indo-Aryan elite in the ancient Near East. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Mitanni.

question: The oldest spoked-wheel chariots ever found come not from India or Egypt but from steppe graves dated to roughly 1950 BC and buried with the first known bridle-bits. Which steppe people left these earliest chariot burials that scholars link to the ancestors of the Vedic Indo-Aryans?
answer: The Sintashta culture
choices: The Sintashta culture
The Mitanni kingdom
The Hittite empire
The Harappan cities
context: The Sintashta culture's graves in the southern Urals of Russia (c. 1950-1880 BC) hold the oldest spoked-wheel chariots ever found, buried with the first known bridles and bits. These Proto-Indo-Iranian steppe peoples are linked by scholars to the ancestors of the Vedic Indo-Aryans. The leading model holds that Indo-Aryan speakers moved into northern India around 1500 BC from the Central Asian steppes — a contested reconstruction from language, archaeology and genetics, not a settled date. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chariot; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Aryan_migrations.

question: On June 28, 1914 in Sarajevo, a young conspirator named Nedeljko Cabrinovic hurled a hand grenade at Archduke Franz Ferdinand's open-topped car. What happened to that grenade?
answer: It bounced off the car's folded roof and blew up under the next car in line
choices: It bounced off the car's folded roof and blew up under the next car in line
It exploded in mid-air directly above the Archduke's head
It landed in the Archduke's lap and he calmly threw it back
It rolled under the seat and failed to go off at all
context: The grenade had a 10-second fuse; it skipped off the convertible's folded-back roof, rolled into the street, and detonated under the following car, wounding roughly 16-20 people but leaving Franz Ferdinand completely unhurt. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Archduke_Franz_Ferdinand

question: Gavrilo Princip killed Archduke Franz Ferdinand with a small semi-automatic handgun that history would remember as the gun that effectively started the First World War. What pistol was it?
answer: A Belgian-made FN Model 1910
choices: A Belgian-made FN Model 1910
A British Webley service revolver
A German Luger P08
A Russian Nagant revolver
context: Princip fired an FN Model 1910 in .380 caliber from about 1.5 metres away. The car itself was a 1911 Graf & Stift open-top Double Phaeton. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Archduke_Franz_Ferdinand

question: Shot in the neck and bleeding to death in the car, Archduke Franz Ferdinand spoke his last words not about himself but to his wounded wife Sophie beside him. What did he say?
answer: "Sophie, Sophie! Don't die! Live for our children!"
choices: "Sophie, Sophie! Don't die! Live for our children!"
"Drive on, the show must go on as planned."
"Now they have what they wanted from us."
"Tell the Emperor I did my duty to the end."
context: He then repeated 'It is nothing' six or seven times before a violent choking from the hemorrhage. Both he and Sophie were dead by about 11:30 a.m. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/gavrilo-princips-sandwich-79480741/

question: Gavrilo Princip had fired the shots that triggered a world war, yet a court could not hang him. Born July 25, 1894, he had missed the law's cutoff for the gallows by just 27 days. What sentence did he get instead?
answer: The maximum prison term of 20 years
choices: The maximum prison term of 20 years
Hard labor for life in a fortress
A 15-year term cut short by his health
Banishment for life to a penal colony
context: Habsburg law set 20 as the minimum age for execution, and Princip was still 19 by less than a month, so he received the maximum 20-year sentence instead of the rope. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavrilo_Princip

question: After Governor Oskar Potiorek shouted that the motorcade had taken a wrong street, chauffeur Leopold Lojka braked and tried to reverse the Archduke's car. In doing so he made one fatal mistake that left the car dead in the road exactly where Gavrilo Princip was standing. What happened?
answer: He accidentally stalled the engine
choices: He accidentally stalled the engine
He backed into the car behind and jammed both
He turned the wheel and hit a lamppost
He flooded the brakes and rolled forward instead
context: The car came to a dead stop in front of Moritz Schiller's delicatessen, the exact spot where Princip happened to be. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/gavrilo-princips-sandwich-79480741/

question: After the failed grenade attack, Franz Ferdinand insisted on visiting the wounded at the hospital, so Governor Oskar Potiorek picked a safer route along the Appel Quay. The cars still ended up turning the wrong way onto Franz Joseph Street. Why did the drivers take the dangerous old route?
answer: No one had told the drivers the route was changed
choices: No one had told the drivers the route was changed
The new route was blocked by the bomb wreckage
The Archduke personally ordered the old turn
A crowd forced the cars off the safer road
context: Potiorek changed the plan but never passed it to the chauffeurs, so Leopold Lojka simply followed the cars ahead onto Franz Joseph Street, straight toward Princip. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Archduke_Franz_Ferdinand

question: His grenade having missed, Nedeljko Cabrinovic swallowed a cyanide capsule and leapt into the Miljacka River to kill himself before capture. Both attempts failed and he was simply dragged out and arrested. Why did they fail?
answer: The old cyanide only made him vomit and the river was barely ankle-deep
choices: The old cyanide only made him vomit and the river was barely ankle-deep
The capsule was a fake and police nets had been strung across the water
He lost his nerve and spat out the poison before reaching the bank
Bystanders pulled him back and forced an antidote down his throat
context: The cyanide had gone stale, and that dry summer the Miljacka was only about 13 cm (4-5 inches) deep, so Cabrinovic survived to be arrested. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Archduke_Franz_Ferdinand

question: A famous story says Gavrilo Princip was eating a sandwich at Schiller's delicatessen when the Archduke's stalled car appeared right in front of him. Historians say this tale grew up long after the fact, with no basis in the trial record. Where does the sandwich story actually come from?
answer: A 2001 Brazilian novel and a 2003 documentary
choices: A 2001 Brazilian novel and a 2003 documentary
A 1990s History Channel segment on the war
A 1920s newspaper interview with Princip himself
A Sarajevo cafe owner's memoir from the 1930s
context: LEGEND, not history: the shooting was around 10:55 a.m., too early for lunch, and sandwiches weren't a Sarajevo custom. The real cool fact is the wrong turn and the stalled engine, not a sandwich. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/gavrilo-princips-sandwich-79480741/

question: Two pistol shots in Sarajevo set off a chain of military alliances. Exactly one month after the assassination, on July 28, 1914, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. What happened over the following week?
answer: Germany, Russia, France, Belgium, and Britain were all dragged into the fighting
choices: Germany, Russia, France, Belgium, and Britain were all dragged into the fighting
Russia and France mobilized briefly, then both backed down and stood aside
Britain, Germany, and Italy brokered a settlement that kept the war between two nations
Serbia quickly surrendered and the great powers stayed out of the quarrel
context: The web of alliances meant Austria's declaration against Serbia dragged in the great powers within about a week, turning two gunshots into the First World War. Germany, Russia, France, Belgium, Montenegro, and Great Britain were all pulled in. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/the-assassination-of-archduke-franz-ferdinand

question: The Bosnian-Serb conspirators chose June 28 on purpose, because it fell on Vidovdan (St. Vitus Day), a sacred Serbian anniversary. What event from 1389 did that date commemorate?
answer: The Battle of Kosovo, where Prince Lazar fell to the Ottomans
choices: The Battle of Kosovo, where Prince Lazar fell to the Ottomans
The coronation of Stefan Dusan as the first Serbian emperor
The treaty by which Serbia broke free of the Habsburg crown
The founding of the Serbian church under the monk Saint Sava
context: Vidovdan marked the 1389 defeat where Prince Lazar died fighting the Ottomans; the date carried enormous symbolic weight for the assassins. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavrilo_Princip

question: The bombs and pistols used in the Sarajevo attack didn't come from the boys themselves. A Serbian secret society, run by Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijevic (code-named 'Apis'), the chief of Serbian military intelligence, supplied and trained them. What was that society called?
answer: The Black Hand
choices: The Black Hand
The Young Bosnians
The Carbonari
The People's Will
context: The Black Hand's agent Major Vojislav Tankosic supplied the FN pistols and bombs and trained the assassins. Apis himself was executed by firing squad in 1917. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Archduke_Franz_Ferdinand

question: At his trial Gavrilo Princip declared himself a Yugoslav nationalist seeking to unite all the South Slavs and free them from Austria. When the court asked by what method he meant to achieve it, what did he answer?
answer: "By means of terror."
choices: "By means of terror."
"Through honest persuasion."
"With a Russian army at our backs."
"By the will of God alone."
context: Princip stated his aim was 'the unification of all Yugoslavs... it must be free from Austria,' and named his method as terror. His co-conspirator Trifko Grabez testified he would never have taken part had he known it would lead to a European war. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Archduke_Franz_Ferdinand

question: Athens and Sparta were the two great rival cities of ancient Greece, and they raised their sons in completely opposite ways. An Athenian boy lived at home and studied music, poetry, and how to argue. But a Spartan boy, at just seven years old, was handed over to the city itself. What happened to a Spartan boy at age seven?
answer: He was taken from his parents to live in army barracks
choices: He was taken from his parents to live in army barracks
He was sent to a temple to be raised as a priest
He was shipped to a colony to farm new land
He was bound to a master to learn a craft trade
context: At seven, Spartan boys entered the 'agoge,' the state's brutal military schooling, and lived in barracks rather than at home — the mirror opposite of the Athenian boy, who stayed home studying music, poetry, and argument. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agoge

question: Sparta lay in a region called Laconia, and the Spartans were famous for using as few words as possible — which is why we still call a short, blunt reply 'laconic.' When the warlord Philip of Macedon sent a message threatening, 'If I invade Laconia, I will raze your city to the ground,' the Spartans sent back a reply just one word long. What was their entire answer?
answer: "If."
choices: "If."
"Never."
"Begone."
"Cowards."
context: Their whole reply was a single word: 'If.' — a dare daring Philip to even succeed at the first step. (This kind of polished one-liner is remembered as legend more than verified record.) Source: https://greekreporter.com/2025/11/03/spartan-wit-history-sharpest-one-liner/

question: Athens grew rich as a city of traders, its harbor packed with merchant ships from across the sea. Sparta wanted the exact opposite — no trade, no merchants, no one hoarding wealth or greedy for it. So Spartans were said to use money made of a material so bulky and worthless that storing a small fortune took a whole room and a team of oxen to haul it. What was Spartan money made of?
answer: Bars of iron
choices: Bars of iron
Tablets of clay
Shells from the sea
Coins of silver
context: Sparta supposedly used heavy iron bars instead of gold or silver, on purpose, so that wealth was too cumbersome to pile up or trade with — killing greed and commerce in one stroke. (Plutarch credits the lawgiver Lycurgus, but the story is part legend; a real later law banning Spartans from owning gold and silver coins is genuinely attested.) Source: http://kiwihellenist.blogspot.com/2018/02/paying-iron-price-spartan-money.html

question: In one single lifetime, golden-age Athens produced the philosophers, the great playwrights, and the first true historians — a burst of genius warlike Sparta never matched. The Athenians even invented a brand-new art form, putting on the world's first plays as part of a yearly religious festival. Which god was that drama festival held to honor?
answer: Dionysus, god of wine
choices: Dionysus, god of wine
Apollo, god of music
Athena, goddess of the city
Zeus, king of the gods
context: Greek theater was born as a festival for Dionysus, the god of wine — so the very first tragedies and comedies were a form of worship. Apollo (music) and Athena (Athens' own patron) are tempting guesses, but the stage belonged to Dionysus. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Athens

question: Pericles was the great statesman of Athens at its height, and over the bodies of the city's war dead he delivered the most famous speech in Athenian history, praising everything that made Athens special. One of his proudest boasts was about how Athens treated strangers and outsiders from other lands. Which boast did Pericles make about Athens and outsiders?
answer: "We throw our city open to all the world"
choices: "We throw our city open to all the world"
"We let no foreigner set foot inside our walls"
"We make the stranger swear to our gods or leave"
"We take the outsider's gold but never his counsel"
context: Pericles boasted Athens 'throws open the city to the world and never by alien acts excludes a foreigner' — the open city. The distractors describe closed-city policies; Sparta really did expel foreigners (a practice called 'xenelasia'), the opposite of what Pericles celebrated. He also called Athens 'the school of Hellas [Greece].' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pericles's_Funeral_Oration

question: Athens ran the boldest experiment in government the world had yet seen. Its great Assembly of citizens met on a bare hill called the Pnyx more than forty times a year to debate and vote on the city's laws. Picture an ordinary Athenian farmer who wants a say in a new law. What does he actually do at the Assembly?
answer: He climbed a platform and argued before the whole Assembly
choices: He climbed a platform and argued before the whole Assembly
He elected a representative to cast the votes for him
He mailed a written petition to a council of old nobles
He whispered his view to a city magistrate once a year
context: Athenian democracy was DIRECT, not representative: any adult male citizen could mount the speaker's platform (the 'bema') on the Pnyx and address the entire Assembly in person — no go-betweens. (Women, slaves, and foreigners, about three-quarters of the people there, had no vote.) Source: https://www.history.com/articles/ancient-greece-democracy

question: Athens had a strange power no other city did: it could banish a man for ten years for no crime at all, just by a vote scratched onto broken pottery shards. At one such vote a citizen who couldn't read handed his shard to a stranger and asked him to scratch on the name 'Aristides' — not knowing the stranger WAS Aristides. Why did the man want this Aristides banished?
answer: He was simply tired of hearing him called "the Just"
choices: He was simply tired of hearing him called "the Just"
He blamed him for a harsh tax that had ruined him
He had lost an important lawsuit that Aristides judged
He bitterly envied Aristides for his famous riches
context: The man didn't even know Aristides by sight — he just said he was sick of everyone forever calling the fellow 'the Just.' Aristides quietly wrote his own name on the shard, handed it back, and was banished. This banishment-by-pottery is where our word 'ostracism' comes from. Source: https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:abo:tlg,0007,024:7

question: You might expect the grim warrior city to crush its women, but the reverse was true: Spartan women trained in sports and were the freest women in all of Greece. When an Athenian woman asked Queen Gorgo why Spartan women were the only ones in Greece who could rule their own husbands, Gorgo gave a famously cutting reply. What did Gorgo answer?
answer: "Because we are the only ones who give birth to real men"
choices: "Because we are the only ones who give birth to real men"
"Because our husbands fear us more than they fear the foe"
"Because we alone are taught to fight beside our husbands"
"Because we alone of Greek women were never raised to obey"
context: Gorgo, wife of King Leonidas, shot back that Spartan women alone gave birth to (real) men. By the 300s BC Spartan women owned nearly two-fifths of all Sparta's land — a freedom the philosopher Aristotle actually blamed for Sparta's decline. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/123/spartan-women/

question: Athenian juries were enormous — often 500 ordinary citizens, sometimes 2,500 — because Athens trusted everyday people, not nobles or judges, to run its courts. In the courthouse stood a clever slab of stone, the 'kleroterion,' fitted with slots for citizens' bronze name-tickets and a tube that dropped black and white balls. What was this stone machine for?
answer: It picked the day's jurors purely at random
choices: It picked the day's jurors purely at random
It tallied the votes the jurors cast at a trial
It decided guilt on its own once evidence was heard
It chose which rich citizens would pay for a trial
context: The kleroterion chose jurors purely by chance: citizens slotted in bronze name-tickets, and a white ball meant a whole row served that day. Random selection meant no bribe could pick a friendly jury — radical trust in ordinary citizens, the opposite of Sparta's rule by a council of elders. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dikasterion

question: Sparta could train every man as a full-time soldier only because enslaved serfs called helots — conquered neighbors — did all the farming. The helots vastly outnumbered their masters, and Sparta lived in terror of a revolt. So every single year, Sparta's rulers did one chilling thing to the helots. What did the Spartan leaders formally do to the helots each year?
answer: Declared war on them, so any Spartan could kill one freely
choices: Declared war on them, so any Spartan could kill one freely
Drafted the strongest of them, to swell the army's ranks
Freed a chosen few of them, to reward their good behavior
Counted every one of them, to track how fast they multiplied
context: Sparta's five magistrates (the ephors) formally declared WAR on the helots every year, so killing one carried no religious guilt — state-sanctioned terror to keep the serfs cowed. At the battle of Plataea there were seven helots for every Spartan soldier. This was the hidden, ugly foundation that 'free' Sparta rested on. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helots

question: The two rival cities finally fought a brutal 27-year war (431-404 BC), and on paper they were mismatched: Athens ruled the sea with the mightiest navy in Greece, while Sparta's strength was its unbeatable army on land. Sparta could not break Athens — until it did the one thing that finally won the war. How did land-power Sparta beat sea-power Athens?
answer: It took Persian gold to build a fleet and beat Athens at sea
choices: It took Persian gold to build a fleet and beat Athens at sea
It marched a huge army over the mountains in deep winter
It burned every farm in the Athenian countryside to starve them
It bribed the Athenian generals into surrendering the city
context: To beat Athens, Sparta had to fight at sea — so it took GOLD from Persia, the very empire Greeks had united to defeat, and built a navy. The Spartan admiral Lysander then destroyed 168 Athenian ships at Aegospotami in 405 BC and starved Athens into surrender. (Burning the Athenian farmland really happened early in the war, but didn't win it.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peloponnesian_War

question: Spartan mothers raised their sons for one purpose: to win or to die, never to flee. A Spartan warrior carried a huge round shield, and a man who ran from battle would throw that heavy shield away to run faster — the ultimate disgrace. As her son left for war, a Spartan mother would hand him his shield with five famous words. What did she tell him?
answer: "With it, or on it"
choices: "With it, or on it"
"Guard it with your life"
"Bring it home to me"
"Win, or do not return"
context: 'With it, or on it' — come home carrying your shield in victory, or come home dead, carried ON it. To drop the shield and run was the deepest shame in Sparta. (Like the other polished Spartan sayings, this is remembered as legend more than documented fact.) Source: https://greekreporter.com/2025/11/03/spartan-wit-history-sharpest-one-liner/

question: When the dictator Julius Caesar was murdered on 15 March 44 BC, his will was opened and stunned everyone: he had adopted his teenage great-nephew, plain young Gaius Octavius, and made him chief heir. The boy instantly seized the single inheritance that mattered most of all. What did he take?
answer: Caesar's name
choices: Caesar's name
Caesar's villa
Caesar's sword
Caesar's crown
context: He became 'Caesar' overnight, the most powerful name in Rome handed to a teenager, along with the fortune. That name carried him to supreme power and outlived him as a title for emperors. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus

question: One month of our calendar is named after the first Roman emperor himself. In 8 BC the Senate renamed the old month Sextilis after him, because it was the month he first became consul, brought Egypt under Rome, and ended the civil wars. Which modern month carries his name?
answer: August
choices: August
March
October
January
context: Sextilis became 'Augustus.' His victories are literally written into the calendar every year. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sextilis

question: Augustus, the first Roman emperor, loved a tidy two-word Latin motto that a kid can still use today. He liked to say 'whatever is done well enough is done quickly enough,' and packed that whole idea into one short saying. What was the motto?
answer: 'Make haste slowly'
choices: 'Make haste slowly'
'Conquer by yielding'
'Win by losing'
'Rest, then strike'
context: 'Festina lente' means 'make haste slowly.' Suetonius records the emperor's fondness for the phrase and his saying that whatever is done well enough is done quickly enough. Source: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Augustus

question: Augustus, then still called Octavian, wanted to be remembered for rebuilding Rome itself. The historian Suetonius recorded his most famous boast: that he had taken over a shabby, flood-prone capital and turned it into a capital fit for an empire. How did Augustus sum up that transformation?
answer: 'I found Rome brick and left it marble'
choices: 'I found Rome brick and left it marble'
'I found Rome poor and left it rich'
'I found Rome small and left it vast'
'I found Rome weak and left it armed'
context: 'I found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble.' In Latin, 'Marmoream relinquo, quam latericiam accepi.' Suetonius adds the boast was 'not without reason,' since Augustus had transformed a city of mud-brick liable to floods and fires. Source: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 28 (perseus.tufts.edu).

question: At the sea battle of Actium in 31 BC, Octavian's fleet had cornered the ships of Mark Antony. Then one ally's squadron suddenly turned and bolted for open water, and Antony abandoned his whole navy to chase after that fleeing ship, throwing the battle and the future of Rome away. Whose flight wrecked Antony?
answer: Cleopatra's
choices: Cleopatra's
Agrippa's
Caesar's
Pompey's
context: Cleopatra's Egyptian squadron broke for the open sea; Antony followed her and left his navy to be destroyed by Octavian's admiral Agrippa. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Actium

question: In 27 BC the Senate retired the name 'Octavian' for good and crowned him with a brand-new title no Roman had ever borne: 'Augustus.' It was not a family name or a place, but an ordinary word lifted into a man's title for the very first time. What did that new word actually mean?
answer: 'the revered one'
choices: 'the revered one'
'the unconquered one'
'the firstborn one'
'the golden one'
context: 'Augustus' meant 'the revered' or 'consecrated one,' a word of religious awe hinting he was edging toward the divine. Granted 16 January 27 BC, the coined word marks the birth of the Empire. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reign_of_Augustus

question: Augustus's worst day came in AD 9, when his general Varus marched three whole legions into Germania's Teutoburg Forest and was ambushed and wiped out. Suetonius says the news so shattered the old emperor that for months he banged his head against a door, crying out one anguished sentence again and again. What did he cry?
answer: 'Varus, give me back my legions!'
choices: 'Varus, give me back my legions!'
'Varus, you have doomed us all!'
'Legions of Rome, avenge yourselves!'
'Forest of Germania, give back my dead!'
context: 'Quintili Vare, legiones redde!' He let his hair and beard grow in grief. The three legions were never re-raised. Source: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 23 (en.wikiquote.org).

question: Augustus died in AD 14 at seventy-five. Suetonius says that near the end the dying emperor calmly called for a mirror and had his hair combed, then asked his gathered friends one strange question about how he had handled his whole long life. He summed it up with one surprising image. How did Augustus describe his life at the very end?
answer: as a part played in a comedy
choices: as a part played in a comedy
as a battle hard fought
as a long road now ended
as a debt at last repaid
context: He asked if he had 'played the part well in the comedy of life,' then quoted Greek comedy: 'clap your hands and send us off with applause.' His true last words were to his wife: 'Livia, live mindful of our marriage; and now, farewell.' Source: Suetonius, Augustus (penelope.uchicago.edu).

question: Augustus carefully avoided the one Roman word that could get a man killed: 'rex' (king), a word Romans had hated ever since they threw out their kings. So instead of a royal title he picked a plain Latin word that dodged that hated name entirely, even as he quietly held all the armies. Which title did Augustus choose?
answer: princeps, 'first citizen'
choices: princeps, 'first citizen'
imperator, 'supreme commander'
dictator, 'absolute ruler'
tribunus, 'champion of the people'
context: 'Princeps,' meaning 'first citizen,' is why his system is called the Principate. The careful word let a king avoid being called a king. He also took 'Pater Patriae,' Father of his Country. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principate

question: In the Roman Forum stood a small shrine with double doors that were flung open in wartime and shut only when the whole empire was at peace, and in seven centuries they had been closed just twice. Augustus boasted he had managed to shut them three times, the great symbol of the Roman Peace. By the name of which god were those famous doors known?
answer: the Gates of Janus
choices: the Gates of Janus
the Gates of Jupiter
the Gates of Mars
the Gates of Saturn
context: The Gates of Janus (the 'Gates of War') were shut three times under Augustus, in 29, 25, and 13 BC, the vivid symbol of the Pax Romana. Janus was the two-faced god of doorways and beginnings. Source: https://www.livius.org/sources/content/augustus-res-gestae/

question: In his old age Augustus wrote his own resume in stone, a first-person list of everything he had done, titled 'The Deeds of the Divine Augustus.' The bronze originals stood at his tomb and are lost, but a near-complete copy survives carved on a temple wall in Ankara. By what Latin name is this stone autobiography known?
answer: Res Gestae
choices: Res Gestae
Pax Romana
Aeneid
Twelve Tables
context: The 'Res Gestae Divi Augusti' was engraved on two bronze pillars at his tomb; the surviving copy is the Monumentum Ancyranum in Ankara, Turkey. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Res_Gestae_Divi_Augusti

question: After his adoptive father Julius Caesar was murdered, Augustus swore revenge, and at the Battle of Philippi he vowed to build a temple if the gods let him pay the killers back. He won, and later crowned his grand new Forum with that promised temple, hailing the god in a brand-new 'Avenger' title to mark the vengeance fulfilled. Which god did Augustus honor as 'the Avenger'?
answer: Mars the Avenger
choices: Mars the Avenger
Bellona the Avenger
Victoria the Avenger
Quirinus the Avenger
context: The Temple of Mars Ultor ('Mars the Avenger') crowned the Forum of Augustus, fulfilling his vow at Philippi to avenge Caesar's murder. Source: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 29 (perseus.tufts.edu).

question: Augustus pulled off the ultimate magic trick of one-man rule. He kept the Senate, the consuls, and the elections, all the Republic's old forms, while really controlling the armies. In the memoir he carved in stone he summed up the trick in a single honest sentence, claiming that in the formal powers of his office he was no greater than his fellow magistrates, yet in one other quality he towered over them all. According to that sentence, what did Augustus have more of than anyone?
answer: authority, not legal power
choices: authority, not legal power
respect, not high office
fame, not armed force
honor, not the vote
context: Res Gestae 34: he 'surpassed all in authority (auctoritas), but had no more power (potestas) than the others.' Auctoritas was personal weight and influence; potestas was the formal legal power of an office. The honest trade in one sentence: the real control without the king's title. Source: https://www.judaism-and-rome.org/printpdf/res-gestae-divi-augusti-chapter-34

question: Augustus's forty-year rule gave Rome peace and stability, but at a price the old Republic had fought for centuries to prevent. When he died in AD 14, power did not return to the Senate and the people; it passed on to one chosen successor. What did the Republic permanently lose in that handover?
answer: its elected leaders, replaced by family succession
choices: its elected leaders, replaced by family succession
its trade routes, replaced by foreign tribute
its old gods, replaced by emperor worship
its standing army, replaced by hired troops
context: Power passed to his stepson Tiberius, setting the pattern that rule would pass within a family, the very thing the Republic had fought to prevent. The Senate declared the dead Augustus a god (divus). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus

question: The Germans built the camp they called Auschwitz right beside a small Polish town named Oswiecim. In which country - then under German military occupation - did the camp stand?
answer: Poland
choices: Poland
Germany
Austria
Czechoslovakia
context: Auschwitz stood about 40 miles west of Krakow, in German-occupied Poland. The original camp, Auschwitz I, opened on May 20, 1940 with its first 30 prisoners. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Auschwitz'.

question: Over the main gate of Auschwitz the SS forced prisoner metalworkers to forge an iron sign reading 'ARBEIT MACHT FREI' - 'Work Sets You Free,' a cruel lie to people being worked to death. As they built it, the prisoners slipped in one tiny, silent act of defiance the guards never caught. What did they do?
answer: Welded the letter B upside down
choices: Welded the letter B upside down
Spelled one whole word wrong
Hid their initials underneath
Bent the whole frame crooked
context: The upside-down B in 'ARBEIT' is still visible today - a small protest hidden in plain sight above the gate. Source: Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum; auschwitz-guide.com, 'The Arbeit Macht Frei Gate'.

question: Of every Nazi camp, only Auschwitz did one particular thing to the prisoners it sent to slave labor - a mark that stayed on survivors' bodies for the rest of their lives. What did the SS do to them?
answer: Tattooed a serial number on the forearm
choices: Tattooed a serial number on the forearm
Branded a triangle on the shoulder
Stamped a number on a metal collar
Shaved a wide stripe through the hair
context: Auschwitz was the only Nazi camp that tattooed prisoners with serial numbers, on the left forearm. SS doctors ran 'selections' on the arrival ramp: those judged fit were tattooed and sent to labor; the elderly, the sick, and most mothers with young children were sent straight to the gas chambers. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Auschwitz Camp Complex'.

question: The poison the SS dropped into the Auschwitz gas chambers, called Zyklon B, was nothing a person had to make in a weapons lab. Before the war it was sold in ordinary stores for an everyday job around farms and buildings. What was Zyklon B normally used for?
answer: Killing insects and rats
choices: Killing insects and rats
Fueling farm tractors
Cleaning factory floors
Preserving canned food
context: Zyklon B was a commercial pesticide - pellets of hydrogen cyanide. An SS man dropped the pellets through openings in the chamber roof, and the gas killed by asphyxiation. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Nazi Gas Chambers / Gassing Operations'.

question: On January 27, 1945, soldiers reached Auschwitz and freed about 7,000 prisoners, most of them so starved and sick they could barely stand. Whose army opened the gates that day - a date the world now keeps as International Holocaust Remembrance Day?
answer: The Soviet Red Army
choices: The Soviet Red Army
The American Army
The British Army
The Polish Home Army
context: Soldiers of the Soviet Red Army entered the camp on January 27, 1945. Most of the prisoners able to walk had already been driven away days earlier; those left behind were the ones too weak to move. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Soviet Forces Liberate Auschwitz'.

question: The Auschwitz complex had three main parts: the original main camp; a huge slave-labor camp built to feed a synthetic-rubber factory; and the killing center, where the gas chambers and crematoria stood. Which of the three was the killing center?
answer: Auschwitz II-Birkenau
choices: Auschwitz II-Birkenau
Auschwitz I
Auschwitz III-Monowitz
Auschwitz-Oswiecim
context: Birkenau, begun in October 1941, was the killing center. Auschwitz III-Monowitz served the I.G. Farben synthetic-rubber factory from October 1942. By spring 1943 four large gas-chamber-and-crematorium complexes were running at Birkenau. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Auschwitz'.

question: The Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum counts about 1.1 million people murdered at the camp. Most belonged to a single people - roughly one million of the dead. Which group was the largest by far?
answer: Jews
choices: Jews
Poles
Roma and Sinti
Soviet prisoners of war
context: The museum's figures: about 1,000,000 Jews, about 70,000 Poles, about 21,000 Roma and Sinti, about 15,000 Soviet prisoners of war, and some 12,000 others. Source: Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum, 'The number of victims'.

question: In the spring and early summer of 1944 one nation's Jews were sent to Auschwitz faster than any group in the camp's whole history - about 426,000 people in barely ten weeks, most gassed within hours of arriving. Which country had they been taken from?
answer: Hungary
choices: Hungary
Poland
Greece
the Netherlands
context: The deportation of the Hungarian Jews, from late April to early July 1944, was the single largest to Auschwitz. At the peak of the killing an average of about 6,000 Jews were gassed every day at Birkenau. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Auschwitz'.

question: At Auschwitz-Birkenau, the people picked to die were marched into a sealed underground room. To keep them calm and moving in an orderly line, the SS told them a gentle, ordinary lie about what was about to happen next. What did the guards say they were going to do?
answer: Take a shower
choices: Take a shower
Get a hot meal
Move to a new camp
Line up for new clothes
context: The victims were told they were going to take a shower; instead the doors were sealed and the Zyklon B was dropped in. The deception kept thousands moving quietly to their deaths. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Auschwitz / Gassing Operations'.

question: In April 1944 two Slovak Jews, Rudolf Vrba and Alfred Wetzler, broke out of Auschwitz and hid three days inside a hollow woodpile while SS guards and tracking dogs hunted them. They had prepared one clever trick to beat the dogs' noses. What had they done around their hiding place?
answer: Scattered tobacco soaked in gasoline
choices: Scattered tobacco soaked in gasoline
Rubbed mud and ash on their skin
Waded a mile down an icy stream
Smeared themselves with raw onion
context: The gasoline-soaked tobacco threw the search dogs off the scent. Once free, the two men dictated the 'Vrba-Wetzler Report' - the first detailed eyewitness account of the gas chambers, complete with maps - sent to warn the world. Source: Britannica, 'Rudolf Vrba'; Wikipedia, 'Vrba-Wetzler report'.

question: The SS doctor Josef Mengele stood on the Auschwitz arrival ramp and, with a flick of his hand, sent some new prisoners to the right and others to the left - and the left meant the gas chamber. The prisoners gave him a grim nickname for it. What did they call him?
answer: the Angel of Death
choices: the Angel of Death
the Butcher of Birkenau
the White Wolf
the Iron Surgeon
context: Mengele took part in at least 74 ramp selections between May 1943 and November 1944. He singled out twins for cruel experiments - drawing their blood and operating on them, often with no anesthetic. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Josef Mengele'.

question: When Soviet soldiers reached Auschwitz in 1945, the SS had fled but left warehouses still piled with the belongings of the murdered, among them thousands of suitcases. One detail painted on many of the cases made them almost unbearable to look at. What was written there?
answer: Their owners' names
choices: Their owners' names
A yellow cloth star
A red warning stamp
The SS skull badge
context: About 3,800 suitcases were found, roughly 2,100 still painted with their owners' names - people who had packed expecting to start a new life. The same warehouses held about 7,000 kg of human hair and around 110,000 shoes. Source: Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum, Historical Collection.

question: On October 7, 1944, the Jewish prisoners forced to work the Birkenau crematoria rose up in revolt. Women slave-laborers had smuggled them gunpowder a pinch at a time from a nearby munitions factory. Before the SS crushed the rising, what did the rebels manage to do with it?
answer: Blew up one of the crematoria
choices: Blew up one of the crematoria
Shot the camp commandant dead
Opened the gate for an escape
Burned down the Kanada warehouses
context: The Sonderkommando rebels destroyed Crematorium IV and killed several SS guards before being overwhelmed. In early January 1945 the SS publicly hanged four young women - including Roza Robota - for supplying the gunpowder. Source: National WWII Museum, 'The Sonderkommando Uprising'.

question: Rudolf Hoss, the commandant of Auschwitz, was asked at the Nuremberg trials how the guards could tell when the people locked in a gas chamber had finally died. He gave a flat, matter-of-fact answer that became one of the most chilling lines of the whole trial. How did Hoss say they knew the people were dead?
answer: The screaming stopped
choices: The screaming stopped
The guards checked pulses
A clock simply ran out
A doctor peered through glass
context: In his testimony Hoss said the Zyklon B took three to fifteen minutes, and that 'we knew when the people were dead because they stopped screaming.' He even boasted he had improved on the camp at Treblinka. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rudolf Hoss', citing his Nuremberg testimony and memoir.

question: After the war Rudolf Hoss, who had run Auschwitz longer than any other commandant, hid under the false name 'Franz Lang' until a Nazi-hunter tracked him down. In 1947 Poland sentenced him to hang. Of all the places they could have built the gallows, where did they choose to hang him?
answer: At Auschwitz, beside the crematorium
choices: At Auschwitz, beside the crematorium
At a prison yard in Warsaw
At Nuremberg, with the others
At an army base in Berlin
context: Hoss was hanged on April 16, 1947 on a small gallows next to the Auschwitz I crematorium - at the very place he had run. The German-Jewish Nazi-hunter Hanns Alexander had found him in 1946. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rudolf Hoss'.

question: Ibn Sina — known in Europe as Avicenna — wrote the Canon of Medicine, a five-book encyclopedia of over a million words. European universities such as Padua and Bologna taught from it for roughly 600 years, right into the 1600s. Doctors trusted this one book so completely that they gave it a nickname. What did they call it?
answer: The Medical Bible
choices: The Medical Bible
The Doctor's Mirror
The Book of Cures
The Healer's Almanac
context: Avicenna's al-Qanun fi al-tibb was translated into Latin in the 12th century and remained a standard medical textbook in European universities for about 600 years, in use as late as 1650 — earning the nickname the 'Medical Bible.' A book written in the Islamic world taught Europe's doctors for six centuries. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avicenna ; https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Avicenna

question: Ibn Sina — known in Europe as Avicenna — boasted he had mastered every science by eighteen. But one book defeated him: he read Aristotle's Metaphysics forty times until he nearly knew it by heart, yet still could not understand it, and fell into despair. What finally broke the riddle open for him?
answer: a cheap little commentary a bookseller talked him into buying
choices: a cheap little commentary a bookseller talked him into buying
a fresh translation a fellow scholar lent him
a vision of Aristotle that came to him in prayer
a debate he won against a famous rival scholar
context: After 40 readings left him stuck, a bookseller talked Ibn Sina into buying al-Farabi's short commentary on the Metaphysics for just three dirhams — and suddenly it all made sense. He was so overjoyed that he gave thanks to God and handed out alms to the poor. The greatest mind of the age was unlocked by a throwaway booklet he almost refused to buy. Sources: https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Avicenna ; https://iep.utm.edu/avicenna-ibn-sina/

question: Ahuitzotl, the greatest conqueror among the Aztec rulers, dedicated the rebuilt Great Temple of Tenochtitlan in 1487. His own name came from a monster of Aztec legend — and his name-glyph was carved as that creature. What did the carving show?
answer: A water-beast with a human hand at the end of its tail
choices: A water-beast with a human hand at the end of its tail
An eagle clutching a writhing serpent in its beak
A jaguar with a obsidian blade for each claw
A feathered serpent swallowing the evening sun
context: The 'ahuizotl' was a mythical aquatic monster said to lurk at the bottom of a lake and grab creatures that came to the water's edge; Ahuitzotl was the 8th Aztec ruler (reigned 1486-1502). Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Ahuitzotl'.  (Legend.)

question: In 1978, electrical workers digging behind the cathedral in Mexico City struck a giant carved stone disk at the foot of the Templo Mayor: the goddess Coyolxauhqui, her body hacked to pieces. The Aztec myth carved here tells how her newborn brother Huitzilopochtli burst from their mother's womb fully grown and armed, and killed her. What became of Coyolxauhqui's severed head afterward?
answer: It was flung into the sky and became the moon
choices: It was flung into the sky and became the moon
It was buried under the temple as an offering
It was turned to stone and became a mountain
It was carried off by her four hundred brothers
context: The Coyolxauhqui Stone is over 11 ft across and shows the goddess naked, beheaded, with arms and legs cut off; the chance find in 1978 sparked the INAH excavation of the buried Templo Mayor. In the myth, Huitzilopochtli sprang fully armed from Coatlicue's womb and struck Coyolxauhqui down, and her severed head was tossed into the sky and became the moon. Source: Wikipedia, 'Coyolxauhqui Stone'; World History Encyclopedia, 'Coyolxauhqui' and 'Templo Mayor.'

question: The Templo Mayor rose about 180 feet over Tenochtitlan, and at its summit stood not one shrine but two side by side — one painted red, one painted blue. Which two gods shared the top of the Great Temple?
answer: Huitzilopochtli, god of war and sun, and Tlaloc, god of rain
choices: Huitzilopochtli, god of war and sun, and Tlaloc, god of rain
Quetzalcoatl, the feathered serpent, and Xipe Totec, the flayed one
Coatlicue, the earth mother, and Coyolxauhqui, the moon
Mictlantecuhtli, lord of the dead, and Tezcatlipoca, the smoking mirror
context: The red shrine honored Huitzilopochtli (war and sun); the blue shrine honored Tlaloc (rain). A double flight of steps climbed the western face of the four-tiered pyramid. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Templo Mayor'.

question: For a heart sacrifice atop the Templo Mayor, four priests pinned the victim spread-eagled on his back across a stone slab while a fifth cut open his chest below the ribs with a stone knife. In that instant, what did the fifth priest do that was the whole point of the rite?
answer: Tore out the still-beating heart and held it up to the sun
choices: Tore out the still-beating heart and held it up to the sun
Pressed a jade bead onto the victim's tongue
Painted the victim's face blue for the rain god
Read the future in the pattern of the spilled blood
context: The knife was the 'tecpatl' (obsidian or flint); the slab was the 'techcatl'. After the heart was offered to the sun, the body was flung down the temple stairs. Source: Wikipedia, 'Human sacrifice in Aztec culture'; 'Tecpatl'.

question: At the climax of the spring festival for Xipe Totec, a brave captive was tethered to a round stone platform and forced to fight elite, fully-armed Eagle and Jaguar warriors — a duel rigged to be unwinnable. To guarantee he could not win, what weapon was the lone captive handed?
answer: A wooden club fitted only with feathers instead of blades
choices: A wooden club fitted only with feathers instead of blades
A single throwing spear with a fire-hardened tip
A short knife chipped from black flint
Nothing at all but his bare hands
context: The 'gladiator' sacrifice (tlahuahuanaliztli) set the feather-clubbed captive against warriors wielding the macuahuitl, a wooden sword lined with razor-sharp obsidian. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Xipe Totec'; Wikipedia, 'Xipe Totec'.

question: For centuries people argued whether Spanish accounts of Aztec skull racks were just propaganda to justify the conquest. Then Mexico's INAH archaeologists dug beside the Templo Mayor and found the Huey Tzompantli itself. What did this excavated structure prove?
answer: That the mass skull racks were real, not Spanish invention
choices: That the mass skull racks were real, not Spanish invention
That the Spanish had built the racks to frame the Aztecs
That the skulls came from a single plague, not sacrifice
That the racks held only carved stone heads, never real ones
context: Built around 1485-1502 in Ahuitzotl's era, the Huey Tzompantli was about 112 ft long, its hundreds of real skulls coated in lime and cemented into a tower — forensic confirmation of the practice. Source: Smithsonian Magazine (2017); NPR (2017).

question: The Aztecs built the Templo Mayor as the sacred mountain Coatepec, where the newborn war-god Huitzilopochtli sprang up fully armed, beheaded his sister the moon-goddess, and threw her dismembered body tumbling down the slope. Bodies cast down the real temple steps landed at a giant carved stone at its base. What did that arrangement deliberately re-enact?
answer: The moon-goddess Coyolxauhqui being hurled down the mountain
choices: The moon-goddess Coyolxauhqui being hurled down the mountain
The drowning of an enemy king beneath the sacred lake
The flooding of the world before the rain god relented
The first sunrise climbing over the eastern horizon
context: The carved disk at the temple foot showed Coyolxauhqui dismembered; every body flung down the stairs replayed Huitzilopochtli's defeat of his sister. Source: Smarthistory, 'The Templo Mayor and the Coyolxauhqui Stone'; Wikipedia, 'Coyolxauhqui Stone'.  (Legend.)

question: When archaeologists sorted the skulls cemented into the Huey Tzompantli tower, they expected captured warriors. By skull size and tooth development they instead found something that stunned them, making anthropologist Rodrigo Bolanos call it 'a first.' Whose remains turned up in the warrior skull tower?
answer: Women and at least three small children
choices: Women and at least three small children
Elderly priests of the rain god
Spanish soldiers killed in the conquest
Foreign kings sent as royal tribute
context: Bolanos said, 'Something is happening that we have no record of, and this is really new, a first in the Huey Tzompantli.' The find showed sacrifice reached beyond captured fighters. Source: NPR (2017); Smithsonian Magazine (2017).

question: The Aztecs believed the sun-god Huitzilopochtli was locked in endless war with the darkness, and that human blood was the debt that kept the sun moving — they called it 'nextlahualli,' the payment of debts. So at the 1487 dedication the friar Diego Duran recorded 80,400 captives killed, a number that would mean roughly 15 deaths every minute, day and night, for four days. Most historians reject that as impossible — what do they estimate the real toll was closer to?
answer: About 20,000
choices: About 20,000
About 250,000
About 500
context: Duran's 80,400 and the Spanish eyewitness claim of 100,000-plus skulls are treated as wild exaggerations; one Aztec source, the Codex Telleriano-Remensis, gives about 4,000. Even the lower estimates describe an enormous death toll. Source: Wikipedia, 'Human sacrifice in Aztec culture'; History.com.

question: Each spring the Aztecs honored a god whose priests flayed sacrificed captives in one whole piece and then wore the human skins for twenty days, calling the dried skin a 'golden garment.' This god, patron of goldsmiths and of spring, carried a name that says exactly what was done. What was he called?
answer: Xipe Totec, 'Our Lord the Flayed One'
choices: Xipe Totec, 'Our Lord the Flayed One'
Tlaltecuhtli, 'the Earth that Devours'
Mictlantecuhtli, 'Lord of the Land of the Dead'
Tezcatlipoca, 'the Smoking Mirror'
context: The festival was Tlacaxipehualiztli, 'the flaying of men'; the skin shed and regrown was likened to a maize seed losing its husk before sprouting, which made Xipe Totec patron of spring and goldsmiths. Source: Wikipedia/Britannica/World History Encyclopedia, 'Xipe Totec'.

question: The honest record runs both ways: as Spanish conquest ended Aztec sacrifice, Spain itself put the conquest on trial. At the Valladolid debate of 1550-51, the scholar Juan Gines de Sepulveda used Aristotle's idea of 'natural slaves' to argue that practices like human sacrifice justified conquering the Indians. The Dominican friar Bartolome de las Casas argued the opposite — what did Las Casas insist the Indians were?
answer: Rational free people who must be won by persuasion, not the sword
choices: Rational free people who must be won by persuasion, not the sword
Lost tribes of Israel owed protection by the crown
Subjects already conquered who owed labor by right
Heathens who could be enslaved until they converted
context: Emperor Charles V even halted new conquests while the question was argued, and no side was declared the clear winner. Las Casas spent his life denouncing the abuse of natives under the 'encomienda' forced-labor system. Source: Wikipedia, 'Valladolid debate'; History Today.

question: Years before that debate, in a 1539 lecture at Salamanca called 'Relectio de Indis,' the Dominican Francisco de Vitoria challenged Spain's right to rule the Americas at all. Because rights flow from human reason and natural law, he taught, not from being Christian, what did Vitoria say the native Americans had been before the Spanish ever arrived?
answer: The true owners of their lands and rightful rulers of their own peoples
choices: The true owners of their lands and rightful rulers of their own peoples
Wandering tribes with no claim to any settled territory
Vassals of a Christian empire they had simply forgotten
Property of whichever Christian king reached them first
context: Vitoria's argument — with later thinkers like Suarez — helped found modern international law, the 'law of nations' (ius gentium), out of the question of how the Indigenous peoples of the Americas should be treated. Source: Wikipedia, 'Francisco de Vitoria'; University of Nevada Reno.

question: At the top of the Templo Mayor, the great pyramid of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan, stood TWO temples side by side. One was painted blue-and-white for Tlaloc, the gentle rain god. The OTHER shrine belonged to the war god Huitzilopochtli. What color was it painted?
answer: Red, the color of blood
choices: Red, the color of blood
White, the color of bone
Green, the color of jade
Gold, the color of the sun
context: The twin shrines split the Aztec world in two: Tlaloc's blue-and-white half for water and life, Huitzilopochtli's red half for blood and war, atop a pyramid about 60 m (180 ft) high. Source: World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Templo_Mayor.

question: The Aztecs did not just build the Templo Mayor as a pyramid — they built it to BE a sacred hill from their myths, the place where their war god was born and crushed his enemies. Carved stone heads of one single animal ran the whole length of its great stairway. What animal's heads lined the stairs?
answer: Serpents
choices: Serpents
Jaguars
Eagles
Wolves
context: The hill was Coatepec, 'Snake Mountain,' where Huitzilopochtli was born and defeated his foes, so its stairway was lined with carved serpent heads — worshippers were climbing a man-made sacred mountain. Source: World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Templo_Mayor.

question: To cut open the chest of a sacrifice, an Aztec priest used a special knife called a tecpatl, chipped to an edge far sharper than steel. What stone were these sacrificial knives chipped from?
answer: Obsidian
choices: Obsidian
Marble
Chert
Granite
context: The tecpatl was knapped from obsidian (volcanic glass), or sometimes flint, to an edge sharper than a modern scalpel. Source: Human sacrifice in Aztec culture / Tecpatl, en.wikipedia.org.

question: In the Aztec creation story, the world was the 'Fifth Sun,' and at Teotihuacan a humble little god covered in sores, Nanahuatzin, threw himself into a sacred fire to become that sun. But the new sun just sat motionless on the horizon and would not move. What did the Aztecs believe finally set it moving across the sky?
answer: The gods feeding it their own blood
choices: The gods feeding it their own blood
A great wind sent by Tlaloc
The beating of a giant drum
The prayers of the first people
context: The sun moved only because the other gods sacrificed themselves to feed it; human sacrifice was understood as repaying that debt to keep the sun moving. Legend, from the Leyenda de los Soles (1558). Source: Five Suns, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Suns.

question: In the standard Aztec sacrifice, four priests held the victim spread-eagled over a stone block while a fifth cut the chest open and tore out the still-beating heart to offer to the sun. The Aztecs gave that torn-out heart a beautiful name. What did they call it?
answer: 'Precious eagle-cactus fruit'
choices: 'Precious eagle-cactus fruit'
'The red dawn-flower'
'The sun's own bread'
'The gift of warm rain'
context: The heart was the 'precious eagle-cactus fruit' and was placed in a carved stone bowl called a cuauhxicalli, the 'eagle vessel.' Source: Human sacrifice in Aztec culture, en.wikipedia.org.

question: During droughts the Aztecs sacrificed young children to Tlaloc, the rain god, and on the road to the altar the priests took great care to make sure each child was WEEPING — the more tears, the better the omen. Why did the priests want the children to cry?
answer: A child's tears were believed to call down rain
choices: A child's tears were believed to call down rain
Crying drove out the evil spirit of the drought
Tears were the only payment Tlaloc would take
A silent child was thought to anger the gods
context: Excavation of 'Offering 48' at the Templo Mayor (1980-81) found at least 42 children, mostly boys aged 2-7, sacrificed during the drought of 1452-1454; many showed signs of anemia and malnutrition. Source: Ancient Origins / La Brujula Verde.

question: After the heart was cut out, Aztec priests rolled the victim's body down the steep temple steps. At the bottom waited a huge round stone carved with the moon goddess Coyolxauhqui — her head, arms, and legs hacked off. Why was the body sent tumbling onto exactly THAT carving?
