answer: To re-enact the war god throwing his sister down Snake Mountain
choices: To re-enact the war god throwing his sister down Snake Mountain
To send the soul down to the moon goddess in the underworld
To feed the blood to the rain god buried beneath the stone
To hide the priests' work from the watching crowd below
context: Coyolxauhqui was Huitzilopochtli's sister, hurled down Snake Mountain in the myth; each falling body repeated her defeat. The 8.5-ton stone was found by electrical workers on 21 February 1978, launching the modern excavation. Source: Coyolxauhqui Stone, en.wikipedia.org.

question: To honor the god Xipe Totec, Aztec priests at the spring festival Tlacaxipehualiztli put something over their own bodies and wore it for twenty days, then shed it like a maize husk to stand for new green shoots bursting up in spring. What did the priests put on and wear?
answer: The flayed skins of sacrificed victims
choices: The flayed skins of sacrificed victims
Cloaks woven from green maize leaves
Masks carved from human skulls
Robes dyed with sacrificial blood
context: Xipe Totec's name means 'Our Lord the Flayed One'; the rotting skins were shed after 20 days to mirror a maize seed shedding its husk, then sealed in containers under the temple to trap the smell. Source: Britannica, britannica.com/topic/Xipe-Totec.

question: At that same Flaying festival came the 'gladiatorial sacrifice': a captive was tied by one ankle to a round stone platform and had to fight elite Aztec jaguar and eagle warriors who carried real obsidian-edged weapons. The fight was designed to be lost — so what was the lone captive given to fight with?
answer: A war club edged with feathers instead of blades
choices: A war club edged with feathers instead of blades
A short spear with no shield to guard himself
Only his bare hands and the rope at his ankle
A blunt wooden club used to train young boys
context: The captive's club (a macuahuitl) had its obsidian blades replaced with feathers; survivors of the tlahuahuanaliztli were rare. Source: World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Xipe_Totec.

question: For the festival Toxcatl, the Aztecs chose one flawless young captive to live for a FULL YEAR as the living image of the god Tezcatlipoca — dressed in gold and turquoise, given four wives, so honored that people kissed the ground as he passed. How did that golden year end for him?
answer: He climbed the temple steps and his heart was cut out
choices: He climbed the temple steps and his heart was cut out
He was set free to wander the land as a holy beggar
He led the army into the next war and fell in battle
He was walled up alive inside the temple as a guardian
context: On the feast day he climbed the steps alone, breaking one clay flute on each step, before the priests seized him and cut out his heart. The captive was the ixiptla, the god's living image. Source: Toxcatl, en.wikipedia.org; Sahagun, Florentine Codex Book 2.

question: Every 52 years the Aztecs held a ceremony they called the Binding of the Years. Every fire in the empire was put out, pots were smashed, and people dreaded that the sun might never rise again. When the Pleiades crossed overhead at midnight, the priests tore out a victim's heart and kindled a brand-new flame, which runners then carried out to relight every hearth in the land. In what unlikely place did the priests kindle that new flame?
answer: Inside the open chest of the victim
choices: Inside the open chest of the victim
On the summit of a high volcano
Inside the great palace of the emperor
On a reed raft out on the lake
context: This was the New Fire Ceremony; priests on the Hill of the Star kindled the flame inside the victim's open chest cavity, and runners carried it out to relight every hearth in the empire. The last such ceremony was in 1507 under Motecuhzoma II. Source: New Fire ceremony, en.wikipedia.org.

question: During the great famine of the 1450s, the Aztec priest-statesman Tlacaelel pushed a strange kind of war on neighbors like Tlaxcala — the 'Flower Wars' — whose goal was NOT to kill the enemy in the field or seize their land. The warriors were sent out to do something else entirely. What were they trying to do?
answer: Capture enemy warriors alive to be sacrificed
choices: Capture enemy warriors alive to be sacrificed
Burn the enemy's temples down to the ground
Steal the enemy's grain during the famine
Win honor in a fight where no one was hurt
context: Diego Duran reports Tlacaelel expanded the xochiyaoyotl and human sacrifice during the famine, keeping Tlaxcala unconquered as a permanent 'farm' for captives. Source: Flower war / Tlacaelel, en.wikipedia.org.

question: The Spanish soldier Bernal Diaz del Castillo left a horrified eyewitness account of the Templo Mayor: he heard its great snakeskin war-drum boom so loud it carried for miles, then watched 62 of his own captured comrades dragged up the temple steps to the altar. He wrote that he dreaded one thing every single day. What was it?
answer: That he would be dragged up those same steps next
choices: That he would be dragged up those same steps next
That the drum was calling the war god down in person
That his ground-up bones would go into the temple walls
That his trapped soul would never leave Snake Mountain
context: Bernal Diaz watched 62 captured comrades have their chests struck open and hearts torn out, and wrote that he feared every day the Aztecs would do the same to him. Source: Bernal Diaz, The History of the Conquest of New Spain.

question: The grandest entrance into ancient Babylon was the Ishtar Gate, a huge gateway sheathed in deep-blue glazed brick and covered with rows of golden animals that seemed to glow against the blue. Which three creatures marched across its face?
answer: A lion, a bull, and a dragon-snake
choices: A lion, a bull, and a dragon-snake
A lion, a horse, and an eagle
A lion, a bull, and a winged bull
A lion, a ram, and a serpent
context: Each beast belonged to a god: the lion to Ishtar, goddess of love and war; the bull to the storm god Adad; and the scaly dragon-snake, the mushhushshu, to Marduk, chief god of Babylon. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Ishtar_Gate/

question: Ancient writers said King Nebuchadnezzar II built the Hanging Gardens of Babylon as a gift to comfort his wife, Amytis of Media, who was homesick on the flat, dusty plain. What did the gardens give her back that she missed from home?
answer: The green forested mountains of her home
choices: The green forested mountains of her home
The salt sea that ringed her old city
The marble palaces of her childhood
The vast deserts she had crossed as a girl
context: The story is legend more than record: no Babylonian text mentions any queen named Amytis at all. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon/

question: The road that led up to Babylon's Ishtar Gate was called the Processional Way, and a visitor walking it was watched the whole way by the same animal, made over and over in glazed brick, striding alongside. More than 120 of which beast lined that avenue?
answer: Lions
choices: Lions
Horses
Bulls
Eagles
context: At New Year, priests carried the statues of the gods down the Processional Way past the watching brick lions. The lion was sacred to Ishtar, whom the gate was named for. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Ishtar_Gate/

question: Nebuchadnezzar's blue Ishtar Gate still stands today, and you can walk through it in person, but not in Iraq. Archaeologists shipped almost 800 crates of its broken glazed bricks out of Babylon and slowly rebuilt the gate piece by piece. In which city can you walk through it now?
answer: In a museum in Berlin
choices: In a museum in Berlin
In a museum in London
In a museum in Munich
In a museum in Paris
context: The German archaeologist Robert Koldewey shipped the fragments to Germany, where over decades they were desalted, cleaned, and reassembled into the towering gate now standing in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin. Source: https://isaw.nyu.edu/publications/newsletters/025/ishtar

question: The Greek historian Diodorus Siculus described the terraces of the Hanging Gardens as a green artificial mountain of trees rising about 20 metres into the sky. He said the planted levels were arranged in one particular shape. How did Diodorus say the terraces were laid out?
answer: Sloping up like the seats of a theatre
choices: Sloping up like the seats of a theatre
Spinning slowly on a great stone wheel
Floating on barges in the river
Hanging from chains off the palace roof
context: Diodorus never saw the gardens himself and wrote centuries after they supposedly stood, so this is a passed-down description, not an eyewitness one. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon/  (Legend.)

question: Towering over Babylon was a giant stepped temple-tower, a ziggurat named Etemenanki, 'House of the Foundation of Heaven and Earth.' Nebuchadnezzar boasted he raised it with baked brick and tar so its top would reach the heavens. By what far more famous name is this tower remembered today?
answer: The Tower of Babel
choices: The Tower of Babel
The Tower of Nimrod
The Temple of Bel
The Ziggurat of Ur
context: Ancient tablets put Etemenanki near 91 metres (about 300 feet) tall in seven stepped terraces with a temple on top. It is the structure the Bible remembers as the Tower of Babel. Source: https://www.historyofinformation.com/detail.php?id=123

question: In 539 BC the Persian king Cyrus the Great took Babylon, the mightiest city on earth, almost without a fight. His soldiers got past walls so huge a chariot could ride along the top. By what trick did Cyrus get his army inside the city?
answer: He drained the Euphrates and waded in under the walls
choices: He drained the Euphrates and waded in under the walls
He battered the bronze gates down with iron rams
He starved the city through a two-year siege
He bribed the wall guards to swing the gates open
context: Cyrus diverted the Euphrates into an old channel, dropping the water in the riverbed until his men could wade along the drained river and walk in through gates left open. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Babylon

question: The Bible says that on the very night Babylon fell, King Belshazzar was throwing a wild feast, drinking wine from golden cups his people had stolen from the Temple in Jerusalem. In the middle of the party, something terrifying happened that gave us a famous saying. What appeared?
answer: A hand appeared and wrote on the wall
choices: A hand appeared and wrote on the wall
A statue stepped down from its pedestal
A star fell burning into the hall
A voice thundered from an empty throne
context: A disembodied hand wrote glowing words on the wall, which is where we get the phrase 'the writing on the wall.' That same night the city was taken and Belshazzar was killed. Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/fall-babylon  (Legend.)

question: In 587 BC the army of Nebuchadnezzar II broke into Jerusalem and carried thousands of the Hebrew people into exile in Babylon, an event called the Babylonian Captivity. Before they were marched away, Nebuchadnezzar's soldiers burned the holiest building in the city to the ground. Which building did they burn?
answer: The Temple of Solomon
choices: The Temple of Solomon
The royal palace of the city
The great granaries by the gate
The library of the old kings
context: Nebuchadnezzar's men carried off the Temple's gold and silver vessels along with the people. Half a century later, in 538 BC, the Persian king Cyrus let the exiles go home. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Nebuchadnezzar-II

question: The priest Berossus, the historian Diodorus, and the geographer Strabo all left vivid written descriptions of the Hanging Gardens of Babylon. Yet when archaeologists dug through the ruins of Babylon for decades, hunting for the famous green mountain, they turned up one startling result. What did they find of the gardens?
answer: Nothing at all, not a single trace
choices: Nothing at all, not a single trace
The cracked stone steps of the terraces
The clay pipes that once watered the trees
The carved sign that named the garden
context: Of all Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, the Hanging Gardens are the only one no archaeologist has ever found a trace of, and not one Babylonian text or dug-up brick mentions them. The greatest wonder may be that they might never have stood in Babylon at all. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon/

question: Because no garden was ever found at Babylon, the British scholar Stephanie Dalley argues the famous Hanging Gardens were real but stood in a different city, built a hundred years earlier by a different king whose own carved inscription brags about planting a great park of mountain trees. Where and by whom does Dalley say the gardens were really built?
answer: At Nineveh, built by the Assyrian king Sennacherib
choices: At Nineveh, built by the Assyrian king Sennacherib
At Nineveh, built by the Egyptian pharaoh Necho
At Ur, built by the Sumerian king Gilgamesh
At Babylon, built by the queen Semiramis
context: Sennacherib boasted he planted 'a great park beside the palace... with all kinds of herbs and fruit trees,' and stone carvings from Nineveh actually show trees growing on tiered, arched terraces. This is Dalley's argued case, still debated. Source: https://www.biblicalarchaeology.org/daily/news/hanging-gardens-of-babylon-in-assyrian-nineveh/

question: A garden of trees stacked high in the air needs constant water lifted up to its top terraces, against gravity. The Greek geographer Strabo claimed the Hanging Gardens hid a clever device that pulled river water all the way up to the highest levels. What did Strabo say did the lifting?
answer: A hidden machine of screws pumping water upward
choices: A hidden machine of screws pumping water upward
A chain of slaves hauling buckets up the steps
A network of clay pipes fed only by rainfall
A deep stone well dug beneath the terraces
context: Strabo described screws inside the gardens drawing water up from the river to keep the high terraces green, an ancient water-lifting machine working against gravity. Like the rest of the gardens, it survives only in such written accounts. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon/  (Legend.)

question: In a Baroque fugue, one voice states a tune all alone, and then each new voice enters in turn and takes up that same tune while the others keep weaving around it. The word 'fugue' comes from the Latin 'fuga.' What does 'fuga' literally mean?
answer: To flee or chase
choices: To flee or chase
To sing in unison
To repeat note for note
To slowly grow louder
context: 'Fuga' = to flee or to chase: the subject is stated, then 'chased' by each entering voice, which is why a fugue feels like music pursuing itself. Source: New World Encyclopedia, 'Fugue' (newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Fugue); San Francisco Bach Choir (sfbach.org/what-is-a-fugue).

question: Johann Sebastian Bach had twenty children across two marriages, first to Maria Barbara and then to Anna Magdalena, though only about ten lived to grow up. What did four of his sons go on to become?
answer: Four became famous composers
choices: Four became famous composers
Four became court painters
Four became sea captains
Four became Lutheran priests
context: Wilhelm Friedemann, Carl Philipp Emanuel, Johann Christoph Friedrich, and Johann Christian Bach all became noted composers in their own right. Source: Classic FM, Bach's children (classicfm.com/composers/bach/guides/children); Britannica, 'Johann Sebastian Bach'.

question: For about eighty years after Bach died, his giant St. Matthew Passion went unperformed and half-forgotten, dismissed as old-fashioned. Then in 1829 a 20-year-old staged it again in Berlin, the first big performance in generations, and relaunched Bach's fame. Who was it?
answer: Felix Mendelssohn
choices: Felix Mendelssohn
Joseph Haydn
Johannes Brahms
Wolfgang Mozart
context: Felix Mendelssohn, only 20, conducted the St. Matthew Passion in Berlin on 11 March 1829, the first major performance in some 80 years, and essentially revived Bach's reputation. Source: Classical Music, 'How Mendelssohn helped bring back the St. Matthew Passion'; Library of Congress, Mendelssohn reviving Bach.

question: In Bach's own beautifully hand-bound manuscript of the St. Matthew Passion, most of the music is in ordinary brown-black ink, but he switched to deep RED ink for certain words so they would stand out on the page. Which words did Bach write in red?
answer: The words of Jesus
choices: The words of Jesus
The name of the king
His own signature
The title at the top
context: Bach inked the words of Jesus and the Gospel text in red and everything else in brown-black, so the sacred words literally stand out on the page. Source: Plough, Marianne Wright, 'Bach's Saint Matthew Passion'; Interlude (interlude.hk).

question: Bach's St. Matthew Passion is built so that two groups of singers and players, placed in the Thomaskirche's two organ lofts, can call back and forth across the church like two crowds answering each other. Going far beyond a single ensemble, what did Bach write it for?
answer: Two full choirs and two orchestras
choices: Two full choirs and two orchestras
Two boys' choirs and two organs
Two brass bands and two drummers
Two solo singers and two lutes
context: Bach scored the St. Matthew Passion for two full choirs and two orchestras at once, using the church's two organ lofts so the ensembles could answer each other across the space. Source: Wikipedia, 'St Matthew Passion'; LA Opera blog, Bach and the St. Matthew Passion.

question: On old keyboard tunings, many keys sounded badly out of tune, so most music stuck to just a few safe keys. To show off a new way of tuning, Bach wrote a matched prelude and fugue in 'The Well-Tempered Clavier' covering how many of the keys?
answer: All 24 keys, major and minor
choices: All 24 keys, major and minor
Only the 12 major keys
Only the 12 minor keys
Only the 7 easiest keys
context: Bach wrote a prelude and fugue in all 24 keys, every major and every minor, to prove a keyboard could be tuned so music sounded good in ANY key. Source: Britannica, 'The Well-Tempered Clavier, BWV 846-893'; Wikipedia, 'The Well-Tempered Clavier'.

question: A famous legend says Bach composed the gentle, looping Goldberg Variations to ease the sleepless nights of Count Keyserlingk, whose young harpsichordist Johann Gottlieb Goldberg supposedly played them when the count could not sleep. As a reward, what is the count said to have given Bach?
answer: A gold goblet of 100 coins
choices: A gold goblet of 100 coins
A silver crown of jewels
A velvet purse of pearls
A carved chest of silks
context: Legend: a golden goblet filled with 100 gold coins. Scholars now think the insomnia tale is mostly a charming myth. Source: Interlude, 'Sleep Gently, Count Keyserlingk' (interlude.hk); Wikipedia, 'Goldberg Variations'.

question: When Bach visited King Frederick the Great at Potsdam in 1747, the king handed him a tricky tune and dared him to invent a complex fugue on it then and there, with no preparation. What did Bach do right at the keyboard?
answer: Improvised a fugue on the spot
choices: Improvised a fugue on the spot
Refused and left the palace
Copied one from a songbook
Asked for a week to prepare
context: Bach improvised the fugue on the spot, then went home and built a whole work, 'The Musical Offering,' from the king's theme, labeling it RICERCAR, an acrostic for a Latin phrase meaning 'the theme given by the king, worked out in canon.' Source: Wikipedia, 'The Musical Offering'; Oxford Frederick the Great project (frederick.mml.ox.ac.uk).

question: Bach could spell his own name in music. In German notation B means B-flat and H means B-natural, so the four notes B-flat, A, C, B spell out B-A-C-H. He slipped this signature in as a theme inside the final fugue of which of his late works?
answer: The Art of Fugue
choices: The Art of Fugue
The Well-Tempered Clavier
The Goldberg Variations
The Musical Offering
context: Bach worked the B-A-C-H motif (B-flat, A, C, B-natural) into the last fugue of 'The Art of Fugue,' hiding his own name in the notes. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Art of Fugue'; Medium, 'The Bach Motif'.

question: In his 'Musical Offering,' Bach wrote a piece where one player performs a line from start to finish while a second player performs the very same line backwards, and the two parts fit together perfectly. Because of the way it works, what animal nickname did this canon get?
answer: The Crab Canon
choices: The Crab Canon
The Spider Canon
The Eagle Canon
The Serpent Canon
context: It is called the Crab Canon (canon cancrizans) because crabs move backwards, just as the second player plays the line in reverse, making it a musical palindrome. Source: Wikipedia, 'Crab canon'; kottke.org, Bach's crab canon.

question: Bach's last, unfinished fugue stops dead in the middle of a phrase, right after the four-note B-A-C-H signature appears in it. On the original manuscript, his son Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach added a note at that exact spot. What did the note say had happened?
answer: That his father died while writing it
choices: That his father died while writing it
That the rest was lost in a fire
That a pupil completed it later
That the ink had run dry
context: C.P.E. Bach wrote that 'where the name BACH was placed in the countersubject, the author died.' Modern scholars doubt Bach literally died mid-note, but the broken-off page is real. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Art of Fugue' (quoting C.P.E. Bach); Slate, 2008, on The Art of Fugue.

question: A famous tale claims the score of the St. Matthew Passion was nearly lost for good. The critic A. B. Marx reported that a Berlin shop was wrapping the goods it sold in pages torn from the score, until Bach's teacher Carl Friedrich Zelter got hold of a copy. What did the shop sell?
answer: Cheese
choices: Cheese
Fish
Bread
Soap
context: The legend says the pages wrapped cheese in a Berlin cheese shop. Scholars think the cheese-shop story is at least exaggerated. Source: Robert Greenberg on Medium (quoting A. B. Marx); skepticism noted at Wikipedia Talk, 'Johann Sebastian Bach'.

question: Bartolomé de las Casas first came to the New World as a Spanish colonist, and was granted an encomienda — a parcel of land worked by forced Indian laborers, handed to him to use as he pleased. Around 1514, after he decided the whole system was unjust, what did he do?
answer: He handed his Indians back to the governor and became the system's fiercest enemy
choices: He handed his Indians back to the governor and became the system's fiercest enemy
He sold his Indians to a wealthier planter and sailed back home to Spain
He doubled his landholding and drove the Indians to mine for gold
He kept his Indians but vowed to the governor to work them gently
context: Las Casas had owned forced laborers on Hispaniola and Cuba before he turned on the encomienda system and spent the rest of his life fighting it — the colonist who became its deadliest enemy. Source: World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/Bartolome_de_las_Casas); Wikipedia 'Bartolomé de las Casas'; Britannica.

question: In 1550 Emperor Charles V did something no monarch had done: he halted Spain's conquests in the Americas and summoned theologians to Valladolid to settle one question — was it just to wage war to subjugate the Indians? Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda argued they were barbarians and, by Aristotle's reckoning, 'natural slaves' fit to be conquered. Arguing in person against him, what was Bartolomé de las Casas's core answer?
answer: That the Indians were fully rational humans, able to govern themselves, so no people are 'natural slaves'
choices: That the Indians were fully rational humans, able to govern themselves, so no people are 'natural slaves'
That the Indians could be conquered, but only by Spanish soldiers who had first been baptized
That the Indians should be left wholly alone, with no Spanish priest or settler ever sent
That the Indians owed Spain nothing until the Pope himself had formally ruled on it
context: Answering Sepúlveda point by point, Las Casas held that 'All the World is Human' — the Indians had reason and could rule themselves, so the category of 'natural slave' was a lie. The judges named no winner and both men claimed victory, but it stands as history's first formal debate over the rights of an indigenous people, and a root of the natural-rights tradition. Source: Gilder Lehrman Institute 'Las Casas debates the subjugation of the Indians, 1550'; History Today 'The Valladolid Debate'.

question: In 1488 the Portuguese captain Bartolomeu Dias became the first European to sail around the southern tip of Africa, but he reached it in such violent tempests and currents that he named the headland for the weather that nearly killed him. What did Dias call it?
answer: Cabo das Tormentas, the 'Cape of Storms'
choices: Cabo das Tormentas, the 'Cape of Storms'
Cabo da Boa Esperanca, the 'Cape of Good Hope'
Cabo Verde, the 'Green Cape'
Cabo do Fim, the 'Cape of the End'
context: Dias named the southern tip Cabo das Tormentas in 1488 for the storms and currents that battered his ships. Portugal's King John II later renamed it the Cape of Good Hope, because rounding it opened the long-sought sea route toward India. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/bartolomeu-dias

question: After rounding Africa's southern tip in 1488, Bartolomeu Dias wanted to keep sailing all the way to India, but his men were exhausted and nearly out of supplies. How did the voyage actually end?
answer: His crew refused to go on, forcing Dias to turn back
choices: His crew refused to go on, forcing Dias to turn back
Dias pressed on alone and reached the coast of India
A rival Portuguese fleet ordered him home
Dias sailed onward and circled the whole continent
context: Dias appointed a council that agreed he could sail just three more days, then he had to turn for home. He returned to Lisbon in December 1488 after an absence of sixteen months and seventeen days. It would be Vasco da Gama, years later, who finished the route to India. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/bartolomeu-dias

question: Frederic Bastiat wrote a mock petition in which French candle and lamp makers beg the government to ban an unfair foreign rival who floods the market with light at an impossibly cheap price, ruining their trade. Bastiat's joke is the identity of that unbeatable rival. Who is it?
answer: The sun
choices: The sun
The Dutch
The English
The moon
context: In Bastiat's satirical 'Petition of the Candlemakers,' the makers demand a law shutting every window, skylight, shutter and curtain so the free light of the sun cannot enter, forcing France to buy candles by day. He used the absurdity to mock protectionist tariffs that punish cheap competition. Bastiat, 'Petition of the Candlemakers' (in Economic Sophisms, 1845). https://monadnock.net/bastiat/petition.html

question: Frederic Bastiat told of a shopkeeper whose son breaks a shop window; bystanders cheer that it's good for business, since the glazier now earns six francs. Bastiat argues the town is no richer at all, because everyone forgets one thing the shopkeeper can no longer do with those six francs. What is it?
answer: Buy new shoes or another book
choices: Buy new shoes or another book
Pay the glazier
Repair the window
Hire the careless boy
context: This is Bastiat's 'seen versus unseen': the SEEN is the glazier's six-franc job; the UNSEEN is that the same six francs would have bought the shopkeeper new shoes or another book for his library. The money is only moved, not created, so destruction never enriches a society. Bastiat, 'What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen' (1850), his last published work. https://www.econlib.org/library/Bastiat/basEss1.html

question: Japan's war planners budgeted just 50 days to capture the Bataan Peninsula in the Philippines in 1942. Starving on quarter-rations, the American and Filipino defenders refused to break on schedule. How many days did they actually hold out before surrendering?
answer: 99 days
choices: 99 days
52 days
75 days
120 days
context: The defenders held Bataan for 99 days before Major General Edward King surrendered on April 9, 1942. Historians link the brutal treatment that followed partly to Japanese commanders being enraged by the unexpectedly long fight and unprepared for tens of thousands more prisoners than they had planned for. Source: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/topics/battle-bataan-death-march

question: Lieutenant General Masaharu Homma commanded the Japanese 14th Army in the Philippines during the 1942 march in which thousands of surrendered American and Filipino prisoners were beaten, bayoneted, and starved to death. After the war he was tried on 43 counts and held answerable for his troops' conduct under command responsibility. What was his fate?
answer: Executed by firing squad
choices: Executed by firing squad
Imprisoned for life
Acquitted of all counts
Released after ten years
context: Homma was sentenced to death and executed by firing squad on April 3, 1946. He was held responsible not for atrocities he personally committed but for failing to control the soldiers under his command. Colonel Masanobu Tsuji, blamed for ordering the Pantingan River massacre of 350-400 captured Filipinos, escaped prosecution entirely and vanished in Laos in 1961. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bataan_Death_March

question: In the summer of 1940, the RAF's fighter pilots held off the entire Luftwaffe, Germany's air force, in the skies over southern England, outnumbered every single day. Winston Churchill honoured them with a one-word nickname so fitting it has stuck ever since. By what name are these pilots remembered?
answer: the Few
choices: the Few
the Brave
the Eagles
the Aces
context: Churchill coined it in his 20 August 1940 speech to the House of Commons. Ever since, the RAF pilots who fought the Battle of Britain have been known simply as 'the Few.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Never_was_so_much_owed_by_so_many_to_so_few

question: The Battle of Britain, fought from July to October 1940, earned a unique place in the whole history of warfare. What made it a genuine first?
answer: It was the first major battle decided entirely in the air.
choices: It was the first major battle decided entirely in the air.
It was the first major battle fought entirely at night.
It was the first major battle decided by aircraft carriers.
It was the first major battle won by tanks alone.
context: No armies clashed on land and no fleets met at sea. After France fell in June 1940, Britain stood as the only major power in Western Europe still fighting Nazi Germany, and the whole campaign was decided overhead. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Britain

question: Two British fighters won the Battle of Britain. The sleek Supermarine Spitfire became the legend everyone still remembers, but a plainer, tougher, easier-to-build plane actually destroyed more enemy aircraft than every other British defence put together. Which fighter did most of the real work?
answer: The Hawker Hurricane
choices: The Hawker Hurricane
The Bristol Blenheim
The Boulton Paul Defiant
The Gloster Gladiator
context: The unglamorous Hurricane shot down about 60 percent of all enemy aircraft destroyed in the battle. In tactics, Spitfires were sent high to tangle with the German fighter screen while Hurricanes tore into the bomber formations. Source: https://www.iwm.org.uk/history/why-the-hurricane-was-a-vital-aircraft-in-the-second-world-war

question: Britain's secret edge in 1940 was a line of tall towers strung along its south and east coasts. Long before German bombers reached the coast, these towers could detect them up to two hundred miles away, even while the raiders were still climbing into formation over France. What was this new invention that let the RAF 'see' the enemy coming?
answer: Radar
choices: Radar
Sonar
Searchlights
Spotter balloons
context: This was Chain Home, the world's first early-warning radar network. Its weakness: the towers faced out to sea, so once raiders crossed the coast the human-staffed Observer Corps had to track them inland by eye and ear. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_Home

question: After watching his outnumbered squadrons turn back raid after raid, Winston Churchill rose in the House of Commons on 20 August 1940 and captured the entire battle in one immortal sentence. How did that famous line go?
answer: Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few.
choices: Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few.
We shall fight on the beaches, and we shall never surrender to the foe.
I have nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears, and sweat.
Let us so bear ourselves that men will call this their finest hour.
context: Four days earlier, watching No. 11 Group's every squadron go up at once from the Uxbridge operations room, Churchill had told General Hastings Ismay in the car, 'Don't speak to me; I have never been so moved.' He turned that feeling into this line. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Never_was_so_much_owed_by_so_many_to_so_few

question: The Junkers Ju 87 'Stuka' dive-bomber had terrified Europe; its screaming dive had helped smash Poland and France in the Blitzkrieg. But over the English Channel in August 1940, the Battle of Britain put the Stuka to the test. What happened to it?
answer: British fighters shot it down so easily it was withdrawn.
choices: British fighters shot it down so easily it was withdrawn.
It smashed the airfields and broke Fighter Command.
It switched to sinking ships in the English Channel.
It was grounded by the autumn storms over France.
context: Over 20 percent of the whole Stuka force was lost between 8 and 18 August 1940, so the Luftwaffe pulled it out of the battle to save it. Its myth of invincibility was shattered over the Channel. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junkers_Ju_87

question: Nearly one in five of the RAF pilots who fought the Battle of Britain were not British at all; Poles, Czechs, New Zealanders, Canadians and others flew with them. The single highest-scoring ace of the entire battle, with seventeen kills, was a Czech sergeant flying inside the famous Polish No. 303 Squadron. Who was this top-scoring pilot?
answer: Josef Frantisek
choices: Josef Frantisek
Douglas Bader
Keith Park
Trafford Leigh-Mallory
context: About 595 of roughly 3,000 aircrew came from abroad, including 145 Poles and 88 Czechoslovaks. No. 303 Squadron joined two months late yet became the top-scoring RAF fighter unit, claiming 126 German aircraft in 42 days. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._303_Squadron_RAF

question: The RAF won the Battle of Britain not only through the courage of its pilots but through a war-winning machine: the world's first integrated air-defence network. It wove together radar stations, the human spotters of the Observer Corps, telephone lines, plotting rooms and radio control, so that precious fighters were scrambled only when a real raid had been detected. Named after the Air Chief Marshal who built it, what was this network called?
answer: The Dowding System
choices: The Dowding System
The Chain Home System
The Fighter Command System
The Bentley Priory System
context: It was named after Air Chief Marshal Sir Hugh Dowding. By scrambling fighters only against confirmed raids, it spared fuel, pilots and planes, the heart of how an outnumbered force kept winning. Source: https://www.iwm.org.uk/history/what-was-the-dowding-system

question: Deep inside Bentley Priory and the group operations rooms, the whole Battle of Britain was tracked on a giant gridded map of Britain. Around the map, plotters used long rods to slide colour-coded counters showing each German formation's position, height and strength, while controllers watched from a raised gallery and gave the order to scramble. Who were these plotters working the map?
answer: Women of the WAAF
choices: Women of the WAAF
Off-duty fighter pilots
Royal Navy sailors
Army signalmen
context: The plotters were members of the WAAF, the Women's Auxiliary Air Force. A wall clock divided into red, blue and yellow five-minute segments matched the counters, so anyone could see at a glance how fresh, or how stale, each plot was. Source: https://bentleypriorymuseum.org.uk/bentley-priory-and-the-battle-of-britain/the-many/

question: By early September 1940 the Luftwaffe believed it had nearly destroyed RAF Fighter Command, the force defending Britain's skies. Then, enraged by a British raid on Berlin, Hermann Goring's airmen made a fateful change of plan that historians count among the great blunders of the war, and it handed the battered RAF the breathing space it needed to recover. What did the Luftwaffe do?
answer: It stopped hitting the airfields and bombed London instead.
choices: It stopped hitting the airfields and bombed London instead.
It gave up daylight raids and attacked only by night.
It pulled its bombers back to France to refit.
It turned its full weight onto the Royal Navy.
context: The switch began on 7 September 1940, the first day of the Blitz on London. By taking the pressure off the airfields and radar stations, it gave Fighter Command exactly the time it needed to rebuild. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Britain

question: Before the war, air forces reckoned they would be lucky to intercept even a third to a half of any incoming raid. Britain's new integrated air-defence network changed that completely: by feeding radar and ground reports through filter rooms to the controllers, it guided fighters onto roughly nine of every ten raids. What did this do to Fighter Command's effective strength?
answer: It roughly tripled it
choices: It roughly tripled it
It roughly doubled it
It barely changed it
It cut it in half
context: The system lifted the interception rate to about 90 percent, against the 30-50 percent thought good before the war. In effect it tripled Fighter Command's strength, letting outnumbered British fighters keep beating larger German formations to the punch. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dowding_system

question: Air Chief Marshal Hugh Dowding had just masterminded the greatest air defence in history. Yet a bitter tactical quarrel, the 'Big Wing' feud, was raging: Trafford Leigh-Mallory and the legless ace Douglas Bader argued for massing whole wings of fighters, against the fast squadron-by-squadron scrambles Dowding and Keith Park had used to win. In November 1940, what became of Hugh Dowding?
answer: He was sacked from Fighter Command.
choices: He was sacked from Fighter Command.
He was promoted to head the whole RAF.
He was knighted by the King for the victory.
He retired quietly to write his memoirs.
context: In a striking twist, the man who built the winning system was relieved of Fighter Command within weeks of victory, partly over the Big Wing feud led by Leigh-Mallory and Bader, who wanted mass wings rather than the fast squadron scrambles Dowding and Park preferred. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Dowding

question: At Gaugamela in 331 BC, Alexander the Great wrenched a gap open in the Persian line. To exploit it he massed his Companion cavalry into one tight, pointed formation with himself riding at the very front. What shape did he drive at the enemy?
answer: A giant wedge, with Alexander at its tip
choices: A giant wedge, with Alexander at its tip
A long thin crescent curling around the flank
A hollow square bristling with spears
A double column splitting left and right
context: Alexander packed his Companion cavalry into a giant wedge with himself at the very point and drove it straight through the gap, aimed directly at King Darius III. When the wedge burst toward him, Darius turned and fled the field in his chariot; the moment his soldiers saw their king run, the Persian army collapsed. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/108/the-battle-of-gaugamela-331-bce/

question: Before Gaugamela, King Darius III chose his ground and had his soldiers level the battlefield plain perfectly smooth, so his cavalry and scythed chariots could charge across it freely. The preparation backfired. Why did the smoothed-out plain end up helping Alexander instead?
answer: The flat ground was ideal footing for Alexander's tight phalanx formation
choices: The flat ground was ideal footing for Alexander's tight phalanx formation
The dust kicked up blinded only the Persian archers
The cleared field left the Persians no walls to retreat behind
The level surface let Greek scouts count the Persian host exactly
context: Darius deliberately had the plain leveled smooth for his cavalry and roughly 200 scythed chariots, but the flat ground turned out to be perfect for Alexander's tightly packed phalanx. Alexander's light troops shot the chariot drivers and grabbed the reins, and the phalanx opened lanes to let the rest rumble harmlessly through, then closed up again. Source: https://www.livius.org/articles/battle/gaugamela-331-bce/

question: The Bayeux Tapestry tells the whole story of the year 1066 across 58 scenes and stretches nearly 70 metres (230 feet) long. Despite its name, it is not a tapestry at all. What kind of object is it really?
answer: A long strip of embroidered wool stitched onto linen
choices: A long strip of embroidered wool stitched onto linen
A woven wool-and-silk tapestry hung on a wall
A painted mural spread across wet plaster
A carved stone frieze set above a doorway
context: A true tapestry is woven on a loom; the Bayeux Tapestry is embroidery — coloured wool thread stitched onto bleached linen, like a 70-metre medieval comic strip. It survives today in a museum in Bayeux, Normandy, France. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayeux_Tapestry

question: After he won England, William the Conqueror built Battle Abbey directly on top of the Hastings battlefield. Tradition says the church's high altar was set down on the exact spot of one particular thing. What spot does it mark?
answer: Where King Harold was killed
choices: Where King Harold was killed
Where William was crowned king
Where the blazing comet first appeared
Where the English line first formed up
context: The battle was fought on 14 October 1066, not at Hastings itself but about 7 miles inland near the town now literally called Battle, in East Sussex. William placed the altar of Battle Abbey where Harold is said to have fallen. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hastings

question: Just 19 days before Hastings, King Harold of England won a huge battle 250 miles to the north at Stamford Bridge, crushing a Viking invasion. With William's fleet now landing in the south, what did Harold's worn-out army immediately have to do?
answer: Force-march roughly 200 miles south
choices: Force-march roughly 200 miles south
Rest and regroup for a full month
Sail the long way round the coast
Wait in London for fresh reinforcements
context: Harold's men had beaten the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada and Harold's own treacherous brother Tostig at Stamford Bridge on 25 Sept 1066, then had to march the length of England to meet William — arriving exhausted. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stamford_Bridge ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hastings

question: At the Battle of Hastings, King Harold's entire English army fought one way that William's Normans did not — and it was the choice that let them hold the hilltop all day. How did the English fight?
answer: Entirely on foot behind a wall of shields
choices: Entirely on foot behind a wall of shields
Mounted on horseback with heavy lances
From small boats along the nearby river
Hidden among the trees of a thick forest
context: Harold's housecarls stood in mail wielding two-handed Danish battle-axes, locked shoulder to shoulder. William's advantage was exactly what Harold lacked: heavy cavalry on horseback and ranks of archers. Harold had to hold the high ground; William had to break it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hastings

question: The Viking invasion that King Harold smashed at Stamford Bridge had crossed the sea in about 300 ships. The defeat was so total that when the few survivors were allowed to sail home, they needed only a tiny fraction of that fleet. About how many ships carried them back?
answer: About 24
choices: About 24
About 70
About 130
About 220
context: Around 300 Norse ships came; survivors needed only 24 to sail home — a measure of how many men never left. Both leaders, Harald Hardrada and the traitor Tostig, were killed. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stamford_Bridge ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hastings

question: In the spring of 1066 a blazing object appeared in the sky over England and was taken as a terrible omen for King Harold. It was later worked into the Bayeux Tapestry above a row of frightened onlookers, with the Latin words 'ISTI MIRANT STELLA' — 'These men marvel at the star.' This is the first known picture in all of history of what?
answer: Halley's Comet
choices: Halley's Comet
A total solar eclipse
An exploding supernova
The planet Venus blazing
context: The same comet returns about every 76 years, but nobody knew that in 1066. Centuries later the British astronomer Edmond Halley worked out its orbit and predicted its return, so it took his name — and the Bayeux Tapestry holds its earliest known image. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayeux_Tapestry ; https://www.physics.unlv.edu/~jeffery/astro/art/bayeux_tapestry.html

question: The English line held firm on the hilltop at Hastings all day, and wave after wave of Norman cavalry failed to break it. According to the chronicler William of Poitiers, the Normans finally cracked it with a single trick they used twice. What was the trick?
answer: They pretended to flee, then wheeled around on the chasers
choices: They pretended to flee, then wheeled around on the chasers
They dug tunnels under the English-held hill
They set the dry grass ablaze before the line
They simply waited the English out through the night
context: The 'feigned retreat': horsemen faked a panicked flight, luring English troops to chase them downhill — then turned and cut the scattered pursuers to pieces. Some historians suspect the story was polished later to disguise a real Norman rout. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hastings

question: Partway through Hastings, a rumor tore through the Norman ranks that Duke William had been killed, and his men began to break and run. To stop the panic, William did one bold thing as he rode along his own lines. What did he do?
answer: Tore off his helmet to show his bare face
choices: Tore off his helmet to show his bare face
Charged out alone straight at King Harold
Called down a fresh storm of arrows
Sounded the horns to retreat and regroup
context: William ripped off his helmet, rode along the line showing everyone he was alive, and shouted that he still lived — turning the panic into a counter-charge. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hastings

question: Before the northern battle, the towering Norwegian king Harald Hardrada — said to stand taller than any man around him — demanded that King Harold of England hand over land. Legend says an English messenger answered with a grim joke about exactly how much land Hardrada would get. What did he offer?
answer: Six feet of ground, or a little more
choices: Six feet of ground, or a little more
A rich earldom in the north
A chest of silver and gold
Half of England to rule
context: The full reply, from Snorri Sturluson's saga: Hardrada would get 'six feet of ground, or as much more as he needs, as he is taller than most men' — meaning a grave. Hours later Hardrada was dead. Told as legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stamford_Bridge

question: Legend says the fighting at Hastings was opened not by a charge but by a single Norman who rode out ahead of the entire army to face the English alone. What did this lone rider do as he closed on the enemy line?
answer: Rode out singing aloud and juggling his sword in the air
choices: Rode out singing aloud and juggling his sword in the air
Knelt to bless the whole army with holy water
Read out William's claim to the crown for all to hear
Planted the Pope's banner on the open hillside
context: The minstrel was named Taillefer. He rode out singing the 'Song of Roland' and tossing his sword, killed an Englishman who charged him, then plunged alone into the English line and was cut down — the first man to die at Hastings. Told as legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taillefer

question: Everyone 'knows' King Harold died with an arrow in his eye. But the earliest written source, the 'Carmen de Hastingae Proelio,' set down within months of the battle, gives a far gorier account with no arrow in it at all. How does the Carmen say Harold was killed?
answer: Four knights cut him down with lance and blade
choices: Four knights cut him down with lance and blade
A single arrow struck him through the eye
A crossbowman shot him from his horse
William himself ran him through with a spear
context: Per the Carmen, four knights set on Harold: one ran him through with a lance, the second cut off his head, the third speared his entrails, the fourth carried off his thigh. The arrow in the famous Bayeux Tapestry scene may itself be an 1800s repair — eighteenth-century drawings of the same figure show a plain shaft, not a fletched arrow. Some scholars think the real arrow-death belonged to Harald Hardrada (shot through the throat weeks earlier) and got transplanted onto Harold over time. Source: https://www.medievalists.net/2022/10/arrow-king-harold-eye/

question: William the Conqueror's whole claim to England rested on a broken promise. The Normans said Harold had once laid his hands on something and sworn to support William — then took the crown himself, which is what made the broken oath a sacred crime. What did Harold supposedly swear upon?
answer: A chest of holy relics
choices: A chest of holy relics
A great stack of gold
The old king's own crown
A Bible held out by William
context: Because Harold was said to have sworn on holy relics and then broken it, William won the backing of the Pope, who (per William of Poitiers) sent a consecrated papal banner to carry into the invasion. Sources: https://www.readingmuseum.org.uk/harold-makes-solemn-oath ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hastings

question: After taking the throne, William the Conqueror crushed rebellions in 1069-70 so savagely that whole villages were burned and starved. Sixteen years later, his great survey of England, the Domesday Book, still recorded estate after estate in those lands with a single grim one-word label. What was that word?
answer: Waste
choices: Waste
Burned
Empty
Cursed
context: The campaign is remembered as the 'Harrying of the North,' and the Domesday Book (1086) marked the ruined estates as 'waste.' By then only about 8% of England's land was still held by English owners — roughly 92% had passed to Normans. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrying_of_the_North ; https://www.thecollector.com/what-domesday-book-tell-norman-conquest/

question: In February 1945 American Marines landed on a tiny volcanic island sitting right on the bomber route to Tokyo. The island's Japanese name, Iōtō, told you exactly what it was made of. What did Iōtō mean?
answer: Sulfur Island
choices: Sulfur Island
Iron Island
Ash Island
Storm Island
context: Iōtō means 'Sulfur Island,' and the name was no exaggeration — the volcanic air on Iwo Jima actually stank of sulfur. The island mattered because it lay about 650 miles from Tokyo with airfields right on the route Allied bombers flew to Japan. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iwo_Jima ; National WWII Museum, nationalww2museum.org/war/topics/battle-iwo-jima

question: When the Marines stormed the beaches of Iwo Jima, the ground itself fought them: the slopes were piled up to fifteen feet deep with a loose material their boots and vehicles sank into, so deep they couldn't even dig a proper foxhole. What were the beaches made of?
answer: Black volcanic ash
choices: Black volcanic ash
Thick gray mud
Loose river gravel
Crushed coral sand
context: The beaches were soft black volcanic ash — men slid backward with every step and vehicles bogged down. It did have one mercy: the deep ash helped smother the blast of incoming Japanese shells. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Iwo_Jima

question: American commanders promised the Marines that taking the little island of Iwo Jima would be fast — they planned for roughly five days of fighting. Lieutenant General Tadamichi Kuribayashi's dug-in defenders had other plans. How long did the battle actually last?
answer: 36 days
choices: 36 days
19 days
12 days
21 days
context: The Marines expected about 5 days; the Japanese held out for 36 (19 February – 26 March 1945). The American codename for the assault was Operation Detachment. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Iwo_Jima ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadamichi_Kuribayashi

question: On 23 February 1945, Associated Press photographer Joe Rosenthal was atop Mount Suribachi when six Marines suddenly began hoisting a large American flag. He had only a split second to react. How did Rosenthal take what became the most famous war photograph in American history?
answer: He fired the shutter without even looking through the viewfinder
choices: He fired the shutter without even looking through the viewfinder
He posed the Marines and took three careful frames
He waited for the smoke to clear and zoomed in close
He climbed a ladder to shoot down from above them
context: Rosenthal swung his bulky Speed Graphic camera up and fired blind — he almost missed the shot entirely. That single frame won the 1945 Pulitzer Prize for Photography, the only photo ever to win in the same year it was taken. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raising_the_Flag_on_Iwo_Jima ; Pulitzer Prizes, pulitzer.org/article/joe-rosenthal-and-flag-raising-iwo-jima

question: The flag in Rosenthal's famous picture was actually the SECOND flag raised on Mount Suribachi that morning. The first was small, and an officer wanted to keep it as a souvenir — so battalion commander Chandler Johnson ordered a replacement raised that every Marine fighting across the island could look up and see. What were Johnson's orders about the new flag?
answer: "Make it a bigger one"
choices: "Make it a bigger one"
"Raise it before nightfall"
"Guard it with your lives"
"Fly it at half-staff"
context: Johnson said "And make it a bigger one," so troops fighting on the far side of Suribachi could see it. The little first flag measured 54x28 inches; the big replacement was 96x56 inches and came from the ship USS LST-779. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raising_the_Flag_on_Iwo_Jima ; military.com/history/story-behind-two-flag-raisings-battle-of-iwo-jima.html

question: After the battle, Fleet Admiral Chester Nimitz looked at the staggering casualty lists from Iwo Jima and summed up the Marines who fought there in a single sentence — a line later carved into the Marine Corps War Memorial. What did Nimitz say about the men of Iwo Jima?
answer: "Uncommon valor was a common virtue"
choices: "Uncommon valor was a common virtue"
"They died so that freedom might live"
"No finer fighting men ever drew breath"
"Their courage outlasted the longest night"
context: Nimitz's line — "Among those who served on Iwo Jima, uncommon valor was a common virtue" — is now engraved on the Marine Corps War Memorial in Arlington. Sources: National Museum of the Marine Corps, usmcmuseum.com/blog/uncommon-valor-was-a-common-virtue ; defensemedianetwork.com

question: The whole reason for taking Iwo Jima was its airfields, sitting right on the bombing route to Japan, and the payoff began while Marines were still fighting and dying for the island: on 4 March 1945 the first crippled American B-29 bomber set down safely on the runway. What was the name painted on that first bomber to be saved by Iwo Jima?
answer: "Dinah Might"
choices: "Dinah Might"
"Enola Gay"
"Bockscar"
"Memphis Belle"
context: The B-29 'Dinah Might' (a pun on 'dynamite') was the first of roughly 2,400 American bombers in trouble that would make emergency landings on Iwo Jima — saving an estimated 27,000 airmen who might otherwise have ditched in the sea. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Iwo_Jima ; National WWII Museum, nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/iwo-jima-sacrifice-and-sanctuary

question: Seventeen-year-old Private First Class Jacklyn 'Jack' Lucas was in a trench on Iwo Jima when two enemy grenades landed among his comrades. With no time to throw them back, Lucas did something that made him the youngest Marine ever to receive the Medal of Honor. What did Jack Lucas do?
answer: He threw himself on top of both grenades
choices: He threw himself on top of both grenades
He kicked them into a flooded shell hole
He hurled his helmet over the nearest one
He shoved his buddies out of the trench
context: Lucas pushed one grenade as deep as he could into the soft black ash; one failed to go off, the other blew up under him. His buddies thought he was dead and left him — but he lived. He had faked his way into the Marines at 14 by forging his mother's signature and stowed away to reach the battle; the blast left 250+ pieces of shrapnel in his body and he endured 26 operations. Truman pinned on his medal on 5 October 1945. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacklyn_H._Lucas ; nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/incredible-story-jack-lucas-youngest-medal-honor-recipient-world-war-ii

question: Gunnery Sergeant John Basilone was already a national hero — he had won the Medal of Honor at Guadalcanal — yet he insisted on returning to combat. On the very first day of Iwo Jima, 19 February 1945, what happened to John Basilone as he pushed his machine-gun section forward toward the airfield?
answer: He was killed by a bursting mortar shell
choices: He was killed by a bursting mortar shell
He was captured leading the assault
He was wounded and shipped home again
He was promoted on the battlefield
context: Basilone was killed on the first day on Red Beach by a bursting mortar shell and was awarded the Navy Cross posthumously — a Medal of Honor hero from one battle, killed in the opening hours of another. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Basilone ; usmcu.edu/Research/Marine-Corps-History-Division

question: During the first two days of the Iwo Jima landings, six U.S. Marines worked around the clock, sending and receiving more than 800 battlefield messages without a single error in a code the Japanese were never able to crack. Their signal officer, Major Howard Connor, said the Marines could never have taken Iwo Jima without them. Who were these six Marines?
answer: Navajo Code Talkers
choices: Navajo Code Talkers
Army cryptanalysts
British signals officers
Naval radio engineers
context: The Navajo Code Talkers built their unbreakable code on their own native language. Connor's exact words: "Were it not for the Navajos, the Marines would never have taken Iwo Jima." Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Iwo_Jima ; Navy history, history.navy.mil/research/library/online-reading-room

question: Lieutenant General Tadamichi Kuribayashi handed his men a written code called the 'Courageous Battle Vows,' copies of which Marines later found inside captured Japanese pillboxes. It spelled out exactly what he expected of every defender of Iwo Jima. How did Kuribayashi's final vow order each of his men to fight?
answer: Kill ten of the enemy before dying
choices: Kill ten of the enemy before dying
Hold the beach until reinforcements come
Surrender only on his direct command
Fall back to the northern caves
context: The last of the vows read: "Each man will make it his duty to kill ten of the enemy before dying." Kuribayashi forbade the wasteful 'banzai' charges other commanders used and instead made his men sell every yard dearly — which is why this tiny island cost so much. Sources: Issuu/Faircount USMC Iwo Jima 75, issuu.com/faircountmedia/docs/iwo_jima_75_marines ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadamichi_Kuribayashi

question: Years before the war, Lieutenant General Tadamichi Kuribayashi — the man who would defend Iwo Jima to the death — had lived in the United States as a military attaché, studying at Harvard and the University of Michigan. Having seen American factories and power up close, what did he repeatedly warn his own family about the United States?
answer: "America is the last country in the world Japan should fight"
choices: "America is the last country in the world Japan should fight"
"America will soon tire of war and seek peace"
"America's soldiers have no stomach for losses"
"America can be beaten if Japan strikes first"
context: Kuribayashi knew American industrial might firsthand and told his family America was the last country Japan should ever take on. He was probably killed leading a final attack in the early morning of 26 March 1945 — and held that grim conviction as he defended the island. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadamichi_Kuribayashi

question: Most likely in the early morning of 26 March 1945, Lieutenant General Tadamichi Kuribayashi led one last attack and was killed somewhere on Iwo Jima. Yet the Americans could never identify his body, and to this day it has never been found. Why couldn't they identify him?
answer: He had stripped off all his officer's insignia
choices: He had stripped off all his officer's insignia
He had burned his own face beyond recognition
He had switched uniforms with a dead private
He had been buried by his men beforehand
context: Kuribayashi deliberately removed every badge of his rank before that final charge, so no enemy could ever identify the commander who had cost them so dearly. His body was never recovered. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadamichi_Kuribayashi

question: In July 1943 the Germans hoped to surprise the Red Army at the Kursk salient, but Soviet forces dug in for weeks beforehand because Moscow already knew the exact attack plan. How did the Soviets learn German intentions so precisely?
answer: The 'Lucy' spy ring in Switzerland and British Ultra decrypts of German radio traffic
choices: A captured German general gave up the whole plan under interrogation
The 'Lucy' spy ring in Switzerland and British Ultra decrypts of German radio traffic
A double agent inside Hitler's bunker smuggled out the orders by courier
Soviet scouts photographed the German maps from a downed reconnaissance plane
context: Moscow learned of Operation Citadel almost as soon as Hitler approved it on 15 April 1943, thanks to Rudolf Roessler's 'Lucy' ring in Switzerland feeding precise German intentions, plus British Ultra decrypts of Enigma traffic. The Soviets fortified exactly where the pincers would strike. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Operation_Citadel; Wikipedia, Battle of Kursk.

question: On 12 July 1943 General Pavel Rotmistrov's tanks took brutal losses at Prokhorovka. Reporting to Stalin, Rotmistrov claimed his crews had destroyed 400 German tanks, including 70 Tigers, in a heroic charge of point-blank ramming. When historian Ben Wheatley later studied Luftwaffe aerial photos of the field, what did they actually show?
answer: The Germans lost only about five tanks while the Soviets lost roughly 250 or more
choices: Rotmistrov had undercounted — the Germans lost closer to 600 tanks
The Germans lost only about five tanks while the Soviets lost roughly 250 or more
Both sides lost almost exactly the same number, about 200 tanks each
The famous battlefield was empty — the clash happened miles away
context: The legend of T-34 crews ramming Tigers was largely invented by Rotmistrov himself to explain his catastrophic losses to Stalin. Many of his T-34s had charged downhill into ground they had not scouted and tumbled into a 4.5-meter anti-tank ditch dug by their own side, exposing their flanks. Aerial-photo study ('Shattered Myths: The Tank Battle at Prokhorovka') put German losses at roughly five. Framed as legend: Rotmistrov's ramming account is testimony, not forensic fact. Source: the-past.com/feature/prokhorovka-the-greatest-tank-battle-in-history/.

question: The very first modern Olympic marathon, run in Athens in 1896, was won by a 23-year-old local named Spyridon Louis. Before he became a national hero, what humble job did Spyridon Louis do for a living?
answer: He was a water-carrier
choices: He was a water-carrier
He was a goat-herd
He was a fisherman
He was a stonemason
context: Spyridon Louis hauled his father's mineral water into Athens, a city with no central water supply. He won by over seven minutes before about 100,000 spectators and ran the final lap flanked by two Greek princes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spyridon_Louis

question: After the Battle of Marathon in 490 BC, the 192 Athenians who had died were cremated and buried on the spot, exactly where they fell on the plain. What still marks that grave today?
answer: A great earthen mound
choices: A great earthen mound
A row of marble pillars
A bronze statue
A stone temple
context: The mound is called the Soros, a roughly 9-meter-high earthwork still standing on the Marathon plain. Herodotus put the dead at 192 Athenians and 11 Plataeans, against 6,400 Persians counted on the field. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Marathon

question: As the huge Persian army landed in 490 BC, the Athenians sent their best professional long-distance runner, Pheidippides, racing off on foot to beg for help. Which city did Pheidippides run to for aid?
answer: Sparta
choices: Sparta
Thebes
Corinth
Argos
context: Herodotus says Pheidippides covered the roughly 150 miles to Sparta in about two days, then ran back. In Herodotus this Sparta run is the ONLY run Pheidippides makes; the famous Marathon-to-Athens death run is not in Herodotus at all. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pheidippides

question: When Pheidippides reached Sparta and begged for help against the Persians, the Spartans said yes in spirit but refused to march yet. What were they waiting for before their army could leave?
answer: For the moon to grow full
choices: For the moon to grow full
For new shields to be forged
For an oracle to be consulted
For the spring floods to fall
context: Spartan religious law forbade marching until the full moon, and it was only the ninth day of the month. They arrived after the battle was over, toured the field, and praised the Athenian dead. Athens essentially won Marathon without them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Marathon

question: Pheidippides came back from his run to Sparta with a strange story: high in the mountains of Arcadia, he said, a god had stopped him, called him by name, and grumbled that the Athenians had been ignoring him. Which god did Pheidippides claim to have met? (told as legend)
answer: The god Pan
choices: The god Pan
The god Hermes
The god Apollo
The god Zeus
context: Pheidippides reported that Pan complained the Athenians neglected him despite his friendliness and past help. After the war the grateful Athenians built Pan a shrine in a cave below the Acropolis. Herodotus relays this as Pheidippides's own testimony. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pheidippides  (Legend.)

question: A marathon is famously 26 miles 385 yards, an oddly exact number. The first 1896 Olympic race was only a round ~40 km, so the strange extra distance came later. What stretched the course to that precise length?
answer: Moving the finish to a royal box
choices: Moving the finish to a royal box
Matching the old run to Athens
A surveyor's measuring error
A rule copied from ancient Greece
context: At the 1908 London Games the course was extended to start at Windsor Castle and finish in front of the royal box, making it 26 miles 385 yards (42.195 km). That distance became the official standard in 1921. Source: https://www.britannica.com/sports/Why-Is-a-Marathon-26-2-Miles

question: The modern marathon's name and its triumphant cry of 'Rejoice, we conquer!' do not come straight from the ancient battle; they come from a Victorian writer. What did Robert Browning's 1879 poem about the runner directly inspire?
answer: A new Olympic race
choices: A new Olympic race
A famous oil painting
A children's adventure novel
A military marching song
context: Frenchman Michel Breal, moved by Browning's poem 'Pheidippides,' proposed a 'marathon' race for the very first modern Olympics in Athens in 1896. The poem, not the ancient record, gave the race its battle-cry. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pheidippides  (Legend.)

question: At Marathon the Athenian general Miltiades had too few men to match the wide Persian line at full strength everywhere. To stretch his front the same width without breaking, how did Miltiades arrange his hoplites?
answer: He thinned the center and kept the wings strong
choices: He thinned the center and kept the wings strong
He stacked every rank evenly across the line
He held most men back in a deep reserve
He spread the strongest fighters in the center
context: Miltiades cut his center to only four ranks deep instead of the usual eight. The center buckled on purpose while the strong wings wheeled inward and surrounded the Persians, a double envelopment. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Marathon

question: At Marathon the Athenians did something no Greek army had ever been recorded doing: instead of advancing slowly, they sprinted across about a mile of open ground straight at the Persian line, with no cavalry or archers of their own. How did the Persians read this charge?
answer: They thought the Athenians had gone mad
choices: They thought the Athenians had gone mad
They mistook it for a surrender
They assumed it was a feint
They believed reinforcements had come
context: Herodotus says this was the first time a Greek army is recorded running into battle. The sprint cut their losses to Persian arrows and shocked the enemy, who could not believe men would charge an empire with no horsemen or bowmen. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Marathon

question: As the beaten Persians fled to their ships at Marathon, an Athenian named Cynaegirus, brother of the playwright Aeschylus, seized the stern of a Persian ship with his bare hands to stop it sailing away. What did a Persian do to him for it?
answer: Hacked off his hand with an axe
choices: Hacked off his hand with an axe
Ran him through with a spear
Dragged him under the waves
Struck him down with an arrow
context: Cynaegirus died this famous death gripping the ship. Also killed that day was Callimachus, the war-archon (polemarch) who had cast the deciding vote to attack in the first place. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Marathon

question: Winning the battle did not end the danger: the Persian fleet rowed around Cape Sounion to grab the city of Athens while it sat undefended. To save their city, what did the exhausted Athenian hoplites do right after the fight?
answer: Force-marched the army back to Athens
choices: Force-marched the army back to Athens
Sent a single runner ahead to warn the city
Sailed a captured Persian ship home
Lit warning fires along the coast
context: The just-victorious hoplites marched roughly 25 miles straight back and lined the shore, so when the Persian ships arrived they gave up and sailed home. THIS desperate march by a whole army, not one runner, is the real 'marathon.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Marathon

question: Everyone 'knows' a runner gasped out the news of victory and dropped dead, yet Herodotus, the earliest source, never tells that story at all. Where does the famous drop-dead version actually first appear? (the death tale is legend, not eyewitness record)
answer: In Lucian, writing 600 years later
choices: In Lucian, writing 600 years later
In a Spartan war monument
In Herodotus's own footnotes
In an Athenian victory hymn
context: The satirist Lucian (2nd century AD) has a runner named 'Philippides' cry 'Nenikekamen' ('We have won!') and die on the spot. Lucian is the only ancient source with every element of the modern legend; over the centuries Herodotus's Pheidippides, Plutarch's Eucles, and Lucian's Philippides got merged into one hero. Source: https://sententiaeantiquae.com/2015/12/06/myths-of-marathons-herodotus-lucian-plutarch-and-us/

question: In the spring of 1942, six months after Pearl Harbor, the Japanese navy steamed toward the tiny American base at Midway atoll meaning to crush the U.S. Pacific Fleet for good. Instead, on June 4, American carrier dive-bombers found the four Japanese fleet carriers and sank every one of them in a single day. Before Midway, Japan had been winning almost everywhere in the Pacific. What did this one day of fighting do to the war?
answer: It turned the tide of the Pacific War
choices: It turned the tide of the Pacific War
It forced Japan to surrender within weeks
It ended all fighting in the Pacific
It captured the Japanese home islands
context: The four sunk carriers were Akagi, Kaga, Soryu, and Hiryu. Japan had used these same ships to attack Pearl Harbor; losing all four in one day cost it the heart of its carrier striking force. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Midway)

question: American codebreakers at Station HYPO in Hawaii kept reading Japanese messages about a coming attack on a place the enemy code-named only "AF" -- but they could not prove where AF was. To unmask it, Captain Wilfred Holmes had the base at Midway radio a fake, plain-language message reporting a sudden shortage at the base. About a day later the codebreakers intercepted a Japanese report that confirmed AF was Midway. What shortage did the faked message invent to bait the trap?
answer: A shortage of fresh water
choices: A shortage of fresh water
A shortage of aircraft fuel
A shortage of ammunition
A shortage of medical supplies
context: Holmes had Midway radio that its fresh-water purification plant had broken down. Within about 24 hours HYPO intercepted a Japanese message reporting that "AF is short of fresh water" -- proving AF was Midway and letting the Americans set their ambush. The codebreaking effort was led by Commander Joseph Rochefort. (nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/battle-midway)

question: Torpedo Squadron 8 flew off the carrier USS Hornet in slow, obsolete TBD Devastator torpedo planes, with no fighter escort to protect them. Japanese Zeros tore into them and shot down all fifteen planes before a single torpedo could hit anything. Of the squadron's thirty aircrew, only one man lived. Ensign George Gay was shot down too, but survived in the open ocean for about thirty hours until a flying boat found him. What kept the wounded Gay afloat and hidden as the battle raged?
answer: A floating seat cushion from his downed plane
choices: A floating seat cushion from his downed plane
A wooden crate of rations from a sunk ship
An empty fuel drum that drifted past him
A life raft dropped by a passing bomber
context: Gay hid under the black rubber seat cushion partly to shelter from the sun and partly to avoid being spotted by Japanese ships; he watched the carriers burn from the water. He was the only aircrew survivor of Torpedo Squadron 8. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._Gay_Jr.)

question: Reading the Japanese code told Admiral Chester Nimitz exactly where the enemy was heading, so he wanted every carrier he could get. The USS Yorktown had been badly mauled a month earlier at the Battle of the Coral Sea, and engineers first estimated months of repairs. Nimitz gave them three days. Pearl Harbor shipyard crews patched her up and sent her back to fight in about 72 hours. What were the workmen still doing when Yorktown sailed for Midway?
answer: Still aboard and working as she put to sea
choices: Still aboard and working as she put to sea
Still waiting on parts that never arrived
Still arguing she was unfit to sail
Still painting her new hull number on
context: The around-the-clock repair brought a third American carrier to the battle that the Japanese believed had already been sunk at Coral Sea -- a surprise that helped even the odds. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Midway)

question: For hours on the morning of June 4, 1942, wave after wave of American attacks on the Japanese carrier fleet failed and were shot to pieces. Then, starting around 10:22, U.S. SBD Dauntless dive-bombers plunged out of the high sky almost unopposed. In roughly five minutes they fatally wrecked three of the four Japanese carriers at once -- Akagi, Kaga, and Soryu. Why did those few minutes turn the carriers into floating infernos so fast?
answer: Their decks were crammed with armed, fueled planes
choices: Their decks were crammed with armed, fueled planes
Their crews had already abandoned the ships
Their fuel tanks had been drained for safety
Their fighters were still parked below decks
context: Caught in the middle of re-arming and refueling, each carrier's deck was packed with bombs, torpedoes, and fuel hoses; a few hits set off chain explosions. Naval historians call this stretch "the five fateful minutes." (usni.org/magazines/proceedings/1955/june/five-fateful-minutes-midway)

question: Lieutenant Commander Wade McClusky led the Enterprise's dive-bombers to the spot where the Japanese fleet was supposed to be -- and found empty ocean. Low on fuel and almost out of time, instead of turning back he kept searching, and spotted a single Japanese destroyer, the Arashi, racing north all alone. McClusky gambled on what that lone ship was doing and followed it straight to the four carriers. What did he bet the Arashi was doing?
answer: Hurrying to rejoin the main carrier fleet
choices: Hurrying to rejoin the main carrier fleet
Fleeing the battle after being damaged
Laying a smoke screen to hide the fleet
Scouting ahead for an American attack
context: Admiral Nimitz later wrote that McClusky's decision to keep searching and his judgment of where the enemy lay "decided the fate of our carrier task force and our forces at Midway." (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._Wade_McClusky)

question: Lieutenant Richard "Dick" Best, flying a Dauntless dive-bomber off the Enterprise, dove almost vertically on the carrier Akagi that morning and put his bomb through her flight deck into the planes packed below. He flew a second mission that same afternoon. By the end of June 4, Best had earned a distinction no other pilot in the entire war would ever match. What did Best alone accomplish?
answer: He helped sink two enemy carriers in one day
choices: He helped sink two enemy carriers in one day
He sank an enemy battleship with one bomb
He shot down five enemy fighters in one day
He led three separate strikes in one day
context: Best's morning bomb helped doom Akagi; that afternoon his bomb was among those that finished off the last Japanese carrier still fighting, the Hiryu. No other pilot in the war helped sink two carriers in a single day. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Halsey_Best)

question: The Hiryu was the last of the four Japanese carriers still afloat, and she fought on alone until American dive-bombers from the Enterprise and Yorktown finally left her ablaze and doomed. Rear Admiral Tamon Yamaguchi, widely regarded as one of Japan's finest carrier commanders, was offered the chance to leave the burning ship and save himself for the war ahead. What did Yamaguchi choose to do?
answer: Go down with his ship and her captain
