choices: Go down with his ship and her captain
Transfer his flag to a nearby cruiser
Order the survivors to ram an American ship
Escape by destroyer to report the defeat
context: Yamaguchi stayed aboard the sinking Hiryu alongside her captain, Tomeo Kaku, rather than be rescued. Japan lost not just four carriers at Midway but many of its most skilled commanders and aircrews. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamon_Yamaguchi)

question: At Midway the American torpedo squadrons in their slow planes were slaughtered almost to the last man without scoring a single hit on a Japanese carrier -- a seemingly pointless massacre. Yet minutes later the U.S. dive-bombers arrived high overhead and found the sky above the carriers wide open, with no fighters to stop them. How had the doomed torpedo runs, though they hit nothing, set up the dive-bombers' success?
answer: They pulled the defending Zeros down to wave-top level
choices: They pulled the defending Zeros down to wave-top level
They knocked out the carriers' anti-aircraft guns
They forced the carriers to scatter out of formation
They used up the last of the Zeros' ammunition
context: To chase the low torpedo planes, the Japanese fighters dove to sea level -- leaving no one to guard the high altitude when the Dauntless dive-bombers tipped over into their attack. The sacrifice bought the decisive opening. (nationalww2museum.org/war/topics/battle-of-midway)

question: Wade McClusky found the Japanese carriers only because he spotted the destroyer Arashi tearing north all alone and followed her wake. But the Arashi was behind the fleet and rushing to catch up for a reason that had nothing to do with McClusky. She had been left behind on a different job entirely, and finishing it sent her racing back along the path the dive-bombers would follow. Why had the Arashi fallen behind the fleet?
answer: She had stayed behind to hunt an American submarine
choices: She had stayed behind to hunt an American submarine
She had stopped to pick up downed Japanese pilots
She had broken down and made hasty repairs
She had been scouting eastward for the American fleet
context: The Arashi had been depth-charging the U.S. submarine Nautilus (Lt. Cdr. William Brockman), which was harassing the carriers; her dash back to rejoin drew the wake McClusky followed. So an American submarine indirectly led the dive-bombers to their targets -- skill and luck braided together. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Nautilus_(SS-168))

question: Vice Admiral Chuichi Nagumo, commanding the Japanese carriers at Midway, had first armed his reserve planes with bombs to hit the island again. Then scouts reported American ships nearby, so he reversed the order and had the crews swap the bombs for torpedoes to attack the fleet instead. With his decks cluttered mid-change, he made one more choice that left them exposed at the worst possible moment. What did Nagumo do that doomed his carriers?
answer: He delayed launching to first recover his returning strike
choices: He delayed launching to first recover his returning strike
He launched his half-armed planes into a storm
He turned the fleet away and split it in two
He ordered all aircraft below to refuel at once
context: Rather than launch a hasty attack, Nagumo waited to land his returning Midway strike planes first, leaving the flight decks jammed with fueled, armed aircraft exactly when the American dive-bombers struck. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Midway)

question: Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto sent against Midway the largest fleet Japan ever assembled, including the battleship Yamato -- the biggest warship in the world. On paper he vastly outnumbered the three American carriers. Yet when the decisive carrier battle was fought, only Nagumo's four carriers were in range to meet the Americans, and the mighty Yamato never fired a shot. What had Yamamoto done with his enormous fleet that wasted his advantage?
answer: He split it into groups too far apart to help each other
choices: He split it into groups too far apart to help each other
He held it all back to bombard the island first
He sent the carriers in without any escorts
He launched the attack before the fleet was ready
context: Yamamoto spread his ships across diversions and separate forces, so his battleships and the Yamato were hundreds of miles from the carrier fight. Only the four carriers were in range -- and they were the ones that were lost. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Midway_order_of_battle)

question: On January 8, 1815, Andrew Jackson's ragtag army shattered a British assault outside New Orleans in about half an hour of fighting — the greatest American land victory of the War of 1812. But there was a strange catch about that war that no soldier on the field that morning knew. What was it?
answer: The peace treaty ending the war had already been signed two weeks earlier
choices: The peace treaty ending the war had already been signed two weeks earlier
The British had already captured and burned the city of New Orleans
Jackson had secretly been ordered to surrender the city without a fight
The American government had already declared the war a lost cause
context: The Treaty of Ghent was signed in Europe on December 24, 1814 — but news couldn't cross the Atlantic faster than a wooden sailing ship, so the armies fought a battle for a war that was technically already over. The U.S. wouldn't even ratify the treaty until February 16, 1815, over a month after the battle. The pointless victory still made Jackson 'Old Hickory' a national hero and put him on the road to the presidency. Source: battlefields.org/learn/war-1812/battles/new-orleans; history.com.

question: Before the battle for New Orleans, the British secretly offered the smuggler-pirate Jean Lafitte $30,000 and a captain's rank in the Royal Navy to help them take the city. Lafitte didn't take the bribe. What did he do instead?
answer: He handed the British letters to the Americans and joined Jackson for a pardon
choices: He handed the British letters to the Americans and joined Jackson for a pardon
He fled the region with his ships and stayed out of the fighting entirely
He pocketed the money and then quietly betrayed the British plans to no one
He demanded twice the sum and a fleet before agreeing to help the British
context: Jackson had once called Lafitte's Baratarian privateers 'hellish banditti' — but he took the deal. About 50 of Lafitte's men worked the cannons in Jackson's defense. The defending army was a wild mix: Tennessee and Kentucky frontier marksmen, Louisiana militia, New Orleans free Men of Color, Choctaw warriors under leaders like Pushmataha, U.S. regulars, sailors, marines, and the pirates. Source: britannica.com/biography/Jean-Laffite; nps.gov.

question: In April 1945, with the Battle of Okinawa raging, Japan sent the Yamato, the largest battleship ever built, steaming toward the island on a mission she was never meant to survive. Her orders were not to win a sea fight but to do what once she arrived?
answer: Run herself aground on the beach and fight until destroyed
choices: Run herself aground on the beach and fight until destroyed
Slip past the fleet and bombard the American landing zones
Ferry reinforcements ashore under cover of darkness
Lure the carriers into a trap for the waiting submarines
context: The Yamato never reached Okinawa. On April 7, 1945, American carrier planes hit her with about a dozen bombs and many torpedoes; she rolled over and exploded, taking roughly 2,498 of her crew down with her. Sources: history.com/this-day-in-history/april-7/japanese-battleship-yamato-is-sunk-by-allied-forces; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_battleship_Yamato

question: The Battle of Okinawa was the bloodiest of the Pacific War: more than 12,000 Americans, roughly 90,000 to 110,000 Japanese soldiers, and somewhere between 94,000 and 150,000 Okinawan civilians died on one island in 82 days. American war planners studied this staggering toll for a specific, fateful reason. What did they use Okinawa's death count to do?
answer: Estimate the cost of invading mainland Japan, weighing the atomic-bomb decision
choices: Estimate the cost of invading mainland Japan, weighing the atomic-bomb decision
Negotiate a ceasefire with the Japanese high command
Redraw the postwar borders of the Ryukyu Islands
Calculate pensions owed to the families of the fallen
context: With civilian and military dead together topping 200,000 on a single island, Okinawa became the bloody preview of what invading the Japanese home islands might cost, a calculation that directly weighed on the decision to drop the atomic bombs instead. Sources: nationalww2museum.org/war/topics/battle-of-okinawa; britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Okinawa

question: At Plataea in 479 BC, the Spartan officer Amompharetus refused his commander Pausanias's order to pull the army back from the Persians, because to a Spartan fleeing the enemy was a disgrace. To cast his vote against retreat, Amompharetus picked up a large object with both hands, set it at Pausanias's feet, and said it stood for his vote not to run. What did he set down?
answer: A large stone
choices: A large stone
His broken spear
His own helmet
A handful of soil
context: Herodotus reports his words: "With this pebble I give my vote not to run away from the strangers." In a Spartan assembly men voted by casting pebbles, so a soldier laying down a boulder-sized 'pebble' was a defiant joke and a vote rolled into one. Source: Herodotus, Histories Book 9.55 (Rawlinson translation).

question: After the Greeks crushed the Persians at Plataea in 479 BC, the Spartan regent Pausanias captured the rich tableware of the dead Persian general Mardonius. He ordered the Persian cooks to lay out the lavish feast they had been preparing, then had a plain Spartan dinner set beside it. Pausanias laughed and pointed to the contrast to make one mocking point about Mardonius. What was his joke?
answer: A man who ate this well was a fool to invade poor Greece to rob it
choices: A man who ate this well was a fool to invade poor Greece to rob it
Spartan food would make the Persians too soft to fight
The gods favored whichever side ate the simpler meal
Greek cooks could never match such Persian splendor
context: Herodotus quotes Pausanias: he summoned the Greeks "to show you the folly of this Median captain, who, when he enjoyed such fare as this, must needs come here to rob us of our penury" (our poverty). The joke is the irony: Mardonius left luxury to conquer a land that had little worth taking. Source: Herodotus, Histories Book 9.82 (Rawlinson translation).

question: At the strait of Salamis in 480 BC, the Persian king Xerxes brought a fleet of perhaps 600 to 800 warships against the Greeks, who could muster only about 370 triremes. Knowing they could never win a fair fight on the open sea, what did the Greek commanders deliberately do with this lopsided matchup?
answer: Lured the huge fleet into a narrow strait where its numbers could not be used
choices: Lured the huge fleet into a narrow strait where its numbers could not be used
Sailed straight out to meet the larger fleet in open water
Split their ships into many tiny squadrons across the coast
Burned half their own triremes to lighten the line
context: Roughly 370-380 Greek triremes (Athens supplied about 180, the largest contingent) faced perhaps 600-800 Persian ships. The Greeks chose the cramped strait precisely so the giant fleet could not bring its numbers to bear. Source: World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/article/671); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Salamis.

question: During the sea battle at Salamis, the Persian king Xerxes did not fight aboard a ship. Instead he had a throne carried up the slopes of Mount Aegaleus overlooking the strait, where he sat in full view of both fleets. What did he keep beside him as he watched?
answer: Scribes ready to write down the names of captains who fought bravely
choices: Scribes ready to write down the names of captains who fought bravely
A cage of war hounds to loose on shipwrecked sailors
A herd of horses saddled for a charge across the water
A chest of gold to throw to the first ship that rammed an enemy
context: Herodotus says Xerxes watched from his throne on Mount Aegaleus with scribes at his side, recording the names of brave captains so they could be rewarded. He expected to be recording a victory. Source: Herodotus, Histories 8.90; World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/article/671).

question: On the night before the battle of Salamis, the Athenian commander Themistocles wanted Xerxes to seal off the narrow strait so the Persian fleet would be trapped. He sent his own children's Persian tutor, Sicinnus, secretly across to the Persian king. What did Sicinnus tell Xerxes to spring the trap?
answer: A lie that the Greeks were quarreling and about to flee, so Xerxes should block the strait now
choices: A lie that the Greeks were quarreling and about to flee, so Xerxes should block the strait now
The true Greek battle plan, hoping Xerxes would reward him richly
A warning that a storm would wreck any ship that entered the strait
A demand that Xerxes surrender before dawn or be destroyed
context: Themistocles sent Sicinnus, the Persian tutor of his own children, with the bluff that the Greeks were breaking apart and would flee. Xerxes believed it and ordered his fleet to seal the narrows, walking straight into the trap. Source: Herodotus, Histories 8.75; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicinnus.

question: Before the Persians came, the Delphic oracle warned the Athenians that only a 'wooden wall' would save them. Some Athenians thought it meant a thorn hedge around the Acropolis. Themistocles argued for a different meaning, and won the city over. What did he say the 'wooden wall' really was?
answer: Their fleet of ships
choices: Their fleet of ships
A new palisade around the harbor
The wooden gates of the Acropolis
A bridge of rafts across the strait
context: Themistocles insisted the 'wooden wall' meant Athens' triremes. He even pointed out that the oracle called the island 'divine Salamis,' not 'hateful Salamis,' so the deaths it foretold must be the enemy's, not Athens'. The Athenians abandoned their city and fought at sea. Source: Herodotus, Histories 7.141-143.

question: Queen Artemisia I of Caria was the only woman commanding a ship in Xerxes' fleet at Salamis. Cornered by a chasing Athenian trireme, she escaped by ramming and sinking a ship of her own Persian-allied side. Xerxes, watching from shore and mistaking the wreck for an enemy's, praised her with what astonished line?
answer: 'My men have become women, and my women men'
choices: 'My men have become women, and my women men'
'Even the gods now fight on the side of Greece'
'Bring me her name, that all Persia may honor it'
'No captain of mine has shown such loyalty today'
context: Artemisia rammed a friendly ship to shake off her pursuer; Xerxes, watching from Mount Aegaleus, assumed she had sunk a Greek and exclaimed that his men had become women and his women men. The irony is that her 'brave' act was sinking one of his own. Source: Herodotus, Histories 8.87-88; TheCollector (thecollector.com/facts-artemisia-caria).

question: In 1925 the Soviet industrial city on the Volga River called Tsaritsyn was given a new name, which later made its capture a point of personal pride for the man it now honored. After which Soviet leader was the city renamed?
answer: Joseph Stalin
choices: Joseph Stalin
Vladimir Lenin
Leon Trotsky
Nikita Khrushchev
context: Renamed Stalingrad, the city carried Stalin's own name, so holding or taking it became a prestige contest for both Stalin and Hitler on top of its value controlling Volga shipping. The battle there (17 July 1942 to 2 February 1943) is often called the deadliest single battle in human history. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stalingrad

question: On 28 July 1942, as German forces drove toward the Volga, Joseph Stalin issued Order No. 227 to halt the Red Army's retreat. The order is remembered for a famous three-word battle cry. Which one was it?
answer: Not one step back!
choices: Not one step back!
Not one inch surrendered!
Hold where you stand!
The Volga is ours!
context: In Russian the cry was 'Ni shagu nazad!' Order No. 227 commanded that panic-mongers and cowards be shot on the spot and forbade any retreat without orders from high command. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_No._227

question: As the battle ground on through Stalingrad's bombed-out ruins, the combat broke down into vicious struggles for single rooms, cellars, and stairwells, with the same building changing hands again and again. German soldiers gave this grinding urban fighting a grim nickname. What did they call it?
answer: the War of the Rats
choices: the War of the Rats
the Iron Harvest
the Meat Grinder
the Devil's Anvil
context: In German it was 'Rattenkrieg.' Streets, single buildings, and even individual floors of one building were lost and retaken over and over in the rubble. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stalingrad

question: In central Stalingrad a platoon that began with only about 25 to 30 men seized a four-story apartment building, ringed it with barbed wire and mines, fired down on German tanks from the roof, and held it for roughly two months. The building became famous under the name of the sergeant who led the defense. What is it called?
answer: Pavlov's House
choices: Pavlov's House
Rodimtsev's House
Lyudnikov's House
Gorishny's House
context: Sergeant Yakov Pavlov led the defense, so the building took his name. Soviet general Vasily Chuikov later boasted the Germans lost more men trying to take Pavlov's House than they did capturing all of Paris, though that vivid claim has no support in the military archives. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavlov%27s_House

question: The Red Army's most celebrated marksman at Stalingrad, Vasily Zaitsev, was credited with about 225 kills in roughly five weeks of fighting, eleven of them enemy snipers. His deadly aim came from the way he was raised in the Ural Mountains. What had the young Zaitsev done up in those mountains?
answer: hunted deer and wolves
choices: hunted deer and wolves
herded reindeer
trapped sable for furs
fished the cold rivers
context: Zaitsev was a former deer and wolf hunter who killed his first wolf at age 12; the 225 confirmed kills were tallied between 10 November and 17 December 1942. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasily_Zaitsev_(sniper)

question: On the southern edge of Stalingrad stood a giant grain elevator, a steel-and-concrete tower so massive the two sides ended up battling through it floor by floor. Holding out inside against three full German divisions was a tiny Soviet force. About how many defenders held the tower?
answer: about 50 men
choices: about 50 men
about 500 men
about 2,000 men
about 10,000 men
context: The elevator was roughly 90 meters long and 35 meters high, and the fighting inside was so close the two sides battled level by level. Source: https://stalingradtours.com/en/sights/articul/stalingrad_grain_elevator

question: Stalin's Order No. 227 did more than forbid retreat. Behind the Red Army's own front lines it posted armed units called 'blocking detachments,' who in their first three months sent 24,000 men to penal battalions. What were these units ordered to do to their own soldiers who tried to fall back?
answer: shoot them on the spot
choices: shoot them on the spot
strip them of all rank
march them home in chains
force them to clear minefields
context: The blocking detachments (zagraditelnye otryady) executed about 1,000 of their own troops in those first three months. Soviet soldiers fought heroically and were driven forward by a murderous regime; both are part of the honest record. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_No._227

question: By November 1942 the German 6th Army was driven deep into Stalingrad, but its long flanks were guarded by weaker allied armies. On 19 November the Soviets launched Operation Uranus, and instead of hitting the Germans head-on, they smashed straight through one ally's lines, linked up near the town of Kalach, and trapped about 290,000 Axis troops. Whose troops did the Soviet pincers tear through?
answer: Romania's
choices: Romania's
Italy's
Hungary's
Bulgaria's
context: The pincers broke the Romanian armies holding the flanks and met near Kalach on 22 November, sealing the 6th Army inside the city. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Uranus

question: With the German 6th Army trapped inside Stalingrad, Hermann Goering promised Hitler the Luftwaffe could keep it supplied entirely by air, vowing 300 tons of cargo a day. Over the 71 days the airlift actually ran, what daily amount did it really average?
answer: about 120 tons a day
choices: about 60 tons a day
about 120 tons a day
about 200 tons a day
about 280 tons a day
context: The airlift averaged only about 117 tons daily, less than half what Goering promised, while losing more than 266 Junkers Ju 52 transport planes, a crippling blow to German air power. Source: https://www.ospreypublishing.com/ca/osprey-blog/2023/the-luftwaffe-s-stalingrad-airlift-the-transport-fleet-that-failed/

question: On 30 January 1943, with the 6th Army doomed in Stalingrad, Adolf Hitler promoted Friedrich Paulus to Field Marshal and pointedly noted that no German field marshal had ever surrendered, a coded order to shoot himself. Paulus surrendered the next morning instead. What did his aide record him saying about killing himself?
answer: I'm not going to do them such a favour.
choices: I'm not going to do them such a favour.
A soldier dies, he does not beg.
Let history judge this defeat.
I serve Germany, not one man.
context: Paulus's surrender made the 6th Army the first of Hitler's field armies ever to capitulate. Of roughly 91,000 frozen, starving Germans taken prisoner, only about 5,000 to 6,000 ever returned home. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Paulus

question: Vasily Zaitsev's fame later grew into a legendary sniper duel, a German marksman supposedly sent to Stalingrad just to hunt him down, a tale eventually turned into movies. The historian Antony Beevor checked the Russian Defence Ministry archives to test the famous story. What did Beevor conclude about the duel?
answer: It never happened, a Soviet propaganda invention.
choices: It never happened, a Soviet propaganda invention.
It happened, but Zaitsev embellished the range.
It happened on a quieter stretch of front.
The truth was lost when the archives burned.
context: Beevor judged the duel a propaganda invention because the Defence Ministry archives contradict it; the dramatic version lives on mainly through films. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasily_Zaitsev_(sniper)  (Legend.)

question: Captured at Stalingrad, Field Marshal Friedrich Paulus turned against the Nazi regime and even testified for the prosecution at the Nuremberg war-crimes trials. In captivity he refused to refer to Adolf Hitler by his title, using instead a contemptuous nickname. What did the captured field marshal call him?
answer: the Bohemian corporal
choices: the Bohemian corporal
the Austrian house-painter
the Berlin butcher
the trench-runner
context: Paulus said he had 'no intention of shooting myself for this Bohemian corporal,' then joined a Soviet-backed anti-Nazi committee and testified at Nuremberg. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Paulus

question: As Britain fought to keep its Atlantic supply line open against Germany's submarines, Winston Churchill later wrote in his war memoir that one threat above all others had haunted him. What did he call 'the only thing that ever really frightened me during the war'?
answer: The U-boat peril
choices: The U-boat peril
The London Blitz
The fall of France
The threat of invasion
context: Churchill feared the U-boats could cut the Atlantic lifeline and starve Britain into surrender. The Battle of the Atlantic ran from the first day of the war, 3 September 1939, to Germany's surrender in May 1945 — the longest campaign of WWII. Source: Imperial War Museum, 'What you need to know about the Battle of the Atlantic'; Churchill, The Second World War.

question: To survive German submarines, Allied merchant ships crossing the Atlantic did not sail alone. They packed together by the dozens — up to about sixty ships in five-ship columns — and were ringed by warship escorts. What was this protective formation called?
answer: A convoy
choices: A convoy
A flotilla
A blockade
A picket line
context: Safety came from sailing together, not alone — the escorts could only guard ships that stayed bunched in the box. The Germans answered the convoy with their 'Wolfpack' tactic, gathering many U-boats to swarm one convoy at night. Source: Imperial War Museum, 'What you need to know about the Battle of the Atlantic'.

question: On the night of 13–14 October 1939, German captain Günther Prien threaded the submarine U-47 past sunken blockships at slack tide, through the narrow Kirk Sound, into Scapa Flow — the Royal Navy's main home base. Once inside, what did he sink in just thirteen minutes?
answer: The battleship HMS Royal Oak
choices: The battleship HMS Royal Oak
An ammunition depot on shore
The base's main fuel tanks
A line of moored destroyers
context: Hitler sent his personal plane to fly Prien's crew to Berlin; Prien became the first U-boat captain to win the Knight's Cross and was nicknamed 'the Bull of Scapa Flow.' Less than 17 months later, on about 8 March 1941, Prien and all 45 of his crew vanished with U-47 attacking a convoy — the sub was never found. Source: Navy History (AU); Osprey Publishing.

question: German U-boats hunted hardest in a roughly 500-mile-wide band of open ocean in the middle of the Atlantic — a stretch so far from any airfield that no Allied aircraft could reach it to guard the convoys. What did the crews and the Allies call this deadly stretch?
answer: The Black Pit
choices: The Black Pit
The Cold Reach
The Devil's Trench
The Iron Triangle
context: Also called the Mid-Atlantic Air Gap, the Black Pit was finally closed in May 1943 when Very-Long-Range Liberator bombers and escort carriers could at last cover the whole crossing — a turning point in the battle. Source: Mid-Atlantic gap references; Canadian Nautical Research Society.

question: On 9 May 1941, British escorts forced the submarine U-110 to the surface and its crew abandoned ship. Sub-lieutenant David Balme led a boarding party down into the dark, possibly-sinking hull. The Bletchley Park codebreakers would soon read German submarine traffic because of what Balme's men hauled out of U-110.
answer: Its intact Enigma cipher machine and codebooks
choices: Its intact Enigma cipher machine and codebooks
A complete map of the convoy routes
A list of every U-boat captain
The submarine's secret fuel reserves
context: U-110's captain Fritz-Julius Lemp had jumped into the sea to swim back and scuttle the boat, but it was too late. Reading this traffic ('Ultra') let the Allies steer convoys around waiting wolfpacks — and German intelligence kept assuring Admiral Dönitz that Enigma was unbreakable. The genuine 'science wins wars' thread linking the Atlantic to Bletchley. Source: ForcesNews; WW2Today.

question: In December 1944 the German army made a sudden push that pressed a huge dent into the Allied line on the war maps — a swelling bulge of enemy-held ground stabbing into territory the Allies had held. American soldiers started calling the fight by a nickname taken straight from that shape on the map. What did they name it?
answer: the Battle of the Bulge
choices: the Battle of the Bulge
the Battle of the Dent
the Battle of the Breakthrough
the Battle of the Wedge
context: The German breakthrough on December 16, 1944 pushed a huge dent into the Allied front line — the bulge that gave the battle its nickname. Over 600,000 American troops were eventually drawn in, making it the largest battle the U.S. Army has ever fought. Source: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/battle-of-the-bulge

question: In December 1944, American paratroopers were surrounded and cut off in the Belgian town of Bastogne. The Germans sent in a written demand for an 'honorable surrender,' expecting the trapped men to give up. Brigadier General Anthony McAuliffe typed his entire reply as a single word. What was that one-word answer?
answer: NUTS!
choices: NUTS!
RETREAT
NEVER
SURRENDER
context: On December 22, 1944, McAuliffe's full typed note read: 'To the German Commander, / N U T S ! / The American Commander.' When the German envoy didn't understand the slang, Col. Joseph 'Bud' Harper explained it meant 'Go to hell.' Source: https://www.army.mil/article/92856/the_story_of_the_nuts_reply

question: On December 16, 1944, Hitler launched a surprise winter attack through the snowy Ardennes Forest, codenamed 'Wacht am Rhein' (Watch on the Rhine). His plan was to smash through Belgium and capture one great prize — a target that, if seized, would cut the Allied armies in two. What was the objective Hitler was driving for?
answer: the port of Antwerp
choices: the port of Antwerp
the city of Paris
the Rhine bridges
the beaches of Normandy
context: Taking the deep-water port of Antwerp would have choked Allied supplies and split the British and American armies. The Ardennes was chosen precisely because it was lightly defended and thought too rugged for a winter offensive. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-the-Bulge

question: During the Battle of the Bulge, English-speaking German commandos in Operation Greif wore captured American uniforms and drove American jeeps behind the lines to spread chaos. Nervous American guards at checkpoints couldn't tell friend from spy by sight, so they grilled each other with one kind of question a real American would know cold but a disguised German might fumble. What did the GIs quiz each other about?
answer: American pop culture, like Mickey Mouse's girlfriend
choices: American pop culture, like Mickey Mouse's girlfriend
the day's secret password
their home addresses and birthdays
the names of their officers
context: GIs asked things like who Mickey Mouse's girlfriend was, which baseball team played where, or state capitals — trivia a homegrown American absorbed by osmosis. Otto Skorzeny led the operation; only about 10 of his men spoke flawless American slang. Source: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/operation-greif-secret-mission-sow-chaos-us-army

question: With the 101st Airborne trapped at Bastogne, the weather grounded the planes that could have dropped supplies — so General George Patton ordered his Third Army chaplain, James O'Neill, to write a prayer for clear skies, and had it printed on cards for the troops. The very next day, December 23, 1944, the skies cleared and the planes flew. How did Patton reward the chaplain?
answer: he pinned a Bronze Star on him
choices: he pinned a Bronze Star on him
he gave him a private's pay raise
he sent him home on leave
he named a tank after him
context: Patton reportedly said, 'God damn! That O'Neill sure did some potent praying,' and pinned a Bronze Star on the chaplain. The clear weather let Allied planes fly and drop supplies to the besieged defenders. Source: https://www.wwiimemorialfriends.org/blog/pattons-prayer

question: The day after the German offensive began, Waffen-SS troops under Joachim Peiper captured a group of unarmed American prisoners at the Baugnez crossroads near Malmedy, Belgium, and machine-gunned them in a field — about 84 men, the largest massacre of U.S. soldiers in Europe during the war. How did more than 50 of the captured Americans manage to survive the shooting?
answer: they fell down playing dead, then ran
choices: they fell down playing dead, then ran
they hid in a nearby barn
they were ransomed back by officers
a German soldier let them go
context: On December 17, 1944, more than 50 GIs survived by dropping as if killed and then running once the SS men moved on. After the war Peiper was sentenced to death for the massacre, but his sentence was commuted and he was released in 1956; in 1976 his house in France was firebombed and he was killed. Source: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/malmedy-massacre

question: At a December 19, 1944 emergency meeting in Verdun, with the 101st trapped at Bastogne, General George Patton stunned the room by promising to counterattack within 48 hours. To keep the promise he pulled off a maneuver generals usually call impossible — physically turning his entire Third Army a quarter-turn in the dead of winter. What did Patton actually do with his 250,000 men and hundreds of tanks?
answer: wheeled them 90 degrees from facing east to driving north
choices: wheeled them 90 degrees from facing east to driving north
dug them into a defensive line and waited
loaded them onto trains heading west
split them into small raiding parties
context: Patton wheeled 250,000 men and hundreds of tanks 90 degrees — from facing east to driving north — through the worst winter in 50 years. His tanks broke the siege and relieved Bastogne on December 26, 1944. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-the-Bulge

question: In the Battle of the Coral Sea in May 1942, two great fleets fought for five days, yet the American and Japanese ships never traded a single shot directly at one another. How is that possible?
answer: The whole battle was fought by carrier aircraft striking ships far over the horizon
choices: The whole battle was fought by carrier aircraft striking ships far over the horizon
The two fleets agreed to a truce and only bombed empty islands
Thick fog hid the ships so completely that no guns could be aimed
The ships fired only at submarines hidden deep beneath the waves
context: Coral Sea (4-8 May 1942) was the first naval battle in history in which the opposing fleets never sighted or fired on each other directly. Aircraft launched from carriers did all the fighting, hitting ships miles away over the horizon. It changed naval warfare forever: the aircraft carrier, not the big-gun battleship, was now the deciding weapon at sea. Source: Naval History and Heritage Command, history.navy.mil.

question: On 7 May 1942 at the Coral Sea, Lieutenant Commander Robert Dixon led Lexington's dive bombers down onto the Japanese carrier Shoho and helped sink her, the first enemy aircraft carrier the United States destroyed in the war. He radioed back four jubilant words that became famous. What did he say?
answer: "Scratch one flat top!"
choices: "Scratch one flat top!"
"The carrier is going down!"
"We have struck the enemy!"
"First blood is ours today!"
context: Lt. Cmdr. Robert E. Dixon's radio call, 'Scratch one flat top!', announced the first Japanese aircraft carrier ever sunk in the war. Shoho was hit by an avalanche of bombs and torpedoes and went down just four minutes after the abandon-ship order at 11:31 on 7 May 1942. Source: Wikipedia, Robert E. Dixon; Wikipedia, Japanese aircraft carrier Shoho.

question: On the morning of 1 July 1916, the British Army lost about 57,470 men killed and wounded on the first day of the Battle of the Somme — its worst single day ever. Many of the dead came from special units the army had built by promising friends from the same town, factory, or street that they could enlist and serve side by side. What were these units called?
answer: The Pals battalions
choices: The Pals battalions
The Iron Brigades
The Home Companies
The Kitchener Lancers
context: Because Pals battalions kept neighbours together, a single bad morning could wipe out the young men of an entire community at once — the Accrington Pals sent about 720 men against the village of Serre and took 585 casualties in roughly half an hour. Source: https://www.historic-uk.com/HistoryUK/HistoryofBritain/Battle-of-the-Somme/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accrington_Pals

question: Two minutes before the British infantry climbed out of their trenches on 1 July 1916, tunnellers detonated 60,000 pounds of explosive packed beneath the German strongpoint at La Boisselle — the Lochnagar mine. The blast threw earth thousands of feet into the air and tore open a hole 330 feet across and 70 feet deep. What record did that single explosion set?
answer: The loudest man-made sound in history to that point
choices: The loudest man-made sound in history to that point
The first shot fired in the First World War
The deepest tunnel ever dug under a city
The first use of poison gas on the Western Front
context: The crater the Lochnagar mine left is still the largest ever made by warfare, and it survives in the French countryside today as a memorial. Source: https://www.lochnagarcrater.org/history/statistics/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lochnagar_mine

question: In 732 the Frankish leader Charles halted a Muslim army pushing north into Gaul at the Battle of Tours. Chroniclers were so struck by how he smashed that advance that they pinned a nickname on him, 'Martel,' which stuck to him ever after. What does 'Martel' mean?
answer: The Hammer
choices: The Hammer
The Shepherd
The Lawgiver
The Wanderer
context: 'Martel' (from the Latin Martellus) is not a family name but an epithet -- 'the Hammer' -- given to Charles Martel for hammering back the Umayyad advance at Tours in 732. His grandson Charlemagne would be crowned in 800. Source: worldhistory.org/article/1809; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tours

question: At the Battle of Tours in 732, Charles Martel's Frankish foot soldiers had held their ground all day against the Umayyad cavalry of Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi. Then a rumor tore through the Muslim camp and the battle line suddenly came apart. What did the rumor claim was happening?
answer: Frankish troops were ransacking their baggage and plunder
choices: Frankish troops were ransacking their baggage and plunder
A second Frankish army was marching up from the south
Their commander al-Ghafiqi had already been slain
A river crossing behind them had been cut off
context: Word spread that Franks were looting the Umayyad baggage train -- the army's accumulated plunder -- and so many men broke off to defend the camp that the line collapsed. Al-Ghafiqi was killed trying to rally his fleeing men. Arab sources call the battle Balat al-Shuhada, the 'Pavement of the Martyrs.' Source: worldhistory.org/article/1809; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tours

question: In 1916 the French army dug in around the fortress town of Verdun, determined to stop the German advance no matter the cost. As the shells rained down, the French defenders adopted a three-word rallying cry that became the spirit of the whole battle. What did they vow?
answer: "They shall not pass!"
choices: "They shall not pass!"
"We will hold the line!"
"France will never kneel!"
"Hold or die here!"
context: "Ils ne passeront pas!" became the watchword of Verdun, associated with General Philippe Petain, who ordered the front line to hold fast. Source: firstworldwar.com/battles/verdun.htm

question: With the rail lines into Verdun cut by 1916, France kept the whole battle supplied along a single narrow road from Bar-le-Duc, soon nicknamed the 'Voie Sacree' (Sacred Way). At its peak in June, just how relentless was the traffic on that one road?
answer: A truck rolled past every 14 seconds
choices: A truck rolled past every 14 seconds
A truck rolled past every 4 minutes
A convoy crossed twice a day
A single train ran each night
context: Up to 12,000 vehicles a day formed an unbroken stream hauling men and shells to the front, since the rail lines were cut and this road was Verdun's only lifeline. Source: worldhistory.org/article/2878/battle-of-verdun/

question: At Fort Vaux in June 1916, Major Sylvain Raynal's French garrison fought the Germans corridor by corridor, dying of thirst under gas attacks with their telephone lines cut. To get one last message out, Raynal turned to an unusual messenger. What did he send?
answer: His last carrier pigeon
choices: His last carrier pigeon
A runner through the sewers
A signal mirror at dawn
A swimmer down the moat
context: The pigeon, named Le Vaillant, carried a message ending 'This is my last pigeon' and delivered it though mortally gassed; it was later awarded the Legion of Honour. Raynal surrendered on 7 June and was honored even by his captors. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Vaillant

question: Fort Douaumont, reputed one of the strongest forts in the world, guarded Verdun behind concrete and steel. On 25 February 1916, only the battle's fifth day, the Germans captured it in a way that shocked France. How did this mighty fort fall?
answer: Without a shot being fired
choices: Without a shot being fired
Under a week-long siege
To a massive flamethrower assault
After its magazine exploded
context: A tiny German raiding party of the 24th Brandenburg Infantry Regiment slipped in through an unguarded passage and captured the surprised garrison of about 57 territorials. The French would not retake the fort until 24 October 1916. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Douaumont

question: The German chief of staff Erich von Falkenhayn chose to attack Verdun knowing French national pride would force France to defend it to the last man. He was not really aiming to capture the town at all; he wanted the killing itself. How did he sum up his grim purpose?
answer: To 'bleed France white'
choices: To 'bleed France white'
To 'break the French spirit'
To 'win by sheer numbers'
To 'starve France of guns'
context: Falkenhayn's aim was attrition itself, compelling the French to throw in every man they had. The battle cost both sides roughly 700,000 casualties, with around 300,000 dead. Source: britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Verdun and worldhistory.org/article/2878/battle-of-verdun/

question: Ludwig van Beethoven had gone so completely deaf that at the 1824 premiere of his Ninth Symphony, after the music ended, he kept beating time and turning pages with no idea the whole audience behind him was on its feet, roaring and waving hats and handkerchiefs. The young singer Caroline Unger stepped over to him so he would finally know. What did she do?
answer: Turned him around to face the cheering crowd
choices: Turned him around to face the cheering crowd
Handed him a written note of praise
Led him gently offstage by the arm
Placed the finished score back in his hands
context: Unger, the contralto soloist, physically turned the deaf composer toward the hall so he could SEE the ovation he could not hear. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._9_(Beethoven); thevintagenews.com/2016/09/10/premiere-symphony-no-9-beethoven-physically-turned-around-see-audience-applaud-even-waved-handkerchiefs/

question: Beethoven's Fifth Symphony opens with what many people call the most famous four notes in all of music. How do those four opening notes go?
answer: Short-short-short-LONG (da-da-da-DUM)
choices: Short-short-short-LONG (da-da-da-DUM)
Long-long-short-short (DUM-DUM-da-da)
Short-long-short-long (da-DUM-da-DUM)
Long-short-long-short (DUM-da-DUM-da)
context: Those four notes, in C minor, open the Fifth and are arguably the most recognizable phrase in Western music. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._5_(Beethoven)

question: The grand finale of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony gives the world one of the most beloved melodies ever written: the tune known as the 'Ode to Joy.' That melody grew so cherished that a major union of nations later adopted it as their official anthem. Which union?
answer: The European Union
choices: The European Union
The United Nations
The British Commonwealth
The International Red Cross
context: The choral finale sets Friedrich Schiller's poem 'An die Freude' ('Ode to Joy'); its melody is today the official anthem of the European Union. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._9_(Beethoven)

question: Before Beethoven's Ninth, a symphony was a work for orchestra alone — strings, brass, woodwinds and drums. In its last movement Beethoven added something no major symphony had ever included, and it astonished the first audiences. What did he add?
answer: A full singing chorus
choices: A full singing chorus
A solo church organ
A band of hunting horns
A military marching drum corps
context: The Ninth was the first major symphony to fold a singing chorus into the music itself, in the choral finale built on Schiller's words. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._9_(Beethoven)

question: At the Ninth's premiere on 7 May 1824, Beethoven stood on stage waving his arms and calling out tempos, but he was stone deaf and could not hear a single note. The real conductor, Michael Umlauf, had secretly told the players to ignore him and follow Umlauf instead. As the deaf Beethoven hurled himself back and forth 'like a madman,' how did his beat end up matching the actual music?
answer: He had fallen several bars behind it
choices: He had fallen several bars behind it
He stayed perfectly in step with it
He raced several bars ahead of it
He stopped beating partway through it
context: Eyewitnesses said Beethoven seemed to play every instrument and sing every chorus part, and by the end was several bars behind the music the orchestra was actually playing under Umlauf. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._9_(Beethoven); history.com/this-day-in-history/may-7/beethoven-ninth-symphony-debuts-vienna

question: The 'short-short-short-long' rhythm that opens Beethoven's Fifth is, by pure coincidence, identical to a single letter in Morse code: dot-dot-dot-dash. The BBC noticed this, and during World War II it broadcast those four Beethoven notes as the signal for one of its most famous wartime campaigns. Which campaign?
answer: The 'V for Victory' campaign
choices: The 'V for Victory' campaign
The 'Dig for Victory' campaign
The 'Keep Calm and Carry On' campaign
The 'Lend and Lease' campaign
context: Dot-dot-dot-dash is Morse for the letter V, matching the Fifth's opening rhythm, so the BBC used the four notes as the audio signal for the Allied 'V for Victory' campaign. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._5_(Beethoven)

question: As his deafness deepened, Beethoven found a strange way to still 'hear' his own piano: he would press one end of a wooden rod against the instrument's soundboard and hold the other end in one particular spot on his body, sensing the music as vibration. Where did he hold that rod?
answer: Clenched between his teeth
choices: Clenched between his teeth
Pressed flat against his ear
Held tight against his chest
Cupped in both of his hands
context: By biting a rod pressed to the piano, Beethoven felt the vibrations carry through his jawbone. (The tale that he sawed off his piano's legs to feel the floor is widely repeated but disputed.) mso.com.au/the-blog/2022-how-did-beethoven-write-one-of-his-greatest-compositions-while-deaf; hearinghealthmatters.org/hearing-international/2023/hearing-beethoven-part-ii-the-medical-conclusion/

question: In 1802, terrified that his deafness was destroying everything he was, Beethoven wrote a despairing private letter to his brothers — a letter found in his drawer only after he died. In it he confessed he had come close to ending his own life, and he named the single thing that had held him back. What was it, in his own account?
answer: His art — the music he still felt called to write
choices: His art — the music he still felt called to write
His faith in God and a life to come
His duty to look after his younger brothers
His hope that a doctor would yet cure him
context: In the Heiligenstadt Testament (6 October 1802) Beethoven wrote that 'only art it was that withheld me... it seemed impossible to leave the world until I had produced all that I felt called upon me to produce.' lvbeethoven.com/biography/the-heiligenstadt-testament/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heiligenstadt_Testament

question: Almost everyone 'knows' that Beethoven called the four-note opening of his Fifth Symphony 'Fate knocking at the door.' Yet historians now doubt he ever said it. Why has that famous quotation fallen under suspicion?
answer: The man who reported it forged entries in Beethoven's notebooks
choices: The man who reported it forged entries in Beethoven's notebooks
The man who reported it admitted he had made the line up
The man who reported it had never actually met Beethoven
The man who reported it was a rival composer with a grudge
context: The phrase comes from Beethoven's secretary Anton Schindler, now known to have forged entries in Beethoven's notebooks, so scholars treat 'Fate knocking' as almost certainly invented rather than the composer's own words. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._5_(Beethoven); classical-music.com/features/works/beethoven-fifth-symphony  (Legend.)

question: Beethoven was dying in Vienna in 1827 when he was told that a long-awaited case of fine wine had just arrived as a gift from his publisher. According to those at his bedside, his reaction became his last words. What did the dying composer say?
answer: 'Pity, pity — too late!'
choices: 'Pity, pity — too late!'
'At last, my dear old friend.'
'Pour it out, and let me rest.'
'Tell them all I forgive them.'
context: Beethoven died on 26 March 1827, aged 56; his documented last words, on hearing of the wine, were reportedly 'Pity, pity — too late!' en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_of_Ludwig_van_Beethoven; popularbeethoven.com/what-were-beethovens-last-words/

question: One romantic legend says Beethoven's true final words were a Latin line — 'Applaud, friends, the comedy is over.' But his friend Anselm Huttenbrenner, who was present at the deathbed, flatly denied in 1860 that Beethoven ever said it. On what grounds did Huttenbrenner reject the story?
answer: He had not been in the room for the rite the line refers to
choices: He had not been in the room for the rite the line refers to
He had never once heard Beethoven speak any Latin
He swore Beethoven had been unconscious for days before
He claimed a rival had invented it to mock the church
context: Huttenbrenner denied the 'comedy is over' line because he was not even present for the religious rite the remark would have followed, so historians treat it as legend, not record. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_of_Ludwig_van_Beethoven; libquotes.com/ludwig-van-beethoven/quote/lbv0f1d

question: Beethoven had asked that his illnesses be studied after his death, but it took until 2023 for scientists to do it the modern way — sequencing his entire genome from authenticated locks of his hair. Alongside a strong inherited risk of liver disease, they found an infection in his final months that, with his heavy drinking, most likely brought on the liver failure that killed him. Which infection did the hair reveal?
answer: Hepatitis B
choices: Hepatitis B
Tuberculosis
Typhoid fever
Malaria
context: The 2023 genome study of five genetically-matched hair locks found a hepatitis B infection plus a genetic risk for liver disease; it also debunked an older 'lead poisoning' claim because that earlier 'Beethoven hair' was not actually his. cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(23)00181-1; phys.org/news/2023-03-dna-beethoven-hair-poor-healthand.html

question: In Boston in 1876, Alexander Graham Bell spilled acid on his clothes and shouted for his assistant through his new invention in the next room. Those few words became the first sentence ever carried down a telephone wire. What did Bell say?
answer: "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you."
choices: "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you."
"Watson, the wire is working at last."
"Can you hear my voice from there?"
"Come quickly, the experiment is done."
context: Boston, March 10, 1876. Thomas Watson, in the next room, heard it clearly and wrote it down in his notebook (now in the Library of Congress Bell Papers). https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/march-10/speech-transmitted-by-telephone

question: In 1877 Thomas Edison built a machine that could record a voice on tinfoil and play it back. He spoke a few words into it as a test, and when the machine repeated them aloud even Edison was astonished. What words did his phonograph speak back?
answer: "Mary had a little lamb"
choices: "Mary had a little lamb"
"Hello, can you hear me"
"Twinkle, twinkle, little star"
"The quick brown fox jumps"
context: His mechanic John Kruesi built the tinfoil phonograph in about 30 hours, and Edison recited the nursery rhyme to test it. https://ethw.org/Phonograph

question: Thomas Edison ran his New Jersey lab like an 'invention factory,' promising a small invention every ten days and a big one every six months. Newspapers gave him a nickname that made him sound like he conjured marvels out of thin air. What was the nickname?
answer: The Wizard of Menlo Park
choices: The Wizard of Menlo Park
The Sage of New Jersey
The Lord of Lightning
The Genius of Greenfield
context: Menlo Park, New Jersey, was the site of his famous lab. Edison's name ended up on 1,093 U.S. patents, still among the most by any single person. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Edison

question: To make his light bulb glow, Thomas Edison's team tested over 1,600 different substances searching for one that could burn bright without melting. On October 21, 1879, one finally glowed for about 13.5 hours. What did they burn inside that first successful bulb?
answer: A carbonized cotton thread
choices: A carbonized cotton thread
A thin strip of copper
A coil of iron wire
A sliver of polished glass
context: Carbonizing (charring) the cotton turned it into a filament that resisted the current and glowed instead of burning up. https://edison.rutgers.edu/life-of-edison/biographical-essays/lighting/the-carbon-filament-lamp

question: After his first bulb worked for only about half a day, Thomas Edison's team kept hunting for a filament that could last far longer. They struck gold with one humble material that burned for over 1,200 hours and lit homes for years. What surprising material was it?
answer: Carbonized bamboo
choices: Carbonized bamboo
Spun sheep's wool
Braided horsehair
Dried seaweed strands
context: Charred bamboo fibers made a tough, long-lasting filament. Edison didn't invent the glowing bulb from nothing, but he built the first practical, long-lasting one plus the wires and generators to actually light a city. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Edison

question: Thomas Edison did not believe great inventions came from sudden flashes of brilliance. He thought they came from relentless trying and failing and trying again, and he summed up that belief in one famous line he confirmed he'd said in a 1927 letter. What did Edison say invention really was?
answer: "One percent inspiration and ninety-nine percent perspiration."
choices: "One percent inspiration and ninety-nine percent perspiration."
"A thousand failures for every single success."
"Equal parts imagination and stubborn hard work."
"Mostly luck, and a little bit of cleverness."
context: The line captures Edison's whole method: test 1,600 materials if that's what it takes. https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Thomas_Edison

question: In the 'War of the Currents,' Thomas Edison championed direct current (DC), which was safe but grew weak after a short distance. His rivals George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla backed a rival kind of electricity that could be pushed for miles over thin wires. That rival won, and it still flows from every wall socket today. What kind of current was it?
answer: Alternating current (AC)
choices: Alternating current (AC)
Stronger direct current (DC)
Static electric charge
Stored battery current
context: Alternating current reverses direction many times a second, which let transformers boost it to high voltage for long trips and then lower it again for safe use in homes. https://www.history.com/articles/what-was-the-war-of-the-currents

question: During the War of the Currents, Thomas Edison's camp wanted the public to dread alternating current as a killer. They coined a creepy new verb meaning 'to execute someone with electricity,' built from the name of the rival inventor who championed AC. What was the made-up word?
answer: "Westinghoused"
choices: "Westinghoused"
"Edisoned"
"Teslated"
"Currented"
context: George Westinghouse was the businessman backing AC, so Edison's camp turned his name into the verb, tying him personally to death by electricity. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/edison-vs-westinghouse-a-shocking-rivalry-102146036/

question: At the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, George Westinghouse used Nikola Tesla's alternating current to switch on more than 100,000 light bulbs at once, more electric light than most people had ever seen in one place. The glowing fairgrounds earned a glittering nickname. What were they called?
answer: The White City
choices: The White City
The Crystal Court
The Golden Mile
The Silver Fair
context: Westinghouse had won the lighting contract by underbidding Edison's people, $399,000 to $554,000. The dazzling display proved AC was safe and practical to the public. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World%27s_Columbian_Exposition

question: On July 30, 1888, Thomas Edison's hired man Harold Brown staged a grim public demonstration at Columbia College, before a hall of electricians and reporters. He shocked the same dog first with Edison's direct current and then with alternating current. What was the shocking result?
answer: It survived 1,000 volts of DC but died at just 330 volts of AC.
choices: It survived 1,000 volts of DC but died at just 330 volts of AC.
It shrugged off 700 volts of DC but died at 700 volts of AC.
It survived 500 volts of AC but died at 1,400 volts of DC.
It died at 250 volts of AC and 250 volts of DC alike.
context: The rigged demo was meant to brand AC as a killer even at low voltage, helping Edison's campaign against Westinghouse. https://www.discovermagazine.com/technology/the-cruel-animal-testing-behind-thomas-edisons-quest-to-show-dangers-of-ac

question: On August 6, 1890, the first electric chair, powered by the alternating current Edison's camp had branded as deadly, was used on William Kemmler, and it went horribly wrong. After the first jolt Kemmler was still breathing and a witness screamed 'Great God! He's alive!' George Westinghouse was appalled by the botched job. What did Westinghouse say afterward?
answer: "They could have done better with an ax."
choices: "They could have done better with an ax."
"This proves my current is the safer one."
"No machine of mine was ever meant for this."
"The fault lies with the men, not the wires."
context: Westinghouse had fought to keep his AC out of executions, and the gruesome failure horrified him. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/edison-vs-westinghouse-a-shocking-rivalry-102146036/

question: A popular story claims Thomas Edison electrocuted Topsy the elephant at Coney Island to scare the public away from alternating current. Historians say that version is false. Which of these is the real story behind Topsy's death?
answer: Topsy died at Coney Island in 1903, after Edison had left his electric company, which only filmed it.
choices: Topsy died at Coney Island in 1903, after Edison had left his electric company, which only filmed it.
Topsy died of old age at the Bronx Zoo in 1910, and Edison's film crew staged a re-enactment afterward.
Topsy was put down by her own circus handlers in 1908, and no film of her death was ever made at all.
Topsy died at Coney Island in 1903, but it was George Westinghouse's company, not Edison's, that filmed it.
context: The War of the Currents was effectively over by the mid-1890s, when AC at Niagara Falls sent power 26 miles to Buffalo. Topsy died on January 4, 1903, ten years after the current war ended; Edison's film company merely recorded it in a short titled 'Electrocuting an Elephant' and did not stage it as anti-AC propaganda. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topsy_(elephant)

question: Benedict Arnold was one of the Continental Army's boldest generals, a hero of the Battle of Saratoga. But bitter over slights and buried in debt, he secretly agreed to betray the Americans for British money and a British command. What did he plot to hand over to the enemy?
answer: West Point, the fort guarding the Hudson River
choices: West Point, the fort guarding the Hudson River
George Washington's personal battle plans
the Continental Army's main gunpowder stores
the harbor defenses of New York City
context: Arnold negotiated 20,000 British pounds and a generalship for surrendering West Point, the fort that controlled the Hudson River. After the plot collapsed he received only about 6,000 of the promised 20,000 pounds. His name became the American synonym for traitor; he died unpopular in London in 1801. Source: history.com, 'Benedict Arnold commits treason' / '9 things you may not know about Benedict Arnold'.

question: As Benedict Arnold's scheme to surrender West Point unraveled, the British officer carrying the secret plans, Major John Andre, was stopped by militiamen near Tarrytown, New York. He tried to bluff his way past, but the men searched him and found the West Point papers in an unexpected hiding place. Where were the plans hidden?
answer: folded inside his boot
choices: folded inside his boot
sewn into his saddle
rolled in his pistol barrel
tucked under his hat
context: Three ordinary militiamen, John Paulding, Isaac Van Wart, and David Williams, caught Andre and found the plans hidden in his boot/stocking. Andre offered them a bribe to let him go; they refused. He asked to die a soldier's death by firing squad rather than the gallows; the request was denied and he was hanged at Tappan, New York on October 2, 1780, at age 29. Source: metmuseum.org collection record; allthingsliberty.com, 'Major Andre's Captors Revisited'; westminster-abbey.org, 'John Andre'.

question: St. Benedict, who organized monastery life in Europe around 529 AD, summed up his whole way of living in just two Latin words — a motto that gave a monk's day its balance, so that it was ruled by neither one thing alone nor the other alone. What was Benedict's famous two-word motto?
answer: Pray and work
choices: Pray and work
Watch and fast
Read and obey
Give and serve
context: 'Ora et labora' — 'pray and work.' Benedict split a monk's day roughly into thirds: about eight hours of prayer, eight of work, and eight of sleep, so a man was ruled by neither prayer alone nor labor alone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ora_et_labora

question: The Rule of St. Benedict is a 73-chapter handbook for how monks should live together. Of all the ways such a rulebook could begin, its very first word is a single, quiet command from the master to the monk. What is the first word of the entire Rule?
answer: Listen
choices: Listen
Obey
Kneel
Pray
context: The Rule opens: 'Listen carefully, my child, to the master's instructions, and incline the ear of your heart.' The Latin is 'Obsculta' / 'Ausculta.' A whole rulebook for the disciplined life begins by telling the monk simply to listen. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_Saint_Benedict

question: Chapter 53 of the Rule of St. Benedict tells the monks how to treat any traveler who knocks at the monastery gate — rich or poor, friend or stranger. According to Benedict, every guest who arrives was to be welcomed as if he were whom?
answer: Christ himself
choices: Christ himself
royal envoy
lost brother
wandering angel
context: 'Let all guests who arrive be received like Christ, for He is going to say: I was a stranger and you welcomed me.' Every traveler at the gate, however poor, was to be greeted as if Christ Himself had come. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_Saint_Benedict

question: Before he ever wrote his Rule, the young Benedict became a hermit at Subiaco, living three whole years alone and unknown to the world in a cliffside cave. A monk named Romanus kept him alive by secretly letting one thing down to the cave on a rope. According to Pope Gregory's account, what did Romanus lower to him?
answer: Bread
choices: Bread
Water
Firewood
Clothing
context: Romanus secretly lowered bread on a rope from the monastery above. The story is told by Pope Gregory the Great in Book II of his 'Dialogues' (c. 593) — the only real biography of Benedict, and the origin point of Western monasticism. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Saint-Benedict-of-Nursia  (Legend.)

question: The Book of Kells, made by Irish monks around 800 AD, is covered in swirling, interlaced patterns so impossibly fine that when the medieval writer Gerald of Wales examined a similar book centuries later, he declared it could not be human work at all. Whose work did Gerald say such a book must be?
answer: Angels'
choices: Angels'
Giants'
Wizards'
Saints'
context: Giraldus Cambrensis (Gerald of Wales), seeing such a book in the 1180s, called it the work 'not of men, but of Angels.' Source: https://www.irishcatholic.com/exploring-the-work-of-angels-in-the-book-of-kells/

question: Monks spent roughly a thousand years as Europe's librarians, hunched in the writing-room — the scriptorium — copying books by hand, one letter at a time. Besides the Bible, Benedict's monks famously preserved a whole body of writing by pagan authors that the Church might easily have let perish. What did they painstakingly copy out and save?
answer: The classical works of Greece and Rome
choices: The classical works of Greece and Rome
The laws of the Frankish kings
The songs of traveling minstrels
The trade records of merchants
context: In the scriptorium, monks copied scripture and the Church Fathers — and crucially the pagan classics of Greece and Rome. Almost everything written that survived to the age of the printing press passed through their hands. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scriptorium

question: Benedict ordered his monks to spend fixed hours of every day at hard manual labor and other fixed hours at sacred reading. Chapter 48 of the Rule gives his blunt reason in one famous opening phrase: one thing, above all, he said, is 'the enemy of the soul.' According to Benedict, what is the enemy of the soul?
answer: Idleness
choices: Idleness
Pride
Greed
Doubt
context: 'Idleness is the enemy of the soul' (Rule, ch. 48). It is the reason Benedict filled the monastic day with labor and reading rather than leaving any hours empty. Source: https://courses.lumenlearning.com/suny-geneseo-humanities1-1/chapter/the-rule-of-st-benedict-chapters-26-50/

question: Around 529 AD Benedict founded his greatest monastery, Monte Cassino, on a mountaintop in southern Italy — the mother-house of all Benedictine monasticism. But the summit was not empty when he arrived, and before he could build, Benedict tore down what already stood there. What did he tear down to make room for the monastery?
answer: A pagan temple to Apollo
choices: A pagan temple to Apollo
A fort built by Caesar
A shrine to the goddess Vesta
A palace of the Lombard kings
context: Monte Cassino was raised on the site of an old pagan temple to Apollo, which Benedict tore down. It became the cradle of Benedictine monasticism. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Saint-Benedict-of-Nursia

question: Copying books by hand was brutal, body-breaking labor — one monk warned that it dimmed the eyes, ached the back, and knit the chest and belly together. Weary scribes sometimes scribbled tiny complaints into the margins of the very books they were copying. One exhausted English scribe wrote a short four-word prayer in Old English. What did he write?
answer: 'God help my hands'
choices: 'God help my hands'
'God grant me sleep'
'God spare my eyes'
'God end this book'
context: An 11th-century English scribe wrote, in Old English, 'God helpe minum handum' — 'God help my hands.' Other real margin-notes: 'Three fingers write, but the whole body labours,' and 'While the fingers write, the rest of the body hardly rests.' Source: https://thijsporck.com/2017/06/12/scribal-complaints/

question: The Rule of St. Benedict is famous for being humane rather than harsh. Benedict even said he was being generous, since stricter custom held that one particular drink 'is not at all proper for monks' — yet he allowed each monk a fixed daily ration of it, with somewhat more on hot days or for heavy work. How much did Benedict permit each monk per day?
answer: Half a pint of wine
choices: Half a pint of wine
A quart of ale
A cup of milk
A jug of cider
context: Each monk was allowed about a 'hemina' of wine — roughly a quarter-litre, or half a pint — even though Benedict admitted 'we read that wine is not at all proper for monks.' On hot days or for hard work the abbot could allow more. The moderation is what made the Rule humane. Source: https://ccel.org/ccel/benedict/rule/rule.xlii.html

question: Dom Pierre Perignon was a real Benedictine monk who worked on the wines of the Champagne region in the 1600s. Everyone 'knows' that on first tasting sparkling champagne he cried, 'Come quickly — I am drinking the stars!' But historians say Perignon never said it, was blind in old age, and did not even invent champagne. Where did this famous fake quote first appear?
answer: In a 19th-century advertisement
choices: In a 19th-century advertisement
In a medieval monk's chronicle
In a French royal decree
In an old drinking song
context: The beloved 'drinking the stars' line is a fiction, invented in a 19th-century advertisement long after Perignon's death. The real Dom Perignon did pioneering work on Champagne wines at Hautvillers Abbey but did not invent sparkling champagne. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dom_P%C3%A9rignon_(monk)  (Legend.)

question: In 2019, scientists studying the skeleton of a medieval nun buried in Germany around the year 1100 found over a hundred specks of brilliant blue trapped in the hardened tartar on her teeth. The blue was ultramarine — ground from lapis lazuli, costlier than gold, carried all the way from Afghanistan. How did this precious blue get inside her mouth?
answer: She licked her paintbrush to a fine point
choices: She licked her paintbrush to a fine point
She chewed the raw stone as medicine
She drank from a blue-glazed cup
She kissed a painted holy book
context: She had repeatedly licked her ultramarine-loaded brush to a fine point while illuminating manuscripts. Her blue-stained teeth are some of the only physical proof that women, too, painted and decorated medieval books. Source: https://www.york.ac.uk/news-and-events/news/2019/research/ultramarine-pigment-reveal-forgotten-female-scribe/

question: Hand-copied books were so precious that monks guarded them with written CURSES against anyone who might steal them. One such curse, copied into a German Bible around 1172, called down a whole storm of torments on the thief. Which of these was actually among the fates that curse wished upon a book-thief?
answer: That he be roasted in a frying pan
choices: That he be roasted in a frying pan
That his hands wither to the bone
That his name be struck from all books
That wolves devour him by night
context: The real curse: 'may he die, may he be roasted in a frying pan, may the falling sickness and fever attack him, and may he be broken on the wheel and hanged. Amen.' Another, shorter, simply spat: 'Out with his eyes, out with his eyes!' Source: https://www.openculture.com/2021/08/medieval-scribes-discouraged-theft-of-manuscripts (Marc Drogin, 'Anathema!')

question: Chapter 7 of the Rule of St. Benedict lays out twelve 'steps of humility' that a monk must climb like rungs on a ladder, each one a harder discipline than the one before. The ninth step tells a monk not to speak until he is spoken to. The tenth step forbids a very ordinary, human thing. According to Benedict, what should a humble monk NOT be quick to do?
answer: Laugh
choices: Laugh
Eat
Sleep
Weep
context: The tenth step of humility is that a monk 'should not be quick to laugh' (the ninth being that he should not speak until spoken to). The twelve steps run from fearing God and surrendering one's own will all the way up to a settled, quiet humility of bearing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_Saint_Benedict

question: In 1723 a hungry 17-year-old named Benjamin Franklin walked off the boat into Philadelphia with barely any money and bought three big puffy rolls. With nowhere to put them, he carried them up the street looking so ridiculous that his future wife Deborah laughed at the sight. How did he carry the three rolls?
answer: He tucked a roll under each arm and ate the third as he walked
choices: He tucked a roll under each arm and ate the third as he walked
He balanced all three rolls on his head and walked slowly
He stuffed the three rolls into his coat and buttoned it shut
He handed two rolls to strangers and ate the last himself
context: Franklin tells this story in his Autobiography: he arrived broke and famished, bought three great rolls, and walked off with one under each arm, eating the third. Deborah Read, watching from her father's doorway, thought he looked absurd — and later married him. Source: Franklin, Autobiography (ushistory.org/franklin/autobiography); Penn Today, 'An inauspicious arrival for the ambitious Benjamin Franklin'.

question: Benjamin Franklin published a wildly popular yearly almanac from 1732 to 1758, packed with sayings still quoted today like 'Early to bed and early to rise makes a man healthy, wealthy and wise' and 'A penny saved is a penny earned.' He never signed his own name to it — instead he invented a folksy character to 'write' it. What was that made-up author's name?
answer: Poor Richard Saunders
choices: Poor Richard Saunders
Honest Abel Trueman
Plain Tom Tickler
Simple Simon Pry
context: Franklin wrote as 'Richard Saunders' — 'Poor Richard' — and the book became Poor Richard's Almanack, one of the best-selling things in the colonies. Many of its sayings are still everyday English. Source: americanliterature.com, 'Poor Richard's Almanack'; worldhistoryedu.com, 'Poor Richard's Almanack'.

question: In 1754 Benjamin Franklin printed the very first American political cartoon in his Pennsylvania Gazette, urging the separate colonies to band together. Under the words 'JOIN, or DIE,' he drew a single picture that became famous across the colonies. What was the image?
answer: A snake chopped into eight pieces, one for each colony
choices: A snake chopped into eight pieces, one for each colony
An eagle clutching eight broken arrows in its claws
A bundle of eight wooden sticks tied tightly together
A heavy iron chain with eight cracked links
context: Franklin drew on an old belief that a snake cut apart could come back to life if its pieces were rejoined before sunset — so the divided colonies, like the divided snake, would die unless they reunited. The 'Join, or Die' snake later reappeared during the Revolution. Source: Join, or Die — Wikipedia; constitutioncenter.org, 'The story behind the Join or Die snake cartoon'.

question: Benjamin Franklin got tired of constantly swapping between his reading glasses and his distance glasses. So he had both kinds of lens sliced in half and fitted into a single frame — distance on top, reading on the bottom — and called them 'double spectacles.' What do we call this invention today?
answer: Bifocals
choices: Bifocals
Binoculars
Monocles
Telescopes
context: Franklin's 'double spectacles' are what we now call bifocals — one lens does two jobs, so the wearer never has to switch glasses. Like his other inventions, he never patented them. Source: The Franklin Institute, 'Benjamin Franklin's Inventions' (fi.edu); science.howstuffworks.com, '10 Ben Franklin Inventions'.

question: In 1761 Benjamin Franklin invented a brand-new musical instrument: a row of 37 nested glass bowls spun on a spindle by a foot pedal, played by touching wet fingertips to the spinning rims. It made such an eerie, beautiful sound that both Mozart and Beethoven later wrote music for it. What did Franklin name this instrument?
answer: The armonica
choices: The armonica
The clavier
The seraphine
The melodeon
context: Franklin called it the glass armonica (from the Italian word for harmony). Spinning glass bowls touched by wet fingers gave it a haunting tone that fascinated Europe's greatest composers. Source: The Franklin Institute, 'Benjamin Franklin's Glass Armonica' (fi.edu); Glass harmonica — Wikipedia.

question: In June 1752 Benjamin Franklin flew a silk kite into a thunderstorm with his son William, having tied a metal key to the bottom of the wet kite string. When he brought his knuckle close to that key, what did he feel?
answer: A spark jumped from the key to his knuckle
choices: A spark jumped from the key to his knuckle
The key turned ice-cold under his finger
A loud crack of thunder right above him
The string yanked hard out of his hand
context: The spark proved that the storm's lightning was the same thing as electricity. Franklin's own Pennsylvania Gazette instructions (Oct. 19, 1752) told readers that once the rain wet the kite and twine, the electric fire 'will stream out plentifully from the Key on the Approach of your Knuckle.' Source: The Franklin Institute, 'Kite-Key Experiment' (fi.edu); Kite experiment — Wikipedia.

question: Buildings in Benjamin Franklin's day often burned down when lightning struck them. Around 1750 Franklin invented a tall, pointed metal rod to bolt onto a rooftop so the building would survive a direct strike — some of the first ones went up on Independence Hall. When lightning hits the rod, what does the rod do with that surge of electricity?
answer: It carries the electricity safely down into the ground
choices: It carries the electricity safely down into the ground
It hurls the electricity back up at the clouds
It locks the electricity away inside itself
It changes the electricity into harmless light
context: This is the lightning rod. The pointed rod catches the strike and a wire runs the electricity harmlessly into the earth, so it never sets the building ablaze. Franklin invented it soon after his electricity experiments. Source: The Franklin Institute, 'Benjamin Franklin's Inventions' (fi.edu); constitutioncenter.org, 'Ben Franklin's best inventions'.

question: When Benjamin Franklin arrived in Paris as America's ambassador, the French treated him like a celebrity. Instead of the fancy powdered wig a gentleman was expected to wear, Franklin showed up in something modest and homespun that the French found irresistibly charming. What did he wear on his head?
answer: A plain fur cap
choices: A plain fur cap
A simple straw hat
A tall silk hat
A red liberty cap
context: The fur cap made Franklin a sensation — fashionable French women piled their hair into a tall style they called the 'coiffure a la Franklin' to imitate it, and his face turned up on snuffboxes and medallions all over France. Source: history.com, 'Ben Franklin in Paris'; benjamin-franklin-history.org, 'Ambassador to France'.

question: Benjamin Franklin invented the lightning rod, the Franklin stove, and bifocals — any one of which could have made him rich. Yet he refused to take out a patent on a single one. In his Autobiography, what reason did he give for letting everyone use his inventions for free?
answer: Since we enjoy others' inventions, we should gladly serve others with ours
choices: Since we enjoy others' inventions, we should gladly serve others with ours
A gentleman should never stoop to selling his clever ideas for coin
An inventor who hoards his ideas insults the God who inspired them
Patents only invite endless lawsuits that he had no time for
