context: Franklin wrote that 'as we enjoy great advantages from the inventions of others, we should be glad of an opportunity to serve others by any invention of ours; and this we should do freely and generously.' He wanted his ideas used by everyone, not locked up for profit. Source: Franklin, Autobiography, quoted by constitutioncenter.org, 'Ben Franklin's best inventions'; The Franklin Institute (fi.edu).

question: Benjamin Franklin's greatest triumph as a diplomat came on February 6, 1778, when he persuaded France to sign a treaty of alliance with the struggling young United States — even a jealous John Adams admitted Franklin was treated like a star in Paris. What did this French alliance give the American cause that made winning the Revolution possible?
answer: Money, weapons, and a powerful navy
choices: Money, weapons, and a powerful navy
Maps, spies, and a promise of secrecy
Settlers, farm tools, and seeds for the frontier
Gold, silk, and fine wine for the generals
context: France's cash, guns, and especially its fleet tipped the war toward American victory; without the French alliance Franklin secured, independence might have failed. Source: history.state.gov, 'Benjamin Franklin: First American Diplomat'; history.com, 'Ben Franklin in Paris'.

question: As the Constitutional Convention finished its work in 1787, the elderly Benjamin Franklin pointed to a sun carved on the back of George Washington's chair. All through the long, uncertain debates, he said, he had wondered about that sun. What did Franklin finally declare about it?
answer: That it was a rising sun, not a setting one
choices: That it was a rising sun, not a setting one
That it should be painted gold for the new nation
That it stood for the king they had thrown off
That no man could tell sunrise from sunset
context: James Madison's convention notes record Franklin saying he had often looked at that half-sun unsure if it was rising or setting, 'but now at length I have the happiness to know that it is a rising and not a setting Sun' — hope for the new republic. Source: James Madison's notes, via teachingamericanhistory.org, 'Benjamin Franklin's Final Remark'; nps.gov, 'September 17, 1787'.

question: Just weeks before he died in April 1790, the 84-year-old Benjamin Franklin made his very last public act: he signed and sent a bold petition to the first United States Congress, asking it to fix what he called a deep 'Inconsistency' in the American character. What did Franklin's petition demand?
answer: That Congress end slavery and the slave trade
choices: That Congress end slavery and the slave trade
That Congress make him the first ambassador to Britain
That Congress build a great university in Philadelphia
That Congress put his face on the new dollar coin
context: Franklin led the Pennsylvania Abolition Society, and its petition asked Congress to end slavery and the slave trade and to 'devise means for removing the Inconsistency from the Character of the American People.' He died a few weeks later. Source: National Archives, 'Benjamin Franklin's Anti-Slavery Petitions to Congress' (archives.gov); constitutioncenter.org, petition document.

question: In October 1723, a broke and hungry 17-year-old Benjamin Franklin walked off the boat into Philadelphia and spent his last pennies on three big puffy rolls at a baker's. With no bag and his pockets stuffed, how did he carry them up Market Street?
answer: With a roll under each arm, eating the third
choices: With a roll under each arm, eating the third
Balanced in a stack on top of his head
Wrapped in his coat slung over his shoulder
Stuffed two in his hat and ate the third
context: Franklin tells the story in his Autobiography: he marched up Market Street 'with a Roll under each Arm, & eating the third' — and a girl who would later become his wife saw him and thought he looked ridiculous. Source: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin (Founders Online; Penn Today, penntoday.upenn.edu; ushistory.org).

question: Benjamin Franklin loved to swim, and at about 11 years old he made his very first invention to go faster in the water. He cut two flat oval pieces of wood with holes for his thumbs and strapped them to his hands. What had he built?
answer: Swim paddles for his hands
choices: Swim paddles for his hands
A wooden diving mask
A pair of webbed wooden flippers
An inflatable leather float
context: The oval paddles were about 10 by 6 inches; Franklin recalled they sped him up by letting him push more water, but they tired out his wrists. He stayed a strong swimmer his whole life. Source: The Franklin Institute, fi.edu/en/science-and-education/benjamin-franklin/inventions; History.com.

question: Benjamin Franklin got tired of swapping between one pair of glasses for reading up close and another for seeing far away. So he had the lenses cut in half and recombined into a single frame — distance on top, reading on the bottom. What do we call the eyewear he invented?
answer: Bifocals
choices: Bifocals
Trifocals
A monocle
The magnifying glass
context: Franklin put two different lenses into one pair of glasses around 1785, so he could look up to see across a room and glance down to read — exactly how bifocals still work today. Source: The Franklin Institute, fi.edu; History.com.

question: After proving that lightning was electricity, Benjamin Franklin designed a simple device to protect buildings: sharp iron points fixed to rooftops to draw the electric fire harmlessly out of a storm cloud before it could strike. Soon these topped buildings all over the colonies. What was this invention?
answer: The lightning rod
choices: The lightning rod
The Franklin stove
The glass armonica
Bifocal spectacles
context: The pointed iron rod carries the charge safely down a wire into the ground instead of letting it blast through the roof — a direct payoff from Franklin's kite work, and still standard on tall buildings today. Source: The Franklin Institute, fi.edu/en/science-and-education/benjamin-franklin/inventions; History.com.

question: In 1752, to prove lightning was the same thing as electricity, Benjamin Franklin flew a silk kite into a storm with a metal key tied to the wet string and a dry silk ribbon he held under shelter to stay safe. As the storm passed, he moved his knuckle close to the key. What happened?
answer: A spark jumped from the key
choices: A spark jumped from the key
The kite caught fire
The key melted in his fingers
The whole string glowed blue
context: A spark leaping to his knuckle showed the storm cloud had charged the key — lightning really was electricity. He also noticed the loose threads of the wet twine standing straight up, repelling each other. Source: The Franklin Institute, fi.edu; Franklin's 19 Oct 1752 letter to Peter Collinson (Pennsylvania Gazette).

question: Paintings and cartoons love to show Benjamin Franklin's kite getting blasted by a forked lightning bolt — but historians say that picture is flat wrong, because the real kite only quietly soaked up charge from the cloud. If an actual bolt HAD struck the kite, why would that have been a catastrophe?
answer: It would almost certainly have killed him
choices: It would almost certainly have killed him
It would have burned the silk kite to ash
It would have shattered the metal key
It would have flung him across the field
context: A direct strike carries enough energy to kill instantly, which is why Franklin was careful to draw charge slowly, not catch a bolt. The danger was real: in 1753 Georg Wilhelm Richmann tried a similar experiment and was killed, reportedly by ball lightning. Source: The Franklin Institute, fi.edu; History.com.

question: At 16, Benjamin Franklin was forbidden to publish in his older brother James's newspaper, the New-England Courant. So he invented a fake author, wrote letters in disguised handwriting, and slipped them under the print-shop door at night — and James printed fourteen of them in 1722. Who was this made-up writer?
answer: A middle-aged widow named Silence Dogood
choices: A middle-aged widow named Silence Dogood
An almanac-maker named Poor Richard
A country preacher named Father Abraham
A busybody named Anthony Afterwit
context: 'Silence Dogood' was a sharp-tongued widow with strong opinions, and her letters were a hit — until James discovered his teenage kid brother was the real author and was furious. Source: Massachusetts Historical Society, masshist.org/online/silence_dogood; ushistory.org/franklin/courant.

question: Benjamin Franklin invented many useful things, but he said one of them 'has given me the greatest personal satisfaction' of all. Which invention did he say he loved most?
answer: The glass armonica
choices: The glass armonica
The lightning rod
Bifocal spectacles
The Franklin stove
context: The glass armonica was a musical instrument: 37 nested glass bowls spun on an iron spindle by a foot pedal, played by touching the wet rims to make 'incomparably sweet' notes. Mozart and Beethoven later wrote music for it. Source: The Franklin Institute, fi.edu; History.com.

question: On May 9, 1754, Benjamin Franklin printed a now-famous picture in his Pennsylvania Gazette: a snake chopped into eight pieces, each piece labeled with a colony's initials, urging the colonies to come together against the French. It is considered the first American political cartoon. What two-word caption ran beneath the snake?
answer: JOIN, or DIE
choices: JOIN, or DIE
UNITE OR FALL
DON'T TREAD ON ME
LIBERTY OR DEATH
context: The idea came from a folk belief that a snake cut in pieces could come back to life if joined before sunset — so a divided America would die, but a united one would live. The image was revived years later during the Revolution. Source: National Constitution Center, constitutioncenter.org/blog/the-story-behind-the-join-or-die-snake-cartoon.

question: Pennsylvania's governor offered Benjamin Franklin a patent that would let him collect a fee from everyone who copied his popular stove — a guaranteed stream of money. What did Franklin do?
answer: Refused it, so anyone could copy it free
choices: Refused it, so anyone could copy it free
Accepted it and made a fortune in fees
Sold it to the governor for a lump sum
Patented it quietly under a false name
context: Franklin never patented any of his inventions. He wrote that 'as we enjoy great advantages from the inventions of others, we should be glad of an opportunity to serve others by any invention of ours.' Source: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, ushistory.org/franklin/autobiography/page55.htm; c4sif.org.

question: Benjamin Franklin's electrical experiments won him the Royal Society's highest honor, the Copley Medal, in 1753 — and along the way he invented plain English words for electricity that we still use every single day. Which set of common electrical words did Franklin coin?
answer: battery, charge, conductor, positive, negative
choices: battery, charge, conductor, positive, negative
volt, watt, ohm, ampere, hertz
atom, molecule, electron, proton, neutron
current, circuit, voltage, resistance, wattage
context: Franklin needed new vocabulary to describe what he was discovering, so he named it — and the words stuck. (The volt, watt, ohm, ampere, and hertz came later, each named after a different scientist.) Source: Library of Congress, loc.gov/exhibits/franklin/franklin-scientist.html; Founders Online (Copley Medal award).

question: As colonial postmaster, Benjamin Franklin was baffled that British mail ships took two weeks longer to cross the Atlantic than American ships. His whaler cousin Timothy Folger explained the reason: the British captains were sailing straight against a powerful warm current. Franklin then charted and named it. What is this current?
answer: The Gulf Stream
choices: The Gulf Stream
The Sargasso Sea
The Humboldt Current
The Labrador Current
context: Franklin published his chart in 1769 and later measured the current with a thermometer, noting it 'is always warmer than the sea on each side of it.' Whalers knew its path because they followed it to find whales. Source: NOAA, oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/bfranklin.html; Smithsonian.

question: The French statesman Turgot summed up Benjamin Franklin's whole life in a single Latin line later carved on busts and engravings — praising him for BOTH taming lightning with his rod AND helping topple a king through the American Revolution. The line said Franklin had snatched two things away. Which two?
answer: The thunderbolt from heaven and the scepter from tyrants
choices: The thunderbolt from heaven and the scepter from tyrants
The fire from the gods and the crown from kings
The lightning from the sky and the throne from emperors
The storm from the clouds and the scepter from Rome
context: The Latin reads 'Eripuit caelo fulmen sceptrumque tyrannis.' It casts Franklin as a kind of Prometheus — stealing fire from the sky — who also helped strip power from a monarch. Source: Oxford Reference, oxfordreference.com; Journal of the American Revolution, allthingsliberty.com.

question: As a younger man, Benjamin Franklin owned enslaved people and ran slave-sale ads in his Pennsylvania Gazette. Late in life he reversed himself completely, becoming president of the Pennsylvania abolition society in 1787. What was his very last public act before his death in 1790?
answer: Signing a petition asking the first Congress to abolish slavery
choices: Signing a petition asking the first Congress to abolish slavery
Freeing the last people he had enslaved
Delivering a speech to Congress against slavery
Leaving his estate to the abolition society
context: The man who once sold enslaved people made ending slavery his dying cause. Weeks before his death he also published a hoax as 'Historicus' — a fake speech by an Algerian, Sidi Mehemet Ibrahim, defending the enslavement of Christians, deliberately mirroring a Georgia congressman's defense of American slavery to expose it as absurd. Source: National Archives, archives.gov/legislative/features/franklin; Bill of Rights Institute.

question: In 1948, American pilot Lt. Gail Halvorsen walked up to a crowd of hungry German children pressed against the fence at Berlin's airfield. All he had to offer was two sticks of chewing gum for the whole crowd. What did the children do that amazed him?
answer: Shared the gum and asked about his plane
choices: Shared the gum and asked about his plane
Fought each other for the first piece
Refused it and demanded real bread
Ran off to tell the Soviet guards
context: Instead of fighting over the gum, the children split it and just wanted to hear about his aircraft. That moment moved Halvorsen so much that he started the famous candy drops. Source: hersheyland.com 'The Berlin Candy Bomber'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gail_Halvorsen.

question: The Berlin children wanted to pick Gail Halvorsen's plane out of the hundreds of supply planes roaring in to land each day. He promised them a signal he would give from the cockpit as he came in on his approach. What was the signal?
answer: He would wiggle his wings
choices: He would wiggle his wings
He would flash his landing lights
He would dip his nose down twice
He would circle the field once
context: Wiggling his wings earned Halvorsen the German nickname 'Onkel Wackelflugel' -- Uncle Wiggly Wings. Source: hersheyland.com 'The Berlin Candy Bomber'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gail_Halvorsen.

question: In 1948 the Americans flew food and coal into blockaded West Berlin around the clock. The British called their share of the effort 'Operation Plainfare.' The American code name wasn't grand or warlike -- it was old soldiers' slang for food. What did the Americans call their operation?
answer: Operation Vittles
choices: Operation Vittles
Operation Lifeline
Operation Stockpile
Operation Freedom Road
context: 'Vittles' is folksy slang for grub or food -- a humble name for the first time in history a whole city would be fed entirely from the sky. Source: history.state.gov 'Berlin Airlift'; amcmuseum.org 'Operation Vittles'.

question: Lt. Gail Halvorsen and his crew wanted to get candy down to the Berlin children without it smashing apart when they dropped it from a moving plane. They tied the chocolate and gum to something small the children could chase across the rubble. What did they tie it to?
answer: Tiny parachutes sewn from handkerchiefs
choices: Tiny parachutes sewn from handkerchiefs
Wooden crates packed with straw
Cloth sacks weighted with sand
Paper kites strung with ribbon
context: They pushed the little candy parachutes out the plane's flare chute as they came in to land. The candy-drop project was officially named 'Operation Little Vittles.' Source: airandspace.si.edu 'Friends Forever'; hersheyland.com 'The Berlin Candy Bomber'.

question: On June 24, 1948, Joseph Stalin's forces moved to choke West Berlin -- two million people stranded deep inside Soviet-controlled territory -- into surrender. They never fired a shot at the city. What did Stalin's forces do to it?
answer: Cut every road, rail line, and canal into it
choices: Cut every road, rail line, and canal into it
Shut off its electricity and water mains
Closed its banks and froze its money
Halted all its mail and telephone lines
context: With every land and water route sealed, West Berlin had only about 36 days of food and roughly six weeks of coal left. Source: history.com 'Soviets Blockade West Berlin'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Blockade.

question: With West Berlin sealed off in 1948, the Western Allies faced two grim options: shoot their way in by land, or abandon two million people to Stalin. They rejected both and chose a third path no one had attempted on this scale. What did they decide to do?
answer: Feed the entire city from the air
choices: Feed the entire city from the air
Tunnel supplies in underground
Smuggle food past the checkpoints
Trade away territory for the city
context: Supplying a city of two million entirely by air had never been done before -- the Allies bet they could outlast the blockade plane-load by plane-load. Source: history.state.gov 'Berlin Airlift'; amcmuseum.org 'Operation Vittles'.

question: A normal busy airport in peacetime might land one plane every minute or two. At the height of the Berlin Airlift, supply planes packed in far tighter than that, pouring into the city in a nonstop stream day and night. About how often did a fully loaded plane touch down?
answer: Every 45 seconds
choices: Every 45 seconds
Every 10 seconds
Every 3 minutes
Every 8 minutes
context: At the peak a loaded plane landed roughly every 45 seconds, and in the busiest spring-1949 stretch the cadence tightened to about one every 30 seconds. Source: history.state.gov 'Berlin Airlift'; historyfacts.com '5 Astonishing Facts About the Berlin Airlift'.

question: A Berlin girl named Mercedes Simon could never reach the crowds where Gail Halvorsen dropped his candy parachutes. So she mailed him a letter with directions to her home near Tempelhof, telling him to look for a landmark in her own yard and drop the candy there. What landmark did she tell him to find?
answer: Her family's white chickens
choices: Her family's white chickens
The tall church steeple
A red roof on the corner
The big oak by the gate
context: Her letter read, 'When you see the white chickens please drop it there, all will be OK.' He never spotted them, so he mailed candy straight to her house -- and when he returned to Berlin in 1972, Mercedes invited him to dinner. Source: airandspaceforces.com '0313halvorsen'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gail_Halvorsen.

question: Planners worked out that West Berlin needed at least 4,500 tons of supplies flown in every single day just to survive. People assume that meant mostly food -- but food was actually the smaller share of the weight. What made up the larger share of the cargo the city needed?
answer: Coal for heat and power
choices: Coal for heat and power
Water in sealed drums
Ammunition for the troops
Timber and cement
context: Of the daily minimum, roughly 3,475 tons was coal versus about 1,500 tons of food -- keeping the lights and furnaces on mattered as much as eating. Source: airandspace.si.edu 'Supplying a City by Air'; historyfacts.com '5 Astonishing Facts About the Berlin Airlift'.

question: On August 13, 1948 -- remembered as 'Black Friday' -- a sudden cloudburst over Berlin's Tempelhof airport turned the airlift into chaos: one plane crashed, another blew its tires, a third skidded off the runway, and the rest stacked up blind in the clouds with the new commander, General William Tunner, trapped overhead. Tunner's response fixed the airlift for good. What rule did he impose on every pilot?
answer: One shot at each landing, with no second try
choices: One shot at each landing, with no second try
Half the planes flying at twice the spacing
Night-only flights to dodge bad weather
A backup runway built at every field
context: Tunner rebuilt the airlift around rigid assembly-line timing: fixed slots, one approach, and a botched landing meant flying home, not circling. Source: historynet.com 'Berlin Airlift Anniversary'; amcmuseum.org 'Operation Vittles'.

question: Two tall Soviet-run radio towers stood right in the flight path of Berlin's brand-new Tegel airport, threatening the airlift planes. In December 1948 the French commander, General Jean Ganeval, simply had the towers blown up. As the story is told, a furious Soviet officer demanded to know HOW he could possibly do such a thing. How did Ganeval reportedly answer?
answer: 'With dynamite!'
choices: 'With dynamite!'
'Very carefully.'
'I lit the fuse myself.'
'The same way you built them.'
context: This famous one-line reply, dated to December 16, 1948, is told as legend -- a great story that may be polished in the retelling. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin-Tegel_radio_transmitter; billdownscbs.com '1948 French Destroy Soviet-Controlled'.

question: By spring 1949 the Berlin Airlift's commanders staged the 'Easter Parade': a furious 24-hour blitz on April 15-16 that flew nearly 13,000 tons into West Berlin in a single day -- about 600 railcars of coal -- without one crash. After a feat like that, what could Stalin no longer believe?
answer: That his blockade could ever starve the city out
choices: That his blockade could ever starve the city out
That the Allies would defend Berlin by force
That the airlift planes would run short of fuel
That winter weather would soon ground the flights
context: The Easter Parade proved the planes could outlast the blockade indefinitely; Stalin lifted it on May 12, 1949. The free world had fed a whole city from the sky for nearly a year. Source: globalsecurity.org 'Berlin Airlift'; history.state.gov 'Berlin Airlift'.

question: On June 12, 1987, President Ronald Reagan stood at the Brandenburg Gate in West Berlin before a crowd of more than 20,000, two panes of bulletproof glass shielding him from snipers in the communist East. He aimed one ringing demand straight at Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev. What did Reagan command him to do?
answer: "Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!"
choices: "Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!"
"Mr. Gorbachev, recall your missiles!"
"Mr. Gorbachev, free your prisoners!"
"Mr. Gorbachev, leave Afghanistan now!"
context: Reagan built to it: "General Secretary Gorbachev, if you seek peace... Mr. Gorbachev, open this gate! Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!" He spoke about 100 yards from the Wall with the Gate at his back. The barrier itself did not fall until November 9, 1989, two and a half years later. Source: Reagan Presidential Library, official speech text, reaganlibrary.gov; Britannica, 'Mr. Gorbachev, Tear Down This Wall!'

question: Before Ronald Reagan spoke at the Brandenburg Gate in 1987, his own State Department and National Security Council fought his most defiant line, handing him seven rewrites with the challenge to Gorbachev stripped out, warning it would embarrass the Soviet leader. Chief of Staff Howard Baker called it "unpresidential." How did Reagan settle the fight?
answer: He overruled them all and kept the line.
choices: He overruled them all and kept the line.
He cut the line to spare Gorbachev.
He let his advisors rewrite the ending.
He softened it into a polite request.
context: On May 18, 1987, Reagan told his speechwriters simply, "I think we'll leave it in." In the limousine to the gate he grinned at aide Ken Duberstein: "It's gonna drive the State Department boys crazy, but I'm gonna leave it in." Deputy National Security Advisor Colin Powell had sided with Baker against the line. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tear down this wall!'; Stanford Report, 2019, 'Reagan's Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall was almost left unsaid.'

question: The sculptor Gian Lorenzo Bernini carved his Apollo and Daphne from a single block of marble, freezing the instant the nymph Daphne escapes the god Apollo by turning into a tree. Bernini's astonishing trick: he let her transformation literally burst out of the stone at her fingertips. What sprouts from the ends of her marble fingers?
answer: Delicate laurel leaves and twigs
choices: Delicate laurel leaves and twigs
A spray of carved seawater
A cluster of golden grapes
A nest of small songbirds
context: Bernini carved real-looking, paper-thin laurel leaves and twigs growing straight out of Daphne's fingertips at the exact moment she becomes a tree. He made the work in his early twenties, between 1622 and 1625, pausing partway to carve his famous David. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_and_Daphne_(Bernini)

question: In his Ecstasy of Saint Teresa, Gian Lorenzo Bernini carved a smiling angel about to plunge a golden arrow into a swooning nun resting on a marble cloud. To make the white marble look as if it were glowing from heaven itself, Bernini built one hidden feature into the chapel above the statue. What was it?
answer: A concealed window letting real daylight pour down
choices: A concealed window letting real daylight pour down
A ring of flickering oil lamps
A ceiling painted with a golden sunburst
A polished silver mirror behind the angel
context: Bernini hid a real window above the Cornaro Chapel so daylight streams down onto gilded bronze rays behind the figures, making the marble appear lit from heaven. The group was carved from white Carrara marble between 1647 and 1652. He was illustrating Teresa of Avila's own written vision of the angel and the spear of gold. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecstasy_of_Saint_Teresa

question: Henry Bessemer's workers thought he was mad: he wanted to blow cold air straight up through a vat of glowing molten iron, and they swore the blast would chill the metal and freeze it into a useless solid lump. Instead, the moment the air rushed in, the iron grew even HOTTER and a roaring flame shot up. What was actually catching fire and burning to drive the temperature higher?
answer: The carbon and silicon already dissolved in the iron
choices: The carbon and silicon already dissolved in the iron
The cold air itself igniting on contact
The clay lining of the vat melting away
Extra coal the workers shoveled in
context: The cold blast burned out the carbon and silicon mixed into the iron, and those elements caught fire and burned as fuel — so the air didn't cool the metal, it turned the whole vessel into a self-heating reaction. Bessemer described the apparatus becoming 'a veritable volcano.' Source: thechemicalengineer.com 'Henry Bessemer – Man of Steel'; HowStuffWorks Bessemer Process.

question: In 1862 a single rail made of Henry Bessemer's cheap new steel was bolted into an English railroad, right beside ordinary iron rails carrying the same trains over the same stretch of track. The soft iron rails kept wearing out and had to be swapped again and again — while the one steel rail just sat there, unworn. By the time that one steel rail finally needed replacing, how many times had the iron rails beside it been replaced?
answer: Eighteen times over
choices: Eighteen times over
Just twice over
Not even once
Exactly once over
context: The single Bessemer steel rail outlasted eighteen replacements of the iron rails next to it. In hard-worn spots, iron rails sometimes wore out in under six months; steel rails carried heavier locomotives and longer trains and lasted for decades — which is why cheap steel rapidly replaced iron across the railroads. Source: cprr.org/Museum/Iron_and_Steel_Rails.html; trains.com 'Rail' / ABCs of Railroading.

question: In the cherished American folk-tale, a committee showed the seamstress Betsy Ross a flag design dotted with six-pointed stars. Ross had a better idea — she folded a scrap of paper and, with a single snip of her scissors, surprised them by cutting out what shape?
answer: A perfect five-pointed star
choices: A perfect five-pointed star
A ring of thirteen stripes
A curled red ribbon
A small blue square
context: The one-snip five-pointed star is the most beloved detail of the Betsy Ross story, and the committee is said to have chosen it for the new flag. It's a treasured national folk-tale, first told publicly by Ross's grandson decades later rather than firmly documented at the time. (ushistory.org/betsy/flagtale.html; historicphiladelphia.org)  (Legend.)

question: The Betsy Ross legend says a small group walked into her Philadelphia upholstery shop in 1776 to ask her to sew the first American flag. According to the story, which famous leader came along on that visit?
answer: General George Washington
choices: General George Washington
King George the Third
Captain John Smith
Governor William Penn
context: In the tale, Washington came with financier Robert Morris and Colonel George Ross (the uncle of Betsy's late husband). The story even says Ross knew Washington already — their church pews at Christ Church sat side by side. A beloved folk-tale, not firmly documented. (ushistory.org/betsy/flagtale.html)  (Legend.)

question: The very first words of the Bill of Rights begin, 'Congress shall make no law...' — and that single First Amendment goes on to protect not one freedom but five of them at once. Which group lists the five freedoms packed into the First Amendment?
answer: Religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition
choices: Religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition
Voting, trial, property, travel, and privacy
Speech, voting, marriage, property, and protest
Religion, arms, trial, voting, and a free press
context: All five ride in one sentence: '...prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances.' Source: National Archives, Bill of Rights Transcript.

question: The Fourth Amendment protects 'persons, houses, papers, and effects' so a home cannot simply be ransacked by the government on a whim. Because of it, what must a government agent generally obtain before entering your house and going through your things?
answer: A warrant signed by a judge
choices: A warrant signed by a judge
A signed note from the mayor
A majority vote of the town council
A written order from the President
context: The amendment bars 'unreasonable searches and seizures,' which is why agents normally need a judge's warrant, based on cause, to come in. Source: National Archives, Bill of Rights Transcript.

question: The Eighth Amendment is the shortest of the rights amendments — it bans three things in a single breath. Two of them are excessive bail and excessive fines. What is the third thing the Eighth Amendment forbids?
answer: Cruel and unusual punishments
choices: Cruel and unusual punishments
Trials held in total secret
Imprisonment with no trial at all
Banishment out of the country
context: The whole amendment reads: 'Excessive bail shall not be required, nor excessive fines imposed, nor cruel and unusual punishments inflicted.' Source: National Archives, Bill of Rights Transcript.

question: One of the Bill of Rights' protections promises that no person can be forced to be 'a witness against himself' — the government cannot make you testify your own way into a prison cell. From this right comes a famous expression people use when they refuse to answer a question that might incriminate them. What is that expression?
answer: Pleading the Fifth
choices: Pleading the Fifth
Taking the stand
Throwing the book
Reading the charges
context: This right against self-incrimination lives in the Fifth Amendment, which also promises 'due process of law' and a grand jury for serious crimes — but its most quoted line is the one that gave us 'pleading the Fifth.' Source: National Archives, Bill of Rights Transcript.

question: Clarence Earl Gideon was too poor to hire anyone to defend him at his trial, so from his prison cell he wrote a five-page plea to the Supreme Court by hand, in pencil, on prison stationery. In Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) the Court ruled unanimously in his favor. What did the justices say states must now provide to any defendant too poor to hire one?
answer: A lawyer paid for by the state
choices: A lawyer paid for by the state
A faster date for the trial
A transcript of the whole case
A jury drawn from his neighbors
context: Gideon's penciled petition turned the Sixth Amendment's promise of counsel into a real right for the poor: if you cannot afford a lawyer, one must be provided. Source: Wikipedia, Gideon v. Wainwright; U.S. Courts case summary.

question: In December 1965, 13-year-old Mary Beth Tinker, her brother John, and their friend Christopher Eckhardt were suspended from their Des Moines schools for a protest against the Vietnam War. They sued, and in Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) the Supreme Court sided with them 7-2. What had these students actually done to get suspended?
answer: Worn black armbands to school
choices: Worn black armbands to school
Walked out of their classes
Refused to say the Pledge
Handed out anti-war leaflets
context: The Court declared that students do not 'shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate' — making the armbands one of the most famous acts of student free speech in American history. Source: Wikipedia, Tinker v. Des Moines; U.S. Courts case summary.

question: George Mason of Virginia, who had written Virginia's own Declaration of Rights, grew so alarmed that the new Constitution contained no bill of rights that he refused to sign it in 1787. He swore he would sooner do something terrible than put his name to the document as it stood. What did George Mason say he would sooner do?
answer: Chop off his own right hand
choices: Chop off his own right hand
Never set foot in Virginia again
Burn down his own great house
Give away his entire fortune
context: Mason said he 'would sooner chop off his right hand than put it to the Constitution as it now stands.' He was one of only three delegates present at the end of the Convention who refused to sign. Source: Wikipedia, George Mason; National Archives 'Pieces of History' blog.

question: George Washington had 14 handwritten copies of the Bill of Rights made — one for the new federal government and one for each state. North Carolina's copy was stolen by a Union soldier in 1865 and vanished for 138 years. In 2003 the FBI finally recovered it. How did agents catch the thief who had it?
answer: They posed as buyers in a sting operation
choices: They posed as buyers in a sting operation
They traced an old letter back to his family
They spotted it hanging in a public museum
They followed a tip from a retired soldier
context: The soldier who first took it had sold it for $5; in 2003 a dealer tried to sell the same document for $5 million, and the FBI sting recovered it for North Carolina. Source: TIME, 'Bill of Rights History: FBI Sting Operation'; NC DNCR.

question: President Franklin Roosevelt created 'Bill of Rights Day' to mark the 150th anniversary of the Bill of Rights, setting it for December 15, 1941. That very first observance fell in the shadow of a national catastrophe just eight days earlier. What had happened on December 7, 1941?
answer: The attack on Pearl Harbor
choices: The attack on Pearl Harbor
The great stock-market crash
The sinking of the Lusitania
The assassination of a president
context: Roosevelt's proclamation of the 150th anniversary collided with the Pearl Harbor attack of December 7, 1941, that pulled the United States into World War II — so the first Bill of Rights Day passed almost unnoticed. Source: National Archives, 'Bill of Rights Day'; Proclamation 2524.

question: During the fight to ratify the Constitution, one group made written protections for individual rights the price of their votes — refusing to approve the new government until a bill of rights was promised. The Massachusetts Compromise, struck by Samuel Adams and John Hancock, became their template. Which faction demanded the Bill of Rights as their price?
answer: The Anti-Federalists
choices: The Anti-Federalists
The Democratic-Republicans
The Federalists
The Sons of Liberty
context: Several states ratified only on the promise that protections would be added at once — the Massachusetts Compromise was the model. Georgia alone thought a bill of rights so pointless it refused to ratify. Source: Wikipedia, United States Bill of Rights; Library of Congress, 'Demand for a Bill of Rights.'

question: Here is the great irony of the Bill of Rights: the man who wrote it and pushed it through Congress, James Madison, had at first argued AGAINST having one at all. He sneered that written guarantees were only feeble 'parchment ____' that angry majorities had trampled in every state. What word did Madison use to dismiss written rights?
answer: 'parchment barriers'
choices: 'parchment barriers'
'parchment promises'
'parchment shadows'
'parchment fences'
context: Madison called written rights mere 'parchment barriers' against overbearing majorities — then changed his mind to win ratification, having pledged amendments to beat James Monroe for a seat in the House. Source: Madison to Jefferson, 17 Oct 1788, Founders Online; Wikipedia, United States Bill of Rights.

question: In 1982 a University of Texas student named Gregory Watson wrote a term paper arguing that a forgotten amendment Madison had proposed back in 1789 — blocking Congress from giving itself a pay raise before the next election — could still be ratified. His professor gave it a C and dismissed the idea as a 'dead letter.' Furious, Watson spent about $6,000 of his own money writing to state legislatures. What did Gregory Watson go on to accomplish?
answer: He got the amendment ratified as the 27th
choices: He got the amendment ratified as the 27th
He had the professor fired by the university
He won a seat in Congress for himself
He rewrote the whole Bill of Rights
context: Watson's 1789 amendment was finally ratified as the 27th Amendment in 1992 — about 203 years after Madison proposed it, the longest gap in U.S. constitutional history. In 2017 the University of Texas went back and changed his grade to an A. Source: National Constitution Center; NPR, 'The Bad Grade That Changed The U.S. Constitution.'

question: Read the lines of the Bill of Rights closely and a pattern appears: 'Congress shall make no law...,' 'shall not be infringed,' 'shall not be violated,' 'No Soldier shall...' Each clause aims at the new federal government. Which description best captures what kind of list the Bill of Rights actually is?
answer: A list of things the government may NOT do
choices: A list of things the government may NOT do
A list of crimes the people may not commit
A list of powers handed to Congress
A list of gifts the government gives the people
context: Every key clause opens with a prohibition aimed at the new federal government, marking where its power must stop — these are negative rights, telling the government what it may not do rather than gifts it bestows. Source: National Archives, Bill of Rights Transcript.

question: James Madison worried that listing certain rights would trick people into thinking the government held every power and every right NOT written down. So the last two amendments answer that fear. The Ninth says rights not listed are still 'retained by the people.' What does the Tenth Amendment say about powers not given to the federal government?
answer: They are reserved to the states and the people
choices: They are reserved to the states and the people
They belong to the President to use as needed
They pass to the Supreme Court to decide
They are surrendered until Congress claims them
context: The Tenth reserves undelegated powers 'to the States respectively, or to the people.' Together the Ninth and Tenth answer the fear that a written list of rights could shrink the rights and powers the people kept. Source: National Archives, Bill of Rights Transcript; Constitution Center, Ninth & Tenth Amendment interpretations.

question: In ancient Athens, when citizens wanted to throw a too-powerful man out of the city for ten years, each voter scratched the man's name onto a scrap surface and dropped it in. What everyday object did an Athenian scratch a name onto to cast this banishment vote?
answer: A broken piece of pottery
choices: A broken piece of pottery
A wax writing tablet
A strip of papyrus
A clay drinking cup
context: The broken potsherd was called an ostrakon -- free, throwaway scrap, used like scrap paper. That is why a vote into exile is called 'ostracism.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostracism

question: The Greek word 'democracy' is built from two Greek words joined together. Athenian citizens gathered on the Pnyx hill to vote laws by a show of hands -- the first 'demos kratos' in the world. What does 'democracy' literally mean?
answer: People-power
choices: People-power
Council-rule
City-law
Noble-voice
context: Demos ('the people') + kratos ('power/rule') = 'people-power.' Eligible citizens met on the Pnyx hill west of the Acropolis and voted by a simple show of hands. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athenian_democracy; https://www.worldhistory.org/Athenian_Democracy/

question: Before Athens had any democracy, an early lawgiver named Draco set such savage penalties that even stealing a cabbage could cost a man his life. The orator Demades later summed up Draco's code in one cutting line about what it seemed to be written with. How did Demades say Draco's laws were written?
answer: Not in ink but in blood
choices: Not in ink but in blood
Not on stone but on sand
Not by men but by gods
Not with care but in haste
context: Draco's code made death the penalty for even minor crimes. When Solon reformed Athens he scrapped all of Draco's laws except the one on murder. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draco_(legislator)

question: Around 594 BC the Athenian reformer Solon freed citizens who had been sold into slavery to pay off their debts, and he banned ever again using a person's own body as security for a loan. Athenians remembered this rescue by a single Greek name. What did that name mean?
answer: The shaking-off of burdens
choices: The shaking-off of burdens
The breaking of the chains
The gift of the poor
The mending of the city
context: The law was the seisachtheia -- literally 'the shaking off of burdens.' It ended Athenian debt-slavery before democracy was even born. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seisachtheia

question: In one of his own poems, Solon bragged about ripping up the horoi -- the mortgage marker-stones farmers had to plant in any field they owed debt on. His most famous line in that poem describes what tearing up those stones did to the land. What did Solon's line say it had done?
answer: Freed the black earth
choices: Freed the black earth
Opened the closed gate
Lit the dark hills
Filled the empty barn
context: Solon's line ran: 'Before, Earth was in bondage, now she is free.' Tearing up the debt-marker stones literally 'freed the black earth.' Sources: Plutarch, Life of Solon (Fragment 36); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solon

question: After Solon rewrote Athens' laws, he made the citizens swear a binding oath to leave them unchanged for ten years -- then he did something drastic so nobody could pester him into softening them. What did Solon do right after the Athenians took the oath?
answer: Sailed away on a long voyage
choices: Sailed away on a long voyage
Burned his only copy of the laws
Handed himself over to a rival
Locked himself inside a temple
context: Solon left Athens for years rather than stay and be begged to change his laws, hoping the city would grow used to ruling itself before he came home. Source: Plutarch, Life of Solon (Perrin trans.)

question: An Athenian statesman was nicknamed Aristides 'the Just' for his fairness. On voting day a citizen who could not even read walked up to Aristides -- not knowing who he was -- and asked him to scratch a name on a potsherd. Told the man wanted to banish Aristides simply because he was sick of hearing him praised as 'the Just,' what did Aristides do with the potsherd (as the story is told)?
answer: Wrote his own name and handed it back
choices: Wrote his own name and handed it back
Tore it in half and walked away
Refused and reported the man
Begged the man to change his vote
context: Told as a famous legend by Plutarch. The man said: 'None whatever, I don't even know the fellow, but I am tired of hearing him everywhere called The Just.' Aristides calmly inscribed his own name. Source: Plutarch, Life of Aristides, ch. 7.

question: In 508/507 BC the reformer Cleisthenes set out to smash the grip of the old noble clans on Athenian politics. Instead of grouping citizens by their ancestral families, he completely re-sorted every citizen by one different thing -- so that no single noble family or region could control a voting bloc. What did Cleisthenes group citizens by instead?
answer: Where each man lived
choices: Where each man lived
How old each man was
Which trade each man worked
How rich each man was
context: Cleisthenes junked the four ancestral tribes and built ten new ones, each deliberately mixing people from the city, the coast, and the inland so no region or clan could dominate. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleisthenes; https://www.britannica.com/place/ancient-Greece/The-reforms-of-Cleisthenes

question: To run the daily business of Athens, Cleisthenes created a Council of 500 (the boule) drawn from across the new tribes. He filled its seats in a way that meant an ordinary farmer, not just a wealthy noble, could end up helping govern the city. How were the 500 councilmen chosen?
answer: Picked by lot
choices: Picked by lot
Elected by vote
Named by the nobles
Chosen by wealth
context: Fifty men from each of the ten tribes were selected by lot, not election -- so governing was open to ordinary citizens. Cleisthenes called the whole system isonomia, 'equality before the law,' not yet 'democracy.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleisthenes

question: Athens' new self-rule was nearly strangled in its cradle: Cleisthenes' rival Isagoras called in the Spartan king Cleomenes, who expelled 700 Athenian families and tried to dissolve the council. But the ordinary Athenians rose up. What did the people of Athens do to Cleomenes and Isagoras?
answer: Besieged them on the Acropolis until they surrendered
choices: Besieged them on the Acropolis until they surrendered
Bribed them with gold to sail home quietly
Put them on public trial before the Assembly
Begged the other Greek cities to drive them out
context: The Athenians trapped Cleomenes and Isagoras on the Acropolis and, after two days, forced them to surrender and leave. Cleisthenes was recalled in triumph. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleomenes_I; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleisthenes

question: In a well near the Acropolis, archaeologists found a buried cache of 190 ostraka all scratched with the single name Themistocles -- looking like 190 separate voters wanting him gone. But studying the handwriting exposed a fraud: those 190 sherds had been inscribed by far fewer people than it appeared. About how many different hands wrote all 190?
answer: About 14 hands
choices: About 14 hands
About 25 hands
About 45 hands
About 70 hands
context: Roughly 14 hands producing 190 ready-to-vote sherds means someone mass-produced ballots in advance -- ancient evidence of ballot-stuffing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostracism

question: Athenian democracy was real, but it was far narrower than the word suggests: only free adult male citizens could vote, while women, enslaved people, and resident foreigners were all shut out. Out of perhaps a few hundred thousand people living in Attica, roughly how many actually held the vote?
answer: Around 30,000 to 40,000 men
choices: Around 30,000 to 40,000 men
Around 3,000 to 4,000 men
Around 100,000 to 150,000 men
Around 250,000 to 300,000 men
context: Only free adult male citizens voted -- women, enslaved people, and resident foreigners (metics) were excluded. The first democracy was genuine but narrow. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athenian_democracy; https://www.worldhistory.org/Athenian_Democracy/

question: Louis Armstrong's boyhood nicknames all poked fun at his enormous mouth. Years later, a British magazine editor named Percy Brooks greeted him by accidentally scrunching one of those mouth-nicknames into a single new word, and Armstrong loved it so much he answered to it for the rest of his life. What was the new nickname?
answer: Satchmo
choices: Satchmo
Gatemouth
Dippermouth
Slidehorn
context: Percy Brooks, editor of the British magazine Melody Maker, accidentally contracted 'Satchelmouth' into 'Satchmo' when greeting him in England. 'Gatemouth' and 'Dippermouth' were two of Armstrong's real earlier nicknames, all of which mocked the size of his mouth. Source: Louis Armstrong House Museum FAQ, 'How did Louis Armstrong get the nickname Satchmo?' (louisarmstronghouse.org).

question: On New Year's Eve in 1912, eleven-year-old Louis Armstrong celebrated by firing his stepfather's pistol into the air on a New Orleans street, and was arrested on the spot. He was locked up in the Colored Waif's Home for Boys. What happened to him inside the Waif's Home?
answer: The home's bandmaster taught him to play the cornet
choices: The home's bandmaster taught him to play the cornet
A wealthy visitor adopted him and paid for his schooling
A riverboat captain hired him on as a deckhand
He escaped over the wall and rode the rails north
context: Bandmaster Peter Davis taught Armstrong the cornet at the Colored Waif's Home for Boys, the spark that turned the arrested boy into a musician. He was released in 1914. Source: Biography.com 'Louis Armstrong'; Louis Armstrong House Museum biography (louisarmstronghouse.org/biography).

question: When Louis Armstrong was a boy of about seven in New Orleans, a Jewish immigrant family, the Karnofskys, hired him to haul coal and junk, fed him at their own table, and even loaned him the money to buy his very first cornet. Armstrong never forgot their kindness. How did he honor them for the rest of his life?
answer: He wore a Star of David around his neck
choices: He wore a Star of David around his neck
He named his first band after them
He learned Yiddish and sang it on records
He sent them money from every concert he played
context: Morris Karnofsky lent young Louis two dollars toward the five-dollar pawnshop cornet, which Louis paid off at fifty cents a week. Armstrong wrote, 'It was the Jewish Family who instilled in me singing from the heart,' and wore a Star of David for the rest of his life. Source: Louis Armstrong, 'Louis Armstrong + the Jewish Family in New Orleans, La., the Year of 1907' (memoir); Aish.com; National Park Service, Karnofsky Tailor Shop (nps.gov).

question: In 1926 Louis Armstrong was recording a song called 'Heebie Jeebies' when, as the legend goes, his lyric sheet fluttered to the floor mid-take. Rather than stop, he kept right on singing, but with no words left he made up a stream of wordless nonsense syllables on the spot. What is that improvised, no-real-words style of singing called?
answer: scat singing
choices: scat singing
crooning
yodeling
the blues holler
context: Armstrong popularized scat singing on 'Heebie Jeebies' (recorded February 26, 1926, in Chicago). Bandmates Kid Ory and Johnny St. Cyr confirmed he dropped the sheet, but scat already existed in New Orleans, so he did not invent it, only made it a sensation. Source: Wikipedia 'Heebie Jeebies (composition)'; Library of Congress NRPB Hot Five/Seven essay; Louis Armstrong House Museum exhibit '100 Years of Heebie Jeebies'.  (Legend.)

question: Louis Armstrong's 1928 recording 'West End Blues' opens with a soaring, unaccompanied trumpet solo he invented himself, about nine bars with no other instrument behind it. The jazz historian Doug Ramsey said three of the greatest classical composers who ever lived 'would have been grateful for the inspiration to compose' that opening. Which three composers did he name?
answer: Mozart, Bartok, and Stravinsky
choices: Mozart, Bartok, and Stravinsky
Bach, Beethoven, and Brahms
Handel, Haydn, and Schubert
Chopin, Liszt, and Wagner
context: The unaccompanied opening cadenza of 'West End Blues' (recorded June 28, 1928) announced that jazz could be art at the highest level. Doug Ramsey wrote that 'Mozart, Bartok, or Stravinsky would have been grateful for the inspiration to compose' it. Source: uDiscoverMusic 'The Day Jazz Changed Forever'; Library of Congress NRPB Hot Five/Seven essay (Doug Ramsey quotation).

question: Ludwig Boltzmann explained why a smashed egg never reassembles itself and why heat always flows from hot to cold, never backward. He said it isn't because a law forbids the reverse — it's a matter of sheer counting. So why does the egg stay smashed?
answer: There are vastly more ways to be a mess than to be whole
choices: There are vastly more ways to be a mess than to be whole
A hidden law of physics forbids broken things from mending
The egg loses weight as it breaks, so it cannot rebuild
Time pushes on objects with a small but constant force
context: This is the heart of Boltzmann's entropy: disordered, jumbled arrangements outnumber tidy ones so overwhelmingly that the orderly outcome essentially never happens by chance. It is also why time seems to have a direction — the universe drifts toward the states there are more ways to be in. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H-theorem ; academic.oup.com/book/34859/chapter/298194940

question: Above Ludwig Boltzmann's grave in Vienna stands a marble wall carved with the one short equation that sums up his life's work — his statistical definition of entropy. What is the formula engraved over his name?
answer: S = k log W
choices: S = k log W
E = m c squared
F = m times a
P V = n R T
context: S is entropy, k is the Boltzmann constant, and W counts how many microscopic arrangements look the same from the outside. The bust and inscribed marble wall were made by sculptor Gustinus Ambrosi and unveiled in 1933, decades after Boltzmann died — the formula was added as a memorial. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boltzmann%27s_entropy_formula ; visitingvienna.com/sights/zentralfriedhoffamousgraves

question: The famous equation S = k log W is carved above Ludwig Boltzmann's grave as the summary of his work — yet Boltzmann himself never wrote it in that exact tidy form. Who first compressed his ideas into that compact equation, around 1900?
answer: Max Planck
choices: Max Planck
Albert Einstein
Ernst Mach
Wilhelm Ostwald
context: Boltzmann developed the underlying idea between 1872 and 1875, but Max Planck put it into the terse form S = k log W around 1900–1901 while working out black-body radiation. The grave honors Boltzmann with a sentence written by someone else. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boltzmann%27s_entropy_formula

question: Ludwig Boltzmann's whole theory of heat depended on atoms being real, countable things — but powerful colleagues like Ernst Mach insisted atoms were a convenient fiction. Worn down and convinced the deniers had won, Boltzmann took his own life in 1906. What happened just two years later?
answer: Jean Perrin measured Brownian motion and proved atoms are real
choices: Jean Perrin measured Brownian motion and proved atoms are real
Ernst Mach published a final book denying atoms once more
The Vienna academy quietly removed Boltzmann's name from its rolls
A rival theory of continuous matter swept across the universities
context: Perrin's 1908 experiments on Brownian motion gave decisive proof that atoms exist, vindicating Boltzmann right after he died believing he had failed. Even Ostwald eventually conceded; Planck and Einstein carried Boltzmann's ideas to victory. Source: kroneckerwallis.com/ludwig-boltzmann-the-physicist-who-proved-atoms-exist-through-statistics ; plato.stanford.edu/entries/statphys-Boltzmann

question: On the island of Java stands Borobudur, the world's largest Buddhist temple: nine stone platforms stacked into a giant mandala that a pilgrim climbs level by level. The builders gave the climb a meaning, so that reaching the top is meant to mirror the Buddhist path. What is a pilgrim's walk up Borobudur supposed to represent?
answer: The journey from worldly desire up toward Nirvana
choices: The journey from worldly desire up toward Nirvana
The voyage of a trader from India home to China
The march of an army up to besiege a hill fort
The flight of a soul up through nine starry heavens
context: Borobudur's tiers map the stages of the Buddhist path: Kamadhatu, the realm of desire, at the hidden base; Rupadhatu, the realm of form, on the square terraces; and Arupadhatu, the formless realm, on the bare circular terraces at the top. So climbing the monument is walking from worldly desire toward Nirvana. Built around 800 AD by the Sailendra dynasty from roughly 2 million andesite blocks fitted without mortar. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur; UNESCO World Heritage #592.

question: On the top three round terraces of Borobudur in Java sit 72 bell-shaped stone cages, each one a stupa pierced with diamond-shaped holes like stone latticework. A visitor who peers through the gaps in one of these stone bells gets a surprise. What is sealed inside, peeking back out through the holes?
answer: A seated stone Buddha
choices: A seated stone Buddha
A bowl of temple ashes
A coiled stone serpent
A casket of royal bones
context: Each of the 72 perforated stupas on the upper circular terraces hides a seated stone Buddha, visible only as a shape glimpsed through the latticework. The whole temple holds 2,672 relief panels and once held 504 Buddha statues. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur; UNESCO #592.

question: On the night of March 5, 1770, a Boston crowd pelted British soldiers with snowballs, ice, and rocks outside the Custom House, and the rattled soldiers fired into the mob, killing five colonists. The first man to fall, shot twice in the chest, was a sailor of African and Wampanoag descent who had escaped slavery years before. He is remembered as the first to die for the American Revolution. What was his name?
answer: Crispus Attucks
choices: Crispus Attucks
Samuel Maverick
James Caldwell
Patrick Carr
context: Crispus Attucks fell first on King Street. A 1750 newspaper ad had once offered a 10-pound reward for a runaway named 'Crispas,' about 6 feet 2 inches tall; he later worked as a sailor and ropemaker and had just returned from the Bahamas. The other four who died that night were Samuel Gray, James Caldwell, 17-year-old Samuel Maverick (who died the next morning), and Patrick Carr (who died of his wounds nearly two weeks later). Sources: nps.gov/articles/000/boston-massacre-trial.htm; historyhit.com/who-was-crispus-attucks.

question: After the Boston Massacre, the people of Boston wanted the British soldiers hanged, and finding any lawyer to defend them in court seemed impossible. Then a fierce patriot stunned the city by agreeing to defend the redcoats himself, telling the jury 'Facts are stubborn things.' He won: six of the eight soldiers were acquitted. Which patriot defended the British soldiers?
answer: John Adams
choices: John Adams
Paul Revere
Samuel Adams
John Hancock
context: John Adams, a future U.S. president, believed every accused person deserved counsel even in a free country that hated them. Captain Thomas Preston and six soldiers were acquitted; only Hugh Montgomery and Matthew Kilroy were convicted of manslaughter and, instead of hanging, had their thumbs branded under 'benefit of clergy.' A free Black witness, Newton Prince, testified Preston stood in front of his men and never ordered them to fire. Sources: nps.gov/articles/000/boston-massacre-trial.htm; masshist.org/features/massacre1770-2020/trials.

question: On the night of December 16, 1773, the colonists who boarded three British ships in Boston Harbor to dump the tea didn't go as themselves. They smeared their faces with soot and lampblack and wrapped in blankets, dressing up as a group they wanted everyone to picture instead. Who did they disguise themselves as?
answer: Mohawk warriors
choices: Mohawk warriors
British redcoats
Spanish sailors
French traders
context: The raiders disguised themselves as Mohawk warriors, smearing their faces with soot and lampblack. The costume partly hid their identities, but it also sent a message: they saw themselves as Americans of this land, not British subjects. Source: American Battlefield Trust, battlefields.org/learn/topics/boston-tea-party; americanrevolution.org/boston-tea-party/

question: During the Boston Tea Party of December 16, 1773, the raiders dumping British tea into the harbor caught one of their own men quietly stuffing tea into his coat to keep for himself. They turned on him hard. What did the raiders do to the man caught pocketing the tea?
answer: Made him run a gauntlet, every person kicking him
choices: Made him run a gauntlet, every person kicking him
Tossed him overboard into the icy harbor
Locked him in the ship's hold overnight
Painted his face and marched him home
context: Stealing the tea instead of destroying it was treated as a betrayal of the whole protest, so the raiders made the thief run a gauntlet through the crowd on the wharf, every person kicking him as he passed. The point was destruction as principle, not personal profit. Source: bostonteapartyship.com/the-destruction-of-the-tea; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Robert_Twelves_Hewes

question: Most people assume the colonists threw the British tea into Boston Harbor in 1773 because the tea had been made too expensive to afford. But the Tea Act of 1773 had just done the opposite to the price of British East India Company tea. What had the new law actually done to that tea's price?
answer: Lowered it, so it would undersell smuggled Dutch tea
choices: Lowered it, so it would undersell smuggled Dutch tea
Doubled it overnight with a steep new duty
Frozen it at the old smugglers' rate
Tied it to the price of British wool
context: The Tea Act cut duties so East India Company tea would actually be cheaper than smuggled Dutch tea. Colonists protested anyway, because the cheap tea was a trap to get them to accept Parliament's right to tax them without their consent. The fight was over the principle of the tax, not its cost. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea_Act; americanrevolution.org/tea-act/

question: In Sandro Botticelli's painting the Birth of Venus, the newborn goddess Venus arrives at the shore fully grown, drifting in balanced on a single huge object. What is she standing on?
answer: A giant scallop shell
choices: A giant scallop shell
A small wooden raft
A bed of floating reeds
A flat slab of marble
context: Botticelli paints the shell 'as pure and as perfect as a pearl' — Venus rides it toward land. Source: https://www.uffizi.it/en/artworks/birth-of-venus

question: In Botticelli's Primavera, the blue-skinned wind god Zephyrus seizes the fleeing nymph Chloris, and the painting shows her changing into Flora, goddess of spring. How does Botticelli paint that transformation happening?
answer: Real flowers spill out of her open mouth
choices: Real flowers spill out of her open mouth
Green vines wrap and bind her wrists
Her bare feet sink and root into the soil
A gold light bursts from her chest
context: As Zephyrus catches Chloris, blossoms pour from her lips — she becomes Flora before the viewer's eyes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primavera_(Botticelli)

question: The orange trees crowded behind the figures in Botticelli's Primavera carry a hidden signature for the family who paid for the painting: their golden fruit copies the round gold balls on a famous Florentine coat of arms. Which family did Botticelli secretly honor this way?
answer: The Medici family
choices: The Medici family
The Borgia family
The Sforza family
The Visconti family
context: The golden oranges echo the gold balls — the 'palle' — on the Medici coat of arms; both Primavera and the Birth of Venus were Medici works. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primavera_(Botticelli)

question: In 1418 the people of Florence had a problem: their great cathedral had a huge eight-sided hole at the top where a roof should go, and not one builder alive knew how to span it. The ancient Romans had once roofed enormous buildings, but why couldn't anyone copy them?
answer: The secret of how the Romans built giant domes had been lost
choices: The secret of how the Romans built giant domes had been lost
The Pope had forbidden anyone to build a dome that tall
No quarry in Tuscany could supply enough white marble
The original architect had died before drawing the plans
context: After Rome fell, the know-how for vast concrete domes like the Pantheon's vanished for a thousand years. In 1418 nobody knew how to roof the octagonal opening at Santa Maria del Fiore. Source: worldhistory.org/Filippo_Brunelleschi; arsartisticadventureofmankind.wordpress.com.

question: Before he dared design the dome, Filippo Brunelleschi went down to Rome with his friend the sculptor Donatello. Obsessed with the giant ancient ruins, he spent his days there doing one strange thing over and over to learn the old builders' tricks. What was it?
answer: He crawled over the ruins measuring the Pantheon
choices: He crawled over the ruins measuring the Pantheon
He prayed at the tomb of Saint Peter for guidance
He bought every Roman statue he could carry home
He copied the frescoes on the old basilica walls
context: Brunelleschi and Donatello clambered over Rome's ruins for years, and he measured the Pantheon again and again, determined to work out how its ancient dome stayed up. Source: worldhistory.org/Filippo_Brunelleschi.

question: Tourists today climb 463 steps to the top of Brunelleschi's dome in Florence — but they don't go up the inside of the church or a ladder on the outside. Brunelleschi built it as a dome inside a dome, so where exactly does the staircase run?
answer: You walk up the curved gap between two domes, one inside the other
choices: You walk up the curved gap between two domes, one inside the other
You ride a wooden cage pulled up the outside by ropes
You climb a straight iron ladder bolted to the inner wall
You wind up a stone tower built against the cathedral side
context: It is a double dome — a shell within a shell — and the 463-step climb spirals up the hollow gap between them. Source: brunelleschi.imss.fi.it (TheDomeOfSantaMariaFiore); duomo.firenze.it.

question: For 130 years the giant gilded ball on top of Brunelleschi's lantern — eight feet across and two tons of copper — sat untouched 350 feet above Florence. Then on a January night in 1601 something hit it and sent it crashing down into the piazza below. What struck it?
answer: A lightning bolt knocked it clean off the top
choices: A lightning bolt knocked it clean off the top
A flock of birds slowly pecked the gold leaf away
An earthquake cracked it loose from the lantern
A careless workman dropped it during a repair
context: Lightning struck the golden ball on 27 January 1601 and knocked it clean off; it crashed into the square and was rebuilt in 1602. A marble disc still marks the spot where it landed. Source: duomo.firenze.it (Verrocchio's golden ball); guidedflorencetours.com.

question: Brunelleschi's biggest trick was that his dome held itself up as it rose, with no wooden scaffold underneath to catch it — impossible, the other masters said. His secret was the clever way he laid each brick, angling them so every new ring locked the one below in place. What was this pattern called?
answer: He laid the bricks in a herringbone, fish-spine pattern
choices: He laid the bricks in a herringbone, fish-spine pattern
He poured liquid Roman concrete over an iron frame
He bolted the stones together with long bronze pins
He froze the mortar with snow so it set rock-hard
context: The herringbone (Italian spina-pesce, 'fish-spine') brickwork let each ring grip the last, so the dome supported itself with no centring scaffold beneath it. Source: brunelleschi.imss.fi.it; science.howstuffworks.com (Brunelleschi's dome).

question: To lift millions of bricks and stones hundreds of feet up to the rising dome, Brunelleschi invented a machine powered by oxen walking in a circle. Its cleverest feature solved a real headache — switching a load from going up to going down used to mean stopping and turning the whole ox team around. How did his machine fix that?
answer: A reversible hoist that could raise or lower without turning the oxen around
choices: A reversible hoist that could raise or lower without turning the oxen around
A water wheel on the river that wound the ropes by current
A spiral ramp the oxen themselves walked up to the rooftop
A counterweight of sand that dropped to lift each load
context: His ox-powered hoist had a gear that reversed the load between rising and lowering without un-hitching the animals. Decades later the young Leonardo da Vinci sketched these machines. Source: bdml.stanford.edu/BrunelleschiNotes; brunelleschi.imss.fi.it.

question: Rival masters demanded Brunelleschi reveal his secret plan for the dome before they would back him. Instead, the story goes, he handed them an egg and challenged them to stand it upright on the smooth marble table. None of them could. So what did Brunelleschi do?
answer: He cracked the egg flat on its base so it stood upright
choices: He cracked the egg flat on its base so it stood upright
He spun the egg fast so it balanced like a top
He nestled the egg in a ring of soft wax
He leaned the egg against a coin on edge
context: In Vasari's tale Brunelleschi tapped the egg's bottom flat so it stood; when the masters scoffed 'we could have done that,' he answered they could likewise build his dome — if he showed them how. Told as legend. Source: Giorgio Vasari, Lives of the Artists; thecritic.co.uk/brunelleschis-egg.

question: Working up on the dome's dizzying heights, Brunelleschi's men risked freezing in fear or falling hundreds of feet. Besides adding railings to the hanging platforms, he did one unpopular thing to the workers' lunches to keep their heads clear and their footing steady. What was it?
answer: Watered down the workers wine so they stayed steady up high
choices: Watered down the workers wine so they stayed steady up high
Tied every worker to a rope fixed at the lantern above
Sent the workers home whenever the wind began to gust
Made the workers climb blindfolded so they felt no fear
context: Brunelleschi watered the men's wine (to grumbling) and added parapets to the suspended platforms so they wouldn't fall or freeze looking down. Source: througheternity.com; firenzemadeintuscany.com.

question: In 1471 Brunelleschi's dome got its crown: a two-ton gilded ball forged in Verrocchio's workshop, hauled 350 feet up to the lantern. One of the workshop's young helpers on that job would grow up to be the most famous mind of the whole age. Who was he?
answer: Leonardo da Vinci
choices: Leonardo da Vinci
Sandro Botticelli
Donatello
Lorenzo Ghiberti
context: The golden ball was made in Andrea del Verrocchio's workshop and hoisted up on 27 May 1471, with the teenage apprentice Leonardo da Vinci helping. Source: duomo.firenze.it (Verrocchio's golden ball); guidedflorencetours.com.

question: Here is the strangest thing about the man who built the most daring dome in the world: Filippo Brunelleschi had never been trained to design buildings at all. What had he actually trained as before he took on the dome?
answer: He was a trained goldsmith and clockmaker, not an architect
choices: He was a trained goldsmith and clockmaker, not an architect
He had built three smaller cathedrals in northern Italy
He had studied dome-building under a master in Rome
He had spent his youth as a stonemason in the quarries
context: Brunelleschi trained as a goldsmith and clockmaker. In 1401 he even lost the famous competition for Florence's bronze Baptistery doors to his lifelong rival Lorenzo Ghiberti — yet it was Brunelleschi who solved the dome. Source: worldhistory.org/Filippo_Brunelleschi.

question: Brunelleschi was forced to share charge of the dome with his old rival Lorenzo Ghiberti, who took the credit but had no idea how the engineering worked. At the most critical moment, the story goes, Brunelleschi exposed him with a trick. What did Brunelleschi do?
answer: He pretended to be sick and stayed home until work ground to a halt
choices: He pretended to be sick and stayed home until work ground to a halt
He tore up the building plans in front of the whole guild
He challenged the rival to a public building contest
He bribed the workers to follow only his orders
context: As the tale is told, Brunelleschi faked an illness and stayed home; with Ghiberti unable to direct the work, it stalled — proving who the real engineer was. Brunelleschi then 'recovered' and took sole charge. Told as legend. Source: britannica.com/biography/Filippo-Brunelleschi; worldhistory.org.

question: Brunelleschi's dome was sealed in 1436. Engineers have built with steel, concrete, and computers in the six centuries since — yet one astonishing claim about his brick-and-stone dome has never been beaten. What is still true of it today?
answer: It is still the largest brick-and-stone dome ever built
choices: It is still the largest brick-and-stone dome ever built
It was the tallest building in the world for a year
It is the only cathedral dome shaped like an egg
It was the first dome ever raised over a church
context: Nearly 600 years on, it remains the largest masonry dome ever built — over 4 million bricks and an estimated 37,000 tons, raised without any centring scaffold. Source: brunelleschi.imss.fi.it (TheDomeOfSantaMariaFiore).

question: Filippo Brunelleschi wanted the job of building Florence's giant cathedral dome, but the judges doubted such a thing could even stand. So he made them a bet: he could stand a raw egg straight up on a smooth piece of marble. Each judge tried and failed. How did Brunelleschi then make the egg stand?
answer: Tapped one end down hard so it cracked flat and stood
choices: Tapped one end down hard so it cracked flat and stood
Balanced it on a pinch of spilled salt
Spun it fast so it stood on its point
Stuck it upright in a blob of wax
context: When the judges complained that they could have done the same, Brunelleschi laughed and said they could also have raised the cupola -- if only they had seen his design. He won the commission. (Legend, told by Giorgio Vasari, 'Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors and Architects': '...giving one end of it a blow on the flat piece of marble, made it stand upright.')

question: When Filippo Brunelleschi began Florence's cathedral dome in 1418, it was the widest brick dome anyone had dared attempt, and the judges feared it would crumble before the mortar even set. Every builder assumed a dome that size needed one thing to hold it up while it was being built. What did Brunelleschi famously do without?
answer: Any wooden scaffolding rising from the ground to hold the dome up as it rose
choices: Any wooden scaffolding rising from the ground to hold the dome up as it rose
Any iron chain wrapped around the base to stop it spreading
Any central stone pillar inside to carry the weight
Any smaller practice dome built first to test the design
context: No one in 1418 knew it was possible to raise a dome that wide with nothing supporting it from below. More than 600 years later it is still the largest masonry (brick-and-stone) dome ever built. (Museo Galileo / IMSS Brunelleschi archive: 'the biggest dome ever built without using centring to support the masonry'; ArchDaily, 'How Did Filippo Brunelleschi Construct the World's Largest Masonry Dome?')

question: In Buddhist teaching, the goal called nirvana (Pali: nibbana) is the perfect peace that arrives once craving is gone. The word itself is not the name of a heavenly place but a plain, homely, physical picture. What does the word 'nirvana' literally describe?
answer: A flame being blown out
choices: A flame being blown out
A river reaching the sea
A bird let out of a cage
A lamp carried into a dark room
context: Nirvana (Pali nibbana) literally means 'to be blown out' or 'extinguished,' like a flame going out. It is not a place but the state reached when the fires of greed, aversion, and delusion are snuffed out -- a perfect peace that can arrive even while one is still alive, once craving ends. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nirvana_(Buddhism)

question: The monk Sona, who had been a musician before he became one of the Buddha's followers, threw himself into meditation so fiercely that he burned out and began thinking about quitting. The Buddha reached for the instrument Sona had once played to show him how spiritual effort should feel. What was the Buddha's advice?
answer: Tune the string neither too tight nor too slack
choices: Tune the string neither too tight nor too slack
Pluck every string as hard as you can
Put the instrument away and rest for good
Play one note over and over until it is perfect
context: To explain balanced effort the Buddha reminded the former musician Sona that a lute string wound too tight will not play, and a string left too slack will not play either -- only a string tuned 'not too tight, not too loose' makes music. Spiritual effort works the same way; the Middle Way is the tuned string. Told as a traditional teaching-story. Source: https://www.middlewaysociety.org/the-lute-strings/  (Legend.)

question: The Buddha taught that physical pain is unavoidable, but most of our misery is something extra we pile on ourselves. He pictured an ordinary person who, when something hurts, is struck not once but twice -- by the hurt itself, and then by a second blow made of grief, resentment, and brooding over the hurt. In the Buddha's image, what is that second blow?
answer: A second arrow they shoot into themselves
choices: A second arrow they shoot into themselves
A wound that never finishes healing
A debt they can never finish paying
A shadow that follows them everywhere
context: In the Sallatha Sutta the Buddha used the image of 'two arrows.' When something hurts, an untrained person is struck twice -- first by the physical pain (the first arrow), then by their own grief, resentment, and storytelling about it (the second arrow), feeling two pains. The trained disciple feels the first arrow but not the second: 'he feels one pain: physical, but not mental.' Source: https://www.accesstoinsight.org/tipitaka/sn/sn36/sn36.006.than.html

question: The Buddha's very first sermon opened by warning against two opposite dead-ends: chasing sensual pleasure, and torturing the body with extreme self-denial.
