Between them he set the Middle Way. The striking thing is that he spoke not as an outsider but as someone describing a road he had personally walked. What had the Buddha done before finding the Middle Way?
answer: He had lived as a pampered prince and then nearly starved himself as an ascetic
choices: He had lived as a pampered prince and then nearly starved himself as an ascetic
He had reigned as a great king and then begged for alms in rags
He had led armies in war and then lived alone in a forest
He had mastered the old scriptures and then debated rival teachers
context: The Buddha opened his first sermon by naming two extremes to avoid: devotion to sensual pleasure ('base, vulgar, common, ignoble, unprofitable') and devotion to self-affliction ('painful, ignoble, unprofitable'). The Middle Way between them was the discovery of a man who had tried both -- he had lived as a pampered prince and then nearly starved himself as an ascetic before finding the road in the middle. Source: https://www.dhammatalks.org/suttas/SN/SN56_11.html

question: The Buddha's Second Noble Truth says suffering is not random -- it has a cause, named by the Pali word tanha. He listed three forms of it: craving pleasure, craving to keep on existing, and even craving to be wiped out of existence. The word tanha is an ordinary bodily word that turns 'craving' into a raw physical urge. What does tanha literally mean?
answer: Thirst
choices: Thirst
Hunger
Fever
Itch
context: The Second Noble Truth pins the cause of suffering on tanha, a Pali word that literally means 'thirst.' The Buddha named three thirsts: craving for sensual pleasure (kama-tanha), craving to keep existing or becoming (bhava-tanha), and craving for non-existence or self-annihilation (vibhava-tanha). Suffering is not random; it is produced by a graspingness that always wants more or wants out. Source: https://inthewordsofbuddha.wordpress.com/2013/12/24/the-second-noble-truth-the-noble-truth-on-the-cause-of-suffering/

question: At Bunker Hill in 1775, the American militia were dangerously short on gunpowder, so legend says their commander barked an order to make every single shot count: hold your fire until the redcoats were almost on top of you. What did he supposedly tell the men to wait to see before pulling a trigger?
answer: The whites of their eyes
choices: The whites of their eyes
The buttons on their coats
The mud on their boots
The fear on their faces
context: 'Don't fire until you see the whites of their eyes' is attributed to Colonel William Prescott and/or General Israel Putnam, but most historians think the line is apocryphal. With little powder, holding fire until the British were close meant no shot was wasted. Source: nps.gov/articles/000/the-battle-of-bunker-hill.htm; armyhistory.org  (Legend.)

question: At Bunker Hill in June 1775, the British army did capture the hill — but only on their third charge, after the colonists ran out of ammunition. So why is this British WIN remembered as the moment that proved the Americans would stand and fight a real war?
answer: The British lost over 1,000 men taking the hill
choices: The British lost over 1,000 men taking the hill
The colonists never actually retreated
The British surrendered their cannon afterward
The fighting lasted for three straight days
context: About 1,054 British casualties (including 89 officers killed or wounded) versus roughly 450 American. The colonists threw back the first two charges with close-range musket fire; the British only stormed the redoubt on the third assault, when the defenders ran out of powder. A victory that bloody showed Britain the colonists would stand and fight. Source: nps.gov/articles/000/the-battle-of-bunker-hill.htm; britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Bunker-Hill

question: At Constantinople's Hippodrome, chariot-racing fans roared a single Greek word to spur their team onward. On 13 January 532 the rival Blue and Green factions turned that same cheer against Emperor Justinian and made it the war-cry of a five-day rebellion. What was the word they chanted?
answer: Nika!
choices: Nika!
Doxa!
Kyrie!
Aetos!
context: 'Nika' is Greek for 'Win!' / 'Conquer!' The race-day cheer became the name of the Nika riot, which burned half the city. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nika_riots

question: When Rome in the West fell in 476, the eastern half of the empire ruled on from Constantinople for almost a thousand more years. Scholars later coined the name 'Byzantine' for these people, but only after the empire was dead and gone. While it lived, what did its people always call themselves?
answer: Romans
choices: Romans
Greeks
Hellenes
Trojans
context: They called themselves Romaioi — 'Romans.' To them, the Roman Empire had never fallen; it simply ruled from a new capital. The word 'Byzantine' was invented by outsiders centuries later. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire

question: Tradition says that when Emperor Justinian first stepped into his finished church of Hagia Sophia in 537 and saw its vast dome, he was so overwhelmed that he boasted he had surpassed the legendary Temple in Jerusalem. According to the famous legend, what did he cry out?
answer: "Solomon, I have outdone thee!"
choices: "Solomon, I have outdone thee!"
"Caesar walks with me today!"
"Heaven itself has descended!"
"Rome is reborn this hour!"
context: Legend — the line is a later tradition, not found in Procopius, who saw the church new. Solomon was the king said to have built the great Temple in Jerusalem; Justinian claimed his church had outshone it. Source: http://gloriaromanorum.blogspot.com/2017/12/o-solomon-i-have-surpassed-thee.html

question: Before she became empress, Theodora was an actress of the lowest class, raised among the chariot-racing crowds of the Hippodrome. Her father held an unusual job there: he trained the animals that performed for the Green racing faction. What animals did Theodora's father keep?
answer: Bears
choices: Bears
Horses
Lions
Hounds
context: Theodora was a bear-keeper's daughter. A Roman law banned a senator from marrying an actress; only after his aunt the empress died did Justinian's uncle repeal it so he could marry her. Source: https://www.ancient-origins.net/history-famous-people/theodora-humble-beginnings-powerful-empress-who-changed-history-002368

question: Justinian was born a peasant boy in a tiny village and raised to rule the Roman world by his uncle Justin I, who adopted him. Justin's own rise was the unlikeliest of all: he had climbed from a lowly trade, to palace guardsman, all the way to emperor. What humble work had Justin done before the throne?
answer: He had kept pigs
choices: He had kept pigs
He had mined silver
He had rowed galleys
He had baked bread
context: Justin I began life as a swineherd. He brought his nephew Justinian — likely the last Roman emperor to speak Latin as his native tongue — from a village called Tauresium to Constantinople. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justinian_I

question: The Nika riot of 532 was set off by a botched execution. Condemned rioters — one a Blue, one a Green — were to be hanged at the Hippodrome, and the rival factions watched as bitter enemies. Then something went wrong at the gallows that suddenly united the two gangs in fury. What happened?
answer: The gallows broke and two men survived
choices: The gallows broke and two men survived
The executioner fled before the crowd
A sudden fire scattered the guards
The emperor's pardon arrived too late
context: The scaffold failed and the two survivors were spirited to a church for sanctuary. The Blues and Greens, normally enemies, united against Justinian and the rebellion began. Source: https://roman-empire.net/constantinople/nika-riots

question: As the Nika rioters burned Constantinople and crowned a rival emperor, Justinian readied a ship to flee. The historian Procopius records that his wife, Empress Theodora, refused to run and steadied him with one defiant saying — that it was better to die a ruler than live as a fugitive. Which saying did she use?
answer: "Royal purple makes a fine burial shroud"
choices: "Royal purple makes a fine burial shroud"
"A throne lost is a life half-spent"
"Better the sword than the open road"
"Crowns are won, never surrendered"
context: Legend — the speech survives only through Procopius. Purple was the color reserved for emperors; she meant she would rather be buried in it than flee. Justinian stayed, and the riot was crushed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nika_riots

question: With Constantinople burning and his soldiers outnumbered, Justinian needed to break the united mob from within. He sent the eunuch Narses, who walked alone into the packed Hippodrome carrying a sack of gold. How did Narses turn the crowd against itself?
answer: He paid the Blues to abandon the Greens
choices: He paid the Blues to abandon the Greens
He freed prisoners to start a brawl
He promised the Greens their own emperor
He set the wooden stands ablaze
context: Narses bribed the Blue faction's leaders to walk out, splitting the alliance. The generals Belisarius and Mundus then sealed the exits; Procopius reports some 30,000 dead in a day, and the rival emperor Hypatius was executed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nika_riots

question: Just weeks after the Nika riot destroyed the old church, Justinian launched a daring new Hagia Sophia and finished it in under six years. For its designers he passed over ordinary builders and instead chose two men from a surprising profession to plan the colossal dome. What were Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus by training?
answer: Mathematicians
choices: Mathematicians
Shipwrights
Sculptors
Bishops
context: Anthemius was a geometer and Isidore a fellow mathematician. Over 10,000 workers raised the church in 5 years and 10 months, dedicated 27 December 537. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia

question: The historian Procopius saw Hagia Sophia when it was brand new and tried to capture how its enormous dome seemed to float without support. He wrote that it did not rest on solid foundations but appeared to hang down from heaven by a single fabled object. What did Procopius say the dome hung from?
answer: A golden chain
choices: A golden chain
An angel's wing
A silver thread
A pillar of light
context: Procopius wrote the dome seemed 'suspended from heaven by the fabled golden chain.' He marveled that the church was so bright you would think the light came from within itself, not the sun. Source: https://www.pallasweb.com/deesis/procopius-description-of-hagia-sophia.html

question: Justinian set his minister Tribonian to a staggering task: take a thousand years of tangled, contradictory Roman law and boil it down into one ordered code. The result became the foundation of legal systems across Europe and is why much of Western law still traces back to Rome. By what Latin name is Justinian's great law code known?
answer: The Corpus Juris Civilis
choices: The Corpus Juris Civilis
The Pax Romana Edicta
The Lex Constantina
The Tabula Imperii
context: The Corpus Juris Civilis ('Body of Civil Law') gathered the Codex, the Digest, and the Institutes textbook. Tribonian led the project, finished around 534. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justinian_I

question: Procopius is the single richest eyewitness for Justinian's whole age — and he led a double life as a writer. In public he produced glowing works on the emperor's wars and buildings, but in secret he penned a venomous tell-all, savaging Justinian and Theodora, that could only be released safely after his death. What is that hidden book called?
answer: The Secret History
choices: The Secret History
The Roman Confessions
The Imperial Annals
The Book of Shadows
context: The Secret History (Greek 'Anekdota,' meaning 'unpublished things') is Procopius's poisonous private account, the dark twin of his official praise. Source: https://www.ancient-origins.net/history-famous-people/theodora-humble-beginnings-powerful-empress-who-changed-history-002368

question: Byzantine churches glow with walls of gold mosaic, and the secret is in each tiny gold tile, or tessera. A craftsman pressed a sheet of real gold leaf between two thin layers of glass, then tilted each finished tile at a slightly different angle as he set it into the wall. In flickering candlelight, what does that tilting trick make the gold wall appear to do as a worshiper walks past it?
answer: Shimmer and ripple, as if the wall itself is moving
choices: Shimmer and ripple, as if the wall itself is moving
Stay a flat, even sheet of unchanging color
Cast colored shadows of red and blue onto the floor
Slowly fade from gold to silver and back again
context: Because every tessera faces a slightly different way, each one catches the candle flame at a different instant, so light seems to chase across the gold as the viewer moves. The gold-leaf-between-glass tile and the angled setting are both deliberate. The gold ground was meant as a window into eternity, not mere decoration. Source: mosaicartstudio.us 'Byzantine Mosaic Art: Detailed Guide'; Smarthistory, San Vitale.

question: At Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai hangs the oldest surviving icon of Jesus, the 6th-century Christ Pantocrator, painted in colored hot wax. Look closely and the two halves of the face do not match: the painter gave each side a different expression on purpose. What two faces of Christ did he paint into that single portrait?
answer: One half a stern judge, the other half a calm, merciful savior
choices: One half a stern judge, the other half a calm, merciful savior
One half a young man, the other half a white-bearded elder
One half awake with open eyes, the other half asleep
One half lit by sun, the other half lost in shadow
context: Cover one side, then the other, and you see two different men: the judge who sees all, and the savior who blesses. The icon was painted in encaustic (pigment in hot wax), a technique that grew rare after the icon-smashing fights. It survived only because remote Sinai sat far from the Byzantine emperors destroying images. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_Pantocrator_(Sinai); mused.com.

question: The Athenian playwright Sophocles wrote about 120 plays during his life. Because a Greek text was lost forever the moment people stopped copying it out by hand, how many of Sophocles's plays still survive today?
context: Just 7 of Sophocles's ~120 plays survive; of Aeschylus's ~90 only 7, and of Euripides's ~80 only about 18. A work vanished the instant the last copy crumbled and no one had made a new one, which is why the thousand-year labor of hand-copyists is the reason any ancient Greek books reached us at all. Source: talesoftimesforgotten.com 'If You Like Ancient Greek Texts, Thank the Byzantines'; potentialdifference.org.uk on the lost Greek tragedies.

question: Almost everything the world knows about the ancient Greek genius Archimedes survived by sheer luck. Byzantine scribes had copied his works into a book around the 10th century, but a later scribe named Johannes Myronas scraped the pages clean, washed them, and wrote Christian prayers across them, finishing his prayer book in 1229. Using special imaging after 1999, what did modern scientists find still hidden beneath the prayers?
answer: His own lost mathematics
choices: His own lost mathematics
A lost Athenian play
A map of the old capital
A gospel written in Greek
context: Beneath the prayers lay Archimedes's lost 'Method of Mechanical Theorems' — the only surviving copy in any language. Recovered only after 1999 with special imaging, this reused book is called the Archimedes Palimpsest. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archimedes_Palimpsest; smithsonianmag.com 'Reading Between the Lines.'

question: By the 1430s the thousand-year Byzantine Empire was almost gone, yet its scholars carried one last treasure west to Italy. When the aged Byzantine philosopher Gemistos Plethon lectured in Florence in 1438, his teaching so inspired Cosimo de' Medici that Cosimo founded a brand-new academy and lent out his own Greek manuscripts to be translated. Which ancient Greek thinker did Plethon's lectures place at the heart of the Italian Renaissance?
answer: Plato
choices: Plato
Homer
Aristotle
Archimedes
context: The Florentines were so dazzled they called Plethon 'the second Plato.' Cosimo de' Medici's new Platonic Academy lent the young scholar Marsilio Ficino its Greek manuscripts of Plato to translate, so the Renaissance's love of Plato was in a real sense a parting gift from a dying empire. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemistos_Plethon; encyclopedia.com 'Florentine Academy'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platonic_Academy_(Florence).

question: At the center of Cahokia, near modern St. Louis, the people piled up a flat-topped pyramid of packed earth, now called Monks Mound — about 100 feet tall, with a base roughly 1,000 by 800 feet. Set against every earthen mound and pyramid ever raised across the Americas, north and south, how does it rank?
answer: the biggest earthen mound anywhere in the Americas
choices: the biggest earthen mound anywhere in the Americas
smaller only than the stone pyramids of Mexico
about equal to several other great American mounds
the biggest in the north but small beside Peru's
context: Monks Mound is the largest earthwork in the Americas and the biggest pyramid north of Mexico — roughly 100 feet tall with a base about 1,000 by 800 feet, a footprint broader than the Great Pyramid of Giza in Egypt. Source: https://www.britannica.com/place/Monks-Mound

question: Inside a mound at Cahokia, archaeologist Melvin Fowler uncovered a powerful man laid to rest on top of more than 10,000 polished shell beads. The beads had not been scattered — workers had carefully arranged them into a single shape beneath his body. They had built the dead man a bed in the form of what?
answer: a falcon, a bird of prey, with outspread wings
choices: a falcon, a bird of prey, with outspread wings
a serpent, a great snake, with a coiling body
a panther, a big cat, with a long tail
a turtle, a river creature, with a broad shell
context: In Mound 72, Melvin Fowler (digging from 1967) found the man on more than 10,000 cut marine-shell beads shaped like a falcon — its head beneath his head, its wings and tail under his arms and legs. He is known as the 'Birdman'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mound_72

question: Crowds at Cahokia gathered around a long, smooth court to watch their favorite sport. One player rolled a polished stone disc skidding across the ground, and the moment it slowed the others hurled their spears, each trying to land closest to where the disc would stop. What was this game called?
answer: chunkey
choices: chunkey
lacrosse
atlatl
shinny
context: Chunkey was Cahokia's signature sport, and the city spread it across the South and Great Plains. Crowds bet so heavily that, by some accounts, ruined losers killed themselves rather than face their debts. A famous stone figurine shows a kneeling chunkey player, disc in one hand and sticks in the other. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Chunkey/

question: Cahokia's builders raised about 120 mounds — including one a hundred feet tall — moving an estimated 55 million cubic feet of soil. They had no wheels, no horses or oxen, and no metal tools. How did they move that mountain of earth?
answer: by hand, hauling it basket by basket on their backs
choices: by hand, hauling it basket by basket on their backs
by floating it downriver on great wooden rafts
by dragging it on stone sledges pulled by dogs
by washing it into place through dug canals
context: Workers dug earth from 'borrow pits' and carried it in woven baskets, moving an estimated 55 million cubic feet over decades — one basket-load at a time, with no wheels, draft animals, or metal tools. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia

question: Around the year 1100, the town of Cahokia near modern St. Louis was home to perhaps 15,000 to 20,000 people. For its time, how did that crowd compare with the cities of Europe?
answer: It held more people than London or Paris did then.
choices: It held more people than London or Paris did then.
It rivaled the world's greatest city, Constantinople.
It was about the size of a small European market town.
It held a few hundred souls, like a country village.
context: Around 1100 Cahokia held roughly 15,000-20,000 people, probably more than London or Paris at the same moment. No city in what is now the United States would grow larger until Philadelphia passed 40,000 in the 1780s. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia

question: The greatest mound at Cahokia is called Monks Mound — yet the people who piled it up over generations had vanished centuries before it ever got that name. So who were the 'monks' it honors?
answer: Trappist monks who later gardened on one of its terraces
choices: Trappist monks who later gardened on one of its terraces
French priests who first dug into the mound for treasure
Spanish friars who built a chapel on its summit
English monks who mapped the ruins for a king
context: The mound is named for a group of Trappist monks who lived nearby and gardened its first terrace in the early 1800s. They never lived on the great mound itself, and the city's true builders had been gone for centuries. Source: https://cahokiamounds.org/mound/mound-38-monks-mound/

question: Digging at Cahokia in the 1960s, archaeologist Warren Wittry kept finding rings of holes where huge wooden posts had once stood. When he worked out that the posts had been arranged to track the rising and setting sun, he nicknamed the place after a famous monument in England. What did he call it?
answer: Woodhenge
choices: Woodhenge
Timberhenge
Cedarhenge
Posthenge
context: Wittry found the post-hole rings during 1960s salvage digging and realized they tracked the sun, nicknaming them 'Woodhenge' after Stonehenge. The main ring was about 410 feet across with 48 tall posts of red cedar, likely painted red with ochre. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia_Woodhenge

question: Cahokia's great ring of sacred posts, nicknamed Woodhenge, was no random circle. Twice a year, on the spring and fall equinox, a watcher standing at its exact center would see the rising sun appear to climb directly out of one particular spot half a mile away. What did the sun seem to rise from?
answer: the front of Monks Mound, the city's great pyramid
choices: the front of Monks Mound, the city's great pyramid
the river, glinting along the Mississippi's bend
a gap notched between two distant hills
the tallest post on the ring's far side
context: At the equinoxes, the sun rose as if emerging from the front of Monks Mound, half a mile away — and the builders kept that alignment even as they raised the mound taller over time. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia_Woodhenge

question: In one grave at Cahokia, archaeologists found a cache of about 700 finely made arrowheads. Testing the stone, they traced it to four far-apart regions — Tennessee, Wisconsin, southern Illinois, and Oklahoma. Which explanation for that four-region haul do scholars actually favor?
answer: trade networks that reached across half a continent into Cahokia
choices: trade networks that reached across half a continent into Cahokia
Cahokia's war parties had raided each of the four regions in turn
Cahokia's own traders had travelled out to all four regions themselves
pilgrims had carried points from their home regions as offerings
context: The roughly 700 arrowheads were sourced to four distant regions — Tennessee, southern Illinois, Wisconsin, and the Oklahoma Caddo — proof of trade networks reaching across half a continent into Cahokia. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mound_72

question: Cahokia, near modern St. Louis, was the largest city of ancient North America. Its people left no writing, so their own name for the city is lost forever. The name we know it by today, 'Cahokia,' was given to it much later. Who did it come from?
answer: a much later, unrelated people who moved into the area after the city fell
choices: a much later, unrelated people who moved into the area after the city fell
the French missionaries who built a chapel among the ruined mounds
an American army surveyor sent to map the strange earthen mounds
Spanish explorers who came up the river valley hunting for gold
context: The builders left no writing, so we do not know what they called their city or themselves. The name 'Cahokia' actually belongs to a much later, unrelated Illiniwek (Illini) people who lived in the area centuries after the city was abandoned. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia

question: Mound 72 at Cahokia held the graves of about 272 people. One pit alone held 53 young women, all roughly 15 to 30 years old, laid out in neat rows in two layers. Studying their bones and how carefully the bodies had been arranged, archaeologists worked out how these women had died. What did they conclude?
answer: they had been strangled and buried as sacrifices
choices: they had been strangled and buried as sacrifices
they had been a chief's wives, buried to follow him in death
they had been warriors fallen in a great battle
they had been travelers lost to a winter storm
context: Mound 72 held about 272 people buried over roughly a century, and scholars estimate nearly 62 percent were sacrificial victims — evidence that Cahokia's rulers held the power of life and death. The 53 young women, ages about 15 to 30, were laid in two layers separated by matting and showed signs of strangulation. A separate pit held 39 people killed violently, with fractured skulls and partial decapitations; some seemed to have been trying to climb out as they were buried. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mound_72

question: By about 1350 the great city of Cahokia stood empty, and no one has ever fully explained why. In 2021 archaeologist Caitlin Rankin dug into the old creek beds beside Cahokia to test the most popular idea — that the people had felled so many trees the bared hillsides washed mud down and ruined their farmland in floods. The layers of soil told her something that upset that whole story. What did her study find?
answer: no real evidence the tree-cutting caused any flooding
choices: no real evidence the tree-cutting caused any flooding
the logging really had triggered the ruinous floods after all
the floods had come, but from far upstream rains, not local logging
the creeks had dried to dust, killing the crops with drought
context: Cahokia was abandoned by about 1350, and why is still a mystery. The 2021 Washington University study led by Caitlin Rankin found no evidence the people caused flooding by overcutting trees, challenging the popular 'deforestation' story and leaving the collapse genuinely unsolved. Source: https://source.washu.edu/2021/04/study-scant-evidence-that-wood-overuse-at-cahokia-caused-collapse/

question: Michelangelo Merisi, the painter known as Caravaggio, made his figures loom out of near-total blackness, lit as if by a single spotlight on a dark stage. This dramatic light came to define the whole Baroque style. What is the name of this technique he is famous for?
answer: Tenebrism
choices: Tenebrism
Sfumato
Pointillism
Impasto
context: Tenebrism comes from the Italian 'tenebroso,' meaning gloomy or dark. It is an extreme form of chiaroscuro (Italian for 'light-dark'): instead of gently shading figures, Caravaggio drowned everything but his lit subjects in black, so they seem caught in a single shaft of theatrical light. Sources: britannica.com/art/tenebrism; thecollector.com/caravaggio-use-light-baroque-art/

question: Michelangelo Merisi, the painter Caravaggio, fled Rome in 1606 as a wanted murderer with a death sentence on his head. Still hunted years later, he painted young David holding the severed, bleeding head of the giant Goliath, and sent the picture toward the papal court as a plea for a pardon. Whose face did he paint onto the dead giant's severed head?
answer: His own
choices: His own
The murdered man's
A rival knight's
The pope's
context: Caravaggio painted his OWN face onto Goliath's severed, bleeding head, casting himself as the defeated villain begging for mercy. The sword in the painting carries the inscription 'H-AS OS,' read as the Latin 'humilitas occidit superbiam' -- 'humility kills pride.' Sources: galleriaborgheseroma.it (David and Goliath); blog.ricksteves.com/blog/caravaggios-david-with-the-head-of-goliath/

question: When Christopher Columbus sailed west in 1492 with three ships, two of them were small, quick caravels and one was a bigger, slower carrack he used as his flagship. The two nimble caravels were the Nina and the Pinta. What was the name of the larger, slower flagship that was NOT a caravel?
answer: The Santa Maria
choices: The Santa Maria
The Nina
The Pinta
The Esmeralda
context: Columbus's flagship, the Santa Maria, was a larger and slower carrack (called a nau), not a caravel. The two caravels, the Nina and the Pinta, were the nimble ones. (Source: exploration.marinersmuseum.org/watercraft/caravel/)

question: The magnetic compass was invented in China, not Europe. A Song-dynasty military manual from the 1040s describes floating a thin, magnetized iron shape in a bowl of water so it would swing around and find direction in the dark. The Chinese did not call its pointing end the 'north' end, the way we do today. What direction did they say their floating needle pointed?
answer: South
choices: South
East
West
Down
context: The Chinese called it the 'south-pointing fish' (or south-pointing needle), not north-pointing. The 1040s manual describes a magnetized iron fish floated in water to find direction 'in the obscurity of the night.' (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_compass)

question: A square sail can only push a ship along with the wind behind it, so an explorer who ran south down the coast of Africa would be stuck unable to get home against the prevailing wind. The caravel solved this with one clever piece of equipment that let it angle close to the wind and zig-zag back toward home. What was the single trick that let a caravel beat against the wind?
answer: A triangular lateen sail
choices: A triangular lateen sail
A deeper iron keel
A second steering oar
A taller mainmast
context: The triangular lateen sail let a caravel point as close as about 55-60 degrees off the wind and tack (zig-zag) toward a goal that lay directly upwind. This is the one trick that let ships explore a coast and still get home against the prevailing wind. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravel)

question: A sailor far out on the open ocean, with no landmarks in sight, could still figure out how far north or south he was by pointing his mariner's astrolabe at one particular star and measuring its angle above the horizon. Because that star sits almost exactly over the North Pole, its height in the sky equals your latitude. Which star did he measure?
answer: Polaris, the North Star
choices: Polaris, the North Star
The planet Venus
The red star Mars
The Dog Star, Sirius
context: Polaris stays within about 1 degree of true north, so its height above the horizon basically equals your latitude. A sailor sighted it at night through the two pinholes of his astrolabe and read the angle off the rim. By day he used the noon sun instead. (Source: exploration.marinersmuseum.org/object/astrolabe/)

question: The mariner's astrolabe was a disc of solid brass or bronze, and its makers deliberately cut large open spokes through it so the wind would blow straight through instead of pushing it around. They also made it surprisingly thick and heavy. On a pitching, rolling ship's deck, why was that heaviness designed in on purpose rather than being a flaw?
answer: A heavy disc hung steadier on a rolling deck
choices: A heavy disc hung steadier on a rolling deck
Heavy metal held the sun's heat to glow at night
The weight let it double as an anchor in a calm
Extra metal stopped the brass from rusting at sea
context: The weight was a feature, not a bug: a heavy disc dangled by its ring hung steadier on a pitching, rolling deck, so the angle could be read. Even so, in high seas it still swung enough to throw a ship off course. (Source: exploration.marinersmuseum.org/object/astrolabe/)

question: In 1503, a Portuguese ship named the Esmeralda wrecked on an island off Oman under Vicente Sodre, an uncle of the explorer Vasco da Gama, and a bronze navigating disc went down with it. Divers found it under the sand in 2014, but its surface looked blank and smooth. A laser scan then revealed faint navigation markings too worn for the eye to see, proving it was the world's oldest known mariner's astrolabe. What did the laser scan reveal on the worn disc?
answer: Degree markings cut every five degrees
choices: Degree markings cut every five degrees
A captain's name scratched into the rim
A map of the African coastline
A row of holes for sighting the stars
context: The laser scan of the 'Sodre astrolabe' revealed degree markings every 5 degrees, too worn to see by eye, plus the Portuguese royal coat of arms and the armillary sphere of King Manuel I. Made between 1496 and 1501 and certified by Guinness World Records as the oldest known mariner's astrolabe. (Source: smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/mariners-astrolabe-recovered-shipwreck-worlds-oldest-180971761/)

question: Baldassare Castiglione, writing his 1528 manual on the perfect courtier, coined a brand-new word for a gentleman's master skill: making something difficult look completely effortless, hiding all the practice behind it. What word did he invent?
answer: Sprezzatura
choices: Sprezzatura
Magnificenza
Disinvoltura
Cortesia
context: Castiglione defined it as 'a certain nonchalance, so as to conceal all art and make whatever one does or says appear to be without effort.' The term first appears in The Book of the Courtier (1528). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sprezzatura

question: In The Book of the Courtier, Count Ludovico da Canossa lays down the 'one universal rule' behind sprezzatura: the courtier must hide every trace of his study and practice. By Castiglione's logic, what happens to a courtier's grace the instant his audience sees the effort behind it?
answer: The grace is destroyed, because true art is the kind that does not look like art
choices: The grace is destroyed, because true art is the kind that does not look like art
The grace is doubled, because the audience admires the labor
The grace is unchanged, since skill speaks for itself
The grace is delayed, until the courtier rests and tries again
context: Canossa urges the courtier 'to avoid affectation to the uttermost' and 'to conceal art, for if it is discovered, it quite destroys our credit' — 'we may call that art true art which does not seem to be art.' Source: https://publicdomainreview.org/collection/baldassare-castiglione-the-book-of-the-courtier/

question: Castiglione's close friend, the painter Raphael, made him immortal in a portrait now hanging in the Louvre. The painting so enchanted later masters that one Dutch genius sketched it at a 1639 Amsterdam auction and let it echo through his own self-portraits for the rest of his life. Which painter studied it that day?
answer: Rembrandt
choices: Rembrandt
Vermeer
Titian
Caravaggio
context: Rembrandt sketched Raphael's Portrait of Baldassare Castiglione (c. 1514-15) at the 1639 auction; Rubens also painted a copy, now at the Courtauld. Castiglione and Raphael had been close friends since about 1504 at Urbino. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait_of_Baldassare_Castiglione

question: In 1304, King Edward I of England ordered the largest siege engine ever built — a colossal trebuchet meant to hurl boulders and crack open the walls of Stirling Castle in Scotland. Edward gave his monster machine its own dreaded name. What was it called?
answer: Warwolf
choices: Warwolf
Stormcrow
Wolfsbane
Ironclaw
context: Warwolf (also called Loup-de-Guerre or Ludgar) took five master carpenters and about fifty workmen roughly three months to build, and when taken apart it was said to fill around 30 wagons. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwolf; blog.historicenvironment.scot/2024/04/the-war-wolf-at-stirling-castle/

question: A portcullis was a heavy grille of oak crossed with iron, dropped on chains to slam a castle gate shut in an instant. The strongest gatehouses had not one but TWO of these grilles, one behind the other. What was the deadly purpose of dropping that SECOND grille?
answer: To trap attackers in the killing space between the two
choices: To trap attackers in the killing space between the two
To double the gate's weight against a battering ram
To give defenders a spare if the first grille jammed
To block arrows shot in through the open gateway
context: Defenders slammed down the inner grille first, then the outer one, sealing attackers in the deadly space between them with no way forward and no way back. Source: medievalchronicles.com/medieval-castles/medieval-castle-parts/castle-portcullis/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portcullis

question: After William the Conqueror seized England in 1066, the Normans needed forts in a hurry. Their answer was a castle so quick and cheap a small one went up in mere weeks: heap up a great mound of earth, plant a wooden tower on its summit, and ring a yard below with a timber fence and a ditch. What is this earth-and-timber castle called?
answer: A motte-and-bailey
choices: A motte-and-bailey
A moat-and-mound
A keep-and-ward
A ring-and-tower
context: William and his barons threw up an estimated 500 to 600 of these motte-and-bailey castles across England between 1066 and 1087, later rebuilding many in stone. The Bayeux Tapestry even shows men shovelling up such a mound. Source: exploring-castles.com/castle_designs/motte_and_bailey/; worldhistory.org/image/8757/

question: When King John besieged Rochester Castle in 1215, his miners dug a tunnel under a corner of the great stone keep and propped its roof with timber — but to topple the tower they had to burn those props away, and needed a fierce-burning fuel. John sent a written order all the way to London for forty of the fattest of one farm animal. Which animal did he send for?
answer: Pigs
choices: Pigs
Oxen
Sheep
Goats
context: John's order asked for 'forty of the fattest pigs, the sort least good for eating.' Their burning fat collapsed the mine, and one whole corner tower of Rochester's keep came crashing down. The starving defenders, by then reduced to eating their horses, surrendered on 30 November 1215. Source: exploring-castles.com/uk/england/rochester_castle/; english-heritage.org.uk/visit/places/rochester-castle/history/

question: In 1304, King Edward I had spent months building an enormous siege engine to batter Stirling Castle. Its tiny garrison of about thirty men, terrified, tried to surrender before the giant machine was even finished — but Edward refused to accept it and made them wait. What was Edward's reason for turning down their surrender?
answer: He wanted to fire his monster engine at them first
choices: He wanted to fire his monster engine at them first
He suspected their surrender was a hidden trap
He demanded a far heavier ransom in gold
He was waiting for more soldiers to arrive
context: Edward I made the garrison wait until his great engine had been tested as a public show of power, accepting the surrender only on 24 July 1304. To feed his thirteen siege engines he even ordered Scottish churches stripped of the lead on their roofs — 22 cartloads came from St Andrews alone. Source: blog.historicenvironment.scot/2024/04/the-war-wolf-at-stirling-castle/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Stirling_Castle_(1304)

question: Old movies love the scene where castle defenders pour boiling OIL down through a 'murder hole' — a gap in the ceiling of the gate passage — onto enemies trapped below. But historians say the boiling-oil part is mostly make-believe. Why did real castle defenders almost never use oil this way?
answer: Oil was far too scarce and costly to waste
choices: Oil was far too scarce and costly to waste
Oil could not be made hot enough to burn
The murder holes were too narrow for oil
Their faith forbade burning enemies alive
context: Through murder holes defenders really did drop stones or pour boiling WATER, heated sand, or quicklime — but oil was too precious to pour away. With the gate sealed behind them, attackers packed into the gatehouse had nowhere to flee. Source: exploring-castles.com/castle_designs/machicolations/; medievalchronicles.com/medieval-castles/medieval-castle-parts/murder-holes/

question: The trebuchet was the most powerful siege engine of the Middle Ages — it could fling a 350-lb stone nearly a thousand feet and smash a castle wall to rubble. What single, simple force gave this giant machine all of its throwing power?
answer: A heavy falling weight
choices: A heavy falling weight
A tightly twisted rope
A bent wooden arm
A charge of gunpowder
context: Earlier catapults stored their punch in twisted ropes or bent wood, but the trebuchet used only gravity — a heavy counterweight box on the short arm falling a little way while the long sling-end whipped around, hurling the stone fast enough to break a wall. Source: history.howstuffworks.com/european-history/trebuchet.htm; medievalchronicles.com/medieval-weapons/castle-siege-weapons/trebuchet-siege-weapon/

question: Later medieval castles replaced their old square corner-towers with ROUND ones — and not for the looks. The change answered one dreaded attack: enemy miners tunnelling under a tower's base, propping the roof with timber, then burning the props so the stone above caved into the pit. Why did a round tower survive this undermining far better than a square one?
answer: It had no corner to undermine and collapse
choices: It had no corner to undermine and collapse
Its curved wall was always far thicker
Its smooth face gave miners nowhere to dig
Its round weight crushed the tunnel shut
context: A square tower has corners that crumble when one is mined out; a round tower has none, so there is no weak point to bring it down. Defenders also fought back by countermining — digging their own tunnels to break into the attackers' mine for a brutal fight in the dark. Source: medievalchronicles.com/medieval-castles/castle-siege/; templarknightstours.com/templar-blog/beneath-the-walls-medieval-sappers-and-the-secret-tactics-of-siege-warfare

question: A concentric castle is a castle inside a castle — a complete ring of walls encircled by a second, lower ring of walls. The clever twist is that the INNER wall is built taller than the outer one. What deadly advantage did making the inner wall higher give the defenders?
answer: Archers on both walls could fire at the same time
choices: Archers on both walls could fire at the same time
The inner keep stayed hidden from outside view
Rocks dropped from it gathered far more speed
Sentries could spot enemies much farther away
context: Because the inner archers stand higher, they fire right over the heads of the outer archers, so anyone caught in the gap between the two walls faces arrows from both at once. Edward I's Beaumaris Castle in Wales, laid out in near-perfect symmetry, is the finest concentric design ever planned — though it was never even finished. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concentric_castle; worldhistory.org/Beaumaris_Castle/

question: Attackers learned to press right against the foot of a castle wall, in a blind spot where defenders leaning over the battlements couldn't hit them — anything dropped just glanced off the wall's sloping base. The cure was a stone gallery that juts OUT beyond the wall, with holes in its floor, so missiles fall straight down onto anyone hugging the base. What is this overhanging stone defence called?
answer: A machicolation
choices: A machicolation
A barbican
A crenellation
A casemate
context: Before stone machicolations, castles used wooden HOARDINGS — galleries bolted onto the wall in wartime — but being timber they could be set alight. Stone machicolations replaced them precisely because masonry will not burn. Source: exploring-castles.com/castle_designs/machicolations/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoarding_(castle)

question: The Byzantine Empire's terror weapon was GREEK FIRE — a liquid flame sprayed from a tube that stuck to ships and men and kept burning even ON WATER, almost impossible to douse. Its recipe was guarded so jealously that Emperor Romanos II named it among the three things that must never fall into foreign hands. What finally became of the recipe for Greek Fire?
answer: It vanished with Byzantium and is lost today
choices: It vanished with Byzantium and is lost today
It survives in a single monastery's old library
It passed to the Crusaders, who copied it down
It is still kept secret by one Greek family
context: Romanos II said three things must never reach foreigners: the imperial regalia, the royal princesses, and Greek Fire. The Byzantines kept the recipe so secret that it was never written plainly, and it stays unknown to this day. Source: worldhistory.org/Greek_Fire/; allthatsinteresting.com/greek-fire

question: Krak des Chevaliers in Syria was so mighty that the Knights Hospitaller holding it almost never lost it to attack. In 1271 the Mamluk Sultan Baibars besieged the fortress for about a month and still could not break in by force. According to the traditional story, what trick finally lured the knights into marching out and surrendering?
answer: A forged letter faking their commander's surrender order
choices: A forged letter faking their commander's surrender order
A secret tunnel dug beneath the chapel floor
A traitor who unbarred the gate one night
A sickness that emptied the fortress of men
context: The forged message pretended to come from the knights' own Grand Master, ordering them to give up; they obeyed and were spared. Historians treat the tale as a traditional story rather than proven fact. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krak_des_Chevaliers; worldhistory.org/Krak_Des_Chevaliers/  (Legend.)

question: Jesús Sosa Blanco, a major under the ousted dictator Batista, was condemned to die before a firing squad at the La Cabaña fortress in Havana for scores of killings. As the squad took aim, Sosa Blanco did something that stunned the men sent to shoot him. What did he do?
answer: He shouted the squad's own commands at them — "Atención! Apunte! Fuego!" — ordering his own death
choices: He shouted the squad's own commands at them — "Atención! Apunte! Fuego!" — ordering his own death
He fell to his knees and begged the young soldiers to spare his life
He read aloud a list of judges he swore would die after him
He stayed silent and refused the blindfold the guards offered him
context: By the recounting, Sosa Blanco — charged with 108 murders — cried out the firing-squad's own orders ('Pelotón, atención! Prepare! Apunte! Fuego!'), commanding the volley that killed him. La Cabaña's condemned were shot in the fortress's dry, floodlit moat, beneath a giant lit statue of Christ; Che Guevara had been placed in command of the tribunals on January 3, 1959. https://magazine.atavist.com/2021/the-butcher-of-havana-cuba-che-castro-aclu

question: On July 13, 1994, a group of Cubans hijacked an old tugboat, the 13 de Marzo, and made a run for the United States. Seven miles off Havana, Cuban government boats caught them and sank the tug, drowning 41 of the 72 people aboard, including 10 children. What did the government boats use to sink it?
answer: High-pressure water hoses, aimed at the people on deck
choices: High-pressure water hoses, aimed at the people on deck
Mounted machine guns firing across the water
Depth charges dropped beneath the hull
Tow cables that dragged it back to port
context: Cuban government boats rammed the hijacked 13 de Marzo and blasted it with high-pressure water hoses until it sank; 41 of the 72 aboard drowned, 10 of them children. The sinking became the defining tragedy of the 1994 'balsero' (rafter) crisis, when tens of thousands of Cubans fled on homemade rafts of inner tubes and planks. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinking_of_tugboat_13_de_Marzo

question: World War II was the deadliest conflict in human history -- some 70 to 85 million people died, roughly one in every thirty alive on Earth at the time. You might picture a war of soldiers, but historians counting the dead found that most of the people killed never carried a rifle. Who made up the majority of the dead?
answer: Civilians, who died in about double the numbers of the soldiers killed
choices: Civilians, who died in about double the numbers of the soldiers killed
Front-line soldiers, who died in about double the numbers of civilians killed
Sailors and airmen, who died in about double the numbers of foot soldiers
Prisoners of war, who died in about double the numbers of civilians killed
context: Civilian deaths totaled roughly 50-55 million while military deaths from all causes were about 21-25 million -- so for every soldier who died, roughly two ordinary people did, killed by bombing, famine, disease, and massacre. Source: Wikipedia, World War II casualties.

question: As German armies drove deep into Soviet territory in 1942, Joseph Stalin grew enraged at Red Army units that fell back. On July 28 he issued a battlefield order that posted special detachments BEHIND his own front lines with instructions to shoot any of his soldiers who tried to retreat. By what name -- both its number and its three-word slogan -- is that order remembered?
answer: Order No. 227, 'Not one step back!'
choices: Order No. 227, 'Not one step back!'
Order No. 270, 'Surrender means treason!'
Order No. 88, 'Hold the motherland!'
Order No. 145, 'Forward without fear!'
context: Order No. 227's blocking detachments shot retreating troops; archives suggest as many as 158,000 Soviet soldiers were executed by their own side over the war, including about 15,000 in a couple of weeks at Stalingrad. A real share of the USSR's enormous losses traces to Stalin's own conduct, not the Germans alone. Source: Wikipedia, Order No. 227; ww2today.com.

question: On March 21, 1861, Confederate Vice President Alexander Stephens gave a speech in Savannah saying the brand-new Confederate government had a 'corner-stone' resting on one 'great truth.' What did Stephens claim that 'great truth' was?
answer: That the negro is not equal to the white man
choices: That the negro is not equal to the white man
That each state could govern its own affairs
That Northern tariffs were crushing the South
That the North had broken the Constitution
context: Stephens's exact words: the cornerstone 'rests, upon the great truth that the negro is not equal to the white man; that slavery -- subordination to the superior race -- is his natural and normal condition.' This is now called the Cornerstone Speech. (American Battlefield Trust, Cornerstone Speech primary source.)

question: When Mississippi voted to leave the Union in January 1861, it published a Declaration of the Immediate Causes -- a list of WHY it was seceding. The very first sentence tied the state's whole position to a single institution, calling that institution 'the greatest material interest of the world.' Which institution did Mississippi name in that opening line?
answer: Slavery
choices: Slavery
Cotton shipping
Free trade
Plantation banking
context: Mississippi's first line: 'Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery -- the greatest material interest of the world.' It added: 'a blow at slavery is a blow at commerce and civilization.' (American Battlefield Trust; National Constitution Center, Mississippi Declaration of the Immediate Causes.)

question: South Carolina was the FIRST state to secede, on December 20, 1860. In its Declaration of Causes it complained that the Northern states had just handed power to one particular man -- a man whose 'opinions and purposes,' the document said, were 'hostile to slavery' -- by winning the autumn 1860 vote at the head of a brand-new anti-slavery party. Whose recent victory was South Carolina calling the last straw?
answer: Abraham Lincoln
choices: Abraham Lincoln
Stephen Douglas
John Brown
Roger Taney
context: South Carolina objected that the North had 'united in the election of a man to the high office of President of the United States, whose opinions and purposes are hostile to slavery.' That man was Abraham Lincoln, who had won weeks earlier but had not yet even taken office. (Avalon Project, Yale Law School, South Carolina Declaration of Causes.)

question: When Mississippi gathered its convention to vote on leaving the Union in January 1861, the men in the room were not neutral judges -- many had a personal stake in slavery. Of the 100 delegates who decided whether Mississippi would secede, how many were themselves slaveholders?
answer: 84 of the 100 delegates
choices: 84 of the 100 delegates
51 of the 100 delegates
39 of the 100 delegates
22 of the 100 delegates
context: 84 of the 100 convention delegates owned slaves, and the ordinance to leave the Union passed 84 to 15. Slavery was no abstraction in Mississippi: enslaved people were roughly 55% of the state's 1860 population, an outright majority. (Wikipedia, Mississippi Secession Convention.)

question: In the Cornerstone Speech, Alexander Stephens did not hint or dance around what had split the country -- he named it outright. He said the new Confederate constitution had 'put at rest, forever, all the agitating questions relating to our peculiar institution,' and called that very thing 'the immediate cause of the late rupture and present revolution.' What was the 'peculiar institution' Stephens said had caused the war?
answer: Slavery
choices: Slavery
Tariffs
Federal courts
States' rights
context: Stephens, the Confederacy's own vice president, used the era's polite phrase 'our peculiar institution' for slavery, and called it 'the immediate cause of the late rupture and present revolution' while the war was just beginning. (American Battlefield Trust, Cornerstone Speech.)

question: Alexander Stephens was not embarrassed by the idea at the heart of the Confederacy -- he bragged that it was brand new in human history. He declared, 'This, our new government, is the first, in the history of the world, based upon this great physical, philosophical, and moral truth.' The 'truth' he was boasting about being the world's first to build on was a claim about which group of people?
answer: Black people, whom he claimed were inferior
choices: Black people, whom he claimed were inferior
Farmers, whom he claimed the North exploited
States, which he claimed were fully sovereign
Christians, whom he claimed the North persecuted
context: Stephens openly claimed the Confederacy was the first government ever founded on the supposed 'truth' of Black inferiority -- not hiding it, but presenting it as an achievement. (American Battlefield Trust, Cornerstone Speech.)

question: Mississippi's secession declaration tried to make slavery sound like a fact of nature rather than a human choice. It argued that the state's crops grew only in a near-tropical climate, and then claimed that 'by an imperious law of nature' only one kind of person could survive working under that hot sun. According to Mississippi's declaration, who alone could 'bear exposure to the tropical sun'?
answer: None but the black race
choices: None but the black race
Only the native-born Southerner
Only the experienced plantation hand
Only those raised in the lowland heat
context: Mississippi dressed up slavery as biology: 'by an imperious law of nature, none but the black race can bear exposure to the tropical sun.' The declaration ended that the state's only options were 'submission to the mandates of abolition, or a dissolution of the Union.' (American Battlefield Trust, Declaration of Causes of the Seceding States.)

question: Texas seceded on February 2, 1861, and its declaration listed several things it called 'undeniable truths.' Among them: that the American governments were 'established exclusively by the white race' and that the African race was 'rightfully held and regarded as an inferior and dependent race.' How did the same Texas document describe the actual system of slavery it was defending?
answer: The beneficent and patriarchal system of African slavery
choices: The beneficent and patriarchal system of African slavery
A sacred trust handed down from their forefathers
A Christian guardianship over a dependent people
The firm foundation of Southern peace and prosperity
context: Texas praised slavery in glowing terms, calling it 'the beneficent and patriarchal system of African slavery,' and condemned the idea of racial equality as 'a doctrine at war with nature.' (Texas State Library, Declaration of Causes, Feb 2, 1861.)

question: The Confederacy did not just defend slavery in speeches -- it wrote slavery into its own constitution, adopted in March 1861, and went one startling step further. The document tied the hands of the Confederacy's OWN lawmakers: it commanded that the Confederate Congress could never pass a certain kind of law, no matter what future Southerners might want. Which law was the Confederate Congress forbidden to ever pass?
answer: A law abolishing slavery
choices: A law abolishing slavery
A law raising tariffs on imports
A law granting the president a second term
A law admitting a free state to the Confederacy
context: The Confederate Constitution barred the Confederate Congress from ever passing 'any law denying or impairing the right of property in negro slaves' (Art. I, Sec. 9) and required that slavery 'be recognized and protected' in all new territories (Art. IV) -- making it legally impossible for the Confederacy to end slavery itself. (Avalon Project, Yale Law School, Constitution of the Confederate States.)

question: In the Cornerstone Speech, Alexander Stephens directly took on the American founders. He admitted the framers had believed slavery 'was wrong in principle, socially, morally, and politically,' and that it rested on the idea 'of the equality of races.' Stephens quoted that founding belief out loud -- and then told his audience exactly what he thought of it. What was Stephens's verdict on the founders' view that slavery was wrong?
answer: That their ideas were 'fundamentally wrong' and rested on 'an error'
choices: That their ideas were 'fundamentally wrong' and rested on 'an error'
That their ideas were noble but impossible for any nation to live up to
That their ideas had been honored by the South better than by the North
That their ideas applied only to white men and never to any other race
context: Stephens broke openly with the founders: 'Those ideas, however, were fundamentally wrong. They rested upon the assumption of the equality of races. This was an error.' He was rejecting the equality principle on purpose, by name. (American Battlefield Trust, Cornerstone Speech.)

question: Alexander Stephens was so confident his claim about Black inferiority was true that he compared it to great scientific discoveries the world had once resisted but later accepted. He predicted his pro-slavery 'truth' would be vindicated just as the world eventually accepted Galileo and Adam Smith's economics -- and, third on his list, the breakthrough of a 17th-century English physician. Which scientist did Stephens name third, alongside Galileo and Adam Smith?
answer: William Harvey
choices: William Harvey
Isaac Newton
Charles Darwin
Louis Pasteur
context: Stephens: 'It was so with the principles announced by Galileo -- it was so with Adam Smith... It was so with Harvey, and his theory of the circulation of the blood.' He genuinely expected his racial 'truth' to be proven right by history. It was not. (American Battlefield Trust, Cornerstone Speech.)

question: After the Confederacy lost, Alexander Stephens tried to rewrite history. In an 1868 book he claimed the war had really been about constitutional questions, not slavery, and that newspaper reporters had simply misquoted his famous 1861 speech. But Stephens did one thing that quietly destroyed his own excuse. What did Stephens do that undercut his claim of being misquoted?
answer: He reprinted the speech in full in his own authorized biography
choices: He reprinted the speech in full in his own authorized biography
He repeated the same racial claims in a later public address
He kept private letters that praised the original speech
He paid the reporters who had first written it down
context: Stephens could not credibly cry 'misquote': he let the entire Cornerstone Speech be reprinted in his own authorized biography. The story that the war was 'really about states' rights' collapses against the secessionists' own published words. (Wikipedia, Cornerstone Speech.)

question: In Cervantes's novel, the aging knight Don Quixote rides across the plain of La Mancha, spots thirty or forty windmills standing in a row, and tells his squire Sancho Panza he means to charge and slay them. What does Don Quixote insist the windmills really are?
answer: Monstrous giants he must fight
choices: Monstrous giants he must fight
A castle of an evil king
A camp of enemy soldiers
A herd of wild bulls
context: Don Quixote calls them 'thirty or more monstrous giants' and charges with his lance lowered, while Sancho protests they are only windmills. Source: Don Quixote, Vol.1 Ch.8 (Ormsby trans.), en.wikisource.org/wiki/Don_Quixote_(Cervantes/Ormsby)/Volume_1/Chapter_8.

question: As Don Quixote prepares to charge the windmills he believes are giants, one companion stays loyally at his side, plainly warning him: 'what we see there are not giants but windmills.' What is the name of this down-to-earth squire?
answer: Sancho Panza
choices: Sancho Panza
Rocinante
Friston
Alonso Quijano
context: Sancho Panza is Don Quixote's earthy, sensible squire, who sees plain windmills where his master sees giants. (Rocinante is the horse; Friston the imagined enchanter; Alonso Quijano the knight's real name.) Source: Don Quixote, Vol.1 Ch.8 (Ormsby trans.), en.wikisource.org/wiki/Don_Quixote_(Cervantes/Ormsby)/Volume_1/Chapter_8.

question: Don Quixote is really a poor aging gentleman who has read so many books of chivalry that his wits dry up. Crowning himself for battle, he jams a barber's brass shaving-basin onto his head and insists it is a famous piece of armor. What does he call this shaving-basin?
answer: The helmet of Mambrino
choices: The helmet of Mambrino
The crown of La Mancha
The shield of Rocinante
The sword of Friston
context: His real name is Alonso Quijano; convinced he is a knight-errant, he treats a barber's brass basin as 'the helmet of Mambrino.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Quixote.

question: Don Quixote dedicates every brave deed to a beloved noble lady named Dulcinea del Toboso, whom he praises endlessly. Who is this 'lady' actually based on?
answer: A sturdy local farm girl he has barely spoken to
choices: A sturdy local farm girl he has barely spoken to
A queen he served as a young soldier
A princess he rescued from a castle
His late wife he still mourns
context: Dulcinea is a noble name Don Quixote invented for Aldonza Lorenzo, a robust farm girl; he never sees her as she really is. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Quixote.

question: When Don Quixote drives his lance into a turning windmill, the sail whirls round with such force that it shatters the lance and sweeps both horse and rider rolling across the plain. Knocked flat, Don Quixote refuses to admit he was wrong. How does he explain his defeat?
answer: An evil enchanter turned the giants into mills
choices: An evil enchanter turned the giants into mills
His horse Rocinante stumbled and threw him
The wind itself was a demon sent against him
He had been tricked by Sancho Panza
context: He blames 'that same sage Friston,' claiming the enchanter turned the giants into mills to rob him of glory. This scene gave English the phrase 'tilting at windmills' -- fighting imaginary enemies. Source: Don Quixote, Vol.1 Ch.8 (Ormsby trans.).

question: Before he wrote his great novel, Miguel de Cervantes was a soldier. At the sea Battle of Lepanto in 1571 he fought though burning with fever and took three gunshot wounds, one of which crippled his left hand for life. What proud nickname did this wound earn him?
answer: El manco de Lepanto -- the one-handed man of Lepanto
choices: El manco de Lepanto -- the one-handed man of Lepanto
El Cid -- the lord of the sea
The captain of La Mancha
The iron knight of Spain
context: Cervantes wore the maiming of his left hand at Lepanto (Oct 7, 1571) as a badge of honor, calling himself 'el manco de Lepanto.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes; britannica.com/biography/Miguel-de-Cervantes.

question: Sailing home from war in 1575, Miguel de Cervantes was captured by Barbary corsairs and enslaved in Algiers for five years. After one of his four failed escape plots, he was dragged before the viceroy Hassan Pasha and threatened with death. What did Cervantes do when he stood before the viceroy?
answer: Took all the blame on himself to shield the others
choices: Took all the blame on himself to shield the others
Betrayed the names of his fellow plotters
Begged on his knees for his own life
Offered the viceroy a secret ransom
context: Cervantes shouldered the entire blame to protect his fellow captives; his bold bearing won a reprieve, and he was finally ransomed in 1580. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes; excellence-in-literature.com/miguel-de-cervantes-biography/.

question: In January 1605, at about 57 years old -- poor, aging, and one-handed -- Miguel de Cervantes published the first part of Don Quixote, and it became an instant sensation. Why is this book given a landmark place in the history of literature?
answer: It is called the first modern novel
choices: It is called the first modern novel
It was the first book ever printed in Spanish
It was the first story written about a king
It was the first book read aloud in churches
context: Don Quixote's instant fame is why it is called the first modern novel; today it is among the most-translated books on earth, with over 500 million copies. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Quixote.

question: In 1614 a rival writer published a fake, unauthorized Part Two of Don Quixote under the false name 'Avellaneda,' stealing Cervantes's characters. How did Miguel de Cervantes respond to this insult?
answer: He finished his own genuine Part Two in 1615
choices: He finished his own genuine Part Two in 1615
He sued the impostor in the king's court
He abandoned the story in disgust
He paid the rival to stop printing it
context: The insult of Avellaneda's fake spurred Cervantes to complete his authentic Part Two in 1615. He died on April 22, 1616 -- the date tradition also links to Shakespeare's death, now marked as World Book Day. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes.

question: High on Fajada Butte in Chaco Canyon, three leaning stone slabs let a thin blade of sunlight fall onto a spiral carved into the rock. At about 11:15 in the morning on the summer solstice, that blade of light does one striking thing to the spiral. What does the 'Sun Dagger' do?
answer: It pierces straight through the center of the spiral
choices: It pierces straight through the center of the spiral
It traces the full outline of the spiral's curve
It splits into a ring of small bright dots
It slowly fades from the top of the spiral down
context: The Sun Dagger on Fajada Butte marks the summer solstice when a single dagger of light cuts the center of the carved spiral around 11:15 a.m.; at the winter solstice TWO daggers frame the spiral's outer edges, and the equinox gets its own mark. Artist Anna Sofaer spotted it in 1977 while recording rock art, and on a later visit watched the light split the spiral. Around 1989 visitor foot traffic shifted one slab and broke the alignment forever. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Dagger

question: At Pueblo Bonito in Chaco Canyon, scientists tested the residue inside tall cylinder-shaped jars and found theobromine, the chemical fingerprint of cacao. That single chemical proved the Chacoans were doing something no one expected of a desert people. What were they doing?
answer: Drinking chocolate carried over 1,200 miles from Mesoamerica
choices: Drinking chocolate carried over 1,200 miles from Mesoamerica
Brewing a bitter tea from a local desert shrub
Trading dried beans they grew in the canyon floor
Grinding seeds into a paint for the great-house walls
context: The cylinder jars from Pueblo Bonito tested positive for theobromine, the signature of cacao, meaning chocolate had traveled more than 1,200 miles up from Mesoamerica. The same long-distance trade brought scarlet macaws and copper bells from far to the south. Source: https://www.sciencenews.org/article/pueblo-traded-chocolate-big-time + https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pueblo_Bonito

question: The Frankish king Charlemagne received an astonishing gift from the far-off Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid: a living Asian elephant, fetched all the way from Baghdad and walked over the Alps to his court at Aachen. What was the elephant's name?
answer: Abul-Abbas
choices: Abul-Abbas
Olifant
Childeric
Durendal
context: The elephant Abul-Abbas was fetched by a Jewish envoy named Isaac, landed in Italy in October 801, wintered at Vercelli, and reached Aachen on 20 July 802. (Royal Frankish Annals 801-802; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abul-Abbas)

question: On Christmas Day in the year 800, in Old St. Peter's in Rome, Pope Leo III set a crown on the kneeling Charlemagne's head and the whole Roman crowd cheered three times -- the first time in over 300 years a man in the West had been hailed with this ancient Roman title. What title did they cry out for Charlemagne?
answer: Emperor of the Romans
choices: Emperor of the Romans
King of the Franks
Duke of Aachen
Consul of Gaul
context: The crowd shouted three times: 'To Charles, Augustus, crowned by God, great and pacifying emperor of the Romans, life and victory!' It was the first imperial coronation in the West in over 300 years. (Royal Frankish Annals c.801; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlemagne)

question: Charlemagne built his capital at Aachen for its natural hot springs and was such an expert swimmer, his biographer Einhard wrote, that nobody could surpass him. He loved company in the warm water so much that on some days a remarkable crowd bathed together with him at once. Roughly how many shared his bath?
answer: A hundred or more men
choices: A hundred or more men
Around a dozen friends
Just three or four guards
Only his two brothers
context: Einhard wrote that Charlemagne was so strong a swimmer that none could surpass him, and that 'a hundred or more persons sometimes bathed with him.' (Einhard, Life of Charlemagne ch.22; Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook)

question: Charlemagne launched the greatest revival of learning Europe had seen in centuries -- yet the mighty emperor himself, who had started far too late in life, never quite got the hang of it and met with poor success. His biographer Einhard reveals a touching secret habit he kept up at night under his pillow, trying to train his own clumsy hand. What was Charlemagne struggling so hard to learn to do?
answer: Form his letters and write
choices: Form his letters and write
Pray in proper Latin
Play the harp like David
Speak the Greek tongue
context: Einhard says Charlemagne kept 'tablets and blanks in bed under his pillow, that at leisure hours he might accustom his hand to form the letters; however... they met with ill success.' The near-illiterate king still drove a learning revival. (Life of Charlemagne ch.25; Fordham)

question: The road to Charlemagne's crown began with a savage assault on a pope. In April 799, a faction of enemies set upon Pope Leo III in the middle of a street procession in Rome and laid hands on him, meaning to leave him too maimed to ever serve as pope again. According to the chronicles, which two parts of Leo did the attackers go for?
answer: His tongue and his eyes
choices: His tongue and his eyes
His right hand and ear
His feet and his knees
His teeth and his nose
context: The attackers tried to cut out Leo's tongue and tear out his eyes; he survived the 25 April 799 attack, fled north to Charlemagne at Paderborn, and a year later crowned him emperor. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Leo_III; Britannica 'Saint Leo III')

question: In August 778, Basque warriors ambushed the rear of Charlemagne's army in a high pass of the Pyrenees and wiped it out, looting its baggage of Spanish gold. Among the dead Einhard names a governor of the Breton March whose name would later swell into the most famous knight's legend in French literature. Who was he?
answer: Roland
choices: Roland
Alcuin
Widukind
Eggihard
context: Einhard lists Eggihard the steward, Count Palatine Anselm, and 'Roland, Governor of the March of Brittany' among the fallen of 15 August 778. The small real defeat became one of history's most famous legends. (Life of Charlemagne ch.9; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Roncevaux_Pass)

question: Three centuries after the real ambush, the poets turned it into 'The Song of Roland,' the oldest great epic of French literature. In the tale a proud Roland refuses to sound the alarm for rescue until it is hopelessly too late, then winds his great war-horn so desperately hard that it bursts and his own temples split. By what name does the legend call Roland's famous ivory horn?
answer: The olifant
choices: The olifant
The Gjallarhorn
The Sackbut
The Buisine
context: In the 11th-century poem the few Basques become 400,000 Saracens; Roland blows the ivory olifant too late, then dies beside his friend Oliver after trying to shatter his sword Durendal on the rocks. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Roncevaux_Pass, Song of Roland section)  (Legend.)

question: Charlemagne brought the English scholar Alcuin of York to run his palace school, and out of that revival came a clean new handwriting. Renaissance printers later copied it, mistaking it for ancient Roman script -- which is why one everyday feature of the very words you are reading now descends straight from Charlemagne's scribes. Which feature of our writing did their new script give us?
answer: The lowercase letters
choices: The lowercase letters
The Roman numerals
The printing press
The exclamation mark
context: The script, Carolingian minuscule, introduced lowercase letters and spaces between words. Renaissance humanists revived it as 'roman' type, thinking it ancient. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolingian_minuscule; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcuin)

question: Around 793 Charlemagne reformed money across his empire on a single silver penny: 12 pennies to the shilling, 240 to the pound -- the pound-shilling-penny system written as L, s, d. In Britain this Carolingian money lasted an astonishing length of time before decimal currency finally replaced it. In what year did Britain abandon it at last?
context: The L/s/d system (the d standing for the Roman denarius) survived in Britain until decimalisation in 1971 -- almost 1,200 years after Charlemagne set it. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolingian_monetary_system)

question: Einhard wrote that Charlemagne stood 'seven times the length of his own foot,' and for a thousand years everyone assumed that was just flattery. Then in 2010 scientists got a chance to test the boast directly against one of his actual bones, kept in Aachen Cathedral, and calculated he really had towered over nearly everyone of his age. Which bone did they measure to prove the legend true?
answer: His shinbone
choices: His shinbone
His skull
His jawbone
His kneecap
context: Measuring his tibia (shinbone), a 2010 study put Charlemagne near 1.84 m -- taller than about 99% of men of his day. The flattering legend turned out literally true. (Ruhli, Blumich & Henneberg, Economics & Human Biology, 2010; Medievalists.net)

question: The darkest stain on Charlemagne's name came in 782 at Verden, where after a Saxon revolt destroyed a Frankish army he is reported to have had about 4,500 captured Saxons killed in a single day. He chose one particular method on purpose, because it was the old Roman penalty for traitors and oath-breakers. How were the Saxon captives put to death?
answer: Beheaded
choices: Beheaded
Burned alive
Hanged
Drowned
context: At Verden, where the Aller meets the Weser, about 4,500 Saxons were beheaded -- the Roman punishment for oath-breakers. It remains the darkest episode of his reign. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_of_Verden; Royal Frankish Annals 782)

question: Charlemagne's dynasty is called 'Carolingian' after an earlier Charles in the family -- the grandfather who in 732 turned back a Muslim army at the Battle of Tours and won a fearsome nickname. By what nickname is that grandfather, Charlemagne's forebear, remembered?
answer: Charles the Hammer
choices: Charles the Hammer
Charles the Bald
Charles the Fat
Charles the Simple
context: Charles Martel ('the Hammer') beat back a Muslim army at Tours in 732; his son Pepin the Short became the first Carolingian king in 751 by deposing the last Merovingian, Childeric III. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolingian_dynasty; Britannica 'Pippin III')

question: In 1927 a young American pilot, Charles Lindbergh, became the first person to fly alone and nonstop across the Atlantic Ocean, from New York all the way to Paris. He flew a small single-engine plane that he had given a famous name. What was his plane called?
answer: The Spirit of St. Louis
choices: The Spirit of St. Louis
The Pride of New York
The Atlantic Arrow
The Paris Comet
context: Lindbergh named the silver monoplane the Spirit of St. Louis after the city whose businessmen helped pay for it. He flew it from New York to Paris on May 20-21, 1927 -- the first solo nonstop crossing of the Atlantic. (Source: britannica.com/topic/Spirit-of-Saint-Louis)

question: Charles Lindbergh's plane, the Spirit of St. Louis, was packed with so much fuel that a gas tank sat right where a front window would normally go -- meaning the pilot had no windshield to look through and could not see straight ahead at all. To watch where he was flying, how did Lindbergh see forward?
answer: He peered through a small periscope on the plane's side
choices: He peered through a small periscope on the plane's side
He flew with his head out the side window the whole way
He steered only by watching his compass needle
He trusted a second pilot to call out the way
context: With a fuel tank filling the nose, the Spirit of St. Louis had no front windshield, so Lindbergh watched the way ahead through a small periscope mounted on the side -- or by banking the plane to peek out a side window. He flew the whole 3,600 miles alone, with no co-pilot. (Source: airandspace.si.edu/stories/editorial/stories-inside-spirit-st-louis)

question: At a time when England's royal court spoke French and the Church wrote its books in Latin, the poet Geoffrey Chaucer made a daring choice for his great collection of pilgrim stories, the Canterbury Tales: he wrote them in the plain spoken tongue of ordinary folk. That decision helped turn a humble language into a literary one. Which of these famous opening lines did Chaucer write to begin his Tales?
answer: Whan that Aprille with his shoures soote
choices: Whan that Aprille with his shoures soote
Nel mezzo del cammin di nostra vita
In principio erat verbum
En l'an de grace mil trois cent
