context: Chaucer wrote the Canterbury Tales in Middle English, the spoken language of ordinary people, while the court used French and the Church used Latin. Its opening line, 'Whan that Aprille with his shoures soote' (When April with its sweet showers), is one of the most famous beginnings in English and helped earn him the title 'Father of English literature.' The other lines are Dante's Italian, the Latin Vulgate, and courtly French. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Canterbury_Tales; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Prologue

question: Among Chaucer's Canterbury pilgrims rides the Pardoner, a smooth-talking swindler who preaches a fierce sermon that greed is the root of all evil -- then turns around and sells his listeners fake holy relics for money. To dupe the faithful, he carries a brass cross set with fake jewels and a pillowcase he swears is the Virgin Mary's veil. But his most brazen fake is a glass jar he passes off as containing the bones of a holy saint. What is actually inside that jar?
answer: the bones of a pig
choices: the bones of a pig
a splinter of the True Cross
a lock of an angel's hair
a vial of holy water
context: The Pardoner sells pig bones in a glass jar as saints' bones, along with a fake-jeweled brass cross and a pillowcase he calls Mary's veil -- all while preaching the Latin text 'Radix malorum est cupiditas' (greed is the root of all evil), the very sin he commits. Source: https://www.litcharts.com/lit/the-canterbury-tales/the-pardoner-s-tale and https://www.shmoop.com/study-guides/literature/pardoners-tale/analysis/relics-and-pardons

question: Deep inside the underground stone maze at Chavin de Huantar in the Peruvian highlands stands the Lanzon, a 15-foot granite shaft carved into a fanged man-jaguar god that pilgrims met face-to-face in pitch darkness. On that snarling god, what are the hair and eyebrows carved as?
answer: Coiled snakes
choices: Coiled snakes
Bird feathers
Curling flames
Twisting vines
context: The Lanzon's hair and eyebrows are carved as snakes, one hand pointing up and the other down, in a cramped cross-shaped chamber at the very heart of the temple labyrinth. Source: https://www.ancient-origins.net/ancient-places-americas/lanzon-0015725

question: At Chavin de Huantar, the polished granite Raimondi Stele shows a Staff God standing upright, gripping a staff in each hand. The carving hides a trick: when you turn the whole stone upside down, the god's tall headdress transforms. Into what?
answer: A stack of grinning fanged faces
choices: A stack of grinning fanged faces
A field of blooming flowers
A circle of dancing condors
A pair of crossed staffs
context: Flipped over, the Raimondi Stele's headdress becomes a stack of grinning fanged faces and the god's face becomes a smiling reptile. The 1.98 m stele packs in 10 sets of eyes, 11 mouths, and 50 snakes; Antonio Raimondi documented it in 1873. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raimondi_Stele

question: In British coal mines the very youngest children, some only five or six, were given the loneliest job of all. Each sat by itself in the pitch dark for up to twelve hours, doing one thing: pulling a rope to open and shut a wooden ventilation door every time a coal cart rumbled past. What were these small children called?
answer: Trappers
choices: Trappers
Sweepers
Stokers
Carters
context: Eight-year-old Sarah Gooder, a trapper in the Gawber pit, told the 1842 Royal Commission: 'I have to trap without a light and I'm scared.' The door she worked controlled the air flow that kept the mine from filling with deadly gas. (Ashley's Mines Commission, 1842; victorianweb.org/history/ashley.html)

question: Chimney sweeps in Britain used 'climbing boys' -- children as small as four, often orphans sold to a master sweep, sent up the narrow soot-choked flues to brush them clean. When a frightened boy froze partway up and would not climb higher, what did the master do to drive him on?
answer: Lit a fire of straw beneath his bare feet
choices: Lit a fire of straw beneath his bare feet
Rang a loud bell to startle him upward
Lowered a rope for him to grab and climb
Sent a second boy up to guide him out
context: Masters lit a fire or jabbed pins at the boy's feet to force him up. The flues could be only seven inches wide; elbows and knees were rubbed raw, and boys could get stuck and suffocate in the dark. (historic-uk.com, History of the Boy Chimney Sweep; daily.jstor.org/chimney-sweeps)

question: In the cotton and flax mills the smallest children worked as 'scavengers.' While the great spinning machines were still running at full speed, a scavenger had to do something most adults would never dare. What was a scavenger's job?
answer: Crawl beneath the running machines to sweep up loose cotton
choices: Crawl beneath the running machines to sweep up loose cotton
Carry heavy buckets of water up to the spinning floor
Stand at the great door and count the finished cloth
Climb the rafters to free threads snagged up high
context: One slip meant a crushed hand or worse. Older children worked as 'piecers,' leaning across the machine to retie snapped threads on their feet 12 to 14 hours a day. (courses.lumenlearning.com, Child Labor; Factory Acts)

question: In the coal fields of Pennsylvania, 'breaker boys' as young as eight sat hunched over chutes of coal thundering past, snatching out chunks of slate by hand all day long. The sharp coal sliced their fingers bloody -- yet the bosses forbade them to wear gloves. Why were gloves banned?
answer: So the boys could feel the rock by touch and pick faster
choices: So the boys could feel the rock by touch and pick faster
Because gloves were far too costly to buy in bulk
So the boys could not hide stolen coal inside them
Because the breaker rules demanded bare hands
context: Breaker boys breathed coal dust all day, and sulphuric acid washed off the wet coal burned and cracked their hands. A boy who slipped could be pulled into the gears. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breaker_boy; wynninghistory.com)

question: Older children in the coal mines worked as 'hurriers,' crawling on hands and knees to drag heavy coal carts called corves through tunnels too low to stand in. A chain pulled the cart along behind the child. To haul it, how was that chain fastened to the hurrier's body?
answer: It ran between the legs to a belt buckled round the waist
choices: It ran between the legs to a belt buckled round the waist
It was looped twice over both of the shoulders
It was gripped tightly in the teeth while crawling
It was tied around one ankle and dragged behind
context: Patience Kershaw, a 17-year-old hurrier near Halifax, said she pushed corves a mile and more underground, hauling eleven of them a day. (speakingwhilefemale.co, Patience Kershaw 1842; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_in_coal_mines)

question: Patience Kershaw, a 17-year-old who hauled coal carts deep under Halifax, was brought before the 1842 Commission with one strange mark on her body that the gentlemen could not stop staring at: a bald patch worn clean across the top of her head. How had years of work rubbed her scalp bare?
answer: From shoving the loaded carts forward with her head
choices: From shoving the loaded carts forward with her head
From a leather strap she wore tight over her hair
From baskets of coal balanced upon her crown
From the low rock ceiling scraping her as she crawled
context: 'The bald place upon my head is made by thrusting the corves,' she testified. Day after day she had pushed the loaded wagons forward with her skull. (speakingwhilefemale.co, Patience Kershaw; sniff.numachi.com, Testimony 1841)

question: Elizabeth Bentley first went to work in a Leeds flax mill at six years old. In the busy season, she told a committee of Parliament in 1832, she stood at the machines from five in the morning until nine at night. Out of that whole sixteen-hour day, how much time was she given to rest and eat?
answer: Forty minutes for all the day's meals
choices: Forty minutes for all the day's meals
Two full hours spread across the day
One long hour at the noon bell
A half-day of rest each Saturday
context: Asked if she was ever 'strapped' -- hit with a leather strap to keep her working -- Bentley answered, 'Yes, severely,' and said the girls were strapped as well as the boys. (history.hanover.edu, Sadler Committee 1832, Elizabeth Bentley testimony)

question: In 1838 at the Huskar Colliery near Silkstone in Yorkshire, twenty-six children drowned underground as they scrambled to escape up the mine drift. The water that killed them came from a single unexpected source. What had let the flood loose into the pit?
answer: A thunderstorm bursting on the surface above
choices: A thunderstorm bursting on the surface above
A pump that broke down during the night
An underground spring the diggers had struck
A canal wall that gave way nearby
context: Eleven girls aged 8 to 16 and fifteen boys aged 9 to 12 drowned when the storm water poured down the drift. The newly crowned Queen Victoria heard of it; an inquiry followed, and the disaster helped push Parliament toward the Mines Act. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mines_and_Collieries_Act_1842)

question: In 1830 a Yorkshire land steward named Richard Oastler fired off a furious letter to the Leeds Mercury. He pointed out that the very men cheering the end of slavery in the West Indies were ignoring the children worked to death in the mills of their own towns. What blistering name did Oastler give that child labor?
answer: 'Yorkshire Slavery'
choices: 'Yorkshire Slavery'
'The White Plague'
'The Mill Tax'
'Leeds Bondage'
context: The phrase lit the fuse of mill reform. Michael Sadler, a Leeds MP, then carried the Ten-Hour Bill and chaired the 1832 committee that gathered the children's testimony. (victorianweb.org/history/yorkslav.html; spartacus-educational.com/IRsadler.htm)

question: Earlier laws against child labor had failed because mill owners simply ignored them. So when Parliament passed the Factory Act of 1833 -- barring children under nine from the textile mills -- it added one thing no factory law had ever had before. What did the 1833 Act add that no earlier law had?
answer: Paid government inspectors sent into the mills
choices: Paid government inspectors sent into the mills
A printed notice nailed to every factory wall
A yearly oath sworn by each mill owner
A reward paid to children who reported abuse
context: The 1833 Act limited 9-to-13-year-olds to eight hours a day and, for the first time, sent salaried Factory Inspectors to enforce the rules -- because owners could not be trusted to obey on their own. (parliament.uk, Factory Act; britannica.com/event/Factory-Act-United-Kingdom-1833)

question: When the great 1842 report on the mines reached respectable Victorian drawing rooms, it caused an uproar far louder than its dry pages of testimony could explain. One feature of the report struck comfortable readers harder than any words and forced Parliament to act. What was it?
answer: Engravings of small children chained to coal carts
choices: Engravings of small children chained to coal carts
A grim county-by-county list of the pit dead
Signed letters of protest from the mine owners
A folding map of every working pit in Britain
context: The pictures of women and small children harnessed to wagons deep underground shocked the public into outrage. The Mines and Collieries Act followed that same year. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mines_and_Collieries_Act_1842, Children's Employment Commission illustrations)

question: The man who drove the 1842 Mines Act through Parliament was Lord Ashley -- later the Earl of Shaftesbury -- a devout Christian reformer in the same line as the anti-slavery champion William Wilberforce. He spent decades fighting the powerful mine and factory owners on behalf of ordinary working families. What nickname did the people give him?
answer: 'The Poor Man's Earl'
choices: 'The Poor Man's Earl'
'The Iron Lord'
'The Mill Baron'
'The People's Knight'
context: Shaftesbury took up the cause, he said, 'after meditation and prayer,' and acted at real political cost. His 1842 Act banned all women and girls from working underground and set a minimum age of ten for boys. (britannica.com, Shaftesbury; christianity.org.uk/article/lord-shaftesbury)

question: In 1775 the London surgeon Percivall Pott noticed that grown men who had been chimney climbing boys kept dying of the same rare cancer, which they called 'soot-wart.' Pott suspected the chimney soot was to blame and set out to prove it. What did Pott establish for the very first time?
answer: That a person's job could give them cancer
choices: That a person's job could give them cancer
That washing the skin could prevent the cancer
That soot was poisonous to breathe in
That the cancer ran in sweeps' families
context: Pott traced the soot-wart to the chimney soot ground into the boys' skin in childhood. His finding launched the science of occupational medicine and helped pass the first Chimney Sweepers Act of 1788, setting a minimum age of eight. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percivall_Pott; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimney_sweeps'_carcinoma)

question: Just outside Jerusalem lay the Valley of Hinnom, where the Bible says children were once burned in fire to the god Moloch. The place became such a byword for horror that its Hebrew name, Ge-Hinnom, was carried straight into Greek as a single word the New Testament then uses as its very image for hell. What is that word?
answer: Gehenna
choices: Gehenna
Tartarus
Hades
Sheol
context: Ge-Hinnom (Valley of Hinnom) became the Greek 'Gehenna' (Geenna), the word Jesus uses in the New Testament as an image for hell. The valley held the Tophet, the burning-ground where the rite was carried out. A real cursed place outside Jerusalem became the language's name for hell itself. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gehenna ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tophet

question: Hebrew scribes who wrote down the name of the god of child sacrifice did not spell it plainly. They started from melekh, 'king,' but punched in the vowels of a different word so the name itself would read as an insult to anyone who knew Hebrew. Which word's vowels did they graft on to twist 'king' into 'the shameful king'?
answer: boshet, meaning 'shame'
choices: boshet, meaning 'shame'
sheker, meaning 'lie'
tame, meaning 'unclean'
ra, meaning 'evil'
context: The name Moloch (Molech) is widely understood as melekh, 'king,' deliberately given the vowels of boshet, 'shame' — so the god's own name was rigged to read 'the shameful king.' The scribes built their verdict on the cult right into its spelling. Sources: jewishvirtuallibrary.org/the-cult-of-moloch ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tophet

question: The Aztecs farmed Lake Xochimilco on long strips of cropland the Spanish later nicknamed "floating gardens." But the nickname is wrong: a chinampa never floated. How did farmers actually build one?
answer: They packed layers of lake mud and rotting plants between staked reeds until solid ground rose above the water
choices: They packed layers of lake mud and rotting plants between staked reeds until solid ground rose above the water
They lashed hollow reed rafts together so the beds rode loose on the lake's surface
They quarried stone blocks and sank them to make islands that broke the waterline
They let mats of tangled waterweed drift until enough silt collected to plant on
context: Farmers staked out a rectangle of shallow lakebed, wove reeds and branches between the stakes, and piled in alternating layers of mud and decaying vegetation until the bed sat solid and rooted to the bottom. "Floating gardens" is a charming mistake. Sources: worldhistory.org/Chinampas/; anthrome.wordpress.com/2011/04/24/chinampa-raised-bed-hydrological-agriculture/

question: A chinampa was a long ribbon of soft mud built up out of a lake, and soft mud at the water's edge wants to wash away. Along every plot's edge the Aztec farmers planted one specific tree whose roots bound the soil and stopped it from eroding. Which tree held the islands together?
answer: The ahuejote willow, grown straight from the construction stakes
choices: The ahuejote willow, grown straight from the construction stakes
The Montezuma cypress, planted in rings around each plot
The mangrove, whose stilt roots gripped the lakebed
The mesquite, set deep to anchor the bank
context: The stakes farmers drove in to build the plot sprouted into ahuejote willows (Salix bonplandiana). Their roots bound the soil against erosion while their canopy shaded the crops and cut evaporation. The willows quite literally held the islands together. Sources: worldhistory.org/Chinampas/; hilo.hawaii.edu/nihopeku/2018/02/02/chinampa-an-ancient-agricultural-system/

question: The Chinese city of Jingdezhen — older name Changnan — made the world's finest porcelain for over a thousand years, and traders carried its wares to kings across the globe. On foreign tongues its name slowly wore down into a short everyday English word we still use. Which word did Changnan become?
answer: China
choices: China
Silk
Jade
Ivory
context: Porcelain was so bound up with the land that one word, 'china', came to mean both the country and any fine ceramic dish. The town was renamed Jingde in 1004 CE after the emperor's reign-name; he prized its ceramics as tribute. Source: MudandLeaves, 'Jingdezhen Porcelain and the name China'; WildChina, 'Jingdezhen: City of Porcelain'.

question: In a Chinese ink landscape — shan shui, meaning 'mountain-water' — the painter leaves large stretches of silk completely bare, no ink at all, and plans these blank gaps as carefully as the inked parts. Some things in the picture are drawn with the brush; others are left to the bare silk to suggest. Which three does the bare silk stand in for?
answer: The mist, the water, and the sky
choices: The mist, the water, and the sky
The cliffs, the pines, and the rocks
The bridges, the boats, and the huts
The herders, the mules, and the carts
context: The empty, unpainted silk IS the mist, the water, and the sky — painters 'paid as much attention to the unpainted areas of their compositions as they did to the detailed sections.' Song masters Ma Yuan ('One-Corner Ma') and Xia Gui ('One-Side Xia') pushed all the detail into one corner and left the rest as open mist. Source: Princeton University Art Museum, 'Chinese Landscape Painting during the Song Dynasty'; Shan shui, New World Encyclopedia.

question: Fan Kuan painted 'Travelers Among Mountains and Streams' around the year 1000, and he hid his own signature in it so well that no one noticed for centuries. Not until August 1958 did the scholar Li Lincan finally spot the two-character name in the lower-right of the silk, at Taipei's National Palace Museum. Where in the picture had Fan Kuan hidden his name?
answer: Among the leaves of a tree
choices: Among the leaves of a tree
Beneath the tiny travelers' feet
Inside a red seal in the corner
Along the bottom edge of the silk
context: Fan Kuan disguised his name among the leaves of a lower-right tree, made to look like a drooping branch, and it went unnoticed for roughly 900 years. In the same painting a single towering mountain fills nearly two-thirds of the picture, while a mule caravan led by two herders is so tiny you can barely find it. Source: China Online Museum / DailyArt Magazine, citing Li Lincan, National Palace Museum Taipei, August 1958.

question: A Chinese master grinds an ink stick with water, loads a soft brush, and paints a mountain on silk. Ink on silk works unlike a Western oil painting in one strict way. Of the four things below, which one can the painter simply NOT do to a brush stroke once it has landed?
answer: Erase a stroke once it's down
choices: Erase a stroke once it's down
Darken a stroke by retracing it
Nudge a stroke while it's still wet
Soften a stroke's edge with water
context: A brush stroke cannot be erased or painted over — the moment the brush touches the silk, the mark is permanent, so the painter must commit with full intention and no hesitation. The same brush, ink, and silk carry the 'Three Perfections' — poetry, calligraphy, and painting together; painting itself was called 'silent poetry'. Source: National Gallery of Victoria, 'Three Perfections: Poetry, Calligraphy and Painting'; ink-and-brush.com.

question: In 353 CE the calligrapher Wang Xizhi sat at a riverside drinking party, brush in hand, and dashed off the 'Orchid Pavilion Preface' while drunk — now honored as the most famous calligraphy ever written. In it, one common character appears 20 times. What did Wang Xizhi do with that one character every one of the 20 times it appears?
answer: Wrote it a different way all 20 times
choices: Wrote it a different way all 20 times
Wrote it bigger each of the 20 times
Left it out and drew a dot instead
Wrote all 20 copies in one breath
context: The character was 'zhi' (之), and Wang Xizhi formed it differently every single time. When he sobered up and tried to rewrite the preface, he could never recapture the same beauty; he is honored as the 'Sage of Calligraphy.' The party itself: 42 scholars along a winding stream, cups of wine floated down the water, and whoever the cup stopped before had to compose a poem or drink. Source: Lantingji Xu, Wikipedia.

question: For centuries Europe could not make true porcelain like China's, no matter how hard they tried. In 1712 a French Jesuit priest, Francois Xavier d'Entrecolles, quietly studied the great Jingdezhen kilns — helped by Catholic-convert workers there — and pulled off one of the earliest acts of industrial spying. What did d'Entrecolles send back to France?
answer: The secret recipe for porcelain
choices: The secret recipe for porcelain
The location of China's finest clay
The names of the kiln masters
The price charged for each vase
context: d'Entrecolles mailed China's closely-guarded porcelain method home to France — one of the earliest cases of industrial espionage. When his letters were published in 1716 they caused a sensation, and Europeans began hunting for kaolin clay of their own. Source: Atlas Obscura, 'One of the Earliest Industrial Spies Was a French Missionary'; Francois Xavier d'Entrecolles, Wikipedia.

question: For about a thousand years in China, parents broke their young daughters' arches and folded the toes under to force the foot down to a prized length of roughly four inches. A foot bound that small was considered the most beautiful feature a woman could have, and it had a poetic name. What were these tiniest, most prized bound feet called?
answer: The golden lotus
choices: The golden lotus
The silver lotus
The iron lotus
The jade lotus
context: The 'golden lotus' (jin lian) was a foot of no more than three Chinese inches, about 10 cm. A pair under four cun were merely 'silver lotuses,' and anything larger was dismissed as an 'iron lotus.' Girls' binding began as young as five, when the four small toes were curled under and pressed until the bones broke. Sources: worldhistory.org/Foot-Binding and chinahighlights.com/shanghai/article-discover-foot-binding.htm.

question: By the late 1800s nearly every upper-class Han Chinese woman had bound feet, and the practice had crippled women for a thousand years. In 1875 a group of about sixty Christian women in the city of Xiamen, led by the missionary John MacGowan, organized one of the first stands against it. They named their group for the kind of foot they were defending. What was their society called?
answer: The Natural Foot Society
choices: The Natural Foot Society
The Bound Daughters League
The Lotus Mercy Mission
The Golden Foot Sisterhood
context: They called it the 'Natural Foot' or 'Heavenly Foot' Society (Tianzu Hui) -- a name defending the unbroken, unbound foot. The Chinese reformer Kang Youwei later built on this: in the 1898 Hundred Days' Reform he sent the throne a memorial titled 'Plea to Forbid Female Foot Binding,' arguing the custom had to end for China to modernize. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavenly_Foot_Society and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foot_Emancipation_Society.

question: Around 105 AD a Chinese court official named Cai Lun cooked up a cheap new writing surface by mashing together a soggy pulp of tree bark, hemp scraps, old rags, and worn-out fishing nets. What everyday material did he just invent?
answer: Paper
choices: Paper
Ink
Silk cloth
Leather parchment
context: Cai Lun, a eunuch official of the Han court, reported his invention to the emperor and was praised for it. His pulp recipe was cheaper and better to write on than the silk and bamboo Chinese scribes had used before. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cai_Lun (Britannica: britannica.com/biography/Cai-Lun).

question: Before Cai Lun's paper, a single long Chinese book was so heavy and bulky that just storing one could mean hauling around roughly what?
answer: A whole wagon-load of bamboo slips
choices: A whole wagon-load of bamboo slips
A whole cart of carved stone tablets
A whole chest of heavy clay bricks
A whole crate of folded silk bolts
context: Chinese writing went on bamboo and wooden tablets that were heavy, bulky, and awkward to store — a single long book could fill a whole cart of bamboo slips. Cai Lun's paper replaced all of it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cai_Lun.

question: Taoist alchemists in China, while mixing saltpeter, sulfur, and charcoal in search of an elixir that would make them live forever, accidentally created an explosive black powder. To this day the Chinese name for it, 'huo yao,' translates literally as what?
answer: Fire medicine
choices: Fire medicine
Black sand
War dust
Dragon ash
context: Gunpowder was a happy accident of immortality-seeking alchemists. The Chinese name huo yao (火药) literally means 'fire medicine' and is still used today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gunpowder; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elixir_of_life.

question: The very first Chinese compass was the si nan, a spoon carved from lodestone — a naturally magnetic rock — that spun on a smooth bronze plate until it slowed and came to rest. Which single direction did the si nan always settle toward?
answer: Pointing south
choices: Pointing south
Pointing north
Pointing east
Pointing toward water
context: The si nan, or 'south-pointing spoon,' was carved from lodestone and spun on a bronze plate. By tradition Chinese compasses point south, not north like the ones we use today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_compass; ancient-origins.net.

question: The oldest dated, complete printed book in the world is a Buddhist text from 868 AD, printed from carved woodblocks onto seven sheets of paper glued into a scroll about 16 feet long with a picture of the Buddha at the front. By what name is this book known?
answer: The Diamond Sutra
choices: The Diamond Sutra
The Dream Pool Essays
The Lotus Scroll
The Book of Changes
context: The Diamond Sutra of 868 AD was printed roughly 600 years before Gutenberg's Bible. Its end note says a man named Wang Jie had it made 'for universal free distribution' to honor his two parents. Source: idp.bl.uk/blog/the-diamond-sutra (British Library); smithsonianmag.com.

question: Sometime between 1039 and 1048, a Song-dynasty commoner named Bi Sheng built the world's first movable type, so that books no longer had to be carved one whole page at a time. He cut each individual Chinese character, one at a time, into thin pieces of what material?
answer: Sticky clay
choices: Sticky clay
Carved jade
Cast bronze
Soft wax
context: Bi Sheng cut each character into sticky clay 'as thin as the edge of a coin,' then baked it hard in a fire — movable type centuries before Gutenberg. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bi_Sheng (Shen Kuo, Dream Pool Essays).

question: The oldest known picture of a gun in the world is Chinese: a painted silk Buddhist banner from around 950 AD, found at Dunhuang, shows a demon aiming a long tube fixed to a pole that shoots flames, while another demon hurls a bomb. What was this early Chinese fire weapon called?
answer: A fire lance
choices: A fire lance
A flame pike
A blaze spear
A dragon lance
context: The Chinese first used gunpowder in fire arrows and fire lances — a tube of powder lashed to a pole — not cannons. The Dunhuang banner (c. 950 AD) is the earliest surviving image of a gun. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gunpowder; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_lance.

question: For hundreds of years after Chinese craftsmen discovered that a lodestone compass settles along the Earth's magnetic force, they did not use it to find their way at all. What did they use it for instead?
answer: Feng shui and fortune-telling
choices: Feng shui and fortune-telling
Healing and medicine
Music and ceremony
Astronomy and stargazing
context: Only later did the compass go to sea. For centuries it lined up houses, graves, and fields with the Earth's magnetic force for feng shui and fortune-telling. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_compass; encyclopedia.com.

question: Cai Lun, the inventor of paper, got tangled in a deadly palace plot and in 121 AD a new emperor ordered him to report to prison to stand trial. Rather than face it, what did Cai Lun do?
answer: He put on his finest robes and drank poison
choices: He put on his finest robes and drank poison
He fled north in disguise and vanished for good
He confessed and begged the emperor for a pardon
He burned his workshop down and turned himself in
context: Cai Lun had passed along a slander that helped cause the death of a consort, the emperor's grandmother. Ordered to prison in 121 AD, he bathed, dressed in his finest formal robes, and chose a dignified death over trial. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cai_Lun (Hou Hanshu).

question: The Diamond Sutra, the world's oldest dated printed book, survived because it spent roughly 900 years sealed inside a hidden cave near Dunhuang, walled up with tens of thousands of other manuscripts. How did this huge trove come to light again around 1900?
answer: By chance, when a monk was clearing drifted sand
choices: By chance, when a monk was clearing drifted sand
By an emperor's officials on a grand treasure hunt
By a farmer breaking in to dig a well
By archaeologists who had searched for it for years
context: The Mogao caves near Dunhuang had been walled up for centuries. Around 1900 the Daoist caretaker-monk Wang Yuanlu uncovered the sealed Library Cave by chance while clearing drifted sand; the explorer Aurel Stein later carried off much of the hoard. Source: idp.bl.uk/blog/the-diamond-sutra; openculture.com.

question: In 1088 the Song-dynasty polymath Shen Kuo described a compass needle magnetized by rubbing iron on a lodestone, and noticed it did not point at true south but sat a little to one side. Shen Kuo was the first person on record to measure this gap between magnetic and true direction. What is that gap called today?
answer: Magnetic declination
choices: Magnetic declination
Magnetic saturation
Polar inversion
Lodestone drift
context: Shen Kuo's note is the first recorded discovery of magnetic declination — the angle between where a compass points and true geographic direction. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_compass (Shen Kuo, Dream Pool Essays).

question: China invented movable type with Bi Sheng's clay characters, yet for centuries Chinese printers kept carving each page as a single solid woodblock instead, and movable type never caught on there. Why was movable type so impractical in China in particular?
answer: Written Chinese needs thousands of separate characters
choices: Written Chinese needs thousands of separate characters
The emperor had banned all clay type
Carved woodblocks outlasted fragile clay type
Woodblocks alone could print in color
context: Cutting a full set of type for thousands of characters cost far more than carving one page as a single block, so woodblock printing stayed dominant. Centuries later the same idea met Europe's roughly 26-letter alphabet and exploded. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bi_Sheng; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_printing_in_East_Asia.

question: On 1 October 1949, Mao Zedong stood atop the Gate of Heavenly Peace in Beijing and announced the new People's Republic of China. As cannon fired a 21-gun salute, a brand-new national flag rose for the first time over the square. What did that red flag carry in its corner?
answer: Five gold stars
choices: Five gold stars
A gold hammer and sickle
A coiled gold dragon
A rising gold sun
context: The five-starred red flag was hoisted for the first time during Mao's proclamation on 1 October 1949, to a 21-gun salute. The one big star with four smaller ones is still China's flag today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China

question: When the Communists won China's civil war in 1949, the Nationalist leader Chiang Kai-shek did not surrender. He loaded ships with roughly two million refugees and most of the country's gold reserves and fled across the sea. Which island did Chiang make his last stronghold?
answer: Taiwan
choices: Taiwan
Hainan
Hong Kong
Okinawa
context: Chiang Kai-shek and the Nationalists fled across the strait to Taiwan with about two million refugees and most of China's gold, which became the backing for the New Taiwan dollar. Source: https://factsanddetails.com/southeast-asia/Taiwan/sub5_1a/entry-3800.html

question: In Mao Zedong's 'Four Pests' campaign, peasants across China were ordered to wipe out sparrows. People banged pots and drums for hours so the terrified birds could never land, until the sparrows dropped dead from exhaustion. With the sparrows gone, what swarmed in and made the coming famine even worse?
answer: Locusts and insects
choices: Locusts and insects
Rats and mice
Crows and vultures
Wild dogs
context: Mao's 'Four Pests' campaign destroyed the sparrows that ate crop-eating bugs; with no predator, locusts and insects exploded and devoured the crops. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Leap_Forward

question: To hit Mao Zedong's impossible steel targets during the Great Leap Forward, ordinary peasants built backyard furnaces and threw in their own pots, pans, and farm tools to be melted down. They even burned the doors and furniture off their houses to feed the fires. What did those backyard furnaces yield?
answer: Brittle pig iron that snapped
choices: Brittle pig iron that snapped
Slag too soft to forge
Cracked iron that rusted fast
Fine tempered steel
context: The backyard furnaces yielded brittle, useless pig iron that snapped under pressure, while the farm tools melted to make it were now gone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backyard_furnace

question: On the night of 1 December 1948, with the Communists closing in, Chiang Kai-shek's men quietly emptied the Bank of China's vaults in Shanghai. A British journalist watching from a hotel saw a line of figures filing through the dark across the waterfront. What did he see those men carrying the gold on?
answer: Long poles slung over their shoulders
choices: Long poles slung over their shoulders
Armored bank trucks
Steel handcarts
Mule-drawn wagons
context: The reporter described 'men with long poles carrying heavy boxes' filing across Shanghai's Bund waterfront to a customs vessel. The first shipment was about 2 million of the 4.6 million taels in the treasury. Source: https://www.scmp.com/article/716329/how-chiang-spirited-chinas-gold-away-reds

question: The Long March of 1934-35 is the retreat that made Mao Zedong a legend. About 86,000 Communist troops set out from Jiangxi in the southeast, trudging some 6,000 miles over snow-capped mountains to reach Shaanxi in the far northwest a year later. Of those 86,000 who started, roughly how many survived to the end?
answer: A few thousand
choices: A few thousand
About sixty thousand
About forty thousand
Almost all of them
context: Of roughly 86,000 troops who set out, only about 4,000-8,000 reached Shaanxi after 368 days, 24 rivers, and 18 mountain ranges. Source: https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/october-20/maos-long-march-concludes

question: Every Chinese schoolchild learns the slogan 'The Chinese people have stood up,' and everyone pictures Mao Zedong roaring it from the gate on 1 October 1949. But the famous proclamation speech contains no such line. Where did those words actually come from?
answer: A different speech ten days earlier
choices: A different speech ten days earlier
A poster pasted up after the parade
A song the crowd sang that night
A letter Mao wrote from prison
context: 'The Chinese people have stood up' was the title of a speech Mao gave on 21 September 1949 to the Political Consultative Conference, not part of the October 1 proclamation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China

question: The largest battle of the Chinese Civil War, the Huaihai Campaign of 1948-49, destroyed roughly 550,000 American-equipped Nationalist troops around Xuzhou. The Communists faced that mechanized army with almost no motor transport, yet over two million ordinary people kept their soldiers fed and armed all the way to the front. Who hauled those supplies?
answer: Peasants pushing wheelbarrows
choices: Peasants pushing wheelbarrows
Mule and camel caravans
River junks poled upstream
Lines of conscripted porters
context: Over 2 million peasants pushing wooden wheelbarrows hauled supplies to the Huaihai front, a peasant supply line that helped crush an American-equipped mechanized army. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huaihai_campaign

question: The most heroic tale of the Long March is the Battle of Luding Bridge in 1935. According to the journalist Edgar Snow, the wooden planks of the bridge over the boiling Dadu River had been ripped out, leaving a deadly gap 50 feet above the water. Snow wrote that a handful of Communist commandos still seized the far side under machine-gun fire. How did they get across?
answer: Swung hand-over-hand along the iron chains
choices: Swung hand-over-hand along the iron chains
Swam the icy river at night
Floated across on bamboo rafts
Built a new rope bridge under fire
context: Edgar Snow wrote that 22 commandos swung hand-over-hand across the bare chains under machine-gun fire and burning planks; he called it 'the most crucial single incident of the Long March.' This is the legendary telling, not settled fact. Source: https://thechinaproject.com/2023/05/31/what-really-happened-at-the-battle-of-luding-bridge/

question: Mao Zedong's Great Leap Forward set off the deadliest famine in human history, killing tens of millions between 1958 and 1962. The most damning detail in the records is not that the harvest failed. While villagers starved and some were driven to eat the dead, what was the Chinese state still doing with its grain?
answer: Exporting it abroad for foreign aid
choices: Exporting it abroad for foreign aid
Burning spoiled stockpiles to hide them
Feeding it to army livestock
Dumping it to keep prices high
context: In 1960 China shipped grain to Albania, Cuba, Vietnam, Indonesia and Poland for hard currency while granaries stayed locked to the hungry. Yang Jisheng documented government records of cannibalism, including 63 cases in Fengyang County alone. Death estimates run from Yang's ~36 million to Frank Dikotter's ~45 million. Source: https://factsanddetails.com/china/cat2/sub6/item2854.html

question: In 1966 Mao Zedong launched the Cultural Revolution and turned millions of teenagers loose as 'Red Guards'; by that November some 11 million had flooded into Beijing waving a little book of his quotations. They dragged teachers and officials onto stages to be beaten and humiliated before screaming crowds. What were these public denunciations called?
answer: Struggle sessions
choices: Struggle sessions
People's tribunals
Self-criticism circles
Reform assemblies
context: Red Guards waving the 'Little Red Book' dragged victims before 'struggle sessions' of public denunciation; the Cultural Revolution killed an estimated 500,000 to 2 million people before Mao died in 1976. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution

question: For decades the Battle of Luding Bridge was Communist China's proudest war story. Then Deng Xiaoping himself told the American adviser Zbigniew Brzezinski that the famous crossing had really been 'a very easy military operation' -- just how the propaganda presents it. According to Deng, the warlord soldiers guarding the far bank were armed with what?
answer: Old muskets
choices: Old muskets
Rusty bolt-action rifles
Belt-fed machine guns
Bamboo spears and swords
context: Deng Xiaoping told Brzezinski the defenders were warlord troops 'armed with old muskets' and that the heroic crossing was 'a very easy military operation' -- 'that is how our propaganda presents it.' Jung Chang and Jon Halliday wrote 'there was no battle at the Dadu Bridge,' citing a witness and Nationalist plans showing the guards had already withdrawn. Source: https://thechinaproject.com/2023/05/31/what-really-happened-at-the-battle-of-luding-bridge/

question: In 2005 the historians Jung Chang and Jon Halliday published 'Mao: The Unknown Story,' a biography of the man who ruled a quarter of the world's people. Its very first sentence makes a staggering charge about Mao Zedong: that in peacetime he was responsible for more deaths than any other leader of the twentieth century. What toll did that opening line put on him?
answer: Well over 70 million
choices: Well over 70 million
About 5 million
Around 20 million
Nearly 200 million
context: Chang and Halliday's opening line states Mao was 'responsible for well over 70 million deaths in peacetime, more than any other twentieth-century leader.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao:_The_Unknown_Story

question: Sophie Scholl, a 21-year-old student at the University of Munich, slipped into the empty main hall one morning in February 1943 with her brother Hans and a case of forbidden anti-Nazi leaflets. With one last batch left over and students about to pour out of the lecture rooms, what did Sophie do with them?
answer: Pushed the stack off the top-floor railing onto the students below
choices: Pushed the stack off the top-floor railing onto the students below
Handed them out at the main doors as the students left
Pinned them one by one on the campus boards
Stacked them on the benches by the lecture halls
context: She sent them fluttering down into the atrium. A custodian, Jakob Schmid, saw her do it, locked the doors, and held her and Hans until the Gestapo came. The White Rose leaflets had declared, 'We will not be silent. We are your bad conscience,' and one had named the crime outright: 'three hundred thousand Jews have been murdered in this country in the most bestial way... a crime against human dignity.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakob_Schmid ; encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/white-rose

question: Sophie Scholl, just 21, was to be beheaded that same morning. Looking up at the sky, she spoke a few quiet words that have been remembered ever since. What did Sophie say?
answer: The sun is still shining.
choices: The sun is still shining.
The sky has never looked clearer.
Let them see I was not afraid.
I would do it all again.
context: 'Die Sonne scheint noch.' She added, 'What does my death matter, if through us thousands of people are awakened and stirred to action?' She, Hans, and Christoph Probst were tried before the screaming Nazi judge Roland Freisler and guillotined the same day, 22 February 1943. Sources: theepochtimes.com/bright/the-suns-still-shining-the-courage-of-sophie-scholl-3665966 ; en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Sophie_Scholl

question: Hans Scholl was made to watch his sister Sophie beheaded, then was laid under the same guillotine moments later. In his last second he shouted something so loudly it rang through the whole prison. What did Hans cry out?
answer: Long live freedom!
choices: Long live freedom!
God will judge you all!
You cannot kill the truth!
Remember our names!
context: 'Es lebe die Freiheit!' Hans and Sophie were medical and philosophy students who, with their friends, had written and mailed six secret leaflets to cities from Hamburg to Vienna. Sources: womenshistorynetwork.org/sophie-scholl ; executedtoday.com/2009/02/22/1943-sophie-scholl-of-the-white-rose

question: Christoph Probst, a 23-year-old medical student, was condemned to die beside Hans and Sophie Scholl. He was married with three small children and had never been christened. In the minutes before he was led to the guillotine, a Catholic priest came to his cell. What did Probst receive there?
answer: Baptism into the church and his first communion
choices: Baptism into the church and his first communion
A blessing and absolution for his sins
A psalm read over him and a wooden cross
The last rites and prayers for the dying
context: Probst had no church baptism, but at the threshold of death he asked for it, and the priest baptized him and gave him communion minutes before he was beheaded. Sources: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Christoph_Probst ; aleteia.org/2018/12/07/this-friend-of-sophie-scholl-became-catholic-moments-before-his-martyrdom

question: Dietrich Bonhoeffer was a Lutheran pastor who had once leaned close to pacifism, believing a Christian should not kill. Yet as Hitler's crimes grew, Bonhoeffer decided his faith now compelled him to act, and he joined a secret group plotting one specific deed. What had this pastor signed on to do?
answer: Assassinate Adolf Hitler
choices: Assassinate Adolf Hitler
Kidnap Heinrich Himmler
Blow up the Reichstag building
Smuggle weapons to the Allies
context: Bonhoeffer used a job in the Abwehr (military intelligence) as cover; under the code name 'Operation 7' he had already helped smuggle a group of Jews into Switzerland. After the failed 20 July 1944 bomb plot was traced to his circle, Hitler personally ordered the conspirators killed. The SS hanged Bonhoeffer at Flossenburg on 9 April 1945, just two weeks before US troops liberated the camp. Sources: history.com/this-day-in-history/april-9/defiant-theologian-dietrich-bonhoeffer-is-hanged ; gedenkstaette-flossenbuerg.de/en/history/prisoners/dietrich-bonhoeffer

question: Dietrich Bonhoeffer, in a famous 1937 book, attacked what he called 'cheap grace' - forgiveness offered with no repentance and no cross, religion made easy. Against it he set a demanding opposite, the grace that claims a person's whole life. What did Bonhoeffer name that opposite?
answer: Costly grace
choices: Costly grace
Saving grace
Hard grace
Pure grace
context: In 'The Cost of Discipleship,' Bonhoeffer wrote that costly grace is the grace that costs a person their life, the call to follow no matter the price. His own death under Hitler became the test of those words. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cost_of_Discipleship ; thegospelcoalition.org/article/great-books-friday-bonhoeffer-cost-of-discipleship

question: In July AD 64 a great fire burned much of Rome for days. Rumors spread that the emperor Nero himself had started it to clear land for a grand new palace. To turn the crowd's anger away from himself, what did Nero do?
answer: He blamed the city's Christians and had them killed
choices: He blamed the city's Christians and had them killed
He blamed the Senate and had them exiled
He blamed the Jewish priests and closed their temple
He blamed foreign sailors and banned them from the port
context: The Roman historian Tacitus (Annals 15.44) is the sole source linking the fire directly to this first persecution; Nero wanted the land for his Domus Aurea, his 'Golden House.' Source: https://brians.wsu.edu/2016/11/14/tacitus-neros-persecution-of-the-christians/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_Rome

question: In the dangerous early years when openly showing a cross could get you arrested, Roman Christians scratched a secret sign to recognize one another. The Greek word for it spelled out a hidden phrase: 'Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior.' What simple creature was this secret sign?
answer: A fish
choices: A fish
A lion
An eagle
A serpent
context: The Greek word ICHTHYS ('fish') worked as an acrostic for the phrase; Christians also carved an anchor as a disguised cross. Both appear on tombs in the Catacomb of Callixtus from the early 2nd century. Source: https://www.ewtn.com/catholicism/library/symbolism-of-the-fish-10733 ; https://www.catacombesancallisto.it/en/simboli-cristiani.php

question: Beneath Rome lies a maze of Christian tunnels — more than fifty sites and roughly 150 km of passages, some four levels deep. People often imagine Christians dug them as secret hideouts from persecution, but historians say that's mostly a myth; their locations were well known. So why did Christians really dig these tunnels?
answer: To bury their dead, because they believed the body would rise again
choices: To bury their dead, because they believed the body would rise again
To stay hidden from Roman soldiers during the persecutions
To hold secret church services away from the emperor's spies
To store the church's gold where thieves could not reach it
context: Believing in bodily resurrection, Christians buried their dead rather than cremating them like most Romans. The tunnels were dug and sold by gravediggers called fossors; bodies were slid into wall shelves called loculi. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catacombs_of_Rome ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catacomb_of_Callixtus

question: Ignatius, the bishop of Antioch, was condemned to be torn apart by wild beasts in Rome's arena (around AD 107). The Christians there had the connections to try to save his life, and he knew it. So he wrote ahead to them — but not to ask for rescue. What did Ignatius beg them to do?
answer: To let him be ground by the beasts like wheat into the pure bread of Christ
choices: To let him be ground by the beasts like wheat into the pure bread of Christ
To care for the poor of Antioch once he was gone
To send word of his death to every church in the East
To bury his bones in the catacombs beside the other martyrs
context: His exact words to the Roman Christians: 'I am the wheat of God, and let me be ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, that I may be found the pure bread of Christ' (Epistle to the Romans 4). Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Saint-Ignatius-of-Antioch ; https://www.franciscanmedia.org/saint-of-the-day/saint-ignatius-of-antioch/

question: Polycarp, the aged bishop of Smyrna, was hauled before a Roman proconsul (around AD 155) and offered his life if he would swear by Caesar and curse Christ. Polycarp refused with a single sentence, pointing to how long he had followed his King. What did the old man say?
answer: Eighty and six years I have served Him, and He has done me no wrong
choices: Eighty and six years I have served Him, and He has done me no wrong
I was born a Christian and a Christian I will die
Caesar rules my body, but my soul belongs to another
Do your worst, for tomorrow I dine in heaven
context: He added, 'How then can I blaspheme my King and my Saviour?' The 'Martyrdom of Polycarp' is the earliest detailed account of a Christian martyrdom outside the New Testament. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polycarp ; https://www.earlychristianwritings.com/text/martyrdompolycarp-roberts.html

question: Vibia Perpetua was a young noblewoman of about 22, still nursing her baby, when she was jailed at Carthage in AD 203. In prison she kept a diary in her own voice — one of the earliest surviving writings by a Christian woman. In it she described a striking dream of how she would reach heaven. What did she write that she saw?
answer: A ladder hung with swords, guarded by a serpent at its foot
choices: A ladder hung with swords, guarded by a serpent at its foot
A river of fire that her enemies could not cross
A white horse waiting to carry her over the city walls
A golden door that opened only when she spoke her name
context: Perpetua's prison diary records several visions before her death; she climbed the bladed ladder past the serpent in the dream. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Passion_of_Saints_Perpetua_and_Felicity ; https://www.britannica.com/biography/Perpetua-Christian-martyr

question: Perpetua's pregnant slave, Felicity, was condemned to die alongside her mistress in the Carthage arena. Yet as the day approached, Felicity grew afraid — not of dying, but that she would be left BEHIND and miss it. What stood between Felicity and the martyrdom she wanted?
answer: Roman law forbade executing a pregnant woman
choices: Roman law forbade executing a pregnant woman
Her owner could pay a fine to free her at the last moment
Slaves were sold off rather than sent to the arena
The governor had pardoned all the women in her cell
context: Felicity gave birth to a daughter in prison just days before the games, and so was allowed to die alongside Perpetua. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Passion_of_Saints_Perpetua_and_Felicity ; https://orthodoxwiki.org/Perpetua_and_Felicitas

question: In the Carthage arena a young, nervous gladiator was sent to finish Perpetua with his sword. His first stroke missed the mark, striking bone, and only made her cry out in pain. What did Perpetua, badly wounded, do next?
answer: She took his shaking hand and guided the blade to her own throat
choices: She took his shaking hand and guided the blade to her own throat
She knelt and prayed aloud until he found the courage to strike
She forgave him before the crowd and asked that he be spared
She seized his sword and turned it against the watching guards
context: Her last words to the watching catechumens were: 'Stand fast in the faith, and love one another, and be not offended at my sufferings.' She and Felicity had first risen to give each other the kiss of peace. Source: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0324.htm (Passion of Perpetua, ch. 21)

question: Lawrence, a deacon of Rome, was martyred in AD 258. Ordered to hand over the church's wealth, he had instead gathered the city's poor and called THEM the treasures of the Church. Tradition says he was then roasted alive on an iron gridiron — and that even there he managed a grim joke. What is he said to have told his executioners?
answer: Turn me over; I am done on this side
choices: Turn me over; I am done on this side
Your fire is cold next to the love of God
I thank you for the warmth on this cold night
Caesar's gold burns hotter than these coals
context: LEGEND: ancient accounts disagree on the details of Lawrence's death, so the gridiron quip is traditional rather than firmly attested fact. His line that the poor were 'the treasures of the Church' is the better-documented part of the story. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Saint-Lawrence ; https://missions.ewtn.com/seasonsandfeastdays/stlawrence/

question: Writing in North Africa around AD 197, the Christian author Tertullian argued that Rome's executions were backfiring: every believer killed in the arena only won the faith MORE converts. He summed up this idea in one famous line that is still quoted today. What did Tertullian write?
answer: The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church
choices: The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church
Rome may kill the body but never the truth
Each death in the arena lights a hundred candles
What the sword cuts down, faith grows back twofold
context: From Tertullian's Apologeticus; the literal Latin reads 'semen est sanguis Christianorum' — 'the blood of Christians is seed.' Tertullian was also an early source of the dramatic lions imagery. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apologeticus ; https://earlychurchtexts.com/public/tertullian_blood_christians_seed.htm

question: Everyone 'knows' the image of Christians thrown to the lions in the Colosseum. But modern historians point out that 'condemnation to the beasts' was a punishment used on all kinds of criminals, rarely lions in particular — Perpetua's group at Carthage faced a boar, a bear, a leopard, and a wild cow. What do these historians say specifically about the Colosseum in Rome?
answer: There is no solid evidence any Christian was martyred there
choices: There is no solid evidence any Christian was martyred there
Only nobles, not commoners, were sent to die there
It was reserved for gladiators and never used for executions
The lions there were too valuable to risk on prisoners
context: 'Damnatio ad bestias' was used on many criminals, not just Christians, and rarely specified lions; despite the long tradition, there is no firm evidence of a Christian martyrdom in the Colosseum specifically. Source: https://www.badancient.com/claims/lions-christians/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damnatio_ad_bestias

question: The fiercest crackdown of all began on 23 February AD 303 under the emperor Diocletian — the last great persecution. Rather than starting with arrests, the authorities opened it with a public act of destruction at the brand-new Christian church in Nicomedia. What did they do first?
answer: They razed the church and burned the Christians' scriptures
choices: They razed the church and burned the Christians' scriptures
They marched every bishop of the East off to the mines
They crucified the clergy along the road into the city
They melted down the empire's coins bearing Christian signs
context: The Diocletianic or 'Great Persecution' opened with razing the Nicomedia church, burning scriptures, and seizing church treasures; later edicts ordered everyone in the empire to sacrifice to the Roman gods. It ended in stages — Galerius's Edict of Toleration (311) and the Edict of Milan (313). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocletianic_Persecution ; https://www.historytoday.com/archive/months-past/diocletians-great-persecution

question: In 43 BC Mark Antony's soldiers hunted down Cicero, Rome's greatest orator, to silence the 14 blistering speeches (the Philippics) he had hurled at Antony. They cut off his head — but Antony wanted to punish the very part of Cicero that had written those speeches. What else did the killers sever and nail beside his head on the Rostra, the speaker's platform in the Forum?
answer: His hands
choices: His hands
His feet
His ears
His eyes
context: Antony ordered Cicero's hands cut off along with his head — the hands that wrote the Philippics — and both were nailed to the Rostra, the very platform where Cicero had given his greatest speeches. Plutarch, Life of Cicero 48; Ancient World Magazine, 'Resigned to fate: the death of Cicero.'

question: After Cicero's severed head was brought to Mark Antony, Antony's wife Fulvia is said to have taken it onto her lap and pulled the pins from her hair — bent on revenge against the orator whose words had savaged her husband. According to Cassius Dio, what did Fulvia then stab with those hairpins?
answer: Cicero's tongue
choices: Cicero's tongue
Cicero's eyes
Cicero's nose
Cicero's lips
context: Legend recorded by Cassius Dio: Fulvia jabbed her hairpins into the dead orator's tongue — final revenge for the speeches it had spoken against Antony. Marked as legend (ancient testimony, not forensic fact). Imperium Romanum, 'Death of Cicero.'

question: In 458 BC a Roman army was trapped by the Aequi tribe in the hills southeast of Rome. The Senate decided that only a dictator could save the city, and sent messengers to bring back a man named Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus. Where did they find him?
answer: Plowing a field on his small farm
choices: Plowing a field on his small farm
Lounging at his villa by the sea
Speaking on the floor of the Senate
Drilling soldiers out on the frontier
context: Cincinnatus was working a tiny plot of about four iugera (a few acres) across the Tiber, called the Quintian Meadows. Livy says the messengers found him 'either pushing upon a stake in a ditch, or busy plowing,' and asked him to put on his toga so they could deliver the Senate's command. Source: Livy, History of Rome 3.26 (elfinspell.com/PrimarySourceCincinnatus.html); worldhistory.org/Cincinnatus.

question: When the Aequi trapped a Roman army in 458 BC, the Senate made the farmer Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus dictator of Rome, handing him absolute command for a term of six months. He raised an army, marched through the night, surrounded the enemy and won. How long did he keep that power before laying it down and walking back to his plow?
answer: About sixteen days
choices: About sixteen days
About four months
The full six months
A little over a year
context: Livy says Cincinnatus 'laid down his dictatorship on the sixteenth day, although he had received it for six months' (some retellings say fifteen). Handed absolute power to save Rome, he beat the Aequi, made their whole army stoop one by one 'under the yoke' of three spears, then gave the power straight back and returned to farming. Source: Livy 3.27-3.29 (elfinspell.com/PrimarySourceCincinnatus.html); worldhistory.org/Cincinnatus.

question: George Washington was nicknamed 'the American Cincinnatus' for doing what the old Roman did: in 1783 he resigned command of the army and went home to his farm instead of seizing power. During the war the painter Benjamin West had told King George III that Washington meant to give up power and go back to farming if he won. What did the King reply?
answer: If he does that, he will be the greatest man in the world
choices: If he does that, he will be the greatest man in the world
Then America will have found itself a king instead
No man alive gives up such power willingly
I shall believe that on the day I see it
context: Washington did exactly that on December 23, 1783, surrendering his commission as commander-in-chief at the Maryland State House in Annapolis and riding home to Mount Vernon. His officers named the Society of the Cincinnati after the same Roman, with Washington as its first president general; the city of Cincinnati, Ohio was renamed for the Society in 1790. Source: americanrevolutioninstitute.org/the-american-cincinnatus; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington's_resignation_as_commander-in-chief.

question: In 48 BC the 21-year-old Cleopatra was locked out of her own palace in Alexandria by her brother's soldiers, but she was desperate to meet the Roman general Julius Caesar inside. With a loyal servant's help, how did she get past the guards and reach Caesar?
answer: Rolled up and carried in past the guards inside a bed-sack
choices: Rolled up and carried in past the guards inside a bed-sack
Disguised herself in the armor of a Roman soldier
Was lowered over the palace wall on a rope at night
Bribed the guards with a chest of Egyptian gold
context: Plutarch says her servant Apollodorus smuggled her in rolled inside a bed-sack (often retold as a carpet); she tumbled out at Caesar's feet, and her sheer audacity won him over — they became allies and lovers. Source: Plutarch, Life of Caesar 49; History.com, '10 Little-Known Facts About Cleopatra.'

question: Everyone pictures Cleopatra as an Egyptian queen, but her family were outsiders who had ruled Egypt for nearly 300 years ever since their ancestor Ptolemy, one of Alexander the Great's own generals, seized the country when Alexander died. By blood, what was Cleopatra?
answer: Greek
choices: Greek
Egyptian
Persian
Phoenician
context: Cleopatra was a Macedonian Greek of the Ptolemaic dynasty, descended from Ptolemy I Soter — not an Egyptian by blood at all. Her real power was political brilliance, not exotic mystery. Source: History.com, '10 Little-Known Facts About Cleopatra'; Britannica, Cleopatra.

question: For nearly 300 years Cleopatra's family ruled Egypt as foreign Greek kings who never tried to connect with the ordinary people they governed in one basic way. Cleopatra broke that streak. What did she become the first of her royal line to do?
answer: Learned to speak Egyptian
choices: Learned to speak Egyptian
Worshipped at Egypt's temples as a native pharaoh would
Took an Egyptian commoner as her husband
Moved her court out of Greek Alexandria
context: Plutarch notes the Ptolemy kings before her 'had not even made an effort to learn the native language'; Cleopatra was the first of her line to learn Egyptian. Source: Plutarch, Life of Antony 27; ASOR, 'Cleopatra's Languages.'

question: Cleopatra had chosen to die rather than be marched through Rome as a captive in Octavian's victory parade. According to the famous tale, the means of her death was slipped past her guards hidden inside an ordinary-looking object. What was it hidden in?
answer: A basket of figs
choices: A basket of figs
The lining of her gown
A sealed jar of wine
A box of her jewels
context: The legend says an asp (an Egyptian cobra) was smuggled to her in a basket of figs; she was found dead on a golden couch in full royal robes. Plutarch passes this on as the famous story, not proven fact. Source: Plutarch, Life of Antony 85-86; Wikipedia, Death of Cleopatra.

question: Cleopatra could deal with foreign envoys face to face — Ethiopians, Arabians, Hebrews, Medes, Parthians and more — rarely needing an interpreter. Plutarch was so struck by this that he compared her speaking tongue to a particular kind of object. What did he compare it to?
answer: An instrument of many strings
choices: An instrument of many strings
A coin stamped with many faces
A river fed by many streams
A key that opened many doors
context: Plutarch wrote that her tongue was 'like an instrument of many strings,' switching to whatever language she pleased — she reportedly commanded around nine. Source: Plutarch, Life of Antony 27.

question: Summoned by Mark Antony in 41 BC, Cleopatra arrived at Tarsus on a barge with a gilded stern and silver oars that rowed in time to flutes. Reclining beneath a gold-spangled canopy, she had costumed herself as one particular deity to overwhelm Antony. Which one?
answer: Venus, goddess of love
choices: Venus, goddess of love
Isis, goddess of magic
Athena, goddess of war
Diana, goddess of the hunt
context: Dressed as Venus (the Greek Aphrodite) with purple sails overhead, she made such a spectacle that word spread 'Aphrodite had come to revel with Dionysus' — and Antony was won. Source: Plutarch, Life of Antony 26; National Geographic, Antony & Cleopatra.

question: To win a bet with Mark Antony over who could throw the costliest banquet, Cleopatra called for one of the two largest pearls in the world and a cup of vinegar. According to Pliny the Elder, what did she then do with the priceless pearl?
answer: Dissolved it in the vinegar and drank it down
choices: Dissolved it in the vinegar and drank it down
Ground it to powder and stirred it into wine
Tossed it into the harbor before the guests
Crushed it over a roasted peacock as seasoning
context: Pliny says the pearl-and-vinegar meal was worth ten million sesterces; the judge Lucius Plancus stopped her before she could destroy the second pearl and declared Antony the loser. It is a famous tale, likely exaggerated. Source: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 9.119-121.  (Legend.)

question: Legend turned Cleopatra into the most beautiful woman in the world, yet coins that her own mint struck with her portrait survive today. Historians look at that profile to judge her real face. What does the nose on those coins actually look like?
answer: A strong hooked nose
choices: A strong hooked nose
A small upturned nose
A broad flat nose
A long straight nose
context: Her coins show a sharp, hooked-nosed profile with a jutting chin — no great beauty. Plutarch agreed her looks were 'not altogether incomparable,' crediting instead her charm, wit, and a 'mellifluous' voice. Source: History.com, '10 Little-Known Facts About Cleopatra'; Plutarch, Life of Antony 27.

question: At a grand ceremony in 34 BC, the Donations of Alexandria, Antony and Cleopatra sat on golden thrones and handed out Rome's eastern lands to her children. They declared her son Caesarion — fathered by Julius Caesar himself — to be Caesar's true heir, and crowned him with a title borrowed from the great emperors of the East. What title?
answer: King of Kings
choices: King of Kings
Pharaoh of Egypt
Son of the Divine
Great King of Asia
context: Proclaiming Caesarion 'King of Kings' and Caesar's real heir was a direct challenge to Octavian (Caesar's adopted heir) and helped trigger the final war of the Roman Republic. Source: Wikipedia, Donations of Alexandria; World History Encyclopedia, Cleopatra & Antony.

question: The struggle between Antony and Octavian was decided at the naval Battle of Actium off western Greece on 2 September 31 BC, a clash that would hand one man the entire Roman world. Mid-battle, Cleopatra's squadron of about sixty ships did something that doomed Antony's side. What did her ships do?
answer: Broke off and sailed away for Egypt
choices: Broke off and sailed away for Egypt
Rammed and sank Octavian's flagship
Set themselves on fire to block the strait
Encircled and trapped the enemy line
context: When Cleopatra's squadron slipped out of the battle, Antony abandoned the fight to follow her; his remaining fleet surrendered and Octavian became master of Rome. Source: Britannica, Battle of Actium; History.com, 'This Day in History: Battle of Actium.'

question: Cleopatra was found dead in her full royal robes and diadem, and her loyal maid Charmion was straightening the dead queen's crown when a guard burst in and shouted, 'Was this well done of your lady, Charmion?' Charmion gave one defiant reply and then dropped dead beside her mistress. What did she say?
answer: 'Extremely well, and as became the descendant of so many kings.'
choices: 'Extremely well, and as became the descendant of so many kings.'
'She has cheated your master of his triumph in Rome.'
'Ask the gods, soldier, for I will not answer you.'
'Better a queen's death than a Roman's chains.'
context: Charmion's last words — pride in Cleopatra's royal Ptolemaic line — are recorded by Plutarch; she collapsed dead the moment she finished. Source: Plutarch, Life of Antony 85 (Dryden); Wikipedia, Charmion.

question: After Cleopatra's death in 30 BC, Octavian wanted no rival left alive and had her son Caesarion — Julius Caesar's only real blood son — hunted down and killed. The scholar Arius Didymus urged him on with a grim joke twisting a line of the poet Homer. What did Arius say?
answer: 'It is not good to have too many Caesars.'
choices: 'It is not good to have too many Caesars.'
'Two suns cannot share a single sky.'
'A dead lion no longer bites.'
'Rome has room for only one heir.'
context: Arius Didymus punned on Homer to justify the killing; with about-17-year-old Caesarion's death ended the last claim of Caesar's true blood-heir. His murder closed the Ptolemaic line and roughly 3,000 years of Egyptian pharaohs as Egypt became a Roman province. Source: Plutarch, Life of Antony 81-82; Wikipedia, Caesarion and Arius Didymus.

question: On a snowy December day in 1888, two cowboys named Richard Wetherill and Charlie Mason were hunting stray cattle along a canyon rim in Colorado when, through the falling snow, they spotted something huge across the gorge that no one had lived in for centuries. What did they see tucked under a single sandstone overhang?
answer: A stone village of about 150 rooms
choices: A stone village of about 150 rooms
A wooden fort ringed by a tall palisade
A mine shaft cut deep into the rock
A row of painted burial caves
context: They named it Cliff Palace -- the largest cliff dwelling in North America, built by the Ancestral Puebloans and packed with about 150 rooms under one overhang. Source: coloradoencyclopedia.org/article/cliff-palace

question: After spotting Cliff Palace across the gorge, Richard Wetherill and Charlie Mason climbed down a makeshift ladder into its empty rooms, where they found pottery and human remains left behind in a village no one had lived in for about 600 years. What single tool did they find that looked as if its owner had just set it down -- still ready to use?
answer: A stone axe still lashed to its wooden handle
choices: A stone axe still lashed to its wooden handle
A loaded bow with its string still drawn
An iron sword resting in a leather sheath
A bronze knife wrapped in woven cloth
context: The Ancestral Puebloans had no metal tools -- the axe head was shaped stone bound to a wooden handle, abandoned with the village around the 1280s. Source: coloradoencyclopedia.org/article/cliff-palace

question: Archaeologists can spot a Clovis spear point at a glance because of one signature feature no later style copies: a long channel was chipped off the base, running a third to half the way up the stone so it could be socketed onto a wooden shaft. What is that named, defining trait called?
answer: A long flute channeled up from the base
choices: A long flute channeled up from the base
A hooked barb notched along each edge
A hollow socket drilled through the center
A serrated saw-edge ground into the tip
context: The 'flute' is the channel flake struck off the base of the point. It is the single trait that distinguishes a Clovis point from every later style. The culture is named for Clovis, New Mexico, where in February 1929 a 19-year-old named Ridgely Whiteman spotted such fluted points lying among the bones of Columbian mammoths at Blackwater Draw. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clovis_culture

question: At the Naco site in Arizona, archaeologists dug up a single Columbian mammoth that had been butchered by Ice Age hunters roughly 12,000 years ago — and found the kill frozen mid-hunt, the weapons still exactly where they had struck the animal. What was lying in and among the mammoth's rib cage?
answer: Eight stone spear points still among its ribs
choices: Eight stone spear points still among its ribs
A clay pot buried beneath its skull
A painted handprint left on a nearby wall
A necklace of carved teeth around its neck
context: Eight Clovis points lay in and among the rib cage of the one butchered mammoth at Naco, caught mid-hunt about 12,000 years ago. The site came to light after a local man, Marc Navarrete, found points while his father dug fossil bones out of Greenbush Draw. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naco_Mammoth_Kill_Site

question: People often say the ancient Maya mysteriously "vanished" around 900 CE, when their great jungle cities in the southern lowlands fell silent and emptied one by one. But the people did not actually disappear. What is true of the Maya today?
answer: About seven million people still speak Mayan languages in Mesoamerica
choices: About seven million people still speak Mayan languages in Mesoamerica
Their language survives only in carvings no living person can read
A single elderly speaker of Mayan remained when Spain arrived
Every Maya community was wiped out within a century of the collapse
context: It was the great Classic-era CITIES that emptied, not the people. Around 800-900 CE the southern lowland cities went quiet one after another until roughly 60,000 square miles of jungle held only deserted pyramids. But millions of Maya descendants still live in the Yucatan, Guatemala, and southern Mexico, and about seven million people speak Mayan languages today. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'The Classic Maya Collapse' (worldhistory.org/article/759).

question: For roughly 700 years the Maya marked their monuments with precise Long Count calendar dates, a counting system carried across the centuries. As their southern cities emptied, the carving of these dates trailed off. The very last Long Count date the Maya ever inscribed sits on Monument 101 at the city of Tonina, reading January 909 CE. After that single carving, what became of the 700-year tradition?
answer: No Maya city ever carved a Long Count date again
choices: No Maya city ever carved a Long Count date again
Northern cities revived it and carved Long Count dates for centuries more
The Spanish recorded it from Maya scribes in the 1500s
It shifted from stone monuments onto painted pottery
context: Monument 101 at Tonina, dated 10.4.0.0.0 (January 909 CE), bears the last Long Count date the Maya ever carved; the 700-year tradition simply stopped. The fall is visible in the numbers: the Maya carved about 40 dated monuments a year around 750 CE, but the count dropped to ten by 800 and to zero by 900. Tikal's last dated stela went up in 869 CE. Sources: Encyclopedia.com 'Tonina'; Wikipedia 'Classic Maya collapse'; American Scientist, 'Climate and the Collapse of Maya Civilization'.

question: Archaeologists still argue about WHY the southern Maya cities were abandoned, and one big clue came from an unexpected place: the mud at the bottom of Lake Chichancanab in the Yucatan. Drilling out long cores of that lake-bed sediment, scientists found a chemical record of exactly what the 9th century was like when the cities were dying. What did the lake mud reveal about those years?
answer: A drought so severe that yearly rainfall fell by half or more
choices: A drought so severe that yearly rainfall fell by half or more
A run of floods that drowned the lowland cornfields
A sudden cold snap that froze the tropical lowlands
A layer of volcanic ash that buried the farmland
context: Sediment cores from Lake Chichancanab (Hodell, Curtis & Brenner, 1995), later refined by gypsum-hydrate analysis (Evans et al., 2018, Science), showed the 9th century suffered drought so severe that annual rainfall dropped 41-54%, and at the worst peaks fell by up to 70%. Drought is only one suspect, though: scholars also blame relentless warfare between rival city-states and soil exhaustion from overpopulation and deforestation, and most now see a chain reaction rather than a single cause. Sources: American Scientist, 'Climate and the Collapse of Maya Civilization'; Eos, 'Severe Drought May Have Helped Hasten Ancient Maya's Collapse'.

question: On the night of December 25, 1991, the Soviet Union ended and the red hammer-and-sickle flag came down over the Kremlin for the last time. As crowds watched, a different flag rose in its place. Which flag was raised over the Kremlin?
answer: The pre-revolutionary white-blue-red Russian tricolor
choices: The pre-revolutionary white-blue-red Russian tricolor
A plain white flag of surrender
The blue-and-yellow flag of Ukraine
A new flag with a golden two-headed eagle
context: At 7:32 p.m. the Soviet flag was lowered and the old Russian tricolor — the white-blue-red banner from before the 1917 revolution — was raised in its place. The empire that built the Gulag was gone; the flag it had buried came back. Source: https://history.state.gov/milestones/1989-1992/collapse-soviet-union

question: On August 19, 1991, hardliners tried to seize power and sent tanks into Moscow to crush Russia's elected leader, Boris Yeltsin. Instead of hiding, Yeltsin walked out to the parliament building and did something that became the symbol of the coup's defeat. What did Yeltsin do?
answer: Climbed on top of one of the tanks to speak to the crowd
choices: Climbed on top of one of the tanks to speak to the crowd
Surrendered himself to the soldiers to spare the city
Ordered Russian jets to bomb the advancing column
Fled Moscow by helicopter to set up a government in exile
context: Yeltsin climbed onto tank No. 110 of the elite Taman Division, outside the Russian White House, and read a defiant decree to the crowd. The photograph went around the world and became the image of the coup collapsing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_Soviet_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat_attempt

question: After seizing power on August 19, 1991, the coup leaders put their acting 'president,' Gennady Yanayev, in front of TV cameras to show they were in command.
