question: Sixty-six years before 476, the blow that Romans truly felt as the 'fall' had already landed: in 410, Alaric and the Visigoths sacked the city of Rome itself, the first time an enemy had breached it in eight hundred years. Far away in Bethlehem, the scholar Jerome wept and wrote a single line that captured the shock. What did Jerome write?
answer: The city which had taken the whole world was itself taken
choices: The city which had taken the whole world was itself taken
Rome has fallen, and with her falls the light of all mankind
Better to die a free Roman than live to see this day
The gods we abandoned have at last abandoned us
context: St. Jerome, hearing of the 410 sack from his monastery in Bethlehem, mourned: 'The city which had taken the whole world was itself taken.' For Romans it was the emotional fall of Rome — the date 476 was the quiet legal one. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(410)

question: Odoacer ruled Italy for years, but in 493 his rival Theodoric the Ostrogoth invited him to a peace banquet at Ravenna and there struck him down with his own hand. According to legend, Theodoric looked at the dead body and made a chilling remark about it. What did he reportedly say?
answer: The man had no bones in his body
choices: The man had no bones in his body
So perishes the last servant of Rome
He died as he lived, betraying his betters
Let no king ever trust a banquet again
context: Legend holds that after killing Odoacer at the banquet — reportedly saying 'This is what you did to my friends' — Theodoric gazed at the corpse and marveled, 'The man had no bones in his body.' Told as legend, not certain fact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odoacer

question: Historians like Edward Gibbon picked 476 as the year the Western Roman Empire 'fell,' but in truth Rome did not so much die as transform — its law became the root of Western law, the Church inherited its structure, and its everyday language never stopped being spoken, only changed shape. Into which living languages did Latin grow?
answer: French, Italian, and Spanish
choices: French, Italian, and Spanish
English, German, and Dutch
Greek, Turkish, and Arabic
Irish, Welsh, and Breton
context: Latin lived on and slowly became French, Italian, and Spanish; Roman law became the foundation of Western law, and the Church took up Rome's organization. The empire transmuted rather than simply vanishing in 476. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historiography_of_the_fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire

question: In Prokofiev's 'Peter and the Wolf', a story written to teach kids the orchestra, every character is played by a different instrument. The hungry wolf comes stalking out of the forest, and to make him sound big and menacing Prokofiev gave him not one instrument but THREE of the same kind playing together. Which instrument did the wolf get three of?
answer: French horns
choices: French horns
violins
flutes
drums
context: Prokofiev assigned each character its own instrument so children would learn the four families by story: the bird is a flute, the duck an oboe, the cat a clarinet, the grumpy grandfather a bassoon, and Peter himself is the whole string section. The wolf gets three French horns (a brass instrument, sounded by buzzing the lips into a cup-shaped mouthpiece). Source: laphil.com/musicdb/pieces/552/peter-and-the-wolf

question: Near the end of Prokofiev's 'Peter and the Wolf', the duck has been gobbled up by the wolf, who was in such a hurry that he swallowed her alive and whole. The narrator says that if you listen very carefully at the finish, you can still hear the duck quacking away INSIDE the wolf's belly. The duck's voice in the music is one particular instrument. Which instrument do you hear quacking from inside the wolf?
answer: the oboe
choices: the oboe
the flute
the clarinet
the bassoon
context: Each animal in the piece is voiced by a fixed instrument: the bird is the flute, the cat the clarinet, the grumpy grandfather the bassoon, and the duck is the oboe. Because the wolf swallowed her whole and alive, Prokofiev keeps the oboe quacking faintly at the end -- the duck is still down there. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_and_the_Wolf

question: Michael Faraday became one of the greatest experimental scientists in history, yet he left school at fourteen and never attended a university. As a poor apprentice, how did he teach himself science?
answer: By reading the very books he was hired to bind
choices: By reading the very books he was hired to bind
By attending free evening lectures at Oxford
By copying out the notebooks of a rich tutor
By memorizing a single encyclopedia given to him
context: Faraday was apprenticed to a bookbinder at 14 and educated himself on the books passing through the shop, becoming one of history's greatest experimentalists without ever going to university. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Faraday

question: Michael Faraday was a bookbinder's son who never learned advanced math, yet his name now sits on a basic electrical measurement used by engineers every day. Which everyday electrical unit is named after him?
answer: The farad
choices: The volt
The watt
The farad
The joule
context: The farad, the unit of electrical capacitance, honors Michael Faraday, the self-taught bookbinder who never learned advanced mathematics. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Faraday

question: Before he was even three years old, James Clerk Maxwell drove the whole household mad demanding to know how doors, locks, streams, and bell-wires actually worked. What single question did the curious toddler repeat over and over?
answer: "What's the go o' that?"
choices: "Where does it all go?"
"What's the go o' that?"
"Who made it move?"
"How can that be true?"
context: As a toddler Maxwell endlessly asked 'What's the go o' that?', demanding the workings of everything around him long before he grew into the century's greatest physicist. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Clerk_Maxwell

question: Queen Victoria offered Michael Faraday a knighthood, and twice he was asked to become president of the Royal Society. Faraday turned all of it down, insisting on staying what instead?
answer: "plain Mr Faraday to the end"
choices: "a free man of science"
"plain Mr Faraday to the end"
"a humble servant of God"
"only a poor bookbinder"
context: Faraday refused the knighthood and twice declined the Royal Society presidency, vowing to remain 'plain Mr Faraday to the end'; he also refused to help make poison gas for the Crimean War on ethical grounds. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Faraday

question: In 1861 James Clerk Maxwell made the world's first true color photograph by shooting the same object three times through red, green, and blue filters, then projecting the three pictures back together. What everyday object did he choose as the subject of that first color photo?
answer: A tartan ribbon
choices: A bowl of fresh fruit
A tartan ribbon
A garden of roses
A stained-glass window
context: Maxwell's three-filter method produced the first color photograph in 1861 using a tartan ribbon, proving any color could be built from red, green, and blue light. Source: https://www.historyofinformation.com/detail.php?id=3666

question: In August 1831 Michael Faraday wound two separate coils of wire onto an iron ring, with only the iron joining them. He switched the current ON in the first coil and watched the meter attached to the SECOND coil, which carried no battery of its own. What did he see happen in that second coil?
answer: Its meter needle twitched, showing a current
choices: Its meter needle twitched, showing a current
Its wire glowed red and began to smoke
Nothing at all, until the iron melted
Its coil flung itself off the ring
context: Switching current on in one coil made Faraday's galvanometer twitch in the other: moving magnetism had created electricity (electromagnetic induction), the principle behind every generator. That iron ring is still on display at the Royal Institution. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Faraday

question: Around 1862 James Clerk Maxwell used his equations to calculate how fast an invisible electromagnetic wave should travel through space. When the number came out, he realized it exactly matched a speed scientists had already measured by completely different means. What had his electromagnetic number turned out to equal?
answer: The speed of light
choices: The speed of sound in air
The speed of light
The speed of the Earth's orbit
The speed of a falling object
context: Maxwell's electromagnetic wave speed equaled the measured speed of light, leading him to conclude light itself is an electromagnetic wave, uniting light, electricity, and magnetism as one phenomenon. Source: https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Maxwell/

question: Maxwell predicted invisible electromagnetic waves on paper but died before anyone made one. In 1887 Heinrich Hertz finally produced and detected them in his lab; asked what use they could possibly be, he reportedly shrugged that they were of no use whatsoever. Within a decade those 'useless' waves became which world-changing invention?
answer: Radio
choices: The telephone
Radio
The electric lightbulb
The X-ray machine
context: Hertz confirmed Maxwell's waves in 1887 and dismissed them as useless; within ten years they became radio. The 'of no use whatsoever' quote is widely retold but only loosely documented, so it is treated as legend. Source: https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Heinrich_Hertz

question: Franklin Roosevelt took the oath of office on March 4, 1933, with the country at the bottom of the Great Depression — a quarter of workers jobless and banks failing by the day. In his inaugural address he tried to calm a panicked nation with one famous sentence. How did it go?
answer: "The only thing we have to fear is fear itself."
choices: "The only thing we have to fear is fear itself."
"Ask not what your country can do for you."
"We have nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears, and sweat."
"Government of the people, by the people, for the people."
context: FDR's 1933 inaugural line — "the only thing we have to fear is fear itself — nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror" — is often credited to adviser Louis Howe, who added it to the draft. The other three quotes belong to John F. Kennedy, Winston Churchill, and Abraham Lincoln. Source: National Archives, FDR's First Inaugural Address (archives.gov); Yale Avalon Project (avalon.law.yale.edu).

question: Franklin Roosevelt's Civilian Conservation Corps paid nearly 3 million young men $30 a month to plant trees and build parks across Depression-era America. But the men did not get to keep most of that pay — the program had a strict rule about the $30. What happened to it?
answer: $25 of it was sent straight home to their families.
choices: $25 of it was sent straight home to their families.
All of it was held back until they finished their service.
Half of it was taxed to pay for the camps' upkeep.
$25 of it was paid in scrip good only at the camp store.
context: Of the CCC's $30 monthly pay, $25 was mailed straight home to the worker's family. The Corps ran from 1933 to 1942 in camps organized like the Army, and its crews together planted more than 3 billion trees. Source: History.com, Civilian Conservation Corps (history.com); Britannica, Civilian Conservation Corps (britannica.com).

question: Two days after Franklin Roosevelt took office in March 1933, with terrified depositors yanking out their savings and banks collapsing in a chain reaction, he made a startling first move to halt the panic. What did he order?
answer: He shut every bank in the country for several days.
choices: He shut every bank in the country for several days.
He seized the failing banks and ran them from Washington.
He sent federal troops to guard the largest banks.
He printed emergency cash to hand out at every bank.
context: FDR's Proclamation 2039 (March 6, 1933) declared a nationwide "bank holiday" that closed every bank, then Congress passed the Emergency Banking Act — the first law of his presidency — to reopen them under federal supervision. In his first radio "fireside chat" the night before they reopened, he told listeners it was safer to keep money in a reopened bank than under the mattress; that week Americans returned about $1 billion in hoarded cash. Source: Federal Reserve History (federalreservehistory.org); Library of Congress, 1933 Bank Holiday (guides.loc.gov).

question: Franklin Roosevelt's Tennessee Valley Authority built 16 dams across seven poor Southern states in the 1930s and '40s. The project finally brought to families on dirt-poor backcountry farms something most of them had never had inside their homes. What was it?
answer: Electric lights
choices: Electric lights
Running water
Telephones
Paved roads
context: TVA power lit up farms that had never had electricity. Its first dam, Norris Dam, was named for Senator George Norris of Nebraska, called "the father of TVA." The bank tells the cost honestly too: Norris Dam flooded the valley, forcing nearly 3,000 people from their homes and requiring the government to relocate some 5,200 graves. Source: History.com, Why the TVA Was the New Deal's Most Ambitious Program (history.com); TVA, Our History (tva.com).

question: When Franklin Roosevelt signed the Social Security Act in 1935, he handed one of the signing pens to his Labor Secretary, Frances Perkins, who had pushed hard for the law. Perkins had already made history the day she joined Roosevelt's Cabinet. How?
answer: She was the first woman ever to serve in a U.S. Cabinet.
choices: She was the first woman ever to serve in a U.S. Cabinet.
She was the first Labor Secretary to rise from a union.
She was the youngest Cabinet member in the nation's history.
She was the first Cabinet member born outside the country.
context: Frances Perkins was the first woman ever to serve in a U.S. Cabinet, and she fought for the Social Security Act before receiving one of FDR's signing pens on August 14, 1935. Source: EBSCO Research Starters, Social Security Act of 1935 (ebsco.com); SSA History (ssa.gov/history).

question: The Works Progress Administration is remembered for putting 8.5 million Depression-era Americans to work building roads and bridges. But it also spent federal money on a kind of worker most people would never picture on a New Deal jobs program. Who else did the WPA put on the payroll?
answer: Out-of-work writers and artists
choices: Out-of-work writers and artists
Retired soldiers and sailors
Schoolchildren and students
Foreign engineers and architects
context: The WPA paid unemployed writers and artists: its Federal Art Project funded 2,566 murals, and its Federal Writers' Project produced the American Guide Series — 378 books and pamphlets describing every state, city, and village in the nation. In all the WPA ran 1.4 million projects from 1935 to 1943. Source: Britannica, Works Progress Administration (britannica.com); Wikipedia, Works Progress Administration (en.wikipedia.org).

question: Ida May Fuller, a retired Vermont schoolteacher, cashed the very first monthly Social Security check in 1940. Over three years of the new payroll tax she had paid in just $24.75 — and then she lived all the way to 100. By the time she died, how much had Social Security paid her in benefits?
context: Ida May Fuller's first check (number 00-000-001, dated January 31, 1940) was for $22.54; against $24.75 in payroll taxes she ultimately collected $22,888.92 — 924 times what she paid in. FDR was candid that the payroll tax was political armor, telling aide Luther Gulick: "With those taxes in there, no damn politician can ever scrap my social security program... they're straight politics." Source: Social Security Administration History, Ida May Fuller and the Gulick Memorandum (ssa.gov/history).

question: The National Industrial Recovery Act was the centerpiece of Franklin Roosevelt's first New Deal — until 1935, when a Brooklyn family that sold food to local markets fought the law's federal rules all the way to the Supreme Court, and a unanimous bench struck the whole act down. By what nickname is that landmark case remembered?
answer: The Sick Chicken Case
choices: The Sick Chicken Case
The Bad Milk Case
The Rotten Meat Case
The Spoiled Egg Case
context: A.L.A. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States (1935), the "Sick Chicken Case," was decided unanimously; the Court ruled the NIRA had handed the President legislative power he could not constitutionally hold. Source: Cornell LII, Schechter Poultry (law.cornell.edu); Wikipedia, A.L.A. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States (en.wikipedia.org).

question: After the Supreme Court kept striking down his New Deal laws, Franklin Roosevelt struck back in 1937 with a bold plan to reshape the bench in his favor. Critics nicknamed it "court-packing." What exactly did Roosevelt's plan propose to do?
answer: Add one new justice for every sitting justice over age 70
choices: Add one new justice for every sitting justice over age 70
Force every justice over age 70 to retire at once
Let the President remove justices who voted against his laws
Send each major law to a public vote instead of the Court
context: Unveiled February 5, 1937, the plan would have let FDR appoint up to six extra justices, ballooning the bench from 9 to as many as 15. The conservative bloc that kept voting the New Deal down — Sutherland, Butler, McReynolds, and Van Devanter — was nicknamed "the Four Horsemen." The bill died in the Senate on July 22, 1937, opposed even by FDR's own Vice President, John Nance Garner; the Court has stayed at nine justices ever since. Source: Wikipedia, Judicial Procedures Reform Bill of 1937 (en.wikipedia.org); Federal Judicial Center (fjc.gov).

question: In the middle of the court-packing fight, Justice Owen Roberts — the swing vote who had been striking down New Deal laws — abruptly reversed himself in 1937 and voted to uphold one, helping drain the life out of Roosevelt's plan to enlarge the Court. A humorist gave Roberts's about-face a nickname that stuck. What was it?
answer: "The switch in time that saved nine"
choices: "The switch in time that saved nine"
"The one vote that kept them nine"
"The turn that spared the bench"
"The change of heart that held the line"
context: Humorist Cal Tinney coined "the switch in time that saved nine" (a pun on "a stitch in time saves nine") after Roberts joined the majority in West Coast Hotel Co. v. Parrish (March 29, 1937), upholding a state minimum-wage law. Historians debate whether the threat actually caused it: records show Roberts had already voted to uphold the law at the justices' private conference on December 19, 1936 — weeks before FDR announced his plan — so the timing may be coincidence, not capitulation. Source: Wikipedia, The switch in time that saved nine (en.wikipedia.org); Constitution Center (constitutioncenter.org).

question: In his 1944 State of the Union, Franklin Roosevelt argued that political freedom meant little to a hungry man — "true individual freedom," he said, "cannot exist without economic security." He proposed guaranteeing every American a job, a decent home, medical care, and an education. What did Roosevelt call this sweeping list of economic guarantees?
answer: A Second Bill of Rights
choices: A Second Bill of Rights
The Four Freedoms
The Fair Deal
The Economic Charter
context: FDR's 1944 "Second Bill of Rights" reframed freedom around economic security — "Necessitous men are not free men" — listing rights to a job, a home, medical care, education, and protection from old age, sickness, and unemployment. The bank presents this positive-rights case at full strength and imposes no verdict. (The Four Freedoms was FDR's earlier 1941 idea; the Fair Deal was Truman's.) Source: FDR Presidential Library, 1944 State of the Union (fdrlibrary.org); Wikipedia, Second Bill of Rights (en.wikipedia.org).

question: The very year Franklin Roosevelt proposed guaranteeing economic security as a right, the economist Friedrich Hayek published the era's sharpest counter-argument. Hayek warned that central economic planning, however good its intentions, slowly erodes freedom — because a guaranteed good is a claim on someone else, and enforcing the plan means silencing those who resist it. What did Hayek title this famous warning?
answer: The Road to Serfdom
choices: The Road to Serfdom
The End of Liberty
The Servile State
The Price of Security
context: F.A. Hayek published The Road to Serfdom in 1944 — the same year as FDR's Second Bill of Rights — arguing that the New Deal's kind of planning was exactly the transformation that erodes liberty. The bank presents the FDR case and the Hayek case at full strength and imposes no verdict on which is right. (The Servile State is a real 1912 book by Hilaire Belloc.) Source: Wikipedia, The Road to Serfdom (en.wikipedia.org); Future of Freedom Foundation (fff.org).

question: Franklin Roosevelt is the only U.S. president ever elected four times — in 1932, 1936, 1940, and 1944. George Washington had started a tradition that Roosevelt broke. What was that tradition he broke?
answer: No president would serve more than two terms
choices: No president would serve more than two terms
No president would run during a war
No president would lead from a wheelchair
No president would leave the capital in wartime
context: FDR broke Washington's unwritten two-term tradition during the Depression and WWII. After he died, the 22nd Amendment (ratified 1951) made the two-term limit actual law, so no one could do it again. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/fdr-four-term-president-22-amendment

question: In a December 1940 radio 'fireside chat,' Franklin Roosevelt told Americans the U.S. would not send soldiers to fight Hitler — instead it would out-build the enemy, flooding Britain and the Allies with American planes, ships, and tanks. What did he call the role America would play?
answer: The great arsenal of democracy
choices: The great arsenal of democracy
The shield of the free world
The workshop of the brave
The fortress of liberty
context: 'We must be the great arsenal of democracy' became the rallying idea: win the war by manufacturing, not by sending troops (yet). Source: https://millercenter.org/the-presidency/presidential-speeches/december-29-1940-fireside-chat-16-arsenal-democracy

question: By late 1940 Britain had run out of money to buy American weapons, and Franklin Roosevelt needed to sell skeptical Americans on lending arms instead of selling them. At a press conference he reached for a homely image: if your neighbor's house is on fire and you have a garden hose, what do you do?
answer: Hand him the hose to fight the fire, no haggling over price
choices: Hand him the hose to fight the fire, no haggling over price
Sell him the hose for fifteen dollars cash up front
Call the fire brigade and wait on your own porch
Lock your hose away so the fire can't spread to you
context: You don't haggle '$15 for the hose' while the fire spreads — you lend it and he replaces it after. That image sold Lend-Lease, which by 1945 shipped about $36.5 billion in war supplies to Britain, the Soviet Union, and China. Source: https://www.fdrlibrary.org/lend-lease

question: Polio paralyzed Franklin Roosevelt's legs in 1921, yet as president he hid it so well a biographer called it a 'splendid deception.' Gripping a cane and an aide's arm, he learned to 'walk' a few steps — and the press agreed to one thing that kept the secret. What did the press agree to?
answer: Never to photograph him in his wheelchair
choices: Never to photograph him in his wheelchair
Never to mention his age in print
Never to report on his fireside chats
Never to film him giving a speech
context: Locking steel braces on his withered legs, FDR swung his hips forward a few agonizing steps. His own wheelchair was a homemade thing — an armless kitchen chair on a bicycle-wheeled frame — and reporters honored the no-photo agreement for years. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/inside-fdrs-lifelong-health-struggles-and-his-sudden-death

question: Drafting his speech to Congress after the Pearl Harbor attack on December 7, 1941, Franklin Roosevelt looked at his own typed phrase 'a date which will live in world history,' crossed out two words, and wrote one word in their place — creating one of the most famous lines in American history. What word did he write?
answer: infamy
choices: infamy
treachery
shame
sorrow
context: He struck 'world history' and wrote 'infamy': 'a date which will live in infamy.' The draft with his handwriting survives at the FDR Library — proof that one word can turn a flat sentence into history. Source: https://prologue.blogs.archives.gov/2011/12/05/crafting-a-call-to-arms-fdrs-day-of-infamy-speech

question: Two months after Pearl Harbor, on February 19, 1942, Franklin Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066. The order never named any group by name, yet in practice it was used almost only against one group of Americans. What did it do to about 120,000 of them?
answer: Forced Japanese Americans from their West Coast homes into incarceration camps
choices: Forced Japanese Americans from their West Coast homes into incarceration camps
Drafted Japanese Americans into segregated combat units overseas
Barred German Americans from holding wartime factory jobs
Stripped Italian Americans of citizenship until the war ended
context: The order's words were neutral, but it was aimed almost entirely at people of Japanese descent — a dark mark on FDR's record that historians have judged harshly ever since. Source: https://www.fdrlibrary.org/executive-order-9066

question: Writing as 'Publius' in Federalist No. 51, James Madison granted that 'if men were angels, no government would be necessary' — but since men are not angels, a government run by men still has to be kept from abusing its own power. What was Madison's mechanism for keeping each branch in check?
answer: Set each branch's ambition to fight the others, so 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition'
choices: Set each branch's ambition to fight the others, so 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition'
Let the people vote out any official who oversteps his constitutional bounds
Bind every officeholder by a sworn oath taken before taking up the post
Appoint a council of wise elders to overrule any branch that abused power
context: Federalist No. 51 (Madison, as 'Publius'): the famous design connects 'the interest of the man' to 'the constitutional rights of the place' — each branch is given both the means and the motive to resist the others, turning selfishness against itself. Source: https://billofrightsinstitute.org/primary-sources/federalist-no-51/

question: In Federalist No. 10, James Madison argued you cannot abolish faction -- rival groups pushing their own interest -- without destroying liberty itself, since 'liberty is to faction what air is to fire.' So if faction can never be removed, the question becomes how to stop any single faction from seizing control. What design did Madison argue was safest against that danger?
answer: A republic spread wide over many people, so rival factions multiply and check each other
choices: A republic spread wide over many people, so rival factions multiply and check each other
A republic kept small and close-knit, where neighbors watch the public good together
A republic that bans political parties of any kind from forming at all
A republic guided by one virtuous leader standing above every faction
context: Federalist No. 10 (1787), James Madison: faction cannot be removed without ending liberty ('liberty is to faction what air is to fire'); the remedy is an extended republic where the multiplicity of factions prevents any single one from dominating.

question: In the homage ceremony that began a feudal bond, a man knelt bareheaded before his lord with no sword or belt, put his clasped hands inside the lord's hands, and the lord closed his own hands around them. What did this hands-inside-hands gesture mean the man had now become?
answer: Wholly his lord's man
choices: Wholly his lord's man
A free citizen of the town
A sworn knight of the realm
An owner of his own land
context: The kneeling, weaponless, bareheaded posture showed submission; the enclosing hands signaled the lord's promise of protection. The man was now 'wholly his man.' Source: Britannica, 'Homage and fealty'; Littleton's Tenures c.1480.

question: After the new vassal placed his clasped hands inside his lord's hands during the homage ceremony, the lord did one more thing to turn this private deal into a public act done in front of witnesses. What did the lord do to seal the bond?
answer: Gave him a kiss on the mouth
choices: Gave him a kiss on the mouth
Handed him a written contract
Struck him on the shoulder with a sword
Poured wine over his clasped hands
context: The kiss on the mouth made the agreement public before witnesses, sealing the bond of homage. Source: Britannica, 'Homage and fealty'; World History Encyclopedia, 'Feudalism'.

question: In the feudal system, a lord granted a vassal a parcel of land of no fixed size; the vassal kept its income, ruled the people on it, and could pass it to his heirs, all in exchange for service (usually fighting for the lord). What was this granted land called?
answer: A fief
choices: A fief
A tithe
A guild
A charter
context: The fief (land-for-service) was the heart of feudalism. 'Vassal' itself comes from a Celtic word *wasso-, meaning 'young man, servant' (Welsh gwas, boy or servant). Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Feudalism'; Wiktionary/Etymonline 'vassal'.

question: The smallest standard fief in England was sized to support exactly one knight, his family, his servants, and his very expensive war-horses, armour, and weapons. In return, that knight owed his lord a fixed amount of military service each year. How many days of fighting did he owe?
answer: 40 days a year
choices: 40 days a year
12 days a year
100 days a year
365 days a year
context: This unit was called a 'knight's fee.' The 40-day cap kept nobles from abandoning their own lands too long; when the lord called, the knight rode to war with his own arms and armour. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Feudalism'; Wikipedia 'Knight's fee'; Britannica 'Knight service'.

question: A knight who didn't want to ride to war could instead pay his lord a special fee to escape the duty, named from the Latin scutum, meaning 'shield' (so it literally meant 'shield-money'). England's King Henry II loved this fee, collecting it seven times between 1157 and 1187 so he could hire paid soldiers loyal only to him. What was this payment called?
answer: Scutage
choices: Scutage
Tithe
Wergild
Danegeld
context: Scutage ('shield-money') let kings swap unreliable feudal levies for cash-paid troops loyal to the crown alone, quietly weakening the old land-for-fighting bargain. Source: Wikipedia 'Scutage'; Britannica 'Scutage'.

question: Bishop Fulbert of Chartres wrote a famous letter in 1020 listing the duties a vassal owed his lord. But Fulbert added a twist that made the bond run both ways: he warned that a lord who failed his faithful vassal in return would be considered guilty of one thing. What did Fulbert say such a lord would be guilty of?
answer: Bad faith
choices: Bad faith
High treason
Mortal sin
Petty theft
context: Fulbert wrote the lord 'ought to act toward his faithful vassal reciprocally in all these things. And if he does not... he will be justly considered guilty of bad faith.' Feudal loyalty was a two-way contract, not one-way servitude. Source: Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook, 'Fulbert of Chartres: On Feudal Obligations, 1020'.

question: On Lammas Day, 1 August 1086, William the Conqueror summoned roughly 170 of his great landholders to Old Sarum near Salisbury and made every one of them swear allegiance directly to him, ahead of their own immediate lords. What is this unprecedented mass act of homage now called?
answer: The Oath of Salisbury
choices: The Oath of Salisbury
The Treaty of Sarum
The Domesday Charter
The Council of Clarendon
context: By making even his vassals' vassals swear personally to him, William bound the whole pyramid to the crown. It was finished the same month as the Domesday Book survey. Source: English Heritage, 'William the Conqueror and the Oath of Sarum'; Anglo-Saxon Chronicle; Wikipedia 'Oath of Salisbury'.

question: In pre-Christian Fiji, a chief or priest was held in a sacred 'tapu' state that forbade him from letting his own hands touch the cooked flesh of a slain enemy. So at these grim feasts, attendants fed the chief using a special object carved just for the purpose. What was it?
answer: A long-pronged wooden fork made only for feeding the chief human flesh
choices: A long-pronged wooden fork made only for feeding the chief human flesh
A clay bowl reserved for the chief's portion of the feast
A woven palm-leaf mat the chief had to kneel upon
A polished whale-tooth ornament worn around the chief's neck
context: The carved wooden fork was called the iculanibokola ('icula ni bakola' = the fork for the bakola, the human victim). Because a chief or priest in a tapu (taboo) state could not touch the flesh with his hands, attendants used it to feed him. Source: Atlas Obscura, 'The Fiji Cannibal Fork'; Finch & Co, 'Fijian Chief's Ritual Flesh or Cannibal Fork Icula Ni Bakola'.

question: Seru Epenisa Cakobau, the paramount chief of Bau and himself a former cannibal, was converted to Christianity by the missionary James Calvert and renounced cannibalism in 1854. A year later, at the Battle of Kaba in 1855, he stood over enemies he had captured — men whom, by the old Fijian custom, a victorious chief would have had killed and eaten. What did the newly Christian Cakobau do instead?
answer: He pardoned his captured enemies on the battlefield and spared their lives
choices: He pardoned his captured enemies on the battlefield and spared their lives
He handed his captured enemies to a rival chief for the customary feast
He demanded a ransom in whale-teeth before releasing his captured enemies
He exiled his captured enemies to a distant island under guard
context: Cakobau (who took the Christian name Epenisa, 'Ebenezer') pardoning his captives reversed the old custom under which they would have become 'long pig'. His conversion prompted tens of thousands of Fijians to adopt Christianity, hastening the end of the practice. Source: Wikipedia, 'Seru Epenisa Cakobau'; Britannica, 'Cakobau'.

question: In June 1790, Thomas Jefferson hosted Alexander Hamilton and James Madison at a private dinner to break a deadlock: the federal government would take over the states' Revolutionary War debts, which Hamilton wanted, in exchange for something the Virginians wanted. What did Jefferson and Madison win at that dinner table?
answer: The permanent national capital moved south to the Potomac
choices: The permanent national capital moved south to the Potomac
A national bank chartered in Philadelphia
A treaty of trade and friendship with Britain
An immediate end to all federal taxes on farms
context: This is the Compromise of 1790. Hamilton got federal assumption of the states' war debts; in return the capital was set on the Potomac River, the future Washington, D.C. Jefferson later wrote that assumption was 'a bitter pill' for the South, so moving the seat of government there 'was a just measure.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compromise_of_1790

question: America's first two political parties were not born from any election campaign. They grew out of a feud between two men who sat at the same table in George Washington's own cabinet: Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton and Secretary of State Thomas Jefferson. What did these two cabinet officers split over?
answer: How strong the central government should be
choices: How strong the central government should be
Whether to keep a standing peacetime army
Where to build the first federal courthouse
Which foreign language to use in treaties
context: Hamilton's Federalists wanted a strong central government, a commerce-and-manufacturing economy, and a 'loose' reading of the Constitution; Jefferson's Democratic-Republicans wanted stronger states, an agrarian economy, and a 'strict' reading where any power not explicitly granted stays with the states. The disagreement, not a campaign, created the parties. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Party_System

question: By 1791 each side fought through its own newspaper. To answer the Federalists' paper, Jefferson and Madison recruited the poet Philip Freneau to Philadelphia to run the 'National Gazette' as their attack organ. George Washington was so stung by its assaults on his administration that in private he railed against the editor with a memorable insult. How did Washington refer to Freneau?
answer: As 'that Rascal Freneau'
choices: As 'that Rascal Freneau'
As 'a most honest journalist'
As 'the conscience of the Republic'
As 'a harmless pamphleteer'
context: The Federalists had John Fenno's 'Gazette of the United States'; the Republicans answered with Freneau's 'National Gazette,' which hammered the administration. Washington fumed in private about 'that Rascal Freneau' — a sign that the party press had turned a cabinet feud into a public, nationwide fight. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Party_System

question: Alexander Fleming came back from his summer holiday to his messy lab at St Mary's Hospital in London and found a blob of mould growing on one of his bacteria dishes. Around the mould was a clear ring with no germs in it. What had the mould done to the bacteria in that ring?
answer: Killed it off
choices: Killed it off
Made it glow
Frozen it solid
Turned it blue
context: 1928. Fleming realized the Penicillium mould was making something that killed germs around it — the clear ring was the first glimpse of the world's first antibiotic. Source: https://www.sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/alexander-fleming/

question: When Alexander Fleming first found that his mould made a substance that killed germs, he didn't have a fancy name for it yet. He just called it by a plain, almost silly nickname. What did Fleming first call it?
answer: Mould juice
choices: Mould juice
Germ soap
Sick water
Bug killer
context: He only gave it the proper name 'penicillin' on 7 March 1929, after the mould Penicillium — mostly so he'd stop having to write out 'mould broth filtrate'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_penicillin

question: Penicillin was so hard to grow that the Oxford scientists turned their whole lab into a makeshift mould factory. They grew the mould in any container they could find. What kind of containers did they end up using?
answer: Biscuit tins and bedpans
choices: Biscuit tins and bedpans
Glass beakers and flasks
Wooden barrels and crates
Sealed steel drums
context: They grew it in biscuit tins, sheep-dip cans, pie dishes, bath tubs, milk churns and hospital bedpans. Gallons of mould broth yielded only a fingernail's worth of penicillin. Source: https://www.sciencemuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/how-was-penicillin-developed

question: The story goes that when Alexander Fleming first noticed the strange mould killing the germs on his dish, he muttered just two words to himself. They became one of the most famous lines in the history of science. What did Fleming reportedly mutter?
answer: "That's funny."
choices: "That's funny."
"At last!"
"How dreadful."
"Run for help!"
context: Remembered as legend, not a recording. Fleming also said, looking back: 'One sometimes finds what one is not looking for.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_penicillin

question: The mould that landed on Alexander Fleming's dish was a rare strain that just happened to drift in by chance. Historians think the spores floated into his cluttered lab from one particular place nearby. Where did the spores most likely come from?
answer: A mould expert's lab one floor below
choices: A mould expert's lab one floor below
An open window facing the street
A bakery across the road
A damp basement under the building
context: The spores most likely floated up from the lab of the Irish mycologist C.J. La Touche, working one floor below Fleming through an open door — the rare strain Penicillium notatum. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_penicillin

question: Alexander Fleming published his penicillin discovery in 1929, but he couldn't purify the fragile stuff or keep it from falling apart, so almost nobody cared. For about ten years it sat unused — until two scientists at Oxford University took his forgotten paper and turned penicillin into a real, usable medicine. Who finished the job Fleming couldn't?
answer: Howard Florey and Ernst Chain
choices: Howard Florey and Ernst Chain
Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch
Marie Curie and Pierre Curie
Edward Jenner and Joseph Lister
context: Discovering penicillin was NOT enough to save anyone — Florey and Chain revived the work in 1939-1940 and made it a drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel Prize with Fleming. Source: https://www.sciencemuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/how-was-penicillin-developed

question: On 25 May 1940 the Oxford team ran the experiment that finally proved penicillin worked. They injected eight mice with deadly streptococci germs, then gave penicillin to only four of them. When the scientists came back the next morning, what did they find?
answer: The four treated mice were alive; the four untreated were dead
choices: The four treated mice were alive; the four untreated were dead
All eight mice had survived the night
All eight mice had died despite the drug
Only one treated mouse had pulled through
context: By the next morning all four untreated mice were dead and the treated ones were alive and well — the proof that penicillin could save a living body, not just a lab dish. Source: https://www.lrb.co.uk/the-paper/v01/n05/peter-medawar/florey-story

question: Albert Alexander, a 43-year-old Oxford policeman, became the very first person ever treated with penicillin on 12 February 1941. He had a terrible facial infection — so bad that one of his eyes had already been removed. Within 24 hours of his first injection, what happened?
answer: His fever dropped and his infection began to heal
choices: His fever dropped and his infection began to heal
His other eye had to be taken out too
He felt nothing different at all
He broke out in a worse new rash
context: The popular tale that he scratched himself on a rose thorn is doubted; the infection more likely began with wounds from a German bombing raid during the Blitz. Source: https://www.phc.ox.ac.uk/blog/on-this-site-penicillin-a-historic-first

question: In 1941 Howard Florey and Norman Heatley sailed to America to get penicillin mass-produced. They were terrified that if the Nazis invaded Britain, the precious mould could be lost forever. To make sure they could secretly carry it out no matter what, what did the two men do with the mould spores?
answer: Rubbed them into the linings of their coats
choices: Rubbed them into the linings of their coats
Swallowed them in sealed capsules
Sewed them inside their shoe heels
Mailed them ahead in a diplomatic bag
context: Even if everything else was lost, they could carry penicillin out hidden in their clothing. Biographer Eric Lax titled his book 'The Mold in Dr. Florey's Coat.' Source: https://www.acponline.org/about-acp/chapters-regions/united-states/tennessee-chapter/about-the-chapter/grand-rounds-in-literature/the-mold-in-dr-floreys-coat-by-eric-lax

question: At a U.S. government lab in Peoria, Illinois, scientists were hunting for a mould that made more penicillin than Fleming's weak original strain. A lab worker nicknamed 'Moldy Mary' Hunt brought in the winner from a local market — an everyday piece of food covered in mould. What was it?
answer: A mouldy cantaloupe
choices: A mouldy cantaloupe
A rotten potato
A spoiled loaf of bread
A bad wheel of cheese
context: Its strain (Penicillium rubens NRRL 1951) made far more penicillin than Fleming's and became the ancestor of mass-production mould — it is now the official state microbe of Illinois. Source: https://www.the-scientist.com/how-a-moldy-cantaloupe-took-fleming-s-penicillin-from-discovery-to-mass-production-72304

question: Penicillin was so scarce in 1941 that Albert Alexander's doctors couldn't bear to waste a single drop. They knew about 80% of the drug passed straight through his body and came out in his urine. To stretch the tiny supply, what desperate thing did the doctors do?
answer: Collected his urine to recover the penicillin and re-injected it
choices: Collected his urine to recover the penicillin and re-injected it
Diluted each dose with ten times the water
Gave him only one injection a week
Switched him to a cheaper sister drug
context: Even so the supply ran out. After improving dramatically, Albert Alexander relapsed and died on 15 March 1941 — there simply wasn't enough penicillin yet to finish the cure. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Alexander_(police_officer)

question: Anne Miller, dying of blood poisoning at New Haven Hospital in March 1942, became the first person whose life penicillin actually saved. The dose flown in to rescue her was only about a tablespoon — yet that tiny amount was a staggering share of something. A tablespoon of penicillin was roughly equal to what?
answer: Half of all the penicillin then existing in the United States
choices: Half of all the penicillin then existing in the United States
A single week's output of one factory
The yearly dose for one small hospital
What a doctor's bag normally carried
context: That's how rare the drug still was in early 1942 — saving one woman took half the nation's entire supply. Source: https://medicine.yale.edu/news-article/who-saved-the-first-life-with-penicillin/

question: Accepting his Nobel Prize on 11 December 1945, Alexander Fleming used his speech to give the world a warning about his own discovery. He said that a careless person who took too little penicillin would expose germs to a weak dose and not kill them. According to Fleming, what would happen to those germs?
answer: They would become resistant to penicillin
choices: They would become resistant to penicillin
They would spread twice as fast
They would turn into a deadlier strain
They would hide inside the body for years
context: Fleming warned: 'the ignorant man may easily underdose himself and by exposing his microbes to non-lethal quantities of the drug make them resistant.' He foresaw antibiotic resistance the very year penicillin was celebrated. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2018/06/fleming-lecture.pdf

question: Norman Heatley devised the extraction methods and improvised equipment that turned penicillin from a lab curiosity into a usable drug, yet when the 1945 Nobel Prize was awarded he was left off it entirely. Heatley was a chemist, not a physician. In 1990 Oxford University finally honoured him, and what it chose to give him was startling for a man who had never trained in medicine. What did Oxford award Heatley?
answer: An honorary Doctorate of Medicine
choices: An honorary Doctorate of Medicine
An honorary chair in the chemistry department
A bronze bust in its medical school's entrance hall
A graduate scholarship established under his name
context: Per Oxford University and Eric Lax's 'The Mould in Dr Florey's Coat', in 1990 Oxford gave Heatley -- a chemist, not a medic -- an honorary Doctorate of Medicine, said to be the first such degree it had awarded a non-physician.

question: At the Scutari army hospital during the Crimean War, the nurse Florence Nightingale walked the wards alone each night, checking on wounded soldiers long after the surgeons had gone to bed. The grateful men gave her a famous nickname for what she carried on those rounds. What was it?
answer: A small lamp
choices: A small lamp
A heavy hammer
A leather ledger
A basket of bread
context: The soldiers called her 'the Lady with the Lamp.' The Times described a 'ministering angel' with 'a little lamp in her hand,' and Henry Wadsworth Longfellow fixed the image forever in his 1857 poem 'Santa Filomena': 'A Lady with a lamp shall stand.' Her actual lamp (c.1856) survives in a museum collection. Sources: https://www.nam.ac.uk/explore/florence-nightingale-lady-lamp ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Nightingale

question: Florence Nightingale was certain that filth and disease — not enemy bullets — had killed most of the British soldiers at the Scutari hospital, and she needed to convince doubtful Parliament officials. Instead of just arguing, she won them over by inventing something that made the truth impossible to ignore. What did she create?
answer: A colored statistical diagram
choices: A colored statistical diagram
A signed petition
A public newspaper letter
A stirring speech
context: She invented the 'coxcomb' or polar-area diagram — now called the 'Nightingale rose' — a circle of twelve wedges, one per month, with big blue areas for deaths from disease and red for battle wounds. The enormous blue swaths made it electrically clear that preventable disease was the real killer, and the chart shrinks dramatically after her sanitary reforms. In 1859 she became the first woman ever elected a Fellow of the Royal Statistical Society. Sources: https://cwfn.uoguelph.ca/short-papers-excerpts/nightingale-statistics-and-the-crimean-war/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Nightingale

question: In July 1777, the Continental Congress made a French volunteer a major general — and a big reason they said yes was the unusual offer this 19-year-old made about his service. What did the young Marquis de Lafayette agree to?
answer: To serve without any pay
choices: To serve without any pay
To command the navy at sea
To bring a regiment from France
To stay only one summer
context: The Marquis de Lafayette was only 19 when Congress commissioned him a major general on July 31, 1777, and his willingness to serve WITHOUT PAY helped win them over. Source: history.com/this-day-in-history/july-31/marquis-de-lafayette-becomes-a-major-general-without-pay

question: When Baron von Steuben reached the Continental Army at Valley Forge, he was disgusted to find the soldiers never fought with their bayonets — they treated the blades as something else entirely. What were the Americans using their bayonets for?
answer: Roasting their beefsteak over the fire
choices: Roasting their beefsteak over the fire
Digging trenches in the snow
Trading them to local farmers
Cleaning mud off their boots
context: Von Steuben was appalled that the men used their bayonets to roast beefsteak over the campfire — or left them behind entirely. He retrained the army to charge with the bayonet as a real weapon. Source: newenglandhistoricalsociety.com/baron-von-steuben-shows-the-army-a-bayonet-is-not-a-grilling-tool/

question: The Marquis de Lafayette came to love George Washington like a father during the Revolution. Years later, Lafayette showed just how deep that devotion ran in the name he chose for his own newborn son. What did he name the boy?
answer: Georges Washington de Lafayette
choices: Georges Washington de Lafayette
Louis Capet de Lafayette
Jean Brandywine de Lafayette
Henri Yorktown de Lafayette
context: Lafayette loved Washington so much that he named his son Georges Washington de Lafayette. Source: Mount Vernon Digital Encyclopedia, 'Marquis de Lafayette' (mountvernon.org)

question: After the French fleet trapped the British at Yorktown, the towering Admiral de Grasse — six foot two — hosted George Washington at a victory dinner aboard his flagship. To the amusement of everyone, what did the French admiral keep doing to the even-taller American commander?
answer: Hugging him and calling him 'my little general'
choices: Hugging him and calling him 'my little general'
Saluting him as 'King of America'
Toasting him with twelve cannon volleys
Offering him command of the French navy
context: The 6-foot-2 Comte de Grasse repeatedly embraced the 6-foot-4 Washington aboard the Ville de Paris, calling him 'mon petit général' — my little general. Source: americanrevolution.org/degrasse.php

question: To get Congress excited about the foreign officer Benjamin Franklin was sending them, Franklin described Baron von Steuben as a Prussian 'lieutenant general' who had served Frederick the Great. The grand title was largely invented. What had von Steuben's actual top rank been?
answer: Captain and aide-de-camp
choices: Captain and aide-de-camp
Field marshal of cavalry
Colonel of the royal guard
Admiral of the Baltic fleet
context: Franklin padded the resume: von Steuben's true top rank had been captain and aide-de-camp to Frederick the Great, and even the 'Baron' title was inflated. He proved a brilliant drillmaster anyway. Source: smithsonianmag.com/history/underappreciated-true-story-prussian-military-office-whipped-patriots-into-shape-valley-forge-180987172/

question: When Confederate cannons ringing Charleston Harbor opened fire on Fort Sumter to begin the Civil War, the gunners used a fearsome trick to burn the fort down. They heated their cannonballs in ovens until the iron glowed, then fired them into Sumter's wooden buildings to set the place ablaze. What was this glowing ammunition called?
answer: Hot shot
choices: Hot shot
Grapeshot
Chain shot
Canister shot
context: Over the 34-hour bombardment beginning at 4:30 a.m. on April 12, 1861, the Confederates hurled more than 3,000 rounds at Sumter's brick walls, and the red-hot 'hot shot' set the fort's wooden barracks on fire. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/fort-sumter

question: The Civil War would become the bloodiest war in American history, yet across the entire 34-hour Confederate bombardment of Fort Sumter, not one soldier on either side was killed. The very first soldier to die in the war, Private Daniel Hough, was killed only after the fighting had already stopped. How did Hough die?
answer: An accidental cannon explosion during a salute to the flag
choices: An accidental cannon explosion during a salute to the flag
A Confederate cannonball that finally found its mark
A bullet to the chest while lowering the fort's flag
A fall from the rampart as the garrison evacuated
context: After Major Robert Anderson surrendered, his men fired a 100-gun salute to the U.S. flag. A spark set off a pile of cartridges, and the explosion killed Private Daniel Hough, the first soldier to die in the war that would kill hundreds of thousands more. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fort_Sumter

question: When Major Robert Anderson surrendered Fort Sumter in April 1861, he lowered its 33-star American flag and carried it north rather than leave it to the enemy. Exactly four years later, in April 1865, with the war won and Charleston retaken at last, Anderson came back to the ruined fort. What did he do there?
answer: Raised the very flag he had carried off in defeat
choices: Raised the very flag he had carried off in defeat
Buried the flag in the rubble where the fort stood
Cut the flag into pieces for his surviving soldiers
Donated the flag to a museum back in the North
context: On April 14, 1865, Robert Anderson hoisted the same flag over the recaptured Fort Sumter and broke down weeping, saying it had been 'the cherished wish of my heart' to restore it. Source: https://emergingcivilwar.com/2020/04/14/190026/

question: The wandering Mexica people were told by their god Huitzilopochtli to build their city wherever they spotted an eagle perched on a prickly-pear cactus. They found that exact sign on a swampy island in Lake Texcoco and founded Tenochtitlan there. Where can you still see that founding image today?
answer: On Mexico's national flag
choices: On Mexico's national flag
On the U.S. dollar bill
On the Olympic rings
On a Roman coin
context: The eagle on the prickly-pear cactus sits at the center of Mexico's flag and coat of arms, making the founding legend a living national symbol. (Legend element: the divine omen.) Source: https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/tenochtitlan/

question: Mexico's flag shows an eagle on a cactus with a snake in its beak, and everyone assumes the snake was always part of the Aztec founding legend. But the oldest Aztec pictures of the scene, like the title page of the Codex Mendoza, show no snake at all; it only crept in a couple of generations after the Spanish conquest. Scholars think the 'snake' began as a misread Aztec glyph drawn near the eagle's beak. What was that glyph?
answer: A glyph of fire-and-water, the Aztec sign for sacred war
choices: A glyph of fire-and-water, the Aztec sign for sacred war
A glyph of falling rain the priests drew beside the eagle
A ribbon of speech, the Aztec sign for a god's command
A coiled rope the eagle stood on in the older drawings
context: The snake first appears in the Codex Aubin around 1576, roughly 50 years after the conquest. Scholars think it is a misread of the atl-tlachinolli glyph (water-and-fire, the sign of sacred war), which sits near the eagle's beak and looks similar. The famous serpent is a post-Conquest add-on. Source: https://www.mexicolore.co.uk/aztecs/ask-us/eagle-and-the-snake

question: The name "United Nations" was being used during World War II, years before the UN actually existed — 26 countries fighting the Axis signed a wartime pact called the "Declaration by United Nations" on January 1, 1942. Who came up with that name?
answer: President Franklin Roosevelt of the United States coined it
choices: President Franklin Roosevelt of the United States coined it
Prime Minister Winston Churchill of Britain coined it
Marshal Joseph Stalin of the Soviet Union coined it
Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek of China coined it
context: Franklin Roosevelt coined "United Nations," and it first appeared in print in the Declaration by United Nations signed by 26 countries on January 1, 1942 — long before the UN itself was founded. Source: https://www.un.org/en/about-us/history-of-the-un/preparatory-years

question: In 1945 the new United Nations made five nations — the United States, Britain, France, China, and the Soviet Union — permanent members of its Security Council and handed them a power no other country received. What was that power?
answer: A single "no" from any one of them blocks any resolution
choices: A single "no" from any one of them blocks any resolution
A guaranteed seat for one of their generals on every mission
The right to host every Security Council meeting in turn
Permanent exemption from paying any UN membership dues
context: Each of the five permanent members got a veto: one "no" blocks a resolution no matter how many other nations agree. This "Yalta formula" was settled by the great powers at the Yalta Conference in early 1945. The great powers had refused to join any body they could be forced to act against — that was the price of getting them to join at all. Source: https://www.securitycouncilreport.org/un-security-council-working-methods/the-veto.php

question: In 1968 the Soviet Union sent tanks into Czechoslovakia to crush the "Prague Spring," and the UN Security Council voted 10 in favor of a resolution condemning the invasion and demanding the troops leave. With ten nations on one side, what happened to the resolution?
answer: The single Soviet veto killed it, and the tanks stayed
choices: The single Soviet veto killed it, and the tanks stayed
It passed, and Soviet troops withdrew within the week
It passed, but the Soviets simply ignored the order
It was tabled because China refused to take part in the vote
context: The Council voted 10-to-1, but one Soviet veto was enough to kill the resolution — exactly the limit built into the veto from the start. The same thing had happened in 1956, when the USSR vetoed action over its crushing of the Hungarian Revolution, calling it merely a "reactionary uprising," and the matter had to be pushed to the General Assembly, where no nation holds a veto. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_veto_power

question: Around 105 AD a Han court official named Cai Lun perfected paper by mashing a wet pulp, then draining it on a screen to dry into sheets. What everyday junk did he throw into that pulp?
answer: Tree bark, hemp, old rags, and worn-out fishing nets
choices: Tree bark, hemp, old rags, and worn-out fishing nets
River clay, crushed shells, sand, and powdered chalk
Sheep's wool, beeswax, animal fat, and dried reeds
Gold leaf, silk thread, jade dust, and lacquer sap
context: Cai Lun mashed bark, hemp, rags, and ragged fishing nets into pulp and drained it on a cloth screen, c. 105 AD. Making paper from cheap scraps is exactly why it could spread to everyone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cai_Lun

question: The Chinese word for gunpowder is 'huo yao.' Today, as in the beginning, it literally translates to which strange-sounding pair of words?
answer: Fire medicine
choices: Fire medicine
Black thunder
Flying sand
Sky powder
context: 'Huo yao' (火藥) means 'fire medicine' or 'fire drug' -- a fossil in the language pointing back to alchemists who were hunting a healing elixir, not a weapon. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gunpowder

question: A Chinese woodblock scroll of the Buddhist Diamond Sutra carries the exact date 11 May 868, stamped right on it. Among all books that survive, that makes it the what?
answer: World's oldest dated printed book
choices: World's oldest dated printed book
World's longest hand-copied scroll
World's first book bound with pages
World's earliest map of the heavens
context: The 5-metre Diamond Sutra scroll ends, 'reverently made for universal free distribution by Wang Jie on behalf of his two parents.' Its printed date makes it the oldest dated printed book known. Source: https://www.bl.uk/collection-items/the-diamond-sutra

question: Daoist alchemists mixing saltpeter, sulfur, and charcoal believed they were brewing an elixir that would let a person live forever. What did the mixture actually do?
answer: It exploded
choices: It exploded
It turned to gold
It froze solid
It glowed silver
context: The recipe for immortality turned out to be the recipe for gunpowder: instead of eternal life, the alchemists got fire and a blast. Source: https://www.chinaxiantour.com/xian-travel-blog/chinese-gunpowder-invention.html

question: Centuries before cannons, the very first gunpowder weapon was the Chinese 'fire lance,' first confirmed in battle at the siege of De'an in 1132. What was a fire lance, in plain terms?
answer: A bamboo tube on a pole that blasted flame into the enemy's face
choices: A bamboo tube on a pole that blasted flame into the enemy's face
A giant crossbow that hurled a barrel of burning oil
An iron ball flung over the walls by a catapult
A spinning wheel of swords pushed at charging horses
context: The huo qiang was a bamboo (or paper) tube tied to a spear that shot out a roar of flame and smoke -- the direct ancestor of the gun. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gunpowder

question: Cai Lun, the man who perfected paper, grew so rich the emperor made him a marquis -- but years later he was ordered to stand trial for an old crime. Rather than face it, what did he do?
answer: He drank poison dressed in his finest robes
choices: He drank poison dressed in his finest robes
He fled on horseback into the far mountains
He burned every sheet of paper he had made
He threw himself down before the emperor
context: Ordered to trial around 121 AD, Cai Lun bathed, put on his best clothes, and drank poison rather than be disgraced -- a quiet, deliberate end for the lord of Longting. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cai_Lun

question: Long before anyone steered a ship by it, Chinese diviners used a 'south-pointing spoon' -- a lodestone carved into a ladle and spun on a polished bronze board. What was the spoon's original job?
answer: Lining up tombs and buildings with cosmic forces
choices: Lining up tombs and buildings with cosmic forces
Guiding fishing boats safely back to shore
Measuring the passing hours of the night
Sniffing out veins of buried iron and gold
context: The 'sinan' was a fortune-telling instrument: spun on a divination board, the lodestone ladle settled pointing south, and diviners used it to align graves and halls with unseen forces -- the compass began as magic, not navigation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_compass

question: The earliest known writing about a gunpowder mixture isn't a weapon design -- it's a 9th-century Daoist text warning alchemists NOT to combine sulfur and saltpeter with honey. What did the warning say would happen if they did?
answer: It burned their hands, faces, and even their houses
choices: It burned their hands, faces, and even their houses
It crumbled away into useless gray ash
It gave off a silent and deadly poison gas
It hardened overnight into unbreakable stone
context: The Zhenyuan Miaodao Yaolue warns that 'smoke and flames result, so that their hands and faces have been burnt, and even the whole house burned down' -- the first gunpowder document is a safety warning. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhenyuan_Miaodao_Yaolue

question: For centuries China kept papermaking a guarded secret. It finally leaked out in 751 at the Battle of Talas, when an Arab Abbasid army won the fight. How did the army walk away with the secret?
answer: It captured Chinese prisoners who knew the craft
choices: It captured Chinese prisoners who knew the craft
It found the recipe written inside a stolen sutra
It was handed the method as a gift for peace
It bought the formula from a wandering merchant
context: Prisoners taken at Talas could make paper, and the first paper mill in the Islamic world soon rose at Samarkand -- from there paper crossed to Europe. Source: https://www.computersmiths.com/chineseinvention/paper.htm

question: In 1900 a monk swung open a door at Dunhuang that had been walled shut for centuries. Scholars expected maybe a small shrine; instead the cave held a hidden library of roughly how many manuscripts?
context: The sealed Dunhuang cave hid about 40,000 manuscripts, including the printed Diamond Sutra. The archaeologist Aurel Stein bought the famous scroll from the monk in 1907. Source: https://www.ancient-origins.net/artifacts-ancient-writings/diamond-sutra-oldest-known-printed-book-world-006185

question: Around 1040, four centuries before Gutenberg, a Chinese commoner named Bi Sheng built the world's first movable type -- one reusable piece for every character. What were his little pieces made of?
answer: Baked clay
choices: Baked clay
Cast bronze
Carved jade
Polished bone
context: Bi Sheng carved each character into sticky clay 'as thin as the edge of a coin,' then fired it hard so it could be used again. He chose clay over wood because wood warped and stuck in the glue. Everything we know of him comes from Shen Kuo's Dream Pool Essays. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bi_Sheng

question: The polymath Shen Kuo, in his Dream Pool Essays of 1088, gave the first description of a true magnetic-needle compass -- and spotted something no one had recorded before. What did he notice the needle did?
answer: It pointed slightly east of true north, not dead on it
choices: It pointed slightly east of true north, not dead on it
It swung harder during a thunderstorm
It lost its pull after many years of use
It pointed the opposite way below the equator
context: Shen Kuo was the first known person to record magnetic declination -- that the compass needle leans a little off true north. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shen_Kuo

question: On 1 September 1870 the French army was trapped in a valley at Sedan, ringed by hills the Germans had crowned with cannon. Rather than die fighting, Emperor Napoleon III of France raised a white flag and surrendered. When the army laid down its arms, something happened that had not happened in modern European history. What was unprecedented about this surrender?
answer: A reigning emperor was captured on the battlefield with his whole army
choices: A reigning emperor was captured on the battlefield with his whole army
A king escaped in disguise and was never found by the enemy
A peace treaty was signed before the first shot was fired
A capital city surrendered without losing a single soldier
context: Roughly 104,000 French soldiers and 558 cannon were taken prisoner, along with Napoleon III himself — the first time in modern European history a reigning emperor was captured on the battlefield with his entire army. He was sent into comfortable captivity at Schloss Wilhelmshöhe, then exile in England, where he died in 1873. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sedan; Britannica summary (ebsco.com).

question: The capture of Napoleon III at Sedan in 1870 destroyed France's Second Empire and won the war for Prussia's chancellor, Otto von Bismarck. To crown his victory, Bismarck staged the proclamation of the new German Empire — deliberately on French soil, in the grandest room of the French kings' own palace. Where did the Germans proclaim their empire?
answer: In the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles
choices: In the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles
In the throne room of the royal palace in Berlin
In the cathedral where French kings were crowned
In a captured fortress on the German border
context: On 18 January 1871 Bismarck, in a cuirassier uniform, read the proclamation in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles as Wilhelm I was hailed Kaiser on French soil. The Treaty of Frankfurt then stripped Alsace-Lorraine from France — the grievance that fed 1914 and 1919. Source: en.chateauversailles.fr/discover/history/key-dates/proclamation-german-empire-1871; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_of_the_German_Empire.

question: Frederick Douglass was born into slavery on Maryland's Eastern Shore around 1818 and was never told the day he was born. As a grown man he picked February 14 to celebrate as his birthday. Why that day?
answer: His mother had called him her 'Little Valentine'
choices: His mother had called him her 'Little Valentine'
It was the day he finally escaped to freedom
It was the day he learned to read his first word
It was the day his first newspaper went to print
context: Douglass wrote in his 1845 Narrative, 'I have no accurate knowledge of my age, never having seen any authentic record containing it.' His enslaved mother had nicknamed him her Little Valentine, so he chose Feb 14. (Britannica, Frederick Douglass; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Douglass, citing his 1845 Narrative)

question: When young Frederick Douglass was a slave in Baltimore, his enslaver Hugh Auld forbade anyone to teach him, warning that letters would 'spoil' a slave. Determined to learn anyway, what did the boy do to keep getting reading lessons?
answer: Traded his own bread to poor white boys for lessons
choices: Traded his own bread to poor white boys for lessons
Hid a spelling book under the floorboards of the kitchen
Practiced writing letters in chalk on the ship timbers
Memorized the sermons the preacher gave each Sunday
context: Sophia Auld had begun teaching him until her husband Hugh forbade it. Douglass kept learning in secret, giving bread to hungry poor white boys on Philpot Street in exchange for lessons; he called it buying 'the bread of knowledge.' (frederick-douglass-heritage.org/biography-early-life; SparkNotes, Narrative ch. VII-IX)

question: Around age twelve, Frederick Douglass spent about fifty cents he had saved shining boots on a single schoolbook. Inside it, a 'Dialogue Between a Master and Slave' — where a captured slave out-argues his owner so well the owner frees him — gave Douglass his first words for arguing his own freedom. Name the book.
answer: The Columbian Orator
choices: The Columbian Orator
The American Spelling Book
The Liberty Almanac
The Freedman's Reader
context: The Columbian Orator was a popular school reader of speeches and dialogues. Its master-and-slave dialogue, in which the slave's arguments win him his freedom, became a model for the young Douglass. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Columbian_Orator; frederickdouglasspapersproject.com, his Narrative ch. VII)

question: When the runaway Frederick Bailey reached New Bedford and needed a new last name to throw off slave-catchers, the abolitionist Nathan Johnson renamed him 'Douglass.' Johnson took the name from one of his favorite stories. Where did the name come from?
answer: A hero in Sir Walter Scott's poem 'The Lady of the Lake'
choices: A hero in Sir Walter Scott's poem 'The Lady of the Lake'
A Baltimore deacon who had once hidden the runaway
The captain of the ship that carried him north
A verse the preacher read from the book of Exodus
context: Nathan Johnson was reading Scott's poem, which features the heroic clan of Douglas, and suggested the name. Frederick Bailey became Frederick Douglass — the name under which the runaway would become world-famous. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Douglass, citing Douglass's own account)

question: On September 3, 1838, Frederick Douglass made his run for freedom, traveling by train and steamboat from Maryland to New York in about a day. How did he get past the slave-catchers watching the rail lines?
answer: He disguised himself as a free Black sailor with borrowed seaman's papers
choices: He disguised himself as a free Black sailor with borrowed seaman's papers
He hid inside a wooden shipping crate nailed shut by a friend
He waited until a snowstorm and walked the rails on foot at night
He bribed a conductor to lock him alone in a baggage car
context: Douglass wore a red shirt, a sailor's hat, and a knotted black cravat, and carried a friend's 'seaman's protection papers.' His future wife Anna Murray, a free woman, had sewn the sailor outfit and sold her own featherbed to help fund the escape. (history.com/articles/frederick-douglass-escapes-slavery; smithsonianmag.com, 'The Hidden History of Anna Murray Douglass')

question: At sixteen, Frederick Douglass was hired out to Edward Covey, a farmer paid to whip rebellious slaves into obedience. One day Douglass refused to take it and fought back, grappling with Covey for nearly two hours until the slave-breaker gave up and never whipped him again. What did Douglass call that fight?
answer: 'The turning point in my career as a slave'
choices: 'The turning point in my career as a slave'
'The first free breath of my whole life'
'The bloodiest hour I ever lived through'
'The day I lost my fear of the lash'
context: Douglass wrote the fight with Covey 'revived within me a sense of my own manhood.' Beating the man hired to break him restored his will to be free. (essentialcivilwarcurriculum.com/frederick-douglass.html; cliffsnotes.com, Narrative ch. X, quoting his 1845 Narrative)

question: In 1847 Frederick Douglass started his own antislavery newspaper in Rochester, New York. He named it after the one thing escaping slaves followed by night to find their way to freedom. What did he call the paper?
answer: The North Star
choices: The North Star
The Liberator
The Freeman's Torch
The Morning Bell
context: Runaways navigated north by the fixed North Star. The paper's masthead read: 'Right is of no Sex — Truth is of no Color — God is the Father of us all, and we are all Brethren.' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Douglass; loc.gov Frederick Douglass Timeline)

question: Frederick Douglass sat for more than 160 photographs, making him the most photographed American of the entire 1800s — ahead of even Lincoln. In almost every one he keeps a stern, unsmiling face. Why did he refuse to smile for the camera?
answer: He would not look like the grinning 'happy slave' of racist cartoons
choices: He would not look like the grinning 'happy slave' of racist cartoons
He thought a smile made a portrait look cheap and unserious
A childhood injury had left him unable to smile evenly
Photographers of the day told everyone to hold a blank face
context: Douglass deliberately used the brand-new technology of photography to broadcast Black dignity, refusing the caricature that pretended slaves were content. His 160-plus portraits beat Lincoln's 126 and Custer's 155. (npr.org/2015/12/13, 'Picture This: Frederick Douglass...'; nbcnews.com/news/nbcblk)

question: In 1852 the citizens of Rochester invited Frederick Douglass to deliver their Fourth of July oration. Douglass agreed to speak, but made one pointed choice to protest celebrating American freedom while millions were still in chains. What did he do?
answer: He gave the speech a day late, on July 5, refusing to honor the Fourth itself
choices: He gave the speech a day late, on July 5, refusing to honor the Fourth itself
He delivered it in total silence, holding up a chained man's irons
He spoke only the words of the Declaration and then walked off
He refused his fee and gave it to a fund for runaway slaves
context: On July 5, 1852, at Corinthian Hall, Douglass told the crowd: 'This Fourth of July is yours, not mine. You may rejoice, I must mourn.' He asked what the day meant to the slave and answered: 'your celebration is a sham... your shouts of liberty and equality, hollow mockery.' (constitutioncenter.org; nmaahc.si.edu, 'A Nation's Story'; americanyawp.com reader)

question: At Abraham Lincoln's second inauguration in 1865, police barred Frederick Douglass from the White House reception simply because he was Black. Douglass got word inside to the president. What did Lincoln do in front of the whole crowded room?
answer: Called out 'Here comes my friend Douglass' and asked his opinion of the speech
choices: Called out 'Here comes my friend Douglass' and asked his opinion of the speech
Quietly slipped out a side door to shake his hand in private
Sent an aide to apologize and pressed money into his hand
Pretended not to notice to spare Douglass any embarrassment
context: Lincoln told him, 'there is no man's opinion that I value more than yours,' and Douglass called the Second Inaugural 'a sacred effort.' After the assassination, Mary Todd Lincoln sent Douglass the president's own walking stick, still kept at the Frederick Douglass National Historic Site. (mrlincolnswhitehouse.org; whitehousehistory.org, 'Frederick Douglass and Abraham Lincoln')

question: Abolitionists were split over the U.S. Constitution: Frederick Douglass's own mentor, William Lloyd Garrison, publicly burned a copy and called it a 'covenant with death' — a proslavery pact best destroyed. Douglass studied it and reached a startling opposite conclusion. What did he come to argue the Constitution was?
answer: Rightly read, a 'glorious liberty document' to be turned against slavery
choices: Rightly read, a 'glorious liberty document' to be turned against slavery
A wicked bargain that honest men were bound to burn
A dead letter with no force until slavery was abolished
A foreign British relic that free Americans should discard
context: Douglass broke with Garrison, arguing the founding document should be wielded for freedom, not surrendered to slaveholders. (reason.com/2015/07/04, 'Douglass on Liberty, Slavery, and the Fourth of July'; californialawreview.org, 'Frederick Douglass and the Two Constitutions')

question: In his 1852 Fourth of July speech, Frederick Douglass called the Declaration of Independence the 'ringbolt to the chain of your nation's destiny.'
