Many in the crowd expected the famous abolitionist to denounce the founders' principles as a lie. What did he urge his listeners to do with those founding principles instead?
answer: Stand by them 'against all foes, and at whatever cost'
choices: Stand by them 'against all foes, and at whatever cost'
Scrap them and start the whole nation over
Admit they had always been an empty boast
Keep them for white citizens only, as written
context: Douglass called the Declaration's principles 'saving principles' and demanded the nation live up to them rather than abandon them — the natural-rights argument that the country must keep its own promise. (billofrightsinstitute.org, Douglass July 5 1852 speech; loveman.sdsu.edu/docs/1852FrederickDouglass.pdf)

question: In January 1610 Galileo pointed his new telescope at the planet Jupiter and, over four nights, watched four tiny points of light travel along with it as it drifted across the sky. What had he discovered?
answer: Four moons orbiting Jupiter
choices: Four moons orbiting Jupiter
Four comets passing near Jupiter
Four new planets beyond Jupiter
Four bright stars behind Jupiter
context: They were the first moons ever found circling another world — today named Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto, and still called the Galilean moons. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilean_moons

question: In March 1610 Galileo rushed a slim book into print in Venice to announce the wonders he had seen through his telescope — the first scientific work in history built entirely on telescope observations. By what name is that book known?
answer: The Starry Messenger
choices: The Starry Messenger
The Book of the Heavens
The Mirror of the Sky
The Wanderer's Almanac
context: Its Latin title was 'Sidereus Nuncius,' published March 13, 1610. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidereus_Nuncius

question: Galileo aimed his telescope at the line dividing the bright and dark halves of the Moon and saw long shadows stretching across it. Measuring those shadows, he concluded the Moon was no smooth, flawless sphere like the old teachers claimed. What did he actually see standing on it?
answer: Mountains and craters
choices: Mountains and craters
Cracks and canyons
Ridges and plains
Dunes and ash fields
context: From the shadow lengths he even estimated the lunar mountains stood about four miles high — a rugged world like Earth, overturning Aristotle's perfect heavens. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidereus_Nuncius

question: Hoping to win a powerful protector, Galileo dedicated his four newly found moons of Jupiter to the ruling family of Florence and printed their name right on his book's title page. After which family did he name those four moons?
answer: The Medici family
choices: The Medici family
The Borgia family
The Sforza family
The Visconti family
context: He called them the 'Medicean Stars,' and the flattery worked: Grand Duke Cosimo II made Galileo his court Philosopher and Mathematician. https://www.lindahall.org/about/news/scientist-of-the-day/galileo-galilei-2/

question: For ages people had called the faint glowing band across the night sky the Milky Way, but no one knew what it truly was. When Galileo turned his telescope on it, he saw something nobody had ever seen. What was the Milky Way really made of?
answer: Countless faint stars
choices: Countless faint stars
One single huge bright star
Glowing dust between the stars
Frozen crystals of ice
context: He described it as 'innumerable stars grouped in clusters' — too faint and tightly packed for the naked eye to split apart. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidereus_Nuncius

question: The hunter Orion is one of the easiest constellations to spot, and to the naked eye Galileo could count just 9 stars in it. When he raised his telescope to the same patch of sky, the number exploded. Roughly how many stars did he then count in Orion?
answer: About 80
choices: About 80
About 15
About 30
About 200
context: The Pleiades did the same: 6 stars to the naked eye became about 35 through his lens. The sky was far fuller than anyone had imagined. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidereus_Nuncius

question: In 1610 Galileo turned his telescope on Saturn and saw something so strange he wrote that the planet 'is not alone but composed of three which almost touch' — it seemed to have bumps or handles on its sides. Two years later those bumps had completely vanished, leaving him baffled. What he had glimpsed was the edge of Saturn's what?
answer: Its rings
choices: Its rings
Its moons
Its storms
Its shadow
context: Galileo's telescope was too weak to resolve them, so the rings looked like 'ears'; when Earth crossed their plane in 1612 they turned edge-on and seemed to disappear. https://www.astronomy.com/today-in-the-history-of-astronomy/july-30-1610-galileo-sees-saturns-rings/

question: Legend says that after Galileo was forced before the Inquisition to deny that the Earth moves, he rose and muttered four defiant words under his breath, insisting on the truth anyway. Which phrase is supposedly his quiet last word on the matter?
answer: 'And yet it moves'
choices: 'And yet it moves'
'God sees the truth'
'The stars do not lie'
'Time will judge me'
context: The Italian is 'Eppur si muove.' It is almost certainly a legend — Galileo's own pupil Viviani never recorded it, and it first appeared in print in 1757, over a century after his death. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/And_yet_it_moves

question: Watching the planet Venus night after night, Galileo saw it run through a full cycle of phases — crescent, half, and full — exactly like the Moon. In the old Earth-centered Ptolemaic system this was flatly impossible, so the phases proved one specific thing about Venus. What did they prove?
answer: That Venus orbits the Sun
choices: That Venus orbits the Sun
That Venus is closer than the Moon
That Venus shines with its own light
That Venus is larger than the Earth
context: Galileo first hid the discovery in a Latin anagram, later decoded as 'The Mother of Love [Venus] imitates the shapes of Cynthia [the Moon].' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phases_of_Venus

question: On June 22, 1633, the ailing, roughly 69-year-old Galileo was made to kneel before the Inquisition in Rome in a white penitential gown and read aloud an oath about the moving Earth that everyone in the room knew was forced from him. What were the words he had to speak?
answer: To curse and detest the idea Earth moves
choices: To curse and detest the idea Earth moves
To beg the Pope's forgiveness in writing
To praise the Earth-centered heavens
To deny he ever owned a telescope
context: He swore to 'abjure, curse, and detest' the belief that the Earth moves, at the convent of Santa Maria sopra Minerva. https://brunelleschi.imss.fi.it/itineraries/itinerary/TheAbjuration.html

question: Pope Urban VIII had been Galileo's friend and even encouraged his great 1632 book, asking only that his own pet argument be tucked inside it. Galileo did include it — but he gave the argument to the dull-witted character named Simplicio, the 'simpleton' who loses every debate. How did the Pope react?
answer: He felt mocked and never forgave Galileo
choices: He felt mocked and never forgave Galileo
He laughed and rewarded the joke
He demanded the book be rewritten
He ignored it and stayed Galileo's friend
context: Putting the Pope's words in a fool's mouth shattered the friendship and helped trigger the 1633 trial — the clash was as much about wounded pride and papal politics as about astronomy. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo_affair

question: After his trial Galileo was sentenced to house arrest for life at his villa near Florence, his books banned and his eyesight failing toward total blindness. Yet in those final years he finished his most important scientific work, the one whose ideas Isaac Newton would later build upon to explain how things fall and fly. What did this last book lay the foundations of?
answer: The science of motion
choices: The science of motion
The mapping of the stars
The grinding of lenses
The measuring of time
context: It was 'Discourses and Mathematical Demonstrations Relating to Two New Sciences' (1638), smuggled out and printed abroad because his writings were forbidden at home. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo_affair

question: In August 1609, Galileo Galilei led the Doge of Venice and the city's senators up the bell tower of St. Mark's and handed them his new spyglass to look out over the lagoon. Pointed at the sea, the instrument let them spot something hours before anyone watching with the naked eye could. What could they suddenly see coming?
answer: Ships still far out at sea
choices: Ships still far out at sea
Storm clouds on the horizon
Fish swimming below the surface
Stars in the daytime sky
context: The grateful Venetian Senate rewarded the 8-power instrument with a lifetime professorship at Padua and doubled Galileo's salary to 1000 florins. Source: Italy On This Day, Galileo demonstrates telescope (Aug 1609); Design World, Galileo Demonstrates Telescope to Venetian Senate.

question: In late November 1609, Galileo Galilei turned his telescope on the Moon. For centuries everyone had 'known' the Moon was a perfect, smooth, polished heavenly ball. Reading the shadows along its surface, Galileo saw the exact opposite of a smooth ball. What did he see covering the Moon?
answer: Mountains, valleys, and craters
choices: Mountains, valleys, and craters
Oceans of dark blue water
Forests of strange grey trees
A glassy, polished surface
context: Trained as a Renaissance artist in chiaroscuro (light-and-shadow shading), Galileo read the moving shadows along the terminator line as real peaks throwing shadows, proving the Moon was a rugged world like the Earth. Source: HISTORY, Galileo begins observing the moon, Nov 30 1609; Linda Hall Library, Mapping the Moon.

question: On January 7, 1610, Galileo Galilei pointed his telescope at the bright planet Jupiter and noticed three tiny 'little stars' lined up beside it. Watching night after night, by January 15 he realized they weren't stars at all — there were four of them, and they were swinging back and forth from one side of Jupiter to the other. What had he actually discovered?
answer: Four little moons circling Jupiter
choices: Four little moons circling Jupiter
A ring of dust around Jupiter
Four comets racing past Jupiter
Spots on the face of Jupiter
context: Galileo named them the 'Medicean Stars' to flatter his patron Cosimo II de' Medici; today we call them the Galilean moons (Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto). Source: NASA, 410 Years Ago: Galileo Discovers Jupiter's Moons; Museo Galileo, Sidereus Nuncius.

question: In 1737, almost a hundred years after Galileo Galilei died, his body was moved to a grand new tomb in Florence. During the move, admirers actually cut pieces off his corpse to keep as treasured relics. One of those keepsakes is still on display today in Florence, sealed inside a little gilded glass egg for visitors to see. What body part is it?
answer: His middle finger
choices: His middle finger
His right ear
His left eye
His tongue
context: Admirers cut off three fingers, a tooth, and a vertebra, joking that they were taking the parts with which 'Galileo wrote so many beautiful things.' His mummified middle finger, pointing upward in a gilded glass egg, is still displayed at the Museo Galileo in Florence. Source: Wikipedia, Galileo's middle finger; Museo Galileo, Galilean iconography and relics.

question: Galileo Galilei did not invent the telescope — the idea came from Dutch spectacle-makers — but he made far better ones by grinding his own lenses, starting at 3-power in spring 1609 and reaching 20-to-30-power by January 1610. In March 1610 he packed all his new sky discoveries into a slim Latin booklet with his own engraved drawings of the cratered Moon. It was the first scientific book in history based on telescope observations. What was it called?
answer: 'The Starry Messenger'
choices: 'The Starry Messenger'
'On the Revolutions'
'The Book of the Heavens'
'Letters on the Sun'
context: In Latin it was 'Sidereus Nuncius.' It made Galileo instantly famous across Europe. Source: Wikipedia, Sidereus Nuncius; Museo Galileo, Sidereus Nuncius facsimile.

question: When Galileo Galilei aimed his telescope at the hazy, milky band of light called the Milky Way, the blur broke apart into separate stars far too faint to see by eye. He then tested the lens on the famous little cluster called the Pleiades, where the naked eye can pick out just six stars. Through his telescope, a whole crowd of extra stars sprang into view there. How many MORE did he see?
answer: About forty more
choices: About forty more
About a dozen more
About a hundred more
About four hundred more
context: Orion told the same story, jumping from nine visible stars to about eighty through the lens. The universe was suddenly vastly more crowded than anyone had imagined. Source: Cloudy Nights, The Discoveries of Galileo Part 5; Sidereus Nuncius (Smithsonian Libraries digital edition).

question: Galileo Galilei's discovery of four moons circling Jupiter struck a quiet blow against the cosmos as everyone then pictured it. People of his day held many fixed beliefs about the heavens, and this one sight quietly broke one of them. Which long-held belief did those four little moons knock down?
answer: That every heavenly body must circle the Earth
choices: That every heavenly body must circle the Earth
That nothing in the heavens ever moves at all
That only the Sun can hold moons of its own
That every planet shines with its own light
context: Here were four objects plainly orbiting Jupiter, not the Earth — so the claim that the Earth must be the one center around which everything turns could no longer hold. Source: Linda Hall Library, Galileo Galilei (Scientist of the Day); Britannica, Telescopic discoveries.

question: Galileo Galilei's eldest daughter entered the convent of San Matteo near Florence and took the name Suor Maria Celeste. As the convent's apothecary she mixed pills and tonics from rose water, aloe, and rue to treat her ailing father, and she wrote to him constantly. Of their correspondence, 124 of her letters survived among Galileo's papers — but something about his side of it is heartbreaking. What happened to his half?
answer: All of his replies are lost
choices: All of his replies are lost
They were burned by the Inquisition
They were written in secret code
They were never written at all
context: Suor Maria Celeste's 124 letters (1623-1633) survive, but every one of Galileo's replies to his devoted daughter is gone. Source: Wikipedia, Maria Celeste; Harvard Magazine, Vita: Suor Maria Celeste.

question: In the autumn of 1610 Galileo Galilei watched the planet Venus slowly run through a full cycle of phases, just like a tiny moon — crescent, then half, then gibbous, then full and round — all while it stayed close to the Sun. Astronomers of the day argued bitterly over what path Venus really took through the sky. Galileo said his full, round Venus settled it. What did that full Venus prove?
answer: That Venus must travel around the Sun, not the Earth
choices: That Venus must travel around the Sun, not the Earth
That Venus must circle the Earth far beyond the Moon
That Venus must hang fixed forever beside the Sun
That Venus must be larger and closer than the Moon
context: Only a Venus that loops around the Sun can swing to the far side and turn its whole sunlit face toward us. It demolished Ptolemy's Earth-centered model (which could never produce a full Venus) and was the strongest physical evidence yet for Copernicus. Source: Royal Belgian Institute for Space Aeronomy, Venus phases not in line with geocentric model; Museo Galileo, Phases of Venus.

question: When Galileo Galilei made a new discovery, he wanted to lock in the credit without revealing it to rivals, so he sent fellow astronomers a deliberately jumbled line of Latin. Unscrambled, it announced his result in a single poetic sentence. What did that hidden message actually say?
answer: That Venus imitates the shapes of the Moon
choices: That Venus imitates the shapes of the Moon
That the Moon borrows its light from Venus
That Venus burns brighter than any fixed star
That Venus and the Sun share one orbit
context: Galileo had discovered the phases of Venus. Unscrambled, his Latin read 'Cynthiae figuras aemulatur mater amorum' — 'The mother of love [Venus] imitates the shapes of Cynthia [the Moon].' Source: Rutgers Physics, Galileo Galilei's Anagram; The Renaissance Mathematicus, Phases of Venus.

question: Galileo Galilei's telescope was too weak to make out the rings of Saturn clearly, so when he saw a bulge sticking out on each side of the planet he thought Saturn had two companions stuck to it. Hiding the find in yet another scrambled-Latin anagram, what funny name did he give those two mysterious bulges?
answer: Its 'ears'
choices: Its 'ears'
Its 'horns'
Its 'wings'
Its 'twins'
context: Galileo thought Saturn was 'triple-bodied'; his anagram spelled 'Altissimum planetam tergeminum observavi.' Kepler misread the same anagram as 'Mars has two moons' — wrong, but by luck Mars really does. Source: Wikipedia, Rings of Saturn; ScienceBlogs/Uncertain Principles, Advent Calendar of Science Stories 10.

question: In 1632 Galileo Galilei published his 'Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems,' written as a debate among three characters. He took one man's own favorite argument against a moving Earth and put it word-for-word into the mouth of a foolish character named Simplicio, making it look ridiculous. That man, once Galileo's friend, felt personally mocked — and his fury helped trigger the trial. Whose argument did Galileo hand to the fool?
answer: Pope Urban VIII's
choices: Pope Urban VIII's
Cardinal Bellarmine's
Ptolemy's
Aristotle's
context: Putting Pope Urban VIII's own anti-Copernican argument in the mouth of 'Simplicio' (literally 'Simpleton') turned a science book into a personal insult, and that wound helped trigger the trial as much as the doctrine did. Source: Wikipedia, Galileo affair; EBSCO Research Starters, Galileo's Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems.

question: On June 22, 1633, a 68-year-old Galileo Galilei was made to kneel in a Roman convent, having been questioned under the threat of torture and found 'vehemently suspect of heresy.' Forced to read a statement aloud, he had to swear that he 'abjured, cursed, and detested' a particular idea. Which idea did the Church force him to renounce?
answer: That the Earth moves around the Sun
choices: That the Earth moves around the Sun
That the Moon has mountains on it
That the stars are too many to count
That Jupiter has four moons
context: At the convent of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, Galileo had to curse and detest the idea that the Earth moves around the Sun — the very thing his telescope had given him reason to believe. Source: Wikipedia, Galileo affair; Documents in the Case of Galileo (Ohio State, Abjuration 1633).

question: Legend says that the very moment Galileo Galilei rose from his knees after being forced to deny that the Earth moves, he muttered a defiant little phrase under his breath. There is no contemporary proof he ever said it; the story only appears about a century after his death. What are those famous defiant words said to be?
answer: 'And yet it moves'
choices: 'And yet it moves'
'Still the stars turn'
'God sees the truth'
'The light remains'
context: In Italian, 'Eppur si muove.' No contemporary evidence shows Galileo said it — but tellingly, a 1640s painting attributed to Murillo already shows the phrase scrawled on a dungeon wall behind him. Source: Wikipedia, Galileo affair ('Eppur si muove' legend, Murillo painting).

question: After his trial, Galileo Galilei was sentenced to house arrest at his villa near Florence, old and going blind, and forbidden to publish. Yet he secretly finished one last masterpiece, on motion and the strength of materials, called 'Two New Sciences.' To get it printed, friends had to do something risky with the manuscript to put it beyond the Inquisition's reach. What did they do?
answer: Smuggled it out of Italy to be printed abroad
choices: Smuggled it out of Italy to be printed abroad
Buried it until the Pope had died
Read it aloud in secret meetings
Hid it inside a religious prayer book
context: Friends smuggled the manuscript to Leiden, Holland, where the Elzevir Press printed it in 1638, beyond the reach of the Inquisition. Source: Wikipedia, Two New Sciences; High Altitude Observatory, Galileo Galilei.

question: Galileo Galilei was condemned at his trial in 1633, but the Catholic Church left the case officially unsettled for generation after generation. Not until 1992 did Pope John Paul II stand up in public and admit the churchmen of Galileo's time had been wrong to demand a strictly literal reading of Scripture, and that Galileo had been right all along about the Sun and the Earth. How long did the Church take to formally admit its error?
answer: 359 years
choices: 359 years
About 50 years
About 150 years
About 700 years
context: From the 1633 condemnation to the 1992 acknowledgment was 359 years. Pope John Paul II conceded that Galileo was right that the Sun, not the Earth, sits at the center. Source: Wikipedia, Galileo affair (1992 John Paul II acknowledgment).

question: In December 1915 the Allies wanted to slip away from Gallipoli at night without the Turks noticing the trenches had emptied. Australian Lance Corporal William Scurry rigged two stacked kerosene tins so water dripping from the top tin into the bottom one slowly grew heavy enough to pull a rifle's trigger by itself. What was Scurry's contraption called?
answer: The drip rifle
choices: The drip rifle
The trench mortar
The smoke screen
The dummy sentry
context: Scurry's 'drip rifle' let abandoned trenches keep firing on their own after the men had crept away, helping screen the secret withdrawal. Source: https://www.awm.gov.au/articles/encyclopedia/gallipoli/drip_rifle

question: As Australian and New Zealand troops scrambled up the cliffs at Anzac Cove on 25 April 1915, the Ottoman commander Mustafa Kemal threw his 57th Regiment straight at them, knowing most would not survive. According to the words remembered from that moment, what did Kemal tell his men he was ordering them to do?
answer: To die where they stood so reinforcements had time to arrive
choices: To die where they stood so reinforcements had time to arrive
To hold the ridge until the very last bullet was spent
To charge downhill and drive the invaders back into the sea
To dig in deep and wait for the enemy guns to fall silent
context: Kemal's order is remembered as: 'Men, I am not ordering you to attack. I am ordering you to die. In the time it takes us to die, other forces and commanders can come and take our place.' He later became Ataturk, founder of modern Turkey. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landing_at_Anzac_Cove

question: In March 1930, the 61-year-old Mohandas Gandhi set out from his ashram and walked 240 miles over 24 days to the seaside village of Dandi. He was protesting a British law that made it a crime for Indians to collect or sell one cheap, everyday thing for themselves. What was that everyday thing?
answer: Salt
choices: Salt
Tea
Cloth
Sugar
context: Gandhi argued, 'Next to air and water, salt is perhaps the greatest necessity of life,' so a tax on it crushed the poorest Indians hardest. The British Salt Act made it illegal for Indians to gather or sell their own salt. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_March

question: At dawn on 6 April 1930, after a 240-mile march to the sea at Dandi, Mohandas Gandhi waded into the surf, bent down, and picked up a lump of natural salt from the mud — breaking British law on the spot. As he held it up, what did he declare he was doing with that one handful of salt?
answer: 'With this, I am shaking the foundations of the British Empire'
choices: 'With this, I am shaking the foundations of the British Empire'
'Today the salt of India belongs again to the people of India'
'Let the Viceroy answer now for the hunger of the poor'
'This grain of salt is worth more than all their guns'
context: He then boiled the mud-salt in seawater to make illegal salt. A single pinch he made at Dandi was later auctioned for 1,600 rupees (about $750) — a worthless clump turned into a precious relic of defiance. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_March

question: Mohandas Gandhi coined a name for his method of resistance, building it from two Sanskrit words — 'satya' (truth) and 'agraha' (firmness, or holding). The march to make salt, where protesters broke the law openly but never lifted a hand to fight back, was an example of it. What did this word he invented literally mean?
answer: 'Holding firmly to truth'
choices: 'Holding firmly to truth'
'The patience of the poor'
'Rule by our own hands'
'Peace without surrender'
context: The word is satyagraha, often translated 'truth-force.' Gandhi built it himself from satya (truth) and agraha (firmness). Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/satyagraha-philosophy

question: On 21 May 1930, about 2,500 of Gandhi's followers walked in rows toward the Dharasana Salt Works and let waiting police club them down without raising an arm to defend themselves. The American reporter Webb Miller stood watching and put the scene into one unforgettable line that ran in some 1,350 newspapers worldwide. How did he describe the way the marchers fell?
answer: 'They went down like ten-pins'
choices: 'They went down like ten-pins'
'They fell as quietly as snow'
'They dropped like wheat before the scythe'
'They sank without a single cry'
context: Miller wrote, 'Not one of the marchers even raised an arm to fend off the blows. They went down like ten-pins.' British telegraph operators first censored his dispatch; he counted 2 dead and roughly 320 wounded, many with fractured skulls, none of whom fought back. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dharasana_Satyagraha

question: One of the most repeated sayings credited to Mohandas Gandhi is 'An eye for an eye leaves the whole world blind.' When historians went looking for it in Gandhi's actual letters, speeches, and writings, what did they discover about this famous line?
answer: No record of Gandhi ever saying or writing it has been found
choices: No record of Gandhi ever saying or writing it has been found
Gandhi first said it to the Viceroy before the Salt March
Gandhi borrowed it word-for-word from an ancient Sanskrit text
Gandhi wrote it in a letter from prison after Dharasana
context: The line seems to trace to biographer Louis Fischer paraphrasing Gandhi's philosophy, not to Gandhi himself — a teachable misattribution rather than a documented quote. Source: https://quoteinvestigator.com/2010/12/27/eye-for-eye-blind/  (Legend.)

question: Gandhi went looking for one weapon to use against the British Empire — something so ordinary that every Indian needed it, rich or poor, Hindu or Muslim, yet the British forced them to buy it from the government and pay a tax on it. He picked the humblest thing he could think of. What did Gandhi choose as his weapon?
answer: Salt
choices: Salt
Cloth
Bread
Lamp oil
context: Indians were forbidden by the Salt Act to gather salt from their own seashore; they had to buy taxed British salt. Gandhi said, 'Next to air and water, salt is perhaps the greatest necessity of life' — which is exactly why a tax on it touched everyone. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_March; history.com/articles/salt-march)

question: To break the salt law without firing a shot, 61-year-old Gandhi set out walking to the sea, with just 78 chosen followers stepping along behind one old man — a tiny band against the whole British Empire. But every night he stopped in a new village to speak against the salt tax, and people joined. By the time Gandhi reached the coast at Dandi, what had that little band of 78 become?
answer: A marching column more than two miles long
choices: A marching column more than two miles long
A handful who quietly turned back home
A few hundred guarded by armed soldiers
A crowd that waited at the shore instead of walking
context: The 24-day march (12 March to 6 April 1930) ran about 240 miles from the Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi, roughly 10–12 miles a day. He started with 78 followers; by the sea the procession was more than three kilometres — nearly two miles — long, and the protest he triggered led to over 60,000 Indians being arrested. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_March; britannica.com/event/Salt-March)

question: At 8:30 in the morning on 6 April 1930, after his long walk to the sea, Gandhi waded onto the wet sand at Dandi, reached down, and lifted a single lump of salty mud. He held it over his head in front of the watching crowd. What did Gandhi declare as he held it up?
answer: "With this, I am shaking the foundations of the British Empire."
choices: "With this, I am shaking the foundations of the British Empire."
"Today the sea itself has joined our struggle."
"Let the King come and take this salt from my hand."
"This grain of salt is worth more than English gold."
context: British officials had tried to cheat him by grinding the seashore salt back into the sand so he couldn't pick any up — but he easily found a salt-crusted lump and raised it in triumph. The protest he triggered led to over 60,000 Indians being arrested, Gandhi included. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_March; history.com/articles/gandhi-salt-march-india-british-colonial-rule)

question: Gandhi had a one-word name for his method: refuse to obey an unjust law, refuse to strike back when you are punished for it, and accept the jail or the blows without ever raising a hand — and beat an empire that way without a single weapon. What was Gandhi's name for this method?
answer: Satyagraha
choices: Satyagraha
Swaraj
Ahimsa
Khadi
context: Satyagraha means 'truth-force' or 'soul-force.' (Swaraj meant self-rule; ahimsa was the broader principle of non-violence; khadi was the homespun cloth Indians wove to boycott British goods.) (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_March; mkgandhi.org/articles/salt_satya.php)

question: After Gandhi was jailed, 2,500 unarmed Indians marched on the Dharasana Salt Works, where police waited with steel-tipped clubs. The American reporter Webb Miller watched row after row of marchers walk straight into the blows. In eighteen years across twenty-two countries he had never seen anything like it — above all because of one thing not a single marcher did, even as the clubs cracked down on their skulls. What did not one marcher do?
answer: Raise an arm to block the blows
choices: Raise an arm to block the blows
Cry out for mercy
Break ranks and run
Shout back at the police
context: Miller wrote, 'I heard the sickening whacks of the clubs on unprotected skulls... They went down like ten-pins,' and counted 320 wounded and 2 dead with not one arm lifted to deflect a blow. The poet Sarojini Naidu had told the marchers beforehand: 'You will be beaten, but you must not resist; you must not even raise a hand to ward off the blows.' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dharasana_Satyagraha)

question: Less than a year after a half-naked Gandhi picked up his lump of salt, the British Viceroy Lord Irwin sat down and signed a pact with him as an equal — the first time the Empire bargained with the Indian Congress that way. Winston Churchill was disgusted that Britain would even talk to Gandhi, and sneered at him with a phrase Indians then wore as a badge of honour. What did Churchill call Gandhi?
answer: A "half-naked fakir" striding up the Viceroy's steps
choices: A "half-naked fakir" striding up the Viceroy's steps
A "barefoot lawyer playing at saints"
A "spinning-wheel rebel" who fooled the crowds
A "penniless pilgrim" begging for an empire
context: Churchill called it 'the nauseating and humiliating spectacle of this one-time Inner Temple lawyer, now seditious fakir, striding half-naked up the steps of the Viceroy's palace... to parley on equal terms with the representative of the King-Emperor.' The Gandhi–Irwin Pact was signed 5 March 1931, and the 'half-naked fakir' insult became Gandhi's badge of honour. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gandhi%E2%80%93Irwin_Pact; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_March)

question: The conqueror the world remembers as Genghis Khan was not born with that name. Around 1162 a boy was born on the Mongolian steppe and named after a Tatar chieftain his father had just defeated in battle. What was that boy's birth name?
answer: Temujin
choices: Temujin
Subutai
Yesugei
Inalchuq
context: He was born Temujin (Temüjin) around 1162, named for a captured Tatar enemy. 'Genghis Khan' came only as a title in 1206. Source: worldhistory.org/Genghis_Khan and britannica.com/biography/Genghis-Khan

question: By the time Genghis Khan and his heirs were done, the Mongol Empire stretched from the Sea of Japan to eastern Europe and covered about a fifth of all the land on Earth. In one respect it still holds the all-time record. What record?
answer: The largest contiguous land empire ever
choices: The largest contiguous land empire ever
The first empire to circle the whole globe
The longest-lasting empire in history
The first empire with a written constitution
context: At its peak it covered about 9 million square miles (~23 million sq km) of unbroken territory — the largest contiguous land empire that has ever existed. Source: britannica.com/place/Mongol-empire and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_Empire  (Legend.)

question: Mongol tradition tells a strange omen about the infant Temujin, the boy who would grow up to be Genghis Khan: when he was born, his tiny fist was already clenched shut around something. According to the legend, what was the newborn gripping in his hand?
answer: A clot of blood
choices: A clot of blood
A shard of bone
A lock of black hair
A scrap of gold cloth
context: The Secret History of the Mongols tradition says he was born clutching a blood clot — read as a sign he would shed blood and rule. Told here as legend, not fact. Source: worldhistory.org/Genghis_Khan

question: When Temujin — the future Genghis Khan — was about nine, his father Yesugei accepted a meal from some Tatars on the road, and they poisoned him for an old grudge. With the father dead, what did his own clan do to the widow and her young children?
answer: Abandoned them on the open steppe to die
choices: Abandoned them on the open steppe to die
Sold them into slavery to a rival tribe
Took them in and raised them as their own
Handed them over to the Tatars as hostages
context: After Tatars poisoned Yesugei, the clan deserted his widow and children, expecting them to perish. The future conqueror of the world grew up an outcast. Source: worldhistory.org/Genghis_Khan and history.com/articles/genghis-khan

question: Early in his rise, the man not yet called Genghis Khan suffered a humiliating blow: a rival tribe, the Merkits, raided his camp and carried off his wife Borte. Rather than accept the loss, what did he do that first made other men want to follow him?
answer: Gathered allies and led a raid to rescue her
choices: Gathered allies and led a raid to rescue her
Paid the Merkits a ransom in horses and gold
Challenged the Merkit chief to single combat
Swore off marriage and vowed lifelong revenge
context: He rallied allies and struck back to recover Borte — a defining moment in his climb and the start of his reputation as a leader men would follow. Source: history.com/articles/genghis-khan and worldhistory.org/Genghis_Khan

question: At a battle in 1202, an enemy archer shot Genghis Khan's horse out from under him with a single arrow. Later the man was captured, and instead of denying it he openly confessed he was the one who fired and offered to serve faithfully. What did Genghis Khan do with the archer who had nearly killed him?
answer: Made him one of his top generals
choices: Made him one of his top generals
Had him shot with arrows in return
Set him free but banished him forever
Kept him as a stable hand for life
context: Genghis spared the archer Jirqo'adai, renamed him Jebe ('the Arrow'), and made him a leading commander — he promoted men by ability, not birth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jebe

question: The Mongol war on the Khwarezmian Empire began over a trade caravan. In 1218 a governor accused about 450 Mongol merchants of spying and had them all killed. Genghis Khan sent envoys demanding justice — and the Khwarezmian Sultan answered in a way that left no path but war. What did the Sultan do to the ambassadors?
answer: Beheaded the chief envoy and shaved the others' beards
choices: Beheaded the chief envoy and shaved the others' beards
Threw all of the envoys into a desert prison
Sent them home with chests of silver and apologies
Forced them to convert before releasing them
context: After the Otrar massacre, the Sultan beheaded the lead ambassador and shaved the beards of the rest — a deliberate insult that unleashed the invasion of Khwarezmia. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otrar_Catastrophe and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inalchuq

question: In February 1220 Genghis Khan rode into the conquered city of Bukhara, climbed into the pulpit of the great Friday mosque, and addressed the terrified people. The Persian chronicler Juvayni recorded the words. How did Genghis Khan describe himself to the crowd?
answer: As the punishment God had sent for their sins
choices: As the punishment God had sent for their sins
As a humble guest who came only to trade
As the rightful heir of their fallen Sultan
As a prophet bringing a new and final law
context: He told them: 'I am the punishment of God. If you had not committed great sins, God would not have sent a punishment like me upon you.' Recorded by Ata-Malik Juvayni. Source: en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Genghis_Khan and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Bukhara

question: The city of Nishapur was destroyed in April 1221 in revenge: an arrow from its walls had killed Toquchar, Genghis Khan's own son-in-law. The Mongols, led by his son Tolui, killed almost the entire population and then did something with the severed heads meant to terrify everyone who came after. What did they do?
answer: Stacked the heads into three great pyramids
choices: Stacked the heads into three great pyramids
Mounted the heads on spears along the road
Threw the heads into the city's wells
Carried the heads back to Genghis as proof
context: The dead — men, women, and children — had their heads piled into three separate pyramids; only about 400 craftsmen were spared. Modern historians estimate 100,000–200,000 killed. Among the dead was the great Persian poet Attar of Nishapur. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Nishapur_(1221)

question: Across the vast Mongol Empire, messengers could cover an astonishing 120 to 190 miles in a single day on horseback, because relay stations stood every 25 to 30 miles with fresh horses always waiting. At its height this network used over 50,000 horses. What was this horseback postal relay called?
answer: The yam
choices: The yam
The paiza
The kurultai
The Yassa
context: The yam relay let a rider hand off to a fresh mount every 25–30 miles, so news crossed the empire at up to ~190 miles a day. (Greatly expanded by Genghis's successor Ogedei from 1234.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yam_(route) and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pax_Mongolica

question: Genghis Khan died in August 1227 while campaigning in the Tangut kingdom, and to this day no one has found his grave. According to Mongol legend, his funeral escort guarded the secret of its location in a chillingly thorough way. What does the legend say the escort did?
answer: Killed everyone they met on the road to the grave
choices: Killed everyone they met on the road to the grave
Burned every map that showed the route
Took a vow of silence and were never seen again
Built a hundred false tombs to confuse searchers
context: Legend (no forensic proof) says the escort killed all they encountered and diverted a river over the grave; the Burkhan Khaldun region became 'Ikh Khorig,' the Great Taboo, sealed on pain of death. Told here as legend. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burial_place_of_Genghis_Khan

question: The Mongol conquest of Persia was not just a string of battles but a true demographic catastrophe, because every town that resisted was wiped out and famine followed the massacres. By one widely cited estimate, Persia's population of about 2,500,000 was reduced to roughly what figure?
answer: About 250,000
choices: About 250,000
About 900,000
context: One cited estimate puts the fall at 2,500,000 down to 250,000 — a tenth — through massacre and famine (the Persia figures are contested). Overall Mongol-conquest death tolls run from ~30 million to 40–60 million. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destruction_under_the_Mongol_Empire

question: Two of Genghis Khan's generals, Jebe and Subutai, took a single army on a scouting expedition that became one of the greatest cavalry feats in history: out of Central Asia, across northern Persia, through the Caucasus, onto the steppe to crush a Rus'–Kipchak army at the Kalka River in 1223, and then all the way home. Roughly how far did that one ride cover?
answer: More than 5,500 miles
choices: More than 5,500 miles
More than 1,200 miles
More than 800 miles
More than 3,000 miles
context: Jebe and Subutai rode over 5,500 miles in about three years, crushing the Rus'–Kipchak coalition at the Battle of the Kalka River on 31 May 1223 before returning home. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subutai and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Kalka_River

question: In 2003 geneticists (Zerjal et al.) discovered a single Y-chromosome lineage carried by about 8% of men across a huge stretch of Asia — and proposed it traced back to Genghis Khan and his sons. Scaled to the whole male population of Earth, roughly how many men alive today share that one lineage?
answer: About 1 in 200 men
choices: About 1 in 200 men
About 1 in 10 men
About 1 in 5,000 men
About 1 in a million men
context: The lineage is carried by roughly 0.5% of all men on Earth — about 16 million people. Later researchers argue it may come from ordinary Mongol warriors rather than Genghis himself, so the direct link is debated. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_descent_from_Genghis_Khan

question: By the end of 1783 George Washington had led America to victory in the Revolutionary War, and he was the most powerful and beloved man in the new country. Right at that peak, he rode hard for his Virginia home, Mount Vernon, arriving on Christmas Eve. What did Washington go home to become?
answer: a farmer working his own fields
choices: a farmer working his own fields
a king crowned by his officers
a general still leading the army
a governor ruling all Virginia
context: He spent Christmas as a private citizen tending his land rather than as a general. This image of the war hero choosing the plow over power became one of the most admired things about him. Source: Wikipedia, 'George Washington's resignation as commander-in-chief'; American Revolution Institute, 'The American Cincinnatus'.

question: When the Revolutionary War was won, General George Washington held the most dangerous thing in the new country: command of its only army. On December 23, 1783, he walked into Congress at Annapolis, Maryland, and stunned the world. What did Washington do with that power?
answer: handed it back to Congress and went home
choices: handed it back to Congress and went home
used it to make himself the new king
kept the army under his own command
demanded that Congress pay him for it
context: He told Congress, 'Having now finished the work assigned me, I retire from the great theatre of Action,' surrendered his commission, and left as a private citizen. Generals who win wars almost never give the power back. Source: Mount Vernon Digital Encyclopedia, 'Resignation of Military Commission'; Wikipedia, 'George Washington's resignation as commander-in-chief'.

question: Because George Washington won a war while holding nearly absolute power and then gave it all up to return to farming, Americans compared him to a famous figure from ancient times who had done the very same thing: called from his plow to lead Rome's army with a dictator's powers, he won the war and then immediately surrendered that power and went back to his fields. Whom did they call Washington?
answer: the American Cincinnatus
choices: the American Cincinnatus
the American Caesar
the American Augustus
the American Hannibal
context: Cincinnatus was the Roman who took total power only to win a war, then handed it back the moment victory came. Washington's officers were so moved by the parallel that they founded the Society of the Cincinnati in his honor. Source: American Revolution Institute, 'The American Cincinnatus'.

question: When King George III of Britain heard that George Washington planned to give up his power and go home to his farm rather than rule the country he had just won, the king reportedly weighed what that would make Washington. According to a story passed down from an American-born court painter, what did George III say about him?
answer: "he will be the greatest man in the world"
choices: "he will be the greatest man in the world"
"he will seize a crown before long"
"he is the boldest traitor of the age"
"he will not last a year at the plow"
context: This treasured anecdote comes from the painter Benjamin West, who told it second-hand; one 1797 version has the king calling Washington 'the greatest character of the age,' so it is a cherished story, not a verified word-for-word royal quote. Source: Library of Congress, 'The Two Georges' exhibition and Unfolding History blog, 'George Washington, "The Greatest Man in the World"?'.  (Legend.)

question: In March 1783 at Newburgh, New York, angry and unpaid officers of the Continental Army were ready to march on Congress, and George Washington came in person to stop them. His prepared speech was not winning them over. Then he did one small, unplanned thing that broke the whole room: hardened soldiers began to weep, and the mutiny collapsed. What did Washington do?
answer: put on a pair of reading glasses no one knew he needed
choices: put on a pair of reading glasses no one knew he needed
drew his sword and dared them to strike him down
tore off his war medals and flung them to the floor
read aloud the names of the men who had died
context: As he fumbled with the spectacles, Washington said, 'Gentlemen, you will permit me to put on my spectacles, for I have not only grown gray but almost blind in the service of my country.' Seeing this private weakness from their commander, the officers wept and abandoned the plot. Source: Wikipedia, 'Newburgh Conspiracy'; Mount Vernon Digital Encyclopedia, 'Newburgh Address'.

question: In 1782, Colonel Lewis Nicola wrote to George Washington with a bold idea: the army was unhappy and the country was shaky, so Washington should make himself king. Washington wrote back the same day. What did he tell Nicola to do with the idea?
answer: to banish such thoughts from his mind forever
choices: to banish such thoughts from his mind forever
to gather the officers and prepare a crown
to keep the plan secret until the time was right
to put the question before Congress instead
context: Washington said he must 'view with abhorrence, and reprehend with severity' the idea, calling it 'big with the greatest mischiefs that can befall my Country.' He flatly refused the crown. Source: Founders Online, 'From George Washington to Lewis Nicola, 22 May 1782'.

question: When the brand-new United States held its very first presidential election in 1789, George Washington won in a way no other president ever has — and then it happened a second time in 1792. How did Washington win?
answer: unanimously, with every single elector voting for him
choices: unanimously, with every single elector voting for him
by a single electoral vote over his rival
only after the House broke a deadlock
by sweeping every state except his own
context: He took all 69 electoral votes in 1789 and all 132 in 1792. No one campaigned against him because everyone wanted him; he remains the only president ever elected unanimously by the Electoral College. Source: Mount Vernon Digital Encyclopedia, 'Presidential Election of 1789'; Britannica, 'United States presidential election of 1789'.

question: George Washington stepped down after two terms as president in 1796, and for the next 150 years every single president who followed did the same — none sought a third term. Here is the strange part: through all those years, what actually forced presidents to stop at two terms?
answer: nothing but Washington's own example
choices: nothing but Washington's own example
a clause in the original Constitution
a law that Congress had passed
an oath sworn at each inauguration
context: No law required it. Washington simply declined a third term in his 1796 Farewell Address, and his example alone held for over a century and a half, until the two-term limit was finally written into the Constitution as the 22nd Amendment in 1951. Source: Mount Vernon Digital Encyclopedia, 'George Washington's Farewell Address'; U.S. State Department Office of the Historian, 'Washington's Farewell Address, 1796'.

question: Every American kid hears the story of young George Washington chopping down his father's cherry tree and bravely confessing, 'I cannot tell a lie.' But Mount Vernon and historians say it never happened. So where did this beloved tale actually come from?
answer: a preacher invented it to sell more biographies
choices: a preacher invented it to sell more biographies
Washington himself told it in his old age
his mother wrote it down in a family diary
British newspapers printed it to mock him
context: A traveling preacher and bookseller named Mason Locke 'Parson' Weems added the cherry-tree scene to the 5th edition of his Washington biography in 1806 to sell copies and teach children virtue. There is no evidence it ever happened. Source: Mount Vernon Digital Encyclopedia, 'Cherry Tree Myth'; National Park Service, 'George Washington and the Cherry Tree'.  (Legend.)

question: George Washington caught a violent throat infection in December 1799 after riding for hours across his farms through snow and sleet. As he lay dying at Mount Vernon, his doctors drained almost half his blood, but nothing helped. Knowing the end was near, Washington gave his secretary one strange, specific instruction about his own body. What did he demand?
answer: that they wait three days before burying him
choices: that they wait three days before burying him
that his heart be buried beside his mother
that no doctor be allowed near him again
that he be buried in his old army uniform
context: Washington was terrified of being buried alive, so he told his secretary Tobias Lear to wait three days. His doctors had drained roughly 40 percent of his blood trying to cure what was likely epiglottitis, and his last words were 'Tis well.' Source: Mount Vernon, 'Death of George Washington' and '8 Facts About George Washington's Death'.

question: George Washington enslaved people at Mount Vernon his entire adult life; in 1799 the estate held 317 enslaved men, women, and children. Of the early presidents who enslaved people, Washington alone did one thing with the 123 he personally owned that none of the others did. What did he do?
answer: ordered them freed in his will
choices: ordered them freed in his will
freed them the day he became president
sold them all before he died
left them to his nephews in his will
context: Washington directed that the 123 he owned be freed after Martha's death, making him the only slaveholding early president to free all of his own enslaved people. He could not legally free the other 153 'dower' slaves tied to the Custis estate. The virtue and this contradiction are part of the same honest record. Source: Mount Vernon, 'Ten Facts About Washington & Slavery' and 'A Decision to Free His Slaves'.

question: Among all the people George Washington enslaved at Mount Vernon, his will singled out one man for special treatment, set apart from everyone else. That man was William 'Billy' Lee, the enslaved valet who had ridden at Washington's side through the entire Revolutionary War. Alone among them all, what did Billy Lee receive?
answer: his freedom at once and a yearly pension
choices: his freedom at once and a yearly pension
a parcel of land near Mount Vernon
a fine horse from the general's stable
a letter of thanks and nothing more
context: Lee was freed immediately and granted $30 a year for life 'as a testimony of my sense of his attachment to me, and for his faithful services during the Revolutionary War.' Source: Wikipedia, 'William Lee (valet)'; Mount Vernon, 'Slavery and George Washington's Will'.

question: George Washington owned many enslaved people at Mount Vernon, but two of them refused to wait for any master's permission to be free. Martha Washington's expert seamstress, Ona Judge, and the household's celebrated cook, Hercules Posey, each won their own freedom while Washington was still alive and still the most powerful man in the country. How did Ona Judge and Hercules Posey become free?
answer: they ran away and were never recaptured
choices: they ran away and were never recaptured
they bought their freedom with saved wages
they petitioned a court and won release
they were freed early in Washington's will
context: Ona Judge escaped in 1796 and Hercules Posey escaped in 1797. Despite Washington's efforts to recover them, both eluded recapture and lived out their lives free. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ona Judge'; Zinn Education Project, 'Hercules Escapes from Enslavement by George Washington'.

question: Otto von Bismarck welded the scattered German states into one empire by deliberately starting three short wars in a row, each one to knock out a rival to Prussia's leadership. Which three countries did Prussia fight, in order?
answer: Denmark, then Austria, then France
choices: Denmark, then Austria, then France
Poland, then Russia, then Britain
France, then Spain, then Italy
Austria, then Russia, then Turkey
context: Bismarck engineered the wars against Denmark (1864), Austria (1866), and France (1870-71) as a planned sequence, each designed to remove a rival to Prussian leadership of the German states. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Koniggratz ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War

question: In January 1871, with German armies besieging Paris, Bismarck proclaimed the new German Empire not in Berlin but inside the palace of the French kings. In which famous room did he stage the ceremony to humiliate France on the site of its greatest glory?
answer: The Hall of Mirrors at Versailles
choices: The Hall of Mirrors at Versailles
The throne room of the Louvre
Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris
The great hall of the Bastille
context: The German Empire was proclaimed on 18 January 1871 in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, Louis XIV's own palace, while German armies besieged Paris. Bismarck chose the spot deliberately to take revenge on France on the site of its greatest glory. Source: https://en.chateauversailles.fr/discover/history/key-dates/proclamation-german-empire-1871

question: Defending the king's army budget before Prussia's parliament in 1862, Bismarck warned that the great questions of the day would not be settled by speeches and majority votes but by something far harsher. What two things did he say would decide them, in the pairing the world came to remember?
answer: Blood and iron
choices: Blood and iron
Faith and fire
Gold and steel
Sword and crown
context: Bismarck actually said 'iron and blood' (Eisen und Blut) on 30 September 1862, calling speeches and majority votes 'the great mistake of 1848 and 1849.' The catchier flipped order, 'blood and iron' (Blut und Eisen), is the version that stuck and earned him the nickname 'the Iron Chancellor.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_and_Iron_(speech)

question: At the Battle of Koniggraetz in 1866, Prussian infantry could fire ten to twelve rounds a minute while lying flat on the ground, while Austrians had to stand up to ram a charge down their muzzle-loaders. What gave the Prussians this roughly five-to-one edge in firepower?
answer: The breech-loading 'needle gun'
choices: The breech-loading 'needle gun'
Heavier cavalry armor
Repeating revolver pistols
Steel-tipped bayonets
context: The Dreyse 'needle gun' loaded at the breech, so a Prussian soldier could fire lying down about five shots to every Austrian one. At Koniggraetz (3 July 1866) Austria lost about 45,000 men, Prussia fewer than 10,000. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dreyse_needle_gun ; https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Koniggratz

question: In July 1870 Bismarck took a telegram his king had sent from Bad Ems and trimmed its wording until a polite report read like a curt insult to France's ambassador. He told his dinner guests the edited version would act like 'a red rag upon the Gallic bull.' What did this doctored message accomplish within six days?
answer: France declared war on Prussia
choices: France declared war on Prussia
Austria rejoined the German states
The French king abdicated his throne
Britain entered the war on Prussia's side
context: By shortening the Ems Dispatch, Bismarck made a parley sound like a challenge. Moltke said the edited version 'sounded before like a parley; now it is like a flourish in answer to a challenge.' France declared war six days later, exactly as Bismarck intended. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ems_dispatch

question: At the 1871 proclamation, King Wilhelm I wanted the grand title 'Emperor OF Germany,' claiming lordship over all German lands, but Bismarck forced the humbler 'German Emperor,' first among equal princes, to avoid offending the southern kings. How did the slighted Wilhelm show his fury at the ceremony itself?
answer: He refused to shake Bismarck's hand
choices: He refused to shake Bismarck's hand
He tore up the proclamation document
He ordered Bismarck arrested on the spot
He cancelled the planned coronation feast
context: Bismarck insisted on 'German Emperor' (first among equals) over Wilhelm's preferred 'Emperor of Germany' to avoid offending the southern kings and Austria. The slighted Wilhelm stepped down from the dais, refused to shake Bismarck's hand, and snubbed him for several days. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_of_the_German_Empire

question: On July 3, 1863, the third day at Gettysburg, about 12,500 Confederate soldiers lined up and marched straight toward the waiting Union army on Cemetery Ridge. What did they have to cross to reach the enemy?
answer: Nearly a mile of open, empty field
choices: Nearly a mile of open, empty field
A deep, fast-moving river crossing
A thick forest tangled with brush
A swamp full of mud and reeds
context: Pickett's Charge sent roughly 12,500 men across almost a mile of open ground with no cover, in full view of Union cannon and rifles the whole way. Source: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/picketts-charge

question: The Battle of Gettysburg raged for three days in July 1863, when two whole armies — Union and Confederate — slammed into each other in Pennsylvania. By the time it ended, what made it stand out in all of American history?
answer: It caused about 50,000 casualties, the most of any battle in North America
choices: It caused about 50,000 casualties, the most of any battle in North America
It lasted longer than any other battle ever fought on the continent
It was the first battle in history to be photographed by cameras
It was the only Civil War battle fought during a heavy snowstorm
context: Three days of fighting, July 1-3, 1863, left roughly 50,000 men killed, wounded, or missing — the bloodiest battle ever fought in North America. Lee's army began retreating south on July 4 and never invaded the North again. Source: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/civil-war/battles/gettysburg

question: On the morning of July 1, 1863, Union cavalry general John Buford had only a thin line of horsemen on the ridges at Gettysburg, and he knew the entire Confederate army was about to arrive. When someone asked him about the situation, what was his famous, grim reply?
answer: "The devil's to pay!"
choices: "The devil's to pay!"
"Not one step backward, boys!"
"We shall hold or we shall fall!"
"God defend the right today!"
context: Buford understood the whole Confederate army was bearing down on his outnumbered cavalry, who had to hold the ridges until Union infantry came up. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Gettysburg,_first_day

question: Buford's cavalry were badly outnumbered on McPherson's Ridge on July 1, so they fought a clever way: every fourth man held the horses while the rest fought on foot. What gave these dismounted troopers the edge that let them stall the Confederates until the infantry arrived?
answer: Their breech-loading carbines fired faster than the enemy's muzzle-loaders
choices: Their breech-loading carbines fired faster than the enemy's muzzle-loaders
They had dug deep trenches across the whole ridge overnight
They were hidden behind a tall stone fort on the hilltop
They greatly outnumbered the Confederate troops attacking them
context: Each Union trooper carried a single-shot breech-loading carbine that reloaded faster than the Confederates' muzzle-loaders — enough of a head start to buy time for the infantry to reach the field. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Gettysburg,_first_day

question: After the Battle of Chancellorsville, President Lincoln offered General John Reynolds command of the entire Army of the Potomac — the top job in the eastern war. Reynolds did something startling with that offer, then was shot through the neck and killed within half an hour of reaching the field on July 1. What had he done with Lincoln's offer?
answer: He turned it down, refusing unless free of Washington's meddling
choices: He turned it down, refusing unless free of Washington's meddling
He accepted it and led the whole army into Gettysburg
He demanded a huge sum of money before he would agree
He passed it to his younger brother, also a general
context: Reynolds refused command unless he could run the army without interference from Washington, so the job went to Meade instead. Reynolds was the highest-ranking soldier on either side killed at Gettysburg. Source: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/biographies/john-f-reynolds

question: On July 2, Union engineer Gouverneur K. Warren climbed Little Round Top and found the hill nearly empty — held by just a tiny signal station. Looking to the southwest, what did he suddenly see that told him an entire enemy column was about to seize the high ground?
answer: The glint of Confederate bayonets shining in the sun
choices: The glint of Confederate bayonets shining in the sun
A long row of campfires already burning on the hill
A signal flag waving the order to retreat
A cloud of smoke from a barn set ablaze
context: Warren spotted the sun flashing off enemy bayonets and realized a whole Confederate column was moving to grab the unguarded hill, so he raced off to find troops to defend it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Round_Top

question: On July 2, Colonel Strong Vincent rushed his brigade up Little Round Top without even waiting for orders. He placed Colonel Joshua Chamberlain's 20th Maine at the very end of the whole Union army's line and gave him one fierce command. What did Vincent tell him?
answer: "You are to hold this ground at all costs!"
choices: "You are to hold this ground at all costs!"
"Fall back the moment they break through!"
"Wait here for the general's next order!"
"March around and strike them from behind!"
context: Vincent told Chamberlain this was the left of the entire Union line and it had to hold. Vincent was mortally wounded and given a deathbed promotion to brigadier general. Source: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/defense-little-round-top

question: On Little Round Top, Colonel Joshua Chamberlain's 20th Maine had beaten back charge after charge by Alabama troops until his men ran out of ammunition and faced being overrun. With the enemy only thirty yards away, what did Chamberlain order that turned the fight?
answer: A downhill bayonet charge straight into the enemy
choices: A downhill bayonet charge straight into the enemy
A quiet retreat back over the crest of the hill
His men to lie flat and play dead until dark
A white flag raised to ask for a truce
context: Out of ammunition, Chamberlain ordered the bayonet; in his official report he wrote the word 'ran like fire along the line' and the charge swept up about 400 prisoners, mostly from the 15th and 47th Alabama. His regiment lost about 136 men, roughly 30 killed. Source: Chamberlain's official report, July 6 1863 (https://ironbrigader.com/2020/06/29/joshua-lawrence-chamberlains-report-on-the-20th-maine-at-gettysburg/)

question: On July 2, a gap tore open in the Union center and General Hancock had only the small 1st Minnesota regiment — 262 men — on hand. He pointed them at an oncoming Confederate brigade to buy five desperate minutes. What was the cost of that near-suicidal charge, which Hancock called the most gallant deed in history?
answer: An 82% casualty rate, the worst of any Union regiment in one action
choices: An 82% casualty rate, the worst of any Union regiment in one action
A complete encirclement that captured the whole regiment alive
A long stalemate that pinned both sides down until nightfall
A quick victory that cost only a handful of wounded men
context: Colonel William Colvill led the charge that bought the five minutes Hancock needed; the 1st Minnesota suffered an 82% casualty rate — the highest of any Union regiment in a single action in the entire war. Hancock wrote, 'there is no more gallant deed recorded in history.' Source: https://www.civilwarmed.org/1st-minnesota-at-gettysburg/

question: On July 3, when General Pickett asked General Longstreet, 'General, shall I advance?', Longstreet was sure the charge across that open mile was doomed. Longstreet later wrote that he could not make himself say the word out loud. How did he give the order to send 12,500 men forward?
answer: He only nodded, unable to speak the command aloud
choices: He only nodded, unable to speak the command aloud
He shouted it eagerly to spur the men onward
He wrote it on paper and handed it over silently
He fired a single pistol shot as the signal
context: Longstreet wrote that 'the effort to speak the order failed, and I could only indicate it by an affirmative bow.' He believed the attack would fail but could not stop it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pickett's_Charge

question: During Pickett's Charge, General Lewis Armistead pushed his Virginians farther into the Union line than anyone else. To keep his men following him through the smoke and fire, he did something to make himself easy to see as he shouted, 'Come on, boys, we must give them the cold steel!' What did he do?
answer: He stuck his black hat on the tip of his sword and held it high
choices: He stuck his black hat on the tip of his sword and held it high
He tied a bright red sash around his waist as a banner
He climbed onto the shoulders of two of his soldiers
He carried the regiment's flag in his own two hands
context: Armistead crossed the stone wall at the Angle and laid his hand on a Union cannon — the deepest point of the whole assault — before he was mortally wounded. Source: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/picketts-charge

question: The Union general defending the spot where Lewis Armistead made his deepest push, Winfield Scott Hancock, turned out to be no stranger to him at all. Before the war the two men had been so close that they parted in tears. What does the story say connected these two enemies who were now wounded only yards apart?
answer: They were dear old friends who had wept as they parted before the war
choices: They were dear old friends who had wept as they parted before the war
They were brothers who had not spoken in many long years
They had once dueled each other over a bitter insult
They had been rival suitors competing for the same woman
context: Story holds that Armistead and Hancock were close friends who parted in tears to 'Auld Lang Syne'; as Armistead lay dying he asked that his regrets be sent to Hancock, wounded nearby at almost the same moment. Armistead died on July 5. (Told as legend — the depth of the friendship is debated by historians.) Source: https://militaryhistorynow.com/2022/11/27/armistead-and-hancock-rethinking-the-storied-friendship-between-opposing-generals-at-gettysburg/

question: Pickett's Charge collapsed in under an hour, costing about 6,555 Confederate casualties — roughly half the men who started. After the war, someone asked General George Pickett why his great charge had failed. What was his famously rueful answer?
answer: "I've always thought the Yankees had something to do with it."
choices: "I've always thought the Yankees had something to do with it."
"We were betrayed by a coward who fled the field."
"The good Lord simply willed us to lose that day."
"Our powder was wet and not a gun would fire."
context: About half the attacking force fell. As the survivors streamed back, Robert E. Lee rode among them taking the blame, repeating 'It's all my fault.' Pickett's dry answer years later became one of the most quoted lines of the war. Source: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/picketts-charge

question: In 1600, after seven years in the Inquisition's prisons, Giordano Bruno stood before his judges in Rome and heard them read out his death sentence. The friar-philosopher looked back at the men who had just condemned him to the fire and threw one defiant line in their faces. What did Bruno say?
answer: "Perhaps you pronounce this sentence with greater fear than I receive it."
choices: "Perhaps you pronounce this sentence with greater fear than I receive it."
"You may burn my body, but my books will outlive every one of you."
"I have served the Church faithfully, and the Church has betrayed me."
"Strike, then, for I no longer fear the power of any man on Earth."
context: The eyewitness Caspar Schoppe recorded nearly the same words in a 1600 letter: "You who pronounce this sentence have more fear than I in hearing it." Bruno was burned at the stake in Rome's Campo de' Fiori on February 17, 1600. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giordano_Bruno; religionnews.com (2000); famous-trials.com/bruno/261-home.

question: Giordano Bruno is often remembered as a martyr burned in 1600 for teaching that the Earth moves and that countless worlds fill an infinite universe. But the Inquisition did not condemn him chiefly for astronomy — the "plurality of worlds" was only one of his eight final propositions. Which charges actually doomed Bruno to the fire?
answer: Denying the Trinity, that Jesus was God, and the bread's change at Mass
choices: Denying the Trinity, that Jesus was God, and the bread's change at Mass
Forging papal letters, selling indulgences, and pocketing the Church's gold
Practicing alchemy, casting horoscopes, and conjuring spirits for hire
Leading an armed revolt of friars against the bishops of Naples
context: The charges that sealed his fate were theological: denying the Trinity, denying that Jesus was God made flesh, denying transubstantiation, and denying the perpetual virginity of Mary. Cardinal Robert Bellarmine — the same theologian who later confronted Galileo — boiled the case down to eight heretical propositions. Bruno was no modern scientist-saint; he was a Hermetic mystic who also believed in the transmigration of souls. Sources: scientificamerican.com ("Was Giordano Bruno Burned at the Stake for Believing in Exoplanets?"); famous-trials.com/bruno/261-home.

question: On October 29, 1969, a UCLA student named Charley Kline sat at a computer trying to send the very first message over the ARPANET, the network that would grow into the internet. He started typing the word 'LOGIN' to a machine at Stanford, but the far computer crashed before he could finish — and only the opening of the word ever arrived. What was that first internet message — the fragment the world actually received?
answer: 'LO'
choices: 'LO'
'LOG'
'LOGI'
'GO'
context: The Stanford machine crashed after just 'L' and 'O', so history's first network message was the unintended 'LO' — as in 'lo and behold'. They fixed the bug and sent the full 'LOGIN' about an hour later. Source: icann.org / samueli.ucla.edu / cyberlaw.stanford.edu.

question: On April 26, 1956, a trucking businessman named Malcolm McLean loaded a converted World War II tanker, the SS Ideal X, at Port Newark, New Jersey with 58 identical metal boxes — each one the size of a truck trailer — and sailed it to Houston. Sliding goods on as whole sealed boxes instead of piece by piece launched a revolution in world trade. What were those 58 boxes the first true example of?
answer: The shipping container
choices: The shipping container
The oil supertanker
The cargo airplane
The railroad boxcar
context: Loose 'breakbulk' cargo had to be carried aboard sack by sack; McLean's 58 boxes loaded in under eight hours instead of days. Marc Levinson called his history of it 'The Box: How the Shipping Container Made the World Smaller and the World Economy Bigger.' Source: porthouston.com / maritime-executive.com.

question: In 1991 the world's first website ran on a single black NeXT computer sitting on Tim Berners-Lee's desk at the CERN physics lab in Switzerland. Switching that one machine off would have shut down the entire World Wide Web, so a colleague stuck a hand-lettered red-ink warning on its case. What did that label on the world's first web server say?
answer: 'This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!!'
choices: 'This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!!'
'CRITICAL: live web server — DO NOT UNPLUG!'
'WARNING: powering this off kills the network!'
'STOP! Keep this machine running at all times!'
context: The whole World Wide Web lived on that one NeXT cube; the first website, info.cern.ch, went live in 1991. Source: home.cern 'The web spreads beyond CERN' / cds.cern.ch.

question: In March 1989 Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist at the CERN physics lab, handed his boss Mike Sendall a paper titled 'Information Management: A Proposal' describing a way to link documents across many computers. Sendall scribbled a two-word verdict at the top of the page — a note that ended up greenlighting the project that became the World Wide Web. What two words did he scrawl?
answer: 'Vague, but exciting…'
choices: 'Vague, but exciting…'
'Brilliant — start now.'
'Strange, but worth trying.'
'Confusing, but promising.'
context: Sendall's 'Vague, but exciting…' note greenlit the project that became the Web. Berners-Lee gave it away free to the world rather than patenting it. Source: info.cern.ch/Proposal.html / home.cern.

question: Malcolm McLean, the man who invented the shipping container, got the idea decades earlier as a young North Carolina truck driver. In 1937 he sat for hours on a dock watching longshoremen haul his cargo onto a ship one bale at a time, and stared at his own loaded trailer with a frustrated thought. What did McLean wish he could simply do with the whole trailer?
answer: Lift the entire trailer straight onto the ship
choices: Lift the entire trailer straight onto the ship
Drive the truck right onto the deck himself
Pay the dockworkers to hurry up
Mail the cargo in smaller parcels
context: That dock-side wish became containerization. McLean founded Sea-Land Service in 1960, and his containers later carried U.S. military supplies in the Vietnam War, proving the system at full scale. Source: maritime-executive.com / americanbusinesshistory.org.

question: The shipping container only conquered the world because one small steel part let any crane lift any box and let boxes stack and lock together — the 'twist-lock' corner fitting, designed in the 1950s by engineer Keith Tantlinger. When it came to the patent on his invention, Tantlinger persuaded Malcolm McLean's company to make one particular choice about who could use it. What did they decide to do with the patent?
answer: Released it royalty-free for anyone to use
choices: Released it royalty-free for anyone to use
Gave it free only to U.S. shipping lines
Published the design in an engineering journal
Donated the patent to the U.S. Navy
context: Because the twist-lock was free for everyone, a box from any port fits any ship, train, or truck — the standardized ISO container measured in 'TEU', the twenty-foot equivalent unit. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twistlock.

question: Cheaper shipping and falling trade barriers powered an extraordinary stretch between 1990 and 2015: even as the world added more than two billion people, the number living in extreme poverty dropped by almost 1.2 billion. At the height of that boom, people were climbing out of extreme poverty at a staggering steady pace. Roughly how many escaped extreme poverty every single day?
answer: About 130,000 a day
choices: About 130,000 a day
About 1,000 a day
About 12,000 a day
About 1 million a day
context: As a share of all humanity, extreme poverty fell from 36% in 1990 to 10% in 2015, and East Asia's rate collapsed from 62% to 2%. The ~130,000-a-day pace met the UN's goal of halving 1990 poverty more than five years early. Source: cato.org / worldbank.org press release 2018-09-19.

question: In 1985 the Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev launched a policy he called glasnost, letting newspapers and ordinary citizens freely discuss and criticize the country's problems for the first time in decades. What does the Russian word glasnost mean?
answer: Openness
choices: Openness
Rebuilding
Equality
Victory
context: Glasnost (literally 'publicity' or 'public voice') relaxed strict government censorship and allowed open public discussion of political and social problems for the first time in decades. Source: britannica.com/topic/glasnost ; time.com/5512665/mikhail-gorbachev-glasnost-perestroika/

question: Alongside glasnost, Mikhail Gorbachev launched a second program in 1985-86 to fix the broken, stagnant Soviet economy and get it moving again. He called this program perestroika. What does that Russian word mean?
answer: Restructuring
choices: Restructuring
Openness
Brotherhood
Friendship
context: Perestroika means 'restructuring' or 'reconstruction' -- Gorbachev's plan to decentralize the economy: weakening the central planners in Moscow, allowing more local decisions, and permitting some private ownership for the first time since the 1920s. Source: alphahistory.com/coldwar/glasnost-and-perestroika/ ; history.com/articles/perestroika-and-glasnost

question: Mikhail Gorbachev, the man who would one day be the last leader of the Soviet Union, grew up in the poor peasant village of Privolnoye in southern Russia. As a teenager he worked on a state farm, where his father Sergei taught him to drive a big machine. What did the future Soviet leader drive as a boy?
answer: A combine harvester
choices: A combine harvester
A threshing machine
A hay wagon
A tractor
context: Gorbachev was born March 2, 1931, in Privolnoye in the Stavropol region; as a teenager he drove a combine harvester at a state farm, a skill taught by his father Sergei. Source: notablebiographies.com/Gi-He/Gorbachev-Mikhail.html ; nobelprize.org/prizes/peace/1990/gorbachev/biographical/
