question: Just two months into power, in May 1985, Mikhail Gorbachev launched a sweeping campaign against drinking -- raising prices, slashing production, and ordering vineyards torn out across Crimea, Moldova, and the Caucasus. Mocking citizens gave him a teasing nickname for it. What did they call him?
answer: The mineral-water secretary
choices: The mineral-water secretary
The empty-bottle secretary
The lemonade secretary
The dry-throat secretary
context: Citizens nicknamed him the 'mineral-water secretary' (mineralny sekretar) instead of General Secretary (generalny sekretar), mocking the anti-alcohol drive. Source: rferl.org/a/russia-gorbachev-admits-botching-anti-alcohol-campaign/27018247.html ; soviethistory.msu.edu/1985/anti-alcohol-campaign/

question: At 1:23 a.m. on April 26, 1986, a catastrophe struck Soviet Ukraine, and the state's first instinct was to hide it -- which collided head-on with Gorbachev's new policy of openness. Gorbachev later said this single disaster was the 'turning point' that opened the way to far greater freedom of expression, so that the old secretive system 'could no longer continue.' Which catastrophe did he mean?
answer: The Chernobyl reactor explosion
choices: The Chernobyl reactor explosion
The Kyshtym nuclear disaster
The sinking of the submarine Komsomolets
The Spitak earthquake in Armenia
context: Gorbachev called Chernobyl -- the reactor that exploded at 1:23 a.m. on April 26, 1986, in northern Ukraine -- a 'turning point' that 'opened the possibility of much greater freedom of expression' so the old system 'could no longer continue.' (Kyshtym 1957, the Komsomolets sinking 1989, and the Spitak earthquake 1988 were other real Soviet catastrophes.) Source: gorby.ru/en/presscenter/2006/04/view-turning-point-at-chernobyl-mikhail-s-gorbachev-kopiya ; slate.com/technology/2013/01/chernobyl-and-the-fall-of-the-soviet-union

question: Visiting East Berlin in October 1989 for East Germany's 40th anniversary, Mikhail Gorbachev pulled aside its hardline Communist boss Erich Honecker and warned him not to resist reform, with a grim line that became famous. Within weeks Honecker was forced out, and on November 9 the Berlin Wall fell. What did Gorbachev tell him?
answer: Life punishes those who come too late
choices: Life punishes those who come too late
The walls of empires fall from within
History forgives the bold and buries the slow
No throne outlasts the people's patience
context: Gorbachev's warning to Honecker -- 'Life punishes those who come too late' -- preceded Honecker's ouster and the fall of the Wall on Nov 9, 1989. Source: ecfr.eu/article/life-punishes-those-who-come-too-late/ ; blogs.loc.gov/international-collections/2019/11/the-rise-and-fall-of-the-berlin-wall/

question: On August 19, 1991, Communist hardliners seized Mikhail Gorbachev at his vacation home and rolled tanks into Moscow to undo his reforms. Russian president Boris Yeltsin answered with one act of defiance, cameras rolling, that became the very image of the coup's collapse -- and within days the plot failed. What did Yeltsin do?
answer: Climbed on top of a tank outside parliament
choices: Climbed on top of a tank outside parliament
Barricaded himself inside the Kremlin walls
Flew to Washington to plead for help
Locked the army out of Red Square
context: Yeltsin climbed atop a tank outside the parliament ('White House'), shook the crew's hands, and read a defiant appeal denouncing the coup; the image symbolized the plot's collapse. Source: rferl.org/a/24300856.html ; cato.org/blog/remembering-boris-yeltsins-finest-moment

question: At the Reykjavik summit of October 1986, Mikhail Gorbachev and U.S. president Ronald Reagan came astonishingly close to abolishing every nuclear weapon on Earth -- when Reagan floated the idea, Gorbachev answered, 'Let's eliminate them.' The deal collapsed only because Reagan refused to give up one program. Which one?
answer: His Star Wars missile-defense program
choices: His Star Wars missile-defense program
His Pershing missiles in West Germany
His B-1 bomber fleet
His underground nuclear tests
context: The Reykjavik deal to abolish all nuclear weapons collapsed when Reagan would not confine his 'Star Wars' missile defense (SDI) testing to the laboratory. Source: nsarchive.gwu.edu/document/22397-document-2-transcript-gorbachev-reagan ; armscontrol.org/act/2011-09/features/reykjavik-when-abolition-was-within-reach

question: Mikhail Gorbachev let the Communist countries of Eastern Europe choose their own paths, abandoning the old Brezhnev Doctrine of crushing dissent with tanks. In October 1989 his spokesman Gennadi Gerasimov joked that Moscow now followed a 'doctrine' named for a Frank Sinatra song. Which Sinatra song gave the policy its nickname?
answer: My Way
choices: My Way
New York, New York
Fly Me to the Moon
Strangers in the Night
context: Gerasimov dubbed the hands-off policy 'the Frank Sinatra Doctrine -- he has a song, My Way, so every country decides on its own which road to take,' replacing the Brezhnev Doctrine. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinatra_Doctrine ; archive.macleans.ca/article/1989/11/6/the-sinatra-doctrine

question: On the evening of December 25, 1991, Mikhail Gorbachev sat down to sign the papers dissolving the Soviet Union -- but his Soviet felt-tip pen ran dry. CNN's president Tom Johnson handed him a fancy Mont Blanc to finish the job. Before he would use it, Gorbachev asked one wry question. What did he ask?
answer: Is it an American pen?
choices: Is it an American pen?
Is the camera still rolling?
Is this the final copy?
Is the whole world watching?
context: Gorbachev asked 'Is it an American pen?' and used the Mont Blanc only after being told it was French or German -- a last small refusal to end the USSR with an American pen. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Johnson_(journalist) ; quote.org/quote/is-it-an-american-pen-in-that-601911

question: Mikhail Gorbachev's 1985 campaign against drinking carried a hidden trap: vodka taxes had quietly supplied a huge share of the entire state budget, so banning drink tore a gaping hole in the government's income. To cover that hole the Soviet government did something that helped wreck the economy in the years that followed. What did it do?
answer: Printed more money
choices: Printed more money
Raised income taxes sharply
Sold off the state gold reserves
Borrowed heavily from Western banks
context: Vodka taxes funded much of the state; with that revenue gone, the government printed more money, fueling the inflation that helped wreck the Soviet economy. Source: soviethistory.msu.edu/1985/anti-alcohol-campaign/ ; euronews.com/my-europe/2021/12/23/mikhail-gorbachev-tried-to-get-russia-on-the-wagon-he-failed

question: Here is the deepest irony of Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms. Glasnost let citizens openly criticize the Soviet system, while perestroika tore down the old central planning -- but the second reform left one fatal gap that produced inflation, empty shelves, and shortages, and the USSR dissolved in 1991. What did perestroika fail to do as it dismantled the old command economy?
answer: Build a working market to replace central planning
choices: Build a working market to replace central planning
Free prices fast enough to refill the shelves
Let farmers freely sell their own grain
Keep the ruble from collapsing in value
context: Perestroika dismantled central planning without building a working market to replace it, producing inflation and empty shelves; a system that could not survive even partial honesty about itself unraveled, and the USSR dissolved in 1991. Source: courses.lumenlearning.com/suny-worldhistory/chapter/37-2-2-gorbachev-and-perestroika/ ; britannica.com/place/Russia/The-Gorbachev-era-perestroika-and-glasnost

question: High under the roof of Notre-Dame de Paris stretched a maze of ancient timber that the builders themselves nicknamed 'the Forest.' They earned that name honestly: to frame the roof in the 1200s, workers felled about 5,000 oak trees. What was special about each single beam up there?
answer: Each beam came from a different oak tree.
choices: Each beam came from a different oak tree.
Each beam was painted with a saint's name.
Each beam was carved into a leafy shape.
Each beam was as old as the cathedral itself.
context: Builders cut roughly 5,000 oaks from 522 hectares of woodland to frame the roof, and because each timber came from its own tree, the carpenters called the whole structure 'the Forest.' The 2019 fire destroyed it almost entirely. Source: notredamedeparis.fr 'The roof structure'; woodcentral.com.au 'How Notre-Dame fully traced oaks for rebuild'.

question: On the night of April 15, 2019, as fire raced through Notre-Dame de Paris, the fire-brigade chaplain Father Jean-Marc Fournier organized a human chain and ran INTO the burning cathedral to rescue its single most sacred relic. What did Father Fournier carry back out through the flames?
answer: The Crown of Thorns.
choices: The Crown of Thorns.
The bishop's golden mitre.
A jeweled silver chalice.
The high altar's gold cross.
context: Father Fournier led a human chain inside and brought out the Crown of Thorns, Notre-Dame's holiest relic, along with the Blessed Sacrament. Source: cbsnews.com 'Notre Dame heroes human chain crown of thorns'; cnn.com 'Notre Dame art saved'.

question: When workers sifted through the charred wreckage after the 2019 Notre-Dame fire, they found the dented copper rooster that had perched on top of the fallen spire. Cracking it open revealed a small surprise sealed inside the bird. What was tucked within the rooster?
answer: Three holy relics.
choices: Three holy relics.
A builder's old coins.
A folded prayer card.
A lock of human hair.
context: Inside the rooster were three relics: a piece of the Crown of Thorns and bone fragments of Saint Denis and Saint Genevieve, the patron saints of Paris. The bird was dented but intact. Source: foxnews.com 'Notre Dame cathedral cross reinstalled'; onejourney.com 'Notre-Dame de Paris complete guide'.

question: About 180,000 honeybees lived in beehives kept on a stone ledge of Notre-Dame's roof when the 2019 fire broke out. The hives sat roughly 30 meters below the main roof that was burning, so when the smoke cleared, their keeper rushed out happy news. What did the keeper announce about the bees?
answer: They were still alive.
choices: They were still alive.
They had flown to safety.
They had made extra honey.
They had moved to a new hive.
context: Because the hives sat about 30 meters below the burning roof, the colonies survived; the keeper announced, 'Our Lady's bees are still alive.' Source: cbsnews.com '180,000 bees were living on top of Notre Dame'; smithsonianmag.com 'Honey bees on Notre Dame's roof survived fire'.

question: As the 2019 fire collapsed the roof of Notre-Dame, people feared the worst for the cathedral's three giant rose windows, the famous wheels of 13th-century stained glass set high in its walls. When the smoke cleared, what had happened to all three rose windows?
answer: All three survived intact.
choices: All three survived intact.
Two shattered, one held.
All three were badly cracked.
Their colors melted in the heat.
context: All three great rose windows came through the fire undamaged, sparing Notre-Dame's most famous artworks even as the roof collapsed below them. Source: catholicnewsagency.com 'Famous rose windows survive massive Notre Dame fire'; newsweek.com 'Notre Dame rose windows fire'.

question: A rounded Roman arch is strong, but it shoves outward against the walls that hold it, so those walls have to be thick and heavy. Gothic builders changed the shape of the arch to a point, and that one change redirected the weight. Where does a pointed arch send most of its load instead?
answer: Straight down its supports.
choices: Straight down its supports.
Outward against the walls.
Sideways along the roofline.
Up toward the arch's peak.
context: A pointed arch funnels weight steeply downward instead of pushing sideways, cutting the outward thrust; it can carry roughly three times the load of a round arch, letting builders raise far taller, thinner walls. Source: architecturecourses.org 'The pointed arch'; aramcoworld.com 'The point of the arch'.

question: On the outside of a Gothic cathedral you can see rows of arched stone 'bridges' leaning against the building. These are flying buttresses, and their job is to catch the outward push of the heavy vaulted ceiling and carry it safely down to a thick pier. Once the walls no longer had to brace all that weight, what could builders finally do with them?
answer: Fill them with vast stained glass.
choices: Fill them with vast stained glass.
Build them far thicker for safety.
Pile them higher into stone towers.
Carve them into deep dark niches.
context: By moving the ceiling's outward thrust onto external buttresses, builders freed the walls from holding up the roof, so they could open them into huge windows of stained glass instead of thick stone. Source: friendsofnotredamedeparis.org 'Flying buttresses'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_buttress.

question: On the night of June 10, 1194, lightning set Chartres Cathedral ablaze and burned nearly all of it to the ground. The townspeople were sure their greatest treasure was lost in the flames. Three days later, priests climbed up out of the crypt, where they had locked themselves behind iron doors, carrying that treasure unharmed. What did they bring back up?
answer: The Veil of the Virgin.
choices: The Veil of the Virgin.
A great golden altar cross.
The bishop's jeweled staff.
A gospel book bound in gold.
context: Told as legend: priests sheltered behind iron trapdoors in the crypt and emerged three days after the 1194 fire with the Veil of the Virgin, Chartres' treasured relic, unharmed. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org 'Chartres Cathedral'; worldhistory.org 'Chartres Cathedral'.

question: Set into the stone floor of Chartres Cathedral is a flat maze, built around the year 1200, with a single winding path more than 260 meters long coiled into a circle. Medieval pilgrims who could not afford the long, dangerous journey to Jerusalem used this floor maze as a stand-in. How did they 'make the pilgrimage' along it?
answer: They shuffled to the center on their knees.
choices: They shuffled to the center on their knees.
They carried a lit candle around it.
They recited a psalm at each turn.
They walked it backward in silence.
context: The labyrinth is nearly 13 meters across with a path 261.5 meters long; pilgrims walked or shuffled on their knees to its center as a symbolic pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Source: worldhistory.org 'Chartres Cathedral'; labyrinthos.net 'Chartres FAQs'.

question: King Louis IX of France paid a fortune for the Crown of Thorns and, between 1241 and 1248, built a jewel-box chapel in Paris just to hold it: the Sainte-Chapelle. Its upper chapel pushed the buttress-and-window idea to its absolute limit, so that the walls themselves nearly vanish. What are the walls of that upper chapel almost entirely made of?
answer: Stained glass.
choices: Stained glass.
Carved oak.
Polished marble.
Gold leaf.
context: The upper chapel is almost solid glass: 15 windows about 15 meters tall holding 1,113 stained-glass panels, the flying-buttress idea taken to its extreme. Source: sainte-chapelle.fr 'A unique set of stained-glass windows'; sainte-chapelle.fr 'History of the Sainte-Chapelle'.

question: The deep cobalt 'Chartres blue' in the cathedral's windows has glowed for 800 years and weathered better than the reds and greens beside it. A romantic story grew up around it: that its recipe was a magical secret, lost forever, that no glassmaker today could ever reproduce. What do historians actually say about that 'lost secret'?
answer: It is a myth; the recipes survive.
choices: It is a myth; the recipes survive.
It is true; the formula died out.
It is true, but only for the cobalt.
It is unknown; no records were kept.
context: The blue was made from sodium-based cobalt oxide, which proved unusually durable, but the tale of a lost, irreproducible secret is a romantic myth: medieval glass recipes actually survive. Told as legend. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Stained glass windows of Chartres Cathedral'; worldhistory.org 'The stained glass windows of Chartres Cathedral'.

question: Gothic builders kept competing to raise their cathedrals higher, and Beauvais Cathedral in France reached the highest of all, with choir vaults about 48 meters tall. But Beauvais had finally reached too far. What happened to that record-setting cathedral?
answer: Its choir collapsed and it was never finished.
choices: Its choir collapsed and it was never finished.
Its bishop ran out of money to roof it.
Its design was copied all across Europe.
Its tower still stands as France's tallest.
context: Beauvais raised the tallest choir vaults in the world, but the choir collapsed in 1284 and its 153-meter tower fell in 1573; the cathedral was never completed. Source: mdpi.com (Heritage journal, Beauvais study); frenchmoments.eu 'Beauvais Cathedral'.

question: On a great medieval cathedral, a true gargoyle isn't just a scary stone carving sticking off the roof - it does a real, practical job. What is that job?
answer: Spouts rainwater out through its mouth
choices: Spouts rainwater out through its mouth
Holds the heavy roof up on its back
Frightens evil spirits from the church
Marks a buried saint down below it
context: A real gargoyle is a waterspout: rain runs through a trough in its back and pours out its open mouth, throwing the water clear of the walls. The name comes from the Old French 'gargouille', meaning throat or gullet - the same root as the word 'gurgle.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gargoyle

question: Chartres Cathedral in France guarded one treasure above all others: the Sancta Camisia, said to have been worn by the Virgin Mary when Jesus was born. What kind of object was this most precious relic?
answer: A veil of silk
choices: A veil of silk
A crown of gold
A robe of wool
A cloak of fur
context: King Charles the Bald, grandson of Charlemagne, gave the silk veil to Chartres in 876. It turned the town into one of medieval Europe's greatest pilgrimage destinations. During the French Revolution the veil was cut into pieces; the largest fragment is still displayed in a side chapel today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chartres_Cathedral

question: The craft guilds of Chartres - its shoemakers, tanners, butchers, and money-changers - paid for the cathedral's stained-glass windows, and they made sure to leave their mark in the glass itself. What did they have pictured in the lower panels?
answer: Themselves at work in their trades
choices: Themselves at work in their trades
The kings who once ruled France
Angels blowing golden trumpets
The walls of the Holy City
context: In the lower 'donor panels' you can still find the shoemakers, the tanners, the butchers, and the money-changers shown plying their trades - the ordinary craftsmen who footed the bill, proudly pictured in the windows they paid for. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stained_glass_windows_of_Chartres_Cathedral

question: On 2 December 1804, Napoleon Bonaparte held his coronation as Emperor inside Notre-Dame de Paris, with the Pope right there at the altar. At the climax, Napoleon did something startling with the crown. What did he do?
answer: Took the crown and crowned himself
choices: Took the crown and crowned himself
Knelt low and let the Pope crown him
Refused the crown and walked away
Passed the crown to his young son
context: By taking the crown from the Pope's hands and placing it on his own head, Napoleon signaled that his power came from himself and the people, not the Church. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notre-Dame_de_Paris

question: Look up at Chartres Cathedral and something seems off: its two great towers don't match - one plain, one a burst of carved stone lace. The reason is time. How far apart were the two spires actually built?
answer: More than three centuries apart
choices: More than three centuries apart
Within the very same single year
Only about a decade apart
Roughly one generation apart
context: The plain south spire (about 105 m) was finished around 1160 in the older Romanesque style. The lacy north spire (about 113 m) was built in flamboyant Gothic by architect Jean Texier between 1507 and 1513 - over 340 years later. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chartres_Cathedral

question: On 10 June 1194 a fire tore through Chartres Cathedral. As it burned, priests grabbed the cathedral's holiest treasure - the Veil of the Virgin - and fled with it behind iron trapdoors into the crypt. Three days later, when the veil was found unharmed, how did the townspeople read that survival?
answer: A sign the Virgin wanted a grander church
choices: A sign the Virgin wanted a grander church
A punishment for the whole town's sins
Proof that the relic had been a forgery
A warning to abandon the ruined site
context: Belief that the Virgin herself willed a greater cathedral fueled an astonishing burst of rebuilding. The crypt, towers, and west facade had survived the fire; the rest rose new around them. Source: https://www.christianity.com/church/church-history/timeline/901-1200/chartres-burned-but-relic-survived-11629810.html

question: Set into the floor of Chartres Cathedral is an 11-ring stone labyrinth, about 261 metres of winding path built around 1200. Medieval pilgrims too poor or too frail to travel would instead walk its single path on their knees, treating it as a stand-in for one specific holy journey. Which journey did walking this path stand in for?
answer: A pilgrimage to Jerusalem
choices: A pilgrimage to Jerusalem
A pilgrimage to Rome
A pilgrimage to Compostela
A pilgrimage to the Jordan
context: Pilgrims called it the 'chemin de Jerusalem' - the road to Jerusalem - a symbolic pilgrimage to the Holy Land for those who could never make the real trip. The labyrinth is about 12.9 metres across. Source: https://www.discover-chartres.com/chartres-labyrinth.html

question: Notre-Dame de Paris hangs a single giant bell, named Emmanuel, that weighs about 13 tonnes - its clapper alone is half a tonne. Cast in 1683 and named by King Louis XIV, this bell is rung only on a handful of days each year. Which kind of day calls for it?
answer: The greatest feasts, like Christmas
choices: The greatest feasts, like Christmas
The funeral day of a French king
The day a new pope is chosen
The city's yearly founding day
context: Emmanuel rings for the greatest feasts and major national events - moments grave enough to deserve the deepest voice in Paris. Source: https://www.friendsofnotredamedeparis.org/cathedral/artifacts/bells/

question: The famous horned, brooding stone monsters perched on Notre-Dame - like 'Le Stryge', the chin-on-hands creature glaring out over Paris - feel utterly medieval. But there's a catch most tourists never learn. What is the surprising truth about them?
answer: Added in the 1800s, not the Middle Ages
choices: Added in the 1800s, not the Middle Ages
Carved by the cathedral's first bishop
Made of solid gold beneath the grime
Given as a gift by England's king
context: These brooding figures are 'chimeras' - pure decoration that drains no water, so not true gargoyles either. They were added during Eugene Viollet-le-Duc's 1844-1864 restoration. Le Stryge became famous through Charles Meryon's 1850s etching. Source: https://www.friendsofnotredamedeparis.org/cathedral/artifacts/grotesques/le-stryge/

question: Notre-Dame de Paris was begun in 1163 and not finished until around 1345. What does that span of roughly 182 years mean for the masons who laid its first stones?
answer: Generations of them died before it was done
choices: Generations of them died before it was done
They finished early and left for other towns
One master oversaw it from start to finish
They rebuilt it twice after it collapsed
context: Building a great cathedral could swallow more than a century of labor, so the men who laid the first stones knew they would never see the towers rise. Notre-Dame's towers reach about 69 metres. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notre-Dame_de_Paris

question: In August 1944, with Chartres just liberated, American artillery was ordered to flatten the cathedral - commanders feared German snipers were hiding in its towers. Colonel Welborn Barton Griffith Jr. refused to accept that on faith. What did he do to save the cathedral?
answer: Climbed the towers himself, found them empty, and stopped the order
choices: Climbed the towers himself, found them empty, and stopped the order
Phoned the German commander and arranged a quiet local truce
Posted his own men to surround and guard the towers all night
Towed the heavy artillery guns far away under cover of darkness
context: Griffith and his driver climbed into the towers, found them empty of snipers, and had the shelling called off - saving the 800-year-old cathedral. Hours later, on 16 August 1944, Griffith was killed directing troops in the nearby town of Leves. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welborn_Griffith

question: The whole point of the Gothic flying buttress was to let cathedral walls turn into walls of glass. A flying buttress is a stone arch that reaches out from high on the wall, across open air, to a heavy pier standing several feet away. What does this stone arm actually accomplish?
answer: Carries the roof's outward push to a pier, freeing the wall
choices: Carries the roof's outward push to a pier, freeing the wall
Adds heavy weight to the wall so it cannot sway in the wind
Funnels rainwater down from the high roof to the street
Hides iron chains that secretly tie the building together
context: The arched arm catches the roof's outward thrust high up and channels it across open air into a massive pier, which sends the force straight down into the ground. Freed from holding itself up, the wall can become a thin curtain pierced by enormous windows. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_buttress

question: Historians can point to roughly one building as the birthplace of the entire Gothic style: the rebuilt choir of a great church near Paris, pushed through by Abbot Suger and dedicated on 11 June 1144. It was the first to fuse the pointed arch, the ribbed vault, and walls of stained glass. Which church was this?
answer: Saint-Denis
choices: Saint-Denis
Notre-Dame
Chartres
Sainte-Chapelle
context: Abbot Suger called the glowing result 'lux nova' - new light. By combining the pointed arch, ribbed vault, and radiating chapels lit by large stained-glass windows, Saint-Denis set the template every later Gothic cathedral would follow. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilica_of_Saint-Denis

question: King Louis IX of France raced to build Sainte-Chapelle in Paris in under seven years, consecrating it in 1248 to house one relic: the Crown of Thorns, bought from the broke emperor of Constantinople. Set against the price he paid for that relic, what did building the dazzling chapel cost?
answer: Less than the relic itself had cost
choices: Less than the relic itself had cost
Roughly ten times the relic's price
About the same as one stained window
Nothing, since monks built it free
context: Louis paid more for the Crown of Thorns than the entire jewel-box chapel cost to build. Its upper chapel is almost all glass - 15 soaring windows holding 1,113 stained-glass scenes that wrap a visitor in colored light. Source: https://www.sainte-chapelle.fr/en/discover/history-of-the-sainte-chapelle

question: In Francisco Goya's painting The Third of May 1808, a poor laborer in a glowing white shirt kneels before a French firing squad and throws his arms wide. Goya posed him exactly like the crucified Christ — and hid one small detail on his outstretched right hand that drives the comparison home. What does a close look at that hand show?
answer: A dark mark like the nail-wound of the crucifixion
choices: A dark mark like the nail-wound of the crucifixion
A wedding ring he is twisting in fear
A scrap of bread he refused to drop
A rosary wound tightly around his fingers
context: The mark echoes the stigmata, the nail-wound of Christ's hand. Goya turned a Napoleonic firing-squad killing into a timeless image of sacrifice — the man's yellow-and-white clothing even matches the papal colors. Yet unlike a saint in old religious art, his face shows raw terror, not holy calm. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Third_of_May_1808 ; artincontext.org/the-third-of-may-1808-francisco-goya/

question: Late in life Francisco Goya — deaf, bitter, and shut away — bought a house outside Madrid already nicknamed the Quinta del Sordo, the 'Villa of the Deaf Man.' There he made 14 nightmarish works he never titled and never meant anyone to see, including Saturn Devouring His Son. What surface did Goya paint these 'Black Paintings' onto?
answer: The bare plaster walls of his own house
choices: The bare plaster walls of his own house
Wooden panels he hid in his cellar
Tattered sheets stretched over his windows
Small canvases he locked away in a chest
context: Goya painted the Black Paintings straight onto his interior plaster walls between 1820 and 1823, for no eyes but his own. Decades after his death they were carefully peeled off the walls and transferred to canvas; they now hang in the Prado in Madrid. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Paintings

question: When the Grand Canal of China was finished in 609, Emperor Yang of Sui celebrated by sailing it in a fleet of imperial dragon-boats so enormous that the procession formed one continuous line of vessels down the waterway. How long did that single line of boats stretch from end to end?
answer: About 65 miles long
choices: About 65 miles long
About 7 miles long
About 20 miles long
About 40 miles long
context: The flotilla reportedly stretched about 105 km (65 miles) as it traveled from the north down to the southern capital — a column of boats longer than many countries are wide. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Canal_(China)

question: Roughly five million people — including women and children — were forced to dig the Grand Canal of China for Emperor Yang of Sui, and ancient records put the death toll from overwork and disease at perhaps two million laborers. On top of failed wars, that crushing cost sparked rebellions. What became of the Sui dynasty that built the canal?
answer: Rebellions toppled it within one generation
choices: Rebellions toppled it within one generation
It ruled on peacefully for three more centuries
It abandoned the canal and moved the capital
It split the empire into rival northern and southern courts
context: The forced labor of the canal and other projects, piled onto failed wars against Goguryeo, ignited revolts that overthrew the Sui within a single generation of the canal's completion — the dynasty was destroyed by the very lifeline it built. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Canal_(China)

question: In 1845 a disease swept Ireland's potato fields, turning healthy plants to dark splotches and the potatoes pulled from the ground into shrunken, inedible mush. What kind of organism caused this rot that wrecked the crop the Irish poor depended on?
answer: A water mold that arrived from North America
choices: A water mold that arrived from North America
A swarm of beetles blown over from France
A frost that froze the fields three winters running
A fungus carried in by infected English seed
context: The blight was Phytophthora infestans, a water mold (not a true fungus) that crossed the Atlantic from North America in 1845. It blackened the leaves and rotted the tubers into slime. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phytophthora_infestans ; history.com/articles/irish-potato-famine

question: Between 1845 and 1852 the Great Famine emptied Ireland. Roughly a million Irish died of starvation and diseases like typhus. What happened to at least another million people during those same years?
answer: They fled their homeland as refugees
choices: They fled their homeland as refugees
They were drafted into the British army
They moved into the cities to find factory work
They were resettled by the government on new farms
context: About one million died and at least another million emigrated. Ireland's population fell from 8,175,124 in the 1841 census to 6,552,385 by 1851 — a drop of over 1.5 million in a decade. Sources: history.com/articles/irish-potato-famine ; britannica.com/event/Great-Famine-Irish-history

question: One year of the Great Famine was so deadly that the Irish gave it a grim nickname that has stuck ever since — the year when close to a million people were starving to death all at once. What did they call 1847?
answer: Black '47
choices: Black '47
The Hungry Forty-Seven
The Lost Harvest
The Great Mortality
context: 1847 was the worst year of the famine, remembered as 'Black '47.' Sources: smithsonianmag.com (Choctaw Nation's gift to the Irish, 2018)

question: In the winter of 1845-46 Prime Minister Robert Peel secretly bought 100,000 pounds' worth of American maize to sell cheaply to the starving Irish. The hard, gritty yellow grain was difficult to cook and digest, and the Irish gave it a bitter nickname. What did they call it?
answer: Peel's brimstone
choices: Peel's brimstone
Peel's penance
The yellow famine
Treasury gruel
context: The Irish nicknamed the imported Indian corn 'Peel's brimstone.' Peel also repealed the Corn Laws in 1846. Sources: historyhome.co.uk/peel/ireland/famine.htm ; rte.ie (Temporary Relief Commission)

question: On New Year's Day 1847 the Cork magistrate Nicholas Cummins carried bread into the village of Skibbereen and entered a hovel where six people lay on filthy straw, alive only by their low moaning. In a letter to the Duke of Wellington, later printed in The Times, what did Cummins say happened the moment he stepped outside?
answer: He was surrounded by at least 200 such phantoms
choices: He was surrounded by at least 200 such phantoms
He found the village priest digging graves alone
He counted forty fresh coffins stacked in the lane
He watched a cart carry off the dead by lamplight
context: Cummins found 'six famished and ghastly skeletons' — four children, a woman, and what had once been a man — and wrote, 'In a few minutes I was surrounded by at least 200 such phantoms.' His letter to the Duke of Wellington was published in The Times. Sources: irishcentral.com (Great Famine workhouse) ; sites.evergreen.edu/ireland1617/texts/history/famine

question: Charles Trevelyan, the Treasury official who controlled Britain's famine relief and ordered Peel's food programs shut down, wrote about the mass death in Ireland in a way that horrifies readers to this day. How did Trevelyan describe the famine?
answer: As 'a direct stroke of an all-wise and all-merciful Providence'
choices: As 'a direct stroke of an all-wise and all-merciful Providence'
As 'a misfortune beyond any government's power to mend'
As 'the gravest trial ever laid upon the Crown'
As 'a debt the empire must labour to repay'
context: Trevelyan, Assistant Secretary to the Treasury (1840-1859), called the famine 'a direct stroke of an all-wise and all-merciful Providence' and 'the sharp but effectual remedy by which the cure is likely to be effected,' blaming 'the selfish, perverse, and turbulent character' of the Irish. He was knighted (KCB) on 27 April 1848 for his famine-relief services. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Charles_Trevelyan,_1st_Baronet ; legallegacy.wordpress.com

question: In 1847, while Irish families starved, ships still carried Irish-grown food across the sea to England — wheat, oats, butter, and nearly ten thousand calves, a third more than the year before — and British troops often guarded the convoys to the ports. Yet historians like Austin Bourke and Christine Kinealy disagree about what this export record proves. What is their core dispute?
answer: Whether scarcity alone, or also policy and profit, drove the death toll
choices: Whether scarcity alone, or also policy and profit, drove the death toll
Whether the exports were larger than Britain officially admitted
Whether the troops were guarding food or hunting rebels
Whether the calves were sold abroad or kept for breeding
context: Ireland exported roughly 39,000 tonnes of wheat, 98,000 tonnes of oats, about a million gallons of butter, and 9,992 calves to England in 1847. Austin Bourke argued grain imports exceeded exports by 1847; Christine Kinealy stresses the deadly 'starvation gap' of winter 1846-47 before imports arrived, and that merchant profit-seeking and laissez-faire ideology — not absolute scarcity alone — shaped the catastrophe. Sources: historyireland.com/food-exports-from-ireland-1846-47 ; usbornefamilytree.com/irishfoodexports.htm

question: Famine refugees crossed the Atlantic on overcrowded vessels so deadly they earned a name that says everything about the voyage. Steerage passengers were let on deck barely an hour a day, and so many of the dead were buried at sea that sharks were said to trail the vessels. What were these emigrant ships called?
answer: Coffin ships
choices: Coffin ships
Fever barques
Hunger packets
The grave fleet
context: At the Grosse Île quarantine station below Quebec, of 98,749 Irish who sailed for Quebec in 1847, 10,820 died at sea or in quarantine — about 11%, a rate on par with slave ships. Sources: amusingplanet.com/2017/11/the-coffin-ships ; rte.ie (Revisiting the coffin ships, 2023)

question: In March 1847, only about 14 years after being driven west on their own Trail of Tears, one Native American nation in Oklahoma took up a collection for the starving people of Ireland, half a world away. Which nation made this gift, still honored between the two peoples today?
answer: The Choctaw Nation
choices: The Choctaw Nation
The Cherokee Nation
The Seminole Nation
The Chickasaw Nation
context: The Choctaw Nation raised $170 (worth several thousand dollars today) for Irish famine relief in 1847. The Irish repaid the kindness with donations to the Choctaw during the 2020 pandemic. Sources: choctawnation.com/about/history/irish-connection ; smithsonianmag.com (2018)

question: The Great Mosque of Cordoba in Spain was begun as a mosque in the 780s, then turned into a Christian cathedral when builders cut a tall stone nave right through the middle of its famous prayer hall. When the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V came to see the finished cathedral, what did he reportedly say?
answer: "You have built here what others might have built anywhere, but you have destroyed something unique in the world."
choices: "You have built here what others might have built anywhere, but you have destroyed something unique in the world."
"You have raised here the grandest house of worship that my whole empire has ever seen."
"You have repaired here a ruin that lay neglected, and given the city back its proud heart."
"You have matched here the great cathedrals of the north, stone for stone and arch for arch."
context: The emperor had approved the cathedral himself, then regretted it on seeing the result. The remark is recorded as testimony (legend), not a verbatim transcript. The mosque's prayer hall had been one of a kind; the inserted cathedral nave could have been built in any city. Source: https://www.emperorcharlesv.com/in-charles-footsteps/spain/cordoba/

question: To build the prayer hall of the Great Mosque of Cordoba, the architects reused old columns scavenged from Roman and Visigothic ruins on the site. These salvaged columns were a problem: too short to hold up a roof at the soaring height the builders wanted. Their clever fix turned that flaw into the hall's most famous sight, a striped red-and-white canopy that seems to march on forever. What did they do to gain the height they needed?
answer: They stacked a second tier of arches on top of the first, doubling them up to reach the roof.
choices: They stacked a second tier of arches on top of the first, doubling them up to reach the roof.
They sank the floor of the hall well below ground level so the short columns would stand taller.
They carved fresh capitals from a single huge block and fitted them between every old column.
They bound the short columns together in clustered bundles to make each one count as taller.
context: At the Great Mosque of Cordoba (begun 785 under Abd al-Rahman I), the reused short columns were extended with a double-tier arcade: a second row of arches stacked atop the first, in alternating red brick and white stone (voussoirs), creating the famous striped two-level arches. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosque-Cathedral_of_Cordoba.

question: In southern Africa stand the ruins of a great medieval city built entirely of stacked granite. The whole country of Zimbabwe later took its name from these ruins -- from the Shona phrase 'dzimba dza mabwe.' What does that phrase mean?
answer: Houses of stone
choices: Houses of stone
City of gold
Walls of the king
Land of the eagle
context: 'Dzimba dza mabwe' means 'houses of stone' (or 'large houses of stone'). When the modern nation became independent it named itself after the ancient stone city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe; The Met (metmuseum.org/essays/great-zimbabwe).

question: At Great Zimbabwe, workers raised towering granite walls up to 11 meters high. The thing that has amazed every visitor for centuries is HOW the stones are held together. What holds the walls up?
answer: Their own weight, with no mortar at all
choices: Their own weight, with no mortar at all
Iron clamps driven between the blocks
Lime-and-sand mortar in every joint
Wooden pegs hidden inside the wall
context: The walls were built with no mortar at all. Each granite block was cut and stacked so precisely that the wall holds together by its own weight. This dry-stone fitting is the city's signature achievement. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe; PanAfroCore (panafrocore.com).

question: Carvers at Great Zimbabwe made eight tall figures out of soapstone, each one perched on top of a stone column. One of these carved figures became the national emblem of modern Zimbabwe -- it sits on the country's flag, coins, and coat of arms. What is the figure?
answer: A bird
choices: A bird
A lion
A crocodile
A spear and shield
context: The soapstone Zimbabwe Bird is the country's emblem, appearing on the flag, coat of arms, banknotes, coins, and the logos of over 100 organizations. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_Bird.

question: The Great Enclosure at Great Zimbabwe is a curving wall about 250 meters around and up to 11 meters high. Among all the ancient stone buildings of Africa south of the Sahara, where does it rank by size?
answer: The largest of them all
choices: The largest of them all
About the tenth-largest
Roughly average-sized
One of the smallest known
context: The Great Enclosure is the largest ancient stone structure in sub-Saharan Africa. Its walls run about 250 meters (820 feet) around and rise up to 11 meters (36 feet). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe.

question: Inside the Great Enclosure stands the Conical Tower -- a rounded stone tower about 9 meters tall and 5.5 meters across. When archaeologists examined it closely, they discovered something strange about the inside of the tower. What did they find?
answer: It is completely solid -- no door, no room inside
choices: It is completely solid -- no door, no room inside
A spiral staircase climbing to the top
A burial chamber holding a king's bones
A hidden well shaft going deep underground
context: The Conical Tower has no entrance and no chamber: it is a solid mass of stone. What it was for is still unknown. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe.

question: Great Zimbabwe sat far inland, yet its court grew enormously rich. Wealth flowed from huge herds of cattle and from one metal mined on the plateau and carried down to the coast for trade. Which metal made the city rich?
answer: Gold
choices: Gold
Copper
Silver
Tin
context: Gold mined on the plateau was carried to the coastal port of Sofala, then north to the Swahili city of Kilwa, and out into the Indian Ocean. Cattle herds were the court's other great source of wealth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe; World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/Kilwa).

question: Great Zimbabwe was laid out in three main areas: the Hill Complex on a rocky outcrop, the great walled compound below it, and the Valley Complex. But the granite walls were not where people actually lived. Inside the walls, the homes were built of what?
answer: Packed earth and clay
choices: Packed earth and clay
Stacked granite blocks
Timber and thatch
Sun-dried mud brick
context: Inside the stone walls, people lived in 'daga' houses made of packed earth and clay. The three main parts are the Hill Complex (oldest), the Great Enclosure, and the Valley Complex. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe.

question: To make building blocks for Great Zimbabwe, masons needed to split solid granite without iron tools to spare. Granite naturally peels apart in flat layers, so the builders used a clever trick to crack the rock into brick-shaped slabs. What did they do to the granite?
answer: Heated it with fire until it cracked apart
choices: Heated it with fire until it cracked apart
Soaked it in vinegar to dissolve it
Froze water in its cracks overnight
Pounded it for days with wooden mallets
context: Workers quarried granite from local outcrops, then heated the rock with fire and cracked it into slabs -- using granite's natural tendency to peel in layers (called exfoliation) -- then shaped and selected each piece to fit. Source: MemoryCherish (memorycherish.com); Smarthistory.

question: The famous Zimbabwe Birds look strange when you study them closely -- they are not ordinary birds at all. Instead of a hooked beak they have human-like LIPS, and instead of talons they have five toes. What does this human-and-eagle blend most likely represent?
answer: A messenger eagle of God and the ancestors
choices: A messenger eagle of God and the ancestors
A guardian spirit set to watch over the dead king
A rain-god summoned to bring the harvest
A trophy from a great royal hunt by the king
context: The birds mix human and eagle features and likely depict the bateleur eagle, called 'chapungu' in Shona, believed to be a messenger from Mwari (God) and the ancestors. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_Bird.

question: Some doubted that an inland African city could really be part of long-distance trade -- until archaeologists dug into the soil of Great Zimbabwe. Buried there they found goods carried from thousands of miles away. Which of these did they pull from the ground?
answer: Chinese porcelain and a coin minted by a sultan of Kilwa
choices: Chinese porcelain and a coin minted by a sultan of Kilwa
Roman silver coins stamped with an emperor
Egyptian hieroglyphic tablets and gold masks
Viking silver arm-rings and amber beads
context: Excavations turned up Chinese porcelain (Longquan green-glazed and blue-and-white ware), Persian glass, beads, and a copper coin minted by a sultan of Kilwa -- proof the inland city was plugged into Indian Ocean trade. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe.

question: The top of the Great Enclosure's outer wall carries the city's most famous decoration: a long band of dark stones set in a repeating geometric pattern, running along the crest of the wall. What pattern is this?
answer: A double-chevron zigzag, often read as a snake
choices: A double-chevron zigzag, often read as a snake
A row of carved human faces
A line of interlocking circles
A spiral coiling around the wall
context: The crest of the outer wall is decorated with a long double-chevron (zigzag) band of dark stone -- the city's most famous pattern, often read as a snake or as a symbol of fertility and continuity. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe; thedarkatlas.com.

question: In 1889 a European hunter named Willi Posselt wanted one of Great Zimbabwe's carved soapstone birds for himself. He cut a bird from the top of its stone column and carried it off. How did he get it from the local chief?
answer: He paid with blankets and a few small goods
choices: He paid with blankets and a few small goods
He traded a rifle and ammunition for it
He won it in a wrestling contest
He bought it for a chest of gold coins
context: Posselt cut the soapstone bird from its column and paid a local chief in blankets and a few goods. The bird ended up at Cecil Rhodes's Cape Town estate, Groote Schuur; a piece of its column was sold to a Berlin museum in 1907. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_Bird.

question: The Conical Tower of Great Zimbabwe is solid stone with no door and no room inside, so scholars have argued for years about why it was built. The leading idea is that the whole tower is a giant stone copy of an everyday Shona object. What everyday object is it thought to copy?
answer: A grain bin (granary)
choices: A grain bin (granary)
A war drum
A king's crown
A cooking pot
context: Legend and scholarly reading: the tower is thought to be a giant stone copy of a Shona grain bin -- a symbol that the ruler, like a generous chief filling his granary, was the provider for his people. Others read it as a fertility symbol; its true purpose is debated. Source: Timbuktu Travel (timbuktutravel.com); AP Art History notes.

question: In 1531 a Portuguese captain named Vicente Pegado wrote the first European account of Great Zimbabwe. He could have described many things about the towering granite city, but he reached for one short phrase that has been quoted ever since. He called it a fortress built of stones of what?
answer: Marvelous size
choices: Marvelous size
Painted gold
Sacred fire
Royal blood
context: Pegado, the first European to write about the city, described 'a fortress built of stones of marvelous size, and there appears to be no mortar joining them.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe.

question: When the German explorer Karl Mauch reached Great Zimbabwe in 1871, he refused to believe Africans had built it. He cut a sliver from a fallen wooden door-beam, sniffed it, and convinced himself it matched a familiar object in his own pocket. What did he compare the wood to?
answer: His cedar pencil
choices: His cedar pencil
His leather boot
His tobacco pipe
His brass compass
context: Mauch decided the lintel smelled and looked like his cedar pencil, declared it Lebanese cedar, and claimed Phoenicians had built the city for the Queen of Sheba as a copy of King Solomon's temple. Source: zimfieldguide.com (Karl Mauch); World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/article/1429).

question: In the era of Cecil Rhodes, an investigator named Richard Nicklin Hall was sent to 'restore' Great Zimbabwe. Instead, he dug out and dumped away the buried archaeological layers -- as much as two meters deep -- which he called the 'filth and decadence' of African occupation. By destroying those layers, what did Hall wipe out?
answer: The dated layers of soil that recorded who built it
choices: The dated layers of soil that recorded who built it
A hidden vault of the kingdom's gold
The foundations holding up the Great Enclosure walls
A library of written records kept by the kings
context: Hall removed up to two meters of archaeological deposits, erasing the dated evidence of who built Great Zimbabwe -- because he wanted to remove signs of African occupation. Source: World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/article/1429).

question: In 1929 the archaeologist Gertrude Caton-Thompson led an expedition to Great Zimbabwe and, by carefully reading the layers of soil, settled the long argument over who built the city. What did her evidence show?
answer: Africans, ancestors of the Shona, built it in medieval times
choices: Africans, ancestors of the Shona, built it in medieval times
Phoenician sailors built it for the Queen of Sheba
Arab traders built it as a coastal trading fort
Portuguese settlers built it in the 1500s
context: Caton-Thompson wrote that the evidence produced 'not one single item that is not in accordance with the claim of Bantu origin and medieval date.' Great Zimbabwe was built by Africans, the ancestors of the Shona. Source: World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/article/1429); Lady Science (ladyscience.com).

question: Even after the science was settled, the white Rhodesian government of the 1960s and 70s pressured archaeologists to keep denying that Africans built Great Zimbabwe. Archaeologist Paul Sinclair said he was personally threatened for telling the truth in public. What did the government threaten to do to him?
answer: Make him lose his job
choices: Make him lose his job
Put him in prison
Deport him from the country
Take away his excavation findings
context: Sinclair said he was threatened with losing his job for stating publicly that Black Africans built Great Zimbabwe. The government also censored radiocarbon dates and printed tourist guidebooks showing Africans bowing to imaginary white 'builders.' Source: World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/article/1429); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe.

question: The word 'alphabet' is just its first two letters' names jammed together: alpha plus beta. The Greeks borrowed those names from the Phoenicians, whose letters were named after everyday things you could point at. Aleph meant 'ox' and bet meant 'house' so taken literally, what does the word 'alphabet' actually mean?
answer: Ox-house
choices: Ox-house
Sun-river
Hand-mouth
Bird-stone
context: Greek alpha and beta came from Phoenician aleph ('ox') and bet ('house'). The Phoenicians named their letters after common objects, so the very word 'alphabet' literally reads as 'ox-house.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleph; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bet_(letter); metmuseum.org Alphabet Origins.

question: Around the early 8th century BC the Greeks borrowed a writing system from the Phoenicians, but that system only wrote consonants and left every vowel sound off the page entirely. To make their own language readable, the Greeks did one thing no writers before them had ever done. What was that breakthrough?
answer: They wrote down the vowels
choices: They wrote down the vowels
They wrote on papyrus scrolls
They carved letters into stone
They read the lines aloud
context: The Phoenician script was an 'abjad' (consonants only). By repurposing spare Phoenician consonants their tongue didn't need (aleph became alpha, He became epsilon, and so on), the Greeks gave every sound on the page a letter the first true alphabet. That line ran Phoenicians to Greeks to Etruscans to Romans, whose Latin letters we still write. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Greek_alphabet; worldhistory.org/Greek_Alphabet.

question: Greek builders crowned their fanciest columns with a capital wrapped in carved, curling leaves. The Roman writer Vitruvius passed down a legend about how the sculptor Callimachus dreamed up that design: he was walking past the grave of a young Corinthian girl when something he saw there gave him the shape. What did Callimachus see growing on the grave?
answer: A spray of acanthus leaves curling out from under a roof tile set atop a basket
choices: A spray of acanthus leaves curling out from under a roof tile set atop a basket
A laurel wreath that a mourner had hung across the headstone that morning
A grapevine that had twisted itself around the marble grave marker
A bed of poppies that had bloomed in a ring around the burial mound
context: The girl's nurse had set a votive basket of the child's toys on the grave and laid a square roof tile on top as a lid. An acanthus plant grew up through the basket, and the tile forced its leaves to curl outward -- the exact shape Callimachus then carved into the Corinthian capital. Told as legend by Vitruvius. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corinthian_order (citing Vitruvius).

question: On the south porch of the Erechtheion, a temple on the Athenian Acropolis, the builders skipped plain stone columns entirely. Instead the heavy roof-beam rests directly on the heads of a row of carved figures, the most famous example of sculpted forms used as pillars in Greek architecture. What are these six load-bearing figures?
answer: Six carved stone women standing as living pillars
choices: Six carved stone women standing as living pillars
Six carved lions seated on their haunches
Six carved warriors holding raised shields
Six carved horses rearing on their hind legs
context: They are called the Caryatids -- six stone women carrying the entablature on their heads, draped in carved robes. They are the best-known case of figures used in place of columns. Source: greektraveltellers.com/blog/caryatids and acropolis.athenstickets.org/erechtheion.

question: A Byzantine warship sprayed a stream of liquid flame across the sea at an enemy fleet, and when sailors tried to douse it the fire only kept burning on top of the water until their wooden ships were ash. What did the Byzantines call this weapon?
answer: Greek fire
choices: Greek fire
Persian oil
Roman pitch
Spartan tar
context: Greek fire was a Byzantine liquid weapon that kept burning even on water, so it could not be splashed out, and it tore through enemy wooden fleets at sea. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Greek_Fire/

question: The recipe for Greek fire was guarded so jealously that Emperor Constantine VII warned his heir it had been revealed by an angel and must never be handed to foreigners. Because no one outside that tiny circle was ever told, what happened to the formula?
answer: It was lost and is still not fully known today
choices: It was lost and is still not fully known today
It was carved into the walls of Constantinople
It was sold to the Arab fleets after the siege
It was published in the emperor's own war manual
context: Constantine VII told his heir the weapon had been 'shown and revealed by an angel' to Constantine the Great and must never be given to foreigners (a legendary claim of divine origin). The secret was kept so well that the formula was eventually lost completely and is still not fully known. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_fire

question: The ancient Greeks pictured their gods living in a palace above the clouds, feasting and quarrelling. But the home they gave the gods was a real mountain you can still climb in northern Greece, and it happens to be the tallest peak in the whole country. Which mountain did the Greeks make the home of the gods?
answer: Mount Olympus
choices: Mount Olympus
Mount Parnassus
Mount Ida
Mount Pelion
context: Mount Olympus sits on the border of Thessaly and Macedonia; its highest peak, Mytikas ('the nose'), rises to 2,917 m (9,573 ft), the tallest in Greece, and the massif has 52 peaks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Olympus

question: Zeus was the king of the Greek gods and ruler of Mount Olympus. When he was angry, he hurled his signature weapon down from the heavens at those who defied him. What was the weapon Zeus threw from the sky?
answer: a thunderbolt
choices: a thunderbolt
a warhammer
a longbow
a battleaxe
context: Zeus's symbols were the thunderbolt (his weapon), the eagle (his royal bird), the bull, and the oak tree. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeus

question: Zeus was struck by a terrible, splitting headache, so the smith-god Hephaestus swung an axe and cracked his skull open to relieve it. Out of the wound leapt the goddess Athena. What was so startling about the way Athena was born?
answer: Fully grown, in armor, and shouting a war-cry
choices: Fully grown, in armor, and shouting a war-cry
As a baby who aged a year every day
As an owl that flew to the Acropolis
As a column of fire that spoke aloud
context: Zeus had earlier swallowed Athena's pregnant mother, the Titaness Metis, because of a prophecy that her child would surpass him, which is why Athena was born straight from his head. Legend. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/athena/

question: Two gods both wanted a great new city named after them, so they held a contest before its king, Cecrops. Poseidon struck the rock of the Acropolis with his trident and made a salt-water spring gush out. The goddess Athena offered a different gift, and the people liked hers better, naming the city Athens after her. What was Athena's winning gift to the city?
answer: the first olive tree
choices: the first olive tree
the first grapevine
the first fig tree
the first rose bush
context: The olive became the wealth of Athens, its oil prized across the ancient world. Legend. Source: https://www.greekmyths-greekmythology.com/athena-vs-poseidon-contest-name/

question: The Greeks called Poseidon the 'Earth-Shaker' and blamed him whenever the ground trembled in an earthquake. The sea-god was also said to have created one particular animal, shaping the very first of its kind from the white crests of the waves. Which animal did Poseidon make?
answer: the horse
choices: the horse
the dolphin
the bull
the eagle
context: Poseidon's chief epithet, Ennosigaios ('Earth-Shaker'), tied earthquakes to him; he was also god of horses. Legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poseidon

question: The goddess Athena carried a fearsome goatskin shield called the aegis, and onto it she fixed the snake-haired head of the Gorgon Medusa, whose gaze turned men to stone. Athena did not kill the monster herself; she was given the severed head as a gift by the mortal hero who had beheaded Medusa. Which hero gave Athena the Gorgon's head?
answer: Perseus
choices: Perseus
Heracles
Theseus
Achilles
context: The snake-fringed head on the aegis was called the Gorgoneion. Athena's other signature symbol was the owl, her bird of wisdom. Legend. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/athena/

question: When Zeus freed the three Cyclopes, the giant one-eyed smiths, from their prison, the grateful giants forged a signature weapon for each of the three ruling brothers. After arming Zeus and Poseidon with theirs, what did the Cyclopes forge for the third brother, Hades, lord of the dead?
answer: a helm that turned its wearer invisible
choices: a helm that turned its wearer invisible
a sword that never missed its mark
a net that could trap any god
a shield that reflected any spell
context: The three Cyclopes were Brontes ('Thunder'), Steropes ('Lightning'), and Arges ('Bright'). Hades's gift was the Helm of Darkness, or Cap of Invisibility. Legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cap_of_invisibility

question: Hephaestus, the lame smith-god, kept his forge beneath the volcanoes and crafted wonders no other god could make. Among his creations were golden servant-women he built to help him in his workshop, and these were no ordinary statues. What was astonishing about Hephaestus's golden handmaidens?
answer: They could think, move, and speak on their own
choices: They could think, move, and speak on their own
They could turn lead into solid gold
They could fly the god across the sky
They could heal any wound with a touch
context: Because they could think and speak, these golden handmaidens are often called literature's first robots. Hephaestus also forged the wonder-worked shield of Achilles. Legend. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Hephaistos/

question: After Zeus, Poseidon, and Hades overthrew the Titans, the three brothers had to split the entire cosmos between them, dividing up the sky, the sea, and the gloomy underworld. They did not let the eldest simply choose, and they did not fight over it. How did the three brothers decide which realm each would rule?
answer: They drew lots for it
choices: They drew lots for it
Zeus chose first and gave the orders
They settled it with a wrestling match
Their mother Rhea divided it up
context: Zeus drew the sky, Poseidon the sea, and Hades the underworld; in the Iliad, Poseidon says the earth and Olympus stayed common to all three. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hades

question: Cronus, the Titan king, had heard a prophecy that one of his own children would one day overthrow him. To stop it, he swallowed each of his babies whole the moment it was born. When her youngest, Zeus, was born, the mother Rhea hid the infant and handed Cronus something else to swallow in the baby's place. What did Rhea trick Cronus into swallowing instead of Zeus?
answer: A stone wrapped in baby clothes
choices: A stone wrapped in baby clothes
A goat dressed in royal robes
A clay doll painted to look real
A loaf of bread shaped like a child
context: Grown Zeus forced Cronus to vomit up his swallowed siblings and the stone; that stone was set up at Delphi as the Omphalos, the 'navel of the world.' Legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cronus

question: The Greeks worshipped twelve supreme gods of Olympus, a group they called the Dodekatheon, or 'Twelve Gods.' Yet there was never one single official list: the twelfth and last place was shared between two gods, and different cities and poets picked one or the other. One claimant was Hestia, goddess of the home and hearth. Who was the other god that ancient sources swapped into that disputed twelfth seat?
answer: Dionysus, god of wine
choices: Dionysus, god of wine
Hades, god of the dead
Eros, god of love
Pan, god of the wild
context: Hades, though brother to Zeus and Poseidon, was never counted among the Twelve at all, because his realm lay far off in the underworld rather than on Olympus. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve_Olympians

question: The sculptor Phidias built a colossal statue of Zeus at Olympia, plated in gold and ivory and counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. The seated Zeus was so vast it nearly filled the whole temple. The geographer Strabo captured its size with a famous remark about what would happen if the statue ever moved. According to Strabo, what would the seated Zeus do if he stood up?
answer: He would smash through the roof of the temple
choices: He would smash through the roof of the temple
He would crush the worshippers at his feet
He would tower higher than Mount Olympus
He would set the whole temple ablaze
context: Strabo wrote that 'if Zeus arose and stood erect he would unroof the temple.' The 12-metre (40-ft) statue held a small figure of Nike, goddess of victory, in one hand. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statue_of_Zeus_at_Olympia

question: The first of Heracles' twelve labors was to kill the Nemean lion, a beast whose golden hide was so tough that arrows bounced off it and no blade could pierce its skin. With every weapon useless against it, how did Heracles finally kill the lion?
answer: He strangled it with his bare arms
choices: He strangled it with his bare arms
He crushed it beneath a boulder
He starved it inside its own cave
He drowned it in a river
context: Because no weapon could harm the invulnerable hide, Heracles wrestled the lion and choked it to death. Apollodorus: 'putting his arm round its neck held it tight till he had choked it.' He later wore the lion's pelt as his signature armor. Source: Apollodorus, Library 2.5.1 (Perseus Tufts).  (Legend.)

question: Princess Ariadne fell in love with the hero Theseus and wanted to help him survive the twisting Labyrinth where the Minotaur waited. The maze was so confusing that no one who entered had ever found the way out again. What did Ariadne give Theseus so he could escape the Labyrinth after the fight?
answer: A ball of thread to unwind behind him
choices: A ball of thread to unwind behind him
A torch to light the dark passages
A trail of white pebbles to drop
A map scratched onto a clay tablet
context: Ariadne told Theseus to tie one end at the entrance and unwind the thread as he went, then follow it back out. Plutarch calls it a 'clue of thread' -- which is literally why the word 'clue' came to mean a hint that leads you to the answer. Source: Plutarch, Life of Theseus (classics.mit.edu).  (Legend.)

question: The city of Athens was forced to send seven young men and seven young women across the sea to Crete, where they were shut in the Labyrinth to be devoured by the Minotaur. When the fourteen victims were being chosen, what did the young prince Theseus do?
answer: He volunteered to go as one of the fourteen
choices: He volunteered to go as one of the fourteen
He hid himself among the temple priests
He begged his father to stop the ships
He paid another man to take his place
context: The tribute was Athens' penalty for the death of Minos' son Androgeos. Theseus put himself among the fourteen on purpose, planning to kill the Minotaur and end the tribute forever. Source: Plutarch, Life of Theseus, and Apollodorus (ancient-greece.org).  (Legend.)

question: When Heracles fought the Lernaean Hydra, he made a horrifying discovery: every time he smashed one of its heads, two new heads grew back in its place, so the monster only got deadlier as he struck. How did Heracles and his nephew Iolaus finally stop the heads from growing back?
answer: They burned each neck-stump with fire
choices: They burned each neck-stump with fire
They froze the necks in cold spring-water
They tied each stump shut with rope
They smeared the wounds with poison
context: As Heracles cut, Iolaus seared each stump with a flaming firebrand so no new heads could sprout. The one head that was immortal, Heracles buried under a heavy rock. Source: Apollodorus, Library 2.5.2 (Perseus Tufts).  (Legend.)

question: Perseus was sent to bring back the head of the Gorgon Medusa, whose face was so horrifying that anyone who looked straight at her was instantly turned to stone. The goddess Athena told him a trick that let him get close enough to cut off her head without being turned to stone himself. What was Athena's trick?
answer: He watched her reflection in his polished shield
choices: He watched her reflection in his polished shield
He fought her with his eyes shut tight
He attacked only after dark had fallen
He wore a blindfold woven by Athena
context: By striking while watching only Medusa's reflection in his bronze shield, Perseus never met her petrifying gaze. Medusa was the only one of the three Gorgon sisters who could be killed at all -- the other two were immortal. Source: Apollodorus, Library 2.4.2; Wikipedia 'Medusa'.  (Legend.)

question: Daedalus built wings of feathers for himself and his son Icarus so they could escape from Crete. Drunk on the thrill of flight, Icarus soared higher and higher toward the sun, ignoring his father's warning to keep to a middle course -- and his wings came apart. What did the sun's heat do to Icarus' wings?
answer: It melted the wax holding the feathers together
choices: It melted the wax holding the feathers together
It scorched the feathers down to bare ash
It dried the feathers until they cracked apart
It set the wooden frame of the wings alight
context: The feathers were fixed with wax; the sun's heat melted it, the feathers fell away, and Icarus dropped into the sea still crying his father's name. The water where he fell was named the Icarian Sea after him. Source: Ovid, Metamorphoses Book 8 (web.sas.upenn.edu/discentes).  (Legend.)

question: An oracle warned King Acrisius of Argos that his own grandson would one day kill him. To make sure his daughter Danae could never have a child, Acrisius locked her away inside a chamber of solid bronze. Yet the god Zeus still reached her, and she gave birth to the hero Perseus. How did Zeus get to Danae inside the sealed chamber?
answer: He poured in as a shower of golden rain
choices: He poured in as a shower of golden rain
He slipped in disguised as a palace guard
He flew in through a crack as an eagle
He tunneled up through the chamber floor
context: Zeus reached Danae as a shower of golden rain pouring through the roof, and Perseus was born despite every precaution -- the prophecy could not be stopped. Source: Apollodorus, Library, and Theoi.com 'Danae'.  (Legend.)

question: For one of his labors, Heracles was ordered to clean the vast stables of King Augeas in a single day -- filthy pens that housed over a thousand cattle and had gone uncleaned for years. The job was impossible by ordinary shoveling. What did Heracles do to clean the stables in one day?
answer: He rerouted two rivers to flood through them
choices: He rerouted two rivers to flood through them
He hauled the dung out on a hundred carts
He set the soiled straw ablaze and burned it
He summoned a storm to rain the filth away
context: Heracles diverted the courses of the rivers Alpheus and Peneus and turned them through the yard, washing it clean in a day. Eurystheus refused to count this labor because the rivers had done the work. Source: Apollodorus, Library 2.5.5 (Perseus Tufts).  (Legend.)

question: On his way to find the Gorgons, Perseus had to get directions from the three Graeae -- ancient witch-sisters who, between all three of them, shared just one single eye and one single tooth, passing them from hand to hand. When the sisters refused to help him, how did Perseus force them to tell him what he needed?
answer: He stole their single shared eye and held it hostage
choices: He stole their single shared eye and held it hostage
He threatened to smash their one shared tooth
He chained the three sisters to a great rock
He offered them a chest of gold for the directions
context: Perseus snatched the eye in the moment it was being passed between them and refused to return it until they revealed where to find the gear he needed -- the winged sandals, the cap of invisibility, and the kibisis bag. Source: Apollodorus, Library 2.4.2; Theoi.com 'Graeae'.  (Legend.)

question: Before sailing to fight the Minotaur, Theseus promised his father, King Aegeus, a signal: the ship would come home flying a white sail if Theseus had survived, but a black sail if he had died. Theseus won -- but in his joy he forgot the promise and left the black sail flying. Watching the sea for his son and seeing black, what did the heartbroken Aegeus do?
answer: He threw himself off the cliff into the sea
choices: He threw himself off the cliff into the sea
He set the returning ship on fire
He sailed out alone to search for the body
He took his own life by the palace altar
context: Seeing the black sail, Aegeus believed his son was dead and hurled himself from the rocks into the water -- which is why that sea has been called the Aegean ever since. Source: Plutarch, Life of Theseus (classics.mit.edu).  (Legend.)

question: Heracles needed the golden apples that grew in a far-off garden, but only the Titan Atlas could pick them -- and Atlas was busy holding the entire sky on his shoulders. So Heracles offered to hold up the sky himself while Atlas fetched the apples. When Atlas returned, he liked his freedom and refused to take the crushing sky back. How did Heracles trick Atlas into taking the sky again?
answer: He asked Atlas to take the sky back while he padded his shoulders
choices: He asked Atlas to take the sky back while he padded his shoulders
He challenged Atlas to a contest to see who could hold it longer
He promised Atlas a generous share of the golden apples
He pretended to be crushed and quietly slipped out from under it
context: Heracles pretended to agree to hold the sky forever, asking Atlas to take it back just for a moment so he could cushion his shoulders -- then picked up the apples and walked away, leaving Atlas stuck again. Source: standard Apollodorus/Pherecydes tradition (Wikipedia 'Labours of Hercules').  (Legend.)

question: The monster of the Crete Labyrinth is known today as the Minotaur, but that word is really just a nickname meaning 'the Bull of Minos.' Few people remember that the beast was actually born with its own real name: Asterion. What does the name Asterion mean?
answer: The starry one
choices: The starry one
The bull-child
The maze-born
The man-eater
context: The beast's real given name was Asterion, which means 'the starry one'; 'Minotaur' simply means 'Bull of Minos.' It was the child of Minos' wife Pasiphae and a white bull sent by Poseidon. Source: Apollodorus, Library (Wikipedia 'Minotaur').  (Legend.)

question: Years earlier, an oracle had warned King Acrisius that his own grandson, the hero Perseus, was fated to kill him -- and despite every effort to prevent it, the prophecy could not be escaped. Long after, a grown Perseus was competing in athletic games when fate caught up in the cruelest, most accidental way. How did Perseus end up killing his grandfather Acrisius, exactly as foretold?
answer: A discus he threw flew wild and struck the old man
choices: A discus he threw flew wild and struck the old man
A javelin slipped from his hand and impaled a bystander
His chariot overturned and crushed a man in the stands
A wrestling throw flung an opponent into the crowd
context: At games in Larissa, a discus Perseus threw veered off course and struck an old spectator who happened to be Acrisius -- fulfilling the prophecy by pure accident, no matter how hard Acrisius had tried to dodge fate. Source: Apollodorus, Library 2.4.4 (Wikipedia 'Acrisius').  (Legend.)

question: Around 2,400 years before modern chemistry, the Greek thinkers Leucippus and his pupil Democritus reasoned that if you keep cutting a piece of matter in half, you must finally reach a smallest piece that can be cut no further. They named that smallest piece 'atomos' — the ancestor of our word 'atom.' What does that Greek word literally mean?
answer: Uncuttable
choices: Uncuttable
Unchanging
Unending
Unseen
context: 'Atomos' comes from a- ('not') + tomos ('cut') — literally 'uncuttable.' Leucippus and Democritus held that everything is built from these indivisible, eternal atoms. They were guessing 2,400 years before chemists confirmed matter is made of tiny particles, and our modern word 'atom' is their word handed down. Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/atomism-ancient/

question: Democritus of Abdera taught that the things our senses report — sweetness, bitterness, heat, cold, colour — are not really out there in the world; they are just how arrangements of atoms strike us. In a fragment that survives in his own words, he finished the thought: 'By convention sweet is sweet, by convention bitter is bitter... but in truth there are only atoms and the ____.' What did Democritus name as the only other real thing besides the atoms?
answer: the void
choices: the void
the gods
the elements
the heavens
context: Democritus and the atomists insisted reality is just two things: indivisible atoms and the empty 'void' they move through. They argued that even 'what is not' — empty space — must be real, because without void the atoms would have nowhere to move or rearrange. The famous fragment is preserved by Sextus Empiricus. Source: en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Democritus

question: Greek plays began at a yearly contest where the winning poet took home a live animal as his prize. The very word for the serious plays, tragoidia, joined the word for 'song' to the name of that prize animal — so 'tragedy' literally means the song of which creature?
answer: A goat
choices: A goat
A bull
A ram
A stag
context: 'Tragedy' = tragos ('goat') + oide ('song') — 'goat-song.' A goat was the original prize handed to the winning playwright at Athens' drama festival. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_ancient_Greece + Britannica 'Great Dionysia'.

question: Greek actors performed in huge open-air theaters before thousands of spectators, wearing stiffened linen masks painted with giant expressions. The most surprising part of every mask was the mouth itself, shaped in an unusual way. How was the mask's mouth shaped?
answer: Flared open wide like a megaphone
choices: Flared open wide like a megaphone
Sewn shut into a thin line
