Fitted with a bronze sound-tube
Carved into a wide grin
context: The masks were built with a flared, megaphone-shaped mouth to project the voice across the open-air theater, and painted with exaggerated expressions readable from the back rows. Source: europe.factsanddetails.com/article/entry-989 + thedramateacher.com 'Role of Masks in Greek Theatre'.

question: Around 534 BC, an Athenian named Thespis did something no one had done before: he stepped out of the singing chorus and spoke alone as a single character, becoming the first true actor in Western theater. Because of him, actors are still called by what name today?
answer: Thespians
choices: Thespians
Choristers
Dramatists
Orators
context: Thespis (around 534 BC) was the first to step out of the chorus and speak as a character — the first actor. Performers have been called 'thespians' after him ever since. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_ancient_Greece + ebsco.com 'Thespis'.

question: Athens built its great stone theater right into the landscape rather than on flat ground, letting the curved rows of seats climb a steep natural hill above the city. Into the side of which famous Athenian height was the Theater of Dionysus carved?
answer: The south slope of the Acropolis
choices: The south slope of the Acropolis
The harbor wall of Piraeus
The summit of Mount Olympus
The marble quarry of Pentelicus
context: The Theater of Dionysus was cut into the south slope of the Acropolis hillside; at its peak under Lycurgus (around 330 BC) it held roughly 16,000–17,000 spectators. Source: worldhistory.org/article/814/theatre-of-dionysos-eleuthereus + en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_Dionysus.

question: The Athenian plays were not just entertainment but a sacred competition staged each spring at the City Dionysia. Three poets each presented tragedies, and judges chosen by lot awarded the prize. The whole festival was held in honor of which god?
answer: Dionysus, the god of wine
choices: Dionysus, the god of wine
Apollo, the god of light
Athena, the city's patron
Hephaestus, the smith god
context: The plays were a religious competition at the City Dionysia, a spring festival for Dionysus, god of wine. Three tragic poets each staged three tragedies plus a satyr play, judged by men chosen by lot. Source: britannica.com/topic/Great-Dionysia + artsedge.kennedy-center.org.

question: At the center of every Greek theater was a flat circular ground where the chorus sang and danced together. The Greeks called this space the 'orchestra' — but to them it had nothing to do with a band of musicians. What did the word orchestra literally mean?
answer: The dancing place
choices: The dancing place
The singing pit
The judges' ring
The actors' door
context: 'Orchestra' came from orcheisthai ('to dance') — it was the circular 'dancing place' at the theater's center where the chorus performed, not a group of musicians. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_ancient_Greece + greektheater8.weebly.com.

question: The front row of the Theater of Dionysus held 67 carved marble thrones, each with a VIP's name cut into the stone. One throne stood grander than all the rest, set in the very center as the most honored seat in the house. To whom did that central throne belong?
answer: The priest of Dionysus
choices: The priest of Dionysus
The richest grain merchant
The winning playwright
The captain of the fleet
context: Among the 67 named marble thrones in the front row, the grandest central seat belonged to the priest of Dionysus — the most honored place in the theater. Source: worldhistory.org/article/814/theatre-of-dionysos-eleuthereus.

question: Early Greek tragedy let only two actors share the stage at once. Sophocles made one change to the stage that transformed how complex a story a poet could tell. What did Sophocles add?
answer: A third actor
choices: A third actor
A second chorus
A trap door in the floor
A musicians' balcony
context: Sophocles' great innovation was adding a third actor (Aeschylus had used two), enabling three-way confrontations; he also pioneered painted scenery (skenographia) behind the action. Source: worldhistory.org/sophocles + en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophocles.

question: In 468 BC the young Sophocles entered the drama contest against Aeschylus, the reigning master of tragedy. The rivalry ran so hot that Athens set aside the usual judges chosen by lot, and an unlikely group already in the city was pulled in to decide the winner instead. Who judged that contest?
answer: The general Cimon and his commanders
choices: The general Cimon and his commanders
The priests of the temple of Apollo
The elders of the Athenian council
The ten archons of Athens
context: Sophocles' first victory (468 BC) defeated Aeschylus. The contest was so charged that, instead of judges chosen by lot, the general Cimon and his fellow commanders — soldiers, not poetry experts — were called in to decide. Source: britannica.com/biography/Sophocles + Plutarch via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophocles.

question: In Sophocles' Oedipus the King, the hero spends the play hunting for the man whose crime has cursed his city — only to uncover the most devastating truth in Greek drama about himself. Aristotle praised this moment of recognition as the perfect tragic reversal. What did Oedipus discover he had done?
answer: He had killed his own father and married his own mother
choices: He had killed his own father and married his own mother
He had stolen the sacred fire from the gods themselves
He had betrayed his own brother to win the throne
He had broken a vow sworn upon his children's lives
context: Oedipus realizes the stranger he killed was his own father and the queen he married is his own mother. Aristotle held up this recognition (anagnorisis) as the perfect example of tragic reversal. Source: britannica.com/biography/Sophocles + fiveable.me 'Aristotle Poetics'.

question: When a Greek plot tangled past any human solution, a god could be brought on to set everything right — lowered over the stage on a crane called the mechane, the actor playing the deity descending from above. This stage trick gave later writers a famous phrase for an out-of-nowhere rescue. What is that phrase?
answer: Deus ex machina
choices: Deus ex machina
In medias res
Anagnorisis
Catharsis
context: A crane called the mechane hoisted the god-actor over the stage to resolve tangled plots — giving us 'deus ex machina,' Latin for 'god from the machine.' Euripides loved the device. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deus_ex_machina + helinika.com 'Greek Stage Machinery'.

question: Aristophanes' comedies mocked real, living Athenians by name. His play The Clouds (423 BC) ridiculed one famous thinker as a babbling fraud who taught students to wriggle out of paying their debts. That same man later claimed the play had helped turn the jury against him at his own trial. Whom did The Clouds mock?
answer: Socrates
choices: Socrates
Euripides
Cleon
Pericles
context: The Clouds (423 BC) ridiculed Socrates as a babbling fraud teaching students to dodge debts; Socrates later said the play helped poison the jury against him at his trial. Source: britannica.com/art/Old-Comedy + fiveable.me 'Aristophanes and Political Satire'.

question: Lord Byron, the most famous poet in Europe, sailed to the besieged Greek town of Missolonghi in 1824 hoping to die a soldier's death fighting for Greek freedom. He never saw a real battle. Instead he caught a fever at 36 -- and what finished him off was not the fever itself but the men treating him. What did they do?
answer: His own doctors bled him over and over with leeches and a lancet
choices: His own doctors bled him over and over with leeches and a lancet
A Turkish sniper picked him off as he inspected the walls
His ship struck rocks and went down in a winter storm
A rival officer challenged him to a duel and shot him dead
context: Byron's doctors, believing bloodletting would break the fever, drained him repeatedly until he was too weak to recover. His reported last words were 'I must sleep now.' He had given the Greek cause both his fortune and his life. Source: https://www.bars.ac.uk/blog/?p=5192

question: On 20 October 1827 a combined British, French and Russian fleet anchored alongside the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet in a bay on the Greek coast. The British admiral Edward Codrington had sailed in only to intimidate the Turks, not to fight -- yet by nightfall about 60 Ottoman ships were sunk or burning. What turned the standoff into a slaughter?
answer: A single musket shot during a quarrel over an Ottoman fireship
choices: A single musket shot during a quarrel over an Ottoman fireship
A planned dawn assault the allied admirals had agreed on in advance
A Greek army attacking the Turkish camp on the shore at the same time
A formal ultimatum that expired at noon and triggered the bombardment
context: When a British boat rowed over to stop an Ottoman crew from lighting a fireship, muskets cracked, a shot rang out, and the anchored fleets erupted into point-blank carnage. Navarino was the last major naval battle fought entirely with wooden sailing ships, most of them blasting each other while still at anchor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Navarino

question: A monk named Guido of Arezzo wanted to help church singers learn melodies faster, so he took a hymn whose every line begins one musical note higher than the line before. By grabbing the first syllable of each climbing line, he named the six rising notes of the scale. What everyday singing-syllables did those names become?
answer: The do-re-mi we still sing today
choices: The do-re-mi we still sing today
The A-B-C note letters
The loud-soft volume marks
The sharp and flat signs
context: The hymn was 'Ut queant laxis,' a song to St. John the Baptist; Guido (c. 991-1033) named the notes ut-re-mi-fa-sol-la, and centuries later 'ut' was changed to 'do,' giving the do-re-mi children still sing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ut_queant_laxis

question: Hildegard of Bingen, a 12th-century German abbess, wrote the Ordo Virtutum, the oldest surviving play set entirely to music. In it the Virtues all sing their parts, but Hildegard gave the Devil one strange limitation, because she believed music itself was the true praise of God. What could the Devil alone never do in her play?
answer: Sing — he can only shriek and shout
choices: Sing — he can only shriek and shout
Speak the name of God aloud
Step into the lighted stage
Touch any of the Virtues
context: Hildegard (1098-1179) shut the Devil out of music entirely: every other character sings, but he only shrieks and shouts, because she held music to be the true praise of God. More chant survives from her than from any other named medieval composer, and she wrote both words and music. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordo_Virtutum

question: In August 1942 the US Marines launched their first big offensive of the Pacific war by landing on Guadalcanal. The plan was officially called Operation Watchtower, but it went ahead so badly under-supplied that Admiral Ernest King had told them to attack 'even on a shoestring.' What bitter nickname did the Marines give the operation?
answer: Operation Shoestring
choices: Operation Shoestring
Operation Watchfire
Operation Lost Cause
Operation Empty Hand
context: Operation Watchtower began August 7, 1942 -- just six months after Pearl Harbor and the first major American ground offensive of the Pacific war. Admiral Ernest King had ordered the invasion forward 'even on a shoestring,' and the under-supplied Marines turned that phrase into a grim nickname for the whole campaign. Source: nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/war-shoestring-fight-guadalcanal

question: In September 1942 on Guadalcanal, Lt. Col. Merritt 'Red Mike' Edson and roughly 800 Marine Raiders and paratroopers dug in on a coral ridge guarding Henderson Field. For three nights about 3,000 Japanese troops charged them, reaching the edge of the runway before being thrown back -- the Japanese lost 700 to 800 men to about 100 Marines. What name did the survivors give that coral ridge afterward?
answer: Bloody Ridge
choices: Bloody Ridge
Shoestring Hill
Watchtower Heights
Henderson Ridge
context: The Battle of Edson's Ridge (Sept 12-14, 1942) was fought south of Henderson Field. During the night fighting Edson stood about 20 yards behind the firing line shouting 'Hold out just one more night,' and Major Kenneth Bailey physically shoved panicking men back into position. The Marines held, and the place was renamed Bloody Ridge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Edson%27s_Ridge

question: For a thousand years the Theodosian Walls of Constantinople had thrown back every army that came at them. In 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II hauled up a single new weapon and smashed those famous walls open. What new weapon finally broke the city's defenses?
answer: A giant bronze cannon
choices: A giant bronze cannon
A thousand scaling ladders
A tunnel under the moat
A fleet of fire-ships
context: Mehmed II's huge bronze bombard, cast by the gun-founder Orban, breached the Theodosian Walls in 1453 — walls that had repelled attackers for a thousand years. The fall proved stone castle-walls were now obsolete against cannon, the iconic moment historians use to open the 'gunpowder empire' age. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunpowder_empires

question: The gun-founder Orban first walked into Constantinople and offered his monster cannon to the Byzantine defenders, not to their enemy. The Emperor Constantine XI wanted it — but Orban ended up casting it for the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II, whose army then used it to shatter the city's walls. What sent Orban over to the other side?
answer: Constantine XI was too poor to pay him
choices: Constantine XI was too poor to pay him
The emperor doubted the gun would work
Mehmed II had captured his family
His foundry inside the city burned down
context: Constantine XI could not afford Orban's price, so Orban took the job for Mehmed II, who 'showered him with gifts.' The defenders' own would-be weapon brought their walls down. Source: https://www.ancient-origins.net/history/orban-man-whose-cannon-brought-down-walls-constantinople-part-i-008056

question: For centuries a rebellious noble could defy his own king almost forever from behind tall stone castle walls. Then huge siege cannon arrived that could shatter those walls in days — but the guns were so enormous and expensive that only a rich central ruler could afford them. Historians argue this single shift is what let the Ottomans, Safavids, and Mughals build their vast 'gunpowder empires.' What did the new cannon do to royal power?
answer: It broke the castle nobles and let kings centralize huge empires
choices: It broke the castle nobles and let kings centralize huge empires
It made open-field cavalry charges the deciding force again
It pushed kings to share power with the castle-holding lords
It ended large land empires in favor of small trading cities
context: Because only wealthy central rulers could afford the giant guns, the old castle-holding nobility collapsed and kings built vast centralized land empires — the Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal states. The Safavid Shah Abbas even tore down Iran's old fortifications and built an artillery corps answering to him alone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunpowder_empires

question: In a courtyard in Delhi stands a black iron column over 23 feet tall, raised about 1,600 years ago under a Gupta emperor. Ordinary iron left out in the rain and sun rusts away within a few years. After sixteen centuries in the open, what state is this ancient pillar in?
answer: It has barely rusted at all
choices: It has barely rusted at all
It has rusted down to a thin stump
It has turned bright green like old copper
It has crumbled into reddish flakes
context: The Iron Pillar of Delhi weighs over 6 tonnes (about 13,000 lb) and is roughly 98% wrought iron, yet after ~1,600 years outdoors it has scarcely corroded — a metallurgical marvel of the Gupta age. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_pillar_of_Delhi

question: The Gupta-era astronomer Aryabhata, born near Pataliputra (modern Patna) in 476 CE, worked out that the Earth spins and measured the heavens with astonishing accuracy. About 1,500 years later, in 1975, India found a very fitting way to honor him. How did India honor Aryabhata?
answer: It named its very first satellite after him
choices: It named its very first satellite after him
It named its first university after him
It put his face on its first banknote
It built him a great marble tomb
context: India's first satellite, launched in 1975, was named 'Aryabhata' after the astronomer born in 476 CE who wrote his masterwork at age 23. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aryabhata

question: Samudragupta, the Gupta conqueror nicknamed the 'Indian Napoleon,' put his own image on his gold coins to tell his people who he was. One celebrated coin type shows him not as a fighter at all, but seated, absorbed in a pastime — proof their warrior-king had another side. What is Samudragupta doing on that coin?
answer: Seated, playing the veena, a lute
choices: Seated, playing the veena, a lute
Seated, playing a board game
Seated, reading from a scroll
Seated, feeding a tame peacock
context: Despite conquests that earned him the 'Indian Napoleon' nickname, Samudragupta's gold coins also show him seated playing the veena — advertising a warrior-king who was also a musician. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samudragupta

question: Around 400 CE the Chinese Buddhist monk Fa-Hien walked across Gupta India and wrote home amazed: the highways were safe and the death penalty was almost never used. In the capital, Pataliputra, he found one charity paid for entirely by donations, where anyone in need was taken in and helped at no cost. What was this remarkable place?
answer: A free hospital
choices: A free hospital
A free library
A free granary
A free travelers' inn
context: Fa-Hien (Faxian) reported that Pataliputra had a free hospital, funded by donations, giving the poor and sick food, shelter, and medicine — in a land so peaceful that criminals were usually just fined. https://byjus.com/free-ias-prep/fa-hien-faxian-337ce-422ce/

question: About 499 CE Aryabhata made a claim most people found impossible: that the Earth itself spins, and the sky only LOOKS like it is turning. Critics objected — if the Earth were really spinning, surely we would feel it whirling. Aryabhata answered with an everyday picture. Which picture did he use?
answer: A man drifting downstream sees the still bank slide backward
choices: A man drifting downstream sees the still bank slide backward
A child on a spinning top feels pinned to its centre
A bird gliding feels the wind hold it perfectly still
A stone dropped from a tower lands far behind the thrower
context: Aryabhata wrote that just as a man in a moving boat sees the stationary shore drift backward, people on the spinning Earth see the still stars sweep toward the west. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aryabhata

question: The Sushruta Samhita, the great Sanskrit surgery manual put into its lasting form in Gupta times, explains how to rebuild a patient's missing nose — real plastic surgery, some 1,500 years ago. Before cutting any skin, the surgeon needed the replacement to be sized exactly right. What simple tool did he use to take that measurement?
answer: A leaf, held up to the face
choices: A leaf, held up to the face
A knotted length of string
A carved wooden mold
A lump of soft clay
context: The surgeon measured the missing nose with a leaf, then cut a matching flap of living skin from the patient's cheek or forehead and stitched it on, propping the new nostrils open with little castor-oil-plant tubes. https://hekint.org/2017/01/22/sushruta-the-ancient-indian-surgeon/

question: The Sushruta Samhita does not only describe ancient Indian operations — it tells the surgeon how to spare the patient before the knife goes in, about 2,000 years before modern medicine. According to the text, what should the patient be given first to ready him?
answer: Wine, to make him insensible to pain
choices: Wine, to make him insensible to pain
A leather strap, to bite down on
A priest's chant, to calm his fear
A cup of cold water, to wet his lips
context: Sushruta's text orders wine before an operation 'to produce insensibility to pain' — a form of anesthesia roughly 2,000 years before modern surgery. https://hekint.org/2017/01/22/sushruta-the-ancient-indian-surgeon/

question: Across Gupta-era India, scholars built the place-value number system the whole world now uses. In 628 CE the mathematician Brahmagupta went a step further and did what no one had managed before: he wrote down the rules for treating one strange quantity as a real number you could add, subtract, and multiply — a quantity older thinkers had refused to call a number at all. Which quantity was Brahmagupta taming?
answer: Zero
choices: Zero
Infinity
One half
The square root of two
context: In his Brahma-sphuta-siddhanta (628 CE), Brahmagupta wrote the first known rules for treating zero as a real number. The digit zero and the decimal place-value system both grew up in Gupta-era India. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brahmagupta

question: The Gupta court's brightest literary star was the poet Kalidasa, later nicknamed 'the Shakespeare of India,' and people still stage his plays 1,500 years on. In his most famous one, King Dushyanta is cursed to utterly forget the woman he loves, Shakuntala. At the climax, a single small keepsake makes the king suddenly remember her and everything that happened. What was the keepsake?
answer: A ring he had given her
choices: A ring he had given her
A lock of her hair
A song she once sang
A scar on her hand
context: Kalidasa's play 'Abhijnanashakuntalam' (The Recognition of Shakuntala) turns on a ring of recognition that restores King Dushyanta's cursed memory — still performed 1,500 years later. https://curiousindian.in/reign-of-chandragupta-ii-vikramaditya/

question: The Iron Pillar of Delhi has stood in the open for roughly 1,600 years and barely rusted, while ordinary iron rots in a few years. In the 1990s a metallurgist at IIT Kanpur, R. Balasubramaniam, finally cracked the riddle: the ancient iron is unusually rich in one element, which over the centuries grew a wafer-thin skin on the surface that locks the rust out. What was different about this iron?
answer: It held far more phosphorus than modern iron
choices: It held far more phosphorus than modern iron
It held far more carbon than modern iron
It held far more sulphur than modern iron
It held a hidden thread of pure silver
context: The pillar's iron carries about 0.25% phosphorus (versus under 0.05% in modern iron), which slowly formed a protective iron-phosphate film called 'misawite,' only about one-twentieth of a millimetre thick. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_pillar_of_Delhi

question: Ancient Indian surgeons in the Sushruta tradition faced a deadly problem: how to close a cut deep inside the body — a sliced intestine — with stitches that would still hold after the patient was sewn shut. Their answer used living creatures as the stitches themselves. What did these surgeons do?
answer: Let black ants bite across the cut, then snipped off their bodies
choices: Let black ants bite across the cut, then snipped off their bodies
Let leeches clamp the cut, then sealed them under hot wax
Held the cut shut with live beetles' pincers, then crushed their shells
Packed the cut with maggots, then bound it tight with silk
context: They let big black ants bite down across the wound with their pincer jaws, then cut off the bodies — leaving the locked heads in place as natural living stitches. https://www.gocuriousmind.com/2024/09/ancient-indian-medicine-live-ants-wound-sutures.html

question: About 499 CE Aryabhata gave a value for pi — the ratio around a circle — of 3.1416, so accurate that no one bettered it for a thousand years. But then he added one careful word, calling the value 'asanna,' meaning 'approaching' or 'approximate.' Scholars believe that single word shows Aryabhata had glimpsed a deep truth about pi. What was he hinting?
answer: That pi can never be written out exactly
choices: That pi can never be written out exactly
That pi changes from one circle to the next
That pi is exactly twenty-two sevenths
That pi had been copied from Greek books
context: Aryabhata gave pi as 62832/20000 = 3.1416 and called it 'asanna' — read by scholars as a hint that pi is irrational and can never be written out exactly. His value went unbeaten for about a thousand years. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aryabhata

question: Around 1455 in Mainz, Germany, Johannes Gutenberg printed his famous Bible using an invention that let a single press do the work of a whole roomful of scribes. What was his great breakthrough?
answer: Casting hundreds of tiny metal letters that could be arranged into a page and then rearranged for the next
choices: Casting hundreds of tiny metal letters that could be arranged into a page and then rearranged for the next
Carving each whole page into a single wooden block that was inked and stamped
Teaching dozens of scribes to copy the same page at the same time
Pressing wet clay tablets against a stone master copy
context: This was movable metal type. Gutenberg cast hundreds of individual letters, locked them into a page, printed, then broke the page apart and reused the same letters for the next — so one press replaced a roomful of hand-copyists. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible

question: Gutenberg did not build his printing machine from nothing. He took a heavy farm device that crushed grapes for wine and olives for oil and rebuilt it to print inked metal letters onto paper. Which farm device did he repurpose?
answer: A screw press
choices: A screw press
A cheese press
A cider press
A cloth press
context: The wine-and-oil screw press already existed on farms across Europe; Gutenberg's clever move was to point that crushing power at a tray of inked type. The machine that made wine became the machine that made books. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press

question: A skilled scribe copying a book by hand could finish only about one page in a day. Gutenberg's press, working the same day, could produce roughly how many printed pages?
context: One scribe: a page a day. One press: about 3,600 pages a day. By 1500, just fifty years after Gutenberg's Bible, around 20 million printed books were already circulating in Europe — versus maybe 100,000 hand-copied manuscripts before. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press

question: Collectors nickname Gutenberg's Bible by counting the lines in each tall column of text on its pages. By what number is the finished Bible known?
answer: The 42-line Bible
choices: The 42-line Bible
The 40-line Bible
The 66-line Bible
The 100-line Bible
context: Each column ended up with exactly 42 lines, so collectors call it the '42-line Bible.' Gutenberg actually began printing with 40 lines per column, then tightened the spacing to squeeze in two more partway through — you can spot the switch, since the earliest pages have fewer, more open lines. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible

question: Before he printed anything, Johannes Gutenberg trained in a craft that became his secret weapon — it let him invent a hand mould and mix a special low-melting alloy of lead, tin, and antimony to cast type cheaply. What was his trade?
answer: Goldsmith
choices: Goldsmith
Blacksmith
Locksmith
Bell-founder
context: As a trained goldsmith, Gutenberg knew how to melt and cast metal precisely. His reusable hand mould could pump out identical letters fast, and his lead-tin-antimony type-metal melted at a low temperature so new letters were cheap to make. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Gutenberg

question: In 1999, looking back over the entire second millennium — the years 1000 to 2000 — the A&E television network ranked the people whose work had changed the world most. They placed Johannes Gutenberg in what position?
answer: The single most influential person of the millennium
choices: The single most influential person of the millennium
Inventor of the year for the 1450s
The richest man of medieval Germany
The first modern celebrity
context: A&E rated Gutenberg the most influential PERSON of the whole millennium — ahead of every king, scientist, and explorer — because cheap printed books spread knowledge to ordinary people for the first time. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Gutenberg

question: Gutenberg's pages came off the press in plain black ink only. The handsome red chapter headings and the painted decorations you see in surviving copies were not printed at all. How did each Bible get them?
answer: The buyer hired scribes and artists to add them by hand afterward
choices: The buyer hired scribes and artists to add them by hand afterward
A second press stamped them in colored ink
Gutenberg painted every copy himself before selling it
They faded from black to red with age
context: After buying the plain black-ink book, owners paid scribes to brush in red headings (called rubrication) and artists to paint decorations. Because every owner hired different hands, no two surviving Gutenberg Bibles are decorated alike. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible

question: Gutenberg printed most of his roughly 180 Bibles on paper, but the finest copies were printed on vellum — fine animal skin. To make the pages for just ONE vellum Bible took the skins of about how many calves?
context: About 170 calfskins went into a single vellum copy — an entire calf herd for one Bible. Of all the copies, only three complete vellum Gutenberg Bibles survive today. Source: https://www.history.com/news/7-things-you-may-not-know-about-the-gutenberg-bible

question: In 1969 a burglar named Vido Aras hid until closing inside Harvard's Widener Library, pried two volumes of its Gutenberg Bible into a knapsack, and tried to rope his way down the outside of the building. What happened to him as he climbed down?
answer: The heavy load dragged him off the wall and he fell six stories
choices: The heavy load dragged him off the wall and he fell six stories
Campus guards spotted his rope and caught him at the bottom
His rope snapped clean and he tumbled into the bushes unhurt
He froze halfway down and had to be talked back up by police
context: The two volumes weighed about 70 pounds — so heavy the load pulled Aras off the building. He plunged six stories and fractured his skull, but he survived, and so did the Bible, which went back on the shelf. Source: https://www.history.com/news/7-things-you-may-not-know-about-the-gutenberg-bible

question: Gutenberg borrowed a fortune from a wealthy moneylender named Johann Fust to finish the Bible. Just as the work was nearly done, in November 1455, Fust sued him and the court ruled for Fust. What did Fust walk away with?
answer: Gutenberg's whole workshop and half of the finished Bibles
choices: Gutenberg's whole workshop and half of the finished Bibles
Only the money he had lent, paid back with interest
A public apology and Gutenberg's promise to repay later
A share of every book Gutenberg printed for life
context: After lending Gutenberg 1,600 guilders, Fust took him to court and won — seizing the print shop and, together with Gutenberg's own foreman Peter Schöffer, keeping half the finished Bibles. Gutenberg lost his life's work right as it succeeded. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Gutenberg

question: School often calls Gutenberg the first person ever to print with movable metal type — but he was beaten to it. A Buddhist book called the Jikji was printed with movable metal type in the Korean city of Cheongju in 1377. How long was that before Gutenberg's Bible?
answer: About 73 years earlier
choices: About 73 years earlier
About 5 years earlier
About 300 years earlier
About the same year
context: The Jikji, printed in Korea in 1377, beat Gutenberg by 73 years and survives as the oldest book printed with movable metal type — now held in Paris and listed in UNESCO's Memory of the World. Gutenberg's leap was building a whole system that flooded a continent with books. Source: https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/689333-oldest-book-printed-using-movable-metal-type

question: Gutenberg Bibles are among the most valuable books on Earth. At a Christie's auction in October 1987, a single volume from the Doheny collection set a record for any printed book ever sold. About how much did that one volume bring?
answer: About $5.4 million
choices: About $5.4 million
About $90,000
About $250 million
context: The buyer, Maruzen of Tokyo, paid about $5.4 million for one volume — a record for any printed book at the time. Experts now estimate a complete two-volume copy would fetch over $35 million. Source: https://www.upi.com/Archives/1987/10/23/Record-49-million-spent-on-Gutenberg-Bible/1356561960000/

question: Johannes Gutenberg needed to push a whole sheet of paper down onto inked metal letters firmly and evenly, all at once. Rather than build a machine from scratch, he took a heavy wooden screw-down press already standing in workshops all over the Rhineland and pointed its crushing power at a tray of type. The press he chose was the same back-breaking kind farmers cranked down each autumn to make their region's most famous drink. Which farm press did Gutenberg convert into the first printing press?
answer: The wine press
choices: The wine press
The olive press
The cider press
The cheese press
context: Gutenberg adapted the wooden screw press used by Rhineland vintners to crush grapes, turning that even, all-at-once pressure onto a tray of inked movable type. The machine that made wine became the machine that made books. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press

question: Gutenberg's masterpiece is nicknamed the '42-line Bible' because almost every tall column holds exactly 42 lines of type. But the very first pages he printed had only 40 lines. Page by page he crammed the lines closer together -- 40, then 41, then 42 -- to make a single change. Why did Gutenberg squeeze in those extra lines?
answer: To save costly paper
choices: To save costly paper
To finish the book faster
To copy a rival's design
To leave room for pictures
context: Paper and vellum were the most expensive part of the job, so fitting more text on each page meant fewer sheets per Bible. The nickname records the squeeze: the 42-line Bible. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible)

question: The man who changed the world by printing books did not start out as a printer or a scholar. Before his great invention, Johannes Gutenberg trained in a craft of cutting tiny shapes into hard steel and casting molten metal by hand -- the very skill that later let him punch and cast thousands of perfectly identical little letters. What was Gutenberg's original trade?
answer: A goldsmith
choices: A goldsmith
A monk
A papermaker
A merchant
context: Goldsmithing taught Gutenberg to cut steel punches and strike copper matrices -- exactly the metalwork needed to mass-produce reusable type. The jeweler's eye for tiny, exact shapes is what made movable type possible. (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Johannes-Gutenberg)

question: For a thousand years, scribes had written with a thin, water-based ink that soaked nicely into paper. But when Gutenberg brushed that same ink onto his smooth metal letters, it beaded up and slid right off, leaving smears instead of crisp print. To make ink that would actually cling to metal, Gutenberg borrowed the recipe painters used for their paints. What was the key ingredient in his new ink?
answer: Oil
choices: Oil
Wax
Sap
Soot
context: Water-based scribal ink would not stick to metal, so Gutenberg made an oil-based ink, closer to a varnish, like the paints of oil painters; analysis shows it was rich in metals like copper, lead, and titanium. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible)

question: When a finished Gutenberg Bible came off the press, it looked oddly incomplete. The machine had stamped the plain black text, but Gutenberg had deliberately left blank gaps at the start of chapters. Skilled artists then went through each copy by hand, filling those gaps -- which is why no two Gutenberg Bibles ended up looking exactly the same. What did the artists add by hand afterward?
answer: The colored initials and red headings
choices: The colored initials and red headings
The page numbers and the index
The wooden covers and clasps
The author's name on the spine
context: The press printed only black text; big colored initial letters and red headings were painted in by hand, so richer buyers paid for fancier decoration and no two copies are identical. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible)

question: Gutenberg printed about 180 copies of his Bible, and most were on paper. But the finest, most expensive copies were not printed on paper at all. For wealthy buyers, Gutenberg used a far costlier writing surface that gave a smoother, more luxurious page -- the same material monks had long used for their grandest hand-copied books. What were the deluxe Gutenberg Bibles printed on?
answer: Fine animal skin
choices: Fine animal skin
Pressed silk cloth
Thin birch bark
Beaten copper sheets
context: Of roughly 180 copies, about 135 were on paper and 45 on the finer animal skin, called vellum -- fine parchment made from calfskin. The vellum copies are the rarest survivors today. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible)

question: We picture Gutenberg's press making his beautiful Bible -- but a Bible took about two years to finish. To bring in money along the way, his workshop churned out thousands of small printed slips for the Church. A buyer paid a fee for one, and in return the Church promised to cancel the heavenly punishment owed for his sins. The 'Cypriot' batch was sold around 1454 to fund a crusade. What were these money-raising slips called?
answer: Indulgences
choices: Indulgences
Crusader maps
Cathedral tickets
Church tax bills
context: Gutenberg's shop printed thousands of paper indulgences for the Church, including Cypriot indulgences issued under Pope Calixtus III around 1454-1455 to fund a crusade -- fast, profitable jobs next to the slow Bible. (https://www.mainz.de/en/microsite/gutenberg/zeit/zeitleiste_gutenberg)

question: To fool the eye, Gutenberg wanted his printed Bible to look exactly like a monk's handwriting, where letters often join and shrink into shorthand. You might guess his type needed only the 26 letters of the alphabet. In fact, to copy every joined letter, every shorthand mark, and both upper and lower case, his B42 typeface held a startling number of different characters. About how many did it have?
answer: About 290
choices: About 290
About 26
About 52
About 75
context: The B42 type had roughly 290 characters: 47 capitals, 63 lowercase, 92 abbreviations, 83 joined-letter ligatures, and 5 punctuation marks -- all to mimic a scribe's hand. (https://oldbookappreciator.com/libraryofhistoricaltype/exhibits/show/gutenbergsb42/b42type)

question: Johannes Gutenberg borrowed a small fortune from a rich Mainz businessman, Johann Fust, to build his shop and print his Bible. Then, just as the long years of work were paying off, Fust dragged Gutenberg to court in 1455 and won. The verdict let Fust walk off with the heart of the whole enterprise, right when Gutenberg should have collected his reward. What did the verdict let Fust carry off?
answer: His press and the finished Bibles
choices: His press and the finished Bibles
His house and his goldsmith's tools
His store of fresh paper and ink
His chest of gold and silver coins
context: On 6 November 1455 Fust sued in the archbishop of Mainz's court and won; he seized Gutenberg's press, equipment, and a share of the finished Bibles just as they were ready to sell -- so Fust, not Gutenberg, reaped the profit. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/Helmaspergersches-Notariatsinstrument)

question: Johannes Gutenberg never put his own name anywhere in his great Bible. For a thousand years no book had ever told a reader a single thing about how it came to be -- who had made it, or when. Then in 1457 came the Mainz Psalter, printed by Johann Fust and his partner Peter Schoeffer. On its very last page they added a short line, a 'first' that printed books have copied ever since. What did that line record?
answer: Who made it and when
choices: Who made it and when
How much it cost
A blessing for readers
A warning to copyists
context: The 1457 Mainz Psalter carried the first printed colophon -- a closing line naming the printers and the date -- plus the first printer's mark and printed colored initials. The names history records there are Fust and Schoeffer (Gutenberg's former assistant), not Gutenberg, whose press they had seized two years earlier. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainz_Psalter)

question: For all his fame, Johannes Gutenberg left behind almost no personal trace -- no diary, no business ledgers, not even a single page he signed. Astonishingly, nearly everything historians know about his business and his invention survives because of just one piece of paper, still kept today at Germany's Goettingen university library. What document is that one precious source?
answer: The court record of Fust's lawsuit against him
choices: The court record of Fust's lawsuit against him
A city tax roll listing his Mainz workshop
An archbishop's account book of his pension
A goldsmiths' guild register bearing his name
context: The Helmasperger Notarial Instrument, recording the 1455 lawsuit, is the only contemporary account of Gutenberg's work -- so our knowledge of the printing revolution rests largely on the document that ruined its inventor. (https://www.mainz.de/en/microsite/gutenberg/zeit/zeitleiste_gutenberg)

question: His invention would reshape the world, yet Johannes Gutenberg himself ended his life poor, his press lost to Fust. Late in 1465, the archbishop Adolf von Nassau took pity and granted the old man a courtier's honor with a yearly gift of grain, wine, and clothing, all of it tax-free. Gutenberg died in Mainz three years later, in 1468, having left behind one strange gap. What do we still not have of Gutenberg today?
answer: A genuine portrait of his face
choices: A genuine portrait of his face
A single copy of his Bible
The city records of his birth
Any printing by his rivals
context: Archbishop Adolf von Nassau gave the impoverished Gutenberg a tax-free pension of grain, wine, and clothing in 1465; he died on 3 February 1468. No genuine likeness of him survives -- every famous 'portrait' was imagined long after his death. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Gutenberg)

question: Around 1450 in the German city of Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg used his new movable metal type to print the first major book ever made this way in Europe — the work that launched the whole age of printed books. Which book was it?
answer: the Bible
choices: the Bible
a grammar book
a book of Psalms
a saints' calendar
context: Gutenberg's first big printed book, made around 1450 in Mainz, was a Latin Bible now famous as the Gutenberg Bible. It is the work that launched the age of printed books in the West. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible

question: Gutenberg's great book is nicknamed the '42-line Bible' because almost every column has 42 lines of type. But his very first sheets had only 40 lines — he then squeezed the lines closer together to cram two more onto each column. Why did he bother packing them in tighter?
answer: to use less paper
choices: to use less paper
to make it easier to read
to copy a rival's design
to leave room for pictures
context: The first sheets had 40 lines (one page even has 41); Gutenberg then tightened the spacing to fit 42, most likely to save costly paper. That is exactly why it is called the 42-line Bible. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible

question: A printed Gutenberg Bible was a real bargain next to one copied by hand — yet a finished copy still cost about 30 gold florins, roughly 100 grams of gold. For an ordinary working man of the time, how much was 30 florins worth?
answer: about three years' wages
choices: about three years' wages
about three weeks' wages
about three days' wages
about thirty years' wages
context: Thirty florins was about three years' pay for a clerk and equal to roughly 100 grams of gold — far cheaper than a hand-copied Bible, but still a small fortune for most people. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible

question: The fanciest copies of Gutenberg's Bible weren't printed on paper at all, but on vellum — fine parchment made from calfskin. To make just ONE of these deluxe Bibles, how many calves' worth of skin did it take?
answer: about 170 calfskins
choices: about 170 calfskins
about 12 calfskins
about 40 calfskins
about 600 calfskins
context: A single vellum Gutenberg Bible needed roughly 170 calfskins. With about 35 vellum copies made, somewhere near 5,950 calves went into the parchment editions. Source: https://sarahemilybond.com/2016/04/04/sacrificial-lambs-livestock-book-costs-and-the-premodern-parchment-trade/

question: Gutenberg cast each tiny printing letter from a special metal mix — soft enough to pour into a sharp shape, yet hard enough to survive being pressed thousands of times. Printers used the very same recipe for centuries afterward. Which three metals were melted together to make it?
answer: lead, tin, and antimony
choices: lead, tin, and antimony
iron, copper, and zinc
gold, silver, and lead
bronze, brass, and pewter
context: Type metal was an alloy of lead, tin, and antimony — soft enough to cast sharply, tough enough to survive thousands of presses. This same recipe was still in use centuries later. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movable_type

question: Copying a Bible by hand was brutally slow: a lone monk bent over his desk in a scriptorium needed roughly a whole year to finish a single copy. In that very same span of about a year, Gutenberg's press turned out — not one Bible, but how many?
answer: about 180
choices: about 180
about 12
about 3
about 40
context: Gutenberg printed the entire run of about 180 Bibles in roughly the time it would take one scribe to hand-copy a single one. That one comparison is the whole revolution. Source: https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Gutenberg_Bible

question: Gutenberg's real secret was a clever hand mould. He hammered a steel punch into soft copper to stamp a backwards letter, making a little mould called a matrix; he dropped the matrix into the hand mould, poured in molten metal, and seconds later popped out one finished letter. The magic was what that single matrix let him do. What was it?
answer: make thousands of identical copies of that one letter
choices: make thousands of identical copies of that one letter
press that one letter straight onto the page
shape an entire page in a single pour
engrave a decorated capital by hand
context: One matrix could cast thousands of identical reusable letters (each called a 'sort'), and each one cooled in seconds. That is what made mass printing possible. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movable_type

question: In March 1455, a churchman named Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini — the future Pope Pius II — saw sheets of Gutenberg's new Bible on display at Frankfurt and wrote the earliest known eyewitness report of printing. What amazed him most about the pages?
answer: so clean and clear you could read it without glasses
choices: so clean and clear you could read it without glasses
so bright with gold paint it lit up the room
so sweet with perfume the whole hall smelled of it
so thin and light you could fold it into a pocket
context: In his letter of 12 March 1455 to Cardinal Carvajal, Piccolomini marveled that the lettering was so neat and correct it 'could be read effortlessly, even without glasses.' It is the first eyewitness account of printing. Source: https://www.historyofinformation.com/detail.php?id=292

question: Gutenberg had borrowed a fortune from a Mainz businessman, Johann Fust, to pay for what he called 'the Work of the Books.' The moment the great Bible was finished, Fust took him to court over the loans — and won. What did the court make Gutenberg hand over?
answer: his printing press and type
choices: his printing press and type
his house and all its furniture
his stable of horses and cart
his title and court pension
context: The Helmasperger Notarial Instrument of 6 November 1455 shows Gutenberg ordered to repay Fust with interest, costing him his press and type. Fust then took over the workshop with Gutenberg's assistant Peter Schoeffer and kept printing — so the inventor lost the very press that made his masterpiece almost the moment it was done. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Johann-Fust

question: In 1921 a New York bookseller named Gabriel Wells owned an incomplete Gutenberg Bible — and did something that scandalized the rare-book world. He pulled the centuries-old Bible apart and sold its loose pages one at a time, each in its own leather case with a scholarly essay. What did he call these single sheets?
answer: "Noble Fragments"
choices: "Noble Fragments"
"Holy Leaves"
"Mainz Relics"
"Gutenberg Shards"
context: Wells sold the dismembered pages as 'Noble Fragments.' The rare-book world was scandalized — but he died rich, because the Bible turned out to be worth more in pieces than whole. Source: https://www.themorgan.org/incunables/145177

question: The printing press didn't just make Bibles — it made the Reformation impossible to stop. When Martin Luther posted his 95 Theses in 1517, printers spread them across Germany within a year, and by 1525 his short pamphlets had sold in such staggering numbers that historians give Luther a title no author had held before him. What is that title?
answer: the first bestselling author in history
choices: the first bestselling author in history
the first man to print a book
the first translator of the Bible
the first to write in German
context: Between 1517 and 1525 Luther published over half a million works — making him the first bestselling author of the modern age. His short German pamphlets were nicknamed Flugschriften, 'flying writings,' because they spread so fast; Luther called printing 'God's highest and extremest act of grace.' Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/2039/the-printing-press--the-protestant-reformation/

question: Gutenberg's press began with a single book. Just fifty years later, by the year 1500, printing presses were running in roughly 282 European towns — and together they had already produced an astonishing mountain of printed books. Roughly how many had Europe printed by 1500?
answer: over nine million
choices: over nine million
over ninety thousand
over nine hundred
over nine billion
context: By 1500 presses in about 282 towns across some 18 countries had produced over nine million books in just fifty years. Books printed before 1501 are called 'incunabula' — Latin for 'cradle' — and about 30,000 distinct editions are known. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incunable

question: Johannes Gutenberg invented printing in the German city of Mainz around 1440. Before his great invention, he earned his living there as a skilled craftsman. What was Gutenberg's trade?
answer: a goldsmith
choices: a goldsmith
a stonemason
a woodcarver
a glassblower
context: As a goldsmith, Gutenberg had spent years cutting, casting, and polishing metal by hand — the exact skills he needed to make thousands of tiny, perfect metal letters. The invention grew straight out of his craft. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Gutenberg

question: Gutenberg needed to press paper down hard and evenly onto his inked metal type. Rather than invent a brand-new machine, he adapted a screw press that workers already used in the food trade. The printing press was a made-over version of a press built to squeeze what?
answer: grapes, to make wine
choices: grapes, to make wine
olives, to make oil
apples, to make cider
barley, to make beer
context: Gutenberg's press was a converted WINE press. He kept the big turning screw that crushed grapes and used it to push a flat plate (the platen) down onto the paper, pressing every letter evenly at once. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press

question: Before Gutenberg, to print a page you had to carve the whole page — every single word — backwards into one wooden block, and that block was useless for any other page. Gutenberg's breakthrough did away with all that carving. What was his key invention?
answer: tiny reusable metal letters, rearranged for each new page
choices: tiny reusable metal letters, rearranged for each new page
a giant iron stamp that pressed a whole page at once
a faster knife for carving wooden blocks quickly
a paint roller that spread ink across the wood
context: This is called movable type: thousands of separate metal letters that you arrange into a page, print, then pull apart and rearrange into the next page — instead of carving a brand-new block every time. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movable_type

question: Gutenberg used his new press to make a book that became the most famous in the world — the first big book in Europe ever produced with mass-made movable metal type. Which book did Gutenberg print in Mainz in the 1450s?
answer: a Latin Bible
choices: a Latin Bible
a book of Greek myths
a royal law code
a book of love poems
context: The Gutenberg Bible, printed in Mainz in the 1450s, was the first major book in Europe made with mass-produced movable metal type. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible

question: Copying a book by hand, a single monk could finish only a handful of pages in a day, and even the older method of printing from carved wooden blocks managed only about 40 a day. Gutenberg's press blew past both. About how many pages could one printing press turn out in a single day?
answer: about 3,600
choices: about 900
about 1,800
about 3,600
about 7,200
context: Roughly 3,600 pages a day — hundreds of times faster than a human copyist. For the first time, books could be made faster than people could hand-copy them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press

question: The watery ink that monks used for writing simply beaded up and slid off Gutenberg's smooth metal letters, leaving a smeared mess. So Gutenberg mixed a brand-new kind of ink that would grip the metal and print crisp, dark letters. What was special about Gutenberg's new ink?
answer: it was oil-based
choices: it was oil-based
it was made from berries
it was scented with perfume
it was mixed with gold dust
context: Gutenberg's oily, oil-based ink clung to the smooth metal type where the old water-based ink could not — printing clean, dark letters. A whole new ink had to be invented just to make the press work. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Gutenberg

question: The Gutenberg Bible is nicknamed the '42-line Bible' because 42 lines of text fill each tall column. Gutenberg's earliest pages actually held only 40 lines per column, but partway through the print run he packed the lines closer together to fit 42. Why did Gutenberg squeeze the lines closer?
answer: to save expensive paper
choices: to save expensive paper
to make the words bigger
to copy a rival printer
to leave room for pictures
context: Paper was costly, so fitting 42 lines instead of 40 in each column meant fewer pages per Bible. The page has two columns, and that 42-line layout gave the book its famous nickname. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible

question: Gutenberg couldn't cast his letters from just any metal. He needed a recipe that melted at low heat, cooled fast, and — thanks to one special ingredient — expanded slightly as it hardened so each letter came out razor-sharp. Gutenberg's 'type metal' was a blend of lead, tin, and which third metal?
answer: antimony
choices: antimony
copper
silver
iron
context: Type metal mixed lead, tin, and antimony. The antimony was the clever part: most metals shrink as they cool, but antimony made the blend expand a touch when setting, so the letters filled the mould completely and came out crisp. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_metal

question: Gutenberg cut each letter backwards onto the tip of a hard steel rod called a punch, then hammered that punch into a soft copper bar to create a small object called a matrix. What was a single matrix used for?
answer: to cast thousands of identical metal letters
choices: to cast thousands of identical metal letters
to press the paper flat against the type
to grind the ink into a fine powder
to carve pictures into wooden blocks
context: One steel punch stamped one copper matrix, and that single matrix could be filled with molten metal again and again to cast thousands of perfectly identical letters. This punch-and-mould system is what made mass-producing type possible. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movable_type

question: When Gutenberg's Bible came off the press, the pages were not actually finished. He had left deliberate blank gaps where the big decorated capital letters and chapter headings belonged, so that more work could be done on each copy afterward. What was done in those blank spaces?
answer: artists hand-painted the initials in red and blue
choices: artists hand-painted the initials in red and blue
buyers wrote their own names in the gaps
Gutenberg pasted in small woodcut pictures
the spaces were filled with gold leaf
context: Human artists came back and painted the big red and blue initials and headings by hand (called rubrication). Because each painter worked a little differently, almost no two surviving Gutenberg Bibles look exactly alike. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible

question: We picture Gutenberg's first printed work as his magnificent Bible — but the earliest item historians can pin to an exact date from his shop was something far humbler, churned out in bulk with a blank space left for a buyer's name. The first precisely dated printing from Gutenberg's shop, known by October 1454, was a batch of what?
answer: church pardon slips
choices: church pardon slips
royal tax forms
school grammar books
merchant trade receipts
context: Before the famous Bible, the first thing precisely dated to Gutenberg's shop was printed indulgences — church pardon slips — with blanks for the buyer's name and date. The 31-line Indulgence is known to have existed by 22 October 1454. Source: https://dpul.princeton.edu/gutenberg/catalog/d217qp581

question: To build his shop and print his Bible, Johannes Gutenberg borrowed a small fortune from a rich Mainz businessman named Johann Fust. In 1455, just as the Bibles were nearly finished, Fust dragged Gutenberg into court and won. When he won the lawsuit, what did Fust take from Gutenberg?
answer: Gutenberg's whole print shop and its presses
choices: Gutenberg's whole print shop and its presses
Gutenberg's house and farmland
Gutenberg's title and good name
Gutenberg's tools and a public apology
context: Fust had lent Gutenberg about 800 guilders for the shop and 800 more for the Bible, then sued, won 2,026 guilders, and seized the print shop and presses — at the very finish line. Gutenberg was ruined while Fust went on to profit from the invention. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Johann-Fust

question: In 1517 a German monk named Martin Luther posted his 95 Theses, a list of complaints against the Church. Luther meant them only for fellow scholars — but printers grabbed them and ran off copies without his permission. Thanks to the printing press, how fast did Luther's 95 Theses spread?
answer: across Germany in about two weeks
choices: across Germany in about two weeks
across Germany in about two years
across Germany in about twenty years
across Germany in about two centuries
context: Within two weeks the Theses had spread across Germany, and within two months across Europe. Historians say bluntly, 'No printing press, no Reformation' — ideas could now multiply faster than any king or church could suppress them. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/2039/the-printing-press--the-protestant-reformation/

question: At Vindolanda, a Roman fort on the northern frontier in Britain, a thin wooden tablet preserved a real letter sending a soldier supplies to survive the cold British weather. Along with two pairs of sandals and two pairs of underpants, what woolen item did the care package include?
answer: Socks
choices: Socks
A cloak
Gloves
A scarf
context: Vindolanda Tablet 346 lists 'pairs of socks from Sattua, two pairs of sandals and two pairs of underpants' — a genuine Roman care package from the edge of empire. Hundreds of these tablets survived ~2,000 years in a waterlogged, oxygen-free rubbish heap and were voted the British Museum's top treasure from Roman Britain in 2003. Source: britishmuseum.org Vindolanda tablets; Antigone Journal.

question: A soldier's note found at Vindolanda sneers at the local British tribesmen, complaining that 'the wretched Britons' don't even climb onto their horses to throw javelins. The note pins a mocking nickname on them — a single Latin word meaning 'wretched little Britons' that appears in no other surviving Latin writing anywhere. What was the insult?
answer: Brittunculi
choices: Brittunculi
Gallunculi
Barbarunculi
Germanunculi
context: Tab.Vindol. 164 (c. AD 97-105) is the only known use of 'Brittunculi' in all of surviving Latin — a contemptuous diminutive coined by a Roman on the frontier. The full line jeers that 'the cavalry do not use swords nor do the wretched Britons mount in order to throw javelins.' Source: romaninscriptionsofbritain.org TabVindol164; penelope.uchicago.edu.

question: The huge domed church Emperor Justinian built in Constantinople is called Hagia Sophia. In Greek, what does that name actually mean?
answer: Holy Wisdom
choices: Holy Wisdom
Holy Cross
Sacred Heart
Blessed Mother
context: Hagia Sophia is Greek for 'Holy Wisdom' — it was dedicated to the Wisdom of God, not to any saint named Sophia. Source: britannica.com 'Hagia Sophia'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia.

question: When Emperor Justinian first walked into his finished Hagia Sophia in 537 and gazed up at its vast dome, tradition says he shouted a boast that his church had outdone the greatest building in the Bible. What did Justinian cry out?
answer: "Solomon, I have surpassed thee!"
choices: "Solomon, I have surpassed thee!"
"Babylon itself would envy me!"
"Behold, a second Eden!"
"Rome has never seen the like!"
context: King Solomon's Temple in Jerusalem was the most famous building in the Bible; Justinian's boast claimed he had outbuilt it. Told as tradition. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia; gloriaromanorum.blogspot.com 'O Solomon, I have Surpassed Thee'.  (Legend.)

question: Eight enormous discs of gold-on-black Arabic calligraphy hang high on the walls of Hagia Sophia, each one about as wide as a city bus is long. Years later, when people wanted to take the giant discs down, they hit one surprising obstacle. What was it?
answer: They were too big to fit through the doors.
choices: They were too big to fit through the doors.
They were too holy to be moved.
They were bolted to the dome itself.
They were promised to stay forever.
context: Each roundel is about 7.5 meters across — among the largest pieces of calligraphy in the world — bearing the names of Allah, Muhammad, the first four caliphs, and Muhammad's two grandsons. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia; thehagiasophia.com 'Medallions'.

question: One marble column inside Hagia Sophia is famous as the 'wishing column.' Visitors press a thumb into a hole worn through the bronze plate over it and slowly turn their hand. According to the legend, what sign tells you your wish will come true?
answer: Your thumb comes out damp.
choices: Your thumb comes out damp.
Your thumb feels suddenly warm.
The hole hums very faintly.
The bronze turns slightly green.
context: Byzantines believed the moisture was the tears of the Virgin Mary, and legend says Justinian once cured a headache by leaning against the column. Told as legend. Source: atlasobscura.com 'Hagia Sophia wishing column'; ayasofyamuzesi.gov.tr 'Wishing Column'.

question: Hagia Sophia exists only because the church standing there before it burned down. In January 532 a furious riot called the Nika Revolt swept Constantinople and set the old church ablaze. What everyday event had first set off that riot?
answer: A chariot race.
choices: A chariot race.
A new royal tax.
A shortage of bread.
A feud between bishops.
context: The Nika Revolt began as a brawl between chariot-racing factions in the Hippodrome, then exploded into a city-wide riot. Justinian ordered the new church rebuilt within weeks. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nika_riots; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia.

question: High in a stone railing of Hagia Sophia's upper gallery, archaeologists in 1964 found graffiti scratched in Norse runes — left by one of the Viking warriors who served as bodyguards to the Byzantine emperor. Roughly translated, what does this 1,000-year-old scratch say?
answer: "Halfdan was here."
choices: "Halfdan was here."
"Olaf owns this seat."
"Glory to the emperor."
"God keep this hall."
context: It was carved by a member of the Varangian Guard, the Norse warriors who served the Byzantine emperor, and was only rediscovered in 1964. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runic_inscriptions_in_Hagia_Sophia; atlasobscura.com.

question: When Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453, the young Sultan Mehmed II rode straight through the conquered city to Hagia Sophia. What did he order be done with the great church that very day?
answer: Turned into a mosque.
choices: Turned into a mosque.
Pulled down for its stone.
Sealed shut forever.
Made into his palace.
context: A scholar climbed the pulpit and recited the shahada, and Mehmed prayed the first Friday prayer there days later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia.

question: The builders of Hagia Sophia faced a tricky problem: how do you rest a perfectly round dome on top of a square hall? The mathematician Anthemius of Tralles and the geometer Isidore of Miletus solved it with curved triangular sails of stone tucked into the four upper corners. What is each of these corner pieces called?
answer: A pendentive.
choices: A pendentive.
A buttress.
A keystone.
An archway.
context: Pendentives let a round dome sit smoothly on a square base — the breakthrough that made Hagia Sophia's vast dome possible. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia; smarthistory.org 'Hagia Sophia, Istanbul'.

question: For centuries Hagia Sophia served as one of the world's grandest mosques. Then in 1934, Turkey's first president, Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, changed its purpose once more, opening it to people of every faith and nation. What did Ataturk turn Hagia Sophia into?
answer: A public museum.
choices: A public museum.
A royal library.
A military fortress.
A national cathedral.
context: As a museum, its Byzantine Christian mosaics and Islamic calligraphy were displayed side by side, and it became Turkey's most-visited tourist site. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia; middleeasteye.net.

question: Forty windows ring the foot of Hagia Sophia's dome, and the daylight pouring through them makes the dome seem to hover weightlessly overhead. A historian named Procopius, who saw it for himself in the 500s, wrote the most famous line ever about that effect: the dome, he said, seems to hang from heaven by what?
answer: A golden chain.
choices: A golden chain.
A silver thread.
An iron rod.
A silken cord.
context: Procopius wrote that the dome 'seems not to rest upon solid masonry, but to cover the space as though suspended from heaven by a golden chain' — the 'dome of heaven' effect the architects wanted. Source: hagiasophia.com 'Hagia Sophia dome'; smarthistory.org.

question: Justinian's first dome on Hagia Sophia cracked in the earthquakes of 553 and 557, and in 558 its eastern half collapsed in a roar of falling stone. The architect Isidore the Younger rebuilt it — and that new dome has stood for more than 1,400 years. How did his dome differ from the one that fell?
answer: It was steeper and taller.
choices: It was steeper and taller.
It was wider and flatter.
It was thicker and heavier.
It was lower and rounder.
context: Isidore the Younger (nephew of the first Isidore) raised the rebuilt dome about 6.25 meters steeper and higher than Justinian's too-flat original. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia; hagiasophia.com 'Hagia Sophia dome'.

question: A golden mosaic in Hagia Sophia shows the Empress Zoe beside her husband — but Zoe married three different emperors in her lifetime. Each time she took a new husband, the mosaic workers updated the picture. How did they change it for the new emperor?
answer: They chiseled out the old face and set in the new one.
choices: They chiseled out the old face and set in the new one.
They added the new husband beside the old one.
They covered the whole panel with fresh paint.
They built a second mosaic on the far wall.
context: When Zoe swapped husbands, workmen cut out the previous emperor's face and name and inserted her new husband, Constantine IX Monomachos — even Christ's and Zoe's own faces were redone. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia; byzantine-world.com 'Zoe Porphyrogenita'.

question: When the leaders of the Haitian Revolution needed their own flag in 1803, they started with the blue-white-red flag of France — the very country they were fighting. What did they do to it to make the flag of Haiti?
answer: Tore out the white middle stripe and sewed the blue and red together
choices: Tore out the white middle stripe and sewed the blue and red together
Added a white star in the corner for each region they had freed
Turned the three stripes sideways and dyed the top one green
Stitched a golden lion across the center of the three stripes
context: The white middle stripe stood for the white colonists, so the leaders cut it out and joined the remaining blue and red. Tradition says Catherine Flon, goddaughter of the general Jean-Jacques Dessalines, sewed the two halves together in May 1803. (Source: Marxists.org, 'Dessalines, the Flag, and Independence'; Wikipedia, Catherine Flon.)

question: Toussaint, the great general of the Haitian Revolution, was born enslaved with no last name at all. Around 1792 he chose the surname 'Louverture' for himself. What does that French word mean?
answer: 'The opening' — the one who opens the way
choices: 'The opening' — the one who opens the way
'The lion' — the one who knows no fear
'The free man' — the one born to no master
'The storm' — the one who never rests
context: 'Louverture' is French for 'the opening.' The name was said to mark his talent for breaking open the enemy's lines in battle. By 1801 this once-enslaved man was the de facto ruler of the whole island and issued a constitution making himself governor-general for life and permanently abolishing slavery. (Source: Wikipedia, Toussaint Louverture.)

question: Toussaint Louverture was born enslaved and worked as a coachman, so skilled with horses that his masters made him their personal driver. He never set foot in a school — he taught himself to read. Which writers did this self-taught enslaved man teach himself to study?
answer: The Stoic philosopher Epictetus and Machiavelli
choices: The Stoic philosopher Epictetus and Machiavelli
The poet Homer and the general Julius Caesar
The explorer Marco Polo and the artist Leonardo da Vinci
The scientist Isaac Newton and the king Louis XIV
context: Teaching himself to read, Toussaint studied the Stoic philosopher Epictetus and the political writer Machiavelli. He was freed around 1776 and even rented a coffee plantation of his own before the revolution — all before becoming the general who drove Napoleon's army out of the island. (Source: Wikipedia, Toussaint Louverture.)

question: In June 1802 the French general Brunet invited Toussaint Louverture to a friendly meeting — then arrested him by treachery and put him on a ship bound for a prison in France. As he boarded, Toussaint is said to have warned his captors with a famous image of a tree. What did he tell them?
answer: "In overthrowing me you have cut down only the trunk of the tree of liberty; it will spring up again by the roots, for they are numerous and deep."
choices: "In overthrowing me you have cut down only the trunk of the tree of liberty; it will spring up again by the roots, for they are numerous and deep."
"You may chain my hands, but a hundred thousand free men will rise where I have fallen to finish what I began."
"Take me to your emperor, and let him look me in the eyes and say that one man may own another."
"The sea you sail me across is wide, but freedom has crossed it ahead of you to reach my island."
context: Toussaint died a prisoner on April 7, 1803, in the cold of Fort de Joux in the Jura Mountains, from illness and neglect — he never lived to see independence, which came less than a year later. His warning proved true: the fight went on without him. (Reported as his words; framed as legend. Source: Wikipedia, Toussaint Louverture; History Today.)

question: Napoleon poured a huge army into the colony of Saint-Domingue to crush the revolution, but the Haitians and yellow fever destroyed it. With his dream of an empire in the Americas in ruins, Napoleon made a sudden decision in 1803 that reshaped the map of North America. What did he do?
answer: Sold the entire Louisiana Territory to the United States, doubling its size
choices: Sold the entire Louisiana Territory to the United States, doubling its size
Invaded Canada to seize a fresh base from the British
Sent his fleet to burn the ports of the United States in revenge
Handed Saint-Domingue back to Spain in exchange for Florida
context: Because losing Saint-Domingue wrecked his plans for an American empire, Napoleon sold the whole Louisiana Territory to the United States in 1803 for about $15 million — doubling the size of the country. The slaves' fight for freedom indirectly reshaped the map of a continent. (Source: History.com, 'The Louisiana Purchase Was Driven by a Slave Rebellion.')

question: On January 1, 1804, Haiti became the only nation ever founded by a successful slave revolt — but France refused to recognize it. In 1825 France sent warships and set one staggering condition before it would admit Haiti was free. What did France force the Haitian people to do?
answer: Pay 150 million francs to repay the former slave-owners for their lost slaves
choices: Pay 150 million francs to repay the former slave-owners for their lost slaves
Return every freed person to their former master within ten years
Give back half the island's land to the French planters who had fled
Swear loyalty to the French king and fly his flag over their ports
context: France made the freed nation pay its former enslavers as the price of being recognized — a crushing 'independence debt' Haiti did not finish paying until 1910, generations later. (Source: Wikipedia, Haitian independence debt; NPR Planet Money, 'The Greatest Heist in History.')

question: Around 1754 BC, King Hammurabi of Babylon had his 282 laws carved top to bottom into a single upright monument over seven feet tall, set up in public so anyone could come and have the laws read aloud to them. Archaeologists have a special word for this kind of tall inscribed pillar. What is it?
answer: a stele
choices: a stele
a tablet
a scroll
a ledger
context: The stele still stands today in the Louvre in Paris. The whole code (about 4,130 lines) is carved in cuneiform in the Old Babylonian dialect of Akkadian. It is the earliest famous written law code -- the deep root of the idea that the law is written down, public, and read aloud to all. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_of_Hammurabi ; https://www.louvre.fr/en/the-code-of-hammurabi

question: Hammurabi's Code is famous for one harsh rule of fairness: the punishment had to mirror the crime exactly. If you blinded a man's eye, your own eye was blinded in return. What is the Latin name for this 'an eye for an eye' principle?
answer: lex talionis
choices: lex talionis
habeas corpus
casus belli
quid pro quo
context: Lex talionis means 'the law of retaliation.' Law 196 states it plainly: 'If a man has blinded the eye of a member of the awilum class, his eye will be blinded.' It is a real, nameable legal principle, not just a saying. Source: https://ehammurabi.org/law/196 ; https://www.louvre.fr/en/the-code-of-hammurabi

question: In the epilogue carved on his stele, Hammurabi did not call himself a warlord or a god. He chose a humble title and wrote, 'I am the ___ who brings peace, with a staff that is straight,' casting himself as one who gently guards and guides his people. Which title fills the blank?
answer: shepherd
choices: shepherd
high priest
judge
father
context: Hammurabi calls himself 'the shepherd' of his people in the epilogue: 'I am the shepherd who brings peace, with a staff that is straight.' The shepherd-with-staff image for a just ruler is one of the oldest in recorded history. Source: https://ehammurabi.org/epilogue ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammurabi

question: At the very top of Hammurabi's stele, a carving shows the king standing before Shamash, the seated Babylonian god of justice, receiving the law from him. How would an ancient viewer know the seated figure was the sun god? He is carved with ___.
answer: flames rising from his shoulders
choices: flames rising from his shoulders
a crown of bright golden rays
a blazing torch in each hand
a glowing disk above his head
context: Shamash is identified by flames bursting from his shoulders and by a footrest shaped like the mountains over which he rises each morning. The relief is the famous 'Shamash handing Hammurabi the law' image. Source: https://www.louvre.fr/en/the-code-of-hammurabi ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_of_Hammurabi

question: Hammurabi's very first law, Law 1, guards against lying in court. If a man accused another of murder but could not prove the charge, what happened to the accuser?
answer: the accuser was killed
choices: the accuser was killed
the accuser was fined
the accuser was branded
the accuser was exiled
context: Law 1: 'If a man accuses another man and charges him with homicide, but cannot bring proof against him, his accuser shall be killed.' Bringing a deadly charge you couldn't prove cost you your own life -- an early version of putting the burden of proof on the accuser. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_of_Hammurabi

question: Around 1158 BC an Elamite king sacked Babylon and hauled Hammurabi's seven-foot law-stele home to his own capital as a war trophy, where it lay buried for roughly 3,000 years until a French team dug it up in 1901. Which conqueror looted it?
answer: Shutruk-Nahhunte
choices: Shutruk-Nahhunte
Tiglath-Pileser
Ashurbanipal
Nebuchadnezzar
context: The Elamite king Shutruk-Nahhunte (reigned c. 1185-1160 BC) carried the stele off as plunder to his capital, Susa, in modern Iran. A French archaeological team under Jacques de Morgan rediscovered it there in 1901; the Louvre has displayed it since 1904. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_of_Hammurabi ; https://www.louvre.fr/en/the-code-of-hammurabi
