context: Between the stuck fuel-transfer pump and the Kokura delay, Bockscar limped to Okinawa with the flight engineer estimating under five minutes of fuel left in the tanks. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bockscar

question: American leaders were planning Operation Downfall — a full invasion of the Japanese home islands set to begin that winter. The just-finished battle for the island of Okinawa had been a horrifying preview, with about a third of the men involved killed or wounded. President Harry Truman said he hoped invading Japan would not turn into what?
answer: An Okinawa from one end of Japan to the other
choices: An Okinawa from one end of Japan to the other
A slaughter with no surrender ever in sight
A second front to rival the whole European war
A grave for a generation of young Americans
context: Okinawa's roughly 35% casualty rate was the grim model. Casualty forecasts for invading Japan ranged enormously — from a June 1945 estimate of about 40,000 US dead, to Truman's later claim of being warned of 250,000 to a million US casualties, with Japanese deaths projected in the millions. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Downfall

question: Historians still argue about exactly what pushed Japan to surrender in August 1945. Many point not only to the two atomic bombs but to a second massive shock that landed on August 8 — the very day between the bombing of Hiroshima and the bombing of Nagasaki. What happened on August 8 that some historians call an equally decisive blow?
answer: The Soviet Union declared war and invaded Japanese-held Manchuria
choices: The Soviet Union declared war and invaded Japanese-held Manchuria
The United States warned it would firebomb Tokyo next
Japan's navy lost its last carriers in a final sea battle
China's armies broke through into the Japanese home islands
context: On Aug 8 the USSR declared war on Japan; the next day over a million Soviet troops poured into Manchuria, crushing the Kwantung Army. Many historians argue the Soviet entry, alongside the atomic bombs, was a decisive shock; a minority (e.g. Ward Wilson) argue it was the bigger factor. This remains a genuinely debated question. Source: history.com/this-day-in-history/august-8/soviets-declare-war-on-japan-invade-manchuria

question: On the night of 8 November 1923, Adolf Hitler led about 600 of his armed SA men to surround a packed Munich beer hall, the Burgerbrau Keller. He shoved inside, leaped onto a chair, and shouted that the national revolution had begun. What dramatic thing did Hitler do to silence the crowd and prove he meant it?
answer: Fired a pistol shot into the ceiling
choices: Fired a pistol shot into the ceiling
Smashed a beer stein on the floor
Threw a burning torch onto the stage
Hung a Nazi banner over the bar
context: Hitler jumped on a chair, fired into the ceiling, and yelled 'The national revolution has broken out! The hall is surrounded by six hundred men.' The takeover, later called the Beer Hall Putsch, collapsed within a day. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beer_Hall_Putsch; USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia.

question: Adolf Hitler's coup failed, and in 1924 he was locked in Landsberg prison. Bored behind bars, he dictated his ranting political testament aloud to a devoted fellow inmate, Rudolf Hess, who wrote it all down. What was this book, which became the Nazi movement's blueprint?
answer: Mein Kampf
choices: Mein Kampf
The Communist Manifesto
The Prince
Das Kapital
context: So the book at the heart of Nazism was literally composed by a convicted coup-plotter sitting in a jail cell, dictated to Rudolf Hess. The title means 'My Struggle.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mein_Kampf; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landsberg_Prison.

question: On the night of 30 January 1933, the day Adolf Hitler was made Chancellor of Germany, tens of thousands of his SA and SS men poured through the streets of Berlin in a massive celebration. What did the marchers carry that made the night so famous and frightening to watch?
answer: Flaming torches
choices: Flaming torches
Black coffins
Iron chains
Brass trumpets
context: The torchlight parades became the iconic image of the night a democracy lit the way for the man who would destroy it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler's_rise_to_power.

question: On the night of 27 February 1933 the German parliament building, the Reichstag, burst into flames in Berlin, and its grand glass dome was gutted. Police rushed in and caught a 24-year-old man inside who confessed he had set the fire alone. Who was this lone arsonist?
answer: A Dutch bricklayer named Marinus van der Lubbe
choices: A Dutch bricklayer named Marinus van der Lubbe
A German general named Erich Ludendorff
An Austrian painter named Adolf Hitler
A Russian agent named Georgi Dimitrov
context: Marinus van der Lubbe, a young Dutch ex-communist bricklayer, was caught inside the burning building and confessed to acting alone. The fire gutted the debating chamber and the gilded glass cupola. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reichstag_fire; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marinus_van_der_Lubbe.

question: The day after the failed 1923 Beer Hall Putsch, about 2,000 Nazis marched into central Munich and were met by police gunfire at the Feldherrnhalle; sixteen of them fell dead. One Nazi banner was soaked in the blood of the men who died beneath it. What did the movement turn this gory banner into?
answer: Its holiest relic, touched to every new flag
choices: Its holiest relic, touched to every new flag
A burial shroud laid over the fallen dead
A war trophy mailed to Berlin headquarters
A velvet curtain hung in Hitler's office
context: The blood-splattered banner became the movement's most sacred object, the 'Blutfahne' (Blood Flag). New SS and SA banners were 'consecrated' by being physically touched to it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beer_Hall_Putsch.

question: In the gun battle at the Feldherrnhalle that ended Hitler's 1923 putsch, his loyal lieutenant Hermann Goring was hit by a bullet in the groin and smuggled out of Germany to escape arrest. The agony of that wound left Goring with a lifelong affliction. What was it?
answer: An addiction to morphine
choices: An addiction to morphine
A permanent limp
Blindness in one eye
A paralyzed arm
context: Goring was given morphine for the pain and became addicted to it for the rest of his life, a habit that dogged him to the Nuremberg trials. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beer_Hall_Putsch.

question: After the Reichstag burned on 27 February 1933, the very next day Adolf Hitler had the aged President Hindenburg sign the Reichstag Fire Decree, using emergency powers to suspend free speech, free press, assembly, and privacy of mail. With those rights gone, what did the Nazi-run police do across Germany overnight, just days before the election?
answer: Arrested thousands of Communists, including every KPD deputy
choices: Arrested thousands of Communists, including every KPD deputy
Shut every newspaper and radio station in the country
Seized all the gold in Germany's banks
Drafted every jobless man into the army
context: Police arrested thousands overnight, jailing every Communist (KPD) member of parliament and gutting the opposition before the 5 March 1933 vote. The Fire Decree was never lifted and became the permanent legal skeleton of the dictatorship. Source: encyclopedia.ushmm.org Reichstag Fire Decree article.

question: After his 1923 coup failed in a hail of police bullets, Adolf Hitler drew a hard lesson: street violence had landed him in prison and gotten his men killed. He decided that to take over Germany he would use a completely different weapon than guns and barricades. What was this new strategy he chose?
answer: Seizing power legally, through elections
choices: Seizing power legally, through elections
Fleeing Germany to lead the party from exile
Allying with the Communists to share power
Petitioning the French occupiers to back him
context: This 'path of legality' is the mechanism the whole story turns on: Hitler never won a majority at the ballot box, but he exploited the democratic system from the inside to dismantle it. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, Beer Hall Putsch article.

question: In 1928 the Nazi Party was a fringe group with about 800,000 votes. Then the Great Depression hit, unemployment climbed sharply, and millions of Germans were thrown out of work. Riding that desperation into the July 1932 election, roughly how far did the Nazi vote climb from that 800,000?
answer: About 14 million votes
choices: About 14 million votes
About 4 million votes
About 8 million votes
About 21 million votes
context: The Depression was the rocket fuel: as unemployment soared from about 8.5% to nearly 30% between 1929 and 1932, the Nazi vote leapt from 800,000 to roughly 14,000,000, making them the largest party in parliament. Source: britannica.com, Nazi Party; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/July_1932_German_federal_election.

question: In the July 1932 election the Nazis became the biggest party in the Reichstag with 37.4 percent, yet still fell short of a majority. So when Adolf Hitler was made Chancellor on 30 January 1933, it was not by winning an election but through a backroom deal struck by ex-Chancellor Franz von Papen. What did Papen convince President Hindenburg that Hitler would be?
answer: A harmless puppet they could control
choices: A harmless puppet they could control
A loyal soldier for the army
A temporary caretaker until new elections
A unifying hero for all Germans
context: Papen persuaded the aged Hindenburg to appoint Hitler, certain he could be controlled; only 3 of the 11 cabinet seats went to Nazis. Papen took the Vice-Chancellorship for himself. Source: history.com, Hitler named Chancellor; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler's_rise_to_power.

question: On 23 March 1933, as SA and SS men packed the hall for the vote on the Enabling Act, which would hand Adolf Hitler dictatorial power, only Social Democrat leader Otto Wels dared rise and tell Hitler to his face the one thing the Nazis could never take from his party. What did Wels say they could never take?
answer: Our honor
choices: Our honor
Our homeland
Our faith
Our children
context: Otto Wels told Hitler, 'Freedom and life can be taken from us, but not our honor.' His 94 Social Democrats cast the only No votes against the Enabling Act, and his speech was the last free speech in the German parliament for twelve years. Source: germanhistorydocs.org, Otto Wels speech, 23 March 1933.

question: The Enabling Act of 23 March 1933 needed a two-thirds majority to hand Adolf Hitler dictatorial powers, and the Nazis did not have the votes alone. The act only passed because one other party swung behind it, fooled by Hitler's spoken promises to its leaders, promises he broke. Which party's swing votes handed Hitler his dictatorship?
answer: The Catholic Centre Party
choices: The Catholic Centre Party
The Communist Party
The German National People's Party
The German Democratic Party
context: The Centre (Catholic) Party voted 72 to 0 in favor after Hitler verbally promised to protect Catholic schools and civil liberties. Without their cooperation the two-thirds majority would have failed and the legal road to dictatorship would have closed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enabling_Act_of_1933.

question: Trapped in the cave of the one-eyed giant Polyphemus, the hero Odysseus gets the Cyclops drunk on wine, then drives a sharpened, fire-hardened stake into the giant's single eye. When Polyphemus bellows for the other Cyclopes to come help, they ask who is hurting him -- and his answer makes them shrug and walk away, because earlier Odysseus had cleverly told the giant his name was something tricky. What name had Odysseus given?
answer: Nobody
choices: Nobody
Stranger
No one of Ithaca
A poor lost sailor
context: Odysseus called himself 'Nobody' (Greek 'Outis'), so the blinded giant screamed 'NOBODY is killing me!' and his neighbors left him to it. Odysseus and his men then escaped clinging to the bellies of the giant's sheep. Homer, Odyssey Book 9 (poetryintranslation.com/PITBR/Greek/Odyssey9.php); sparknotes.com Odyssey Book 9; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outis

question: Odysseus wanted to be the one man alive who had HEARD the deadly, irresistible song of the Sirens and still lived to tell it. He plugged every crewman's ears with beeswax so they would row on deaf, leaving him the only one who could hear. To keep himself from steering toward the song, what did Odysseus do to himself?
answer: Had himself lashed upright to the ship's mast
choices: Had himself lashed upright to the ship's mast
Had the crew chain his wrists but leave him standing
Tied a rope from his own waist to the steering-oar
Gripped the prow-rail tightly with both his hands
context: He ordered the crew to bind him TIGHTER if he begged to be freed -- and as the Sirens sang he writhed and pleaded, while his deaf men only roped him down harder until they were safely past. Homer, Odyssey Book 12 (poetryintranslation.com/PITBR/Greek/Odyssey12.php); litcharts.com Odyssey Book 12

question: After twenty years away, Odysseus finally reaches his home of Ithaca disguised as a ragged beggar so his enemies won't know him. Before any human being sees through the disguise, one old, half-forgotten creature lying on a dung-heap, covered in fleas, lifts its head and knows him at once. Who recognized Odysseus first?
answer: His old hunting dog, Argos
choices: His old hunting dog, Argos
His baby son, grown to manhood
An aged beggar at the gate
A swineherd tending the pigs
context: Argos had waited twenty years just to see his master return; he wagged his tail one last time, and Odysseus -- unable to greet him without blowing his cover -- secretly wiped away a tear as the old dog died. Homer, Odyssey Book 17; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argos_(dog); cliffsnotes.com Odyssey Book 17

question: After ten years of siege the Greeks could not break into Troy by force, so they tried a trick: they pretended to give up and sail home, leaving one enormous gift behind on the beach for the Trojans to find. What was the gift the Trojans dragged inside their own walls?
answer: A giant hollow wooden horse
choices: A giant hollow wooden horse
A towering bronze statue of a god
A great altar piled with treasure
A huge ship loaded with grain
context: Greek warriors were hidden inside; that night they climbed out and opened the gates. The priest Laocoon had warned against it -- the origin of 'I fear the Greeks, even when they bear gifts' -- but he and his two sons were strangled by sea-serpents, so the Trojans trusted the horse. (That famous Latin line is from Virgil's Aeneid; Homer's Odyssey mentions the horse only briefly.) britannica.com/topic/Trojan-horse; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beware_of_Greeks_bearing_gifts

question: Odysseus has to sail a narrow strait guarded by two monsters: on one side Charybdis, a whirlpool that swallows whole ships, and on the other Scylla, a many-headed monster reaching down from a high cliff. He chooses to pass close to Scylla -- and as his ship slips by, what does she do?
answer: Snatches and eats six of his men, one in each mouth
choices: Snatches and eats six of his men, one in each mouth
Drags the whole ship down beneath the waves
Wraps the mast in her coils and snaps it
Sings until half the crew leap overboard
context: Scylla had six heads, and her victims screamed his name as she devoured them, one per mouth. The phrase 'between Scylla and Charybdis' still means an impossible choice between two dangers. Homer, Odyssey Book 12; cliffsnotes.com / sparknotes.com Odyssey Book 12

question: In the most tender scene of the Iliad, the Trojan prince Hector says goodbye to his wife at the city gate and reaches out to hold their baby son Astyanax. But the infant suddenly shrieks and shrinks back in terror, hiding his face. What frightened the baby?
answer: The bronze helmet with its nodding horsehair crest
choices: The bronze helmet with its nodding horsehair crest
The great bronze shield strapped to his father's arm
The strangers crowding around the gate
The great war-horse stamping behind Hector
context: Hector laughed, lifted the gleaming helmet off his head, set it shining on the ground, and kissed his son -- a flash of gentleness from the war's greatest defender, who would soon die. Homer, Iliad Book 6 (poetryintranslation.com/PITBR/Greek/Iliad6.php); litcharts.com The Iliad Book 6

question: At the end of the Odyssey a contest is set in the great hall: string the mighty bow of Odysseus, a bow he alone could ever draw. One by one the arrogant suitors strain to bend it, even warming it at the fire to soften the wood, and every one of them fails. Then the ragged 'beggar' quietly asks to try. What does the beggar do with the bow?
answer: He strings it easily and shoots an arrow through a row of axe-heads
choices: He strings it easily and shoots an arrow through a row of axe-heads
He braces it on the floor and snaps the string trying to bend it
He warms it longer at the fire until the wood finally gives way
He hands it back, unable to bend it any more than the suitors could
context: The 'beggar' was Odysseus himself, home at last. He bent the great bow as easily as a singer strings a lyre, sent his arrow clean through the long line of axe-heads set up in the hall, and then turned the bow on the suitors. Homer, Odyssey Book 21; litcharts.com / cliffsnotes.com Odyssey Book 21

question: Odysseus comes home disguised as a beggar, and his old nurse Eurycleia kneels to wash the stranger's feet. Suddenly she gasps, drops his foot so the basin clangs and water spills, and almost cries out his name -- not because she saw his face, but because she felt one thing on his leg. What gave him away?
answer: A scar from a wild boar's tusk
choices: A scar from a wild boar's tusk
A ring carved with his family's crest
A tattoo from his sailing days
A birthmark shaped like a star
context: The boar had gored him long ago while he hunted as a boy with his grandfather Autolycus. Odysseus seized Eurycleia's throat and hushed her so his secret would hold. Homer, Odyssey Book 19; sparknotes.com Odyssey Books 19-20; cliffsnotes.com Odyssey Book 19

question: The Greek hero Achilles refuses to fight at Troy until his dearest companion Patroclus borrows Achilles' own armor, marches out to frighten the Trojans, and is killed -- the god Apollo striking him from behind before Hector finishes him. When the news reaches Achilles, how does he react?
answer: He pours ashes over his head and lies face-down in the dust
choices: He pours ashes over his head and lies face-down in the dust
He arms instantly and charges the walls alone
He calls the Greek kings together to plan revenge
He sails out to beg his mother for new armor
context: Mad with grief, Achilles tore his hair and vowed to kill Hector -- the death that finally brought him roaring back into the war. Patroclus had even prophesied with his dying breath that Hector too would soon die. Homer, Iliad Books 16 & 18; standardebooks.org Iliad Book 18; americanliterature.com Iliad Book 16

question: The very FIRST word of the Iliad in Greek is 'menis' -- the rage of Achilles that launches all 24 books of the poem. What makes this striking is that Homer uses 'menis' nowhere else for ordinary human anger; he saves this one word for the anger of a very different kind of being. Whose anger does Homer otherwise reserve the word 'menis' for?
answer: The immortal gods
choices: The immortal gods
Kings and great generals
The dead in the underworld
Wild beasts and monsters
context: The Greek word menis opens the poem: 'Sing, goddess, the rage of Achilles, son of Peleus...' By giving a mortal man's anger the very word he reserves elsewhere for divine wrath, Homer frames Achilles' rage as almost more than human. Homer, Iliad Book I; poets.org Iliad Book I lines 1-16; sententiaeantiquae.com 'Beginning the Iliad'

question: The Greek hero Achilles is famous for the 'Achilles' heel,' his one fatal weak spot. Legend gives him a body almost no weapon can harm. But anyone who reads Homer's actual Iliad meets a different Achilles: in Book 21, the Trojan warrior Asteropaios hurls his spear and grazes Achilles on the forearm. What does Homer say happens?
answer: Black blood spurts forth from the wound
choices: Black blood spurts forth from the wound
The spear shatters against his unscarred skin
It glances off him and leaves no mark
The cut closes over and heals at once
context: In Homer, Achilles is an ordinary mortal who can be cut and bleed -- 'black blood spurted forth.' The dipped-in-the-Styx, held-by-the-heel invulnerability tale first appears in the Roman poet Statius's Achilleid, written around AD 90 -- some 800 years after Homer. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achilles%27_heel; talesoftimesforgotten.com on Statius, Achilleid

question: Helen of Troy is remembered as 'the face that launched a thousand ships.' That ringing phrase sounds ancient, but it never appears anywhere in Homer. The poet who actually coined it was writing in England in 1604, in a play about a man who sells his soul to the devil. Who wrote 'the face that launched a thousand ships'?
answer: Christopher Marlowe
choices: Christopher Marlowe
Homer himself
Virgil of Rome
Geoffrey Chaucer
context: The line is from Marlowe's play Doctor Faustus: 'Was this the face that launch'd a thousand ships, / And burnt the topless towers of Ilium?' In Homer, a Greek fleet of about a thousand ships did sail for Troy to win Helen back after she left with the prince Paris. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_of_Troy; interestingliterature.com on Marlowe

question: Achilles' fury in the Iliad grows so monstrous that he kills until he clogs an entire river with the bodies of the Trojans he has slain. The river itself fights back -- its god rises up, first as a man and then as a towering flood, and chases Achilles, who runs uphill for his life. Which river god rose against Achilles?
answer: Scamander
choices: Scamander
Styx
Oceanus
Acheron
context: The river Scamander's channels choked with corpses until the river-god flooded to drown Achilles; the goddess Hera saved him by sending Hephaistos, god of fire, whose flames boiled the river until it surrendered. Homer, Iliad Book 21; sparknotes.com The Iliad Books 21-22; etc.usf.edu Lit2Go Iliad Book 21

question: The Iliad is the great epic of the ten-year Trojan War, yet Homer does NOT tell the whole war. He drops the reader into its final year and stops at a single funeral -- never narrating the wooden horse or the fall of the city at all. About how much of that ten-year war does all 24 books of the Iliad actually cover?
answer: Only about fifty days
choices: Only about fifty days
All ten years from start to finish
Roughly the first five years
Exactly one year, day by day
context: The whole poem spans some fifty days near the war's end -- the bulk of it just four days and two nights of fighting -- and closes with Hector's funeral, BEFORE the Trojan Horse. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iliad; cliffsnotes.com 'About the Iliad' (E.V. Rieu)

question: Tradition pictures Homer as a blind wandering poet, and scholars still argue whether one man named Homer ever existed -- the 'Homeric Question.' The strongest clue is hidden in the poems' repeated stock phrases: 'swift-footed Achilles' (21 times), 'rosy-fingered Dawn,' 'the wine-dark sea.' Scholar Milman Parry argued these repeated phrases prove what about how the epics were first made?
answer: They were sung aloud from memory before being written down
choices: They were sung aloud from memory before being written down
They were copied by hand from a single master scroll
They were translated from an older Egyptian poem
They were written down slowly over several centuries
context: Parry's oral-formulaic theory showed the stock phrases were memory-pegs that let a bard improvise the poem live in its strict dactylic-hexameter rhythm. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epithets_in_Homer; britannica.com/biography/Homer-Greek-poet; classicalia.co.uk 'The Homeric Question'  (Legend.)

question: Convinced the Iliad described a REAL city, the businessman-turned-archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann dug into a mound at Hisarlik in Turkey in the 1870s and uncovered buried ruins -- evidence that a real city had stood where Homer set Troy. Digging at Mycenae in 1876 he lifted a golden death-mask and announced what?

choices: I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon
I have found the tomb of Achilles
Here lie the walls of Troy itself
This is the helmet of great Hector
context: Schliemann claimed the gold 'Mask of Agamemnon,' though scholars now date it centuries before any Trojan War. He had proven a real city stood at Troy -- but his most famous mask belonged to no one from Homer. smithsonianmag.com on Schliemann; worldhistory.org 'Discovery of Troy'; archive.archaeology.org 'Behind the Mask of Agamemnon'

question: After ten years besieging Troy, the Greeks could not break in by force, so Odysseus dreamed up a trick. The Greeks burned their camp and sailed off as if giving up, leaving behind one enormous gift for the Trojans to haul through their gates in triumph. That night, soldiers hidden inside it crept out and threw the gates open. What had the Trojans dragged into their own city?
answer: A giant hollow wooden horse
choices: A giant hollow wooden horse
A great bronze battering ram
A towering siege catapult
A tall wooden watchtower
context: Odysseus' Trojan Horse is the most famous trick in the ancient world: hidden Greeks climbed out at night, opened the gates, and Troy fell. (Legend.) Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trojan_Horse; worldhistoryedu.com/trojan-horse/

question: Trapped in the cave of the man-eating Cyclops Polyphemus, the hero Odysseus told the one-eyed giant a strange false name. He got the giant drunk, then drove a fire-hardened stake into his single eye. Later that one odd name was what saved the men's lives, by making the blinded giant's cry for help sound absurd to his neighbors. What name had Odysseus given?
answer: Nobody
choices: Nobody
Stranger
Captain
Hunter
context: In Greek the name was 'Outis' — 'Nobody.' So when the other Cyclopes asked who was hurting him, Polyphemus howled 'Nobody is killing me!' — and they just shrugged and walked away. (Legend.) Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outis; ancientworldmagazine.com/articles/blinding-polyphemus/

question: The morning after blinding the Cyclops Polyphemus, Odysseus and his men still had to slip past the giant out the cave mouth. Polyphemus, now blind, sat in the doorway and ran his hands carefully over every big woolly ram as it filed out to pasture, so no man could ride out on one. How did Odysseus and his crew get past those searching hands?

They drove the rams out ahead as a screen
They squeezed out one by one at a run
They tossed meat to lure the giant away
context: Each man hung beneath a ram's belly while Polyphemus felt only the wool on top — and never caught them. (Legend.) Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyphemus; greekmyths-greekmythology.com/odysseus-and-cyclops-myth/

question: With Odysseus gone twenty years and presumed dead, more than a hundred suitors crowded his palace in Ithaca demanding his wife Penelope pick one of them. She agreed to choose the day she finished weaving a burial shroud — and wove at her loom all day in plain sight for about three years. How did Penelope keep the shroud from ever being finished?
answer: She secretly unraveled her weaving each night

She wove in a hidden flaw and restarted
context: Penelope pulled out every day's work after dark, so the cloth never grew — until a servant gave away the trick. Her cunning matches her husband's. (Legend.) Sources: britannica.com/topic/Penelope-Greek-mythology; ebsco.com/research-starters

question: Odysseus finally reached home in Ithaca disguised in rags after twenty years away, careful to let no one know him while his wife's suitors filled the palace. As he passed, one figure lying neglected on a dung-heap lifted its head, knew him at once after all those years — and then died on the spot. Who recognized the disguised Odysseus first?
answer: His old hunting dog, Argos
choices: His old hunting dog, Argos
His childhood nurse, Eurycleia
His aging father, Laertes
His loyal swineherd, Eumaeus
context: Argos the dog had waited twenty years; flea-bitten on the dung-heap, he pricked up his ears and wagged his tail at his master's voice, then died. Odysseus had to look away to hide his tears from the watching suitors. (Legend.) Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odysseus; greekmyths-greekmythology.com/odysseus-return-to-ithaca/

question: Odysseus was warned that the Sirens' singing lured every passing sailor to steer onto the rocks and die — yet he wanted to hear that song and survive to tell of it. He had his whole crew stop their ears with beeswax so the song could not reach them. What did he have the deaf crew do to him so that he alone could listen and live?

choices: Tie him to the mast and ignore his pleas
Lock him below deck behind the cargo
Bind his own hands to the steering oar
Lower him in a barrel over the side
context: With his ears open Odysseus heard the Sirens and begged to be freed; the deaf crew only roped him tighter until they were past. (Legend.) Sources: litcharts.com/lit/the-odyssey/book-12; sparknotes.com/lit/odyssey/section7/

question: For hundreds of years before anyone wrote them on a page, the Iliad and the Odyssey existed only as performances by singing poets called bards. Together the two epics run close to 28,000 lines of strict metered verse. How did the bards keep and pass down these enormous poems, generation after generation, before they were ever written?
answer: Carried entirely in the bards' memory
choices: Carried entirely in the bards' memory
Re-improvised fresh by each singer every time
Memorized word-for-word as one fixed text
Sung only once a year at a single festival
context: Composed and performed from memory, the epics were passed mouth to mouth for centuries — not rigidly word-for-word, but rebuilt each time from stock formula-phrases. An astonishing feat of ordinary human skill before writing. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeric_Question; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iliad

question: Sailing a narrow strait, Odysseus was caught between two horrors: on one side Charybdis, a whirlpool that swallowed entire ships, and on the other Scylla, a many-headed monster waiting on the cliff. Told he could not escape both and must lose something either way, he steered well clear of the whirlpool. What did that choice cost him?

choices: Scylla plucked his sailors off the deck
Scylla cracked the hull against the cliff
Scylla tore the mast and sail away
Scylla swept his food stores overboard
context: Better to lose a few men than the whole ship to Charybdis: Scylla's heads each snatched a sailor — six of his men in all — as Odysseus watched, unable to stop it. (Legend.) Sources: litcharts.com/lit/the-odyssey/book-12; timelessmyths.com

question: Home at last but still disguised as a beggar, Odysseus faced a hall full of suitors he meant to defeat. He set a contest at his own massive bow that not one of them could even perform — they could not so much as bend the bow enough to string it. What did the disguised Odysseus do that none of the suitors could?
answer: Strung the bow and shot one arrow through twelve axe-heads
choices: Strung the bow and shot one arrow through twelve axe-heads
Bent the bow double and snapped its great string
Drew the bow and split a shield across the hall
Lifted the bow overhead and roared out a challenge
context: He strung it as easily as a musician fits a string to a lyre, then fired a single arrow clean through a row of twelve lined-up axe-heads — and turned the bow on the suitors. (Legend.) Sources: poetryintranslation.com/PITBR/Greek/Odyssey21.php; cliffsnotes.com

question: People often assume the Iliad tells the whole Trojan War, right up to the Wooden Horse and the burning of the city. In fact it covers only a few weeks of the war's tenth year, and the Horse and the fall of Troy are not in it at all. The poem closes instead on a single event, with Troy still standing. What does the Iliad end with?
answer: The funeral of the Trojan prince Hector
choices: The funeral of the Trojan prince Hector
The death of the Greek hero Achilles
The burning and sack of the city
The Greeks sailing home from Troy
context: The Iliad ends not in triumph but in grief, with Hector's burial — Troy still standing, Achilles still alive. The famous sack of the city, and Achilles' own death, come only in later stories. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iliad

question: Achilles had killed the Trojan prince Hector and was dragging his body in the dust, refusing to give it back for burial. Then in the dead of night Hector's old father, King Priam, slipped alone and unarmed into the enemy camp and knelt before Achilles. What did the grieving Priam do that broke even Achilles?
answer: Kissed the hands that had killed his son
choices: Kissed the hands that had killed his son
Offered his own life in his son's place
Cursed the Greek gods to their faces
Drew a hidden blade against Achilles
context: Priam kissed the very hands that slew Hector; the two enemies wept together — Priam for his son, Achilles for his dead friend Patroclus — and Achilles gave the body back. The Iliad's most human moment. Sources: litcharts.com/lit/the-iliad/book-24; americanliterature.com

question: For a long time scholars doubted Homer's Troy had ever been a real place. In the 1870s the German Heinrich Schliemann began digging at a great mound called Hisarlik in Turkey and uncovered ruined city built on ruined city, stacked in layers, plus a hoard of gold he proudly named 'Priam's Treasure.' What turned out to be wrong with Schliemann's prize gold?
answer: He had dug too deep, to gold far older than Troy
choices: He had dug too deep, to gold far older than Troy
The gold was a fake planted by a rival
The gold was Roman coins from centuries later
The hoard was actually made of painted bronze
context: The treasure was about 1,250 years too old for the Trojan War — Schliemann had cut straight past Homer's Troy to a far earlier city. Still, he had found the real buried site Homer sang about. Sources: smithsonianmag.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priam%27s_Treasure

question: In Budapest on October 23, 1956, a crowd of about 200,000 Hungarians swarmed the giant bronze statue of Stalin. Workers drove up in trucks with oxygen cylinders and metal-cutting blowtorches, looped a thick steel rope around its neck, and pulled. An hour later the towering figure crashed down. When the dust settled, what was the only part of the statue still standing on its pedestal?
answer: Only his boots
choices: Only his boots
Only his head
Only his right arm
Only his bronze coat
context: The blowtorches and rope severed the figure at the ankles, leaving the giant bronze boots planted on the limestone base. Hungarians mockingly renamed the spot 'Boots Square.' The statue had stood about 25 meters (82 feet) tall, unveiled in 1951 as a 'gift' for Stalin's 70th birthday. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stalin_Monument_(Budapest)

question: On October 23, 1956, protesters at Bem Square in Budapest were sick of the communist coat of arms — the hated Rakosi red star — that the government had stamped into the center of every Hungarian flag. Wanting that symbol gone, what did the demonstrators do to their flags that became the lasting emblem of the whole uprising?
answer: They cut the communist seal out, leaving a hole
choices: They cut the communist seal out, leaving a hole
They dyed the whole flag a defiant blood red
They flew it upside down as a signal of distress
They burned it on the steps of the radio building
context: They snipped the red-star emblem out of the flag's middle with scissors, and the ragged 'flag with a hole' (Lyukas zaszlo) became the symbol of the revolution — still honored in Hungary today. Source: https://www.freedomfirst1956.com/the-1956-revolutions-symbol-the-hole-with-a-flag-in-the-center/

question: Imre Nagy, the reform prime minister who led Hungary's 1956 uprising, took refuge in the Yugoslav embassy in Budapest after Soviet tanks stormed back in to crush the revolt. He was coaxed out only by a written promise of safe passage. Once he stepped outside trusting that promise, what happened to Imre Nagy?
answer: He was seized, secretly tried, and hanged
choices: He was seized, secretly tried, and hanged
He was exiled to live out his years abroad
He was pardoned and allowed to retire quietly
He escaped to the West and told his story
context: The safe-conduct was a trap: Nagy was arrested, deported to Romania, secretly tried for treason, and hanged on June 16, 1958 — the same day as Colonel Pal Maleter, who had been arrested while negotiating under a flag of truce. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Imre-Nagy

question: In 1325 a 21-year-old scholar named Ibn Battuta left Tangier in Morocco for what he expected to be a single pilgrimage to Mecca. He did not come home for 24 years, and over about three decades of wandering he crossed three continents and some 40 countries. Roughly how far did he travel in all?
answer: About 75,000 miles
choices: About 75,000 miles
About 7,000 miles
About 25,000 miles
About 50,000 miles
context: Ibn Battuta covered roughly 75,000 miles (120,000 km) across some 40 countries and three continents over about 30 years -- around three times the distance of Marco Polo, making him the greatest traveler of the pre-modern world. He set out at 21 for a single hajj and stayed away 24 years. Source: Britannica biography (via worldhistory.org) and islamicity.org, '75,000 Miles of Travel by Ibn Battuta'; theconversation.com (Jan 2025).

question: The Sultan of Delhi sent Ibn Battuta as his envoy to the emperor of China in 1341, loading him with lavish gifts: 200 slaves, singers and dancers, 100 horses, and piles of cloth and swords. Off the Malabar Coast near Calicut his ship was wrecked, and Ibn Battuta lost all his own property and every gift meant for the Chinese emperor. Too afraid of the sultan to return to Delhi empty-handed, where did Ibn Battuta go instead?
answer: To the Maldive Islands, where he became a judge
choices: To the Maldive Islands, where he became a judge
Back to Mecca, where he became a pilgrim again
Home to Tangier, where he became a merchant
To Constantinople, where he became an envoy
context: Afraid to face Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq after losing the imperial gifts in the shipwreck, Ibn Battuta fled to the Maldive Islands and served as a qadi (judge) there for nearly two years. He complained that the local women wore clothing only from the waist down and that, as judge, he 'was quite unable to get them covered entirely.' Source: worldhistory.org/Ibn_Battuta and ORIAS Berkeley, 'Escape from Delhi to the Maldive Islands'; Britannica.

question: In 1325 a 21-year-old named Ibn Battuta left his home city of Tangier completely alone, meaning to make the hajj to Mecca and come straight back. Instead he kept going for nearly 30 years and about 75,000 miles. When he finally returned, he dictated the whole journey from memory to a scribe, and the book got a name that simply means 'The Journey.' What is that famous book called?
answer: The Rihla
choices: The Rihla
The Muqaddimah
The Almagest
The Periplus
context: Ibn Battuta kept no diary on the road; around 1352-1355 he dictated the entire 30-year account from memory to a scribe named Ibn Juzayy. 'Rihla' means 'The Journey' or 'The Travels' and became the title. Sources: worldhistory.org/Ibn_Battuta/ ; britannica.com/biography/Ibn-Battuta

question: Young Ibn Battuta had set out from Tangier with no companions at all, and the loneliness hit him hard early in the trip. Reaching the city of Tunis, he later wrote that he did something that a tough explorer might be embarrassed to admit, until a kind stranger finally took him in. What did he confess he did?
answer: He wept bitterly from loneliness
choices: He wept bitterly from loneliness
He turned back toward Tangier
He sold his horse for passage
He prayed through the night
context: In Tunis he wrote that he 'wept bitterly' because he had 'neither fellow-traveller in whose companionship I might find cheer,' until a stranger befriended him. The greatest traveler in the world began in tears. Source: worldhistory.org/Ibn_Battuta/

question: On a bandit-haunted desert stretch on the road to Mecca, Ibn Battuta came down with a fever so violent he could barely stay upright in the saddle. Rather than stop and let the caravan leave him behind in dangerous country, he did something desperate to keep himself on his horse. What did he do?
answer: He tied himself to his saddle with a turban-cloth
choices: He tied himself to his saddle with a turban-cloth
He swallowed a handful of dried herbs
He paid a guard to hold him upright
He chained his wrists to the reins
context: Falling behind a caravan in bandit country could mean death, so the feverish Ibn Battuta lashed himself to the saddle with his turban-cloth to keep from collapsing off the horse. Source: history.com/articles/why-arab-scholar-ibn-battuta-is-the-greatest-explorer-of-all-time

question: Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq of Delhi chose Ibn Battuta to carry a staggering gift to the emperor of China: about 200 slaves, singers and dancers, 100 horses, and heaps of cloth, dishes, and swords. The whole grand mission ended in disaster off the coast near Calicut, before Ibn Battuta had even sailed. What wrecked it?
answer: A storm destroyed his ships in port
choices: A storm destroyed his ships in port
Pirates seized the treasure fleet
The emperor refused the envoy
Plague swept through the crew
context: A storm smashed his ships in the harbor near Calicut (Kozhikode), drowning companions and sinking the sultan's treasure-gifts. Ibn Battuta was left empty-handed and too afraid to return to the brutal sultan. Sources: britannica.com/biography/Ibn-Battuta/Time-in-India-and-later-journeys ; history.com

question: Stranded after the China mission failed, Ibn Battuta drifted to the Maldive Islands, where the rulers were desperate for someone who could read Arabic and Islamic law. Rather than help him sail onward, the islanders did the opposite to keep this rare scholar from ever leaving. What did they do?
answer: They refused to let his ship leave so he would stay as their judge
choices: They refused to let his ship leave so he would stay as their judge
They hid his maps and charts at sea
They jailed him until he swore loyalty
They burned the only ship in the harbor
context: Desperate for an Arabic-speaking Islamic judge, the Maldive rulers showered Ibn Battuta with pearls and gold and refused to let his ship depart so he would serve as their qadi (judge). Source: orias.berkeley.edu/resources-teachers/travels-ibn-battuta/journey/escape-delhi-maldive-islands-and-sri-lanka-1341-1344

question: After crossing the Sahara, Ibn Battuta reached the wealthy Empire of Mali and watched its subjects approach the ruler, the mansa, in a startling way. To show their submission, the people would grovel low, beat the ground with their elbows, and do one more thing to their own heads. What did they do to themselves?
answer: They threw dust and ashes over their heads
choices: They threw dust and ashes over their heads
They shaved their heads bald
They covered their heads with gold cloth
They struck their heads on stone
context: Ibn Battuta left the first eyewitness account by an outside traveler of a West African kingdom, the court of Mansa Sulayman (brother of the famous Mansa Musa). Subjects groveled, beat the ground with their elbows, and threw dust and ashes over their own heads in submission. Sources: orias.berkeley.edu ; faculty.buffalostate.edu Ibn Batuta on Mali

question: In 1521 a young Spanish soldier named Inigo of Loyola was defending the fortress of Pamplona when an enemy projectile smashed into him, shattering one leg and tearing open the other and ending his fighting days forever. What kind of weapon struck him down?
answer: A cannonball
choices: A cannonball
A crossbow bolt
A cavalry lance
A thrown spear
context: The wound left Ignatius of Loyola with a lifelong limp. Jesuits still celebrate 'Cannonball Day' because that single shot, on May 20, 1521, redirected his whole life from soldiering toward founding a religious order. Source: jesuits.org/stories/celebrating-cannonball-day; gonzaga.edu/about/our-mission-jesuit-values/gonzagas-history.

question: Recovering in bed, Ignatius of Loyola wanted the chivalry-and-adventure tales he had always loved, but the castle held only a Life of Christ and a book about the saints. Forced to read those instead, he began catching himself wondering whether he could match the holy deeds of one famous figure. Which figure's life did the saint-book set him dreaming of imitating?
answer: Saint Francis
choices: Saint Francis
Charlemagne
Julius Caesar
King Arthur
context: Reading the only books on hand, Ignatius thought, 'What if I should do what St. Francis or St. Dominic did?' That daydream was the start of his conversion. Source: worldhistory.org/Ignatius_of_Loyola; jesuits.org/stories/celebrating-cannonball-day.

question: When Ignatius of Loyola's broken leg healed crooked, with a knob of bone jutting out below the knee, the vain ex-soldier could not bear how it ruined the look of a courtier's tight stockings. With no anesthesia existing yet, he ordered the surgeons to do something to the leg that he himself called 'butchery' — yet he never cried out, only clenching his fists. What did he have them do?
answer: Saw off the protruding bone and stretch the leg straight
choices: Saw off the protruding bone and stretch the leg straight
Pack the wound in salt and ice for a week
Amputate the leg at the knee entirely
Bind the leg in iron splints for a year
context: Surgeons sawed off the bony lump and stretched the leg on traction, all while Ignatius was fully awake. He suffered it silently out of vanity about his appearance. Source: International Orthopaedics (2025), link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00264-025-06591-4; worldhistory.org/Ignatius_of_Loyola.

question: At the mountain abbey of Montserrat in 1522, Ignatius of Loyola kept an all-night knightly vigil before the altar of the Black Madonna. At dawn he gave his fine clothes to a beggar and dressed himself in rough sackcloth. To mark that he was done with war for good, what did he hang up by the altar as he walked away?
answer: His sword and dagger
choices: His sword and dagger
His war horse's saddle
His soldier's helmet
His captain's banner
context: Hanging his weapons by the Black Madonna's altar was Ignatius's deliberate surrender of the soldier's life. He left Montserrat dressed as a pilgrim in sackcloth. Source: covamanresa.cat/en/march-21-22-vigil-st-ignatius-montserrat-and-pilgrimage-manresa; worldhistory.org/Ignatius_of_Loyola.

question: Riding toward Jerusalem, Ignatius of Loyola fell in with a Muslim traveler who insulted the Virgin Mary's purity. The old soldier in him itched to ride the man down and stab him, but he could not decide whether killing him would be right. Unable to choose, how did Ignatius settle whether to pursue and kill the man?
answer: He dropped the reins and let his mule pick the road at the fork
choices: He dropped the reins and let his mule pick the road at the fork
He drew his sword and prayed for a sign before striking
He challenged the traveler to a formal duel
He waited overnight to see if his anger would cool
context: Ignatius let the mule choose at a fork in the road; it took the path away from the man, and he was spared. The half-converted soldier still trusted a beast to decide a killing. Source: worldhistory.org/Ignatius_of_Loyola; covamanresa.cat.

question: Alone in a cave at Manresa for nearly a year, Ignatius of Loyola fasted, let his hair and nails grow wild, and was at times so tormented by despair that he thought of suicide. Out of that ordeal he wrote a step-by-step program of guided meditations that Jesuits still lead people through on silent retreats today. What is this book called?
answer: The Spiritual Exercises
choices: The Spiritual Exercises
The Confessions
The Imitation of Christ
The Rule of Saint Benedict
context: In the cave at Manresa (1522-1523) Ignatius worked out the Spiritual Exercises, the meditation program at the heart of every Jesuit retreat to this day. Source: worldhistory.org/Ignatius_of_Loyola; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cave_of_Saint_Ignatius.

question: Reaching Japan in 1549 as the first Catholic priest the country had ever seen, the Jesuit missionary Francis Xavier needed to win an audience with its rulers. He did it by presenting marvels never before seen there — a chiming clock, a glass mirror, spectacles, muskets, and oil paintings. Which of these was among the wonders Xavier brought to open Japan's doors?
answer: A mechanical chiming clock
choices: A mechanical chiming clock
A printing press
A telescope
A steam-driven pump
context: Xavier, one of Ignatius's first six companions and the first Jesuit missionary east, dazzled Japanese rulers with European marvels including a chiming clock, a music box, a mirror, muskets, spectacles, and port wine. Source: ebsco.com/research-starters/history/father-xavier-introduces-christianity-japan; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Xavier.

question: The Jesuit missionary Francis Xavier died in 1552 on a tiny island within sight of China, and sailors buried him in a chest packed with quicklime meant to dissolve his flesh for easier transport. When the coffin was opened months later, the corpse stunned everyone. What had become of Xavier's body?
answer: It was fresh and undecayed, as if newly dead
choices: It was fresh and undecayed, as if newly dead
It had turned entirely to white bone
It had been reduced to ash by the lime
It had been stolen and replaced with stones
context: The quicklime had not destroyed the body; it was found fresh and 'incorrupt,' reportedly sweet-smelling. Xavier's body still lies in a glass casket in the Basilica of Bom Jesus in Goa, India. Source: daily.jstor.org/the-incorruptible-body-of-francis-xavier; atlasobscura.com/places/body-st-francis-xavier.

question: Francis Xavier was said to have baptized tens of thousands of people across Asia with his right hand. In 1614 the head of the Jesuit order decided that very arm deserved special honor and ordered it removed from the long-dead body. What did he have done with Xavier's right forearm?
answer: Cut it off and sent it to Rome as a relic
choices: Cut it off and sent it to Rome as a relic
Buried it separately under the altar at Goa
Cast it in gold as a statue
Returned it to Xavier's family in Spain
context: The Jesuit superior had Xavier's forearm cut off at the elbow and carried to Rome, where it is still displayed in a silver reliquary in the Gesu, the Jesuit mother church. Source: liquisearch.com/francis_xavier/burials_and_relics; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Xavier.

question: The Lindisfarne Gospels are one of the most beautiful books of the Middle Ages, packed with painted birds, knots and color. A monk named Eadfrith, who later became Bishop of Lindisfarne, made it. How much of the book did Eadfrith do himself?
answer: He wrote and painted the entire book alone
choices: He wrote and painted the entire book alone
He painted the pictures but others wrote the words
He drew the outlines and apprentices colored them in
He copied the words and other monks added the pictures
context: A single scribe-artist, Eadfrith, produced the whole Lindisfarne Gospels by his own hand. He became Bishop of Lindisfarne in 698 and died in 721. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindisfarne_Gospels

question: In 1007 thieves broke into the stone church at Kells in Ireland one night and stole the Book of Kells for its gold-and-jeweled cover. The Annals of Ulster record that two months and twenty nights later the book was found again. Where had it been left?
answer: Buried under a sod of earth with its gold cover ripped off
choices: Buried under a sod of earth with its gold cover ripped off
Floating in a river with its pages soaked through
Hidden in a hollow oak with its cover still on
Sold to a trader in a market across the sea
context: The thieves wanted the precious shrine, not the book itself, so they tore off the gold cover and abandoned the pages buried under a sod of earth. The Book of Kells survived; the gold did not. Source: https://ireland-calling.com/when-the-priceless-book-of-kells-was-discarded-under-a-sod/

question: To paint a glittering yellow that shone like real gold, the monks of the Book of Kells used a pigment called orpiment. There was a hidden danger in grinding it. What was the monk who prepared orpiment actually handling?
answer: Poison, because orpiment is made of arsenic
choices: Poison, because orpiment is made of arsenic
Crushed gold flakes, which were rare and costly
Burning lime, which scorched the fingers
Rotting plant dye, which carried disease
context: Orpiment is arsenic sulphide. It glittered like gold but was genuinely poisonous, so a monk grinding it to fake the look of gold was handling real poison. Source: https://www.tcd.ie/library/research-collections/book-of-kells.php

question: The Book of Kells, a gospel book painted by Irish monks around 800 AD, hides tiny living creatures in the swirls of its most famous page. Hunt carefully and you find two cats pinning down two mice that are nibbling a communion wafer, and one other animal lying on its back. What is that animal holding?
answer: An otter holding a fish
choices: An otter holding a fish
A raven holding a ring
A hound holding a bone
A serpent holding an egg
context: On the Chi-Rho page of the Book of Kells, hidden among the spirals, an otter lies on its back gripping a fish, while two cats pin the tails of two mice nibbling a wafer and two more mice ride on the cats' backs. The monks tucked a whole little zoo into a page about the name of Christ. Source: https://www.futurelearn.com/info/courses/book-of-kells/0/steps/50086

question: Around 1185 the traveling writer Giraldus Cambrensis, also called Gerald of Wales, was shown a dazzling illuminated gospel book in Ireland, its pages crowded with spirals and interlace too fine to seem human. Giraldus wrote one line of praise that has stuck to the Book of Kells ever since. What did he say it looked like?
answer: The work of an angel, not of a man
choices: The work of an angel, not of a man
A garden grown from gold and ink
The dream of a sleeping saint
A window into the next world
context: Giraldus Cambrensis declared the book seemed 'the work of an angel, not of a man' — a line later attached to the Book of Kells, whose density still astonishes viewers. This is testimony, Giraldus's own awed reaction, not a forensic claim about who painted it. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Book_of_Kells/  (Legend.)

question: The word 'Impressionism' did not start as a compliment. After the painters' first 1874 show, the critic Louis Leroy mocked Claude Monet's hazy harbor picture and titled his whole sneering review 'The Exhibition of the Impressionists.' What did the painters do with that jeer?
answer: They adopted the insult and made it the name of their movement
choices: They adopted the insult and made it the name of their movement
They sued the critic and forced a printed apology
They painted over the picture he had mocked
They never exhibited their work in public again
context: Leroy coined the jeer in Le Charivari, April 25, 1874, riffing on Monet's 'Impression, Sunrise.' The rebels seized the slur and wore it as their banner. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impression,_Sunrise

question: Claude Monet's 1872 painting 'Impression, Sunrise' shows the foggy port of Le Havre at dawn, with ghostly ships and cranes barely sketched in the gray morning mist. What is the one blazing thing your eye jumps to in the middle of all that gray?
answer: A small burning orange sun and its rippling reflection on the water
choices: A small burning orange sun and its rippling reflection on the water
A tall white lighthouse flashing above the docks
A red sail crossing in front of the harbor
A golden church spire rising over the rooftops
context: The little orange sun and its broken reflection streaking down the gray water are the heart of the picture, with everything else dissolved into fog. Source: https://www.claude-monet.com/impression-sunrise.jsp

question: Before the little metal paint tube was invented, painting outdoors was a mess, because there was no clean way to carry wet oil paint into a field. What disgusting container did artists squeeze their oil paint out of in the years before the tube?
answer: Tied-off pig's bladders that you pricked with a pin
choices: Tied-off pig's bladders that you pricked with a pin
Hollow cow horns stoppered with wax
Sealed clay jars dug into the ground
Folded squares of oiled leather
context: You pricked the bladder with a pin, squeezed, then tried to patch the hole; they leaked, burst, and dried out within a day or two. American artist John Goffe Rand's collapsible tin tube (patented 1841) fixed all of it. Source: https://uk.winsornewton.com/blogs/articles/winsor-newton-archive-pigs-bladders

question: When the Impressionists held their very first show in 1874, the official Paris Salon was the place everyone went, pulling in about 400,000 visitors that same year. Roughly how many people bothered to come see the Impressionists' rival show?
answer: About 3,500
choices: About 3,500
About 90,000
About 200,000
About 500,000
context: Only about 3,500 came against the Salon's 400,000. The rebels' 'Anonymous Society of Painters, Sculptors and Engravers' lost money and was dissolved by December 1874 before the name caught on. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Impressionist_Exhibition

question: Instead of premixing one smooth blended tone, the Impressionists laid down lots of small separate dabs of pure color right next to each other. Step back from the canvas and the dabs seem to melt into shimmering light. Where does that final blending of the colors actually happen?
answer: In the viewer's own eye
choices: In the viewer's own eye
On the artist's palette
In the drying coat of varnish
Under the warm studio lamplight
context: This is the 'broken color' trick: the separate dabs of pure color combine in your eye as you step back, so the picture shimmers instead of going flat. The mixing happens in your eyeball, not on the palette. Source: https://www.jacksonsart.com/blog/2015/04/24/impressionist-painting-techniques/

question: From about 1912 Claude Monet kept painting even as cataracts clouded his eyes so badly he could barely tell one color from another. To know which paint he was reaching for, what did the half-blind Monet have to do at his easel?
answer: Read the printed labels on his paint tubes
choices: Read the printed labels on his paint tubes
Have an assistant call out each color aloud
Arrange the tubes by smell instead of sight
Mix every color himself the night before
context: With his color vision gone, Monet relied on the labels to tell his tubes apart; his pictures from those years turned muddy red and brown until he finally had eye surgery in 1923. Source: https://hekint.org/2017/01/24/monet-and-his-cataracts/

question: The Inca built a stone highway they called the Qhapaq Nan, the 'Royal Road,' running about 40,000 km (25,000 miles) through the mountains of Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Chile, and Argentina. Laid end to end, that much road was long enough to do what?
answer: Circle the whole Earth
choices: Circle the whole Earth
Reach partway to the Moon
Cross the Sahara Desert
Span the Atlantic Ocean
context: About 40,000 km is roughly the distance around the planet. The Inca built it with no iron, no wheeled vehicles, and only wooden, stone, and bronze tools, rivaling the Roman road network built a thousand years earlier. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_road_system; worldhistory.org/article/757/the-inca-road-system/

question: Across the vast Inca empire a royal order could travel from the coast deep into the high Andes in a single day, faster than any one person could possibly run it. How did the Inca move a message that fast?
answer: Fresh runners each sprinted a short leg and handed it on
choices: Fresh runners each sprinted a short leg and handed it on
A single rider galloped through on a fast horse
Watchmen flashed it peak to peak with mirrors
Fast canoes rushed it up the rivers
context: These relay messengers were the chasquis, posted in small cabins only about 2.5 km apart. Each ran his short stretch flat-out, so a message could cover roughly 240 to 300 km a day. The Spanish historian Bernabe Cobo called the chasqui post 'one of the great accomplishments of the Inca kings.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chasqui; worldhistory.org/article/757/the-inca-road-system/

question: An Inca chasqui sprinting his leg of the relay needed the next runner already moving before he arrived, so no time was lost at the handoff. As he came pounding up to the cabin, how did he signal the fresh runner to take off?
answer: He blew a conch-shell trumpet
choices: He blew a conch-shell trumpet
He waved a burning torch
He rang a heavy bronze bell
He shouted out a secret password
context: The trumpet was a pututu, a sea-conch shell. The chasqui also wore a white feather headdress so he could be spotted coming from far off, and often carried a knotted-string record called a quipu. We can still see one drawn from life in Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala's 1615 manuscript. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chasqui; trexperienceperu.com/blog/chasquis-ancient-messengers

question: To carry their roads across the deep Andean canyons, the Inca hung swaying suspension bridges hundreds of feet above the rivers, bridges so alarming that Spanish conquistadors were often terrified to step onto them. What were these bridges actually woven from?
answer: Twisted mountain grass
choices: Twisted mountain grass
Iron chain links
Split bamboo poles
Stretched ox hides
context: The cables were braided from ichu, a thin Andean bunchgrass that is feeble by itself but enormously strong when twisted by the hundreds. One survives today, the Q'eswachaka over the Apurimac River, rebuilt by hand by four Quechua communities every June in a four-day ceremony unbroken for about 500 years. UNESCO named it Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2013. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_rope_bridge; atlasobscura.com/articles/last-inca-rope-bridge-qeswachaka-tradition

question: The chronicler Martin de Murua recorded that the Inca emperor, sitting in his palace in the high mountains many days' travel from the Pacific, sometimes craved ocean fish. His chasqui runners sprinted it up from the coast in relays. In what condition did Murua say the fish arrived?
answer: Still alive and fresh
choices: Still alive and fresh
Dried hard and salted
Smoked over a fire
Pickled in brine
context: Murua wrote that the fish was carried roughly 350 to 400 km up into the Andes 'so that it would still be alive.' Garcilaso de la Vega tells the same story. The relay delivered live seafood to the mountains in under two days, on foot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chasqui; kimmacquarrie.com/how-inca-postal-runners-delivered-their-emperor-fresh-fish-from-the-sea/

question: The Inca ran an empire of about 12 million people, taxing harvests and tracking storehouses, yet they never invented an alphabet or any writing at all. What did their record-keepers use instead to hold all those accounts?
answer: Bundles of knotted strings
choices: Bundles of knotted strings
Clay tablets pressed with marks
Rows of painted symbols
Carved wooden tally sticks
context: This was the quipu (khipu): a main cord with dozens or hundreds of hanging cords, some quipus carrying as many as 1,500 strings, the knots encoding numbers in base-10. Source: worldhistory.org/Quipu/; britannica.com/technology/quipu

question: Inca armies could march for weeks far from any farm because the Inca had found a way to make potatoes that would keep for years. To turn a fresh potato into that long-keeping food, called chuno, what did they do to it?
answer: Froze it on cold nights, then stomped it underfoot by day
choices: Froze it on cold nights, then stomped it underfoot by day
Buried it deep in dry desert sand
Boiled it down into a thick paste
Smoked it for days over a slow fire
context: They left potatoes to freeze in the Andean night, then trampled them by foot in the warm day to squeeze out water and skins, repeating it until the potato became chuno, essentially freeze-drying centuries before electricity. Black chuno is sun-dried as is; white chuno is washed and peeled first. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chu%C3%B1o; atlasobscura.com/foods/chunos-potatoes-feet

question: The masons of Machu Picchu shaped each huge polygonal block of stone, using bronze chisels, stone hammers, and sand, to lock against its neighbors with no mortar between them. Their joints are so famously tight that even today a visitor cannot do what at many of the walls?
answer: Slide a knife blade between the stones
choices: Slide a knife blade between the stones
Find where one block ends
Tell the wall is hundreds of years old
Hear an echo off the surface
context: The walls were built completely dry, stone fitted to stone. That same mortar-free style is why the site rides out earthquakes: the interlocking blocks shift slightly and resettle instead of cracking, and engineers have found over 130 drainage holes built in from the start to carry off the heavy mountain rain. Source: history.com/articles/machu-picchu-construction; blog.viajesmachupicchu.travel

question: At the very top of Machu Picchu the Inca carved a single upright stone pillar they used to follow the sun through the year. Around the equinoxes the noon sun stands so nearly straight over it that the pillar casts almost no shadow. What did the Inca call this stone?
answer: The Hitching Post of the Sun
choices: The Hitching Post of the Sun
The Throne of the Emperor
The Stone of Sacrifice
The Cornerstone of the City
context: Its Quechua name is the Intihuatana. When American explorer Hiram Bingham was guided up to the overgrown, then-unknown ruins in 1911 and brought them to the world's attention, he named the nearby curved enclosure the 'Temple of the Sun' for its astronomical alignment. Source: worldhistory.org/Machu_Picchu/; inkayniperutours.com/blog/intihuatana-stone-in-machu-picchu

question: What makes the 40,000 km Inca road system astonishing is what the builders did NOT have: no wheeled carts, no horses, no oxen, and no other large beast to pull or haul. Just one animal carried their loads, about 30 kg for some 20 km a day. Which animal was it?
answer: The llama
choices: The llama
The donkey
The water buffalo
The reindeer
context: Everything beyond what a llama could carry moved on human backs and human feet. With only the llama and people, the Inca still built and ran a road network that rivaled Rome's. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_road_system

question: Near Cusco at a place called Moray, the Inca dug giant bowls of concentric circular terraces down into the ground. Because each ring sits at a different depth, the temperature from the top ring to the bottom can differ by as much as 15 C, making about twenty little climates in one spot. What do archaeologists think Moray was used for?
answer: A laboratory to test which crops grew best
choices: A laboratory to test which crops grew best
A temple for sun-worship ceremonies
A reservoir to store mountain rainwater
An arena to stage public games
context: The twenty mini-climates would let Inca farmers see which crops thrived at which altitude before planting them across the empire's terraced mountainsides, an open-air agricultural laboratory. Source: leadingperutravel.com/blog/moray-peru; mdpi.com/2571-9408/9/2/56

question: On an Inca quipu, the place of a knot along a cord set its value, the ones, then tens, then hundreds, up to ten-thousands, in a base-10 system. So a number was read by where the knots sat. On that cord, what did a bare stretch with NO knot at all mean?
answer: Zero
choices: Zero
One
Start over
Unknown amount
context: A position left empty stood for zero. The Inca were recording the idea of zero centuries before it reached Europe from India, all in knotted string. Source: worldhistory.org/Quipu/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quipu

question: Most surviving Inca quipus can no longer be read. Spanish colonists, suspecting the knotted strings hid idolatry, deliberately destroyed huge numbers of them, and the trained 'knot-keepers' who alone understood each one were a hereditary class. What was lost that leaves the surviving knots unreadable today?
answer: The spoken key, passed keeper to keeper, that explained each quipu
choices: The spoken key, passed keeper to keeper, that explained each quipu
The original cords, which all rotted away in the damp
The bright dyes that once colored every string
A master alphabet the Spanish carried back to Europe
context: The keepers were quipucamayocs, and the story explaining a quipu was passed father to son; a keeper whose count was wrong could be severely punished, even executed. Gary Urton's Harvard Khipu Database has catalogued more than 900, about 700 well-formed enough to study, yet most still cannot be read because the code died with its keepers. Source: worldhistory.org/Quipu/; atlasobscura.com/articles/khipus-inca-empire-harvard-university-colonialism

question: The Inca built the giant stone walls of their city Cusco without any mortar or cement at all, just stones cut to fit. So perfectly do the blocks lock together that, even today, if you walk up and try to push something thin into the seam between two stones, what happens?
answer: A sheet of paper will not slide into the joint
choices: A sheet of paper will not slide into the joint
A thin trickle of rainwater always seeps through
The stones rock loosely until you steady them
A faint line of crumbled mortar rubs off
context: Inca masons fitted their blocks so tightly that not even a knife blade or a sheet of paper can slip between them. Britannica notes of the great fortress Sacsayhuaman that 'not even a sheet of paper can slip between them.' Sources: casadelsolhotels.com (Inca ashlar masonry); Britannica /place/Sacsayhuaman.

question: On a street in Cusco, set into the wall of Inca Roca's old palace, sits a single famous green block that has drawn visitors for centuries. The Inca masons carved its edges so that it interlocks with every neighboring stone — count the precisely cut corners on it and you find how many?
answer: Twelve angles, each matched to a neighbor
choices: Twelve angles, each matched to a neighbor
Four clean right-angle corners
A single curved, polished face
Seven shallow grooves for ropes
context: The Twelve-Angled Stone of Hatun Rumiyoc is a single green diorite block carved with twelve precisely matched corners that lock it into its neighbors with no mortar — so solid the Spanish could not pry it loose, and it stands intact after 500-plus years. Sources: peruforless.com/blog/twelve-angle-stone; ticketmachupicchu.com/stone-twelve-angles.

question: When the Spanish built churches in Cusco on top of Inca foundations, Andean earthquakes cracked and toppled the newer Spanish work — yet the older mortarless Inca walls underneath kept standing. What is it about the loose-fitted Inca blocks that let them outlast the quakes?
answer: The interlocking blocks shift and resettle, so the wall 'dances' instead of cracking
choices: The interlocking blocks shift and resettle, so the wall 'dances' instead of cracking
A hidden iron frame ran through the core of each wall
The stones were fused together by intense heat
Deep mortar channels absorbed the shaking
context: Because the mortarless blocks interlock like a 3-D jigsaw, they can shift slightly and resettle during a tremor — the walls 'dance' through earthquakes instead of cracking, surviving centuries of Andean quakes that toppled later Spanish buildings. Sources: peru-explorer.com (earthquake-resistant techniques); History.com/articles/machu-picchu-construction.

question: Around 825 AD the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi wrote one of the first books teaching Europeans a powerful new way to write numbers and calculate with them. His own name, mashed and mangled as it passed into Latin, hardened into an everyday word we still use all the time. Which word grew out of al-Khwarizmi's name?
answer: algorithm
choices: algorithm
decimal
cipher
digit
context: al-Khwarizmi's book survives in Latin as 'Algoritmi de numero Indorum' -- 'al-Khwarizmi on the Numerals of the Indians.' Scribes turned 'al-Khwarizmi' into 'Algoritmi,' and centuries later that became 'algorithm,' the word for any step-by-step calculation procedure. Source: https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/Arabic_numerals/

question: The oldest written zeros we have survive on the Bakhshali manuscript -- 70 fragile leaves of birch bark that a farmer turned up while digging a field near Peshawar in 1881. When Oxford scientists carbon-dated the pages, some proved as old as the 200s-300s AD, far older than anyone had guessed. On those ancient pages the zero is not the round '0' we write today. How does zero appear there instead?
answer: as small dots
choices: as small dots
as tiny crosses
as open squares
as short dashes
context: Oxford's 2017 carbon dating pushed parts of the Bakhshali manuscript back to roughly 224-383 AD, about 500 years earlier than scholars had thought. On its birch-bark leaves, zero is written as hundreds of little dots -- the symbol slowly rounding out into the '0' shape over later centuries. Source: https://www.glam.ox.ac.uk/article/carbon-dating-finds-bakhshali-manuscript-contains-oldest-recorded-origins-symbol-zero

question: Negative numbers are hard to picture -- what does 'less than nothing' even mean? Around 628 AD the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta cracked the idea with an everyday image: he gave positive and negative numbers two names borrowed straight from the world of money, so that even a minus-times-a-minus made plain sense. What pair of money words did Brahmagupta use for positive and negative numbers?
answer: fortunes and debts
choices: fortunes and debts
profits and losses
riches and ransoms
savings and fines
context: In his Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628 AD), Brahmagupta wrote the first rules for arithmetic with zero and negative numbers, calling positives 'fortunes' and negatives 'debts.' One rule, 'the product or quotient of two debts is one fortune,' is the ancient way of saying a minus times a minus makes a plus. Source: https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Brahmagupta/

question: Borobudur in central Java is the largest Buddhist temple in the world, raised around 800 AD from roughly 2 million blocks of volcanic stone. What is the surprising thing about how its builders fit those 2 million blocks together?
answer: They used no mortar at all, locking the stones by shape alone
choices: They used no mortar at all, locking the stones by shape alone
They poured molten iron into channels between the stones
They glued the stones with rice paste and tree resin
They left every stone loose so the temple could be rebuilt
context: Borobudur (c. 780-850 AD, built under the Sailendra dynasty) was assembled from about 2 million stone blocks fitted together WITHOUT mortar. It also carries 2,672 carved relief panels - laid end to end nearly 6 km, the longest continuous stone narrative on Earth - and 504 Buddha statues. https://www.nationalgeographic.com/travel/world-heritage/article/borobudur-temple

question: Most ocean winds blow steadily one way, which can strand a sailing ship far from home with no breeze to carry it back. But the great seasonal wind of the Indian Ocean, the monsoon, does something unusual that let traders sail all the way to Southeast Asia AND get home again on a single trip. What does the monsoon do?
answer: It flips direction with the seasons, blowing one way then the opposite way
choices: It flips direction with the seasons, blowing one way then the opposite way
It blows twice as hard one way, fast enough to outrun the return
It dies away completely each night so ships drift gently home
It curves ships around in a giant circle back to where they began
context: The southwest monsoon blows June-September from Africa/India toward Southeast Asia; the northeast monsoon blows back October-March. Sailors timed voyages to ride one wind out and the other home - going and returning on a single trip without ever rowing against the wind. https://www.britannica.com/place/Indian-Ocean/Trade-winds-zone

question: Gajah Mada, the powerful prime minister of the Hindu-Buddhist Majapahit empire of Java, made a famous public vow - the Sumpah Palapa - that he would deny himself one specific pleasure until he had united the whole archipelago under Majapahit. According to the legend, what did he swear to give up until then?
answer: Eating any food flavored with spices
choices: Eating any food flavored with spices
Sleeping under any roof made of wood
Speaking to his own family members
Riding any horse into battle
context: Legend: Gajah Mada, prime minister under King Hayam Wuruk (ruled 1350-1389), swore the Palapa Oath - to eat no spiced food until all of Nusantara (the archipelago) was united under Majapahit. The court poem Nagarakretagama (1365) claimed Majapahit's reach spanned 98 territories from Sumatra to New Guinea. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palapa_oath

question: Angkor Wat in Cambodia, built by the Khmer king Suryavarman II in the 1100s, is the largest religious monument on Earth. The king raised it as a temple to one god, whose carved scenes fill its long galleries. Which god was Angkor Wat first dedicated to?
answer: The god Vishnu
choices: The god Vishnu
The god Shiva
The god Brahma
The god Indra
context: Suryavarman II (1113-1150 AD) built Angkor Wat as a HINDU temple to Vishnu; its galleries carry carved scenes from the Mahabharata and the Ramayana. Only from the late 1200s did it gradually become the Buddhist temple it remains today - so the largest religious monument on Earth began as a Hindu, not a Buddhist, temple. https://www.worldhistory.org/Angkor_Wat/

question: Indian culture - Hindu and Buddhist gods, Sanskrit, temple art - spread across Southeast Asia, and historians have a name for the process: 'Indianization.' Yet they stress it spread in a way that did NOT involve any Indian army marching in to impose it. So how, according to these scholars, did it actually take hold?
answer: Indian merchants and holy men settled in ports, and local rulers invited them to court
choices: Indian merchants and holy men settled in ports, and local rulers invited them to court
Indian rulers paid the local chiefs tribute in gold to adopt their gods
Local rulers each sailed to India and copied whatever they saw there
An older shared religion already linked India and the islands beforehand
context: In 'Indianization,' Indian merchants settled in coastal ports bringing Brahmin priests and Buddhist monks; impressed local rulers invited these holy men to their courts, because a ruler surrounded by Indian gods, Sanskrit, and ceremony was seen as more powerful and legitimate. Culture carried by trade and prestige, not conquest. https://www.britannica.com/topic/Hinduism/The-spread-of-Hinduism-in-Southeast-Asia-and-the-Pacific

question: The Dominican friar Johann Tetzel traveled the German lands selling indulgences — slips that promised to spring a dead loved one's soul out of purgatory.
