To close the sale he chanted a little rhyme: the moment your coin dropped into his chest, your loved one was freed. How did the rhyme go?
answer: "When the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs."
choices: "When the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs."
"Give to the Pope and the gates of heaven open wide."
"Pay the friar his fee and your sins are washed away."
"A penny for the church buys a pardon for the soul."
context: Tetzel's reported sales-jingle is often rendered "As soon as the gold in the casket rings, the rescued soul to heaven springs." The instant the buyer's money clinked into the secured metal chest — the famous "Tetzel chest" — he promised the dead loved one's soul shot out of purgatory. Sources: worldhistory.org/Johann_Tetzel; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Tetzel; reformation500.csl.edu/johannes-tetzel.

question: Most Germans dropping coins in Johann Tetzel's chest believed every penny was sailing to Rome to rebuild St. Peter's Basilica — and Tetzel himself believed it too. But a secret deal sent half the German proceeds somewhere else entirely. Where did that hidden half actually go?
answer: To repay a loan from the banker Jacob Fugger that had bought Albert of Mainz his archbishopric
choices: To repay a loan from the banker Jacob Fugger that had bought Albert of Mainz his archbishopric
To fund a new Crusade the Pope was quietly preparing against the Turks
To pay the wages of the Swiss Guard protecting the Pope in Rome
To purchase a private collection of relics for the papal treasury
context: Albert of Mainz had borrowed roughly 20,000 guilders from the banker Jacob Fugger to buy his archbishopric. By a secret arrangement, half the German indulgence money went to repay that Fugger loan while the other half went toward rebuilding St. Peter's. Sources: britannica.com/biography/Johann-Tetzel; christianhistoryinstitute.org/magazine/article/selling-forgiveness-sparked-protestant-reformation.

question: Long before archaeologists realized a 4,500-year-old city lay buried under it, people in the Sindh region of Pakistan had already given the lonely mound an ominous name. What does that name, Mohenjo-daro, mean in the local Sindhi language?
answer: Mound of the Dead
choices: Mound of the Dead
City of the River
Hill of the Kings
Gate of the Sun
context: Locals named it 'Mound of the Dead' because they kept turning up human and animal bones along with old artifacts there, ages before anyone knew a Bronze-Age city was underneath. Source: World History Encyclopedia, https://www.worldhistory.org/Indus_Valley_Civilization/

question: Around 4,000 years ago an Indus artist cast a tiny bronze figure of a girl, barely four inches tall, standing with one hand cocked on her hip, chin lifted, and bangles stacked all the way up her left arm. By what nickname do archaeologists know this confident little statue from Mohenjo-daro?
answer: the Dancing Girl
choices: the Dancing Girl
the Snake Charmer
the Bangle Maiden
the River Maiden
context: The 'Dancing Girl,' about 10.5 cm tall, was cast by the lost-wax method (c. 2300-1750 BCE) and found by Ernest Mackay in 1926 -- one of the earliest metal castings ever made. She wears about 24-25 bangles on her left arm and only 4 on her right. Mortimer Wheeler said: 'She stands there with bangles all the way up her arm and nothing else on.' Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dancing_Girl_(prehistoric_sculpture) ; https://smarthistory.org/dancing-girl-mohenjodaro/

question: At the heart of Mohenjo-daro's raised citadel sits a watertight brick pool about 40 feet long, with wide staircases leading down into it from two ends -- the oldest public water tank ever found anywhere on Earth. What do archaeologists call this 4,000-year-old structure?
answer: the Great Bath
choices: the Great Bath
the Royal Cistern
the Sun Temple
the Council Hall
context: The Great Bath is the oldest known public water tank in the world -- about 12 m by 7 m and 2.4 m deep (40 x 23 x 8 ft), reached by two wide brick staircases descending from the north and south ends. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Bath ; worldatlas.com Great Bath article

question: Archaeologists digging at Mohenjo-daro found that Indus children played with real toys made of clay: little bullock carts with wheels that actually turned, animals with heads that nodded, and bird-shaped whistles. One clay figurine was built to do a trick when you pulled a string through it. What was that toy?
answer: a monkey that slid down it
choices: a monkey that slid down it
a snake that reared up
a bull that charged ahead
a bird that flew in circles
context: Among the Mohenjo-daro toys was a little monkey figurine posed to slide down a string like a vine, alongside terracotta bullock carts with detachable oxen and clay animals with movable nodding heads. Sources: https://www.amarchitrakatha.com/history_details/toys-of-indus-valley-civilization/ ; https://www.harappa.com/blog/toys-and-civilization

question: More than 4,500 years ago, the engineers of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa laid out their cities not as a tangle of alleys but with a deliberate plan that makes them among the earliest planned cities on Earth. How were their main streets arranged?
answer: in a strict grid, north-south and east-west
choices: in a strict grid, north-south and east-west
in winding rings around a hilltop
in spokes spreading from a harbor
in terraces climbing a hillside
context: Straight streets ran north-south and east-west, oriented to the compass, with main avenues twice the width of the side lanes -- among the earliest grid-planned cities ever built. Sources: https://www.worldhistory.org/Indus_Valley_Civilization/ ; https://www.thearchaeologist.org/blog/sanitation-of-the-indus-valley-civilisation

question: In most ancient cities people threw their waste into the open street, but more than 4,000 years ago almost every house in Mohenjo-daro had its own toilet -- making this the world's first city-wide sanitation system. What carried the waste away beneath the roads?
answer: covered brick sewers
choices: covered brick sewers
hollow wooden pipes
open roadside gutters
a diverted stream
context: Household toilets drained into covered brick sewers running under the streets -- the world's first urban sanitation system. National Geographic called it the 'ancient world's best plumbing,' in some ways ahead of what Rome built two thousand years later. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanitation_of_the_Indus_Valley_Civilisation ; https://humanprogress.org/centers-of-progress-pt-3-mohenjo-daro-2/

question: Among the thousands of small carved seals the Indus people pressed into clay, one creature appears far more often than any other -- on roughly half of every inscribed seal found, for some 700 years -- always shown in profile facing right, with a strange ritual object standing before it. Scholars still cannot say for certain what real animal it was. What do they nickname this single most common Indus seal creature?
answer: the unicorn
choices: the unicorn
the griffin
the phoenix
the sphinx
context: The 'unicorn' -- a one-horned bull facing right with a ritual object before it -- appears on roughly half to 60% of the inscribed seals (thousands of them) across c. 2600-1900 BCE. The single horn gave it the nickname; scholars still argue over what real animal, if any, it represents. Sources: https://imp-art.org/perspectives/dispatches/the-unicorn-seals-an-indus-valley-mystery/ ; https://www.harappa.com/slide/unicorn-seal-0

question: Indus merchants in Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, hundreds of miles apart, weighed their goods on identical little cube-shaped stone weights -- and no king's stamp forced them to match. The weights climbed in one exact mathematical pattern. What was it?
answer: each weight double the one before (1, 2, 4, 8, 16...)
choices: each weight double the one before (1, 2, 4, 8, 16...)
each weight one more than the last (1, 2, 3, 4, 5...)
each weight ten times the last (1, 10, 100, 1000...)
each weight a square number (1, 4, 9, 16, 25...)
context: Indus traders used cubical chert weights cut to an exact binary doubling system -- 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 -- with a base unit of about 0.86 grams. A trader in Harappa and a trader in Mohenjo-daro weighed goods on the identical standard, with no king's stamp needed to enforce it. Sources: https://www.sizes.com/units/harappan_weights.htm ; https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/social-science/chapter-1-seals-script-weights-class-12-history-notes/

question: Egypt left pyramids and giant statues for its pharaohs and Mesopotamia left royal tombs, but when archaeologists dug through Mohenjo-daro and Harappa they found something startling missing. Across both great cities, what did they never find?
answer: any palace, royal tomb, or name of a king
choices: any palace, royal tomb, or name of a king
any clay pot, bead, or bronze tool
any house, well, or workshop
any drain, brick, or doorway
context: Unlike Egypt or Mesopotamia, the Indus cities left no palaces, no temples, no royal tombs, no giant statues of kings, and not one name of any ruler -- a vast civilization with no visible monarchy. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Indus_Valley_Civilization/

question: For years a famous theory held that invaders stormed Mohenjo-daro and slaughtered its people, pointing to scattered skeletons as 'massacre victims.' Then the archaeologist George Dales re-examined those very bones. What did he discover that demolished the invasion-massacre story?
answer: the skeletons bore no wounds at all
choices: the skeletons bore no wounds at all
the skeletons were soldiers in armor
the skeletons came from a much later age
the skeletons belonged to wild animals
context: George Dales showed the skeletons once read as 'battle victims' had no wounds at all, demolishing the old 'Aryan invasion massacre' story. The Indus cities show almost no signs of war. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Indus_Valley_Civilization/

question: At the Indus city of Dholavira, archaeologists uncovered ten huge Indus signs set over the north gate -- each more than a foot tall, cut from white gypsum and inlaid into a wooden board about three metres long, like mosaic tiles. What nickname did this giant 4,000-year-old line of writing earn?
answer: the world's oldest billboard
choices: the world's oldest billboard
the world's oldest sundial
the world's oldest milestone
the world's oldest tombstone
context: The Dholavira signboard -- 10 large signs about 37 cm tall, inlaid in a roughly 3 m board over the citadel's north gate -- has been called the world's oldest billboard. We can see it, but still cannot read a word of it. Sources: https://www.harappa.com/blog/dholavira-and-its-mysterious-sign-board ; https://atlasobscura.com/articles/oldest-billboard-in-world

question: For a hundred years scholars have tried and failed to read the Indus script -- more than 400 signs that no one alive can translate, because no 'Rosetta Stone' was ever found to unlock it. In January 2025, marking the centenary of the cities' discovery, a leader in India put up a reward for anyone who could finally crack the code. How big was the prize?
answer: one million US dollars
choices: one million US dollars
one hundred thousand dollars
ten thousand dollars
one thousand dollars
context: In January 2025, on the centenary of the civilization's discovery, Tamil Nadu's chief minister M.K. Stalin offered a US $1 million prize to anyone who can decipher the Indus script. The script has a little over 400 distinct signs, written mostly right-to-left, with inscriptions averaging about 5 signs (none longer than 26) and no bilingual key -- still unread after 100 years. Sources: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/officials-are-offering-1-million-to-anyone-who-can-decode-this-ancient-script-180985922/ ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Indus_Script/

question: On a stone seal barely an inch and a half across, found at Mohenjo-daro, sits a horned figure cross-legged like a yogi, ringed by wild animals -- an elephant, a tiger, a rhino, and a buffalo. In 1931 the archaeologist John Marshall proposed that this figure was an early ancestor of a great Hindu god, the Lord of Animals. Which god did he have in mind?
answer: Shiva
choices: Shiva
Vishnu
Brahma
Ganesha
context: On the 'Pashupati seal' (~3.5 cm square, found 1928-29), Marshall in 1931 called the cross-legged horned figure a 'proto-Shiva,' an ancestor of the Hindu Lord of Animals -- though that reading is still debated, not settled fact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pashupati_seal  (Legend.)

question: James Hargreaves built a machine in the 1760s called the spinning jenny to make thread faster. Where one old spinning wheel turned a single spindle of thread at a time, how many spindles could one worker spin on Hargreaves' new frame at once?
answer: Eight spindles at once
choices: Eight spindles at once
Two spindles at once
A hundred at once
Three spindles at once
context: The spinning jenny (1764-65) was a metal frame holding eight wooden spindles, so one worker did the work of eight spinning wheels. Later versions pushed it to 120 spindles from a single operator. Source: britannica.com/biography/James-Hargreaves ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinning_jenny

question: In 1771 Richard Arkwright built a cotton-spinning mill on the River Derwent, powered by the river turning a water wheel instead of by human hands. Hundreds of workers came to one building to run rows of machines on a fixed clock — a way of working so new that Arkwright is remembered by a single famous title. What is he called?
answer: The Father of the Factory System
choices: The Father of the Factory System
The Father of British Cotton
The Master of the Mills
The Father of the Spinning Frame
context: Cromford Mill (1771) was the world's first water-powered cotton spinning mill, employing about 200 people. It was one of the first workplaces where the working day was set by the CLOCK instead of by daylight. Source: scienceandindustrymuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/richard-arkwright ; britannica.com/biography/Richard-Arkwright

question: Around 1779 Samuel Crompton built a spinning machine by combining two earlier inventions, the spinning jenny and the water frame, into one. His machine had no name of its own at first; it earned a nickname because it was a cross of those two earlier machines. What was Crompton's machine called?
answer: The spinning mule
choices: The spinning mule
The spinning griffin
The spinning ox
The spinning hawk
context: A mule is the cross of a horse and a donkey, so Crompton's cross of the jenny and the water frame took the same name. It spun thread fine enough for delicate muslin, and a single operator could eventually work over 1,000 spindles at once. Source: britannica.com/biography/Samuel-Crompton ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Crompton

question: From 1811, English workers who blamed the new spinning and weaving machines for their poverty smashed those machines and signed their threatening letters in the name of a single leader, 'Ned Ludd' — the man they all claimed to follow. What do historians say about this Ned Ludd?
answer: He almost certainly never existed
choices: He almost certainly never existed
He was secretly Lord Byron
He owned the largest mill in Nottingham
He was hanged at York in 1813
context: The machine-breakers became known as the Luddites, after the imaginary 'Ned Ludd' they signed their letters in the name of. They carried out at least 100 attacks and destroyed about 1,000 frames. Source: nationalarchives.gov.uk/explore-the-collection/stories/the-proclamation-of-ned-ludd/ ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ned_Ludd  (Legend.)

question: In 1812 Parliament passed the Frame Breaking Act to stop the Luddites from smashing textile machines. The Act set one penalty for destroying a textile machine, even when no person had been harmed. What could a frame-breaker now be sentenced to?
answer: Death by hanging
choices: Death by hanging
A fine of five pounds
A year in prison
Banishment from England
context: Breaking a frame became a capital crime. At York in January 1813, 14 convicted Luddites were hanged in two batches of seven, and others were transported to Australia. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destruction_of_Stocking_Frames,_etc._Act_1812 ; ludditebicentenary.blogspot.com

question: In February 1812, as Parliament debated hanging the Luddites for smashing textile machines, the famous poet Lord Byron rose in the House of Lords to give the very first speech of his life there. Byron used that maiden speech to argue what?
answer: That hunger, not hatred of machines, drove the men
choices: That hunger, not hatred of machines, drove the men
That every last machine-breaker fully deserved to hang
That England ought to ban all of the new spinning machines
That the king himself should personally tour the cotton mills
context: Byron's maiden speech (27 February 1812) defended the Luddites against the new hanging law. He told the Lords that in Nottingham 'not twelve hours elapsed without some fresh act of violence' — forty frames broken in a single evening. Source: ludditebicentenary.blogspot.com/2012/02/27th-february-1812-lord-byrons-maiden.html ; historyofinformation.com/detail.php?id=4654

question: A 1788 survey of 143 water mills across England and Scotland counted who actually ran two-thirds of the machines — a finding that later shocked Parliament into passing the 1833 Factory Act. Who were they?
answer: Children
choices: Children
Whole families together
Skilled master weavers
Irish migrant workers
context: Children made up two-thirds of the workforce in the 1788 survey. The Factory Act of 1833 finally banned mill work under age 9 and created paid inspectors to actually enforce it. Source: britannica.com/event/Factory-Act-United-Kingdom-1833 ; galbithink.org/child.htm

question: Alexander Fleming came back to his cluttered London lab in 1928 to find a stray blue-green mould had killed every colony of bacteria in a ring around itself. Before he ever settled on the name 'penicillin,' what plain, unglamorous nickname did Fleming first give the germ-killing liquid the mould oozed out?
answer: mould juice
choices: mould juice
germ broth
blue water
spore milk
context: Fleming called it 'mould juice' before naming penicillin after the mould Penicillium notatum that made it; the mould may have drifted up a stairwell from a lab below. He was famously modest: 'I did not invent penicillin. Nature did that. I only discovered it by accident.' (Science History Institute biography, sciencehistory.org; American Chemical Society penicillin landmark, acs.org; Asimov Press 'The Penicillin Myth,' asimov.press)

question: A 1927 gathering of scientists in Brussels produced what's been called 'the most intelligent photo ever taken' — 29 of the world's greatest physicists in one frame, most of them Nobel Prize winners. Only one woman sits among them, and she stood out for another reason too: she alone had won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. Who was she?
answer: Marie Curie
choices: Marie Curie
Lise Meitner
Emmy Noether
Dorothy Hodgkin
context: Marie Curie won the Nobel Prize in physics and again in chemistry — the only person at the 1927 Solvay Conference, and the only person there, to have won in two different sciences. (Rare Historical Photos 'The Solvay Conference, 1927,' rarehistoricalphotos.com; University of Antwerp PLASMANT, uantwerpen.be)

question: In 1927 a Belgian named Georges Lemaître worked out, straight from Einstein's own equations, that the whole universe is expanding — that distant galaxies fly apart faster the farther away they are — a full two years before Edwin Hubble measured it. Apart from being a trained physicist, what was Lemaître, by ordination back in 1923?
answer: a Catholic priest
choices: a Catholic priest
a Lutheran pastor
a Baptist preacher
an Anglican vicar
context: Georges Lemaître, ordained a Catholic priest in 1923, published the expanding-universe law in 1927, two years before Hubble's measurement — a priest at the root of what became the Big Bang. (Encyclopaedia Britannica 'Georges Lemaître,' britannica.com; University of Navarra Science, Reason and Faith, unav.edu)

question: On a night in October 1923, Edwin Hubble photographed a faint star in the Andromeda nebula and first marked his glass plate 'N' for a nova. Then he studied it again, realized what the star truly was, crossed out the 'N' — and in red ink scrawled one triumphant word that meant Andromeda was a whole separate galaxy beyond the Milky Way. What word did Hubble write?
answer: VAR!
choices: VAR!
FAR!
NEW!
RED!
context: 'VAR!' marked it as a variable star — the kind whose brightness let Hubble measure distance and prove Andromeda lay far outside the Milky Way. The plate has been called 'the only scientific artifact I know of that shows human emotion.' (Live Science 'Edwin Hubble uncovers the vastness of the universe,' livescience.com; Carnegie Science 'Hubble's Famous M31 VAR! plate,' carnegiescience.edu)

question: When Georges Lemaître showed Albert Einstein his radical new paper arguing the universe is expanding, at the 1927 Solvay Conference in Brussels, Einstein granted that the young Belgian's mathematics was flawless — yet flatly rejected the idea anyway. What stinging verdict did Einstein deliver on Lemaître's work?
answer: Your calculations are correct, but your physics is abominable.
choices: Your calculations are correct, but your physics is abominable.
Your numbers add up, but your conclusion is impossible.
Your equations are elegant, but your universe is a fantasy.
Your logic is sound, but your imagination has run wild.
context: Einstein said it in French: 'Vos calculs sont corrects, mais votre physique est abominable.' Years later, after a 1933 seminar, he reversed himself and called Lemaître's idea 'the most beautiful and satisfactory explanation of creation that I have ever heard.' (University of Navarra Science, Reason and Faith, unav.edu; Big Think 'The priest who proved Einstein wrong,' bigthink.com)

question: The everyday name for the theory that the universe burst out of a single explosive beginning was actually coined by an astronomer who thought the whole idea was nonsense — he backed a rival 'Steady State' universe and used the phrase while describing the explosive-origin theory he opposed, on a 1949 BBC radio broadcast. Which household term did this skeptic, Fred Hoyle, hand to the theory he was mocking?
answer: the Big Bang
choices: the Big Bang
the Cosmic Egg
the First Flash
the Great Burst
context: Fred Hoyle used 'Big Bang' on BBC radio on 28 March 1949 to describe an idea he rejected; the name stuck to the very theory he spent his career arguing against. (Popular Science 'The big bang got its name from a man who thought the theory was total nonsense,' popsci.com; BBC Radio 4 / SciHi Blog, scihi.org)

question: In February 1941 an Oxford policeman named Albert Alexander became the first human ever treated with penicillin, and within a day his life-threatening infection began to heal. But wartime penicillin was so scarce that, to keep the tiny supply going, his doctors did something desperate and ingenious to recover the drug from his own body. What did they do to reuse it?
answer: Filtered it from his urine and re-injected it
choices: Filtered it from his urine and re-injected it
Recovered it from his sweat and re-injected it
Drained it from his wounds and re-injected it
Distilled it from his blood and re-injected it
context: Even filtering the drug back out of his urine wasn't enough — the supply ran out, and Albert Alexander died on 15 March 1941. The old story that a rose-thorn scratch caused his infection is probably legend; recent research points instead to a German bombing raid that hit his police station on 30 November 1940. (Wikipedia 'Albert Alexander (police officer),' en.wikipedia.org; University of Oxford Nuffield Dept, phc.ox.ac.uk; The Conversation 'Guns, not roses,' theconversation.com)

question: At dawn on September 1, 1939, the old German battleship Schleswig-Holstein opened fire on the tiny Polish garrison at Westerplatte in Danzig, firing some of the first shots of World War II. The ship had sailed into the harbor days earlier flying festive flags, pretending to be there for a friendly anniversary visit. What was that 'celebration' really hiding?
answer: More than 200 German marines waiting below deck
choices: More than 200 German marines waiting below deck
A cargo of food aid for the starving city
A delegation of diplomats seeking peace talks
A shipment of coal bound for the harbor
context: The pre-dreadnought Schleswig-Holstein had arrived under cover of a WWI-anniversary courtesy visit, with the assault troops concealed aboard. At 04:45 its guns opened on the Westerplatte depot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_Poland; polishhistory.pl 'The Defence of Westerplatte'.

question: German Ju 87 Stuka dive-bombers became infamous for the unearthly howl they made as they fell out of the sky onto Polish troops in 1939. That scream was no accident — engineers had bolted small wind-driven propellers onto the planes for the sole purpose of making noise to terrify people below. What were these screaming sirens called?
answer: The Jericho Trumpets
choices: The Jericho Trumpets
The Valkyrie Bells
The Berlin Whistles
The Thunder Pipes
context: The 'Jericho-Trompete' sirens were ~0.7 m propellers mounted on the landing gear; the drag actually cost the plane 12-15 mph, but the panic was worth it. The idea is usually credited to Ernst Udet. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junkers_Ju_87.

question: At Westerplatte, Major Henryk Sucharski's garrison of about 200 Polish soldiers was told to hold their position for just 12 hours until reinforcements arrived. The reinforcements never came, and about 3,400 Germans kept attacking. Instead of folding, how long did Sucharski's men actually hold out?
answer: For seven days, through thirteen assaults
choices: For seven days, through thirteen assaults
For about three hours, then they fled
For a single afternoon of fighting
For exactly the twelve hours ordered
context: Ordered to last 12 hours, the garrison repelled thirteen assaults and held until September 7. The German commander, General Friedrich Eberhardt, was so impressed he let Sucharski keep his Polish saber into captivity. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Westerplatte.

question: The small Polish town of Wielun has been called the first town destroyed in World War II. Around 04:40 on September 1, 1939, German Stukas appeared over it and pounded it for hours, wiping out about 70 percent of the town. What made this attack especially chilling?
answer: The town was undefended, with no guns and no soldiers
choices: The town was undefended, with no guns and no soldiers
The town had just surrendered the day before
The bombs were meant for a different city entirely
The pilots dropped leaflets warning people first
context: Wielun had no anti-aircraft guns and no garrison. About 90 percent of its center was destroyed in roughly nine hours; one of the first buildings hit was the hospital. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombing_of_Wielu%C5%84.

question: People remember 1939 as a hopeless slaughter for Poland, but on the very first day the Poles actually won a battle at Mokra. The Wolynska Cavalry Brigade fought alongside a weapon that rolled right up to the German Panzers and blasted them at point-blank range, helping destroy over 50 tanks. What was this unusual weapon?
answer: An armored train, No. 53
choices: An armored train, No. 53
A captured German Panzer
A fleet of motorcycle scouts
A row of buried land mines
context: Armored Train No. 53 fired on the Panzers at point-blank range while the cavalry brigade held; together they inflicted about 800 casualties and forced the 4th Panzer Division back to its start line. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mokra; nationalww2museum.org.

question: The most famous image of the 1939 campaign — brave Polish horsemen charging German tanks with lances — is a myth. At Krojanty on September 1, the 18th Pomeranian Uhlans did charge, but not at tanks. According to the story, what did they actually do?
answer: They drew sabers and scattered German infantry resting on foot
choices: They drew sabers and scattered German infantry resting on foot
They galloped straight into a column of heavy tanks
They threw their lances at low-flying Stukas
They surrendered the moment the shooting started
context: The Uhlans routed German infantry on foot and were winning until armored cars arrived. Italian reporter Indro Montanelli later saw the dead horses, assumed they had charged tanks, and the lance-versus-tank legend was born. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charge_at_Krojanty.

question: The German tactic in Poland, later called Blitzkrieg or 'lightning war', worked by making different weapons act as a single team: fast tanks punched holes in the line, radios kept everyone talking, and the Stuka dive-bombers played one special role above the battlefield. In this combined attack, what job did the Stukas do for the tanks below?
answer: They served as flying artillery, smashing targets ahead of the tanks
choices: They served as flying artillery, smashing targets ahead of the tanks
They dropped supplies and fuel to the advancing tanks
They scouted quietly and reported enemy positions by radio
They evacuated wounded crews back behind the lines
context: Stukas dived near-vertically as precision 'flying artillery' clearing the way for the Panzers, while the Luftwaffe bombed rail lines, bridges and airfields so the Poles could never concentrate a defense. Source: nationalww2museum.org; historyskills.com.

question: Hitler wanted the world to believe Germany was the victim, not the attacker. The night before the invasion, in an operation codenamed Himmler, German agents pulled off a staged 'attack' so he could claim he was only striking back. What did the agents actually stage?
answer: SS men in Polish uniforms faked an assault on a German radio station
choices: SS men in Polish uniforms faked an assault on a German radio station
A Polish ship was reported sinking a German fishing boat
A bomb was set off in a crowded Berlin train station
A border guard was photographed tearing down a German flag
context: At Gleiwitz, SS men in Polish uniforms staged the attack and left a body in a Polish uniform as 'proof', giving Hitler his pretext to claim Germany was returning fire. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_Poland; nationalww2museum.org.

question: Most tellings of 1939 say Poland was crushed by Germany — and stop there. But while Polish soldiers were still fighting the Germans in the west, on September 17 more than 600,000 troops suddenly poured across Poland's eastern border too. Who launched this second invasion from the east?
answer: The Soviet Union
choices: The Soviet Union
The kingdom of Hungary
The Czechoslovak army
The forces of Romania
context: Under the secret Molotov-Ribbentrop pact that had already carved Poland in two, the Red Army invaded from the east. Molotov claimed the Polish state 'had ceased to exist' and the Soviets were merely 'protecting' Ukrainians and Belarusians. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_invasion_of_Poland; ushmm.org.

question: After Germany and the Soviet Union both invaded Poland in 1939, the two conquerors met at the captured fortress of Brest-Litovsk on September 22. German General Heinz Guderian and Soviet Brigadier Semyon Krivoshein even shared breakfast. To mark handing the fortress over at the agreed dividing line, what did the two armies stage together?
answer: A joint military parade
choices: A joint military parade
A signing of a peace treaty
A prisoner exchange ceremony
A funeral for the fallen
context: The Germans and Soviets held a joint parade in Brest-Litovsk before the Germans handed the fortress to the Red Army, a striking image of the two totalitarian powers cooperating to dismember Poland. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German%E2%80%93Soviet_military_parade_in_Brest-Litovsk.

question: When the Soviet Union invaded eastern Poland in 1939, the Red Army captured up to 450,000 Polish soldiers. Most ordinary troops were eventually let go, but thousands of Poland's army officers, police, and educated leaders were never freed. What did Stalin's secret police, the NKVD, do to them in 1940?
answer: They shot about 22,000 of them at Katyn and other sites
choices: They shot about 22,000 of them at Katyn and other sites
They drafted them into the Soviet army by force
They put them on trial and then released most of them
They sent them home in exchange for grain shipments
context: The NKVD murdered roughly 22,000 Polish officers and elites at Katyn and elsewhere, then for decades the Soviets blamed the Germans. The eastern invasion fed directly into one of the war's great hidden massacres. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_invasion_of_Poland.

question: Poland fought the 1939 invasion with brains as well as soldiers. Just weeks before the war, in July 1939 near Warsaw, three Polish mathematicians — Marian Rejewski, Jerzy Rozycki and Henryk Zygalski — quietly handed the British and French a secret that would help win the whole war. What did they give away?
answer: Their reverse-engineered Enigma machines and the methods to read them
choices: Their reverse-engineered Enigma machines and the methods to read them
A complete map of every German airfield and supply dump
A new diesel engine design for faster Allied tanks
The location of Germany's planned invasion routes
context: At Pyry, the Polish cryptologists revealed they had already broken the German Enigma cipher and shared their machines and techniques, the secret gift that later powered Britain's codebreakers at Bletchley Park. Source: history.blog.gov.uk (26 July 1939); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_machine.

question: In January 1077, the German king Henry IV came to the castle of Canossa to beg Pope Gregory VII to lift the excommunication that had cost him his throne. For three days, what did Henry do at the castle gate?
answer: Stood barefoot in the snow, wearing only rough wool
choices: Stood barefoot in the snow, wearing only rough wool
Waited on horseback in full armor and his crown
Knelt on a carpet of gold beneath a silk canopy
Was chained to the gate by his own soldiers
context: Henry IV, the most powerful king in Europe, humbled himself completely. Pope Gregory VII later wrote that Henry, 'having laid aside all the belongings of royalty, wretchedly, with bare feet and clad in wool,' stood three days before the gate. This is the most famous penance in medieval history. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_to_Canossa

question: The whole fight between Henry IV and Pope Gregory VII was over 'investiture' — the right to install a new bishop by handing him the two symbols of his office. Which two objects did a new bishop receive?
answer: A ring and a staff
choices: A ring and a staff
A crown and a sword
A scroll and a key
A chalice and a candle
context: The staff was called a crozier (shaped like a shepherd's crook), and the ring marked the bishop's bond to his church. The real quarrel was over who got to do the handing — king or pope — which meant a fight over who outranked whom. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/Investiture-Controversy

question: A year before Canossa, Henry IV fired back at Pope Gregory VII with a furious letter (1076). He refused to even call Gregory 'pope' — addressing him instead by his birth name, Hildebrand. Henry ended the letter with a thundering command to the pope. How did he sign off?
answer: "Descend, descend, and be damned throughout the ages."
choices: "Descend, descend, and be damned throughout the ages."
"Kneel, kneel, and repent before your king."
"Be silent and obey the crown of Germany."
"Surrender your throne or perish in disgrace."
context: Henry's letter opened by calling Gregory 'not pope but FALSE MONK' and ordered him off the papal throne. Gregory's answer was to excommunicate Henry and release every Christian from their oath of loyalty to him — which is exactly why Henry later had to crawl to Canossa. Source: https://historyofthegermans.com/2021/10/lettertogregory/

question: Henry IV's surrender at Canossa became so famous that 'going to Canossa' turned into a phrase across Europe for humbling yourself completely before an enemy. In 1872, during his own power struggle with the Catholic Church, the German chancellor Otto von Bismarck threw the phrase back in defiance. What did Bismarck declare?
answer: "We will not go to Canossa!"
choices: "We will not go to Canossa!"
"Let them remember Canossa!"
"Berlin is not Canossa!"
"Canossa shall be avenged!"
context: The idiom is so deeply rooted that it survives in German, Dutch, Danish, Swedish, French, Italian, Hungarian, Hebrew, and Polish. Bismarck's full boast was 'We will not go to Canossa, neither in body nor in spirit' — 800 years after a king stood barefoot in the snow. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_to_Canossa

question: Two years before Canossa, Pope Gregory VII set down the 'Dictatus Papae' (1075) — 27 blunt claims of papal power, including that the pope alone could depose an emperor. One clause spelled out the submission Gregory expected from the world's rulers. According to the Dictatus, what were all princes to do?
answer: Kiss the feet of the pope alone
choices: Kiss the feet of the pope alone
Send their crowns to Rome each year
Swear their oaths upon the pope's ring
Kneel before any bishop they met
context: The Dictatus Papae was a stunning assertion that spiritual authority outranked every king and emperor. The collision between this claim and royal power is a deep root of the Western distinction between sacred and secular authority — a separation the later tradition of liberty inherited. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dictatus_papae

question: Canossa did not end the war between Henry IV and Pope Gregory VII. Henry later marched on Rome, drove Gregory out, and installed a rival 'antipope.' Gregory died far from Rome in 1085, and the bitter line later carved on his tomb summed up how he saw his fall. What were Gregory's dying words?
answer: "I have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile."
choices: "I have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile."
"Rome has fallen, but Heaven remembers her servant."
"Let no king ever again raise his hand against God."
"I forgive Henry, as I hope to be forgiven."
context: Gregory died at Salerno, exiled by the very king who had once knelt barefoot before him — so Canossa was a setback for Henry, not a true defeat. The defiant epitaph casts the dying pope as the righteous loser. Source: https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/06791c.htm

question: On March 5, 1946, Winston Churchill stood in a small Missouri college gym and told the world that a barrier had slammed down across Europe — running from Stettin on the Baltic Sea to Trieste on the Adriatic — sealing the Soviet-ruled East away from the free West. What did Churchill call that barrier?
answer: An iron curtain
choices: An iron curtain
A steel wall
An iron gate
A stone barrier
context: Churchill titled the address 'The Sinews of Peace,' but history remembers it as the 'Iron Curtain Speech.' The line he drew — Stettin on the Baltic to Trieste on the Adriatic — marked off the Soviet-controlled captives from the free West, naming a divide that would define the next forty years. Source: America's National Churchill Museum (nationalchurchillmuseum.org); Wikipedia 'Fulton Speech.'

question: When Winston Churchill handed reporters advance copies of his March 1946 Missouri speech, the lines that would become its most famous — and give it the name history remembers — were nowhere on the printed pages. How did those unforgettable words end up in the speech he delivered?
answer: He ad-libbed them past his prepared text
choices: He ad-libbed them past his prepared text
He memorized them and recited from notes
An aide cued them to him from the wings
He read them from a hidden index card
context: Churchill spoke past his typed text, so the stenographers in the hall had to reconstruct his most famous lines from their shorthand notes — the words the whole world would quote were improvised on his feet and pieced back together afterward. Source: Wikipedia 'Fulton Speech.'

question: In 1943 the British archaeologist Bernard Fagg, working near Jos in Nigeria, was handed a terracotta head that a farmer had perched atop a scarecrow in his yam field. Fagg realized the clay face matched no civilization anyone had catalogued. What did this scarecrow head become?
answer: The namesake first find of the lost Nok culture
choices: The namesake first find of the lost Nok culture
A burial mask traded down from ancient Egypt
A toy carved by a bored colonial soldier
A medieval charm left by passing merchants
context: Named the Jemaa Head after the nearby village, it launched the study of the Nok culture of central Nigeria, whose terracottas are the oldest known figurative sculptures made south of the Sahara. Source: Archaeology Magazine, 'The Nok of Nigeria'.

question: Nok artists drilled open the nostrils, mouths, and ears of their hollow clay heads, and pierced tiny holes through the pupils of the stylized eyes. Beyond the bold look, those open holes served a hidden purpose when the figure was baked. What did the holes do?
answer: Let trapped heat escape so the figure wouldn't crack
choices: Let trapped heat escape so the figure wouldn't crack
Held strings so the heads could be worn as pendants
Drained rainwater so the clay would not rot
Whistled in the wind to scare birds from the field
context: The pierced nostrils, ears, and pupils doubled as air vents: as the hollow clay was fired, heat and steam escaped through them instead of building up and shattering the sculpture. Function and style in one move. Source: Metropolitan Museum of Art, 'Nok Terracottas'; World History Encyclopedia, Nok Culture.

question: Across most of the ancient world, metalworking climbed a ladder: stone tools first, then bronze, then iron. At Taruga in central Nigeria, archaeologists found about thirteen iron-smelting furnaces, with charcoal inside radiocarbon-dated to the centuries before 200 BCE, sitting among old stone tools. What was unusual about how the Nok climbed that ladder?
answer: They skipped bronze entirely, jumping from stone tools straight to iron
choices: They skipped bronze entirely, jumping from stone tools straight to iron
They mastered bronze first, then slowly worked their way up to iron
They learned iron-smelting from Egyptian traders crossing the Sahara
They used bronze and iron side by side for hundreds of years
context: Charcoal from the Taruga furnaces radiocarbon-dates the smelting to the 4th-2nd centuries BCE, making the Nok among the earliest iron-smelters in sub-Saharan Africa. They jumped from stone tools straight to iron hoes, hand-axes, and cleavers, with no Bronze Age in between. Source: World History Encyclopedia, Nok Culture.

question: Isaac Newton was born early and so tiny on Christmas Day 1642 that his mother Hannah said the newborn could have fit inside what small household container?
answer: A quart mug
choices: A quart mug
A cooking pot
A wooden pail
A soldier's helmet
context: His mother Hannah Ayscough said the premature baby was so small he could have fit inside a quart mug; his father had died three months before he was born, at Woolsthorpe Manor in Lincolnshire. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton (also National Trust, Woolsthorpe Manor history).

question: Sitting in the garden at Woolsthorpe, Isaac Newton watched a piece of fruit drop straight down and wondered why it never fell sideways or upward. What fruit set him thinking about gravity?
answer: An apple
choices: An apple
A pear
A plum
A cherry
context: The apple story is real and in Newton's own words: his friend William Stukeley recorded Newton saying the idea of gravity came to him 'occasion'd by the fall of an apple... Why should it not go sideways or upwards, but constantly to the earth's centre?' Source: William Stukeley, Memoirs of Sir Isaac Newton's Life (1752); https://blogs.royalsociety.org/history-of-science/2012/02/22/newtons-apple-tree/.

question: Isaac Newton's great leap was realizing that the very same force that pulls an apple to the ground is also responsible for doing what far out in the sky?
answer: Holding the Moon in its orbit
choices: Holding the Moon in its orbit
Lighting the Sun each morning
Pushing the clouds across the sky
Making the wind blow over the sea
context: This was the unification of the heavens and the earth: one law of universal gravitation governs both the falling apple and the orbiting Moon, set out in his 1687 book the Principia. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophi%C3%A6_Naturalis_Principia_Mathematica.

question: In 1665 a deadly outbreak forced Cambridge University to close, sending the young Isaac Newton home to Woolsthorpe for nearly two years. What disease emptied the city?
answer: The plague
choices: The plague
Cholera
Smallpox
Typhoid
context: Those years home from the plague (summer 1665 to spring 1667) became his 'year of wonders,' when he invented calculus, split sunlight with a prism, and began his theory of gravity. He later said, 'For in those days I was in the prime of my age for invention.' Source: https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/nottinghamshire-lincolnshire/woolsthorpe-manor/history-of-woolsthorpe-manor.

question: Home from the plague, Isaac Newton let a thin beam of sunlight pass through a glass prism in his darkened room. What appeared on the wall beyond the prism?
answer: A band of rainbow colors
choices: A band of rainbow colors
A single bright white dot
A blurry gray smear
Two crossed beams of light
context: By splitting white sunlight with a prism, Newton discovered that it is made of all the colors of the spectrum, one of three breakthroughs of his 'year of wonders' at Woolsthorpe. Source: https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/nottinghamshire-lincolnshire/woolsthorpe-manor/history-of-woolsthorpe-manor.

question: A cartoon shows an apple bonking Isaac Newton on the head. The one firsthand account of the moment was written by his friend William Stukeley, who heard it straight from Newton. According to Stukeley, what did Newton actually do?
answer: He simply watched the apple fall to the ground
choices: He simply watched the apple fall to the ground
He was struck on the head by the apple
He caught the apple just before it landed
He picked the apple up and ate it
context: The apple-on-the-head detail is a later embellishment. Stukeley's primary account only has Newton watching an apple fall to the ground while sitting in the garden; no version from Newton himself has it hit him. Source: https://www.todayifoundout.com/index.php/2013/10/origin-apple-falling-newtons-head-story/.  (Legend.)

question: An apple tree still grows in the orchard at Woolsthorpe Manor, and visitors are told it is the very tree that inspired Isaac Newton. But the original blew down in an 1820 storm, so how can it still be standing today?
answer: It grew back from the original tree's roots
choices: It grew back from the original tree's roots
A cutting was replanted in the same spot
Newton's family propped it upright for years
It was a different tree planted nearby
context: Dendrochronology confirms a tree there is over 400 years old, having regrown from the roots of the original after the storm of 1820, so it can genuinely be called the same tree. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolsthorpe_Manor (also National Trust).  (Legend.)

question: Isaac Newton's masterpiece almost never got printed. His friend Edmond Halley, of comet fame, ended up paying for the printing out of his own pocket because the Royal Society had just blown all its money on what?
answer: A lavish book about fish
choices: A lavish book about fish
A new telescope for the king
A grand banquet for its members
A voyage to chart the stars
context: When Halley visited in 1684 and asked what curve a planet follows under an inverse-square force, Newton instantly replied 'an ellipse.' Halley coaxed him to write it all up, then paid for printing himself because the Royal Society had run out of money after spending its budget on a book about fish. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophi%C3%A6_Naturalis_Principia_Mathematica.

question: Isaac Newton's law of gravity says the pull between two objects weakens fast as they move apart. If you DOUBLE the distance between two bodies, the force does not simply drop to a half. It drops all the way to what?
answer: One quarter
choices: One quarter
One third
One eighth
One sixteenth
context: Universal gravitation is an inverse-square law: the force falls off with the square of the distance. Doubling the distance squares to four, so the pull drops to one-quarter. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophi%C3%A6_Naturalis_Principia_Mathematica.

question: As Isaac Newton was finishing his great book, the Principia, the scientist Robert Hooke loudly accused him of stealing the idea of gravity's inverse-square law and demanded credit. Newton was so enraged that he did what to the manuscript?
answer: Went through it deleting nearly every mention of Hooke
choices: Went through it deleting nearly every mention of Hooke
Burned the whole manuscript in a fit of rage
Added a page openly mocking Hooke by name
Refused to let it be published for ten years
context: Hooke conceded the mathematical proof was entirely Newton's, but Newton went through the manuscript striking out nearly every mention of Hooke's name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton-Hooke_priority_controversy_for_the_inverse_square_law.

question: Isaac Newton and the German mathematician Gottfried Leibniz waged a bitter war over who really invented calculus. As President of the Royal Society, Newton set up a committee to judge the dispute. How did he rig the outcome?
answer: He wrote the committee's verdict himself
choices: He wrote the committee's verdict himself
He bribed two of the committee members
He fed secret evidence to a chosen ally
He destroyed Leibniz's oldest letters
context: Newton stacked the supposedly impartial committee with his own supporters and anonymously wrote its 1713 verdict (the Commercium Epistolicum), ruling in his own favor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leibniz%E2%80%93Newton_calculus_controversy.

question: Most people picture Isaac Newton as the founder of cold, clear science. But when the economist John Maynard Keynes studied a hoard of Newton's secret papers (a million words on alchemy, half his writing on religion), he called Newton not the first man of reason but the last of what?
answer: The last of the magicians
choices: The last of the magicians
The last of the prophets
The last of the alchemists
The last of the philosophers
context: Of roughly 10 million words Newton left in manuscript, about a million are on alchemy and about half is religious writing. After buying these papers in 1936, Keynes declared, 'Newton was not the first of the age of reason. He was the last of the magicians.' Source: https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Extras/Keynes_Newton/ (Keynes, 'Newton, the Man', 1936).

question: In 1665 the plague forced Cambridge University to close, so the young Isaac Newton went home to the family farm at Woolsthorpe in Lincolnshire. Cut off from school for about a year and a half, he quietly worked out the foundations of gravity, light, and a whole new kind of math. Scholars gave this astonishing stretch a Latin nickname. What is it called?
answer: His annus mirabilis, or 'wonderful year'
choices: His annus mirabilis, or 'wonderful year'
His tempus fugit, or 'time that flies'
His terra incognita, or 'unknown land'
His casus belli, or 'cause for war'
context: With Cambridge shut for the plague (1665-1666), Newton at Woolsthorpe Manor laid the groundwork for gravity, optics, and calculus all at once -- the 'annus mirabilis.' Source: thonyc.wordpress.com 'Isaac and the Apple'; Linda Hall Library scientist-of-the-day.

question: Isaac Newton darkened a room and let a single thin sunbeam pass through a triangular glass prism. Until then most people thought white light was plain and colorless. When the beam came out the other side and struck the wall, what did Newton see it had become?
answer: A spread-out band of every rainbow colour
choices: A spread-out band of every rainbow colour
A single narrow beam of pure white light
One round, bright white spot of sunlight
Two thin beams of plain white light
context: The prism fanned white light into a band of colours -- Newton called this spreading 'dispersion.' Source: livescience.com on Newton's light experiments; testbook.com Newton's prism experiment.

question: Everyone has heard that an apple bonked Isaac Newton on the head and gravity popped into his mind. The truth comes from Newton himself: on 15 April 1726 the old man sat under his apple trees over tea with his friend William Stukeley and told the story. According to Stukeley's written memoir, what did Newton say happened that long-ago day?
answer: He watched an apple fall straight to the ground
choices: He watched an apple fall straight to the ground
An apple struck him hard on the top of the head
He caught a falling apple in his open hand
He shook the tree until apples rained down
context: William Stukeley's 'Memoirs of Sir Isaac Newton's Life' (1752) records Newton saying a falling apple set him wondering about gravity; the apple-on-the-head version is later myth. Source: gethistories.com 'The Apple of His Eye'; amusingplanet.com on Newton's apple tree.

question: The famous apple tree still stands in the orchard at Woolsthorpe, and it is a rare old variety called a 'Flower of Kent.' A storm knocked the tree over in 1816 -- yet visitors today can still see it, now more than 350 years old. How did this very tree live through being blown flat?
answer: Part of the toppled tree re-rooted and kept growing
choices: Part of the toppled tree re-rooted and kept growing
Gardeners propped it upright again with iron posts
Fresh shoots sprang up straight from the old stump
New bark slowly grew over the cracked, fallen trunk
context: After the 1816 storm, part of the fallen 'Flower of Kent' re-rooted, so the same tree -- over 350 years old -- still grows in the orchard. Source: york.ac.uk on Newton's apple tree; amusingplanet.com.

question: Glass lenses smeared starlight into ugly false-colour fringes, so in 1668 Isaac Newton built a brand-new kind of telescope that beat the problem -- and it became the first working telescope of its type ever made. The little instrument so impressed England's scientists that they carried it before King Charles II and made Newton a member of the Royal Society. What did Newton put inside to gather the starlight?
answer: A curved polished mirror
choices: A curved polished mirror
A second, thicker glass lens
A hollow polished cone of brass
A spinning disc of clear quartz
context: Newton's reflecting telescope (1668) used a curved mirror instead of a lens to dodge the colour-smearing of glass; the Royal Society showed it to Charles II and elected Newton a Fellow in January 1672. Source: en.wikipedia.org, Newton's reflector.

question: Watching an apple drop, Isaac Newton asked a daring question: the apple always falls straight down toward the center of the Earth -- so does that same downward pull reach higher, and higher still, until it stretches off the Earth entirely? His great leap was to claim one single force explains a falling apple AND something else entirely. What did Newton say that same force was also doing?
answer: Holding the Moon in its orbit around the Earth
choices: Holding the Moon in its orbit around the Earth
Making the ocean tides rise twice each day
Streaming a comet's bright tail out behind it
Turning the whole sky of stars once a night
context: Newton's unification: the same gravity that pulls an apple down also holds the Moon around the Earth and the planets around the Sun -- one law for heaven and Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org, universal gravitation; Conduitt account via thonyc.wordpress.com.

question: Fire a cannon and it lurches violently backward the instant the ball flies out the front. In his masterwork the Principia, Isaac Newton wrote down three laws of motion, and one of them is the rule behind that backward lurch. Which of these is the law Newton actually wrote down?
answer: To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction
choices: To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction
A moving body keeps moving until some force stops it
The push on a body equals its mass times its speeding-up
Every body pulls every other body with the force of gravity
context: Newton's third law: 'To every action there is always opposed an equal reaction... directed to contrary parts.' (The other choices paraphrase his first and second laws and his law of gravity -- all real, but not the one behind recoil.) Source: en.wikipedia.org, Newton's laws of motion.

question: In 1684 the astronomer Edmond Halley visited Isaac Newton with a puzzle that had stumped London's finest minds: what shape would a planet's path be if the Sun pulled it with a force that weakens with distance? Newton answered at once that it would be an ellipse. Astonished, Halley asked how he could possibly know. What did Newton reply?
answer: That he had already calculated it years before
choices: That he had already calculated it years before
That he had read the answer in Kepler's books
That he had simply guessed the likeliest shape
That he would need many more years to find out
context: Per Abraham De Moivre's memorandum, Newton said 'I have calculated it' -- then couldn't find the paper and had to work it out again. Source: newtonproject.ox.ac.uk (De Moivre); pbs.org NOVA on the Principia.

question: Isaac Newton's law of universal gravitation says the pull between two objects depends on how far apart they are -- but not in the simple way you might guess. Imagine you move twice as far from the Earth's center. You might expect gravity's pull to drop to one-half. According to Newton's inverse-square law, what does the pull actually drop to?
answer: One-quarter of what it was
choices: One-quarter of what it was
One-half of what it was
Exactly the same as before
Twice as strong as before
context: Gravity follows an inverse-square law: double the distance and the force falls to a quarter, because it depends on the square of the distance. Source: en.wikipedia.org, Newton's law of universal gravitation.

question: After his prism split sunlight into colours, Isaac Newton ran a test he called his 'crucial experiment.' He took just one colour from the spread-out band and sent it alone through a SECOND prism -- and it came out exactly the same colour, never changing. Newton said this single result proved a surprising truth about white light. What did he conclude?
answer: The colours were already hidden inside the white light
choices: The colours were already hidden inside the white light
The prism itself was painting fresh colours onto the light
Glass slowly stains any light that passes through it
White light has no real colours, only tricks of the eye
context: Because a single colour passed unchanged through a second prism, Newton argued the prism does not create colours -- they are already present in white light, and the prism only separates them. Source: testbook.com Newton's prism experiment; livescience.com.

question: By 1687 Isaac Newton had finished the Principia, but the Royal Society told him it had no money left to print it. Newton's friend Edmond Halley believed in the book so much that he paid the whole printing bill out of his own pocket. Later, when the Society owed Halley part of his salary and still had no cash, it paid him in a very strange currency instead. What did the broke Society hand him?
answer: Leftover copies of its costly picture-book about fishes
choices: Leftover copies of its costly picture-book about fishes
A gold medal struck specially in his honour
A lifetime seat on the Society's ruling council
A share of every future copy of the Principia sold
context: The Society had blown its whole book budget on 'De Historia Piscium' (History of Fishes), a lavish flop, leaving nothing to print the Principia -- so Halley funded it, and was later 'paid' part of his salary in unsold fish books. Source: royalsociety.org 'the fishy blunder'; en.wikipedia.org, De Historia piscium.

question: Isaac Newton and the German thinker Gottfried Leibniz both claimed to have invented calculus first, and the feud turned bitter. The Royal Society set up a committee to judge who deserved the credit, and in 1713 it ruled firmly in Newton's favour. Decades later, historians uncovered why the verdict was so one-sided. What had Newton, the Society's own president, secretly done?
answer: He had secretly written much of the committee's report himself
choices: He had secretly written much of the committee's report himself
He had quietly paid each committee member to back him
He had hidden Leibniz's earliest letters from the committee
He had forged a diary to make his discovery look older
context: The 'Commercium Epistolicum' committee was packed with Newton's allies, and Newton himself secretly wrote much of the supposedly impartial report -- and even an anonymous review praising it. (Calculus itself belongs to the math story.) Source: maths.tcd.ie Commercium account; sites.math.rutgers.edu.

question: Long before Isaac Newton, the astronomer Johannes Kepler had discovered three separate rules describing how the planets move -- including that each planet sweeps out an ellipse around the Sun. They seemed like three unrelated facts of nature. In the Principia, Newton showed something deeper about Kepler's three rules. What did he prove?
answer: They all follow automatically from his one law of gravity
choices: They all follow automatically from his one law of gravity
They were wrong and had to be completely replaced
They applied only to Earth, not the other planets
They were three different forces, not one
context: Newton proved Kepler's laws are not separate rules but consequences of the single inverse-square law of gravity -- the planets obey Kepler because they obey Newton. Source: en.wikipedia.org, universal gravitation; britannica.com, Principia.

question: One of the most beloved sayings credited to Isaac Newton has him comparing himself to a child: 'I seem to have been only like a boy playing on the seashore... finding a smoother pebble or a prettier shell, whilst the great ocean of truth lay all undiscovered before me.' Schoolbooks quote it everywhere. What do careful scholars say about this lovely line?
answer: It is found nowhere in any of Newton's own writings
choices: It is found nowhere in any of Newton's own writings
A Victorian schoolbook editor first put the words in his mouth
It was actually a saying of the older scientist Robert Boyle
It first turns up in a biography written long after he died
context: LEGEND: the 'pebbles and shells on the seashore' humility quote is traditionally attributed to Newton but appears nowhere in his own writings -- it is fond tradition, not a documented saying. (The other choices are plausible-sounding stories, but the sourced truth is simply that it is absent from everything he wrote.) Source: todayinsci.com on Newton 'playing on the seashore.'

question: Islamic sacred art avoided pictures of people and animals, so artists poured their genius into pattern and design instead. Because Muslims treated the Quran as God's own speech, demanding the most beautiful possible form, one art form rose above all others as the most respected in the Islamic world. Which one was it?
answer: Beautiful writing, called calligraphy
choices: Beautiful writing, called calligraphy
Woven wool carpets
Glazed pottery bowls
Carved wooden doors
context: With figures off-limits in sacred art, Muslim artists pushed three crafts to dazzling heights: geometric patterns, flowing plant designs called arabesques, and calligraphy. Because the Quran was treated as the literal word of God, writing itself became the most honored art form of all. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_ornament + https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aniconism_in_Islam

question: The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, finished around 691 CE, is the oldest surviving work of Islamic architecture in the world: an eight-sided building crowned by a golden dome. What single object sits at its very center, the thing the whole golden building was raised to shelter?
answer: A bare rock
choices: A bare rock
A golden coffin
A carved throne
A stone tablet
context: The Dome of the Rock was built under the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik (691-692 CE), about 60 meters wide with a golden dome roughly 20 meters across, raised to shelter one bare stone. Three faiths hold that rock sacred: Muslims tie it to Muhammad's Night Journey, while Jewish and Christian tradition link it to Abraham's near-sacrifice and the ancient Temple. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dome_of_the_Rock

question: At the Alhambra palace in Granada, the poet Ibn Zamrak did something startling: he carved verses into the walls written in the room's OWN voice, so the building speaks to you in the first person. In the Hall of the Two Sisters, what does the room itself announce?
answer: "I am a garden adorned by beauty."
choices: "I am a garden adorned by beauty."
"I am the gate to paradise."
"I am the throne of kings."
"I am stronger than stone."
context: Ibn Zamrak (1333-1393) made the Alhambra's walls literally speak. On the lions' fountain he wrote of the water and marble that 'you cannot tell which of them is flowing,' and in the Hall of the Two Sisters the room declares itself a garden. Source: https://www.alhambradegranada.org/en/info/epigraphicpoems.asp

question: Look up in the Hall of the Two Sisters at the Alhambra and the ceiling becomes a glittering sky: more than 5,000 tiny niche-like cells cascade down from a central star into sixteen miniature domes. What is the name for this honeycomb, 'stalactite'-style plaster vaulting prized across the Islamic world?
answer: Muqarnas
choices: Muqarnas
Arabesque
Minaret
Mihrab
context: Muqarnas was invented around the 10th century in northeastern Iran or North Africa to solve a real engineering puzzle: how to fit a round dome on top of a square room. Stacks of small prism-like cells bridge the corners and hide the join, turning a structural problem into pure decoration. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muqarnas

question: In the 1890s mathematicians finally proved that there are only a fixed number of different ways a flat pattern can repeat across a wall, and not one more is possible. Then they studied the hand-cut tilework of the Alhambra, built centuries earlier by Nasrid artisans with nothing but compass and ruler, and got a shock: the craftsmen had already used EVERY one of them. How many of these possible repeating patterns does the Alhambra contain?
answer: 17 of them
choices: 17 of them
9 of them
24 of them
40 of them
context: Mathematicians call them the 17 'wallpaper groups' (plane crystallographic groups) and proved in the 1890s that exactly 17 exist. The Nasrid artisans hit all 17 by eye, centuries earlier, using only compass, ruler, and medieval set-squares called cartabones. Source: https://euromathsoc.org/magazine/articles/246

question: The Dome of the Rock was built by the caliph Abd al-Malik, who dated his inscription to the year 72 in the Islamic calendar. More than a hundred years later the caliph al-Ma'mun tried to steal the credit: he scraped out Abd al-Malik's name and carved in his own, but left one detail untouched that exposes the whole lie. What detail betrays his forgery to anyone who reads the inscription?
answer: A date a century too early
choices: A date a century too early
A misspelling of his name
A crack down the gold dome
A verse quoted wrong
context: The Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun (early 800s) swapped in his own name but forgot to change the date, which still reads 'year 72' (692 CE), more than a century before his reign. That same inscription band, about 240 meters of Kufic script, carries some of the oldest surviving verses of the Quran anywhere. Source: https://www.islamic-awareness.org/history/islam/inscriptions/dotr

question: In Islamic sacred art, artists avoided drawing people and animals out of fear of idol-worship. So instead of painting pictures, they poured their highest devotion into one surprising thing, treating its making and even its viewing as a form of worship. What became the supreme Islamic art form?
answer: Beautiful Arabic calligraphy of the Quran's verses
choices: Beautiful Arabic calligraphy of the Quran's verses
Lifelike portraits of the prophets and caliphs
Stained-glass windows showing scenes from heaven
Carved marble statues of angels and guardians
context: With figural images off-limits in sacred settings (aniconism), writing itself became the highest art. Arabic calligraphy of Quranic verses is ranked above all other Islamic arts, and crafting or contemplating it counts as worship and meditation. Source: metmuseum.org/essays/geometric-patterns-in-islamic-art; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_calligraphy

question: On the wall of the Darb-i Imam shrine in Isfahan, Iran, finished in 1453, medieval tile-makers laid out a geometric pattern using their five girih tile shapes — and the pattern never exactly repeats itself. Centuries later, scientists were stunned to find these craftsmen had already built what Western mathematicians (Roger Penrose) only worked out around 500 years afterward. What had the Isfahan artisans created so far ahead of the West?
answer: A non-repeating 'quasicrystal' tiling
choices: A non-repeating 'quasicrystal' tiling
A perfectly symmetrical mirror grid
A spiral that shrinks toward its center
A repeating checkerboard of square tiles
context: In 2007 Harvard physics student Peter Lu recognized the Isfahan tiling as a near-perfect 'quasicrystal' — a pattern that fills space forever without ever repeating. He was so gripped he said he couldn't sleep for days and skipped Christmas break to study it. The craftsmen had anticipated Penrose's quasicrystal geometry by roughly five centuries. Source: sciencenews.org/article/ancient-islamic-penrose-tiles-0 (Lu & Steinhardt 2007)

question: Around the year 820, the Persian scholar al-Khwarizmi sat in Baghdad and wrote a mathematics book whose Arabic title used the word 'al-jabr' — the move of carrying a subtracted term across to the other side of an equation. A whole branch of mathematics still carries that word as its name. Which branch?
answer: Algebra
choices: Algebra
Geometry
Arithmetic
Calculus
context: ALGEBRA comes straight from al-Khwarizmi's word 'al-jabr' (restoration — moving terms across an equation), paired with 'al-muqabala' (balancing — cancelling like terms). His book was the first to teach solving equations as its own subject. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Khwarizmi.

question: The physician Avicenna (Ibn Sina), born around 980, was such a prodigy that by the age of just ten he had already learned one whole enormous book perfectly by heart. Which book had the ten-year-old memorized?
answer: The entire Quran
choices: The entire Quran
Aristotle's works
Euclid's Elements
Homer's Iliad
context: Avicenna had memorized the whole Quran by age 10 and was practicing as a physician by about 16–17. As a teenager he cured the Samanid ruler Nuh ibn Mansur when the royal doctors couldn't, and his reward was the run of the prince's magnificent library. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avicenna.

question: In 9th-century Baghdad the Abbasid Caliph al-Ma'mun ran a great library and translation center called the House of Wisdom, hungry for the lost knowledge of the Greeks. By tradition, he rewarded scholars who translated a Greek manuscript with a famously lavish payment. According to that tradition, how was a translator paid?
answer: The book's weight in gold
choices: The book's weight in gold
A house in the city
A seat on his council
Freedom from all taxes
context: Tradition says al-Ma'mun (ruled 813–833) paid the weight of each translated book in gold, and even sent envoys to the Byzantine Empire to buy Greek manuscripts. The gold-by-weight detail is widely repeated but not found in primary records — a legend. Source: middleeasteye.net/discover/iraq-baghdad-house-wisdom-uniting-east-west.

question: When al-Khwarizmi's mathematics reached Latin Europe, scribes turned his name into a brand-new word — the everyday term for a step-by-step recipe of exact steps that always reaches the right answer, the kind a machine can follow without thinking. Which word grew out of his name?
answer: Algorithm
choices: Algorithm
Logarithm
Diagram
Theorem
context: ALGORITHM is literally named after al-Khwarizmi: his Latinized name 'Algoritmi'/'Algorismi' became the word for a step-by-step procedure, and a modern computer algorithm is named for a 9th-century Baghdad mathematician. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Khwarizmi.

question: Most medical textbooks are replaced within a generation as knowledge moves on. Yet Avicenna's five-volume Canon of Medicine, finished around 1025, stayed the standard textbook in both the Islamic world and the universities of Christian Europe far longer than that. For roughly how long did the Canon remain the doctor's bible?
answer: About 600 years
choices: About 600 years
About 300 years
About 900 years
About 1,200 years
context: The Canon of Medicine (al-Qanun fi al-Tibb, c.1025) was THE standard medical textbook in European universities until roughly 1650 — about 600 years as the doctor's bible across both the Islamic world and Christian Europe. It even argued, centuries before microscopes, that some diseases spread by tiny tainted particles, recommending a 40-day isolation — an early quarantine. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avicenna.

question: Studying how light travels, Ibn al-Haytham let a single pinpoint of light through a small hole into a sealed, pitch-dark room, and watched a full upside-down picture of the street outside glow on the opposite wall. He named this 'the dark room' in Arabic — and scholars later carried its name into Latin. What is that Latin name?
answer: Camera obscura
choices: Camera obscura
Lucerna magica
Speculum solis
Vitrum opticum
context: Ibn al-Haytham (c.965–c.1040, known in Europe as Alhazen) called the darkened room 'Albait Almuzlim,' Latinized as CAMERA OBSCURA — the ancestor of the photographic camera. Through the pinhole he even watched an eclipsed sun appear as 'the form of a moonsickle.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_al-Haytham.

question: Ibn al-Haytham had boasted to Egypt's dangerous Caliph al-Hakim that he could build a dam to tame the Nile's yearly floods — then discovered the job was impossible, and that failing the Caliph meant death. To stay alive for years until the Caliph finally died, what did Ibn al-Haytham do?
answer: He feigned complete madness
choices: He feigned complete madness
He fled in secret disguise
He bribed the palace guards
He hid inside the great library
context: To escape execution Ibn al-Haytham feigned madness, and spent the house-arrest years writing his seven-volume Book of Optics (Kitab al-Manazir, 1011–1021) in Cairo. His creed: the seeker after truth 'suspects his faith' in the ancients and questions what he reads. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_al-Haytham.

question: Ibn al-Haytham used careful experiments to settle one of the oldest questions about sight — how seeing actually works. In doing so he overturned a belief the great Greek thinkers Euclid and Ptolemy had taught for centuries: a now-famous mistake about what the eyes do. What had the Greeks believed about sight?
answer: The eyes shoot out beams
choices: The eyes shoot out beams
The brain blends all colors
The eye makes its own light
Sight needs total darkness
context: Euclid and Ptolemy taught that rays shoot OUT of the eyes like beams. Ibn al-Haytham proved the reverse with experiments rather than argument — light reflects off objects into the eye — which is why he is often called the 'first true scientist' and a father of the scientific method. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_al-Haytham.

question: The Golden Age came to a brutal end in 1258, when Hulagu Khan's Mongol army stormed Baghdad, killed tens of thousands of people, and wrecked the House of Wisdom. Survivors said so many books were hurled into the River Tigris that the water itself changed color for days. What color did the Tigris run, according to that account?
answer: Black, from the ink
choices: Black, from the ink
Red, from the blood
Gold, from the covers
Green, from the bindings
context: By survivors' accounts the Tigris ran BLACK with the ink of countless drowned books — some said the volumes piled up enough to bridge the river. The sack and the destruction of the House of Wisdom are historical fact; the river-ran-black detail is a survivors' tradition (legend). Source: historyofinformation.com/detail.php?entryid=294; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Wisdom.

question: Around the year 820 in Baghdad, scholars under the Abbasid caliphs gathered in one famous place to translate Greek, Persian, and Sanskrit science into Arabic — part library, part study hall, part observatory. It was the engine room of the whole Golden Age. What was this center called?
answer: The House of Wisdom
choices: The House of Wisdom
The Hall of Mirrors
The Tower of Scholars
The Court of Stars
context: The House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikma) in Baghdad was a library, study center, and observatory rolled into one, where al-Khwarizmi himself worked under Caliph al-Ma'mun. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Wisdom

question: The astrolabe was a flat brass disc fitted with a movable openwork map of the heavens — a whole model of the sky you could hold in one hand. Spin it to match the night, and it told you the time and your location. Its name is Greek, and it means what?
answer: Star-taker
choices: Star-taker
Sky-wheel
Sun-reader
Night-glass
context: From Greek astron (star) + lambanein (to take). The astrolabe has been called a 'mathematical jewel.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astrolabe

question: The word 'algebra' comes from the Arabic 'al-jabr' in the title of al-Khwarizmi's book around the year 820. But before it ever meant math, 'al-jabr' was a medical word — a man who did this work was called an 'algebrista.' What did 'al-jabr' originally mean?
answer: Setting broken bones
choices: Setting broken bones
Mixing healing potions
Reading the stars
Weighing gold coins
context: 'Al-jabr' meant the restoration or reuniting of broken parts — it was the word for bone-setting. Al-Khwarizmi borrowed it because his method 'restores' an equation by moving terms to make it whole again. Source: https://www.wnycstudios.org/podcasts/science-diction/articles/algebra-from-broken-bones-to-twitter-feuds

question: When al-Khwarizmi's work spread west, Europeans took the Arabic word 'sifr' along with the round symbol that holds an open place in a number — so that 105 isn't mistaken for 15. That one Arabic word gave English both 'cipher' and 'zero.' What did 'sifr' actually mean?
answer: Empty
choices: Empty
Round
Hidden
Endless
context: 'Sifr' (empty) became Latin 'cifra,' then split into both 'cipher' (a secret code) and 'zero.' Al-Khwarizmi's book popularized this Hindu place-holder idea. Source: https://www.todayifoundout.com/index.php/2015/09/the-story-of-zero/
