question: Al-Khwarizmi also wrote a book on the Hindu-Arabic numerals, which reached Europe in a Latin translation. The Latin title turned his name into the word that now means any step-by-step calculation procedure. Which everyday word is literally al-Khwarizmi's own name?
answer: Algorithm
choices: Algorithm
Equation
Decimal
Calculus
context: The Latin translation was titled 'Algoritmi de numero Indorum' — 'Algoritmi' is just the Latinized form of al-Khwarizmi, and the word stuck. Source: https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Al-Khwarizmi/

question: Ibn al-Haytham noticed that light passing through a tiny pinhole into a sealed, lightless chamber throws an upside-down picture of the whole outside world onto the far wall. He named his chamber 'al-bayt al-muzlim.' Translated into Latin, that name became the direct ancestor of the photographic camera. What does the name mean?
answer: The dark room
choices: The dark room
The seeing box
The hidden eye
The light trap
context: 'Al-bayt al-muzlim' (the dark room) became Latin 'camera obscura' — the ancestor of the camera. Ibn al-Haytham gave the first clear scientific description of how it works. Source: https://www.ibnalhaytham.com/discover/who-was-ibn-al-haytham/

question: Around the year 1020 Ibn al-Haytham overturned a theory of eyesight that the ancient Greeks Euclid and Ptolemy had taught for centuries. His careful experiments proved their explanation of how human sight works was flat wrong. What had those ancient Greeks believed the eye did when it looked at something?
answer: Shot out rays to feel distant objects
choices: Shot out rays to feel distant objects
Soaked up light reflected off objects
Caught thin films shed by objects
Stirred the air between itself and objects
context: Euclid and Ptolemy held that the eye sends out rays to 'feel' the world. Ibn al-Haytham proved the opposite — we see because light bounces OFF objects and travels INTO the eye. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_al-Haytham

question: In the Islamic world the astrolabe was a holy instrument as much as a scientific one: from the Sun's position it could fix the five daily prayer times, and it pointed a worshipper toward one exact spot on Earth to face while praying. Which direction was the astrolabe used to find?
answer: The direction of Mecca
choices: The direction of Mecca
The direction of sunrise
The direction of the North Star
The direction of the nearest river
context: That direction is called the qibla. The 10th-century astronomer al-Sufi wrote a text of 386 chapters describing more than 1,000 uses for the astrolabe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astrolabe

question: Mariam al-Astrulabi, working in 10th-century Aleppo for the ruler Sayf al-Dawla, was one of history's first famous female engineers — she designed astrolabes so intricate they astonished her contemporaries. A thousand years later, in 1990, astronomers honored her with a very fitting kind of monument. What did they name after her?
answer: An asteroid
choices: An asteroid
A university
A bridge
A festival
context: The main-belt asteroid 7060 Al-'Ijliya, discovered in 1990, is named for Mariam al-Astrulabi (al-'Ijliyya) — a fitting tribute to a maker of star-finding instruments. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-%CA%BBIjliyyah

question: Ibn al-Haytham argued that a real scientist must test claims by experiment instead of simply trusting the great writers of the past. In one famous line he wrote that the true seeker after knowledge must take a startlingly combative attitude toward the books he studies. According to that line, what must the truth-seeker make himself?
answer: The enemy of all that he reads
choices: The enemy of all that he reads
The servant of all that he reads
The mirror of all that he reads
The heir of all that he reads
context: Ibn al-Haytham wrote that a truth-seeker 'must make himself the enemy of all that he reads' — questioning every authority. His Book of Optics drew conclusions from controlled experiments centuries before the term 'scientific method' existed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_al-Haytham

question: Ibn al-Haytham was summoned to Egypt by Caliph al-Hakim with a grand promise: to build a dam that would tame the Nile's yearly flooding. Standing at the riverbank he realized the river was far too vast and the plan was hopeless — and he feared the caliph would have him executed for failing. According to the famous story, how did he escape that fate?
answer: He faked being insane
choices: He faked being insane
He fled across the desert
He bribed the caliph's guards
He swore a binding oath of secrecy
context: Legend holds that madness was legally protected, so Ibn al-Haytham pretended to lose his mind and was kept under house arrest for about ten years — and used that confinement to write his Book of Optics. Source: https://www.ibnalhaytham.com/discover/who-was-ibn-al-haytham/

question: In February 1258 the Mongol army under Hulagu Khan stormed Baghdad and destroyed the House of Wisdom, ending the Golden Age in blood. So many books were hurled from its shelves into the river Tigris that chroniclers described a horrifying sight in the water itself. According to those chroniclers, what happened to the river?
answer: It ran black with ink
choices: It ran black with ink
It rose over its banks
It caught fire from end to end
It froze solid overnight
context: Chroniclers said so many books were thrown into the Tigris that the water ran black with the ink washing off them — a vivid image of the loss. (A later 'bridge of books' claim, historians note, was an exaggeration of Mongol barbarity, not documented fact.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Wisdom  (Legend.)

question: In the Pacific war, instead of invading every Japanese-held island one by one, American commanders skipped the heavily fortified ones, grabbed weakly-defended islands nearby, and used the captured airfields to choke off the strongholds they had passed. What word did they use for what would happen to the cut-off Japanese garrisons, left bombed and starving but never stormed?
answer: They would wither on the vine
choices: They would wither on the vine
They would melt into the sea
They would burn to the ground
They would sink without a trace
context: The leapfrogging strategy bypassed fortified islands and let their garrisons 'wither on the vine' — useless to Japan's war effort, cut off from supply and reinforcement. Source: nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/pacific-strategy-1941-1944 ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leapfrogging_(strategy)

question: American Pacific commanders summed up their whole island-skipping strategy with a line borrowed from baseball hitter Willie Keeler, who was famous for poking the ball into the gaps the fielders left open. What was the saying they used to mean 'strike the weak spots, skip the strong ones'?
answer: "Hit 'em where they ain't"
choices: "Hit 'em where they ain't"
"Keep your eye on the ball"
"Swing for the fences"
"Three strikes and you're out"
context: Willie Keeler's hitting motto became the commanders' shorthand for leapfrogging: the goal was speed and saving lives, not capturing every island for its own sake. Source: warhistory.org/article/island-hopping-and-leap-frogging-u-s-strategies-part-i ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leapfrogging_(strategy)

question: The American advance toward Japan came as two converging spears. General Douglas MacArthur pushed northwest along the New Guinea coast in the Southwest Pacific. Who drove the second spear straight across the Central Pacific, leaping through the Gilbert, Marshall, and Mariana Islands?
answer: Admiral Chester Nimitz
choices: Admiral Chester Nimitz
General George Patton
Admiral William Halsey
General Omar Bradley
context: MacArthur and Nimitz ran two parallel drives — MacArthur up through New Guinea, Nimitz across the Central Pacific island chains — both aimed at Japan. Source: nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/pacific-strategy-1941-1944 ; macarthurmemorial.org Island Hopping Primary Resources

question: Rabaul was Japan's mightiest base in the South Pacific, ringed by guns and packed with about 100,000 soldiers and workers. Rather than storm it, the Allies surrounded it with captured airbases and bombed it into uselessness. So how did the Allies finally take Rabaul, in September 1945?
answer: They walked in to accept its surrender
choices: They walked in to accept its surrender
They stormed the beaches at dawn
They burned it with carrier fire-raids
They blew its harbor with submarines
context: Rabaul was never invaded. Its roughly 69,000 soldiers and 20,000 civilian workers were cut off from late 1943 to war's end, and the Allies simply accepted the surrender in September 1945. Source: history.com/topics/world-war-ii/battle-of-new-britain-rabaul ; historytools.org/stories/the-neutralisation-of-rabaul-a-turning-point-in-the-pacific-war

question: In November 1943, before bypassing became the rule, U.S. Marines assaulted the fortified speck of Betio in the Battle of Tarawa head-on. In just 76 hours they took over 3,000 casualties — a toll rivaling the six-month Guadalcanal campaign. What lesson did later commanders draw from that bloody day?
answer: Bypass the strongholds instead of charging them
choices: Bypass the strongholds instead of charging them
Land only after a week of bombing
Attack at night to hide the landing
Never assault an island without tanks
context: Tarawa cost 1,027 Marines killed and 2,292 wounded in 76 hours on tiny Betio. The slaughter is exactly why later commanders leapfrogged fortified islands rather than assaulting them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tarawa ; history.com/articles/battle-of-tarawa

question: Japanese commanders called Truk Lagoon the 'Gibraltar of the Pacific' — their main forward fleet base. In Operation Hailstone (February 17–18, 1944), American carrier planes sank about 45 ships there, over 220,000 tons in two days, the war's record. Having wrecked it from the air, what did the Allies then do about Truk?
answer: Sailed past it and left it to starve
choices: Sailed past it and left it to starve
Landed Marines to seize the lagoon
Towed away its damaged warships
Garrisoned it as a new airbase
context: Task Force 58 destroyed about 45 ships and 250–275 aircraft at Truk, then the fleet simply bypassed it. Its roughly 28,000-man garrison was left cut off until surrender. Source: the-past.com/feature/operation-hailstone-17-18-february-1944-the-task-force-58-raid-on-the-japanese-fortress-of-truk/

question: Nimitz's Central Pacific drive aimed at the Mariana Islands for one specific reason, not just because they lay in the path toward Japan. What made the Marianas the prize that gave the whole leapfrog a destination?
answer: They put the new B-29 bombers in range of Japan
choices: They put the new B-29 bombers in range of Japan
They held Japan's largest oil refineries
They guarded the only route to the Philippines
They sheltered the deepest fleet anchorage
context: The Marianas were close enough to bring the new B-29 Superfortress bombers within range of the Japanese home islands — the leapfrog had a target, not just a direction. Source: nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/pacific-strategy-1941-1944

question: The 'wither on the vine' plan did not always work as drawn up. At some bypassed bases the trapped Japanese troops stayed surprisingly well-organized and well-fed, surviving far better than the Allies expected. How did those cut-off garrisons feed themselves?
answer: They grew gardens from submarine-delivered seeds
choices: They grew gardens from submarine-delivered seeds
They raided Allied supply ships at night
They fished the lagoons with stolen nets
They bartered gold for rice from traders
context: Some bypassed garrisons planted gardens from seeds shipped in by submarine and worked with local labor, surviving better than expected. The strategy still worked: the men were useless to Japan's war effort even when they lived. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leapfrogging_(strategy)

question: Giuseppe Garibaldi led a band of about a thousand volunteers to conquer Sicily in 1860. His fighters all wore the same eye-catching piece of clothing, which became their nickname. What were they called?
answer: the Redshirts
choices: the Redshirts
the Ironsides
the Blackcaps
the Greycloaks
context: Garibaldi's volunteers were the Redshirts (Camicie Rosse). The red shirts traced back to his years in South America — reportedly from a Montevideo factory that had meant to export them to the slaughterhouses of Argentina. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Garibaldi

question: Giuseppe Garibaldi had fought as a soldier on two different continents — in the wars of South America and then in Europe. Italians gave him a grand nickname celebrating this. What was he called?
answer: the Hero of the Two Worlds
choices: the Hero of the Two Worlds
the Lion of the North
the Sword of Italy
the Father of the People
context: Garibaldi was nicknamed 'the Hero of the Two Worlds' for fighting in both South America and Europe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Garibaldi

question: In May 1860 Giuseppe Garibaldi's roughly one thousand volunteers needed ships to cross to Sicily, but they had none. His lieutenant Nino Bixio solved the problem the night they sailed from near Genoa. How did the expedition get its two steamships, Il Piemonte and Il Lombardo?
answer: Bixio seized them from a private shipping company
choices: Bixio seized them from a private shipping company
the king of Piedmont lent them from his navy
British merchants donated them to the cause
the volunteers bought them with pooled savings
context: Nino Bixio seized the two steamships Il Piemonte and Il Lombardo from the Rubattino shipping company to carry the roughly 1,089 volunteers. They slipped away by night on 5 May 1860 from the rocky beach of Quarto, near Genoa. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_of_the_Thousand

question: On 15 May 1860 Giuseppe Garibaldi's Redshirts charged uphill at Calatafimi against entrenched Bourbon troops dug in on a hill. As the attack faltered, Garibaldi is remembered for turning to Nino Bixio and saying which words?
answer: 'Here we make Italy, or we die'
choices: 'Here we make Italy, or we die'
'God will know His own'
'Not one step backward'
'Victory or the grave'
context: By tradition (legend), at Calatafimi, attacking uphill against entrenched Bourbon troops on the Pianto dei Romani hill, Garibaldi told Nino Bixio: 'Qui si fa l'Italia o si muore' — 'Here we make Italy, or we die.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Calatafimi

question: By October 1860 Giuseppe Garibaldi had conquered Sicily and Naples with his volunteers — a whole kingdom won by his own sword. At the meeting at Teano on 26 October he met Victor Emmanuel II. What did the romantic hero do with everything he had conquered?
answer: he handed it all to the king and took no crown
choices: he handed it all to the king and took no crown
he had himself crowned king of the south
he split the conquered land among his officers
he demanded a great fortune as his reward
context: At Teano on 26 October 1860, Garibaldi greeted Victor Emmanuel II as 'King of Italy' and handed over his entire conquest. He then retired to the rocky island of Caprera, refusing any reward, title, or pay — the romantic hero who took no crown. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Garibaldi

question: Count Camillo di Cavour was the diplomat who engineered Italy's unification by careful maneuvering rather than the battlefield, and he became the new kingdom's first prime minister. Dying of malaria in June 1861 after only months in office, he is said to have murmured which last words?
answer: 'Italy is made. All is safe'
choices: 'Italy is made. All is safe'
'I have done my duty'
'Let the work go on without me'
'The peninsula is whole at last'
context: Cavour engineered unification by diplomacy — at the secret Plombières meeting (July 1858) he and Napoleon III agreed France would help Piedmont fight Austria in exchange for Nice and Savoy. He became united Italy's first prime minister but died of malaria on 6 June 1861 after about three months; on his deathbed he is said (legend) to have murmured 'Italy is made. All is safe.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camillo_Benso,_Count_of_Cavour

question: When the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in March 1861, its first king had ruled Piedmont-Sardinia as 'Victor Emmanuel II.' Rather than restyle himself the first King of Italy, he kept the number 'II.' What did historians say that telling choice hinted about the new kingdom?
answer: that Piedmont had taken over the peninsula rather than truly merging into it
choices: that Piedmont had taken over the peninsula rather than truly merging into it
that he wished to honor a beloved earlier king of the same name
that he meant to rule only as a temporary caretaker
that he expected a third Victor Emmanuel to complete the work
context: Victor Emmanuel II kept the 'II' from his Sardinian title instead of becoming Victor Emmanuel I of Italy — a choice that hinted Piedmont had taken over the peninsula rather than truly merging into it. He became the first king of a united Italy since the 6th century when the kingdom was proclaimed on 17 March 1861. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Emmanuel_II

question: Jacques-Louis David's painting 'The Death of Marat' (1793) shows the murdered French revolutionary Jean-Paul Marat slumped dead in his bathtub, one arm hanging limply over the tub's edge. David posed that drooping arm to copy a famous earlier image of a sacred body, so the slain politician would look like a holy martyr taken down from the cross. Whose famous sculpture of a dead body did David echo to make Marat look like a fallen Christ?
answer: Michelangelo's 'Pietà', the dead Christ across Mary's lap
choices: Michelangelo's 'Pietà', the dead Christ across Mary's lap
Leonardo da Vinci's 'Last Supper', painted on a wall
Donatello's 'David', a young bronze warrior boy
Botticelli's 'Birth of Venus', a goddess on a shell
context: David borrowed the limp, hanging arm from Michelangelo's 'Pietà' (and Caravaggio's 'Entombment of Christ'), turning a real political murder into a secular pietà — a martyr's image for the Revolution. He even idealized the body: the real Marat had a chronic skin disease that forced him to soak for hours, but David painted his skin smooth and unblemished. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Death_of_Marat

question: King Louis XVI's government hired the painter Jacques-Louis David to make 'Oath of the Horatii' (1784) — three Roman brothers raising their arms toward three swords, swearing to die for their country — as a grand picture about loyalty to the king and state. A few years later David himself sat in France's revolutionary assembly during the Terror. What did this same royal-commissioned painter then do to King Louis XVI?
answer: He voted to execute King Louis XVI
choices: He voted to execute King Louis XVI
He painted a flattering new portrait of the king
He fled France to go on painting for the king
He hid the king's family inside his Paris studio
context: David voted for the king's death in January 1793 and signed the death warrant. The same man who painted a royal loyalty-allegory became the Revolution's image-maker, then later switched again to serve Napoleon — spending three years on 'The Coronation of Napoleon' as First Painter to the Emperor. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Jacques-Louis-David-French-painter and https://www.biography.com/artist/jacques-louis-david

question: Jain monks hold ahimsa — harming no living thing — as 'the pure, unchangeable, eternal law,' and they carry the rule to a startling extreme. A strict Jain monk walking down a path does one small thing again and again, before nearly every step he takes. What is it?
answer: He gently sweeps the ground ahead with a soft broom so he won't crush an ant
choices: He gently sweeps the ground ahead with a soft broom so he won't crush an ant
He scatters a handful of grain to feed any hungry creatures
He rings a small bell to warn animals that a person is coming
He bows toward the rising sun and whispers a short prayer
context: Devout Jains carry ahimsa to its limit: monks sweep the path before each step with a soft broom so as not to crush an ant, wear a small cloth over the mouth (the muhpatti) to avoid inhaling an insect, and strain their drinking water to spare the tiniest lives in it. The strictest will not even swat a mosquito. Sources: https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/jainism/ ; https://www.thecollector.com/who-was-mahavira/

question: Mahavira, the 'Great Hero' revered by Jains, gave up his throne and renounced even his clothing, going naked through twelve and a half years as a wandering ascetic. Centuries later Jainism split in two over exactly this point. The 'sky-clad' Digambara monks went naked as Mahavira had; how did the rival Svetambara branch differ?
answer: Their monks and nuns wear simple white robes
choices: Their monks and nuns wear simple white robes
Their monks shave their heads but keep beards
Their monks live in temples rather than wandering
Their monks may marry and keep a household
context: The names say it: Digambara means 'sky-clad' (naked, as Mahavira lived) and Svetambara means 'white-clad.' The two branches divided largely over whether a monk must renounce clothing entirely. Mahavira, born Vardhamana around 599 BCE into a royal family, is counted as the 24th and last Tirthankara ('ford-maker'), a Jina or 'conqueror' over the self. Source: https://www.thecollector.com/who-was-mahavira/

question: In the year before the Constitutional Convention, James Madison crammed for it like a student. His friend Thomas Jefferson, living in Paris, shipped him two whole trunks of books on the history of failed republics and broken confederacies so Madison could study where past governments had gone wrong. When the books arrived, Madison wrote back to thank Jefferson for what?
answer: The literary cargo
choices: The literary cargo
The borrowed library
The Paris parcels
The scholar's bounty
context: Madison thanked Jefferson for the 'literary cargo' — two trunkfuls of books on ancient and modern confederacies that Jefferson bought for him in Europe. Madison's homework on why earlier republics collapsed became the backbone of his plan for the convention. Source: monticello.org/encyclopedia/james-madison; Madison-to-Jefferson letters, founders.archives.gov.

question: James Madison reached Philadelphia for the Constitutional Convention before most of the other delegates even showed up — and unlike them, he wasn't arriving empty-handed. He carried a fully drafted blueprint for a brand-new national government with three branches that would check each other. Edmund Randolph laid it before the convention on May 29, 1787, and it became the framework the entire Constitution was argued out from. What was this blueprint called?
answer: The Virginia Plan
choices: The Virginia Plan
The Randolph Charter
The Philadelphia Frame
The Federal Compact
context: Madison's draft was the Virginia Plan, proposing a strong central government split into three branches that would check and balance one another. Because the whole convention debated from it, Madison earned the nickname 'Father of the Constitution.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Plan; montpelier.org/learn/the-life-of-james-madison.

question: To convince people that a government had to be built to restrain its own officials, James Madison wrote one of the most quoted explanations in American politics. In Federalist No. 51 he argued that since rulers are not perfect beings, power has to be split so that each branch can hold the others back. Which line of his sums it up?
answer: 'If men were angels, no government would be necessary.'
choices: 'If men were angels, no government would be necessary.'
'Power yields nothing without a demand.'
'A government of laws, and not of men.'
'Liberty is the right to do as the law permits.'
context: Madison's line from Federalist No. 51 — paired with 'Ambition must be made to counteract ambition' — became his classic argument for checks and balances: because people aren't angels, government must be designed to check itself. Source: avalon.law.yale.edu/18th_century/fed51.asp; founders.archives.gov.

question: In 1763 the University of Glasgow gave the young instrument-maker James Watt a broken machine and asked him to repair it. Tinkering with this barely-working device is what set him on the path to his famous improvements. What had he been handed to fix?
answer: a small working model of an early steam engine
choices: a small working model of an early steam engine
a brass telescope with a cracked lens
a ship's compass that pointed the wrong way
a church clock that kept losing time
context: The model was of Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric engine. It ran so poorly that fixing it exposed to Watt how much heat the design wasted, pointing him toward his great improvement. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Watt.

question: A beloved legend says that as a boy, James Watt first dreamed up the steam engine while sitting by the fire and watching steam from a boiling kettle push something up and down again and again. According to the story, what was the steam making jump?
answer: the kettle's lid
choices: the kettle's lid
a spoon in a teacup
the iron poker
a candle flame
context: Watt's cousin Marion Campbell told this tale, and his son helped polish it, but it is almost certainly a charming myth. Watt himself said a Dr. John Robison first turned his attention to steam engines in 1759. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Watt; David Philip Miller, 'True Myths: James Watt's Kettle' (2004).  (Legend.)

question: James Watt needed a partner who could actually sell his engines, and he found one in Matthew Boulton, owner of the great Soho works near Birmingham. When the visitor James Boswell toured the factory in 1776, Boulton boasted that he sold there the one thing all the world wanted to buy. What was it?
answer: power
choices: power
gold
glory
weapons
context: Boulton's full line: 'I sell here, sir, what all the world desires to have - POWER.' He meant the work his steam engines could do for mines and mills. Source: britannica.com/biography/Matthew-Boulton; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Boulton.

question: In March 1776 the very first Boulton & Watt steam engine sold to a customer was set to work at the Bloomfield Colliery, a coal mine at Tipton. What did that first engine do for the mine?
answer: it pumped the water up out of the mine
choices: it pumped the water up out of the mine
it wound the coal cages up the shaft
it pumped fresh air down into the tunnels
it hauled loaded wagons along the surface
context: Deep mines filled with water, and pumping them dry by hand or horse was brutal, so the engine was built to drain the floodwater. A month later a second engine started at John Wilkinson's ironworks. Between 1775 and 1800 the partnership built roughly 450 to 500 engines. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watt_steam_engine; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boulton_and_Watt.

question: More than sixty years after James Watt died, scientists wanted to honor him by attaching his name to something every person on Earth now uses without thinking. In 1882 they gave his name to the standard unit of one particular thing. The name was his; what does it measure?
answer: power - the rate at which work is done
choices: power - the rate at which work is done
distance - how far apart two places are
temperature - how hot something is
weight - how heavy an object is
context: One watt equals one joule of work every second. C. William Siemens proposed the name in 1882, over sixty years after Watt's death in 1819. The bulbs and appliances rated in watts all carry his name. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watt.

question: The older Newcomen engine had a fatal flaw: every single stroke, it sprayed cold water inside the cylinder to make the piston drop, then had to reheat that whole cylinder for the next stroke - burning about three-quarters of its coal just doing that. James Watt's great fix let the cylinder do roughly twice the work on the same fuel. What was his idea?
answer: let the steam rush into a separate vessel to be condensed there, so the working cylinder never had to be chilled
choices: let the steam rush into a separate vessel to be condensed there, so the working cylinder never had to be chilled
add a second cylinder that took over the work while the first one cooled down
build a much hotter fire so the cylinder could be reheated twice as fast
line the inside of the cylinder with copper so it shed and regained heat faster
context: This is the 'separate condenser,' patented in 1769 - the single insight that made steam power efficient enough to remake the world. Watt also wrapped the cylinder in an outer 'steam jacket' to keep it hot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Watt; thenewatlantis.com/publications/the-most-useful-man-who-ever-lived.

question: James Watt remembered exactly when the answer came to him: strolling home through the heart of Glasgow on a Sunday in May 1765, the whole plan for his engine fell into place in his head before he had even finished the walk. Across what Glasgow place was he walking when the idea struck?
answer: Glasgow Green, the city's common
choices: Glasgow Green, the city's common
the deck of a Clyde river ferry
the floor of his own workshop
the nave of Glasgow Cathedral
context: By his own much-later account: 'I had not walked further than the Golf-house when the whole thing was arranged in my mind.' He recalled this about fifty years afterward, recorded by the Hart brothers, so it is vivid memory rather than a contemporaneous record. Source: thenewatlantis.com/publications/the-most-useful-man-who-ever-lived; Robert Hart, 1859.

question: James Watt had a salesman's problem: his customers already powered their mills with teams of living animals, and had no way to judge whether a clanking machine was a good deal. So Watt invented a brand-new unit of work, pegged to how much one such animal could haul in a minute, and priced his engines by how many of them they replaced. What did he call his unit?
answer: horsepower
choices: horsepower
the foot-pound
the kilowatt
the joule
context: Watt set one horsepower at 33,000 foot-pounds per minute - lifting 33,000 pounds one foot in one minute. He got the figure in 1782 from watching draft horses walk a mill wheel and rounded it to a clean number the next year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horsepower; britannica.com/science/horsepower.

question: James Watt's engine nearly failed for a clumsy reason: no workshop could carve a cylinder round enough, so steam leaked past the loose piston and the engine wheezed. The man who rescued it, John Wilkinson, normally made a very different iron product, and pointed that same precise machine at Watt's cylinders. What did Wilkinson's machine usually bore out?
answer: the barrels of cannon
choices: the barrels of cannon
the pipes for city wells
the links of anchor chain
the rims of carriage wheels
context: Wilkinson's cannon-boring machine (1774) bored Watt's cylinders so accurately that Boulton marveled a 50-inch cylinder 'does not err the thickness of an old shilling in any part.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watt_steam_engine; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wilkinson_(industrialist).

question: James Watt understood why reheating the cylinder wasted so much coal because his friend, the Glasgow professor Joseph Black, had discovered the hidden reason. Black showed that turning water into steam swallows up a huge, invisible amount of heat - heat that is dumped right back out the instant the steam condenses. What did Black name this hidden heat?
answer: latent heat
choices: latent heat
specific heat
radiant heat
sensible heat
context: Latent heat is exactly why condensing steam inside the cylinder threw away so much fuel - and why moving the condensing into a separate vessel saved it. Black's science underpinned Watt's engineering. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Watt.

question: A steam engine left to itself can run faster and faster until it tears itself apart. In 1788 James Watt fitted a device with two metal balls that spin on a spindle: as the engine speeds up, the balls fly outward, and their swing automatically pinches the steam valve to slow things down - one of the first machines that controlled itself. What is this self-regulating device called?
answer: the centrifugal governor
choices: the centrifugal governor
the connecting rod
the boiler gauge
the drive piston
context: Watt borrowed the idea from devices that regulated the speed of windmills. The spinning balls form an early feedback loop - the engine sensing and correcting its own speed. Source: britannica.com/biography/James-Watt; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Watt.

question: For all his genius with machines, James Watt was an anxious worrier who dreaded the haggling side of business. In a 1772 letter he confessed he would rather face one particular danger than settle an account or strike a bargain - which is exactly why he needed the steady, sales-minded Matthew Boulton beside him. What did Watt say he would rather face?
answer: a loaded cannon
choices: a loaded cannon
a winter at sea
an angry mob
a long illness
context: His words: he 'would rather face a loaded cannon than settle an account or make a bargain.' The perfectionist inventor and the confident salesman made an ideal pair - Watt built the engines, Boulton sold them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Watt (1772 letter to William Small).

question: In December 1606 three small ships sailed from London for Virginia, and the colonists they carried founded Jamestown the next spring. What were the three ships named?
answer: the Susan Constant, the Godspeed, and the Discovery
choices: the Susan Constant, the Godspeed, and the Discovery
the Mayflower, the Speedwell, and the Fortune
the Golden Hind, the Pelican, and the Squirrel
the Matthew, the Trinity, and the Christopher
context: The Susan Constant was the largest (about 71 aboard), the Godspeed mid-sized, and the Discovery a tiny pinnace of about 21. They were funded not by the king but by the Virginia Company of London, a for-profit business hoping to strike gold. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Constant

question: At Jamestown many of the colonists were 'gentlemen' who thought manual labor was beneath them and refused to work while others starved. To force them, Captain John Smith laid down one blunt rule. What was it?
answer: "He that will not work shall not eat."
choices: "He that will not work shall not eat."
"Idle hands invite the enemy in."
"A gentleman digs, or a gentleman dies."
"No man rests until the fort is raised."
context: Smith's full order was that the labor of thirty or forty honest men should not be spent to feed 150 idle loiterers. The line echoes the New Testament (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Source: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/John_Smith_(explorer)

question: During the terrible winter of 1609-1610 the trapped Jamestown colonists ate every animal they could find: snakes, rats, mice, cats, dogs, and horses. When even those ran out, what did the starving survivors boil and eat?
answer: their own leather boots and shoes
choices: their own leather boots and shoes
the bark stripped from pine trees
sawdust ground up into bread
candle wax melted in water
context: That winter is remembered as 'the Starving Time.' Of the roughly 240 to 500 colonists alive when winter began, only about 60 were left by spring. Source: https://encyclopediavirginia.org/entries/starving-time-the/

question: The famous girl the English called Pocahontas was actually named Amonute, with a private name of Matoaka. 'Pocahontas' was only a nickname her people used. What did that nickname mean?
answer: the playful or mischievous one
choices: the playful or mischievous one
the bright morning star at dawn
the laughing daughter of the river
the small and fearless feather
context: She was a daughter of Wahunsenaca, the paramount chief the English called Powhatan, who ruled a chiefdom of more than 30 tribes. Source: https://www.nps.gov/jame/learn/historyculture/pocahontas-her-life-and-legend.htm

question: For years Jamestown lost money and nearly died. Then in 1612 the colonist John Rolfe planted sweeter Spanish seeds and grew a strain he called 'Orinoco.' What crop finally made the colony profitable and saved it?
answer: tobacco
choices: tobacco
cotton
sugarcane
indigo
context: The first four barrels shipped to England in 1614, and within a few years tobacco was Virginia's cash crop. Demand was so high that colonists planted it in the streets of Jamestown. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Rolfe

question: By June 1610 the starving Jamestown survivors gave up completely, boarded their ships, and began sailing down the James River to abandon Virginia for good. A few miles downstream, what happened that saved the colony by days?
answer: they met an incoming relief fleet that turned them back
choices: they met an incoming relief fleet that turned them back
a sudden storm wrecked their boats on the shore
the Powhatan ambushed the boats from the riverbank
their leaking ships ran aground on a sandbar
context: The fleet carried the new governor, Lord De La Warr, who ordered the colonists back to Jamestown and refused to let them leave. The settlement survived almost by accident. Source: https://historicjamestowne.org/history/history-of-jamestown/the-starving-time/

question: The single year 1619 gave America two founding firsts at Jamestown. One of them met in the Jamestown church that July: a body of elected colonists gathered to make laws together. What was this gathering, the first of its kind in English America?
answer: the first elected representative assembly
choices: the first elected representative assembly
the first royal court of colonial justice
the first gathering of company shareholders
the first open town hall meeting
context: It was called the House of Burgesses, the first elected lawmaking body in English America and a direct ancestor of later American self-government. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/jamestown-colony-settlement-facts

question: Long before Jamestown, John Smith had already lived an adventure novel: fighting the Turks in Hungary he was wounded, captured, and sold as a slave. By his own account, before he turned 25 he won his freedom in dramatic fashion. How did he claim he escaped?
answer: he killed his master and fled on foot across Russia and Poland
choices: he killed his master and fled on foot across Russia and Poland
he was ransomed by an English merchant trading in Constantinople
he was freed by a Tartar princess who had fallen for him
he stowed away on a galley sailing for Venice and Italy
context: Smith's whole life read like fiction, which is part of why later historians question some of the dramatic stories he told about himself. Source: https://www.livescience.com/40898-captain-john-smith.html

question: August 1619 brought the second American founding fact to Jamestown: the ship White Lion arrived carrying '20 and odd' Angolans, the first enslaved Africans in English North America. How had the ship come to be carrying these people?
answer: English privateers had seized them from a Portuguese slave ship
choices: English privateers had seized them from a Portuguese slave ship
the Virginia Company had bought them directly in Angola
a Dutch trading post had sold them as indentured servants
they had been captured in a war between Powhatan tribes
context: These men and women had been taken from a Portuguese vessel by privateers and brought to Virginia. The same year that English America got its first elected assembly, it also got its first enslaved Africans. Source: https://blackpast.org/african-american-history/first-africans-in-the-jamestown-colony-1619/

question: In 2013 a Smithsonian forensic team led by Douglas Owsley examined the skull and shin bone of a 14-year-old English girl from the Starving Time, whom they nicknamed 'Jane.' Four hatchet chops to her forehead and fine cut marks on the bones gave the team the first hard proof of what at an early American colony?
answer: that the dead were eaten by starving colonists
choices: that the dead were eaten by starving colonists
that a settler was murdered by another colonist
that the Powhatan raided inside the Jamestown fort
that a deadly plague had swept through the colony
context: The forehead chops were tentative, then deeper blows struck the back of her head; knife marks on the jaw showed flesh being removed. It is the first hard physical evidence that desperate colonists ate the dead. Source: https://www.si.edu/stories/survival-cannibalism-historic-jamestown

question: In 1613 the English kidnapped Pocahontas and held her for ransom. While captive she was baptized a Christian and renamed 'Rebecca,' and in April 1614 she married an English colonist, beginning several years of calm known as 'the Peace of Pocahontas.' Whom did she marry?
answer: John Rolfe
choices: John Rolfe
John Smith
Christopher Newport
Lord De La Warr
context: John Rolfe was the planter whose 'Orinoco' tobacco had begun to save the colony. His marriage to Pocahontas linked the English and the Powhatan and bought a fragile peace. Source: https://historicjamestowne.org/history/pocahontas/john-rolfe/

question: The most famous Jamestown story has Pocahontas, about 10 years old, throwing herself over the captured John Smith to stop his execution. Historians now doubt there was ever a real near-execution at all. What do many think the ceremony actually was?
answer: an adoption ritual that 'killed' Smith and reborn him as a chief
choices: an adoption ritual that 'killed' Smith and reborn him as a chief
a staged feast meant to frighten Smith into serving Powhatan
a war dance that Smith wrongly took to be his own execution
a weapons trade that Smith later dressed up as a brush with death
context: In this view Smith was ceremonially 'killed' and 'reborn' as a weroance under Powhatan. Smith may have written the dramatic rescue version years later, only after Pocahontas was famous, to boost his own legend. At the time she was a child and Smith was 27; there was no romance. Source: https://www.nps.gov/jame/learn/historyculture/pocahontas-her-life-and-legend.htm

question: Taken to England in 1616 as 'Lady Rebecca,' Pocahontas met John Smith again, after years of being told he was dead. By Smith's own written account she reminded him that her father had called him 'father,' then made a sharp remark about the English. What did she say of his countrymen?
answer: that "your Countriemen will lie much"
choices: that "your Countriemen will lie much"
that "your God has not kept his word"
that "your king is no king of mine"
that "your ships bring only sorrow"
context: She told Smith, 'you shall call mee childe, and so I will bee for ever and ever your Countrieman.' Pocahontas never made it home: she fell ill as the return voyage began, was taken ashore at Gravesend, and died there in March 1617, around age 21. Source: https://encyclopediavirginia.org/primary-documents/john-smith-and-pocahontas-in-england-an-excerpt-from-the-generall-historie-of-virginia-new-england-and-the-summer-isles-by-john-smith-1624/

question: Jan van Eyck's 1434 Arnolfini Portrait shows a wealthy merchant and his wife standing in their room. On the back wall hangs a small round mirror that bulges outward, and van Eyck used it to reveal something the couple's bodies would otherwise hide from the viewer. What does the curved mirror show?
answer: The whole room seen from behind, including two figures who have just stepped into the doorway
choices: The whole room seen from behind, including two figures who have just stepped into the doorway
A second couple posing in an identical room next door
A burning candle multiplied into a ring of tiny flames
The street and rooftops of Bruges through an open window
context: The convex mirror reflects the entire room from the far side — you see the backs of the couple plus two extra people standing in the doorway facing them. One, dressed in red, may be van Eyck himself arriving as a visitor or witness. Source: nationalgallery.org.uk/paintings/jan-van-eyck-the-arnolfini-portrait ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnolfini_Portrait

question: Jan van Eyck's paintings glow as if lit from inside, and people once credited that magic to a secret: many writers, following the Italian Giorgio Vasari, claimed van Eyck flat-out invented oil paint. Historians now reject the invention story — oil was already in use. So what did van Eyck actually do to make his colors seem to shine from within the panel?
answer: He built the picture from many thin see-through layers of oil so light sinks in, bounces off the panel, and shines back out
choices: He built the picture from many thin see-through layers of oil so light sinks in, bounces off the panel, and shines back out
He mixed crushed gemstones into every color to make them sparkle
He coated the finished panel in a thick varnish of melted amber
He painted onto a sheet of polished silver that mirrored light through the paint
context: Van Eyck perfected — did not invent — the oil medium, tinkering with his recipes for life. He stacked translucent glazes over a careful underdrawing; light passes through the layers, reflects off the panel, and seems to light the picture from inside, something fast-drying egg tempera could never do. Vasari's invention claim in his 'Lives of the Artists' stuck around into the 1800s. Source: vaia.com/en-us/explanations/art-and-design/art-and-design-theory/jan-van-eyck/ ; theartstory.org/artist/van-eyck-jan/ ; news.artnet.com/art-world/art-bites-jan-van-eyck-oil-paint-2631103

question: In the spring of 1942 the U.S. Army gave Japanese-American families on the West Coast as little as 48 hours to leave their homes. Soldiers pinned numbered tags on them like baggage and herded them onto buses bound for fairgrounds and racetracks. How much of their belongings were the families allowed to bring?
answer: Only what they could carry in their own hands
choices: Only what they could carry in their own hands
One steamer trunk for each family
Whatever would fit inside a single car
Everything, shipped ahead of them by the Army
context: Families lost homes, farms, and businesses in a weekend. They were first held at hastily fenced 'assembly centers' -- some in horse stalls at racetracks -- before being shipped to ten remote camps. Source: National Archives, https://www.archives.gov/education/lessons/japanese-relocation

question: The day after the Pearl Harbor attack, Oakland grocer Tatsuro Masuda hung a huge banner across his store window. In March 1942 the photographer Dorothea Lange snapped it just as Masuda was forced to shut the store and report to the Gila River camp in Arizona. What four words did the banner say?
answer: "I AM AN AMERICAN"
choices: "I AM AN AMERICAN"
"GOD BLESS THIS COUNTRY"
"WE ARE LOYAL CITIZENS"
"CLOSED BY GOVERNMENT ORDER"
context: Lange's photograph of the shuttered Wanto Co. store became one of the most famous images of the incarceration -- a citizen declaring his loyalty on the very day his country imprisoned him for his ancestry. Source: Library of Congress, https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/2004665381/

question: While their own parents and siblings sat behind barbed wire in American camps, thousands of young Japanese-American men volunteered to fight for the United States and formed the 442nd Regimental Combat Team. For their motto they took a gambler's phrase meaning to bet everything on one roll to win big. What was that motto?
answer: "Go For Broke"
choices: "Go For Broke"
"Double or Nothing"
"All or Nothing"
"Win or Die"
context: For its size and length of service the 442nd became the most decorated unit in U.S. military history -- earned by men whose families remained imprisoned at home. Source: National WWII Museum, https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/442nd-regimental-combat-team

question: Fred Korematsu, a 23-year-old American citizen, refused to report to the camps -- he wanted to stay with his girlfriend. To dodge the roundup, he disguised himself before the FBI finally caught him in May 1942. What did Korematsu do to try to pass as someone else?
answer: He had minor plastic surgery and called himself 'Clyde Sarah'
choices: He had minor plastic surgery and called himself 'Clyde Sarah'
He slipped across the border and posed as a Canadian
He shaved his head and posed as a wandering monk
He forged papers naming him a Filipino merchant sailor
context: Under the alias Clyde Sarah, Korematsu claimed Spanish-Hawaiian descent. His arrest set up the most infamous Supreme Court case of the whole episode. Source: Korematsu Institute, https://korematsuinstitute.org/freds-story/

question: On February 19, 1942, President Franklin Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066, and the Army locked away about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry -- no charges, no trials. The single fact that most shocked later generations was the legal status of most of those prisoners. What was true of the majority of them?
answer: About two-thirds were American citizens
choices: About two-thirds were American citizens
Nearly all were citizens of Japan
About half had been born in Japan
Hardly any had any U.S. citizenship
context: Roughly two-thirds were U.S. citizens, most born on American soil, never charged with any crime. Not one Japanese American was ever found guilty of sabotage or espionage. Source: National Archives, https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/executive-order-9066

question: On April 21, 1945, near San Terenzo, Italy, Lieutenant Daniel Inouye of the 442nd was already shot through the stomach when a German rifle grenade nearly tore his right arm clean off -- with his own live grenade still clenched in that ruined hand. What did Inouye do next?
answer: He pried the grenade loose with his left hand and threw it into the German bunker
choices: He pried the grenade loose with his left hand and threw it into the German bunker
He smothered the grenade against the trench wall to shield his men
He ordered his squad back and lost consciousness in the mud
He rolled into a shell hole and signaled frantically for a medic
context: Inouye kept firing one-handed, telling his men only, 'Nobody called off the war!' He lost the arm and later served 50 years as a U.S. Senator from Hawaii. Source: National Park Service, https://www.nps.gov/articles/inouyeww2.htm

question: In December 1944 the Supreme Court ruled on Fred Korematsu's case and, by a 6-3 vote, sided with the government -- one of the only times in American history the Court allowed citizens to be imprisoned by race. What two-word justification did the majority give for upholding the camps?
answer: "Military necessity"
choices: "Military necessity"
"National emergency"
"Public safety"
"Wartime loyalty"
context: Korematsu v. United States (December 18, 1944) accepted the Army's claim of 'military necessity' at face value. The ruling has never been formally praised since, and the Court repudiated it only in 2018. Source: U.S. Courts, https://www.uscourts.gov/about-federal-courts/educational-resources/educational-activities/facts-and-case-summary-korematsu-v-us

question: In 1982 a federal Commission on Wartime Relocation finished its investigation into the camps -- and confirmed that not one Japanese American had ever been convicted of espionage or sabotage. Rather than military need, the Commission blamed three things for the whole disaster. What three causes did it name?
answer: Race prejudice, war hysteria, and a failure of political leadership
choices: Race prejudice, war hysteria, and a failure of political leadership
Naval weakness, coastal raids, and pressure from foreign allies
Supply shortages, faulty maps, and slow battlefield communication
Port congestion, fuel rationing, and confused chains of command
context: The Commission's verdict -- 'race prejudice, war hysteria, and a failure of political leadership' -- became the official judgment that the imprisonment was never justified by military necessity. Source: National Archives, https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/executive-order-9066

question: In October 1944, in France's Vosges Mountains, the 442nd was ordered to rescue the 'Lost Battalion' -- more than 200 Texas soldiers surrounded by German forces. The Japanese-American troops fought through the woods for five days and broke through. How did their own losses compare with the number of trapped men they saved?
answer: Their casualties outnumbered the men they rescued
choices: Their casualties outnumbered the men they rescued
Their losses were far lighter than anyone expected
They freed every man without losing a single soldier
They lost almost exactly as many as they saved
context: The 442nd saved over 200 men of the Texas 36th Division's 1st Battalion, 141st Regiment -- and took several times that many casualties doing it. The unit earned 21 Medals of Honor and over 4,000 Purple Hearts. Source: Densho Encyclopedia, https://encyclopedia.densho.org/442nd_Regimental_Combat_Team/

question: On April 29, 1945, scouts of the all-Japanese-American 522nd Field Artillery Battalion reached the barbed-wire gates of a Nazi concentration camp near Hurlach, Bavaria, broke them open, and helped free about 3,000 prisoners of a Dachau sub-camp. Where had some of these very soldiers come from only months before they freed those prisoners?
answer: America's own internment camps for Japanese families
choices: America's own internment camps for Japanese families
A prisoner-of-war swap with the surrendering Japanese army
Segregated training bases deep in the American South
Merchant ships interned at the start of the war
context: Some of the men who broke open the gates of a Nazi camp had themselves enlisted straight out of America's barbed-wire camps -- soldiers who freed prisoners abroad while their own families were imprisoned at home. Source: Densho Encyclopedia, https://encyclopedia.densho.org/522nd_Field_Artillery_Battalion/

question: When the Supreme Court upheld the imprisonment of Japanese-American citizens in 1944, Justice Robert Jackson refused to go along and wrote a famous warning. He said the ruling would now lie waiting -- ready for the hand of any future leader who could claim an urgent need. Lie waiting like what, in his words?
answer: A loaded weapon
choices: A loaded weapon
A sleeping fire
An unlocked door
A poisoned well
context: Jackson warned the decision would lie 'about like a loaded weapon, ready for the hand of any authority that can bring forward a plausible claim of an urgent need.' Justice Frank Murphy, also dissenting, said the exclusion fell 'into the ugly abyss of racism.' Source: dissents in Korematsu v. United States (1944).

question: In 1943 the government forced every camp prisoner over 17 to fill out a 'loyalty questionnaire.' Its Question 28 demanded they swear off any allegiance to the Emperor of Japan. But American law already barred the older immigrant prisoners -- the Issei -- from ever becoming U.S. citizens. For them, what trap did answering 'yes' to Question 28 spring?
answer: Renouncing Japan would leave them citizens of no country at all
choices: Renouncing Japan would leave them citizens of no country at all
It would have drafted them straight into combat overseas
It would have stripped their American-born children of citizenship
It would have sent the whole family to a harsher camp
context: Since U.S. law forbade the Issei from naturalizing, swearing off Japan would have made them stateless. Meanwhile the American-born Nisei had never owed the Emperor any allegiance to renounce. About 12,000 of 78,000 answered 'no-no' and were segregated at the Tule Lake camp. Source: Densho Encyclopedia, https://encyclopedia.densho.org/Questions_27_and_28/

question: Decades after Korematsu lost in 1944, researcher Aiko Herzig-Yoshinaga and lawyer Peter Irons dug through the National Archives in 1981 -- and found the Navy's own intelligence report, which had concluded almost no Japanese Americans were a threat. What did they prove the government had done with that report and the Army's case for the camps?
answer: Hidden and altered them to win the case before the Supreme Court
choices: Hidden and altered them to win the case before the Supreme Court
Lost them in a wartime filing error and never recovered them
Destroyed every copy shortly after the war ended
Published them openly but simply chosen to ignore them
context: The suppressed Ringle Report contradicted the Army's claims. On November 10, 1983, Judge Marilyn Hall Patel erased Korematsu's conviction in the same San Francisco courthouse where he was convicted 40 years earlier. Korematsu's words: 'One person can make a difference, even if it takes forty years.' In 1988 Congress apologized and paid $20,000 to each surviving prisoner. Source: Densho Encyclopedia, https://encyclopedia.densho.org/Coram_nobis_cases/

question: Hokusai's 'Great Wave off Kanagawa' shows a huge wave curling over three little fishing boats. But look down through the hollow under the wave's crest and you spot one small thing sitting far off in the distance. What is back there, dwarfed by the wave?
answer: Tiny Mount Fuji
choices: Tiny Mount Fuji
A passing sailing ship
A small shore temple
A second snowy peak
context: The towering wave is the foreground, but framed inside its curl sits Mount Fuji — the highest mountain in Japan — made tiny and serene in the far distance. The whole print is really about Fuji. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_Wave_off_Kanagawa

question: Most artists make their most famous work when they are young and at their peak. Katsushika Hokusai designed the 'Great Wave,' the single most reproduced image he ever made, around 1831. Roughly how old was he when he created it?
answer: About 70
choices: About 30
About 50
About 70
About 90
context: Hokusai was around 70 when he made his masterpiece, signing it 'Hokusai, who changed his name to Iitsu.' He called himself the Old Man Mad About Drawing and believed his best work was still ahead of him. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_Wave_off_Kanagawa

question: Today the 'Great Wave' hangs in famous museums, but in Hokusai's own time it was a mass-produced woodblock print, cranked out by the thousand and sold to ordinary people on the streets of Edo (old Tokyo). About how much did one cost back then?
answer: About the price of a bowl of soba noodles
choices: About the price of a bowl of soba noodles
About the price of a folding paper fan
About the price of a few grilled-chicken skewers
About the price of a cup of sake
context: The Great Wave sold for roughly the price of a bowl of soba noodles — pocket-change street art for commoners. So many were used up that of the estimated 8,000 printed, only about 113 first-edition impressions are known to survive today. nippon.com/en/japan-topics/g02414

question: Japanese woodblock prints like the 'Great Wave' first reached Europe in the 1850s — not hung in galleries, but doing a humble job nobody remembers ordering them for. How did they actually arrive on European shores?
answer: Stuffed in as packing paper around crates of porcelain
choices: Stuffed in as packing paper around crates of porcelain
Lining the inside of imported tea chests
Wrapped around bundles of fine Japanese silk
Pasted onto folding screens sold to tourists
context: The prints showed up crumpled around shipments of Japanese porcelain as cheap packing paper. Around 1856 the French artist Felix Bracquemond found Hokusai prints used as packaging and was electrified — helping spark the 'Japonisme' craze that reshaped European art. nippon.com/en/column/g00284

question: The Dutch painter Vincent van Gogh was stunned by the 'Great Wave' and wrote to his brother Theo about it, marveling that you could be so terrifying with just blue and green. Pointing at the curling foam reaching down toward the boat, what did he say the waves were?
answer: Claws
choices: Claws
Mountains
Dragons
Smoke
context: Van Gogh wrote: 'these waves are claws, the boat is caught in them, you can feel it.' The wave's crest really does break into spreading white fingers that reach down toward the boats like grasping hands. theartnewspaper.com / dailyartmagazine.com/great-wave-hokusai

question: Joan of Arc was about thirteen, a farm girl in the village of Domremy, when she began hearing voices in her father's garden — often just after the church bell rang. The voices told her to drive the English out of France. Who did Joan say was speaking to her?
answer: Saint Michael, Saint Catherine, and Saint Margaret
choices: Saint Michael, Saint Catherine, and Saint Margaret
Saint Peter, Saint Paul, and Saint Andrew
Saint George, Saint Denis, and Saint Martin
Saint Anne, Saint Agnes, and Saint Cecilia
context: Joan testified that the archangel Michael came first, followed by the virgin-martyrs Catherine and Margaret, guiding her for years. Source: Wikipedia 'Joan of Arc'; SparkNotes 'Joan of Arc: Voices'; saint-joan-of-arc.com 'Her Voices'.

question: Joan of Arc was burned at the stake in the Old Marketplace at Rouen at about nineteen years old. As the flames rose, a friar named Isambart held a crucifix up high so she could keep her eyes on it. Joan died crying out one single name, three times. What was the name?
answer: "Jesus! Jesus! Jesus!"
choices: "Jesus! Jesus! Jesus!"
"France! France! France!"
"Michael! Michael! Michael!"
"Charles! Charles! Charles!"
context: An English soldier was so moved he broke a stick in two, tied the pieces into a little cross, and handed it to her before the fire took her. She died on 30 May 1431; the Catholic Church canonized her as a saint in 1920. Source: famous-trials.com Joan of Arc account; thecatholicthing.org 'The Martyrdom of Joan of Arc'.

question: When the seventeen-year-old Joan of Arc reached the castle of Chinon after an eleven-day ride through enemy country, the prince Charles tested her: he dressed in plain clothes, hid in the crowd, and put another man on the throne in his place. According to the legend of the meeting, what did Joan do?
answer: She walked past the throne and picked the hidden prince out of the crowd
choices: She walked past the throne and picked the hidden prince out of the crowd
She knelt before the false king on the throne and called him her lord
She demanded the whole court remove their hats so she could choose
She refused to enter until the real prince was announced by name
context: Called 'La Reconnaissance' — the Recognition. The story is told in the early accounts but cannot be proven from the trial record, so it is remembered as legend rather than certain fact. Source: jeanne-darc.info 'Chinon'; maidofheaven.com 'Charles VII First Meeting'.

question: At the siege of Orleans, Joan of Arc was standing in the trench holding her banner when an arrow struck her between the neck and the shoulder. The wound was real and bloody. What did Joan do that very same day?
answer: She went back and led the final assault that broke the siege
choices: She went back and led the final assault that broke the siege
She was carried off the field and did not fight again for a week
She handed her banner to a knight and prayed in her tent
She ordered a retreat to spare her exhausted soldiers
context: The English abandoned the siege of Orleans on 8 May 1429 — only about nine days after Joan arrived. Source: Wikipedia 'Joan of Arc'; warfarehistorynetwork.com 'Joan of Arc, Siege of Orleans'.

question: Joan of Arc went into battle carrying a sword she had never laid eyes on. She told her followers exactly where to find it — buried in the church of Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois, a place she said her voices had revealed to her. Where in the church was the sword hidden?
answer: Behind the altar, beneath the floor
choices: Behind the altar, beneath the floor
Inside the bishop's locked treasure chest
Walled up in the bell tower
Wrapped in cloth under a saint's statue
context: When her men dug exactly where Joan described, the rusted sword was there — and she had never seen the church. Source: Wikipedia 'Joan of Arc'; jeanne-darc.info 'Sword' page.

question: Joan of Arc kept her promise to the prince: the city of Reims opened its gates and Charles VII was crowned king of France on 17 July 1429. Joan stood beside the new king at the ceremony, holding her white banner. When asked why the banner deserved a place of honor, what did Joan say?
answer: That it had borne the burden, so it deserved the honor
choices: That it had borne the burden, so it deserved the honor
That it was painted by the finest Scotsman in France
That the king himself had commanded her to raise it
That the saints had woven it for her in a dream
context: Joan had carried the banner herself through every battle. Her white silk banner, painted at Tours, showed Christ holding the world between two angels and bore the words 'JHESUS MARIA.' Source: Wikipedia 'Joan of Arc'; jeanne-darc.info 'Banner' page.

question: Before the fighting at Orleans, Joan of Arc dictated a letter to the English army, signing herself 'the Maid' and ordering them in God's name to go home. To warn them what would happen if they stayed, she made a bold prophecy. What did Joan promise was coming?
answer: A clash of arms so great France had not seen one like it in a thousand years
choices: A clash of arms so great France had not seen one like it in a thousand years
A plague sent by the saints to empty every English camp
A flood of soldiers from every corner of Christendom
A fire from heaven that would burn their siege towers
context: She dictated the letter during Holy Week, March 1429, and could neither read nor write it herself. Source: archive.joan-of-arc.org 'Letter to the English, 22 March 1429' (primary-source transcript).

question: Joan of Arc's luck ran out at Compiegne on 23 May 1430, when Burgundian troops pulled her from her horse and captured her. They later sold her to the English for money. While she was held prisoner in the tower of Beaurevoir, Joan did something desperate. What did she do?
answer: She leapt from the top of the tower and survived the fall
choices: She leapt from the top of the tower and survived the fall
She set fire to the castle gate and fled in the smoke
She bribed a guard with her banner to unlock her cell
She starved herself until the lord agreed to free her
context: Joan jumped trying to escape and lived; she was handed over to the English that November. Source: Wikipedia 'Joan of Arc' (jumps from tower in escape attempt).

question: After Joan of Arc was dead, the executioner Geoffroy Therage raked back the fire so the watching crowd could see for certain she had been a woman. Then he gathered up her ashes. The English had ordered him to make sure no follower could ever keep a scrap of her as a holy relic. What did Therage do with the ashes?
answer: He threw them into the river Seine
choices: He threw them into the river Seine
He sealed them inside the cathedral wall
He scattered them across an unmarked field
He buried them secretly at the city gate
context: By throwing the ashes into the river, the English meant to erase her forever — instead her legend only grew. Source: famous-trials.com Joan of Arc account ('ashes tossed into the Seine').

question: The man who carried out Joan of Arc's execution at Rouen was an executioner named Geoffroy Therage. Soon afterward he came to the friars Martin Ladvenu and Isambart de la Pierre, deeply shaken by what he had done that day. What did Therage confess to them?
answer: That he greatly feared damnation, for he had burned a saint
choices: That he greatly feared damnation, for he had burned a saint
That the English had forced his hand against his will
That he would never light another execution fire
That Joan had forgiven him with her dying breath
context: The man paid to kill her walked away convinced he had murdered a holy woman. Source: thecatholicthing.org 'The Martyrdom of Joan of Arc'; historyweblog.com (consistent across multiple accounts).

question: As the story of Joan of Arc's death spread across France, the executioner himself was said to have made an astonishing claim about her burning. He swore that, no matter how the fire raged, one part of Joan's body refused to burn and was found whole among the ashes. What part of her was it?
answer: Her heart
choices: Her heart
Her right hand
Her face
Her feet
context: This is told as legend — the executioner's later claim as Joan's fame grew — not as a proven fact. Source: historysphere.com 'Joan of Arc death'; thecatholicthing.org martyrdom account (reported as the executioner's claim).

question: At her trial, the learned judges set Joan of Arc a trap of a question: were she in God's grace? To say 'yes' would be the sin of presumption; to say 'no' would condemn herself out of her own mouth. The illiterate teenager answered so cleverly that the court notary said the room was left stupefied. What did Joan say?
answer: "If I am not, may God put me there; and if I am, may God keep me in it."
choices: "If I am not, may God put me there; and if I am, may God keep me in it."
"Only God may judge that, and no man in this room."
"I am, and you cannot prove otherwise before God."
"That is a question for the saints, not for me to answer."
context: The notary Boisguillaume testified the judges were stunned that a farm girl had slipped their theological trap. Source: famous-trials.com Joan of Arc account; Wikipedia 'Trial of Joan of Arc'.

question: Joan of Arc was finally condemned to death as a 'relapsed' heretic over the clothes she wore. She had agreed to put on a dress, which should have saved her life. While she slept in her cell, her jailers did one thing that doomed her. What did Joan's jailers do?
answer: They took her dress away and left her only the forbidden men's clothes
choices: They took her dress away and left her only the forbidden men's clothes
They forged her name on a fresh confession of heresy
They told the judges she had cursed the king of England
They burned the pardon that the bishop had already signed
context: Forced to choose between nakedness and the banned clothing, Joan put the men's clothes back on — and was condemned. She said of the pardon she had signed, 'What was in the schedule of abjuration I did not understand.' Source: famous-trials.com 'Joan's Relapse and Final Adjudication'; rehabilitation testimony of Massieu and Manchon.

question: Twenty-five years after Joan of Arc was burned, the Church reopened her case in a fresh trial, and her aged mother Isabelle Romee pleaded for her in person at Notre-Dame. The new court ruled the 1431 verdict 'null, invalid, worthless, and annihilated.' To prove it, the public executioner at Rouen did something dramatic to the original record. What did he do?
answer: He tore out the pages of her death sentence and burned them
choices: He tore out the pages of her death sentence and burned them
He carved her innocence into the courthouse door
He returned her ashes to her family for burial
He paraded the guilty bishop's body through the streets
context: The dead judge, Bishop Cauchon, was branded the real heretic, and Joan's mother lived to hear her daughter cleared. Source: Wikipedia 'Rehabilitation trial of Joan of Arc'; archive.joan-of-arc.org 'Declaration of Innocence, July 7th 1456'.

question: In 1770 British soldiers fired into an angry Boston crowd, killing five colonists in what became known as the Boston Massacre. When the soldiers were put on trial for murder, the patriot lawyer John Adams stunned his neighbors by taking a job none of them would touch. What did Adams do?
answer: He served as the defense lawyer for the accused British soldiers
choices: He served as the defense lawyer for the accused British soldiers
He signed up as a witness for the grieving Boston families
He printed pamphlets demanding the soldiers be hanged at once
He sailed to London to argue the case before the king
context: John Adams believed even hated enemies deserved a fair trial. He won acquittals for six of the eight soldiers; the jury convicted only two, of manslaughter. Adams later called it 'one of the best pieces of service I ever rendered my country.' Source: U.S. National Park Service, nps.gov/articles/000/boston-massacre-trial.htm; Adams' autobiography.

question: As President, John Adams signed the 1798 Sedition Act, which made it a federal crime to print 'false, scandalous and malicious' attacks on the government or the president. Vermont congressman Matthew Lyon was the very first man tried under it, jailed four months for mocking Adams's 'unbounded thirst for ridiculous pomp.' From behind bars, what did Lyon do that turned the punishment against Adams?
answer: He ran his re-election campaign from his cell and won in a landslide
choices: He ran his re-election campaign from his cell and won in a landslide
He smuggled out a confession admitting his writings were false
He begged the president for a pardon and was quietly released
He fled across the border into Canada before his sentence ended
context: The Alien and Sedition Acts criminalized criticism of the government Adams led — a real assault on the free-speech principle the founding professed. Federal courts prosecuted at least 26 people, mostly Jeffersonian newspaper editors. Matthew Lyon's jailhouse landslide made him a symbol of the backlash that helped sink Adams in 1800. Source: Bill of Rights Institute, billofrightsinstitute.org/essays/the-alien-and-sedition-acts; Britannica, britannica.com/event/Alien-and-Sedition-Acts.

question: John Cabot sailed west from Bristol in 1497 in a small ship called the Matthew, hunting a shortcut to Asia for King Henry VII of England. He never reached Asia, but his crew came home raving about the fish off the new land. How thick were the cod, they boasted?
answer: So thick they could scoop them up in baskets lowered over the side
choices: So thick they could scoop them up in baskets lowered over the side
So thick the ship could barely push through the water
So thick they leapt onto the deck on their own
So thick the sea looked silver from the masthead
context: Cabot's men said the cod on the Grand Banks were so plentiful they only had to lower baskets weighted with stones into the water — and boasted England would have 'no further need of Iceland' for fish. Source: https://www.heritage.nf.ca/articles/exploration/cabot-1497.php ; https://www.worldhistory.org/John_Cabot/

question: John Cabot found land for England on June 24, 1497, somewhere on the coast of what is now Canada. He went ashore and saw clear signs that people lived there — old fire sites, simple tools, and carvings on trees. But one strange thing was true of his whole landing. What was it?
answer: He never met a single person face to face
choices: He never met a single person face to face
He could not find any fresh water
He never went more than a few steps from his boat
He left without planting a flag
context: Cabot saw fire pits, snares, and carved or cut trees, but in his brief landing he encountered no people at all. He planted a cross and flew three banners: King Henry VII of England, the Pope, and Saint Mark of Venice. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/John_Cabot/

question: Martin Frobisher, the first Englishman to hunt the Northwest Passage, brought home a heavy black stone in 1576 that he was sure was gold. Three experts called it worthless, but a fourth swore it was real, so England sent fleets back for more — about 1,225 tons of ore in all. Then the truth came out. What was the 'gold' really worth?
answer: Nothing — it was fool's gold, and some was dumped to pave streets
choices: Nothing — it was fool's gold, and some was dumped to pave streets
A fortune, but pirates stole it before it could be melted
Enough to fund one more voyage, then it ran out
Less than the cost of the ships sent to fetch it
context: Frobisher's ore was iron pyrite — fool's gold — worth nothing. After years trying to melt gold out of it, England gave up; some of the worthless rock was reportedly dumped as gravel to pave streets and patch walls. Source: https://www.rmg.co.uk/stories/topics/martin-frobisher-north-west-passage-expedition-1576-78

question: Henry Hudson, still hunting the passage in 1611, got his ship frozen fast in the ice of a vast northern bay. His starving crew turned on him. What did the mutineers do to Hudson, his teenage son, and seven other men?
answer: Set them adrift in a small open boat and cut them loose
choices: Set them adrift in a small open boat and cut them loose
Locked them below deck until the ship sank
Marched them onto the ice and sailed away
Left them on a barren island with no supplies
context: The mutineers shoved Hudson, his son John, and seven sick or loyal men into a small open boat and cut the rope. They were never seen again. The water is now called Hudson Bay. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Passage

question: For over a century, British officials brushed off Inuit accounts of where Sir John Franklin's two lost warships had gone down in the Arctic ice. Then the wrecks were finally found in 2014 and 2016 — exactly where the Inuit had said. How well had HMS Terror survived on the sea floor?
answer: So well its drawers were still shut and cabins intact
choices: So well its drawers were still shut and cabins intact
Crushed flat, with only the keel recognizable
Buried so deep in silt that divers nearly missed it
Scattered in pieces across miles of seabed
context: The Inuit were right all along. HMS Erebus was found in 2014 and HMS Terror in 2016, the Terror so well preserved that drawers were still closed and cabins intact underwater. Franklin's 128 men had all died after their ships froze fast near King William Island. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/the-shipwrecks-from-john-franklins-doomed-arctic-expedition-were-exactly-where-the-inuit-said-they-would-be-180986627/

question: John Calvin is remembered as the great reformer of the Swiss city of Geneva, but he was not born Swiss at all. He grew up in Noyon, in France, and before he ever joined the Reformation he trained at Orleans for an entirely different profession. What had young Calvin studied to become?
answer: A lawyer
choices: A lawyer
A sea captain
A blacksmith
A painter
context: Born Jehan Cauvin on July 10, 1509 in Noyon, Picardy, Calvin studied law at Orleans before joining the Reformation. He was French; Geneva was only his adopted city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Calvin; Britannica 'John Calvin'.

question: John Calvin spent his life building a famous reformed church in Geneva, yet when he died on May 27, 1564 he gave one strange order about his own funeral: he asked to be buried in an unmarked grave, the exact spot left secret to this day. Why did Calvin want no marker on his grave?
answer: So no one could turn his tomb into a shrine
choices: So no one could turn his tomb into a shrine
So his enemies could not find his body
So the city would not have to pay for a stone
So he could be moved back to France later
context: Calvin worked himself to death in poor health and died at age 54. At his own request he was buried in the Cimetiere des Rois with no marker, so no one could make his tomb a place of pilgrimage; the spot is unknown today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Calvin.
