question: Taharqa was one of the Black Pharaohs — a Nubian king who ruled Egypt. Around 701 BC he led his army north to fight the powerful Assyrian Empire. Centuries later, where would a reader be surprised to come across Taharqa mentioned by name?
answer: In the Hebrew Bible
choices: In the Hebrew Bible
On the Rosetta Stone
In Homer's Iliad
On Trajan's Column
context: He appears in 2 Kings 19:9 as 'Tirhakah, king of Cush,' marching to fight the Assyrian king Sennacherib, who was besieging Jerusalem. Source: https://www.biblicalarchaeology.org/magazine/representing-cush-in-the-hebrew-bible/

question: When the Nubian king Piye captured the Egyptian city of Hermopolis, his victory stela records that he was furious with the defeated prince Nimlot. Yet Piye declared that one thing pained his heart more than any of Nimlot's crimes. What had upset Piye the most?
answer: That Nimlot had let his horses go hungry
choices: That Nimlot had let his horses go hungry
That Nimlot had looted a temple of Amun
That Nimlot had broken a sworn oath
That Nimlot had burned the city's grain
context: Piye's stela quotes him: 'it is more painful in my heart that my horses have been starved than any other crime you have committed.' He loved horses so much that four favorites were buried standing near his own pyramid at El-Kurru. Source: https://www.attalus.org/egypt/piye.html

question: In 1834 an Italian treasure-hunter named Giuseppe Ferlini went to the pyramids of Meroë hunting for gold, and he found the golden jewelry of a Kushite queen. But how did Ferlini get into the pyramids in the first place?
answer: He blew their tops off with explosives
choices: He blew their tops off with explosives
He dug long tunnels under their bases
He paid local villagers to break them open
He lowered himself inside on ropes
context: Ferlini wrecked around 40 pyramids and found the gold of Queen Amanishakheto — but when he tried to sell it, Europeans refused to believe such fine work could have been made in sub-Saharan Africa. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Ferlini

question: A medieval boy who wanted to become a knight started training around age seven, learning manners and riding in a lord's household. Around age fourteen he moved up to the next rank, carrying a knight's shield and lances and caring for his armor and horses. What was this teenage knight-in-training called?
answer: A squire
choices: A squire
A herald
A marshal
A varlet
context: The path ran page (about 7) to squire (about 14) to knight (about 18-21). A squire was a knight's working apprentice on and off the battlefield. Source: World History Encyclopedia, Medieval Knight (worldhistory.org/Medieval_Knight/).

question: In the most glamorous tournament event, two armored knights on horseback thundered straight at each other down a fenced track called the lists, each trying to shatter his long wooden lance on the other man or knock him clean out of the saddle. What was this contest called?
answer: The joust
choices: The joust
The melee
The pas d'armes
The tilt
context: Galloping head-on, the two knights closed at a combined speed near 30 mph. A later wooden barrier between them, the tilt, kept the horses from colliding. Source: World History Encyclopedia, Medieval Tournament (worldhistory.org/Medieval_Tournament/).

question: At a tournament, a lady watching from the stands might single out the knight she was cheering for and give him a small love-token to tie to his arm or lance. The fact sheet says this could be a veil, a sleeve, or a ribbon. What was such a token called?
answer: A favour
choices: A favour
A pennon
A garland
A streamer
context: Carrying a lady's favour, a knight fought in her honor. Winners might be awarded a gold crown, a jewel, a falcon, a fine horse, or a lady's kiss. Source: World History Encyclopedia, Medieval Tournament (worldhistory.org/Medieval_Tournament/).

question: Most people picture a knight's sword as his proudest mark of rank, but the true badge that proved he had really earned knighthood was something else entirely. Earning knighthood was even called 'winning' this gear. What was the real badge of a knight?
answer: His spurs
choices: His spurs
His helm
His banner
His belt
context: Knights and royalty wore golden (gilded) spurs, squires wore silver, and pages wore tinned ones, which is why earning the rank was called 'winning your spurs.' Source: royalspurs.com, History of Spurs.

question: The single act that turned a man into a knight was the accolade: his lord tapped or struck him a light blow on the shoulders or neck with the flat of a sword. Tradition gave this blow a famous meaning. What did people say made it so special?
answer: It was the last blow he should ever take without striking back.
choices: It was the last blow he should ever take without striking back.
It was the only blow a knight could ever give to a king.
It had to be struck hard enough to leave a lifelong scar.
It needed to be returned threefold before the next dawn.
context: The accolade (also called the colee or the dubbing) made the knight. From that day a knight was a fighting man who answered a blow with a blow. Source: World History Encyclopedia, Medieval Knight; Wikipedia, Medieval accolade.

question: The night before he was knighted, a squire first took a ritual bath to wash away his sins. Then he spent the whole night alone, kneeling in a dark church and watching over his weapons laid out on the altar until dawn. What was this all-night ceremony called?
answer: The vigil of arms
choices: The vigil of arms
The investiture
The girding
The blessing of arms
context: Bath then vigil readied the squire body and soul. He knelt watching his arms on the altar until first light, when the dubbing followed. Source: English Heritage, '5 Things You Might Not Know About Knights'; Wikipedia, Vigil of arms.

question: To practice the charge, a squire rode at a quintain: a spinning post with a shield on one arm and a heavy sandbag hanging from the other. The trick was to strike the shield dead-center. If he hit it off-center instead, what happened to him?
answer: The sandbag whipped around and knocked him off his horse.
choices: The sandbag whipped around and knocked him off his horse.
The shield sprang open and showered him with blunt arrows.
The post toppled over and pinned his horse to the ground.
The swinging arm snapped off and the splinters cut his hands.
context: A bad hit spun the bag around to clout the rider, so a squire had to strike true AND keep riding past it. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'How to Become a Medieval Knight'; Wikipedia, Quintain (jousting).

question: A knight did not actually ride his warhorse to the battlefield. This massive, specially trained stallion, around sixteen hands and over half a ton, was so precious that it was led there by hand and only mounted for the fighting itself. What was a knight's warhorse called?
answer: The destrier
choices: The destrier
The palfrey
The courser
The rouncey
context: The destrier was the 'great horse,' saved for combat alone. A knight rode a lesser horse to the field and switched mounts to fight. Source: horsesandpeople.com.au, The Great Horse of the Middle Ages.

question: Chivalry asked a knight to be brave and skilled with a blade, but also to be loyal, honest, merciful, courteous, and generous. When a new knight's sword was blessed in church, the priest gave him one duty above all the rest. What was a knight charged to always do?
answer: Protect the poor and the weak.
choices: Protect the poor and the weak.
Obey his king before his God.
Avenge every insult to his honor.
Win glory in every tournament.
context: The blessing of the sword charged the knight to 'always protect the poor and the weak.' Defending those who could not defend themselves was the beating heart of the chivalric ideal. Source: World History Encyclopedia, Medieval Knight; medievalchronicles.com, Code of Chivalry.

question: William Marshal, whom the Archbishop of Canterbury called 'the greatest knight that ever lived,' was so dominant that after one tournament he had been hit so many times his iron helmet was battered out of shape and jammed fast onto his head. How did he finally get the wrecked helm off?
answer: He knelt at a blacksmith's anvil and had it hammered and pried off.
choices: He knelt at a blacksmith's anvil and had it hammered and pried off.
He soaked his head in a horse-trough until the dented metal slipped free.
He had two squires haul on it with a rope rigged to a pulley.
He cut the leather straps and split the helmet open with an axe.
context: The greatest knight of his age had to kneel at a smith's anvil to be freed from his own helmet. He claimed he never lost and captured 500 knights for ransom over his career. Source: World History Encyclopedia, Sir William Marshal (worldhistory.org/Sir_William_Marshal/).

question: In 1559, King Henry II of France rode in a celebration joust feeling perfectly safe inside his full armor. But his opponent's lance shattered against him, and one flying piece did something no armor could stop: it slipped through the narrow slit of the king's visor. What did that splinter do?
answer: It pierced his eye and drove on into his brain.
choices: It pierced his eye and drove on into his brain.
It tore open his throat just below the chin-guard.
It snapped his neck with the force of the strike.
It punched through his breastplate and into his heart.
context: King Henry II lingered in agony for ten days before he died. The horror of it helped push France to give up jousting for good. Source: historytoday.com, 'Henry II of France Dies of Tournament Wounds'; Wikipedia, Gabriel de Lorges, Count of Montgomery.

question: In 1434 the Spanish knight Suero de Quinones held a bridge against all challengers for a whole month, calling himself a 'prisoner of love.' To prove his devotion to his lady, he vowed to wear one heavy thing around his neck every Thursday until he had broken 300 lances. What did he wear?
answer: An iron collar
choices: An iron collar
A silken blindfold
A golden chain
A black veil
context: This bridge-defense was a 'pas d'armes,' where a knight held a spot against all comers. Suero de Quinones wore a real iron collar every Thursday as a token of love until his 300 lances were spent. Source: Wikipedia, Suero de Quinones; fascinatingspain.com, 'The Passage of Arms by Suero de Quinones'.

question: Knights swore to show mercy and to spare a beaten foe, yet the ideal and the real world often clashed. At the Battle of Agincourt in 1415, with the fighting still uncertain, the English king gave a brutal order about the French knights his army had already taken alive. What did he command his men to do?
answer: Kill the helpless prisoners.
choices: Kill the helpless prisoners.
Ransom them back for gold.
March them home in chains.
Set them all free unharmed.
context: Ransoming captured knights was the normal, profitable custom, which is what makes the order so shocking. Men spoke of honor even as they burned villages, showing the code was a goal to aim at, not a guarantee. Source: historyskills.com, Code of Chivalry; English Heritage.

question: A Korean Buddhist book called the Jikji was printed at Heungdeok Temple in 1377 using cast metal letters that could be reused. That was 78 years before Johannes Gutenberg printed his Bible in Europe. So among all the world's books, what record does the Jikji hold?
answer: The oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type
choices: The oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type
The longest book ever copied by hand in one monastery
The first book translated into a hundred languages
The heaviest religious book ever bound in one volume
context: The Jikji was printed at Heungdeok Temple in the city of Cheongju in July 1377, predating Gutenberg's Bible by 78 years. It is the oldest surviving book in the world made with movable metal type. Source: https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/689333-oldest-book-printed-using-movable-metal-type

question: In 1443 the Korean ruler Sejong the Great gave his people something brand new: a writing system designed so that even ordinary commoners, not just trained scholars, could learn to read. He called it 'The Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People.' What did Sejong create?
answer: Korea's alphabet, Hangul
choices: Korea's alphabet, Hangul
A new tax law for farmers
A royal library in the capital
A network of mountain temples
context: King Sejong the Great invented Hangul in 1443, naming it Hunminjeongeum, 'The Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People.' He built it so commoners could learn to read, not only scholars. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hangul

question: King Sejong's Korean alphabet, Hangul, has a clever trick built into the very shapes of its letters. The letter for the 'm' sound is drawn as a square, and the letter for the 'k/g' sound shows the back of the tongue blocking the throat. What do the letter shapes actually picture?
answer: The position of the mouth and tongue making each sound
choices: The position of the mouth and tongue making each sound
The phases of the moon over a single month
The strokes used to paint each Chinese character
The footprints of animals from a royal hunt
context: Hangul's consonant letters are shaped like the mouth making the sound: the 'm' letter is a square like closed lips; the 'k/g' letter shows the back of the tongue blocking the throat. The letters are pictures of how you say them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hangul

question: Only one of the Jikji's two volumes survives today, and it is not in Korea. Around 1900 a French diplomat named Victor Collin de Plancy bought the book in Seoul and carried it home with him. Where can the surviving Jikji be found now?
answer: In the National Library of France in Paris
choices: In the National Library of France in Paris
Back at Heungdeok Temple in Cheongju
In a sealed vault beneath Seoul's palace
On a touring exhibit that never stops moving
context: The surviving second volume of the Jikji sits in the National Library of France in Paris. Victor Collin de Plancy, a French diplomat, bought it in Seoul around 1900 and took it to France. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jikji

question: King Sejong of Korea once took a man who had been born a palace slave and lifted him into his royal court of scientists, purely because of his talent. In 1441 that man, Jang Yeong-sil, built the world's first standardized version of a particular weather instrument. What did Jang Yeong-sil invent?
answer: The first standardized rain gauge
choices: The first standardized rain gauge
The first compass for sea voyages
The first telescope for the stars
The first thermometer for cold winters
context: Jang Yeong-sil, born a palace slave, was raised into King Sejong's court of scientists on talent alone. In 1441 he invented the world's first standardized rain gauge, the cheugugi, along with water clocks and sun clocks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jang_Yeong-sil

question: In 1444, just after King Sejong unveiled his new Korean alphabet, a Confucian scholar named Choe Manri and six others sent the king an angry petition. They argued that a country inventing its own script was something only 'barbarians' did and would bring ridicule from Ming China. How did Sejong respond to the petition?
answer: He kept the alphabet and spread it anyway
choices: He kept the alphabet and spread it anyway
He burned the alphabet to please the scholars
He fled the capital to avoid the dispute
He handed the throne to Choe Manri
context: Choe Manri and six other Confucian scholars petitioned King Sejong in 1444, calling an independent script the mark of 'barbarians' that would invite Ming China's ridicule. Sejong made and spread the alphabet anyway. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choe_Malli

question: In June 1953 a Brooklyn newsboy was delivering the Brooklyn Eagle when he dropped a nickel and it split in two on the sidewalk. Hidden inside was a tiny photograph of coded numbers — the loose thread that the FBI eventually pulled to expose Soviet spy Rudolf Abel. What everyday object was the spy hiding his secret message inside?
answer: A hollowed-out nickel
choices: A hollowed-out nickel
A rolled newspaper
A leather coin purse
A folded delivery receipt
context: The 'Hollow Nickel Case': the coin held a microphotograph of a coded cipher. The FBI cracked it years later with help from Abel's defecting partner Reino Hayhanen, unravelling the spy ring. Source: FBI history 'Hollow Nickel / Rudolph Abel'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollow_Nickel_Case

question: Early on February 10, 1962, two governments met at the middle of the Glienicke Bridge over the Havel river between West Berlin and Potsdam to trade prisoners. At 8:52 a.m. a white line was painted across the middle, and at the same instant each side waved its man across to the other. Captured American U-2 pilot Francis Gary Powers walked one way — who walked the other way to the Soviets?
answer: KGB colonel Rudolf Abel
choices: KGB colonel Rudolf Abel
Physicist Klaus Fuchs
Defector Reino Hayhanen
Courier Harry Gold
context: The exchange gave the Glienicke crossing its nickname, the 'Bridge of Spies.' Powers had been freed after the swap; Abel was the Soviet spy whose ring the hollow nickel had helped expose. Source: history.com 'Spies Swapped'; biography.com 'Rudolf Abel'

question: When the Soviets shot down Francis Gary Powers' U-2 spy plane on May 1, 1960, the CIA had given him a way out: a hollowed-out silver dollar concealing a tiny needle. Powers chose not to use it and let himself be taken alive. What had the CIA hidden on that needle for him?
answer: A dose of deadly shellfish poison
choices: A dose of deadly shellfish poison
A microfilm of his orders
A miniature lock-pick
A radio homing beacon
context: The needle was tipped with saxitoxin, a poison drawn from Alaskan shellfish — a suicide weapon Powers refused to use. He was captured and later traded on the Glienicke Bridge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1960_U-2_incident; historynet.com 'CIA Poisoner in Chief'

question: Kim Philby rose to become a senior officer of Britain's own spy service, MI6 — while secretly working for the Soviets as the 'Third Man.' In 1951 he learned that two fellow Soviet agents he had been recruited with at Cambridge were about to be caught. What did Philby do that let Donald Maclean and Guy Burgess slip away to Moscow?
answer: He tipped them off to flee before arrest
choices: He tipped them off to flee before arrest
He forged their exit visas himself
He hid them inside the Soviet embassy
He bribed the officers tailing them
context: Warned by Philby, Maclean and Burgess fled to Moscow on May 25, 1951. Philby escaped prosecution, was publicly cleared in 1955, and finally defected to Moscow himself in 1963. They were part of the 'Cambridge Five.' Source: history.co.uk 'Who Were the Cambridge Five'; historyhit.com 'Facts About Kim Philby'

question: For decades supporters insisted Julius Rosenberg, executed in 1953, had been framed for spying. Then beginning in 1995 the United States released the decoded Venona cables — intercepted Soviet wartime messages — and they settled the question of whether he was really a spy. What did those decrypts reveal that nailed Julius Rosenberg?
answer: His Soviet codename, 'LIBERAL,' running a spy ring
choices: His Soviet codename, 'LIBERAL,' running a spy ring
A signed confession he had recanted
A Soviet payment ledger in his name
His fingerprints on stolen bomb plans
context: The Venona decrypts named Julius as 'LIBERAL' and documented the espionage ring he ran — confirming the spying was real, even as scholars still debate how much his wife Ethel was involved. Source: ahf.nuclearmuseum.org 'Rosenberg Trial'; commentary.org 'The Venona Men'

question: In August 1945 Japan suddenly surrendered, and two young U.S. Army colonels were given about half an hour to draw a line splitting Korea into a Soviet half and an American half. With no time to study, they grabbed the handiest thing in the room and picked the 38th parallel. What did they pull out to draw the line that still divides Korea today?
answer: A National Geographic map
choices: A National Geographic map
A captured Japanese battle plan
An old Russian railway chart
A British naval atlas
context: One of the colonels was Dean Rusk, a future U.S. Secretary of State. The 38th parallel was meant to be a temporary line just for accepting the Japanese surrender. (National Geographic, 'National Geographic, Korea, and the 38th Parallel'; NEH, 'Korea and the Thirty-Eighth Parallel')

question: Before dawn on June 25, 1950, about 135,000 North Korean soldiers came storming south across the 38th parallel in a surprise attack on South Korea. Spearheading the assault was a Soviet-made weapon the South had little to stop. What rolled at the front of the invasion?
answer: T-34 tanks
choices: T-34 tanks
Heavy siege cannons
Armored gunboats
Cavalry squadrons
context: The attack began at 4 a.m. The Soviet-built T-34 had been a war-winning tank for the USSR in World War II, and South Korea had almost nothing that could knock it out. (U.S. National Archives, 'US Enters the Korean Conflict'; U.S. Army, 'North Korea attacks across 38th parallel')

question: The North Korean invasion of 1950 moved so fast that within weeks the surviving United Nations and South Korean troops had been pushed back into the far southeast corner of the country, fighting with their backs to the sea and almost nowhere left to retreat. What was this last-ditch pocket called?
answer: The Pusan Perimeter
choices: The Pusan Perimeter
The Yalu Salient
The Hungnam Line
The Osan Pocket
context: Holding the Pusan Perimeter kept the war alive until MacArthur's Inchon landing in September 1950 broke the siege from behind. (Military.com, 'Task Force Smith...Pusan Perimeter'; TheCollector, 'The American Defeat at Taejon That Saved South Korea')

question: NASA's nighttime satellite photos of the Korean peninsula show South Korea blazing with electric light, while right beside it a huge zone sits almost pitch black, as if nobody lived there at all. Yet deep inside that darkness glows a single dot of light — one lone city still lit up. Which city is that one point of light?
answer: Pyongyang
choices: Pyongyang
Hamhung
Chongjin
Wonsan
context: That dark zone is North Korea, so short of electricity that at night it nearly vanishes, while its capital Pyongyang glows as a single tiny island of light. (NASA Earth Observatory, 'The Korean Peninsula at Night'; National Geographic, 'New Space Station Photos Show North Korea at Night')

question: On July 5, 1950, the first American ground unit thrown into the Korean War — 'Task Force Smith,' just 540 lightly-armed men — dug in at Osan against a North Korean column of about 5,000 troops and 36 tanks. Badly outnumbered, they were finally overrun. Before they broke, what did those 540 men manage to do?
answer: Held on for about seven hours and bought precious time
choices: Held on for about seven hours and bought precious time
Knocked out every one of the 36 enemy tanks
Captured the North Korean column's commanding general
Forced the entire enemy column to turn back north
context: Task Force Smith took 181 casualties and was overrun, but its desperate seven-hour delaying action bought time that helped save the South. (Military.com, 'Task Force Smith: How the 24th Infantry Division Saved South Korea'; johnsmilitaryhistory.com)

question: General Douglas MacArthur's September 1950 plan to land troops at Inchon was such a wild gamble that his own planners thought it nearly impossible. The single biggest reason was a problem with Inchon's harbor itself — one that could leave the whole fleet helpless. What was that harbor problem?
answer: Its extreme tides
choices: Its extreme tides
Its drifting mines
Its blinding fog
Its hidden reefs
context: Inchon's tidal range was so huge that ships could only land during a few hours at high tide before being stranded in the mud. MacArthur gambled anyway, landed behind enemy lines, broke the war wide open, and lost only about 225 men killed. (Naval History Magazine, 'Operation Chromite: Target INCHON'; Britannica, 'Inchon landing')

question: At the frozen Chosin Reservoir in late 1950, a messenger told Marine Colonel Lewis 'Chesty' Puller that the enemy had completely encircled his men. Instead of panicking, Puller fired back a now-legendary line. What did Chesty Puller say?
answer: 'We're surrounded. That simplifies the problem.'
choices: 'We're surrounded. That simplifies the problem.'
'Then we shall fight in the shade.'
'Nuts! We will never surrender.'
'Hold the line at any cost.'
context: His full reply: 'We've been looking for the enemy for some time now. We've finally found him. We're surrounded. That simplifies the problem.' Surrounded, the Marines could attack the enemy in any direction. (19FortyFive, "'We're Surrounded. That Simplifies the Problem.'"; military-quotes.com)

question: During the December 1950 evacuation at Hungnam, the American cargo ship SS Meredith Victory — a freighter built to carry only 12 passengers — crammed in as many desperate Korean refugees as it possibly could for a three-day voyage to safety. No one died, and five babies were born along the way. How many refugees did that one ship rescue?
answer: More than 14,000
choices: More than 14,000
About 900
About 3,500
About 7,000
context: It set the Guinness record for the largest sea rescue ever by a single ship, earning the name 'Ship of Miracles.' (Korean War Memorial Foundation, 'SS Meredith Victory: The Ship of Miracles'; Washington Post, 'Korean War Christmas miracle')

question: On November 27, 1950, near Korea's Chosin Reservoir, about 30,000 United Nations troops — most of them the 1st Marine Division — were suddenly surrounded in cold that dropped to roughly 30 degrees below zero, so frigid that weapons jammed and blood plasma froze solid. How many Chinese soldiers had encircled them?
answer: About 120,000
choices: About 120,000
About 25,000
About 45,000
About 60,000
context: The survivors proudly call themselves 'The Frozen Chosin.' In the brutal cold the dead were stacked like cordwood. (Britannica, 'Battle of the Chosin Reservoir'; Bill of Rights Institute, 'The Korean War and the Battle of Chosin Reservoir')

question: As his surrounded Marines fought their way out of the Chosin Reservoir toward the sea, reporters asked Marine General Oliver P. Smith whether his division was retreating. Smith bristled and rejected the word 'retreat' outright with a defiant one-liner. What did Oliver P. Smith snap back?
answer: 'Retreat, Hell! We're just attacking in another direction.'
choices: 'Retreat, Hell! We're just attacking in another direction.'
'A Marine never takes one step backward.'
'We came to win, not to run.'
'There is no retreat in this Corps.'
context: Smith's division then fought about 70 miles through the mountain passes to the sea at Hungnam. The line is often misquoted as 'advancing in a different direction.' (Wikipedia, 'Oliver P. Smith'; U.S. Marine Corps Museum, 'O.P. Smith – Savior of Chosin')

question: The Korean War's enormous fighting — over a million combat casualties and millions of civilian deaths — finally stopped on July 27, 1953 when commanders met at a village called Panmunjom and signed a document that ended the shooting. More than seventy years later, what does that 1953 signing still mean for North and South Korea?
answer: They are technically still at war, never having made peace
choices: They are technically still at war, never having made peace
They signed a full peace treaty that settled the war for good
They reunited into a single country a few years afterward
They agreed the North would slowly absorb the South
context: What was signed at Panmunjom was only an armistice — a cease-fire — not a peace treaty, so the two Koreas remain officially at war, divided by the heavily-mined DMZ. (Britannica, 'Korean War – Armistice'; USFK, official Armistice Agreement text, Panmunjom, 1953)

question: North and South Korea began from the same ruined starting point in the 1950s — and into the early 1970s the communist North was actually the richer of the two per person. Then the South's 'Miracle on the Han River' transformed it while the North stayed desperately poor. Today, how does the South compare to the North in wealth per person?
answer: More than 50 times wealthier
choices: More than 50 times wealthier
About twice as wealthy
About five times wealthier
About ten times wealthier
context: South Korea reached roughly $35,000 per person while North Korea sits near $640 — a more than fiftyfold gap from the same beginning. (Brilliant Maps, 'North Korea vs South Korea GDP Per Capita'; CSGEF, 'South Korea: The Miracle on the Han River')

question: On the night of November 9-10, 1938, mobs across Germany set fire to more than 1,400 Jewish synagogues during the pogrom the Nazis called Kristallnacht, the 'Night of Broken Glass.' German firefighters rushed to the scene. But what were their orders?
answer: Protect only the neighboring non-Jewish buildings
choices: Protect only the neighboring non-Jewish buildings
Protect the synagogues and arrest the arsonists
Protect the worshippers trapped inside the synagogues
Protect the fire crews from the rampaging mob
context: The firefighters stood by and let the synagogues burn to the ground; their orders were only to keep the flames from spreading to nearby 'Aryan' (non-Jewish) property. Around 7,500 Jewish-owned businesses were also smashed and looted that night. Source: https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/the-night-of-broken-glass

question: After Kristallnacht, the 1938 'Night of Broken Glass,' insurance companies owed money to the Jewish shopkeepers whose windows had been smashed. But Hermann Göring's regime flipped the whole thing on its head. When the enormous bill for the damage came due, who did the Nazi government force to pay it?
answer: The Jewish community, made to pay for all of it
choices: The Jewish community, made to pay for all of it
The insurance companies that owed the claims
The mobs and rioters who smashed the shops
The Nazi Party that had ordered the attack
context: The Nazis fined the entire Jewish community one billion Reichsmarks as an 'atonement payment' (Suhnezahlung) for the death of diplomat Ernst vom Rath, forced Jewish owners to pay for their own repairs, and confiscated the insurance money they were owed, handing it to the Reich. The victims were punished for the crime committed against them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kristallnacht

question: When Marco Polo came home from Kublai Khan's China, he told of people digging black stones out of the mountains that caught fire and held their heat far better than wood. Europeans, who still heated their homes with firewood, could barely believe it. What was this strange burning rock?
answer: Coal
choices: Coal
Peat
Amber
Sulfur
context: Marco Polo's report of coal astonished Europeans, who at the time burned wood for heat. Source: https://charactorium.com/en/character/marco-polo

question: Marco Polo reported that in Kublai Khan's China, ordinary people walked into a shop and bought everything they needed without a single gold or silver coin. Back in Europe, people still lugged around heavy metal coins. What did the Chinese hand over instead?
answer: Paper money
choices: Paper money
Strings of shells
Carved jade tokens
Bars of salt
context: The Yuan paper note was called the chao, one of the first nationwide paper currencies in the world. Source: https://historyofinformation.com/detail.php?id=243

question: Twice Kublai Khan launched gigantic fleets to conquer Japan, and twice a sudden typhoon smashed them apart — in 1281 a storm wrecked roughly 4,400 ships carrying about 140,000 men, drowning at least half of them. Grateful Japanese gave those storms a name they would remember forever. What did they call them?
answer: Kamikaze, the divine wind
choices: Kamikaze, the divine wind
Bushido, the warrior's way
Tsunami, the harbor wave
Shogun, the great general
context: Kamikaze means 'divine wind' — the storms that twice destroyed Kublai Khan's invasion fleets. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1415/the-mongol-invasions-of-japan-1274--1281-ce/

question: At Xanadu, his summer capital, Kublai Khan kept a second palace built entirely of gilded cane and bamboo, painted all over with beasts and birds. Marco Polo marveled most at one feature: a single remarkable thing that could be done with the whole structure. What was it?
answer: The entire palace could be taken to pieces and carried away wherever he commanded
choices: The entire palace could be taken to pieces and carried away wherever he commanded
The entire palace floated out onto the lake on wooden rafts each summer
The entire palace slowly turned to follow the sun across the sky
The entire palace was burned and rebuilt fresh every single spring
context: The cane palace was braced against the wind by more than 200 silk cords and could be dismantled and moved at the Khan's command. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Xanadu/

question: Kublai Khan's Yuan dynasty sorted everyone into four legal classes by privilege, with the Mongols on top and the native Chinese of the former Southern Song at the very bottom, where the same crime brought a harsher punishment. Besides those harsher punishments, what were the two bottom classes flatly forbidden to do?
answer: Own weapons or keep dogs and hunting eagles
choices: Own weapons or keep dogs and hunting eagles
Ride horses or wear robes of colored silk
Travel beyond the province where they were born
Learn to read or write the Chinese script
context: Under the Yuan four-class system, northern Han and Southerners could not own weapons or keep dogs or hunting eagles — an honest record of foreign rule ranking native Chinese lowest. Source: https://www.travelchinaguide.com/intro/history/yuan/four-class-system.htm

question: Marco Polo's book was so packed with marvels that Venetians mockingly nicknamed it 'Il Milione' — 'The Million,' as in a million tall tales. Centuries later the historian Frances Wood argued he may never have set foot in China at all, pointing to famous Chinese things his book never once mentions. Which three did he completely leave out?
answer: The Great Wall, tea, and chopsticks
choices: The Great Wall, tea, and chopsticks
Paper money, coal, and the city of Dadu
Silk, the Grand Canal, and pagodas
Horses, archery, and felt tents
context: Frances Wood ('Did Marco Polo Go to China?') notes Polo never mentions the Great Wall, tea, chopsticks, or foot-binding, and suggests he may have compiled his account from Persian guidebooks and other travelers. Source: https://www.asianstudies.org/publications/eaa/archives/debunking-the-myth-did-marco-polo-go-to-china/

question: Marco Polo, a Venetian who had only ever seen wood burned for heat, was amazed to watch the people of China dig up 'black stones' from the ground and set them alight to warm their homes. What were these 'black stones' that Europe barely knew?
answer: Coal
choices: Coal
Amber
Flint
Jade
context: Polo described coal — dug from the ground and burned in place of firewood — a fuel almost unknown in 13th-century Europe, where he had grown up burning only wood. Source: history.com 'Marco Polo'; factsanddetails.com China.

question: Twice Kublai Khan launched huge fleets to invade Japan, and twice — in 1274 and again in 1281 — his ships were smashed and tens of thousands of his men drowned at sea. The Japanese gave the storms that saved them a name meaning 'divine wind.' What did the Japanese believe wrecked the Mongol fleets?
answer: Twin typhoons they called the kamikaze
choices: Twin typhoons they called the kamikaze
A chain of underwater reefs
A surprise fleet of fire-ships
A traitor who burned the harbor
context: In 1281 an armada of some 4,400 ships and 140,000 men was wrecked; at least half the warriors drowned. 'Kamikaze' means 'divine wind.' Source: World History Encyclopedia 'Mongol Invasions of Japan'; Britannica.

question: Marco Polo reported that Kublai Khan paid for goods and labor not with gold or silver coins but with slips of paper money — and the bills were all made from one strange material harvested from a single kind of tree. What were Kublai Khan's banknotes made from?
answer: The white inner bark of the mulberry tree
choices: The white inner bark of the mulberry tree
Pressed and dried lotus petals
The boiled pulp of bamboo shoots
Thin sheets hammered from pine resin
context: The bills used the fine white inner bark — the thin skin between the wood and the rough outer bark — of the mulberry tree. Source: factsanddetails.com; fee.org 'Marco Polo on Money'; historyofinformation.com.

question: Marco Polo described a cloth he called 'salamander' that would not burn — when it got dirty, you threw it into the fire and it came out white as snow. Europeans believed it was the skin of a fire-living lizard, but Polo reported the truth of where it really came from. Where did the fireproof 'salamander' cloth actually come from?
answer: It was mined from rock in the ground and spun into thread
choices: It was mined from rock in the ground and spun into thread
It was woven from the hair of mountain goats
It was the molted skin of a desert serpent
It was dyed silk soaked in a secret oil
context: Polo correctly reported the 'salamander' was asbestos — dug from the ground, spun into thread, and cleaned by fire. Kublai Khan reportedly sent a bolt of it to the Pope in Rome. Source: factsanddetails.com; thehistorianshut.com.

question: Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis Khan, became the first foreign ruler ever to conquer and unify all of China. For his new dynasty he chose a name drawn from the ancient I Ching, the same word he wanted his rule to embody. The name 'Yuan' meant what?
answer: Origin, or primal source
choices: Origin, or primal source
Heaven's chosen sword
The eternal mountain
Conqueror of the four seas
context: Kublai proclaimed the 'Yuan' dynasty in 1271; the name from the I Ching means 'origin' or 'primal source.' His 1279 naval victory at Yamen destroyed the Song and unified China. Source: World History Encyclopedia 'Kublai Khan'; Britannica.

question: On the green of Tolpuddle village in Dorset stands an ancient sycamore, alive since the 1680s, where in the autumn of 1833 six poor farm laborers gathered to hear union organizers. What is that sycamore called today?
answer: The Martyrs' Tree
choices: The Martyrs' Tree
The Hanging Oak
The Charter Elm
The Gallows Ash
context: The Tolpuddle Martyrs' Tree still lives on the village green, now pollarded and cared for by the National Trust. Court testimony shows the men's secret oath was actually sworn inside Thomas Standfield's cottage, not under the tree, but the sycamore became the movement's emblem. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolpuddle_Martyrs_Tree)  (Legend.)

question: In 1834 the ploughman and Methodist preacher George Loveless gathered six Dorset farm laborers into a society to stop their pay being cut. Their wages had already been driven down toward six shillings a week. What weekly wage did they band together and refuse to work below?
answer: Ten shillings
choices: Ten shillings
Three shillings
Twenty shillings
Forty shillings
context: George Loveless led the six men to form the Friendly Society of Agricultural Labourers, swearing not to work for less than ten shillings a week as farmers pushed pay toward six. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolpuddle_Martyrs ; britannica.com/event/Tolpuddle-Martyrs)

question: The six Tolpuddle laborers had broken no strike law in 1834 — banding together for higher pay was not itself the charge that doomed them. The court instead reached for a 1797 statute first written to punish naval mutineers. So what exactly did the prosecutors convict the six men of doing?
answer: Swearing a secret oath to their society
choices: Swearing a secret oath to their society
Burning a landlord's hay ricks
Smuggling a pamphlet from France
Marching armed on the county jail
context: In March 1834 the six men were sentenced to seven years' transportation to Australia — not for organizing, but for the secret oath of loyalty they had sworn, prosecuted under a 1797 law aimed at mutineers. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolpuddle_Martyrs)

question: Awaiting transportation to Australia, the Tolpuddle martyr James Brine was set to brutal labor. He later recalled digging post-holes barefoot until his feet were too cut to press to the spade — and then a second ordeal washing sheep that he said went on for seventeen straight days. What did he describe enduring through those seventeen days?
answer: Standing up to his breast in cold water
choices: Standing up to his breast in cold water
Chained to a wall in solitary darkness
Hauling stone blocks in the noon sun
Locked below a ship's flooded deck
context: Five of the martyrs were first held on the rotting prison hulks York and Leviathan off Portsmouth — 500-600 men per ship, swept by cholera and smallpox. Brine recalled standing 'up to my breast in water' for seventeen days washing sheep. (tolpuddlemartyrs.org.uk/story/transportation)

question: The People's Charter of 1838, drawn up by William Lovett, listed six demands for reforming Parliament. Five are now British law — votes for all men over 21, the secret ballot, paid MPs, no property qualification for MPs, and equal-sized constituencies. Which sixth demand was the one point Britain never adopted?
answer: Yearly elections for Parliament
choices: Yearly elections for Parliament
Votes for all women over 21
Abolishing the House of Lords
A written national constitution
context: The Charter's six points became the program of the Chartist movement. Five eventually became law; only annual parliaments was never adopted. (newportrising.co.uk/sixpoints ; parliament.uk Chartists overview)

question: In 1848 the Chartist leader Feargus O'Connor presented Parliament a petition he claimed carried 5,736,000 names. The Commons clerks recounted and found barely two million — and scattered among them obvious forgeries that made the whole roll a laughingstock. What kind of names did the clerks turn up among the signatures?
answer: Joke names like 'Victoria Rex' and 'Mr. Punch'
choices: Joke names like 'Victoria Rex' and 'Mr. Punch'
Names of men long dead in the churchyards
The same clerk's hand copied a thousand times
Whole pages left blank but counted as signed
context: O'Connor claimed 5,736,000 signatures; clerks counted only 1,975,496 and found fakes including 'Victoria Rex' and 'Mr. Punch.' The 1842 petition, by contrast, was a genuine 6-mile roll of 3,315,752 names that the Commons still refused even to hear. (parliament.uk Chartist petitions)

question: Richard Oastler, a Tory reformer, opened the campaign for a ten-hour working day in 1830 with a furious letter to the Leeds Mercury. He charged that small children laboring in the Bradford mills were treated worse than West Indian slaves, and gave his letter a title that branded the mills with that very word. What did he title it?
answer: 'Yorkshire Slavery'
choices: 'Yorkshire Slavery'
'The Factory King'
'The Cry of the Children'
'Bradford's Shame'
context: Oastler's 1830 'Yorkshire Slavery' letter launched the ten-hours movement; he himself became known as 'the Factory King.' The Ten Hours Act of 1847, steered by Lord Ashley and the mill-owner John Fielden, finally capped women and young workers at ten hours a day. (britannica.com/biography/Richard-Oastler)

question: Blue-collar real wages in Britain roughly doubled between 1810 and 1850, and working hours fell. Economic historians note that for decades before 1830, output per worker had raced ahead while wages barely moved — a gap that closed only once one particular thing finally began to grow after 1830. According to these historians, what grew after 1830 that let wages and conditions rise?
answer: Capital and tools invested per worker
choices: Capital and tools invested per worker
The number of trade-union members
The harshness of the factory laws
The size of the protest marches
context: Historians call the early gap 'Engels' pause' — wages rose only ~12% from 1780-1840 while output per worker climbed 46%. The gap closed after 1830 as capital per worker grew, suggesting rising wages and shorter hours came chiefly from capital accumulation and productivity, not from agitation alone. (econlib.org Industrial Revolution and the Standard of Living ; nuff.ox.ac.uk Allen, engelspause.pdf)

question: At Lalibela in the Ethiopian highlands, King Lalibela's eleven churches around 1200 AD were not built up from stacked stone blocks the way a cathedral is. Workers shaped each church a stranger way, starting from a single mass of volcanic bedrock. How did they make a church out of it?
answer: They cut trenches around a block of bedrock, then hollowed it out from the roof down into a finished church
choices: They cut trenches around a block of bedrock, then hollowed it out from the roof down into a finished church
They poured a mortar of crushed rock into carved wooden molds and let it harden into walls
They quarried the rock into bricks elsewhere and hauled them back to stack on the site
They tunneled sideways into a cliff face and propped the long hall up with stone pillars
context: Each church was carved DOWNWARD into living volcanic rock: chisel a deep trench all the way around a block, freeing it from the mountain, then hollow the freed block into a finished church roof-first, top to bottom. No stacking, no mortar — a whole church carved out of one piece of the ground, still in use for Ethiopian Orthodox worship ~800 years later. Source: metmuseum.org/essays/the-rock-hewn-churches-of-lalibela; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock-Hewn_Churches,_Lalibela.

question: The last of King Lalibela's eleven Ethiopian churches, Bete Giyorgis, was cut down into the ground from a single block of rock so cleanly that when you stand at the rim of the pit and look down at its roof, the whole church reads as one enormous shape pressed into the earth. What shape is it?
answer: A perfect cross
choices: A perfect cross
A round dome
A six-pointed star
A square keep
context: Bete Giyorgis ('House of St. George') is carved as a perfect Greek cross sunk into the earth, sitting in a courtyard roughly 72 by 72 feet and 36 feet deep — so from the rim it looks like a giant cross cut into the ground, its roof carved with a pattern of nested crosses, all from the one solid block. It was the last of the eleven built. Source: biblicalarchaeology.org/daily/ancient-cultures/ancient-near-eastern-world/rock-hewn-churches-of-lalibela/.

question: Bartolomé de las Casas believed Native peoples could be won over by preaching alone, with no soldiers at all. To prove it, he and his fellow Dominican friars walked unarmed into a region of Guatemala the Spanish had named 'Tuzulutlán' — the Land of War — and converted its people peacefully. Impressed, the Spanish gave the region a hopeful new name. What was it renamed?
answer: Verapaz — 'True Peace'
choices: Verapaz — 'True Peace'
Nueva Sevilla — 'New Seville'
Santa Cruz — 'Holy Cross'
Buenaventura — 'Good Fortune'
context: The Land of War became Verapaz, 'True Peace.' Las Casas had insisted for years that conversion at swordpoint was both cruel and false; Verapaz was his proof that it could be done by persuasion instead. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartolomé_de_las_Casas

question: After Bartolomé de las Casas began speaking out against the colonists' treatment of Native peoples, Cardinal Cisneros, then ruling Spain as regent, appointed him to a brand-new royal office in 1516 with a salary of 100 pesos a year. What title did this office give him?
answer: Protector of the Indians
choices: Protector of the Indians
Bishop of the New World
Confessor to the King
Apostle of the Caribbean
context: He was named 'Protector of the Indians' — an official crown post created to give his advocacy real standing. Decades later, as Bishop of Chiapas in 1545, he refused absolution to colonists who would not free their slaves; they fired shots at him and he left, never to return. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartolomé_de_las_Casas

question: On a Sunday in Advent 1511, a Dominican friar named Antonio de Montesinos climbed into the pulpit on Hispaniola and told the stunned Spanish colonists that their cruelty to the Taíno people had put them in mortal sin. He hammered them with one burning question about the people they were working to death. The colonists were so furious they demanded he take it back. What did Montesinos thunder at them?
answer: 'Are these not men? Do they not have souls?'
choices: 'Are these not men? Do they not have souls?'
'Have you no fear of the King's justice?'
'Will the gold buy back your honor?'
'Who gave you this land to plunder?'
context: Montesinos demanded, 'Are these not men? Do they not have rational souls? Are you not obliged to love them as yourselves?' The congregation was outraged and ordered him to retract it. He refused — and the sermon helped set the young Las Casas on the path that defined his life. Source: summitdominicans.org, '500th Anniversary of the Sermon of Friar Montesinos'

question: In Cuba in 1512, the Spanish captured a Taíno chief named Hatuey who had led the resistance against them and condemned him to be burned at the stake. As the fire was readied, a friar promised Hatuey he could go to heaven if he accepted baptism first. Hatuey asked whether Spaniards went to heaven too. Told that good ones did, what did the chief reply — according to the account Las Casas later recorded?
answer: He would rather go to hell than share heaven with such cruel people
choices: He would rather go to hell than share heaven with such cruel people
He would accept baptism only if his people were freed first
He had no fear of the fire, for his gods would carry him home
He forgave the friar but cursed the men who lit the flames
context: By Las Casas's account, Hatuey chose hell over an eternity beside the Spaniards. He became Cuba's first national hero. This comes down to us as Las Casas's recorded testimony rather than a verified transcript, so it is remembered as legend. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hatuey

question: Bartolomé de las Casas became Spain's fiercest defender of Native peoples — but as a young settler on Hispaniola and Cuba he had a very different life, one he later renounced in shame. Before his change of heart, he profited directly from the colonial system he would spend the rest of his days trying to tear down. What had Las Casas himself been?
answer: A slave-owning landholder worked by Native laborers
choices: A slave-owning landholder worked by Native laborers
A royal tax-collector for the Caribbean colonies
A ship's captain in the conquest fleets
A gold-mine overseer in the Cuban interior
context: Las Casas held an encomienda — a royal grant of Native laborers forced to work his land — and even owned African slaves, and had served as a chaplain on the 1513 conquest of Cuba. That he had once lived off the very system he later condemned gave his attacks on it a weight no outsider's could match. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartolomé_de_las_Casas

question: In 1514, the settler Bartolomé de las Casas — who still owned Native laborers himself — was preparing a sermon when a single line of Scripture struck him so hard he freed his slaves and changed his life forever. The verse said an offering made from goods taken wrongfully is worthless. How did that verse end?
answer: 'The bread of the needy is the life of the poor.'
choices: 'The bread of the needy is the life of the poor.'
'What you do to the least of these, you do to me.'
'The laborer is worthy of his wages.'
'Let justice roll down like waters.'
context: The line was from Sirach 34: an offering 'from what has been wrongfully obtained' is blemished, for 'the bread of the needy is the life of the poor.' Las Casas read it as God Himself condemning the encomienda, gave up his own laborers, and never turned back. Source: uscatholic.org, 'The conversion of Bartolomé de las Casas'

question: Early in his crusade, Bartolomé de las Casas made one suggestion he would spend the rest of his life regretting: to spare Native laborers, he proposed bringing enslaved Africans to the colonies instead. Years later, writing his 'History of the Indies,' he confronted his own mistake in print. What did Las Casas conclude?
answer: That African slavery was every bit as unjust as Native slavery
choices: That African slavery was every bit as unjust as Native slavery
That he had damned his own soul beyond any forgiveness
That Spain should abandon the colonies altogether
That he himself deserved to be enslaved in recompense
context: He wrote that he 'soon repented and judged myself guilty of ignorance,' recognizing that 'black slavery was as unjust as Indian slavery.' That he condemned his own worst idea in writing is part of why historians read him as honest rather than self-serving. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartolomé_de_las_Casas (Historia de las Indias, Vol. II)

question: To shock the conscience of Prince Philip, Bartolomé de las Casas wrote down the atrocities he had witnessed in a book, 'A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies' (1552). In one passage he described Spaniards building gallows sized to hang Native people in batches and lighting fires beneath them — and gave the blasphemous reason they offered for choosing that exact number. How many did each gallows hang at once, and why?
answer: Thirteen — in honor of Christ and his twelve Apostles
choices: Thirteen — in honor of Christ and his twelve Apostles
Seven — one for each of the deadly sins
Twelve — one for each month they had labored
Forty — for the days Christ fasted in the desert
context: Las Casas recorded that they hanged the Taíno thirteen at a time — 'in honour and reverence (as they said blasphemously) of our Redeemer and his Twelve Apostles' — then lit fires beneath them. Dressing mass murder in the language of devotion was, to Las Casas, the deepest horror of all. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Short_Account_of_the_Destruction_of_the_Indies

question: In 1550 the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V summoned a remarkable gathering at Valladolid — the first time in European history that a public assembly was called to judge whether a conquered people had any rights at all. The scholar Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda opened by arguing his side for three hours. Then the friar Bartolomé de las Casas rose to answer, and kept going. For how long did Las Casas read out his reply?
answer: Five days straight
choices: Five days straight
Six straight hours
Two straight days
Half a day
context: Against Sepúlveda's three hours, Las Casas read aloud from his written 'Apologia' for five days running. Oddly, the two men never argued face to face — they addressed the judges in separate sessions. The Dominican Domingo de Soto wrote a neutral summary, and the panel deliberated privately but never issued a verdict, so both sides claimed they had won. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valladolid_debate

question: While Las Casas fought in the field, a Dominican professor at the University of Salamanca named Francisco de Vitoria built the legal case in the lecture hall. In his 1539 lecture 'On the American Indians,' Vitoria argued that the Native peoples truly OWNED their lands, 'just like Christians.' He then made a claim startling for his day about the one authority everyone assumed could simply hand the New World to Spain. What did Vitoria argue?
answer: Not even the Pope had the authority to give away their lands
choices: Not even the Pope had the authority to give away their lands
Only a council of bishops could approve such a transfer
The land belonged to whichever crown first mapped it
The Emperor alone could redistribute conquered territory
context: Vitoria called the Indians 'veri domini' — true owners — and ruled that not even the Pope could give away other people's lands. He went on to knock down the other excuses for conquest one by one, arguing that mere unbelief 'does not render it lawful to make war on them.' His vision of a 'republic of the whole world' under a law of nations made him a father of international law. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_de_Vitoria

question: The Salamanca thinkers' ideas reached their boldest form in the Jesuit Francisco Suárez. In his 1612 work 'On Laws,' Suárez took on a belief most of Europe held without question — the 'divine right of kings,' the idea that a king's power comes straight from God to him alone. Suárez argued that political power does come from God, but by a completely different route. Where, said Suárez, does a king's authority actually begin?
answer: From God to the people, who then consent to be governed
choices: From God to the people, who then consent to be governed
From the eldest bloodline God has chosen to rule
From the Church, which crowns kings in God's name
From conquest, which God permits the strong to keep
context: Suárez argued power flows from God to the PEOPLE, who consent to be governed — and who, in extreme cases, may depose a tyrant. This Salamanca-rooted idea of popular sovereignty would echo through later political thought, including the arguments that justified resisting absolute kings. Source: iep.utm.edu/suarez/

question: Bartolomé de las Casas's great opponent at Valladolid, the humanist scholar Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda, argued that Native Americans were 'natural slaves' — leaning on Aristotle's old idea that some people are born to be ruled — and that conquering them was therefore just. He laid it all out in a book called 'Democrates Alter.' But before the debate even began, Spain's two greatest universities, Salamanca and Alcalá, passed their own judgment on that book. What did they do?
answer: Refused to license it for publication
choices: Refused to license it for publication
Ordered every copy publicly burned
Demanded he rewrite it in Latin
Awarded it their highest honor
context: Salamanca and Alcalá refused to license the book — the establishment's own universities would not let Sepúlveda's case for conquest be printed. Las Casas's reply was that even if a few simple people fit Aristotle's 'natural slave,' such people existed in Spain too, so it could never justify enslaving whole nations — and Domingo de Soto, summarizing, sided against the natural-slavery doctrine. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Ginés_de_Sepúlveda

question: In 1940, four teenagers exploring the woods near Montignac in southwest France slipped down a hole beside an uprooted tree and dropped into a hidden chamber whose walls were covered in painted animals — the cave now called Lascaux. What had led them to that hole in the first place?
answer: A dog named Robot
choices: A dog named Robot
A fox named Renard
A goat named Bisou
A horse named Comet
context: On September 12, 1940, the boys (the first one down was 18-year-old Marcel Ravidat) followed a dog named Robot down the hole. The paintings inside are roughly 17,000 years old. Source: iflscience.com (2024); history.com, This Day in History, Sept 12.

question: When Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola showed scholars the herd of bison painted on the ceiling of the Altamira cave in Spain in 1880, they refused to believe ancient cave people had made them and accused him of a fraud. What about the bison convinced the experts they had to be a modern forgery?
answer: The paintings were too skillful and too well-preserved to be ancient
choices: The paintings were too skillful and too well-preserved to be ancient
The cave floor held coins stamped with a recent date
A local painter confessed to sketching them for money
The pigments smelled of fresh oil paint still drying
context: Sautuola's eight-year-old daughter María, small enough to look straight up, first spotted the bison overhead in 1879. Scholars ridiculed him at the 1880 Lisbon Prehistoric Congress — the work was simply too good to be 'primitive,' and Sautuola couldn't explain the lack of soot on the walls. He died in 1888 still disbelieved; in 1902 his loudest doubter, Emile Cartailhac, publicly confessed his error. The ceiling is now called the 'Sistine Chapel of Paleolithic Art.' Source: en.wikipedia.org, Cave of Altamira; britannica.com.

question: In 1204 the soldiers of the Fourth Crusade smashed and looted Constantinople and carried their plunder home to Venice. Their single most spectacular prize -- four life-size figures cast in gilded bronze, ripped from the top of the city's great racing-arena -- was bolted up over the front of St. Mark's Basilica, where it still stands today. What did the Venetians mount above the door?
answer: A team of four bronze horses
choices: A team of four bronze horses
A pair of bronze temple doors
A golden bronze sun-disc
A bronze statue of an emperor
context: The Horses of Saint Mark are the only surviving four-horse chariot team (quadriga) in bronze from the ancient world. Crusaders looted them from the Hippodrome, Constantinople's chariot-racing stadium, in 1204. To ship them, workers severed the heads -- then hid the cuts by fastening collars around the horses' necks, collars you can still see. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horses_of_Saint_Mark

question: The Fourth Crusade set out to fight for Jerusalem by first invading Muslim-held Egypt -- yet it never reached the Holy Land and never traded a single blow with any Muslim army. Instead, in April 1204, the crusading army turned its swords on the largest and wealthiest Christian city on earth, storming its walls and looting and killing for three days. Which Christian city did these Crusaders sack?
answer: Constantinople
choices: Constantinople
Jerusalem
Antioch
Alexandria
context: Constantinople, capital of the Christian Byzantine Empire, fell to fellow Christians on April 12-15, 1204. The Crusaders then crowned one of their own, Baldwin of Flanders, as emperor rather than restoring a Byzantine ruler. Pope John Paul II formally apologized for the sack 800 years later, in 2004. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Constantinople_(1204)

question: After leading the wars that drove Spain out of South America, Simon Bolivar was honored with a single sweeping title that he carried for the rest of his life. What was he called?
answer: The Liberator
choices: The Liberator
The Conqueror
The Protector
The Emperor
context: Bolivar earned the title 'the Liberator' for leading the fight that freed six future nations from Spanish rule: Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Panama, and Bolivia. Bolivia is named after him. https://www.britannica.com/event/Guayaquil-Conference

question: In 1817 Jose de San Martin marched an army 500 km over the freezing peaks of the Andes to surprise the Spanish holding Chile, a feat so audacious that historians compare it to one ancient general's legendary march over the mountains into Italy. Which ancient crossing is San Martin's compared to?
answer: Hannibal crossing the Alps
choices: Hannibal crossing the Alps
Caesar crossing the Rubicon
Xerxes bridging the Hellespont
Alexander crossing the Hydaspes
context: San Martin's Army of the Andes departed the El Plumerillo camp near Mendoza on January 19, 1817 and entered Santiago on February 13 -- a 21-day crossing at elevations averaging 3,000 meters, compared to Hannibal's Alpine march. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossing_of_the_Andes

question: To haul men, guns, and supplies over the Andes, Jose de San Martin's Army of the Andes leaned overwhelmingly on one kind of pack animal -- they gathered roughly 9,000 of them, far outnumbering the horses and cattle. Which animal carried the army over the mountains?
answer: Mules
choices: Mules
Camels
Oxen
Elephants
context: The crossing needed roughly 9,000 mules, about 1,600 horses, and hundreds of cattle; the army even learned to cast its own cannons. Roughly a third of the 4,000 soldiers were lost on the crossing. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_of_the_Andes

question: Two years after San Martin's crossing, Simon Bolivar attempted his own impossible march in 1819, leading about 2,400 men through swamps and over a freezing pass the Spanish were sure no army could ever take. He sprang the trap on August 7, 1819, crushing the royalists and capturing their commander in a battle that opened the road to Bogota. What was this decisive battle?
answer: The Battle of Boyaca
choices: The Battle of Boyaca
The Battle of Carabobo
The Battle of Ayacucho
The Battle of Junin
context: After crossing the Paramo de Pisba, Bolivar's victory at Boyaca captured about 1,800 prisoners including the Spanish commander; three days later he marched into Bogota and was hailed as the Liberator of New Granada. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Boyac%C3%A1

question: In July 1822 the continent's two great liberators, Simon Bolivar and Jose de San Martin, met face to face at Guayaquil to decide South America's future. They quarreled over what kind of governments the freed colonies should have: Bolivar wanted republics modeled on the United States, while San Martin pushed for the opposite. What kind of government did San Martin argue the new nations should adopt?
answer: Constitutional monarchies under a European prince
choices: Constitutional monarchies under a European prince
Direct democracies run by town assemblies
A single empire ruled by Bolivar
Military councils of the liberating generals
context: San Martin even proposed bringing a European prince to be King of Peru. Soon after the secret Guayaquil Conference of July 26-27, 1822 -- held with no witnesses and a vow that no record be kept -- San Martin quietly handed everything over to Bolivar and left South America for good. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guayaquil_Conference

question: Simon Bolivar freed half a continent, yet his dream of one united Gran Colombia fell apart as region after region broke away. Dying of tuberculosis in 1830, the bitter Liberator summed up his despair in a single famous line about the futility of his life's work. What did he write?
answer: 'He who serves a revolution is plowing the sea'
choices: 'He who serves a revolution is plowing the sea'
'I die without seeing the dawn I fought for'
'A king's crown was always within my reach'
'The mountains alone were honest with me'
context: Weeks before his death on December 17, 1830, the disillusioned Bolivar wrote that 'America is ungovernable' and that 'he who serves a revolution is plowing the sea.' https://www.history.com/articles/simon-bolivar-liberator-south-america-venezuela

question: Antoine Lavoisier set out to test the reigning theory of his day — phlogiston, an invisible 'fire-stuff' that was supposed to escape from anything as it burned, which meant a burned thing should end up lighter. He sealed a metal in a vessel, weighed it, burned it, and weighed it again. What did his balance actually show happened to the metal's weight?
answer: It weighed more than before it burned.
choices: It weighed more than before it burned.
It weighed less than before it burned.
It weighed the same as before it burned.
It weighed almost nothing after it burned.
context: The metal GAINED weight because burning is the metal combining with oxygen from the air, not losing a fire-stuff. That weight increase was the death blow to phlogiston theory and helped Lavoisier establish that in a chemical change matter is neither created nor destroyed. Source: https://study.com/academy/lesson/antoine-lavoisier-atomic-theory-contribution.html

question: Antoine Lavoisier had turned chemistry into a science of the balance, but on 8 May 1794, during the Reign of Terror, the Revolution he had served sent him to the guillotine — not for his science, but because he had once helped collect the king's taxes. The day after the blade fell, the great mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange mourned the loss in a single famous line. What did Lagrange say?
answer: It took them only an instant to cut off that head, but a hundred years may not produce another like it.
choices: It took them only an instant to cut off that head, but a hundred years may not produce another like it.
France has murdered her finest mind today, and history itself will never forgive this blade.
They have silenced the one balance that weighed the whole world; let no man call this justice.
A nation that beheads its own scholars has surely signed the warrant for its own ruin.
context: Lagrange's actual words: 'It took them only an instant to cut off that head, and a hundred years may not suffice to reproduce its like' ('Il ne leur a fallu qu'un moment pour faire tomber cette tête, et cent années peut-être ne suffiront pas pour en reproduire une semblable'). Lavoisier was 50; his father-in-law Jacques Paulze went to the same blade just ahead of him. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine_Lavoisier

question: In 1917 the Ottoman guns guarding the Red Sea port of Aqaba all pointed out to sea, ready for any ship that dared approach. T. E. Lawrence and the Howeitat chieftain Auda abu Tayi took the town anyway. How did they beat those fixed seaward guns?
answer: They crossed hundreds of miles of open desert and stormed the port from its undefended landward side
choices: They crossed hundreds of miles of open desert and stormed the port from its undefended landward side
They smuggled men aboard fishing boats and seized the harbor guns at dawn
They shelled the fortress from warships until the garrison ran out of water
They tunneled beneath the walls and blew open the seaward gate with mines
context: The march began on 9 May 1917 with about 45 Howeitat and Ageyl camel men and swelled to roughly 1,000 as desert tribes joined; Aqaba surrendered on 6 July 1917. The decisive fight was inland at Aba el Lissan, where Auda's charge wiped out the Ottoman force for the loss of only two Arab dead. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Aqaba ; smithsonianmag.com/history/true-story-lawrence-arabia-180951857

question: As T. E. Lawrence fought beside the Arabs in the desert revolt, Britain had pledged them their independence once the Ottomans were beaten. Yet the year before, in May 1916, Britain and France had quietly signed the Sykes-Picot Agreement. What did that secret deal actually do to the lands the Arabs were fighting to free?
answer: It divided the Ottoman Arab lands between Britain and France as their own spheres
choices: It divided the Ottoman Arab lands between Britain and France as their own spheres
It promised the same territory twice over to both the Arabs and the Russians
It handed every Ottoman province to a new League of Nations to govern jointly
It pledged the entire region to a single independent Arab kingdom under Hussein
context: The Arabs only learned of the carve-up when the new Soviet government published the secret text in late 1917. The lines drawn by Mark Sykes and Francois Georges-Picot helped seed the borders and grievances of the modern Middle East, contradicting the independence promised in the McMahon-Hussein letters. Source: britannica.com/event/Sykes-Picot-Agreement ; theconversation.com/what-was-the-sykes-picot-agreement-246332

question: Georges Lemaitre, a Belgian Catholic priest who wore a Roman collar, worked out in 1927 that the whole universe is expanding. When he explained the idea to Albert Einstein at a conference in Brussels, Einstein admitted the priest's math was correct -- but what did Einstein say about the physics?
answer: That his physics was 'abominable.'
choices: That his physics was 'abominable.'
That his physics was 'preposterous.'
That his physics was 'unconvincing.'
That his physics was 'muddled.'
context: Einstein's full reply in 1927 was 'Your calculations are correct, but your physics is abominable' (French: 'Vos calculs sont corrects, mais votre physique est abominable'). He came around: in 1933, after hearing Lemaitre present the theory in California, Einstein stood up and applauded, calling it 'the most beautiful and satisfactory explanation of creation to which I have ever listened.' The father of the Big Bang was a priest. Sources: catholiceducation.org 'A Day Without Yesterday'; bigthink.com/13-8/lemaitre-priest-proved-einstein-wrong.

question: In 1951 Pope Pius XII announced that the new Big Bang theory seemed to prove the creation story in the book of Genesis. The scientist who had first proposed the Big Bang was Georges Lemaitre -- who was himself a Catholic priest. What did Lemaitre do about the Pope's announcement?
answer: He quietly persuaded the Pope to drop the claim.
choices: He quietly persuaded the Pope to drop the claim.
He publicly thanked the Pope for his support.
He pushed the Pope to make it Church doctrine.
He resigned his priesthood in open protest.
context: Lemaitre, the priest, argued that a scientific theory must never be used to prove -- or disprove -- a matter of faith, and he privately convinced Pius XII to stop making the claim. He had imagined the universe beginning as a single super-dense 'primeval atom' that shattered and expanded; shortly before he died in 1966 he learned that Penzias and Wilson had detected the cosmic microwave background, the leftover glow that confirmed his idea. Sources: inters.org/pius-xii-lemaitre; vaticanobservatory.org 'Priests in Science: Georges Lemaitre.'

question: The Soviet secret police set up their first big prison camp in 1923 on freezing islands in the White Sea, and gave it the short name SLON. By an odd coincidence, that same word SLON is the ordinary Russian word for what animal?
answer: An elephant
choices: An elephant
A bear
A wolf
A fox
context: SLON stood for the Solovetsky Camp of Special Purpose, built inside an ancient Russian Orthodox monastery on the Solovetsky Islands; the acronym just happens to spell the Russian word for 'elephant.' Source: Anne Applebaum, Gulag: A History (erenow.org/modern/gulagahistoryanneapplebaum/4.php).

question: Lenin's new secret police, the Cheka, was created in December 1917 to hunt down enemies of the revolution, and its first chief Felix Dzerzhinsky ran it from the Lubyanka building in Moscow. His feared reputation earned him a one-word nickname that stuck for the rest of Soviet history. What was it?
answer: Iron Felix
choices: Iron Felix
Red Felix
Black Felix
Steel Felix
context: The Cheka's full name was the All-Russian Extraordinary Commission for Combating Counter-Revolution and Sabotage; 'Iron Felix' Dzerzhinsky headed it from the Lubyanka. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheka.

question: On 30 August 1918 a woman named Fanny Kaplan shot and wounded Lenin as he left a Moscow factory, and the shock of it triggered the official Red Terror. Kaplan was not a monarchist but a member of a rival socialist party. When interrogators asked her why she did it, what did she tell them?
answer: I shot Lenin because I consider him a traitor to the Revolution
choices: I shot Lenin because I consider him a traitor to the Revolution
I shot Lenin because he made a shameful peace with the Germans
I shot Lenin to avenge the murdered Tsar and his children
I shot Lenin on the orders of the British and their spies
context: Fanny Kaplan was a Socialist Revolutionary; she told interrogators 'I shot Lenin... I consider him a traitor to the Revolution' and was executed days later. The same day, Petrograd's Cheka chief Moisei Uritsky was assassinated. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Terror.

question: In a July 1918 newspaper interview, Felix Dzerzhinsky was asked plainly what his Cheka secret police was actually for. What did Dzerzhinsky answer?
answer: We stand for organized terror -- it is absolutely necessary in revolution
choices: We stand for organized terror -- it is absolutely necessary in revolution
We act only on solid proof and only against the truly guilty
We guard the people against ordinary criminals and foreign spies
We serve as the sword and shield of the honest workers' state
context: In an interview in Novaya Zhizn (14 July 1918) Dzerzhinsky said: 'We stand for organized terror -- this should be frankly admitted. Terror is an absolute necessity during times of revolution.' Source: spartacus-educational.com/RUSterror.htm.

question: New prisoners stumbling off the boats at a remote prison camp on an island in the freezing White Sea were met by the commander with a single chilling sentence, meant to strip away every right they thought they still had. What did he tell them?
answer: Here there is no Soviet power -- only Solovetsky power
choices: Here there is no Soviet power -- only Solovetsky power
Here the law of the old Tsar no longer protects you
Here you will work hard and one day return to your home
Here every man stands equal before the revolution
context: The camp was Solovki; the greeting -- that even Soviet law did not reach here, only the camp's own authority -- became its grim motto. Source: Anne Applebaum, Gulag: A History (erenow.org/modern/gulagahistoryanneapplebaum/4.php).

question: The worst punishment block at the Solovki camp was Sekirka, an old hilltop church reached by climbing 365 wooden steps. Survivors remembered one torment above all others: for as long as 18 hours at a stretch, prisoners were forced to do what?
answer: Sit dead still on a thin pole with their feet off the floor
choices: Sit dead still on a thin pole with their feet off the floor
Stand at rigid attention facing a bare stone wall
Kneel on the freezing stone with both arms held up
Lie face-down and motionless on the cold church floor
context: At Sekirka prisoners were also left tied and stripped in unheated bell towers in the Arctic winter, and some were thrown down the 365 steps as staged 'accidents.' Source: Anne Applebaum, Gulag: A History (erenow.org/modern/gulagahistoryanneapplebaum/4.php).

question: Metropolitan Vladimir of Kiev was the first bishop the Bolsheviks killed -- beaten and dragged outside the Monastery of the Caves on 25 January 1918. As his captors hauled him from the monastery, Vladimir did something that became the story people told ever after. What did he do?
answer: Prayed for his killers to be forgiven
choices: Prayed for his killers to be forgiven
Called down God's judgment upon them
Sang a psalm as they dragged him out
Shouted out the names of his killers
context: Vladimir was beaten and shot on 25 January 1918, praying for his killers to be forgiven before he died. Between mid-1918 and early 1919, Bolshevik forces killed 1 metropolitan, 18 bishops, and over 100 priests. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-religious_campaign_during_the_Russian_Civil_War_(1917-1921).

question: In August 1918 Lenin sent a telegram to officials in Penza, ordering them to hang at least one hundred 'kulaks' in public 'so that the people might see and tremble' and to publish the victims' names. Then he added a postscript. What did Lenin's P.S. say?
answer: Find some tougher people
choices: Find some tougher people
Spare the women and the children
Send me word when it is done
Burn their farms to the ground
context: Lenin's order said to hang 'no fewer than one hundred known kulaks, fatcats, bloodsuckers' in full view 'so that for hundreds of miles around the people might see and tremble,' and closed: 'Yours, Lenin. P.S. Find some tougher people.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenin's_hanging_order (U.S. Library of Congress translation).

question: People often picture the Soviet system of mass imprisonment as Stalin's invention of the 1930s. In fact the government's own decree 'On Red Terror,' issued on 5 September 1918, already spelled out in plain words what should be done with 'class enemies.' What did that 1918 decree order?
answer: Isolate them in concentration camps
