He ruled that William Marbury truly deserved his commission and had been wronged — but then declared the Court had no power to order it delivered, because the very law letting Marbury sue there clashed with the Constitution. By giving away that small power, the Court claimed a far greater one for the first time. What power did the Court seize?
answer: To strike down an act of Congress as void
choices: To strike down an act of Congress as void
To order the President to appoint new judges
To remove a sitting Secretary of State from office
To rewrite a law that Congress had passed badly
context: This is judicial review — the authority of the Supreme Court to declare a law passed by Congress unconstitutional and refuse to enforce it. Marbury v. Madison was the first time the Court struck down an act of Congress (Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789) as void. Marshall: 'No legislative act... contrary to the Constitution, can be valid.' Source: https://www.fjc.gov/history/cases/cases-that-shaped-the-federal-courts/marbury-v-madison

question: Marco Polo lay dying in Venice in 1324, and his friends gathered at his bed begging him to save his soul by admitting that the wonders in his famous book had all been lies. According to the story, what did the old traveler say back to them?
answer: "I have not told half of what I saw."
choices: "I have not told half of what I saw."
"Forgive me, for I have deceived you all."
"Burn the book and forget my name."
"The Khan himself will avenge these words."
context: On his deathbed (he died Jan 8, 1324), friends urged Marco Polo to confess his book was full of lies; he refused with this line. Recorded as tradition, so it is told as legend, not a verified quote. Source: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Marco_Polo ; 'The Travels of Marco Polo, the Venetian' (J.M. Dent, 1926).

question: When the Polos left Kublai Khan's court to journey home across the whole Mongol empire, the Khan gave them a foot-long object inscribed with a warning: anyone who refused to honor its bearers should be killed. Everywhere they showed it, officials had to hand over horses, food, and lodging. What did this object work as for the travelers?
answer: A passport that commanded help across the empire
choices: A passport that commanded help across the empire
A map of every road back to Venice
A treaty ending the wars along the route
A list of the Khan's enemies to avoid
context: The golden tablet, a paiza about a foot long and three inches wide, was a magic passport across the Mongol empire. Its inscription read: 'By the strength of the eternal Heaven, holy be the Khan's name. Let him that pays him not reverence be killed.' Source: https://erenow.org/biographies/marco-polo-from-venice-to-xanadu/3.php

question: In his book Marco Polo described a strange thing the people of Cathay dug out of beds in the mountains in lumps and then set on fire to heat their homes. Most Europeans had never heard of such a thing and could hardly believe a rock would burn. What was this fuel that Polo called 'black stones'?
answer: Coal
choices: Coal
Amber
Charcoal made from oak
Dried river mud
context: Polo amazed Europe by describing coal, then unknown to most Europeans. His chapter was titled 'Concerning the Black Stones That Are Dug in Cathay, and Are Burnt for Fuel,' and he marveled that lumps kindled at night were 'still alight in the morning.' Source: https://factsanddetails.com/china/cat2/4sub8/entry-5456.html

question: Marco Polo never actually wrote down his own famous book. After Venice lost a sea battle to Genoa, he was thrown in a Genoese prison in 1298, and there he told his adventures aloud while someone else put them on paper. Who was that writer who took down Polo's tale?
answer: A fellow prisoner, the romance-writer Rustichello of Pisa
choices: A fellow prisoner, the romance-writer Rustichello of Pisa
A monk sent by the Pope to record him
His own father, Niccolo Polo
A scribe in the service of Kublai Khan
context: Captured after the naval defeat, Marco Polo dictated his travels to his cellmate Rustichello da Pisa, a writer of Arthurian romances, who wrote it all down (Genoa prison, 1298-1299). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Travels_of_Marco_Polo ; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/polo-marco/

question: Marco Polo reported that Kublai Khan paid for things across his whole empire with sheets made from the bark of the mulberry tree, pressed flat and stamped with the Khan's red seal — and refusing to take them was punished by death. Because the Khan could spend tree bark as if it were treasure, what did Polo say the Khan possessed?
answer: The secret of the alchemists
choices: The secret of the alchemists
The blessing of the eternal Heaven
A mountain of buried gold
The loyalty of every merchant
context: Polo described Kublai Khan's paper money, made from mulberry bark stamped in red vermilion, and said the Khan thereby 'possessed the secret of the alchemists' because he could make money out of tree bark. Source: https://factsanddetails.com/china/cat2/4sub8/entry-5456.html ; https://fee.org/articles/marco-polo-on-money/

question: On December 12, 1901, Guglielmo Marconi and his assistant George Kemp stood on Signal Hill in Newfoundland, holding a receiving wire aloft on a kite in the wind, straining to catch a signal beamed more than 2,000 miles across the Atlantic from Cornwall. The faint taps in Marconi's earpiece spelled out a single Morse letter, sent over and over. Which letter was it?
answer: S
choices: S
E
T
A
context: Marconi heard the letter 'S' — three faint dots in Morse. They chose 'S' on purpose: three quick dots were the easiest pattern to pick out of the Atlantic static at extreme range. (An earlier balloon antenna had blown away in the gale, so the kite was the improvised fix to get the wire high.) Some later scientists doubted the 1901 reception was even physically possible at that wavelength and wondered if Marconi heard lightning static instead of the real signal — an honest doubt, while the milestone still stands. Source: https://ethw.org/Milestones:Reception_of_Transatlantic_Radio_Signals,_1901

question: On Christmas Eve 1906, wireless operators on U.S. Navy and United Fruit Company ships far out in the Atlantic sat at their sets expecting the usual Morse code — the dots-and-dashes clicking that was all radio had ever carried. Then, from Reginald Fessenden's station at Brant Rock, Massachusetts, something none of them had heard before came out of their headphones. What did the astonished operators suddenly hear?
answer: A human voice and a violin
choices: A human voice and a violin
A faster string of Morse code
A ship's bell ringing the hour
A burst of crackling static
context: Fessenden made the leap from code to sound: he played Handel's 'Largo' on a phonograph, played 'O Holy Night' on his own violin and sang, and read from the Bible — the first broadcast of voice and music. Men used to hearing only clicks suddenly had a human voice in their ears, hundreds of miles out at sea. Source: https://ethw.org/Milestones:First_Wireless_Radio_Broadcast_by_Reginald_A._Fessenden,_1906

question: The boy who became emperor Marcus Aurelius was born Marcus Annius Verus - and 'Verus' meant 'true.' The old emperor Hadrian, charmed by how serious and honest the boy was, played on that name with a nickname that stuck. What did Hadrian call him?
answer: Verissimus, 'the truest'
choices: Verissimus, 'the truest'
Optimus, 'the best'
Probus, 'the upright'
Pius, 'the dutiful'
context: Hadrian punned on the boy's family name Verus ('true') to call him Verissimus, 'the truest' or 'most truthful' - a sign of how seriously honest the young Marcus already seemed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Aurelius

question: It is strange that we can read the Meditations at all: the most powerful man in the world, Marcus Aurelius, scribbled it as private jottings and gave it no title, never publishing a word. Centuries later, copyists added a plain two-word Greek heading that stuck: 'Ta eis heauton.' What does that Greek phrase mean?
answer: 'To Himself'
choices: 'To Himself'
'Notes by Night'
'A Soldier's Diary'
'The Emperor's Book'
context: 'Ta eis heauton' (the Greek heading later added by copyists) literally means 'Things to Himself' or 'To Himself.' Marcus wrote it as a private notebook with no real title, never meaning anyone else to read it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meditations

question: Marcus Aurelius was the Roman emperor and a native Latin speaker. In which language did he write his private notebook, the Meditations?
answer: Greek
choices: Greek
Latin
Egyptian
Aramaic
context: Though he was Rome's emperor and a native Latin speaker, Marcus wrote the Meditations in Greek - the language of philosophy in the ancient world. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meditations

question: A note tucked inside Book 1 of the Meditations records exactly where Marcus Aurelius was sitting when he wrote it: 'in the country of the Quadi, at the Granua,' a river on the empire's edge. For the ruler of the whole Roman world, where was that?
answer: An army tent at the front
choices: An army tent at the front
A captured enemy hill-fort
A torch-lit riverside barge
A frontier supply depot
context: A note in Book 1 records that Marcus wrote 'in the country of the Quadi, at the Granua' - a war tent on the Hron river in modern Slovakia; Book 2 was written at Carnuntum, a fort on the Danube frontier. The most powerful man alive wrote his philosophy on campaign. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meditations

question: In the Meditations, Marcus Aurelius thanks the philosopher Rusticus for the gift that shaped his life most: lending him his personal copy of the teachings of Epictetus, a man who had once been a Roman slave. That single loaned book carried one ancient school of philosophy from a slave to an emperor. Which school was it?
answer: Stoicism
choices: Stoicism
Epicureanism
Cynicism
Platonism
context: Marcus calls Rusticus's loan of Epictetus's discourses the most important gift of his life. Epictetus, born a slave, was a great teacher of Stoicism; that loaned book carried Stoicism from a slave to the emperor - the Athens-to-Rome line of the tradition. Source: iep.utm.edu/marcus-aurelius

question: Marcus Aurelius was the last of Rome's 'Five Good Emperors,' a run of rulers each picked by adoption on merit rather than by blood. Marcus broke that streak himself by handing the empire instead to his own son - who became one of Rome's worst emperors. Who was the son?
answer: Commodus
choices: Commodus
Lucius Verus
Avidius Cassius
Hadrian
context: Marcus ended the merit-by-adoption streak of the Five Good Emperors by leaving the throne to his own son, Commodus, remembered as one of Rome's worst rulers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Aurelius

question: With the treasury drained by plague and endless war, Marcus Aurelius refused to crush his suffering people with higher taxes. Instead he held a weeks-long public auction in Trajan's Forum, selling off the palace treasures to pay his soldiers. What did Marcus put up for sale at this imperial yard sale?
answer: His own wife's silk-and-gold robes
choices: His own wife's silk-and-gold robes
Old Hadrian's marble garden statues
The crown jewels of conquered kings
Slaves taken in the German wars
context: Rather than tax his plague-stricken people harder, Marcus auctioned off imperial treasures in Trajan's Forum - gold and crystal vessels, jewels from Hadrian's private sanctum, and even his own wife's silk-and-gold robes - to fund his army for the German wars. An imperial yard sale. Source: medium.com/of-pasta-and-plagues

question: During Marcus Aurelius's war against the Quadi, the surrounded soldiers of the Thundering Legion were dying of thirst when a sudden downpour broke over them. The historian Cassius Dio describes what the desperate men did as the rain fell. What was it?
answer: They drank and fought at the same time
choices: They drank and fought at the same time
They threw down their shields to surrender
They built a dam to trap the floodwater
They fled the field under cover of the storm
context: Cassius Dio writes that the parched soldiers 'turned their faces upwards and received the water in their mouths,' caught rain in their shields and helmets, and 'drank and fought at the same time' - some gulping rainwater mixed with blood from their own wounds - while hail and thunderbolts struck the enemy. Source: livius.org - Cassius Dio on the Rain Miracle

question: After that life-saving downpour rescued Marcus Aurelius's trapped legion, ancient writers split over who had really summoned the storm. The historian Cassius Dio credited an Egyptian magician in the camp who called on the gods. What rival explanation did the North African writer Tertullian give for the very same rain?
answer: The prayers of the legion's Christian soldiers
choices: The prayers of the legion's Christian soldiers
A sacrifice burned on the altar of Jupiter
A vow Marcus swore to the goddess Minerva
A spell cast by a captured Quadi shaman
context: Cassius Dio credited an Egyptian magician named Harnouphis, who summoned the god Mercury; Tertullian claimed the storm answered the prayers of Christian soldiers in the legion. Same storm, rival miracle stories. Source: livius.org - Cassius Dio on the Rain Miracle

question: When the general Avidius Cassius rebelled and declared himself emperor on a false rumor that Marcus Aurelius had died, his own officers soon killed him and a centurion brought the rebel's severed head to Marcus. How did the philosopher-emperor respond to the trophy?
answer: He refused to look at it and had it buried
choices: He refused to look at it and had it buried
He had it displayed on the Forum gates
He sent it back to Cassius's family in disgrace
He kept it as proof of the traitor's fate
context: Cassius's revolt lasted three months and six days before his officers killed him. When the centurion brought his head, Marcus refused even to look at it and ordered it buried; sources say he had hoped Cassius would be taken alive so he could show mercy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avidius_Cassius

question: More than twenty bronze statues of Roman emperors were melted down for coins over the centuries, but Marcus Aurelius's giant bronze horseman survived - the only one of a pre-Christian emperor still standing. It was spared only because medieval Christians wrongly believed it showed a different, beloved ruler. Who did they think it was?
answer: Constantine, the first Christian emperor
choices: Constantine, the first Christian emperor
Julius Caesar, the first dictator
Augustus, the first Roman emperor
Charlemagne, the first Holy Roman Emperor
context: Medieval Christians spared the statue because they mistook the rider for Constantine, the first Christian emperor; more than twenty other bronze emperor-statues were melted down for coin. It is the only surviving full bronze statue of a pre-Christian Roman emperor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equestrian_statue_of_Marcus_Aurelius

question: One of the most quoted 'Marcus Aurelius' lines is 'What we do in life echoes in eternity' - printed on posters and credited to the Stoic emperor himself. But those words are not his at all. Where do they really come from?
answer: A blockbuster movie about a Roman general
choices: A blockbuster movie about a Roman general
A Renaissance forgery of a lost letter
A Victorian book of moral self-help
A medieval monk's collection of sayings
context: The line was written for the 2000 film Gladiator and given to the fictional general Maximus - not the real Marcus Aurelius. His genuine lines run plainer, like 'Waste no more time arguing about what a good man should be. Be one.' Labeled as legend because it is a popular misattribution, not a real quote. Source: en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Marcus_Aurelius

question: Marie and Pierre Curie discovered a brand-new element and got to name it. Marie chose a name to honor her homeland, a country that had been swallowed up by its neighbors and wiped right off the map of Europe. Which country did she name the element after?
answer: Poland
choices: Poland
Russia
Bohemia
Lithuania
context: They named it POLONIUM, 'after the name of the country of origin of one of us.' At the time Poland had been partitioned among Russia, Germany, and Austria and erased from the map, so naming an element for it was a defiant patriotic act. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/themes/marie-and-pierre-curie-and-the-discovery-of-polonium-and-radium/

question: Marie Curie was studying the strange, invisible rays that pour out of elements like uranium and radium, and there was no word for what these elements were doing. So she invented one. What new word did Marie Curie coin for this?
answer: Radioactivity
choices: Radioactivity
Luminescence
Phosphorescence
Fluorescence
context: Marie Curie coined the very word 'radioactivity' to describe the rays given off by elements like uranium, polonium, and radium. It is now used everywhere, but she made it up. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Curie

question: Marie Curie wrote that one of her greatest joys was to slip into her workroom late at night and look at the test tubes of radium she had made. What did the test tubes do that delighted her?
answer: Glowed on their own
choices: Glowed on their own
Froze solid
Floated upward
Changed color
context: Radium glows in the dark. In her biography of her husband, 'Pierre Curie,' Marie described seeing 'on all sides the feebly luminous silhouettes' of the tubes — 'the glowing tubes looked like faint, fairy lights.' Source: https://womenslegacyproject.com/iconic-f-fairy-lights-marie-curie/

question: During World War I, Marie Curie built a fleet of about twenty trucks fitted with X-ray machines and drove them to the front so doctors could find bullets and shrapnel inside wounded soldiers. What affectionate nickname did the soldiers give these trucks?
answer: The petites Curies (Little Curies)
choices: The petites Curies (Little Curies)
The radium wagons
The bullet-finders
The iron angels
context: Soldiers called them the 'petites Curies.' Marie taught herself to drive and repair the vehicles, trained 150 women to operate them, and over one million wounded soldiers were helped. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/how-marie-curie-brought-x-ray-machines-to-battlefield-180965240/

question: Hundreds of people have won a Nobel Prize, and a handful have even won two. But Marie Curie holds a record that, to this day, no one else has ever matched. What did she alone achieve?
answer: Won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences
choices: Won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences
Won Nobel Prizes in three different sciences
Won a Nobel Prize on three separate occasions
Won a Nobel Prize and refused two others
context: Marie Curie won Physics in 1903 (with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel) and Chemistry in 1911 (for discovering polonium and radium). She is the only person ever to win Nobels in two different sciences, and was also the first woman ever to win a Nobel at all. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/1911/marie-curie/facts/

question: To prove radium was real, Marie Curie spent four years boiling, stirring, and sifting roughly seven tons of pitchblende ore — by hand, in a shed. After all that backbreaking work, how much pure radium did she manage to pull out of those seven tons?
answer: About one-tenth of a gram
choices: About one-tenth of a gram
About two kilograms
About half a pound
About fifty grams
context: Seven tons of ore slag yielded just one-tenth of a gram of pure radium chloride, in 1902. Marie wrote of the labor: 'I had to spend a whole day mixing a boiling mass with a heavy iron rod nearly as large as myself.' Source: https://www.kroneckerwallis.com/four-years-in-a-shed-how-marie-curie-isolated-radium/

question: Marie Curie made one of history's greatest discoveries not in a grand laboratory but in a borrowed shed. When the famous chemist Wilhelm Ostwald saw the place where she worked, how did he describe it?
answer: A cross between a stable and a potato shed
choices: A cross between a stable and a potato shed
A drafty cellar fit only for storing coal
A cramped attic piled high with dusty junk
A crumbling barn with a slowly sagging roof
context: The shed had no ventilation and even let in the rain. Ostwald said that if he had not seen the worktable and apparatus, he 'would have thought I was being played a practical joke.' Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/themes/marie-and-pierre-curie-and-the-discovery-of-polonium-and-radium/

question: As a young woman in Russian-occupied Warsaw, Marie was forbidden to attend university simply because she was female. So she joined secret night classes that kept moving from house to house to dodge the Russian authorities. What was this illegal underground school called?
answer: The Flying University
choices: The Flying University
The Midnight Academy
The Hidden Sorbonne
The Warsaw Free School
context: The 'Flying University' constantly changed locations to evade the police. Later, Marie and her sister Bronya made a pact: Marie worked as a governess to fund Bronya's Paris medical studies, then Bronya funded Marie's turn at the Sorbonne — where Marie graduated first in her physics class. Source: https://www.openculture.com/2016/07/marie-curie-attended-a-secret-underground-flying-university-when-poland-blocked-her-other-women-from-advancing-their-education.html

question: Marie Curie kept glowing vials of radium in her coat pockets and in her desk drawer, with no idea how dangerous they were. In 1934 she died of a disease of the bone marrow. What had made Marie Curie so ill?
answer: The radiation from her own discovery
choices: The radiation from her own discovery
A sudden fever from influenza
A fall in her laboratory
A failing and weakened heart
context: She died on 4 July 1934 of aplastic anaemia, a bone-marrow disease caused by decades of radiation exposure. The very discovery that made her famous is what killed her. Source: https://www.britannica.com/question/How-did-Marie-Curie-die

question: Marie Curie had worked out a method for isolating radium that the whole world wanted, and patenting it could have made her rich. Instead she made a very different choice about her hard-won method. What did Marie Curie decide to do with it?
answer: Refused to patent it so all could use it free
choices: Refused to patent it so all could use it free
Sold it to the highest bidder for a fortune
Patented it and licensed it to companies
Hid it and let the secret die with her
context: Marie deliberately refused to patent the radium-isolation process so the entire scientific and medical community could use it freely. She gave away the secret rather than get rich from it — even though it left her too poor to afford radium herself. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Curie

question: In 1995, more than sixty years after her death, France dug up Marie Curie's body to rebury her with honor in the Panthéon among the nation's greatest minds. When they opened her grave, they discovered an unusual precaution had been taken with her remains. What had she been buried in?
answer: A lead-lined coffin
choices: A lead-lined coffin
A sealed glass case
A solid gold casket
An unmarked wooden box
context: Her remains were still radioactive, so she had been buried in a lead-lined coffin. She was the first woman entombed in the Panthéon on her own merits. Source: https://www.iflscience.com/marie-curies-body-was-so-radioactive-she-was-buried-in-a-lead-lined-coffin-69080

question: Marie and Pierre Curie tested a rock called pitchblende and got a baffling result: the whole rock gave off MORE rays than the pure uranium they could pull out of it. The uranium alone could not account for all that energy. What did the Curies reason must be true?
answer: Hidden, more powerful new elements were inside the rock
choices: Hidden, more powerful new elements were inside the rock
The instruments measuring the rays were broken
The uranium itself was somehow impure and weak
Sunlight was charging the rock with extra energy
context: This reasoning — that something more radioactive than uranium was hidden in the ore — led them to announce polonium and then radium in December 1898. Source: https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/200412/history.cfm

question: In 1948 the economist Ludwig Erhard scrapped Germany's old price controls overnight, freeing prices without first asking the Allied generals who governed occupied Germany. When the American military governor General Lucius Clay confronted him -- "My advisers tell me you're making a terrible mistake" -- how did Erhard answer?
answer: "Don't listen to them, General. My advisers tell me the same thing."
choices: "Don't listen to them, General. My advisers tell me the same thing."
"Then your advisers have never gone hungry, General."
"You may court-martial me, but the order stands."
"History will decide which of us was mistaken."
context: Erhard freed prices and gutted Nazi-era controls on a Sunday in June 1948 on his own authority. His quip to General Lucius Clay became famous because he was admitting his own experts opposed him too -- and pressing on anyway. The gamble launched West Germany's Wirtschaftswunder (economic miracle). Source: fee.org, 'The German Economic Miracle and the Social Market Economy.'

question: For years under price controls, German shopkeepers had hidden their goods rather than sell at fake official prices, and a black market thrived. On a Sunday in June 1948 the economist Ludwig Erhard abolished those price controls overnight and let prices float freely. What happened across West Germany the very next morning?
answer: Hoarded goods reappeared on the store shelves and the black market collapsed.
choices: Hoarded goods reappeared on the store shelves and the black market collapsed.
Riots broke out as prices on bread and coal shot far out of reach.
The Allied generals jailed Erhard and reinstated the old controls.
Shopkeepers kept their goods hidden, distrusting the sudden change.
context: Once merchants could sell at real prices, goods hoarded for years filled the shelves by Monday, June 21, 1948, and the black market vanished almost overnight -- the seen-vs-unseen verdict made visible. West German industrial output jumped from 51% of its 1936 level in May 1948 to 78% by December. Source: econlib.org, 'German Economic Miracle.'

question: On June 5, 1947, U.S. Secretary of State George Marshall first laid out the whole plan to rebuild war-shattered Europe. He gave the press no warning, and even Harvard's president had no idea a major announcement was coming. Where did Marshall unveil one of the most consequential ideas of the century?
answer: In a brief 11-minute commencement speech at Harvard
choices: In a brief 11-minute commencement speech at Harvard
In a televised address from the White House lawn
In a special joint session of the U.S. Congress
In a worldwide radio broadcast carried across Europe
context: Marshall buried it in an unadorned 11-minute graduation talk that nobody expected to matter. One of history's most consequential speeches was almost a throwaway. Source: https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2017/05/70-years-ago-a-harvard-commencement-speech-outlined-the-marshall-plan-and-calmed-a-continent/

question: The U.S. Congress ordered that a red-white-and-blue shield be stamped on every crate of Marshall aid that reached Europe -- every sack of flour, drum of fuel, and machine -- so no one across the ocean could mistake who had sent it. What did the shield say?
answer: Supplied by the United States of America
choices: Supplied by the United States of America
A Gift from the Free Peoples of the World
Property of the United Nations Relief Fund
Donated by the Allied Powers of Europe
context: The full label read 'For European Recovery -- Supplied by the United States of America.' Congress wanted the credit visible on every shipment. Source: https://www.loc.gov/exhibits/marshall/marsh-exhibition.html

question: In 1947, even before the official aid began, ordinary Americans launched the 'Friendship Train' to gather donated food for hungry France and Italy. It left Hollywood with just 8 freight cars -- but people kept piling on food at every stop across the country. How many boxcars had it grown into by the time it reached New York?
answer: 270 boxcars
choices: 45 boxcars
130 boxcars
270 boxcars
540 boxcars
context: Eight cars in Hollywood snowballed into 270 boxcars of supplies by New York -- a grassroots wave of generosity ahead of the government program. Source: https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/in-1947-friendship-train-crossed-us-gathering-food-for-hungry-europe/2019/05/18/95d9aa66-77f9-11e9-b7ae-390de4259661_story.html

question: At Harvard, George Marshall gave the line that became the heart of his plan. America's policy, he said, was directed 'not against any country or doctrine, but against' four enemies. Which four?
answer: Hunger, poverty, desperation and chaos
choices: Hunger, poverty, desperation and chaos
Fascism, hatred, ruin and despair
Tyranny, famine, ignorance and fear
War, plague, want and disorder
context: That one sentence framed the whole program as a fight against suffering itself, not against an enemy nation -- the line most quoted from the speech ever since. Source: https://www.marshallfoundation.org/the-marshall-plan/speech/

question: President Harry Truman believed that putting his own name on the rebuilding bill would kill it -- so he gave the whole thing away to General George Marshall instead. What did Truman expect the general's name to buy him?
answer: The votes of even the worst Republicans in Congress
choices: The votes of even the worst Republicans in Congress
The lasting gratitude of the European public
A guaranteed second term in the White House
The Soviet Union's agreement to take part
context: Truman told an aide that anything bearing his name would 'quiver a couple of times, turn belly up and die,' but 'the worst Republican on the Hill can vote for it if we name it after the General.' Source: https://www.marshallfoundation.org/articles-and-features/the-marshall-plan-in-10-minutes/

question: In 1953 George Marshall received an honor that no other career army general in history has ever won -- given for the plan that rebuilt Europe. Which honor?
answer: The Nobel Peace Prize
choices: The Nobel Peace Prize
The Presidential Medal of Freedom
The Pulitzer Prize for History
The Nobel Prize in Literature
context: A lifelong soldier won the Nobel PEACE Prize -- the only professional general ever to do so. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/peace/1953/marshall/facts/

question: The man Truman picked to run the Marshall Plan day to day, Paul Hoffman, had never been a diplomat. Before taking charge of rebuilding a continent, he had been president of which American institution?
answer: The Studebaker automobile company
choices: The Studebaker automobile company
The Chase National Bank
The U.S. Steel Corporation
The Pennsylvania Railroad
context: A carmaker ran the rescue of Europe: Hoffman, the former Studebaker chief, headed the Economic Cooperation Administration that delivered the aid. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Cooperation_Administration

question: Of the roughly $13 billion the United States poured into 16 Western European nations, one country received the single biggest share -- about a quarter of the entire program. Which country got the most?
answer: Britain
choices: Britain
France
West Germany
Italy
context: Britain took about $3.3 billion, ahead of France (~$2.3B), West Germany (~$1.4B), and Italy (~$1.2B). The biggest industrial powers got the most, because reviving them was seen as the key to all of Europe. Source: https://www.statista.com/statistics/1227834/distribution-marshall-plan-by-country/

question: American generosity had a hard strategic edge. In France and Italy after the war, Communist parties feeding on the misery were pulling 20-30% of the vote. Above all else, what was the Marshall Plan racing to accomplish?
answer: Revive prosperity before Communists could win power at the ballot box
choices: Revive prosperity before Communists could win power at the ballot box
Keep the defeated Axis nations poor and disarmed for good
Repay America's wartime loans out of European treasuries
Merge Western Europe into one federal state under Washington
context: The deeper fear was political: aid was meant to revive prosperity before communism could win the vote in Western democracies. The free West was, in effect, inoculated against it. Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/marshall-plan

question: The Marshall Plan's aid was offered to the Soviet Union as well. Stalin sent his foreign minister, Vyacheslav Molotov, and nearly 100 economic experts to Paris in 1947 to hear the terms. What did Molotov do?
answer: He stormed out and rejected the plan outright
choices: He stormed out and rejected the plan outright
He signed on and brought the USSR into the program
He demanded the aid be doubled for the East
He stalled for months without ever giving an answer
context: On July 2, 1947, Molotov walked out, calling the plan 'totally unsatisfactory' and fearing it would let Eastern Europe slip out of Soviet control. Stalin turned down free money to keep his grip on the East. Source: https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/july-2/soviet-union-rejects-marshall-plan-assistance

question: Shut out of the Marshall Plan, Stalin built a rival economic bloc for Eastern Europe -- first the 'Molotov Plan,' then in 1949 a permanent organization that locked the satellite states into Soviet-controlled trade and cut them off from Western technology. What was that organization called?
answer: Comecon
choices: Comecon
Warsaw Pact
Cominform
Comintern
context: Comecon (the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance), founded in January 1949, was Stalin's mirror-image answer to the Marshall Plan -- binding the East to Moscow instead of opening it to the West. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molotov_Plan

question: On a single Sunday in June 1948, the German economist Ludwig Erhard made a move so bold he never cleared it with the Allied occupation authorities running his country first. What had he done?
answer: He abolished the wartime price controls overnight
choices: He abolished the wartime price controls overnight
He seized control of every bank in the country
He cancelled all of Germany's wartime debts
He printed a billion fresh banknotes in a week
context: The same week a new Deutsche Mark replaced the worthless Reichsmark, Erhard scrapped the Nazi-era price controls without asking. The black market vanished, shelves filled, and the German recovery took off -- Marshall aid working hand in hand with sound money and free markets. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_Erhard

question: West Germany's recovery under the Marshall Plan was so spectacular that Germans gave it a single name: the 'Wirtschaftswunder.' What does that word mean?
answer: The economic miracle
choices: The economic miracle
The iron curtain
The people's car
The year zero
context: Aided West Germany's 'economic miracle' outpaced France and Britain within a decade. Meanwhile command-economy East Germany stagnated -- four decades later the East still had not reached the prosperity the West hit by the early 1960s. The contrast made the case for free markets visible across one divided country. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Wirtschaftswunder

question: Martin Luther's fight with the Church began over a paper certificate it sold to people in 1517. According to the sellers, what did buying one of these certificates do for you?
answer: Shortened a dead loved one's time in purgatory
choices: Shortened a dead loved one's time in purgatory
Guaranteed you a place on the next crusade
Made you a full member of the priesthood
Let you read the Bible in your own language
context: These certificates were called indulgences. The Church claimed they cancelled the punishment for sins and shortened a soul's time in purgatory. Luther's core objection was simple and explosive: forgiveness was being SOLD for money. Source: https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/october-31/martin-luther-posts-95-theses ; https://www.christian-history.org/john-tetzel.html

question: The friar Johann Tetzel sold these certificates with a catchy sales jingle. The first half went, 'As soon as the coin in the coffer rings...' -- how did the rhyme finish?
answer: ...the soul from purgatory springs
choices: ...the soul from purgatory springs
...your sins are washed by holy kings
...the bell up in the steeple sings
...an angel lends the sinner wings
context: In German: 'Wenn das Geld im Kasten klingt, die Seele aus dem Fegefeuer springt.' This was the exact sales pitch that provoked Luther -- the idea that you could buy a dead relative's release from purgatory the instant your coin hit the box. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninety-five_Theses ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Johann_Tetzel/

question: Years before any of this, in 1505, a young Martin Luther was caught walking in a violent thunderstorm when a lightning bolt struck the ground right beside him. Terrified, he cried out a promise on the spot -- what did he vow?
answer: 'Help! Saint Anna, I will become a monk!'
choices: 'Help! Saint Anna, I will become a monk!'
'Spare me, Lord, and I will sail for Rome!'
'Save me, and I will give all I own away!'
'Mercy! I will build a church on this spot!'
context: The storm struck on July 2, 1505. True to his terrified vow, Luther sold his books and entered the Augustinian monastery at Erfurt -- the decision that set the whole story in motion. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther ; https://www.ligonier.org/posts/luther-and-thunderstorm

question: After the Church declared Luther an outlaw, his protector Frederick the Wise had soldiers stage a FAKE kidnapping and hide him away in Wartburg Castle. There Luther grew out a beard and lived under a disguised name. What was the alias?
answer: Junker Joerg, meaning 'Knight George'
choices: Junker Joerg, meaning 'Knight George'
Bruder Hans, meaning 'Brother John'
Pilger Max, meaning 'Pilgrim Max'
Vater Klaus, meaning 'Father Klaus'
context: Frederick the Wise staged the ambush so Luther's enemies would believe he had been seized, when really he was safe. Disguised as the knight 'Junker Joerg,' Luther hid in the Wartburg in plain sight. Source: https://www.luther.de/en/wartburg.html ; https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1900/luthers-speech-at-the-diet-of-worms/

question: Luther wrote his Ninety-five Theses in Latin, meaning them only as topics for a small scholarly debate among professors. Within weeks, though, they were translated into German and racing across the whole country. What carried them so far, so fast?
answer: The new printing press
choices: The new printing press
Friars traveling on foot
Merchants' private letters
Criers in the town square
context: The recently invented printing press spread the Theses faster and farther than Luther ever intended -- copies were soon being printed in Basel, Leipzig, and Nuremberg. A debate meant for scholars became a movement for everyone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninety-five_Theses ; https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/october-31/martin-luther-posts-95-theses

question: The indulgences Tetzel sold were not raising money for nothing -- officially, the cash was for rebuilding St. Peter's Basilica in Rome for Pope Leo X. But half of it was secretly being funneled somewhere else. Where?
answer: To Archbishop Albert, to repay his debt for buying his church office
choices: To Archbishop Albert, to repay his debt for buying his church office
To the town of Wittenberg, to pay for its growing university
To Tetzel himself, to reward him for his record sales
To the German princes, to buy their continued loyalty
context: Archbishop Albert of Mainz had gone into debt to purchase his high church office, and half of Tetzel's indulgence money was quietly diverted to pay it off. So the certificates promising to cleanse sins were partly settling the bill for a man who had bought his way to power. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninety-five_Theses ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Johann_Tetzel/

question: Pope Leo X issued an official order called 'Exsurge Domine' -- 'Arise, O Lord' -- giving Luther sixty days to take back his writings or face the consequences. On December 10, 1520, before cheering students at Wittenberg's Elster Gate, Luther answered the pope's order with a single public act. What did he do with the document?
answer: Threw it into a bonfire and burned it
choices: Threw it into a bonfire and burned it
Nailed it shut across the church doors
Mailed it back to Rome unopened
Read it aloud and then signed it
context: 'Exsurge Domine' was the papal bull that demanded Luther recant. Instead, with students and faculty cheering, Luther burned it in a bonfire at the Elster Gate -- an open declaration that he would not bow to Rome. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exsurge_Domine ; https://lutheranreformation.org/history/burning-papal-bull/

question: In 1521, Emperor Charles V summoned Luther to the Diet of Worms and ordered him to take back everything he had written. Luther refused -- and gave one reason for why he could not back down. What was it?
answer: He could not, in good conscience, speak against his own conscience
choices: He could not, in good conscience, speak against his own conscience
He had already sworn a public oath never to recant
He feared the German princes would rebel if he did
He believed an emperor had no power over a monk
context: Luther's recorded words: 'I neither can nor will retract anything, for it cannot be either safe or honest for a Christian to speak against his conscience.' Standing alone before the most powerful ruler in Europe, he made conscience itself the final authority. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1900/luthers-speech-at-the-diet-of-worms/ ; https://www.britannica.com/biography/Martin-Luther/Diet-of-Worms

question: Luther dared to travel to the Diet of Worms only because the emperor granted him a 'safe-conduct' -- a sworn promise he could come and go unharmed. Yet everyone remembered why that promise was chilling: a reformer named Jan Hus had been given the very same guarantee at Constance in 1415. What had happened to Hus anyway?
answer: He was burned at the stake despite the promise
choices: He was burned at the stake despite the promise
He was locked in a dungeon for life despite the promise
He was banished from every Christian land despite the promise
He was forced to recant on his knees despite the promise
context: A 'safe-conduct' was a ruler's sworn guarantee of safe passage. A century earlier, Jan Hus had trusted exactly such a promise at Constance and was burned at the stake regardless. Every person at Worms knew Luther might be walking into the same trap. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diet_of_Worms ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Diet_of_Worms/

question: While hiding from the emperor's outlaw order inside Wartburg Castle, Luther took on a staggering task: translating Scripture out of Greek and into everyday German so ordinary people could finally read it for themselves. How much did he translate, and how fast?
answer: The entire New Testament, in just eleven weeks
choices: The entire New Testament, in just eleven weeks
The four Gospels only, in about three years
A single Gospel, in roughly six months
The whole Bible cover to cover, in one year
context: Luther translated the complete New Testament from Greek into German in only eleven weeks. His German Bible was printed so widely it helped standardize the modern German language -- one admirer called him 'the German Cicero.' Putting Scripture in the people's own tongue is one of the Reformation's lasting achievements. Source: https://www.luther.de/en/wartburg.html ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luther_Bible

question: The very first of Luther's Ninety-five Theses set the tone for all the rest. Taking Jesus' command to 'Repent,' it argued that true repentance was not a single act a person could simply pay their way out of. What did that opening thesis say repentance should be?
answer: A task lasting a believer's entire life
choices: A task lasting a believer's entire life
A duty owed only to an ordained priest
A burden that faith alone removes
A matter for the pope alone to settle
context: Thesis 1 reads: 'When our Lord and Master Jesus Christ said, Repent, he willed the entire life of believers to be one of repentance.' Repentance as a whole life turned toward God -- not a payment dropped in Tetzel's coffer -- struck at the very heart of the indulgence trade. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninety-five_Theses

question: The most famous image of the Reformation shows Luther hammering his Ninety-five Theses onto the Wittenberg church door. But historians aren't sure it ever happened -- the nailing story comes from Philip Melanchthon, who hadn't even arrived in Wittenberg yet in 1517. According to Luther's OWN account, how did he first send the Theses out?
answer: He mailed them in a letter to Archbishop Albert
choices: He mailed them in a letter to Archbishop Albert
He read them aloud from the cathedral pulpit
He pinned them to the town hall notice board
He handed them straight to a printer to publish
context: Legend, not forensic fact: the dramatic hammer-and-nail scene comes from Melanchthon, who wasn't present in 1517. Luther's own surviving account says he sent the Theses by letter to Archbishop Albert of Mainz. The image may capture the spirit of the moment without being literally true. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninety-five_Theses ; https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/blogs/justin-taylor/what-was-luther-doing-when-he-nailed-his-95-theses-to-the-wittenberg-door/

question: In July 1505, a young law student named Martin Luther was caught in the open when a thunderstorm rolled in and a lightning bolt struck the ground right next to him. Terrified, he shouted a desperate promise to a saint. What did he cry out?
answer: "Help me, Saint Anne, and I will become a monk!"
choices: "Help me, Saint Anne, and I will become a monk!"
"Spare me, Saint Peter, and I will sail to Rome!"
"Save me, Saint George, and I will take up the sword!"
"Hear me, Saint Paul, and I will give up my books!"
context: Luther kept the vow that the lightning bolt scared out of him. Within weeks he sold his law books and entered the Augustinian monastery at Erfurt (July 17, 1505), which enraged his father, who had wanted him to be a lawyer. Source: LutherCountry, 'July 2nd: The day Martin Luther was thunder struck'; Ligonier, 'Luther and the Thunderstorm'.

question: On October 31, 1517, the monk Martin Luther finished writing out ninety-five complaints against the Church in the town of Wittenberg. By tradition, what did he famously do with the list that very day?
answer: Nailed it to the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg
choices: Nailed it to the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg
Read it aloud from the steps of Saint Peter's in Rome
Buried it beneath the altar of the cathedral at Mainz
Tossed it from the bell tower over the crowd in Leipzig
context: The list was his Ninety-five Theses, written in Latin as 'Disputation on the Power and Efficacy of Indulgences' — meant as points for an academic debate, not a public revolt. The church door served as the university's bulletin board. That same day he also mailed a copy to Archbishop Albert of Brandenburg, the man in charge of the sales he was protesting. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ninety-five Theses'.

question: In 1523 Martin Luther arranged for twelve nuns to flee the Nimbschen convent in a merchant's covered wagon on the night before Easter. To get them past the gates unnoticed, what did he hide them among?
answer: Empty herring barrels
choices: Empty herring barrels
Bolts of dyed wool
Sacks of milled grain
Crates of clay jugs
context: One of the twelve smuggled-out nuns was Katharina von Bora, who married Luther on June 13, 1525 — the runaway nun and the renegade monk. The union scandalized Europe but became a genuine partnership. Source: Wikipedia, 'Katharina von Bora'.

question: The spark for Luther's protest was a friar named Johann Tetzel, who went from town to town selling the Church's paper certificates called indulgences. What did the Church claim a person got for buying one?
answer: A reduction in the punishment owed for their sins
choices: A reduction in the punishment owed for their sins
A guaranteed seat at the next Church council
A blessing on their crops for the coming harvest
A pardon from taxes owed to the local bishop
context: Tetzel's sales were partly meant to fund the rebuilding of Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome — and secretly to pay off Archbishop Albert's debts to the Fugger bankers for buying his church office. Promising forgiveness for cash is exactly what Luther attacked. Source: Wikipedia, 'Johann Tetzel'.

question: To sell more indulgences, the friar Johann Tetzel used a catchy rhyme promising that a dead relative would be sprung from purgatory the instant the buyer paid. What was his notorious jingle?
answer: "As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs."
choices: "As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs."
"Pay the priest and bend the knee, and Heaven's gate will open free."
"A silver crown laid on the stone buys back a sin you might atone."
"Light a candle, say a prayer, and find your loved one waiting there."
context: In the original German it rhymes too: 'Sobald das Geld im Kasten klingt, die Seele aus dem Fegefeuer springt.' The idea that you could buy a dead parent's way out of purgatory with a few coins is what enraged Luther into writing his Theses. Source: Wikipedia, 'Johann Tetzel'; aphorismen.de (German original).

question: After the emperor declared Luther an outlaw whom anyone could kill, his protector Frederick the Wise of Saxony staged a fake ambush and hid him inside Wartburg Castle. Luther grew out a beard and disguised himself as a minor nobleman. What knightly alias did he take?
answer: Junker Jörg
choices: Junker Jörg
Ritter Konrad
Junker Friedrich
Herr Wolfgang
context: 'Junker Jörg' means roughly 'Knight George.' Disguised as a bearded knight, the most wanted heretic in Europe lived hidden in plain sight at the Wartburg for almost a year. Source: Lutheran Witness, 'Junker Jörg Translates the Bible'.

question: On June 15, 1520, Pope Leo X issued a document titled 'Exsurge Domine' ('Arise, O Lord') giving Luther sixty days to take back his writings or be excommunicated. On the sixtieth day, Luther gathered students at the Elster Gate in Wittenberg and did what to the pope's document?
answer: Threw it into a bonfire
choices: Threw it into a bonfire
Nailed it shut in a wooden box
Mailed it back to Rome unopened
Read it aloud and signed it
context: He fed the papal bull to the flames along with books of Church law, in front of a crowd of students and faculty on December 10, 1520. There was no clearer way to say he would not back down. Source: Wikipedia, 'Exsurge Domine'; Lutheran Reformation, 'The Burning of the Papal Bull'.

question: Hidden at Wartburg Castle under his knight's disguise, Martin Luther spent about eleven weeks at a single huge project, even inventing brand-new German words for ideas the language did not yet have. What did he produce in those weeks?
answer: A German translation of the entire New Testament
choices: A German translation of the entire New Testament
A new hymn book for German village churches
A complete history of the German monasteries
A German dictionary of Latin Church terms
context: He translated it straight from the original Greek into everyday German. Legend says he once hurled an inkwell at the devil there — but the phrase really meant he 'fought the devil with ink,' that is, by translating; caretakers re-painted an 'ink stain' on the wall for centuries of tourists anyway. Source: Wikipedia, 'Luther Bible'; luther.de.

question: Summoned in 1521 before Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Worms, Martin Luther was shown a table piled high with his own books and ordered to take back what he had written. He refused unless someone could prove him wrong from Scripture, saying his conscience was held prisoner by what?
answer: The Word of God
choices: The Word of God
The will of the emperor
The judgment of Rome
The laws of the empire
context: His full line was that his conscience was 'captive to the Word of God.' To recant against his own conscience, he said, would be neither safe nor right. Refusing the emperor to his face was an act of staggering nerve. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Luther's Speech at the Diet of Worms'.

question: Martin Luther's defiant stand at the Diet of Worms is remembered by four short sentences traditionally quoted as his closing words — though most scholars believe they were polished and added in the earliest printed version rather than spoken exactly on the spot. Which famous line is it?
answer: "Here I stand. I can do no other. God help me. Amen."
choices: "Here I stand. I can do no other. God help me. Amen."
"Let the world burn before I yield a single page."
"No crown nor mitre shall command my soul."
"I answer to Heaven alone, and to no man here."
context: Treat this as legend rather than a perfect transcript: the dramatic 'Here I stand' may have been sharpened by the first printers, but it captures the spirit of a lone monk refusing to back down before an emperor. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Luther's Speech at the Diet of Worms'; Crossway, 'Luther at the Diet of Worms'.

question: Because the printing press was new, Luther's Ninety-five Theses raced across the German lands within two weeks and across Europe within two months — all without his permission. In the few years after, of every book rolling off the printing presses in Germany, how large was Luther's own share?
answer: About half of everything printed
choices: About half of everything printed
About a tenth of everything printed
About a fifth of everything printed
Nearly all of everything printed
context: Between 1517 and 1520, thirty of his pamphlets ran through 370 editions — roughly 400,000 copies — making him the era's runaway bestseller. He claimed he had 'no wish or plan to publicize these Theses,' but the presses spread them anyway. Source: Christian History Institute, 'Preaching From the Print Shop'.

question: When Luther's German New Testament flooded the country, his enemy Johann Cochlaeus complained in disgust that even the most ordinary working people were now reading it eagerly, 'as if it were a fountain of all truth.' Which humble tradesfolk did he name as devouring the new Bible?
answer: Tailors and shoemakers
choices: Tailors and shoemakers
Bakers and butchers
Farmers and shepherds
Miners and blacksmiths
context: Cochlaeus meant it as an insult — that uneducated commoners had no business reading Scripture for themselves — but it stands as vivid eyewitness proof of how hungrily ordinary Germans took up the printed Bible. Source: Christian History Institute, 'Preaching From the Print Shop'.

question: In late February 1848 a small German pamphlet went on sale in London, and it opened with one of the most famous first lines ever written about politics. What did that opening sentence say was 'haunting Europe'?
answer: A spectre — the spectre of communism
choices: A spectre — the spectre of communism
A hunger that no king could feed
A fire lit in the heart of Paris
A storm gathering over the factories
context: The Communist Manifesto (Manifest der kommunistischen Partei) opened: 'A spectre is haunting Europe — the spectre of communism.' Published anonymously around February 21, 1848, as a 23-page pamphlet. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Communist_Manifesto ; https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/february-21/marx-publishes-manifesto

question: Karl Marx's three daughters never called their father 'Karl.' At university he had earned a nickname for his dark complexion and jet-black hair, and his family used it his whole life. What was the name?
answer: Moor
choices: Moor
Bear
Professor
Raven
context: His daughters called him 'Moor' for his dark hair and complexion. His close friend Friedrich Engels carried a nickname too — 'the General.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx ; https://mhoefert.blogspot.com/2018/05/happy-birthday-moore.html

question: Karl Marx ends the Communist Manifesto with a rallying cry to the working class — a single short line that became one of the most quoted political slogans in the world. What is that closing call?
answer: Workers of all lands, unite!
choices: Workers of all lands, unite!
Down with every crown in Europe!
Take the factories, and take them now!
Let no man labour for another!
context: The Manifesto closes 'Working Men of All Countries, Unite!' (often rendered 'Workers of all lands, unite!'). The sentence just before it: 'The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win.' 'Proletarians' is Marx's own term for the working class. Source: https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/february-21/marx-publishes-manifesto

question: Friedrich Engels first drafted the communist program a few months before the Manifesto, in an odd schoolroom format — a 'catechism' of 25 questions, each with its answer, which Marx then reworked into flowing prose. What was Engels' question-and-answer draft called?
answer: Principles of Communism
choices: Principles of Communism
The Workers' Catechism
A Confession of Faith
Letters to the League
context: Engels' 'Principles of Communism' laid out the program as 25 questions each with an answer. Marx reworked it into the Manifesto. The first edition had a dark-green cover and was printed at 46 Liverpool Street in London. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Communist_Manifesto

question: The Communist Manifesto sold in late February 1848 and at first almost nobody read it. Then, within a single day of its appearance, an event broke out in one European capital and set off a wave of upheaval across the continent. What happened?
answer: Revolution erupted in France
choices: Revolution erupted in France
A general strike shut down London
The King of Prussia abdicated
Workers seized the Vienna mint
context: Revolution broke out in France on February 22, 1848 — within a day of the Manifesto's publication — then spread in the wave known as the Revolutions of 1848. The pamphlet nobody read landed exactly as Europe caught fire. Source: https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/february-21/marx-publishes-manifesto

question: Friedrich Engels led a double life. By day he was a wealthy executive at a Manchester cotton mill, earning over £1,000 a year and even riding to hounds with the local gentry; by night he secretly funneled thousands of pounds to the broke Marx household. What did that mill money pay for?
answer: The research and writing of Das Kapital
choices: The research and writing of Das Kapital
A printing press hidden in Brussels
Marx's escape from the Prussian police
A network of couriers across Europe
context: Engels, an executive at the Ermen & Engels mill, funneled roughly £3,000–£4,000 over about twenty years to Marx — the money behind Das Kapital, the book attacking the very capitalism that earned it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Engels

question: Friedrich Engels needed firsthand sight of Manchester's worst slums for his 1845 book on the working class, but the 'Little Ireland' district was too dangerous for a well-dressed German to enter alone. A spirited Irish factory worker walked him through it. Who was his guide?
answer: Mary Burns
choices: Mary Burns
Jenny von Westphalen
Helen Macfarlane
Eleanor Marx
context: Mary Burns, an Irish factory worker, led Engels through Manchester's 'Little Ireland,' giving him the material for 'The Condition of the Working Class in England' (1845). He called his own years as a cotton merchant 'purgatory' and wrote, 'Huckstering is too beastly.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Engels

question: Karl Marx wrote the last pages of Das Kapital's first volume standing up, because a painful affliction made sitting unbearable, and he cursed his enemies over it: 'I hope the bourgeoisie will remember the carbuncles until their dying day.' What condition forced him to his feet?
answer: An eruption of boils on his rear
choices: An eruption of boils on his rear
A broken hip from a bad fall
Gout swelling both his knees
A wound that would not heal
context: Marx finished Volume 1 standing, driven up by carbuncles (boils) on his rear, cursing: 'What a swine they are!' He drafted much of it at desk G7 in the British Museum's Round Reading Room. Source: https://www.marxists.org/history/etol/newspape/isj2/1999/isj2-085/morgan.htm ; https://opinion.inquirer.net/115074/warming-seat-marx-wrote-das-kapital

question: The very first English version of the Manifesto (1850), translated by Helen Macfarlane, did not begin with the famous word 'spectre.' She chose a stranger, eerier creature that 'stalks throughout Europe.' What was it?
answer: A frightful hobgoblin
choices: A frightful hobgoblin
A pale wandering ghost
A hungry grey wolf
A nameless dread
context: Helen Macfarlane's 1850 translation opened: 'A frightful hobgoblin stalks throughout Europe.' It ran in George Julian Harney's paper The Red Republican in November 1850. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Communist_Manifesto

question: Living in real poverty in Soho, Karl Marx lost several children to illness worsened by want. His son Edgar — a boy who loved to belt out the Marseillaise at the top of his voice — died on 6 April 1855. Where was the boy when he died?
answer: In his father's arms
choices: In his father's arms
In a charity hospital ward
On the boat to England
Alone in the night
context: Edgar died in Marx's arms; Marx wrote to Engels, 'I feel broken down.' Only three of the seven children Jenny Marx bore survived to adulthood. The family at 28 Dean Street sometimes lived on bread and potatoes. Source: https://www.marxists.org/history/etol/newspape/isj2/1999/isj2-085/morgan.htm ; https://buddhistsocialism.weebly.com/karl-marx-ndash-life-at-28-dean-street-ndash-soho-london-w1-2016.html

question: Only about eleven mourners came to Karl Marx's burial at Highgate in 1883. Friedrich Engels, who paid for the funeral, gave the graveside speech and reached for the grandest scientist of the age to measure his friend — saying Marx had done for human history what this man did for nature. Whom did Engels name?
answer: Charles Darwin
choices: Charles Darwin
Isaac Newton
Galileo Galilei
Michael Faraday
context: Engels said: 'Just as Darwin discovered the law of development of organic nature, so Marx discovered the law of development of human history.' He opened, 'the greatest living thinker ceased to think,' and closed, 'His name will endure through the ages.' Source: https://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1883/death/burial.htm

question: Karl Marx's most-quoted line on faith is usually clipped to a sneer, but in full (1844) it is gentler — he calls religion 'the sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world.' How does Marx finish the thought, the phrase everyone remembers?
answer: It is the opium of the people
choices: It is the opium of the people
It is a chain forged by kings
It is the dream of the defeated
It is a lie sold to the poor
context: Marx wrote that religion 'is the opium of the people' — meaning partly with sympathy, as a real cry of suffering and a painkiller for a hard life, not only as a sneer. From his journal the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opium_of_the_people ; https://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1843/critique-hpr/intro.htm

question: Karl Marx opens the Manifesto with the engine he claims drives all of history: 'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of...' By Marx's argument, what force moves history forward?
answer: The struggle between economic classes
choices: The struggle between economic classes
The will of great men and kings
The march of reason and ideas
The hand of God over the nations
context: Marx argued history is driven by class struggle — part of his theory of historical materialism, that how a society produces and trades its goods shapes its politics, law, and ideas. This is Marx's claim, a serious idea in the philosophy of history, not a settled fact. Source: https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/february-21/marx-publishes-manifesto ; https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/marx/

question: Marx's tomb in Highgate is carved with the line he is most remembered for, the last of his 1845 'Theses on Feuerbach.' It draws a sharp contrast: the philosophers have only interpreted the world in various ways — but what, Marx says, is the real point?
answer: The point is to change it
choices: The point is to change it
The point is to understand it
The point is to record it
The point is to endure it
context: The 11th Thesis on Feuerbach: 'The philosophers have only interpreted the world, in various ways; the point, however, is to change it.' Marx never published the theses; Engels printed them in 1888, five years after Marx's death. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theses_on_Feuerbach ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_Karl_Marx

question: In August 1800, a woman named Elizabeth Haskings stood under an elm tree at Lyme Regis holding a 15-month-old baby, watching a horse show, when a bolt of lightning struck the tree and killed all three grown women standing there. The baby alone lived. Rushed home limp and lifeless, how was the infant Mary Anning brought back to life?
answer: She was bathed in a tub of hot water
choices: She was bathed in a tub of hot water
She was carried up to the church altar
She was wrapped in the skin of a lamb
She was rowed straight out to sea
context: Mary Anning (born 21 May 1799) was the only survivor; her family said the sickly baby afterward 'seemed to blossom,' and for years Lyme Regis credited her sharp curiosity to that lightning bolt. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: In 1811, on the crumbling sea-cliffs of Lyme Regis, Mary Anning's older brother Joseph dug out a strange four-foot skull that looked like a crocodile's. A few months later, 12-year-old Mary went back to the same cliffs and found the rest of it. What did she pull out of the rock?
answer: The whole 17-foot skeleton of the beast
choices: The whole 17-foot skeleton of the beast
A chest of gold the tide had buried
The bones of a drowned sailor
A nest of giant speckled eggs
context: It was the first ichthyosaur ever recognised. The British Museum bought it, and people argued for years over what kind of animal it even was. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: The dolphin-shaped sea reptile that Mary Anning found in the Lyme Regis cliffs had enormous eyes and rows of teeth, and naturalists needed a name for it. Charles Konig of the British Museum coined the word 'ichthyosaur.' What does that name mean?
answer: Fish-lizard
choices: Fish-lizard
Storm-runner
Dragon-king
Sea-ghost
context: The creature swam like a fish but was a reptile that breathed air, so 'fish-lizard' captured the puzzle of it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: For years Mary Anning worked the Lyme Regis cliffs with a little black-and-white terrier named Tray at her side. On a stormy October day in 1833 a landslide thundered down. Mary just escaped, but what happened to Tray?
answer: The falling cliff crushed him in an instant
choices: The falling cliff crushed him in an instant
He swam out to a fishing boat and was saved
He ran off and was never seen again
He dug Mary free from the rubble
context: Mary wrote to her friend Charlotte Murchison: 'the cliff that fell upon him and killed him in a moment before my eyes... it was but a moment between me and the same fate.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: Mary Anning's family dug out the first complete ichthyosaur skeleton ever recognised, a 17-foot sea-monster that scholars across England would soon fight to study. With her father dead and the family near starving, they sold this world-first find for about 23 pounds to the gentleman who held the manor near Lyme Regis. Which gentleman walked off with the sea-monster?
answer: Henry Hoste Henley
choices: Henry Hoste Henley
William Bullock
Thomas Birch
William Buckland
context: They sold it to Henry Hoste Henley, lord of the manor of Colway near Lyme Regis, for roughly 23 pounds; he then resold it to the collector William Bullock, who displayed it in London. The Annings hunted fossils not for science but to keep from starving. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: On 10 December 1823 Mary Anning prised a brand-new kind of monster out of the Lyme Regis rock — a creature so strange it would soon be nicknamed a 'sea-dragon.' What made this Plesiosaurus look so impossible?
answer: An enormously long neck of about 35 vertebrae
choices: An enormously long neck of about 35 vertebrae
A single eye set in the middle of its skull
A shell as wide across as a cartwheel
A double row of leathery bat-like wings
context: The four-flippered Plesiosaurus had a neck so long that experts who only saw drawings refused to believe it was real. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: In December 1828 Mary Anning dug a creature out of the Lyme Regis cliffs that had never been seen before anywhere in Britain, and it caused a public sensation. William Buckland gave it the Latin name Pterodactylus macronyx. What kind of animal had Anning uncovered?
answer: The first pterosaur known outside Germany
choices: The first pterosaur known outside Germany
The first woolly mammoth found in Britain
The first giant turtle of the Dorset coast
The first armoured fish of the deep past
context: Buckland named it Pterodactylus macronyx; Richard Owen later renamed it Dimorphodon macronyx. A reptile from the deep past stunned the public. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: Inside the ichthyosaur skeletons she dug up, Mary Anning kept finding odd polished lumps that scholars called 'bezoar stones.' Anning cracked them open and worked out what they truly were. What had these lumps been when the animal was alive?
answer: Its fossilised droppings
choices: Its fossilised droppings
Its swallowed eyeballs
Eggs it had been carrying
Pearls it had eaten from the sea floor
context: Anning saw they were packed with fish bones and scales. William Buckland named them 'coprolites' and, in a rare act of fairness, credited 'Miss Mary Anning' by name in his paper. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: In 1824 the geologist William Conybeare stood before the scientific world and presented Mary Anning's astonishing long-necked plesiosaur — the very specimen she had dug from the cliffs and sketched with her own hand. How did Conybeare treat Anning in that presentation?
answer: He left her name out of it entirely
choices: He left her name out of it entirely
He named her as his equal partner
He brought her on stage to speak
He gave her half of the prize money
context: Anning found the fossil and drew the sketch Conybeare used, yet the gentleman geologist presented it as his own triumph and never mentioned her. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: In 1830 Mary Anning was facing financial ruin. Her friend the geologist Henry De la Beche painted a crowded Dorset scene — ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs and pterosaurs all built from her discoveries — called 'Duria Antiquior,' then sold prints of it and handed her the proceeds. Beyond the gift of money, why did that painting matter to the wider world?
answer: It was the first widely circulated picture of 'deep time'
choices: It was the first widely circulated picture of 'deep time'
It was the first map ever drawn of the Jurassic Coast
It was the first life-size model of an ichthyosaur
It was the first museum guidebook to ancient reptiles
context: 'Duria Antiquior' let ordinary people picture a vanished world of ancient monsters for the first time — prehistory made visible, paid for to rescue the woman who found the bones. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: When the great French anatomist Georges Cuvier — the most powerful naturalist in Europe — saw drawings of Mary Anning's impossibly long-necked plesiosaur, he went public with a stinging charge against her. What did Cuvier accuse Anning of?
answer: Gluing bones from different animals into a fake
choices: Gluing bones from different animals into a fake
Smuggling the fossil out of a French collection
Inventing a Latin name she had no right to
Hiding the skull to drive up the price
context: Cuvier called the long neck impossible and branded the specimen a forgery — until a Geological Society meeting examined it in 1824 and he admitted he was wrong: the skeleton was real. A poor self-taught woman had out-observed the greatest anatomist alive. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: Mary Anning supplied the fossils and observations that gentleman geologists published under their own names, and she felt the sting of it. Her friend Anna Pinney wrote down how Anning described the way the learned men had treated her. In Anning's own bitter words, what had those men done?
answer: 'These men of learning have sucked her brains'
choices: 'These men of learning have sucked her brains'
'These men of learning have stolen my gold'
'These men of learning have burned my letters'
'These men of learning have barred my door'
context: The full quote: the world 'has used her ill... these men of learning have sucked her brains, and made a great deal of publishing works, of which she furnished the contents, while she derived none of the advantages.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: Lots of people will tell you the tongue-twister 'She sells seashells by the seashore' was written about Mary Anning, the woman who sold fossils on the Dorset coast. A Library of Congress folklorist, Stephen Winick, traced where the rhyme really came from. What did he find?
answer: The song came long after her and never names Anning
choices: The song came long after her and never names Anning
A Lyme Regis fishmonger first shouted it as her cry
Anning's own brother Joseph composed it for her shop
Anning painted it as the slogan on her shop window
context: Winick showed the phrase was already common folklore before Terry Sullivan's 1908 song — written more than 60 years after Anning's birth — and that song never even mentions her. A charming legend, but not history. Source: https://blogs.loc.gov/folklife/2017/07/she-sells-seashells-and-mary-anning-metafolklore-with-a-twist/

question: In 1792 Mary Wollstonecraft published 'A Vindication of the Rights of Woman,' arguing that women only seemed inferior because they were denied the education men received. Her most-quoted line begins 'I do not wish them to have power over men; but...' -- power over what?
answer: over themselves
choices: over the home
over the law
over themselves
over the purse
context: Wollstonecraft's goal was self-mastery through education, not dominance over men: '...but over themselves.' She wanted women equipped to reason and govern their own lives. Source: https://digitalcommons.chapman.edu/vocesnovae/vol5/iss1/4/

question: Mary Wollstonecraft's 'A Vindication of the Rights of Woman' (1792) was a direct rebuttal of Rousseau's 'Emile,' whose model woman 'Sophie' was to be educated only for a man's pleasure. After quoting one of Rousseau's passages on Sophie, Wollstonecraft dismissed it in a single tart phrase -- she called it the philosophy of what?
answer: the philosophy of lasciviousness
choices: the philosophy of tyranny
the philosophy of lasciviousness
the philosophy of cowardice
the philosophy of idleness
context: Wollstonecraft's argument was that reason is not sexed: if rights rest on rational nature, denying women the same education is incoherent. Rousseau's vision of training a girl purely for a man's pleasure she branded 'the philosophy of lasciviousness.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Vindication_of_the_Rights_of_Woman

question: Atop one of Ashoka's stone pillars at Sarnath stood a carving of four lions standing back-to-back. More than two thousand years later, the modern nation of India adopted that exact carving for an official role it still holds today. What did the four-lion capital become?
answer: The national emblem of India
choices: The national emblem of India
The national flag of India
The national anthem of India
The national tree of India
context: The Lion Capital of Ashoka, four life-sized lions back-to-back, is the official National Emblem of India. The pillar marked the spot at Sarnath where the Buddha is said to have preached his first sermon, roughly two centuries before Ashoka. Source: Wikipedia, Lion Capital of Ashoka; Smarthistory; World History Encyclopedia.

question: The four-lion capital that crowned Ashoka's pillar at Sarnath was cut from a single block of sandstone about 2,300 years ago. One feature of its surface still astonishes people who see it today. What still survives on the stone?
answer: A mirror-like polish that still shines
choices: A mirror-like polish that still shines
Painted colors that still glow
Carved words that still read clearly
Gold leaf that still glints
context: The capital is carved from a single block of Chunar sandstone and given the famous 'Mauryan polish,' a mirror-like shine that still gleams after about 2,300 years. The whole capital stands roughly 2.1 metres (7 feet) tall. Source: Wikipedia, Lion Capital of Ashoka; GKToday; Smarthistory.

question: Ashoka used his stone edicts to brag not about battles but about restraint. Rock Edict 1 records that where the royal kitchen had once slaughtered many thousands of animals every day for the king's table, now only three were killed. Which three animals did the edict say were now the only ones killed?
answer: Two peacocks and a deer
choices: Two peacocks and a deer
Two pheasants and a goat
Two swans and a boar
Two cranes and a hare
context: Rock Edict 1 boasts that where thousands of animals were once slaughtered daily for the royal table, now 'only three creatures, two peacocks and a deer, are killed, and the deer not always' -- and even those killings would stop. Source: World History Encyclopedia, Edicts of Ashoka (Rock Edict 1).

question: Legend says the adviser Chanakya secretly mixed tiny doses of a slow killer into the food of the first Mauryan emperor, Chandragupta, day after day, hardening the king's body so no assassin could ever finish him that way. One evening the king shared that food with his pregnant queen, who collapsed and died -- but the baby was saved and grew up to rule as Ashoka's father. They named him for the very thing that had nearly killed him: Bindusara. According to the legend, what does the name 'Bindusara' mean?
answer: Drop of poison
choices: Drop of poison
Gift of the gods
Son of the serpent
Born in sorrow
context: In this tradition Chanakya laced the king's food in tiny doses to build immunity; the unborn child was saved as the queen died and was named Bindusara, 'drop of poison.'
