He became the next emperor and Ashoka's father. The story is legend, not documented fact. Source: Sankalp India Foundation, Poisoning the King; Medium, Bindusara (Stories of Aryavarta).

question: Ashoka conquered the kingdom of Kalinga, and on his Rock Edict 13 he carved the human cost of that one war in hard numbers: one hundred thousand slain, one hundred and fifty thousand carried off, and many times as many dead afterward. Historians point to this edict as almost unique in the ancient world -- not for the size of the toll, but for who was reporting it. What made Ashoka's edict so extraordinary?
answer: He recorded the death toll of his own victory in stone
choices: He recorded the death toll of his own victory in stone
He blamed the entire slaughter on his defeated enemy
He demanded a matching toll of prisoners every year
He ordered the dead counted to set the size of his reward
context: Edict 13 states that in the Kalinga conquest 150,000 were deported, 100,000 were slain, and 'many times as many' died afterward. A king carving the body count of his OWN victory into a monument -- rather than only his glory -- is almost unique in ancient history. Source: Wikipedia, Major Rock Edicts (E. Hultzsch translation, 1925); World History Encyclopedia.

question: Beneath the four lions on Ashoka's pillar sits a carved wheel, the Dharma Chakra or 'Wheel of Law.' When India became independent, its people took a 24-spoke version of Ashoka's wheel and placed it onto one national object, where it still appears today. Where is the Ashoka Chakra found now?
answer: India's national flag
choices: India's national flag
India's highest war medal
Every Indian coin
India's parliament building
context: The 24-spoke Ashoka Chakra sits at the centre of India's national flag -- a Mauryan emperor's symbol flying over a modern nation. The wheel beneath the Sarnath lions is the Wheel of Law. Source: Wikipedia, Lion Capital of Ashoka; Wikipedia, State Emblem of India.

question: Ashoka sent his own children to spread the Buddha's teaching. His daughter Sanghamitta, a young Buddhist nun, sailed to the island of Sri Lanka carrying in a golden vase a living sapling cut from the very tree the Buddha had sat under to reach enlightenment. She planted it at Anuradhapura, where it still grows today. Among all the trees on Earth, what record does this one hold?
answer: The oldest planted tree on record anywhere
choices: The oldest planted tree on record anywhere
The tallest living tree in all of Asia
The only tree with its own armed guard
The widest tree trunk ever measured
context: That tree, the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi at Anuradhapura, still lives and is the oldest historically authenticated planted tree in the world -- a tree whose exact planting was recorded. Sanghamitta carried it across the sea in a golden vase. Source: Tricycle, Sanghamitta; AmazingLanka, Sri Maha Bodhi.

question: Chandragupta Maurya, who founded the Mauryan Empire, lived in constant terror of being murdered. By Greek and later accounts, he took one strange precaution every single night to stay alive. What did Chandragupta do each night out of fear of assassination?
answer: He slept in a different bedroom every night
choices: He slept in a different bedroom every night
He burned every letter he read that day
He wore heavy armor to bed each night
He had a new cook prepare every meal
context: Tradition holds that Chandragupta never slept in the same bedroom two nights running, was guarded inside his palace by armed women, and had every dish tasted before he ate -- fear so deep it became legend. Source: Oxford History of India; HistoryDiscussion, Administration of Chandragupta Maurya.

question: Around 305 BCE the Mauryan founder Chandragupta fought and defeated Seleucus, a Greek king who had been one of Alexander the Great's own generals. To seal the peace, Chandragupta handed Seleucus a gift of war animals so valuable that Seleucus used them to win a great battle back in the Greek world. What did Chandragupta give Seleucus?
answer: Five hundred war elephants
choices: Five hundred war elephants
One thousand war horses
Three hundred war chariots
Two hundred war camels
context: The treaty handed the Mauryans huge lands including Kandahar and eastern Afghanistan and sealed a marriage alliance; in return Chandragupta gave Seleucus 500 war elephants -- which Seleucus used to win the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE. Source: Wikipedia, Seleucid-Mauryan War.

question: Ashoka had just conquered the kingdom of Kalinga. The war was won and his enemy was crushed. On his great stone edicts, where a victorious king might record his triumph, Ashoka instead carved his own feelings about the Kalinga war. According to Rock Edict 13, what did Ashoka express?
answer: Deep remorse and grief over the slaughter
choices: Deep remorse and grief over the slaughter
Fierce pride in his crushing victory
Eager plans to conquer the next land
Warm thanks to the gods for the win
context: Edict 13 reads, 'This is the repentance of Beloved of the Gods on account of his conquest,' and declares that even 'the hundredth part or the thousandth part' of those killed would now be deeply deplorable to him. The conqueror publicly grieved the war he himself had won. Source: Wikipedia, Major Rock Edicts (Hultzsch translation, 1925).

question: After the Kalinga war, Ashoka swore off armed conquest for good. From then on, he said, he would pursue only one kind of victory -- a moral one that 'bears fruit in this world and the other world,' won not with armies but by teaching people to live rightly. What did Ashoka name this new kind of conquest?
answer: Conquest by Dhamma
choices: Conquest by Dhamma
Conquest by Wisdom
Conquest by Faith
Conquest by Virtue
context: Ashoka renounced war for what he called 'conquest by Dhamma' -- conquest by morality -- which he said 'bears fruit in this world and the other world.' Dhamma was his word for living and ruling rightly, and it is the line that turns a war monument into a peace manifesto. Source: Wikipedia, Major Rock Edicts; World History Encyclopedia, Edicts of Ashoka.

question: In every one of his stone inscriptions, the great emperor we call Ashoka never once wrote the name 'Ashoka.' He called himself only by a royal title, Devanampiya Piyadasi -- 'Beloved of the Gods.' After his empire fell, no one could match this 'Beloved of the Gods' to a known king, and the carvings kept their secret author for a staggering length of time. For roughly how long did Ashoka's true identity stay lost?
answer: About two thousand years
choices: About two thousand years
About two hundred years
About five hundred years
About fifty years
context: Because he called himself only Devanampiya Piyadasi, 'Beloved of the Gods, of gracious gaze,' Ashoka's real identity was lost for almost two thousand years. His empire had collapsed within about 50 years of his death, and even the script of his edicts became unreadable. Source: World History Encyclopedia, Edicts of Ashoka; Wikipedia, Devanampriya / Priyadasi.

question: By the 1800s the Brahmi script on Ashoka's pillars had become unreadable, and the emperor behind them was forgotten. In 1837 the British scholar James Prinsep finally cracked the script -- but the carvings only named a mysterious 'Beloved of the Gods,' not Ashoka. What let Prinsep prove that this mysterious king was actually the long-lost emperor Ashoka?
answer: An old Sri Lankan chronicle that named the same king
choices: An old Sri Lankan chronicle that named the same king
A row of coins stamped with Ashoka's portrait
A Greek letter describing Ashoka by name
A family tree carved on the Sarnath lions
context: James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in 1837; pointed by George Turnour to a Sri Lankan Pali chronicle, he realized the mysterious 'Devanampiya Piyadasi' of the pillars was the lost emperor Ashoka, who had been forgotten for nearly two thousand years. Source: World History Encyclopedia, Edicts of Ashoka; GKToday; Scroll.in (James Prinsep).

question: The Maya wrote every number they ever needed using only three marks: a dot, a bar, and one more shape they had invented to stand for nothing at all. What was that third mark?
answer: A drawing of a shell
choices: A drawing of a shell
A drawing of a feather
A drawing of an eye
A drawing of a hand
context: A dot meant one, a bar meant five, and the shell stood for zero. With just those three symbols the Maya could write any number. The shell-zero is one of the few zero symbols ever invented from scratch. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_numerals

question: Long before Arabic numerals carried the idea of zero into Europe, the Maya had already invented their own symbol for nothing on the other side of the world. Roughly how far ahead of Europe were they?
answer: More than a thousand years
choices: More than a thousand years
About fifty years
About one century
A few decades
context: The Maya invented their shell-shaped zero independently, more than a thousand years before zero reached Europe through Arabic numerals. Inventing zero from scratch happened only a handful of times in all of human history. Source: https://www.mexicolore.co.uk/maya/home/the-maya-and-zero

question: In 1562 the Spanish bishop Diego de Landa gathered up thousands of Maya bark-paper books and burned them in a single bonfire at Mani. Only four Maya books survived the conquest at all. Which one is the finest that escaped the flames?
answer: The Dresden Codex
choices: The Dresden Codex
The Mani Bonfire Scroll
The Landa Codex
The Yucatan Folio
context: Bishop Diego de Landa burned thousands of codices at Mani in 1562. Just four Maya bark-paper books survived, and the Dresden Codex is the finest of them. It later turned up in a library in Dresden, Germany, which gave it its name. Source: https://mayan.org/civilization/dresden-codex/

question: The Dresden Codex, the finest surviving Maya book, escaped Bishop de Landa's 1562 bonfire only to face a second brush with fire centuries later. What nearly destroyed it the second time?
answer: The Allied firebombing of Dresden in 1945
choices: The Allied firebombing of Dresden in 1945
A flood of the river Elbe in 1845
A library lamp fire in 1745
A lightning strike in 1645
context: During the Allied firebombing of Dresden in February 1945 the codex took water damage but stayed readable. A Maya astronomy book had survived both a Spanish bishop's fire and a 20th-century war. Source: https://mayan.org/civilization/dresden-codex/

question: Reading the numbers hidden in the Dresden Codex, modern scholars found the Maya had measured how long Venus takes to cycle through its appearances in the sky: 583.92 days. Set against the true modern value of 583.93 days, how far off were they?
answer: By about one hundredth of a day
choices: By about one hundredth of a day
By about three days
By nearly a week
By roughly a month
context: The Maya value of 583.92 days misses the modern 583.93 days by only about one hundredth of a day. They tracked Venus this precisely with the naked eye, and even built in a leap-year-style correction so the count would not drift. Source: https://www.sci.news/astronomy/dresden-codex-venus-table-discovery-04110.html

question: In 1562 the Spanish friar Diego de Landa burned almost every Maya book he could find, destroying a written language nobody in Europe could read. Yet de Landa himself later left behind the very thing that would one day help scholars crack the Maya script. What did he write down?
answer: A list matching Maya glyphs to the letters of the Spanish alphabet
choices: A list matching Maya glyphs to the letters of the Spanish alphabet
A grammar book teaching Spanish friars to speak the Maya language
A confession admitting he had burned the books out of fear
A map showing where the surviving Maya books were hidden
context: In his 'Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan,' the man who burned the books recorded a list of Maya glyphs paired with Spanish letters — the so-called 'de Landa alphabet,' which became the key that eventually helped decipher Maya writing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Landa_alphabet

question: For centuries Diego de Landa's glyph list looked useless, because the Maya signs paired to single Spanish letters never matched up. In 1952 the Soviet scholar Yuri Knorozov saw why: de Landa had misunderstood his own informant. When de Landa said the letter 'b,' the Maya scribe had drawn the glyph for a whole spoken sound, not a letter. What kind of writing system did Knorozov realize Maya script actually was?
answer: A syllabary, where each glyph stands for a spoken syllable like 'be'
choices: A syllabary, where each glyph stands for a spoken syllable like 'be'
A picture-writing of symbols that each stand for a whole idea
A counting system of dots and bars with no link to speech
An alphabet borrowed directly from the Spanish friars
context: Knorozov realized de Landa's 'alphabet' was really a syllabary: asked for 'b,' the scribe wrote the glyph for the syllable 'be.' That insight turned de Landa's list into the 'Rosetta Stone' of Maya writing — and Knorozov cracked it from photographs in Moscow, not seeing a Maya ruin until 1990. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuri_Knorozov

question: During the 1954 televised Army-McCarthy hearings, Senator Joseph McCarthy attacked a young lawyer named Fred Fisher who worked in Army counsel Joseph Welch's own law firm. Welch, voice shaking, stopped him cold with one question that turned the room against McCarthy. What did Welch ask?
answer: "Have you no sense of decency, sir?"
choices: "Have you no sense of decency, sir?"
"Where is the list you promised us?"
"Will you swear that under oath?"
"Do you speak for the Republican Party?"
context: Welch said: 'Let us not assassinate this lad further, Senator. You've done enough. Have you no sense of decency, sir? At long last, have you left no sense of decency?' The gallery burst into applause and McCarthy's popularity collapsed. Source: U.S. Senate, 'Have You No Sense of Decency?' senate.gov.

question: In December 1948, ex-communist Whittaker Chambers led congressional investigators onto his Maryland farm to prove that State Department official Alger Hiss had passed secrets to the Soviets. There Chambers produced rolls of 35mm spy film from a bizarre hiding place. Where had he stashed the film?
answer: Inside a hollowed-out pumpkin
choices: Inside a hollowed-out pumpkin
Under a loose floorboard
Sewn into a scarecrow
Buried beneath the barn
context: The film, wrapped in waxed paper inside a pumpkin, became known as the 'Pumpkin Papers.' Prosecutors also matched documents to Hiss's own Woodstock typewriter (No. N230099), and Hiss was convicted of perjury in 1950. Source: Wikipedia 'Pumpkin Papers'; famous-trials.com/algerhiss.

question: To swap atomic secrets at Los Alamos, Soviet courier Harry Gold needed to be sure spy David Greenglass was his real contact and not a trap. They used a torn-in-half object as a secret recognition signal: Gold held one jagged piece, and Greenglass produced the matching piece from his wife's purse so the two edges fit together. What was the torn object?
answer: A Jell-O box top
choices: A Jell-O box top
A dollar bill
A playing card
A train ticket
context: The jagged halves of a Jell-O box top matched, proving each man was who he claimed. Greenglass then handed over sketches of the plutonium bomb's high-explosive lenses, one of its most crucial secrets. Source: Science History Institute 'Harry Gold: Spy in the Lab'; National Archives 'Fat Man, Little Boy, A Packet of Jell-O.'

question: In October 1947, ten Hollywood screenwriters and directors, including Dalton Trumbo, were hauled before the House Un-American Activities Committee and asked, 'Are you now or have you ever been a member of the Communist Party?' These 'Hollywood Ten' refused to answer the question. What happened to them for refusing?
answer: They were jailed and blacklisted from films
choices: They were jailed and blacklisted from films
They were fined and quietly let go
They were deported from the country
They were cleared and praised as heroes
context: The Hollywood Ten were cited for contempt of Congress, sent to federal prison, and blacklisted by the studios. Many never worked under their own names again. Source: History.com 'Who Were the Hollywood 10?'; todayinclh.com on Dalton Trumbo.

question: Blacklisted screenwriter Dalton Trumbo could not be hired under his own name, so he wrote movies under fake ones for a fraction of his old pay. When his script 'The Brave One' won the 1956 Best Story Oscar credited to 'Robert Rich,' no one walked up to accept it, and gossip columnist Hedda Hopper blurted out a question that exposed the whole sham. What did she ask?
answer: "Who the hell is Robert Rich?"
choices: "Who the hell is Robert Rich?"
"Where did the studio find him?"
"Why won't the winner stand up?"
"Has anyone read this man's contract?"
context: 'Robert Rich' was a front name for the blacklisted Trumbo, who also secretly wrote 'Spartacus' and 'Exodus.' His real name was restored to those films in 1960 and the Oscar reissued to him in 1975. Source: Hollywood Reporter on 'The Brave One'; Britannica 'Dalton Trumbo.'

question: On February 9, 1950, Senator Joseph McCarthy stood before a women's Republican club in Wheeling, West Virginia, waved a piece of paper, and announced he held the names of communists hiding inside the State Department. Over the following weeks the count he gave kept shrinking, from 205 down to 57, then 81, then 10. What never happened with that paper?
answer: He never showed the list or proved one name
choices: He never showed the list or proved one name
He never repeated the charge in public again
He never named the State Department again
He never spoke to reporters about it
context: McCarthy waved the paper but never made the list public, and the number on it kept changing. He never produced solid evidence against even one person, yet the speech launched his crusade. Source: McCarthy's Wheeling speech text (uoregon.edu); History.com 'This Day in History: Feb 9, 1950.'

question: On March 9, 1954, broadcaster Edward R. Murrow used Senator McCarthy's own filmed words to expose him on the program 'See It Now.' Murrow closed by looking straight into the camera and refusing to let Americans be ruled by fear. How did Murrow finish?
answer: "We are not descended from fearful men."
choices: "We are not descended from fearful men."
"The fault lies not in our stars."
"Fear is the enemy of a free press."
"Good night, and trust your neighbors."
context: Murrow said: 'We will not walk in fear, one of another... we are not descended from fearful men.' The broadcast was a turning point that helped move the public against McCarthy. Source: CBS News on Murrow's McCarthy report; plosin.com 'See It Now' transcript, March 9, 1954.

question: Senator Millard Tydings had called Joseph McCarthy's communist charges 'a fraud and a hoax,' so McCarthy's staff set out to destroy him before his 1950 re-election. They printed hundreds of thousands of copies of a single fake image to ruin him. What did that faked image show?
answer: Tydings chatting with a U.S. Communist leader
choices: Tydings chatting with a U.S. Communist leader
Tydings burning an American flag
Tydings asleep during a Senate vote
Tydings shaking hands with Stalin
context: The doctored composite spliced a 1938 photo of Tydings with a 1940 photo of Communist leader Earl Browder to fake a friendly chat; 300,000-500,000 copies circulated. Tydings lost, and a Senate panel called the campaign 'despicable, back-street.' Source: Time.com on the doctored photo; Wikipedia 'Tydings Committee.'

question: German-born physicist Klaus Fuchs worked at Los Alamos on the Manhattan Project from 1944 to 1946, then handed the Soviets detailed plans for the atomic bomb and later the hydrogen bomb. The secret Venona decrypts unmasked him, and he was arrested in Britain in early 1950. According to experts, what did his spying buy the Soviet Union?
answer: Its first atomic bomb one to two years sooner
choices: Its first atomic bomb one to two years sooner
Its first atomic bomb three to four years sooner
Working plans for the U.S. hydrogen bomb
A head start on a Soviet jet bomber
context: Experts estimate Fuchs's intelligence let the USSR build and test its first atomic bomb one to two years earlier than it otherwise could have. He proved the spies in the Red Scare were not all imaginary. Source: Atomic Heritage Foundation 'Klaus Fuchs'; Smithsonian 'Spies Who Spilled Atomic Bomb Secrets.'

question: On June 19, 1953, Julius and Ethel Rosenberg went to the electric chair at Sing Sing prison, the only American civilians executed for espionage during the Cold War. Julius died after three jolts of 2,000 volts. With Ethel, the first two jolts failed to stop her heart. How many jolts did it finally take to kill Ethel Rosenberg?
answer: Five jolts
choices: Five jolts
Three jolts
Four jolts
Six jolts
context: Ethel survived the first jolts, and a fifth had to be ordered to kill her. Both Rosenbergs proclaimed their innocence to the end. Source: History.com 'Julius and Ethel Rosenberg executed, June 19, 1953'; UPI Archives 1953.

question: The whole Army-McCarthy showdown that destroyed Senator McCarthy did not start with spies at all. Starting in July 1953, McCarthy's chief counsel Roy Cohn spent six months leaning on the U.S. Army over a single drafted private, even threatening to 'expose the Army in its worst light' when it refused him. What was Cohn actually demanding?
answer: A cushy posting for his friend Schine
choices: A cushy posting for his friend Schine
A weekend pass for a young aide
A fast promotion for a former staffer
An early discharge for a buddy
context: Cohn pressured the Army to give cushy treatment to his friend G. David Schine, a former McCarthy aide drafted as a private. The Army's counter-charge triggered the televised hearings that ended McCarthy. Source: Wikipedia 'Army-McCarthy hearings.'

question: The top-secret Venona project, which decoded intercepted Soviet cables, named Julius Rosenberg in 21 messages under the codenames ANTENNA and LIBERAL and showed he really ran a spy ring. Yet prosecutors never used a single one of these cables against him in court. Why were the decoded cables kept out of his trial?
answer: The cables were still classified secrets
choices: The cables were still classified secrets
Revealing them would expose the broken codes
The cables named only his codename
The code-breakers refused to testify
context: Venona stayed classified until July 1995, so the public, and the courtroom, never saw the cables proving Julius passed the proximity fuze and P-80 jet data. The case shows the witch-hunt and real spying tangled together: Julius truly spied. Source: NSA 'The Venona Story'; Wikipedia 'Venona project.'

question: Ethel Rosenberg was sent to the electric chair largely on the word of her own brother, David Greenglass, who testified he had watched her type up atomic secrets. Decades later, in 2001, Greenglass made a confession to author Sam Roberts and on '60 Minutes' that cast doubt on her execution. What did he admit?
answer: He had lied and never saw her type anything
choices: He had lied and never saw her type anything
He had been a Soviet agent himself all along
He had forged her signature on the documents
He had been paid by the FBI to accuse her
context: Greenglass admitted he never actually saw Ethel type and had lied to spare his own wife, Ruth, from prison so she could raise their children. So Julius truly spied, yet his wife may have gone to the chair on her brother's perjury. Source: Sam Roberts, 'The Brother'; CBS '60 Minutes' 2001.

question: On December 2, 1954, the U.S. Senate voted 67 to 22 to formally condemn Senator Joseph McCarthy for conduct that 'tended to bring the Senate into dishonor and disrepute.' He kept his seat but lost his subcommittee chairmanship and his power, and less than three years later he was dead at 48. His death certificate said acute hepatitis, but friends knew the real cause. What was it?
answer: Alcoholic liver failure
choices: Alcoholic liver failure
Heart disease from years of strain
Untreated diabetes
Long-term kidney failure
context: After the censure, McCarthy declined steeply into drink and died on May 2, 1957, of alcoholic liver failure, though his death certificate said acute hepatitis. Source: constitutioncenter.org 'The Senate censures Joseph McCarthy'; History.com 'May 2, 1957.'

question: Every year about two million Muslims travel to the city of Mecca for the hajj pilgrimage, where they all crowd around one building at the center of the Grand Mosque and walk in circles around it. What is that cube-shaped stone building called?
answer: The Kaaba
choices: The Kaaba
The minaret
The basilica
The ziggurat
context: The Kaaba is a cube about 15 metres (50 feet) tall at the centre of the Grand Mosque in Mecca; the Arabic word ka'bah literally means 'cube.' Muslims everywhere face its direction, the qibla, when they pray. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Kaaba-shrine-Mecca-Saudi-Arabia

question: When a man arrives in Mecca for the hajj, he takes off his ordinary clothes and puts on the ihram: two plain unstitched white sheets, one wrapped at the waist and one over the shoulder. With millions of pilgrims dressed exactly the same, what striking thing happens in the crowd?
answer: You cannot tell a king from a beggar
choices: You cannot tell a king from a beggar
Each tribe forms its own line
The wealthy lead the procession
Pilgrims are sorted by their age
context: Because rich and poor, prince and pauper all wear the same simple white cloth, no one can tell who is powerful and who is poor, all standing equal before God. Source: https://hisartravel.com.au/symbolism-of-white-ihram-all-you-need-to-know-before-hajj-2026/

question: In January 930 CE a raiding sect called the Qarmatians stormed Mecca and carried off the Black Stone set in the Kaaba's corner, hauling it away to eastern Arabia. About 22 years later it was finally returned, but it came back changed in a way that left a permanent mark. How did it come back?
answer: Broken into seven pieces
choices: Broken into seven pieces
Painted a deep gold
Wrapped in royal silk
Sealed inside a clay jar
context: The Black Stone returned around 952 CE shattered into seven fragments, which is why to this day it is cemented together and bound inside a silver frame, with a visible face only about 20 cm by 16 cm. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Stone

question: In Venice in 1516, the city council forced every Jew to live on one cramped little island, locking the gates from outside each night. That island had once been a metal-casting works, and the Venetian word for such a foundry gave the new walled quarter its name — a word the whole world still uses for a forced minority neighborhood. What was that word?
answer: ghetto
choices: ghetto
bazaar
commune
quarantine
context: The Venetian word for a foundry or casting-works was 'geto' (or 'getto'). Each evening the gates of the island were locked from the outside, and each morning they were reopened only when the marangona — the great bell of St Mark's Campanile — rang. Source: britannica.com/place/Venetian-Ghetto; myjewishlearning.com/article/a-brief-history-of-the-venice-ghetto/

question: Moses Maimonides (1138–1204) fled Cordoba as a boy when conquerors gave Jews the choice of convert, leave, or die; he grew into a physician for Saladin's court and wrote the 'Guide for the Perplexed,' which married Aristotle's philosophy to the Torah. Later generations judged him the greatest Jewish thinker since the prophet himself, and carved a single line on his tomb in Tiberias to say so. What does that line say?
answer: "From Moses to Moses there arose none like Moses."
choices: "From Moses to Moses there arose none like Moses."
"Here lies the physician who healed both body and soul."
"He brought the wisdom of Greece into the house of Israel."
"The light of Cordoba, extinguished but never darkened."
context: The first 'Moses' is Moses the prophet, the last is Maimonides; the line ranks him as the greatest Jewish mind since the Torah's own lawgiver. Born in Cordoba in 1138, he fled when the Almohads conquered the city in 1148, settled in Fustat, Egypt, served Saladin's court as a physician, and wrote the 'Guide for the Perplexed.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maimonides

question: A knight in full plate armour had a special name for every steel piece. What was the sabaton, the part shaped to a long point at the very front?
answer: The steel shoe that covered his foot
choices: The steel shoe that covered his foot
The steel collar that guarded his neck
The steel cap that covered his knee
The steel glove that covered his hand
context: The sabaton was the pointed steel shoe. Plate armour had a whole vocabulary of named parts: the gauntlet (hand), gorget (neck), poleyn (knee), greave (shin), pauldron (shoulder), and the fauld (the skirt of overlapping steel hoops at the waist). Source: worldhistory.org/article/1244/the-armour-of-an-english-medieval-knight/

question: For hundreds of years a sword stood wedged into a cliff face above a chapel at Rocamadour in France, said to be the legendary blade Durendal. What finally happened to it in June 2024?
answer: Someone stole it out of the rock
choices: Someone stole it out of the rock
Lightning shattered it in a storm
The cliff crumbled and buried it
A flood swept it down the river
context: The blade that vanished was a replica; the legend it honoured says Durendal belonged to the knight Roland. In June 2024 it was stolen straight out of the cliff. Source: smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/fabled-sword-from-medieval-french-folklore-disappears-180984682/

question: In the old legend, the dying knight Roland tried to destroy his sword Durendal by smashing it against a rock so no enemy could ever take it. According to the tale, what happened when blade met stone?
answer: The rock split apart, but the blade stayed whole
choices: The rock split apart, but the blade stayed whole
Both the sword and the rock shattered to pieces
The sword bent double but would not break
Sparks set the dry grass around him ablaze
context: Legend, not fact. Durendal was said to be unbreakable because its golden hilt held holy relics: a tooth of Saint Peter, the blood of Saint Basil, the hair of Saint Denis, and a scrap of the Virgin Mary's robe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durendal

question: People love to picture a medieval knight so weighed down by his armour that a crane had to hoist him onto his horse. In real life, how did a knight in full plate get into the saddle?
answer: He climbed up himself using just the stirrup
choices: He climbed up himself using just the stirrup
A team of squires lifted him by the arms
A wooden ramp was built up to the horse
He was strapped on while the horse knelt
context: A full suit of plate weighed only about 20-25 kg (45-55 lbs) spread evenly over the whole body, not piled in one spot. The crane was a myth: its first known version appeared in the magazine Punch in 1843 and was cemented by a 1944 Henry V film scene that horrified the Master of the Armouries at the Tower of London. Source: worldhistory.org/article/1244/the-armour-of-an-english-medieval-knight/

question: Heraldry — the coats of arms painted on knights' shields — followed a strict 'rule of tincture': you could never put metal on metal or colour on colour, such as a gold shape on a silver background. What was this rule really for?
answer: So the design stayed readable across a battlefield
choices: So the design stayed readable across a battlefield
So no two families could ever share a shield
So the paint would not flake off in the rain
So only the richest knights could afford one
context: A coat of arms had to be recognised instantly from far away, so the design needed strong contrast — that is why the rule (stated by Humphrey Llwyd in 1568) banned metal on metal or colour on colour. Heraldry even had its own colour names: red is gules, blue is azure, black is sable, gold is or, silver is argent. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_tincture

question: The red-and-white striped pole that still spins outside barbershops today is a leftover from when barbers also did surgery and bloodletting. What did the two colors originally stand for?
answer: Red for blood, white for the bandages
choices: Red for blood, white for the bandages
Red for fire, white for ice water
Red for wine, white for clean linen
Red for the king, white for the church
context: Medieval barber-surgeons let blood, pulled teeth, and lanced boils. By legend the very first poles were the used bloody bandages themselves, hung outside to dry and twisting in the wind into a red-and-white spiral that was later just painted on. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/why-are-barber-poles-red-white-and-blue

question: In the medieval peasant year, each season's work was timed by a Church feast day. The autumn feast of Michaelmas, on September 29, marked the end of the harvest. What else fell due on that day?
answer: The rents owed to the lord
choices: The rents owed to the lord
The first snowfall blessing
The spring ploughing
The midsummer bonfire
context: The whole farming calendar ran on feast days: Candlemas (Feb 2) was when ploughing could begin, and Lammas (Aug 1) was the first-loaf harvest festival when bread from the first wheat went to the lord and the priest. Michaelmas closed the harvest and was rent day. Source: https://nicolaa5.tripod.com/articles/feast.html

question: Medieval doctors believed your health and mood came from four body fluids called 'humors' — blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile — that had to stay in balance. We still describe people with words straight from that theory. The word for a cheerful, ruddy person traces to an excess of which fluid?
answer: Blood
choices: Blood
Phlegm
Yellow bile
Black bile
context: A cheerful, ruddy person was 'sanguine,' from the Latin for blood. The others gave us 'phlegmatic' (sluggish, pale), 'choleric' (angry, from yellow bile), and 'melancholic' (sad and creative, from black bile). It was a coherent system reasoned from observation, not foolishness. Source: https://becker.wustl.edu/news/humors-and-you/

question: During a 1537 battle the French barber-surgeon Ambroise Pare ran out of the boiling oil everyone used to seal gunshot wounds, so for the rest of the men he slapped on an improvised salve of egg yolk, oil of roses, and turpentine. The next morning, what did he find?
answer: The salve men were resting comfortably while the boiled men were in agony
choices: The salve men were resting comfortably while the boiled men were in agony
Both groups had died of their wounds overnight
The salve had hardened into a useless crust
The boiled men had recovered far faster
context: The accident taught Pare that the gentle dressing beat the brutal cautery. He summed up his humble view of medicine in a famous line: 'Je le pansai, Dieu le guerit' — 'I bandaged him, and God healed him.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambroise_Par%C3%A9

question: In 2015 scientists brewed up a 1,000-year-old eye-salve recipe from the Anglo-Saxon 'Bald's Leechbook' — garlic, an onion-family plant, wine, and cow bile, aged nine nights in brass — and tested it in the lab. What did the ancient recipe do?
answer: It killed MRSA, a modern antibiotic-resistant superbug
choices: It killed MRSA, a modern antibiotic-resistant superbug
It dissolved harmlessly with no effect at all
It turned out to be mildly poisonous
It only worked once the wine was removed
context: Strikingly, only the full mixture worked — none of the single ingredients killed the bacteria on their own, which suggests the medieval recipe-maker had genuinely tuned the combination. Medieval willow-bark tea for headaches was another real hit: willow contains salicin, the compound aspirin is made from. Source: https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/mbio.01129-15

question: At the University of Bologna in the Middle Ages, the students banded together into a guild and ran the whole school themselves. They even elected one of their own students as Rector to give the orders. What surprising power did these students hold over the scholars who taught them?
answer: They hired the professors and paid their wages
choices: They hired the professors and paid their wages
They wrote the professors' lectures for them
They chose which subjects the city could teach
They granted the professors their final degrees
context: At Bologna the students WERE the university — a 'universitas scholarium,' a guild of scholars who hired and paid the masters out of their own pockets and elected a student Rector with authority over them. The professors worked for the students, not the other way around. Source: Catholic Encyclopedia (newadvent.org/cathen/02641b.htm); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_university.

question: Because the students of Bologna paid their professors' wages, they ran their teachers like hired employees — and they did not tolerate a master who turned up late or strolled in unprepared for the morning lecture. When a professor slacked off, what did the students do to him?
answer: Fined him a sum of money out of his pay
choices: Fined him a sum of money out of his pay
Locked him out of the lecture hall
Forced him to teach an extra year free
Reported him to the bishop for trial
context: Bologna's students fined their own professors — a master who failed to start a lecture promptly was docked nine Bolognese pounds. They even elected official 'denouncers' to report a professor's misdeeds, and masters had to leave a cash deposit the students could seize for bad behavior. Source: History of Education Society, 'Puncta for Professors' (historyofeducation.org.uk/puncta-for-professors); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bologna.

question: When Thomas Aquinas was a young student he was enormous in size and so quiet in class that he almost never spoke up. His sharp-tongued classmates decided he must be slow and stupid, and they pinned a cruel mocking nickname on him. What did they call the silent giant?
answer: The Dumb Ox
choices: The Dumb Ox
The Sleeping Bear
The Stone Saint
The Lazy Monk
context: Classmates mocked the big, silent Aquinas as 'the Dumb Ox.' His teacher Albert the Great shut them down: 'You call him the Dumb Ox; I tell you this Dumb Ox will bellow so loud that his bellowing will fill the whole world.' Aquinas went on to write the 'Summa Theologica,' and the prediction came true. Source: World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/Thomas_Aquinas); Christianity.com.

question: When the young nobleman Thomas Aquinas announced he was joining the Dominicans — friars who lived by begging — his rich family was horrified and determined to stop him by force. They seized him and held him prisoner for about a year, trying to break his resolve. Where did his own family keep him locked up?
answer: In a tower of the family castle
choices: In a tower of the family castle
In a monastery far across the sea
In the dungeon of a rival lord
In a hermit's cave in the hills
context: Aquinas's family kidnapped him and locked him in a tower of the family castle (Monte San Giovanni / Roccasecca) for roughly a year to make him quit the begging friars. He refused, kept his vows, and became the greatest theologian of the age. Source: World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/Thomas_Aquinas).

question: Our word 'university' sounds like it should mean a place of universal, all-embracing learning. But that is not where the word came from at all. In the Middle Ages 'universitas' was the everyday Latin word for the same thing a guild of merchants or craftsmen was. What did the word 'universitas' originally name?
answer: A guild or corporation of people
choices: A guild or corporation of people
A library holding all knowledge
A walled town with its own laws
A grand hall built for teaching
context: 'Universitas' simply meant a guild or corporation — the same word used for tradesmen. A medieval university was a 'universitas magistrorum et scholarium,' a guild of masters and scholars; the word named the PEOPLE, not the buildings. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_university; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Paris.

question: Peter Abelard was the rock-star logician of early Paris — students flocked to watch him out-argue every rival, and his fame helped turn the city into a university. He fell in love with his brilliant pupil Héloïse, and when they had a son the couple gave the boy a startling name borrowed from an astronomical instrument. What did they name their son?
answer: Astrolabe
choices: Astrolabe
Quadrant
Lodestar
Meridian
context: Peter Abelard (1079–1142) and Héloïse named their son 'Astrolabe,' after the instrument used to measure the stars. Abelard's dazzling skill in logic drew crowds to Paris and helped make it a great university. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Abelard; Britannica (britannica.com/biography/Peter-Abelard).

question: In 1209, after scholars at Oxford clashed violently with the local townspeople, a frightened group of masters and students packed up and fled the city for good. They settled in a new town and started teaching there, founding England's second-oldest university. Which famous university was born from that flight out of Oxford?
answer: Cambridge
choices: Cambridge
Durham
Winchester
Canterbury
context: A town-and-gown riot drove Oxford scholars to flee in 1209; they regrouped and founded Cambridge. (Oxford itself had surged in 1167 when Henry II, feuding with Thomas Becket, barred English students from Paris and sent them home.) A riot literally created Cambridge. Source: University of Oxford, 'Our history' (ox.ac.uk/about/organisation/history); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford.

question: In a medieval university classroom there were almost no books, because every book had to be copied by hand and cost a fortune. So a 'lecture' was something very literal: the master sat before the class and performed a single action, after which he added his own commentary. What did the master actually do that gave the lecture its name?
answer: Read the text aloud word for word
choices: Read the text aloud word for word
Wrote the whole text on a great board
Recited the entire text from memory
Acted out the story in the text
context: The master read the set text aloud while students copied it down, then gave his commentary — the birth of the lecture itself. The word comes from Latin 'lectio,' a reading. 'Ordinary' lectures by master teachers ran from about 6 a.m. to 9 a.m. Source: Serious Science, 'Student Life in the Medieval Universities' (serious-science.org/...10575); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_university.

question: In the medieval university a scholar climbed from student to bachelor to master, but the key step was earning the 'licentia docendi' — the license to teach. Here is the strange part: the university itself did not hand out that license. Who actually granted a scholar the right to teach?
answer: The Church, through the local chancellor
choices: The Church, through the local chancellor
The king, through his royal court
The city, through its town council
The students, by their own vote
context: The 'licentia docendi' was granted by the Church — the chancellor of the diocese — so a medieval degree was literally a license to teach in the Church's name. Our words 'license' and 'licentiate' come straight from it. The Third Lateran Council of 1179 ordered the license given FREE to every qualified applicant. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Licentia_docendi; Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Master of Arts'.

question: The first great student strike in history broke out at the University of Paris in 1229, and it started over something astonishingly petty. During the carnival before Lent, a band of students got into a furious quarrel that turned into a riot, then a deadly crackdown by the queen's guards. What trivial dispute set the whole thing off?
answer: An argument over a tavern bill
choices: An argument over a tavern bill
A fight about a stolen cloak
A quarrel over a girl at a dance
A row about the price of bread
context: Students brawled with a tavern keeper over the bill for sweet wine, returned with clubs and wrecked the place; guards under regent Blanche of Castile then killed several students. The masters suspended all lectures and scattered for over two years — winning the 1231 bull 'Parens Scientiarum' (Mother of Sciences), the university's 'Magna Carta.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1229_University_of_Paris_strike.

question: In 1277 Étienne Tempier, the Bishop of Paris, struck back against the boldest philosophers at the university by condemning a long list of forbidden ideas drawn from Aristotle and his Arab commentators. The most shocking forbidden claim denied that each person has their own soul. Which dangerous idea did the bishop forbid Christians to hold?
answer: That all humans share one single intellect
choices: That all humans share one single intellect
That the soul dies with the body's blood
That the stars decide every human choice
That only priests possess a true soul
context: Tempier condemned 219 propositions, the most dramatic faith-and-reason clash of the medieval university. Among the 'Latin Averroist' claims he forbade: that the world is eternal, that philosophy is the highest life, and that there is one shared intellect for all humanity — which denied personal immortality and free will. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (plato.stanford.edu/entries/condemnation/); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condemnations_of_1210%E2%80%931277.

question: Thomas Aquinas built his 'Summa Theologica' as a series of structured debates, and the method has a surprising twist for anyone who expects a writer to attack his enemies first. Before Aquinas gives his own 'reply' to a question, he opens each one by doing something unexpected with the views he is about to refute. What does he do first?
answer: States the opposing arguments at their strongest
choices: States the opposing arguments at their strongest
Lists every thinker who ever erred
Mocks the opposing side as foolish
Quotes only Scripture and nothing else
context: Each scholastic 'quaestio' opens with the OBJECTIONS — the best case for the wrong side — then 'sed contra' (an authority for the other view), then Aquinas's own 'respondeo' (reply), then answers to each objection one by one. Steelman the opponent first, then refute: this 'disputatio' is the engine of scholastic reasoning. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scholasticism; Encyclopedia.com, 'Scholastic Method'.

question: Eleanor of Aquitaine was the most powerful woman in 12th-century Europe. First she married King Louis VII and became queen of France; then, after that marriage was annulled, she married Henry II and became queen of a second country. Which one?
answer: England
choices: England
Spain
Scotland
Sicily
context: Her marriage to Louis was annulled in March 1152, and she married Henry just two months later, on 18 May 1152 — making her the wife of two kings and queen of both France and England. Source: Britannica, Eleanor of Aquitaine; World History Encyclopedia.

question: In the Middle Ages, brewing beer was treated as women's work — nearly every peasant woman knew how, and women who sold it from their own homes earned a part-time living of their own. What were these beer-selling women called?
answer: Alewives
choices: Alewives
Goodwives
Midwives
Fishwives
context: Selling ale gave ordinary women rare financial independence at a time when most trades were closed to them. Source: Medievalists.net, 'The Village Ale-Wife'; JSTOR Daily, 'A Pint for the Alewives'.

question: When the Second Crusade set out for the Holy Land in 1147, Queen Eleanor of Aquitaine joined the march herself rather than ruling from home. In what way did she travel with the crusade?
answer: She rode toward the Holy Land with her own entourage of Aquitanian ladies
choices: She rode toward the Holy Land with her own entourage of Aquitanian ladies
She sailed ahead with a fleet and seized a port to await the army
She rode in the armored vanguard alongside the Knights Templar
She marched at the rear commanding the baggage train and its guards
context: Eleanor travelled through Constantinople with her own company of Aquitanian ladies; her conduct at her uncle Raymond's court in Antioch later sparked her husband Louis VII's jealousy. Source: National Geographic, 'Life of the Lioness'; Britannica.

question: Christine de Pizan was widowed in her mid-twenties when her husband died of the plague in 1389, leaving her with three children, her mother, and a niece to support. Instead of remarrying, she did something almost no one in Europe had done before. What?
answer: She earned her living as a professional writer
choices: She earned her living as a professional writer
She joined a convent and took vows
She ran her late husband's law practice
She became a lady-in-waiting at court
context: Christine de Pizan (c.1364–c.1430) is considered the first person in Europe to make a living by her pen. Source: National Geographic, 'France's first woman of letters'; World History Encyclopedia.

question: Around age 60, the abbess Hildegard of Bingen did something ordinarily forbidden to women: between 1158 and 1170 she went on four tours to cities like Cologne and Trier and stood up to do one particular thing before crowds of men. What?
answer: She preached sermons to male audiences
choices: She preached sermons to male audiences
She heard the confessions of monks
She crowned local bishops
She led armies of pilgrims into battle
context: Hildegard also corresponded with popes, with Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, with St. Bernard of Clairvaux, and with King Henry II of England. Source: Encyclopedia.com; World History Encyclopedia, Hildegard of Bingen.

question: Hilda of Whitby, an Anglo-Saxon abbess, ran a great double monastery and held nearly the power of a bishop. In 664 King Oswiu of Northumbria chose her abbey to host a famous meeting where the English Church settled whether to follow Roman or Irish custom. What was the key practice they argued over how to fix?
answer: The proper date for Easter
choices: The proper date for Easter
The language of the Mass
The age for baptizing infants
The number of feast days a year
context: The synod settled how to date Easter, in favor of Roman over Irish custom; the king choosing Hilda's abbey to host it was a mark of the prestige of her position. Five future bishops trained at her abbey, and people of every class called her 'mother.' Source: World History Encyclopedia, Hilda of Whitby; Wikipedia, Synod of Whitby.

question: Christine de Pizan was tired of poets like Jean de Meun painting women as 'vile temptresses.' In 1405 she answered with a book in which she builds a walled refuge page by page, filling it with the great and virtuous figures she had drawn from history. What is the book called?
answer: The Book of the City of Ladies
choices: The Book of the City of Ladies
The Romance of the Rose
The Mirror of Princes
The Garden of Earthly Delights
context: She also publicly debated The Romance of the Rose, attacking its portrayal of women. The distractor 'Romance of the Rose' is the very poem she was arguing against. Source: World History Encyclopedia; Open University, 'World-Changing Women: Christine de Pizan'.

question: The abbess Hildegard of Bingen wrote music, medical books, and a record of 26 visions. Around 1150 she made a bold move to win her nuns their independence: she broke away from a man's authority and set up something of her own. What did she do?
answer: She founded her own monastery at Rupertsberg
choices: She founded her own monastery at Rupertsberg
She petitioned the king to grant her a title
She sold the abbey's lands to fund a hospital
She left religious life to marry a nobleman
context: Hildegard broke from the abbot Kuno's authority so her community of nuns could flourish independently, and later founded another house at Eibingen in 1165. Source: Encyclopedia.com; World History Encyclopedia, Hildegard of Bingen.

question: Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar, spent eight years in his monastery garden in Brno patiently crossbreeding and counting about 28,000 plants to uncover the hidden rules of heredity. What humble crop did this friar grow and cross by the tens of thousands?
answer: Pea plants
choices: Pea plants
Grape vines
Wheat stalks
Apple trees
context: From 1856 to 1863 Mendel grew and crossbred about 28,000 plants, mostly peas, in the garden of St. Thomas Monastery in Brno. He chose peas because they were cheap, bred quickly and abundantly, and produced hundreds of observable peas per plant; he tracked seven clear traits including seed shape, seed color, pod shape, and stem length. Born Johann Mendel in 1822 to peasant farmers, he took the name Gregor when he entered the monastery. Sources: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/gregor-mendel-genetics ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregor_Mendel

question: In 1865 Gregor Mendel presented the hidden math of heredity to about 40 people at the Brno Natural History Society, and the world ignored it for roughly 35 years. Near his death in 1884 Mendel reportedly told a colleague that his vindication was still coming. What did he say?
answer: "My time will come"
choices: "My time will come"
"The peas never lie"
"Let the monks judge me"
"Count, and you will see"
context: The line ('Meine Zeit wird schon kommen') is reported testimony, framed as legend. Sixteen years later it came true: in 1900 three botanists — Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns, and Erich von Tschermak — independently rediscovered Mendel's laws and finally gave him credit, a generation after he published in 1866. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregor_Mendel ; https://www.vaticanobservatory.org/education/gregor-mendel-planting-seeds-genetics/ ; https://www.genome.gov/25520238/online-education-kit-1900-rediscovery-of-mendels-work

question: Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar, spent years crossing pea plants in his monastery garden in Brno. When he bred a round-seeded pea with a wrinkled-seeded pea, every single offspring came out round and the wrinkled seeds vanished completely. Then he let those round hybrid plants pollinate themselves. What happened to the wrinkled seeds in that next generation?
answer: The wrinkled form reappeared in about a quarter of the plants
choices: The wrinkled form reappeared in about a quarter of the plants
The wrinkled form stayed gone for good
Every plant produced seeds that were half-round, half-wrinkled
The plants grew wrinkled pods instead of wrinkled seeds
context: The wrinkled trait had been hidden, not erased. Mendel called the form that shows up 'dominant' (round) and the one that hides 'recessive' (wrinkled), and the recessive form returned in a roughly 3-to-1 ratio. Proving the trait was hidden, not blended away, is Mendel's signature result. Sources: https://www.sciencelearn.org.nz/resources/2000-mendel-s-principles-of-inheritance ; https://www.khanacademy.org/science/ap-biology/heredity/mendelian-genetics-ap/a/mendel-and-his-peas

question: Gregor Mendel read out his eight years of pea-breeding results to about 40 members of a small science society in 1865, and almost no one understood what they had heard. He died in 1884 with his work still ignored. Sixteen years later, in 1900, three botanists chasing the very same puzzle of heredity made the same discovery, then dug up Mendel's forgotten old paper. What did they find?
answer: Mendel had reached the same laws 35 years before them
choices: Mendel had reached the same laws 35 years before them
Mendel had reached the opposite conclusion entirely
Mendel had studied roses, not the question they were solving
Mendel had given up and never finished the work
context: Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns, and Erich von Tschermak each independently re-derived Mendel's laws in 1900 and discovered he had beaten them by decades. The patient, honest pea-counting of a monastery friar, unrewarded in his own lifetime, had quietly founded the science of genetics. Sources: https://www.genome.gov/25520238/online-education-kit-1900-rediscovery-of-mendels-work ; https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/gregor-mendel-genetics

question: Before dawn on September 16, 1810, Miguel Hidalgo, the village priest of Dolores in Spanish-ruled Mexico, ran to his church and rang the bell to wake every townsperson, then stood before them and called on them to rise up and throw off Spanish rule. That ringing speech, which launched Mexico's war for independence, is remembered by a single name. What is it called?
answer: The Grito de Dolores, the Cry of Dolores
choices: The Grito de Dolores, the Cry of Dolores
The Reconquista, the reconquest of Spain
The Cortes of Cadiz, the Spanish assembly
The Edict of Nantes, a royal decree
context: The 'Grito de Dolores' (Cry of Dolores) is Hidalgo's call to arms on Sept. 16, 1810. Mexico still celebrates Independence Day on Sept. 16 to mark it, even though independence was not actually won until 1821. Every year the President re-rings Hidalgo's bell from the National Palace balcony and shouts 'Viva Mexico!' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grito_de_Dolores ; https://www.britannica.com/event/Grito-de-Dolores

question: The day after he called his town to revolt, the priest Miguel Hidalgo and his ragtag army stopped at the church in Atotonilco, and Hidalgo grabbed a banner off its wall to carry into battle as his army's standard. His fighters then marched and fought under it, shouting their war cry. Whose image was on the banner Hidalgo seized?
answer: The Virgin of Guadalupe, patron saint of Mexico
choices: The Virgin of Guadalupe, patron saint of Mexico
King Ferdinand VII, the Spanish monarch
Saint James, the warrior patron of Spain
Hernan Cortes, the Spanish conqueror
context: Hidalgo seized a banner of the dark-skinned Virgin of Guadalupe (the 'virgen morena') and made it his army's standard; the insurgents' battle cry was roughly 'Long live the Virgin of Guadalupe! Death to bad government!' The image rallied thousands of Indian and mestizo fighters to his side. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banner_of_the_Virgin_of_Guadalupe ; https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/september-16/mexican-war-of-independence-begins

question: Michelangelo's statue of David in Florence is carved from one single block of marble. Standing far taller than a grown man, about how tall does it rise?
answer: About 17 feet

About 5 feet
About 9 feet
About 40 feet
context: The David stands roughly 17 feet (5.17 m) tall and weighs around 6 tons, all from a single block of Carrara marble. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_(Michelangelo)

question: People love to picture Michelangelo lying flat on his back to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling, but that story is a myth. How did he actually paint it?

question: In 1991 a man named Piero Cannata walked up to Michelangelo's David in Florence with a weapon hidden under his jacket and damaged the statue before he was stopped. What did he carry and what did he break?

question: Before Michelangelo touched it, the enormous marble block for the David had a nickname Florentines gave it. Two earlier sculptors had already given up on it and left it weathering in the cathedral yard for years. What did they call the block?
answer: il Gigante, 'the Giant'
choices: il Gigante, 'the Giant'

la Rovina, 'the Ruin'
il Re, 'the King'
context: The block was nicknamed 'il Gigante.' Agostino di Duccio roughed out the legs in 1464-66, Antonio Rossellino quit, and the half-worked block lay abandoned for decades before Michelangelo took it on. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_(Michelangelo)

question: For decades a single colossal block of Carrara marble lay on its side in the courtyard of Florence's cathedral workshop. It stood nearly seventeen feet tall, two earlier sculptors had already gouged into it and walked away, and the whole city had a nickname for the scarred, half-ruined slab that nobody could finish. In 1501 the 26-year-old Michelangelo asked for that very block and carved the most famous statue in the world from it. What did Florentines call the marble before he claimed it?
answer: The Giant
choices: The Giant
The Tower
The Mountain
The Whale
context: Florentines called the seventeen-foot block 'il Gigante' (the Giant). Agostino di Duccio roughed it out around 1464 and abandoned it; Antonio Rossellino briefly took it on next; it then lay weathering in the Opera del Duomo yard for about 25 years until Michelangelo began carving on 13 September 1501. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_(Michelangelo)

question: In the Sistine ceiling's most famous panel, the Creation of Adam, God reaches toward Adam and Adam reaches back. What is true of their two outstretched fingers?
answer: They do not touch; a small gap holds them apart
choices: They do not touch; a small gap holds them apart
They are firmly clasped together
Adam's hand covers God's entirely
God touches Adam's shoulder, not his hand
context: The fingers come within a few centimeters but never meet, holding the scene in suspense. In 1990 physician Frank Meshberger argued the shapes around God form the outline of a human brain. Source: https://www.thecollector.com/michelangelo-creation-of-adam-meaning/

question: Once the 17-foot David was finished, getting it out of Michelangelo's workshop and across Florence was its own ordeal. Workers had to knock down an archway just to free it, then move the 6-ton statue to the town hall. How did they haul it through the streets?
answer: Rolling it on fourteen greased logs

Floating it down the river on a barge
Lifting it with a giant crane
Dragging it on an iron sledge with oxen
context: More than 40 men took four days to roll the David on fourteen greased logs to the Palazzo della Signoria, unveiled on 8 September 1504. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_(Michelangelo)

question: When Michelangelo started the Sistine ceiling, the architect Bramante designed a scaffold for him that hung from the ceiling on ropes. Michelangelo threw the plan out for one specific reason and built his own self-supporting wooden bridge instead. What was wrong with Bramante's design?

context: Bramante's hanging scaffold needed anchor points in the vault itself; Michelangelo refused to scar the painting surface and braced his own bridge against the side walls. Source: https://www.archeoroma.org/sites/sistine-chapel/ceiling/

question: Early in the Sistine project disaster struck Michelangelo's very first big scene, the Flood. His Florentine plaster recipe did not suit Rome's damp air, and something appeared across the fresh paint that forced him to destroy months of work and redo the whole panel. What ruined it?
answer: A bloom of mold growing across the plaster
choices: A bloom of mold growing across the plaster

context: A lime-mold fungus bloomed because the plaster mix was wrong for Rome's humidity; Michelangelo chipped the panel back to bare wall and started over. Source: https://stephaniestorey.com/blog/top-10-little-known-facts-about-the-sistine-ceiling

question: Michelangelo's David has a head and right hand that look slightly too big for the body. This was not a mistake but a deliberate choice made for the spot the statue was first meant to stand. Where was it originally going to be placed?
answer: High up on the roofline of Florence Cathedral

context: The David was meant for the cathedral roofline, so the upper body was enlarged to read correctly from far below. Once finished, Florence judged it too magnificent to hoist up and set it at ground level by the town hall. Source: https://selectitaly.com/blog/florence/11-things-you-didnt-know-about-michelangelos-david/

question: Earlier Florentine sculptors like Donatello and Verrocchio had shown David standing in triumph over Goliath's severed head. Michelangelo broke with them and chose a completely different moment for his David to capture. Which moment did he freeze in marble?
answer: The tense instant before the fight, sling on his shoulder

question: Pulled off his beloved marble to paint, a miserable Michelangelo scribbled a comic poem to his friend Giovanni da Pistoia, complaining his beard pointed at heaven and dribbled paint splattered his face. He ended the poem with one curt line. What was it?

Source: https://agnionline.bu.edu/poetry/to-giovanni-da-pistoia-when-the-author-was-painting-the-vault-of-the-sistine-chapel

question: Michelangelo painted the Sistine ceiling's nine Genesis scenes out of order, in fact backwards. The first panel he painted was the Drunkenness of Noah, over the door, and he worked toward the altar. As he painted scene after scene in this reverse sequence, how did his figures change?

context: Working backward from the Drunkenness of Noah to the Creation, Michelangelo's figures grew larger and more confident as his skill on the vault deepened. Source: https://library.biblicalarchaeology.org/sidebar/genesis-in-reverse-the-hidden-meaning-of-the-sistine-chapel-ceiling/

question: Some scholars believe Michelangelo modeled the prophet Zechariah on Pope Julius II, the impatient pope who had once struck him with a stick. According to this reading, Michelangelo hid a small revenge in the painting. What is the boy behind Zechariah said to be doing?

This is interpretive tradition, not proven fact. Source: https://stephaniestorey.com/blog/top-10-little-known-facts-about-the-sistine-ceiling

question: Michelangelo's giant marble statue of David shows the young shepherd at a very particular instant. Earlier sculptors had carved David as a victor standing over Goliath's severed head. What moment does Michelangelo's David capture instead?

question: Michelangelo was so admired in his own lifetime that people gave him a single awe-struck nickname, and they spoke of the 'terribilita' -- the overwhelming power -- of his work. What did they call the man himself?

question: The huge block of Carrara marble that became David had a grim reputation before Michelangelo touched it. question: A famous legend says Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling flat on his back for four years. The legend is false. How did he actually reach the ceiling to paint it?

question: Around age 15, Michelangelo was training in the Medici sculpture garden in Florence. A jealous fellow pupil named Pietro Torrigiano attacked him, leaving a mark Michelangelo carried in every portrait for the rest of his life. What did Torrigiano do to him?

question: When the finished David was ready, Florence had to move the 8.5-ton statue just half a mile from the cathedral workshop to the Piazza della Signoria. question: Michelangelo thought of himself as a sculptor, not a painter, and resisted the Sistine ceiling commission. His biographer Condivi claimed a rival, the architect Bramante, had schemed to hand him that very job. What was Bramante secretly hoping would happen?

question: In 1509, miserable from months of overhead work on the Sistine ceiling, Michelangelo poured out his suffering in a comic sonnet to his friend Giovanni da Pistoia -- describing a goiter swelling in his throat, his beard pointing at heaven, and paint dripping onto his face. question: Michelangelo longed to be buried in Florence, but he died in Rome, where the Church wanted to keep his body. To get him home, his nephew Lionardo had the corpse carried out of Rome past the guards using a clever disguise. How was the body smuggled out?

question: In 1414 the admiral Zheng He's treasure fleet sailed home to the Ming court carrying a live giraffe, a gift from the African coast that no one in China had ever seen. Yongle had a court artist paint it — the only animal in his menagerie so honored — yet publicly insisted it was 'more important to maintain good government than to be concerned with supernatural signs.' Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/peculiar-story-giraffes-medieval-china-180963737/

question: Zheng He's Ming treasure fleets reached the East African coast in the early 1400s — decades before Columbus crossed the far smaller Atlantic in 1492. China stood poised to rule the oceans. Sent the fleet west to seek a sea route around to Europe
context: After 1433 the Ming court abandoned the treasure fleets, passed Haijin (sea-ban) laws forbidding private maritime trade and restricting shipbuilding to small coastal vessels, and Confucian officials set about destroying the records of the voyages. Having reached Africa first, China deliberately turned inward — the Yongle Emperor's cosmopolitan vision replaced by the Confucian ideal of a self-sufficient agrarian realm. Source: https://www.thecollector.com/zheng-he-closing-ming-china/

question: The Ming dynasty's founder, Zhu Yuanzhang, was born in 1328 to a dirt-poor peasant family. Plague killed his father, mother, and eldest brother within weeks, leaving him orphaned at 16. Before he ever dreamed of a throne, how did this future emperor keep himself alive?

question: For nearly 500 years, the great palace at the heart of Beijing was called the Forbidden City. What happened to an ordinary commoner who walked in or out of it without the emperor's express permission?

question: When Christopher Columbus sailed to the Americas, he crossed with three ships and fewer than a hundred men. Yet decades earlier the Ming emperor Yongle had already sent the eunuch admiral Zheng He across the Indian Ocean to Arabia and the coast of East Africa. Compared to Columbus's three ships, how big was just one of Zheng He's fleets?

context: Zheng He's treasure fleets (1405-1433) dwarfed anything in Europe; his flagships may have been several times the length of Columbus's Santa Maria. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1334/the-seven-voyages-of-zheng-he/

question: Legend says the builders of the Forbidden City stopped just short of giving it 10,000 rooms, the number in the Heavenly Emperor's palace, so the earthly emperor's home would never rival heaven's. According to that legend, how many rooms did they build instead?
answer: 9,999 and a half
choices: 9,999 and a half

context: That is the legend; a 1973 survey counted the real total at 980 buildings and 8,707 rooms across 90 courtyards. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbidden_City

question: The Forbidden City's Chinese name, Zijincheng, means 'Purple Forbidden City' even though the walls are red, not purple. The 'purple' pointed to the heavenly home of the celestial emperor, which Chinese astronomers tied to one particular star. Which star was it?

The Dog Star, Sirius

Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/history-magazine/article/emperors-ruled-from-chinas-forbidden-city-for-nearly-5-centuries

question: The floors of the Forbidden City's grand throne halls were paved with what the Chinese called 'golden bricks,' carried 1,000 miles up the Grand Canal from kilns near Suzhou. They were not actually made of gold. What earned them the name?

They glitter with real gold dust

They never crack under any weight
context: They are special clay tiles fired for months in the imperial kilns; the dense bake gives them their metallic ring. Source: https://www.chinahighlights.com/beijing/forbidden-city/

question: Yongle (Zhu Di) seized the Ming throne by waging civil war against his own nephew, the Jianwen Emperor. When Yongle's army took Nanjing in 1402, the palace caught fire and Jianwen vanished, his body never confirmed. What does legend say became of him?
answer: He escaped disguised as a wandering monk and lived nearly 40 more years
choices: He escaped disguised as a wandering monk and lived nearly 40 more years
He drowned trying to cross the Yangtze that same night
He fled north and raised a second army against Yongle
He was captured at sea aboard one of Zheng He's ships
context: This is the enduring legend; no body was ever confirmed, and the vanished Jianwen became one of China's great unsolved royal mysteries. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Yongle_Emperor/

question: At the Forbidden City's Meridian Gate, the great central doorway was reserved for the emperor alone. The empress passed through it exactly once, on her wedding day. One other group earned the right to walk that imperial path, just once each. Who were they?
answer: The top three scholars in the empire-wide civil-service exam
choices: The top three scholars in the empire-wide civil-service exam
Foreign kings arriving to pay tribute
The emperor's eldest son and heir
Generals returning from a great victory
context: In a society that prized learning above almost all else, scoring at the very top of the grueling imperial exam bought you a walk through the emperor's own door. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/history-magazine/article/emperors-ruled-from-chinas-forbidden-city-for-nearly-5-centuries

question: In 1414 Zheng He's fleet brought a strange long-necked, one-horned beast back to the Ming court from East Africa. The court, eager to flatter the usurper-emperor Yongle, decided it was a famous creature from Confucian tradition said to appear only when a perfectly wise and virtuous ruler sits on the throne. What did they declare the animal to be?
answer: A qilin
choices: A qilin
A phoenix
A dragon
A divine tortoise
context: The animal was really a giraffe, but calling it a qilin handed Yongle a heaven-sent stamp of legitimacy for a throne he had taken by force. Source: https://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/history/worldspring09/giraffe.html

question: The first Ming emperor, Hongwu, ruled by terror; after he suspected his chancellor Hu Weiyong of plotting in 1380, more than 15,000 officials and their relatives were executed. Which line is the one Hongwu himself is recorded as saying about the endless plotting around him?
answer: In the morning I punish a few; by evening others commit the same crime
choices: In the morning I punish a few; by evening others commit the same crime
Trust no minister, for every smile at court hides a knife
Spies whisper in my walls, and sleep has become my enemy
Cut down one traitor and ten more sprout in his place
context: The full line ends 'Day and night I cannot rest,' a chilling glimpse of a ruler who trusted almost no one. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Hongwu_Emperor/

question: The Yongle Emperor put about 2,000 scholars to work compiling the Yongle Encyclopedia, gathering roughly 22,937 chapters into 11,095 volumes by 1408, so vast it was never even printed. It held the title of largest encyclopedia on Earth for almost 600 years, until what finally surpassed it in 2007?
answer: Wikipedia
choices: Wikipedia
Encyclopaedia Britannica
The Library of Congress catalog
The complete works of the Qing court
context: A web project written by volunteers finally outgrew the handwritten masterpiece of 2,000 imperial scholars. Source: https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Yongle_Encyclopedia

question: After Yongle died, Confucian officials condemned Zheng He's costly ocean voyages as wasteful folly, and around 1477 an official named Liu Daxia is said to have taken a drastic step to make sure no future emperor could ever repeat them. What did he do?
answer: He hid or burned Zheng He's voyage records
choices: He hid or burned Zheng He's voyage records
He sank the last treasure ships in harbor
He had Zheng He's name struck from all histories
He sold the fleet's maps to foreign traders
context: In 1436 the Ming even banned building seagoing ships; China turned inward just as Europe began sailing outward, a turning point with consequences for centuries. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haijin

question: Zheng He's fleet sailed home from Africa carrying a live giraffe, an animal no one at the Chinese court had ever seen. When the towering creature was led before the Yongle Emperor, the court declared it was no ordinary beast but a legendary creature whose appearance proved that Heaven blessed the throne. Which mythical creature did they say the giraffe was?
answer: A qilin, the gentle unicorn of legend
choices: A qilin, the gentle unicorn of legend
A phoenix, the firebird of rebirth
A dragon, the bringer of rain
A tortoise, the bearer of long life
context: The qilin was a unicorn-like beast said to appear only under a wise and virtuous ruler, so a real giraffe arriving from overseas in 1414 (routed through the king of Bengal) was the perfect propaganda gift for the throne-usurping Yongle Emperor. Court painters made scrolls titled 'The Eulogy of the Qilin, an Auspicious Omen.' (Smithsonian Magazine, 'The Peculiar Story of Giraffes in 1400s China'; Sally K. Church, 'The Giraffe of Bengal,' 2004.)

question: Zheng He's largest 'treasure ships' were so colossal that Christopher Columbus's flagship, the Santa Maria, at about 85 feet long, would have looked like a rowboat beside one. According to the traditional Ming records, just how vast was one of Zheng He's greatest ships?
answer: Every ship of Columbus and Vasco da Gama combined could fit on its deck
choices: Every ship of Columbus and Vasco da Gama combined could fit on its deck
Its anchor alone weighed more than the entire Santa Maria
It took a full week just to sail all the way around a small island
A thousand horses could gallop across its open deck at once
context: By the traditional dimensions in Ming sources, Zheng He's longest ships ran about 400 feet, carrying nine masts and twelve sails. When archaeologists dug at the Longjiang shipyard in Nanjing in 1957 they unearthed a single rudder post about 36 feet long, longer than half of Columbus's whole ship, hinting at just how enormous the real vessels were. (Association for Asian Studies / National Geographic, 'Seven Voyages of Zheng He'; TheCollector, 'Admiral Zheng He.')

question: History classes often credit European sailors with opening the Age of Exploration: Columbus crossing the Atlantic in 1492 and Vasco da Gama reaching India in 1498. Yet Zheng He's treasure fleets had already crossed the Indian Ocean and reached the coast of East Africa. How long before Columbus's famous 1492 voyage did Zheng He's expeditions set sail?
answer: Roughly 60 to 90 years earlier
choices: Roughly 60 to 90 years earlier
Roughly 5 to 10 years earlier
About the same time, give or take a year
Only a few months earlier
context: Zheng He's seven voyages ran from 1405 to 1433, about 60 years before Columbus crossed the Atlantic and roughly 80 years before da Gama reached India. China explored the Indian Ocean first, on a scale Europe would not match for generations, and then stopped. (Crash Course World History #21; TheCollector, 'Admiral Zheng He.')

question: After Zheng He's death, China's scholar-officials judged the treasure voyages a ruinous waste, and the empire turned away from the sea. The expeditions' priceless navigation charts and logbooks, the maps of the greatest navy on Earth, came into the hands of a War Ministry official named Liu Daxia, who reportedly feared that future generations 'might imitate them.' What did Liu Daxia do with the fleet's records?
answer: He destroyed them, and the maps were lost forever
choices: He destroyed them, and the maps were lost forever
He locked them away in the imperial library
He sealed them inside his family's tomb
He handed them in secret to the next admiral
context: Liu Daxia is recorded as having destroyed or hidden the fleet's logs and charts 'fearing future generations might imitate them.'
