The Xuande emperor banned the building of ocean-going ships, Confucian officials framed the voyages as extravagance, and the records of history's greatest navy were erased, a civilization deliberately abandoning its own lead. (Yan Congjian, 'Shuyu Zhouzi Lu'; World History Encyclopedia; Wikipedia, 'Haijin.')

question: In 1409, Zheng He's expedition set up a stone tablet in Galle, on the island of Ceylon (today Sri Lanka). What makes this single stone astonishing is its writing: the same monument carries an inscription in three different languages, each one offering thanks and gifts to a completely different god. Which three did the stone honor side by side?
answer: The Buddha, the Hindu god Vishnu, and Allah
choices: The Buddha, the Hindu god Vishnu, and Allah
The Buddha, the Hindu god Shiva, and Allah
The Buddha, the Hindu god Vishnu, and the Jade Emperor
Confucius, the Hindu god Vishnu, and Allah
context: The Galle Trilingual Inscription praises the Buddha in Chinese, the Tamil-Hindu god Tenavarai Nayanar (Vishnu) in Tamil, and Allah in Persian, the only known inscription in those three languages together, and it promised offerings of 1,000 pieces of gold, 5,000 of silver, and tons of scented oil. The stone vanished for centuries and was rediscovered in 1911 lying face down, being used as a cover for a roadside drain in Galle; it now sits in the Colombo National Museum and is on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register. (Wikipedia, 'Galle Trilingual Inscription'; UNESCO Memory of the World.)

question: Before the Spanish came, the Aztec emperor was Moctezuma II, also called Moctezuma Xocoyotzin. He had been a war-leader and the high priest of the war-god Huitzilopochtli. What does the name 'Moctezuma' roughly mean?
answer: he frowns like a lord
choices: he frowns like a lord
he speaks for the sun
he walks among eagles
he holds the obsidian
context: Roughly 'he frowns like a lord' or 'he who is angry in a noble manner.' Before taking the throne he served as a tlacatecuhtli (war-leader) and as high priest of Huitzilopochtli, the Aztec war-god. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moctezuma_II

question: When the Spanish soldiers crossed the mountains and first saw the city of Tenochtitlan rising out of its lake, with towers and temples shining on the water, the eyewitness Bernal Diaz wrote that it looked so unreal that some men asked if they were dreaming. What did Diaz compare the sight to?
answer: the enchanted cities in the legend of Amadis
choices: the enchanted cities in the legend of Amadis
the golden halls in the tales of King Arthur
the hanging gardens of ancient Babylon
the lost island kingdom of Atlantis
context: Bernal Diaz del Castillo wrote that the towers and temples on the water 'seemed like an enchantment... like the things of which they tell in the legend of Amadis' (a hugely popular chivalric romance), and that some soldiers asked whether what they saw was real or a dream. Source: https://www.pbs.org/conquistadors/cortes/cortes_e02.html

question: When Moctezuma II and Hernan Cortes finally met on the great causeway into Tenochtitlan in November 1519, the two rulers traded necklaces. Cortes gave a collar of pearls and cut glass; Moctezuma gave back collars of red snail-shells, and from each one hung eight little objects of gold, each about a foot and a half long. What were the gold objects shaped like?
answer: golden shrimp
choices: golden shrimp
golden eagles
golden skulls
golden serpents
context: By Cortes's own account (his Second Letter), Moctezuma gave two collars of red snail-shells, from each of which hung eight golden prawns/shrimp 'finished in a very perfect manner, about a foot and a half in length.' Source: https://www.historians.org/resource/cortes-on-meeting-moctezuma/

question: For the final siege of Tenochtitlan, Cortes's shipwright Martin Lopez built thirteen small sailing warships far inland, nowhere near the water. How did the Spanish get these ships onto Lake Texcoco to fight the Aztec war-canoes?
answer: carried them overland in pieces, then rebuilt them
choices: carried them overland in pieces, then rebuilt them
floated them down a river to the lakeshore
dug a long canal out to the lake
waited for the rains to flood the plain
context: Martin Lopez built thirteen brigantines inland, and they were carried and dragged overland in pieces and reassembled on the shore of Lake Texcoco. The ships let the Spanish smash the Aztec war-canoe fleet and dominate the water during the siege. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Tenochtitlan

question: When Tenochtitlan fell in 1521, the Aztecs' last emperor had led the defense to the bitter end. His name was Cuauhtemoc. What does the name 'Cuauhtemoc' mean?
answer: Descending Eagle
choices: Descending Eagle
Smoking Mirror
Speaking Stone
Obsidian Serpent
context: 'Cuauhtemoc' means 'Descending Eagle.' He led the defense of Tenochtitlan to the very end before the city fell on 13 August 1521. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Cuauhtemoc

question: La Malinche (Marina), a Nahua noblewoman who had been sold into slavery, was Cortes's indispensable interpreter; Bernal Diaz said that without her the Spanish could not have understood the Aztecs at all. But Malinche did not speak Spanish. So when Cortes spoke to the Aztecs, how did his words reach them?
answer: a relay through two interpreters and three tongues
choices: a relay through two interpreters and three tongues
a priest who had mastered the Nahuatl language
hand signs the two sides agreed in advance
letters drafted and read aloud in Latin
context: The chain ran: Cortes spoke Spanish to the shipwreck survivor Geronimo de Aguilar, who rendered it into Maya for Malinche, who then spoke Nahuatl (including the elite court register) to the Aztecs, and back again. Bernal Diaz: 'Without Dona Marina we could not have understood the language of New Spain and Mexico.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Malinche

question: The popular story says a few hundred Spaniards toppled the Aztec Empire. In truth Cortes marched with tens of thousands of Indigenous warriors who had their own reason to hate the Aztecs: they were sick of paying Aztec tribute. Which people, never themselves conquered by the Aztecs, became Cortes's great ally?
answer: the Tlaxcalans of Tlaxcala
choices: the Tlaxcalans of Tlaxcala
the Maya of the Yucatan
the Tarascans of Michoacan
the Zapotecs of Oaxaca
context: The Tlaxcalans, never conquered by the Aztecs and resentful of their tribute, supplied warriors in the tens of thousands (estimates run up toward 100,000+ across the campaign), plus food, guides, and safe haven. The conquest was an Indigenous alliance against the Aztecs, not a handful of Europeans. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_conquest_of_the_Aztec_Empire

question: The Spanish are remembered for their steel swords and their horses. But the deadliest force in the conquest of the Aztecs was something they brought without meaning to, something the people of Mexico had never met before. What was it?
answer: smallpox
choices: smallpox
typhus
cholera
measles
context: The 1520 smallpox epidemic killed an estimated 5 to 8 million people across Mesoamerica, far more than Spanish weapons; among the dead was Moctezuma's successor Cuitlahuac, emperor for only about 80 days. The Florentine Codex describes the sores in agonizing detail: 'Sores erupted on our faces, our breasts, our bellies... agonizing sores from head to foot.' Source: https://www.doaks.org/resources/online-exhibits/epidemics/epidemics-english/fall-of-tenochtitlan/smallpox

question: While Cortes was away from Tenochtitlan, his captain Pedro de Alvarado feared a revolt and attacked the unarmed Aztec nobles dancing at the festival of Tezcatlipoca, in May 1520. Aztec accounts say the killing began with one particular man. What did the Spanish do first?
answer: cut the arms off the man beating the great drum
choices: cut the arms off the man beating the great drum
set fire to the wooden steps of the temple
shot the high priest down from the gateway
seized the gold piled on the temple altar
context: The Toxcatl Massacre (22 May 1520). Aztec sources (Florentine Codex Book 12, Codex Aubin) say the Spanish first cut off the arms/hands of the man playing the great drum, then beheaded him, then slaughtered the dancers, having blocked the temple exits. Two drums appear in the codex images: the upright huehuetl and the horizontal teponaztli. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_in_the_Great_Temple_of_Tenochtitlan

question: On the night of 30 June 1520, the Night of Sorrows, the Spanish tried to sneak out of Tenochtitlan along a causeway in the dark and were caught and slaughtered. Many soldiers had stuffed their clothes full of looted Aztec gold. What happened to those men?
answer: they drowned, dragged under by the gold
choices: they drowned, dragged under by the gold
they were dragged off to be sacrificed
they turned back and gave up their gold
they were trampled in the fleeing crowd
context: La Noche Triste, 30 June 1520: roughly 400 Spaniards and about 4,000 Indigenous allies were killed, along with many horses, as the Spanish fled along the causeway. Soldiers weighed down with looted gold sank and drowned in the lake. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_conquest_of_the_Aztec_Empire

question: When Tenochtitlan finally fell on 13 August 1521, the last emperor, Cuauhtemoc, tried to escape across the lake by canoe with his family but was intercepted by a Spanish ship and brought before Cortes. Having done everything he could to defend his city, what did Cuauhtemoc reportedly do before Cortes?
answer: asked Cortes to kill him with his own dagger
choices: asked Cortes to kill him with his own dagger
begged Cortes to spare his wife and children
cursed Cortes and the Spanish in open court
offered Cortes the city's last hidden gold
context: Cuauhtemoc was intercepted by a brigantine under Garcia Holguin/Sandoval. Brought before Cortes, he reportedly touched the dagger at Cortes's belt and said, 'Take that dagger... and kill me with it,' having done all he could to defend Tenochtitlan. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Cuauhtemoc

question: Everyone 'knows' that when Hernan Cortes landed in Mexico in 1519 he burned his ships so his men could not turn back. But that story comes from a painting made decades later. To strand his men, what did Cortes actually do to his fleet?
answer: ran them aground and stripped them bare
choices: ran them aground and stripped them bare
burned them down to the waterline
sailed them home across the sea
handed them over to Governor Velazquez
context: Cortes did NOT burn his ships. At Veracruz he had them stripped of anchors, sails, and cables and run aground/scuttled (keeping the parts) so his men could not sail home; he wrote to the king that he 'ran the ships ashore under the pretext that they were no longer fit to sail.' The 'burning ships' image comes from a 1558 funerary painting. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hern%C3%A1n_Cort%C3%A9s

question: Aztec accounts written down decades after the conquest tell of eight omens that warned of doom, including a strange ashen bird brought to Moctezuma with a mirror set in its head. When Moctezuma looked into that mirror, what did he reportedly see?
answer: warriors riding strange deer
choices: warriors riding strange deer
the city of Tenochtitlan in flames
two suns rising over the lake
a serpent swallowing the moon
context: In the omen, Moctezuma saw warriors riding 'deer', that is, men on horses, animals the Aztecs had never seen. These 'eight omens' survive mainly in the Florentine Codex, compiled by friar Bernardino de Sahagun about 50 years after the conquest; historians treat them, and the famous claim that Moctezuma thought Cortes was the returning god Quetzalcoatl, as largely a post-conquest construction rather than reliable contemporary evidence. Source: https://mexicounexplained.com/8-omens-montezuma-end-aztec-empire/  (Legend.)

question: Moctezuma II died in Spanish custody in June 1520, and exactly how he died is still genuinely disputed. The Spanish soldier Bernal Diaz wrote that three stones struck Moctezuma on the head, arm, and leg as he was brought out before the city. By Diaz's telling, who had thrown those stones?
answer: his own Aztec people
choices: his own Aztec people
the Spanish soldiers
Pedro de Alvarado
the Tlaxcalan warriors
context: By Bernal Diaz's Spanish account, Moctezuma was struck by stones thrown by his own people and then refused food and treatment and died of the wounds. But the death is genuinely contested: some Indigenous sources (e.g. Chimalpahin) say the Spanish killed him, and report that his body bore sword wounds. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moctezuma_II ; https://www.mexicolore.co.uk/aztecs/ask-us/moctezumas-death

question: The conqueror the world calls Genghis Khan was not born with that name. His father, the chieftain Yesugei, named the newborn boy Temujin, after a Tatar warrior he had just captured. What did that birth-name, Temujin, mean?
answer: Of iron, or blacksmith
choices: Of iron, or blacksmith
Son of the open sky
Wolf of the cold steppe
Lord of a thousand horses
context: Temujin meant 'of iron' or 'blacksmith.' 'Genghis Khan,' likely meaning 'universal ruler,' was a title given to him only in 1206. Sources: worldhistory.org/Genghis_Khan; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genghis_Khan

question: A Mongol warrior could gallop at full speed and still strike a target hundreds of yards away. What was this signature weapon, light enough to fire from the saddle yet pulling more than a hundred pounds?
answer: A composite bow of horn and sinew
choices: A composite bow of horn and sinew
A long iron-tipped cavalry lance
A curved single-edged saber
A heavy wooden siege crossbow
context: The Mongol composite bow was built from layers of sinew, horn, and wood; it could exceed 100-pound draw weights and strike at roughly 350 yards. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_bow; coldsiberia.org/monbow.htm

question: By the time Genghis Khan died in 1227, the realm he had built was already twice the size of the Roman Empire at its height. Among all the empires the world has known, what extent record does the Mongol Empire still hold today?
answer: The largest connected stretch of land ever ruled
choices: The largest connected stretch of land ever ruled
The most separate kingdoms ever held at once
The widest sweep of ocean ever controlled
The greatest number of walled cities ever taken
context: It became the largest contiguous land empire in history, peaking near 23.5 million square kilometers under Kublai Khan around 1294. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_Empire

question: Across the vast Mongol Empire, an urgent message could travel 200 miles in a single day. The secret was a chain of stations every 20 to 40 miles, each holding what ready for the next leg of the journey?
answer: A relay of fresh horses and riders
choices: A relay of fresh horses and riders
A chain of signal fires on hills
A fleet of fast river boats
A line of trained carrier pigeons
context: This postal relay was called the yam (or ortoo): a rider handed off his message and rested while a fresh rider raced on, like a pony express spanning a continent. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yam_(route); warriorsandlegends.com

question: At the Battle of Mohi in 1241 the Mongols faced a large Hungarian army drawn up for battle. What favorite battlefield trick did they use to break it apart?
answer: They pretended to flee, then turned and fired
choices: They pretended to flee, then turned and fired
They crossed the river in a night march
They set their own camp ablaze as a lure
They locked their shields into a wall
context: The feigned retreat: the 'fleeing' horsemen suddenly wheeled around and showered their disorganized pursuers with arrows. They used it to shatter the Hungarians at Mohi on 11 April 1241. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mohi

question: A messenger crossing the Mongol Empire carried a special object that entitled him to fresh horses, food, and lodging at every station. Its inscription opened 'By the power of eternal Heaven' and warned that anyone who disrespected the bearer 'shall die.' What was this object?
answer: A metal passport tablet
choices: A metal passport tablet
A sealed wax letter
A painted silk banner
A carved bone whistle
context: The paiza (gerege): rank showed in the metal, from wood and bronze up to silver and gold for the highest. It opened 'By the power of eternal Heaven.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paiza; rubinmuseum.org

question: Under the peace the Mongols enforced, called the Pax Mongolica, the Silk Road grew so orderly that travelers like Marco Polo crossed from China to Europe. People summed up that order with a famous saying. What did the saying claim a traveler could do on those roads?
answer: A maiden could carry gold across it unharmed
choices: A maiden could carry gold across it unharmed
A lone child could cross it without any fear
A merchant could sleep in the open and wake untouched
A pilgrim could walk it for a year and meet no thief
context: It was said 'a maiden bearing a nugget of gold on her head could wander safely throughout the realm.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pax_Mongolica; education.nationalgeographic.org

question: For the most urgent dispatches, a Mongol relay rider carried something that the next station, still far off, would hear, so a fresh horse and rider stood waiting the instant he arrived. What did the rider use to announce himself from a distance?
answer: A belt of jingling bells
choices: A belt of jingling bells
A horn he sounded as he rode
A drum strapped to his saddle
A whistle carved from bone
context: These 'arrow messengers' rode with head and torso bandaged against the pace; for top-priority mail a rider wore a belt of bells whose jingling warned the next station from far off. Sources: warriorsandlegends.com; tldrhistory.com

question: Genghis Khan's greatest general, Subutai, is credited with conquering 32 nations and winning 65 pitched battles, yet he had no family tie to the Khan at all. He joined the army at about fourteen and rose to supreme command. What was he when he started out?
answer: A blacksmith’s son with no royal blood
choices: A blacksmith’s son with no royal blood
A captured prince of a rival clan
A cousin born into the Khan’s family
A hired captain from a foreign land
context: Subutai was the son of a blacksmith from the Uriankhai tribe near Lake Baikal, with no blood tie to the Khan, and ended his life as a herdsman, living proof the Mongol army rewarded merit. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subutai; historyfacts.com

question: Genghis Khan's huge western war did not begin over land or a throne. In 1218 he had sent a trading caravan of about 450 merchants to the Khwarazmian city of Otrar, expecting peaceful commerce. What did the city's governor, Inalchuq, do to that caravan and unleash the Mongol army?
answer: He killed every merchant and seized their goods
choices: He killed every merchant and seized their goods
He let them pass but taxed them into ruin
He jailed the merchants and held them for ransom
He turned the caravan back at the city gate
context: Inalchuq accused the merchants of spying, killed them all, and seized their goods; when Genghis sent envoys for justice, the Shah beheaded the lead ambassador, so Genghis invaded. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otrar_Catastrophe; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inalchuq

question: When Genghis Khan died in 1227, his followers hid his burial place so completely that it has never been found to this day. Tradition says the funeral escort even killed travelers they met along the way. What did they do at the grave itself to erase every trace of it?
answer: Riders trampled the grave flat to hide it
choices: Riders trampled the grave flat to hide it
He was buried at sea in a stone coffin
His tomb was filled with molten gold
His body was burned on a great pyre
context: Tradition holds that the escort had horses trample the grave flat so no mound or marker remained. The tomb has never been located. Sources: worldhistory.org/Genghis_Khan; history.com/topics/asian-history/genghis-khan  (Legend.)

question: In 1258 Genghis Khan's grandson Hulegu took Baghdad, the seat of the Abbasid Caliphate. Because the Mongols feared spilling royal blood on the ground, they chose an unusual way to kill the captured caliph, al-Musta'sim. How did they execute him?
answer: He was rolled in a carpet and trampled by horses
choices: He was rolled in a carpet and trampled by horses
He was strangled with a silk bowstring
He was sealed inside a wall to starve
He was smothered under heavy felt rugs
context: Baghdad's House of Wisdom library was destroyed; chroniclers say the Tigris ran black with ink and red with blood. To avoid shedding royal blood on the earth, the caliph was rolled in a carpet and trampled. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Baghdad; warhistoryonline.com

question: The Persian city of Nishapur had killed Genghis Khan's son-in-law Toquchar with an arrow. In April 1221 his son Tolui stormed the city and ordered every inhabitant put to the sword, including the famous poet Attar. What did the Mongols build there as a lasting warning to anyone who might resist?
answer: Three pyramids stacked from the severed heads
choices: Three pyramids stacked from the severed heads
Fields sown with salt so nothing would grow
The great mosque burned down to bare stone
A pillar carved with the Khan's victories
context: The severed heads were reportedly built into three separate pyramids, one of men, one of women, one of children, as a warning. The poet Attar, about 78, was among the dead. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Nishapur_(1221)

question: In 2003 geneticists studying men across the lands of the old Mongol Empire found one Y-chromosome lineage shared far more widely than chance allows, and they proposed it traced back to Genghis Khan and his sons. Roughly how many living men were estimated to carry it?
answer: About 16 million men across the old empire
choices: About 16 million men across the old empire
About 1 in 5,000 men on the whole planet
About every man descended from the Khan
About a few thousand men in Mongolia alone
context: The 2003 study found the lineage in about 8% of men across the former empire, roughly 16 million. Later researchers have questioned whether it truly belongs to Genghis specifically. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_descent_from_Genghis_Khan; nationalgeographic.com

question: In April 1241 the Mongol general Subutai sent two armies hundreds of miles apart to crush two separate European armies almost at once - the Poles at Legnica on April 9 and the Hungarians at Mohi on April 11. Both times his lightly-armed horse-archers used the same trick to wreck the heavily-armored European knights. What was the trick?
answer: They pretended to flee, luring the knights into a hidden ambush
choices: They pretended to flee, luring the knights into a hidden ambush
They dug a deep trench across the front of the battlefield
They poisoned the rivers the knights drank from before the fight
They bribed the knights' own commanders to switch sides
context: The 'feigned retreat' was the Mongol signature: horse-archers would attack, then turn and gallop away, baiting the European knights into breaking formation and charging straight into a pre-set ambush. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Battle-of-Legnica-1241

question: By late 1241 the Mongol armies under Subutai had smashed every force sent against them and were marching on Vienna, meaning to ride all the way to the 'Great Sea' - the Atlantic. No European army had stopped them. Yet that winter they suddenly turned around and rode east, never to come back. What turned the Mongols back?
answer: The Great Khan Ogedei died far away in Mongolia, recalling the princes
choices: The Great Khan Ogedei died far away in Mongolia, recalling the princes
A massive blizzard froze and starved the Mongol horses in the passes
The Pope's crusading army finally united and met them outside Vienna
The Mongol princes caught a plague sweeping through their camp
context: Ogedei Khan died on December 11, 1241, after a night of heavy drinking. By Mongol custom his death summoned the princes and their armies thousands of miles back to Karakorum for the kurultai - the assembly to choose the next Great Khan. Europe was saved not by a victory but by the timing of a drinking bout an empire away; it was the farthest west the Mongols ever reached. Source: https://www.ancient-origins.net/history-famous-people/ogedei-khan-0010837

question: In March 1862 the U.S. Navy launched the strangest-looking warship anyone had seen: the USS Monitor was a low flat iron deck riding almost level with the water, with one fat round revolving gun-tower rising from the middle and nothing else on top. What did sailors nickname this odd vessel?
answer: A cheesebox on a raft
choices: A cheesebox on a raft
A floating barn roof
An iron coffin afloat
A turtle in armor
context: The Monitor's single 20-foot cylindrical turret rising from a nearly flat deck gave it that look. The turret could rotate to fire its two 11-inch Dahlgren guns in any direction without the whole ship turning. (battlefields.org/learn/articles/uss-monitor-cheesebox-raft)

question: On March 8, 1862, the day before the famous ironclad duel at Hampton Roads, the Confederate ironclad CSS Virginia charged straight at the wooden U.S. sloop Cumberland and drove its 1,500-pound iron ram into her side, tearing a hole one officer said was wide enough to drive in a horse and cart. As the Cumberland sank, what happened to the Virginia's iron ram?
answer: It snapped off and stuck inside the sinking Cumberland
choices: It snapped off and stuck inside the sinking Cumberland
It bent backward and jammed the Virginia's own bow
It glanced off the hull and shattered into pieces
It dragged the Virginia down with the Cumberland
context: Virginia's chief engineer Ashton Ramsay compared his ship to 'a wasp we could sting but once, leaving the sting in the wound.' The Cumberland's crew kept firing as she went down with her flag still flying; about 121-123 sailors went down with her. (marinersmuseum.org/2021/10/uss-cumberland-sink-before-surrender)

question: Charles-Louis de Secondat, Baron de Montesquieu, designed the idea of splitting government into three branches so no one could grab all the power. But at home near Bordeaux he was a working country nobleman with a very ordinary day job he cared about deeply. Besides writing, how did Montesquieu actually make his living?
answer: He grew and sold wine
choices: He grew and sold wine
He bred warhorses
He sailed trading ships
He minted the king's coins
context: Montesquieu was a real wine-grower at the moated Chateau de La Brede, where he wrote most of his great books. He fussed over his grape harvests and the sales of his renowned Graves wine. The man who engineered the separation of powers was, day to day, a merchant-winemaker. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (plato.stanford.edu/entries/montesquieu); Chateau de la Brede official site.

question: In his masterwork The Spirit of the Laws (1748), Montesquieu argued that a government's power is really three different kinds of power, and that freedom survives only if those three are kept in separate hands. Which three powers did Montesquieu say must never be held by the same person?
answer: The lawmaking, the law-enforcing, and the law-judging powers
choices: The lawmaking, the law-enforcing, and the law-judging powers
The military, the religious, and the merchant powers
The royal, the noble, and the common powers
The tax, the trade, and the treaty powers
context: In Book XI Montesquieu names them the legislative (which enacts laws), the executive (which carries out public resolutions), and the judicial (which tries the causes of individuals). Keep them in separate hands and liberty lives; merge them and it dies. This is the blueprint the Framers wired into the U.S. Constitution. Source: Online Library of Liberty, 'Montesquieu and the Separation of Powers' (Spirit of the Laws Bk XI Ch 6).

question: Before his book on government, Montesquieu became famous overnight in 1721 with a sly bestseller he published anonymously in Holland. To mock French and Christian society without being punished for it, he wrote the whole book as letters from two outsiders touring Paris and writing home about how strange the French seemed. Who were the two travelers Montesquieu used to poke fun at France?
answer: Two Persian visitors
choices: Two Persian visitors
Two shipwrecked sailors
Two country priests
Two runaway princes
context: The book is the Persian Letters. Two Persians, Usbek and Rica, roam Paris and mock French and Christian customs in letters home, while back east Usbek's seraglio of five wives slowly falls into revolt. It ran through about ten editions in a single year. Source: Wikipedia, 'Persian Letters'.

question: In his last years Montesquieu was losing a battle with cataracts and going nearly blind, yet he refused to stop working on his books. To keep writing once he could no longer see the page, what did Montesquieu do?
answer: He dictated his words to secretaries
choices: He dictated his words to secretaries
He learned to write with his eyes shut
He had the text read back to him in court
He carved the words into wax by feel
context: Going nearly blind, Montesquieu dictated to scribes until he died of a fever in Paris on 10 February 1755. Some of his surviving manuscripts are partly in the handwriting of the secretaries who wrote for him during his blindness. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (plato.stanford.edu/entries/montesquieu).

question: Montesquieu did not trust rulers to behave themselves. In The Spirit of the Laws he warned that 'every man invested with power is apt to abuse it, and to carry his authority as far as it will go.' So instead of hoping for good rulers, what did Montesquieu say was needed 'from the very nature of things'?
answer: That power should be a check to power
choices: That power should be a check to power
That kings should be chosen by lottery
That the people should rise up and revolt
That rulers should swear a sacred oath
context: Montesquieu's remedy was not better men but a better machine: 'it is necessary from the very nature of things that power should be a check to power.' Don't trust rulers to be good; arrange the branches so each one blocks the others. Source: Founders' Constitution, Univ. of Chicago Press (Spirit of Laws Bk XI).

question: There is a startling twist in Montesquieu's life: the very thinker who argued the judges must be walled off from the rest of the government had once held that exact power himself. In 1716 he inherited from his uncle a high office in the Parlement of Bordeaux and ran its criminal court for about eleven years. Before he became a writer, what had Montesquieu actually been?
answer: A judge over criminal trials
choices: A judge over criminal trials
A general of the king's army
A bishop of Bordeaux
A tax collector for the crown
context: As President a Mortier in the Parlement of Bordeaux, Montesquieu presided over the Tournelle, its criminal court, for about eleven years. The man who designed the separation of judicial power had actually been a judge. He sold the office in 1726 to devote himself to writing. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (plato.stanford.edu/entries/montesquieu).

question: When The Spirit of the Laws appeared anonymously in 1748, it spread across Europe so fast, and challenged kings and priests so boldly, that one powerful institution struck back in 1751 by formally branding it dangerous. How did the Roman Catholic Church punish Montesquieu's book?
answer: It placed the book on the list of forbidden books
choices: It placed the book on the list of forbidden books
It excommunicated everyone who read it
It ordered every copy publicly burned
It fined the printers who had sold it
context: In 1751 the Church added The Spirit of the Laws to the Index Librorum Prohibitorum, its official list of forbidden books. Montesquieu fired back with a 'Defense of the Spirit of the Laws.' Being banned only helped the book's fame spread further. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Spirit of Law'.

question: Montesquieu did not think all governments were alike. He sorted them into three kinds, each kept alive by a different driving passion in its people. A republic, he said, runs on virtue; a monarchy runs on honor; and the third and darkest kind runs on a single emotion, where 'a single person directs everything by his own will and caprice.' What did Montesquieu say a despotism runs on?
answer: Fear
choices: Fear
Greed
Pride
Faith
context: Montesquieu paired each government with its animating principle: republic with virtue (love of country and the laws), monarchy with honor, despotism with fear. A government dies, he warned, when it loses its animating principle. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (plato.stanford.edu/entries/montesquieu).

question: When James Madison defended the new U.S. Constitution in Federalist No. 47 (1788), he leaned on Montesquieu so heavily that he gave the Frenchman a single grand title, calling him the great authority everyone turns to on the separation of powers. What did Madison call Montesquieu in Federalist No. 47?
answer: The oracle always consulted on this subject
choices: The oracle always consulted on this subject
The father of the American republic
The first true friend of liberty
The wisest king's counselor in Europe
context: Madison wrote: 'The oracle who is always consulted and cited on this subject is the celebrated Montesquieu.' Madison reported that Montesquieu treated England's constitution as the very 'mirror of political liberty,' and credited him with displaying the principle of separated powers to mankind 'most effectually.' The line from 1748 Paris to the 1787 Convention runs straight through this one Frenchman. Source: Avalon Project, Yale Law School, Federalist No. 47.

question: A scholar named Donald Lutz once counted up every author the American founders quoted in their political writing from 1760 to 1805 to see who shaped them most. Among all named human authorities, Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws came out on top, beaten by only a single source the founders cited even more. What was the one source quoted more than Montesquieu?
answer: The Bible
choices: The Bible
The Magna Carta
The works of Aristotle
The English common law
context: In Lutz's famous citation survey, The Spirit of the Laws was the single most-cited secular source on government in American founding-era writing. The founders quoted Montesquieu more than any author except the Bible itself. Source: Wikipedia, 'Montesquieu' (citing Donald Lutz's citation survey).

question: James Madison turned Montesquieu's warning into one of the most quoted sentences in American government. In Federalist No. 47 he wrote that piling all the lawmaking, law-enforcing, and judging power into one set of hands 'may justly be pronounced' a single terrible thing. What did Madison say that accumulation of all powers in the same hands was?
answer: The very definition of tyranny
choices: The very definition of tyranny
The seed of every civil war
The death of all commerce
The end of religion itself
context: Madison wrote that 'the accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands... may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny.' It is the American restatement of Montesquieu's warning that liberty cannot survive when the branches merge. Source: Avalon Project, Yale Law School, Federalist No. 47.

question: Montesquieu insisted that judges should never get to soften or stiffen a law to suit themselves; their job was only to apply it exactly as written. To drive this home he gave judges a haunting image, saying they should be no more than one thing that simply 'pronounces the words of the law.' What did Montesquieu say a judge should be no more than?
answer: The mouth that speaks the law
choices: The mouth that speaks the law
The shield that guards the law
The sword that enforces the law
The scale that weighs the law
context: Montesquieu's image (Spirit of the Laws Bk XI Ch 6): judges should be 'no more than the mouth that pronounces the words of the law, mere passive beings, incapable of moderating either its force or rigour.' The judicial branch applies the law; it does not make or bend it. Source: Online Library of Liberty, 'Montesquieu and the Separation of Powers'.

question: Montesquieu's cold-eyed insight was to stop hoping rulers would be good and instead let the branches of government check each other. James Madison turned that idea into a single rule in Federalist No. 51: he named one human passion and ordered it set against its own twin, so each office's hunger blocks the next. Which passion did Madison pit against itself?
answer: Ambition
choices: Ambition
Greed
Envy
Pride
context: Madison's line: 'Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.' Because people are not angels, each branch's appetite for power is used to block the others — the engineering principle behind the Constitution and the direct heir of Montesquieu's 'power should be a check to power.' Source: Founders' Constitution / Avalon Project (Madison, Federalist No. 51; Montesquieu Bk XI).

question: In 1607 the composer Claudio Monteverdi staged L'Orfeo, retelling the Greek myth of Orpheus, who walks into the land of the dead to win back his bride. To get past Charon, the grim ferryman who guards the river into Hades, Orpheus does not fight, bribe, or trick him. In the great aria 'Possente spirto' ('Powerful spirit'), what does Orpheus use to get across?
answer: His own singing, so beautiful it charms the ferryman into rowing him over
choices: His own singing, so beautiful it charms the ferryman into rowing him over
A golden coin pressed into the ferryman's hand as payment for the crossing
A sword drawn against the ferryman to force him back from the oars
A secret password the gods had taught him to speak at the river's edge
context: In 'Possente spirto,' Monteverdi piled on chitarrone, organ, two violins, two cornetts and a double-harp to make the singing itself the magic that opens the underworld. L'Orfeo, premiered 24 February 1607 for the Gonzaga court in Mantua, is the earliest opera still regularly staged today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'Orfeo

question: At the Council of Trent (1545-1563), Catholic churchmen argued bitterly over church music: one faction wanted to BAN all the new tangled, many-voiced polyphony from worship as too worldly, fearing it buried the sacred words. A beloved legend, written down decades later, claims one piece settled the fight all by itself. What does the legend say Giovanni Palestrina's Missa Papae Marcelli did?
answer: Proved polyphony could be holy and clear, saving the whole tradition from the ban
choices: Proved polyphony could be holy and clear, saving the whole tradition from the ban
Was the first music ever sung in the new Sistine Chapel before the assembled cardinals
Converted a Protestant prince who heard it and returned his lands to the Church
Was composed overnight on a dare and performed for the pope the very next morning
context: This is a beloved legend, not fact: it was first claimed by the theorist Agostino Agazzari in 1607 and dramatized by biographer Giuseppe Baini in 1828; modern scholars say Palestrina's name probably never even came up in the Council's debates. The Mass is written for six voice parts, but its trick was clarity: he often had the voices move together in chords so every word could be understood. Source: ebsco.com/research-starters/music/pope-marcellus-mass

question: Inside a mosque, one wall has a small niche carved into it that all the worshippers turn to face when they pray. The niche has a single job: it points the way to one specific place far away. What does the mihrab niche point toward?
answer: The Kaaba in Mecca
choices: The Kaaba in Mecca
The grave of the local imam
The tallest minaret in town
The rising sun at dawn
context: The mihrab is a niche cut into the qibla wall, and its only purpose is to show the qibla, the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca, so the whole congregation faces the same way. The earliest mosques had no niche at all, just a painted line or a wooden staff in the ground to mark the way. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mihrab (Wikipedia, Mihrab); https://www.britannica.com/topic/mihrab (Britannica).

question: In January 630 CE, after Muslim forces took the city of Mecca, the Prophet Muhammad gave his herald Bilal ibn Rabah, a freed man with a famously beautiful voice, an order to sound the call to prayer from one dramatic spot for the first time. Where did Muhammad order Bilal to climb to make the call?
answer: To the top of the Kaaba
choices: To the top of the Kaaba
To the gate of the city
To a hill outside Mecca
To the roof of his own house
context: Bilal ibn Rabah, an Ethiopian-descended freed slave, was the very first muezzin. Before towers existed the muezzin simply climbed onto the highest nearby rooftop to be seen and heard; the minaret tower came later. Muhammad had Bilal climb the Kaaba itself to give the call there for the first time. Source: https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/the-history-of-the-muezzin--74007 (Hurriyet); https://archive.mpac.org/article/bilal-ibn-rabah-the-voice-of-resilience/ (MPAC). Confidence: medium.

question: The Atlantic slave trade ran as a three-cornered voyage. European ships carried manufactured goods — cloth, brass, knives, guns, gunpowder, and alcohol — south to the coast of West Africa. From the Americas they carried plantation crops — sugar, tobacco, cotton, and rum — back home to Europe. What did the ships carry on the long middle leg, west across the ocean to the Americas?
answer: Captive Africans
choices: Captive Africans
Ivory and gold dust
Salt and dried fish
Copper and palm oil
context: That middle leg was called the Middle Passage. The cycle fed itself: the guns sold in Africa were used to take more captives, and the crops the captives grew were sold for money to buy more guns. Between about 1517 and 1867 roughly 12.5 million Africans were forced onto these ships. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangular_trade ; Britannica 'Triangular trade')

question: To rally ordinary people against the slave trade, the English potter Josiah Wedgwood designed a small ceramic medallion in 1787 showing a kneeling African man in chains, looking up. Around the rim ran a short motto that became the most famous image of the whole anti-slavery cause. What did the motto ask?
answer: Am I not a man and a brother?
choices: Am I not a man and a brother?
No man is born to be a slave
Remember those who are in chains
Let the oppressed go free at last
context: Wedgwood made the design the seal of the Abolition Society and produced it as fashionable jasperware cameos. Middle-class women wore it as pendants, hairpins, and snuffbox inlays — turning the cause into a thing you wore. It is called the most recognizable piece of antislavery imagery ever made. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wedgwood_anti-slavery_medallion ; vam.ac.uk)

question: On 25 March 1807, after a debate that ran ten hours, the British House of Commons voted 283 to 16 to make the slave trade illegal across the entire British Empire. As the members rose to their feet and cheered the man who had fought for the ban for twenty years, what did William Wilberforce do?
answer: He sat and wept for joy
choices: He sat and wept for joy
He gave a long victory speech
He slipped out of the chamber alone
He knelt and led the House in prayer
context: Wilberforce had brought abolition bills to Parliament year after year and lost again and again before this night. The 1807 Act outlawed the trade in human beings throughout the Empire, though slavery itself in the colonies would not be abolished until 1833. (historic-uk.com 'West Africa Squadron' ; historyskills.com 'William Wilberforce')

question: Olaudah Equiano was an Igbo boy taken from his home in Africa around the age of ten and carried to the coast, where for the first time in his life he saw a slave ship, white sailors, and the open sea all at once. In the autobiography he later wrote, he says he was seized by one terror above all. What did the boy fear was about to happen to him?
answer: That the white men were going to eat him
choices: That the white men were going to eat him
That he would never see his home again
That the sea was a living monster
That he was being carried off to die
context: Equiano wrote that he saw 'a multitude of black people of every description chained together, every one of their countenances expressing dejection and sorrow,' and asked whether 'we were not to be eaten by those white men with horrible looks, red faces, and loose hair.' His 1789 book became one of the most powerful weapons of the abolition campaign. (https://www.worldhistory.org/article/2672/olaudah-equianos-account-of-the-middle-passage/)

question: In 1788 the abolitionist Thomas Clarkson published a printed diagram of the slave ship Brookes that showed more than 400 human beings drawn lying side by side, packed across its lower deck like rows of goods. The picture's power came from one number: the width of deck allotted to each grown person. About how wide was the space given to each captive?
answer: Sixteen inches
choices: Sixteen inches
Thirty inches
Forty inches
Sixty inches
context: Each person had about sixteen inches (40 cm) of width and roughly two and a half feet of headroom — too little to sit up or stand. The Quaker printer James Phillips ran off 7,000 copies in 1789. Clarkson called the diagram's effect 'intelligible and irresistible' and carried it on his lecture tours. (abolitionseminar.org 'Brookes')

question: After 1808 the Royal Navy sent a squadron of warships to West Africa to hunt down slave ships and free the people aboard. Its single most successful hunter was a small, fast vessel called HMS Black Joke — but she carried a dark irony in her own history before the Navy ever flew the British flag from her mast. What was true of the Black Joke?
answer: She had herself been a slave ship
choices: She had herself been a slave ship
She had once been a royal yacht
She was built from a captured warship
She was seized from French smugglers
context: Built as the Baltimore clipper Henriqueta, she had carried about 3,040 enslaved people to Brazil before the Navy captured her in 1827 and turned her against the trade. She caught around a dozen slavers — once taking the Vengador with 645 captives aboard — before her rotten timbers forced the Navy to burn her in 1832. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Black_Joke_(1827))

question: From the early 1700s the Asante Empire of West Africa grew rich by capturing people in war and raids and selling them to British and Dutch traders waiting on the coast. In exchange the Asante kings wanted one kind of European good above the rest: firearms. What did the Asante use those guns to do?
answer: Seize more land and capture more people
choices: Seize more land and capture more people
Defend their coast from European raiders
Hunt elephants for the ivory trade
Guard the gold mines from rival kingdoms
context: Historians call this the 'gun-slave cycle': captives bought guns, and guns let the Asante conquer neighbors and take more captives to sell for still more guns. The wars that filled the slave ships were African wars, fought with European weapons. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asante_Empire ; Britannica 'Asante empire')

question: European slavers rarely marched inland to seize people themselves. Instead they anchored on the coast and bought captives from African kingdoms such as Dahomey, who had taken them in raids and wars and traded them for guns, gunpowder, cloth, and cowrie shells. Why did the Europeans leave the actual capturing to the African kingdoms?
answer: They thought raiding inland too dangerous
choices: They thought raiding inland too dangerous
They lacked the men to march inland
Their own kings had forbidden it
They had promised the chiefs they would not
context: This is the part of the story often left untaught: the internal African slave trade came first and fed the Atlantic one. Coastal kingdoms did the capturing and sold the captives to waiting European ships, who judged the interior too deadly to enter themselves. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dahomey ; africanhistoryextra.com 'Kingdom of Dahomey and the Atlantic')

question: In his account of the Middle Passage, Olaudah Equiano described the hold as so foul and crowded that each chained person had 'scarcely room to turn himself.' He then recorded the most desperate act he witnessed: two captives, chained together and choosing death over the voyage, did one thing rather than go on living. What did the two men do?
answer: Jumped through the netting into the sea
choices: Jumped through the netting into the sea
Refused all food until they died
Broke their chains and fought the crew
Begged the captain to turn the ship back
context: Equiano wrote that the two men, 'preferring death to such a life of misery, somehow made through the nettings and jumped into the sea' to drown rather than continue — a documented act of suicide-resistance on the Middle Passage. Crews strung netting along the rails precisely to stop such escapes. (https://www.worldhistory.org/article/2672/olaudah-equianos-account-of-the-middle-passage/)

question: In November 1781 the Liverpool slave ship Zong, blundering off course and running low on drinking water, became the scene of one of the trade's most infamous crimes: over several days the crew killed about 132 enslaved Africans — first 54 women and children, then 42 men, then more. How did the crew kill them?
answer: They threw them alive into the sea
choices: They threw them alive into the sea
They left them chained below deck
They put them ashore to starve
They sold them at the nearest port
context: The owners then filed an insurance claim of 30 pounds a head for the drowned, treating murdered people as lost cargo — which is what dragged the case into court and into history. The formerly-enslaved Olaudah Equiano carried news of it to the abolitionist Granville Sharp, who coined the word 'massacre' for what had been done. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zong_massacre ; Britannica 'Zong massacre')

question: When the owners of the slave ship Zong sued their insurers in 1783 to be paid for the roughly 132 drowned Africans, the case was argued not as murder but as a routine loss of property. The Lord Chief Justice, Lord Mansfield, summed up the legal question in a single chilling comparison. How did Mansfield say the law should treat the killings?
answer: As if horses had been thrown overboard
choices: As if horses had been thrown overboard
As a tragic but honest mistake
As the worst crime of the age
As a matter for the church to judge
context: Mansfield said 'the Case of Slaves was the same as if Horses had been thrown over board.' The crew's water-shortage excuse later collapsed when records showed the Zong reached port with 420 gallons to spare and rain had refilled the casks mid-killing. Granville Sharp made the case a cornerstone of the abolition fight. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zong_massacre)

question: Afonso I, the Christian king of Kongo, watched Portuguese merchants go behind his back and buy captives straight from his own nobles, until even his relatives were being seized. In 1526 he wrote a letter to King Joao III of Portugal protesting the trade, describing the precise mark the slavers put on his stolen people. What did Afonso say was being done to them?
answer: Branded with a red-hot iron
choices: Branded with a red-hot iron
Sold to lands across the sea
Worked until they dropped dead
Torn from their mothers at birth
context: Afonso (born Nzinga Mbemba) wrote that traders were 'kidnapping our people — children of this country, sons of our nobles and vassals, even people of our own family,' who were then 'branded with a red-hot iron.' He is a rare example of an African ruler protesting the trade from inside it — and being ignored. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_I_of_Kongo ; worldhistorycommons.org)

question: When Wolfgang Mozart was baptized in Salzburg in 1756, his parents gave him the Greek name Theophilus — the same name we now know in its Latin form, Amadeus. What does that name actually mean?
answer: "Beloved of God"
choices: "Beloved of God"
"Born in winter"
"Son of the court"
"Master of the keys"
context: Theophilus is Greek for 'lover of God' / 'beloved of God'; its Latin equivalent is Amadeus, the name history remembers him by. Source: mozartproject.org/the-many-names-of-wolfgang-amadeus-mozart/ ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozart's_name

question: Wolfgang Mozart was composing music before he was old enough to read well. His father Leopold wrote the boy's earliest little pieces down in his sister Nannerl's music notebook. What kind of piece was the very first one Mozart composed, around age five?
answer: A short minuet
choices: A short minuet
A church hymn
A drum march
A sea shanty
context: His first surviving piece is a tiny Minuet in G, later catalogued as K.1, written when he was five. Source: mozartproject.org/mozarts-first-composition-a-minuet-and-trio/ ; classicfm.com/composers/mozart/first-piano-music-minuet/

question: Wolfgang Mozart was a child prodigy who could already play a full keyboard instrument by the age of three — before many children can even tie their shoes. Which instrument was the little boy playing at three?
answer: The harpsichord
choices: The harpsichord
The church organ
The clavichord
The fortepiano
context: Mozart could play the harpsichord by age 3 and was composing by 4-5. Source: britannica.com/biography/Wolfgang-Amadeus-Mozart

question: As a small boy, Wolfgang Mozart was taken on tour across Europe by his father and sister, and crowds were astonished by what this child could do. What was the prodigy doing that amazed everyone?
answer: Performing for kings and queens at the grandest courts
choices: Performing for kings and queens at the grandest courts
Conducting full armies on the battlefield
Painting royal portraits from memory
Sailing trading ships between cities
context: As a child he played at Versailles for the French king and in London for King George III and Queen Charlotte, where he met Johann Christian Bach. Source: britannica.com/biography/Wolfgang-Amadeus-Mozart ; ebsco.com/research-starters/history/mozart-tours-europe-child-prodigy

question: In London an English scientist, Daines Barrington, tested eight-year-old Wolfgang Mozart for the Royal Society — and the boy sight-read a hidden manuscript flawlessly and improvised songs on command. Yet partway through, this genius-child did something that reminded everyone he was still only eight. What did he do?
answer: He wandered off to play with his pet cat
choices: He wandered off to play with his pet cat
He fell asleep at the keyboard
He demanded a bag of sweets
He started crying for his mother
context: Barrington recorded that the child would sometimes abandon the harpsichord to play with his favourite cat. Source: royalsociety.org/blog/2015/03/meeting-mozart-in-london/ ; publicdomainreview.org/collection/account-of-a-very-remarkable-young-musician-1769/

question: At fourteen, Wolfgang Mozart visited the Sistine Chapel in Rome and heard a famous nine-voice choral work the Vatican guarded so jealously that copying it could get you excommunicated. Mozart went back to his room and wrote the entire thing out from memory after hearing it just once. Which work did he steal with his ears?
answer: Allegri's 'Miserere'
choices: Allegri's 'Miserere'
Bach's 'Mass in B Minor'
Handel's 'Messiah'
Vivaldi's 'Four Seasons'
context: Mozart transcribed Gregorio Allegri's 'Miserere' from memory after a single hearing during Holy Week 1770. Source: classicfm.com/composers/mozart/transcribed-allegri-miserere-sistine-chapel/ ; mymodernmet.com/mozart-miserere-gregorio-allegri/

question: In Wolfgang Mozart's opera Don Giovanni, the villain mockingly invites a statue of a man he murdered to come to supper — and the statue actually arrives, knocks at the door, and seizes his hand, demanding he repent. When Don Giovanni refuses, how does the opera end for him?
answer: The statue drags him down to hell through the burning floor
choices: The statue drags him down to hell through the burning floor
He flees toward the harbour but drowns in the escape
He repents in terror and the statue spares his life
Soldiers seize him and wall him up alive in a tower
context: The murdered Commendatore returns as a stone statue; when Don Giovanni refuses to repent, the floor opens and flames and demons drag him down to hell. Source: metopera.org/discover/education/educator-guides/don-giovanni/the-operas-plot-creation/ ; thelistenersclub.com/2020/10/30/ghostly-mozart-the-commendatore-scene-from-don-giovanni/

question: The night before Don Giovanni was to premiere, Wolfgang Mozart realized he had never written the opera's overture — the music that opens the whole show. With the orchestra needing the parts by morning, how did Mozart get the overture done in time?
answer: He composed the whole overture overnight in about three hours
choices: He composed the whole overture overnight in about three hours
He borrowed the overture from an older opera
He told the orchestra to make it up on the spot
He delayed the premiere by a week
context: Legend says Mozart wrote the overture in roughly three hours the night before, his wife Constanze keeping him awake with stories; copyists barely finished and the orchestra sight-read it cold. (Famous but unverified.) Source: cmuse.org/mozart-midnight-masterpiece-don-giovanni-overture/ ; classicalwonders.com/2024/10/22/mozarts-last-minute-overture-for-don-giovanni/

question: As the story goes, after hearing one of Wolfgang Mozart's operas, Emperor Joseph II complained that the music had 'too many notes.' How did Mozart supposedly answer the emperor of Austria to his face?
answer: "Exactly as many as are necessary, Your Majesty"
choices: "Exactly as many as are necessary, Your Majesty"
"Then I shall compose for the French instead"
"Your Majesty's ears are simply too small"
"I will gladly return your payment"
context: The retort is famous but unverified, popularized by the film Amadeus, tied to The Abduction from the Seraglio (1782). Source: flowingprose.com/2015/08/too-many-notes-my-dear-mozart/ ; interlude.hk/mozart-die-entfuhrung-aus-dem-serail-k-384-premiered-today-1782/  (Legend.)

question: In 1791 a stranger dressed all in black came to Wolfgang Mozart with an anonymous commission: write a Requiem, a mass for the dead. The eccentric secrecy unnerved the sick, exhausted Mozart so deeply that he formed a haunting belief about the piece. What did Mozart come to believe he was writing?
answer: A requiem for his own death
choices: A requiem for his own death
A secret coded message to the emperor
Music that would make him immortal
An opera disguised as a mass
context: The Requiem was secretly commissioned by Count Franz von Walsegg (who meant to pass it off as his own) via a black-clad messenger; the ailing Mozart came to believe he was composing a requiem for himself. Source: classical-music.com/features/works/requiem-mozart ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_von_Walsegg

question: Wolfgang Mozart died at only 35 with his Requiem still unfinished — his pen stopped mid-piece, and his pupil had to complete the rest in his style. The last music in Mozart's own hand runs just eight bars into one movement, the very place where he set down his pen for good. Which movement is where his writing fell silent?
answer: The 'Lacrimosa'
choices: The 'Lacrimosa'
The 'Hallelujah'
The 'Gloria'
The 'Magnificat'
context: The last music in Mozart's own hand is the first eight bars of the 'Lacrimosa'; his pupil Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed the Requiem. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacrimosa ; classicfm.com/composers/mozart/music/requiem/

question: In barely 35 years Wolfgang Mozart wrote an astonishing flood of music — symphonies, operas, concertos and more. To keep it all straight, scholars label every single Mozart work with a special catalogue number, running from his childhood minuet all the way to the unfinished Requiem. What is that numbering system called?
answer: The Köchel (K.) number
choices: The Köchel (K.) number
The Salzburg index
The Vienna stamp
The Amadeus code
context: Ludwig von Köchel catalogued Mozart's works; the numbers run from K.1 (the minuet he wrote at five) to K.626 (the Requiem). A 2024 revision pushed his documented output past 700 pieces. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Köchel_catalogue ; mozarteum.at/en/presentation-of-the-new-koechel-catalogue

question: The play and film 'Amadeus' fixed one idea in everyone's head: that the Vienna court composer Antonio Salieri so envied Mozart that he murdered him. But the real Salieri and Mozart actually worked together. In 1785 the two of them, joining a third musician, did what as colleagues?
answer: Jointly composed a cantata to celebrate a singer recovering her voice
choices: Jointly composed a cantata to celebrate a singer recovering her voice
Co-conducted a full opera season at the Vienna court theater
Shared one apartment near the cathedral through a hard winter
Traded their best pupils back and forth between their classes
context: The 1785 cantata 'Per la ricuperata salute di Ofelia' was co-written by Salieri, Mozart, and a man named Cornetti, to a text by Lorenzo Da Ponte, to celebrate the singer Nancy Storace getting her voice back. Salieri wrote the outer parts, Mozart the middle. The score was thought lost until musicologist Timo Jouko Herrmann found it in a Prague archive in 2015-2016. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_la_ricuperata_salute_di_Ofelia

question: The story of Antonio Salieri as the jealous nobody who poisoned Mozart is a fiction grown from drama, not history. The real Salieri was Vienna's Imperial Royal Kapellmeister for 36 years, and he trained the next generation of composers. Which trio of his pupils later became giants of music?
answer: Beethoven, Schubert, and Carl Czerny
choices: Beethoven, Schubert, and Carl Czerny
Bach, Handel, and Antonio Vivaldi
Chopin, Liszt, and Johannes Brahms
Haydn, Gluck, and Niccolo Paganini
context: Salieri's pupils read like a who's-who of music: Beethoven, Schubert, Carl Czerny, Giacomo Meyerbeer, and Mozart's own son Franz Xaver Wolfgang Mozart. Beethoven dedicated his three Violin Sonatas, Op. 12, to Salieri. An orphan from Legnago, Italy, Salieri often taught for free. Historians find no evidence anyone poisoned Mozart, whose 1791 death certificate listed 'severe miliary fever.' Source: https://www.thecollector.com/antonio-salieri-misjudged-italian-composer/ ; https://www.classicfm.com/composers/mozart/guides/did-salieri-murder-mozart-mythbuster/

question: Long before he was a prophet, the young Muhammad drove trading caravans across the deserts of Arabia for the merchants of Mecca. He kept his word and his accounts so faithfully that the Meccans gave him a proud nickname, 'al-Amin.' What does that nickname mean?
answer: The Trustworthy
choices: The Trustworthy
The Wanderer
The Merchant
The Fearless
context: Muhammad's reputation for honesty on the Syria caravan routes earned him the title 'al-Amin' -- the Trustworthy. People reportedly cried 'There he is, al-Amin! There is Muhammad!' when he arrived to settle a quarrel. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad and https://lastprophet.info/6-the-ka-ba-arbitration

question: When Muhammad and his followers fled Mecca, they found a new home in the city of Yathrib. The people there honored him so highly that they renamed the whole city after him: 'Madinat al-Nabi,' the City of the Prophet. What is that city called today, for short?
answer: Medina
choices: Medina
Mecca
Baghdad
Damascus
context: Yathrib was renamed Madinat al-Nabi, 'the City of the Prophet,' shortened to Medina ('the City'). It became the base from which Islam grew into an organized community and an Arabian power. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijrah and https://www.britannica.com/event/Hijrah-Islam

question: Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina in 622 mattered so much that the Muslim community later made that year the start of their whole calendar -- Year One. To this day Muslims count their years from that journey. What is this famous migration called?
answer: The Hijra
choices: The Hijra
The Hajj
The Jihad
The Sunna
context: The Hijra (the word means to depart or break ties and move away) became Year One of the Islamic calendar. The caliph Umar fixed the count in 639, starting from the first day of the month Muharram -- corresponding to 16 July 622. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijrah

question: At 25, Muhammad went to work running caravans for a wealthy 40-year-old widow named Khadija. She was so impressed by how he handled her business that she did something bold and unusual for the time. What did Khadija do?
answer: She proposed marriage to him
choices: She proposed marriage to him
She made him head of her household guards
She gave him half of her caravans
She sent him to study in Syria
context: Khadija bint Khuwaylid, impressed by his competence, proposed marriage to Muhammad. He stayed married only to her until she died, and she became the very first person to believe him when revelation came. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad

question: When the leaders of Mecca rebuilt the Kaaba, they nearly came to blows over which clan would get the honor of setting the sacred Black Stone back in place. Muhammad settled the quarrel without a fight, in a way that let EVERY clan share the honor at once. What was his solution?
answer: He laid the stone on a cloak and had each clan lift a corner together
choices: He laid the stone on a cloak and had each clan lift a corner together
He drew lots and let blind chance choose the one winning clan
He simply gave the honor to the oldest and most senior clan
He marched the stone to the wall and set it there single-handed
context: Around 605, Muhammad laid the Black Stone on a cloak and had an elder of each clan lift a corner together to carry it to the wall, then set it into place with his own hands -- so no clan was slighted. Reported in Ibn Ishaq's biography. Source: https://lastprophet.info/6-the-ka-ba-arbitration

question: Around 610, Muhammad was alone in a cave on the mountain Jabal al-Nour when he said the angel Gabriel seized him and gave him a single command. Muhammad, who could not read, protested that he could not -- but the angel pressed him three times with the same word. What was that first command?
answer: 'Recite!'
choices: 'Recite!'
'Kneel!'
'Believe!'
'Write!'
context: In the Cave of Hira the command was 'Iqra!' -- 'Recite!' The first words of the Quran followed: 'Recite in the name of your Lord who created... who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know' (Surah Al-Alaq, 96:1-5). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad's_first_revelation

question: Bilal ibn Rabah, an enslaved early Muslim, was dragged onto the burning sand of Mecca by his master and pinned under a heavy boulder on his chest to force him to give up his new faith. Through the torture he answered only with the same word, repeated again and again. What did Bilal keep saying?
answer: 'One, One' (God is One)
choices: 'One, One' (God is One)
'Mercy, Mercy'
'Never, Never'
'Free me, free me'
context: Bilal repeated only 'Ahad, Ahad' -- 'One, One.' Abu Bakr bought his freedom, and Bilal later became Islam's first muezzin, the caller to prayer. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilal_ibn_Rabah

question: The leaders of Mecca leaned on Muhammad's uncle and protector, Abu Talib, to make him drop his preaching. Muhammad refused with a famous vow, swearing he would never abandon his course even if they handed him the greatest bribe imaginable. What did he say they could offer and still not stop him?
answer: The sun in his right hand and the moon in his left
choices: The sun in his right hand and the moon in his left
Every last camel and caravan in the whole of Arabia
The crown and kingship of Mecca and of its temple
A high throne set above all the clans of the Quraysh
context: 'By God, if they put the sun in my right hand and the moon in my left on condition that I abandon this course, I would not abandon it until God makes it victorious or I perish.' Reported in Ibn Ishaq's Sira. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_and_third_deputation_with_Abu_Talib

question: On the night Muhammad escaped Mecca, the clans had agreed to surround his house and kill him in his bed. To buy time and slip away unseen, Muhammad asked one of his own people to lie down in his place. Who took the prophet's bed as a decoy that night?
answer: Ali ibn Abi Talib
choices: Ali ibn Abi Talib
Abu Bakr al-Siddiq
Bilal ibn Rabah
Ja'far ibn Abi Talib
context: Muhammad's young cousin Ali ibn Abi Talib slept in his bed as a decoy while he slipped out. Ali also stayed behind to return the goods people had entrusted to Muhammad for safekeeping. The plotters had planned one man from each clan to strike together, so blood-guilt would be shared. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijrah

question: Fleeing Mecca, Muhammad and his companion Abu Bakr hid in the Cave of Thawr while search parties hunted them. When pursuers came so close that Abu Bakr feared they would look down and see the two of them, Muhammad calmed him with a few words, later set into the Quran. What did Muhammad tell him?
answer: 'Do not grieve, for God is with us'
choices: 'Do not grieve, for God is with us'
'Be still, and God will turn their eyes'
'Fear not, for God has hidden our path'
'Take heart, for God will not forsake us'
context: Muhammad said, 'Do not grieve, for God is with us' -- words later set in the Quran (9:40). They hid three days in the Cave of Thawr, about an hour's walk south of Mecca, while the Quraysh searched. Source: https://www.islamweb.net/en/article/154942/the-cave-of-thawr

question: Years earlier, to escape persecution, Muhammad had sent a band of his followers across the Red Sea to seek refuge with a Christian king of Aksum, the Negus. When Meccan envoys demanded the refugees back, Muhammad's cousin Ja'far recited the Quran's verses about Mary and Jesus aloud to the king. How did the Christian king respond?
answer: He wept until his beard was wet and refused to surrender them
choices: He wept until his beard was wet and refused to surrender them
He sent the refugees home again to keep his peace with Mecca
He demanded that they convert to his own Christian faith first
He locked the refugees away until Mecca should pay him a ransom
context: The Negus 'wept until his beard was wet and the bishops wept until their scrolls were wet,' then said Jesus was no more than what Ja'far had said by even the width of a stick he picked up -- and refused to hand the refugees over. Reported by Ibn Ishaq. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ja'far_ibn_Abi_Talib

question: The Quraysh put a bounty of 100 camels on Muhammad as he fled, and a tracker named Suraqa ibn Malik nearly caught him -- until Suraqa's horse stumbled and its legs sank deep into the sand. Reading it as an omen, Suraqa let him go, and Muhammad made him a strange prophecy: that one day Suraqa would wear the bracelets of Kisra, the emperor of Persia. What finally happened with that prophecy?
answer: When Persia fell, Caliph Umar made him wear the captured bracelets
choices: When Persia fell, Caliph Umar made him wear the captured bracelets
He was buried in honor wearing a pair of plain golden bracelets
He wore the bracelets a single time and then gave them all away
The prophecy went unfulfilled to the very end of Suraqa's life
context: 'How will it be, Suraqa, when you wear the bracelets of Kisra?' Years later, after Muslims conquered Persia, Caliph Umar made Suraqa wear the captured bracelets of the Persian emperor (Sahih al-Bukhari 3906). Suraqa's horse had sunk into the sand 'up to its belly.' Source: https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3906 and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suraqa_bin_Malik

question: Once safe in Medina, Muhammad faced a hard problem: the emigrants from Mecca had arrived with nothing, while the local 'helpers' had homes and trade of their own. His answer bound the two groups tightly into one community. What did Muhammad set up between them?
answer: A bond of 'brotherhood' pairing each emigrant with a local helper
choices: A bond of 'brotherhood' pairing each emigrant with a local helper
A standing tax on the local helpers to feed the new arrivals
A lottery to share out the emigrants' future spoils of war
A ruling council in which only the Meccan emigrants could vote
context: Muhammad paired each Meccan emigrant (the Muhajirun) with a local helper (the Ansar), who shared their homes, trade, and wealth -- welding two groups into one. He also drew up the Constitution of Medina, often called one of the earliest written constitutions, binding emigrants, helpers, and the city's Jewish tribes into a single umma. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Medina

question: A beloved tradition tells how the search parties hunting Muhammad walked right up to the Cave of Thawr where he was hiding -- yet never even looked inside, because two quiet signs at the mouth made it seem no one could possibly have gone in. In the tradition, what two signs turned the hunters away?
answer: A spider's web across the entrance and a dove nesting on its eggs
choices: A spider's web across the entrance and a dove nesting on its eggs
A serpent coiled on the threshold and a hornet's nest overhead
A thornbush grown over the gap and wild bees humming inside
A swallow's nest under the lip and an ants' trail across the floor
context: LEGEND. By pious tradition a spider had spun a web across the entrance and a dove had laid eggs in a nest there, so the pursuers assumed no one had passed. The hadith scholar al-Albani stated there is no authentic (sahih) hadith for the spider-and-dove detail. Source: https://islamqa.info/en/answers/27224

question: To prepare a body for eternity, ancient Egyptian embalmers had to deal with the soft, perishable brain. They considered it useless garbage. So what did they do with it?
answer: Pushed a hook up the nose, churned the brain to liquid, and threw it away
choices: Pushed a hook up the nose, churned the brain to liquid, and threw it away
Lifted off the top of the skull, studied the brain, and wrapped it in linen
Soaked the brain in honey and sealed it in a jar beside the body
Burned the brain on an altar as an offering to the gods
context: A long crooked iron hook went up the nostrils and broke through the thin ethmoid bone behind the nose; the brain was churned to liquid, poured out, and discarded as worthless. Source: worldhistory.org/article/44/mummification-in-ancient-egypt + sciencefocus.com/nature/egyptians-octopuses-brain

question: Before an Egyptian body could be wrapped, every drop of moisture had to be drawn out so it could never rot. Embalmers buried the body for weeks in a natural drying powder scraped from dry desert lakebeds, which they called netjry, the 'divine salt.' What was this drying powder?
answer: Natron
choices: Natron
Sawdust
Chalk
Sand
context: Natron is a natural mix of sodium carbonate and bicarbonate, scraped from the dried lakebeds of the Wadi Natrun. The Egyptians called it netjry, 'divine salt'; it sucked the body completely dry. This was sophisticated applied chemistry, not superstition. Source: worldhistory.org/article/44/mummification-in-ancient-egypt

question: When Howard Carter opened Tutankhamun's coffin, the boy king's face was covered by a famous object made of two sheets of metal hammered together and weighing about 22.5 pounds. What was it?
answer: A solid-gold death mask
choices: A solid-gold death mask
A painted clay portrait
A silver crown of feathers
A bronze battle helmet
context: Tutankhamun's death mask was two sheets of solid gold hammered together, about 22.5 pounds (10.2 kg). His mummy also carried roughly 150 amulets and jewels tucked between its wrappings. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Tutankhamun + en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tutankhamun's_mummy

question: Egyptian embalmers threw the brain away as garbage, yet they carefully left one organ inside the body, believing it was the seat of thought, character, and memory and would be needed at the final judgment. Which organ did they keep?
answer: The heart
choices: The heart
The liver
The stomach
The lungs
context: The Egyptians believed the heart (the 'Ab'), not the brain, held thought and character, and the dead needed it for judgment. Centuries later Aristotle agreed, calling the heart the seat of intelligence and the brain merely a cooling organ. Source: worldhistory.org/article/44/mummification-in-ancient-egypt + en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiocentric_hypothesis

question: The lungs, liver, stomach, and intestines were pulled out and sealed in four special containers, each lid carved as the head of one of the Four Sons of Horus. What are these four organ containers called?
answer: Canopic jars
choices: Canopic jars
Reliquary urns
Funeral amphorae
Burial cauldrons
context: Four canopic jars held the organs, each guarded by a Son of Horus: human-headed Imsety (liver), baboon-headed Hapy (lungs), jackal-headed Duamutef (stomach), and falcon-headed Qebehsenuef (intestines). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_sons_of_Horus + metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/550773

question: As he cut open the body and lifted out the organs, the chief embalmer-priest wore a mask to make himself into the god of the dead. Whose head did the mask copy?
answer: The jackal-headed god Anubis
choices: The jackal-headed god Anubis
The falcon-headed god Horus
The ibis-headed god Thoth
The ram-headed god Khnum
context: The chief embalmer, the hery-seshta ('He Who Is Over the Mystery'), wore a jackal-headed Anubis mask to embody the god of the dead during the cutting. A real cartonnage Anubis mask survives in the Roemer-Pelizaeus Museum in Hildesheim. Source: egyptfuntours.com/blog/the-ancient-egyptian-embalmer + mylearning.org/resources/anubis-mask

question: The Greek traveler Herodotus wrote that packing a body in natron was governed by a strict rule of exactly so many days, and 'for a longer time than this it is not permitted to embalm it.' How long did the whole drying process take?
answer: 70 days
choices: 70 days
40 days
100 days
365 days
context: Herodotus recorded that mummification took exactly 70 days, with the body packed in natron, and that embalming longer than that was forbidden. Seventy days was the rule, never more. Source: worldhistory.org/article/89/herodotus-on-burial-in-egypt

question: In the Egyptian judgment of the dead, jackal-headed Anubis placed the dead person's heart on one pan of a great scale. A monster named Ammit crouched nearby, waiting to devour the heart if it failed. What sat on the other pan, that the heart had to balance against?
answer: A single ostrich feather
choices: A single ostrich feather
A lump of pure gold
A clay model of the body
A bowl of the Nile's water
context: The heart was weighed against the single ostrich feather of Maat (truth), while Thoth recorded the result. If the heart was light, the soul passed on; if heavy with sin, Ammit devoured it and the person was annihilated forever.
