Source: egypt-museum.com/the-weighing-of-the-heart-ceremony + worldhistory.org/article/42/the-egyptian-afterlife--the-feather-of-truth

question: Ammit, the 'Devourer of the Dead,' was the monster that ate the heart of anyone judged guilty at the scales. The Egyptians built her body out of the three biggest man-eaters they feared. Which three animals made up Ammit?
answer: Crocodile, lion, and hippopotamus
choices: Crocodile, lion, and hippopotamus
Cobra, leopard, and elephant
Vulture, jackal, and bull
Scorpion, hyena, and rhinoceros
context: Ammit was a chimera with the head of a crocodile, the front of a lion, and the back of a hippopotamus, the three deadliest creatures Egyptians knew. Source: worldhistory.org/article/42/the-egyptian-afterlife--the-feather-of-truth + egypt-museum.com/the-weighing-of-the-heart-ceremony

question: Egyptians feared the heart would blurt out the dead person's sins at the weighing and doom the soul. So they wrapped a green stone amulet over the chest, inscribed with a spell begging the heart, 'do not rise up against me as a witness.' What was this amulet meant to do?
answer: Bribe the heart into staying silent at the scales
choices: Bribe the heart into staying silent at the scales
Make the heart beat one last time before judgment
Replace the heart if it had been damaged
Weigh the heart down so it sank on the scale
context: The green heart scarab, carved over the chest and inscribed with Spell 30B of the Book of the Dead, was a magical bribe to keep the heart from confessing sins to the Lord of Things at the scales. Source: ancientegyptonline.co.uk/heartscarab + en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_scarab

question: The famous human-headed jars that held a mummy's organs are called 'canopic' jars, but historians say the name is flat-out wrong. How did these Egyptian jars end up with a mistaken name?
answer: Early European travelers confused them with a Greek legend about a helmsman worshipped as a jar
choices: Early European travelers confused them with a Greek legend about a helmsman worshipped as a jar
Egyptians themselves later forgot the original word and guessed at a new one
A famous translator misread the hieroglyph for 'organ' as a place-name
The jars were first dug up in a Greek town and named after its founder
context: Early travelers mixed up the human-headed organ jars with a Greek legend about Canopus, the helmsman of Menelaus, supposedly worshipped at the Egyptian town of Canopus in the shape of a jar. The wrong name stuck. Source: etymonline.com/word/Canopic + encyclopedia.com/humanities/.../canopic-jar

question: Egyptian embalmers tossed the brain out as worthless trash. Yet around 1700 BC, an Egyptian medical scroll, the Edwin Smith Surgical Papyrus, did something with that same organ that no one in the world is known to have done before. What was that first?
answer: It gave the first known written description of the brain and its folded surface
choices: It gave the first known written description of the brain and its folded surface
It was the first to remove a living patient's brain in surgery
It was the first to claim the brain controlled the heart
It was the first to draw a detailed map of the brain's blood vessels
context: The same culture that discarded the brain during mummification produced, around 1700 BC, the Edwin Smith Surgical Papyrus, the first known description of the brain and its folded surface, and the first known use of the word 'brain.' Source: brainhq.com/brain-connection/think-like-an-ancient-egyptian + en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_neuroscience

question: The word 'fascism' comes from the fasces, an emblem the ancient Romans carried in front of a magistrate as a sign of his power to punish. Benito Mussolini named his blackshirt movement, the Fascio di Combattimento, after this old Roman symbol. What object was the fasces?
answer: a bundle of wooden rods strapped around an axe
choices: a bundle of wooden rods strapped around an axe
a bronze eagle clutching a thunderbolt
a laurel wreath set with a gold spike
a short sword crossed over a round shield
context: The bundle meant 'strength through unity': one rod snaps easily, but a whole bundle bound together cannot be broken. Mussolini took both the name and the emblem straight from ancient Rome. Source: Britannica 'Fasces'; Wikipedia 'Fasces'; etymonline.com 'fasces'.

question: Benito Mussolini invented fascism, but he began as a fierce socialist: the son of a blacksmith who rose to edit Avanti!, Italy's most important socialist newspaper, in Milan in 1912. In 1914 his own Socialist Party expelled him. What had Mussolini done to get himself thrown out?
answer: demanded that Italy enter World War I
choices: demanded that Italy enter World War I
converted to the Catholic Church
fled the country with party funds
called for the king to be crowned emperor
context: The socialists wanted Italy to stay neutral; Mussolini broke ranks and pushed for war, so they cast him out. He then built fascism as a rival movement of his own. Source: Britannica 'Benito Mussolini'; Encyclopedia.com 'Benito Mussolini'.

question: Fascist propaganda built Benito Mussolini into a near-godlike figure called 'Il Duce' (The Leader), even painting the boast 'Mussolini is always right' on walls across Italy. One famous stunt involved the windows of his office after dark. What did his handlers do with them each night?
answer: left the office lights burning all night long
choices: left the office lights burning all night long
projected his face onto the windows in light
kept the shutters bolted tight day and night
draped a huge portrait banner across them
context: With the lights left on, passers-by would believe Il Duce was still hard at work at 4 a.m. The whole cult was manufactured, right down to the slogan that he was never wrong. Source: Granger Historical Picture Archive; History of the Twentieth Century podcast ep. 255; Study.com 'Italian Fascist Propaganda'.

question: In October 1922 roughly 25,000 Blackshirts tramped through pouring rain toward the capital in the famous 'March on Rome' that swept the Fascists into power. Their leader Benito Mussolini, though, was nowhere among the marchers. Where was Mussolini while his men advanced on Rome?
answer: relaxing at the opera in Milan
choices: relaxing at the opera in Milan
hiding in a monastery near Rome
rallying a crowd in Naples
waiting aboard a warship off Genoa
context: Mussolini stayed in Milan and went to the opera two nights running, positioned near the Swiss border so he could bolt abroad if the bluff collapsed. The march itself was mostly theater. Source: Wikipedia 'March on Rome'; Britannica 'March on Rome'; World Socialist Web Site retrospective.

question: By April 1945, with the Allies overrunning Italy, Benito Mussolini tried to slip across the Swiss border hidden inside a German army convoy, wearing a German overcoat and helmet as a disguise. Partisans stopped the convoy at Dongo on Lake Como and recognized him anyway. What gave the disguised Mussolini away?
answer: his bald head and heavy jaw from the posters
choices: his bald head and heavy jaw from the posters
a diary of state secrets in his pocket
his thick country accent from Predappio
a fasces ring worn on his finger
context: Decades of propaganda posters had made his shaved bald head and heavy jaw too famous to hide; he was even still wearing general's riding pants with a red stripe. He was shot the next day at Giulino di Mezzegra. Source: History.com 'Mussolini's Final Hours'; War History Online 'Benito Mussolini Execution'.

question: In 1932 Benito Mussolini, helped by the philosopher Giovanni Gentile, set down 'The Doctrine of Fascism' to spell out what fascism actually stood for. At its heart lay a single claim about the relationship between the individual person and the State. What did the Doctrine declare?
answer: the State stands above the individual, who exists to serve it
choices: the State stands above the individual, who exists to serve it
the individual holds rights the State may never touch
the State should wither away once the workers rule
the individual and the State are equal partners by contract
context: The Doctrine made the State the highest good and reorganized the economy into 'corporazioni' (state-controlled guilds) meant to fuse workers and bosses under government command: ultranationalist, anti-liberal, and anti-communist. Knowing this real creed is how you recognize fascism, rather than treating the word as a vague insult. Source: Wikipedia 'The Doctrine of Fascism'; Political Research Associates 'Mussolini on the Corporate State'.

question: Two rival military alliances split Cold War Europe. NATO came first — 12 free nations signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington, D.C. in April 1949. The Soviet bloc did not answer with its own alliance, the Warsaw Pact, until six years later. What finally triggered Moscow to create the Warsaw Pact in 1955?
answer: West Germany was allowed to join NATO
choices: West Germany was allowed to join NATO
The United States tested its first hydrogen bomb
Britain and France invaded Egypt over the Suez Canal
Stalin died and a new leader took power in Moscow
context: West Germany joined NATO on May 9, 1955; just five days later, on May 14, eight Eastern-bloc states signed the Warsaw Pact — all placed under a single Soviet commander. It was a reaction, not a partnership of equals. Source: kafkadesk.org, 'On this day in 1955.'

question: Lord Hastings 'Pug' Ismay, NATO's first Secretary General, summed up the whole point of the alliance in one famous, blunt line about three different groups of people. According to Ismay, NATO existed to do what?
answer: keep the Russians out, the Americans in, and the Germans down
choices: keep the Russians out, the Americans in, and the Germans down
outspend the Soviets until their whole economy collapsed
guard the iron curtain from Berlin all the way to the sea
unite the kings of Europe under one crown against Moscow
context: Ismay's quip captured NATO's threefold purpose: block Soviet expansion, anchor America to Europe's defense, and prevent a militarized Germany from rising again. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hastings Ismay, 1st Baron Ismay.'

question: NATO's Article 5 is the heart of the alliance: an armed attack on one member is treated as an attack on all. In NATO's entire history this all-for-one clause has been formally invoked exactly once — and not for a war in Europe. What attack triggered it?
answer: the September 11, 2001 attacks on the United States
choices: the September 11, 2001 attacks on the United States
the Soviet shooting-down of a Korean airliner in 1983
the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979
the Berlin Wall going up overnight in August 1961
context: The one time NATO's collective-defense clause was ever invoked, it was Europe coming to America's aid after 9/11 — not the other way around. Source: nato.int, 'Collective defence and Article 5.'

question: In August 1968 the Warsaw Pact turned its tanks on its OWN member, pouring a quarter-million troops into Czechoslovakia to crush the 'Prague Spring' reforms. The Czechs had no army to match them, so they fought back with cleverness instead of guns. What was their trick to leave the Soviet tank columns lost and wandering?
answer: they tore down and painted over the street signs
choices: they tore down and painted over the street signs
they jammed every radio frequency the tanks used
they flooded the roads by blowing up a river dam
they disguised their soldiers in Soviet uniforms
context: Czechs erased and repainted street signs so the tanks got lost, gave soldiers wrong directions, and argued with the bewildered young troops in the street to prove there was no 'counter-revolution' — only people who wanted freedom. Source: Swarthmore Global Nonviolent Action Database.

question: The difference between the two alliances showed starkly in 1956. When Hungarian Prime Minister Imre Nagy announced on the radio that Hungary would QUIT the Warsaw Pact, Soviet tanks rolled into Budapest three days later and crushed the country, killing around 2,500 Hungarians. What did Moscow ultimately do to Nagy himself?
answer: hanged him and buried him in an unmarked grave
choices: hanged him and buried him in an unmarked grave
exiled him to a remote village in Siberia for life
forced him to denounce his own reforms on live radio
let him flee west, where he died years later in Paris
context: No NATO member was ever invaded by its own allies for trying to leave — but Nagy was hanged and dumped in an unmarked grave for it. In his last radio message he warned the world that 'the imperialism of Moscow does not know borders.' Source: Britannica, 'Hungarian Revolution of 1956.'

question: To send secret battlefield orders in WWII, the Marines used the Navajo language as a code, hiding war machines behind everyday Navajo words for animals and things. A tank became 'tortoise,' a battleship became 'whale,' and a fighter plane became 'hummingbird.' What everyday creature did the Code Talkers use to mean a submarine?
answer: The iron fish
choices: The iron fish
The thunder eagle
The river snake
The mud crab
context: Submarine was 'besh-lo' — 'iron fish.' A dive-bomber was a 'chicken hawk.' Each English letter also had its own cover word (A = 'ant,' B = 'bear'), so a speller could shuffle words to hide common letters. (National WWII Museum; encyclopedia.com; Multo (Ghost) blog 'Turtles, Pregnant Airplanes, and Iron Fish')

question: The Japanese captured Sergeant Joe Kieyoomia, a Navajo soldier, on the Bataan Death March, and when they realized he spoke Navajo they tortured him and forced him to translate the Marines' intercepted coded messages. Kieyoomia was a native Navajo speaker — so why could he NOT tell them what the messages meant?
answer: The coded words were nonsense to him because he had never been trained in the secret code
choices: The coded words were nonsense to him because he had never been trained in the secret code
The messages were transmitted too fast for any human ear to follow
He had forgotten his Navajo after years away at an English-only school
The Marines were actually speaking a different, unrelated tribal language
context: The code wasn't just Navajo — it was Navajo words standing in for other meanings, memorized only by the trained Code Talkers. A fluent speaker who didn't know the code heard only gibberish. The Japanese never broke it. (Deseret News, 'Neither Navajo Captive Nor Code Was Broken,' 1995; encyclopedia.com)

question: At the battle for Iwo Jima, six Navajo Code Talkers worked around the clock through the brutal first 48 hours, sending and receiving more than 800 messages — orders that could send Marines into fire or call down artillery on the wrong men if garbled. Major Howard Connor, the 5th Marine Division's signal officer, marveled at one thing about those 800 messages. What was it?
answer: Not a single one contained an error
choices: Not a single one contained an error
Every one was sent in under ten seconds
Each was written down in a secret codebook
All were relayed by a single exhausted man
context: More than 800 messages in 48 hours without one mistake. Connor said, 'Were it not for the Navajos, the Marines would never have taken Iwo Jima.' There were no codebooks in the field — every one of the 400-plus code terms had to be memorized. (history.navy.mil Navajo Code Talkers Fact Sheet; soledadmemorial.org)

question: Dr. Janusz Korczak ran a Warsaw ghetto orphanage of nearly 200 children. In August 1942, as the Germans were rounding up the ghetto's Jews for the death trains, Polish friends on the outside got him forged papers and offered to smuggle him to safety. What did Korczak do?
answer: led the children onto the train and died with them
choices: accepted the papers and slipped out of the ghetto alone
led the children onto the train and died with them
hid the children in the orphanage cellar for the night
bribed a guard to spare the youngest orphans
context: Korczak refused to abandon his orphans. He lined them up in orderly rows and walked with them to the cattle cars bound for the Treblinka killing center, and died there with them. (USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Janusz Korczak'; National WWII Museum, 'Defiance in the Face of Death')

question: On January 18, 1943, German troops marched into the Warsaw ghetto to renew the deportations to the death camps. This time, Jewish fighters who had smuggled in a few weapons opened fire on them. After a few days of this unexpected resistance, what did the Germans do?
answer: the German troops pulled back out of the ghetto
choices: the German troops pulled back out of the ghetto
the wall around the ghetto was rebuilt overnight
the orphanage was reopened for the children
the deportation trains switched to a new schedule
context: That small success was the turning point: it convinced the ghetto that armed defense was actually possible, and the fighters spent the next months preparing for the bigger fight to come. (Jewish Virtual Library, 'The Warsaw Ghetto Uprising'; USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia)

question: When the SS marched in on April 19, 1943 to destroy the Warsaw ghetto, the main Jewish fighting force — the Jewish Combat Organization, or ZOB — was led by Mordecai Anielewicz, a commander strikingly younger than the German generals sent against him. How old was Anielewicz?
answer: 24 years old
choices: 24 years old
19 years old
35 years old
45 years old
context: Anielewicz was just 24 when he commanded the uprising. A second group, the Jewish Military Union (ZZW), founded by Revisionist Zionists, fought alongside the ZOB. (USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia; Britannica, 'Mordecai Anielewicz')

question: On the afternoon of April 19, 1943, fighters of the Jewish Military Union seized a stronghold on Muranowski Square and raised two banners over it that flew for about four days, visible across Warsaw — even SS commander Jurgen Stroop noted them in his report. Which two flags did they raise?
answer: the Zionist flag and the Polish flag
choices: the Zionist flag and the Polish flag
the Polish flag and a red Soviet flag
a white truce flag and the Zionist flag
the German war flag flown upside down
context: The blue-and-white Zionist flag flew beside the red-and-white Polish flag over the burning ghetto — a deliberate act of defiance and of solidarity with Poland, plainly visible to the city below. (Israel Forever Foundation; Warsaw Ghetto Museum, 1943.pl)

question: In the April 1943 uprising, the ghetto fighters faced over 2,000 German soldiers backed by artillery and tanks. By one fighter's account, each member of the ZOB went into that battle armed with almost nothing. What was a single fighter's typical arsenal?
answer: one pistol, five grenades, and five Molotov cocktails
choices: one pistol, five grenades, and five Molotov cocktails
one rifle, two pistols, and a box of bullets
three grenades, a knife, and a smoke bomb
two pistols, one grenade, and a length of pipe
context: Pistols, homemade grenades, and Molotov cocktails against tanks and artillery — yet on the first day this handful of fighters drove the German column back out of the ghetto. (National WWII Museum, 'The Warsaw Ghetto Uprising')

question: After the lightly armed Warsaw ghetto fighters beat back the Germans in open street battles in April 1943, SS commander Jurgen Stroop changed tactics. Unable to defeat them gun-to-gun, how did the Germans finally force the fighters and hidden civilians out?
answer: they burned the ghetto down around the fighters
choices: they burned the ghetto down around the fighters
they poisoned the ghetto wells over many weeks
they starved the fighters by cutting off all food
they shelled the ghetto from across the river
context: The Germans torched the ghetto block by block and pumped gas into the sewers to seal the escape routes. The ZOB's deputy commander Marek Edelman later said simply: 'We were beaten by the flames, not the Germans.' (USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia; Marek Edelman via Holocaust Historical Society)

question: SS commander Jurgen Stroop expected to clear out the Warsaw ghetto in three days, deporting some 60,000 Jews. Instead, the fighters and the civilians hiding in bunkers held his far larger, better-armed force off far longer. From April 19 to May 16, 1943, how long did they hold out?
answer: nearly a month
choices: nearly a month
three days
a single afternoon
an entire year
context: About 27 days. A few hundred starving, near-unarmed fighters paralyzed thousands of German troops for almost a month — far longer than several national armies had lasted against the Wehrmacht in 1939-1940. (USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia; Holocaust Memorial Day Trust)

question: On April 23, 1943, with the ghetto in flames and the end near, Mordecai Anielewicz wrote a last letter to his deputy Yitzhak Zuckerman. He did not write of defeat — he wrote that the dream of his life had come true. What was the dream he said had been fulfilled?
answer: his lifelong dream of armed Jewish self-defense had come true
choices: his lifelong dream of armed Jewish self-defense had come true
word had arrived that the Allies were sending them weapons
a secret tunnel out of the ghetto had finally been finished
the German commander had quietly agreed to a ceasefire
context: Anielewicz wrote that he had lived to see Jewish armed self-defense in the ghetto 'in all its greatness and glory.' Days later he was dead, but he died believing the fight itself was the victory. (Jewish Virtual Library, 'The Last Letter from Mordechai Anielewicz')

question: When the fighting in the Warsaw ghetto ended in May 1943, SS commander Jurgen Stroop wrote an official report to Heinrich Himmler boasting that the job was done. What did Stroop title that report?
answer: 'The Jewish Quarter of Warsaw Is No More!'
choices: 'The Jewish Quarter of Warsaw Is No More!'
'Order Restored in the Eastern District'
'A Brief Disturbance, Now Ended'
'The Cleansing of the City Is Complete'
context: Stroop's report survived the war and became evidence of the crime he was bragging about — including the famous photograph of a small boy raising his hands at gunpoint. Stroop was later tried and hanged in Warsaw. (USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia; Library of Congress; Wikipedia, 'Stroop Report')

question: On May 16, 1943, to mark the destruction of the Warsaw ghetto as a symbol of his triumph, SS commander Jurgen Stroop ordered one last, deliberate act of destruction in the city. What did he do?
answer: dynamited Warsaw's Great Synagogue
choices: dynamited Warsaw's Great Synagogue
renamed the city's main street after Hitler
melted down the synagogue's bells for scrap
paraded the captured fighters through the square
context: Stroop personally gave the order and blew up the Great Synagogue of Warsaw as his finishing flourish — turning a place of worship into rubble to crown his report that 'The Jewish Quarter of Warsaw Is No More!' (USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia; Wikipedia, 'Stroop Report')

question: Marek Edelman, a ZOB deputy commander, was asked why a few hundred starving fighters would take up arms against the SS when they all knew they could not possibly win. They were not trying to survive, he said — they were trying to take one thing back from the Germans. What was it?
answer: so the Germans could not pick the time and place of their deaths
choices: so the Germans could not pick the time and place of their deaths
so that the history books would record every fighter by name
so the watching world would be shamed into finally helping
so the children still in hiding could slip away to safety
context: Edelman said: 'We knew perfectly well that we had no chance of winning. We fought simply not to allow the Germans alone to pick the time and place of our deaths.' The fight was a refusal to be murdered passively. (Marek Edelman via Holocaust Historical Society and explorethearchive.com)

question: The historian Emanuel Ringelblum ran a secret archive inside the Warsaw ghetto, codenamed 'Oneg Shabbat,' to record everything the Germans were doing. Knowing the ghetto would be destroyed, his team made sure the testimony would outlast them. How did they save roughly 35,000 pages of records?
answer: sealed them in milk cans and buried them underground
choices: sealed them in milk cans and buried them underground
smuggled them out of the ghetto hidden inside a coffin
memorized the pages and recited them after the war
mailed them to relatives living in America
context: They packed the records into milk cans and metal boxes and buried them. Two milk cans and the boxes were dug up after the war at 68 Nowolipki Street (1946 and 1950) — so the ghetto's own people preserved the record of what was done to them. (USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Oneg Shabbat Archive'; Yad Vashem)

question: By May 8, 1943, the Germans had traced the ZOB's main command bunker to 18 Mila Street, where Mordecai Anielewicz and about 100 fighters were hiding, and began pumping gas inside. Rather than be captured by the SS, what did Anielewicz and many of the fighters do?
answer: took their own lives rather than be captured
choices: took their own lives rather than be captured
surrendered once their ammunition ran out
escaped through a tunnel into the forest
were marched out and sent to Treblinka
context: Anielewicz and roughly 100 fighters died at 'Mila 18,' many by their own hand rather than fall into German hands. A mound still marks the spot in Warsaw today. (USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia; Jewish Virtual Library; Wikipedia, 'Mordechai Anielewicz')

question: On the night of November 9-10, 1938, mobs across Germany burned more than 1,400 synagogues, smashed thousands of Jewish shops, and dragged tens of thousands of Jewish men off to concentration camps. So much glass lay shattered in the streets that the night got a grim nickname. What was it?
answer: Kristallnacht -- 'Night of Broken Glass'
choices: Kristallnacht -- 'Night of Broken Glass'
Blutnacht -- 'Night of Blood'
Pogromnacht -- 'Night of the Pogrom'
Scherbennacht -- 'Night of Shards'
context: Kristallnacht was set off when 17-year-old Herschel Grynszpan shot the German diplomat Ernst vom Rath in Paris on November 7, 1938; after Rath died, Joseph Goebbels gave a Munich speech signaling Nazis to 'spontaneously' attack -- violence that was in fact ordered from the top. About 100 Jews were killed directly (roughly 400 counting suicides) and some 26,000-30,000 men were sent to Dachau, Buchenwald, and Sachsenhausen. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Kristallnacht'.

question: At 10 a.m. on April 1, 1933, in the first nationwide, state-organized action against Germany's Jews, SA storm troopers planted themselves outside Jewish-owned shops and the offices of Jewish doctors and lawyers, holding up signs to turn customers away. What did the signs say?
answer: Germans! Defend yourselves! Don't buy from Jews!
choices: Germans! Defend yourselves! Don't buy from Jews!
Germany awake! Cast out every foreigner now!
Workers, rise! Take your nation back today!
Buy German always! Keep the Reich pure!
context: This 1933 boycott came more than two years before the Nuremberg Laws and showed the regime testing how far it could go in public. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Boycott of Jewish Businesses'.

question: Julius Streicher ran the antisemitic tabloid Der Stürmer, mounting it in glass display cases on street corners and outside factories until it reached nearly 500,000 readers. Every single issue carried the same slogan across it. Which one did it run?
answer: The Jews are our misfortune.
choices: The Jews are our misfortune.
The Jew is the ruin of nations.
Without the Jew, Germany is free.
Trust no Jew, in word or deed.
context: In German the slogan read 'Die Juden sind unser Unglück.' Streicher founded Der Stürmer in 1923; at Nuremberg in 1946 he was sentenced to death for his propaganda. Source: Wikipedia, 'Der Stürmer'; USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Julius Streicher: Biography'.

question: From September 1941, by an order from Reinhard Heydrich, every Jew in Germany aged six and older was forced to wear one particular marker on their outer clothing any time they appeared in public, so they could be identified on sight. What did they have to wear?
answer: A yellow Star of David marked 'Jude'
choices: A yellow Star of David marked 'Jude'
A red armband stamped with 'Jude'
A blue cloth triangle on the sleeve
A black diamond patch on the chest
context: The badge was one rung in a ladder of marking: in August 1938 Jews were forced to add the names 'Israel' or 'Sara' to their own, and in October 1938 a red letter 'J' was stamped on their passports. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Jewish Badge: During the Nazi Era'; National WWII Museum, 'The Nuremberg Race Laws'.

question: In 1938 Julius Streicher's publishing house printed a cartoon picture book aimed straight at children, training them to fear and 'spot' Jews. The whole book turned on one comparison: a Jew was supposedly like one particular dangerous thing. What was the Jew compared to?
answer: A poisonous mushroom hidden among safe ones
choices: A poisonous mushroom hidden among safe ones
A rotten apple buried in a good barrel
A weed creeping through a flowerbed
A snake coiled in the tall grass
context: The book was 'Der Giftpilz' ('The Poisonous Mushroom'), text by Ernst Hiemer with cartoons by Philipp Rupprecht ('Fips'); about 40,000 copies were printed. One page told children, 'The Jewish nose is crooked at its tip. It looks like the number 6.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Der Giftpilz'; USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Julius Streicher: Biography'.

question: After Kristallnacht left Jewish homes, shops, and synagogues in ruins, the Nazi regime declared that the Jews themselves were to blame for the destruction. Instead of any help, what did the regime then do to the German-Jewish community?
answer: Fined them a billion Reichsmarks and seized their insurance
choices: Fined them a billion Reichsmarks and seized their insurance
Deported them all eastward and seized their homes
Made them rebuild the synagogues and pay the workers
Marked their shops and barred them from all trade
context: The collective 'atonement' fine was one billion Reichsmarks, and the state confiscated the insurance money the Jewish owners were owed for their own smashed property -- punishing the victims twice over. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Kristallnacht' / 'Night of Broken Glass'.

question: The second Nuremberg Law of 1935, the Law for the Protection of German Blood and German Honor, banned both marriage and relationships between Jews and other Germans -- and the Nazis invented a special crime-name for any such relationship, sending thousands to concentration camps under it. What did they call this supposed crime?
answer: Rassenschande -- 'race defilement'
choices: Rassenschande -- 'race defilement'
Blutschuld -- 'blood guilt'
Rassenkampf -- 'race struggle'
Volksverrat -- 'betrayal of the people'
context: The same Blood Law also forbade Jewish households from employing German women under 45 as servants, and barred Jews from flying the German flag or showing the Reich colors -- stripping them even of the symbols of their own country. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Nuremberg Laws'; Wikipedia, 'Nuremberg Laws'.

question: On September 15, 1935, the first of the two Nuremberg Laws -- the Reich Citizenship Law -- struck at the most basic legal standing of every German Jew. What did it do to them?
answer: Demoted them from citizens to mere 'subjects' of the state
choices: Demoted them from citizens to mere 'subjects' of the state
Barred them from voting in any national election
Required them to register all property with the state
Banned them from holding any government job
context: Only a person 'of German or related blood' could now be a Reich citizen (Reichsbürger) with full political rights; a Jew became a mere subject (Staatsangehörige) -- no longer a citizen of the country they had been born in. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Nuremberg Laws'; Wikipedia, 'Nuremberg Laws'.

question: To sort the whole population by 'race,' the Nazis printed an official blood-purity chart that split everyone into three groups by ancestry and marked each group with a coded symbol. On that chart, how were people marked?
answer: White circles for 'German blood', black circles for Jews
choices: White circles for 'German blood', black circles for Jews
Gold stars for Aryans, red stars for Jews
Blue squares for Germans, yellow squares for Jews
Green checks for the pure, black crosses for Jews
context: People of mixed ancestry got shaded circles. The chart counted grandparents: three or four Jewish grandparents made you a full 'Jew' (Jude), two a 'Mischling of the first degree', one a 'Mischling of the second degree'. The regime classified about 502,200 Germans as full Jews. Source: National WWII Museum, 'The Nuremberg Race Laws'; EHRI / USHMM blood-purity teaching chart.

question: In 1935 Hitler summoned the German parliament, the Reichstag, to assemble at the giant annual Nazi Party rally and rubber-stamp the new race laws. That single sitting holds a strange record: in all twelve years of Nazi rule, no other Reichstag session was ever like it. What made it the only one of its kind?
answer: It was the only one ever held outside Berlin
choices: It was the only one ever held outside Berlin
It was the only one ever held after dark
It was the only one Hitler did not attend
It was the only one opened to the public
context: It was a one-off parliament summoned to the party rally in Nuremberg for the sole purpose of passing the race laws. The laws were thrown together in a frantic rush -- officials Bernhard Loesener and Franz Albrecht Medicus were hurried to Nuremberg on September 14, and around 2:30 a.m. on the 15th Hitler was handed several drafts, one scrawled on the back of a restaurant menu, and picked one only hours before announcing it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Nuremberg Laws'; National WWII Museum, 'The Nuremberg Race Laws'.

question: The entire Nazi system insisted that Jews were a separate RACE, detectable in the blood -- yet scientists had no test that could find any such thing. So to decide whether a person's grandparent had been 'Jewish,' the regime quietly fell back on one ordinary kind of record. What did they actually use to define a 'Jewish' grandparent?
answer: Whether that grandparent had belonged to the Jewish religion
choices: Whether that grandparent had belonged to the Jewish religion
Whether that grandparent had carried a Jewish surname
Whether that grandparent had lived in a Jewish quarter
Whether that grandparent had looked Jewish in photographs
context: This is the hidden absurdity at the core of the laws: a system that claimed to be about 'blood' secretly rested on religious records, not biology -- it could not define a Jew by race at all without pointing to who had practiced the Jewish faith. Source: National WWII Museum, 'The Nuremberg Race Laws'.

question: Julius Streicher, who ran the antisemitic paper Der Stürmer for over twenty years, was sentenced to death at the Nuremberg war-crimes trials for his propaganda and hanged in 1946. On the gallows he shouted twice -- first 'Heil Hitler!', then one last defiant cry that turned a Jewish festival into a sneer at his executioners. What was that final shout?
answer: Purimfest 1946!
choices: Purimfest 1946!
Bolschewismus 1946!
Deutschland, erwache!
Heil Deutschland!
context: Streicher was the first man at such a tribunal condemned for words alone -- a newspaper, not a single ordered killing. His shout 'Purimfest 1946!' twisted the Jewish festival of Purim, which celebrates the downfall of the ancient persecutor Haman, into a bitter jab as he himself was about to hang on October 16, 1946. Source: Wikipedia, 'Julius Streicher'; Nuremberg executions records.

question: On the night of August 23, 1939, Germany and the Soviet Union signed a pact in Moscow dividing eastern Europe between them. At the banquet afterward, Joseph Stalin rose with a glass of Crimean sparkling wine to toast a man whose entire ideology he had spent years denouncing as his mortal enemy. Whose health did Stalin drink to?
answer: Adolf Hitler, the German Fuhrer
choices: Adolf Hitler, the German Fuhrer
Vyacheslav Molotov, his foreign minister
Vladimir Lenin, the founder of the USSR
Winston Churchill, the British leader
context: Stalin said, 'I know how much the German nation loves its Fuhrer; I should therefore like to drink to his health.' He also gave his 'word of honor that the Soviet Union would not betray its partner' Germany. The toast survives in the German Foreign Office's own memorandum of the banquet. (Avalon Project, Yale Law School, Nazi-Soviet Relations 1939-1941, doc ns053; https://avalon.law.yale.edu/20th_century/ns053.asp)

question: After Germany invaded Poland from the west on September 1, 1939, Stalin sent the Red Army in from the east on September 17, and the two powers split the conquered country between them. On September 28 they signed a follow-up treaty finalizing the new border. With Polish cities still smoking, what single word did Hitler and Stalin actually put in that treaty's title alongside 'Boundary'?
answer: Friendship
choices: Friendship
Conquest
Neutrality
Partition
context: The German-Soviet Boundary and Friendship Treaty of September 28, 1939 finalized the carve-up of Poland and traded the USSR's claim on most of Lithuania for a bigger slice of central Poland (the Lublin region and eastern Warsaw province). The two totalitarian powers were collaborators years before they were enemies; Stalin only 'switched sides' once Hitler invaded him in June 1941. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German%E2%80%93Soviet_Boundary_and_Friendship_Treaty)

question: In August 1939, Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union — bitter ideological enemies — shocked the world by signing a non-aggression pact. At the signing dinner inside the Kremlin, the communist dictator Joseph Stalin raised his glass for a toast. Whose health did Stalin drink to?
answer: Adolf Hitler's health
choices: Adolf Hitler's health
Vyacheslav Molotov's health
The Red Army's health
The Russian people's health
context: Stalin toasted the German dictator, reportedly saying he knew 'how much the German people love their Fuehrer.' The leader of world communism drank to the health of the leader of fascism — the clearest sign the two regimes were now partners, not opposites. Source: history.com (Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact); EBSCO Research Starters: German-Soviet Nonaggression Pact.

question: On August 23, 1939, the foreign ministers Joachim von Ribbentrop of Germany and Vyacheslav Molotov of the Soviet Union signed a public non-aggression treaty in Moscow — the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact. But the treaty hid a secret protocol that the Soviet Union would go on denying ever existed for the next fifty years. What did that secret protocol actually do?
answer: Secretly divided Poland and the Baltic states between the two powers
choices: Secretly divided Poland and the Baltic states between the two powers
Secretly pledged the two armies to attack Britain together
Secretly promised Soviet oil and grain to fund Germany's war
Secretly set a date for Germany to invade the Soviet Union
context: The hidden protocol carved Eastern Europe into 'spheres of influence,' splitting Poland along the Narew, Vistula, and San rivers and handing Estonia, Latvia, Finland, and Bessarabia to the Soviet sphere. Within weeks both powers acted on it: Germany invaded Poland from the west on September 1, the Red Army from the east on September 17, and the USSR went on to seize the Baltics and attack Finland. Moscow denied the protocol existed until 1989. Source: encyclopedia.ushmm.org (German-Soviet Pact); Wilson Center Digital Archive (text of the protocol).

question: The Declaration of Independence (1776) says people are 'endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights.' It names three: life, liberty, and a third. The Founders chose that third one's wording with great care — they pointedly did NOT write 'a right to happiness.' What did they write instead?
answer: The pursuit of happiness
choices: The pursuit of happiness
The guarantee of happiness
The right to own property
The right to lifelong comfort
context: The exact phrase is 'Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness' — the right to CHASE happiness, not a promise that anyone will hand it to you. A right to try, not a thing you are owed. (John Locke's older trio had been life, liberty, and ESTATE — property — which is why 'property' is such a tempting wrong answer here.) This is the heart of an 'unalienable' freedom: it asks others only to leave you alone while you pursue your own life, costing no one anything. Source: National Archives transcription, https://www.archives.gov/founding-docs/declaration-transcript ; ushistory.org on 'unalienable.'

question: Frederic Bastiat, a French writer, attacked what he called 'legal plunder' in his 1850 book 'The Law' — using the law to take from one person and hand it to another. Picture it his way: you cannot walk into your neighbor's house and carry off his bread — do that and you'd be hauled before a judge. Now suppose a law is passed that takes your neighbor's bread and gives it to someone else. What did Bastiat say that law had become?
answer: Theft, just done through the law instead of by hand
choices: Theft, just done through the law instead of by hand
Charity, a lawful way of helping those with less
Justice, the law evening out who has too much
Progress, society outgrowing old ideas of property
context: Bastiat's test for a fake right: 'See whether the law takes from some persons that which belongs to them, to give to others what does not belong to them... an act that this citizen cannot perform without committing a crime.' If an act would be a crime when YOU do it, passing a law to do it for you doesn't make it just — it makes it legal plunder. This is the negative-vs-positive rights line: your life, speech, and property ask only that others leave you alone (everyone can hold those at once, free of charge), but a 'right' to the baker's bread can't be filled unless someone is forced to bake. The strongest case for the other side is Franklin Roosevelt's 1944 'Second Bill of Rights' (a job, a home, medical care as rights) — argued in good faith, but it requires conscripting a provider, which is exactly what Bastiat warned against. Source: Bastiat, 'The Law' (1850), Project Gutenberg #44800.

question: The future emperor Gaius grew up as a toddler in his father Germanicus's army camp on the Rhine, where the soldiers dressed him in a tiny version of the legionary's leather boot, the caliga, and gave him a nickname from it. What did the troops call the little boy?
answer: Caligula, 'Little Boots'
choices: Caligula, 'Little Boots'
Brutus, 'the Heavy One'
Maximus, 'the Great'
Corvus, 'the Raven'
context: The nickname 'Caligula' means 'Little Boots,' from the caliga the soldiers fitted on him in the Rhine camp. As an adult emperor he hated the name and punished anyone who used it. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/7-things-you-may-not-know-about-caligula

question: The Great Fire of Rome broke out on the night of 19 July, AD 64, and tore through the city for about six days. Tacitus records that of Rome's fourteen districts, only four came through unharmed. What part of the city did the fire start in?
answer: The shops full of flammable goods by the Circus Maximus
choices: The shops full of flammable goods by the Circus Maximus
The granaries beside the river harbor
The marble Senate house in the Forum
The aqueduct arches outside the walls
context: The fire began in shops packed with flammable goods at the foot of the Palatine and Caelian hills, by the Circus Maximus. Three of Rome's fourteen districts were destroyed utterly and seven left in scorched ruins. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_Rome

question: Everyone 'knows' that the emperor Nero fiddled while Rome burned in AD 64. But careful historians call this picture impossible for one simple reason about the instrument itself. Why could Nero NOT have fiddled?
answer: The fiddle had not been invented yet, by over a thousand years
choices: The fiddle had not been invented yet, by over a thousand years
Nero was away from Rome at the coast that whole week
Nero could not play any musical instrument at all
Roman law forbade music during a public disaster
context: The fiddle (violin) did not exist in the ancient world; it appeared more than a thousand years later. The phrase comes from much later writers. Tacitus reports only a RUMOR that Nero sang of the fall of Troy, and flags it as rumor; Suetonius and Cassius Dio later repeated it as fact. Source: http://kiwihellenist.blogspot.com/2017/04/the-fire-of-rome-nero-and-fiddle.html  (Legend.)

question: After the Great Fire, a rumor spread that the emperor Nero had started it himself. To shift the blame onto someone else, Nero picked out a small religious group in Rome and had them tortured and killed. According to the historian Tacitus, which group did Nero blame for the fire?
answer: Rome's Christians
choices: Rome's Christians
Rome's grain merchants
The senators of the old families
The priests of the Vestal order
context: Tacitus, no friend of Christians, says Nero 'contrived' the charge against them, and records the punishments: victims wrapped in animal skins and torn by dogs, nailed to crosses, or burned as nightly torches. Tacitus also notes here that 'Christus' had been executed under Tiberius by the procurator Pontius Pilate. Source: https://www.livius.org/sources/content/tacitus/tacitus-on-the-christians/

question: By AD 68 the Senate had declared the emperor Nero a public enemy and his own Praetorian Guard had abandoned him for a rebel governor. Cornered and about to take his own life, Nero spoke a line that Suetonius preserved as his dying boast. What did Nero say as he died?
answer: 'What an artist dies in me!'
choices: 'What an artist dies in me!'
'I have lived as Rome deserved.'
'Let them fear me still.'
'Bury me with the eagles.'
context: Suetonius gives Nero's last words as 'Qualis artifex pereo' — 'What an artist dies in me.' His death on 9 June, AD 68, ended the Julio-Claudian dynasty and triggered the chaotic 'Year of the Four Emperors.' Source: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Nero

question: On 22 April 1915 at the Second Battle of Ypres, German troops opened the valves on thousands of buried steel cylinders and let a greenish-yellow cloud drift on the wind toward the French and Algerian line. It was the first large-scale poison-gas attack of the war. What gas rolled across no man's land that day?
answer: Chlorine
choices: Chlorine
Phosgene
Mustard gas
Tear gas
context: About 160-168 tons of chlorine drifted from roughly 6,000 cylinders; the troops in its path broke and fled, tearing a gap several kilometres wide in the line. Source: National WWI Museum and Memorial (theworldwar.org); IWM 'Second Battle of Ypres'.

question: At Flers-Courcelette on the Somme on 15 September 1916, the British rolled out a brand-new machine that crushed barbed wire and crawled across trenches that stopped every other vehicle. What carried the diamond-shaped Mark I tank over a trench instead of getting stuck in it?
answer: Caterpillar tracks running all the way around the hull
choices: Caterpillar tracks running all the way around the hull
A pair of oversized rubber balloon tires
Folding steel bridges it dropped ahead of itself
Spinning drums of cable that winched it across
context: The Mark I's tracks looped right around its rhomboid body, letting it span the cratered, trench-cut ground. This was the first time in history tanks went into battle. Source: The Tank Museum 'Tanks at Flers'; historyofwar.org 'Battle of Flers-Courcelette'.

question: At Second Ypres in 1915 the Allies had no gas masks yet, so when the chlorine cloud came, Canadian soldiers were given one desperate improvised defense to breathe through. One officer reportedly bellowed the order down the line. What were the men told to do with their handkerchiefs?
answer: Urinate on them and tie them over their faces
choices: Urinate on them and tie them over their faces
Soak them in rum and stuff them up their nostrils
Burn them and breathe through the smoke
Bury their faces in them against the wet ground
context: The ammonia in urine partially neutralised the chlorine. The shouted order was reportedly 'Piss on your handkerchiefs and tie them over your faces!' Source: Veterans Affairs Canada '2nd Battle of Ypres'; Warfare History Network 'Salient of Death'.

question: A water-cooled Maxim-type machine gun could fire around 600 rounds a minute, and commanders placed these guns so their bullet-streams crossed in no man's land rather than pointing straight ahead. What did this 'interlocking fields of fire' do to a soldier who tried to dodge one gun by veering sideways?
answer: It walked him straight into the next gun's kill zone
choices: It walked him straight into the next gun's kill zone
It let him slip through a safe gap between the streams
It drew the gunners' aim away toward the louder gun
It bought him cover until the water jackets overheated
context: The crossing streams swept advancing men from the side (enfilade) in a continuous wall of lead with no gap. On 1 July 1916, the Somme's first day, this fire helped inflict ~57,000-60,000 British casualties, the bloodiest single day in the army's history. Source: Swampfox Optics 'The Devil's Paintbrush'; Warfare History Network.

question: Early WWI pilots could not fire a forward machine gun without shredding their own wooden propeller. In 1915 the Dutch designer Anthony Fokker delivered a device that solved it and handed Germany the skies. How did his synchronization gear let bullets pass a spinning blade unharmed?
answer: A cam tied to the engine stopped the gun the instant a blade crossed the muzzle
choices: A cam tied to the engine stopped the gun the instant a blade crossed the muzzle
Steel wedges on the blades simply bounced any bullet that struck them
The gun was angled to fire just outside the propeller's circle
The blades were slotted with gaps the bullets were timed to find
context: Now a pilot aimed the whole aircraft at his target. Fitted to the Fokker Eindecker, it gave such dominance from mid-1915 that Allied airmen called themselves 'Fokker Fodder' during the 'Fokker Scourge.' (The bouncing-wedge distractor was a real earlier fix: Roland Garros bolted deflectors to his blades before Fokker's gear existed.) Source: Wikipedia 'Synchronization gear'; RAFA.

question: Before Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492, Italian cooks had no tomatoes, Irish farmers grew no potatoes, and kitchens in India and Korea had never tasted a chili pepper. All of these now-iconic foods came from the very same part of the world. Where did they originally come from?
answer: the Americas
choices: the Americas
Africa
China
the Middle East
context: Every one of these foods is native to the Americas and only crossed the Atlantic after 1492 as part of what historians call the Columbian Exchange. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbian_exchange

question: Maize, the crop we call corn, was bred over about 9,000 years by farmers in southern Mexico who slowly turned a scrawny wild grass called teosinte into fat ears of corn. They planted it in the same mound as beans and squash. What did farmers call this trio of crops grown together?
answer: the Three Sisters
choices: the Three Sisters
the Golden Harvest
the Sacred Grains
the Field Brothers
context: The corn stalk gave the beans something to climb, the beans fed the soil, and the squash leaves shaded out weeds. After 1492 maize spread so far that the world now grows more of it than wheat or rice. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Sisters_(agriculture)

question: When the tomato first arrived in Europe, people feared it as a deadly poison for more than 200 years. Their fear came from the plant's family tree: the tomato is cousin to a notorious killer plant, and the tomato's own leaves really are toxic. Which poisonous plant is the tomato's relative?
answer: deadly belladonna
choices: deadly belladonna
poison hemlock
monkshood
foxglove
context: Belladonna, also called deadly nightshade, gave the whole nightshade family its scary reputation. The tomato FRUIT is perfectly safe, but its leaves are genuinely toxic, which made the suspicion stick. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/how-the-misrepresentation-of-tomatoes-as-stinking-poison-apples-that-provoked-vomiting-made-people-afraid-of-them-for-more-than-200-years-863735/

question: French pharmacist Antoine-Augustin Parmentier wanted to convince suspicious peasants that potatoes were good to eat. So he planted a patch of potatoes outside Paris, posted armed guards around it all day long, and then quietly pulled the guards away every night. What was he hoping the villagers would do?
answer: sneak in at night to steal the 'precious' guarded crop
choices: sneak in at night to steal the 'precious' guarded crop
march to the king to demand a share of the harvest
plant their own potato fields to copy the rich man
burn the patch down out of fear of poison
context: Parmentier bet that if a crop looked valuable enough to guard, villagers would assume it was worth stealing and growing themselves. The story is told as legend, but potatoes did catch on in France soon after. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/how-the-potato-changed-the-world-108470605/

question: Italians don't really call the tomato a 'tomato' at all. Their word for it, 'pomodoro', was first put into print by the botanist Pietro Andrea Mattioli in 1554, and it probably described an early yellow-skinned variety. What does the Italian word 'pomodoro' literally mean?
answer: golden apple
choices: golden apple
red jewel
love apple
sun fruit
context: 'Pomo d'oro' means 'golden apple', a hint that the first tomatoes Italians saw may have been yellow rather than red. Centuries later, in 1889, Naples gave the world Pizza Margherita with red tomato, white cheese, and green basil. Source: https://italysegreta.com/pomi-doro-the-tomato-is-italys-golden-apple/

question: By the late 1700s, about 40% of Ireland's people ate the potato as their ONLY solid food, because it grew on tiny plots in poor soil. Then, starting in September 1845, a water mold called late blight rotted the potato crop in the fields. What happened to Ireland after the crop failed?
answer: over a million people died and about two million more emigrated, mostly to America
choices: over a million people died and about two million more emigrated, mostly to America
the government banned potatoes and forced farmers to grow only wheat
famine ended within a year once farmers switched back to grain
the Irish abandoned farming and moved entirely into coastal fishing towns
context: The mold was Phytophthora infestans. Because so many people depended on a single crop, its failure became one of history's deadliest famines, and the wave of Irish emigrants reshaped America. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/how-the-potato-changed-the-world-108470605/

question: Erwin Rommel, the German general who led the Afrika Korps across the open North African desert in 1942, used cunning hit-and-run tank raids that struck and vanished before his enemies could pin him down. What fitting nickname did his own countrymen give him for this?
answer: The Desert Fox
choices: The Desert Fox
The Iron Lion
The Sand Eagle
The Steel Wolf
context: Germans called him the 'Wuestenfuchs' -- the Desert Fox -- for his cunning. Even his British enemies, the 'Desert Rats' of the Eighth Army, respected him. Source: history.com, This Day in History, Oct 14.

question: As General Bernard Montgomery's army prepared to attack at El Alamein, Erwin Rommel had buried about half a million mines in belts up to five and a half miles deep across the desert. His own German troops gave these deadly fields a chilling nickname. What did they call them?
answer: the Devil's Gardens
choices: the Devil's Gardens
the Iron Curtain
the Dead Sea
the Gates of Dust
context: Rommel's troops nicknamed the vast minefields the 'Devil's Gardens.' Source: worldhistory.org, Second Battle of El Alamein.

question: After Montgomery's Eighth Army finally beat Rommel at El Alamein in November 1942 -- Britain's first land victory of the war -- Winston Churchill was so overjoyed he ordered a celebration across the whole country that had been silent for years. What did Churchill order done to mark the win?
answer: the church bells of Britain rung
choices: the church bells of Britain rung
a parade through London held
a national holiday declared
the king's portrait flown everywhere
context: Churchill ordered Britain's church bells rung in celebration. He later wrote in 'The Hinge of Fate' (1951): 'Before Alamein we never had a victory. After Alamein we never had a defeat.' Source: winstonchurchill.org.

question: Bernard Montgomery code-named his opening infantry attack at El Alamein 'Operation Lightfoot' -- a grim joke aimed at the soldiers who had to advance first through Rommel's half-million mines. What did the name 'Lightfoot' darkly mean for those men?
answer: step so lightly the mines wouldn't go off
choices: step so lightly the mines wouldn't go off
march faster than the enemy could aim
carry no packs to move quickly
leave their boots behind in the sand
context: Infantry were meant to step lightly enough not to trigger the mines, leaving the heavier tanks to set them off. Source: worldhistory.org, Second Battle of El Alamein.

question: When the Battle of El Alamein opened in October 1942, Erwin Rommel -- the Afrika Korps's brilliant commander -- wasn't even on the battlefield; he was sick in Germany. Worse, his stand-in, General Georg Stumme, met a sudden fate near the front on the battle's second day. What happened to Stumme?
answer: he dropped dead of a heart attack
choices: he dropped dead of a heart attack
he was captured by a British patrol
he deserted back across the lines
he was court-martialed by Berlin
context: Stumme died of a heart attack on 24 Oct 1942 while driving near the front, forcing Rommel to fly back to a battle already going wrong. Source: worldhistory.org, Second Battle of El Alamein.

question: Before El Alamein the British ran 'Operation Bertram' to fool Erwin Rommel about when and where they would strike: they hid tanks under canvas 'sunshields' to look like trucks, built dummy tanks facing the wrong way, and even faked a slow-growing water pipeline. The captured German general Wilhelm von Thoma later admitted what about the trick?
answer: he had been fooled on both timing and place
choices: he had been fooled on both timing and place
he had warned Rommel but was ignored
he had spotted the dummies from the air
he had refused to believe the pipeline
context: 772 'sunshields' disguised tanks as trucks and a fake pipeline 'grew' 5 miles a day. Von Thoma admitted he was deceived on both the timing and the location of the attack. Source: Wikipedia, Operation Bertram.

question: Two years after El Alamein, on 14 October 1944, Erwin Rommel was implicated in the July plot to kill Hitler. Two generals came to his home and offered him a choice: a public treason trial with reprisals against his family, or a quieter end that would be hidden behind a hero's state funeral. What was that second option Rommel chose?
answer: a cyanide capsule
choices: a cyanide capsule
a quiet exile abroad
a transfer to the eastern front
a confession in writing
context: Rommel took the poison; his death was publicly blamed on his earlier war wounds and he was given a state funeral. Source: historynet.com, 'Rommel's Last Day.'

question: A NASA night-time satellite photo of the Korean peninsula shows South Korea blazing with electric light, while the whole country north of the DMZ is an almost total black void. In all that darkness there is exactly one bright spot. Which place is the single lit dot in North Korea's night?
answer: Pyongyang
choices: Pyongyang
Hamhung
Wonsan
Kaesong
context: The capital, Pyongyang, is the only place the regime keeps reliably lit. After the Soviet Union collapsed in the early 1990s, North Korea lost the subsidized fuel and spare parts that ran its power plants, and electricity generation nosedived — the blackness in the photo is a country that stopped being able to keep the lights on. Source: National Geographic, 'New Space Station Photos Show North Korea at Night, Cloaked in Darkness'; NBC News, 'Satellites document North Korea's dark ages'.

question: When mass starvation swept North Korea in the 1990s and the state ration system collapsed, the government did not call it a famine. Instead it branded the disaster with a heroic name borrowed from a legend of Kim Il Sung's guerrilla days marching through 20-below snow under a red flag. What glorious name did the state give the famine?
answer: the Arduous March
choices: the Arduous March
the Great Leap
the Red Banner Trek
the Iron Harvest
context: Gonanui Haenggun, the 'Arduous March' — the regime turned mass death into propaganda about a glorious struggle. By 1997 official daily rations had fallen to about 128 grams of food per person, and the UN estimated wild foraged foods made up roughly 30 percent of the diet; a 2011 U.S. Census Bureau study put excess deaths from 1993-2000 at roughly 500,000-600,000. Source: Wikipedia, '1990s North Korean famine'.

question: North Korea runs a 'guilt by association' rule, traced to a 1972 line attributed to Kim Il Sung that the 'seed' of an enemy must be eliminated. So when one person is accused of a political crime, the state does not punish that person alone. How far across a family does it reach when it sends them to the prison camps?
answer: three generations — grandparents, parents, and children
choices: three generations — grandparents, parents, and children
only the accused person
the accused and their spouse
the entire home village
context: Under the three-generations rule, grandparents, parents, and children of one accused person can all be sent to the kwan-li-so camps, in most cases for life. The 1972 line attributed to Kim Il Sung read: 'Factionalists and enemies of class, whoever they are, their seed must be eliminated through three generations.' The camp network holds an estimated 80,000 to 120,000 prisoners. Source: Wikipedia, 'Yodok concentration camp'; Freedom House, 'Concentrations of Inhumanity'.

question: On November 1, 1952, the United States tested the first true hydrogen bomb, code-named Ivy Mike, on a small island called Elugelab in the Pacific. When the smoke cleared, what had happened to the island?
answer: It had completely vanished, leaving a mile-wide crater of ocean where the island had been
choices: It had completely vanished, leaving a mile-wide crater of ocean where the island had been
It had been split cleanly in two by the blast
It had been buried under a mountain of fallen ash
It had been pushed several miles out to sea by the shockwave
context: Ivy Mike's 10.4-megaton blast vaporized Elugelab entirely, leaving a crater about 6,300 feet wide and 160 feet deep. The 'bomb' was actually an 82-ton experimental device the size of a building, not a usable weapon — its blast was over 600 times more powerful than the Hiroshima bomb. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivy_Mike

question: On October 30, 1961, the Soviet Union dropped the Tsar Bomba, the most powerful bomb ever built, over the Arctic island of Novaya Zemlya. Its mushroom cloud climbed so high it dwarfed the tallest mountain on Earth. How tall did the cloud rise?
answer: About 67 kilometers — nearly eight times the height of Mount Everest
choices: About 67 kilometers — nearly eight times the height of Mount Everest
About 9 kilometers — roughly the height of Mount Everest
About 20 kilometers — about twice the height of Mount Everest
About 150 kilometers — into outer space itself
context: The Tsar Bomba's mushroom cloud rose about 67 km (42 miles) high and its base spread 40 km wide. The flash was visible nearly 1,000 km away. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsar_Bomba

question: The Tsar Bomba was so enormous — 27,000 kg and 8 meters long — that the Soviets ran into a strange problem just getting it off the ground in their Tu-95 bomber. What did they have to do to carry it?
answer: Remove the bomb-bay doors so it hung half-exposed beneath the plane
choices: Remove the bomb-bay doors so it hung half-exposed beneath the plane
Strap it to the top of the fuselage above the cockpit
Tow it behind the plane on a long steel cable
Break it into two halves and carry it in separate aircraft
context: The bomb couldn't fit inside the bomber's bay, so the bomb-bay doors and a fuel tank were removed and it hung half-exposed underneath. To give the crew a chance to escape, it was lowered on an 800-kg parachute the size of 1,600 square meters. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsar_Bomba

question: At the 1955 banquet celebrating the first Soviet hydrogen bomb, the lead designer Andrei Sakharov rose with a toast that startled the room. He raised his glass and wished that all their devices would explode as successfully as that day's — but he added one condition. What did he wish?
answer: That they explode 'always over test sites and never over cities'
choices: That they explode 'always over test sites and never over cities'
That they explode 'only when the motherland truly needs them'
That they explode 'far from the eyes of our enemies'
That they explode 'with even greater force next time'
context: Marshal Nedelin answered Sakharov's toast with a crude joke to mock him. Sakharov later wrote, 'Many years have passed, but I still feel as if I had been lashed by a whip.' That same RDS-37 test had killed real people far away — a soldier and a two-year-old girl in collapsed shelters. https://blog.nuclearsecrecy.com/2014/01/31/sakharovs-turning-point-first-soviet-h-bomb-test/

question: Andrei Sakharov, the 'father of the Soviet hydrogen bomb,' turned against the system he had armed and became its most famous dissident. In 1975 the Nobel committee awarded him the Peace Prize — but Soviet authorities refused to let him leave the country to accept it. So who delivered his acceptance speech in Oslo?
answer: His wife, Yelena Bonner, read it aloud in his place
choices: His wife, Yelena Bonner, read it aloud in his place
The Nobel committee chairman read it on his behalf
No one — the prize was accepted in silence
A fellow Soviet scientist who had defected to the West
context: Sakharov was barred from leaving the USSR, so Bonner read his speech for him. After he protested the 1979 Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, the man who had built their most powerful weapon was arrested in 1980 and exiled to the closed city of Gorky, where he staged hunger strikes for years. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrei_Sakharov

question: When Sputnik 1 beeped overhead on October 4, 1957, Americans were not just impressed — they were frightened. The very same rocket that launched the satellite, the Soviet R-7 'Semyorka,' was something the United States did not yet have. What was it?
answer: The world's first intercontinental ballistic missile
choices: The world's first intercontinental ballistic missile
The world's first reusable space rocket
The world's first nuclear-powered engine
The world's largest cargo aircraft
context: The R-7 that lofted Sputnik was the first ICBM, which meant the beeping satellite proved the USSR could now drop a nuclear warhead on any American city. The panic spawned a feared 'missile gap' — but it was largely a myth: analysts imagined the Soviets leading 16-to-1, while the real Soviet ICBM count was just four. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R-7_(rocket_family)

question: The Cold War doctrine that neither superpower dared strike first — because the other could always strike back and destroy it — came to be known by the grim acronym MAD: Mutual Assured Destruction. Surprisingly, the name was coined by Donald Brennan, a military analyst who opposed the policy. Why did he choose that particular acronym?
answer: To mock the idea of guaranteeing peace by promising mutual annihilation
choices: To mock the idea of guaranteeing peace by promising mutual annihilation
To honor the mathematician who first proved the theory
To stand for the three cities the doctrine was designed to protect
To disguise the policy's true purpose from the public
context: Brennan, an opponent of the policy, chose 'mad' deliberately as a jab — the acronym spelling out the English word for insanity. Defense Secretary Robert McNamara argued the logic in numbers: just 400 warheads on Soviet cities would destroy a third of the population and half of industry, enough to make any attack suicidal. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutually_assured_destruction

question: The Tsar Bomba was originally designed to release 100 megatons of energy. But the Soviet engineers deliberately cut its power roughly in half before the test by swapping out one component. Why did they cripple their own super-weapon?
answer: The full design would have doused the bomber crew and a quarter of the USSR in fallout
choices: The full design would have doused the bomber crew and a quarter of the USSR in fallout
They ran out of time to build the full-power version
International treaty had capped the legal yield at 50 megatons
The bomber could not physically lift the heavier full-power design
context: The Soviets replaced the bomb's uranium tamper with lead, roughly halving the yield to 50 megatons and cutting fallout by about 97%. Even so, pilot Andrei Durnovtsev and his crew were given only a 50% chance of surviving the test. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsar_Bomba

question: When the four victorious Allies decided where to put Germany's captured Nazi leaders on trial in 1945, they chose one German city on purpose: the very place the Nazis had staged their enormous annual party rallies. Which German city did the Allies pick, turning the Nazis' old showcase into the scene of their judgment?
answer: Nuremberg
choices: Nuremberg
Berlin
Munich
Frankfurt
context: Nuremberg was where the Nazis had held their giant yearly rallies, so trying them there was deliberately symbolic. The city's Palace of Justice was also chosen because it had survived Allied bombing fairly intact and had a prison attached where the defendants could be held between sessions. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuremberg_trials

question: Hermann Goering, the highest-ranking Nazi leader put on trial at Nuremberg, was sentenced to hang. But in the early hours of October 1946, only about two hours before he was due on the gallows, guards found him dead in his cell. How had Goering cheated the hangman?
answer: He bit down on a smuggled cyanide capsule
choices: He bit down on a smuggled cyanide capsule
He hanged himself with a torn bedsheet
He starved himself to death over weeks
He provoked a guard into beating him fatally
context: Guards found crushed glass particles on Goering's lips from the poison capsule. How he obtained the cyanide stayed a mystery for decades. Source: https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/roadshow/articles/hermann-goering-whats-the-explanation-for-glass-on-the-lips/

question: Just over a week into the Nuremberg trial, in November 1945, the prosecutors did something no courtroom had done before: they dimmed the lights and screened an hour-long film. When it ended and the lights came back up, the whole courtroom, defendants and judges alike, sat in stunned silence. What had the film shown them?
answer: Footage of the just-liberated Nazi concentration camps
choices: Footage of the just-liberated Nazi concentration camps
Hitler's private home movies and family scenes
Maps animating Germany's planned invasions
Recordings of the huge Nazi party rallies
context: The film, 'Nazi Concentration Camps,' was shot by Allied troops as they liberated places like Buchenwald, Dachau, and Belsen. Screened on 29 November 1945, it brought the Holocaust itself into evidence. Source: https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/we-will-show-you-their-own-films-film-at-the-nuremberg-trial

question: Gustave Gilbert, the American prison psychologist at Nuremberg, secretly gave the captured Nazi leaders IQ tests, and the results surprised him. Far from being the dull brutes some people had imagined, how did the Nazi defendants score?
answer: In the genius and near-genius range
choices: In the genius and near-genius range
Far below average, as expected
Right at average, like ordinary men
Too erratic and scattered to measure
context: The top scorer, Hjalmar Schacht, reached 143, while Goering and Karl Doenitz each scored 138. Gilbert recorded his cell-block conversations with the prisoners in his book 'Nuremberg Diary.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustave_Gilbert

question: Rudolf Hess, once Hitler's deputy, spent the opening days of the Nuremberg trial insisting he had completely lost his memory, baffling the judges and even his own defense lawyer. Then, on 30 November 1945, Hess suddenly stood up and announced the truth about his amnesia. What did he reveal?
answer: He had faked the amnesia as a tactic, and his memory was fine
choices: He had faked the amnesia as a tactic, and his memory was fine
A war injury had genuinely wiped out his memory
Doctors had drugged him into the confusion
Hitler had ordered him to stay silent in court
context: Hess told the court: 'Henceforth my memory will again respond to the outside world. The reasons for simulating loss of memory were of a tactical nature.' He admitted he had even fooled his own lawyer. Source: https://avalon.law.yale.edu/imt/v1-29.asp

question: Hermann Goering, the highest-ranking defendant, nearly wrecked the Nuremberg trial right from the dock. When the American prosecutor Robert Jackson accused Germany of secretly preparing for war, Goering fired back so sharply that Jackson lost his temper and the court had to adjourn for the rest of the day. What was Goering's stinging reply?
answer: He didn't recall reading America's own published war-mobilization plans either
choices: He didn't recall reading America's own published war-mobilization plans either
He had never read a single military document in his life
Hitler alone had planned every campaign without him
The Allies, not Germany, had truly started the war
context: Goering's defiant comeback was broadcast across Germany and actually lifted some German spirits. It was later the British prosecutor, Sir David Maxwell Fyfe, not Jackson, who finally pinned Goering down with cold, methodical cross-examination. Source: https://www.spectator.com.au/2025/12/how-goring-almost-derailed-the-nuremberg-trials/

question: The Nazi crimes were so vast that the world had no single word for the deliberate destruction of an entire people, until a Polish-Jewish lawyer, Raphael Lemkin, coined one in his 1944 book and then fought to get it into the Nuremberg case. What was Lemkin's brand-new word?
answer: Genocide
choices: Genocide
Holocaust
Extermination
Pogrom
context: Lemkin built the word in 'Axis Rule in Occupied Europe' by fusing the Greek 'genos' (race or tribe) with the Latin '-cide' (killing). Though he got it into the conversation, no defendant was actually convicted of 'genocide' as a named crime at Nuremberg. Source: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/defining-genocide-after-world-war-ii

question: Hermann Goering and the other captured Nazi leaders could simply have been lined up and shot. Instead the four Allied nations chose to put them on trial. The American chief prosecutor, Robert H. Jackson, opened the case by saying that staying the hand of vengeance this way was 'one of the most significant tributes that Power has ever paid' to what?
answer: Reason
choices: Reason
Mercy
Victory
Justice
context: Jackson's full opening line, delivered 21 November 1945, was: 'That four great nations, flushed with victory and stung with injury, stay the hand of vengeance and voluntarily submit their captive enemies to the judgment of the law is one of the most significant tributes that Power has ever paid to Reason.' Source: https://famous-trials.com/nuremberg/1897-jacksonopen

question: The judges at Nuremberg laid down a rule that has echoed through every war-crimes trial since: a soldier or official who commits an atrocity cannot wipe away the blame just by offering one particular excuse. What excuse did the Nuremberg court declare could never, by itself, clear a man of a crime against humanity?
answer: That he was only following his superiors' orders
choices: That he was only following his superiors' orders
That he had not personally killed anyone
That his country had been losing the war
That he had not known the law existed
context: Article 8 of the London Charter put it this way: acting 'pursuant to order of his Government or of a superior shall not free him from responsibility, but may be considered in mitigation of punishment.' This birthed the rule that 'I was just following orders' cannot excuse such a crime. Source: https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/how-were-the-crimes-defined

question: Julius Streicher, a vicious Nazi propagandist, was among the men hanged at Nuremberg. On the gallows he shouted 'Heil Hitler!' and then sneered 'Purimfest 1946!', a jab at the Bible's Book of Esther, in which the ten sons of the villain Haman are hanged. Why did Streicher choose that particular taunt as he faced the rope?
answer: Exactly ten Nazis were hanged that night, matching Haman's ten sons
choices: Exactly ten Nazis were hanged that night, matching Haman's ten sons
Purim happened to be the date the trial had first opened
The Book of Esther had been his favorite story as a boy
He believed the Jews had laid a curse on him to hang
context: Streicher's final words before the hood dropped were for his wife: 'Adele, my dear wife!' The ten condemned men were hanged in the early hours of 16 October 1946. Source: https://www.thetorah.com/article/purimfest-1946-the-nuremberg-trials-and-the-ten-sons-of-haman

question: At Nuremberg the Soviet Union sat as one of the four judging nations, yet the Soviets pressed the court to convict the Germans of the Katyn massacre, the murder of thousands of Polish officers. The American and British judges quietly declined to pin Katyn on any defendant. Why did the Western judges hold back from convicting on that charge?
answer: The Soviets themselves had actually committed that massacre
choices: The Soviets themselves had actually committed that massacre
The victims' bodies had never once been found
Katyn had taken place before the war even began
No Polish witnesses had survived to testify to it
context: The killings at Katyn were carried out by the Soviet NKVD, not the Germans. After Soviet prosecutor Roman Rudenko pressed the charge, the tribunal left it unresolved rather than convict. The USSR finally admitted its own guilt in 1990. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katyn_massacre

question: Most of the Nazi leaders at Nuremberg flatly denied any guilt, but Albert Speer, Hitler's architect and armaments minister, did the opposite: he stood up and publicly accepted a share of responsibility for the regime's crimes. Historians believe this single move helped Speer do what, even though men who had worked under him were hanged?
answer: Avoid a death sentence, drawing 20 years in prison instead
choices: Avoid a death sentence, drawing 20 years in prison instead
Win an early release after just five years
Have every charge against him quietly dropped
