Be freed to testify openly against Goering
context: Historians later argued that Speer used vague talk of 'collective' guilt to mask his real, direct responsibility for slave labor. His admission of shared responsibility is widely credited with helping him escape the gallows. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Speer

question: Seventeen giant stone heads carved by the Olmec of Mexico's Gulf coast have survived, and no two are alike: each has its own fleshy cheeks, its own flat nose, its own particular face. From those individual features, what have scholars concluded the heads actually are?
answer: Portraits of specific real Olmec rulers
choices: Portraits of specific real Olmec rulers
Statues of the Olmec rain and storm gods
Carved guardians set to watch the city gates
Faces of the founding ancestors as a group
context: Because every head is a distinct individual face rather than a repeated divine type, scholars read them as portraits of particular Olmec rulers, not images of gods. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olmec_colossal_heads

question: To carve their colossal heads, the Olmec needed single basalt boulders weighing many tons. The nearest source of that stone, the Sierra de los Tuxtlas, lay more than 100 kilometers from their cities, and the Olmec had no wheels and no draft animals. How did they move the multi-ton boulders all that way?
answer: By river rafts and log rollers
choices: By river rafts and log rollers
By teams of harnessed oxen
By carving them where they fell
By dragging them on iron sledges
context: With no wheels and no beasts of burden, the Olmec floated the basalt downriver on rafts and rolled it overland on logs to cover the 100-plus kilometers from the Cerro Cintepec source. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olmec_colossal_heads

question: At dawn on Sunday, 22 June 1941, more than 3.8 million Axis troops poured into the Soviet Union along a front that stretched roughly 2,900 km, all the way from the Baltic Sea to the Black Sea. In the record books, what does Operation Barbarossa stand as?
answer: the largest land invasion in human history
choices: the largest land invasion in human history
the largest amphibious landing in human history
the largest tank battle in human history
the largest aerial bombing in human history
context: Three German army groups attacked at once across a 1,800-mile front. No bigger ground invasion has ever been launched before or since. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Barbarossa; USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/invasion-of-the-soviet-union-june-1941)

question: Hitler codenamed his 1941 invasion of the Soviet Union 'Barbarossa,' borrowing the nickname of the medieval Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I. What did that famous nickname mean?
answer: Redbeard
choices: Redbeard
Blackbeard
Greybeard
Ironbeard
context: 'Barbarossa' is Italian for 'Redbeard.' Hitler first committed Germany to the invasion with Fuhrer Directive 21 on 18 December 1940. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Barbarossa)

question: On the western border, the Brest Fortress was the very first place struck on 22 June 1941. Its roughly 9,000 defenders were cut off and outgunned, with no orders to retreat, yet they held out for over a week. What did one of them scratch into a fortress wall?
answer: I am dying, but I am not surrendering! Goodbye, Motherland.
choices: I am dying, but I am not surrendering! Goodbye, Motherland.
They shall not pass while one of us still stands here.
Avenge us, comrades; remember that we did not run.
We few will hold this gate or die here together.
context: The inscription is dated '20/VII-41.' One commander, Major Pyotr Gavrilov, was finally taken, gravely wounded, on 23 July. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defense_of_Brest_Fortress)

question: Winston Churchill and Stalin's own spies warned him that Hitler was about to attack, but Stalin refused to believe Germany would break their 1939 pact while still fighting Britain. When the invasion struck on 22 June 1941, how did the stunned Soviet leader react?
answer: he withdrew to his dacha in isolation for days
choices: he withdrew to his dacha in isolation for days
he ordered an immediate counter-invasion of Germany
he went on the radio that night to rally the nation
he had the spies who warned him arrested and shot
context: The Red Army was caught completely unprepared. Reports say Stalin retreated to his country house and went silent for days before re-emerging to lead. (History.com, history.com/this-day-in-history/june-22; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Barbarossa)

question: In the first hours of Barbarossa the Luftwaffe wiped out roughly 40% of the Soviet air force's front-line strength — over a thousand aircraft in a single day. How were so many Soviet planes destroyed so quickly?
answer: they were caught lined up on their airfields and bombed on the ground
choices: they were caught lined up on their airfields and bombed on the ground
they were shot down in huge dogfights over the border
they ran out of fuel and crashed behind the lines
their pilots defected and flew them away to Germany
context: At least 1,136 Soviet aircraft were destroyed on the first day alone, most of them sitting neatly parked on their airfields. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German-Soviet_air_war_22_June_1941)

question: The Germans expected a quick summer victory, so their soldiers still wore summer uniforms when the Russian autumn mud froze into a savage winter. To survive temperatures that caused some 100,000 frostbite cases, what did the freezing German troops resort to?
answer: stuffing their coats with newspaper and straw
choices: stuffing their coats with newspaper and straw
skinning local horses to wear the hides
burning their own trucks to stay warm
marching only at midday to keep moving
context: The frostbite epidemic led to about 15,000 amputations. The army had simply never been equipped for a Russian winter. (History.com, history.com/articles/operation-barbarossa; Britannica)

question: By early December 1941, Army Group Centre had clawed to within about 15 to 20 miles of central Moscow before the offensive froze in its tracks and could go no farther. According to legend, what could the closest German soldiers glimpse on the horizon?
answer: the spires of the Kremlin
choices: the spires of the Kremlin
the smoke of the burning capital
Soviet tanks rolling out to meet them
the frozen surface of the Volga River
context: It is told that advancing soldiers believed they could see the Kremlin's towers in the distance — the closest the Germans ever came to Moscow. This is legend, not confirmed fact. (Britannica, britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Moscow; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Moscow)

question: When the autumn rains came in 1941, the dirt roads of the Soviet Union dissolved into bottomless mud that swallowed tanks, trucks, and horses and brought the German advance to a crawl. Russians have a single name for this twice-yearly season of impassable mud. What is it?
answer: the rasputitsa
choices: the rasputitsa
the taiga
the steppe
the tundra
context: The 'rasputitsa' strikes each spring and autumn. The taiga is northern forest, the steppe is open grassland, and the tundra is the frozen far-north plain. (History.com, history.com/articles/operation-barbarossa; Britannica)

question: In August 1941 Hitler overruled his generals — who wanted to drive straight for Moscow — and turned his tank armies south instead. The result was a colossal encirclement around Kiev that trapped over 600,000 Soviet troops, the largest encirclement of soldiers in the history of warfare. What did Hitler call this victory?
answer: the biggest battle in the history of the world
choices: the biggest battle in the history of the world
the final death blow to the Bolshevik state
the open road to the Caucasus oil fields
the greatest act of revenge for the last war
context: The Battle of Kiev ended on 26 September 1941 with about 452,700 troops trapped and over 600,000 Soviet losses. Diverting south to win it, though, cost Hitler the time he needed to take Moscow. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kiev_(1941); Hoover Institution, hoover.org/research/great-battle-kiev-september-1941)

question: Barbarossa was planned as a war of annihilation, and even the regular German army was ordered to take part. Days before the invasion, the German high command issued the so-called Commissar Order. What did it direct German troops to do?
answer: shoot captured Soviet political officers instead of taking them prisoner
choices: shoot captured Soviet political officers instead of taking them prisoner
burn every Soviet village they marched through to the ground
ship all captured Soviet soldiers back to German war factories
execute any German soldier who retreated without written orders
context: The Commissar Order of 6 June 1941 turned the Wehrmacht itself into an instrument of ideological murder, ordering the summary shooting of captured Soviet commissars rather than treating them as prisoners of war. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissar_Order; USHMM, encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/commissar-order)

question: Behind the front lines came four SS mobile killing squads, the Einsatzgruppen, who in the first nine months of the invasion shot about half a million people, overwhelmingly Jews — at first only men, then, after Himmler ordered it, women and children too. By what grim name is this campaign of mass shootings remembered?
answer: the Holocaust by bullets
choices: the Holocaust by bullets
the Night of Broken Glass
the Warsaw Uprising
the Long March
context: Unlike the later death camps, this earlier phase of the Holocaust was carried out face to face with rifles and machine guns across the occupied Soviet Union. (Imperial War Museums, iwm.org.uk/blog/partnerships/2021/09/operation-barbarossa-part-two; USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia)

question: Outside Kiev in late September 1941, the SS posted an order luring the city's Jews to a ravine called Babyn Yar, forced them to undress, and machine-gunned them in small groups at the edge of the gorge. In just two days — 29 and 30 September — how many Jewish men, women, and children did the killers murder there?
context: The exact figure comes from the killers' own report — Sonderkommando 4a of Einsatzgruppe C, under SS-Standartenfuhrer Paul Blobel. In all, about 100,000 people were murdered at Babyn Yar during the occupation. (USHMM, encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/kiev-and-babi-yar; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babi_Yar)

question: The word 'parliament' comes straight from an Old French verb. Long before 'parliament' ever meant an assembly of lords and townsmen, what did 'a parliament' literally mean?
answer: A talking-place (a speaking)
choices: A talking-place (a speaking)
A judging-place (a court)
A praying-place (a chapel)
A trading-place (a market)
context: 'Parliament' descends from Old French 'parler', 'to speak' — so the word literally means a talking-place. It meant 'a speaking, a talk' before it ever named an assembly of representatives. Source: https://www.etymonline.com/word/parliament

question: In January 1265 Simon de Montfort did something no English ruler had done before: he ordered every major town to send two ordinary townspeople to help decide how England was ruled, sitting beside the barons and bishops at Westminster. What were these new town representatives called?
answer: Burgesses
choices: Burgesses
Knights
Aldermen
Reeves
context: The two townsmen from each town were 'burgesses' — the first time town-dwellers, not just lords and knights, were summoned to a parliament. De Montfort's 1265 assembly met at the Palace of Westminster from 20 January until mid-March. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_de_Montfort's_Parliament

question: Before the Battle of Lewes in 1264, Simon de Montfort's rebels marked their tunics with a symbol meant to make their cause feel blessed by God, like an army on a holy mission. What did they sew onto their chests?
answer: White crosses
choices: White crosses
Red dragons
Golden lions
Black eagles
context: De Montfort's men sewed on white crosses as though they were crusaders, giving the army a sense of a divine, holy-war mission. They went on to win the battle and capture the king. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lewes

question: After Simon de Montfort's rebels won at Lewes in 1264, the king's own brother Richard of Cornwall — a man who had even been crowned King of the Romans in Germany — was dragged out of the windmill where he had hidden. How did the jeering rebels mock him as he came out?
answer: "Come down, come down, thou wicked miller!"
choices: "Come down, come down, thou wicked miller!"
"Long live the King of the Romans!"
"God save our noble emperor!"
"Run, run, the prince is coming!"
context: A would-be emperor caught cowering in a windmill was jeered as a 'wicked miller'. Chroniclers report the taunt, so it is best treated as legend rather than certain fact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lewes

question: At the Battle of Lewes in 1264, young Prince Edward — the future Edward I — smashed the London militia on his part of the field, then galloped off chasing the fleeing men for about four miles. What did this reckless pursuit cost him?
answer: His father the king was beaten and captured behind him
choices: His father the king was beaten and captured behind him
His warhorse collapsed and died beneath him in the chase
His own knights deserted to go and join the rebels
The Londoners turned and ambushed his scattered men
context: By the time Edward returned from chasing the Londoners four miles, his father King Henry III had been defeated and taken prisoner. Reckless pursuit lost the whole battle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lewes

question: Simon de Montfort is remembered as a founder of England's Parliament — yet he was not even English, born in France around 1208. What was his startling personal connection to Henry III, the king he would one day rise in rebellion against?
answer: He had married Eleanor, King Henry's own sister
choices: He had married Eleanor, King Henry's own sister
He was Henry's long-lost younger brother
He had once been the young king's tutor
He was Henry's chosen heir to the throne
context: Simon de Montfort, a Frenchman born around 1208 at Montfort-l'Amaury, had married Eleanor, the sister of Henry III — the very king he would later overthrow. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_de_Montfort,_6th_Earl_of_Leicester

question: From each county Simon de Montfort summoned two knights, and from each town two burgesses. Sitting together, this pairing of county knights and town burgesses grew into the more populous of Parliament's two chambers. Which chamber did it become?
answer: The House of Commons
choices: The House of Commons
The House of Lords
The House of Bishops
The House of Burgesses
context: Knights of the shire plus town burgesses are the seed that grew into the House of Commons — which is why de Montfort is often called the founder of the Commons. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_de_Montfort's_Parliament

question: At the Battle of Evesham in 1265, Prince Edward closed in to destroy Simon de Montfort and had his soldiers fly banners they had captured from Kenilworth Castle. When the old earl saw those banners approaching, what did he believe?
answer: That his own reinforcements had finally come to save him
choices: That his own reinforcements had finally come to save him
That the king had escaped and was leading a rescue
That Edward's army was retreating in surrender
That a truce party was riding out to make peace
context: The captured Kenilworth banners fooled de Montfort into thinking allies were arriving — when really it was Edward's army coming to kill him. The battle was fought during a thunderstorm. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Evesham

question: At the Battle of Evesham in 1265 the captured King Henry III was forced onto the battlefield dressed in the colours of his enemy Simon de Montfort. This disguise nearly got the king cut down — by whom?
answer: By his own son Edward's soldiers, who mistook him for the enemy
choices: By his own son Edward's soldiers, who mistook him for the enemy
By de Montfort's bodyguards, taking revenge for their lord
By Welsh archers fighting on the rebel side that day
By looters stripping the fallen bodies after the battle
context: Wearing de Montfort's colours, Henry III was nearly killed by his own son's troops, who took him for the enemy. The knight Roger de Leybourne saved him at the last moment by crying out who he was. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Evesham

question: Thirty years after Simon de Montfort, King Edward I made knights-and-burgesses a permanent rule with his 1295 'Model Parliament.' In the writ summoning it, Edward justified calling commoners with a ringing Latin maxim. What did that maxim declare?
answer: "What touches all should be approved by all"
choices: "What touches all should be approved by all"
"The king's will alone has the force of law"
"Render unto the crown what is the crown's"
"He who pays the tax shall make the law"
context: Edward I's 1295 writ cited 'Quod omnes tangit ab omnibus approbari debet' — 'what touches all should be approved by all' — making knights and burgesses the rule and echoing the principle of consent. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_Parliament

question: Fifty years before de Montfort's parliament, Magna Carta (1215) already planted the seed that a king could not simply help himself to his subjects' money. Its clause 12 said no major tax could be raised in the kingdom except by what?
answer: The common counsel of the kingdom
choices: The common counsel of the kingdom
The blessing of the Pope in Rome
The sworn oath of the royal knights
The consent of the King of France
context: Magna Carta clause 12 (1215): 'No scutage or aid is to be imposed in our kingdom except by the common counsel of our kingdom' — the textual ancestor of 'no taxation without consent.' Source: https://magnacarta.cmp.uea.ac.uk/read/magna_carta_1215/Clause_12

question: In 1258 England's barons forced Henry III to accept the Provisions of Oxford, putting him under a council and ordering Parliament to meet three times every year. The reforms were so radical that a Latin chronicler gave that assembly a mocking nickname. What was it called?
answer: The Mad Parliament
choices: The Mad Parliament
The Iron Parliament
The Boy Parliament
The Hungry Parliament
context: A chronicler called the 1258 Oxford assembly 'insane parliamentum' — the 'Mad Parliament' — because the Provisions of Oxford put the king under a Council of Fifteen and made Parliament meet three times a year. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_Parliament_(1258)

question: Simon de Montfort was hacked apart as a traitor at Evesham in 1265, and the crown wanted him forgotten — it even banned visits to his grave. What did ordinary people do anyway at his grave at Evesham Abbey?
answer: Pilgrims secretly crept there to venerate him as a saint
choices: Pilgrims secretly crept there to venerate him as a saint
Looters dug it up hunting for buried treasure
It was washed away by a flood within a year
Monks quietly moved his bones to unmarked ground
context: Despite the ban, pilgrims crept to de Montfort's grave to honour him as a saint, and a medieval 'miracle book' recorded around 200 miracles credited to him between roughly 1266 and 1280. This cult is testimony, not proven fact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_de_Montfort,_6th_Earl_of_Leicester  (Legend.)

question: The Roman writer Vitruvius explained where the Greeks got the shape of their oldest and plainest column, the Doric. He said its proportions were copied straight from the body of which figure?
answer: A strong man
choices: A strong man
A graceful woman
A tall tree
A galloping horse
context: Doric is the oldest of the three Greek orders — short, thick, no base, set right on the floor with a plain cushion-and-slab top. Vitruvius (Book IV) said its sturdy proportions copied a man's body, while the slimmer Ionic copied a woman's. Source: penelope.uchicago.edu Vitruvius Book IV; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doric_order.

question: Inside the Parthenon stood a colossal statue of the goddess Athena, nearly 40 feet tall, built by the sculptor Phidias over a core of cypress wood. To finish her, he sheathed that core in two costly materials — one for her skin, one for her clothing and armor. Which two materials?
answer: Ivory and gold
choices: Ivory and gold
Marble and bronze
Silver and pearl
Copper and glass
context: The Athena Parthenos used carved ivory for her skin and gold for her robes and armor, over a wooden frame, standing about 12 meters tall. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athena_Parthenos; worldhistory.org/article/785.

question: Phidias' giant Athena inside the Parthenon was so enormous that the figure resting in her open right hand was itself a complete statue — a winged one, standing as tall as a grown adult in her palm. Which winged figure did she hold out?
answer: Nike, the goddess of Victory
choices: Nike, the goddess of Victory
Eros, the boy-god of love
Hermes, the winged messenger
Pegasus, the flying horse
context: In her right hand Athena held a Nike (Victory) about 2 meters tall — 4 cubits, the size of a real person. Source: worldhistory.org/article/785; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athena_Parthenos.

question: The Ionic order is the slim, elegant Greek column — taller and more graceful than the heavy Doric. You can spot it instantly by its capital, the carved top of the column, which is shaped into a pair of matching curls on each side. People said those curls looked most like what?
answer: Curled-up rams' horns
choices: Curled-up rams' horns
Rolling ocean waves
A coiled serpent
An open lotus flower
context: The paired spirals atop an Ionic column are called volutes — likened to rolled-up rams' horns or curly ringlets. Vitruvius said the whole column copied a graceful woman, the volutes her curls and the flutes the folds of her gown. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionic_order; Vitruvius Book IV.

question: We picture ancient temples like the Parthenon as gleaming white marble. But modern scientists scanning the sculptures discovered the Greeks had originally done something to them that 2,500 years of weather later wiped away. What had the Greeks done to the sculptures?
answer: Painted them in bright colors
choices: Painted them in bright colors
Coated them in gold leaf
Polished them mirror-smooth
Wrapped them in fine cloth
context: Imaging found traces of vivid Egyptian blue, plus white and purple, and intricate painted patterns on the figures — the Parthenon was never bare white. Source: King's College London / Antiquity, Oct 2023; Smithsonian Magazine.

question: The gleaming marble Parthenon was actually the second temple on that spot. An older, half-built temple to Athena stood on the Acropolis until 480 BC — the year the Persian king Xerxes captured Athens. How did Xerxes' army wreck that first, unfinished temple?
answer: Burned it to the ground
choices: Burned it to the ground
Toppled its columns into the sea
Carted its marble back to Persia
Smashed it with siege engines
context: Xerxes burned the half-built older temple in 480 BC. The marble Parthenon we know (447-438 BC) was the rebuild, raised under Pericles by the architects Iktinos and Kallikrates with Phidias over the sculpture. Source: GreekReporter, 'When Persians Destroyed Athens'; ebsco.com, Building of the Parthenon.

question: The builders of the Parthenon knew a hard truth: a column built with perfectly straight sides does not actually read as straight to the human eye. So they gave each column a subtle shaping the Greeks called 'entasis' that makes the eye accept it as truly straight. What shaping did they give the columns?
answer: A gentle outward bulge in the middle
choices: A gentle outward bulge in the middle
A sharp taper to a point at the top
A deep inward dent near the base
A slow twist along its whole height
context: Entasis is a swelling of only about 2 cm, peaking around a third of the way up — a deliberate trick, since a truly straight shaft reads as concave to us. Source: thearchaeologist.org; Study.com Entasis lesson.

question: The Parthenon looks rigidly straight and square, but almost none of its lines actually are. Every outer column, for one, leans very slightly inward. If you extended all those leaning columns straight up as imaginary lines into the sky, what would those lines do?
answer: Meet at a single point about a mile and a half overhead
choices: Meet at a single point about a mile and a half overhead
Stay perfectly parallel and never cross at all
Cross low, just above the temple roof
Spread apart, growing wider the higher they go
context: The inward-leaning columns, projected upward, converge at one point roughly 1.5 miles (2.4 km) above the temple. None of the building's 'straight' lines is truly straight. Source: thatsmaths.com, Optical Refinements at the Parthenon, 2018.

question: Athena's statue wore over a ton of gold for her robes — a fortune just standing in the temple. Phidias deliberately built every gold panel so it could be lifted off the statue. According to the historical record, what did this let the Athenians do with that gold in an emergency?
answer: Strip it off and spend it to fund a war
choices: Strip it off and spend it to fund a war
Melt it down to cast more statues
Trade it to Persia in exchange for peace
Bury it in the ground beneath the temple
context: About 44 talents (~1,140 kg, over a ton) of gold made up the robes. The panels were removable on purpose — so the city could weigh the gold to prove none was stolen, and strip it for emergency wartime treasure. Source: worldhistory.org/article/785; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athena_Parthenos.

question: On the shield of his giant Athena, the sculptor Phidias is said to have carved a battle of Greeks against Amazons — and to have secretly slipped two real, living Athenians into that holy scene: himself as a bald old man heaving a rock above his head, and his friend, the city's leader Pericles. When Athenians recognized the faces, what happened to Phidias?
answer: He was put on trial for impiety
choices: He was put on trial for impiety
He was ordered to grind the faces off the shield
He was banished from Athens before any trial
He was fined and made to repay the gold
context: Sneaking real people into a sacred image was treated as a sacrilege; ancient writers say Phidias was tried for impiety and may have died in prison or exile. Told as legend (ancient testimony). Source: thearchaeologist.org, 'He Hid Pericles on Athena's Shield'; britannica.com/biography/Phidias.

question: The sculptor Callimachus passed the grave of a young Corinthian girl. On it sat a basket of her belongings with a roof-tile laid on top, and a wild acanthus plant had grown up around it, its leaves curling outward where the tile blocked them. Back in his workshop, what did Callimachus make from what he had seen?
answer: A stone basket ringed with curling leaves
choices: A stone basket ringed with curling leaves
A marble wreath of flowers for her tomb
A clay pot painted with twisting vines
A woven crown of real acanthus leaves
context: In Vitruvius' tale, that grave-side basket of curling acanthus became the Corinthian capital — a deep basket of carved acanthus leaves, the youngest and most ornate of the three orders, grown out of the Ionic. Told as legend. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callimachus_(sculptor); Vitruvius Book IV.

question: Along the top of a Doric temple like the Parthenon runs a band of grooved stone blocks alternating with carved panels. Architects nickname this band 'petrified woodwork.' These grooved marble blocks are actually stone copies of which part of the much older wooden temples that came before?
answer: The exposed ends of the wooden roof-beams
choices: The exposed ends of the wooden roof-beams
The painted doors of the inner shrine
The woven reed mats on the floor
The carved wooden idols of the gods
context: The grooved blocks are triglyphs — marble imitations of the sawn-off ends of timber roof-beams from the original wooden temples. Vitruvius says carpenters painted those beam-ends blue, which is why triglyphs were painted blue and the metope panels red. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triglyph; penelope.uchicago.edu Doric.

question: In May 1881, at a farm called Pouilly-le-Fort, the French scientist Louis Pasteur made a very public bet: he vaccinated 24 sheep against deadly anthrax, left an equal flock unvaccinated, then weeks later injected EVERY animal with the killer germ while a crowd of farmers and vets watched. Two days after that injection, what did the crowd find when they returned to the farm?
answer: Every unvaccinated sheep was dead and every vaccinated sheep was alive
choices: Every unvaccinated sheep was dead and every vaccinated sheep was alive
Every sheep on the farm had survived the injection unharmed
Every sheep on the farm had died from the anthrax injection
Both flocks were sick but slowly starting to recover
context: It was a flawless, very public victory for vaccination — the unprotected sheep died, the vaccinated ones stayed healthy. Pasteur had staged the test as an open dare in front of officials, betting his reputation on it. Source: https://www.sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/louis-pasteur/

question: In July 1885 a 9-year-old boy named Joseph Meister was carried to Louis Pasteur after a rabid dog bit him 14 times — and rabies, once its symptoms appear, kills more than 99 of every 100 people it strikes. Pasteur, who was not even a licensed doctor, gambled on an untested vaccine he had grown from the dried spinal cords of rabid rabbits. What happened to the boy?
answer: He never developed rabies and became the first person ever saved from it
choices: He never developed rabies and became the first person ever saved from it
He developed rabies but survived it after months of fever
He died of rabies despite the full course of shots
He recovered from the bites but lost the use of his arm
context: Dr. Grancher gave Meister a series of shots over about ten days, each from a more virulent rabbit cord than the last. The boy lived — the first human ever rescued from a disease that almost always kills. Source: https://www.pasteur.fr/en/research-journal/news/history-first-rabies-vaccination-1885

question: Joseph Meister, the boy Louis Pasteur saved from rabies in 1885, grew up and took a job at the Pasteur Institute in Paris — the very institute the rabies cure had made famous. For the rest of his life he served as its gatekeeper, personally guarding one thing inside the building. What was he guarding?
answer: Pasteur's tomb in the crypt below
choices: Pasteur's tomb in the crypt below
The original swan-neck flasks on display
The laboratory where the rabies vaccine was made
The records of every patient Pasteur had treated
context: The boy whose life Pasteur saved spent his own life as gatekeeper of the institute, guarding the building and Pasteur's tomb in its crypt. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Meister

question: To prove that germs ride in on the air rather than springing to life inside a broth, Louis Pasteur boiled broth in glass flasks whose necks he had stretched and bent into long curving 'swan necks.' The broth stayed perfectly clear for as long as he left the flask upright. Then he simply tipped one flask — and the broth clouded with growth within a day. Why did tipping the flask change everything?
answer: It let trapped dust slide down the curved neck into the broth
choices: It let trapped dust slide down the curved neck into the broth
It let air rush in for the first time and feed the broth
It cooled the broth fast enough to wake the germs inside
It cracked the glass so outside water could seep in
context: The curved neck trapped airborne dust and germs in its bend, so the boiled broth stayed sterile forever — until Pasteur tipped the flask and let that trapped dust slide into the broth, which then clouded. Germs came from the air, not from the broth itself. Source: https://medicalmuseum.org.uk/medical-science-pasteurs-swan-neck-flask

question: Louis Pasteur told the public he had weakened the anthrax germs for his famous 1881 vaccine using oxygen. A century later, the historian Gerald Geison opened Pasteur's sealed private notebooks and found the public story was false. According to those notebooks, what had Pasteur actually done?
answer: He had used a rival's chemical method and never credited the rival
choices: He had used a rival's chemical method and never credited the rival
He had bought the working vaccine from a German laboratory
He had used animals already immune and faked the results
He had never tested the vaccine on sheep at all before the trial
context: The Pouilly-le-Fort vaccine was actually made with potassium dichromate, a chemical method pioneered by the veterinarian Henri Toussaint — Pasteur's rival, whom he never credited. Geison revealed this from Pasteur's own sealed notebooks a hundred years later. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthrax_vaccine

question: On the night of April 18, 1775, patriots in Boston arranged a secret signal in the steeple of the Old North Church to warn how the British army was leaving town: ONE lantern would mean the soldiers were marching out by land. How many lanterns meant they were crossing by water instead?
answer: Two lanterns
choices: One lantern
Two lanterns
Three lanterns
Four lanterns
context: 'One if by land, two if by sea.' Robert Newman, the church sexton, hung two lanterns in the steeple because the British regulars were rowing across the Charles River. The lanterns were lit for less than a minute so the British would not spot them. Source: https://oldnorth.com/blog/robert-newman/ and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Revere's_midnight_ride

question: When American militia and British regulars first traded fire in the spring of 1775, the Revolutionary War had begun. Years later the poet Ralph Waldo Emerson gave that opening volley at Concord's North Bridge a famous name in his 'Concord Hymn.' What did Emerson call it?
answer: The shot heard round the world
choices: The shot heard round the world
The blast that woke the world
The first fire of freedom
The volley that freed a nation
context: In the 1837 'Concord Hymn,' Emerson wrote of the militia firing 'the shot heard round the world' and called the militiamen the 'embattled farmers.' The line refers to the fight at Concord's North Bridge. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shot_heard_round_the_world and https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/lexington-and-concord-shot-heard-round-world

question: On April 18, 1775, two lanterns were hung in the Old North Church steeple for less than a minute before being taken down so the British would not see them. Remarkably, one object from that famous signal still survives about 250 years later and sits in a museum you can visit. What survives?
answer: One of the actual lanterns
choices: One of the actual lanterns
The original church keys
Paul Revere's leather saddle
The steeple's wooden door
context: A small tinned-iron-and-glass lantern made around 1770, one of those hung in the steeple that night, can be seen today at the Concord Museum. Source: https://concordmuseum.org/collection/paul-revere-lantern/

question: Before Paul Revere ever climbed onto a horse on the night of April 18, 1775, two friends first had to get him out of Boston and over to Charlestown, slipping past an anchored British warship in the dark. How did they move him across?
answer: They rowed him across the river in a small boat
choices: They rowed him across the river in a small boat
They smuggled him out hidden in a hay cart
They led him over the long bridge on foot
They floated him across on a wooden raft
context: Two friends rowed Revere across the Charles River in a small boat, slipping past the anchored British warship HMS Somerset, before he borrowed a horse in Charlestown. Source: https://www.paulreverehouse.org/the-real-story/ and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Revere's_midnight_ride

question: Paul Revere is remembered in legend for galloping through the countryside shouting 'The British are coming!' But he almost certainly never said that: in 1775 most colonists still thought of themselves as British, and his ride was meant to be secret. What did Revere actually call out to warn people?
answer: The regulars are coming out
choices: The regulars are coming out
The king's men are upon us
To arms, the soldiers march
Wake and arm, the troops ride
context: Revere's real warning was 'the regulars are coming out.' 'Regulars' meant the British army troops. Shouting it openly would also have given the secret mission away. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Revere's_midnight_ride and https://www.paulreverehouse.org/the-real-story/

question: Robert Newman, the church sexton who climbed the Old North Church steeple and hung the two warning lanterns, then had to get away before the British discovered who had lit them. How did Newman slip out of the church that night?
answer: He climbed out a back window
choices: He climbed out a back window
He hid inside the great church bell
He rowed himself across the Charles
He dressed as a British soldier
context: Newman escaped through a back window. The next day the British arrested him because he held the church keys; he was released after blaming Captain John Pulling, who had already fled Boston. Source: https://oldnorth.com/blog/robert-newman/

question: Paul Revere did not even own a horse — he borrowed one for his midnight ride from Deacon John Larkin of Charlestown, who described it only as 'a very good horse.' A family tradition later gave the mare a famous name, Brown Beauty. Where does that name actually come from?
answer: A family story written down generations later
choices: A family story written down generations later
Paul Revere's own written account of the ride
Deacon Larkin's record of the loan
A British patrol officer's report
context: Revere never named the horse. 'Brown Beauty' first appears in a family tradition written down in 1930 — 155 years after the ride — so historically the horse is anonymous. The name is testimony, not record. Source: https://www.paulreverehouse.org/frequently-asked-questions-about-the-midnight-ride-of-paul-revere/ and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Larkin_(Deacon_of_Charlestown)  (Legend.)

question: In Longfellow's poem, Paul Revere rides in triumph all the way to Concord. The real night went differently — his ride ended before he ever got there. What actually happened to Revere on the road that stopped him?
answer: A British patrol captured him at a roadblock
choices: A British patrol captured him at a roadblock
His own horse threw him into a deep ditch
He turned back to carry word to Boston
A redcoat shot him out of his saddle
context: A British patrol stopped Revere, William Dawes, and Dr. Samuel Prescott at a roadblock in Lincoln. The British captured Revere, questioned him, and took his horse; Dawes fell off his horse and escaped on foot. Source: https://www.paulreverehouse.org/frequently-asked-questions-about-the-midnight-ride-of-paul-revere/ and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Prescott

question: As Paul Revere set out on his ride, a British sergeant warned him to stop making so much noise. Revere fired back a defiant reply that has come down from his own account of the night. What did Revere snap at the sergeant?
answer: Noise! You'll have noise enough before long
choices: Noise! You'll have noise enough before long
Quiet yourself, the king has lost this land
Stand aside, I ride for honest men
Hush now, redcoat, your time is short
context: By Revere's own deposition he answered: 'Noise! You'll have noise enough before long. The regulars are coming out!' Source: https://www.paulreverehouse.org/the-real-story/

question: At dawn on April 19, 1775, roughly 70 Lexington militiamen — mostly local farmers — lined up on the village green to face hundreds of advancing British regulars. Among the militia stood one man whom history makes a point of naming, because he was wounded there. Who was he?
answer: Prince Estabrook, a Black man who was then a slave
choices: Prince Estabrook, a Black man who was then a slave
Deacon John Larkin, who had lent out his horse
Robert Newman, the sexton from the Old North Church
Hugh Earl Percy, the British relief commander
context: Prince Estabrook, a Black man enslaved at the time, served in Captain John Parker's Lexington company and was wounded in the fight — among the very first to bleed in the Revolution. The British volley killed eight militiamen and wounded ten that morning. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battles_of_Lexington_and_Concord

question: On the night of the ride a young doctor, Samuel Prescott, joined Paul Revere and William Dawes on the road home from visiting a lady friend. When a British patrol trapped all three, Prescott pulled off a bold move that made him the ONLY rider to reach Concord and raise the alarm. What did he do?
answer: He jumped his horse over a stone wall
choices: He jumped his horse over a stone wall
He swam his horse across a cold river
He hid in a dark farmhouse cellar
He outran the whole patrol on the open road
context: Prescott jumped his horse over a stone wall to escape the patrol, rode on to Concord, and rang the town bell to sound the alarm — the one rider of the three who got through. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Prescott and https://www.nps.gov/places/paul-revere-capture-site.htm

question: At Lexington Green, Captain John Parker had ordered his outnumbered militia to disperse, and as they turned to leave, the first shot of the Revolutionary War cracked across the green. More than two centuries later, what do historians say about who fired that opening shot?
answer: No one knows which side fired it
choices: No one knows which side fired it
A British officer gave the order to fire
A Lexington farmer fired the first shot
Major Pitcairn fired his own pistol first
context: As the militia dispersed, an unknown person fired first — to this day no one knows whether it was a colonist or a British soldier. Major John Pitcairn had ridden forward shouting 'Disperse, ye rebels! Lay down your arms!' Source: https://research.colonialwilliamsburg.org/Foundation/journal/Summer06/lex.cfm and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battles_of_Lexington_and_Concord

question: Captain John Parker drew up his small Lexington militia to face the British column, and tradition holds that he steadied them with a single line now carved on a plaque at Lexington Battle Green. According to that tradition, what did Parker tell his men?
answer: If they mean to have a war, let it begin here
choices: If they mean to have a war, let it begin here
Hold the green or die where you stand
Fire first and fire fast, my friends
God and liberty, follow me forward
context: By tradition Parker said: 'Stand your ground. Don't fire unless fired upon, but if they mean to have a war, let it begin here.' Historians dispute the exact words, but the line is carved at Lexington Battle Green. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Parker_(captain) and https://emergingcivilwar.com/2015/02/18/and-if-they-mean-to-have-a-war-let-it-begin-here-the-real-words-of-captain-john-parker/  (Legend.)

question: At Concord's North Bridge, about 400 colonial militia advanced on roughly 90 British regulars. When the British fired into them and killed a man, Major John Buttrick of Concord roared an order — and for the first time Americans volleyed back in formation and drove the redcoats back. What did Buttrick shout?
answer: Fire, for God's sake, fellow soldiers, fire
choices: Fire, for God's sake, fellow soldiers, fire
Charge them, boys, the bridge is ours
Steady now, and aim for the officers
Avenge him, men, and give no ground
context: Buttrick's cry — 'Fire, for God's sake, fellow soldiers, fire!' — opened the volley at the North Bridge, the moment Emerson later called 'the shot heard round the world.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_North_Bridge and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battles_of_Lexington_and_Concord

question: The day after Japanese planes attacked the American fleet at Pearl Harbor, President Franklin D. Roosevelt stood before Congress and gave December 7, 1941, a single word it has been remembered by ever since. He called it a date that would live as what?
answer: infamy
choices: infamy
tragedy
treachery
disgrace
context: FDR's first dictated draft read 'a date which will live in world history'; he crossed out 'world history' by hand and wrote 'infamy.' The line opened his war message asking Congress to declare war on Japan. Source: https://www.archives.gov/education/lessons/day-of-infamy ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_Infamy_speech

question: The battleship USS Arizona was sunk at Pearl Harbor and still rests on the harbor bottom, and more than 80 years later a thin sheen of oil still rises from her hull to the surface every day. What have people come to call this oil?
answer: the tears of the Arizona
choices: the tears of the Arizona
the blood of the fleet
the sorrow of Oahu
the ashes of December
context: The wreck is now a memorial built over the sunken ship, and the daily seep is one of its most haunting sights. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/USS-Arizona ; https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/fallen-crew-uss-arizona-and-operation-85

question: As the Japanese planes caught the American fleet completely by surprise, the lead pilot, Commander Mitsuo Fuchida, radioed three identical code words back to the carrier Akagi to report that total surprise had been achieved. What three words did he send?
answer: Tora! Tora! Tora!
choices: Tora! Tora! Tora!
Banzai! Banzai! Banzai!
Totsugeki! Totsugeki! Totsugeki!
Kogeki! Kogeki! Kogeki!
context: Fuchida sent it at 7:53 a.m. 'Tora' literally means 'tiger,' but here it stood as shorthand for the Japanese words for 'charge' and 'torpedo attack.' The 1970 film about the attack took its name from this signal. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitsuo_Fuchida ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tora!_Tora!_Tora!

question: USS Nevada's band was up on deck playing 'The Star-Spangled Banner' for the morning flag-raising at 8 a.m. when the first Japanese fighter roared in and sprayed bullets across the deck all around them. What did the band do?
answer: kept playing the anthem to the very end, only faster
choices: kept playing the anthem to the very end, only faster
dropped their instruments and ran below for cover
switched to a quick march to rally the crew
scattered at once to their battle stations
context: Nevada was the only battleship to get underway during the attack. To keep from sinking and blocking the harbor channel, her crew deliberately ran her aground. Source: https://www.military.com/off-duty/history/pearl-harbor-uss-nevada-band.html ; https://www.war.gov/News/Feature-Stories/Story/Article/3879225/uss-nevada-was-the-only-battleship-to-get-underway-during-pearl-harbor-attack/

question: Two young Army pilots, George Welch and Kenneth Taylor, had been up all night at an all-night dance and a poker game when the bombs began to fall. They jumped into a car, raced to the Haleiwa airstrip, and took off in P-40 fighters straight into the swarm of attackers, never stopping to change. What were they still wearing as they fought?
answer: their formal tuxedo mess dress
choices: their formal tuxedo mess dress
their issued flight suits
their dress khaki uniforms
their cotton sleeping clothes
context: Between them Welch and Taylor shot down several enemy planes and both earned the Distinguished Service Cross. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Welch_(pilot) ; https://www.history.com/articles/heroes-of-pearl-harbor-george-welch-and-kenneth-taylor

question: Doris 'Dorie' Miller was a mess attendant aboard USS West Virginia, a cook with no gunnery training in the segregated Navy of 1941. When the attack came he carried his mortally wounded captain to safety, then manned a .50-caliber anti-aircraft gun he had never been taught to fire and shot back at the planes. Miller became the first Black American ever awarded which military honor?
answer: the Navy Cross
choices: the Navy Cross
the Medal of Honor
the Silver Star
the Purple Heart
context: Admiral Chester Nimitz pinned the Navy Cross on Miller in person on May 27, 1942. He had also been the ship's heavyweight boxing champion. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doris_Miller

question: The battleship USS Oklahoma was hit by five torpedoes and rolled completely upside-down in minutes, trapping sailors alive inside the overturned hull. A civilian shipyard worker named Julio DeCastro heard them banging wrenches against the steel in SOS. What did DeCastro and his rescue crew do?
answer: cut through the hull and pulled the trapped men out
choices: cut through the hull and pulled the trapped men out
pumped fresh air inside to keep them alive
rolled the ship upright using harbor cranes
marked the spot and waited for Navy divers
context: DeCastro's crew cut through the steel and rescued 32 survivors, even as 429 men aboard Oklahoma were lost. It was the most successful rescue of the day. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/the-civilian-worker-who-spearheaded-pearl-harbors-most-successful-rescue-mission-180979167/ ; https://www.history.navy.mil/our-collections/photography/wars-and-events/world-war-ii/pearl-harbor-raid/

question: The deadliest blow of the whole attack fell on the battleship USS Arizona, when a single 1,800-pound armor-piercing bomb punched through her deck and detonated deep inside the ship. What happened next?
answer: her forward ammunition magazine went up and the ship blew apart
choices: her forward ammunition magazine went up and the ship blew apart
her engines flooded and she slowly capsized
she caught fire but was towed to safety
her hull split and she settled upright on the bottom
context: Arizona sank with 1,177 of her crew killed -- nearly half of all the Americans who died that day. Aboard her, 23 sets of brothers died together, along with the only father-and-son pair, Thomas Free and his son William. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/USS-Arizona ; https://www.nps.gov/perl/learn/historyculture/brothersassignedarizona.htm

question: About an hour before the attack, two privates at the new Opana radar station on Oahu spotted a huge blip of planes 132 miles out and phoned it in. The duty officer, Lieutenant Kermit Tyler, told them not to worry about it. What did Tyler believe the blip was?
answer: a flight of American B-17 bombers due that morning
choices: a flight of American B-17 bombers due that morning
a flock of seabirds confusing the new radar
a Navy patrol returning toward Pearl Harbor
a thunderstorm building out over the ocean
context: The privates were Joseph Lockard and George Elliott; the blip was the incoming Japanese first wave. A flight of B-17s really was expected from California that morning, which is why Tyler waved it off. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radar_warning_of_Pearl_Harbor_attack ; https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/kermit-tyler-call-would-live-infamy

question: Japan planned to hand the United States a long, 14-part message breaking off peace talks exactly 30 minutes before the attack, meant to serve as a final warning. But decoding and typing the long document took the Japanese embassy in Washington far longer than planned. When did the United States actually receive the message?
answer: only after the bombs had already fallen
choices: only after the bombs had already fallen
a full hour before the first plane arrived
exactly 30 minutes ahead, as planned
the day before the attack began
context: Because the envoy did not deliver it until after the strike, the attack came with no warning at all -- which fixed it in American memory as a sneak attack. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_on_Pearl_Harbor ; https://www.iwm.org.uk/history/what-happened-at-pearl-harbor

question: Japan's attack sank or damaged all eight American battleships at Pearl Harbor, but it missed the targets Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto wanted most. The U.S. Navy's three Pacific aircraft carriers -- Enterprise, Lexington, and Saratoga -- were all away from the harbor that Sunday morning and came through untouched. What would those three surviving carriers go on to do?
answer: carry the war back across the Pacific to Japan
choices: carry the war back across the Pacific to Japan
guard the U.S. West Coast against invasion
ferry fighter planes to help defend Australia
escort supply convoys across the Atlantic
context: Battleships were the old measure of naval power, but the war in the Pacific would be won by carriers -- the very weapon the raid failed to touch. America's shipyards and factories then poured out the planes, ships, and supplies that became the 'arsenal of democracy.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_on_Pearl_Harbor

question: One of the most quoted lines of the whole war has Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto saying, 'I fear all we have done is to awaken a sleeping giant and fill him with a terrible resolve.' Historians have searched, and no diary, letter, or speech of Yamamoto's has ever been found containing those words. Where does the famous line actually come from?
answer: the 1970 film Tora! Tora! Tora!
choices: the 1970 film Tora! Tora! Tora!
a 1943 American wartime newsreel
a popular postwar biography of Yamamoto
a Tokyo radio broadcast during the war
context: Because there is no record of him ever saying it, historians treat the 'sleeping giant' line as words the movie put in Yamamoto's mouth -- powerful, fitting, but legend rather than documented fact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isoroku_Yamamoto's_sleeping_giant_quote

question: Pericles led Athens through its Golden Age, and his speeches in the assembly were so overpowering that comic poets said he seemed to thunder and flash lightning, 'wielding a dread thunderbolt in his tongue.' What grand nickname did they pin on him?
answer: the Olympian
choices: the Olympian
the Golden Tongue
the Lion of the Pnyx
the Voice of Athens
context: The comic playwrights' jab stuck: 'the Olympian' likened Pericles to Zeus himself, ruling Athens from on high with words instead of lightning. Source: Plutarch, Life of Pericles (penelope.uchicago.edu); Wikipedia 'Pericles'.

question: Comic poets in Athens loved to mock Pericles, even giving him the rude nickname 'Squill-head' after a knobby sea-onion. Sculptors got around the problem by almost always carving him in a Corinthian helmet pushed back on his head. What were they politely hiding?
answer: the unusual, elongated shape of his skull
choices: the unusual, elongated shape of his skull
a deep battle scar across his brow
that he had gone completely bald
a birthmark covering one cheek
context: Pericles really is shown helmeted in nearly every surviving portrait, the artists' tactful fix for a head the comedians wouldn't stop teasing. Source: Plutarch, Life of Pericles (penelope.uchicago.edu); Wikipedia 'Pericles'.

question: Around 447 BC Pericles launched a huge building program to rebuild the Acropolis of Athens. Its crown was a brilliant new marble temple to the goddess Athena that became the most famous building of the ancient world. Name that temple.
answer: the Parthenon
choices: the Parthenon
the Erechtheion
the Pantheon
the Temple of Olympian Zeus
context: The Parthenon (built 447-432 BC) was designed by the architects Ictinus and Callicrates, with the sculptor Phidias directing all of its art. Source: worldhistory.org/Phidias; Perseus (Martin, Overview of Classical Greek History); thecollector.com/pericles-athenian-golden-age.

question: Inside Athens' great temple of Athena towered Phidias' statue of the goddess: about forty feet tall, sheathed in ivory and over a ton of gold. On the floor right in front of her, Phidias kept a shallow pool of one liquid, both to protect the ivory and to mirror her image. What filled the pool?
answer: olive oil
choices: olive oil
fresh spring water
sweet wine
scented perfume
context: The statue was Athena Parthenos ('Athena the Virgin'), dedicated in 438 BC, holding a small winged Victory (Nike) in her hand; the oil kept the ivory from cracking and threw her golden reflection back up at her. Source: worldhistory.org/Phidias.

question: Phidias directed all the sculpture of Athena's great temple, and on the goddess's shield he carved a battle of the Amazons. But he slipped in something personal that later got him dragged into court. What did he secretly work into the figures?
answer: small portraits of himself and Pericles
choices: small portraits of himself and Pericles
a hidden curse aimed at Sparta
his own name spelled out in gold
a deliberate flaw to skim the gold
context: Phidias, who also made the gold-and-ivory Zeus at Olympia (one of the Seven Wonders), was accused of impiety for sneaking mortal faces among the sacred figures. Source: worldhistory.org/Phidias.

question: The builders of Pericles' great marble temple on the Acropolis played a trick on the eye: the columns actually lean slightly inward and swell gently at the middle. With almost no truly straight lines in it, how does the finished building appear to a viewer standing below?
answer: perfectly straight and upright
choices: perfectly straight and upright
slightly tilted to one side
taller than it really is
as if it is leaning toward you
context: The gentle bulge is called entasis; the curves correct the distortions of human eyesight, so a temple of subtle curves reads as flawlessly straight. Source: medium.com/time-chronicles 'Pericles: The Architect of Athens' Golden Age'; studedu.org Parthenon article.

question: Pericles' Athens led the Delian League, an alliance of Greek cities that paid yearly tribute into a common war-fund (kept on the sacred island of Delos) to defend against Persia. In 454 BC Athens moved that fund home and began spending the allies' money on temples for itself. What had the alliance quietly turned into?
answer: an empire ruled by Athens
choices: an empire ruled by Athens
a free league of equals
a religious brotherhood
a trading partnership
context: Moving the treasury from Delos to Athens 'for safekeeping' let Pericles fund the Acropolis with the allies' tribute, converting allies into subjects. Source: Wikipedia 'Delian League'; pbs.org/empires/thegreeks/keyevents/454_c.html; Britannica 'Delian League'.

question: Rivals accused Pericles of decking out Athens with the allies' gold 'like a vain woman, hung round with precious stones.' He called their bluff and offered to pay for every building himself, on one condition that made the assembly instantly shout for him to spend public money instead. What did he demand in return?
answer: that his own name be carved on the temples
choices: that his own name be carved on the temples
that he be given command of the army for life
that he receive a share of all future tolls
that a statue of him stand in the marketplace
context: Rather than let Pericles claim the glory, the assembly told him to spend freely from the public treasury, exactly as he had wanted. Source: Plutarch, Life of Pericles (classics.mit.edu/Plutarch/pericles.html).

question: In 431 BC Pericles gave a famous funeral speech for Athens' war dead, recorded by the historian Thucydides, who heard it. Defining the city's government, he said: 'Its administration favours the many instead of the few; this is why it is called ___.' Fill in Pericles' word.
answer: a democracy
choices: a democracy
a republic
an oligarchy
a commonwealth
context: This line from the Funeral Oration is a founding statement of the Western idea that government should rest with the many citizens, not a privileged few. Source: Thucydides 2.37, Crawley translation (en.wikisource.org/wiki/History_of_the_Peloponnesian_War/Book_2).

question: A rude man followed Pericles around the Athenian marketplace cursing and abusing him for an entire day, while Pericles said nothing and bore it in silence. When night fell and Pericles finally went home, what did he order a servant to do for the man?
answer: take a torch and walk him safely home
choices: take a torch and walk him safely home
throw him out of the city gates
fetch him a fine dinner as a joke
write down every insult he had shouted
context: Plutarch's best-loved Pericles story shows the self-control that fit his nickname 'the Olympian.' Told as a famous anecdote rather than a documented event. Source: Plutarch, Life of Pericles (penelope.uchicago.edu).  (Legend.)

question: In 451 BC Pericles passed a strict law: only a child of two Athenian parents could be a citizen. Years later a plague killed both his lawful sons, leaving only his son by Aspasia of Miletus, a foreign woman. To make that boy a citizen, what did Pericles have to do before the assembly?
answer: beg them to set aside his own law
choices: beg them to set aside his own law
pay a huge fine from his fortune
marry an Athenian wife in old age
adopt a full citizen as his heir
context: In a bitter irony, the assembly took pity and suspended the very citizenship law Pericles himself had written. Source: Plutarch, Life of Pericles (penelope.uchicago.edu); thecollector.com/pericles-athenian-golden-age.

question: Pericles is honestly remembered for helping start the catastrophic Peloponnesian War. His war plan was to abandon the Athenian countryside, pack everyone behind the Long Walls down to the port of Piraeus, and let the navy do the fighting. Cramming the city helped a terrible plague spread in 430 BC that killed perhaps a quarter of Athens, and in 429 BC killed whom?
answer: Pericles himself
choices: Pericles himself
the king of Sparta
most of the Athenian navy
his rival Cleon
context: Pericles' own strategy backfired tragically, the plague it worsened took his life along with so many others. Source: Britannica 'Pericles'; ebsco.com 'Plague of Athens'; thecollector.com/pericles-athenian-golden-age.

question: In July 1761 a frail child stepped off a schooner in Boston, and the family who bought her gave her a first name no one expected. What did the Wheatley family name Phillis Wheatley after?
answer: The slave ship that had carried her
choices: The slave ship that had carried her
The auctioneer who sold her
A daughter of the Wheatley family
The Boston church the family attended
context: The schooner that delivered her to Boston in July 1761 was itself named Phillis, and the Wheatleys gave her the vessel's own name. They guessed she was about seven because she was shedding her front teeth. Source: worldhistory.org/Phillis_Wheatley/ ; massmoments.org (John Wheatley Purchases a Slave Child).

question: In 1773 a young enslaved woman in Boston, Phillis Wheatley, had written poems so accomplished that many refused to believe a Black slave girl could have composed them. To settle it, eighteen of the most prominent men in Boston — including Governor Thomas Hutchinson and John Hancock — examined her and signed an attestation. When her book was published in London that year, what milestone did Phillis Wheatley become?
answer: The first African American to publish a book of poetry
choices: The first African American to publish a book of poetry
The first woman admitted to Harvard College
The first slave to win her freedom in a Boston court
The first colonist to be printed in three languages
context: 'Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral' came out in London in 1773 — no colonial printer would take it. The eighteen signers attested the poems were genuinely 'written by PHILLIS, a young Negro Girl.' Source: britannica.com/biography/Phillis-Wheatley ; smithsonianmag.com ; massmoments.org.

question: Late in 1775 Phillis Wheatley wrote a poem honoring General George Washington, and in it she coined a goddess-figure to personify the new American nation — a name that later became a poetic nickname for America itself. What did Phillis Wheatley name her nation-goddess?
answer: Columbia
choices: Columbia
Liberty
Britannia
Minerva
context: Wheatley wrote 'Columbia's scenes of glorious toils I write.' Washington wrote back from Cambridge on Feb 28, 1776, praising her 'great poetical Talents' and inviting her to visit — which she did, meeting him in person in March 1776. The poem ends: 'A crown, a mansion, and a throne that shine, / With gold unfading, WASHINGTON! be thine.' Source: hamilton.gilderlehrman.org ; mountvernon.org.

question: For thousands of years "royal purple" was the most expensive color on earth, worn only by kings and emperors. The Phoenician city of Tyre made the famous dye from a living creature crushed by the thousands -- it took about 10,000 of them to color one garment. What creature gave up the royal purple?
answer: The murex, a spiny sea-snail
choices: The murex, a spiny sea-snail
The squid, an inky deep-sea hunter
The sea-urchin, a spined shellfish
The whelk, a coiled tide-pool snail
context: Tyrian purple was squeezed from the crushed mucus glands of murex sea-snails. About 10,000 snails dyed a single garment, and 12,000 yielded barely 1.4 grams of dye -- only enough to trim a robe. Under Rome a pound of it cost roughly three pounds of gold, making the color literally worth more than gold by weight. Sources: worldhistory.org/Tyrian_Purple/ ; history.com/articles/purple-ancient-phoenicians

question: The Phoenicians were the master sea-traders of the ancient Mediterranean, sailing from Lebanon all the way to Spain and founding Carthage. The Greeks did not call them by their own name for themselves -- they named them after the costly purple dye the traders sold everywhere. The Greek word phoinix that gave us "Phoenician" actually meant which of these?
answer: Reddish-purple
choices: Reddish-purple
Far-wandering
Sea-faring
Cedar-scented
context: "Phoenician" likely comes from the Greek phoinix, meaning roughly "reddish-purple" -- so the Phoenicians were literally "the Purple People," named by the Greeks for the murex dye they carried across the sea. Tyre founded Carthage around 814 BC, the city that would later challenge Rome. Sources: nationalgeographic.com ("Purple reign"); encyclopedia.com ("the Purple People")

question: Pablo Picasso, born in Malaga, Spain in 1881, would grow up to be one of history's most famous painters. According to family legend, his very first word as a baby was 'piz' -- his way of saying the Spanish word 'lapiz.' What was the little boy already asking for?
answer: A pencil
choices: A pencil
A paintbrush
His mother
Some bread
context: 'Piz' was baby-talk for 'lapiz,' Spanish for pencil. Told as a family legend, not documented fact. Source: cigaraficionado.com/article/saved-by-the-cigar-242

question: When Pablo Picasso was baptized as a baby in Malaga, the priest wrote down a name that went on and on: 'Pablo Diego Jose Francisco de Paula Juan Nepomuceno ... Ruiz y Picasso,' a long chain honoring saints and relatives. Roughly how many given names did his baptism pile onto him?
answer: More than a dozen
choices: More than a dozen
Around half a dozen
Exactly two
Just one
context: Spanish baptismal custom piled on saints' names; Picasso's stretched past a dozen given names. Source: historyfacts.com/famous-figures/fact/pablo-picassos-full-name/

question: Pablo Picasso helped invent a startling new way of painting. Stand before one of his portraits and a single nose can sit beside a profiled ear, the parts of one head jumbled together onto the flat canvas, refusing to settle into a normal view. What did this new style let a single picture do?
answer: Show an object from several angles at once
choices: Show an object from several angles at once
Paint a person's emotions as bright colors
Capture one frozen instant of time
Blur shapes to suggest fast motion
context: This is the core trick of Cubism: many viewpoints fused into one image, the form broken into flat planes and reassembled. Source: metmuseum.org/essays/cubism

question: Pablo Picasso painted 'Guernica,' a huge mural mourning a bombed town, and wanted it to hit a viewer with the front-page shock of a war photograph splashed across the morning paper. Which palette did he limit himself to for the entire painting?
answer: Only grey, black, and white
choices: Only grey, black, and white
Sepia and faded brown
A range of blues only
Charcoal grey with blood red
context: The monochrome grey-black-white palette gives Guernica the immediacy of a black-and-white newspaper photograph; his partner, photographer Dora Maar, helped push it that way. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guernica_(Picasso)

question: During World War II, in Nazi-occupied Paris, a Gestapo officer pushed his way into Pablo Picasso's apartment, spotted a photograph of the anti-war painting 'Guernica,' jabbed at it and demanded, 'Did you do that?' How did Picasso answer him?
answer: 'No -- you did.'
choices: 'No -- you did.'
'Yes, and I am proud of it.'
'I have never seen it before.'
'A friend of mine painted it.'
context: Picasso meant the Nazis made the horror the painting records. Recounted as legend in a Guardian editorial. Source: openculture.com/2017/05/the-gestapo-points-to-guernica-and-asks-picasso-did-you-do-this.html

question: On 26 April 1937 -- market day -- German planes of the Condor Legion, sent by Hitler to help Franco, bombed the Basque town of Guernica in Spain for about three hours. When Pablo Picasso painted his mural to mourn the dead of that day, who made up most of the bodies in the rubble?
answer: Women and children
choices: Women and children
Basque militiamen
Retreating soldiers
The town's mayors
context: Most of the town's men were away at the front, so the bombing fell on the women and children left behind -- the atrocity Guernica witnesses. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guernica_(Picasso)

question: Pablo Picasso filled his mural 'Guernica' with horror -- a screaming horse, a wailing mother, a fallen soldier. On the ground the dead soldier's severed arm still grips a broken sword, and from the snapped blade Picasso painted one living thing rising as a hint of hope. What did Picasso paint sprouting from the broken blade?
answer: A flower
choices: A flower
An olive sprig
A wheat stalk
A rose
context: Amid the slaughter, a sprout of hope: a lone flower grows from the broken blade in the fallen fighter's hand. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guernica_(Picasso)

question: Pablo Picasso's painting of five women with mask-like faces is known today as 'Les Demoiselles d'Avignon' -- 'The Young Ladies of Avignon.' But Picasso never chose that gentle title; the poet Andre Salmon swapped it in against his wishes, and Picasso always resented the change. What blunt name had Picasso given the picture himself?
answer: 'The Brothel of Avignon'
choices: 'The Brothel of Avignon'
'The Streetwalkers of Barcelona'
'The Five Sisters'
'The Dancers of Avignon'
context: Picasso named it 'Le Bordel d'Avignon' after Carrer d'Avinyo, a red-light street in Barcelona; Salmon's tamer title stuck against his wishes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Demoiselles_d'Avignon

question: Around 1908 a French critic named Louis Vauxcelles looked at Georges Braque's blocky, geometric landscapes and sneered at them with a mocking phrase. The jeer caught on, and it ended up giving a name to a whole art movement that Braque and Picasso had never named themselves. What did Vauxcelles say the paintings were made of?
answer: 'Little cubes'
choices: 'Little cubes'
'Little bricks'
'Paper triangles'
'Flat playing cards'
context: The insult 'bizarreries cubiques' (cubic oddities), echoing Matisse's jab about 'little cubes,' gave Cubism its name; Picasso and Braque never chose the label. Source: metmuseum.org/essays/cubism

question: Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque built Cubism together from about 1908 to 1914, working so closely that Braque said they were 'like mountain-climbers roped together.' In 1912 the two friends did something no serious painter had dared before, inventing a whole new technique that artists still use today. What technique did Picasso and Braque invent?
answer: Collage
choices: Collage
Oil painting
Fresco
Etching
context: In 1912, during their Synthetic Cubism phase, they glued real-world scraps -- newspaper, wallpaper, and labels -- straight onto the canvas, inventing collage. Source: sothebys.com/en/articles/from-picasso-to-present-the-origins-of-cubism

question: For decades people pressed Pablo Picasso to explain what the bull and the horse in 'Guernica' secretly stand for, expecting him to hand over a tidy code. He famously refused to give them one neat key. How did Picasso wave the question away?
answer: 'This bull is a bull and this horse is a horse.'
choices: 'This bull is a bull and this horse is a horse.'
'Only the dead know what they mean.'
'I painted them from a dream.'
'The critics may decide for me.'
context: He resisted a fixed reading, allowing elsewhere only that the bull suggests brutality and darkness and the horse the people. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guernica_(Picasso)

question: After painting 'Guernica' in 1937, Pablo Picasso swore the canvas would not hang in his Spanish homeland until 'liberty and democracy' had returned there, naming no other condition. So for decades it stayed safe in a New York museum while Spain stayed under the dictator Francisco Franco. By 1981 something had finally changed in Spain, and the painting at last went home. What had happened?
answer: The dictator had finally died
choices: The dictator had finally died
A new constitution outlawed all art bans
The painting had been sold abroad
A grand museum was built to house it
context: Franco died in 1975; Guernica then left New York's Museum of Modern Art and reached Spain on 10 September 1981. Source: history.com/this-day-in-history/guernica-returned-to-spain

question: In November 1532 the Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro marched into the Inca town of Cajamarca with a tiny force, while the Inca emperor Atahualpa camped on the hills above with an army fresh from winning a civil war. How small was Pizarro's whole band against that army of roughly 80,000?
answer: About 168 men
choices: About 168 men
About 1,600 men
About 5,000 men
About 12,000 men
context: Just 62 horsemen and 106 foot soldiers. The Inca thought so tiny a group of strangers was no real threat. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cajamarca (and Britannica).

question: At Cajamarca, a Dominican friar named Vicente de Valverde walked up to the Inca emperor Atahualpa and handed him a Christian holy book, demanding that he submit to Spain and to God. Atahualpa turned the strange object over, listened, and said it 'told him nothing.' What did he then do that the Spanish seized on as their excuse to attack?
answer: He threw the book to the ground
choices: He threw the book to the ground
He tore his own robe in half
He drew a knife on the friar
He ordered the friar seized
context: To Atahualpa a book that did not speak was worthless. The Spanish treated tossing the holy book down as an insult to God and a signal to open fire. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cajamarca; historyskills.com.

question: Captured by Pizarro and held prisoner, the Inca emperor Atahualpa noticed how the Spanish hungered for gold, and he made them an astonishing offer to buy his freedom. What did he promise to give them?
answer: A whole room filled to a high red line with gold, then twice over with silver
choices: A whole room filled to a high red line with gold, then twice over with silver
A mountain whose veins of pure gold ran straight to the sea
A fleet of llamas loaded with every jewel in the empire
His own weight measured out three times in melted gold
context: The Ransom Room still stands in Cajamarca; the red line marked how high Atahualpa could reach, about 8-9 feet up the wall. It became the richest ransom ever paid. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ransom_Room.

question: When Pizarro's men charged the packed square at Cajamarca, they hacked at the eighty nobles carrying Atahualpa's litter to topple the emperor to the ground. According to the Spanish chroniclers, even after swords cut off the bearers' hands and arms, what did those men keep doing?
answer: Holding the litter aloft with their bleeding stumps
choices: Holding the litter aloft with their bleeding stumps
Singing the emperor's name as they fell
Crawling to shield Atahualpa with their bodies
Hurling their severed arms at the horses
context: The chroniclers say the maimed bearers refused to let the emperor fall until they were killed. Pizarro himself took a sword cut to his own hand stopping a soldier from killing Atahualpa, who was worth far more alive. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cajamarca.

question: Atahualpa paid the ransom in full, yet the Spanish staged a sham trial, convicted him, and sentenced him to be burned alive. To the Inca a burned body could never pass into the afterlife, so a terrified Atahualpa accepted Christian baptism to escape the flames. What was then done to him instead in the very square where he had been captured?
answer: He was strangled with an iron garrote
choices: He was strangled with an iron garrote
He was beheaded with a Spanish sword
He was hanged from the town gallows
He was sent in chains to Spain
context: Baptized as 'Francisco,' Atahualpa avoided the fire but was throttled by the iron collar on July 26, 1533. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atahualpa; historyskills.com.

question: People often imagine Pizarro's 168 men toppling a united empire by sheer nerve. But the Inca world was already broken when he arrived: emperor Huayna Capac had died of disease, and his two sons had torn the realm apart. What had really just happened that Pizarro exploited?
answer: A five-year civil war in which Atahualpa's generals had just beaten and captured his brother Huascar
choices: A five-year civil war in which Atahualpa's generals had just beaten and captured his brother Huascar
A famine that had emptied the granaries across the whole empire
A revolt of the southern provinces that had cut Cuzco off from the coast
A failed harvest that had broken the empire's network of roads
context: Disease, the civil war, and the loss of the god-emperor, not any magic, let so few men topple so vast an empire. Even from his cell, Atahualpa secretly had the captive Huascar killed, fearing his brother would offer the Spanish a bigger ransom. Source: ticketmachupicchu.com; worldhistory.org/Atahualpa.

question: In 1532 the Inca emperor Atahualpa was held prisoner by Francisco Pizarro's tiny band of Spaniards. To buy his freedom, Atahualpa reached high up the cell wall, drew a line, and promised to fill that whole room once over with one single thing. What did he promise to fill it with?
answer: Gold
choices: Gold
Salt
Grain
Cloth
context: Atahualpa drew a line about 8-9 feet up the wall and promised to fill the room once with gold and a smaller room twice with silver. The Ransom Room (Cuarto del Rescate) still stands in Cajamarca, Peru, with a red line marking the height. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ransom_Room

question: The Inca empire was already collapsing before Francisco Pizarro ever reached it. The previous emperor, Huayna Capac, died around 1527 from a sickness that had raced ahead of the Spanish through the Americas faster than any soldier could march. What killed him?
answer: Smallpox
choices: Smallpox
Starvation
A spear wound
Old age
