context: Smallpox swept through the Americas ahead of the Spanish themselves. Huayna Capac's death threw the throne into a civil war between his sons Huascar and Atahualpa, gutting the empire before Pizarro arrived. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huayna_Capac

question: When the two armies finally met at Cajamarca in 1532, a Spanish friar, Vicente de Valverde, walked up to the Inca emperor Atahualpa and handed him a Christian holy book. The Inca had no writing and heard their gods through spoken oracles, so Atahualpa held the book up to his ear, heard nothing, and reacted in a way that helped trigger the attack. What did he do with the book?
answer: Threw it on the ground
choices: Threw it on the ground
Tore out its pages
Handed it to a priest
Slipped it into his robe
context: Because the Inca heard their gods through spoken oracles, Atahualpa held the breviary to his ear, heard nothing, and threw it down. Valverde shouted to attack, Pizarro waved a white scarf as the signal, and a cannon fired. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cajamarca

question: At Cajamarca in 1532, Francisco Pizarro sprang his ambush on an Inca army of roughly 80,000 battle-tested troops camped nearby. To take the Inca emperor and butcher thousands of his attendants in the plaza, how many Spaniards did Pizarro actually have with him?
answer: About 168
choices: About 168
About 1,500
About 9,000
About 40,000
context: Pizarro had only 168 Spaniards: 62 on horseback, 106 on foot, with 4 small cannons and 12 harquebuses, against an Inca army of roughly 80,000 outside Cajamarca. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/704/pizarro-and-atahualpa-the-curse-of-the-lost-inca-g/ and Wikipedia 'Battle of Cajamarca'

question: To pay Atahualpa's ransom, Inca llama caravans hauled gold to Cajamarca for months. Much of it was peeled off one sacred building in Cusco that had literally been sheathed in plates of solid gold. Which building did they strip bare?
answer: Coricancha
choices: Coricancha
Sacsayhuaman
Ollantaytambo
Machu Picchu
context: The Coricancha (Qorikancha) was the Temple of the Sun in Cusco, sheathed in gold. The Inca stripped its gold plating, and caravans carried golden statues and life-sized model llamas across the empire to Cajamarca over about four months. Source: https://www.cuscoperu.com/en/travel/cusco/archaeological-centers/qoricancha/

question: During the ambush at Cajamarca, Atahualpa rode in on a royal litter carried high by his servants. As the Spanish swarmed it, they hacked at the bearers with swords to bring the emperor down. According to the eyewitness Pedro Pizarro, what did the mutilated bearers do?
answer: Held the litter up on their stumps and shoulders
choices: Held the litter up on their stumps and shoulders
Dropped it and fled into the crowd
Drew hidden daggers and fought back
Threw their emperor clear to save him
context: The Spanish hacked the arms and hands off the litter-bearers, yet the mutilated men kept holding the litter aloft with their shoulders and stumps until they were killed. Pizarro took a sword-cut to his own hand from one of his own men because he needed Atahualpa alive. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cajamarca (citing Pedro Pizarro)

question: Folk memory holds that before the ambush, the conquistador Hernando de Soto galloped his warhorse straight at the Inca emperor Atahualpa, who had never seen a horse in his life, and reined to a sudden halt only a few feet from the emperor's face to terrify him. As the story is told, how did Atahualpa react?
answer: He did not flinch a muscle
choices: He did not flinch a muscle
He fell backward off his stool
He drew a ceremonial axe
He ordered his guards to fire
context: This is told as legend. Atahualpa reportedly held perfectly still; some accounts say warriors of his who DID recoil were later executed for showing fear. Source: https://heatherpringle.com/2010/03/15/the-emperor-and-the-horse/

question: After Atahualpa's ransom of gold was fully delivered, the Spanish broke their word and condemned him to be burned alive. The emperor dreaded the fire because the Inca believed a burned body could not pass on. Atahualpa found one way to escape the flames, and the Spanish then strangled him by garrote instead. What did he do to avoid the fire?
answer: He accepted Christian baptism
choices: He accepted Christian baptism
He named where the lost gold was
He challenged Pizarro to a duel
He drank a hidden poison
context: Atahualpa accepted baptism, taking the name Francisco after Pizarro, so his body would not be burned. He was executed by garrote (strangling) on Aug 29, 1533. The charges included ordering the murder of his brother Huascar and plotting an uprising. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_conquest_of_the_Inca_Empire

question: A famous tale says the captive Atahualpa learned Spanish, chess, and cards in about twenty days. Watching Hernando de Soto play a tense game of chess, the emperor supposedly leaned over and whispered a single move that led straight to checkmate. According to the legend, which piece did he tell Soto to move?
answer: The rook
choices: The rook
The queen
The king
A pawn
context: Told as legend, retold by Ricardo Palma from chronicler Juan de Betanzos. Atahualpa reportedly whispered 'No, captain - the rook,' and gave chess the Quechua name 'taptana' (surprise attack). Source: https://adventuresinhistoryland.com/2019/03/10/atahualpas-rook/

question: Three years after Atahualpa died, the emperor the Spanish had set up as their puppet, Manco Inca Yupanqui, secretly turned against them and raised a huge army to besiege them in Cusco. From May 1536 his forces held the siege for nearly a year, and the Spanish kept marching relief columns up from Lima to break it. What became of those four relief columns?
answer: His forces wiped out all four
choices: His forces wiped out all four
They broke the siege and freed the city
They lost their way in the mountains
They switched sides and joined the rebels
context: Manco Inca besieged Cusco from May 1536 with an army said to number around 100,000. His forces destroyed all four relief columns the Spanish marched up from Lima, but the siege lasted nearly a year and ultimately failed to drive the Spanish out. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Cusco

question: The story of a handful of conquistadors toppling the Inca on their own is a myth. Beyond disease and the Inca civil war, Pizarro's march on Cusco was reinforced by tens of thousands of native peoples who had been brutalized under Inca rule and saw the Spanish as a chance to throw off Cusco's grip. Which two peoples were the great native allies of the Spanish?
answer: The Canari and the Chachapoya
choices: The Canari and the Chachapoya
The Huascar and the Quito
The Aztec and the Maya
The Olmec and the Toltec
context: The Canari (led by Vilchumlay) and the Chachapoya, along with the Huanca, joined the Spanish drive on Cusco, having been brutalized under Inca rule. The conquest was a coalition, not a lone-conquistador feat. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_conquest_of_the_Inca_Empire

question: Francisco Pizarro, an illiterate man risen from a poor Spanish family, won the largest ransom in history but did not enjoy it for long. The conquistadors fell to fighting over the spoils, his partner Diego de Almagro was executed in 1538, and in 1541 Almagro's vengeful supporters stormed his palace in Lima. What happened to Pizarro there?
answer: He was assassinated
choices: He was assassinated
He was shipped back to Spain in chains
He escaped into the mountains
He was crowned governor for life
context: Pizarro was assassinated in his Lima palace in 1541 by supporters of Diego de Almagro, whom Pizarro's faction had executed in 1538. The conquerors turned on each other in their own civil war. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_conquest_of_the_Inca_Empire

question: The Greek thinker we call Plato was actually born Aristocles, named after his grandfather. As a young man he was a real competitive wrestler, said to have fought in the Isthmian Games, and it was his wrestling coach who pinned the nickname 'Plato' on him. What feature of the young athlete earned him that nickname?
answer: His broad, powerful shoulders
choices: His broad, powerful shoulders
His unusually long legs
His loud booming voice
His thick curly hair
context: 'Plato' comes from the Greek 'platon,' meaning 'broad.' His coach reportedly named him for his build. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/plato/ (citing Diogenes Laertius via Britannica).

question: Around 387 BC, Plato founded a school just northwest of Athens, traditionally counted as the first university in the Western world. He set it in a sacred park of old olive trees that already had a name, honoring a legendary local hero. Plato's school took its name straight from that spot — and from it we get a word every student still uses today. What word?
answer: Academy
choices: Academy
Library
Lecture
Diploma
context: The grove was named for the hero Akademos (archaic 'Hekademia'). 'Academy' and 'academic' trace directly back to that patch of olive trees outside Athens; the site lasted roughly 900 years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platonic_Academy.

question: Plato wrote about 35 'dialogues' — written-out conversations that read like little plays — yet in nearly all of them Plato himself never speaks a single line. Instead he puts the leading arguments in the mouth of his own old teacher, a man who in real life never wrote anything down. Which teacher is the lead speaker in almost all of Plato's dialogues?
answer: Socrates
choices: Socrates
Aristotle
Pythagoras
Homer
context: The real Socrates left no writings, so most of what we 'hear' from him comes through Plato's dialogues. In the Republic, Plato even casts his own two brothers, Glaucon and Adeimantus, as the men arguing with Socrates. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/plato/.

question: The legend of Atlantis — a mighty island-empire swallowed by the sea — has launched countless treasure hunts and movies. But historians can trace it to exactly one origin: it appears for the very first time in two dialogues, Timaeus and Critias, written around 360 BC, with no earlier source anywhere. Who first told the story of Atlantis?
answer: The philosopher Plato
choices: The philosopher Plato
The poet Homer
The historian Herodotus
Egyptian temple priests
context: Scholars generally think Plato invented Atlantis as a fictional example to dramatize his political ideas. No source older than Plato mentions it. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/atlantis/.

question: In the most famous image in Plato's Republic, prisoners have been chained by the neck and legs since childhood, facing a blank cave wall they can never turn from. Behind them a fire burns, and people carry carved figures of animals and objects along a walkway. The prisoners spend their whole lives naming and arguing about the only things they can see on that wall. What are those things they mistake for the whole of reality?
answer: Flickering shadows cast on the wall
choices: Flickering shadows cast on the wall
Paintings left by older prisoners
Carved statues set into the rock
Reflections in an underground pool
context: This is the Allegory of the Cave (Republic Book VII, 514a). The prisoners take the shadows for real things because they have never seen anything else. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegory_of_the_cave.

question: Plato once defined a human being as a 'featherless biped' — a two-legged creature without feathers. According to a story told centuries later, the sharp-tongued rival philosopher Diogenes the Cynic decided to mock that definition. He plucked a live chicken, marched it into Plato's Academy, and held it up with a one-line jab. What did Diogenes say as he presented the bald bird?
answer: 'Behold, Plato's man!'
choices: 'Behold, Plato's man!'
'Here is your philosopher!'
'Diogenes salutes Plato!'
'This is wisdom itself!'
context: Legend, reported by Diogenes Laertius long afterward and likely satirical. Plato supposedly answered by adding 'with broad, flat nails' to his definition. Source: https://www.laphamsquarterly.org/animals/miscellany/plato-and-diogenes-debate-featherless-bipeds.

question: At the heart of Plato's Republic is one bold claim about who should hold power. Plato argues that war, injustice, and human misery will never end in our cities until political power and genuine understanding finally belong to the very same person — the one who rules must also be the one who truly knows. He gives this fused ruler a famous name. What kind of ruler does Plato insist a just city requires?
answer: A philosopher-king
choices: A philosopher-king
A conquering war-hero
A high priest of the gods
The richest man in the city
context: Republic 473c-e: 'There is no end to suffering... unless either philosophers become kings... or kings become real, true philosophers.' Plato's term for the ruler who unites power with knowledge is the philosopher-king. Source: https://jaredhenderson.substack.com/p/either-philosophers-become-kings.

question: In Plato's ideal city, Kallipolis ('the beautiful city'), people are sorted into three classes — ruler-guardians, soldiers, and workers. To make citizens accept their station as natural and permanent, Plato has the rulers spread a single founding story he openly calls a useful falsehood, the 'noble lie.' It claims that everyone was born from the earth with a different substance mixed into their very soul. What does the story say is inside each person's soul?
answer: A metal — gold, silver, or bronze
choices: A metal — gold, silver, or bronze
A color — gold, blue, or grey
An animal spirit guiding them
A god's personal blessing
context: The Myth of the Metals (Republic 414b–415c): gold souls rule, silver souls soldier, bronze and iron souls work. Plato presents it as a deliberate fiction to make the class system feel divinely fixed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_lie.

question: Plato's Republic has inspired thinkers for 2,400 years — but not all of them as a hero. The 20th-century philosopher Karl Popper, writing in 'The Open Society and Its Enemies,' read Plato's ideal state as a warning rather than a dream. He argued it was history's first detailed blueprint of one particular kind of society, and called Plato all the more dangerous because he was a genuinely great mind. Which kind of society did Popper argue the Republic first sketched?
answer: A closed, totalitarian society
choices: A closed, totalitarian society
A militarized, conquering empire
A pious, priest-run theocracy
A rigid, caste-bound oligarchy
context: Popper subtitled the section 'The Spell of Plato' and named Plato an originator of totalitarian thought, describing the ideal state as the first 'closed society.' Presented here as one serious modern reading of the Republic, not a final verdict on Plato. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Open_Society_and_Its_Enemies.

question: In Plato's Cave, a prisoner is finally freed and dragged up out of the darkness into the open daylight. At first the glare blinds him; only slowly can his eyes handle reflections, then real objects, until at last he can look at the brightest thing of all, high in the sky. Plato says that blazing source of light stands for the highest object of all knowledge. In his philosophy, what does the Sun represent?
answer: The Form of the Good
choices: The Form of the Good
The soul of the world
The mind of the gods
The fire of reason
context: The escaped prisoner's painful climb toward the Sun pictures the philosopher's journey toward the Form of the Good (Republic Book VII). Brought back below, he is mocked and re-blinded by the dark. Source: https://www.sparknotes.com/philosophy/republic/section7/.

question: Plato refuses to let his ideal city be ruled by the young or the ambitious. In Athens a man could speak in the assembly as a youth and hold real office in his thirties — but Plato's guardian must spend decades first in hard study and then in junior public posts, and is barred from real power until an age when most Athenian men were nearing the end of public life. At what age does a guardian finally qualify to rule?
context: Britannica and Plato's Republic: roughly 35 years of education plus 15 years of service in lower offices means a guardian reaches the top only at about 50 — a deliberately brutal filter for power. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/philosopher-king.

question: For centuries no one knew exactly where Plato was buried or how he died. Then in 2024, scientists used new imaging technology to read a scroll charred solid when Vesuvius buried Herculaneum in 79 AD. It revealed Plato's resting place — a private garden at the Academy — and a startling detail of his final night: dying in bed at about 80, lucid to the very end, he spent some of his last breath on one sharp, oddly specific criticism. What was that deathbed criticism?
answer: A flute-girl's poor sense of rhythm
choices: A flute-girl's poor sense of rhythm
A student's sloppy, ill-made argument
A wrongly copied line of his own writing
A house-slave's clumsy, noisy serving
context: Deciphered via the Vesuvius Challenge, research led by Prof. Graziano Ranocchia. The scroll says Plato, dying near a shrine to the Muses, criticized a Thracian flute-girl's rhythm. Source: https://www.euronews.com/culture/2024/04/30/platos-death-revealed-from-charred-remains-of-vesuvius-eruption-scroll.

question: Two teams raced to be first to the South Pole in 1911. The British team under Robert Scott brought motor sledges that broke down and ponies that struggled in the cold and had to be shot. Roald Amundsen's Norwegian team ran on skis behind teams of sled dogs, and Amundsen reached the Pole first with a cold-blooded plan he had worked out in advance. What was the ruthless plan that gave Amundsen his edge?
answer: He planned exactly which dogs to shoot along the way to feed the rest
choices: He planned exactly which dogs to shoot along the way to feed the rest
He planned to abandon any man who could not keep the pace
He planned to leave all his supplies behind and travel with nothing
He planned to wait out the worst storms inside buried snow caves
context: Amundsen took 52 dogs and scheduled in advance the exact day each dog would be shot once it had hauled its load — the dead dogs were fed to the surviving dogs and the men. He had learned dog-driving and the use of fur clothing from the Inuit in the Arctic. Scott instead relied on motor sledges that broke down and ponies that had to be shot. Source: livescience.com, science history of the South Pole race.

question: Ernest Shackleton sailed his ship Endurance toward Antarctica, but the pack ice of the Weddell Sea closed around it and held it fast. For months the trapped ship drifted with the ice, while the slow grip of the frozen sea pressed harder on its wooden hull. On 21 November 1915, after all those months, what became of the Endurance?
answer: The ice crushed it and it sank
choices: The ice crushed it and it sank
The thawing ice set it free in the spring
The crew chopped it loose and sailed on
The ice carried it gently onto solid land
context: The Endurance was crushed by the pack ice of the Weddell Sea and sank on 21 November 1915, marooning Shackleton's 28 men on the drifting ice with no ship. Source: coolantarctica.com, Shackleton Endurance Trans-Antarctic Expedition.

question: His ship gone, Ernest Shackleton was stranded on bleak Elephant Island with his men and knew no rescue ship would ever happen upon them there. So on 24 April 1916 he and five hand-picked men climbed into the James Caird, a 22-foot open lifeboat barely longer than a rowboat, and pushed off into the Southern Ocean. What was their desperate plan with that little open boat?
answer: To sail 800 miles across the stormiest ocean to reach help on South Georgia
choices: To sail 800 miles across the stormiest ocean to reach help on South Georgia
To row a few miles out and wait for a passing ship
To paddle around the island hunting seals for food
To ride out the winter sleeping aboard the boat near shore
context: Shackleton left 22 men under Frank Wild on Elephant Island and set out in the 22-foot James Caird on 24 April 1916 to cross 800 miles of the Southern Ocean to South Georgia and bring back rescue. Source: Wikipedia, 'Voyage of the James Caird'.

question: On the death-march home from the South Pole, Captain Lawrence Oates was crippled by frostbite and slowing his starving companions down, and he knew it. One night, in a blizzard, he rose and stepped out of the tent on purpose — never to be seen again. What did Oates quietly say as he went out to die so the others might live?
answer: 'I am just going outside and may be some time'
choices: 'I am just going outside and may be some time'
'Tell my wife I love her dearly'
'Go on without me and save yourselves'
'I will return before the storm breaks'
context: Captain Lawrence Oates, frostbitten and unable to keep pace, walked out of the tent into a blizzard to spare his companions, saying 'I am just going outside and may be some time.' He was never seen again. Source: Wikipedia, 'Terra Nova Expedition'.

question: Robert Peary announced he had reached the North Pole on 6 April 1909 — but just days before, Dr. Frederick Cook claimed HE had stood at the Pole a year earlier. The two men fought bitterly over who was first. Cook's whole claim collapsed when investigators caught him in a separate lie about a famous mountain. What earlier boast unraveled and destroyed Cook's credibility?
answer: His claim to be first to summit Denali (Mt. McKinley)
choices: His claim to be first to summit Denali (Mt. McKinley)
His claim to have crossed Antarctica alone
His claim to have discovered a new continent
His claim to have sailed around the world twice
context: Dr. Frederick Cook claimed he reached the North Pole in April 1908, a year before Peary. Peary denounced him as a fraud, and Cook's credibility collapsed when it emerged he had also lied about being first to summit Denali (Mt. McKinley). Peary's own claim remains disputed to this day. Source: beyondpenguins.ehe.osu.edu, 'Who Got There First: The North Pole Controversies'.

question: In 1938 Czechoslovakia's mountain borderland was home to about three million ethnic Germans, and Adolf Hitler demanded it. At the Munich conference Britain and France agreed to hand this region straight to Germany. What was this borderland called?
answer: The Sudetenland
choices: The Sudetenland
The Rhineland
The Saarland
East Prussia
context: The Sudetenland was Czechoslovakia's fortified mountain rim. German troops were to occupy it starting 1 October 1938 and finish by 10 October. In return Hitler 'promised peace.' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Agreement; encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/timeline-event/holocaust/1933-1938/munich-agreement)

question: Neville Chamberlain, Britain's Prime Minister, became so linked with the policy of appeasing Hitler that one ordinary object he was always pictured with turned into the mocking symbol of the whole policy. Which everyday object became that symbol?
answer: His umbrella
choices: His umbrella
His top hat
His walking cane
His pocket watch
context: Cartoonists and Hitler alike fixed on Chamberlain's umbrella. An MI5 file even recorded Hitler's sneer that if 'that silly old man comes interfering here again with his umbrella, I'll kick him downstairs and jump on his stomach in front of the photographers.' (foreignpolicy.com/2006/10/13/the-umbrellas-shadow/; nationalarchives.gov.uk/education/resources/chamberlain-and-hitler/)

question: On the evening of 30 September 1938 Neville Chamberlain stood at a window of 10 Downing Street, having just returned from signing the Munich Agreement, and told the cheering crowd to 'go home and get a nice quiet sleep.' Which four-word promise did he make to them that night?
answer: Peace for our time
choices: Peace for our time
Peace for a generation
An honourable lasting peace
Peace across all Europe
context: His full line: 'for the second time in our history a British Prime Minister has returned from Germany bringing peace with honour. I believe it is peace for our time.' The 'peace with honour' part deliberately echoed Disraeli in 1878. (encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/timeline-event/holocaust/1933-1938/chamberlains-peace-for-our-time-speech; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_for_our_time)

question: With Britain mobilizing its Navy and handing out gas masks, Neville Chamberlain told the nation by radio on 27 September 1938 how strange it was to be digging trenches at home over a distant dispute. How did he describe Czechoslovakia in that broadcast?
answer: A far-away country between people of whom we know nothing
choices: A far-away country between people of whom we know nothing
A small state caught between two great and hostile empires
A loyal friend we are honour-bound to stand beside
A powder keg that could set the whole continent alight
context: Full line: 'How horrible, fantastic, incredible it is that we should be digging trenches and trying on gas-masks here because of a quarrel in a far away country between people of whom we know nothing.' (encyc.org/wiki/Chamberlain's_Radio_Broadcast,_September_27,_1938)

question: During the September 1938 crisis the 69-year-old Neville Chamberlain did something no British Prime Minister had done before: he climbed into an aeroplane three times in two weeks to go bargain with Hitler in person. The very first trip took him to Hitler's private retreat high in the Bavarian Alps. Where did Chamberlain fly first?
answer: Berchtesgaden
choices: Berchtesgaden
Nuremberg
Berlin
Hamburg
context: The three flights came in quick succession: Berchtesgaden (Hitler's mountain retreat, 15 Sept), Bad Godesberg (~22-23 Sept), then Munich (29-30 Sept). Flying to a summit was almost unheard of for a leader then. (nationalarchives.gov.uk/education/resources/chamberlain-and-hitler/; historyhit.com/neville-chamberlains-three-flying-visits-to-hitler-in-1938/)

question: The Munich Agreement was signed at about 1:30 a.m. on 30 September 1938 by Adolf Hitler, Neville Chamberlain, Edouard Daladier, and Benito Mussolini. They were carving up Czechoslovakia. Of those signing leaders, how many represented Czechoslovakia, the country being dismembered?
answer: None — not one Czechoslovak was at the table
choices: None — not one Czechoslovak was at the table
One — only their president was allowed to sign
Two — their president and foreign minister
Three — a small Czech delegation took part
context: Czechoslovakia's fate was decided entirely by Germany, Britain, France, and Italy. Two Czech envoys, Vojtech Mastny and Hubert Masarik, were not in the room — they were kept waiting nearby. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Agreement)

question: While the four powers decided Czechoslovakia's fate at Munich, the two Czech envoys, Vojtech Mastny and Hubert Masarik, were made to wait in an adjoining room for hours, then summoned at 1:30 a.m. to simply be handed the verdict. Masarik wrote down how Neville Chamberlain behaved while their country was being sentenced. What did he record Chamberlain doing?
answer: Yawning openly, without trying to hide it
choices: Yawning openly, without trying to hide it
Studying his papers in tense silence
Apologizing quietly to the two envoys
Pacing the room unable to sit still
context: Masarik wrote: 'The atmosphere was oppressive; sentence was about to be passed,' and that Chamberlain 'was yawning continuously, without making any effort to conceal his yawns.' (Shirer, The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich, erenow.org/ww/risefallthirdreich/66.php; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Agreement)

question: Less than six months after 'peace for our time,' Hitler's troops marched into Prague on 15 March 1939 and seized the rest of Czechoslovakia. Hermann Goring threatened President Emil Hacha that the Luftwaffe would flatten Prague unless he gave in. What did Hacha do when faced with that threat?
answer: He collapsed, then signed his country away
choices: He collapsed, then signed his country away
He refused and was arrested that night
He fled the capital before dawn
He ordered the army to fight
context: Hacha physically collapsed under the pressure and signed at 3:55 a.m., handing the last of Czechoslovakia to Hitler and shattering the Munich promise. (history.com/this-day-in-history/march-15/nazis-take-czechoslovakia; nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/appeasement-and-peace-our-time)

question: Edouard Daladier, France's premier, flew home from Munich braced to be booed by an angry mob for handing the Sudetenland to Hitler. Instead the Paris crowd cheered him and threw flowers, relieved that war had been avoided. Watching them celebrate, Daladier muttered bitterly to his aide through his teeth. What did he say?
answer: Ah, the fools!
choices: Ah, the fools!
We are lost.
God save France.
They will learn soon enough.
context: In French: 'Ah, les cons!' Daladier knew the deal was a defeat even as the crowds celebrated it as a triumph. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89douard_Daladier; Shirer, erenow.org/ww/risefallthirdreich/66.php)

question: Defenders of Neville Chamberlain make their strongest case like this: in autumn 1938 Britain was simply not ready to fight. Fighter Command had just 25 squadrons, mostly obsolete biplanes, and RAF chief Hugh Dowding himself advised buying time. During the delay before war came, Britain built a system later called the war's single most important force-multiplier. What was it?
answer: A coastal radar network (Chain Home)
choices: A coastal radar network (Chain Home)
A fleet of new battleships
A long-range bomber force
A fortified wall along the coast
context: The Chain Home radar chain was funded and built on Chamberlain's watch; by the 1940 Battle of Britain, Fighter Command had grown to 58 squadrons of modern Spitfires and Hurricanes. This is appeasement's strongest defense: it bought Britain time to prepare. (newstatesman.com/politics/2018/04/did-neville-chamberlain-create-conditions-raf-win-battle-britain; warhistory.org/article/chamberlain-prudent-appeasement-i)

question: On 5 October 1938 Winston Churchill rose in a House of Commons that was about to approve the Munich Agreement by 366 votes to 144, and refused to celebrate it — Nancy Astor heckled that he was talking 'nonsense.' In the speech's blunt opening, what did Churchill call what Britain had just done at Munich?
answer: A total and unmitigated defeat
choices: A total and unmitigated defeat
A regrettable but necessary peace
A triumph of patient diplomacy
A fair bargain honestly struck
context: Churchill: 'we have sustained a total and unmitigated defeat,' and of Czechoslovakia, 'Silent, mournful, abandoned, broken, Czechoslovakia recedes into the darkness.' He warned it was 'only the first sip... of a bitter cup.' No Conservative voted against the deal; Churchill's group only abstained. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_total_and_unmitigated_defeat; winstonchurchill.org/resources/speeches/1930-1938-the-wilderness/the-munich-agreement/)

question: Alfred Duff Cooper, First Lord of the Admiralty, had ordered the Royal Navy mobilized during the crisis — and he became the only member of Chamberlain's cabinet to resign over the Munich Agreement, quitting on 3 October 1938. Explaining why, he said he could have lived with some hard outcomes but not the one Britain had chosen. How did he draw the line in his resignation speech?
answer: War with dishonour — that was too much
choices: War with dishonour — that was too much
Peace at this price I cannot defend
Surrender is not a policy I will sign
Honour has been traded for a quiet sleep
context: Duff Cooper said he could accept 'War with honour or peace with dishonour... but war with dishonour — that was too much.' The famous line 'you were given the choice between war and dishonour; you chose dishonour and you will have war' is usually pinned on Churchill, but it does not appear in his verified 5 October speech — its likeliest true root is Duff Cooper's documented resignation. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duff_Cooper; winstonchurchill.hillsdale.edu/alfred-duff-cooper/)

question: Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of miles of open Pacific, finding tiny islands lost in a vast ocean. Archaeologists who searched their voyaging canoes for the tools that guided them found that the navigators sailed with which of these aboard?
answer: None of them — no instruments at all
choices: None of them — no instruments at all
A magnetic compass and a sandglass
A sextant for reading the sun
A rolled chart of the islands
context: No compass, no sextant, no charts — archaeologists have found no evidence of any navigational device ever carried on a Polynesian voyaging canoe. Everything was held in the navigator's memory and senses. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_navigation

question: On the tiny island of Satawal, the master navigator Mau Piailug began learning the sea as a baby, before he could even walk. To start teaching him, his family did what with the infant Mau?
answer: Set him in tide pools to feel the pull of the sea
choices: Set him in tide pools to feel the pull of the sea
Tied him to the mast of a canoe
Read him the names of the stars at night
Floated him on a raft of coconut fronds
context: As a boy Mau then learned the stars from chunks of coral laid out in the sand. To teach, navigators drew a circle in the sand for the sky, used stones for stars, shaped coconut fronds into a canoe, and laid single fronds for the swells. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mau_Piailug

question: White terns roost on land each night, then fly far out to sea at dawn to fish and stream back at dusk. A Polynesian navigator far from any island spots a flock of these terns at DAWN, beating out to sea. To steer toward land, which way should the navigator turn the canoe?
answer: Back along the path the birds just flew out from
choices: Back along the path the birds just flew out from
Out toward the fishing grounds, following the birds
Straight ahead, keeping the birds dead in line
Wait for dusk, then trail the birds back to land
context: White terns (manu-o-Ku) fly up to about 120 miles out to sea to fish, turning a pinpoint island into a target hundreds of miles wide. The trick is the direction depends on the time: at DAWN the birds are leaving land, so land lies BEHIND them — you sail toward where they came FROM; at DUSK they are heading home, so you follow them. https://www.tetiaroasociety.org/biosphere-tetiaroa/white-tern

question: On 1 May 1976 the double-hulled canoe Hokule'a left Maui for Tahiti, navigated only by Mau Piailug reading stars, swells, and birds. After 34 days at sea the canoe sailed into Tahiti — and to greet it on the shore came what?
answer: Half the island — about 17,000 people
choices: Half the island — about 17,000 people
A handful of colonial officials
A single welcoming chief
No one, the harbour was empty
context: On the 31st day Mau predicted land was near; the next day they sighted white terns, then the atoll Mataiva, reaching Tahiti on 4 June. Roughly 17,000 people — half of Tahiti's population — came down to greet the canoe. https://archive.hokulea.com/holokai/1976/ben_finney.html

question: The Marshall Islanders wove the only 'maps' in the whole Pacific — delicate lattices of coconut ribs and cowrie shells, the curving sticks showing how ocean swells bend around islands. What did they do with these stick charts?
answer: Studied them onshore but never took them to sea
choices: Studied them onshore but never took them to sea
Lashed them to the prow to steer by
Traded them to passing European ships
Burned them after each voyage as offerings
context: The Marshall Islands stick charts were memorization aids used onshore. The curving sticks showed how ocean swells bend and meet around islands; the cowrie shells marked the islands. The chart stayed home — the knowledge went to sea in the navigator's head. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_navigation

question: When clouds blacked out the stars, the master navigator Mau Piailug could still hold his course by ocean swells — he could tell eight separate swell patterns apart at once. To read them, how did Mau sense the swells?
answer: By the canoe's motion against his own body as he lay in the hull
choices: By the canoe's motion against his own body as he lay in the hull
By trailing his hand over the side to feel the water
By the sound the waves made striking the bow
By the spray's taste, salty from the open sea
context: Lying flat inside the hull, Mau read the canoe's roll, pitch, and yaw through his own body. A sudden change in roll meant the canoe had drifted off course. He could distinguish eight separate swell patterns at once. https://daily.jstor.org/pius-mau-piailug-master-navigator-of-micronesia/

question: Sailing toward the low Tuamotu islands, a Polynesian navigator could spot an atoll before the land itself rose into view — by reading a clue painted across the sky. What did the navigator watch for overhead?
answer: A faint green tint thrown onto the clouds by the lagoon below
choices: A faint green tint thrown onto the clouds by the lagoon below
A ring of dark storm clouds circling the island
A bright halo around the moon at night
A column of smoke from the islanders' fires
context: The shallow lagoon of an atoll reflects a greenish glow onto the underside of the clouds above it. Sailing toward the Tuamotus, navigators watched for the green tint from the lagoon of Anaa atoll before the island itself was visible. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_navigation

question: In 1769 Captain James Cook met Tupaia, a priest-navigator from Raiatea, and asked him about the Pacific. From memory alone, Tupaia produced something that astonished Cook. What was it?
answer: A chart of about 130 islands, naming 74 of them
choices: A chart of about 130 islands, naming 74 of them
A logbook of his past voyages in writing
A wooden globe carved with the islands
A list of every star in the night sky
context: Tupaia drew Cook a chart covering about 130 islands within a 2,000-mile radius, naming 74 from memory. Even after Cook's Endeavour sailed all the way around New Zealand and on toward Indonesia, Tupaia could still point accurately back toward Tahiti the whole time. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tupaia_(navigator)

question: Polynesian settlers did not just sail to a barren new island — they arrived ready to build a home from nothing, carrying what they called a 'transported landscape' in the hulls. What did that cargo consist of?
answer: Live pigs, dogs, and chickens with taro, breadfruit, and coconut
choices: Live pigs, dogs, and chickens with taro, breadfruit, and coconut
Stone tools and weapons for conquest
Gold and shells to trade with whoever they found
Timber and rope to build a fort on landing
context: Settlers carried the animals and plants of life so a barren island could be turned into home. A large Tongan double canoe was reputed to carry up to 100 people along with this living cargo. https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1586/polynesian-navigation--settlement-of-the-pacific/  (Legend.)

question: A star sits in the right spot to steer by for only a short while before it climbs too high in the sky to use. To navigate through a whole night, a Polynesian navigator memorized a 'star path' — the greatest of them carrying how much in their heads?
answer: Over 150 stars and the exact bearing of each
choices: Over 150 stars and the exact bearing of each
The single brightest star to follow all night
A dozen constellations and their shapes
The phases of the moon for a full year
context: A 'star path' is a memorized sequence of stars: as one climbs out of position, the navigator switches to the next. The greatest navigators carried over 150 stars and their bearings entirely in memory. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_navigation

question: Across Polynesia, gardeners were growing the kumara, the sweet potato, centuries before any European ship reached the Pacific. That fact stunned historians, because the sweet potato is native to one place far across the sea. Where?
answer: South America
choices: South America
Southeast Asia
West Africa
Australia
context: The sweet potato is native to South America, yet was grown across Polynesia from around AD 1200-1300 — long before Europeans arrived. It is strong evidence that Polynesian voyagers reached the Americas and sailed all the way back. https://phys.org/news/2024-09-unexpected-discovery-early-sweet-potato.html

question: Polynesian navigators passed down stories of te lapa, something strange they said could appear in the deep ocean sometimes a hundred miles from any land and help them point the canoe toward islands they could not yet see. How did the navigators describe te lapa?
answer: Streaks of light darting toward land from under the water
choices: Streaks of light darting toward land from under the water
A wind that always blew in from the nearest shore
A taste of fresh water rising in the open sea
A low humming that came up through the hull
context: Legend, told as the navigators' own testimony: te lapa ('the flashing') is described as underwater light-flashes that dart toward land from below the surface, used to re-orient toward unseen islands. The phenomenon is still not fully explained by science. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_navigation

question: Without any instrument to clock the canoe's speed, a navigator still needed to know how far along the voyage he was. The Caroline Islanders solved this with a mental trick called etak. In etak, the navigator pictures the scene how?
answer: The canoe sits still while an unseen island slides backward past the stars
choices: The canoe sits still while an unseen island slides backward past the stars
The canoe races forward while the stars stay frozen above
The whole ocean tilts and pours the canoe toward land
The island sends out ripples the canoe rides inward
context: Etak (the word means 'refuge') has the navigator imagine the canoe motionless while a reference island slides backward, passing under one star bearing after another. By tracking how far the imaginary island has 'moved,' he always knows his progress — without ever measuring his own speed. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etak_(navigation)

question: Polynesian navigators across the Pacific steered by what they called a 'star compass.' A young Hawaiian named Nainoa Thompson spent years relearning the lost system in the 1970s before he could use it to find Tahiti. What was a star compass, really?
answer: A memorized map of where each star rises and sets around the horizon
choices: A memorized map of where each star rises and sets around the horizon
A carved wooden ring notched with the positions of the stars
A wide bowl of water that mirrored the night sky back up
A bundle of pointing sticks aimed at the brightest stars
context: The star compass is a mental map, not an object. The navigator memorizes the point on the horizon where each star rises and sets; in the Hawaiian version revived by Nainoa Thompson, the horizon is divided into 32 'houses' (11.25 degrees apart), and a star that rises in one house always sets in the matching house opposite. https://hokulea.com/polynesian-wayfinding/

question: The 17-year-old Pliny the Younger watched Mount Vesuvius erupt across the Bay of Naples and later wrote that the enormous cloud rising over the mountain looked exactly like one particular thing. What did he say the towering cloud most resembled?
answer: An umbrella pine tree
choices: An umbrella pine tree
A giant stone tower
A coiled black serpent
A crashing ocean wave
context: Pliny the Younger wrote that the cloud 'more closely resembled a pine-tree than anything else, for what corresponded to the trunk was of great length and height, and then spread out into a number of branches' — the tall, flat-topped Italian stone pine. Source: Pliny the Younger, Letter 6.16.

question: When Vesuvius buried Pompeii in 79 AD, people who could not escape were entombed where they fell. The ash hardened around their bodies, which slowly rotted away over the centuries and left empty body-shaped hollows in the rock. In 1863 the archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli figured out a clever way to bring those vanished people back into view. What did he do?
answer: He poured liquid plaster into the hollows
choices: He poured liquid plaster into the hollows
He carefully dug out their preserved bones
He photographed the bodies before they decayed
He wrapped the remains in cloth bandages
context: Fiorelli poured plaster of Paris into each cavity, let it harden, then chipped away the surrounding ash — recovering the exact final shape of the person, down to faces, folds of clothing, and dying positions. The famous 'casts' of Pompeii are plaster, not bone. Source: Giuseppe Fiorelli; historyskills.com.

question: Set in the floor at the entrance of the House of the Tragic Poet in Pompeii is a mosaic of a snarling black dog on a chain, with three Latin words spelled out in tiles between its paws. It is one of the world's earliest known versions of a sign you still see on gates today. What do the words CAVE CANEM mean?
answer: Beware of the Dog
choices: Beware of the Dog
Welcome to Our Home
Wine Sold Here
Closed for the Holiday
context: CAVE CANEM — 'Beware of the Dog' — was laid in mosaic tiles at the doorway, excavated in 1824. Source: history.com; Wikipedia, House of the Tragic Poet.

question: One of the most famous plaster casts from Pompeii is a chained guard dog from the House of Orpheus. Its owners fled the eruption and left it tied up, and as the ash kept rising the dog fought to climb above it. What does the cast show the dog frozen in the act of doing?
answer: Twisting onto its back straining against its collar
choices: Twisting onto its back straining against its collar
Curled up asleep beside the front door
Leaping clear over the garden wall
Calmly guarding a bowl of food
context: Found in 1874, the dog had climbed atop the deepening ash and twisted onto its back with legs in the air, straining against the bronze ring on its collar — the cast froze it in that exact pose, and the bronze ring is still on the collar. Source: seepompeii.com; pompeiiinpictures.com.

question: Excavators digging out a Pompeii bakery found an oven that had been sealed shut by the eruption with the day's baking still inside — about 80 round loaves abandoned mid-bake. After nearly 2,000 years, what had Vesuvius's heat done to the bread?
answer: Baked it black and rock-hard like charcoal
choices: Baked it black and rock-hard like charcoal
Turned it to fine grey powder
Left it soft and perfectly fresh
Melted it into a sticky paste
context: The carbonized loaves survive, baked black and stone-hard. The round flat loaf (panis quadratus) was scored into 8 wedges; one surviving loaf is even stamped 'Celer, slave of Quintus Granius Verus' — the baker's mark. Source: historyandarchaeologyonline.com.

question: Pompeii's stone streets get deep with mud and water, so the Romans set tall flat stepping stones across them, spaced with gaps in between. A pedestrian could cross without stepping in the muck, while the gaps let one particular thing pass straight through. What were the gaps sized to let through?
answer: The wheels of carts and chariots
choices: The wheels of carts and chariots
Herds of grazing sheep
Streams of rainwater downhill
Marching ranks of soldiers
context: The gaps were spaced so cart and chariot wheels rolled straight between the stones. Generations of wheels carved ruts five to ten inches deep into the paving, and Pompeii has about twenty times more crossing stones than any other known Roman city. Source: world-archaeology.com.

question: Almost everything we know about the day Vesuvius erupted comes from one person: Pliny the Younger, who watched from across the bay as a teenager and, 25 years later, wrote two letters about it to the historian Tacitus. Among all the people in all the towns Vesuvius struck, what makes Pliny's letters so prized by historians?
answer: They are the only eyewitness account that survives
choices: They are the only eyewitness account that survives
They are the only letters of Pliny that survive
They name every town the eruption destroyed
They were copied into Rome's imperial archive
context: Pliny the Younger's Letters 6.16 and 6.20 to Tacitus are the sole surviving eyewitness record of the disaster — the named primary source for the whole event. Source: Pliny the Younger, Letters 6.16 and 6.20; ancientworldmagazine.com.

question: As Vesuvius erupted, the famous naturalist Pliny the Elder commanded the Roman fleet across the bay and got a message from a woman named Rectina begging for rescue. Instead of fleeing the danger, he ordered his ships to sail straight toward the burning mountain. According to his nephew, what did Pliny the Elder say to his helmsman as he gave the order?
answer: 'Fortune favours the bold'
choices: 'Fortune favours the bold'
'All is now lost'
'Let the gods decide'
'Save yourselves and run'
context: 'Fortes Fortuna iuvat' — 'Fortune favours the bold; try to reach Pomponianus.' Pliny the Elder sailed across the bay to Stabiae to rescue his trapped friend Pomponianus, where he later died. Source: Pliny the Younger, Letter 6.16.

question: When Pliny the Elder reached the town of Stabiae, burning stones and pumice were falling out of the sky onto everyone there. To shield their heads as they moved through the deadly rain of stones, what did Pliny the Elder and his companions tie on?
answer: Pillows fastened down with cloths
choices: Pillows fastened down with cloths
Bronze army helmets
Wooden shields held overhead
Wet leather hoods
context: 'They placed pillows on their heads and secured them with cloths, as a precaution against the falling stones.' Source: Pliny the Younger, Letter 6.16.

question: Lining the streets of Pompeii were more than 80 shops called thermopolia, each with an L-shaped marble counter set with big round holes. Terracotta jars sat down in those holes, and a Roman could walk up, stand at the counter, and get served on the spot. What were these shops for?
answer: Selling hot food and wine to go
choices: Selling hot food and wine to go
Storing the town's tax records
Washing and dyeing wool
Renting out chariots and horses
context: Thermopolia were ancient fast-food bars — the round counter holes held jars of hot food and wine, and Romans grabbed quick meals of stewed legumes, meat skewers, and wine standing at the counter, like a modern takeaway shop. Source: contexttravel.com.

question: At Herculaneum, near Pompeii, a young man died in an instant on a wooden bed when a blast of gas heated his town past 500 degrees. In 2020 researchers led by Pier Paolo Petrone opened his skull and found something never seen in any other human remains, formed from his own brain by the heat. What had the extreme heat turned his brain into?
answer: Black glass, like obsidian
choices: Black glass, like obsidian
Solid white salt crystals
A lump of pure gold
Fine drifting ash
context: The brain was heated above roughly 510 °C, then cooled so fast it vitrified into glass — the only known case of a vitrified human brain, published in the New England Journal of Medicine. Source: NEJM 2020; CNN.

question: The eruption charred the 1,800 papyrus scrolls of Herculaneum's library into fragile black lumps that crumble if anyone tries to unroll them, so for 250 years no one could read a word. Then in 2023 a $1 million contest, the Vesuvius Challenge, set students loose on CT scans to find faint ink without opening the scrolls. The 21-year-old Luke Farritor pulled out the first whole word ever recovered. What did that first word mean?
answer: Purple
choices: Purple
Soldier
River
Silence
context: Farritor decoded the Greek word 'porphyras' — 'purple' — from an unopened scroll using AI to detect ink traces in CT scans; a team then recovered over 2,000 letters of ancient Greek philosophy. Source: scrollprize.org; Smithsonian Magazine.

question: For centuries everyone dated the eruption to August 24, 79 AD — but that date survives only through a copied manuscript of Pliny's letter, and Pompeii itself holds physical clues that the traditional summer date is wrong. Besides a charcoal inscription scratched with an October date, what did excavators find at Pompeii that points to a colder season?
answer: Carbonized fruit and heavy clothing on the victims
choices: Carbonized fruit and heavy clothing on the victims
Wine jars sealed for the new vintage
Olive presses left full mid-pressing
Shutters closed against the cold
context: Carbonized autumn fruit, the heavy clothing worn by victims, and charcoal heaters set up in houses all point to a colder season — so many scholars now argue for October. The August date survives only through Pliny's letter. Source: getty.edu; National Geographic.

question: In the 1500s the Spanish dug a mountain of silver out of Cerro Rico in the Andes and minted it into a big silver coin that was accepted on every continent — the first truly global money, the way the dollar is today. People called this famous eight-real coin by what nickname?
answer: Pieces of eight
choices: Pieces of eight
Crowns of Castile
Wheels of silver
Lions of Madrid
context: The eight-real Spanish dollar, minted from Potosí silver, became the first global currency. The modern dollar sign ($) probably descends from the peso symbol stamped on those very coins. Sources: sites.google.com/site/100objectsbritishmuseum (British Museum, pieces of eight); ncvgrading.com/the-piece-of-eight/.

question: The Andean city of Potosí grew so fabulously rich from its silver mountain that the city put a boast right into its own coat of arms. What did Potosí declare itself to be?
answer: Treasure of the world, king of the mountains, envy of kings
choices: Treasure of the world, king of the mountains, envy of kings
First daughter of Spain, jewel of the southern sea
Guardian of the Andes, shield of the Inca
Gate of the Pacific, market of two oceans
context: Potosí's coat of arms boasted in words: 'I am rich Potosí, treasure of the world, king of the mountains, envy of kings.' Sources: sldinfo.com/2020/12/potosi-and-its-silver-the-beginnings-of-globalization/; globaltrademag.com/as-rich-as-potosi/.

question: Miguel de Cervantes, who wrote Don Quixote, helped make famous a Spanish saying that means 'worth a fortune' — and Spaniards still use it today whenever something is fabulously valuable. Which of these is the real saying?
answer: Vale un Potosí (worth a Potosí)
choices: Vale un Potosí (worth a Potosí)
Rico como el Perú (rich as Peru)
El oro del rey (the king's gold)
La plata del cielo (silver from heaven)
context: 'Vale un Potosí' — 'it's worth a Potosí' — still means 'worth a fortune' in Spanish, the silver mountain's name standing in for boundless wealth. Sources: thenaturalsapphirecompany.com/education/.../potosi/; context.reverso.net (vale un Potosí).

question: To force workers up Cerro Rico, the Spanish viceroy Francisco de Toledo signed a 1573 decree creating a rotating forced-labor draft — about 13,500 Indigenous men hauled up the mountain at a time, pulled from sixteen Andean provinces, each village owing its turn of men. What was this dreaded labor draft called?
answer: The mita
choices: The mita
The encomienda
The repartimiento
The corvée
context: Viceroy Francisco de Toledo's 1573 decree established the mita; the Spanish took the name from the Inca word mit'a, meaning 'a turn.' Source: dokumen.pub/potosi-the-silver-city... ; andeanroadperu.com/mita-system....

question: So many Indigenous and African workers died inside Cerro Rico's shafts and in the deadly mercury refining that historians estimate the dead in the millions over the colonial centuries. The silver mountain earned a grim nickname that captured what it did to its workers. What was the mountain called?
answer: The mountain that eats men
choices: The mountain that eats men
The widow's hill
The graveyard peak
The devil's furnace
context: The death toll from the mines and mercury amalgamation was so staggering that Cerro Rico became known as 'the mountain that eats men.' Estimate is medium-confidence. Sources: sciencedirect.com/.../S2214790X16300764; realsafetyai.org/.../potosi-silver-mercury-mining.

question: Spanish galleons carried Potosí's silver across the Pacific on yearly voyages between Acapulco and Manila from 1565 onward, pouring New World silver into Asian markets for two and a half centuries. Scholars estimate that an astonishing share of ALL the silver ever dug from the New World — somewhere between a third and a half of it — ended up absorbed into a single country's taxes and trade. Which country swallowed that silver?
answer: China
choices: China
India
Persia
The Ottoman Empire
context: Carried on the Manila galleons (1565–1815), between one-third and one-half of all New World silver ended up in China, where it was absorbed for taxes and trade. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_silver_trade...; bulliontradingllc.com/blog/spanish-silver-fleets/.

question: In August 1968, half a million Warsaw Pact troops and over 6,000 tanks poured into Czechoslovakia to crush its reforms. The Czechs and Slovaks refused to shoot back -- instead they fought the tank columns without a single weapon. What did they do to make the invaders lose their way?
answer: They repainted the road signs so the tank columns got lost
choices: They repainted the road signs so the tank columns got lost
They flooded the streets to bog the tank columns down
They blocked the bridges so the tank columns turned back
They cut the power so the tank columns drove blind
context: Czechs and Slovaks tore down house numbers and repainted road signs to confuse the invaders -- famously leaving the sign for 'Moscow' pointing the soldiers back the way they came. They argued with the troops in the streets rather than firing on them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Pact_invasion_of_Czechoslovakia.

question: On January 16, 1969, a 20-year-old Charles University student named Jan Palach walked to the top of Prague's Wenceslas Square, poured petrol over himself, and set himself on fire to protest his nation's surrender to the Soviet occupation. He left a letter signing himself with a chilling name and warning that others would follow. What name did he give himself?
answer: "Torch No. 1"
choices: "Torch No. 1"
"The Last Czech"
"Free Prague"
"Student Zero"
context: Palach signed his protest letter 'Torch No. 1' and claimed a secret group of volunteers would keep burning themselves until censorship ended -- though investigators found that group never existed; the threat was meant to wake the nation. Burned over about 85% of his body, he died three days later on Jan 19, 1969. His self-immolation helped forge the dissident playwright Vaclav Havel, who would lead the 1989 Velvet Revolution. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Palach; english.radio.cz/czech-martyr-jan-palachs-enduring-legacy.

question: Tourists call the giant stone figures on Easter Island 'the heads,' because heads are all you can see poking out of the grassy slope of the Rano Raraku volcano. When archaeologists dug down around the base of about 150 of them, what did the diggers find under the soil?
answer: Full bodies buried up to the shoulders
choices: Full bodies buried up to the shoulders
Tunnels linking the statues underground
Rows of smaller statues beneath them
The carvers' stone tools left behind
context: The Easter Island 'heads' (moai) actually have full torsos and arms, buried over centuries by erosion. From 2010 Jo Anne Van Tilburg's Easter Island Statue Project excavated the hidden bodies and found crisp carvings that had been protected underground while the exposed faces above weathered smooth. Source: https://www.livescience.com/20580-easter-island-heads-bodies.html ; https://www.eisp.org/ (Easter Island Statue Project).

question: El Castillo, the great pyramid at Chichen Itza, was built so that twice a year — on the spring and autumn equinox — the late-afternoon sun lines up exactly with its northern staircase. For just a few minutes, sunlight and the pyramid's own shadow paint a shape onto the steps. What appears on the great staircase?
answer: A snake of light slithering down the stairs
choices: A snake of light slithering down the stairs
A cross of light spreading across the stairs
A ladder of light climbing the stairs
A ring of light circling the stairs
context: The triangles of light and shadow connect to a stone serpent's head carved at the foot of the staircase, so a giant feathered snake (Kukulkan) seems to slither down the pyramid. El Castillo is also a calendar in stone: its four sides have 91 steps each, which with the top platform total 365 — one per day of the year. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/travel/world-heritage/article/chichen-itza ; https://popular-archaeology.com/article/chichen-itzas-shadows/.

question: For centuries no one could explain how the people of Easter Island moved their giant stone figures, the moai, weighing many tons, miles from the quarry — with no wheels, no animals, and no metal tools. In 2012 archaeologists Carl Lipo and Terry Hunt tested an old island legend using a 4.35-ton replica and just 18 people pulling on three ropes. How did they move it?
answer: They rocked it upright and walked it forward
choices: They rocked it upright and walked it forward
They rolled it along on a bed of logs
They dragged it flat on a wooden sled
They floated it around the coast by raft
context: Rapa Nui oral tradition long held that the moai 'walked' to their platforms, and the 2012 experiment showed how: three rope teams rocked the upright statue side to side so it waddled forward like a refrigerator being shuffled, covering 100 meters in 40 minutes. The road-statues were engineered for it — a wide D-shaped base and a forward lean of 5-15 degrees that makes them tip and step. Lipo: 'Once you get it moving, it isn't hard at all.' Source: https://www.binghamton.edu/news/story/5830/easter-islands-statues-actually-walked-and-physics-backs-it-up (Lipo & Hunt, Journal of Archaeological Science).

question: The Aztec Sun Stone is a 24-ton basalt disk that packs a whole cosmology into rings carved inside rings. Four square panels set around its center are labeled Four Jaguar, Four Wind, Four Rain, and Four Water. In Aztec belief, what did these four panels record?
answer: Four earlier worlds, each one destroyed
choices: Four earlier worlds, each one destroyed
Four gods who hold up the sky
Four directions of the Aztec compass
Four great festivals of the year
context: Each panel names a previous age and how it ended: Four Jaguar (eaten by jaguars), Four Wind (blown away by hurricanes), Four Rain (consumed by fire), and Four Water (drowned by flood). They frame the present, fifth age — Nahui Ollin, 'Four Movement' — which the Aztecs believed was prophesied to end in earthquakes. The whole disk is rimmed by two fire serpents (Xiuhcoatl) meeting snout-to-snout. Source: https://www.mexicolore.co.uk/aztecs/calendar/calendar-stone ; https://artsandculture.google.com/story/decoding-the-sun-stone/CwUBgE-UXSRhLw.

question: In 1978, electric-company workers digging beneath Mexico City struck a huge carved stone disk — a find that led archaeologists to unearth the buried Aztec Templo Mayor. The disk shows the moon goddess Coyolxauhqui, and the carving freezes one violent moment from a myth in which her own brother, the sun-god Huitzilopochtli, turns on her. What does the stone show?
answer: Her body decapitated and hacked into pieces
choices: Her body decapitated and hacked into pieces
Her body chained to the face of the moon
Her body turned to stone where she stood
Her body cast into the burning underworld
context: Coyolxauhqui ('Bells-Her-Cheeks') is shown beheaded and dismembered, her head, arms, and legs hacked off and scattered after Huitzilopochtli defeats her. The workers struck the monolith on February 21, 1978, which triggered the full excavation of the Templo Mayor at the heart of old Tenochtitlan. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coyolxauhqui_Stone ; https://smarthistory.org/templo-mayor-at-tenochtitlan-the-coyolxauhqui-stone-and-an-olmec-mask/.

question: On the West African coast there was a low headland that fourteen Portuguese expeditions reached and then turned back from in terror, without ever rounding it. Sailors called the water just beyond it the "Sea of Darkness" and swore it boiled and hid monsters at the edge of the world. Which dreaded cape was the wall of fear they would not pass?
answer: Cape Bojador
choices: Cape Bojador
Cape Verde
Cape of Good Hope
Cape Finisterre
context: Cape Bojador was a low, unremarkable headland, but the legend of boiling seas and monsters beyond it stopped fourteen expeditions cold. The 'edge of the world' turned out to be just more coastline. (legend — the boiling seas and monsters were sailors' belief, not fact) Source: https://fathomsdeepbeyond.substack.com/p/beyond-the-cape-of-fear

question: In 1434 the Portuguese captain Gil Eanes finally sailed past Cape Bojador, the cape everyone swore was the edge of the world. To prove to doubters back home that he had truly walked the desert shore beyond it, he carried home one ordinary piece of evidence from that far shore. What did Gil Eanes bring home as his proof?
answer: A handful of "St. Mary's roses"
choices: A handful of "St. Mary's roses"
A jar of the boiling seawater
A captured sea monster
A fragment of the world's edge
context: Gil Eanes brought back the little desert flowers the Portuguese called Rosa de Santa Maria — 'St. Mary's roses.' A fistful of flowers was the proof that the terrifying edge of the world was nothing but ordinary coastline. Source: https://www.encyclopedia.com/science/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/gil-eannes-passes-point-no-return-cape-bojador-and-inaugurates-new-era-exploration

question: An old square-rigged ship could only run with the wind pushing it from directly behind — face a headwind and it was stuck. The caravel borrowed a triangular sail from the Arab dhow that changed everything: a ship could now zig-zag its way FORWARD against a wind blowing at it. What was this game-changing triangular sail called?
answer: The lateen sail
choices: The lateen sail
The mainsail
The spinnaker
The topsail
context: The triangular lateen sail let a caravel sail within five points of the wind and tack — zig-zagging forward against a headwind. That one change is what let ships fight their way home instead of waiting for a tailwind that might never come. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Caravel/

question: Everyone calls Dom Henrique of Portugal (1394–1460) 'Henry the Navigator,' yet he barely went to sea — he stayed home, planned the voyages, and took a 20% cut of their profits. Stories still say he ran a great navigation school at Sagres that taught Portugal's captains. What is the surprising truth about that famous Sagres school?
answer: It never existed — the story was invented a century after he died
choices: It never existed — the story was invented a century after he died
It trained only mapmakers, never actual sea captains
It was secretly run by his brother, not by Henry
It burned down before a single voyage set sail
context: The famous 'navigation school at Sagres' is a myth invented in the 1600s, long after Henry's death — Sagres isn't even a usable port, and the real expeditions sailed out of Lagos. Henry organized the Age of Exploration from a chair, paying for voyages and taking his 20% cut. Source: https://kids.kiddle.co/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator

question: For Portuguese ships, sailing OUT was easy but getting HOME was the killer — north of the equator the wind and current shove a coast-hugging ship the wrong way. The navigators cracked it with a trick they named the volta do mar, the 'turn of the sea.' How did a captain actually use the volta do mar to get home?
answer: Sail boldly out into the open Atlantic, loop northwest to catch westerly winds, then turn east for home
choices: Sail boldly out into the open Atlantic, loop northwest to catch westerly winds, then turn east for home
Hug the coastline north, then cut inland and portage the ship past the worst of the contrary current
Run far south first to gather speed, then loop back along the steady coastal trade winds to the north
Wait at anchor for the seasonal winds to reverse, then ride the new tailwind straight up the coast
context: The volta do mar meant steering AWAY from home to get home: out into the open ocean, looping northwest until you hit the westerlies, then riding them east. Gil Eanes used the same out-to-sea logic to slip past Cape Bojador's reefs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volta_do_mar

question: Early Portuguese navigators found their latitude with a beautifully simple trick: sail until the Pole Star sits at the same height it sat at your home port, then turn and run straight home. But as they pushed south down Africa, the trick suddenly stopped working near the equator. What had gone wrong, forcing them to measure the sun instead?
answer: The Pole Star had sunk below the horizon and vanished from view
choices: The Pole Star had sunk below the horizon and vanished from view
The Pole Star had grown too dim to see clearly
The Pole Star had drifted to a new spot in the sky
The Pole Star had been hidden by the southern haze
context: The Pole-Star trick only works in the north. Crossing toward the equator, the star dropped below the horizon and disappeared. So in 1485 the Portuguese assembled a navigator, a mathematician and an astronomer to build the first daily tables of the sun's height — the sun became the new compass for southern seas. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariner's_astrolabe

question: Below the Canary Islands lay Cape Bojador, which sailors called a wall of fear — they swore the sea beyond it boiled into storms and that no ship rounding it would ever come home. For a dozen years Prince Henry's captains kept turning back. In 1434 his squire Gil Eanes finally swung boldly out into the open ocean, sailed past the cape, and found calm water. To prove he had truly landed on the far side, what did Gil Eanes carry back to Portugal?
answer: Wild roses he had picked there
choices: Wild roses he had picked there
A chunk of the cape's red rock
A jar of the strange dark seawater
A feather from an unknown bird
context: Gil Eanes, born in Lagos, beat Cape Bojador by using the volta do mar — swinging away from the coast into open sea instead of hugging the shore. He reported the water beyond was 'as easy to sail in as the waters at home' and brought back wild St. Mary's roses (rosemary-like plants) as proof he had set foot on land past the cape. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Eanes; worldhistory.org/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator.

question: Off the Guinea coast of Africa, Portuguese ships could sail OUT easily with the wind but then could not get home against it, so crews were terrified of going too far. Prince Henry's shipwrights answered with a small, shallow ship called the caravel. Instead of the usual big square sail, what shape of sail did they rig on it — the feature that let it claw its way back against a headwind?
answer: Triangular sails
choices: Triangular sails
Round bag-shaped sails
Double-decked square sails
Folding fan-shaped sails
context: The caravel's triangular (lateen) sails let it tack within about five points of a headwind, so it could sail not just WITH the wind but against it — finally letting ships return home against the Atlantic winds and currents off Guinea. The shallow draft also let it work close to coasts. Source: worldhistory.org/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator.

question: Around 552 CE, King Seong of the Korean kingdom of Baekje sent the Japanese court a gift that would change Japan forever: a gleaming bronze statue and a set of holy scriptures. What religion arrived on Japan's shores inside that gift?
answer: Buddhism
choices: Buddhism
Confucianism
Hinduism
Daoism
context: King Seong of Baekje sent the bronze Buddha and Buddhist scriptures around 552 CE — a foreign god landing on Japanese shores. It split the court into clans who wanted to worship it and clans who feared the native kami. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism_in_Japan; worldhistory.org/Prince_Shotoku/

question: In 604 CE Prince Shotoku of Japan built a new system to mark a court official's rank — so a man could rise by his own merit instead of the family he was born into. He gave each of the 12 ranks its own badge. What did an official wear to show his rank?
answer: A hat of a certain color
choices: A hat of a certain color
A bronze arm-ring
A jade belt-buckle
A tattoo on his cheek
context: Shotoku's 'cap rank' system (604 CE) showed an official's rank by the COLOR of his hat. With 12 ranks open to merit, a talented man no longer needed noble birth to climb. Source: worldhistory.org/Prince_Shotoku/

question: Prince Shotoku of Japan (574-622 CE) ran the government and reformed its laws for nearly thirty years — yet he was never the ruler himself. In whose name did he govern as regent from 594 to 622 CE?
answer: His aunt, Empress Suiko
choices: His aunt, Empress Suiko
His brother, a Soga lord
His father, the old emperor
His cousin, a Baekje prince
context: Shotoku served as regent for his aunt, Empress Suiko, governing in her name from 594 to 622 CE. He never sat on the throne, but the cap-rank system, the Seventeen Articles, and the great temples all came from his regency. Source: worldhistory.org/Prince_Shotoku/

question: In 607 CE Prince Shotoku of Japan sent his envoy Ono no Imoko to the mighty Sui emperor of China carrying a letter. Its opening line named the two countries by the sun — a pairing that put their rulers on the same plane. How did the letter name the two countries?
answer: The land of the rising sun, to the land of the setting sun
choices: The land of the rising sun, to the land of the setting sun
The land of the morning star, to the land of the evening star
The land of the eastern sea, to the land of the western mountains
The land of the high heavens, to the land of the wide earth
context: The 607 letter began: 'The Son of Heaven where the sun rises, to the Son of Heaven where the sun sets, may good health be with you.' Calling Japan the rising sun and China the setting sun put the two rulers on the same plane. Emperor Yang of Sui was angered that a small island called its ruler 'Son of Heaven' — yet still sent an envoy back, because he wanted Japan's friendship against the kingdom of Goguryeo. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ono_no_Imoko

question: Prince Shotoku's Seventeen-Article 'constitution' (604 CE) was not a list of laws but a code of governing ethics for Japan's officials. Its final article, Article XVII, gives one piece of advice to anyone who holds power. What does it warn against?
answer: Deciding important matters by one person alone
choices: Deciding important matters by one person alone
Punishing a man harder than his crime deserves
Raising a man's rank above the one he was born to
Letting officials grow rich off the people's taxes
context: Article XVII warns: 'Decisions on important matters should not be made by one person alone' — they should be discussed with many. The Seventeen Articles wove Confucian and Buddhist ethics into a code for how Japan's new centralized state should govern. Source: worldhistory.org/Prince_Shotoku/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventeen-article_constitution

question: After the 18th Amendment took effect in 1920 and shut down America's legal saloons, a new kind of bar appeared -- hidden behind an unmarked door you could enter only by giving the right password. What were these illegal hidden bars called?
answer: A speakeasy
choices: A speakeasy
A bootleg hall
A rum house
A blind tavern
context: By 1925 an estimated 100,000 speakeasies were operating in New York City alone -- where one legal saloon used to stand -- each entered by giving a password at the door. Source: Ken Burns PBS Prohibition: Unintended Consequences, https://www.pbs.org/kenburns/prohibition/unintended-consequences

question: Al Capone, the most feared crime boss of Chicago's bootlegging era, was known by a one-word nickname that came from the deep marks on the left side of his face. What was that nickname?
answer: Scarface
choices: Scarface
Big Al
The Enforcer
Iron Jaw
context: Capone earned 'Scarface' in a knife fight at the Harvard Inn in Coney Island: after Capone insulted Frank Galluccio's sister, Galluccio slashed his face three times, leaving scars that took eighty stitches and never healed. Source: https://www.biography.com/crime/al-capone and https://www.todayifoundout.com/index.php/2015/03/al-capone-nicknamed-scarface/

question: On February 14, 1929, four men strode into a Chicago garage where seven of Bugs Moran's gang were waiting, and within seconds the gang lined up calmly with their backs turned and their hands raised -- then about 70 machine-gun rounds tore into them. What trick had made hardened gangsters line up so meekly?
answer: The killers were dressed as policemen, so the men thought it was a raid
choices: The killers were dressed as policemen, so the men thought it was a raid
The killers claimed to be delivering a shipment of whiskey
The killers said Moran had called a peace meeting
The killers flashed badges stolen from a real detective
context: Because the gunmen wore police uniforms, Moran's men assumed it was an arrest and lined up against the wall to be searched -- then were cut down inside the S-M-C Cartage garage at 2122 North Clark Street. The day gave the killing its name: the St. Valentine's Day Massacre. Source: https://themobmuseum.org/exhibits/massacre-wall/ and https://www.britannica.com/event/Saint-Valentines-Day-Massacre

question: George 'Bugs' Moran was the real target of the St. Valentine's Day Massacre, the rival gang boss the killers had come to gun down. Yet his name is not among the seven dead. What saved Bugs Moran's life that morning?
answer: He was running late and turned back when he spotted the 'police' car outside
choices: He was running late and turned back when he spotted the 'police' car outside
He had skipped town the night before after a tip-off
He was hidden in a back office during the shooting
He had already made peace with Capone's gang
context: Moran arrived late, saw what he thought was a real police car parked outside the garage, and turned away -- missing the slaughter of his own men by minutes. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/Saint-Valentines-Day-Massacre and https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/february-14/the-st-valentines-day-massacre

question: Al Capone's bootlegging empire murdered rivals and earned him an estimated $60 million a year, yet the law could never pin a killing on him. When the government finally convicted him on October 18, 1931, and sent him to prison for 11 years, what was the charge that actually brought him down?
answer: Income tax evasion
choices: Income tax evasion
Ordering the garage massacre
Running illegal breweries
Bribing Chicago police
context: IRS Special Intelligence agents traced cash from his gambling profits and proved he reported no taxable income; Capone got 11 years, a $50,000 fine, and $215,000 in back taxes -- not a single bootlegging or murder charge. Source: https://prologue.blogs.archives.gov/?p=6083 and https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/october-17/capone-goes-to-prison
