question: During Prohibition a small squad of agents led by Eliot Ness raided Al Capone's breweries in Chicago. They earned a famous nickname after they publicly turned down huge bribes from Capone's gang, proving they could not be bought. What were Ness and his men called?
answer: The Untouchables
choices: The Untouchables
The Iron Squad
The Dry Agents
The Capone Busters
context: The name stuck because they refused Capone's bribes in public; their raids smashed his breweries, but it was IRS tax agents -- not Ness -- who actually put Capone behind bars. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Eliot-Ness and https://www.atf.gov/our-history/eliot-ness

question: Around 150 CE in Alexandria, Claudius Ptolemy wrote the book that ruled astronomy for over a thousand years. He titled it the plain Greek 'Mathematike Syntaxis' (The Mathematical Composition), but the world remembers it by a half-Arabic name its later translators stuck on it. What does that famous name, the 'Almagest,' literally mean?
answer: The Greatest
choices: The Greatest
The Heavens
The Composition
The Almanac
context: Arab translators called it 'al-majisti' — 'al-' ('the') plus a mangled Greek 'megiste' ('greatest') — and that accidental name stuck instead of Ptolemy's own duller title. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almagest

question: Ptolemy's Earth-centered model already had planets riding small circles (epicycles) on bigger circles (deferents), yet earlier versions still ran slightly off the real sky. His cleverest fix was an imaginary off-center point, set opposite Earth, from which a planet sweeps equal angles in equal times — the device his predecessors lacked that finally made the forecasts match. What is that point called?
answer: the equant
choices: the equant
the epicycle
the deferent
the eccentric
context: The equant let a planet's apparent speed vary while keeping the math accurate — so accurate the model lasted until Copernicus, who rejected the equant on philosophical grounds because it broke perfect uniform circular motion, pushing him toward the Sun-centered view. Source: https://www.britannica.com/science/Ptolemaic-system

question: Pythagoras ran a real secret brotherhood in ancient Greece. To join, a new follower had to obey one strange rule for five whole years before they were even allowed to meet Pythagoras face to face. What did the rule demand for those five years?
answer: Total silence — no speaking at all
choices: Total silence — no speaking at all
Sleeping outdoors every night
Walking everywhere barefoot
Giving away all their money
context: New initiates kept complete silence for five years before they could meet Pythagoras in person. The brotherhood was a genuine secret society with strict laws. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagoras

question: In the brotherhood of Pythagoras, breaking the community's laws got a member expelled. But the others did something eerie to mark the expulsion, as if the person were no longer alive. What did they do to a member they cast out?
answer: Built a tombstone for them as if they had died
choices: Built a tombstone for them as if they had died
Burned all of their writings in the square
Shaved their head and marked their face
Forbade anyone to ever say their name
context: When a member was expelled, the brotherhood erected a tombstone for them as though they had died. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagoras

question: Pythagoras forbade his followers to eat fava beans. Legend says this very rule cost him his life: chased by attackers, he reached the edge of a field of fava beans and refused to escape through it, because running through the beans would break his own law. What happened to Pythagoras at that field?
answer: He stopped at the edge and was killed there
choices: He stopped at the edge and was killed there
He hid among the bean plants until dawn
He turned and fought the attackers off
He bargained to be spared the beans
context: In the legend (LEGEND), Pythagoras halted rather than trample the sacred beans, and his pursuers caught and killed him there. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagoras

question: Aristotle recorded a wild claim about Pythagoras: that he had a GOLDEN body part, which Pythagoras would show off in public at the Olympic Games as proof he was no ordinary man — even a god of the far north in human form. Which body part was said to be made of gold?
answer: His thigh
choices: His thigh
His left hand
His forehead
His heart
context: Aristotle wrote that Pythagoras displayed a golden thigh (LEGEND) at the Olympics and to Abaris the Hyperborean, claiming to be Apollo of the north in human form. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagoras

question: The Pythagoreans treated one shape as sacred enough to swear their secret oath upon it: a triangle built from ten dots, arranged in rows of one, two, three, and four. They called it 'nature's eternal fountain' and held ten to be the perfect number. What was the name of this holy triangle of ten dots?
answer: The tetractys
choices: The tetractys
The monad
The gnomon
The decad
context: The tetractys (1+2+3+4 = 10) was so sacred the initiates swore their oath by it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetractys

question: The Pythagoreans believed whole numbers ruled the entire universe. Then a follower named Hippasus let out a discovery that shattered that belief — that some numbers are 'irrational' and can't be written as a whole-number fraction. The legend says what fate befell Hippasus for letting this secret out?
answer: He drowned at sea, a punishment from the gods
choices: He drowned at sea, a punishment from the gods
He was struck blind and wandered into exile
He was buried alive beneath the meeting hall
He was turned to stone where he stood
context: In the famous legend (LEGEND), Hippasus drowned at sea for revealing the irrationals. Historically the story is shaky — no ancient writer actually credits Hippasus with discovering irrational numbers. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippasus

question: Every kid learns the right-triangle rule as 'the Pythagorean theorem.' But a clay tablet called Plimpton 322, written around 1800 BC, already lists whole-number right-triangle side-sets. Why does that tablet cast doubt on the idea that Pythagoras discovered the rule?
answer: Babylonian scribes knew the rule a thous-plus years before Pythagoras was born
choices: Babylonian scribes knew the rule a thous-plus years before Pythagoras was born
It proves the rule was first carved by Egyptian temple builders
It shows the rule was copied from a lost Chinese manual
It reveals Pythagoras bought the rule from a Persian trader
context: Plimpton 322 (c. 1800 BC) lists Pythagorean triples over a thousand years before Pythagoras lived, showing Babylonian scribes knew the right-triangle rule first. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plimpton_322

question: Buried in pits near the city of Xi'an, China, stands an entire army of about 8,000 life-sized clay soldiers built to guard the First Emperor in death. For more than two thousand years no one knew it was there. In March 1974, who stumbled onto it?
answer: Farmers digging a well
choices: Farmers digging a well
Monks repairing a temple
Soldiers digging a trench
Builders laying a railway
context: Local farmers hit the buried army by accident while digging a well near Xi'an. The pits held some 8,000 clay warriors plus 130 chariots and over 600 horses. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army

question: Qin Shi Huang, China's First Emperor, replaced the many different coins of the conquered states with one official coin called the banliang. What did this new coin look like?
answer: A round coin with a square hole in the middle
choices: A round coin with a square hole in the middle
A square coin stamped with the emperor's face
A triangle of bronze strung on a cord
A flat gold bar marked with a dragon
context: The round disc stood for round heaven and the square hole for the square earth. That round-coin-with-a-square-hole shape became THE shape of Chinese money for over two thousand years, lasting into the 20th century. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banliang

question: China's dirt roads were worn with deep wheel ruts, and a cart built in one region could get stuck on a road in another. To fix this across his whole empire, Qin Shi Huang standardized one surprising measurement so every wagon fit the same ruts. What did he make the same for all carts?
answer: The width of every cart's axle
choices: The width of every cart's axle
The number of horses per cart
The color painted on each wagon
The size of each cart's load
context: One axle-width for the entire empire meant a cart from any region rolled smoothly down any rutted road. He standardized this the way he standardized coins and writing. https://www.nationalgeographic.com/culture/article/qin-shi-huangdi

question: Older Chinese kingdoms had each built their own stretches of border wall against the northern raiders. After Qin Shi Huang united China, what did he do with those scattered walls?
answer: Joined and extended them into one long northern wall
choices: Joined and extended them into one long northern wall
Tore them all down to open the trade roads
Left them exactly as the old kingdoms had built them
Replaced them with a line of wooden watchtowers
context: He linked the older walls into a continuous defense said to run more than 10,000 li -- the origin of what became the Great Wall. He drove hundreds of thousands of soldiers and convicts to build it, and countless workers died in the work. https://www.nationalgeographic.com/culture/article/qin-shi-huangdi

question: Qin Shi Huang named himself the First Emperor and decreed his heirs would rule as Second Emperor, Third Emperor, and onward for 'ten thousand generations' -- and in Chinese, 'ten thousand' means forever. After he died, how long did his forever-dynasty actually last?
answer: It collapsed within about four years
choices: It collapsed within about four years
It ruled for three more centuries
It lasted a thousand more years
It held the throne for ten more generations
context: The dynasty he meant to last ten thousand generations fell apart within roughly four years of his death in 210 BCE. https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Qin_Shi_Huang

question: In 227 BCE the assassin Jing Ke came before the King of Qin pretending to offer him a gift, so he could get close enough to strike. He had smuggled a poisoned dagger into the throne room. Where was the blade hidden?
answer: Rolled up inside a map
choices: Rolled up inside a map
Sewn into his left sleeve
Sunk in a jar of wine
Strapped beneath his boot
context: As the map was unrolled to its end, the dagger appeared; Jing Ke grabbed it and lunged. The king tore free, but his ceremonial sword was so long he couldn't draw it -- until a court physician hurled his medicine bag at Jing Ke, buying the king the moment he needed to draw and cut the assassin down. https://history.followcn.com/2019/02/14/jing-kes-failed-assassination-attempt-of-qin-king/

question: Desperate to live forever, in 219 BCE Qin Shi Huang sent the alchemist Xu Fu sailing east across the sea toward the mythical Mount Penglai to bring back an elixir of immortality from the immortals. According to legend, what did the emperor load onto Xu Fu's fleet to send with him?
answer: Three thousand young boys and girls
choices: Three thousand young boys and girls
Three hundred trained war elephants
A thousand bars of carved jade
Two hundred chests of silver coins
context: Legend says the fleet carried some 3,000 young boys and girls plus many craftsmen. Xu Fu never came back -- one tale says he landed in a far country and made himself its king. https://kids.kiddle.co/Xu_Fu

question: When you look across the thousands of terracotta soldiers in Qin Shi Huang's tomb pits, something is true of every single warrior's face that you would never expect from mass-produced clay. What is it?
answer: No two faces look exactly alike
choices: No two faces look exactly alike
Every face wears the same calm smile
All the faces copy the emperor's own
Each face is left blank and unfinished
context: Scholars found roughly ten base facial molds that were then individualized so no two soldiers match. They were originally painted bright -- malachite green, azurite blue, cinnabar red -- but in Xi'an's dry air the paint can flake off in under four minutes once a figure is uncovered. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army

question: The historian Sima Qian wrote that inside Qin Shi Huang's sealed tomb, craftsmen made the rivers and seas of China 'flow' across a model of the land. Centuries later, scientists tested the soil of the still-unopened mound and found one substance far above natural levels -- highest exactly where Sima Qian said the rivers ran. What was it?
answer: Mercury
choices: Mercury
Melted gold
Sea salt
Black tar
context: Sima Qian wrote that 'Mercury was used to fashion imitations of the hundred rivers, the Yellow River and the Yangtze, and the seas... in such a way that they seemed to flow.' Modern soil tests of the unopened mound found mercury concentrated just where he said the rivers were -- an ancient text confirmed by the dirt. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mausoleum_of_Qin_Shi_Huang

question: In 213 BCE Qin Shi Huang ordered the books of his empire burned -- poetry, the histories of the other states, and philosophy. Yet a few kinds of books were deliberately spared. Which books were allowed to survive?
answer: Useful guides to medicine and farming
choices: Useful guides to medicine and farming
Poems and songs of the old kingdoms
Histories of the states he conquered
Teachings of the Confucian scholars
context: On his chancellor Li Si's advice, only useful books were spared -- medicine, divination, agriculture and forestry, and the records of Qin itself. Anyone caught keeping a banned book was branded and sent as a convict to labor on the wall. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burning_of_books_and_burying_of_scholars

question: The historian Sima Qian recorded that in 212 BCE Qin Shi Huang had about 460 scholars at the capital killed and announced it across the empire as a warning. His own eldest son, Fusu, protested that this cruelty would stir up rebellion. How did the emperor answer his son's protest?
answer: He exiled Fusu to the northern frontier
choices: He exiled Fusu to the northern frontier
He named Fusu his heir on the spot
He spared the rest of the scholars
He put Fusu in charge of the capital
context: Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian says roughly 460 scholars were buried alive in pits at the capital, Xianyang. When Fusu warned this would cause unrest, his father banished him to the far northern border -- a decision that would doom Fusu after the emperor's death. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burning_of_books_and_burying_of_scholars

question: After the First Emperor died, the eunuch Zhao Gao seized the real power and wanted to know which officials would obey him no matter what. He brought a deer into the court and loudly insisted it was a horse, watching who dared correct him. What became of this trick?
answer: It became a Chinese saying for forcing a lie
choices: It became a Chinese saying for forcing a lie
It became a court game played at banquets
It became a test that new judges had to pass
It became a children's riddle about animals
context: Officials who honestly called it a deer were later executed. 'Point at a deer and call it a horse' is still a Chinese idiom for using raw power to make everyone repeat a lie they know is false. https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chinese_Stories/Calling_a_deer_a_horse

question: The Great Exhibition of 1851 was held in a gigantic building of glass and iron in London's Hyde Park, raised in just nine months. The building was so enormous that, rather than cut down the park's full-grown elm trees, the builders simply enclosed something inside it. What did the glass palace swallow whole?
answer: The park's full-grown elm trees
choices: The park's full-grown elm trees
A row of royal carriage stables
A small stone parish church
The bandstand and its musicians
context: The building was nicknamed the 'Crystal Palace,' designed by the gardener Joseph Paxton and raised in only nine months; living elms of Hyde Park stood inside it. Source: https://www.royalparks.org.uk/read-watch-listen/great-exhibition-1851-hyde-park

question: Queen Victoria and Prince Albert had nine children, and as those children grew up they married into royal houses all across Europe — so that decades later a huge share of the continent's kings, queens and emperors were her descendants. What nickname did this web of royal grandchildren earn Victoria?
answer: The Grandmother of Europe
choices: The Grandmother of Europe
The Iron Queen of London
The Mother of Parliaments
The Empress of the Seas
context: Her nine children — including the future Edward VII — married across the continent, spreading her bloodline through Europe's thrones. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Victoria

question: On 14 December 1861 Prince Albert died of typhoid, and his widow Queen Victoria was so shattered that she dressed in black mourning for the rest of her life — another forty years — and hid away from the public almost completely. What mournful nickname did the people give her in those years?
answer: The Widow of Windsor
choices: The Widow of Windsor
The Lady of the Lamp
The Queen of Sorrows
The Veiled Regent
context: Victoria wore black for the remaining 40 years of her life and withdrew so far from public view that she became known as 'the Widow of Windsor.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Victoria

question: On 2 March 1882 a man named Roderick Maclean fired a pistol at Queen Victoria at Windsor railway station, furious that she had ignored a poem he had sent her. A crowd of boys from nearby Eton College was on hand — and they did not wait for the police. How did the Eton schoolboys deal with the gunman?
answer: They beat him down with their umbrellas
choices: They beat him down with their umbrellas
They tackled him into the railway carriage
They pinned him with a coil of station rope
They pelted him with stones from the track
context: The Eton schoolboys set upon Maclean with their umbrellas. His was the eighth and last of the assassination attempts on Victoria. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roderick_Maclean

question: After Roderick Maclean shot at Queen Victoria in 1882, a jury took only five minutes to find him 'not guilty, but insane' — and that wording so enraged Victoria that she pushed Parliament to rewrite the law on insane defendants. What change did the Trial of Lunatics Act of 1883 make to the verdict's wording?
answer: It changed 'not guilty' to 'guilty, but insane'
choices: It changed 'not guilty' to 'guilty, but insane'
It abolished the insanity defence entirely
It moved such cases to military tribunals
It required two juries to agree on a verdict
context: Victoria objected that a would-be assassin should not walk free as 'not guilty'; the 1883 Act recast the verdict as 'guilty, but insane,' which stood in British law for decades. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roderick_Maclean

question: The Aztec god Quetzalcoatl is called the "feathered serpent": coatl is the Nahuatl word for serpent, and quetzalli names the brilliant, shimmering green feather his image borrows. From which creature does that emerald feather come?
answer: The long tail-feather of the quetzal bird
choices: The long tail-feather of the quetzal bird
The wing-feather of a golden eagle
The crest-feather of a scarlet macaw
The plume of a great horned owl
context: Quetzalli was the iridescent emerald tail-feather of the quetzal bird; fused with coatl, "serpent," the name means literally "feathered serpent." The same god was worshipped under other names across Mexico. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quetzalcoatl (etymology).

question: In 2003 archaeologists found a sealed tunnel running beneath the Temple of the Feathered Serpent at Teotihuacan. Alongside jade masks and jaguar bones, by 2015 they had uncovered a miniature mountain landscape built to represent the underworld and, shockingly, glittering pools of a liquid metal. What metal pooled in that buried underworld?
answer: Liquid mercury, lying in shimmering pools
choices: Liquid mercury, lying in shimmering pools
Molten gold, poured into shallow basins
Liquid silver, cooled into bright sheets
Melted copper, set in carved channels
context: Excavators of the sealed tunnel reported pools of liquid mercury, a startling find that with the miniature mountain landscape seems meant to evoke the underworld. The Temple of the Feathered Serpent itself bristles with roughly 260 carved stone serpent heads. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_the_Feathered_Serpent,_Teotihuacan.

question: The Inca ran a sprawling empire — census, taxes, armies, storehouses — with no writing system at all. To keep their records they instead used the quipu: a main horizontal cord with dozens of thinner strings hanging off it. What did the strings carry the numbers in?
answer: Tied knots, read by their height on the string
choices: Tied knots, read by their height on the string
Painted symbols brushed onto the fibers
Carved marks notched into wooden tags
Stamped clay beads strung along the cord
context: The quipu (khipu) worked like a three-dimensional spreadsheet of colored string — a main cord with dozens to hundreds of hanging strings, each tied with knots. The Inca recorded numbers this way despite having no script of any kind. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Quipu/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quipu

question: On an Inca quipu the knots encoded numbers in base-10, and the trick was that the same knot meant a different amount depending on WHERE you tied it. A knot near the free bottom end of the string and an identical knot higher up stood for different things. What told you a knot's value?
answer: Its height on the string set its place value
choices: Its height on the string set its place value
Its color set whether it counted at all
Its distance from the next string over
Its thickness set how many it stood for
context: The ones digit sat at the bottom near the free end, tens above it, hundreds higher still, with a gap between each place — exactly like our columns. Zero was shown by simply leaving a gap with no knot. To write 586 you'd tie six knots near the free end, leave a space, eight for the tens, a space, then five for the hundreds. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quipu ; https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/Inca_mathematics/

question: In 1976 the 3,000-year-old mummy of the pharaoh Ramesses II had to fly from Egypt to Paris so French scientists could treat a fungus eating away at it. Before the dead king could legally enter France, the Egyptian government handed him something no other ancient corpse has ever held. What was it?
answer: A real passport, listing his occupation as 'King (deceased)'
choices: A real passport, listing his occupation as 'King (deceased)'
A gold burial mask sealed inside a guarded crate
A new linen wrapping woven by temple priests
A diplomatic letter signed by the Egyptian president
context: Egypt issued Ramesses II's mummy a genuine modern passport with the occupation line reading 'King (deceased)' so it could legally travel. When the plane landed at Le Bourget airport, the French Republican Guard presented arms with full royal military honors, treating the dead pharaoh like a visiting head of state. Source: https://www.ancient-origins.net/history-famous-people/mummy-passport-0010944

question: At the Battle of Kadesh in 1274 BCE, the pharaoh Ramesses II fought the Hittites to a bloody standstill by the Orontes River — the Hittites kept the city, and neither side truly won. Back home in Egypt, Ramesses turned that draw into one of history's earliest pieces of war propaganda. What did he do?
answer: He carved it across his temple walls as a glorious solo victory
choices: He carved it across his temple walls as a glorious solo victory
He paid the Hittite king tribute to keep the peace quiet
He banned his soldiers from ever speaking of the battle
He abandoned the northern border and pulled his army home
context: Ramesses II had the battle written up in the 'Poem of Pentaur' and the 'Bulletin' and carved across multiple temple walls, even claiming he singlehandedly smashed thousands of Hittite chariots. About fifteen years later he and the Hittite king Hattusili III signed the Treaty of Kadesh, regarded as the world's earliest surviving peace treaty. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/78/the-battle-of-kadesh--the-first-peace-treaty/

question: John Rabe was a German businessman running the Siemens office in Nanjing in 1937 - and a member of the Nazi Party. When the Japanese army began slaughtering civilians, Rabe led a committee that turned part of the city into a protected Safety Zone, and more than 200,000 Chinese crowded into it. When Japanese warplanes roared overhead to bomb the city, Rabe and his workers raced to do one desperate thing to make the pilots spare the people below. What did they spread over the refugees like a giant canopy?
answer: A Nazi swastika flag, gambling Japan's German allies would spare it
choices: A Nazi swastika flag, gambling Japan's German allies would spare it
A bright red painted cross to mark the camp as a hospital
A plain white bedsheet raised on poles as a flag of surrender
A captured Chinese banner taken from the city's old garrison
context: Japan was allied to Nazi Germany, so Rabe bet the pilots would not bomb anything flying the swastika. He draped buildings in it and unfurled a huge one as a canopy; over 600 refugees also camped in his own house and garden. A Nazi Party man used the swastika to shield Chinese civilians from Japan's army. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Rabe and https://www.northcountrypublicradio.org/news/npr/127482829/shelter-under-the-swastika-the-john-rabe-story

question: Minnie Vautrin was an American missionary teacher at Ginling Girls' College in Nanjing in 1937. As Japanese soldiers hunted for women to drag off, she turned her campus into a refuge for up to 10,000 women and children and would step her own body directly between the soldiers and the women they came for. The grateful Chinese refugees gave her a name they used for her ever after. What did they call Minnie Vautrin?
answer: The Goddess of Mercy
choices: The Goddess of Mercy
The Iron Schoolmistress
The American Empress
The Lady of the Locked Gate
context: The refugees called Vautrin the 'Goddess of Mercy' for shielding them with her own body. The horror of what she witnessed broke her: she took her own life in 1941, exactly one year to the day after leaving Nanjing, leaving a note that her life 'was a failure.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnie_Vautrin

question: At the dead center of Raphael's fresco The School of Athens, the two greatest Greek philosophers stand side by side. Plato lifts one finger straight up toward the heavens, pointing to his world of perfect ideas. His student Aristotle stands beside him making a very different gesture with his hand. What is Aristotle doing?
answer: Holding his hand flat, palm down toward the earth
choices: Holding his hand flat, palm down toward the earth
Lowering one hand to rest on a marble pillar
Pressing both palms together in front of his chest
Tucking one hand inside the fold of his robe
context: Plato points up to his ideal world of forms; Aristotle holds his palm down toward the real, touchable world. The single most copied gesture in art history sums up the whole split between the two men. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_School_of_Athens

question: Raphael finished his great painting the Sistine Madonna but thought the bottom edge looked too empty. As an afterthought he doodled in two little figures leaning on a railing along the bottom. Those two became one of the most copied images on Earth, printed on countless postcards, mugs, and pillows. What did he add?
answer: Two cherubs
choices: Two cherubs
Two white doves
Two laurel garlands
Two golden trumpets
context: The two cherubs leaning on the railing at the bottom of the Sistine Madonna were a last-second addition, yet they escaped the painting entirely to become a global decoration. Source: https://www.dailyartmagazine.com/raphael-cherubs-sistine-madonna/

question: For the wise old face of Plato at the heart of The School of Athens, Raphael did not invent a face. Instead he painted the features of the great aging master of the generation before his own, the legend he admired most among living artists. Which real man did Raphael use as the face of Plato?
answer: Leonardo da Vinci
choices: Leonardo da Vinci
Sandro Botticelli
Andrea Mantegna
Giovanni Bellini
context: Legend holds that Raphael gave Plato the face of the aging Leonardo da Vinci, so the great master of the previous generation stands forever at the center of the fresco. Source: https://www.thecollector.com/raphael-school-athens-painting/

question: In 1511, after sneaking next door to see the just-finished Sistine Chapel ceiling that all Rome was talking about, Raphael went back and added one last figure to The School of Athens: a lonely man slumped and brooding alone on the marble steps. As a sly dig, he gave this gloomy figure the scowling face of a particular rival. Whose face did Raphael paint onto him?
answer: Michelangelo's
choices: Michelangelo's
Leonardo da Vinci's
Pope Julius II's
Donatello's
context: The brooding, isolated philosopher (Heraclitus) was the last figure Raphael added, and he is widely identified as wearing the scowling face of his great rival Michelangelo, whose Sistine Chapel ceiling Raphael had just seen. Source: https://www.thecollector.com/raphael-school-athens-painting/

question: Raphael died young, on Good Friday in 1520, and was buried inside the ancient Roman Pantheon, an honor almost unheard of for a painter. At his grand funeral, the cardinals carried his body, and then the Pope himself bent down and did something stunning for the dead 'prince of painters'. What did the Pope do?
answer: Kissed the dead painter's hand
choices: Kissed the dead painter's hand
Laid his own crown on the coffin
Wept and tore his ceremonial robe
Carried the coffin on his own shoulder
context: At Raphael's funeral the Pope himself kissed his hand, an honor almost unheard of for a painter, who in his own lifetime was called 'the prince of painters'. He was buried in the Pantheon. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raphael

question: British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher gave a 1976 speech warning that the Soviets were 'bent on world domination.' Soon after, she picked up the nickname that stuck to her for life: the 'Iron Lady.' Who first called her that?
answer: A Soviet army newspaper
choices: A Soviet army newspaper
A British tabloid editor
An American news magazine
Her own Conservative Party
context: The Soviet army paper Krasnaya Zvezda (Red Star) ran a piece on Jan. 24, 1976 headlined 'Zheleznaya Dama' — 'Iron Lady' — meaning it as an insult after her 'Britain Awake' speech. Thatcher seized it: on Feb. 6, 1976 she told her constituency, 'Yes, I am an iron lady... if that's how they wish to interpret my defence of values and freedoms fundamental to our way of life,' and regarded the name 'with amusement and pride.' The enemy named her, and she made the insult her badge. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Britain_Awake

question: At Berlin's Brandenburg Gate in 1987, U.S. President Ronald Reagan stared at the Wall and demanded, 'Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!' Beforehand, one group fought repeatedly to cut that line, calling it 'extreme,' 'too provocative,' and even 'unpresidential.' Who tried to delete it?
answer: His own White House advisers
choices: His own White House advisers
The Soviet leadership in Moscow
The East German government
West Germany's own chancellor
context: It wasn't the enemy who wanted the line gone — it was Reagan's own side. The State Department and National Security Council tried again and again to strike it; Chief of Staff Howard Baker called it 'unpresidential' and Colin Powell agreed. Reagan overruled them all and kept it in. Speechwriter Peter Robinson had gotten the idea from West Berliner Ingeborg Elz, who said of Gorbachev, 'If this man is serious with his talk of glasnost and perestroika, he can prove it by getting rid of this wall.' Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tear_down_this_wall! ; https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2019/11/reagans-mr-gorbachev-tear-down-this-wall-was-almost-left-unsaid

question: Around 1802 an English clergyman named William Paley imagined a man walking across an empty heath. If the man's foot struck a plain stone, he might suppose it had lain there since the beginning of time and think nothing more of it. But Paley said that finding one particular object on the ground would force a completely different conclusion: that someone had designed it on purpose. What was that object?
answer: A watch
choices: A watch
A coin
A key
A buckle
context: Paley opened 'Natural Theology' (1802) with the watch-on-the-heath image: a stone could have lain there forever, but a watch's parts are fitted together for a purpose, so it must have had a maker. He then argued that nature's contrivances, like the eye, point the same way. This 'watchmaker' picture became the concrete handle for the whole design argument. Source: Paley, Natural Theology (1802), Ch. I; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watchmaker_analogy.

question: In the winter of 1819-1820 the 77-year-old Thomas Jefferson sat down with six copies of the New Testament, in Greek, Latin, French, and English. He wanted to keep only the moral teachings of Jesus and meant to throw out every miracle and the resurrection. How did Jefferson assemble his own private gospel from those six books?
answer: He sliced the verses he wanted out with a razor and pasted them into a blank book
choices: He sliced the verses he wanted out with a razor and pasted them into a blank book
He copied the verses he wanted out by hand into a leather travel journal
He dictated the verses he wanted to a young secretary each evening
He marked the verses he wanted in the margins with red ink
context: Jefferson literally took a razor to the six volumes and pasted the surviving passages into 'The Life and Morals of Jesus of Nazareth'; his version ends with Jesus laid in the tomb and the stone rolled across, no resurrection. He said picking out the real teachings was like finding 'diamonds in a dunghill.' For the deist, reason was the sieve: keep the ethics, cut what reason could not accept. Source: smithsonianmag.com 'Why Thomas Jefferson Created His Own Bible'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_Bible.

question: While the deists were trimming religion down to reason, the same century blazed with a religion of the heart. On the evening of 24 May 1738, at a meeting on Aldersgate Street in London, a young preacher named John Wesley sat listening to a reading of Luther's preface to Romans when he felt a sudden certainty that Christ had saved him. Wesley recorded the moment in four famous words. What did he say happened to him?
answer: His heart was strangely warmed
choices: His heart was strangely warmed
A great light shone around him
The ground beneath him shook
A clear voice called his name
context: Wesley wrote in his journal, 'I felt my heart strangely warmed,' and that instant helped launch Methodism and the great Evangelical Revival. Reason did not sweep faith away; alongside the clockmaker God of the deists ran this fire of heart-religion, revelation answering the age of reason. Source: christianhistoryinstitute.org 'Strangely Warmed'; Wesley's Journal, 24 May 1738.

question: Isaac Newton, who worked out the laws of motion and gravity, was no skeptic about God; he was a convinced believer. In 1713 he added a closing passage declaring that 'this most beautiful system of the sun, planets, and comets could only proceed from the counsel and dominion of an intelligent and powerful Being.' Where did Newton place this argument that the orderly heavens prove a Designer?
answer: In the Principia, his masterwork of physics
choices: In the Principia, his masterwork of physics
In a letter found among his private papers
In a sermon delivered at his parish church
In the margins of his own personal Bible
context: The passage is the General Scholium, added to the second edition of the Principia in 1713, where Newton also named God 'Lord God Pantokrator, Universal Ruler,' known by his dominion rather than his substance. The greatest scientist of the age read the regular orbits of the planets, all moving the same way in nearly the same plane, as the fingerprint of that Ruler, building the design argument straight into the masterpiece of physics. Source: Newton's General Scholium, newtonproject.ox.ac.uk/view/texts/normalized/NATP00056.

question: Voltaire was the Enlightenment's sharpest scourge of the Catholic Church, so people are often surprised that he believed firmly in a Creator and was no atheist. In a 1772 poem he made his case with one homely image: he simply could not believe, he wrote, that a certain familiar machine could exist and have no maker. Which machine did Voltaire pick to argue that the universe must have been designed?
answer: A clock
choices: A clock
A loom
A mill
A ship
context: In 'Les Cabales' (1772) Voltaire wrote that the universe baffled him, 'que cette horloge existe et n'ait point d'horloger' - that this clock exists and has no clockmaker. He also penned the line 'If God did not exist, it would be necessary to invent him,' and added in a letter weeks later that 'all nature cries aloud that he does exist.' Same clockwork image as Paley's watch, reached for by the man who mocked the Church hardest. Source: Voltaire, Les Cabales (1772); en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Voltaire.

question: Even at its height the design argument had a brilliant critic. In David Hume's 'Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion,' published in 1779 after his death, a character named Philo grants that similar effects do point to similar causes, then attacks the whole watch-and-watchmaker comparison at its root. What flaw did Philo say wrecks the analogy between a watch and the universe?
answer: A watch we can actually catch a craftsman making, but no one has ever caught the universe being made
choices: A watch we can actually catch a craftsman making, but no one has ever caught the universe being made
A watch will wear out and stop in time, but the universe keeps running on and on without ending
A watch holds only a handful of parts, but the universe holds far more parts than anyone could count
A watch is clearly built to serve a human user, but the universe was plainly not built for human use
context: Philo's point is about evidence: we infer a watchmaker because we have repeatedly watched men build watches, but we have never once observed a world being built, so the comparison has no track record to stand on. Hume put the strongest case against the design argument into the mouth of a character and never settled the matter, leaving the reader to weigh Newton, Voltaire, and Paley on one side against Philo on the other. Source: Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Part II; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dialogues_Concerning_Natural_Religion.

question: After the Civil War, the United States added three amendments to the Constitution to remake the country. The very first of them, the Thirteenth Amendment, was ratified in December 1865. What one big thing did it do?
answer: Abolished slavery throughout the United States
choices: Abolished slavery throughout the United States
Gave women the right to vote
Created the national income tax
Set a term limit for the president
context: Ratification was completed on Dec 6, 1865, when Georgia became the 27th state to approve it. The 13th was the first of the three Reconstruction Amendments; the 19th (women's vote), 16th (income tax), and 22nd (presidential term limit) all came decades later. Source: National Archives milestone documents (archives.gov) + Reconstruction Amendments, Wikipedia.

question: The Fourteenth Amendment, ratified in 1868, declared that everyone 'born or naturalized in the United States' — including the freed slaves — is a citizen. It also promised every person one famous guarantee, the phrase courts would later use to strike down segregation. What guarantee was that?
answer: The equal protection of the laws
choices: The equal protection of the laws
The freedom of speech and the press
The right to a speedy public trial
The right to keep and bear arms
context: The 14th's citizenship clause overturned the old Dred Scott logic that Black Americans could never be citizens, and its 'equal protection of the laws' became the legal engine of later civil-rights cases. Source: National Archives (archives.gov/milestone-documents/14th-amendment) + Constitution Annotated (constitution.congress.gov).

question: After the Civil War, freed Black families across the South longed for land of their own to farm as free people. General William T. Sherman's wartime order to settle them on confiscated coastal plantations gave its name to a famous promise of that dream. What was the promise?
answer: Forty acres and a mule
choices: Forty acres and a mule
A cabin and a cornfield
A plow and a promise
A homestead and a horse
context: The phrase comes from Sherman's Special Field Orders No. 15 (Jan 16, 1865), which set aside 400,000 acres and settled about 18,000 freed families on plots of up to 40 acres; Sherman later lent army mules. President Andrew Johnson reversed it within months, pardoning ex-Confederates and ordering the freed families evicted so the land could return to its former owners — pushing most into sharecropping. Source: Forty acres and a mule, Wikipedia + Georgia Historical Society (georgiahistory.com).

question: By 1870 the freed slaves were citizens, but in most states they still could not vote. The Fifteenth Amendment, ratified that year, attacked the problem head-on: it said the right to vote could not be denied 'on account of' three things. What three things did it name?
answer: Race, color, or previous condition of servitude
choices: Race, color, or previous condition of servitude
Age, wealth, or amount of land owned
Religion, language, or country of origin
Sex, schooling, or record of military service
context: The 15th (ratified Feb 3, 1870) protected the vote 'on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude' — that last phrase meaning a man could not be barred just because he had once been a slave. Its fatal flaw: it banned denying the vote for these reasons but never affirmatively guaranteed anyone the vote, a loophole Southern states would later exploit. Source: National Archives (archives.gov) + Constitution Annotated.

question: In 1866 six bored Confederate veterans in a law office in Pulaski, Tennessee started a secret club with silly costumes and mock-Greek names — but it soon curdled into a terror group that hunted freed Black families. In 1867 a former Confederate cavalry general took command of it under a chilling title. What was that title?
answer: Grand Wizard
choices: Grand Wizard
Supreme Commander
High Marshal
Imperial Regent
context: The club was the Ku Klux Klan, and the general was Nathan Bedford Forrest, named its first Grand Wizard in 1867. What began as a prank-and-costume social club became one of American history's most violent terror organizations. Source: Tennessee Encyclopedia (tennesseeencyclopedia.net) + Britannica (Nathan Bedford Forrest).

question: In 1870 Hiram Revels of Mississippi became the first Black man ever to sit in the United States Senate. In a stroke of poetic justice, he was sworn into one of two Mississippi Senate seats that had sat empty since 1861 — the very seat one famous Southerner gave up when he resigned to join the rebellion. Whose abandoned seat did Revels fill?
answer: Jefferson Davis, a senator from Mississippi
choices: Jefferson Davis, a senator from Mississippi
Robert Toombs, a senator from Georgia
Judah Benjamin, a senator from Louisiana
Clement Clay, a senator from Alabama
context: Davis resigned his Mississippi Senate seat in 1861 and went on to become president of the Confederacy — so a formerly enslaved race's representative took the Senate seat of the man who had tried to build a nation on slavery. Nevada Senator James Nye marked the moment on the floor: 'In the place of that proud, defiant man... comes back one of that humble race whom he would have enslaved forever... What a magnificent spectacle of retributive justice is witnessed here today!' Source: U.S. Senate (senate.gov) + history.com This Day in History.

question: On Easter Sunday 1873, a White mob of more than 300 attacked the courthouse in Colfax, Louisiana, firing a cannon and setting it ablaze — the bloodiest single act of racial slaughter of the entire Reconstruction era, with between 62 and 153 Black men killed. When the trapped Black defenders raised white flags of surrender, what did the mob do?
answer: Shot them down anyway
choices: Shot them down anyway
Burned them inside the courthouse
Hanged them from the courthouse oaks
Dumped them in the Red River alive
context: Many of the attackers were Confederate veterans; the dead were so numerous that bodies were dumped in the Red River. Historian Eric Foner called Colfax 'the bloodiest single instance of racial carnage in the Reconstruction era.' Only 3 White men died. Source: Colfax massacre, Wikipedia + Smithsonian Magazine + 64 Parishes (64parishes.org).

question: In 1892 New Orleans activists deliberately got a man named Homer Plessy arrested on a whites-only railcar to test Louisiana's segregation law in court. They picked Plessy on purpose to expose how arbitrary the color line was — in fact, the conductor had to be told in advance to arrest him. Why did Plessy need pointing out?
answer: He was seven-eighths White by ancestry
choices: He was seven-eighths White by ancestry
He was a well-known local White lawyer
He was dressed as a railway worker
He was traveling with White friends
context: Plessy was seven-eighths White and one-eighth Black — light enough to pass as White, so his arrest made the point that segregation rested on an arbitrary color line. His case became Plessy v. Ferguson. Source: Plessy v. Ferguson, Wikipedia + Britannica (britannica.com/event/Plessy-v-Ferguson-1896).

question: Blanche K. Bruce of Mississippi was born into slavery in Virginia, yet won a full six-year term in the United States Senate. On February 14, 1879, he did something no Black American — and no former slave — had ever done in that chamber. What first did Bruce achieve that day?
answer: He presided over the United States Senate
choices: He presided over the United States Senate
He cast the deciding vote on a bill
He delivered the Senate's opening prayer
He swore in a newly elected senator
context: Bruce was the first Black senator to serve a full six-year term (1875-1881) and, on Feb 14, 1879, the first Black American — and the only former slave — ever to preside over the U.S. Senate. During Reconstruction, 17 Black men served in Congress, 15 in the House and 2 in the Senate, both from Mississippi. Source: Blanche Bruce, Wikipedia + Emerging Civil War (emergingcivilwar.com).

question: After Reconstruction, Southern states wanted to stop Black men from voting without openly breaking the Fifteenth Amendment's ban on denying the vote 'on account of race.' So they invented a trick: a man could skip the poll tax and literacy test if one ancestor had been eligible to vote before the Civil War. Since the ancestors of freed slaves had been enslaved and barred from voting, this let illiterate Whites vote while blocking Black men — with no race word in the law. What is this notorious loophole called?
answer: The grandfather clause
choices: The grandfather clause
The poll-tax exemption
The literacy waiver
The heritage rule
context: By 1908 every former Confederate state had adopted some version of the grandfather clause. Combined with Mississippi's 1890 'Mississippi Plan' of poll taxes and literacy tests, it collapsed Black registration in Mississippi from about 87,000 (97% of eligible men) in 1869 to fewer than 9,000 by 1892 — racism with no race word in the law. Source: Disfranchisement after the Reconstruction era, Wikipedia + US Legal (civilrights.uslegal.com).

question: When the case of the Colfax massacre reached the Supreme Court in 1876 as United States v. Cruikshank, the justices ruled that the federal laws protecting freed people restrained only state governments — not a private mob like the one that had stormed the courthouse. Given that holding, what became of the men who carried out the killings?
answer: They all walked free
choices: They all walked free
They were jailed for life
They were retried by Louisiana
They were pardoned by Grant
context: By holding that the federal Enforcement Acts could only restrain state governments, not private paramilitary mobs, the Court left Washington unable to prosecute the Colfax killers — so they walked free. The ruling gutted federal power to protect freedmen and emboldened White paramilitary groups across the South. Source: Colfax massacre, Wikipedia + EBSCO Research Starters (ebsco.com).

question: In 1896 the Supreme Court voted 7 to 1 in Plessy v. Ferguson to bless segregation, inventing the 'separate but equal' doctrine that locked in Jim Crow for nearly 60 years. Only one justice, John Marshall Harlan, dissented — and his words were later vindicated by history. Which famous line was Harlan's?
answer: "Our Constitution is color-blind"
choices: "Our Constitution is color-blind"
"We are a government of laws, not men"
"The Constitution follows the flag"
"All men are created equal"
context: Harlan's full line: 'Our Constitution is color-blind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens.' He stood alone against the 'separate but equal' doctrine, which ruled until Brown v. Board of Education in 1954. Source: National Archives (archives.gov/milestone-documents/plessy-v-ferguson) + Plessy v. Ferguson, Wikipedia.

question: Frederick Douglass, who escaped slavery to become the nation's most powerful Black voice, insisted the ballot was no favor granted by the powerful but a natural right on which every other freedom rested — the single power that won and kept all the rest. In his own ringing words, what did Douglass call the right to vote?
answer: The one great power by which all civil rights are obtained, enjoyed, and maintained
choices: The one great power by which all civil rights are obtained, enjoyed, and maintained
The surest safeguard against the return of the slave power
The badge and proof of a free man's standing in the republic
The first fruit gathered from the great emancipation
context: Douglass framed the 15th Amendment's promise as fulfilling the founding's own creed — that all men are created equal — not overturning it. He warned that to deny a man the ballot was to 'declare before the world that we are unfit to exercise the elective franchise.' Source: Frederick Douglass, 'What the Black Man Wants' (1865) and 'Appeal to Congress for Impartial Suffrage' (1867), via BlackPast.org + Teaching American History (teachingamericanhistory.org).

question: Poland had vanished from the map of Europe for 123 years — its land swallowed and split up by Russia, Prussia, and Austria. After World War I, the peacemakers in Paris finally put Poland back. What happened to the country in 1918?
answer: It was reborn as an independent nation
choices: It was reborn as an independent nation
It was renamed but stayed Russian
It was split between two new kingdoms
It was governed by a League council
context: After 123 years partitioned among Russia, Prussia (Germany), and Austria, Poland reappeared as an independent country at the 1919 Paris Peace Conference. Source: https://www.albert.io/blog/ap-european-history-versailles-conference-peace-settlement/

question: The seaport city of Danzig was nearly 90% German-speaking, yet the peacemakers took it from Germany and would not let Poland have it either. Instead they invented a strange in-between status for it, run by the League of Nations. What did Danzig become?
answer: A Free City of its own
choices: A Free City of its own
A province of new Poland
A neutral German port
A League military base
context: Danzig (modern Gdansk) became a 'Free City' under the League of Nations, with its own flag, anthem, currency, and postage stamps — but it was not a country. Source: https://www.thecollector.com/history-free-city-danzig-gdansk/

question: World War I toppled four ancient royal houses in a single stroke: the Romanovs of Russia, the Hohenzollerns of Germany, the Ottomans of Turkey, and one more dynasty whose emperor Karl I was dethroned in 1918 and died in exile at 34. Which centuries-old ruling house fell with him?
answer: The Habsburgs of Austria-Hungary
choices: The Habsburgs of Austria-Hungary
The Bourbons of France
The Savoys of Italy
The Wittelsbachs of Bavaria
context: Four empires collapsed at once after WWI — Russian (Romanov), German (Hohenzollern), Ottoman, and Austro-Hungarian (Habsburg). Karl I, the last Habsburg to rule, was dethroned in 1918 and died in exile in 1922 at just 34. Their lands were carved into new nations at the 1919 Paris Peace Conference. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Paris_Peace_Conference/

question: To give reborn Poland its own outlet to the sea, the Paris treaty sliced a strip of German land — West Prussia and the province of Posen — right through the middle of Germany. The strip ran all the way to the Baltic and cut one German region off from the rest of the country by land. What was the lasting wound this 'Polish Corridor' left on Germany's map?
answer: It left East Prussia stranded, separated from Germany
choices: It left East Prussia stranded, separated from Germany
It handed Berlin itself over to Poland
It merged two German states into one
It gave France a foothold on the Baltic
context: The 'Polish Corridor,' carved from West Prussia and Posen (Poznan) to honor Wilson's call for Polish sea access, physically separated East Prussia from the rest of Germany. Source: https://www.britannica.com/place/Polish-Corridor

question: The peacemakers drew Czechoslovakia's borders around the old Kingdom of Bohemia — and in doing so they trapped about 3 million German-speakers inside the new Czech country. Twenty years later a German leader would point to those very people as his reason to seize Czechoslovakia. Who were these stranded Germans whose grievance Hitler exploited in 1938?
answer: The Sudeten Germans
choices: The Sudeten Germans
The Danzig Germans
The Saar Germans
The Tyrolean Germans
context: Bohemia's borders left roughly 3 million 'Sudeten Germans' inside Czechoslovakia — the population Hitler used as his pretext to dismember the country in 1938. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudetenland

question: President Woodrow Wilson preached 'self-determination' — the idea that each people should choose its own nation. But Europe's peoples were mixed together in a patchwork, so granting it to some meant denying it to others. As the new borders went up, millions of Germans and Hungarians faced a fate that, historians argue, helped set up the next war. What happened to them?
answer: They woke up as minorities inside foreign countries
choices: They woke up as minorities inside foreign countries
They were granted their own small republics
They were allowed to vote to rejoin Germany
They were resettled back to their homelands
context: Because the map was a patchwork, 'self-determination' for some meant millions of Germans, Hungarians, and others became minorities inside new foreign states — roughly 10 million people were displaced overall — planting grievances that fed the next war. Source: https://retrospectjournal.com/2025/02/16/why-woodrow-wilson-didnt-actually-support-self-determination/

question: On September 1, 1939, the German warship Schleswig-Holstein opened fire on a small Polish garrison at Westerplatte — the opening shots of World War II. The target was the same disputed seaport Germany had been forced to give up twenty years earlier. Over which 'Free City' did the new war first explode?
answer: Danzig
choices: Danzig
Vienna
Trieste
Warsaw
context: WWII began with German fire on the Polish garrison at Westerplatte in Danzig on Sept 1, 1939 — Hitler's demand to retake Danzig and the Polish Corridor had finally erupted into war. Source: https://www.thecollector.com/history-free-city-danzig-gdansk/

question: In 1786 the Virginia assembly debated Thomas Jefferson's Statute for Religious Freedom, and some legislators moved to insert the name 'Jesus Christ' before 'the holy author of our religion' so the law would shield only Christians. The assembly voted the insertion down. Jefferson said that refusal proved the protection was meant to cover whom?
answer: The Jew and the Gentile, the Christian and the Muslim, the Hindu, and the unbeliever of every kind
choices: Only Virginians who owned property and could vote
Christians of every church but no one outside the faith
The Jew and the Gentile, the Christian and the Muslim, the Hindu, and the unbeliever of every kind
Anyone who swore an oath of loyalty to the new republic
context: Jefferson wrote that by striking the words 'Jesus Christ' the assembly meant the law to embrace 'the Jew and the Gentile, the Christian and Mahometan [Muslim], the Hindoo, and infidel of every denomination.' Freedom of conscience was for every faith and for none. Source: https://encyclopediavirginia.org/entries/virginia-statute-for-establishing-religious-freedom-1786/

question: What Virginia did for one state in 1786, the First Amendment did for the whole nation when it was ratified in 1791. Packed into a single line, it set down two rules about the government and religion at once. What were those two rules?
answer: There is no official national church, and everyone is free to practice their own faith
choices: The country must stay Christian, but no single church may be favored
There is no official national church, and everyone is free to practice their own faith
Each state picks its own established church, and citizens must support it
Religion is a private matter that government may regulate when needed
context: The First Amendment reads, 'Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof' — no established national church AND free exercise for all. The new United States was deliberately founded with no established religion at all, a genuine break from every European model. Source: https://billofrightsinstitute.org/primary-sources/bill-of-rights/

question: Rembrandt's most famous painting is nicknamed The Night Watch. But when restorers finally scrubbed off centuries of darkened varnish in the 1940s, they uncovered a surprise about the scene it actually shows. What did the cleaned-up painting reveal?
answer: It happens in broad daylight, not at night
choices: It happens in broad daylight, not at night
It happens at dawn, with the militia just waking
It happens by torchlight inside a guardhouse
It happens at sunset, as the company heads home
context: For centuries, thick yellowed varnish darkened the canvas so badly that everyone assumed it was a night scene, and the nickname 'The Night Watch' stuck. In truth it shows a militia company surging forward in full daylight. The varnish was cleaned off in the 1940s, but the misleading nickname never went away. Source: https://www.dutchamsterdam.nl/139-rembrandt-night-watch

question: In the swirling crowd of The Night Watch, Rembrandt tucked in a small girl who glows in gold like a tiny beacon amid the shadows. She is the company's mascot, and dangling from her belt is one strange object that also works as a hidden pun on the militia's name. What hangs there?
answer: A dead chicken
choices: A dead chicken
A brass drinking horn
A silver hunting knife
A leather powder flask
context: The chicken's claws are the joke: the company was the Kloveniers (arquebusiers), whose emblem was a golden claw. So the dead bird's clutching feet are a visual pun on the militia's own name, glowing in gold right in the middle of the painting. Source: https://www.singulart.com/blog/en/2019/10/11/rembrandts-night-watch-and-the-dutch-golden-age/

question: Rembrandt van Rijn left behind a strange forty-year diary in paint: the same face, captured roughly a hundred times, aging from a cocky young star draped in fur and gold into a worn, plainly-dressed old man. Art historians call it the most relentless record of a single human face from before modern times. Whose face did he return to, again and again?
answer: His own
choices: His own
His wife Saskia's
His son Titus's
His teacher's
context: Rembrandt painted, etched, and drew his own face about 80 to 100 times across his life, more than any artist before him. The series runs from the swaggering young star of the 1630s to his final self-portrait, painted the year he died, 1669. As a young man he even used his own face to practice expressions, etching himself grimacing and wide-eyed so he could paint real emotion into other people's portraits. Source: https://www.thecollector.com/rembrandt-self-portrait/

question: In 1715 The Night Watch was moved into Amsterdam's Town Hall, where it had to fit a narrow spot between two marble columns. The painting was too big. Rather than change the wall, officials solved the problem by doing something drastic to Rembrandt's canvas itself, and two whole militiamen on the left vanished forever as a result. What did they do?
answer: They sliced strips off all four sides
choices: They sliced strips off all four sides
They folded the spare canvas behind the frame
They painted over the crowded left edge
They had the extra figures scrubbed out
context: The Night Watch was simply cut down on all four sides, with the biggest slice taken off the left, lopping off two whole militiamen plus the top arch, a balustrade, and a step. The cut-off strips were thrown away and never seen again. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Night_Watch

question: Rembrandt's first great group portrait, The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp, shows surgeons gathered around a real corpse as Dr. Tulp lifts the muscles of its forearm with forceps. By law, Amsterdam permitted only one public dissection a year, and the body had to be that of an executed criminal. The corpse was a real, named man, a thief called Aris Kindt, hanged in Amsterdam for mugging a stranger for his cloak. How long after his hanging was his body dissected for this scene?
answer: The same day
choices: The same day
About a week later
About a month later
Nearly a year later
context: Aris Kindt (real name Adriaen Adriaensz), a repeat thief, was hanged in Amsterdam on January 31, 1632, and his body was dissected publicly that very same day, because the city was allowed only one public dissection a year and it always had to be an executed criminal. The painting was Rembrandt's breakthrough, made at age 26. Source: https://www.executedtoday.com/2012/01/31/1632-aris-kindt-rembrandt-anatomy-lesson-dr-nicolaes-tulp/

question: In 2021, three centuries after The Night Watch was trimmed down, Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum showed it whole again, yet the lost strips of canvas were never found. Instead the museum filled in Rembrandt's missing edges with a surprising helper, one that studied a small 17th-century copy of the full painting and recreated the cropped sections stroke by stroke. What did the museum use to paint back the missing edges?
answer: An artificial-intelligence program
choices: An artificial-intelligence program
A team of master forgers
Rembrandt's surviving sketches
A modern Dutch painter
context: Scientist Robert Erdmann led a convolutional neural network (an AI) that studied a small 17th-century copy of the full Night Watch made by Gerrit Lundens, then recreated the missing edges stroke by stroke. The new sections were printed and mounted around the original, making the painting whole for the first time in 300 years. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/lost-edges-rembrandts-night-watch-are-restored-using-artificial-intelligence-180978056/

question: The Renaissance scholars who hunted for lost Greek and Roman books had a Latin rallying cry: 'ad fontes.' It told students to stop trusting the centuries of medieval summaries and commentaries piled up between them and the ancient world, and to do what instead?
answer: Back to the original sources
choices: Back to the original sources
Back to the holy scriptures
Back to the village schools
Back to the king's library
context: 'Ad fontes' literally means 'to the fountainheads' -- go drink from the spring, not the muddy stream downstream. It meant reading Cicero, Homer, and the rest in the original Greek and Latin rather than trusting centuries of medieval commentary. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ad_fontes; Association of Classical Christian Schools, classicalchristian.org/what-is-ad-fontes/.

question: On 26 April 1336 the poet Petrarch climbed Mont Ventoux, a tall peak in southern France, dragging his brother along. Near the bottom an old shepherd tried to wave them back, grumbling that he had gone up fifty years before and gotten nothing but 'rocks and brambles' for the trouble. Why was Petrarch climbing it anyway, a thing he claimed nobody had done since ancient times?
answer: Simply to enjoy the view from the top
choices: Simply to enjoy the view from the top
To pray at a shrine on the summit
To hunt the wild goats that lived there
To escape a plague in the valley
context: Petrarch said he was the first person since antiquity to climb a mountain purely for the pleasure of the view -- not for hunting, war, or pilgrimage. The grumbling shepherd who had found only 'rocks and brambles' is part of his own written account. Source: Petrarch, Familiares IV.1; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascent_of_Mont_Ventoux.

question: On Easter Sunday, 8 April 1341, the poet Petrarch stood on Rome's Capitoline Hill to receive an ancient Roman honor for poets and victors that no one had been given for over a thousand years, revived just for him. What did they place on his head?
answer: A wreath of laurel leaves
choices: A wreath of laurel leaves
A circlet of beaten gold
A bishop's tall white mitre
A helmet of a Roman general
context: The honor was being crowned 'poet laureate' -- 'laureate' comes straight from the laurel wreath, the ancient prize for poets and victors. Petrarch was the first man of the Renaissance to receive it, an honor unused for more than a thousand years. Source: Academy of American Poets, poets.org/poet/petrarch; World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Petrarch/.

question: In July 1374 the old poet Petrarch was found dead at his desk in his house at Arqua, his head come to rest on an open book, having died (as the story goes) still at work among his beloved ancient authors. Whose ancient manuscript was his head resting on?
answer: Virgil
choices: Virgil
Homer
Aristotle
Augustine
context: Petrarch reportedly died with his head on a manuscript of Virgil, the Roman poet he loved above all others. (Homer was Greek, Aristotle a Greek philosopher, and Augustine a Christian bishop -- all authors Petrarch prized, but the deathbed book was Virgil.) Told as a fond legend. Source: World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Petrarch/.

question: In 1345 Petrarch dug a lost bundle of Cicero's private letters out of a cathedral library in Verona and copied them by hand. Stirred to the bone, he wrote a personal letter back to Cicero himself, who had been dead about 1,400 years. He even dated the letter, teasing the old Roman that he was reckoning the year from the birth of a God 'whom thou never knewest.' Why could the pagan Cicero never have known that God?
answer: Cicero died decades before Jesus was born
choices: Cicero died decades before Jesus was born
Cicero worshipped only the old Greek gods
Cicero had been struck blind in old age
Cicero lived his whole life far from Rome
context: Petrarch dated his reply 'in the land of the living... in the thirteen hundred and forty-fifth year from the birth of that God whom thou never knewest' -- a gentle dig that Cicero, who died in 43 BC, had lived and died before Jesus was ever born. Petrarch's Verona discovery is the reason we know Cicero's private letters at all today. Source: Petrarch, 'Letters to Classical Authors' (trans. Cosenza), Project Gutenberg #47859.

question: Around 1416 the book-hunter Poggio Bracciolini, raiding monastery libraries on breaks from a church council, reached the abbey of St Gall and found the only complete copy of Quintilian's great handbook on how to speak well, mouldy and dust-caked but whole. Where in the abbey had this priceless book been shut away?
answer: In a foul tower dungeon
choices: In a foul tower dungeon
Behind a bricked-up altar
Under the abbot's own bed
Inside a hollow stone pillar
context: Poggio wrote that the book sat in a grim tower prison 'where not even men convicted of a capital offence would have been confined' -- yet 'safe and sound, though filthy with mould and dust.' He then copied the whole thing out by hand over about 54 days. Source: Poggio's letter to Guarino da Verona; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poggio_Bracciolini.

question: In January 1417, in a German monastery, the book-hunter Poggio Bracciolini recovered the last surviving copy of a lost 7,400-line poem by the Roman writer Lucretius, recognizing it only because he recalled Cicero quoting the name. The poem argued a startling idea about what everything in the world is really made of. What did it claim?
answer: Everything is built from tiny atoms
choices: Everything is built from tiny atoms
Everything is spun from a world-soul
Everything is shaped by the gods' hands
Everything is born from eternal fire
context: The poem was 'De rerum natura' ('On the Nature of Things'), which taught that all matter is made of tiny invisible particles -- atoms -- colliding in empty space, an idea far ahead of its time. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poggio_Bracciolini; Harvard Magazine, harvardmagazine.com/2011/06/swerves.

question: Coluccio Salutati ran Florence as its chancellor for 31 years, and his weapon was his elegant Latin: he could wound an enemy with a single well-aimed letter. Florence's great foe, Duke Giangaleazzo Visconti of Milan, is said to have complained that one of Salutati's letters could do more harm than what?
answer: A thousand Florentine horsemen
choices: A thousand Florentine horsemen
A fleet of armed war-galleys
A winter of failed harvests
A plague loosed on the city
context: The line -- that a single Salutati letter outdid 'a thousand Florentine horsemen' -- is the most famous tribute to how the humanists turned polished classical Latin into real political power. Told as legend. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coluccio_Salutati; Britannica 'Coluccio Salutati'.

question: In 1397 the Florentine chancellor Coluccio Salutati sent all the way to Constantinople and brought the Byzantine scholar Manuel Chrysoloras to Florence. Chrysoloras began doing something in public that, astonishingly, no one had done in Italy since the Roman Empire fell roughly seven centuries earlier. What was he teaching?
answer: The ancient Greek language
choices: The ancient Greek language
The casting of bronze statues
The laws of the old Republic
The building of domed roofs
context: Chrysoloras gave the first public lectures in ancient Greek in Italy since the fall of Rome; his grammar book, the 'Erotemata' ('Questions'), remained the standard Greek textbook for over a hundred years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Chrysoloras; Britannica 'Manuel Chrysoloras'.

question: The poet Petrarch looked back on the long stretch of centuries between the fall of Rome and his own day with scorn, seeing only ruin and clumsy, 'barbarous' Latin where once there had been glory. He coined a gloomy name for that whole era, a name people still use today. What did Petrarch call it?
answer: The Dark Ages
choices: The Dark Ages
The Iron Age
The Age of Faith
The Great Silence
context: Petrarch was the first to brand those centuries 'tenebrae' -- darkness -- giving us the idea of a 'Dark Age' standing between two ages of light. Historians now treat the label as far too harsh, but the phrase stuck. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Ages_(historiography); Mommsen, Speculum 17.2 (1942).

question: Niccolo Niccoli, a friend of the book-hunter Poggio, copied out the rediscovered classics so fast that he developed a swift, slanting style of handwriting all his own. Printers later cast that very hand into metal type, and it is still on every computer today. What kind of lettering grew out of Niccoli's hand?
answer: Italic type
choices: Italic type
Boldface type
Gothic blackletter
Capital lettering
context: The slant we call 'italic' traces back to humanist scribes racing to reproduce rediscovered ancient books; printers modeled the new cursive type on that hurried, leaning hand. Source: historyofinformation.com/detail.php?id=3218; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poggio_Bracciolini.

question: In the medieval Italian universities, students had a habit of nicknaming each professor after the subject he taught: the law teacher was the 'jurista,' the canon-law teacher the 'canonista,' the arts teacher the 'artista.' By the same trick they tagged one professor the 'umanista,' the root of our word 'humanist.' What subject did that professor actually teach?
answer: The Greek and Latin classics
choices: The Greek and Latin classics
The healing of the sick
The building of great churches
The motions of the planets
context: The 'umanista' taught the 'studia humanitatis' -- grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history, and moral philosophy, all from the Greek and Latin classics. 'Humanist' started as plain student slang for this kind of teacher, NOT the modern secular worldview the word later picked up. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studia_Humanitatis; Britannica 'umanisti'.

question: Around 1567 an Italian motet written for forty separate voices reached London, and an English duke asked whether none of his own countrymen could write a song as good. The composer Thomas Tallis answered with his own forty-voice motet, Spem in alium. When it was sung, the delighted duke is said to have rewarded Tallis on the spot. What did the duke do?
answer: Pulled the gold chain from his own neck and hung it on Tallis
choices: Pulled the gold chain from his own neck and hung it on Tallis
Knighted Tallis with a sword borrowed from the queen's guard
Granted Tallis a country manor with its own private chapel
Ordered the motet carved in stone above the palace gate
context: Per Thomas Wateridge's account (c.1611), the duke 'tooke his chayne of Gold from his necke & putt yt about Tallice his necke.' Tallis split his 40 voices into eight choirs of five (soprano, alto, tenor, baritone, bass) for a roughly 10-minute wall of polyphony; the Latin title means 'I have never put my hope in any other.' Framed as legend. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spem_in_alium

question: When the Italian composer Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina died, he was buried beneath the floor of St. Peter's Basilica in a lead coffin, and the Spanish master Tomás Luis de Victoria walked in his funeral procession. Two Latin words were inscribed on his coffin to crown his life's work. What did they call him?
answer: Musicae Princeps — 'Prince of Music'
choices: Musicae Princeps — 'Prince of Music'
Pater Harmoniae — 'Father of Harmony'
Vox Ecclesiae — 'Voice of the Church'
Magister Sacer — 'Holy Master'
context: Palestrina's lead coffin under St. Peter's was inscribed 'Musicae Princeps.' Legend (a myth first told in 1607) credits his crystal-clear Missa Papae Marcelli with saving sacred polyphony from a supposed ban at the Council of Trent. https://www.britannica.com/biography/Giovanni-Pierluigi-da-Palestrina

question: The Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe fought a sword duel in the dark at age 20 over who was the better mathematician, and lost part of his body to his opponent's blade. He wore a metal replacement for it, glued on, for the rest of his life. Which part of Tycho Brahe did he wear in metal?
answer: The bridge of his nose
choices: The bridge of his nose
The tip of one ear
The end of a finger
Two of his front teeth
context: Tycho lost the bridge of his nose in a December 1566 duel and wore a metal prosthetic (often said gold or silver; chemical tests on his remains suggest copper) that he reattached using paste from a small flask. Source: Mental Floss, 'Pee, Poison, and Prosthetic Noses'; Gizmodo, 'The crazy life and crazier death of Tycho Brahe.'

question: On his island observatory, the astronomer Tycho Brahe kept an unusual tame pet that roamed the halls. As the story goes, the animal drank too much beer at a nobleman's feast, tumbled down a staircase, and died. What kind of beer-loving pet did Tycho Brahe keep?
answer: A tame elk
choices: A tame elk
A tame bear
A tame wolf
A tame stag
context: The tale of Tycho's pet elk dying after a drunken fall down the stairs is a famous legend told about his estate. His island observatory, Uraniborg, was granted to him by King Frederick II of Denmark. Source: Gizmodo, 'The crazy life and crazier death of Tycho Brahe'; Maidens and Manuscripts, 'Of Dwarves, Pet Elk, and Gold Noses.'

question: Nicolaus Copernicus, the churchman who first dared to place the Sun at the center of the heavens, was so afraid of mockery that he held back his life's work for decades. According to tradition, on the very day he died, May 24, 1543, he was handed something that let him die in peace. What did the dying Copernicus receive?
answer: The first printed copy of his book
choices: The first printed copy of his book
A pardon from the Emperor
A blessing carried from Rome
A new map of the stars
context: Tradition holds that Copernicus saw the finished On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres on his deathbed the day he died. Historians treat the exact deathbed timing as partly legend, but he did die that month as the book was published. Source: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (Wikipedia); 'The Great Myths 6: Copernicus' Deathbed Publication' (History for Atheists).

question: In 1604 the astronomer Johannes Kepler tracked a brilliant new star that suddenly blazed up in the constellation Ophiuchus and outshone every other star in the night sky. What was the most astonishing thing about how bright this 'new star' became?
answer: It was bright enough to see in broad daylight
choices: It was bright enough to see in broad daylight
It was bright enough to read a book by at night
It slowly changed color from red to blue
It drifted across the sky a little each hour
context: Kepler's Star (the supernova SN 1604) was visible in daytime for over three weeks. Kepler charted it for a full year and wrote it up in De Stella Nova (1606). It remains the last naked-eye supernova seen in our own galaxy. Source: Wikipedia, 'Kepler's Supernova'; NASA, '420 Years Ago: Astronomer Johannes Kepler Observes a Supernova.'

question: Nicolaus Copernicus, who first put the Sun at the center of the universe, was not an enemy of the Church at all but a canon of Frombork Cathedral. When he finally published On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres in 1543, he aimed it high: to whom did Copernicus dedicate the book?
answer: Pope Paul III
choices: Pope Paul III
Emperor Charles V
