The Bishop of Krakow
King Sigismund of Poland
context: Copernicus dedicated his great book to Pope Paul III. In the dedication he says he feared mockery from Aristotelian philosophers, not from the Church. Source: Vatican Observatory, 'Religious Scientists: Canon Nicolaus Copernicus'; HTI Ohio State, 'Dedication... to Pope Paul III.'

question: For 2,000 years everyone 'knew' the planets moved in perfect circles. Studying Tycho Brahe's exact observations of Mars, Johannes Kepler proved the planets actually trace a different shape around the Sun, with the Sun sitting off-center at one point inside the curve. What shape did Kepler show the orbits really are?
answer: An ellipse, a stretched oval
choices: An ellipse, a stretched oval
A tight inward spiral
A figure-eight loop
A teardrop shape
context: Kepler's First Law (Astronomia Nova, 1609): planets orbit the Sun in ellipses, with the Sun at one focus rather than the center. He derived it from Tycho Brahe's precise Mars data, breaking two millennia of perfect-circle dogma. Source: Wikipedia, 'Kepler's laws of planetary motion'; AMNH Ology card, 'Johannes Kepler.'

question: While Johannes Kepler served as the Holy Roman Emperor's own mathematician, his elderly mother Katharina was jailed for over a year on a charge of witchcraft. At one hearing the executioner showed her the torture instruments to scare a confession out of her. How did Katharina Kepler answer that threat?
answer: She refused, swearing they could pull every vein from her body before she would confess
choices: She refused, swearing they could pull every vein from her body before she would confess
She broke down at once and confessed to everything they named
She fainted at the sight and had to be carried back to her cell
She begged the judges to summon her son Johannes to save her
context: Katharina Kepler was jailed for 405 days (arrested August 7, 1620). At a July 1621 hearing the executioner used the 'territio verbalis,' showing her the instruments, and she defied them, saying they could pull every vein from her body and she would still have nothing to confess. Source: Wikipedia, 'Katharina Kepler'; APS News, 'August 1620: Kepler's Mother Imprisoned for Witchcraft.'

question: Long before space travel, Johannes Kepler wrote a carefully reasoned tale of a voyage to the Moon, describing how the Earth would look hanging in the sky as seen from the lunar surface. Writers like Isaac Asimov and Carl Sagan later honored this story with a bold title. What was Kepler's 'Somnium' often called?
answer: The first work of science fiction
choices: The first work of science fiction
The first map of the Moon
The first textbook of astronomy
The first book of fairy tales
context: Somnium ('The Dream', written about 1608, published after Kepler's death in 1634) is often called the first science-fiction story. Its witch-mother character resembled Kepler's own mother Katharina, and Kepler believed a leaked draft helped spark the real witchcraft rumors against her. Source: Wikipedia, 'Somnium (novel)'; Medium, 'Somnium: The forgotten father of Science Fiction.'

question: Johannes Kepler's very first big idea about the heavens was beautiful, and completely wrong. He thought he had found the literal geometric blueprint God used to build the solar system, by nesting five perfect three-dimensional shapes one inside another like Russian dolls. What did Kepler nest together in this early model?
answer: The five Platonic solids, like the cube and pyramid
choices: The five Platonic solids, like the cube and pyramid
The five known planets, painted on glass globes
The five rings he imagined around the Sun
The five metals the ancients tied to the planets
context: In Mysterium Cosmographicum (1596) Kepler nested the five Platonic solids to explain why there were exactly six planets and why their orbits were spaced as they are. The model was elegant but false, an early sign of his lifelong faith that God built the cosmos on geometry. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Johannes Kepler'; Wikipedia, 'Mysterium Cosmographicum.'

question: In his 1619 book Harmonices Mundi, Johannes Kepler announced his third law of planetary motion, a precise rule linking how long a planet takes to circle the Sun to its distance from the Sun. But Kepler did not see this as cold arithmetic. He believed the order he had uncovered in the heavens was literally what?
answer: Real cosmic music, the song of the spheres
choices: Real cosmic music, the song of the spheres
A coded message left by the ancient Greeks
A warning that the world would soon end
Proof that the Earth was hollow inside
context: Kepler's Third (Harmonic) Law states that the square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of its distance from the Sun. He treated it as literal cosmic music, the 'harmony of the world' that gives Harmonices Mundi its title. Source: Wikipedia, 'Kepler's laws of planetary motion'; Inters.org, 'Kepler's Third Law and the Harmonices Mundi.'

question: Galileo Galilei argued that true faith and true science can never really clash, because God had written not one book but two: Scripture, and the universe itself. And that second 'book' of nature, Galileo said, was written in one particular language. In what language did Galileo say the book of nature is written?
answer: The language of mathematics
choices: The language of mathematics
The language of the angels
Plain Latin and Greek
The language of music
context: Galileo held that the 'grand book of the universe is written in the language of mathematics' (The Assayer), laying out the 'two books' idea in his Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina. Source: The Renaissance Mathematicus, 'The Book of Nature...'; Physics World, 'The book of nature'; Galileo's Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina.

question: Isaac Newton explained the motion of the planets and comets with his laws of gravity in his masterwork the Principia. Yet he chose to end the 1713 edition not with an equation but with a claim about where 'this most beautiful system of the sun, planets, and comets' came from. According to Newton, such a system could only have proceeded from what?
answer: The counsel of an intelligent and powerful Being
choices: The counsel of an intelligent and powerful Being
The blind churning of endless chance
The eternal spinning of the distant stars
A vast invisible machine slowly winding down
context: Newton ended the Principia's General Scholium (1713) arguing that the cosmos 'could only proceed from the counsel and dominion of an intelligent and powerful Being.' He spent as much effort on theology and Scripture as on physics. Source: Vatican Observatory, 'Isaac Newton, God and the Universe in the General Scholium'; Newton Project, Oxford.

question: Oskar Schindler was a member of the Nazi Party who protected over a thousand Jewish workers by running a factory in Krakow that the German army labeled 'war-essential.' What everyday goods did that factory mainly turn out, giving it the 'essential' stamp that shielded his workers?
answer: Enamel pots and pans for the army
choices: Enamel pots and pans for the army
Leather boots for the army
Wool uniforms for the army
Glass bottles for the army
context: Schindler's Deutsche Emailwarenfabrik, nicknamed 'Emalia,' made enamelware (pots and pans, and later munitions) for the German military. He staffed it with Jewish forced laborers and used its 'war-essential' status as the shield that let him protect them. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/oskar-schindler.

question: Raoul Wallenberg, a Swedish diplomat sent to Budapest in 1944, invented an official-looking document, printed in blue and gold with Sweden's triple-crown emblem, that the Nazis actually honored. This single piece of paper is credited with saving about 20,000 Jews. What was it?
answer: A protective passport called the Schutzpass
choices: A protective passport called the Schutzpass
A forged German army exit visa
A Red Cross hospital release letter
A church baptismal certificate
context: Recruited by the American War Refugee Board, Wallenberg designed the 'Schutzpass' to look official enough that Nazi officials respected it; on its strength alone roughly 20,000 Jews were saved. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/raoul-wallenberg-and-the-rescue-of-jews-in-budapest.

question: As the war ended, Oskar Schindler had to flee because the Allies now wanted him as a war criminal for his Nazi ties. His Jewish workers melted down a prisoner's gold dental crown into a ring and engraved it in Hebrew with a single line from the Talmud. What did the line say?
answer: Whoever saves one life saves the world entire
choices: Whoever saves one life saves the world entire
Blessed is the one who shelters the stranger
Let justice flow down like rivers of water
Remember the days of old, and do not forget
context: The ring, made from a survivor's own gold crown, carried the Talmudic line 'Whoever saves one life saves the world entire.' Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia + SparkNotes, sparknotes.com/film/schindlerslist/quotes/page/5.

question: In Budapest, Raoul Wallenberg rented 32 buildings, declared them Swedish territory the Nazis were forbidden to enter, and sheltered nearly 10,000 Jews inside. What did he do to the outside of those buildings to sell the bluff that they were a slice of neutral Sweden?
answer: Flew huge Swedish flags and hung signs like 'The Swedish Library'
choices: Flew huge Swedish flags and hung signs like 'The Swedish Library'
Stationed armed Swedish soldiers at every door
Walled off the streets around them with barbed wire
Repainted them all in Sweden's blue and yellow colors
context: Wallenberg draped the houses with giant Swedish flags and official-sounding signs ('The Swedish Library' and the like) and declared them off-limits Swedish soil; these 'safe houses' sheltered nearly 10,000 people. Source: Raoul Wallenberg, Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raoul_Wallenberg.

question: In March 1943 the Nazis liquidated the Krakow ghetto in a deadly overnight action. Oskar Schindler gave his Jewish workers one order that night that carried them through it alive. What did he tell them to do?
answer: Stay overnight at the factory instead of going back to the ghetto
choices: Stay overnight at the factory instead of going back to the ghetto
Slip out of the city and hide in the surrounding forests
Report to the train station and wait for transfer papers
Burn their identity badges and pose as Polish gentiles
context: By keeping his workers at the factory overnight rather than letting them return to the ghetto, Schindler kept them out of reach during the lethal liquidation. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/oskar-schindler.

question: Oskar Schindler spent his whole fortune on bribes and food for his Jewish workers and died poor in Germany in 1974. At his own request he became the only former Nazi Party member ever buried in honor in one particular place. Where is his grave?
answer: On Mount Zion in Jerusalem
choices: On Mount Zion in Jerusalem
On the grounds of the Auschwitz memorial
In a war-heroes cemetery in Germany
In the old Jewish cemetery of Krakow
context: Schindler asked to be buried in Jerusalem; his tomb on Mount Zion makes him the only former member of the Nazi Party laid to rest there in honor. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia + See The Holy Land, seetheholyland.net/schindlers-grave.

question: Raoul Wallenberg refused to let trains of Budapest Jews reach Auschwitz. As Arrow Cross gunmen fired (aiming deliberately over his head to scare him off), he ignored the shots and physically got his protective passes into the prisoners' hands, then pulled dozens off the train. How did he deliver the passes?
answer: He climbed onto the boxcar roofs and handed them down through the doors
choices: He climbed onto the boxcar roofs and handed them down through the doors
He bribed the train guards to pass them out car by car
He hid them inside food parcels tossed onto the platform
He mailed them ahead to the camp's receiving office
context: By his driver Sandor Ardai's account, Wallenberg clambered onto the roofs of the boxcars and passed the documents down through the openings while marksmen fired over his head, then walked dozens of pass-holders off the train. Source: Raoul Wallenberg, Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raoul_Wallenberg.

question: In January 1945 two cattle cars from a sub-camp of Auschwitz rolled into Schindler's Brunnlitz factory, frozen and sealed shut, with about a dozen people already dead inside. Oskar Schindler's wife, Emilie, refused to let the SS send the survivors on to die. What did she do for the roughly 100 still alive?
answer: Had the iced-over doors cut open with a soldering iron and nursed the frostbitten survivors back to life
choices: Had the iced-over doors cut open with a soldering iron and nursed the frostbitten survivors back to life
Quietly hid them among the registered factory workers under fake names
Drove them by truck across the border to a neutral country at night
Paid the SS guards to record them as already dead and gone
context: Emilie Schindler had a factory engineer cut the ice-locked doors open with a soldering iron and personally nursed about 100 frostbitten survivors, rather than let the SS deport them to their deaths. Source: Brunnlitz labor camp, Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Br%C3%BCnnlitz_labor_camp + USHMM.

question: After moving his factory to Brunnlitz in late 1944, Oskar Schindler kept his workers 'essential' only by having Itzhak Stern and Mietek Pemper fake the production ledgers so the SS believed the plant was churning out munitions. What was the truth about the factory's actual war output?
answer: It barely produced a single usable shell the whole time
choices: It barely produced a single usable shell the whole time
It quietly redirected its shells to anti-Nazi partisans
It met its quota but shipped the shells out defective
It produced nothing but melted the metal down for bribes
context: The faked figures hid the fact that Brunnlitz barely turned out one usable shell; the sham kept the prisoners classified as essential war workers and therefore alive. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/oskar-schindler.

question: In January 1945, days before Soviet troops arrived, the SS planned to dynamite the Budapest ghetto and murder the roughly 70,000 Jews trapped inside. Raoul Wallenberg got a message to the German general in charge, Gerhard Schmidhuber, and the massacre was called off. What threat did Wallenberg send?
answer: That he would personally see the general hanged as a war criminal
choices: That he would personally see the general hanged as a war criminal
That Sweden would immediately declare war on Germany
That Soviet tanks were already inside the city's edge
That he would pay the general a fortune in Swedish gold
context: Through the Arrow Cross officer Pal Szalai, Wallenberg warned General Schmidhuber that he would personally ensure he was hanged as a war criminal if the ghetto was destroyed; the planned slaughter of about 70,000 people was abandoned. Source: Raoul Wallenberg, Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raoul_Wallenberg.

question: Oskar Schindler died penniless in 1974, having spent everything to keep his Jews alive. By the 1990s a startling comparison showed just how much that mattered: the living descendants of the 'Schindler Jews' (over 6,000) had come to outnumber what other group?
answer: All the Jews still living in the whole of Poland
choices: All the Jews still living in the whole of Poland
All the Jews still living in the city of Krakow
All the survivors of the Plaszow camp combined
All of Schindler's original factory workers combined
context: By the 1990s there were more than 6,000 descendants of the Schindlerjuden alive, more than the fewer than 4,000 Jews left living in all of Poland. Source: Schindlerjuden, Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schindlerjuden.

question: Raoul Wallenberg saved tens of thousands from the Nazis, then on January 17, 1945 was summoned to the Soviet Red Army headquarters and seized by Soviet counter-intelligence on suspicion of spying. His last recorded words named where he was being taken: 'I'm going to Malinovsky's... whether as a guest or prisoner I do not know yet.' What happened to him after that?
answer: He vanished into the Soviet prison system and was never seen free again
choices: He vanished into the Soviet prison system and was never seen free again
He was quietly released and lived out his life back in Sweden
He was executed by the retreating SS within the week
He was traded back to Sweden in a prisoner exchange
context: The man who saved a hundred thousand people from one totalitarian regime disappeared into another. The Soviets later claimed he died in Lubyanka prison in 1947, but eyewitnesses reported seeing him alive years afterward, and Sweden did not formally declare him dead until 2016, 71 years after he vanished. Source: USHMM + Raoul Wallenberg, Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raoul_Wallenberg.

question: The film 'Schindler's List' shows Oskar Schindler personally typing out the famous list of Jews to be saved. Historians say the real typed list was actually drawn up by someone else entirely, redrawn several times, with some prisoners bribing their way onto it. Who really compiled it?
answer: A Jewish SS clerk named Marcel Goldberg
choices: A Jewish SS clerk named Marcel Goldberg
Schindler's accountant Itzhak Stern alone
The Plaszow commandant Amon Goeth
A committee of the Krakow Jewish council
context: The real list was compiled by Marcel Goldberg, a Jewish clerk working for the SS, not hand-typed by Schindler as the movie dramatizes; the lists were redrawn more than once and some names were bought. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/oskar-schindler.

question: In spring 711, the Berber commander Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed from North Africa and landed at the great rock on Iberia's southern tip. Worn down over the centuries, the Arabic name his soldiers gave that rock — Jabal Tariq, 'the mountain of Tariq' — survives today as the name of what landmark?
answer: Gibraltar
choices: Gibraltar
Granada
Constantinople
Damascus
context: Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed the strait with about 7,000 men in spring 711. 'Jabal Tariq' wore down over centuries into 'Gibraltar' — the rock still carries the name of the general who landed there. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tariq_ibn_Ziyad

question: In 622, warned that the Quraysh of Mecca were plotting to kill him, Muhammad slipped out of the city with his companion Abu Bakr and migrated about 200 miles north to the town of Yathrib. This migration — the Hijra — was so important that a later ruler made it Year 1 of a whole calendar. What did the welcoming town of Yathrib become renamed?
answer: Medina, 'the City'
choices: Medina, 'the City'
Mecca, 'the Sanctuary'
Cairo, 'the Victorious'
Baghdad, 'the Gift'
context: Yathrib was renamed Medina, 'the City.' The caliph Umar later set the Hijra of 622 as Year 1 of the Islamic calendar (in 639). Source: https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/september-27/muhammad-completes-hegira

question: Muslim tradition tells that around 610, Muhammad — then about 40 — was meditating in the Cave of Hira on Mount Jabal al-Nour, the 'Mountain of Light,' near Mecca, when the angel Gabriel gripped him and commanded one word. Muhammad protested, 'I cannot read.' What was the single command the angel kept repeating?
answer: 'Recite!'
choices: 'Recite!'
'Kneel!'
'Believe!'
'Follow!'
context: The angel commanded 'Iqra!' — 'Recite!' Muhammad answered that he could not read; tradition holds the first revealed words became the opening of Surah 96: 'Recite in the name of your Lord who created.' This account is preserved as Muslim tradition. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad's_first_revelation  (Legend.)

question: At Yarmuk on the Syria-Jordan border in August 636, the Arab general Khalid ibn al-Walid faced Emperor Heraclius's much larger Byzantine army. As the battle turned, a blinding storm blew straight into the Byzantines' faces and broke them, and they were driven backward into the steep Wadi al-Ruqqad ravine. What happened to the fleeing Byzantines there?
answer: They plunged off the cliffs onto the rocks below
choices: They plunged off the cliffs onto the rocks below
They surrendered and were marched to Damascus
They regrouped and counterattacked at dawn
They escaped across the river by boat
context: A blinding sandstorm blew into the Byzantines' faces; when they broke, they were driven into the steep Wadi al-Ruqqad ravine, where some plunged off the cliffs and others were smashed on the rocks of the river below. The defeat ended Byzantine rule in Syria forever. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Yarmuk

question: The Muslim advance into Europe reached its high-water mark in 732, when the emir Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi pushed north into Gaul and burned Bordeaux. Near Tours, a Frankish leader held a solid wall of infantry against charge after charge of cavalry until the emir himself was killed and the advance was turned back. Who was the Frankish leader who held that line?
answer: Charles Martel
choices: Charles Martel
Tariq ibn Ziyad
King Roderic
Khalid ibn al-Walid
context: Charles Martel held a solid infantry phalanx against repeated cavalry charges near Tours on 10 October 732. Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi was killed, and the northward expansion into Europe was turned back at its very edge. Source: https://www.historyhit.com/day-battle-tours/

question: In the German Middle Ages, a runaway serf who lived inside a chartered town for a year and a day could never again be dragged back to his lord. A proverb captured this escape route in three words. What did Germans say town air does to a person?
answer: Town air makes you free
choices: Town air makes you free
Town air makes you rich
Town air makes you holy
Town air makes you wise
context: "Stadtluft macht frei" - "town air makes you free." An unfree serf who lived in a chartered town for a year and a day could no longer be reclaimed by his lord and became a free man. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadtluft_macht_frei

question: In a medieval craft like baking or smithing, a boy started around age 12 as an apprentice and later became a wage-earning journeyman. To climb to the top rank of master, he had to make one single perfect example of his trade and submit it to be judged by the guild masters. What was that perfect example called?
answer: His masterpiece
choices: His masterpiece
His warrant
His indenture
His tribute
context: The French term was chef d'oeuvre. The judged trial-piece is exactly where the modern word 'masterpiece' comes from - and if the masters rejected it, the man could stay a journeyman for life. Sources: https://news.artnet.com/art-world/art-bites-medieval-masterpiece-2437859 ; https://brewminate.com/the-medieval-guild-apprentice-journeyman-and-master/

question: In many German market towns, a giant stone statue of one of Charlemagne's knights stood in the market square, holding a drawn sword, as the town's public boast that it was free and ran its own market. Bremen's, raised in 1404, towers 10.21 metres - the largest free-standing statue of the German Middle Ages. Which knight stood guard over the market?
answer: Roland
choices: Roland
Lancelot
Siegfried
Galahad
context: Roland was a paladin of Charlemagne; a stone Roland with a drawn sword in the square signalled a town's freedom and market rights. Bremen's 10.21-metre Roland of 1404 is the largest free-standing statue of the German Middle Ages. Source: https://www.welterbe.bremen.de/discover/roland-bremen-s-symbol-of-freedom-21305

question: German teenage merchant trainees sent to the Hanseatic wharf at Bryggen, Norway, faced three brutal initiation ordeals. In one of them, a boy was stripped, had a rope tied round his waist, and was thrown three times into the harbour while older merchants in a rowing boat clubbed him with sticks every time his head broke the surface. What were these three ordeals collectively known as?
answer: The Bergen Games
choices: The Bergen Games
The Bergen Reckoning
The Bryggen Rites
The Bryggen Trials
context: The Bergen Games were the Water Games (the harbour beating described here), the Smoke Games (boys hung over a smoky fire to choke while being quizzed), and the Flogging Games (keel-hauling - dragging a boy by rope under a ship's hull). Source: https://thehiddennorth.com/the-most-haunted-places-in-bergen/

question: A medieval commune turned an ordinary town into a self-governing body that could own property and make its own laws - flipping the whole feudal pyramid upside down. It was created by a single act: every townsman swore an oath. But to whom did each man swear it?
answer: A sworn oath of mutual defense to each other
choices: A sworn oath of mutual defense to each other
A sworn oath of obedience to their lord
A sworn oath of fealty to the bishop
A sworn oath of homage to the king
context: The commune was born from a sworn mutual oath of defense among equals - the opposite of a vassal's oath of obedience to a lord above him. That horizontal oath made the town a legal body that could own property and make laws. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_commune

question: A medieval town's charter of liberties did not come free - the townsmen had to buy it. They usually paid not their own resentful local lord at all, but a more powerful ruler instead. Who usually received the payment for a town's freedom?
answer: The king or emperor
choices: The king or emperor
The pope in Rome
The abbot of the nearest monastery
The richest guild in the town
context: Towns frequently purchased their charter of liberties not from the resentful local lord but from the king or emperor over his head - using the higher power to escape the lower one. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_commune

question: When Japan seized Manchuria in 1931 and turned it into a puppet state called Manchukuo, it needed a famous face to sit on the throne while the Japanese army really ran everything. Who did the Japanese install as the figurehead 'emperor' of Manchukuo?
answer: Puyi, the last emperor of China, who had been deposed as a small child
choices: Puyi, the last emperor of China, who had been deposed as a small child
Hirohito, the reigning emperor of Japan, sent to rule from abroad
Chiang Kai-shek, the Chinese general who had unified the south
Sun Yat-sen, the founder who had led China's republican revolution
context: Puyi had been emperor of China as a toddler before the 1911 revolution removed him. Japan made him 'emperor' of Manchukuo in 1934 under the era name Kangde, but real power lay with the Kwantung Army commander, who doubled as Japan's ambassador and could veto Puyi's decisions. He was a figurehead and nothing more. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchukuo

question: On February 24, 1933, the League of Nations voted 42 to 1 that Japan was the aggressor in Manchuria and that the conquest should not be recognized. Rather than obey, Japan's chief delegate Yosuke Matsuoka walked his whole delegation out of the assembly hall. What did Matsuoka say as he left?
answer: "We are not coming back."
choices: "We are not coming back."
"History will be our judge."
"Japan acts only in self-defense."
"The League has signed its own death warrant."
context: Japan was the lone 'no' vote against the Lytton Report. Matsuoka led his delegation out and said simply, 'We are not coming back.' Japan gave formal notice of withdrawal on March 27, 1933. Source: https://www.upi.com/Archives/1933/02/24/Japan-stuns-world-withdraws-from-league/2231840119817/

question: On May 15, 1932, the young naval officers who murdered Japan's prime minister had a second target on their list that day: the world's most famous movie star, Charlie Chaplin, who had arrived in Japan the day before. What happened to spare Chaplin's life?
answer: He was at a sumo match with the prime minister's son when the attack came
choices: He was at a sumo match with the prime minister's son when the attack came
He had already boarded a ship and left the country that morning
He talked the officers down by performing for them at the door
He was mistaken for an ordinary tourist and waved through a checkpoint
context: The plotters had planned to kill Chaplin too, hoping to provoke war with the United States. At the moment of the assassination, the prime minister's son was at a sumo match WITH Chaplin, which likely saved both their lives. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_15_incident

question: Full-scale war between Japan and China began at the Marco Polo Bridge near Beijing on July 7, 1937. Japanese troops on maneuvers said one of their soldiers, Private Shimura Kikujiro, had gone missing and demanded to search a nearby town. What was strange about that demand?
answer: The missing soldier had already returned to his own lines
choices: The missing soldier had already returned to his own lines
The town they named was empty and had no garrison at all
The soldier had deserted to the Chinese side days before
No soldier by that name was ever on the unit's roster
context: Even though Private Shimura had already come back, the Japanese pressed their demand to enter Wanping, shooting started, and it became the opening of the Second Sino-Japanese War. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Polo_Bridge_incident

question: On the night of September 18, 1931, Japanese officers set off a charge on their OWN railway near Mukden and blamed Chinese soldiers, giving Japan its excuse to invade Manchuria. But the blast was so weak that one detail instantly exposed the 'attack' as fake. What gave it away?
answer: A scheduled train rolled over the very same track minutes later and arrived on time
choices: A scheduled train rolled over the very same track minutes later and arrived on time
The Chinese garrison was found unarmed and still asleep in its barracks
Japanese newspapers printed the story a full day before the blast happened
The charge had been bought from a shop whose receipts the police recovered
context: The explosion damaged only a 1.5-meter section of one rail. A train from Changchun rolled over the same track minutes later and reached Shenyang on time at 10:30 p.m. The staged 'Mukden Incident' became the pretext to seize all of Manchuria. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mukden_incident

question: On the morning of September 19, 1931, about 500 Japanese troops stormed the Chinese garrison at Mukden, which had roughly 7,000 soldiers inside. The fight ended with around 500 Chinese dead and only two Japanese killed. Why was the much larger Chinese force crushed so easily?
answer: The Chinese soldiers had been ordered not to resist
choices: The Chinese soldiers had been ordered not to resist
The Chinese soldiers had run out of ammunition weeks earlier
The Japanese had secretly poisoned the garrison's water
The Japanese attacked with tanks the defenders had never faced
context: Chinese leader Chiang Kai-shek hoped to avoid a war Japan was spoiling for, so the garrison was ordered to stand down. About 500 Chinese died against two Japanese dead. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mukden_incident

question: On May 15, 1932, eleven young naval officers burst into the official residence of Prime Minister Inukai Tsuyoshi to assassinate him. He tried to reason with them, saying, 'If I told you, you would understand.' How did the officers answer before they shot him?
answer: "Dialogue is useless."
choices: "Dialogue is useless."
"You have already said too much."
"We understand you all too well."
"There is nothing left to explain."
context: Inukai said 'hanaseba wakaru' ('if I told you, you would understand'); the officers answered 'mondo muyo' ('dialogue is useless') and killed him. The assassins received astonishingly light sentences, a signal that civilian rule over Japan was collapsing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_15_incident

question: During the February 26 Incident of 1936, about 1,400 rebel army officers seized snowbound central Tokyo and hunted down government leaders to kill. Prime Minister Keisuke Okada survived the attack in a way that sounds almost comic. How did he escape the assassins?
answer: He hid in a closet while his brother-in-law was mistaken for him and killed
choices: He hid in a closet while his brother-in-law was mistaken for him and killed
He slipped out a back gate disguised in a maid's clothing
He convinced the rebels he was only a household servant
He climbed down a drainpipe and walked to a police station
context: The rebels assassinated Finance Minister Takahashi Korekiyo, former PM Saito Makoto, and General Watanabe Jotaro. Okada lived only because his brother-in-law was mistaken for him and shot. The rebels surrendered on February 29. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_26_incident

question: After the Chinese capital Nanjing fell to Japanese troops on December 13, 1937, the army carried out one of the worst atrocities of the century, murdering civilians and prisoners of war over roughly six weeks. How many people did the postwar Tokyo tribunal find were killed in the Rape of Nanking?
answer: More than 200,000
choices: More than 200,000
About 50,000
About 8,000
About 2,000
context: The International Military Tribunal for the Far East found more than 200,000 killed; estimates commonly range from 200,000 up to 300,000. This is established historical fact, accepted by the postwar tribunals. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanjing_Massacre

question: During the Rape of Nanking, an American missionary named Minnie Vautrin turned Ginling Girls College into a refuge for some 10,000 women and girls fleeing Japanese soldiers. When soldiers came to drag victims away, what did Vautrin physically do?
answer: She stood at the gate to keep the soldiers out
choices: She stood at the gate to keep the soldiers out
She hid the girls beneath the floorboards of the chapel
She marched the girls out of the city by night
She paid the soldiers in silver to turn them away
context: Vautrin sheltered about 10,000 women and girls inside Ginling Girls College in the Nanking Safety Zone, standing at the gate to block Japanese soldiers. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanjing_Massacre

question: As the Rape of Nanking raged, a German businessman named John Rabe sheltered roughly 200,000 Chinese civilians in a protected 'Safety Zone.' The strange part is what he used to keep Japanese soldiers away from his refugees. What was Rabe's improbable shield?
answer: His Nazi Party membership and swastika flag, which Japan's ally Germany backed
choices: His Nazi Party membership and swastika flag, which Japan's ally Germany backed
A papal letter from the Vatican declaring the zone neutral ground
A unit of armed German marines on loan from a warship
A fortune in gold he used to buy off the Japanese commanders
context: Rabe was a Nazi Party member; because Germany was Japan's ally, his swastika flag carried weight. The refugees called him a 'living Buddha,' and he is remembered as 'the Oskar Schindler of China.' His diary is one of the fullest records of the massacre. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Rabe

question: The postwar Tokyo tribunal hanged General Iwane Matsui, who had commanded the Nanjing operation, for failing to stop the massacre. But the prince who held field command IN the city during the killing was never put on trial at all. Why did Prince Yasuhiko Asaka escape justice?
answer: He was granted immunity as a member of the imperial family
choices: He was granted immunity as a member of the imperial family
He had died before the tribunal could be convened
No witness would testify that he had been in the city
He fled to a country that refused to extradite him
context: Matsui was hanged in 1948 for failing to prevent the atrocities, yet Prince Asaka, the emperor's uncle who held field command during the massacre, received immunity as a member of the imperial family and was never tried. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanjing_Massacre

question: In 1937 Japanese newspapers thrilled readers with a 'contest to kill 100 people with a sword,' cheering two officers, Toshiaki Mukai and Tsuyoshi Noda, as they raced toward a body count. Most modern historians do not treat those breathless reports as straight reporting. What do historians say the newspaper 'contest' really was?
answer: War-glorifying propaganda; Noda later said he killed only a handful in real combat
choices: War-glorifying propaganda; Noda later said he killed only a handful in real combat
A coded military order to execute exactly one hundred prisoners
A complete fabrication invented decades later by foreign critics
An accurate sporting tally the two officers kept in a private diary
context: Legend, as reported by the press, not forensic fact. The Osaka Mainichi and Tokyo Nichi Nichi (Nov 30 - Dec 13, 1937) reported a tally of 106 to 105 and proposed extending the contest to 150. Most historians treat the reports as war-glorifying propaganda; Noda himself later said he had killed only four or five in actual combat, and that prisoners, not battlefield enemies, were involved. Both officers were tried and executed at Nanjing in 1948. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contest_to_kill_100_people_using_a_sword

question: Benito Mussolini named his political movement after an ancient Roman symbol of state power: a tool that attendants called lictors carried over the shoulder, walking ahead of Roman magistrates. What did this symbol look like?
answer: An axe bound inside a bundle of wooden rods
choices: An axe bound inside a bundle of wooden rods
A silver eagle perched on a tall pole
A laurel wreath woven from olive branches
A short sword crossed over a round shield
context: The bundle was the Roman fasces, and 'fascism' takes its name from it (punning on the Italian 'fascio,' a bundle or political group). The rods stood for the power to flog, the axe for the power to behead -- state authority itself. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fasces ; https://www.livius.org/articles/concept/fasces/

question: On 23 March 1919, Benito Mussolini launched the very first fascist movement -- the Fasci Italiani di Combattimento -- at a meeting in Milan. Within two years it would grow into a national party that ruled Italy. How many people were actually there at the start?
answer: About two hundred people
choices: About two hundred people
About fifty thousand people
About ten thousand people
About five hundred thousand people
context: The founding meeting in Milan's Piazza San Sepolcro drew only around 200 people, yet it became the National Fascist Party within two years -- the first fascist regime in the world. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benito_Mussolini ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Benito_Mussolini/

question: Benito Mussolini's father, a blacksmith and committed socialist, gave his son a first name borrowed from a foreign revolutionary he admired. Who was Benito named after?
answer: A Mexican president, Benito Juarez
choices: A Mexican president, Benito Juarez
A French emperor, Napoleon Bonaparte
A Russian novelist, Leo Tolstoy
An American inventor, Thomas Edison
context: His father Alessandro named him Benito after Mexican president Benito Juarez, and added the middle names Andrea and Amilcare after two Italian agitators, Andrea Costa and Amilcare Cipriani. Mussolini was raised on revolutionary heroes. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benito_Mussolini

question: Once in power, Benito Mussolini took a single title that became his defining name -- the very image of the all-powerful leader that later dictators would copy. What was that title?
answer: Il Duce
choices: Il Duce
El Caudillo
Der Kaiser
Le Premier
context: 'Il Duce' means 'The Leader' (from the Latin 'dux,' a military commander). It became the model for other strongmen, including Hitler's 'Fuhrer' -- which also means 'leader.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benito_Mussolini ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Benito_Mussolini/

question: Before he was a fascist, Benito Mussolini was a star of the revolutionary LEFT -- editor of Avanti!, the Italian Socialist Party's newspaper, whose circulation he drove from 20,000 up to 100,000. In November 1914 he broke with the party by demanding Italy enter World War I. How did the Socialists respond?
answer: They expelled him from the party
choices: They expelled him from the party
They jailed him for the campaign
They sued him over the newspaper
They banned him from public speaking
context: His own party threw him out in November 1914 over his war stance. The first fascist began as a leading socialist -- a reminder that fascism's roots ran partly through the revolutionary left, not a cartoon villainy. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benito_Mussolini ; https://www.britannica.com/biography/Benito-Mussolini

question: Benito Mussolini's squads, the Blackshirts, had a signature way of humiliating a socialist, journalist, or union man they wanted to break. They pinned the victim to a chair and forced his mouth open. What did they pour down his throat?
answer: A litre of castor oil
choices: A litre of castor oil
A dose of bitter purgative salts
A flask of turpentine
A pint of sea-water brine
context: Up to a litre of castor oil -- a violent purgative -- left the victim losing control of his bowels in front of crowds. Their methods were summed up as 'truncheon and castor oil' (manganello e olio di ricino). https://historyoftotalitarianism.com/mussolini-and-his-thugs/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squadrismo

question: On 24 October 1922, days before the March on Rome, Benito Mussolini stood before 60,000 Blackshirts gathered in Naples and stated his real intention in one blunt sentence. What did he tell the Naples crowd his aim was?
answer: 'Our program is simple: we want to rule Italy.'
choices: 'Our program is simple: we want to rule Italy.'
'Our purpose is simple: we want Rome to fear us.'
'Our goal is simple: we will end the old parties.'
'Our path is simple: we answer to no one.'
context: He named the aim plainly to a roaring crowd in Naples four days before the march -- raw power, openly stated. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_on_Rome

question: Newsreels show Blackshirts pouring into Rome at the end of October 1922, and the story is often told as a violent fascist conquest. But Benito Mussolini himself did not lead the columns into the capital. Where was he while the March on Rome happened?
answer: Safe in Milan, arriving by train afterward
choices: Safe in Milan, arriving by train afterward
At the front of the column on horseback
Negotiating in person inside the royal palace
Hiding in exile across the Swiss border
context: Fewer than 30,000 poorly armed Blackshirts marched under four 'Quadrumvirs' (Balbo, De Bono, De Vecchi, Bianchi). Mussolini stayed in Milan and travelled to Rome by train only AFTER the King had already invited him to form a government. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_on_Rome ; https://www.britannica.com/biography/Benito-Mussolini/Rise-to-power

question: As the Blackshirts approached Rome in October 1922, Prime Minister Luigi Facta drew up an emergency decree declaring a state of siege, which would have unleashed the army to stop them cold. The army was ready and likely able to win. Why was the decree never carried out?
answer: King Victor Emmanuel III refused to sign it
choices: King Victor Emmanuel III refused to sign it
The army generals defected to the Blackshirts
A general strike shut down the railways
Facta resigned before he could issue it
context: The King would not sign -- fearing bloodshed and possibly a rival claimant to his throne -- and instead asked Mussolini to become Prime Minister. The march 'succeeded' because the King blinked, not because the Blackshirts won a battle. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_on_Rome ; https://www.history.com/articles/mussolini-italy-fascism

question: On 30 May 1924, the socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti rose in Parliament and denounced fascist election fraud and violence to the fascists' faces. Eleven days later a fascist squad under Amerigo Dumini answered him. What did they do to Matteotti?
answer: They kidnapped and murdered him
choices: They kidnapped and murdered him
They stripped him of his seat
They exiled him to a island
They fined and silenced him
context: The killing of Matteotti nearly toppled Mussolini. In protest, 123 opposition deputies walked out of Parliament -- the 'Aventine Secession.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giacomo_Matteotti ; https://www.britannica.com/event/Matteotti-Crisis

question: The 1923 Acerbo Law, written under Benito Mussolini's direction, was built to hand fascism a permanent grip on Parliament. Under it, whichever party list won the most votes -- needing only to clear 25 percent -- would automatically receive how many of the seats?
answer: A full two-thirds of all seats
choices: A full two-thirds of all seats
An exact one-quarter of all seats
A simple majority of one seat
A guaranteed half of all seats
context: Clearing just 25% of the vote delivered two-thirds of Parliament. The 1924 election held under this law was the last competitive election in Italy until 1946. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acerbo_Law ; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Acerbo-Law

question: Speaking in Milan on 28 October 1925, Benito Mussolini compressed fascism's whole creed into a single formula -- the line that became the motto of his regime. Which slogan was it?
answer: 'Everything in the State, nothing outside the State, nothing against the State.'
choices: 'Everything in the State, nothing outside the State, nothing against the State.'
'The State serves the people, answers to the people, and may be unmade by the people.'
'Workers control the State, abolish the State, and need no State at all.'
'A small State, a free market, and a citizen left alone.'
context: 'Tutto nello Stato, niente al di fuori dello Stato, nulla contro lo Stato.' The core of fascism: the State, not the individual, is supreme -- the structure kids should learn to recognize. https://polyarchy.org/basta/documenti/mussolini.milano.html

question: Visitors who toured fascist Italy were often told of its brutality, yet many waved the criticism away with one cheerful boast about Mussolini's efficiency -- a boast the journalist George Seldes found people repeating everywhere. Historians say this famous claim was largely propaganda, not fact. What was the boast?
answer: That he made the trains run on time
choices: That he made the trains run on time
That he had wiped out all poverty
That he had ended every street crime
That he had drained the Roman marshes
context: LEGEND, mostly false: much rail repair predated the fascists, and only big tourist expresses ran punctually while smaller lines stayed late. Seldes mocked how tourists, told of oppression, always replied, 'But the trains run on time!' https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/loco-motive/ ; https://professorbuzzkill.com/2022/01/10/mussolini-didnt-make-the-trains-run-on-time/

question: On the night of 31 August 1935, Soviet coal miner Alexei Stakhanov went down a Donbas mine and the Party announced he had hewed 102 tons of coal in a single shift — 14 times his quota — and made him the face of a whole 'Stakhanovite' hero movement. Decades later the Soviet press admitted the record was a setup. What was the trick behind Stakhanov's 102 tons?
answer: A support team did the hauling; he got all the credit
choices: A support team did the hauling; he got all the credit
He used a secret new German cutting machine
He had simply worked three shifts back to back
The mine's coal was unusually soft that night
context: It was staged: a support team did the loading and timbering through the 5-hour-45-minute shift while the entire tonnage was tallied to Stakhanov alone. In 1988 the Soviet paper Komsomolskaya Pravda finally admitted the feat was puffery. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexei_Stakhanov ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stakhanovite_movement

question: When Stalin launched the first Five-Year Plan in 1928, the regime grew fixated on raising a single plant, dam, or steelworks so colossal it would out-build anything in the capitalist West, as a point of pure national pride. Western observers mocked this obsession with one coined word. What did they call it?
answer: Gigantomania
choices: Gigantomania
Colossalism
Stakhanovism
Maximalism
context: 'Gigantomania.' The 1928 plan demanded gigantic jumps — coal from 35 to 75 million tons, pig iron from 3.3 to 10 million, electricity from 5 to 22 billion kWh — to prove a peasant country could out-build the West in a decade. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_five-year_plan_(Soviet_Union) ; spartacus-educational.com/RUSfive.htm

question: To prove the Five-Year Plan could conjure modern industry from nothing, Stalin ordered an entire steel city raised from bare ground in the Ural Mountains — a showpiece meant to out-produce anything in the West. What was this brand-new steel city called?
answer: Magnitogorsk
choices: Magnitogorsk
Stalingrad
Vladivostok
Sevastopol
context: Magnitogorsk — built from scratch as a whole steel complex in the Urals. Its twin showpiece was the Dnieper Hydroelectric Dam; together they were meant to prove a backward peasant country could out-build the capitalist West in a single decade. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_five-year_plan_(Soviet_Union) ; britannica.com/money/Five-Year-Plans

question: The Great Purge of 1936-38 is nicknamed the 'Yezhovshchina' after Nikolai Yezhov, the NKVD secret-police chief who ran the killing at its peak. Among the secret police he carried a sinister underworld nickname that made his name a thing of dread. What was Yezhov called?
answer: The Bloody Dwarf
choices: The Bloody Dwarf
The Iron Marshal
The Red Tsar
The Steel Commissar
context: The 'Bloody Dwarf' — Yezhov stood barely five feet tall. The terror is named the 'Yezhovshchina,' literally 'the Yezhov era,' after him. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Purge ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolai_Yezhov

question: At the Moscow show trials, prosecutor Andrei Vyshinsky put almost no real evidence before the court — only confessions beaten out of the old Bolshevik defendants and a stream of pure abuse. He ended one tirade with a blunt courtroom command that became infamous. What did Vyshinsky demand the judges do?
answer: Shoot the mad dogs!
choices: Shoot the mad dogs!
Bury the secrets forever!
Spare these broken men!
Exile the traitors east!
context: Vyshinsky called the defendants 'mad dogs of Trotskyism,' 'accursed vermin' and 'dregs of society,' and demanded the court 'shoot the mad dogs.' The three big trials (1936, 1937, 1938) destroyed Lenin's old guard — Zinoviev, Kamenev, then Bukharin — almost all shot in the Lubyanka cellars. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_trials ; spartacus-educational.com/RUSshow.htm

question: A famous 1937 photograph showed NKVD chief Nikolai Yezhov strolling cheerfully at Stalin's side. After Yezhov was shot, Soviet censors took airbrushes and scalpels to the picture and erased him completely. In the doctored version that the public saw, what now stands where Yezhov had been?
answer: An empty stretch of water
choices: An empty stretch of water
A pair of armed guards
A waving red banner
A row of marble statues
context: The two had been walking beside the Moscow-Volga Canal; the retouchers replaced Yezhov with a blank patch of water. It is the most famous case of Soviet photo-faking, catalogued in David King's 1997 book 'The Commissar Vanishes.' Sources: rarehistoricalphotos.com/stalin-photo-manipulation-1922-1953/ ; grokipedia.com/page/The_Commissar_Vanishes

question: Vasily Blokhin, the NKVD's chief executioner, personally shot tens of thousands of people — the most prolific official executioner in recorded history. He dressed for the job in a particular outfit so that none of the blood would spatter his uniform. What did Blokhin pull on before his killing shifts?
answer: A leather butcher's apron
choices: A leather butcher's apron
A grey army greatcoat
A white doctor's smock
A black canvas raincoat
context: Blokhin wore a leather butcher's apron, a leather cap, and shoulder-length leather gloves to keep the blood off. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasily_Blokhin ; allthatsinteresting.com/vasily-blokhin

question: The Gulag was not an excess but a whole system of slave-labor camps, named and damned by Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn in 'The Gulag Archipelago.' Its first showpiece, the White Sea-Baltic Canal, was clawed out of the earth by 126,000 prisoners between 1931 and 1933 — using what to dig it?
answer: Only primitive hand tools
choices: Only primitive hand tools
Imported American excavators
German tunneling machines
Steam-powered dredgers
context: Only picks, shovels and wheelbarrows — no real machinery. An estimated 12,000-25,000 prisoners died digging the Belomorkanal. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Sea%E2%80%93Baltic_Canal ; allthatsinteresting.com/white-sea-baltic-canal

question: During the Ukrainian famine, a starving peasant who bent down in a collective-farm field and picked up a few stray ears of grain the harvest had left behind could be SHOT for it — those few stalks counted as stealing socialist property. The Soviet regime passed this brutal 1932 decree under a formal title, but it is remembered by a shorter name. What is that 1932 law called?
answer: The Law of Spikelets
choices: The Law of Spikelets
The Iron Harvest Decree
The Bread Requisition Act
The Collective Granary Law
context: The 1932 'Law of Spikelets,' whose formal title was the Law of Five Ears of Grain. By early 1933 about 54,645 people had been tried under it, while the man-made famine — the Holodomor — killed roughly 3.9 million Ukrainians by the most detailed studies. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causes_of_the_Holodomor ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor

question: In June 1937 Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky — the gifted officer who had invented the Red Army's 'deep battle' tank doctrine — was convicted in a secret one-day trial of a German plot he never committed, and shot within hours. Decades later investigators reopened his interrogation file and found a grim physical sign of how the confession had been obtained. What stained the pages?
answer: His own spattered blood
choices: His own spattered blood
A forged German seal
Stalin's red signature
A faded prison stamp
context: Tukhachevsky's blood was spattered across the file — the confession had been tortured out of him. His killing began the decapitation of the Red Army on the eve of war: 3 of 5 marshals, 13 of 15 army commanders and 154 of 186 division commanders were shot or removed. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Tukhachevsky ; militaryhistorynow.com/2023/01/08/the-enemy-within-five-little-known-facts-about-stalins-purge-of-the-red-army-2/

question: In 1920, before the Five-Year Plans even began, the economist Ludwig von Mises argued that a fully socialist economy was doomed to chaos for one fundamental reason. His argument turned on what a planning ministry like Gosplan would be missing once it abolished private property. According to Mises, what made rational planning impossible?
answer: Without market prices, planners could not know what anything was truly worth
choices: Without market prices, planners could not know what anything was truly worth
Without foreign loans, the state could not buy enough machinery to start
Without a strong army, the planners could not enforce their quotas on workers
Without good weather, the harvest targets could never realistically be met
context: Mises (1920, 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth') argued that with no private property there are no real prices, so planners cannot calculate what anything is worth. Friedrich Hayek added that the knowledge to run an economy is scattered among millions and can never be gathered in one ministry. The Plans' bottlenecks, faked reports and shortages were the prediction coming true. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_calculation_problem ; aier.org/article/mises-and-hayek-two-complementary-critiques-of-central-planning/

question: People who downplay Stalin's Great Purge of 1937-38 reach for a vague 'about half a million.' But the killing was bureaucratic, and the Soviet state's own secret files recorded the executions of those two years down to the last person. What was that documented figure?
answer: 681,692 executed
choices: 681,692 executed
504,117 executed
250,431 executed
947,206 executed
context: The NKVD's own records log 681,692 executions in 1937-38 alone (plus about 116,000 Gulag deaths), which is why the honest scholarly range is 700,000 to 1.2 million killed. The soft 'about half a million' shrinks a documented massacre — the bodies were counted. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Purge ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excess_mortality_in_the_Soviet_Union_under_Joseph_Stalin

question: Robert Boyle, a founder of the new Royal Society, had his young assistant Robert Hooke build him a strange machine in 1659: a great glass globe over a brass cylinder that could suck the air out of itself. To prove that air was the thing keeping creatures alive, Boyle sealed a living bird inside and pumped. The bird drooped and convulsed and died. Then he tried it again, racing to let fresh air rush back in. What happened the instant the air returned?
answer: The bird revived and stirred back to life
choices: The bird revived and stirred back to life
The glass globe cracked from the pressure
The bird caught fire and burned up
The brass cylinder filled with water
context: Boyle's air-pump (built by Hooke, ~30-quart glass receiver over a brass cylinder, 1659) let him make a near-vacuum, which most people thought impossible. A bird died when the air was pumped out but revived if air came back quickly; a mouse went giddy, staggered, and collapsed, then revived too. The demonstrations showed dramatically that animals cannot live without air. Source: https://www.sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/full-boyle/

question: For two thousand years scholars had taught that everything in the world was built from four 'elements' — earth, water, air, and fire — while alchemists swore by three secret 'principles' of salt, sulfur, and mercury. In 1661 Robert Boyle published a book written as a sharp debate between characters who argue the whole idea to pieces, insisting that chemistry must rest on observation and repeatable experiment, not on secret authority. What was Boyle's combative book called?
answer: The Sceptical Chymist
choices: The Sceptical Chymist
The Wealth of Nations
The Starry Messenger
The Praise of Folly
context: In 'The Sceptical Chymist' (1661) Boyle attacked both the four classical elements and the alchemists' three principles, demanding evidence over authority. He is often called a father of modern chemistry for dragging it out of secretive alchemy into public, repeatable experiment. Source: https://iep.utm.edu/robert-boyle/

question: Robert Boyle wanted to prove a hidden rule about gases, so he built a tall glass tube bent into a J-shape, trapping a pocket of air in the short sealed end. Then he poured heavy liquid metal into the long open end, more and more, watching the trapped air get crushed into a smaller and smaller space. He found that squeezing the gas into half the room doubled its push-back. In Boyle's Law, when you halve a gas's volume at a fixed temperature, what happens to its pressure?
answer: It doubles
choices: It doubles
It stays the same
It is cut in half
It drops to zero
context: Boyle's Law: pressure times volume stays constant at fixed temperature, so halving the volume doubles the pressure. Boyle proved it with a J-shaped tube, pouring in mercury to crush a trapped pocket of air and measuring the shrinkage. Published in the 1662 second edition of 'New Experiments Physico-Mechanicall, Touching the Spring of the Air.' Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Robert_Boyle/

question: In the Robin Hood legend, the outlaw enters an archery contest and a rival's arrow is already dead center in the bullseye. Robin shoots anyway — and his arrow strikes the back of the rival's arrow, splitting it right down the middle. To this day, archers who split an arrow already in the target call the shot what?
answer: a Robin Hood
choices: a Robin Hood
a Sherwood
a Nottingham
a Little John
context: Splitting an arrow that is already buried in the target is still called 'a Robin Hood' by archers worldwide. The dramatic version of the feat was made iconic by Sir Walter Scott in his 1819 novel Ivanhoe. LEGEND. Source: https://www.worldarchery.sport/news/178452/archery-history-legend-robin-hood

question: In the legend, an old and dying Robin Hood has been betrayed and bled to death by the Prioress of Kirklees. With his last strength, Little John puts the great longbow in Robin's hand and holds him up to a window so he can shoot one final arrow. What does Robin ask of his Merry Men as that arrow flies?
answer: to be buried where the arrow lands
choices: to be buried where the arrow lands
to burn Kirklees to the ground
to crown Little John as their new leader
to carry his body home to Sherwood
context: Robin asks to be buried where his last arrow falls, 'within bow-shot' of Kirklees. A mound marked as Robin Hood's Grave can still be visited there today. LEGEND. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood's_Grave

question: Auguste Rodin's most famous statue shows a muscular man hunched on a rock, chin on his fist, lost in thought — the world knows it as 'The Thinker.' But it started as a small figure of a real poet, perched at the top of Rodin's giant bronze doors and leaning down to brood over the damned souls of Hell carved below him. Which poet was that brooding little figure?
answer: Dante, author of the journey through Hell
choices: Dante, author of the journey through Hell
Homer, who sang of the fall of Troy
Virgil, who wrote of Rome's founding
Ovid, who told tales of the gods
context: The Thinker began as a roughly 70 cm figure called 'The Poet' — Dante Alighieri, seated on the tympanum atop Rodin's 'The Gates of Hell,' brooding over the damned in the circles of his Inferno. Foundry workers nicknamed it 'The Thinker' because it reminded them of Michelangelo's brooding statue of Lorenzo de' Medici. Rodin later enlarged it to colossal size (1904) into the standalone icon. Source: https://www.musee-rodin.fr/en/musee/collections/oeuvres/thinker

question: For his monument to the Burghers of Calais — six citizens who in 1347 walked out to King Edward III barefoot with nooses around their necks, expecting to die for their city — Auguste Rodin refused the usual proud hero on a tall pedestal. He sculpted all six at human size and demanded one radical placement so that passersby would almost bump into the condemned men and meet them eye to eye. Where did Rodin want the figures set?
answer: Directly on the ground, at the viewer's own level
choices: Directly on the ground, at the viewer's own level
High on a column above the town square
Inside a sealed glass memorial case
Atop the city's tallest Gothic spire
context: Rodin broke every rule of the heroic monument: no pedestal, six men at life size with different emotions — resignation, defiance, despair — placed on the ground so viewers meet the condemned eye to eye. Calais first rejected this and mounted them on a tall Gothic base anyway; only in 1924 did the city honor Rodin's wish and lower the Burghers to ground level before the town hall, where they still stand. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Burghers_of_Calais

question: In November 1895 Wilhelm Roentgen discovered invisible rays in his Wurzburg lab that could pass straight through black cardboard and through human flesh. He had no idea what they actually were, and that very uncertainty decided the name he gave them. Why did Roentgen call his discovery 'X-rays'?
answer: X was the mathematical symbol for an unknown quantity
choices: X was the mathematical symbol for an unknown quantity
X marked the spot on his lab bench where they appeared
X was the first letter of the screen's glowing chemical
X stood for the experiment number in his lab notebook
context: Because he could not say what the rays were, Roentgen borrowed the algebra symbol 'X' that stands for an unknown value. The name stuck worldwide, even though others called them 'Roentgen rays' to honor him. Sources: nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1901/perspectives; time.com/3649842/x-ray.

question: In December 1895 Wilhelm Roentgen made an image of his wife Anna Bertha's left hand, and the picture showed the dark shadows of her finger bones with the ring still circling one of them. No living person had ever looked inside their own body before. When Bertha saw the skeleton of her own hand, what did she cry out?
answer: "I have seen my death!"
choices: "I have seen my death!"
"Take it away from me!"
"That is not my hand!"
"It is the work of the devil!"
context: The image is called 'Hand mit Ringen' (Hand with Rings). Bertha recoiled at the ghostly bones of her living hand, the first time any human had seen inside a living body. Sources: pbs.org/newshour/health/i-have-seen-my-death-how-the-world-discovered-the-x-ray; worldhistory.org/article/2497.

question: The dome of the Pantheon in Rome stood as the widest dome on Earth for over 1,300 years — across that whole span no builder anywhere could match it. The record finally broke in 1436. Which building's new dome at last beat Rome's?
answer: Florence Cathedral
choices: Florence Cathedral
Cologne Cathedral
Westminster Abbey
Notre-Dame de Paris
context: Filippo Brunelleschi completed the dome on Florence Cathedral in 1436, ending the Pantheon's 1,300-year reign as the world's widest. He had studied the Pantheon closely before designing his own. Source: Engineering & Technology Magazine (eandt.theiet.org); EngineeringRome.org 'Studying Domes'.

question: Roman concrete is full of little white chunks called lime clasts. For years experts thought they were just sloppy mixing — a sign Roman workers were careless. In 2023, MIT's Admir Masic and Linda Seymour cracked a Roman-style sample and an ordinary one, then watched. The Roman sample sealed itself in two weeks; the ordinary one stayed broken. What were the white chunks secretly doing?
answer: healing the concrete's own cracks
choices: healing the concrete's own cracks
letting the concrete set underwater
making the concrete glow faintly
keeping the concrete from freezing
context: When a crack lets water in, the lime clast dissolves and its calcium recrystallizes as calcium carbonate, filling the gap — self-healing concrete. The Romans made these clasts by 'hot mixing' quicklime with volcanic ash; the recipe was lost, and modern concrete has none. Source: MIT News (news.mit.edu/2023/roman-concrete-durability-lime-casts-0106); Science Advances, Jan 2023.

question: The Appian Way was the first of Rome's great paved highways, begun in 312 BC and eventually running 335 Roman miles down to the port of Brindisi. The Romans gave it a proud nickname that the poet Statius recorded. What did they call it?
answer: The queen of roads
choices: The queen of roads
The spine of Italy
The soldier's path
The merchant's mile
context: 'Regina viarum' — the queen of roads. It was begun by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus, the same man who built Rome's first aqueduct, the Aqua Appia, in that same year. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appian_Way

question: In southern France stands the tallest Roman aqueduct bridge ever built, a three-tier wall of arches rising 48.8 metres above the river it crosses. Which famous bridge is this?
answer: The Pont du Gard
choices: The Pont du Gard
The Ponte Sant'Angelo
The Aqua Claudia
The Trajan's Bridge
context: The Pont du Gard carried water toward Nimes. Its three rows hold 6 arches on the bottom, 11 in the middle, and 35 small ones on top, built from limestone blocks (some weighing 6 tonnes) cut so precisely they hold by friction with almost no mortar. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pont_du_Gard

question: We still say 'all roads lead to Rome,' and the saying is literally true: in 20 BC the emperor Augustus put up a single gilded bronze post in the Roman Forum, and every road's distance was measured from it. What was this post called?
answer: The Golden Milestone
choices: The Golden Milestone
The Victory Column
The Stone of Romulus
The Triumphal Gate
context: The Milliarium Aureum, the Golden Milestone, was inscribed with the distances from Rome to the great cities of the empire. The roads were all measured from this one golden post. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milliarium_Aureum

question: Almost 1,900 years after the emperor Hadrian built it, one Roman building in Rome still holds a world record: it has the largest dome made of plain concrete, with no steel inside it, anywhere on Earth. Which building is it?
answer: The Pantheon
choices: The Pantheon
The Colosseum
The Baths of Caracalla
The Circus Maximus
context: The Pantheon's concrete dome (c. AD 113-125) has no steel rebar at all and is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome on the planet. Its inside is a perfect sphere: the height to the top and the width across are exactly equal, both 43.3 metres. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome

question: When people picture a Roman aqueduct they imagine those towering rows of stone arches marching across the land. But of roughly 780 km of channel feeding the city of Rome, only about 47 km rode on arches. Where did the other 94% of the water travel?
answer: Hidden in tunnels and trenches in the ground
choices: Hidden in tunnels and trenches in the ground
Inside hollow columns along the road
Through pipes laid on the open hillsides
Across floating wooden walkways
context: About 94% of Rome's aqueduct channel was buried. The famous arcades were the rare exception, used only to carry the water across valleys where the ground dropped away. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_aqueduct

question: In 2023, MIT researchers led by Admir Masic deliberately cracked a slab of replica Roman concrete and ran water through the crack to see what would happen. A modern concrete slab kept leaking. What did the Roman one do within two weeks?
answer: The crack sealed itself and stopped the water
choices: The crack sealed itself and stopped the water
It crumbled apart at the broken edge
It turned soft and spongy when wet
It changed colour but kept on leaking
context: Within two weeks the crack in the Roman concrete had sealed and water could no longer pass — it heals its own cracks. The work was published in Science Advances in January 2023. Source: https://news.mit.edu/2023/roman-concrete-durability-lime-casts-0106

question: A Roman stone arch holds itself up with no mortar at all, but while it is being built it must rest on a wooden frame until one special wedge of stone is set into place. Once that one stone is in, the whole ring locks solid and the frame can come away. What is that final locking stone called?
answer: The keystone
choices: The keystone
The cornerstone
The lintel
The pediment
context: The wedge-shaped stones of an arch (voussoirs) turn the weight on top into sideways squeezing force. The keystone locks the ring so the arch carries its load as a single block of stone, enormously strong in compression. Source: https://oldentech.com/ancient-roman-arches/

question: After the Roman general Crassus crushed the great slave revolt of Spartacus in 71 BC, he wanted everyone who travelled the Appian Way to see the price of rebellion. What did Crassus do to the 6,000 captured rebels?
answer: He crucified them in a line all along the road
choices: He crucified them in a line all along the road
He sold them to the mines in Spain
He branded them and set them free
He marched them in chains through Rome
context: Crassus had the 6,000 captured rebels crucified in a line that stretched from Rome toward Capua, left along the queen of roads as a warning to anyone who passed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appian_Way

question: For decades scientists looked at the little white chunks scattered through Roman concrete, called 'lime clasts,' and dismissed them as proof the Romans mixed their concrete sloppily. The 2023 MIT study found the 'flaw' was actually the secret to the concrete's long life. What do the lime clasts do when a crack lets water in?
answer: They dissolve and recrystallise to plug the gap
choices: They dissolve and recrystallise to plug the gap
They swell up and push the crack wider
They wash away and leave the concrete weaker
They harden into a slippery glassy film
context: When a crack admits water, the lime clast dissolves and recrystallises as calcium carbonate, plugging the gap — a built-in repair kit hiding inside what looked like a mixing mistake. Source: https://news.mit.edu/2023/roman-concrete-durability-lime-casts-0106

question: At the very top of the Pantheon's dome is a great round hole, the oculus, left permanently open to the sky and the rain. Besides being the only window, it solved a structural problem for the builders. How did cutting that hole help hold the dome up?
answer: It removed the heaviest, most dangerous part of the dome
choices: It removed the heaviest, most dangerous part of the dome
It let hot air escape so the stone would not crack
It made the dome lighter by drying out the concrete
It let workers lower the stones from above
context: Removing the crown of the dome got rid of its heaviest, most dangerous part and gave the ring of concrete around the opening something to push against. The 30-Roman-foot oculus is the building's only source of light. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome

question: To build concrete that lasts, the Romans did something that sounds reckless: instead of safely soaking their lime in water first, they tossed in dry quicklime, the same caustic powder that burns skin, so the wet mix hit scorching temperatures as it was made. MIT's Admir Masic argues that searing heat was no accident. What did it leave behind in the hardened concrete?
answer: Baked-in lime lumps that crack open and dissolve in rain to fill the gap
choices: Baked-in lime lumps that crack open and dissolve in rain to fill the gap
A glassy waterproof skin where the volcanic ash had melted together
Stiff air pockets that let a wall flex a little instead of snapping clean
A bone-dry inner core baked far harder than the stone around it
context: Masic's team found the heat baked in reactive 'lime clasts'; when a crack forms and water reaches them, they dissolve and recrystallise to fill the gap. He explained the heat 'allows chemistries that are not possible if you only used slaked lime.' Source: https://news.mit.edu/2023/roman-concrete-durability-lime-casts-0106

question: Modern concrete piers standing in the sea crumble within a few decades, eaten away by the waves. Roman harbour walls have stood in salt water for 2,000 years and are actually tougher now than when they were poured. What does seawater do to Roman concrete over the centuries?
answer: It keeps reacting to grow new interlocking crystals
choices: It keeps reacting to grow new interlocking crystals
It coats the surface in a hard layer of salt
It cools the concrete so it never expands
It washes out the weak parts and leaves the strong
context: The volcanic ash (pozzolana) keeps reacting with seawater for centuries, growing rare interlocking crystals — aluminous tobermorite and stratlingite — inside the concrete, so Roman seawater concrete grows stronger over time. Source: https://www.chemistryworld.com/news/romans-hot-recipe-for-self-healing-concrete-unravelled-in-pompeii/4022682.article

question: For generations the common people of Rome, the plebeians, kept losing cases in court and could never tell beforehand how a dispute would be judged. So in 451 BC they forced the city to appoint ten men, the decemviri, to write the law down at last in what became the Twelve Tables. What had Roman 'law' actually been before that, the thing the plebeians were finally tearing open?
answer: An unwritten custom that only the patrician priests knew
choices: An unwritten custom that only the patrician priests knew
A foreign code copied from a rival Greek city
A list of debts the patricians secretly kept
Spoken commands the consuls invented case by case
context: Until 451 BC Roman law was unwritten custom guarded by a small circle of patrician priests, who could bend it against the common people. The plebeians demanded it be written and made public; a board of ten men, the decemviri, produced the Twelve Tables in 451-450 BC (two plebeians were added to the second commission). This is the deep root of the idea that the law must be WRITTEN and KNOWABLE, not a secret of the elite. Source: Britannica, 'Law of the Twelve Tables' (britannica.com/topic/Law-of-the-Twelve-Tables); Wikipedia 'Twelve Tables'.

question: Rome's first written law code, the Twelve Tables, was inscribed on bronze and posted in the Forum so every citizen could read it. Then around 387 BC a disaster destroyed the original tablets, yet the laws themselves were never repealed and stayed the bedrock of Roman law for centuries. What happened to the original bronze tablets?
answer: The Gauls sacked Rome and burned the tablets
choices: The Gauls sacked Rome and burned the tablets
A flood of the Tiber washed the tablets away
A fire in the Senate house melted the tablets
Rioting plebeians smashed the tablets in protest
context: When the Gauls under Brennus sacked and burned Rome (traditionally 387/390 BC), the original bronze tablets were destroyed. No original text survives -- everything we know of the Twelve Tables is reconstructed from quotations in later Roman writers. Yet the laws were never formally repealed: the CODE outlived its own monument. Source: World History Encyclopedia 'Twelve Tables' (worldhistory.org/Twelve_Tables); Wikipedia 'Twelve Tables'.

question: Cicero recorded that when he was a boy's grandfather's age, Roman schoolboys had to learn the entire Twelve Tables -- the whole law code -- by heart, though by Cicero's own day in the first century BC nobody bothered anymore. What exactly did those earlier schoolboys treat the law code as?
answer: A required song they chanted from memory
choices: A required song they chanted from memory
A riddle contest held in the Forum
A copying drill done on wax tablets
A series of mock trials they acted out
context: Cicero (De Legibus 2.59) says that in his grandfathers' day schoolboys learned the Twelve Tables as a 'carmen necessarium' -- a 'required song' -- chanting the entire law code from memory. By Cicero's own time the practice had died out. An entire law code memorized aloud was once simply how a Roman child was schooled. Source: Wikipedia 'Twelve Tables' (citing Cicero, De Legibus 2.59).

question: By the 500s AD, a thousand years of Roman law had piled up into a tangled, contradictory mess. The emperor Justinian I put the brilliant jurist Tribonian in charge of a commission to sort it all out, and the result became the foundation of European civil law for centuries afterward. What is the name of that great four-part collection of Roman law?
answer: The Corpus Juris Civilis
choices: The Corpus Juris Civilis
The Edict of Milan
The Justinianic Codex alone
The Theodosian Synthesis
