context: Justinian's commission under Tribonian produced the Corpus Juris Civilis ('Body of Civil Law') in four parts: the Codex (imperial decrees, first issued 529), the Digest or Pandects (jurists' opinions, 533), the Institutes (a student textbook, 533), and the Novellae (Justinian's new laws). It became the law of the Byzantine Empire and the foundation of European civil law. Source: Wikipedia 'Corpus Juris Civilis'; Lumen Learning 'The Justinian Code'.

question: Justinian's Digest -- the part of his law collection that preserved the opinions of Rome's greatest legal minds -- survives today almost entirely thanks to one object made within a generation of the original. It was held at Amalfi, seized as war booty and taken to Pisa in 1155, then carried to Florence in 1406, where it still rests. What did the survival of Roman legal civilization come down to?
answer: A single hand-copied manuscript
choices: A single hand-copied manuscript
A single carved stone slab
A single bronze tablet of decrees
A single bound roll of scrolls
context: The manuscript is the Littera Florentina, made within a generation of Justinian's original. A 13th-century account says it was held at Amalfi, seized as war booty and taken to Pisa in 1155, then carried to Florence in 1406, where it rests in the Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana. Western legal civilization hung on this one book. Source: Wikipedia 'Littera Florentina'; History of Information 'Pandectarum codex Florentinus'.

question: The Twelve Tables could be savage to debtors. Table III dealt with a man who owed money and could not pay: he was held, displayed in the market on three successive market days, and if still no one paid his debt, his creditors gained a final, gruesome right -- so shocking that Romans themselves argued for centuries over whether it was meant literally. What did Table III let the creditors do on the third market day?
answer: Cut the debtor into pieces between them
choices: Cut the debtor into pieces between them
Brand the debtor on the forehead with iron
Seize the debtor's children as their payment
Nail the debtor to the gate of the Forum
context: Table III's notorious line is 'partis secanto' -- 'let them cut him in pieces,' adding that if they cut more or less than their share, it was no crime. Even Romans debated whether this meant literal dismemberment or merely dividing his property; the alternative penalty was being sold into slavery 'across the Tiber.' Source: Yale Avalon Project, 'The Laws of the Twelve Tables', Table III; en.wikipedia 'Twelve Tables' (Aulus Gellius 20.1).

question: Table IV of the Twelve Tables gave the Roman father, the paterfamilias, terrifying power over his household -- including a rule that a father could sell his own son into bondage. But the same rule hid a loophole the son could turn against his father: if a father sold his son a third time, the third sale carried a consequence the father never intended. What did the third sale do?
answer: The son went free of his father forever
choices: The son went free of his father forever
The son could buy his way out for one as
The son inherited his father's whole estate
The son owed his father triple the price
context: Table IV: 'If a father sells his son three times, the son shall be free of the father.' Roman jurists later turned this three-sales clause into the legal ritual used to deliberately free a son from his father's power -- the origin of emancipation. The same harsh table also ordered that a 'dreadfully deformed child shall be quickly killed.' Source: Yale Avalon Project, 'The Laws of the Twelve Tables', Table IV.

question: One of the deepest gifts Rome left the modern courtroom is captured in a Latin maxim from the jurist Julius Paulus, preserved in Justinian's Digest: 'Ei incumbit probatio qui dicit, non qui negat.' It is the direct ancestor of the rule that a person is innocent until proven guilty. What does that maxim say about who has to prove a charge?
answer: The accuser must prove the case, not the accused
choices: The accuser must prove the case, not the accused
Both sides share the burden of proof equally
The judge must gather the proof himself
The accused must prove that he is innocent
context: 'Ei incumbit probatio qui dicit, non qui negat' -- 'the burden of proof is on the one who asserts, not on the one who denies.' Attributed to the jurist Julius Paulus (2nd-3rd c. AD) and preserved in Justinian's Digest at 22.3.2, it is the direct ancestor of the rule that the accuser, not the accused, must prove the case. Source: Wikipedia 'Presumption of innocence' (citing Digest 22.3.2, Julius Paulus); LawTimesJournal 'Ei incumbit probatio qui'.

question: The emperor Trajan went further than just demanding proof: in a ruling preserved in Justinian's Digest, he wrote that no one should be condemned on mere suspicion, and he put into Roman law a principle that the English jurist Blackstone would later echo. Which principle did Trajan make Roman law?
answer: Better a guilty man go free than an innocent be condemned
choices: Better a guilty man go free than an innocent be condemned
No man may be tried for the same crime twice
A confession outweighs any other evidence
Punishment must always fit the gravity of the crime
context: Trajan's rescript, preserved at Digest 48.19.5 (Ulpian): 'satius esse impunitum relinqui facinus nocentis quam innocentem damnari' -- 'it is better that the crime of a guilty man go unpunished than that an innocent be condemned' -- adding that no one should be condemned on mere suspicion. Blackstone's famous 'better that ten guilty escape than one innocent suffer' is a direct descendant. Source: UCLA Law, A. Volokh 'n Guilty Men' (law.ucla.edu/Volokh/guilty.htm), quoting Digest 48.19.5 (Ulpian, De officio proconsulis 7).

question: When Justinian's team finished the Digest, they had crushed the writings of nearly forty classical jurists -- some two thousand books -- down into a single fifty-book work, and Justinian declared it the only law anyone could cite in court. Determined that his perfect law should never be twisted or argued with again, he then issued an extraordinary command meant to freeze the law forever. What did Justinian forbid?
answer: He forbade anyone to write commentaries on it
choices: He forbade anyone to write commentaries on it
He had every older law book publicly burned
He ordered it recited aloud in every court
He let only senators keep private copies
context: Tribonian's team distilled roughly 2,000 books and millions of lines from about 38-39 jurists down to some 150,000 lines (a 50-book work). Justinian declared the Digest the SOLE source of citable law and forbade anyone to write commentaries on it, hoping to freeze the law forever -- a hope that of course failed once later scholars got hold of it. Source: Wikipedia 'Corpus Juris Civilis'.

question: Around 1070-1100, scholars in the Italian city of Bologna got hold of Justinian's Digest, which had been almost forgotten in the West. A teacher named Irnerius would read the text aloud and squeeze short remarks between the lines and in the margins to make its meaning clear; his successors built a whole curriculum on them and turned Bologna into Europe's first true university of law. What were those between-the-lines remarks called?
answer: Glosses
choices: Glosses
Compurgations
Disputations
Recitations
context: Irnerius read the rediscovered Digest aloud and added explanatory notes called 'glosses'; his successors, the glossators, built a curriculum around it. This revival turned Bologna into Europe's first true university of law and re-seeded Roman law across the continent -- the bridge by which Justinian's code became the backbone of modern European civil law. Source: Wikipedia 'Corpus Juris Civilis'; Visit Bologna 'Irnerius: Founder of the School of Glossators'.

question: Roman jurists argued that beyond the written statutes of any one city there exists a higher standard of justice -- one that is true for every people on earth, whether their own laws recognize it or not. They coined a term for it, and modern thinkers point to it as a root of human rights and international law. What did the Romans call this universal justice?
answer: Natural law
choices: Natural law
Statute law
Sacred law
Common law
context: The Romans coined 'ius naturale' (natural law) -- the idea that some standards of justice are universal, binding on all peoples regardless of any state's written statutes. Alongside it stood 'ius gentium,' the 'law of nations' applied between Romans and foreigners; both are acknowledged roots of modern human-rights and international law. Source: Wikipedia 'Jus gentium'; iusromanum.eu 'Roman Law Revisited'; Ernst Levy 'Natural Law in the Roman Period' (Notre Dame).

question: Cicero gave natural law its most famous words in his book On the Republic: 'True law is right reason in agreement with nature... it is not allowed to alter this law, nor to repeal any part of it.' Yet On the Republic itself was lost for centuries, so this passage should have vanished with it. How did Cicero's definition of true law survive at all?
answer: A Christian writer quoted it long after
choices: A Christian writer quoted it long after
A monk recopied it in a monastery
A rival senator entered it into the record
An emperor had it carved onto a column
context: Cicero's natural-law passage in De Republica Book III ('True law is right reason in agreement with nature; it is of universal application, unchanging and everlasting...') survives only because the Christian writer Lactantius quoted it after the Republic itself was lost for centuries. The idea outlived the book that contained it. Source: nlnrac.org 'On the Republic (De Republica)'; Lex Christianorum 'Natural Law in Cicero's De republica' (citing Lactantius).

question: The grandest temple in ancient Rome was named with two Greek words stuck together: 'pan' and 'theon.' Those two words spell out exactly who the whole building was raised to honor. So the Pantheon was a temple built to honor what?
answer: All the gods of Rome at once
choices: All the gods of Rome at once
Every emperor who had ever ruled
All the heroes of the legions
All the rivers and seas of the empire
context: 'Pantheon' = Greek pan (all) + theon (gods) — a temple meant to honor every god of Rome together, not just one. Source: https://www.turismoroma.it/en/places/pantheon

question: Step inside the Pantheon in Rome and look straight up: there are no side windows at all. Instead, at the very crown of the huge dome there is a single round hole, almost nine meters across, left wide open to the sky. What did the Romans call that one round opening that is the building's only source of daylight?
answer: The oculus
choices: The oculus
The atrium
The forum
The vault
context: The oculus (Latin for 'eye') is about 8.8 m (29 ft) across — the Pantheon's only window and only natural light source. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Pantheon/

question: The Pantheon's great dome has a hole open to the sky at its center, so when a storm rolls over Rome, rain pours straight down through it onto the marble floor inside. Yet the floor never floods. How did the Roman builders keep the water from pooling?
answer: A raised floor with hidden drains cut into it
choices: A raised floor with hidden drains cut into it
A glass pane stretched across the opening
Slaves posted to bail it out with buckets
A sloped dome that shed the rain outside
context: Rain falls through the open oculus, but the marble floor is gently humped in the middle and about 22 hidden drain holes carry the water away so it never pools. Source: https://thepantheonrome.com/pantheon-oculus/

question: Big bold letters carved across the front of the Pantheon name Marcus Agrippa as the man who 'made this.' But Agrippa's own Pantheon had burned to the ground long before the building we see today went up. The dome standing now was actually raised under a later emperor who kept Agrippa's name on the front instead of carving in his own. Which emperor really built today's Pantheon?
answer: Emperor Hadrian
choices: Emperor Hadrian
Emperor Augustus
Emperor Constantine
Emperor Trajan
context: Today's Pantheon was finished under Hadrian around 125–128 CE, but he left Agrippa's old inscription on the front — an act of imperial modesty that confused people for centuries about who really built it. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/pantheon

question: Most pagan temples of Rome were torn apart for their stone after the empire fell, but the Pantheon came through nearly whole. In 608 CE its fate changed in a way that gave it caretakers instead of looters: it stopped being a temple to the old gods and became something else entirely. What did the Pantheon become in 608 that saved it?
answer: A Christian church
choices: A Christian church
A military fortress
A public marketplace
A senate meeting hall
context: In 608 CE the Pantheon was consecrated as the church of Santa Maria ad Martyres (St. Mary of the Martyrs), so unlike most pagan temples it was cared for instead of quarried for stone. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Pantheon/

question: The space inside the Pantheon hides a piece of secret geometry. Measure from the floor up to the open hole at the dome's top — about 43 meters — and you get the exact same number as the dome's width across. Because those two measurements match perfectly, what shape could you imagine fitting snugly inside the Pantheon, just kissing the floor and the top of the dome?
answer: A perfect sphere
choices: A perfect sphere
A tall pyramid
A long cylinder
A wide cube
context: The interior height (about 43.3 m) equals the dome's diameter, so a giant ball would fit exactly inside, touching both the floor and the crown of the dome. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Pantheon/

question: To keep their enormous dome from crushing itself, the Roman builders changed the recipe of the concrete as the dome climbed: dense, heavy stone packed in low down, then lighter material in the middle. At the very top they mixed in a strange volcanic rock so riddled with holes that, oddly for a stone, it floats. Which featherweight rock did they save for the crown of the dome?
answer: Pumice
choices: Pumice
Granite
Marble
Basalt
context: Heavy travertine and basalt sit in the concrete at the base, lighter brick and tufa in the middle, and featherweight pumice — a volcanic rock so full of holes it floats on water — at the very top. Source: https://www.thearchaeologist.org/blog/the-roman-pantheon-the-secret-of-the-unreinforced-concrete-dome

question: Look up inside the Pantheon's dome and you see rings of sunken square hollows marching toward the opening at the top, shrinking as they climb. There are 28 of these recessed panels in each ring, and they are gorgeous to look at — but the Romans cut them for a hard engineering reason, not just beauty. What practical job do those sunken panels do?
answer: They scoop dead weight out of the dome
choices: They scoop dead weight out of the dome
They let rainwater drain through the roof
They lock the marble facing in place
They channel echoes down to the floor
context: The five rings of 28 sunken panels are called coffers; they look beautiful but their real job is to remove weight from the dome so it doesn't crush itself. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Pantheon/

question: Roman concrete could do something ordinary mortar cannot: it would set rock-hard even underwater, through a chemical reaction rather than just drying out in the air. The secret ingredient was a gray volcanic ash dug from the hills near Mount Vesuvius. What is that volcanic ash, the key to Roman concrete, called?
answer: Pozzolana
choices: Pozzolana
Gypsum
Quartz
Slag
context: Pozzolana — volcanic ash from Pozzuoli near Vesuvius — mixed with lime and water sets through a chemical reaction and can even harden underwater, unlike ordinary mortar. Source: https://ancientengrtech.wisc.edu/roman-concrete/

question: The Pantheon's bronze was stripped twice over the centuries, the second time in 1625 when Pope Urban VIII, head of a powerful Roman family, tore the bronze out of the porch to be melted into cannons. Romans were so disgusted that they coined a biting line about it. What did that famous Roman jab say?
answer: What the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did
choices: What the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did
A pope who melts bronze will answer to God
Rome was looted by friends, not enemies
The cannons of the Pope guard an empty shell
context: Pope Urban VIII was a Barberini; the looting prompted the Roman quip 'Quod non fecerunt barbari, fecerunt Barberini' — 'What the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did.' Most of the bronze became cannons for Castel Sant'Angelo. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Peter's_Baldachin

question: For ages, builders sneered at the little white lumps scattered through Roman concrete, calling them proof of careless mixing. Then in 2023 MIT scientists studied those very lumps and found they give the ancient concrete a power no modern concrete has. What can Roman concrete do that ours cannot?
answer: Heal its own cracks shut
choices: Heal its own cracks shut
Glow faintly in the dark
Float on top of seawater
Bend without ever snapping
context: In 2023 MIT researchers found that 'lime clasts' — long dismissed as sloppy mixing — let Roman concrete heal itself: water in a crack dissolves the lime, which re-crystallizes to glue the crack closed. Source: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/ancient-roman-concrete-has-self-healing-capabilities/

question: The Pantheon held the world record for the largest dome for roughly 1,300 years — no builder could match it. The man who finally beat it raised the colossal dome over Florence Cathedral in the 1420s and 1430s, and to crack the problem he traveled to Rome and studied the Pantheon's ancient ruins firsthand. Who finally built a dome to rival the Pantheon's?
answer: Filippo Brunelleschi
choices: Filippo Brunelleschi
Leonardo da Vinci
Michelangelo Buonarroti
Lorenzo Ghiberti
context: Filippo Brunelleschi raised the dome of Florence Cathedral in the 1420s–1430s, ending the Pantheon's ~1,300-year reign as the world's largest dome — and he studied the Pantheon's ruins in Rome to figure out how. Source: https://www.novatr.com/blog/worlds-biggest-dome-by-filippo-brunelleschi

question: As Frederic Chopin lay dying of tuberculosis in Paris, terrified of being buried alive, he begged that one thing be done to his body after death: his heart cut out of his chest. The physician did exactly that during the autopsy. How did the doctor keep Chopin's heart preserved?
answer: Sealed in a jar of cognac
choices: Sealed in a jar of cognac
Buried in a small lead box
Wrapped tightly in silk cloth
Set in a block of beeswax
context: The physician Jean Cruveilhier removed Chopin's heart and sealed it in a crystal jar of cognac. Chopin's dread of premature burial drove the request. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_of_Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Chopin

question: Pyotr Tchaikovsky's 1812 Overture celebrates Russia driving Napoleon's invading army back out of the country. To make the music roar like the battle itself, Tchaikovsky scored in a sound no concert orchestra had ever used before. What did he put into the 1812 Overture?
answer: Blasts of live cannon fire
choices: Blasts of live cannon fire
A galloping troop of horses
A booming thunder machine
A set of blaring trumpets
context: The score calls for sixteen real cannon shots in all (five during the battle, eleven in the finale), alongside the pealing church bells of Moscow, to depict Russia's victory over Napoleon. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1812_Overture

question: Frederic Chopin died far from home, exiled in Paris, but his last wish was for his heart to rest in his native Poland. His sister Ludwika promised to carry it home, yet the route ran through guarded Austrian and Russian border posts where officers searched travelers' bags. How did Ludwika smuggle the sealed jar holding her brother's heart across the borders?
answer: Hidden under her own cloak
choices: Hidden under her own cloak
Packed inside a wine barrel
Sewn into a feather pillow
Bribed past with gold coins
context: Ludwika hid the cognac-preserved heart under her cloak or skirt to get it past customs officers. It now rests sealed in a pillar of the Holy Cross Church in Warsaw. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_of_Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Chopin

question: Richard Wagner wrote 'The Ride of the Valkyries' for the moment his warrior sky-maidens gather to carry slain heroes up to Valhalla. Almost a century later a famous war film bolted loudspeakers onto its attack helicopters and blasted that same galloping music over a village as the choppers swept in. In which film do helicopters roar in to Wagner's Valkyries?
answer: Apocalypse Now
choices: Apocalypse Now
Full Metal Jacket
Black Hawk Down
Saving Private Ryan
context: 'Ride of the Valkyries' opens Act 3 of Die Walkure; the Valkyries are warrior maidens who carry the slain to Valhalla. The same music blares from helicopter loudspeakers during the village attack in Apocalypse Now (1979). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ride_of_the_Valkyries

question: Richard Wagner built his own theater at Bayreuth so his operas could be staged exactly his way, and there he placed the orchestra somewhere no other opera house ever had. Other houses seat the musicians out front, level with the audience. Where did Wagner put his orchestra at Bayreuth?
answer: In a covered pit below the stage
choices: In a covered pit below the stage
On a balcony above the audience
Behind a curtain at the back
Inside a glass booth onstage
context: Wagner hid the entire orchestra in a sunken, hooded pit beneath the stage, invisible to the audience, a design he called the 'mystic gulf' so nothing would distract from the drama onstage. King Ludwig II of Bavaria paid for the Festspielhaus, dedicated solely to Wagner's works. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayreuth_Festspielhaus

question: To paint a real blizzard at sea for 'Snow Storm: Steam-Boat off a Harbour's Mouth' (1842), the English Romantic painter J.M.W. Turner said he didn't sketch it from shore. He claimed he had himself tied to the mast of a steamboat and held there through the worst of the storm. According to his own account, how long did he stay lashed up there in the freezing spray?
answer: Four hours, not expecting to escape alive
choices: Four hours, not expecting to escape alive
One quick gust before going below
A full day and a night at sea
Just long enough to make a sketch
context: Turner, then about 67, said: 'I got the sailors to lash me to the mast to observe it; I was lashed for four hours, and I did not expect to escape, but I felt bound to record it if I did.' The steamboat was named the Ariel. The story is his own testimony — some scholars doubt it is literally true, so it is told as legend. A critic mocked the swirling result as 'soapsuds and whitewash,' but John Ruskin in 1843 called it 'one of the very grandest statements of sea-motion, mist and light, that has ever been put on canvas.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snow_Storm:_Steam-Boat_off_a_Harbour%27s_Mouth ; news.artnet.com/art-world/art-bites-turner-mast-snow-storm-2561636

question: In Eugène Delacroix's 'Liberty Leading the People' (1830), the figure charging forward over the bodies sprawled across the barricade is not a soldier or a king. People often mistake the scene for the famous 1789 French Revolution, but it shows the July Revolution of 1830 that toppled King Charles X. Who is the central figure striding over the dead and waving the French tricolore flag onward?
answer: A bare-breasted woman in a red cap, half-goddess, half-fighter
choices: A bare-breasted woman in a red cap, half-goddess, half-fighter
An armored general on a rearing warhorse
King Charles X surrendering his crown
A robed bishop blessing the fallen
context: She is both an allegory of Liberty and a robust woman of the people — an early image of Marianne, the symbol of France. She wears a red Phrygian cap and carries a bayoneted musket in one hand and the tricolore in the other; the towers of Notre-Dame rise in the smoke behind her. The fighters span the social classes — a top-hatted gentleman with a shotgun, a worker, and a boy with two pistols who later inspired Victor Hugo's street urchin Gavroche in 'Les Misérables.' The French government bought the painting in 1831 but hid it for years, nervous about its raw revolutionary energy; it now hangs in the Louvre, and reappeared as the cover art of Coldplay's 2008 album 'Viva la Vida.' Sources: dailyartmagazine.com/liberty-leading-the-people/ ; uen.pressbooks.pub/arth2720/chapter/1004/

question: In the Roman founding legend, two newborn twin boys named Romulus and Remus were left to die on the bank of the River Tiber. Before any human found them, a wild animal kept the babies alive. What did that animal do?
answer: A she-wolf let them suckle her milk
choices: A she-wolf let them suckle her milk
A great eagle carried them to its nest
A herd of wild deer sheltered them
A serpent coiled warmly around them
context: The she-wolf (Latin lupa) nursing the twins is the single most iconic image of the Roman founding myth, told as legend. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Romulus_and_Remus/

question: After the twins Romulus and Remus survived their abandonment by the river, they were taken in and raised by ordinary country folk who never knew the boys had royal blood. As whom did the brothers grow up?
answer: As shepherds tending flocks
choices: As shepherds tending flocks
As fishermen on the river
As blacksmiths at a forge
As soldiers in the army
context: A shepherd named Faustulus and his wife Acca Larentia found the twins and raised them as their own; the boys grew up herding sheep, unaware they were royal-blooded. Told as legend. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Romulus_and_Remus/

question: In the legend, the baby twins Romulus and Remus were sealed in a basket and set on the River Tiber to drown on the orders of King Amulius. Instead of sinking, the basket caught and held fast. What stopped it at the foot of the Palatine Hill?
answer: The roots of a wild fig tree
choices: The roots of a wild fig tree
A fisherman's tangled net
A sandbar of pale silt
A fallen marble column
context: The basket snagged in the roots of a wild fig tree at the foot of the Palatine Hill, right by the cave (the Lupercal) where the she-wolf lived. Told as legend. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Romulus_and_Remus/

question: Grown to manhood, Romulus began building the walls of his new city. His twin brother Remus mocked the work by leaping over the half-built wall. According to the Roman historian Livy, how did Romulus answer that insult?
answer: He killed his brother Remus in anger
choices: He killed his brother Remus in anger
He banished Remus from the city forever
He challenged Remus to a footrace
He tore the new wall back down
context: Livy (Book 1.7) records Romulus striking Remus down and shouting 'So perish whoever else shall leap over my walls!' The fratricide that founded Rome is told plainly as the legend has it; Plutarch preserves a rival version in which a man named Celer dealt the blow. Source: http://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:1999.02.0151:book%3D1:chapter%3D7

question: The legend gives Romulus and Remus a half-divine birth: their mother was Rhea Silvia, a Vestal Virgin forced into that vow so she could bear no heirs. Yet she bore the twins anyway, the stories say, because of who had fathered them. Who did?
answer: Mars, the god of war
choices: Mars, the god of war
Jupiter, the king of the gods
Neptune, the god of the sea
Apollo, the god of the sun
context: The war-god Mars was said to have fathered Romulus and Remus on Rhea Silvia, making the twins half-divine. Told as legend. Source: https://www.unrv.com/culture/romulus-and-remus.php

question: To settle which twin would found the city, Romulus and Remus held a contest of augury, reading the gods' will in the flight of birds. Remus looked first and counted six vultures, and thought he had won. Then Romulus looked. How many vultures did he count?
answer: Twelve vultures
choices: Twelve vultures
Seven vultures
Three vultures
Twenty vultures
context: Remus saw six vultures first, but Romulus then saw twelve, and each claimed victory, deepening the quarrel that ended in Remus's death. Told as legend. Source: http://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:1999.02.0151:book%3D1:chapter%3D7

question: On 22 January 1879, just over 150 British soldiers turned a mission station called Rorke's Drift into a fort, holding off 3,000 to 4,000 Zulu warriors for more than twelve hours. With no time to build proper defences, what did the defenders stack into walls to shoot from behind?
answer: Maize bags and biscuit boxes
choices: Maize bags and biscuit boxes
Tree trunks and wagon ropes
Sandbags and earth baskets
Rock slabs and timber beams
context: The garrison piled up mealie (maize) bags, biscuit boxes and tinned-meat crates from their stores, and cut loopholes in the buildings to fire through. Lieutenants John Chard and Gonville Bromhead chose to stand and fight after Commissary James Dalton warned that fleeing into open country with the wounded meant death. Source: https://www.nam.ac.uk/explore/defence-rorkes-drift

question: The defence of Rorke's Drift in 1879 became the most decorated single action in British military history. How many Victoria Crosses, the highest award for bravery, were handed out for that one night's fight?
answer: Eleven
choices: Eleven
Three
Five
Twenty
context: Eleven Victoria Crosses were awarded for Rorke's Drift, the most ever for a single action, plus five Distinguished Conduct Medals. Only about 17 of the roughly 150 defenders were killed against some 400 Zulu dead, yet nearly every man in the garrison was wounded. Source: https://www.nam.ac.uk/explore/defence-rorkes-drift

question: Earlier the same day Rorke's Drift began, a Zulu army of about 20,000 wiped out a British camp of 1,800 men at Isandlwana, the Empire's worst defeat in Africa. The Zulu won by sweeping in a battle formation named after an animal. Which formation crushed the British?
answer: The horns and chest of the buffalo
choices: The horns and chest of the buffalo
The jaws and tail of the crocodile
The wings and beak of the eagle
The coils and head of the serpent
context: In the 'horns and chest of the buffalo' formation, the two horns swept around to encircle the enemy while the chest pressed in the centre. At Isandlwana around 20,000 Zulu overran roughly 1,800 British, colonial and native troops, killing over 1,300. A partial solar eclipse darkened the field at the height of the battle; a survivor recalled 'the camp looked dark, just as if a shadow was passing over it.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Isandlwana

question: Jean-Jacques Rousseau opened his 1762 book The Social Contract with one of the most famous first sentences in all of political philosophy. He claimed every human enters the world in one condition but then spends his whole life held fast in its opposite. Which famous pairing did Rousseau open the book with?
answer: born free, and everywhere he is in chains
choices: born free, and everywhere he is in chains
born equal, and everywhere he is ruled
born noble, and everywhere he is debased
born wild, and everywhere he is tamed
context: The full line runs: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.' Rousseau's point was NOT that chains are natural, but that he wanted to show how authority could be made legitimate. Source: Britannica, The Social Contract; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Rousseau.

question: Within weeks of publishing The Social Contract and Emile in 1762, Rousseau saw both books condemned as dangerous and irreligious. The authorities did not merely ban them in Paris and in Rousseau's own home city of Geneva. What did they do to the books in the public squares of both cities?
answer: burned them
choices: burned them
chained them shut
stamped them counterfeit
sealed them in crates
context: Both The Social Contract and Emile were publicly burned in 1762 in Paris AND in Geneva, condemned as subversive and religiously heterodox. Source: EBSCO Research Starters, Rousseau Publishes The Social Contract; SparkNotes context.

question: Rousseau became the great theorist of childhood's natural goodness and wrote Emile, a whole book on how to raise a child well. Yet with his own five children he made a very different choice soon after each was born. Where did Rousseau send all five of his own children?
answer: to a Paris foundling hospital
choices: to a Paris foundling hospital
to a wet-nurse far from Paris
to a convent orphanage
to his mother's poor relatives
context: Rousseau handed all five of his children to a Paris foundling hospital, where in the 1700s survival was bleak -- an almost certain death sentence. The author of the era's great book on tender education abandoned his own. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Rousseau.

question: In The Social Contract, Rousseau argued a state is legitimate only when its laws express the 'general will' of the whole people aimed at the common good. In Book 1, Chapter 7 he pushed this to a chilling edge: anyone who refuses to obey the general will, he wrote, should be compelled by the whole community. What striking phrase did Rousseau use for that compulsion?
answer: forced to be free
choices: forced to be free
broken to the yoke
schooled by the rod
bound to the crowd
context: Rousseau wrote that such a person may be 'forced to be free.' Revolutionaries would later seize on the line. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Rousseau.

question: Rousseau died before the French Revolution, but he became known as 'the muse of the Jacobins.' Maximilien Robespierre and Saint-Just saw themselves as building Rousseau's ideal republic of the general will. In his 1794 speech defending the Revolution's bloodiest year, Robespierre fused two things together, claiming one without the other is murderous and the other without the first is powerless. Which pair did Robespierre bind together?
answer: virtue and terror
choices: virtue and terror
faith and fire
duty and silence
law and exile
context: Robespierre declared 'virtue, without which terror is murderous; terror, without which virtue is powerless,' calling terror 'swift, severe, indomitable justice.' Those who resisted the general will were branded enemies and sent to the guillotine. Hegel argued Rousseau's doctrine led 'inevitably' to the Terror, though some scholars insist Rousseau himself would have condemned it. Source: Robespierre, On Political Morality, 1794; Wikipedia, General will; Notre Dame Philosophical Reviews.

question: On 23 February 1917 (by Russia's old calendar), striking textile workers and huge crowds in the capital, Petrograd, flooded the streets demanding bread, and within a day about 200,000 people had joined them. That date also happened to be a holiday being marked around the world. Which one?
answer: International Women's Day
choices: International Women's Day
International Workers' Day
the Russian Orthodox New Year
the Tsar's official name-day
context: This was the start of the February Revolution. Working-class women, joined by striking workers from the giant Putilov factory, marched against bread shortages and rationing; the crowd swelled to roughly 200,000 within a day. (Petrograd was the wartime name for St. Petersburg.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_Revolution ; https://www.iwm.org.uk/history/what-was-the-february-revolution

question: When the revolutionary Vladimir Lenin returned to Petrograd in April 1917, he boiled his whole program down to a three-word promise that ordinary Russians, sick of war and hunger, could chant in the streets. What were the three things he promised them?
answer: Peace, Land, and Bread
choices: Peace, Land, and Bread
Liberty, Equality, Fraternity
Work, Family, Fatherland
Faith, Tsar, and Country
context: Lenin laid out this slogan, along with 'All power to the Soviets,' in his 'April Theses' right after returning from exile. It promised an end to the war, land for peasants, and food for the cities. Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/politics-and-government/april-theses ; https://easy-to-read.eu/peace-land-and-bread-lenins-return-from-exile-and-the/

question: By the night the Bolsheviks moved on the Winter Palace in October 1917, most of the government's soldiers had drifted away, hungry and leaderless. Among the very last defenders still guarding the palace was one unit that has stuck in memory ever since. Who were they?
answer: a battalion of women
choices: a battalion of women
a regiment of Cossacks
the Tsar's old palace guard
a company of foreign mercenaries
context: The 2nd Russian Women's Battalion of Death, roughly 137 to 139 women, stood among the last guards of the Winter Palace alongside a few hundred military cadets after most of the male troops had melted away. Source: https://www.thevintagenews.com/2017/01/31/the-womens-battalion-of-death-were-the-last-guards-of-the-winter-palace-during-the-bolshevik-revolution/ ; https://spartacus-educational.com/Wdeath.htm

question: By March 1917 Tsar Nicholas II had lost the loyalty of his own generals, who told him the army would no longer fight for him. He gave up the throne, ending 300 years of Romanov rule, in a strangely undignified spot. Where was Nicholas when he abdicated?
answer: aboard his royal train
choices: aboard his royal train
inside the Winter Palace
locked in a prison cell
on a warship at sea
context: Nicholas II abdicated on 2 March 1917 (old calendar) stranded on his imperial train at Pskov, after his generals advised him he had lost the army. His brother, Grand Duke Michael, refused the throne the next day, ending Romanov rule. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_Revolution ; https://www.iwm.org.uk/history/what-was-the-february-revolution

question: In late February 1917 Tsar Nicholas II ordered the soldiers of his Petrograd garrison to put down the bread riots. The Volynsky Regiment faced that order on 27 February, and what its soldiers did next turned the tide. What did they do?
answer: turned their guns around and joined the protesters
choices: turned their guns around and joined the protesters
opened fire and scattered the protesters
surrounded and arrested the Duma
marched out of the city to the war front
context: On 27 February (old calendar) the Volynsky Regiment mutinied and refused to fire on the crowds, pulling the Semyonovsky, Preobrazhensky, and Moskovsky regiments into the uprising. General Khabalov soon reported only about 600 infantry and 500 cavalry still loyal. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_Revolution

question: When the Tsar fell in 1917, the revolutionary Vladimir Lenin was stranded in exile in Zurich, Switzerland. Germany, eager to knock Russia out of World War I, helped him race home to Petrograd. How did the Germans move him across their own territory?
answer: in a sealed train
choices: in a sealed train
aboard a hospital ship
hidden on a submarine
disguised as a diplomat
context: Swiss socialist Fritz Platten brokered the deal; a chalk line on the carriage floor marked the extraterritorial 'no-man's-land' separating the Russians from their German escorts. Germany also approved millions of marks for revolutionary propaganda, much of it routed through the businessman Alexander Parvus, though historians still debate how much reached the Bolsheviks. Source: https://blog.nationalmuseum.ch/en/2017/04/by-train-to-the-revolution/ ; https://blogjamesmorris.wordpress.com/2018/11/15/german-gold-for-the-bolsheviks-an-examination/

question: On the night of 24 October 1917, Vladimir Lenin crept through Petrograd to Bolshevik headquarters in disguise: a workman's coat, a wig that kept slipping off, and a dirty handkerchief over his face so he could claim a toothache if stopped. A comrade who saw him said he looked like what?
answer: a schoolmaster or a second-hand book dealer
choices: a schoolmaster or a second-hand book dealer
a soldier or a sailor home on leave
a village priest or a wandering monk
a banker or a wealthy grain merchant
context: Lenin slipped into Bolshevik HQ at the Smolny Institute in this getup to direct the coup. The Bolshevik organizer Antonov-Ovseyenko said he looked like 'a schoolmaster or a second-hand book dealer.' Source: https://lenin.shm.ru/en/v-i-lenin-in-smolny-in-makeup-october-1917/ ; https://spartacus-educational.com/RUSprovisional.htm

question: The cruiser Aurora is tied to the assault on the Winter Palace on the night of 25 October 1917, and popular memory pictures it bombarding the palace with its big guns. In reality, what did the Aurora actually fire?
answer: a single blank shell
choices: a single blank shell
a full broadside of live rounds
a volley of signal rockets
nothing at all that night
context: At 9:40 p.m. the Aurora, crewed by mutinous sailors, fired one blank shell over the Neva River as the signal to attack. It never actually bombarded the building, contrary to the famous image. Source: https://www.historytoday.com/archive/cruiser-aurora-and-russian-revolution ; https://www.rbth.com/arts/2014/11/07/aurora_the_cruiser_that_sparked_a_revolution_or_did_it_41229.html

question: The October 1917 takeover was not a vast popular uprising but a tightly organized seizure of a few key buildings, carried out while Lenin stayed in hiding until the final hours. Who actually planned and directed the operation, as head of the Petrograd Soviet's Military Revolutionary Committee?
answer: Leon Trotsky
choices: Leon Trotsky
Joseph Stalin
Alexander Kerensky
Grigory Zinoviev
context: Trotsky ran the Military Revolutionary Committee that planned and directed the insurrection while Lenin stayed hidden until the last moment. The 'storming' that followed was nearly bloodless; the Provisional Government's ministers were simply arrested in the palace and jailed in the Peter and Paul Fortress. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_Revolution

question: In January 1918 Russia's freely elected Constituent Assembly, the parliament chosen in the country's first free national vote, met for a single 13-hour session and defied the Bolsheviks. The anarchist sailor in charge of the soldiers on duty, Anatoli Zheleznyakov, shut the parliament down for good with one short sentence. What did he say?
answer: "The guard is tired."
choices: "The guard is tired."
"By order of the Soviet, disperse."
"This session is now over."
"Long live the revolution."
context: When the assembly refused Bolshevik demands and elected the Socialist-Revolutionary Viktor Chernov as its president, Zheleznyakov ended Russia's democratic experiment with this line. The Bolsheviks then locked the doors, and the assembly never met again. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatoli_Zhelezniakov ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Constituent_Assembly

question: Soon after seizing power, the Bolsheviks allowed Russia's first free national election, held in November 1917 with nearly 47 million votes cast. The result undercut their claim to speak for the people. Which party actually won the most seats?
answer: the Socialist-Revolutionaries
choices: the Socialist-Revolutionaries
the Bolsheviks
the Mensheviks
the Constitutional Democrats
context: The Socialist-Revolutionaries won with 324 seats (about 37.6%); Lenin's Bolsheviks came second with 183 seats (about 23%). The Bolsheviks were a minority faction, which is why they dissolved the elected assembly by force weeks later. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1917_Russian_Constituent_Assembly_election

question: The dramatic scenes everyone pictures of the Winter Palace being 'stormed' in 1917, surging crowds and blazing guns, were largely manufactured after the fact. The real event was almost bloodless and left barely any record. Where did that famous heroic image mostly come from?
answer: a 1927 movie by Sergei Eisenstein
choices: a 1927 movie by Sergei Eisenstein
a 1930 painting by Isaak Brodsky
a 1925 newsreel by Dziga Vertov
a 1928 poem by Vladimir Mayakovsky
context: The dramatic image comes largely from Sergei Eisenstein's 1927-28 film 'October' and a 1920 mass re-enactment watched by about 100,000 people, both of which used more men, more ordnance, and produced more injuries than the real 1917 event. Myth literally replaced the memory. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October:_Ten_Days_That_Shook_the_World ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Storming_of_the_Winter_Palace

question: Andrei Sakharov was the lead designer of the Soviet hydrogen bomb. A scaled-up version of his design was detonated over the Arctic in October 1961 and remains the most powerful nuclear device ever exploded. By what name is that 50-megaton monster known?
answer: Tsar Bomba
choices: Tsar Bomba
Fat Man
Castle Bravo
Little Boy
context: Sakharov's 'Third Idea' (using radiation to symmetrically compress the fusion fuel) was first tested as RDS-37 in 1955; the scaled-up Tsar Bomba reached 50 megatons. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrei_Sakharov

question: During Czechoslovakia's Velvet Revolution, hundreds of thousands packed Prague's Wenceslas Square at 6 PM on November 25, 1989. To ring the Communist regime out and tell it its time was up, the whole crowd reached into their pockets and did one thing together. What did they do?
answer: Jingled their keys
choices: Jingled their keys
Lit white candles
Threw down flowers
Stood in total silence
context: The jingling keys symbolized unlocking the regime's doors and ringing it a bell to say 'Goodbye.' Source: https://www.expats.cz/czech-news/article/unlocking-freedom-why-did-czechs-jingle-their-keys-during-the-velvet-revolution

question: In 1975 the Nobel committee gave Andrei Sakharov its Peace Prize, calling him 'a spokesman for the conscience of mankind.' But the Soviet government would not let him leave the country to collect it in Oslo. So who travelled to the Oslo podium and read his Nobel lecture aloud in his place?
answer: His wife
choices: His wife
His daughter
A diplomat
The chairman
context: His wife was Yelena Bonner, his partner in dissent; he later staged hunger strikes to force the regime to let her travel abroad for heart surgery. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/peace/1975/sakharov/facts/

question: Vaclav Havel insisted his revolution had one guiding motto, and he proclaimed it while ending a Prague speech on December 10, 1989. The line is now carved on memorials to him. Which motto was it?
answer: Truth and love must prevail over lies and hatred
choices: Truth and love must prevail over lies and hatred
Workers of the world must unite against their masters
Liberty and equality must be won by fraternity
Peace and bread and land must be given to the people
context: Havel made non-violence and honesty the creed of the Velvet Revolution. Source: https://www.nybooks.com/online/2009/11/24/love-and-truth-vaclav-havel-in-bratislava/

question: Before he was a dissident, Vaclav Havel was an absurdist playwright. In his 1965 play The Memorandum he mocked communist officialdom by inventing a ridiculous fake bureaucratic language that no one could actually speak. What did he name this invented office gibberish?
answer: Ptydepe
choices: Ptydepe
Newspeak
Volapuk
Esperanto
context: Havel started as a stagehand at Prague's Theatre on the Balustrade before writing The Garden Party (1963) and The Memorandum (1965). Source: https://english.radio.cz/czech-books-you-must-read-8506310/13

question: On December 29, 1989, the Czechoslovak Federal Assembly - still 93% Communist deputies, the very men who had jailed Vaclav Havel - voted on whether to make him president. The playwright had gone from a prison cell toward Prague Castle in a single year. How did that vote come out?
answer: Unanimous, with not one vote against
choices: Unanimous, with not one vote against
A slim majority squeaked him through
A deadlocked tie the chairman broke
A first-ballot rejection, then a retry
context: Not a single vote against and no abstentions - the assembly that had imprisoned him elected him unanimously. Source: https://english.radio.cz/december-29-1989-vaclav-havel-elected-president-first-time-8838384

question: Charter 77, the human-rights manifesto Vaclav Havel co-authored, was set off by one 1976 trial in particular. The defendants weren't politicians - they were a long-haired underground rock band, convicted of 'extreme vulgarity with an antisocialist impact.' Whose trial sparked the Charter?
answer: The Plastic People of the Universe
choices: The Plastic People of the Universe
The masked riot-punks Pussy Riot
The New York band Velvet Underground
The metal act Rage Against the Machine
context: Outrage at jailing musicians for their music galvanized intellectuals; Charter 77 was published January 6, 1977 with 242 founding signatories. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter_77

question: Andrei Sakharov had been exiled to the closed city of Gorky for condemning the invasion of Afghanistan. One December evening in 1986, a KGB officer and two electricians showed up at his flat and installed a telephone with no explanation. The next day it rang. Who was on the line?
answer: Mikhail Gorbachev, ending his exile
choices: Mikhail Gorbachev, ending his exile
A KGB interrogator, with new threats
An American reporter, seeking a quote
His old bomb-lab director, pleading
context: Gorbachev personally told Sakharov he could return to Moscow; Sakharov immediately used the call to press him to free other prisoners of conscience. Source: https://www.upi.com/Archives/1986/12/19/Freedom-came-with-a-phone-call/9238535352400/

question: On December 14, 1989, Andrei Sakharov - by then an elected deputy - was resting at home before returning to Congress to fight the Communist Party's monopoly on power. He died that evening of heart failure. What had he just told his wife, in his last words?
answer: Tomorrow will be a battle
choices: Tomorrow will be a battle
I have done all my duty
Let me sleep a while now
The long work is finished
context: He died still in the fight, expecting to argue against one-party rule the next day. Source: https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2002/12/death-andrei-sakharov-1989

question: Jailed for 'subversion' in 1979, Vaclav Havel was allowed just one four-page letter a week to his wife Olga - and the prison banned cross-outs, quotation marks, foreign words, underlining, even humor. For which single act of defiance did his jailers throw Havel into solitary confinement?
answer: Defending an illiterate Roma prisoner
choices: Defending an illiterate Roma prisoner
Hiding a sharpened spoon in his boot
Refusing to put on the prison uniform
Leading the inmates in a hunger strike
context: He was thrown in solitary for writing on behalf of an illiterate Roma fellow prisoner; those restricted weekly letters were later published as the book 'Letters to Olga.' Source: https://www.themarginalian.org/2025/02/06/vaclav-havel-letters-to-olga/

question: At the first Congress of People's Deputies in June 1989, Andrei Sakharov ran past his time at the microphone, and Mikhail Gorbachev cut his mic off, snapping, 'Time's up. Don't you respect the Congress?' How did Sakharov answer him?
answer: Yes, but I respect the country and the people more
choices: Yes, but I respect the country and the people more
Yes, but the truth will not be hurried by a clock
No, for this Congress has not yet earned my respect
No, and history will remember who silenced me here
context: The exchange captured Sakharov's stance: institutions answer to the people, not the reverse. Source: https://time.com/archive/6702744/ussr-presiding-over-a-new-soviet-congress-gorbachev-gets-a-clamorous-lesson-in-democracy/

question: At the banquet after his hydrogen bomb's 1955 test, Andrei Sakharov stood and toasted that the devices would only ever explode over test sites, 'never over cities.' A marshal cut him off with a crude parable and toasted instead to using the weapons in war. Sakharov said the feelings from that night never left him and turned him against the regime. What had his toast shown was awakening in him?
answer: A conscience about the weapon he had built
choices: A conscience about the weapon he had built
A secret wish to defect to the West
Regret that the bomb was still too small
Pride at having beaten the Americans
context: Sakharov wrote that the emotions kindled that night 'completely altered my thinking' and never diminished - the seed of the dissident he became. Source: https://blog.nuclearsecrecy.com/2014/01/31/sakharovs-turning-point-first-soviet-h-bomb-test/

question: Europeans called the great Muslim sultan Saladin, but that was their shortening of his honorific Salah ad-Din. What does that title mean?
answer: Righteousness of the Faith
choices: Righteousness of the Faith
Sword of the Prophet
Lion of the Desert
Shadow of the Caliph
context: His full name was al-Nasir Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub; he was an ethnic Kurd born around 1137 in Tikrit, in modern Iraq. 'Salah ad-Din' means 'Righteousness of the Faith,' which Europeans clipped to 'Saladin.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saladin

question: At the Battle of Hattin in 1187, Saladin's army captured the Crusaders' holiest relic, which the bishop of Acre had carried into the battle. What was it?
answer: the True Cross
choices: the True Cross
the Spear of Longinus
the Crown of Thorns
the Ark of the Covenant
context: The relic was believed to be wood from the cross of Jesus. After Hattin it was reportedly fixed upside-down on a lance and paraded to Damascus. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hattin

question: Saladin gave away so much of his wealth that his own treasurers hid money from him. When he died in Damascus in 1193, what was left in his treasury?
answer: one gold coin and forty-seven silver pieces
choices: one gold coin and forty-seven silver pieces
one full chest of jewels and gold bars
one sealed strongroom no one could open
one hidden hoard of two thousand dinars
context: His treasury held only one piece of Tyre gold and forty-seven dirhams of silver, not even enough to pay for his own funeral. His treasurers had learned to hide reserves, because he gave away anything he found out about. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Saladin/

question: By legend, when Richard the Lionheart lay sick with fever during the Third Crusade, his enemy Saladin sent him a gift to help him recover. What did Saladin send?
answer: fresh fruit and mountain snow
choices: fresh fruit and mountain snow
warm furs and spiced wine
a tent of skilled physicians
a flask of healing waters
context: The snow was to cool Richard's drinks. Whether or not it happened exactly so, this act of courtesy toward an enemy became legendary in Europe and helped build Saladin's reputation for chivalry. Source: https://historychronicles.org/richard-the-lionheart-and-saladin/

question: In 1187 the Crusader lord Reynald of Chatillon seized a rich Muslim caravan during a truce and refused to return it, saying he was lord of his own land. How did Saladin respond to the broken truce?
answer: he swore a personal oath to kill Reynald himself
choices: he swore a personal oath to kill Reynald himself
he demanded twice the caravan's value in gold
he appealed to the king of Jerusalem for justice
he ordered a blockade of the Crusader ports
context: Reynald had already enraged Saladin years earlier by raiding pilgrim ships bound for Mecca and Medina. The caravan seizure made it personal, and Saladin vowed to kill him with his own hand. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raynald_of_Ch%C3%A2tillon

question: At Hattin in 1187, Saladin trapped the Crusader army on a waterless plateau by the twin-peaked Horns of Hattin and let them roast through a thirsty night. What did his men do at dawn to finish the trapped knights?
answer: set the dry grass alight so smoke blinded them
choices: set the dry grass alight so smoke blinded them
loosed a cavalry charge straight up the slope
rolled boulders down from the twin peaks
poisoned the last springs behind the lines
context: Saladin's men had beaten drums and chanted through the night; at dawn they fired the dry grass so the smoke blinded and choked the thirst-maddened knights. The Crusader army was destroyed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hattin

question: When Saladin took Jerusalem in 1187 he did not massacre the people but let them buy their freedom by ransom, set at ten dinars for a man. How did the price change for a woman and for a child?
answer: cheaper still, five dinars and two
choices: cheaper still, five dinars and two
the same ten dinars for everyone
free for women, ten for children
double for women, triple for children
context: The ransom was 10 dinars per man, 5 per woman, and 2 per child. The deliberately low, sliding price was a contrast with what had happened when the Crusaders first took the city. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Jerusalem_(1187)

question: After Hattin, Saladin offered the captured King Guy of Lusignan a cup of iced rose-water. Guy drank and passed the cup to Reynald of Chatillon beside him. Why did Saladin then refuse to let Reynald drink from it?
answer: so the laws of hospitality would not protect Reynald from him
choices: so the laws of hospitality would not protect Reynald from him
because the cup was meant only for a crowned king
because Reynald had insulted him by reaching for it
so that Guy would be forced to watch his ally die
context: By custom, a prisoner offered food or drink by his captor could not then be killed. Saladin said, 'I did not ask this evil man to drink,' and struck Reynald down himself, fulfilling his oath. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hattin

question: Saladin spared the captured King Guy of Lusignan after Hattin, telling him 'a king does not kill a king.' But he ordered death for one group of his roughly 200 prisoners in particular. Which prisoners did he have beheaded?
answer: the Templar and Hospitaller knights
choices: the Templar and Hospitaller knights
the foot-soldiers who had fled
the priests who blessed the army
the lords who had broken the truce
context: Saladin saw the military-order knights as his most implacable enemies and had them beheaded, sparing only the Templar Grand Master. King Guy he kept alive. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hattin

question: By the legend of the Third Crusade, Richard the Lionheart's horse was killed under him at the Battle of Jaffa in 1192, leaving the king on foot in the middle of the fight. What did Saladin have sent out to him across the battlefield?
answer: two Arabian horses, so brave a king need not fight on foot
choices: two Arabian horses, so brave a king need not fight on foot
a guard of his own knights to escort the king to safety
a banner of truce calling an immediate halt to the battle
a challenge to settle the war in single combat between them
context: Saladin, through his brother al-Adil, reportedly sent two horses across the lines. He and Richard traded gifts and courtesies through the whole crusade yet never once met face to face. Source: https://templarblog.com/blogs/media-and-culture-of-knights-templar/saladin-richard-the-lionheart-meeting  (Legend.)

question: Once Jerusalem surrendered in 1187, Saladin had the golden Christian cross pulled down from the Dome of the Rock. How did he then have the Al-Aqsa Mosque restored for Muslim worship?
answer: washed with rose-water and recarpeted
choices: washed with rose-water and recarpeted
torn down and rebuilt from the foundation
sealed shut for a year of mourning
painted over with the sultan's banners
context: Saladin had Al-Aqsa ritually washed with rose-water, recarpeted, and re-decorated with Quranic verse to restore it as a mosque after decades of Crusader use. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1553/saladins-conquest-of-jerusalem-1187-ce/

question: Saladin's mercy at Jerusalem in 1187 was remembered partly because of what had happened when the First Crusade took the same city in 1099. By the accounts that set the contrast, what had the Crusaders done in 1099?
answer: massacred Muslims and Jews across the city
choices: massacred Muslims and Jews across the city
levied a heavy yearly tribute on the city
expelled every non-Christian from the walls
burned the markets but spared the people
context: The 1099 accounts describe Crusaders killing Muslims and Jews even as they sheltered in the Al-Aqsa Mosque. Many modern historians think the toll was exaggerated, but those accounts set the contrast Saladin's restraint was measured against. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_of_Jerusalem_(1099)

question: When Balian of Ibelin negotiated Jerusalem's surrender in 1187, Saladin at first resisted a gentle ransom. What threat did Balian use to force Saladin to agree to the ransom terms?
answer: to destroy the Muslim holy places and kill the Muslim prisoners
choices: to destroy the Muslim holy places and kill the Muslim prisoners
to hold the city until a Crusader relief army arrived
to poison the wells before the gates were opened
to surrender only to Saladin's rival in Damascus
context: Balian threatened that the defenders would burn the city's treasures, kill their 5,000 Muslim prisoners, and destroy the holy places including the Dome of the Rock. Only then did Saladin agree to ransom the inhabitants. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1553/saladins-conquest-of-jerusalem-1187-ce/

question: Several of Saladin's own generals urged him to destroy the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, the Christians' holiest site in Jerusalem, after the city fell in 1187. What did Saladin do with it instead?
answer: let Christians keep visiting it for a fee
choices: let Christians keep visiting it for a fee
converted it into a second mosque
gave it to his brother as a prize
stripped its gold and sealed the doors
context: Against his generals' wishes, Saladin refused to destroy the church and let Christians keep visiting, and he permitted native Christians and Jews to go on living in the city. Source: https://www.historyhit.com/saladin-re-enters-jerusalem/

question: Richard I of England won a famous nickname during his own lifetime, sung by troubadours for his fierce courage in battle even before he sailed for the crusade. What was that byname?
answer: the Lionheart
choices: the Lionheart
the Hammer
the Unready
the Conqueror
context: Coeur de Lion. The troubadour Bertran de Born was praising Richard's lion-like valor in verse as early as the 1180s, before he ever left for the Holy Land; the name is first recorded in Ambroise's chronicle 'L'Estoire de la Guerre Sainte.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_I_of_England

question: The Muslim sultan the Crusaders called Saladin was born Yusuf, a Kurd from Tikrit. 'Salah ad-Din' was not really his name but an honorific he had earned. What does that title mean?
answer: Righteousness of the Faith
choices: Righteousness of the Faith
Sword of the Desert
Shield of the East
Lion of the Sands
context: Born around 1137, Saladin rose to become the first sultan of both Egypt and Syria and founded the Ayyubid dynasty. 'Salah ad-Din' is a laqab, an honorific title, meaning 'Righteousness of the Faith.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saladin

question: During the campaign Richard the Lionheart fell gravely ill with a burning fever. Though the two kings were enemies at war, Saladin sent a remarkable gift across the lines to ease his suffering. What did he send?
answer: snow from the mountains and fresh fruit
choices: snow from the mountains and fresh fruit
a chest of gold and fine silk
a captured banner and sword
a fine suit of armor
context: Richard's fever was severe, possibly scurvy. Saladin sent fresh fruit and snow carried down from the mountains to cool him, and is reported to have offered his own personal physician. It is the wonder-moment of honor reaching across the religious line. Source: https://templarblog.com/blogs/media-and-culture-of-knights-templar/saladin-richard-the-lionheart-meeting

question: After crushing the Crusader army at Hattin, Saladin had the captured King Guy of Lusignan brought before him and handed him a cup of snow-chilled rose-water to drink. What did Saladin say to him?
answer: Kings do not kill kings.
choices: Kings do not kill kings.
Drink, and be my servant.
Your sword is mine now.
Kneel, and keep your crown.
context: Among Saladin's people, offering a captured enemy a drink was a gesture meaning his life was safe. He reassured Guy with words recorded as 'it is not the wont of kings to kill kings.' He spared the ordinary king. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hattin

question: At the Battle of Jaffa in 1192, Richard the Lionheart's horse was struck down and he fought on foot among his men. Saladin's brother al-Adil, watching from the enemy side, sent something out to the struggling king in the thick of the fight. What did he send?
answer: two fine Arab warhorses
choices: two fine Arab warhorses
a flag of truce
a cup of cold water
his own bodyguard
context: Al-Adil, whom the Crusaders called Saphadin, saw Richard unhorsed and sent him two fine Arab horses in the middle of the battle. Richard accepted them as a gift between worthy enemies. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Jaffa_(1192)

question: On the burning hot morning of 4 July 1187, Saladin's army had trapped the Crusaders at Hattin and seized the only springs, leaving the Christian soldiers parched and desperate for water. Overnight Saladin ordered something done to the dry hillsides to torment their thirst even more. What did his men do?
answer: set the brush ablaze so the smoke choked their throats
choices: set the brush ablaze so the smoke choked their throats
poisoned the muddy pools left within their reach
beat war-drums through the night to rob them of sleep
dammed the streams high up in the distant hills
context: Saladin used heat as a weapon. Having already taken the springs of Hattin, his men set the dry summer grass and brush alight overnight so the smoke blew into the exhausted, parched Crusaders at dawn, making their dry throats even drier. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hattin

question: Into the Battle of Hattin the Crusaders carried their holiest relic, a fragment of the True Cross, borne at the front of the army by the bishop of Acre. When Saladin's men captured it, what did they do with this prize as they took it to Damascus?
answer: fixed it upside-down on a lance and paraded it
choices: fixed it upside-down on a lance and paraded it
locked it away inside a golden shrine in Damascus
burned it in front of the captured Christian soldiers
buried it deep beneath the great city walls
context: According to the chroniclers, the captured relic was fixed upside-down on a lance and paraded in triumph to Damascus. The Kingdom of Jerusalem never got it back. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hattin

question: When the first Crusaders stormed Jerusalem in 1099, they massacred its inhabitants in the streets. Saladin retook the city in October 1187 after its defenders surrendered. What did Saladin do with the Christian people of Jerusalem?
answer: he spared the city and let its people ransom their freedom
choices: he spared the city and let its people ransom their freedom
he razed the walls and sold every survivor into slavery
he put the entire garrison and clergy to the sword
he burned the Christian quarter down to its foundations
context: Saladin's recapture was nearly bloodless, a deliberate and famous contrast to the 1099 slaughter. The ransom was set at 10 dinars per man, 5 per woman, and 2 per child; when many could not pay, Saladin and his brother al-Adil let thousands of the poor go free. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Jerusalem_(1187)

question: By Saladin's custom, giving a captured enemy a drink meant his life would be spared. After Hattin, King Guy passed his cup of chilled water to a second prisoner, Raynald of Chatillon, who had broken a truce by raiding Muslim pilgrim caravans bound for Mecca. What did Saladin do to Raynald?
answer: struck the cup away and then killed Raynald himself
choices: struck the cup away and then killed Raynald himself
freed Raynald in exchange for a heavy ransom
handed Raynald to the Templars for judgment
let Raynald keep the cup but seized his lands
context: Saladin struck the cup from Raynald's hands and declared, 'I did not ask this evil man to drink, and he would not save his life by doing so,' then executed him personally. The mercy of the cup was deliberately withheld from the truce-breaker. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hattin

question: Desperate to end the war without more slaughter, Richard the Lionheart floated an astonishing peace plan: rather than fight on for Jerusalem, the city would be ruled jointly by a married couple. Who did Richard propose should marry to seal the deal?
answer: his sister Joan to Saladin's brother al-Adil
choices: his sister Joan to Saladin's brother al-Adil
his niece Eleanor to the Byzantine emperor's son
his cousin Constance to a prince of Antioch
his ward Isabella to Saladin's son al-Afdal
context: Richard proposed marrying his own sister Joan to al-Adil and letting the couple rule Jerusalem together. In a letter dated 12 November 1191 he begged off, saying 'The Christian people disapprove of my giving my sister in marriage without consulting the Pope' (recorded by Roger of Hoveden). Source: https://medieval.substack.com/p/the-letters-of-richard-and-saladin

question: Saladin had ruled as sultan of both Egypt and Syria, master of a vast realm. He gave so much of his wealth away in charity that when he died at Damascus in 1193, his servants counted what was left in his personal treasury. What did they find?
answer: one gold coin and forty-odd silver pieces
choices: one gold coin and forty-odd silver pieces
a thousand gold coins and chests of jewels
forty mule-loads of silver and silk
gold enough to ransom a hundred knights
context: There was not enough money left to pay for his own funeral. Accounts say his treasury held only one piece of gold and about forty-seven silver dirhams. Chided for his giving, he reportedly smiled, 'There are people for whom money is no more important than sand.' He was buried beside the Umayyad Mosque. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saladin

question: After the Crusaders took Acre in 1191, Saladin was slow to pay the agreed ransom of the True Cross, gold, and Christian prisoners. His patience worn through, Richard the Lionheart had some 2,700 Muslim prisoners marched to a hill called Ayyadieh. What did Richard do to them there, in full view of Saladin's army?
answer: had them all beheaded in sight of Saladin's army
choices: had them all beheaded in sight of Saladin's army
sold them into slavery to recover his losses
marched them back to Acre to labor on the walls
held them all for a second, far larger ransom
context: On 20 August 1191 about 2,700 Muslim prisoners were beheaded at Ayyadieh where Saladin's men could see, and Saladin retaliated by executing his own Christian captives. The two 'chivalrous' rivals were also capable of mass slaughter. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_at_Ayyadieh

question: On May 24, 1844, Samuel Morse sat at the U.S. Capitol and tapped out the very first official telegraph message down the wire to Baltimore. What four words did he send?
answer: "What hath God wrought"
choices: "What hath God wrought"
"Come at once please"
"The wire is open"
"Greetings from the Capitol"
context: The line comes from the Bible (Numbers 23:23). It was chosen by Annie Ellsworth, the teenage daughter of the patent commissioner, as a fitting first thing to send across a wire that could carry words in an instant. Source: https://www.senate.gov/about/images/documents/telegraph-message-1844-loc.htm

question: A ship in trouble taps out the most famous distress call in Morse code. It was picked because its pattern is short, rhythmic, and almost impossible to mistake for anything else. What is the SOS signal?
answer: three dots, three dashes, three dots
choices: three dots, three dashes, three dots
one long dash repeated nine times
a dot and a dash, over and over
five dots followed by five dashes
context: ... --- ... — three dots, three dashes, three dots. The simple, even rhythm is what made it almost impossible to garble or confuse with ordinary message traffic. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morse_code

question: When Alfred Vail built Morse's code, he wanted the most common English letters to have the shortest signals. To learn which letters were most common, he walked into a Morristown, New Jersey newspaper office and counted something the printers kept on hand. What did he count?
answer: how many metal type pieces they had of each letter
choices: how many metal type pieces they had of each letter
how many newspapers were printed each day
how many words fit on a single page
how many letters were in the alphabet
context: Printers stocked far more of the letters they used most, so Vail's tally told him which letters mattered. That is why E, the most common English letter, gets the shortest signal of all — a single dot. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morse_code

question: In the Japan of the Tokugawa age, the emperor lived in Kyoto as a sacred figurehead, honored but powerless. The man who actually commanded the armies and ruled the whole country held a different title. What was the real ruler of Japan called?
answer: The shogun
choices: The shogun
The emperor
The daimyo
The samurai
context: Under the Tokugawa system the emperor reigned in name from Kyoto while the shogun -- the supreme military ruler -- held the real power. The man who reigned was not the man who ruled. Source: japanesesword.net 'Life in Feudal Japan'; Britannica.

question: In feudal Japan you could tell a samurai at a glance by what he wore at his waist: a matched pair of blades, the long katana and the shorter wakizashi, mounted to look alike. Farmers, merchants, and monks were forbidden to carry both. What was this two-sword pair, the walking badge of the warrior class, called?
answer: The daisho
choices: The daisho
The tatara
The hagakure
The sankin
context: Only samurai could wear the daisho -- 'big-little' -- the matched katana and wakizashi. The two-sword pair was a badge of rank no commoner was allowed to carry. Source: Wikipedia 'Daisho'; samurai-katana-shop.nl.

question: A samurai condemned to die by seppuku knelt and cut open his own belly with a short sword -- a slow, agonizing death. So a trusted swordsman stood behind him to end his suffering the instant the cut was made. What did that second do to grant this mercy?
answer: Struck off the dying man's head
choices: Struck off the dying man's head
Bound the dying man's wound
Handed him the short sword
Recited the death poem aloud
context: The kaishakunin stood behind the condemned samurai and beheaded him the moment the cut was made -- a mercy stroke that demanded great skill. Seppuku spared samurai the disgrace of execution by a common headsman, and was practiced until 1873. Source: Wikipedia 'Kaishakunin'; Britannica 'seppuku'.

question: To keep his lords too weak to rebel, the shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu in 1635 forced every daimyo to spend alternate years living in his capital, Edo, paying for two grand households and ruinous processions. But one rule above all guaranteed obedience: what did each lord have to leave behind in Edo, permanently, when he went home?
answer: His wife and heir, as hostages
choices: His wife and heir, as hostages
His swords and armor
Half of his rice harvest
His personal bodyguard
context: Under sankin-kotai ('alternate attendance'), the daimyo's wife and heir stayed in Edo as permanent hostages while he shuttled back and forth, bankrupted by the double cost. Rebel, and your family died first. Source: Wikipedia 'Sankin-kotai'; academic.mu.edu.

question: After Lord Asano was forced to commit seppuku, his 47 leaderless samurai secretly swore to avenge him on the official who had wronged him. To fool the official's spies, their leader Oishi Kuranosuke spent over a year doing one shameful thing so everyone would believe he had abandoned the vendetta. What was Oishi's disguise?
answer: Playing a drunken wastrel in the pleasure quarters
choices: Playing a drunken wastrel in the pleasure quarters
Becoming a monk in a mountain temple
Hiring himself out as a common farmer
Fleeing Japan aboard a merchant ship
context: Oishi spent over a year acting as a drunkard in the pleasure quarters of Kyoto so Kira's spies would think the ronin had given up. Then on the snowy night of January 30, 1703, the 47 stormed Kira's Edo mansion and killed him. The shogun praised their loyalty -- then ordered all 47 to commit seppuku. Source: Britannica '47 ronin'; Wikipedia.

question: People imagine bushido, the 'way of the warrior,' as an ancient medieval rulebook samurai carried into battle. But the most famous text of it, the Hagakure -- which opens 'The Way of the Samurai is found in death' -- was dictated around 1709 by the retired samurai Yamamoto Tsunetomo during a long peace. What surprising thing was true of the man whose words shaped the warrior code?
answer: He had never fought in a real battle
choices: He had never fought in a real battle
He had been exiled for cowardice
He could not read or write
He was not himself a samurai
context: Bushido was largely codified and idealized during the peaceful Edo period (1600-1868), when warfare had nearly vanished -- written by administrators looking back, not men fighting wars. Tsunetomo dictated the Hagakure having never seen a real battle, and the book was then forgotten for two centuries before being revived around 1900. Source: Wikipedia 'Hagakure'; the-pamphlet.com 'bushido'.

question: In October 1777 the British general John Burgoyne marched south from Canada to split the rebelling colonies in two, but the Americans trapped him at Saratoga, New York, and he handed his whole army over to General Horatio Gates. Why did this surrender stun every court in Europe?
answer: No entire British field army had ever surrendered to anyone, anywhere
choices: No entire British field army had ever surrendered to anyone, anywhere
Burgoyne was the king's own cousin and heir to the throne
The British had never before lost a battle on American soil
Saratoga was the largest army Britain had ever put in the field
context: It was the first time in history a complete British field army laid down its arms — Burgoyne surrendered on October 17, 1777. Source: American Battlefield Trust, '10 Facts: The Battle of Saratoga' (battlefields.org).

question: When word of General John Burgoyne's surrender at Saratoga reached Paris in December 1777, France had been quietly cheering the American rebellion but staying out of the open. The news changed everything within weeks. What did France do that turned a colonial uprising into a global war Britain could lose?
answer: Signed a formal alliance and entered the war openly on America's side
choices: Signed a formal alliance and entered the war openly on America's side
Sent a private loan of gold but kept its troops and fleet at home
Demanded Canada from Britain as the price of staying neutral
Offered to mediate a peace that would keep the colonies British
