context: News reached Paris on December 4, 1777; foreign minister Vergennes moved fast, and France signed the Treaty of Alliance and the Treaty of Amity and Commerce on February 6, 1778 — secured by Benjamin Franklin's diplomacy. That is what Saratoga DID: it brought France in. Source: U.S. State Dept Office of the Historian, 'French Alliance' (history.state.gov).

question: A legend told on a Babylonian clay tablet says the baby who would grow up to be Sargon of Akkad, the world's first emperor, was born to a priestess who could not reveal she had a child. To hide him, she sealed him inside a basket with tar and set it floating down the Euphrates River. A gardener named Akki, drawing water, found the basket and raised the boy as his own. More than a thousand years later, a nearly identical story would be told about which other famous baby in a river basket?
answer: Moses, drawn from the Nile
choices: Moses, drawn from the Nile
Romulus, suckled by the wolf
Cyrus, left on the mountain
Oedipus, exposed on the hillside
context: Sargon's birth legend, recorded on a clay tablet kept in the Library of Ashurbanipal, predates the story of baby Moses in the bulrushes by over a thousand years. It is told here as legend, not forensic fact. Source: worldhistory.org/Sargon_of_Akkad; The Legend of Sargon (clay tablet).

question: Sargon of Akkad, who built the world's first empire, made his daughter the high priestess of the moon god Nanna at the city of Ur. There she composed hymns to the goddess Inanna and did something no one in history is known to have done before her: she signed her poems with her own name, roughly 4,300 years ago, long before Homer. What is this daughter of Sargon remembered as today?
answer: The world's first author known by name
choices: The world's first author known by name
The first queen to rule alone
The first woman to read and write
The first priestess of any temple
context: Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon, signed works such as 'The Exaltation of Inanna,' making her the earliest author in history whose name we know. Her image and the words 'Enheduanna... daughter of Sargon, king of the world' survive on a carved calcite disk dug up at Ur by Sir Leonard Woolley in 1927. Source: worldhistory.org/Enheduanna; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enheduanna.

question: The Second Punic War ended in 202 BC at the Battle of Zama, in North Africa near Carthage. There the Roman general Scipio finally beat the Carthaginian commander who had crushed Roman armies for 15 years. Which famous enemy did Scipio defeat at Zama?
answer: Hannibal
choices: Hannibal
Masinissa
Pyrrhus
Cato
context: Zama (202 BC) was the decisive battle of the Second Punic War. Scipio beat Hannibal on Hannibal's own home ground near Carthage. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama

question: At Zama in 202 BC, Hannibal lined up 80 war elephants to smash the Roman front. Instead of forming a solid wall to meet them, Scipio left wide empty lanes between his soldiers and had his men blow bugles and bang their weapons on their shields. What did the panicked elephants do?
answer: They bolted harmlessly down the empty lanes
choices: They bolted harmlessly down the empty lanes
They knelt down and refused to move
They charged straight through the Roman line
They swam back across the river
context: The noise terrified the elephants, which stampeded down the corridors Scipio had left open; some even turned and trampled Hannibal's own cavalry. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama

question: Hannibal had once won battles using fast Numidian horsemen against Rome. At Zama, Scipio's secret weapon was that those same Numidian cavalry now fought FOR Rome, swept Hannibal's cavalry off the field, and smashed into the rear of his infantry. Which Numidian king led that cavalry for Scipio?
answer: King Masinissa
choices: King Masinissa
King Pyrrhus
King Polybius
King Aemilianus
context: Masinissa's Numidian cavalry turned the battle: the very kind of horsemen Hannibal had once used to destroy Roman armies now broke his own. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama

question: Decades after Zama, the elder statesman Cato hated Carthage so fiercely that he ended EVERY speech he gave in the Roman Senate the same way -- whatever the topic, even a debate about sewers. What line did Cato tack onto the end of every speech?
answer: 'Carthage must be destroyed'
choices: 'Carthage must be destroyed'
'Rome was not built in a day'
'Let the consuls decide'
'The Senate has spoken'
context: In Latin: 'Ceterum censeo Carthaginem esse delendam.' Cato repeated it relentlessly until his side won the argument for war. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthago_delenda_est

question: To prove to the Senate that Carthage was still a dangerous, thriving rival, Cato did not give a speech of numbers. Instead, mid-debate, he let a single fresh fig fall from the folds of his toga onto the Senate floor. As senators admired the fig's size, what did Cato tell them about it?
answer: It had grown only three days' sail from Rome
choices: It had grown only three days' sail from Rome
It had been blessed by the gods of Carthage
It was the last fig left in all of Italy
It had been sent as a gift by Hannibal's heirs
context: The point: a country rich enough to grow such fruit, and close enough to reach in three days, was no spent force. Plutarch tells the fig story in his Life of Cato. Source: Plutarch, Cato 27, https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:2008.01.0013:chapter=27

question: In the Third Punic War (149-146 BC) Rome besieged Carthage for three years and finally stormed it after six days of house-to-house fighting up to the citadel; the survivors were enslaved and the city burned. The general who razed Carthage was Scipio Aemilianus -- and his family connection made it poetic. Who was he to the Scipio who beat Hannibal at Zama?
answer: His adopted grandson
choices: His adopted grandson
His older brother
His battlefield rival
His Carthaginian hostage
context: Scipio Aemilianus was the adopted grandson of Scipio Africanus. The family that began the war's end at Zama also delivered Carthage's final destruction in 146 BC. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War , https://www.historyskills.com/classroom/ancient-history/scipio-aemilianus/

question: As Carthage burned in 146 BC, Scipio Aemilianus did not cheer his victory -- he wept. Standing beside the historian Polybius, he quoted Homer's lines about doomed Troy, 'A day will come when sacred Troy shall perish,' and told Polybius he feared the same fate would one day fall on which city?
answer: Rome itself
choices: Rome itself
Athens
Alexandria
Jerusalem
context: Polybius was an eyewitness and recorded the moment. Scipio Aemilianus feared Rome, too, would someday meet Carthage's end. Source: Polybius, via https://www.historyskills.com/classroom/ancient-history/scipio-aemilianus/

question: A famous claim says that after destroying Carthage the Romans plowed the ground and 'sowed it with salt' so nothing would ever grow there again. Historians who searched the ancient record reached what conclusion about this salt-the-earth story?
answer: No ancient source mentions it; it is likely a 19th-century invention
choices: No ancient source mentions it; it is likely a 19th-century invention
Roman soldiers really did spread tons of salt over the ruins
Hannibal's heirs salted the fields themselves in revenge
Cato ordered the salting in his final Senate speech
context: The salt legend appears in no ancient writer. The plain ancient record is harsh enough on its own: the city was burned and its people enslaved. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War

question: At the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention, Elizabeth Cady Stanton wrote a Declaration of Sentiments modeled on the Declaration of Independence. To make her point, she took Thomas Jefferson's most famous line, 'all men are created equal,' and added just two words. Which two?
answer: 'and women'
choices: 'and women'
'and equal'
'and free'
'and slaves'
context: Stanton's line read 'all men and women are created equal.' By adding two words to the most famous sentence in American politics, she claimed the founders' own natural-rights principle for women rather than rejecting it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_of_Sentiments

question: On the first morning of the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention, the organizers reached the Wesleyan Chapel and found the door locked, with no one holding a key. How did they get inside to begin the meeting?
answer: They boosted a boy through an open window to unbar the door from within
choices: They boosted a boy through an open window to unbar the door from within
They broke the lock with a stone from the road
They moved the whole convention to a nearby barn
They waited until a passing carpenter cut a new key
context: Stanton's eleven-year-old nephew, Daniel Cady Eaton, was lifted through an open window and opened the door from inside. Source: https://home.nps.gov/wori/learn/historyculture/harriet-cady-eaton.htm

question: At the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention, the women had organized the whole meeting themselves, but when it came time to open the session, they handed the gavel to a man, Lucretia Mott's husband James Mott. Why did they choose a man to preside?
answer: In 1848 none of them thought it proper for a woman to run a public meeting
choices: In 1848 none of them thought it proper for a woman to run a public meeting
James Mott was the only one who had memorized the rules of order
The chapel owners required a male chairman to let them use the hall
The local sheriff would only permit the meeting under a man's name
context: James Mott presided because, even among these reformers, it was not yet considered proper in 1848 for a woman to chair a public meeting. The convention was claiming a right its own organizers had not yet fully exercised. Source: https://www.nps.gov/wori/learn/historyculture/convention-officers-and-committees.htm

question: Every resolution at the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention passed unanimously except one, which nearly failed: the demand that women be granted the vote. It survived only after one man rose to argue for it, calling the denial of the vote 'the maiming and repudiation of one-half of the moral and intellectual power of the government of the world.' Who was that man?
answer: Frederick Douglass, the formerly enslaved abolitionist
choices: Frederick Douglass, the formerly enslaved abolitionist
James Mott, the convention's presiding officer
Henry Stanton, Elizabeth's husband
Daniel Eaton, who had opened the chapel door
context: Douglass, a formerly enslaved man and the only Black person present, edited the abolitionist paper The North Star, whose masthead read 'Right is of no Sex — Truth is of no Color.' He made the same natural-rights case for women that he made for himself. Source: https://utahwomenshistory.org/2018/10/the-suffrage-resolution-at-seneca-falls/

question: When Elizabeth Cady Stanton insisted on putting a demand for the vote into the 1848 Declaration of Sentiments, even her ally Lucretia Mott begged her to drop it, warning, 'Why Lizzie, thee will make us ridiculous.' Stanton refused. What was her argument for keeping the demand for the ballot in?
answer: The ballot was the right that secured all the others
choices: The ballot was the right that secured all the others
The newspapers would ignore a convention with no bold demand
Property rights meant nothing without a man's consent
The other resolutions were too weak to stand on their own
context: Mott feared the suffrage demand would make the movement a laughingstock — and the press did mock it fiercely. But Stanton held that the vote was the right that protected every other right, so she kept it in. Source: https://utahwomenshistory.org/2018/10/the-suffrage-resolution-at-seneca-falls/

question: One hundred people signed the 1848 Declaration of Sentiments, among them Charlotte Woodward, a nineteen-year-old glovemaker who sewed at home for pennies and wanted the right to keep her own wages. By 1920, when the Nineteenth Amendment finally gave American women the vote, what was remarkable about Charlotte Woodward?
answer: She was the only one of the 100 signers still alive
choices: She was the only one of the 100 signers still alive
She had become the first woman elected to Congress
She had personally delivered the amendment to the Senate
She had outlived every president who once opposed her
context: Woodward was the sole survivor of the 100 signers in 1920 — but too ill to cast the ballot she had waited 72 years for. She had signed because she wanted to choose her own work and keep her own wages. Source: https://www.nps.gov/wori/learn/historyculture/charlotte-woodward.htm

question: On the morning of September 11, 2001, as office workers streamed DOWN the stairwells of the burning Twin Towers to escape, one group kept climbing UP into the smoke and fire to reach the trapped people above. Who were they?
answer: New York City firefighters
choices: New York City firefighters
Television news reporters
Off-duty airline pilots
City sanitation workers
context: 343 New York City firefighters died on September 11, 2001 — the single greatest loss of life in the FDNY's history. They were climbing up the stairwells of the burning towers as office workers came down. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Mychal-Judge and FDNY/9-11 Memorial reporting (343 FDNY deaths).

question: During the attacks of September 11, 2001, a 24-year-old equities trader and volunteer firefighter named Welles Crowther stayed inside the burning South Tower, calmly leading trapped strangers down to a stairwell and going back up for more. Survivors couldn't see his face through the smoke and never learned his name — but they all remembered him by the same nickname. What was it?
answer: The man in the red bandana
choices: The man in the red bandana
The voice in the dark
The runner on the stairs
The whistle on 78
context: Welles Crowther had carried a red handkerchief since boyhood and used it to cover his face against the smoke. Survivors remembered only 'the man in the red bandana' who calmly guided them to a stairwell. He made three trips up to the 78th-floor sky lobby to lead people down before the tower fell with him inside. Source: https://www.911memorial.org/connect/blog/remembering-man-red-bandana.

question: On Flight 93 on September 11, 2001, flight attendant Sandra Bradshaw phoned her husband to say goodbye, then went to work in the galley helping the passengers ready themselves to storm the cockpit. When he asked what she was doing, she told him one specific thing. What was it?
answer: Heating water to throw at the hijackers
choices: Heating water to throw at the hijackers
Stacking food carts to block the aisle
Gathering knives and forks from the trays
Wedging a fire extinguisher under a seat
context: Sandra Bradshaw told her husband she was in the galley 'heating water to throw at the hijackers.' The passengers and crew were arming themselves with whatever they had before storming the cockpit. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Airlines_Flight_93.

question: On Flight 93 on September 11, 2001, passenger Todd Beamer was on the phone with airline operator Lisa Jefferson when the passengers decided to rush the hijackers in the cockpit. The last thing she heard him say became one of the most remembered lines of the entire day. What did Todd Beamer say?
answer: "Let's roll."
choices: "Let's roll."
"God help us."
"Tell them I tried."
"We're going home."
context: Before the passengers rushed the cockpit, operator Lisa Jefferson heard Todd Beamer say: 'Are you ready? Okay. Let's roll.' 'Let's roll' became one of the most remembered lines of September 11. Investigators believe Flight 93's target was the U.S. Capitol; it crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania before reaching Washington. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Airlines_Flight_93; https://www.americanheritage.com/remembering-flight-93-okay-lets-roll.

question: On September 11, 2001, FDNY chaplain Father Mychal Judge, a Franciscan priest, ran into the North Tower with the firefighters and was killed by falling debris while praying over the dying. Firefighters carried his body out, and one grim record attached to his name forever. What was it?
answer: The first certified death, Victim 0001
choices: The first certified death, Victim 0001
The 343rd firefighter to be lost
The only priest inside the towers
The last body to be recovered
context: Father Mychal Judge ran into the North Tower to be with the firefighters and was killed by falling debris when the South Tower collapsed, after praying and giving last rites. His body was carried out by firefighters, and he was officially recorded as Victim 0001 — the first certified death of 9/11. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Mychal-Judge; https://allthatsinteresting.com/mychal-judge.

question: After the rubble at Ground Zero was cleared following September 11, 2001, workers found a charred Callery pear with snapped roots and broken branches. New York City parks workers tended it for years and replanted it at the memorial in 2010, where it now carries a one-word name New Yorkers know it by. What is that name?
answer: The Survivor Tree
choices: The Survivor Tree
The Liberty Oak
The Remembrance Ash
The Founders' Elm
context: The burned Callery pear was nursed back to health by New York City parks workers and replanted at the 9/11 Memorial in 2010. It is known today as the 'Survivor Tree.' Source: https://www.911memorial.org/visit/memorial/survivor-tree.

question: The Zulu king Shaka armed his warriors with a new weapon for close-up fighting: a short spear with a long broad blade, made for stabbing instead of throwing. What was this signature Zulu stabbing-spear called?
answer: The iklwa
choices: The iklwa
The katana
The trident
The halberd
context: The iklwa had a roughly 24-inch (610 mm) shaft and a sword-like blade about 12 inches (300 mm) long. It replaced the long thrown assegai so warriors had to close in and fight hand-to-hand. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assegai

question: Shaka's army won battles with a formation called the 'bull horns': older veteran warriors held the enemy head-on as the 'chest,' while two groups of fast young warriors did what?
answer: Raced around both sides to surround the enemy
choices: Raced around both sides to surround the enemy
Climbed nearby hills to throw rocks down
Retreated to lure the enemy into a swamp
Lit grass fires to blind the enemy
context: The Zulu name was 'impondo zenkomo' (the bull horns). The two 'horns' of fast young men encircled the enemy while the 'chest' pinned them, and a reserve called the 'loins' waited behind to plug any gaps. Source: https://ditsong.org.za/en/shaka-zulus-famous-impondo-zenkomo-the-bull-horns-tactical-battle-formation/

question: The Zulu name for Shaka's stabbing-spear, 'iklwa,' was not a description of the blade or its maker. Warriors named it for a sound. What sound gave the iklwa its name?
answer: The wet sucking noise as the blade was pulled from a wound
choices: The wet sucking noise as the blade was pulled from a wound
The whistle the spear made flying through the air
The crack of the shaft against an enemy's shield
The chant warriors shouted as they charged
context: 'Iklwa' is onomatopoeia — the word imitates the sound the broad blade made coming back out of a victim's body. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assegai

question: At the Battle of Gqokli Hill around 1818, Shaka's Zulu were outnumbered about two to one by Zwide's Ndwandwe army, yet Shaka won. What turned the enemy's greater numbers into a fatal weakness?
answer: Packed too tightly to throw their long spears, they were stabbed by Shaka's short-spear men charging downhill
choices: Packed too tightly to throw their long spears, they were stabbed by Shaka's short-spear men charging downhill
A sudden rainstorm soaked the Ndwandwe gunpowder and silenced their muskets
The Ndwandwe king Zwide was captured at dawn before the fighting began
Shaka's men dug pits overnight that swallowed the front ranks
context: Crammed together, the Ndwandwe could not throw their long assegais in the crush, while Shaka's men closed in and stabbed with the new short iklwa, routing a force twice their size. Source: https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Gqokli_Hill

question: When Shaka's mother Nandi died in 1827, his grief turned the whole kingdom into a nightmare — he banned planting crops and using milk, and had thousands killed for not weeping hard enough. He even ordered cows slaughtered for one chilling reason. Why kill the cows?
answer: So the calves would also know what losing a mother felt like
choices: So the calves would also know what losing a mother felt like
So the smoke from the meat would carry his grief to the sky
So no milk could ever be drunk in the kingdom again
So the herders would have time to mourn instead of working
context: Shaka had cows killed so their calves would feel the loss of a mother just as he had. The mourning frenzy after Nandi's death is remembered as one of the most extreme episodes of his reign. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaka

question: The 1810s-1840s upheaval Shaka is linked to is remembered by a Zulu word meaning 'the crushing' or 'scattering' — a wave of war, famine, and forced migration across southern Africa. Out of that chaos new nations were forged. Which kingdom did the leader Moshoeshoe build by gathering mountain clans on a fortified plateau?
answer: Lesotho
choices: Lesotho
Egypt
Carthage
Ethiopia
context: The upheaval is the Mfecane (Zulu, 'the crushing'; Sesotho 'Difaqane'). Moshoeshoe gathered clans on a mountain stronghold to found what became Lesotho, while Shaka's renegade general Mzilikazi led the Ndebele north to found Bulawayo in present-day Zimbabwe. Modern historians argue drought, the slave trade, and other powers — not Shaka alone — drove the Mfecane, and that the old death tolls of 1-2 million were exaggerated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mfecane

question: At Shakespeare's Globe theatre in London, the cheapest ticket cost just one penny — about the price of a loaf of bread. But that penny bought no seat at all: you stood packed against the stage in the open-air pit, called the yard. What were these standing spectators nicknamed?
answer: Groundlings
choices: Groundlings
Gallants
Pittites
Stagers
context: 'Groundlings' were the poorest theatergoers, standing for a penny in the yard right below the stage, rain or shine, while wealthier playgoers paid more to sit in the covered galleries. Source: Shakespeare's Globe (shakespearesglobe.com), 'Audiences'.

question: In Shakespeare's day, English law barred women from acting on the public stage. So every great female role — Juliet, Lady Macbeth, Cleopatra — had to be performed by someone else entirely. Who played all the heroines in his plays?
answer: Teenage boys
choices: Teenage boys
Veiled noblewomen
Older married men
Masked foreign dancers
context: Audiences watched boys and young men play the heroines, since women were forbidden on the English stage until 1660. Source: Colorado State University, 'Why weren't women allowed to act in Shakespeare's plays?'; Shakespeare's Globe.

question: Shakespeare's plays hold the first written record of more than 1,700 English words we still use every single day. One of them is a body part you're using right now to read this. In his play Henry VI, he was the first to write down which word?
answer: Eyeball
choices: Eyeball
Eyebrow
Eyelid
Eyelash
context: Scholars are careful to say these are the FIRST RECORDED uses — Shakespeare may have coined some and merely been the first to write others down. 'Eyeball' first appears in Henry VI, Part 1. Source: Shakespeare Birthplace Trust (shakespeare.org.uk), 'Shakespeare's Words'.

question: Around a steaming cauldron in Macbeth, three witches brew a spell and throw in grotesque ingredients — 'eye of newt and toe of frog, wool of bat and tongue of dog.' What two famous lines do they chant over and over as they brew?
answer: Double, double toil and trouble; fire burn and cauldron bubble
choices: Double, double toil and trouble; fire burn and cauldron bubble
Round about the kettle creeping; pour the venom, set it steeping
Thrice the brindled cat hath mewed; gather darkness, fate be brewed
Smoke and shadow, bone and bramble; through the night the spirits ramble
context: It is the most famous witches' chant in all of literature, from Macbeth, Act 4, Scene 1. Source: Folger Shakespeare Library, Macbeth Act 4 Scene 1 (exact text).

question: In the graveyard scene of Hamlet, a gravedigger turns up a skull from the earth. Prince Hamlet lifts it and says, 'Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio.' Who had Yorick been to the prince when Hamlet was a small child?
answer: The court jester, who carried little Hamlet on his back a thousand times
choices: The court jester, who carried little Hamlet on his back a thousand times
The old king, his father, now murdered and turned to bare bone
The royal tutor, who first taught him to read as a boy
The king's huntsman, who first set him upon a horse
context: Holding the skull of the jester who once made him laugh and gave him piggyback rides, Hamlet sees how death reduces everyone — king or clown — to dust. Hamlet, Act 5, Scene 1. Source: SparkNotes Hamlet; nosweatshakespeare.com 'Alas Poor Yorick'.

question: Juliet's most famous line is 'O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?' To modern ears it sounds like she's calling out to find him in the dark. But 'wherefore' is an old English word that does NOT mean 'where.' What does it actually mean?
answer: Why
choices: Why
Where
When
How
context: Juliet isn't asking where Romeo is — she's despairing at WHY the boy she loves had to be a Montague, her family's sworn enemy. Romeo and Juliet, Act 2, Scene 2. Source: Folger Shakespeare Library; interestingliterature.com.

question: In the opening Prologue of Romeo and Juliet, Shakespeare calls the young couple 'star-crossed lovers.' In his day people believed the stars controlled human fate. So what does that single phrase warn the audience from the very first minute of the play?
answer: That fate itself was set against them, dooming their love from the start
choices: That fate itself was set against them, dooming their love from the start
That they were born under the same lucky star and meant to wed
That they would wander across many distant lands before finding peace
That their feuding families would soon be joined by the marriage
context: 'Star-crossed' means the stars — fate — were crossed against them, so the audience knows the lovers are doomed before the story even begins. Source: Wikipedia 'Star-crossed'; SparkNotes Romeo and Juliet prologue analysis.

question: The phrase 'wild-goose chase' — meaning a hopeless hunt for something you'll never catch — first appears in Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet. But the original 'wild-goose chase' had nothing to do with hunting birds. What was it really?
answer: A horse race where riders followed a leader in a V, like flying geese
choices: A horse race where riders followed a leader in a V, like flying geese
A village game where children chased a goose around the green
A hunt where hounds were loosed after a single wild goose
A market day when farmers raced their geese to the fair
context: A real 'wild-goose chase' was a horse race in which every rider had to follow the leader's twisting path in single file, spread out like a skein of flying geese. Romeo and Juliet, Act 2, Scene 4. Source: Merriam-Webster '10 Phrases Invented by Shakespeare'; Shakespeare Birthplace Trust.

question: Near the end of Macbeth, Lady Macbeth — who helped plan a king's murder — begins sleepwalking at night, frantically rubbing her hands and crying 'Out, damned spot! Out, I say!' What does she believe is staining her hands and will never wash clean?
answer: King Duncan's blood, which she imagines is still on her hands
choices: King Duncan's blood, which she imagines is still on her hands
The black soot from the castle's midnight fires
The dark ink from the letters that revealed the plot
The poison she once mixed for the king's two guards
context: Driven mad by guilt, she hallucinates the murdered king's blood on her hands — a stain her conscience can never scrub away. Macbeth, Act 5, Scene 1. Source: Folger Shakespeare Library; interestingliterature.com sleepwalking-scene analysis.

question: Hamlet's line 'To be, or not to be, that is the question' is the most famous line in all of English drama. In the speech, Prince Hamlet is wrestling with one enormous choice. What is the question he is really asking himself?
answer: Whether to keep enduring life's pain, or to escape it through death
choices: Whether to keep enduring life's pain, or to escape it through death
Whether to avenge his father now, or wait for stronger proof
Whether to trust Ophelia's love, or push her away forever
Whether to seize the crown himself, or let his uncle keep it
context: Hamlet is weighing whether life's suffering is worth bearing, or whether death would be a release. Hamlet, Act 3, Scene 1. Source: Wikipedia 'To be, or not to be'; SparkNotes Hamlet.

question: At the start of Henry V, Shakespeare has the Chorus apologize that one tiny round playhouse must somehow stage the vast battle of Agincourt, and begs the audience to fill the gap with their imagination. What does the Chorus call the Globe theatre itself?
answer: This wooden O
choices: This wooden O
This painted box
This hollow crown
This empty ring
context: 'This wooden O' captures the round, open-roofed shape of the Globe — and the Chorus's plea that the audience imagine kingdoms and armies inside it. Henry V, Prologue. Source: Folger Shakespeare Library; interestingliterature.com 'O for a Muse of Fire' analysis.

question: On 29 June 1613, during a performance of Henry VIII, a stage cannon fired to announce the king and set the Globe's thatched roof alight; the whole theatre burned to the ground within an hour. Yet an eyewitness reported only one injury — a man whose breeches caught fire. How did he put out the flames?
answer: With a bottle of ale
choices: With a bottle of ale
With buckets from the well
With a wet woolen cloak
With handfuls of river mud
context: The eyewitness Sir Henry Wotton wrote that the man would have been broiled 'if he had not by the benefit of a provident wit, put it out with a bottle of ale.' Source: Sir Henry Wotton, letter of 2 July 1613 (Folger / Shakespeare Documented).

question: For the whole of Shakespeare's life, English law kept women off the stage, so boys played every heroine. The theatres reopened in 1660, and on 8 December a woman named Margaret Hughes became the first professional actress ever to perform on the English stage. Which Shakespeare heroine did she play that day?
answer: Desdemona, in Othello
choices: Desdemona, in Othello
Juliet, in Romeo and Juliet
Cleopatra, in Antony and Cleopatra
Ophelia, in Hamlet
context: After decades of boys in the women's roles, the first real actress on the English stage stepped out as Desdemona in Shakespeare's Othello. Source: Wikipedia 'Margaret Hughes'; EBSCO 'Women on the 17th-Century English Stage'.

question: Roughly half of Shakespeare's plays — including Macbeth, The Tempest, and Julius Caesar — had never been printed during his lifetime. Seven years after he died, two of his actor friends, John Heminges and Henry Condell, gathered them into a single book called the First Folio. What would have become of those plays if the two friends had not collected them?
answer: They would have been lost forever
choices: They would have been lost forever
They would have been rewritten by rival poets
They would have been performed only in France
They would have been banned by the church
context: About 18 of the 36 plays in the 1623 First Folio had never been printed before, so without Heminges and Condell's book, masterpieces like Macbeth and The Tempest would simply not exist today. Source: Wikipedia 'First Folio'; Shakespeare Birthplace Trust 'Shakespeare's First Folio'.

question: When the First Folio was printed in 1623, Shakespeare's rival playwright Ben Jonson wrote a tribute poem for the front of it. In that poem Jonson gave Shakespeare a nickname tying him to his birthplace by the river Avon. What did Jonson call him?
answer: The Sweet Swan of Avon
choices: The Sweet Swan of Avon
The Bard of the Thames
The Bright Star of London
The Nightingale of Stratford
context: In the same poem Jonson predicted Shakespeare's fame would never fade, declaring 'He was not of an age, but for all time!' Source: Ben Jonson, 'To the Memory of My Beloved... Mr. William Shakespeare' (First Folio, 1623), via Wikisource and the University of Illinois Rare Book & Manuscript Library.

question: At Shakespeare's Globe theatre in London, the cheapest tickets cost a single penny and let you stand in the open-air yard right in front of the stage, packed in shoulder to shoulder while you snacked on hazelnuts and oranges. What were these penny-paying standing playgoers called?
answer: Groundlings
choices: Groundlings
Pennyfolk
Yardmen
Stinkards
context: Archaeologists digging up the old Globe yard found cracked hazelnut shells and orange peel left behind by the groundlings. Source: shakespearesglobe.com/discover/shakespeares-world/audiences/ ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groundling

question: In Shakespeare's London, every part in a play was acted by males only. Juliet, Lady Macbeth, and Cleopatra — his great women — were therefore all first played on stage by whom?
answer: Boys whose voices had not yet broken
choices: Boys whose voices had not yet broken
Choirboys borrowed from the cathedral
Retired soldiers from the city guard
Foreign actors touring through town
context: Women were forbidden from the public English stage in Shakespeare's day, so the company used boys and young men with unbroken, higher voices for every female role. Source: shakespearestaging.berkeley.edu/topics/gender-in-performance ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_Shakespeare's_works

question: On 29 June 1613, during a performance of Henry VIII, a real cannon was fired on stage to announce the king's entrance. A spark caught the Globe's thatched roof, and the whole theatre burned to the ground within an hour. Astonishingly, no one was killed — what was the only injury?
answer: A man's breeches caught fire, and he put them out with ale
choices: A man's breeches caught fire, and he put them out with ale
A man's cloak caught fire, and he smothered it in mud
An actor's wig caught fire, and he flung it in the river
A boy's sleeve caught fire, and a friend beat it out
context: The eyewitness Sir Henry Wotton wrote that the man would have been 'broyled' if he had not, by a 'provident wit,' doused his burning breeches with bottle ale. Source: ebsco.com/research-starters/history/burning-globe-theatre ; shakespearedocumented.folger.edu

question: William Shakespeare was baptized at Holy Trinity Church in Stratford-upon-Avon on 26 April 1564, and since babies were christened a few days after birth, his birthday is traditionally fixed at 23 April 1564. Fifty-two years later, in 1616, what was strange about the date on which he died?
answer: He died on 23 April, the very same date as his birthday
choices: He died on 23 April, the very same date as his birthday
He died on 23 April, but aged 80, not 52
He died on 24 April, one day after turning 52
He died in London, not in Stratford at all
context: By tradition Shakespeare was born and died on the same day of the year, 23 April — his 52nd birthday. Source: shakespeare.org.uk/explore-shakespeare/shakespedia/william-shakespeare/when-was-shakespeare-born/ ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare

question: Above Shakespeare's Globe, a flag flew over the roof on performance days to tell Londoners a play was on. By old tradition the picture on that flag matched the theatre's grand name: a single mighty figure from Greek myth bearing the whole round world on his shoulders. Who was shown carrying the globe?
answer: Hercules
choices: Hercules
Atlas
Apollo
Zeus
context: Tradition holds the Globe's flag showed Hercules carrying the world, supposedly matching a motto meaning 'all the world's a playhouse' — though some scholars doubt the motto was really used in Shakespeare's own day. Source: shakespeare.org.uk/explore-shakespeare/shakespedia/shakespeares-globe-theatre/ ; research.birmingham.ac.uk  (Legend.)

question: Shakespeare's company once owned a London playhouse simply called 'The Theatre,' but their landlord owned the land it stood on and the lease ran out. Because they still owned the actual timber, what did the company do over a few nights in December 1598 to keep their wood?
answer: They took the building apart beam by beam and carried it across the Thames
choices: They took the building apart beam by beam and carried it across the Thames
They bought the patch of land back from the landlord overnight
They burned it down so no rival company could ever use it
They sued the landlord in court and won the whole plot
context: They ferried the recycled timber across the river by barge and rebuilt it on the south bank as the first Globe, finished in 1599. Source: shalt.dmu.ac.uk/locations/globe-1599-1642/indepth.html ; historyhit.com/locations/shakespeares-globe/

question: When William Shakespeare wrote his will in 1616, he left most of his wealth to his daughter. For his wife, Anne Hathaway, he squeezed in just one short, odd bequest crammed between the other lines. What single item did he leave her?
answer: His second-best bed
choices: His second-best bed
His best velvet gown
His silver drinking cup
His pair of gold rings
context: Historians think the 'second-best bed' was the couple's own marriage bed — the best bed was kept for guests. Source: shakespeare.org.uk/explore-shakespeare/shakespedia/william-shakespeare/second-best-bed/ ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespeare's_will

question: Theatre people believe one of Shakespeare's tragedies — the one with the three witches and a king murdered in his sleep — is so cursed that speaking its real title inside a theatre brings disaster. What do superstitious actors call it instead, to dodge the bad luck?
answer: The Scottish Play
choices: The Scottish Play
The Cursed King
The Dark Tragedy
The Northern Play
context: If someone slips and says the real name, tradition says they must leave the room, turn around three times, spit, and ask to be let back in. Source: rsc.org.uk/macbeth/about-the-play/the-scottish-play ; folger.edu/blogs/shakespeare-and-beyond/macbeth-curse-scottish-play/  (Legend.)

question: Two of the most quoted lines in English are 'To be, or not to be' and 'All the world's a stage.' Many people assume both come from Hamlet. In fact only the first does — Prince Hamlet speaks it. Which play does 'All the world's a stage' actually open a speech in?
answer: As You Like It
choices: As You Like It
Romeo and Juliet
A Midsummer Night's Dream
Twelfth Night
context: In As You Like It the gloomy lord Jaques begins his speech 'All the world's a stage,' so the two most famous lines come from two different plays. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_the_world's_a_stage ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/To_be,_or_not_to_be

question: William Shakespeare is the most-quoted author in the entire Oxford English Dictionary, and scholars credit him with inventing or first recording roughly 1,700 English words. Which set of everyday words below all first appear in his writing?
answer: Frugal, obscene, bedazzle, puppy-dog
choices: Frugal, obscene, bedazzle, puppy-dog
Galaxy, tractor, sandwich, helicopter
Telephone, jungle, robot, gravity
Pizza, soccer, cartoon, weekend
context: Shakespeare often made new words by 'functional shift' — turning a noun into a verb, like 'bedazzle' — and ordinary words such as 'frugal,' 'obscene,' 'horrid,' and 'puppy-dog' are first recorded in his work. Source: litcharts.com/content/shakespeares-literature-creating-words ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Influence_of_William_Shakespeare

question: After Shakespeare died, two of his actor friends, John Heminges and Henry Condell, gathered 36 of his plays into one great book in 1623, now called the First Folio. For about 18 of those plays — including Macbeth, The Tempest, and Twelfth Night — that book mattered enormously. Without it, what would have become of those 18 plays?
answer: They would be lost today, with no other copy surviving
choices: They would be lost today, with no other copy surviving
They would survive only in old Italian translations
They would be remembered just from their titles
They would exist only as scribbled Globe stage scripts
context: Roughly 18 plays, Macbeth and The Tempest among them, were never printed anywhere else, so they exist now only because Heminges and Condell saved them in the First Folio. Source: shakespeare.org.uk/explore-shakespeare/shakespedia/shakespeares-works/shakespeares-first-folio/ ; folger.edu/explore/shakespeare-in-print/first-folio/

question: William Shakespeare is buried inside Holy Trinity Church in Stratford-upon-Avon, beneath a flat stone carved with four rhyming lines that are thought to be his own warning. The verse promises a curse on anyone who does one particular thing to him. What does the rhyme threaten a curse for?
answer: Digging up and moving his bones
choices: Digging up and moving his bones
Speaking ill of his good name
Selling off his family's land
Copying his plays without paying
context: The stone reads, in old spelling, 'Blese be ye man yt spares thes stones, / And cvrst be he yt moves my bones' — a curse meant to stop his grave being dug up. Source: nosweatshakespeare.com/resources/life/shakespeares-grave/ ; historyhit.com/the-curse-on-shakespeares-grave/

question: William Shakespeare wrote a famous tragedy about a grief-stricken prince. Years earlier, in 1596, his own only son had died at age 11 and was buried in Stratford. Some scholars find it haunting that the boy's name was almost identical to that prince's. What was the dead boy's name?
answer: Hamnet
choices: Hamnet
Gilbert
Edmund
Richard
context: Shakespeare's son Hamnet, a twin to his sister Judith, died at 11 in 1596; some scholars link the loss to the later tragedy Hamlet, whose hero's name is nearly the same. Source: shakespeare.org.uk/explore-shakespeare/shakespedia/william-shakespeare/william-shakespeares-family/hamnet-shakespeare/ ; smithsonianmag.com/history/the-real-history-behind-hamnet-180987733/

question: Legend offers a chilling origin for the 'curse' on Shakespeare's Macbeth. The story goes that at the very first performance the boy actor cast in one role died suddenly, forcing Shakespeare himself to rush on stage and fill the part. Which role was the dead boy supposed to play?
answer: Lady Macbeth
choices: Lady Macbeth
King Duncan
One of the three witches
The ghost of Banquo
context: This tale — a boy dying on opening night so Shakespeare had to step in as Lady Macbeth — is one of several legends invented to explain the play's reputation for bad luck, not a recorded fact. Source: study.com/learn/lesson/curse-macbeth-superstition-incidents.html ; rsc.org.uk/macbeth/about-the-play/the-scottish-play

question: Daniel Shays fought at Bunker Hill, Saratoga, and Stony Point, then went home in 1780 unpaid and was dragged into court for debt. The Marquis de Lafayette had honored his service with a fine ceremonial sword. Broke and desperate for cash, what did Shays do with that sword that left his fellow officers ashamed of him?
answer: He sold it for money
choices: He sold it for money
He buried it on his farm
He gave it to his son
He mounted it over his door
context: Lafayette had given Daniel Shays an ornamental ceremonial sword for his Revolutionary War service. Broke and in debt, Shays sold it for cash — to his fellow officers a shameful act, but the perfect emblem of how the new republic left its veterans destitute. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Shays / https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ354858

question: In 1786 indebted Massachusetts farmers led by the veteran Daniel Shays shut down courts and stormed the Springfield arsenal, and the government was nearly too weak to stop them — the Articles of Confederation gave it no power to tax or raise an army. That helplessness terrified leaders like George Washington. What did the scare push them to do?
answer: Call the Constitutional Convention
choices: Call the Constitutional Convention
Disband the Massachusetts militia
Cancel all the farmers' debts
Crown a king to restore order
context: The rebellion convinced America's leaders that the Articles of Confederation were too weak to survive, giving decisive momentum to the Constitutional Convention that met in Philadelphia in May 1787. The 'what it triggered' is the whole point — the scare, not the farmers, is what frightened the founders into building a stronger government. Source: https://constitutioncenter.org/education/classroom-resource-library/classroom/3.1-topic-primer-summary-of-shays-rebellion / https://www.mountvernon.org/library/digitalhistory/digital-encyclopedia/article/shays-rebellion

question: In January 1936 Stalin sat in his box at the Bolshoi watching Dmitri Shostakovich's opera 'Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District' — and walked out before the end. Two days later the Soviet Party newspaper Pravda printed an unsigned editorial tearing the opera apart as a 'cacophony' and a 'wilderness of musical chaos.' In Stalin's USSR, being attacked by name in Pravda was a threat to your life. What was the headline over that editorial?
answer: Muddle Instead of Music
choices: Muddle Instead of Music
Clamor Instead of Music
Disorder Instead of Music
Bedlam Instead of Music
context: 'Muddle Instead of Music' ran on 28 January 1936; it warned the music was 'a game of clever ingenuity that may end very badly.' Archival research credits the Soviet propagandist David Zaslavsky as the author (the rumor that Stalin wrote it himself is now thought unlikely). When Shostakovich came out to bow after the performance Stalin walked out of, witnesses said he went 'white as a sheet.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muddle_Instead_of_Music

question: After Stalin's newspaper denounced Dmitri Shostakovich in 1936, the composer lived in nightly terror that the secret police would come for him in the dark. His son Maxim later described one strange thing his father did to prepare, every single night. What was it?
answer: Slept fully dressed with a packed suitcase beside the bed
choices: Slept fully dressed with a packed suitcase beside the bed
Hid his finished scores inside the walls of the apartment
Kept a loaded pistol under his pillow within easy reach
Burned his letters in the stove before going to sleep
context: By his son Maxim's account, Shostakovich went to bed clothed on top of the blankets with a small packed suitcase on the floor — and some nights waited by the apartment-building lift watching the elevator doors, so that if the NKVD came they would not drag him away in his pajamas in front of his wife and children. The story traces chiefly to Maxim, so the precise details are uncertain. Source: https://www.dailyo.in/arts/julian-barnes-booker-prize-2011-the-sense-of-an-ending-the-noise-of-time-dmitri-dmitriyevich-shostakovich-stalin-ussr-8994  (Legend.)

question: Dmitri Shostakovich's Fifth Symphony, written in 1937 while Stalin's secret police were dragging his friends into the Gulag, ends in a blaring major-key victory that Soviet officials applauded as loyal celebration. But in a disputed memoir published years later, Shostakovich is quoted explaining what that triumph really felt like to him. How did he describe it?
answer: Like being beaten with a stick and forced to march off cheering
choices: Like being beaten with a stick and forced to march off cheering
Like a soldier saluting a flag he had stopped believing in
Like singing a hymn whose words he no longer believed
Like cheering at a parade while the police studied his face
context: The quotation comes from Solomon Volkov's 'Testimony' (1979): 'The rejoicing is forced, created under threat... It is as if someone were beating you with a stick and saying, Your business is rejoicing... and you rise up, shaky, and go marching off muttering, Our business is rejoicing.' Testimony's authenticity is disputed, but this reading of the hollow, coerced finale took hold worldwide. How triumphant it sounds depends partly on speed — Leonard Bernstein in 1959 took the ending more than twice as fast as premiere conductor Yevgeny Mravinsky, who always kept it slow and grim. Source: https://thelistenersclub.com/2020/11/11/shostakovichs-fifth-symphony-the-unlikely-triumph-of-freedom/  (Legend.)

question: During the worst winter of the 872-day German siege of Leningrad, the daily bread ration for an ordinary citizen collapsed to about 125 grams — a quarter-pound a day. As real grain ran out, what did bakers stretch the 'bread' with to keep it from running out entirely?
answer: Sawdust, cellulose, and chaff
choices: Sawdust, cellulose, and chaff
Salted fish and dried peas
Crushed acorns and honey
Powdered milk and lard
context: At the siege's nadir an ordinary Leningrader got ~125 g of 'bread' a day, padded with sawdust, cellulose, and chaff once real grain ran out. The siege lasted 872 days (Sept 8, 1941 – Jan 27, 1944) and killed roughly a million people, most of them civilians who died of starvation and cold. Source: allthatsinteresting.com/siege-of-leningrad; explorethearchive.com/siege-of-leningrad.

question: With Leningrad encircled, the only way in or out was across the frozen surface of Lake Ladoga — the route the city called the 'Road of Life.' The ice was so thin that more than 300 trucks broke through and sank over two winters. What did the drivers do to give themselves a chance when the ice cracked under them?
answer: Kept the cab doors open to leap clear
choices: Kept the cab doors open to leap clear
Drove only at night with headlights off
Roped each truck to the one behind it
Strapped empty barrels to the running boards
context: The Road of Life across Lake Ladoga opened Nov 22, 1941; drivers kept cab doors open to jump free if the ice gave way. Despite losing 300+ trucks through the ice, the route evacuated roughly 1.4 million people and carried over 1.5 million tonnes of supplies into the starving city. Source: tass.com/society/985484; gw2ru.com/history/3038.

question: Eleven-year-old Tanya Savicheva kept a tiny notebook in besieged Leningrad, recording each family death in one flat line — her sister, her grandmother, her mother. Its last three pages are the most quoted words of the whole siege. What do they say?
answer: 'The Savichevs are dead. Everyone is dead. Only Tanya is left.'
choices: 'The Savichevs are dead. Everyone is dead. Only Tanya is left.'
'God has forgotten this street and this house.'
'Spring is coming and no one is here to see it.'
'I will write again when the war is over.'
context: Tanya Savicheva logged each death in flat lines ('Mama on May 13th at 7:30 in the morning, 1942'), ending: 'The Savichevs are dead.' / 'Everyone is dead.' / 'Only Tanya is left.' Evacuated out, she died of intestinal tuberculosis in 1944 at age 14; her diary is displayed at the State Museum of the History of St. Petersburg. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanya_Savicheva.

question: On August 9, 1942, conductor Karl Eliasberg led a performance of Shostakovich's Seventh ('Leningrad') Symphony inside the besieged city and broadcast it over loudspeakers at the German lines. Of the 40-member Leningrad Radio Orchestra only about 14 musicians were still alive in the city. How did Eliasberg fill the empty chairs?
answer: Soldiers were pulled from the front line to play
choices: Soldiers were pulled from the front line to play
Recordings were piped in behind the live players
Children from the conservatory took the open seats
Wax figures were seated to fill out the stage
context: The 252-page score was flown into the encircled city from Kuibyshev; only ~14 of 40 orchestra members were alive, so soldiers were pulled from the front to fill the seats. Three musicians died of starvation during rehearsals, and Eliasberg, weakened by 'dystrophy,' had to be hauled to rehearsals on a sledge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leningrad_première_of_Shostakovich's_Symphony_No._7.

question: Soviet General Leonid Govorov refused to let German guns drown out the broadcast of Shostakovich's Seventh Symphony from inside Leningrad. He launched 'Operation Squall,' firing about 3,000 shells onto the German artillery so the music could play uninterrupted. Afterward Govorov told conductor Karl Eliasberg one line about his own role that day. What did he say?
answer: 'We played our instrument in the symphony, too.'
choices: 'We played our instrument in the symphony, too.'
'Let them remember who owns this sky.'
'The guns have earned their silence tonight.'
'Tell Shostakovich the front kept time for him.'
context: Govorov's 'Operation Squall' put ~3,000 shells onto German batteries so the symphony could be broadcast unbroken; he told Eliasberg, 'we played our instrument in the symphony, too.' Eliasberg later met German soldiers who said the concert convinced them they could never take Leningrad. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leningrad_première_of_Shostakovich's_Symphony_No._7.

question: At Leningrad's Vavilov Institute — the world's first seed bank — staff sat through the famine guarding roughly 380,000 seed samples of grain, rice, and nuts. Nine of them chose the same fate rather than touch the collection. What happened to those nine?
answer: They starved to death surrounded by edible seeds
choices: They starved to death surrounded by edible seeds
They smuggled the seeds out across the ice
They burned the records to hide them from the Germans
They were shot for hoarding state food
context: Nine Vavilov Institute scientists starved to death rather than eat the ~380,000-sample seed bank; one died holding a packet of peanuts, refusing to consume what he saw as the future of Russia's harvests. Source: sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/the-tragedy-of-the-worlds-first-seed-bank.

question: Nikolai Vavilov was the botanist who built Leningrad's seed bank and spent his life trying to end famine for good. He did not die at German hands during the siege. Where and how did he die in January 1943?
answer: Starved on cabbage and mouldy flour in a Soviet prison
choices: Starved on cabbage and mouldy flour in a Soviet prison
Shot by a German sniper on the city wall
Lost on the ice of the Road of Life
Killed by a shell while guarding his seeds
context: Stalin had Vavilov arrested in 1940; he was starved on mashed cabbage and mouldy flour and died in a Soviet prison in January 1943 at age 55 — a famine-fighter killed by hunger inside his own country's jail. The endurance of Leningrad's people and the cruelty of Stalin's regime are separable truths. Source: sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/the-tragedy-of-the-worlds-first-seed-bank.

question: On 7 May 1915 the German submarine U-20 fired a single torpedo into the side of the Lusitania, a Cunard ocean liner as long as four city blocks, off the Irish coast. People assumed a ship that huge would stay afloat for hours, giving everyone time to reach the lifeboats. Instead, how fast did the Lusitania go under?
answer: In about 18 minutes
choices: In about 18 minutes
In about 3 hours
In about 9 hours
In about 30 hours
context: The Lusitania sank in roughly 18 minutes off the Old Head of Kinsale, far faster than anyone expected. 1,198 people died and only about 763 survived; 128 of the dead were Americans, which helped turn U.S. opinion toward entering World War I. Source: https://www.iwm.org.uk/history/18-minutes-that-shocked-the-world ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinking_of_the_RMS_Lusitania

question: U-20's commander, Kapitanleutnant Walther Schwieger, fired just one torpedo at the Lusitania at 2:10 pm and watched her go down in only 18 minutes. In his war diary he recorded the ship 'heels over to starboard' but admitted he was puzzled: a single torpedo should not have sunk such a giant liner that fast. Historians still argue over the real cause of the speed. What had erupted inside the ship moments after the torpedo struck?
answer: A violent second explosion deep inside her
choices: A violent second explosion deep inside her
A jammed and useless steering rudder
A mutiny among her frightened crew
A fire racing through the dining saloon
context: A second, far bigger explosion deep inside the Lusitania is what doomed her so quickly, and its cause is still debated: coal dust igniting, a boiler bursting, a ruptured steam line, or the war munitions in her cargo hold. The ship really did carry war supplies for the Western Front, including about 4.2 million rounds of Remington rifle ammunition and 1,250 cases of shrapnel shells. Source: https://www.historyhit.com/facts-about-the-sinking-of-rms-lusitania/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Schwieger ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinking_of_the_RMS_Lusitania

question: Many diseases crossed from Europe to the Americas after 1492 - measles, influenza, and typhus among them - but one killed far more Native Americans than any other. It covered its victims in pustules, and those who lived through it were left pitted with permanent scars. Which disease was the great killer of the Americas?
answer: Smallpox
choices: Smallpox
Measles
Influenza
Typhus
context: Smallpox (Variola major) was the deadliest of the Old World 'crowd diseases' for Native peoples. It scarred survivors deeply (pockmarks) and could blind them. Source: https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/how-smallpox-devastated-the-aztecs-and-helped-spain-conquer-an-american-civilization-500-years-ago

question: Stories of the conquest of the Americas usually feature armored Spaniards with guns, cannon, and horses. But historians say the soldiers and their weapons killed only a small share of the Native Americans who died in the century after contact - so many that some estimates reach 90% of the population. What did the overwhelming majority actually die from?
answer: Old World epidemic diseases
choices: Old World epidemic diseases
Spanish guns and cannon
Starvation in the silver mines
Battles against the colonists
context: Disease, not warfare, did the overwhelming majority of the killing. One widely cited estimate is about 56 million deaths by the year 1600 out of a pre-contact population as high as ~60 million. This 'germs killed more than swords' fact is real history, not a story staged for effect. Source: https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2019/feb/great-dying-americas-disturbed-earths-climate

question: The Pilgrims' settlement at Plymouth is famous, but the ground was not untouched wilderness when they arrived in 1620. They moved into a place where dwellings already stood and human bones lay unburied. What had Plymouth been, just a few years before the Pilgrims built their town?
answer: A Native village emptied by an epidemic
choices: A Native village emptied by an epidemic
A Spanish fort abandoned after a mutiny
A French trading post burned in a raid
An island the Pilgrims reached by mistake
context: An epidemic of 1616-1619 (often called the 'Great Dying') killed as much as 90% of the Native people of coastal southern New England before the Pilgrims landed. They settled the abandoned Patuxet village and renamed it Plymouth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patuxet

question: In the summer of 1837 a steamboat called the St. Peter carried smallpox up the Missouri River to the Mandan, who lived in earth-lodge towns near Fort Clark. That July the Mandan numbered about 2,000 people. How many were left alive by that October?
answer: About 25
choices: About 1,000
About 500
About 200
About 25
context: The Mandan were reduced from about 2,000 to roughly 23-27 survivors in three months - a death rate of at least ~93%. More than 17,000 Indigenous people died along the Missouri. Trader Francis Chardon, watching from Fort Clark, gave up counting the dead, writing that they died too fast for it to be possible; the chief Four Bears (Mato-Tope) gave a bitter final speech before dying on July 30, 1837. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1837_Great_Plains_smallpox_epidemic

question: Smallpox killed perhaps a third of the Europeans it infected, but in the Americas the very same disease could kill half a population - sometimes nearly all of it. Why were Native Americans so much more likely to die of smallpox than Europeans were?
answer: They had never been exposed, so had no acquired immunity
choices: They had never been exposed, so had no acquired immunity
They lived in larger and far more crowded cities
They had no written knowledge of medicine
They had been weakened by long ocean voyages
context: Native populations had no acquired immunity because they had never been exposed to Old World crowd diseases. Historians call these 'virgin soil' epidemics (a term popularized by historian Alfred Crosby) - outbreaks in a population with zero prior immunological resistance, which is why the death rates ran so catastrophically high. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_American_disease_and_epidemics

question: After the Aztecs drove Cortes out of Tenochtitlan on the 'Night of Sorrows,' the warrior who had led that uprising, Cuitlahuac, became the new emperor in triumph. He never really got to rule. What ended his reign after only about 80 days?
answer: Smallpox, caught in the 1520 epidemic
choices: Smallpox, caught in the 1520 epidemic
A Spanish ambush during the retreat
A revolt led by rival Aztec nobles
Starvation during the siege of the city
context: Cuitlahuac took the throne after Moctezuma's death and led the revolt that drove Cortes out, but died of smallpox after a reign of only about 80 days. He was succeeded by his nephew Cuauhtemoc, the last Aztec emperor. The epidemic also gave Cortes a crucial respite to regroup before the final siege. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuitl%C3%A1huac

question: Tisquantum - the man the Pilgrims called Squanto - is remembered for helping them survive their first year. Years earlier he had been kidnapped and taken to Europe, and when he finally made his way home to his people, the Patuxet, in 1619, he made a terrible discovery. What did Squanto find?
answer: He was the only Patuxet left alive
choices: He was the only Patuxet left alive
His village had moved far inland
His people had all been taken as slaves
A rival tribe had seized his home
context: Squanto returned in 1619 to find he was the last surviving Patuxet - his entire people had died in the 1616-1619 epidemic. The Pilgrims later settled on the empty Patuxet village site, which they renamed Plymouth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patuxet

question: The Taino of Hispaniola were the first people Columbus met in 1492, and the first to be destroyed by contact. A census in 1508 counted about 60,000 Taino; after enslavement, warfare, and then the first New World smallpox epidemic in 1518, their numbers collapsed. To roughly what figure had the Taino fallen by the mid-1500s?
answer: About 400
choices: About 4,000
About 2,000
About 900
About 400
context: The Taino count fell from about 60,000 (1508) to about 23,000 by 1518, and to fewer than 500 by the mid-1500s - effectively the extinction of a people within about two generations of Columbus's arrival. The smallpox epidemic of December 1518-1519 killed up to 90% of those who remained. Source: https://www.science.org/content/article/how-europeans-brought-sickness-new-world

question: When Francisco Pizarro reached the Inca empire in the 1530s with fewer than 200 Spaniards, he found it already torn apart by a civil war between two royal brothers, Huascar and Atahualpa. What had triggered that ruinous war of succession?
answer: Smallpox had killed the emperor and his chosen heir
choices: Smallpox had killed the emperor and his chosen heir
A failed harvest had starved the highlands
The two brothers had long been bitter rivals
An earthquake had destroyed the capital Cusco
context: Smallpox very likely killed the Inca emperor Huayna Capac (around 1524-1527) and his named heir Ninan Cuyochi - the disease apparently raced ahead of the Spanish down the Andes. Their deaths triggered the succession war between Huascar and Atahualpa; Atahualpa won but was captured and executed by Pizarro's tiny force in 1533, so the empire was already shattered by disease before the conquest. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_Civil_War

question: An Aztec who lived through the 1520 smallpox plague described it for the friar Bernardino de Sahagun: the sick were so covered in agonizing sores they 'could only lie on their beds like corpses.' But the witness explained that many people who actually survived the disease itself still died soon afterward. Why did so many survivors die?
answer: No one was well enough to bring them food, so they starved
choices: No one was well enough to bring them food, so they starved
The Spanish killed them as they lay helpless
The disease returned a second time and finished them
They were driven out of the city into the cold
context: Because entire families fell sick at once, there was often no one left healthy to fetch water or food, so people who might have survived the disease died of dehydration and starvation. The eyewitness account survives in the Florentine Codex, recorded by Sahagun from Nahua elders. Source: https://www.doaks.org/resources/online-exhibits/epidemics/epidemics-english/fall-of-tenochtitlan/smallpox

question: The 1545 'cocoliztli' epidemic killed millions in New Spain - its victims suffered high fever, black tongues, and bleeding from the eyes and mouth - yet for centuries no one knew exactly which disease it was. In 2018, a team led by Johannes Krause finally identified the killer from DNA preserved in victims' teeth. What did the ancient DNA reveal the pathogen to be?
answer: A Salmonella bacterium causing a typhoid-like fever
choices: A Salmonella bacterium causing a typhoid-like fever
The smallpox virus, as had long been assumed
A strain of the bubonic plague
An early and unusually deadly measles
context: Krause's team (Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2018) found Salmonella enterica Paratyphi C in the teeth of cocoliztli victims buried at Teposcolula-Yucundaa in Oaxaca - the first molecular identification of a 1545 pathogen. The Spanish physician Francisco Hernandez had described the symptoms: high fever, black tongue, dark urine, and bleeding from the nose, eyes, and mouth. The 1545-1548 outbreak killed an estimated 5 to 15 million people. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/article/cocoliztli-salmonella-outbreak-mexico-dna-spd

question: In 1634 the Puritan governor John Winthrop wrote a letter noting that the Native people near the new Massachusetts colony had nearly all died of smallpox. He read the epidemic as a sign of God's favor toward the settlers. Which of these is the actual line Winthrop wrote?
answer: "The Lord hath cleared our title to what we possess"
choices: "The Lord hath cleared our title to what we possess"
"God hath given these lands to His chosen people"
"Providence hath spared us to tame this wilderness"
"Heaven smiles upon our errand in the new world"
context: From Winthrop's letter of May 22, 1634: 'For the natives, they are near all dead of the smallpox, so the Lord hath cleared our title to what we possess.' This is real primary-source history showing how colonists understood the epidemics, presented plainly. The other three quotations are invented as decoys. Source: https://www.gilderlehrman.org/history-resources/spotlight-primary-source/john-winthrop-describes-life-boston-1634

question: During Pontiac's War in 1763, with the British fort at Fort Pitt under siege, the defenders tried a grim scheme on two visiting Delaware envoys. A trader named William Trent recorded the act and wrote, 'I hope it will have the desired effect.' What had the British handed the envoys?
answer: Blankets taken from their smallpox hospital
choices: Blankets taken from their smallpox hospital
Rifles that had been rigged to misfire
Food that had been deliberately spoiled
Whiskey that had been laced with poison
context: A Fort Pitt ledger records the supplies, and Trent's journal hoped they would 'have the desired effect.' General Jeffery Amherst separately urged Colonel Bouquet to 'inoculate the Indians by means of blankets' to 'extirpate this execrable race.' Historians caution that smallpox was already circulating in the area, so the blankets' actual effect is uncertain - what is documented is the intent. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/colonists-native-americans-smallpox-blankets

question: A 2019 study led by Alexander Koch argued that the deaths of tens of millions of Native Americans had an effect that reached far beyond the Americas - it may even have changed the planet's climate. According to the study, how could so many human deaths have helped cool the whole Earth?
answer: Abandoned farmland regrew into forests that absorbed CO2
choices: Abandoned farmland regrew into forests that absorbed CO2
Fewer cooking fires put less smoke into the sky
Rotting bodies released gases that blocked the sun
Empty cities reflected more sunlight back into space
context: Koch's University College London study argued the 'Great Dying' depopulated so much farmland - about 56 million hectares, roughly the size of Texas - that regrowing forests pulled enough CO2 out of the air to deepen the coldest part of the Little Ice Age around 1600. This is presented as a scientific argument (confidence is moderate), not a settled fact. Source: https://eos.org/articles/european-contact-with-the-americas-may-have-triggered-global-cooling

question: In February 1899 the writer Rudyard Kipling published a poem in the New York Sun urging the United States to seize and rule the Philippines. It described the people there as 'new-caught, sullen peoples, half-devil and half-child' — and gave a famous name to the supposed job of ruling them. What did Kipling title the poem?
answer: The White Man's Burden
choices: The White Man's Burden
The Conqueror's Crown
The Saxon's Charge
The Empire's Errand
context: Kipling's 'The White Man's Burden' (subtitle: 'The United States and the Philippine Islands') ran just as the Philippine-American War began, casting empire as a thankless duty owed to 'your captives' need.' Then-governor Theodore Roosevelt mailed it to Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, calling it 'rather poor poetry, but good sense from the expansionist standpoint.' Source: americanliterature.com/author/rudyard-kipling/poem/the-white-mans-burden ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_White_Man%27s_Burden

question: The slogan 'survival of the fittest' is almost always credited to the naturalist Charles Darwin. But Darwin never wrote those words first. A British philosopher coined the phrase in his 1864 book 'Principles of Biology' after reading Darwin's 'On the Origin of Species,' and only later did Darwin himself borrow it. Who actually invented the phrase 'survival of the fittest'?
answer: Herbert Spencer
choices: Herbert Spencer
Thomas Huxley
Alfred Russel Wallace
Thomas Malthus
context: Herbert Spencer wrote that his 'survival of the fittest' was 'that which Mr. Darwin has called natural selection.' The famous catchphrase was a philosopher's gloss bolted onto biology and then stretched onto human society — Darwin only adopted it later, and as a metaphor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Survival_of_the_fittest ; smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/herbert-spencer-survival-of-the-fittest-180974756

question: On March 28, 1884, France's prime minister Jules Ferry rose in the Chamber of Deputies to defend French conquests overseas. Ferry insisted that empire was really a favor to the conquered, and he compressed the whole justification into one sentence about what he called the 'superior races.' What did Ferry tell the deputies?
answer: They have a right because they have a duty
choices: They have a right because they have a duty
They rule because God has chosen them
They conquer because commerce demands it
They lead because none else can
context: Ferry's full line — 'The superior races have a right because they have a duty. They have the duty to civilize the inferior races' — is the textbook statement of the 'mission civilisatrice,' the civilizing mission: empire reframed as a gift to the people it conquered. Source: web.viu.ca/davies/H479B.Imperialism.Nationalism/Ferry.Fr.imperialism.1884.htm

question: When Jules Ferry told the French Chamber in 1884 that France's conquests were a gift to the peoples it called 'inferior races,' deputy Camille Pelletan refused to let it stand. Right there in the chamber, Pelletan demanded to know what kind of civilization it could be if you had to deliver it with cannonballs — and he gave the conquest its true name. What did Pelletan call it?
answer: another form of barbarism
choices: another form of barbarism
a mask for plain greed
a crime dressed as charity
the rich man's adventure
context: Pelletan answered Ferry in the same room: 'What is this civilization which you impose with cannonballs? What is it but another form of barbarism? Don't these populations, these inferior races, have the same rights as you? Aren't they masters of their own houses?' The rationalization was challenged in real time, by a contemporary, to the proponent's face. Source: web.viu.ca/davies/H479B.Imperialism.Nationalism/Ferry.Fr.imperialism.1884.htm ; digfir-published.macmillanusa.com/Lauldi4e/lauldi4e_ch23_2.html

question: The American sociologist William Graham Sumner argued that 'survival of the fittest' proved which people and nations deserved to rule — that whoever ended up on top must be nature's 'fittest.' But biologists say that twists the science, because the word 'fitness' in biology does not mean what it sounds like in everyday speech. To a biologist, an animal's 'fitness' is simply a measure of one thing — what?
answer: how many offspring it leaves
choices: how many offspring it leaves
how strong and fierce it grows
how clever it becomes
how long it manages to live
context: In biology 'fitness' just means reproductive success — leaving more offspring — not being strongest, smartest, or morally better, and never a ranking of which people or nations 'deserve' to rule. Wikipedia calls social Darwinism 'pseudoscientific' and 'discredited'; thinkers like Steven Pinker flag it as the 'appeal to nature' fallacy — what exists in nature does not tell us what is right. The leap from biology to group moral worth was always illegitimate. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Survival_of_the_fittest ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Darwinism

question: The Black Death killed roughly a third of everyone in Europe. With so many workers suddenly dead, the survivors who could still swing a scythe or plow a field discovered something about their own labor. What changed for them?
answer: They could demand far higher pay than before
choices: They could demand far higher pay than before
They were forced to work for free as punishment
They were sent away from the farms to the cities
They had to share their wages with the dead men's families
context: With a third of Europe dead, surviving workers were scarce, and scarce things command a high price. The medieval body-count turned labor into a seller's market, and serfdom began to crack. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_of_Labourers_1351

question: In 1381 a tax collector named John Bampton rode into Brentwood in Essex to squeeze an unpaid poll tax out of the villagers. He had the law and the king behind him. What did the villagers of Brentwood do to him?
answer: They drove him off, and the revolt spread within days
choices: They drove him off, and the revolt spread within days
They paid the tax twice over to be left alone
They elected him as their new local lord
They marched with him to collect from the next village
context: On 30 May 1381 the men of Brentwood ran Bampton out of town over a third poll tax, and the Peasants' Revolt blazed across southeast England within days. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peasants%27_Revolt

question: On 12 June 1381, on the open ground of Blackheath outside London, the radical preacher John Ball fired up the gathered rebels with a single rhyming question. He meant that since the very first man and woman both dug and spun with their own hands, nobody was born a lord. What was Ball's famous line?
answer: "When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?"
choices: "When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?"
"Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's"
"The meek shall inherit the earth before the proud"
"No king but the King of Heaven shall rule over us"
context: John Ball's couplet became the rallying cry of the revolt: if Adam dug and Eve spun, the noble class had no birthright over the common worker. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peasants%27_Revolt

question: On 14 June 1381 the rebels of the Peasants' Revolt broke into the Tower of London itself, the king's own fortress, and seized two of the most powerful men in England: Archbishop Simon Sudbury and Treasurer Robert Hales. What did the rebels do to these two officials?
answer: They beheaded them and paraded their heads on London Bridge
choices: They beheaded them and paraded their heads on London Bridge
They locked them in the Tower's deepest cell for ransom
They forced them to sign away their lands and exiled them
They put them on trial before a jury of peasants
context: The rebels dragged Sudbury and Hales out of the Tower, beheaded them, and displayed their heads on London Bridge — striking at the very top of church and treasury. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peasants%27_Revolt

question: During the 1381 revolt the rebels burned and tore down John of Gaunt's lavish Savoy Palace in London, which held treasure worth about 10,000 pounds. Calling themselves "zealots for truth and justice, not thieves and robbers," they did something startling with all that wealth. What did they do?
answer: They stole almost nothing from it
choices: They stole almost nothing from it
They split the gold evenly among every rebel
They hauled the treasure back to their villages
They sold it off to pay the hated poll tax for everyone
context: To prove they fought for justice and not plunder, the rebels destroyed the Savoy's riches rather than pocket them — a point of honor declared aloud as the palace burned. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peasants%27_Revolt

question: At the Smithfield meeting on 15 June 1381, the rebel leader Wat Tyler had just been cut down in front of 14-year-old King Richard II, and the angry crowd readied their bows to fire. Instead of fleeing, the boy-king rode straight out toward the leaderless rebels. What did Richard do that defused a massacre?
answer: He told the crowd to follow him as their leader
choices: He told the crowd to follow him as their leader
He drew his own sword and challenged Tyler's men
He promised to lower the poll tax on the spot
He ordered his archers to fire the first volley
context: Chroniclers say the 14-year-old Richard II rode out and told the leaderless mob he would be their captain, turning a powder-keg into a procession. The mercy did not last — within weeks he revoked every promise. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peasants%27_Revolt
