question: During the 1381 revolt Richard II signed charters that abolished serfdom and freed the rebels, and they went home believing they had won. But the boy-king's promises did not hold. What did Richard II do to those charters once the danger had passed?
answer: He formally revoked every one of them weeks later
choices: He formally revoked every one of them weeks later
He had them read aloud in every parish forever
He expanded them to free serfs across all of France
He locked them in the Tower as a sacred record
context: On 2 July 1381 Richard II revoked all the freedom charters he had signed under pressure; by November at least 1,500 rebels had been executed, and John Ball was hanged, drawn and quartered on 15 July. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peasants%27_Revolt

question: In 1349 and 1351, as wages shot up after the Black Death, England's rulers under Edward III passed the Ordinance and Statute of Labourers making it a crime to ask for or pay more than the old pre-plague wages. By 1352 Parliament was complaining the law had failed completely. What were workers doing despite the law?
answer: Demanding double and treble the old rate anyway
choices: Demanding double and treble the old rate anyway
Fleeing England to work in France instead
Refusing to work any land at all
Secretly paying the lords to keep their old wages
context: Scarcity beat the statute: with workers few, supply and demand drove pay to double and treble the old rate no matter what Parliament decreed — a real seen/unseen lesson written into law and then broken. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_of_Labourers_1351

question: Around Michaelmas in 1349, as the Black Death raged, the chronicler Robert of Avesbury watched a procession of over 600 men arrive in London from Flanders. Twice a day they stripped to the waist and whipped their own bare backs with iron-knotted scourges until they bled. Why were these flagellants whipping themselves?
answer: To beg God to lift the Black Death
choices: To beg God to lift the Black Death
To train their bodies for war against France
To punish the tax collectors among them
To mourn a king who had died of the plague
context: The Brethren of the Cross believed self-inflicted suffering might persuade God to spare humanity from the plague; their scourges held sharp iron nails, and each man wore a red cross front and back. Source: https://fathertheo.wordpress.com/2013/05/07/flagellants-in-london-1349/

question: The flagellant Brethren of the Cross spread so fast across plague-stricken Europe that the Church itself grew alarmed at the unsanctioned movement. On 20 October 1349 the Pope acted against them with a formal decree. What did the Pope's papal bull do to the Brethren of the Cross?
answer: It denounced them as an impious sect and ordered them suppressed
choices: It denounced them as an impious sect and ordered them suppressed
It welcomed them into the Church as a holy order
It made their 33-day whipping marches official law
It excused all their followers from paying tithes
context: The flagellants marched town to town in 33-day cycles — one day for each year of Christ's life — until the movement grew so large that on 20 October 1349 the Pope condemned the Brethren of the Cross as an impious sect to be stamped out. Source: https://medium.com/never-stop-writing/the-black-death-part-three-faith-fear-and-the-flagellants-1ef4b2415690

question: France had its own great peasant rising, the Jacquerie, in 1358. Its leader was Guillaume Cale, a well-off farmer from near Beauvais. When Charles II of Navarre invited him to truce talks near Mello, Cale came to parley — and the nobles seized him. They argued the rules of chivalry did not protect a mere peasant. What did they do to Guillaume Cale?
answer: They tortured him and cut off his head
choices: They tortured him and cut off his head
They held him for a king's ransom in gold
They made him swear loyalty and set him free
They exiled him across the sea to England
context: Lured to truce talks near Mello on 10 June 1358, Guillaume Cale was seized, tortured, and decapitated by nobles who held that chivalry's rules did not apply to a peasant. The Jacquerie was crushed with at least 20,000 peasants killed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guillaume_Cale

question: Socrates was an old philosopher put on trial in Athens in 399 BC, accused of two crimes. One charge was impiety — not honoring the city's gods. What was the second charge his accusers brought against him?
answer: Corrupting the young men of Athens
choices: Corrupting the young men of Athens
Stealing money from the city treasury
Spying for the enemy city of Sparta
Refusing to fight in Athens' army
context: His accusers claimed his constant questioning was teaching Athens' youth to doubt and disrespect their elders and gods. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_Socrates

question: Socrates is one of the most famous thinkers who ever lived, yet historians face a strange problem: we have no books, no letters, and no essays in his own hand. Why must everything we know about Socrates come secondhand, from his students Plato and Xenophon?
answer: Socrates never wrote anything down himself
choices: Socrates never wrote anything down himself
A fire destroyed all of his writings
His enemies burned his books after the trial
He wrote only in a secret code no one solved
context: Socrates taught entirely by talking and questioning in the streets and marketplace of Athens; his pupils Plato and Xenophon later wrote down what he said. Source: https://iep.utm.edu/socrates/

question: Socrates told the Athenians that the god had fastened him onto their sleepy, self-satisfied city to sting it awake out of its lazy sluggishness. What stinging creature did Socrates call himself?
answer: A gadfly
choices: A gadfly
A guard dog
A honeybee
A war-horse
context: In Plato's Apology (30e) Socrates says the city is 'a great and noble horse which was somewhat sluggish because of its size and needed to be stirred up,' and he is the gadfly sent by the god to do the stirring. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_unexamined_life_is_not_worth_living

question: Convicted and facing execution, Socrates told the court he would rather die than give up his lifelong habit of questioning everything and everyone. What famous reason did he give for why a life without questioning was no life at all?
answer: The unexamined life is not worth living
choices: The unexamined life is not worth living
A man should always obey the city's laws
Knowledge is the only true form of wealth
Death is nothing to be feared by the wise
context: Plato's Apology (38a) records the line; the original Greek is 'ho de anexetastos bios ou biotos anthropoi.' For Socrates, examining your own beliefs was the whole point of being human. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_unexamined_life_is_not_worth_living

question: Socrates said his whole life of questioning began with one baffling answer from the Oracle at Delphi. His friend Chaerephon had asked the oracle whether any man alive was wiser than Socrates. What did the priestess answer?
answer: That no one was wiser than Socrates
choices: That no one was wiser than Socrates
That the gods alone held true wisdom
That Chaerephon himself was the wiser man
That wisdom would bring Socrates ruin
context: Socrates felt he knew nothing, so the oracle's answer puzzled him. He spent his life questioning politicians, poets, and craftsmen to test it — and kept finding men who only thought they knew things. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apology_(Plato)

question: After the jury convicted him, Socrates was allowed to propose his own punishment instead of death. Rather than beg, he mockingly insisted he deserved a great reward — the very honor Athens gave to Olympic champions and heroes of the city. What did he say he deserved?
answer: Free meals for life at public expense
choices: Free meals for life at public expense
A statue raised in the marketplace
A general's command in the army
A golden crown from the assembly
context: He suggested dining for life at the Prytaneum, the honor reserved for Olympic victors. Only when his friends Plato and Crito offered to pay did he grudgingly propose a fine of thirty minae instead. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apology_(Plato)

question: Socrates was executed by being made to drink a cup of hemlock. Told to walk about until his legs grew heavy, he lay down to wait for the end. How did the hemlock kill him?
answer: A cold numbness crept slowly up toward his heart
choices: A cold numbness crept slowly up toward his heart
A burning fever spread through his whole body
Violent convulsions seized him within moments
A deep sleep took him before any pain began
context: Hemlock causes a slow, creeping paralysis. The executioner pressed his foot and asked if he could feel it; Socrates said no. The cold rose from his feet up his shins and abdomen, and when it reached his heart, he would be gone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phaedo

question: Years before his trial, the brutal Thirty Tyrants who ruled Athens ordered Socrates and four other men to go arrest an innocent named Leon of Salamis so he could be put to death. The other four men went and did it. What did Socrates do?
answer: He simply turned and went home
choices: He simply turned and went home
He warned Leon and helped him escape
He arrested Leon but pleaded for mercy
He fled Athens that same night
context: Disobeying the Tyrants could have cost Socrates his life, but he refused to help murder an innocent man and just walked home. He told this story at his trial as proof he had never bent to unjust power. Source: https://iep.utm.edu/socrates/

question: Socrates' execution did not happen right after his trial — it was held up for about a month, even though he was already condemned. A religious rule forbade any execution in Athens during this time. What caused the long delay?
answer: A sacred ship was away on a holy voyage
choices: A sacred ship was away on a holy voyage
A festival of games had filled the city
A plague had shut the prison gates
An eclipse was read as an evil omen
context: Each year a sacred ship sailed to the island of Delos to honor Apollo, and no execution was permitted until it returned. That year contrary winds stretched the usual two-week trip into a month. Source: https://law.hofstra.edu/sites/law.hofstra.edu/files/2024-08/fall-2024-jurisprudence-sinha-crito.pdf

question: As the hemlock's cold numbness climbed toward his heart, Socrates spoke his very last words — not a grand speech, but a small final instruction to his friend Crito. What did Socrates say with his dying breath?
answer: That they owed a rooster to the healing god
choices: That they owed a rooster to the healing god
That his children should be raised by Crito
That the jury would one day be ashamed
That his books should be given to Plato
context: 'Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius; pay it and do not neglect it.' Asclepius was the god of healing, and such an offering thanked him for a cure — as if Socrates were thanking the god for curing him of life itself. Crito then closed his eyes and mouth. Source: https://classical-inquiries.chs.harvard.edu/the-last-words-of-socrates-at-the-place-where-he-died/

question: On the night before the poison, Socrates' old friend Crito crept into the prison at dawn with an escape fully arranged — guards bribed, a hiding place ready. Socrates refused to run. In Plato's Crito, what imagined confrontation did he use to explain why he would not escape?
answer: The Laws of Athens themselves rising up to accuse him
choices: The Laws of Athens themselves rising up to accuse him
His dead father returning to shame him
The gods of Olympus weighing his soul
A future Athens cursing his cowardice
context: Socrates pictured the Laws of Athens confronting him: he had lived his whole life under them and accepted their protection, so he could not break the city's verdict just because it now harmed him. Crito had no answer and gave in. Source: https://law.hofstra.edu/sites/law.hofstra.edu/files/2024-08/fall-2024-jurisprudence-sinha-crito.pdf

question: The phrase 'I know that I know nothing' is the saying most people attach to Socrates, but it is a later paraphrase, not his actual words. In Plato's Apology, Socrates explains he is wiser than other men for one precise reason. What was it?
answer: He alone knew the full extent of his own ignorance
choices: He alone knew the full extent of his own ignorance
He alone had been blessed by the Oracle at Delphi
He alone had read every poet and lawmaker
He alone could win any argument he entered
context: The real line (Apology 21d) is that Socrates 'neither knows nor thinks he knows' what he does not know, while other men think they know when they don't. Knowing the limits of his own knowledge was the whole of his wisdom. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_know_that_I_know_nothing

question: After the Battle of Solferino in 1859, the women of the Italian town of Castiglione carried the wounded into their church and nursed them through the night — French, Italian, and Austrian soldiers side by side, never asking which army a dying man had fought for. The Swiss traveler Henri Dunant watched, and he never forgot the two words the women kept repeating as they worked. What did they say?
answer: "Tutti fratelli" — all are brothers
choices: "Tutti fratelli" — all are brothers
"Veni, vidi, vici" — I came, I saw, I conquered
"Ora pro nobis" — pray for us
"Avanti, Italia" — forward, Italy
context: Henri Dunant, a 31-year-old Swiss businessman, had stumbled into the aftermath of Solferino while traveling to meet Napoleon III about an Algerian land deal. The scene of the Castiglione women caring for friend and enemy alike — 'Tutti fratelli' — became the seed of his idea for a neutral society to aid the wounded of any side, the future Red Cross. Source: nationalgeographic.com/history/article/red-cross-founder-jean-henri-dunant; ifrc.org/article/world-red-cross-and-red-crescent-day-message-our-movement

question: When delegates met at Geneva in 1864 to design an emblem for Henri Dunant's new society for the wounded — the Red Cross — they wanted a symbol that would honor the movement's home country, neutral Switzerland. So they took the Swiss flag and flipped its colors exactly. The Swiss flag is a white cross on a red background — so what did the Red Cross emblem become?
answer: A red cross on a white background
choices: A red cross on a white background
A white cross on a red background
A red cross on a blue background
A gold cross on a green background
context: The red-cross-on-white emblem chosen in 1864 was deliberately the exact color-reverse of neutral Switzerland's flag, honoring the Swiss origins of the movement Henri Dunant founded. Source: ifrc.org/who-we-are/international-red-cross-and-red-crescent-movement/emblems-and-logo; nationalgeographic.com/history/article/red-cross-founder-jean-henri-dunant

question: On August 14, 1980, Lech Walesa was an unemployed electrician when workers occupied the Lenin Shipyard in Gdansk and shut the gates against the outside. How did Walesa get inside to join the strike that would grow into Solidarity?
answer: He climbed over the twelve-foot perimeter fence
choices: He climbed over the twelve-foot perimeter fence
He bribed a guard to open a side gate
He swam across the harbor to the docks
He hid in the back of a delivery truck
context: Walesa scaled the roughly 12-foot fence to join the strikers, who promptly elected him head of their strike committee — the fence-climb is the iconic founding image of Solidarity. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Lech-Walesa

question: On August 31, 1980, Lech Walesa signed the Gdansk Agreement, winning Polish workers the right to form free trade unions — the first such right anywhere in the Soviet bloc. He marked the moment with an oversized souvenir pen. What was printed on the pen he used to sign it?
answer: A portrait of Pope John Paul II
choices: A portrait of Pope John Paul II
The red-and-white Polish eagle crest
The Solidarnosc logo in bold red letters
An image of the Gdansk shipyard cranes
context: Walesa signed the historic accord with a giant souvenir pen bearing the face of the Polish-born pope — fusing the workers' movement with the faith that had helped fuel it. Source: https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/august-31/polish-government-signs-accord-with-gdansk-shipyard-workers

question: In the Song dynasty's civil service exams, a candidate was locked alone for days in a tiny brick cell, open to the sky and barely three feet wide, bringing his own food, ink, bedding, and even a chamber pot. The cell was furnished with only two wooden boards. What were the two boards for?
answer: One was his desk; the other was both his seat and his bed.
choices: One was his desk; the other was both his seat and his bed.
One was his door; the other sealed the cell shut at night.
One held his lamp; the other propped up a small cooking fire.
One was a shelf for his books; the other a board to kneel on.
context: By day the candidate wrote at one board; by night he slept on the other — for days on end, sealed in alone. (The cell dimensions are best documented from the later imperial exam halls of the same continuous tradition, not from measured Song halls.) Source: New World Encyclopedia, 'Imperial Examinations (Keju)'; Wikipedia, 'Imperial examination.'

question: In Song China, the single best scholar in the whole empire — the man who placed first in the empire-wide Palace Exam — earned the title 'zhuangyuan,' and his name was brushed onto the imperial 'Golden List.' How was this brand-new top scholar then honored in public?
answer: He was paraded through the streets on horseback.
choices: He was paraded through the streets on horseback.
He was carried to the palace temple to be blessed.
He was handed the keys to the city's main gate.
He was seated beside the emperor at a banquet.
context: The 'zhuangyuan' (top graduate) was a celebrity overnight: his name on the yellow 'Golden List,' then a parade on horseback through the streets. Source: Wikipedia, 'Zhuangyuan'; Baidu Baike (EN), 'Zhuangyuan, the top graduate in the imperial examination.'

question: Song China produced the world's first government paper money, the 'jiaozi,' which the state began issuing from an office in Chengdu in the 1020s. What problem in the southwestern region of Sichuan had first driven local merchants to invent paper notes?
answer: The local coins were made of iron and too heavy to carry.
choices: The local coins were made of iron and too heavy to carry.
The local mines had run completely out of copper and silver.
Bandits on the roads kept robbing every shipment of coins.
The region lay too far from the capital's official mints.
context: Sichuan used bulky IRON coins, so merchants there issued lightweight paper notes instead; the state then took it over, opening the Jiaozi office (Jiaozi wu) in Chengdu in 1023 and issuing official notes by 1024. Source: Wikipedia, 'Jiaozi (currency)'; South China Morning Post, 'how China's Song dynasty pioneered global fiat currency.'

question: The Song exams were so grueling that candidates, sealed alone in their cells for days, sometimes died at their desks mid-test. In this exam tradition the sealed compound gates could not be opened until the whole exam ended. So when a candidate died inside, what did officials do with his body?
answer: They wrapped it in a mat and threw it over the compound wall.
choices: They wrapped it in a mat and threw it over the compound wall.
They laid it in his cell until the gates opened days later.
They burned it at once in a brazier out in the courtyard.
They carried it out through a small door kept for the dead.
context: Rather than break the seal on the gates, officials wrapped the body in a mat and pitched it over the high wall. (Documented from the later halls of the same continuous exam tradition, not from Song-specific records.) Source: New World Encyclopedia, 'Imperial Examinations (Keju)'; The History Reader, 'Examination Time in Early Qing Dynasty Beijing.'

question: Emperor Taizu, the general who founded the Song dynasty by seizing the throne, deliberately raised scholars above soldiers. In 973 he created a brand-new final round of the civil service exam — and kept one extraordinary part of it for himself. What was it?
answer: He personally tested the top candidates and ranked them himself.
choices: He personally tested the top candidates and ranked them himself.
He chose which Confucian classics every candidate would study.
He selected the graders who would mark all of the papers.
He wrote out the questions for that first exam by hand.
context: By creating the Palace Examination and presiding over it, Taizu made the emperor the final examiner of his own future officials, announcing the ranked list himself. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Emperor Taizu of Song'; Britannica, 'Taizu — Reform of the examination.'

question: Four centuries before Gutenberg, a Song commoner named Bi Sheng invented movable type — individual characters that could be set, inked, printed, and then reused for the next page. Out of what surprising material did Bi Sheng make his tiny reusable characters?
answer: Baked clay, each piece thin as a coin's edge.
choices: Baked clay, each piece thin as a coin's edge.
Cast bronze, each piece filed smooth by hand.
Carved jade, polished to a mirror shine.
Hardened bamboo, split into narrow slips.
context: Around 1041–1048 Bi Sheng carved characters into sticky clay 'as thin as the edge of a coin,' baked them hard, and set them on an iron plate coated with pine resin, wax, and paper ash. We know this only because Shen Kuo wrote it down. Source: Wikipedia, 'Bi Sheng' and 'Movable type'; HistoryofInformation.com, 'The Invention of Movable Type in China.'

question: The earliest known gunpowder recipes were written down in a Song military manual, the 'Wujing Zongyao' of 1044. Song soldiers soon strapped a tube of gunpowder onto a spear and carried it into battle. This weapon — the 'fire lance' — is remembered today as the ancestor of what?
answer: Every gun and firearm later carried into battle.
choices: Every gun and firearm later carried into battle.
Every cannon later mounted on a city's walls.
Every rocket later launched up into the sky.
Every land mine later buried beneath a road.
context: The fire lance — a spear with a gunpowder tube strapped on — is the ancestor of every gun on earth; defenders used fire lances at the siege of De'an in 1132. The same manual named early bombs like the 'thunderclap bomb.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Gunpowder weapons in the Song dynasty' and 'History of gunpowder'; Asia for Educators (Columbia), 'Gunpowder — Song Dynasty China.'

question: By 1094 the Song official Su Song had finished a forty-foot, water-powered astronomical clock tower at the capital, Kaifeng — driven by a giant water wheel and topped by a slowly turning bronze sphere that tracked the stars. What did this clock do on every hour to mark the time?
answer: Little costumed figurines popped out of doors to ring bells and beat drums.
choices: Little costumed figurines popped out of doors to ring bells and beat drums.
A bronze dragon's mouth dropped a metal ball into a bowl with a clang.
A bank of bronze bells swung out and rang across the whole city.
A painted sun and moon slid across the open face of the tower.
context: 133 little costumed figurines popped from doors to ring bells and beat drums on the hour; the wheel was 11 feet across with 36 scoops, and the bronze armillary sphere on top weighed 10 to 20 tons. Source: Wikipedia, 'Su Song'; Instituto Português de Relojoaria, 'Su Sung's Clock.'

question: In 1127 the invading Jurchen Jin armies sacked Kaifeng and carted Su Song's famous astronomical clock tower north, piece by piece. But the machine was so intricate that no one could ever make it run again. When the emperor ordered Su Song's own son to rebuild his father's clock and he too failed, what did the son conclude?
answer: That his father had deliberately left out essential parts.
choices: That his father had deliberately left out essential parts.
That the Jin had lost crucial pieces on the journey north.
That the design had only ever worked by sheer luck.
That the water in the north was wrong for the great wheel.
context: The Jin could never reassemble the tower; Su Song's son Su Xie failed too, and concluded his father had purposely omitted essential parts. Source: Wikipedia, 'Su Song' (Jurchen dismantling 1127; Su Xie's failed reconstruction).

question: Determined to stamp out favoritism, the Song made the exams anonymous: from 992 a candidate's name on his paper was hidden and replaced with a number. But a grader might still recognize a candidate's handwriting — so from 1015 the Song added an extraordinary second safeguard. What was it?
answer: Clerks recopied every single exam by hand before it was graded.
choices: Clerks recopied every single exam by hand before it was graded.
Graders were reassigned to a different province every year.
Candidates were forced to write in one stiff official script.
Each paper was read aloud so the grader never saw the writing.
context: A whole team of clerks recopied every paper by hand so a grader couldn't recognize the writing; two graders then scored each paper and a third broke ties. Source: Wikipedia, 'Imperial examination' (anonymity reforms 992/1007/1015/1032); SonomaSage Substack, 'The Exams of China: The Song Dynasty.'

question: The Song civil service exam was a real ladder out of obscurity, not just a club for the well-born. Surveys of the degree-holders in 1148 and 1256 found that about 57% came from families that had never held official rank. Because rank now came from the exam and not from birth, what became possible for a farmer's son who mastered the Confucian books?
answer: He could outrank a general's son who had not passed.
choices: He could outrank a general's son who had not passed.
He was given command of the army's western border.
He was guaranteed a post in his own home county.
He was excused from ever paying the imperial taxes.
context: In 1148 and 1256, about 57% of degree-holders came from families with no prior official rank — so a farmer's son who mastered the books really could outrank a general's son who hadn't. Source: Wikipedia, 'Imperial examination' (citing Hartwell/Chaffee social-mobility data for 1148 and 1256).

question: In his 'Dream Pool Essays' of 1088, the Song scholar-official Shen Kuo gave the world's first clear account of a magnetic compass for navigation: rub a steel needle on lodestone, then hang it from a single silk thread. Watching his needle closely, Shen Kuo noticed something Europe would not grasp for centuries. What did he notice?
answer: The needle pointed slightly east of true south, not exactly south.
choices: The needle pointed slightly east of true south, not exactly south.
The needle swung faster the closer it was carried to the sea.
The needle lost its pull entirely during a passing thunderstorm.
The needle pointed straight down when held above buried iron ore.
context: Shen Kuo recorded that the needle points slightly EAST of due south — the discovery of magnetic declination, unknown in Europe for centuries. He also explained rainbows as sunlight through rain and read marine fossils high in the Taihang Mountains as proof the land had changed over vast time. Source: Wikipedia, 'Shen Kuo' and 'Dream Pool Essays'; HistoryofInformation.com, 'Shen Kuo Provides the Earliest Description of the Compass.'

question: The Songhai Empire's capital, Gao, sat on a great river that fed its farms and carried its trade canoes. On which river did Gao stand?
answer: The Niger River
choices: The Niger River
The Nile River
The Congo River
The Zambezi River
context: Gao stood on the Niger River in West Africa, and under Askia Muhammad it swelled to about 100,000 inhabitants, one of the largest cities in the region. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Songhai_Empire/

question: Under the Songhai Empire, one city became so famous as a center of trade and Islamic learning that it held around 100,000 people and roughly 150 to 180 Koranic schools. Which city was this?
answer: Timbuktu
choices: Timbuktu
Cairo
Baghdad
Mecca
context: Timbuktu, on the edge of the Sahara, was Songhai's jewel of scholarship, with scholars teaching at the Sankore Mosque. Its name still means 'the ends of the earth' to many. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Songhai_Empire/

question: On his 1497 pilgrimage to Mecca, the Songhai ruler Askia Muhammad traveled with hundreds of cavalry and a fortune in gold, giving 100,000 pieces to charity in the holy cities. What honorary title did the last Abbasid caliph grant him there?
answer: 'Caliph of the Sudan'
choices: 'Caliph of the Sudan'
'King of the Niger'
'Lion of Gao'
'Sultan of Timbuktu'
context: In Mecca the last Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil named Askia Muhammad 'Caliph of the Sudan' (West Africa). On his way home he recruited scholars from Egypt and Morocco to teach at the Sankore Mosque in Timbuktu. Source: owlcation.com via WebSearch

question: Askia Muhammad seized the Songhai throne by beating the old king's son at the Battle of Anfao in 1493, then ruled for about 37 years. He built a professional standing army and a government of specialized ministers. Where in Gao was he finally buried?
answer: In a stepped pyramid of mud and earth
choices: In a stepped pyramid of mud and earth
In a marble mosque domed with gold
Beneath the Sankore Mosque floor
In a cave carved into a cliff
context: The Tomb of Askia is a stepped pyramid of mud and earth, just over 10 meters tall, bristling with protruding acacia-wood stakes (toron) used as permanent scaffolding for re-plastering. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004. Source: https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Tomb_of_Askia

question: In 1591 a Moroccan army crossed the whole Sahara to attack Songhai. At the Battle of Tondibi the huge Songhai cavalry, armed only with spears, swords and bows, charged the smaller Moroccan force. What weapon did the Moroccans have that decided the battle in about two hours?
answer: Firearms — arquebuses and cannon
choices: Firearms — arquebuses and cannon
Heavier armored war-elephants
A surprise river ambush by canoe
Vastly greater numbers of horsemen
context: Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur's roughly 2,000 arquebusiers and 6 cannon, led by the Spanish-born eunuch Judar Pasha, decimated the gunless Songhai. Gunpowder ended the largest empire in West African history; the region fragmented into dozens of smaller kingdoms. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tondibi

question: At the Battle of Tondibi in 1591, the Songhai tried a desperate trick to break the Moroccan line: they drove a herd of 1,000 cattle to stampede straight into the enemy. What went wrong with the plan?
answer: The gunfire and cannon noise turned the herd back into the Songhai's own ranks
choices: The gunfire and cannon noise turned the herd back into the Songhai's own ranks
The cattle bogged down in the Niger's mud and never reached the line
Moroccan horsemen simply rode around the slow-moving herd
The Moroccans drove their own larger herd to meet it head-on
context: The roar of arquebuses and cannon panicked the cattle, which stampeded backward into the Songhai. Some Songhai soldiers reportedly sat on their shields rather than flee and were killed where they sat. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tondibi

question: Most people learn that Germany invaded Poland on September 1, 1939, to start World War II in Europe. But just over two weeks later, on September 17, a second army poured across Poland's OTHER border under a secret pact that carved the country in two. Whose army was it?
answer: The Soviet Red Army, from the east
choices: The Soviet Red Army, from the east
The Italian Royal Army, from the south
The Austrian Landwehr, from the west
The Hungarian Honved, from the north
context: The secret Molotov-Ribbentrop pact carved Poland in two between Hitler and Stalin. For eastern Poland and the Baltic states, the war's end did not mean liberation but a SECOND tyranny. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_transfer_in_the_Soviet_Union

question: As the Red Army advanced through Eastern Europe in 1944-45, its soldiers became infamous for grabbing so many of one small item that they were seen wearing several at once -- many had grown up too poor to ever own even one. What did they prize above almost any other loot?
answer: Wristwatches
choices: Wristwatches
Wedding rings
Fountain pens
Leather boots
context: Red Army soldiers became notorious across Eastern Europe for wearing watches up each arm. A December 1944 decree letting Soviet soldiers mail parcels home was read across the army as an open invitation to grab whatever they could carry. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_plunder

question: The most famous victory photo of the war, 'Raising a Flag over the Reichstag' (1945), was secretly doctored in two ways before it was published. Besides darkening the smoke over Berlin to make the scene more dramatic, what did photographer Yevgeny Khaldei scratch out of the negative?
answer: A wristwatch on the soldier's second arm
choices: A wristwatch on the soldier's second arm
A second soldier slumped on the rooftop
A swastika banner still flying nearby
A street sign naming the ruined building
context: In the original negative a soldier was wearing a wristwatch on EACH arm -- exactly the looting reputation the Soviets did not want their triumphant image to advertise -- so Khaldei scratched the second one off. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_plunder

question: A Soviet official summed up the plan for the Baltic states in one chilling line that became infamous. Which line did he use?
answer: "There will be Lithuania -- but without Lithuanians"
choices: "There will be Lithuania -- but without Lithuanians"
"There will be a Latvia -- but without its bourgeoisie"
"There will be an Estonia -- but without its borders"
"There will be a Baltic -- but without its old masters"
context: Between 1940 and 1953 over 200,000 Balts were deported -- roughly a tenth of the adult population. Estonian deportee mortality has been estimated at around 60 percent. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/June_deportation

question: On the freezing night of February 10, 1940, the NKVD hammered on doors across Soviet-occupied eastern Poland and gave families minutes to pack 500 kg before loading them onto cattle trains for Siberia -- about 139,794 people in one night. What stands out about who was loaded onto those trains?
answer: Nearly half were children under 16
choices: Nearly half were children under 16
Most were retired army generals
Almost all were Catholic priests
Nearly all were over 70 years old
context: This was the first of four deportation waves. Settlers, foresters, and refugees were packed off to 'special settlements' in Siberia and the Arctic north. Source: https://kresy-siberia.org/museum-galleries/soviet-mass-deportations-1940-41/soviet-mass-deportations/

question: In May 1944 Stalin's regime did not just deport individual 'enemies' -- it loaded an ENTIRE nation onto cattle trains in a single operation, sending about 183,000 people to Uzbekistan, where roughly a fifth were dead within 18 months. Which whole people was uprooted that month?
answer: The Crimean Tatars
choices: The Crimean Tatars
The Cossacks of the Don
The Karelian Finns
The Georgian Mingrelians
context: The Volga Germans, the Chechens, and others met the same fate -- whole peoples uprooted at once. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_transfer_in_the_Soviet_Union

question: During the eight weeks of Soviet occupation in 1945, an anonymous Berlin woman secretly kept a diary. Shunned in 1950s Germany for being too honest, it was reissued after its author Marta Hillers died and became a bestseller and one of the rawest eyewitness records of the occupation. What was the diary actually titled?
answer: "A Woman in Berlin"
choices: "A Woman in Berlin"
"Diary of a Berlin Woman"
"A Berlin Woman's War"
"Notes of a Woman in Berlin"
context: Hillers published it anonymously; German readers of the 1950s rejected its honesty about what the occupation did to women, and only after her death did it find its audience. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Woman_in_Berlin

question: On March 5, 1940, NKVD chief Lavrentiy Beria wrote a note asking permission to give 22,000 captured Polish officers, police, and professionals 'the maximum penalty -- execution.' What did the dictator do to Beria's note that sealed the men's fate?
answer: Stalin signed his approval across the top
choices: Stalin signed his approval across the top
Stalin had it read aloud to the Politburo
Stalin ordered it backdated to look legal
Stalin passed it to Molotov to sign first
context: The men were shot one by one with a pistol to the back of the head -- some 4,400 of them in Katyn Forest -- and dumped in mass graves. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katyn_massacre

question: After Soviet secret police shot roughly 22,000 captured Poles in 1940 and buried them in mass graves at Katyn, the USSR maintained a single lie about the killings for FIFTY years -- until Moscow finally released documents naming 21,857 victims in 1990. Whom had the Soviets blamed for the graves all that time?
answer: The Germans
choices: The Germans
The Poles themselves
Ukrainian partisans
Anti-Stalin rebels
context: The 1990 documents named victims killed across Katyn Forest, the Kharkiv NKVD prison, and Kalinin (Tver); the men were buried at Katyn, Piatykhatky, and Mednoye. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katyn_massacre

question: When Germany invaded the USSR in late June 1941, the retreating NKVD chose to murder its political prisoners in western Ukraine rather than free them -- an estimated 10,000 to 40,000 killed in eight days by shootings, grenades, and burning cells. How did Nazi propagandists cynically exploit this Soviet atrocity?
answer: They blamed it on Jews to incite pogroms
choices: They blamed it on Jews to incite pogroms
They staged it to mimic a German victory
They blamed it on the prisoners' own riots
They credited it to advancing German troops
context: The Soviet atrocity was exploited by linking 'Jews' with 'communism' to provoke mob massacres -- a libel that cost still more innocent lives. Source: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/1941-nkvd-prison-massacres-western-ukraine

question: Historian Antony Beevor concluded that the Red Army's 1944-45 advance produced what he called the greatest phenomenon of mass rape in history -- at least 1.4 million women in East Prussia, Pomerania, and Silesia alone, plus about 100,000 in Berlin. Where did Beevor draw his enormous figure from?
answer: The Soviets' own internal reports
choices: The Soviets' own internal reports
Captured German Red Cross files
Western war correspondents' notebooks
Interrogated Wehrmacht officers
context: Of the roughly 100,000 women raped in Berlin, an estimated 10,000 died afterward. Beevor drew his numbers from the NKVD's own archive reports, not enemy claims. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rape_during_the_occupation_of_Germany

question: After the 1941 Sikorski-Mayski pact, Stalin granted Poland's surviving deportees a brief 'amnesty,' and General Wladyslaw Anders led over 110,000 of them -- including orphans whose parents had died in the Gulag -- out of the Soviet Union through Persia. From there the freed Poles ended up resettled in some startlingly far-flung places. Where did many of them scatter to?
answer: As far as New Zealand, Mexico, and British Africa
choices: As far as New Zealand, Mexico, and British Africa
Mostly to France, Spain, and the United States
Chiefly to Canada, Australia, and Argentina
Largely to Egypt, Greece, and South Africa only
context: The exodus of over 110,000 Poles -- including 36,000 women and children -- escaped through Persia (Iran) and then scattered as far as Iran, India, New Zealand, Mexico, and British Africa: a diaspora born of the Gulag. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evacuation_of_Polish_civilians_from_the_USSR_in_World_War_II

question: Of all the weapons the Soviets brought to Afghanistan, the mujahideen fighters dreaded one most: a heavily armored attack helicopter that shrugged off rifle fire as bullets bounced off its hull. They called it a flying tank. What was this dreaded Soviet helicopter?
answer: The Mi-24 'Hind' gunship
choices: The Mi-24 'Hind' gunship
The B-52 'Stratofortress' bomber
The T-72 'Ural' battle tank
The MiG-21 'Fishbed' fighter
context: The Mi-24 'Hind' was so heavily armored that small-arms fire bounced off it, earning the 'flying tank' nickname from the fighters it hunted. Breaking the Hind's dominance became the central problem of the war for the mujahideen. Source: https://smallwarsjournal.com/2023/11/25/cobra-and-mongoose-legacy-mi-24-and-stinger-missile-soviet-afghan-war/

question: After nearly ten years of fighting, the Soviet war in Afghanistan finally ended on 15 February 1989. The last Soviet commander, General Boris Gromov, marked the end with a single symbolic act as the final soldier to leave. What did Gromov do to end the war?
answer: He walked on foot across the Friendship Bridge into Soviet territory
choices: He walked on foot across the Friendship Bridge into Soviet territory
He signed the surrender at a table inside Kabul
He fired the war's last shot into the air
He raised the Soviet flag over the capital one last time
context: General Boris Gromov crossed the Friendship Bridge over the Amu Darya River on foot, the symbolic last man out. When TV crews asked how he felt, he swore at the camera; he later said the curses were aimed at 'those who start wars while others have to clean up the mess.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_withdrawal_from_Afghanistan

question: The war opened on 27 December 1979 with a 40-minute Soviet special-forces assault on the Tajbeg Palace in Kabul, code-named Operation Storm-333. The commandos came for one man, the Afghan leader Hafizullah Amin. What was the point of the entire palace raid?
answer: To kill the Afghan leader Hafizullah Amin
choices: To kill the Afghan leader Hafizullah Amin
To capture the palace treasury intact
To rescue Soviet hostages held inside
To photograph Amin's secret war plans
context: Operation Storm-333 took only about 40 minutes and ended with Hafizullah Amin dead inside the Tajbeg Palace. Eleven days earlier the KGB had tried to poison Amin's lunch, but a Soviet doctor who knew nothing of the plot treated him and saved his life, forcing the commandos to storm the palace instead. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Storm-333

question: By 1986 the Mi-24 'Hind' gunship ruled the skies over Afghanistan. Then on 25 September 1986 near Jalalabad, a mujahideen engineer named Ghaffar fired five new American shoulder-launched missiles and changed the war in minutes. What did Ghaffar accomplish with those missiles?
answer: He downed three Mi-24 helicopters in quick succession
choices: He downed three Mi-24 helicopters in quick succession
He destroyed a column of Soviet supply trucks
He drove off a Soviet ground patrol unharmed
He scattered a formation of Soviet jet fighters
context: Ghaffar fired five FIM-92 Stinger missiles and downed three Mi-24 'Hinds' in their combat debut. The shoulder-fired, heat-seeking Stinger was light enough for one fighter to carry. The CIA had funneled the missiles to the mujahideen through Pakistan in a secret program called Operation Cyclone. Source: https://smallwarsjournal.com/2023/11/25/cobra-and-mongoose-legacy-mi-24-and-stinger-missile-soviet-afghan-war/

question: Ahmad Shah Massoud, the guerrilla commander nicknamed the 'Lion of Panjshir,' became the Soviets' most stubborn enemy in the Panjshir Valley north of Kabul. Between 1980 and 1985 the Soviets launched nine separate offensives to drive him out. How did Massoud frustrate them each time?
answer: He returned to the valley the moment the Soviets left
choices: He returned to the valley the moment the Soviets left
He surrendered the valley and fought elsewhere
He retreated permanently across the border into Pakistan
He negotiated a lasting truce after the first offensive
context: Massoud, the 'Lion of Panjshir,' held the valley against nine Soviet offensives between 1980 and 1985. The Soviets could push him out but never hold the ground; he simply came back the instant they withdrew, making the valley a symbol of how the war could not be won. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panjshir_offensives_(Soviet%E2%80%93Afghan_War)

question: In February 1986, at the 27th Party Congress, Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev did something no Soviet leader was supposed to do: he publicly admitted the mighty USSR was trapped in a war it could not win in Afghanistan. What two-word phrase did Gorbachev use to describe that war?
answer: A 'bleeding wound'
choices: A 'bleeding wound'
A 'glorious duty'
A 'minor setback'
A 'foreign adventure'
context: Gorbachev called Afghanistan a 'bleeding wound' before the Party Congress, a stunning public admission of failure. Roughly 15,000 Soviet soldiers would die over the decade, which is why the conflict became known as the 'Soviet Vietnam.' Source: https://soviethistory.msu.edu/1985/afghans/afghans-texts/gorbachev-statement-on-afghanistan/

question: Historians point to the Soviet war in Afghanistan as one of the blows that brought down a superpower: a drained treasury, thousands of dead soldiers, and a humiliating defeat. How soon after the last Soviet troops crossed the bridge home did the Soviet Union itself collapse?
answer: Less than three years later, in 1991
choices: Less than three years later, in 1991
Almost twenty years later
Within a few months
Not for another generation
context: The last troops left in February 1989, and the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, fewer than three years later. The cost was staggering on both sides: Afghan civilian dead are estimated from around 850,000 to over a million, with more than five million refugees fleeing into Pakistan and Iran. Source: https://faculty.washington.edu/aseem/afganwar.pdf

question: On April 26, 1937, German and Italian planes firebombed the Basque town of Guernica, and three-quarters of its wooden buildings burned to the ground. Yet beside the spared Basque assembly house, one ancient thing came through the flames untouched -- the very spot where, for centuries, Basque lords had sworn to respect their people's freedoms. What survived the fire there?
answer: An ancient oak tree
choices: An ancient oak tree
A carved stone cross
An old stone well
A bronze church bell
context: The Gernikako Arbola -- the sacred Tree of Gernika -- and the Casa de Juntas (the Basque assembly house) both survived the firestorm. The oak had stood for centuries as the symbol of Basque liberties, the place where lords swore to honor the people's ancient freedoms. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombing_of_Guernica

question: About 40,000 idealistic young foreigners from some 52 countries -- including roughly 2,800 Americans, most of them students who had never fired a rifle -- crossed into Spain to fight Franco's fascists in the International Brigades. The fiery communist orator Dolores Ibarruri, nicknamed 'La Pasionaria,' gave them a battle cry that became the slogan of the whole Republican cause. What was the cry?
answer: 'No pasaran!' (They shall not pass!)
choices: 'No pasaran!' (They shall not pass!)
'Viva la muerte!' (Long live death!)
'Arriba Espana!' (Up with Spain!)
'No rendirse!' (We will not yield!)
context: 'No pasaran!' became the rallying cry of the defenders of Madrid and the International Brigades. The Americans formed the Abraham Lincoln Battalion. 'Viva la muerte!' and 'Arriba Espana!' were in fact Nationalist (Franco's side) cries. Source: alba-valb.org/who-we-are/about/history-the-abraham-lincoln-brigade-and-the-spanish-civil-war/

question: The German officer who planned and directed the bombing of Guernica was Wolfram von Richthofen, who coldly wrote in his diary that the burning of the town had been 'a complete success.' He carried one of the most famous surnames in all of Germany. Which of his relatives had made the name von Richthofen legendary?
answer: His cousin, the WWI ace the Red Baron
choices: His cousin, the WWI ace the Red Baron
His brother, a famous opera singer
His father, a Prussian war minister
His uncle, a noted polar explorer
context: Wolfram von Richthofen was the younger cousin of Manfred von Richthofen, the 'Red Baron,' the top-scoring fighter ace of World War I. Wolfram ran the raid under the code name 'Operation Rugen'; the attackers dropped about 22 tonnes of bombs, including incendiaries that set the town ablaze. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombing_of_Guernica

question: The British writer George Orwell came to Spain a hopeful socialist and joined a left-wing militia called the POUM to fight Franco. But during the Barcelona street fighting of May 1937 he watched something done by his own side that filled him with disgust and helped inspire his later novel '1984.' What did Orwell see happen in the streets of Barcelona?
answer: Communists turning their guns on their own allies
choices: Communists turning their guns on their own allies
Fascist bombers leveling the whole city of Barcelona
Anarchists looting and torching the city's churches
Hungry militiamen deserting the front lines in droves
context: The Soviet-backed Communists fired on their fellow Republicans -- the anarchists and Orwell's own POUM -- then branded them 'Fascist traitors.' The POUM was outlawed, and Orwell and his wife had to flee Spain by train to avoid being jailed by their own side. He wrote it all in 'Homage to Catalonia.' Source: litcharts.com/lit/homage-to-catalonia/summary

question: In June 1937 Andreu Nin, a leader of Orwell's POUM party and once a secretary to Leon Trotsky, was seized in Barcelona, handed to Stalin's secret police the NKVD, and secretly tortured to death. To hide the murder, the Soviets faked an 'escape' and smeared him as a Nazi agent. When people scrawled 'Where is Nin?' on the walls demanding the truth, how did the regime mockingly reply?
answer: 'In Salamanca or in Berlin'
choices: 'In Salamanca or in Berlin'
'Safe in Moscow with his friends'
'At rest in a Barcelona grave'
'Free across the French border'
context: Salamanca was Franco's headquarters and Berlin was Hitler's capital, so the jeer implied Nin had run off to join the fascists -- the very lie the NKVD had planted with forged German documents. His real fate stayed hidden until Moscow's archives briefly opened in the 1990s. The order is linked to NKVD agent Alexander Orlov. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreu_Nin

question: The Spanish Civil War is often called the 'dress rehearsal' for World War II, because Hitler used it to combat-test his newest aircraft and tactics. When his Condor Legion airmen came home, he threw them a giant victory parade in Berlin on June 6, 1939. Barely three months after that parade, Hitler launched the real war his pilots had been rehearsing for. What did he do?
answer: Invaded Poland to the east
choices: Invaded Poland to the east
Invaded Norway to the north
Invaded France to the west
Invaded Greece to the south
context: Germany invaded Poland on September 1, 1939, starting World War II -- less than three months after the Condor Legion's homecoming parade. In Spain, Hitler had combat-tested his Messerschmitt Bf 109 fighter, and pilot Werner Molders had perfected the two-plane 'Rotte' that became the worldwide 'finger-four' formation; about 19,000 German airmen rotated through to gain real combat experience. Source: airandspaceforces.com/article/0213condor/

question: For 250 years a single Spanish galleon, nicknamed 'La Nao de China,' made one round-trip a year across the Pacific between Manila and Acapulco. New World silver sailed west to Manila to buy the cargo that sailed back east. Which Asian good was the prize of that return cargo, worth about ten times more in the Americas than it cost in Manila?
answer: Chinese silk
choices: Chinese silk
Persian carpets
African ivory
Indian pepper
context: A roll of Chinese silk fetched roughly ten times its Manila price once it reached the Americas, which is why silk was by far the most valuable thing aboard the homebound galleon (porcelain, ivory, and spices came too). The whole loop ran on silver-for-silk: as much as a third of all the silver mined in Spanish America flowed to China through Manila. Source: Met Museum essay 'The Manila Galleon Trade'; World History Encyclopedia.

question: Sailing a galleon from Mexico to Manila was easy with the trade winds, but for years nobody could find a way to sail BACK east across the Pacific. In 1565 the Basque friar-navigator Andres de Urdaneta cracked it on the San Pedro. What was his counterintuitive trick for catching a current that would carry the ship home?
answer: Sail far north, almost to the latitude of Japan
choices: Sail far north, almost to the latitude of Japan
Hug the equator straight east the whole way
Sail south below Australia into the cold seas
Wait in port for the winds to simply reverse
context: Urdaneta sailed north from the Philippines nearly to Japan's latitude, caught the Kuroshio Current and the North Pacific westerlies, and rode them east to California and down to Acapulco. That 'tornaviaje' (return voyage) took his first crossing 129 days and opened the route for 250 years. Source: Guampedia 'Andres de Urdaneta'; Wikipedia 'Manila galleon'.

question: Sparta was a tiny warrior elite ruling a vast enslaved majority called helots, who outnumbered them about seven to one and were always one revolt away from overthrowing their masters. To thin out the helots most likely to lead such a revolt, the Spartans once announced that the helots who had fought bravest in war would be set free. About two thousand stepped forward, crowned themselves with garlands, and paraded through the temples celebrating. What did the Spartans then do to these two thousand newly-'freed' men?
answer: They made every one of them vanish, and no one ever learned how each had died
choices: They made every one of them vanish, and no one ever learned how each had died
They shipped every one of them off to colonize a distant island
They drafted every one of them into a special front-line regiment
They taxed every one of them into handing back half their land
context: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 4.80, reports the Spartans promised freedom to the ~2,000 helots judged bravest in war; the chosen men garlanded themselves and toured the temples in celebration, and soon after the Spartans made them all disappear, with 'no one ever knowing how each of them perished.' It was a deliberate trap to eliminate exactly the helots most capable of leading a rebellion. Source: Thucydides 4.80 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crypteia).

question: Every year, when Sparta's ruling magistrates called the ephors took office, their very first official act was a strange declaration aimed at the helots, the enslaved majority who farmed Spartan land. The point of this annual declaration was to make sure that if any Spartan killed a helot, he carried no blood-guilt and brought no religious pollution on himself. What did the incoming ephors formally declare each year?
answer: War on the helots, so that killing one counted as a clean act of the state
choices: War on the helots, so that killing one counted as a clean act of the state
A census of the helots, so that each could be assigned to a master
A tax on the helots, so that each owed half of his harvest
A festival for the helots, so that each could honor the gods of Sparta
context: Aristotle, preserved through Plutarch's Life of Lycurgus 28, recorded that the ephors declared war on the helots upon taking office each year, so that any Spartan could kill a helot without incurring blood-guilt or religious pollution. It turned the routine killing of slaves into a legally and ritually 'clean' act of the state. Source: Aristotle via Plutarch, Lycurgus 28 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crypteia).

question: In ancient Sparta, what happened to a boy on his seventh birthday?
answer: The state took him from his family to be raised as a soldier
choices: The state took him from his family to be raised as a soldier
He was given his father's farm and a team of oxen to work it
He chose a trade and began an apprenticeship in the city
He sailed with the navy to learn seamanship and trade
context: At age 7 Spartan boys were taken from home and enrolled in communal 'herds' (agelai) to be raised in the agoge, the state's military upbringing. They were taught only enough reading and writing 'to serve their turn' -- the rest of the training was to make them obey orders, endure hardship, and win battles. Source: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus 16-17.

question: Spartan boys in the agoge were kept hungry and were expected to steal food to survive -- stealing was a skill the state wanted them to learn. So a boy was only flogged and disgraced for one thing. What was it?
answer: Getting caught in the act
choices: Getting caught in the act
Stealing from another Spartan
Eating more than his share
Sharing his food with a friend
context: Theft itself was not the crime -- being caught was. A boy who was caught was 'soundly flogged, as a careless and unskilful thief.' Underfeeding the boys and forcing them to steal was meant to make them cunning and resourceful. Source: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus 17.

question: As her son marched off to war, a Spartan mother handed him his heavy shield with a grim warning about how she expected to see it again. What did she say?
answer: 'Either this or upon this'
choices: 'Either this or upon this'
'Strike first and strike hard'
'Bring me gold or bring me glory'
'Fight for your brothers in the line'
context: 'Either this or upon this' meant: come home carrying your shield (victorious) or be carried home dead ON it. To drop the shield was to throw it away and run -- the ultimate disgrace. The saying is attributed to Queen Gorgo. Treated as legend. Source: Plutarch, Moralia: Sayings of Spartan Women.

question: Every night Spartan men ate together at a common mess, and the signature dish there -- the famous 'black broth' -- was prized above all. What was this black broth actually made of?
answer: Pork boiled in its own blood, with vinegar and salt
choices: Pork boiled in its own blood, with vinegar and salt
Barley and lentils simmered slowly with wild herbs
Octopus stewed in dark red wine and good olive oil
Goat's milk curdled with mountain honey and figs
context: The black broth (melas zomos) was so prized that the old men gave up their share of meat just to drink it. A visitor from Sybaris who tasted it joked that now he understood why the Spartans did not fear death -- they would sooner die than swallow a second bowl. Source: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus 12; Moralia.

question: A Spartan boy had stolen a young fox and hidden it alive under his cloak. While he stood talking to some men, the trapped fox began to claw and bite at him. According to the famous story, what did the boy do?
answer: Let the fox tear out his insides rather than be caught with it
choices: Let the fox tear out his insides rather than be caught with it
Cried out for help and dropped the fox at the men's feet
Killed the fox through his cloak with a small hidden knife
Let the fox loose and bolted for the river to get away
context: Plutarch's words: the boy 'suffered the animal to tear out his bowels with its teeth and claws, and died rather than have his theft detected.' Told as the ultimate proof of trained Spartan endurance -- treated as legend. Source: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus 18.1.

question: At Thermopylae the Persian king Xerxes sent word to the Spartans under King Leonidas: lay down your weapons. Leonidas sent back a short answer that became one of history's great lines of defiance. What was it?
answer: 'Come and take them'
choices: 'Come and take them'
'We will not kneel'
'Sparta does not yield'
'Death before surrender'
context: In Greek, 'Molon labe.' Leonidas and his small force held the pass against Xerxes' enormous army and died there. The phrase has been a slogan of defiance ever since. Source: Plutarch, Moralia 225D (Sayings of Spartans).

question: Philip II of Macedon sent a threat to Sparta: 'If I invade Laconia, I will raze your city to the ground.' Famous for never wasting words, the Spartans wrote back a reply just one word long. What was the word?
answer: 'If'
choices: 'If'
'Never'
'Try'
'When'
context: Their whole reply was the single word 'If.' This terse style is why we still call a few cutting words 'laconic' -- from Laconia, Sparta's region. Treated as legend. Source: Plutarch, Moralia (Sayings of Spartans); Wikiquote 'Laconic phrases.'

question: Sparta was ruled by a small warrior class who were vastly outnumbered -- by roughly seven to one -- by their own slaves, the helots. Where had this huge enslaved population come from?
answer: A whole neighbouring people Sparta had conquered and enslaved on its own land
choices: A whole neighbouring people Sparta had conquered and enslaved on its own land
Captives shipped in and sold by Phoenician slave-traders from over the sea
Prisoners of war taken in raids on many different Greek cities
Poor men who had sold themselves into bondage to pay off their debts
context: The helots were chiefly the Messenians, conquered by Sparta in the 8th-7th century BC and held in collective serfdom on their own land. They kept their own families, gods and Messenian identity -- which is exactly why Sparta lived in permanent dread of revolt and built a terror-state to control them. Source: Helots (Wikipedia); Paul Cartledge.

question: According to the Spartan tradition, a newborn baby was carried before the tribal elders to be inspected. A strong, sturdy child was allowed to live. What does the tradition say was done with a baby judged sickly or deformed?
answer: It was left to die in a chasm at the foot of Mount Taygetus
choices: It was left to die in a chasm at the foot of Mount Taygetus
It was given to a helot family to be raised as a servant
It was sent away by ship to be raised in another city
It was kept at home but barred from ever becoming a soldier
context: The place was called the Apothetae. Plutarch reports this, but no infant remains have ever been found there, and many scholars treat the detail as part of the semi-legendary tradition around Sparta's lawgiver, Lycurgus -- so it is told here as legend, not proven fact. Source: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus 16; Bad Ancient.

question: Living in dread of a slave revolt, Spartan officials ran a brutal secret operation called the krypteia: they armed picked young men with daggers and sent them out into the countryside by night. What were these young men sent to do?
answer: Murder any helots they came across, especially the strongest ones
choices: Murder any helots they came across, especially the strongest ones
Spy on neighbouring cities and report back on their armies
Guard the mountain passes against foreign invaders
Hunt wild game to stock the soldiers' common mess
context: Plutarch: 'in the night they came down into the highways and killed every Helot whom they caught,' and by day they killed the strongest helots in the fields. It was a state-run program of terror against the enslaved Messenian population. Source: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus 28; Crypteia (Wikipedia).

question: Spartan women had freedoms no other Greek women had: alone in Greece they could own and inherit land, were trained as athletes in the open air, and spoke their minds in public. Asked why Spartan women were the only ones who 'ruled' their men, Queen Gorgo answered with one cutting line. What did she say?
answer: 'Because we are the only women who give birth to real men'
choices: 'Because we are the only women who give birth to real men'
'Because we alone are taught to read and to reason'
'Because our husbands fear the gods we serve'
'Because we hold the keys to every house in Sparta'
context: Gorgo's full reply: 'Because we are the only women who are mothers of [real] men.' Spartan girls were schooled and trained athletically to bear strong children, and Spartan women were the freest in all of Greece. Source: Plutarch, Moralia: Sayings of Spartan Women; World History Encyclopedia.

question: The Spartans announced that the helots who had fought most bravely for them in war would be rewarded with their freedom, and about 2,000 of them put on garlands and went round the temples celebrating as free men. The historian Thucydides records what happened next. What became of those 2,000?
answer: They all secretly vanished, and no one ever knew how each died
choices: They all secretly vanished, and no one ever knew how each died
They were settled together in a new town of their own
They were drafted as full soldiers into the Spartan army
They were sold overseas to buyers in distant cities
context: Thucydides: 'a little afterwards all disappeared, more than two thousand of them, and no man knew how each of them perished.' Sparta had singled out the bravest helots precisely because they were the most dangerous, then murdered them. Source: Thucydides 4.80.

question: For generations Sparta's army was thought unbeatable in open battle. In 371 BC the Theban general Epaminondas crushed it at Leuctra, then marched into Messenia and did one thing that broke Sparta's power for good. What did he do?
answer: Freed the helots, destroying the slave labour Sparta depended on
choices: Freed the helots, destroying the slave labour Sparta depended on
Burned the undefended city of Sparta itself to the ground
Captured both of Sparta's two kings and held them for ransom
Cut off Sparta's grain supply and starved the city into surrender
context: After Leuctra (371 BC), Epaminondas marched into Messenia (369 BC) and freed the helots after centuries of bondage, founding the fortified city of Messene at Mount Ithome. With its enslaved workforce gone, Sparta's whole warrior system collapsed and it never recovered as a great power. Source: World History Encyclopedia; Britannica.

question: In 73 BC about 70 gladiators were training at Lentulus Batiatus's fighting school in Capua when they decided to break out. The real swords were locked away, so before fighting past their guards the men raided one room of the school and grabbed whatever they could swing. Which room did they raid, and what did they arm themselves with?
answer: The kitchen — cooking knives and roasting spits
choices: The kitchen — cooking knives and roasting spits
The chapel — bronze idols and altar candlesticks
The stable — horse whips and iron bridle bits
The armory — wooden practice swords and shields
context: Plutarch says the gladiators seized cleavers and spits from the kitchen, fought their way out, and on the road captured a wagon of real gladiator weapons. They chose Spartacus as their leader. (Plutarch, Life of Crassus 8; worldhistory.org/article/871)

question: After three years of war, Marcus Licinius Crassus finally crushed Spartacus's slave army in 71 BC and captured 6,000 of the survivors alive. Crassus wanted every slave in Italy to see what rebellion cost. What did he do with the 6,000 prisoners?
answer: Crucified them along the Appian Way, the whole road from Capua to Rome
choices: Crucified them along the Appian Way, the whole road from Capua to Rome
Sold them at auction in the great slave market on the island of Delos
Branded their foreheads and sent them back to their old masters
Shipped them to die in the silver mines of Spain
context: Crassus left the 6,000 crosses standing along the road as a warning to any slave who might think of rebelling. Roman slavery and crucifixion were institutions, stated here as fact. (Appian, Civil Wars 1.120; worldhistory.org/article/871)

question: Early in the revolt the Roman commander Gaius Claudius Glaber trapped Spartacus's men on the slopes of Mount Vesuvius, blocking the one path down so he could starve them out. He thought the rest of the mountain was a sheer, impossible cliff. Spartacus's men used the one plant growing all over those slopes to get down it. How did they escape?
answer: They wove ladders from wild grapevines and climbed down the cliff
choices: They wove ladders from wild grapevines and climbed down the cliff
They dug a tunnel through the soft volcanic rock by night
They built rafts and floated down a swollen mountain stream
They disguised themselves in dead Romans' armor and walked out
context: Having climbed down the 'impossible' cliff, they circled behind Glaber's camp and wiped out his force in a surprise attack. Vesuvius's slopes were covered in wild vines. (Plutarch, Life of Crassus 9; Third Servile War)

question: Just before his final battle against Crassus, Spartacus had his warhorse brought to him in front of his men. Instead of mounting it, he drew his sword and killed the horse on the spot. By his own account, why did he do it?
answer: If he won he would take fine horses from the enemy, and if he lost he would have no need of one
choices: If he won he would take fine horses from the enemy, and if he lost he would have no need of one
To feed his starving men one last meal before the fighting began
To honor an old Thracian custom of sacrificing a horse before battle
To prove to his men that there would be no retreat and no escape
context: Plutarch records his words. In the battle Spartacus charged straight for Crassus himself, cut down two centurions who attacked him together, and was finally surrounded and killed; his body was never found. (Plutarch, Life of Crassus 11)

question: Roman generals staged gladiator games where captured enemies and slaves were forced to die for a Roman crowd. When Spartacus's lieutenant Crixus was killed in battle, Spartacus held funeral games for him and turned that whole spectacle upside down. What did he make about 300 captured Roman prisoners do at the funeral?
answer: Fight each other to the death as gladiators, while slaves watched
choices: Fight each other to the death as gladiators, while slaves watched
Dig the mass grave and then march away unarmed and free
Kneel and swear an oath of loyalty to the slave army
Carry Crixus's body in procession and sing Roman funeral songs
context: Spartacus forced Roman captives to die in the arena for slave spectators — the Roman spectacle reversed, Romans now dying for the entertainment of slaves. Crixus had been killed by the consul Gellius near Mount Garganus. (Appian, Civil Wars 1.117)

question: In 629 CE the monk Xuanzang slipped out of the Tang capital Chang'an in secret, breaking Emperor Taizong's ban on travel to the west. What was Xuanzang setting out alone to do?
answer: Bring the original Buddhist sutras back from India
choices: Bring the original Buddhist sutras back from India
Map a new trade road for the emperor's merchants
Carry a peace treaty to a rival western king
Find a legendary spring that cured any sickness
context: Xuanzang defied Taizong's imperial travel ban (issued for border security) and set off alone for India to recover the original Buddhist scriptures. Source: https://iep.utm.edu/xuanzang/

question: Centuries later, Xuanzang's real 16-year pilgrimage to India was rewritten into one of China's most beloved fantasy novels, where the monk travels guarded by magical companions. In that novel, who is the monk's most famous bodyguard?
answer: The Monkey King, Sun Wukong
choices: The Monkey King, Sun Wukong
The dragon-emperor of the eastern sea
The white tiger of the western mountains
The thunder-god who forges his staff
context: The Ming novel 'Journey to the West' turned the historical Xuanzang into 'Tripitaka,' guarded by the Monkey King Sun Wukong, a pig-demon, and a sand-spirit. Legendary retelling, not history. Source: https://iep.utm.edu/xuanzang/

question: Alone in the 800-li Gashun Gobi, Xuanzang spilled his water bag and the water vanished into the sand. He then went four days and five nights with no water at all, surrounded by camel dung and bones, until something saved him. What carried the half-dead monk to water?
answer: His horse, which bolted on its own to a spring
choices: His horse, which bolted on its own to a spring
A sudden rainstorm that filled the dry hollows
A cool night wind that uncovered a buried stream
Circling vultures whose path led him to a pool
context: After four days and five nights without water, with no birds or animals around him, Xuanzang's horse bolted on its own and carried the half-dead monk to a spring. Source: https://en.minghui.org/html/articles/2019/7/13/178423.html

question: Dying of thirst in the Gobi and tempted to turn back to safety in China, Xuanzang made a vow he kept repeating to himself. What did he swear?
answer: He would not go east even one step without the true scriptures
choices: He would not go east even one step without the true scriptures
He would press south to the warmer passes before the snows came
He would reach the western kingdoms or die in the sand
He would never set foot toward home until he saw the sea
context: His vow: 'I will not go back toward the east even one step without obtaining the true Buddhist scriptures.' He would rather die pushing west than live by turning back. Source: https://en.minghui.org/html/articles/2019/7/13/178423.html

question: King Qu Wentai of Gaochang loved Xuanzang so much he tried to keep the monk at his court forever as head monk. Xuanzang refused to stay — how did he force the king to let him go?
answer: He refused all food in a hunger strike until the king relented
choices: He refused all food in a hunger strike until the king relented
He fled at night over the city wall on a stolen horse
He threatened to burn the sutras he already carried
He sat in silent meditation and would not speak for days
context: Xuanzang refused all food until King Qu Wentai gave in; the two then swore an oath of brotherhood, and Xuanzang promised to return and teach there for three years. Source: https://iep.utm.edu/xuanzang/ ; https://factsanddetails.com/china/cat2/4sub8/entry-5450.html

question: Crossing the ice of the Tian Shan over the high Bedel Pass took Xuanzang's party about eight days. How heavy was the toll the frozen pass took on his men?
answer: Three or four of every ten froze to death
choices: Three or four of every ten froze to death
One in twenty was lost in a single avalanche
Half the party turned back before the summit
Every man survived but all the horses died
context: Crossing the Bedel Pass (about 4,284 m) over roughly eight days, Xuanzang lost 30 to 40 percent of his men to the cold, along with countless horses and oxen. Source: https://nembutsu.cc/2024/06/25/the-journeys-of-xuanzang-part-two-onward-and-upward/

question: In 630 Xuanzang passed through Bamiyan and wrote down what he saw carved into its cliffs — giant standing Buddhas towering over a valley of monasteries. Why is his written record of those Bamiyan statues so precious to historians today?
answer: It is the earliest written record of statues the Taliban later destroyed
choices: It is the earliest written record of statues the Taliban later destroyed
It contains the only surviving map of the lost city
It proves the statues were once painted in gold
It names the sculptor who carved them into the cliff
context: Xuanzang reached Bamiyan on 30 April 630 and recorded its giant cliff Buddhas and over a thousand monks — the earliest textual evidence for the statues the Taliban dynamited in 2001. Source: https://en.bharatpedia.org/wiki/Great_Tang_Records_on_the_Western_Regions

question: At an 18-day grand religious assembly that King Harsha convened at Kanauj in 643, Xuanzang stood up to debate the assembled scholars of every rival faith. What did the foreign monk reportedly accomplish there?
answer: He out-argued 500 Brahmins, Jains, and rival Buddhists
choices: He out-argued 500 Brahmins, Jains, and rival Buddhists
He converted the king himself to his school
He recited every sutra he had collected from memory
He settled a war between two Indian kingdoms
context: At King Harsha's 18-day assembly at Kanauj in early 643, Xuanzang reportedly out-argued 500 Brahmins, Jains, and rival Buddhists in open debate. Source: https://iep.utm.edu/xuanzang/

question: After 16 years and roughly 10,000 miles, Xuanzang returned to Chang'an in 645 — and the very emperor who had banned his trip welcomed him as a hero. To house the treasure of sutras he hauled home, what was built in Chang'an in 652?
answer: The 64-meter Big Wild Goose Pagoda
choices: The 64-meter Big Wild Goose Pagoda
A walled translation college beside the palace
A new western gate named for the pilgrim
A royal tomb shaped like a desert dune
context: Xuanzang returned with 657 Sanskrit texts in 520 cases loaded onto twenty-two horses; the 64-meter Big Wild Goose Pagoda was built in 652 to house them, and he spent the rest of his life (he died in 664) translating them into Chinese. Source: https://www.visitourchina.com/xian/attraction/big-wild-goose-pagoda.html ; https://iep.utm.edu/xuanzang/

question: Francis of Assisi, the son of a rich cloth merchant, staged the very first live nativity scene at Greccio in 1223 to let ordinary people picture the birth of Jesus. What did he set up in the manger so people could see it for real?
answer: A real ox and a real donkey beside a straw-filled manger
choices: A real ox and a real donkey beside a straw-filled manger
A painted wooden altar lit by candles
A choir of robed boys singing carols
A golden statue carried through the town
context: Francis filled a manger with straw and set it between a live ox and a live donkey at Greccio in 1223 so villagers could vividly contemplate the birth of Christ. This is the origin of the Christmas crib (presepio / creche) tradition. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_of_Assisi

question: Around 1206 Francis of Assisi was dragged before the Bishop of Assisi by his furious father, a wealthy merchant demanding his money back. In the public square Francis stripped off all his fine clothes, handed them to his father, and gave up his inheritance with a single declaration. What did he say?
answer: From now on he would say only 'Our Father who art in heaven'
choices: From now on he would say only 'Our Father who art in heaven'
He would repay every coin within a single year
He would leave Assisi and never return
He would build a great church with his own hands
context: Naked in the square, Francis declared he would no longer call Pietro di Bernardone 'my father' but say only 'Our Father who art in heaven.' The bishop covered the young man with his own cloak. Underneath his merchant's robes Francis had been wearing a rough penitential hairshirt. Source: https://www.vaticanstate.va/en/state-and-government/general-informations/saint-of-the-day/778-4-october-saint-francis-of-assisi-patron-saint-of-italy.html

question: Donato Bramante was hired to build the new St. Peter's, but first he tore down the 1,200-year-old church that had stood on the spot since the days of the Emperor Constantine — pulling down the nave so fast that Mass was still being said in the ruins. The Romans gave him a mocking nickname for all this knocking-about. What did they call him?
answer: Master Wrecker
choices: Master Wrecker
The Stone Thief
The Church Breaker
The Roman Hammer
