context: In Italian the nickname was 'Maestro Ruinante' — a pun on Bramante, twisting his name into 'Master Wrecker.' He demolished Old St. Peter's, built by Constantine, so eagerly the joke stuck. Source: worldhistory.org/Donato_Bramante + theartstory.org.

question: In 1547 the 71-year-old Michelangelo was put in charge of finishing St. Peter's Basilica, the largest building project in Christendom. He took the job on one remarkable condition, and kept to it until he died at 88 with the work still unfinished. What was that condition?
answer: He would accept no payment
choices: He would accept no payment
He would carve his own tomb there
He would answer to no pope
He would never sign the plans
context: Michelangelo refused all pay, saying he took the work on 'only for the love of God and in honour of the Apostle.' He lived to see the great drum of his dome rise, but not the dome itself. Source: basilicasanpietro.va/the-dome + thehistoryofart.org.

question: In 1586 Pope Sixtus V had a 350-ton Egyptian obelisk hauled upright in St. Peter's Square using 900 men, 140 horses, and 44 winches. He ordered total silence on pain of death so the crew could hear the commands. As the great ropes began to smoke and stretch under the strain, a sailor named Benedetto Bresca broke the silence with a shout that saved the lift. What did he shout?
answer: "Water to the ropes!"
choices: "Water to the ropes!"
"Pull for the Pope!"
"Stand clear, men!"
"Cut it loose!"
context: The story says Bresca shouted 'Acqua alle funi!' — wetting the smoking ropes tightened them and saved the obelisk. As a reward Sixtus V is said to have granted Bresca's town of Bordighera the lasting right to supply the Vatican's Palm Sunday palms. Told as a beloved legend. Source: joansrome.wordpress.com + turismoroma.it.

question: Around the inside base of Michelangelo's enormous dome, in gold mosaic letters taller than a man, runs a line of Latin from Matthew's Gospel: the words Jesus speaks to the apostle Peter. The whole sentence turns on a pun, because in Greek the name 'Peter' is also a plain, everyday word. What does the name 'Peter' mean?
answer: Rock
choices: Rock
Shepherd
Fisherman
Servant
context: The inscription reads 'TU ES PETRUS ET SUPER HANC PETRAM AEDIFICABO ECCLESIAM MEAM' — 'Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church.' Peter (petra) means rock, so Jesus is punning on his name. Catholics read this as the source of the popes' authority. Source: stpetersbasilica.info + walksinrome.com.

question: Gianlorenzo Bernini ringed St. Peter's Square with a sweeping oval colonnade four rows deep — 248 columns carrying 140 over-life-size statues of saints along the top. He explained the unusual curving shape with one famous image: the colonnade, he said, was the Church itself doing something to everyone who stepped into the square. In Bernini's own words, what was the colonnade?
answer: The arms of the Church, embracing all who enter
choices: The arms of the Church, embracing all who enter
The crown of the Church, raised over Rome
The shield of the Church, guarding the faithful
The gateway of the Church, opened to the world
context: Bernini said the colonnade was the 'maternal arms of Mother Church,' reaching out to gather in the faithful, the heretics, and the unbelievers alike. Built 1656-1667 under Pope Alexander VII. Source: en.wikipedia.org/St._Peter's_Square + roma-nonpertutti.com.

question: To help pay the staggering cost of the new St. Peter's, Pope Leo X let the friar Johann Tetzel travel through Germany selling indulgences -- certificates claimed to shorten a dead soul's time in purgatory. Tetzel was a showman, and his pitch was a short rhyming couplet that promised a grieving family their loved one could be sprung loose the very instant they paid. The catchy line stuck in people's heads and outraged a monk named Martin Luther. Which couplet did Tetzel chant to hawk the certificates?
answer: As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs
choices: As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs
Drop your silver, speak the prayer, and your dead shall leave despair
Buy the parchment, pay the friar, and your kin escapes the fire
Give your gold to ease their woe, and to heaven their soul shall go
context: The couplet long attributed to Tetzel renders as 'As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs' (German: 'Sobald das Geld im Kasten klingt, die Seele aus dem Fegefeuer springt'). Luther attacked the idea in his 1517 theses; some scholars doubt Tetzel personally coined the line. Source: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Johann_Tetzel

question: In 1765 Britain made the American colonists pay a new tax just to use paper — and it reached into everyday life in a way that surprised people. Besides legal documents, newspapers, and wills, what two playthings also had to carry the tax stamp?
answer: Playing cards and dice
choices: Playing cards and dice
Marbles and spinning tops
Toy soldiers and kites
Hoops and wooden horses
context: The Stamp Act of 1765 taxed paper itself — every legal document, newspaper, pamphlet, will, marriage license, diploma, and almanac needed a stamp, and even playing cards and dice were taxed. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Stamp_Act/ and https://www.ushistory.org/us/9b.asp

question: On August 14, 1765, a Boston crowd hung a straw effigy of stamp distributor Andrew Oliver from a great elm tree, then beheaded and burned it and tore down his office. That elm earned a famous name that the colonists used for the rest of the Revolution. What did they call it?
answer: The Liberty Tree
choices: The Liberty Tree
The Charter Oak
The Treason Elm
The Gallows Tree
context: The crowd marked the effigy 'A.O.' for Andrew Oliver; the great elm became the Liberty Tree, and Oliver resigned his post three days later. Source: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/biographies/andrew-oliver and https://www.masshist.org/beehiveblog/2024/08/the-259th-anniversary-of-bostons-liberty-tree/

question: Patrick Henry, a brand-new 29-year-old Virginia legislator, raged against the Stamp Act so fiercely that a 22-year-old law student stood in the doorway listening — and decades later still remembered hearing 'torrents of sublime eloquence from Mr. Henry.' Who was that young student in the doorway?
answer: Thomas Jefferson
choices: Thomas Jefferson
George Washington
John Adams
James Madison
context: Jefferson, then a 22-year-old law student, witnessed Henry forcing his Virginia Resolves through the House of Burgesses and never forgot the speech. Source: https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Jefferson/03-07-02-0369-0002 and https://tenthamendmentcenter.com/2024/05/28/patrick-henrys-virginia-resolves-bedrock-principles-of-american-liberty/

question: When Patrick Henry attacked the Stamp Act in the Virginia House of Burgesses, the Speaker leapt up and cried 'Treason!' — and legend says Henry shot back without flinching. According to the famous story, how did Henry finish his thought?
answer: 'If this be treason, make the most of it.'
choices: 'If this be treason, make the most of it.'
'Give me liberty, or give me death.'
'I know not what course others may take.'
'We must all hang together, or hang separately.'
context: Henry had warned that George III might meet the fate of Caesar; when the Speaker cried treason, Henry reportedly finished with this defiant line. It is preserved as legend — a retold story, not a verbatim transcript. Source: https://encyclopediavirginia.org/1658hpr-9260362296ba000/ and https://cardinalnews.org/2024/02/13/dispatch-from-1765-stamp-act-protest-prompts-house-speaker-to-accuse-new-legislator-patrick-henry-of-treason/

question: What lit the 'Treason!' cry against Patrick Henry was the chilling pair he named just before George III. He warned that 'Caesar had his Brutus, Charles the First his Cromwell, and George the Third...' — pointedly listing two rulers who had been killed or executed. Which two doomed rulers did Henry invoke as a warning to the King?
answer: Caesar and Charles the First
choices: Caesar and Charles the First
Caesar and Nero
Charles the First and Richard the Third
Henry the Eighth and Charles the First
context: By naming Caesar (assassinated by Brutus) and Charles the First (executed under Cromwell), Henry was implicitly threatening that George III could meet the same fate. The Speaker's cry of 'Treason!' came mid-sentence. Source: https://cardinalnews.org/2024/02/13/dispatch-from-1765-stamp-act-protest-prompts-house-speaker-to-accuse-new-legislator-patrick-henry-of-treason/  (Legend.)

question: The colonists who organized resistance to the Stamp Act took their name straight from an insult-turned-compliment in Parliament. When Charles Townshend called the colonists 'children planted by our care,' Isaac Barre fired back that they were no such thing. What did Barre call them instead — the name they proudly adopted?
answer: Sons of Liberty
choices: Sons of Liberty
Friends of America
Patriots of the Crown
Defenders of the Charter
context: Isaac Barre's retort in Parliament gave the resistance its name; chapters of the Sons of Liberty sprang up across the colonies to enforce the boycotts and intimidate the stamp distributors. Source: http://www.stamp-act-history.com/sons-of-liberty/ and https://www.britannica.com/event/Stamp-Act-Great-Britain-1765

question: On the night of August 26, 1765, a Boston mob stormed the mansion of Lt. Governor Thomas Hutchinson and tore it apart room by room. Beyond the furniture and the 900 pounds in cash and silver they carried off, they destroyed something Hutchinson could never replace — 30 years of his collected manuscripts. What irreplaceable work-in-progress was lost in that wreckage?
answer: His notes for a history of Massachusetts
choices: His notes for a history of Massachusetts
His maps of the colonial coastline
His letters to the King of England
His ledgers of the colony's accounts
context: The mob cut down the cupola, beat down walls, stripped slate from the roof, slit the beds open to scatter the feathers, and destroyed three decades of Hutchinson's manuscripts, including the notes for his history of Massachusetts. Source: https://newenglandhistoricalsociety.com/1765-rebels-sack-boston-mansion-thomas-hutchinson/

question: The Stamp Act gave its own stamps a terrifying power over colonial life: any document written on un-stamped paper was treated as legally worthless. Rather than buy the hated stamps, colonial courts and ports across America responded with a drastic, defiant act. What did they do?
answer: They shut their doors and stopped operating
choices: They shut their doors and stopped operating
They printed their own counterfeit stamps
They paid the tax under loud protest
They petitioned the King for an exemption
context: A deed, will, or contract on un-stamped paper would not stand in any court — so courts and ports closed rather than legitimize the stamps, freezing legal and commercial life. Source: https://www.ushistory.org/us/9b.asp and https://legalclarity.org/november-1765-the-stamp-act-crisis-and-colonial-resistance/

question: In October 1765, delegates from nine colonies gathered at Federal Hall in New York for what became known as the Stamp Act Congress — a milestone moment in American history. What made this meeting so significant?
answer: It was the first time the colonies acted together
choices: It was the first time the colonies acted together
It was the first colonial army ever raised
It was the first time the colonies declared independence
It was the first colonial currency ever printed
context: The Stamp Act Congress issued a Declaration of Rights and Grievances asserting the colonists could be taxed only with the consent of their own elected representatives — the first time the separate colonies acted in concert. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Stamp-Act-Congress and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stamp_Act_Congress

question: When colonists protested the Stamp Act, their core complaint was not that the tax was too high. They argued from an 'essential principle of the English constitution' — a right of Englishmen they said only their own colonial assemblies could honor. What was the principle they insisted Parliament had violated?
answer: No subject can be taxed without his own consent
choices: No subject can be taxed without his own consent
No subject can be jailed without a trial
No subject can be forced to quarter soldiers
No subject can be denied a seat in Parliament
context: The grievance was constitutional, not about the rate: a subject could not be taxed without his consent, and the colonists held that only their elected assemblies — not a distant Parliament — could grant that consent. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Considerations_on_the_Propriety_of_Imposing_Taxes_in_the_British_Colonies and https://alphahistory.com/americanrevolution/daniel-dulany-british-taxation-1765/

question: Parliament defended taxing America with a doctrine called 'virtual representation' — the claim that every member of Parliament somehow spoke for all British subjects everywhere, even colonists who voted for no one. Marylander Daniel Dulany demolished this in an influential 1765 pamphlet. What was the crux of his argument against it?
answer: No English voter would ever feel a tax laid on America
choices: No English voter would ever feel a tax laid on America
Colonists already paid more tax than Englishmen did
Parliament had never claimed such a power before
The colonies were too distant for laws to reach them
context: Dulany argued that since not a single voter in England would ever be affected by a tax on America, Parliament could not truly 'represent' the colonists' interests when taxing them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Considerations_on_the_Propriety_of_Imposing_Taxes_in_the_British_Colonies and https://alphahistory.com/americanrevolution/daniel-dulany-british-taxation-1765/

question: The Stamp Act collapsed before it could really work. By the day it took effect, November 1, 1765, every appointed stamp distributor in the colonies had been intimidated into resigning or fleeing — but what truly forced Parliament's hand was economic, not violent. What pressure finally drove Parliament to repeal the tax?
answer: Colonial merchants boycotted British goods until London merchants begged for repeal
choices: Colonial merchants boycotted British goods until London merchants begged for repeal
Colonial militias threatened to seize British ships in the harbors
The colonies refused to send any food to the British army
Colonial assemblies voted to stop paying the King's salary
context: The non-importation boycott bankrupted some London merchants, who then petitioned Parliament for repeal — money, not muskets, killed the Stamp Act. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/Stamp-Act-Great-Britain-1765 and https://constitutioncenter.org/blog/on-this-day-the-stamp-act-plants-seeds-of-the-revolution

question: On March 18, 1766, Parliament finally repealed the hated Stamp Act — but on that very same day it passed a second law that made the victory hollow. This new act declared Parliament's full power to make laws binding the colonies 'in all cases whatsoever,' setting up the next fight. What was this same-day law called?
answer: The Declaratory Act
choices: The Declaratory Act
The Townshend Act
The Quartering Act
The Sugar Act
context: The Declaratory Act asserted Parliament's authority over the colonies 'in all cases whatsoever' on the same day the Stamp Act was repealed — repeal with one hand, a fresh claim of power with the other. Source: https://www.americanhistorycentral.com/documents/stamp-act-repeal-1766-text/ and https://constitutioncenter.org/blog/on-this-day-the-stamp-act-plants-seeds-of-the-revolution

question: On the night of September 14, 1814, the lawyer Francis Scott Key was stuck on a ship in Baltimore harbor, watching British warships pound Fort McHenry with shells and rockets for hours. When the smoke cleared at dawn, one sight hit Key so hard he scribbled the poem that became 'The Star-Spangled Banner.' What did he see by the dawn's early light?
answer: The enormous American flag still flying over the fort
choices: The enormous American flag still flying over the fort
The British fleet sailing away in defeat
The fort's stone walls cracked and smoking
A line of American soldiers marching out
context: That single image -- the huge garrison flag still there after a night of bombardment -- is the moment that inspired the national anthem. A smaller storm flag had flown through the rainy night; the giant flag Key saw was likely raised that morning. Source: https://www.nps.gov/fomc/learn/historyculture/the-star-spangled-banner.htm ; https://www.battlefields.org/learn/war-1812/battles/fort-mchenry

question: The flag Francis Scott Key saw over Fort McHenry was a monster: a garrison banner 30 by 42 feet, with 15 stars and 15 stripes, reportedly the largest flag flown in combat at that time. Major George Armistead had ordered such a giant flag back in 1813 for one blunt reason. What did he say he wanted?
answer: A flag the British would have no trouble seeing from a distance
choices: A flag the British would have no trouble seeing from a distance
A flag every soldier in the fort could salute at once
A flag that could be seen from the city of Baltimore
A flag big enough to wrap a fallen man for burial
context: On that flag, each star and each stripe measured a full two feet across. Armistead, the fort's commander, wanted no doubt about whose fort it was. Source: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/star-spangled-garrison-banner

question: The giant Fort McHenry flag was so big that the woman hired to sew it -- Mary Pickersgill, a 37-year-old widow and professional flagmaker -- couldn't lay it out in her own house. Working about seven weeks with her young daughter, two nieces, and a teenage servant named Grace Wisher, where did Pickersgill finally spread the flag out to finish stitching it?
answer: On the floor of a nearby brewery
choices: On the floor of a nearby brewery
On the deck of a docked ship
Across the lawn of the fort itself
In the loft of a church meeting hall
context: The women spread the flag at night on the floor of Claggett's brewery to assemble it. Pickersgill was paid $405.90 for the work -- more than most Baltimoreans earned in a whole year. Source: https://amhistory.si.edu/starspangledbanner/making-the-flag.aspx

question: Francis Scott Key was only out on the water that September night because of a rescue. He had sailed to the British fleet under a flag of truce to free Dr. William Beanes, a captured American civilian doctor. The British agreed to release Beanes -- but they refused to let Key and his companions go just yet. Why did the British hold all three men until the bombardment was over?
answer: The men had seen the fleet's strength before the attack on Baltimore
choices: The men had seen the fleet's strength before the attack on Baltimore
The men had not yet signed the formal release papers
The men were suspected of carrying secret messages
The men owed a ransom that had not been fully paid
context: Because Key and prisoner-agent John Skinner had been aboard the British flagship Tonnant as the fleet prepared to strike Baltimore, the British wouldn't let them leave until it was done -- forcing Key to watch the entire bombardment from behind enemy lines. Source: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/biographies/francis-scott-key

question: Today an "epicure" means a rich gourmet who chases fancy food and wine. But the philosopher the word is named after, Epicurus of Athens, taught almost the opposite: he warned that overindulgence just leads to pain. What did Epicurus say true pleasure actually was?
answer: A calm mind, plain bread and water, and the company of friends
choices: A calm mind, plain bread and water, and the company of friends
A table of roasted meats, honeyed wine, and rare imported spices
A grand house, fine robes, and a name everyone in Athens knew
Endless gold, so a man would never again have to want for anything
context: Epicurus prized philosophical conversation with friends over feasts; he taught that the untroubled mind he called ataraxia, not luxury, was the goal. The modern word 'epicure' completely flips his meaning. Source: IEP Epicurus https://iep.utm.edu/epicur/ ; Stanford SEP https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/epicurus/

question: Around 300 BC the philosopher Zeno of Citium taught in the Athenian marketplace, gathering students under a long covered walkway in the agora that was painted with murals of famous battles. His followers ended up named after that very spot rather than after Zeno. What was the place his school was named for?
answer: The Painted Porch, a colonnade lined with battle murals
choices: The Painted Porch, a colonnade lined with battle murals
The Marble Temple, where the city kept its sacred treasure
The High Tower, which looked out over the whole harbor
The Long Bridge, which carried the road into the city
context: The walkway was the Stoa Poikile, Greek for 'Painted Porch.' Zeno's followers were first called Zenonians, then 'the people of the Stoa' the Stoics. The everyday word 'stoic,' meaning someone who endures pain or bad news calmly, is literally named after a porch, and it has kept that meaning for over 2,000 years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoa_Poikile ; IEP Stoicism https://iep.utm.edu/stoicism/

question: On the night of March 9-10, 1945, 279 American B-29 Superfortresses firebombed Tokyo in Operation Meetinghouse, dropping over 1,665 tons of napalm and killing roughly 100,000 people in a single night. How did this raid compare with the atomic bombs America would drop on Japan months later?
answer: It killed more people in one night than either atomic bomb did
choices: It killed more people in one night than either atomic bomb did
It killed about the same number as a single atomic bomb
It killed roughly a tenth as many as one atomic bomb
It killed fewer people than any other raid of the war
context: Operation Meetinghouse remains the single most destructive air raid in history -- deadlier than the bombing of either Hiroshima or Nagasaki. The U.S. Strategic Bombing Survey officially counted 87,793 killed and 40,918 injured. The raid razed 16 square miles and left over a million people homeless. Source: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/hellfire-earth-operation-meetinghouse

question: General Curtis LeMay, nicknamed 'Iron Ass,' planned the Tokyo firebombing by gambling that Japan had no effective low-altitude anti-aircraft defense. To bet on that hunch, what did he order done to his B-29 bombers before sending them in at night?
answer: He stripped off their guns and armor so they could fly low and slow
choices: He stripped off their guns and armor so they could fly low and slow
He doubled their armor and gun crews to survive the run
He fitted them with extra fuel tanks to bomb from far higher up
He sent them in daylight in a tight defensive formation
context: LeMay sent the bombers in at just 5,000 to 9,000 feet instead of the usual 32,000. Lighter and lower, each plane could blanket Tokyo's dry wooden houses with napalm. Pathfinders first burned an X across the target to aim the fleet, and 65-mph firestorm winds did the rest -- the city had only 8,000 firemen and 'exactly three' firefighting extension ladders. Source: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/hellfire-earth-operation-meetinghouse

question: After the Allies firebombed Dresden in February 1945, the death toll became fiercely contested: Nazi minister Joseph Goebbels claimed 250,000 dead, and writer David Irving later pushed figures of 150,000 to 200,000. After six years of forensic and archival work, what did a German historians' commission set up by the city conclude in 2010?
answer: That about 25,000 people had died
choices: That about 25,000 people had died
That about 100,000 people had died
That Goebbels's figure of 250,000 was accurate
That the true toll could never be estimated
context: The 2010 commission's forensic count came in roughly ten times lower than Goebbels's wartime propaganda figure. Historian Donald Miller noted that most Dresden victims did not burn -- about 70 percent suffocated on carbon monoxide as the firestorm sucked the oxygen out of the cellars where they hid. American POW Kurt Vonnegut survived in an underground meat locker -- 'Slaughterhouse-Five' -- and later turned the raid into his famous anti-war novel. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/bombing-of-Dresden

question: On 29 May 1913 in Paris, Igor Stravinsky's ballet The Rite of Spring opened with pounding, jarring rhythms and dancers stamping pigeon-toed instead of leaping gracefully. As the music hammered on, what did the audience itself end up doing?
answer: Breaking into a brawl, fighting each other in the seats
choices: Breaking into a brawl, fighting each other in the seats
Walking out quietly in a long, silent stream
Demanding their ticket money back at the box office
Falling asleep in the warm, crowded theatre
context: The premiere at the new Théâtre des Champs-Élysées split the crowd into two screaming camps shouting over the music — one side yelling 'Marvelous, magnificent!' and the other 'Abominable, ridiculous!' — until they came to blows. A ballet that started a fight. Source: history.com 'This Day in History — Le Sacre du printemps.'

question: The Rite of Spring's 1913 Paris premiere ended in a brawling riot, with spectators throwing punches over Stravinsky's pounding music. Conductor Pierre Monteux led the very same score again just one year later, in 1914 — this time as a concert with no dancers. How did that 1914 audience react?
answer: They cheered it rapturously, and it became a celebrated classic
choices: They cheered it rapturously, and it became a celebrated classic
They rioted again, even more violently than before
They sat in stunned, total silence the whole way through
They walked out before the first movement had finished
context: The surprise reversal: strip away Nijinsky's jarring choreography and the very music the crowd had rioted over became a beloved 20th-century masterpiece. The scandal, it turned out, was as much about the stamping dancers as the notes. Source: classical-music.com 'Stravinsky: Rite of Spring.'

question: On July 26, 1956, Egypt's leader Gamal Abdel Nasser gave a three-hour speech in Alexandria and secretly signaled his engineers to seize the Suez Canal as he spoke. The signal was a code word his commandos were listening for, and to be sure they caught it he repeated it 14 times in about ten minutes. What was the code word?
answer: The name of the canal's French builder, de Lesseps
choices: The name of the canal's French builder, de Lesseps
The Arabic battle cry his soldiers chanted
The name of the dam he wanted to build, Aswan
The single word 'Egypt' shouted to the crowd
context: Ferdinand de Lesseps was the Frenchman who built the Suez Canal, opened in 1869. When engineer Mahmoud Yunis heard Nasser say 'de Lesseps,' he began the takeover. Nasser, denied US/British money for his Aswan High Dam, said the canal's tolls would pay for it instead. Source: historynewsnetwork.org 'Sixty Years After the Suez Crisis'; Wilson Center Digital Archive, Nasser's Alexandria speech, July 26 1956.

question: After Britain and France invaded Egypt in 1956 to retake the Suez Canal, they were winning on the ground, but US President Dwight Eisenhower was furious his allies had never told him and refused to back them. His weapon against Britain wasn't soldiers. What did Eisenhower threaten that forced Britain to quit within days?
answer: To dump America's British pound bonds and crash the pound
choices: To dump America's British pound bonds and crash the pound
To bomb the British fleet sitting off the Egyptian coast
To recognize Nasser's Egypt as the canal's rightful owner
To expel Britain from the United Nations Security Council
context: Eisenhower blocked roughly $561 million in IMF credit and about $600 million in Export-Import Bank credit to Britain, refused the dollars Britain needed to buy oil after the canal closed, and threatened to sell US-held sterling bonds, which would have crashed the pound as Britain's reserves were already collapsing. Britain and France accepted a UN ceasefire on November 6, 1956. Suez is seen as the symbolic end of Britain as a global superpower. Source: IMF WP/00/192 'Northwest of Suez'; mises.org 'Financial Warfare and the Declining Dollar'; history.state.gov/milestones, Suez.

question: Spanish colonists in the New World were handed a royal grant called an encomienda: a group of Indigenous people were assigned to a colonist to work for him, and in return he was supposed to protect them and pay for a priest to convert them. The very name came from the Spanish verb 'encomendar.' What did that verb mean?
answer: To entrust
choices: To entrust
To conquer
To purchase
To baptize
context: The word 'encomienda' comes from 'encomendar,' to entrust. The grim joke is in the name: the colonist was supposedly being 'entrusted' with the people's care and souls, while in practice it became a license to work them to death. The first encomiendas were set up on Hispaniola in 1502 by the governor Nicolas de Ovando. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Encomienda' (worldhistory.org/Encomienda).

question: On a colonial sugar plantation, workers crushed the cane, then boiled the juice down for hours over roaring fires until it thickened. They poured the hot syrup into clay molds to cool and harden. When a mold was broken open, what shape of sugar came out?
answer: A tall cone-shaped loaf
choices: A tall cone-shaped loaf
A flat brown brick
A bag of loose crystals
A thin pressed sheet
context: The molds were cone-shaped, so the sugar hardened into 'loaves' shaped like tall cones, each weighing about 15 to 20 pounds. A colonial sugar mill was one of the most technologically complex industries of its day. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Life on a Colonial Sugar Plantation' (worldhistory.org/article/1795).

question: The first sugar mill in the New World was built on the island of Hispaniola in 1516, and it made sugar the crop that would drive the whole brutal plantation system. The sugar cane itself was not native to the Americas at all; the colonists shipped it across the Atlantic from islands they already farmed. Which islands did that first cane come from?
answer: The Canary Islands
choices: The Canary Islands
The Cape Verde islands
The islands of the Azores
The island of Madeira
context: The cane for that first 1516 mill was carried over from the Canary Islands, off the coast of Africa. Sugar was the most labor-hungry crop in the colonies, and its demand for workers is what drove the whole forced-labor machine. Source: HistoryAtlas, 'The Indigenous Taino Have Nearly Disappeared' (historyatlas.com).

question: The machine at the heart of a sugar mill was a set of three heavy rollers that squeezed the juice from the cane. Once it was turning it could not be stopped quickly, so if a worker's fingers were caught and dragged in with the cane, the rollers would keep pulling until the whole person was crushed. To prevent that, another worker was always stationed right beside the rollers. What did that worker do to save the trapped person's life?
answer: Chop off the trapped arm with a hatchet
choices: Chop off the trapped arm with a hatchet
Wrench the worker free by main force
Cut the worker's clothes loose from the cane
Drag the worker back with a rope
context: Because the three-roller crusher could not be stopped in time, a worker stood by with a cutlass or hatchet to chop off a trapped arm before the rollers dragged the whole person in and killed them. Losing an arm was the merciful outcome. Source: 'Slaves' Work on Sugar Plantations' (runaways.gla.ac.uk).

question: The labor in a sugar mill was so deadly, between the crushing heat of the boiling house, the exhaustion, the disease, and the maimings, that a worker was not expected to last long at all. Set to work as a young adult, how long was the average working life of a sugar-mill hand said to be before the work killed him?
answer: About seven years
choices: About seven years
About thirty years
A full lifetime
About fifteen years
context: The average working life of a sugar-mill hand was said to be only about seven years before overwork, heat, disease, and injury killed them. The crop that sweetened Europe's tables was among the deadliest work in the colonial world. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Life on a Colonial Sugar Plantation' (worldhistory.org/article/1795).

question: When Spain handed out encomienda grants of Indigenous labor, the biggest went to the great conquerors. The conquistador Hernan Cortes, who toppled the Aztec empire, was awarded a single encomienda in Mexico. How many families of Indigenous laborers did that one grant cover?
answer: Over 23,000 families
choices: Over 23,000 families
About 8,000 families
Around 15,000 families
Nearly 40,000 families
context: Cortes received a single encomienda covering well over 23,000 family units of Indigenous laborers. A grant was not a few servants; it could be the forced labor of tens of thousands of people handed to one man. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Encomienda' (worldhistory.org/Encomienda).

question: Before a Spanish force attacked an Indigenous town, the law required them to read aloud a document called the Requerimiento, demanding the people submit to the Pope and the Spanish crown. It became infamous for the circumstances in which soldiers read it. In one such habit, where and how would Spanish soldiers read the Requerimiento?
answer: To empty beaches and from the decks of ships
choices: To empty beaches and from the decks of ships
To kneeling chiefs gathered in the town square
Through an interpreter, slowly, village by village
Nailed to a post as a written proclamation
context: The Requerimiento (written 1513 by the jurist Juan Lopez de Palacios Rubios) was a pure legal fig-leaf. It was read to barren beaches and empty villages after the people had fled, to prisoners after they were captured, and even from the decks of ships once the coast was merely sighted. The 'offer' was a formality nobody was meant to accept. Source: Wikipedia, 'Spanish Requirement of 1513'.

question: Spanish soldiers would read the Requerimiento, a long legal demand to submit to a foreign Pope and king, in Spanish or Latin to Indigenous people who could not understand a single word of it, and then attack. The friar Bartolome de las Casas, who saw it done, said the whole thing left him torn between two reactions. What did Las Casas say he did not know whether to do?
answer: Whether to laugh or to weep
choices: Whether to laugh or to weep
Whether to fight or to flee
Whether to pray or to curse
Whether to stay or to sail home
context: Las Casas said of the absurd Requerimiento that he 'did not know whether to laugh or to weep' at it. A document read in Latin to people who spoke neither Latin nor Spanish was the conquest's legal cover, and one of its own friars saw straight through it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Spanish Requirement of 1513'.

question: In his eyewitness account of the conquest, the friar Bartolome de las Casas described the Spanish breeding and training one kind of animal as a weapon of terror against the Indigenous people. Which animal did the Spanish train for this?
answer: War-mastiffs set loose on them
choices: War-mastiffs set loose on them
Falcons flown at their faces
Bulls driven through their fields
Horses ridden into their ranks
context: Las Casas wrote that the Spanish 'hunted them with their Hounds, whom they bred up and taught to pull down and tear the Indians like beasts.' These war-mastiffs were trained specifically to hunt and savage people. Source: Bartolome de las Casas, 'A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies' (faculty.chass.ncsu.edu/slatta/hi216).

question: A Taino chief named Hatuey saw the Spanish destroying his home island of Hispaniola and decided to warn the next island in their path before the conquerors arrived. He gathered his people and set out to reach Cuba and raise the alarm. How did Hatuey and his people make the crossing to Cuba?
answer: They paddled across by canoe
choices: They paddled across by canoe
They walked across a land bridge
They drifted across on rafts of reeds
They sailed a captured Spanish ship
context: Hatuey fled Hispaniola by canoe to warn Cuba, then fought the Spanish there with guerrilla raids. Tracked down with the help of war-mastiffs, he was captured and burned at the stake at Yara in 1512, becoming one of the first heroes of resistance in the Americas. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hatuey'.

question: Reformers finally pushed Spain's King Charles V to act: in 1542 he issued the New Laws, declaring that Indigenous people were free subjects who could not be enslaved. The laws also struck at the encomienda itself with one rule the colonists hated most. What did the New Laws say must happen to an encomienda?
answer: It could not be passed down to an heir
choices: It could not be passed down to an heir
It had to be sold to the crown for gold
It must be split evenly among the workers
It could cover only half as many workers
context: The New Laws (Leyes Nuevas), issued by Emperor Charles V on November 20, 1542, ordered that an encomienda could no longer be inherited; when its holder died, it reverted to the Crown. The idea was to let the system wither away as the current holders died off. Source: Wikipedia, 'New Laws'.

question: When the New Laws threatened to end the encomienda, the colonists who held those grants were furious. In Peru the encomenderos rose up in open revolt under Gonzalo Pizarro against the first viceroy, Blasco Nunez Vela, who had come to enforce the new rules. In 1546 their rebellion reached its climax. What did Pizarro's rebels do to the viceroy?
answer: They killed him in battle
choices: They killed him in battle
They shipped him to Spain in chains
They locked him in a mountain fortress
They forced him to sign a surrender
context: Gonzalo Pizarro's encomenderos killed the first viceroy of Peru, Blasco Nunez Vela, in 1546 rather than give up their grants. The Crown blinked first: it had already revoked the no-inheritance clause in 1545. Even a king could not simply override the colonists who profited from the system. Source: Wikipedia, 'Blasco Nunez Vela'.

question: As the old encomienda fell out of favor, Spain replaced it with a new labor system called the repartimiento, known as the 'mita' in Peru. Instead of handing a colonist a body of people to own outright, this system drew its workers in a different way. How did the repartimiento supply labor?
answer: Villages had to send a rotating quota of workers for set periods
choices: Villages had to send a rotating quota of workers for set periods
Colonists paid a wage to any worker who chose to come
Each village owed a yearly payment in gold instead of labor
Workers were shipped from Africa to replace the natives
context: The repartimiento (the 'mita' in Peru, the 'cuatequil' in New Spain) forced Indigenous communities to rotate a quota of laborers for set periods, rather than granting a colonist a body of people outright. It was meant to be a reform, but for the workers rotated into the silver mines it was often just as deadly. Source: Britannica, 'repartimiento' (britannica.com/topic/repartimiento).

question: Around 3100 BCE, one settlement in southern Mesopotamia swelled to perhaps 40,000 people packed inside its walls, making it the largest city on Earth and the first place humans ever built that we can truly call a city. Which city was it?
answer: Uruk
choices: Uruk
Babylon
Memphis
Jericho
context: Uruk, around 3100 BCE, held perhaps 40,000 people inside its walls (80,000-90,000 in the surrounding area) and sprawled across about 6 square kilometers of temples, workshops, and packed neighborhoods - a 'mega-city' before any other existed. Source: worldhistory.org/uruk and metmuseum.org/essays/uruk-the-first-city.

question: Writing itself was invented in Sumer around 3200 BCE, scratched into wet clay by the world's first scribes. Think of everything those first writers could have chosen to set down. What did those earliest clay tablets actually keep track of?
answer: Grain and livestock - who owed what
choices: Grain and livestock - who owed what
A king's orders to his officials
The boundaries of farmers' fields
Spells to ward off evil spirits
context: The very first thing humans ever wrote down was not poetry but accounting: cuneiform began as tallies of grain, livestock, and goods - who owed what to whom. Source: worldhistory.org/uruk and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kushim_(Uruk_period).

question: In the first cities of Sumer, the main title for a king was the word 'lugal.' It is a wonderfully blunt word that tells you exactly how people pictured their ruler. What does 'lugal' literally mean?
answer: Big man
choices: Big man
Bright star
High priest
Good shepherd
context: 'Lugal' literally means 'big man.' Rulers also went by 'en' (lord/priest-king) and 'ensi' (governor), and the king was usually the high priest of the city's god too - the first government in history, one person bound to the gods over the land and the people. Source: worldhistory.org/Sumerians.

question: In the ruins of an ancient Sumerian city, archaeologists found beautiful game boards inlaid with shell and blue lapis lazuli, made around 2600 BCE. A British Museum scholar even cracked the rules from a 2,000-year-old clay tablet, so it can still be played today. What is this, the oldest playable board game known to the world?
answer: The Royal Game of Ur
choices: The Royal Game of Ur
The game of Senet
Nine Men's Morris
Snakes and Ladders
context: The Royal Game of Ur (boards from about 2600-2400 BCE, dug up at Ur by Leonard Woolley) is the oldest playable game we know - a race to get seven pieces across the board, moves set by tetrahedral dice. Curator Irving Finkel decoded its rules from a Babylonian tablet written in 177 BCE. Source: britishmuseum.org and tradgames.org.uk/games/Royal-Game-Ur.htm.

question: The oldest personal name in all of human history belonged to someone in the city of Uruk around 3100 BCE, a person named Kushim. We even know exactly what Kushim did for a living, because that job is the very reason the name got written down at all. What did Kushim do?
answer: Tallied the barley for a beer brewery
choices: Tallied the barley for a beer brewery
Baked the bread for the temple kitchen
Carved the seals for the city's merchants
Herded the sheep on the temple's land
context: History's first named person was not a king or warrior but an accountant: Kushim managed barley for the brewery at the Temple of Inanna in Uruk. One tablet records 134,813 liters of barley owed to Kushim's brewery over 37 months. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kushim_(Uruk_period) and guinnessworldrecords.com.

question: We count in tens, but the Sumerians built their whole number system around 60 instead - a number they liked because it divides cleanly by 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6. That ancient choice never left us; it is still quietly hiding in things you use every single day. Which of these everyday measures did the Sumerians' counting give us?
answer: The minutes in an hour and the degrees in a circle
choices: The minutes in an hour and the degrees in a circle
The days in a week and the weeks in a month
The inches in a foot and the feet in a yard
The letters in the alphabet and the vowels among them
context: The Sumerians counted in base 60 (sexagesimal), which is why an hour has 60 minutes, a minute has 60 seconds, and a circle has 360 degrees. They chose 60 because it divides cleanly by 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 - handy for trade. The system passed to Babylon and never left us. Source: library.fiveable.me and worldhistoryedu.com.

question: For thousands of years written words were anonymous - nobody signed them. Then, around 2300 BCE at the city of Ur, one person became the first author in history to carve their own name into their work and claim the words as their own. Each of these four served a god and wrote in the temples. Which one signed her own name into hymns for the goddess Inanna?
answer: Enheduanna, a high priestess of the moon god Nanna
choices: Enheduanna, a high priestess of the moon god Nanna
Ur-Lama, a high scribe of the sky god Anu
Geme-Sin, a high priestess of the sun god Utu
En-shakush, a high priest of the storm god Ishkur
context: The world's first named author was a woman: Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon of Akkad and high priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur. She wrote hymns to the goddess Inanna and signed her name into them, and composed a set of 42 temple hymns. The other three names here are not real authors. Source: worldhistory.org/Enheduanna.

question: The Epic of Gilgamesh, one of the oldest poems on Earth, opens in a surprising way - not with a battle or a god, but with a dare aimed straight at the listener. The poem credits King Gilgamesh with a mighty building project at Uruk, then turns and challenges the listener face to face. What does the poem dare you to do?
answer: Climb the walls and check that the bricks are kiln-fired
choices: Climb the walls and check that the bricks are kiln-fired
Sail downriver to find the secret of eternal life
Wrestle the wild man Enkidu in the city square
Count every soldier in the king's great army
context: The prologue dares you to inspect Uruk yourself: 'Go up, pace out the walls of Uruk... examine the brickwork. Is not its masonry of kiln-fired brick?' Tradition says Gilgamesh built the wall, which ran about 9.5 km (6 miles) around the city. Source: Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet I (Foster translation) and ancientpages.com.  (Legend.)

question: Around 2100 BCE, King Ur-Nammu began a colossal step-pyramid of mud brick at the city of Ur - about 30 meters tall, with three great staircases climbing to a small shrine at the summit. The Sumerians held a striking belief about why that shrine sat so high. In their eyes, what was the top of the ziggurat?
answer: The home on earth of the moon god himself
choices: The home on earth of the moon god himself
The closest point to the sun's daily path
The throne room of the city's living king
The burial chamber of the first great king
context: The Great Ziggurat of Ur, begun by Ur-Nammu and finished by his son Shulgi, was about 64 m long, 46 m wide, and 30 m tall, climbed by three staircases to a temple for the moon god Nanna. People believed it was the very spot on earth where the god chose to live. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ziggurat_of_Ur and smarthistory.org/ziggurat-of-ur.

question: The world's oldest war monument, carved around 2475 BCE, shows King Eannatum of Lagash crushing the rival city of Umma. This broken stone slab earned a grisly nickname from one image carved along its top edge. What are the creatures in that carving doing?
answer: Flying off with the severed heads of the enemy dead
choices: Flying off with the severed heads of the enemy dead
Dragging a war-chariot over the trampled fallen
Tearing into the bodies left on the battlefield
Dropping heavy stones onto the fleeing soldiers
context: The Stele of the Vultures (about 2475 BCE) is the earliest war monument in the world, named for the vultures carved carrying off the heads of the defeated. The Lagash-Umma fight is history's first well-documented war between states, and it ended in one of the earliest known boundary treaties. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stele_of_the_Vultures and britannica.com.

question: Archaeologists digging at Uruk keep unearthing the same crude clay bowl by the thousands - all roughly the same size, all mold-made, the first object in history ever mass-produced. Why would a city need thousands of identical cheap bowls? What were these 'bevel-rim bowls' for?
answer: Doling out a fixed daily food ration to each worker
choices: Doling out a fixed daily food ration to each worker
Mixing the paints for the temple's bright murals
Burning oil to light the city streets at night
Catching rainwater that ran off the temple roofs
context: The bevel-rim bowl was churned out in huge numbers to dole out daily grain rations to workers. The standardized bowl is the first evidence of organized division of labor - people specializing in jobs and being paid in measured portions of food. Source: worldhistory.org/uruk and metmuseum.org/essays/uruk-the-first-city.

question: At the city of Ur, the excavator Leonard Woolley uncovered a grave he named the 'Great Death Pit': 68 women in scarlet gowns and gold headdresses laid out in neat rows, with six men holding weapons posted by the entrance. None of them had been robbed. Woolley believed all these people had died together for a single reason. What did he conclude they were?
answer: Servants who followed a dead royal master into the grave
choices: Servants who followed a dead royal master into the grave
Soldiers killed defending the city from invaders
Plague victims buried quickly in a single pit
Slaves who had risen up and been put to death
context: In grave PG 1237, Woolley believed the 68 attendants and six armed guards had followed a royal master into death - possibly poisoned, with some skulls showing they were struck on the head. It remains his interpretation of the evidence, not a settled fact. Source: ancient-origins.net/ancient-places-asia/death-pit-of-ur-mesopotamia-0010297.

question: Around 4000 BCE, Sumerian potters in the city of Uruk invented a spinning device, but its very first job was NOT moving carts or loads. What did they spin on this first wheel?
answer: Wet clay, to shape smoother and thinner pots
choices: Wet clay, to shape smoother and thinner pots
Heavy stones, to grind grain into flour
Raw wool, to twist it into woven cloth
Copper ore, to polish it into bright mirrors
context: The potter's wheel came centuries before anyone stood a wheel on its edge and put it under a cart. The oldest surviving potter's wheel was found at Ur, in modern Iraq, dated to about 3100 BCE. Source: thepotterywheel.com/potters-wheel-history; World History Encyclopedia.

question: More than 4,000 years ago the Sumerians counted in a base-60 system called sexagesimal, and we still live by it every single day. What everyday thing did that base-60 counting give us?
answer: An hour of 60 minutes and a minute of 60 seconds
choices: An hour of 60 minutes and a minute of 60 seconds
A week of 7 days, each named for a planet
A year split into 12 months of equal length
A foot divided into 12 inches for measuring
context: The same base-60 system is why a full circle has 360 degrees. Source: Britannica, sexagesimal number system; Wikipedia, Sexagesimal.

question: The Sumerian seed-plow was a clever machine that did two farm jobs at the same time as oxen dragged it down the field. As the blade cut a furrow, what poured down a narrow funnel attached to the plow?
answer: Seeds, dropping straight into the fresh furrow
choices: Seeds, dropping straight into the fresh furrow
Water, soaking the soil before planting
Ash, fertilizing the ground as it opened
Sand, marking a straight line to follow
context: One machine plowed and sowed in a single pass. Steering it took a whole team: one farmer leading the oxen, a second gripping the plow, and a third pouring the seed. Source: 180days.blog/day-12-the-seed-plough; study.com Mesopotamian Technology.

question: Sumerians used sailboats to push trade goods up the Tigris and Euphrates against the current. One story of how people first got the idea points to an everyday household sight. What is said to have sparked the invention of the sail?
answer: Wet laundry billowing and tugging in the wind as it dried
choices: Wet laundry billowing and tugging in the wind as it dried
A leaf skittering fast across the surface of a pond
Smoke from a cook-fire bending sideways in a gust
A bird gliding upstream without flapping its wings
context: People likely noticed wet cloth hung to dry caught the wind, and reasoned a bigger cloth could push a boat upriver. This origin tale is plausible but not certain. Source: timelessmyths.com/stories/sumerian-inventions; study.com.  (Legend.)

question: In 1949 archaeologists in Iraq dug up a tiny Sumerian clay tablet, just 3 by 4.5 inches, now nicknamed the 'Farmer's Almanac.' It records a father's farming advice to his son, including how deep to drop the seed. How deep did it say to plant?
answer: About the width of two fingers into the furrow
choices: About the width of two fingers into the furrow
About the length of a man's forearm down
About as deep as an ox's hoof sinks
About one full hand-span below the surface
context: The tablet gives nuts-and-bolts plow instructions and was found on a joint University of Chicago / University of Pennsylvania expedition. Source: en-academic.com (Sumerian Farmer's Almanac); Kramer, History Begins at Sumer.

question: In the founding epic of the Mali Empire, the hero's name comes from joining his mother Sogolon's name to the word 'jata.' His mother's people called him the Lion because 'jata' means lion. So when West Africans call him by his epic name, what are they calling him?
answer: Sogolon's Lion
choices: Sogolon's Lion
Sogolon's Eagle
Sogolon's Spear
Sogolon's Shadow
context: His birth name was Sogolon Djata (Mari Djata); 'Sundiata' fuses 'Sogolon' with 'jata' (lion) — the Lion of Mali. His royal title was Mansa, meaning king or emperor in Mandinka. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundiata_Keita

question: The epic of Sundiata Keita opens with a shock: the future founder of the Mali Empire spent his early childhood unable to do one ordinary thing, crawling on the ground while a rival queen mocked him and his mother. What could the young Sundiata not do?
answer: Walk
choices: Walk
Speak
See
Hear
context: The boy who could not walk rising to found an empire is the heart of the story; the co-wife Sassouma Bereté mocked him and his mother Sogolon. Told as legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundiata_Keita

question: In the legend, after years of crawling, young Sundiata Keita was handed a huge iron rod so heavy that six men could barely lift it, and he used it to haul himself upright for the very first time. As he stood, the legend says, the iron bar in his grip bent into the shape of one thing under his strength. What did the iron rod become?
answer: A bow
choices: A bow
A crown
A throne
A chain
context: His mother Sogolon had been insulted because no one would fetch her baobab leaves; the bending iron rod is the epic's signature image of Sundiata's hidden power awakening. Told as legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_of_Sundiata

question: Sundiata Keita's great enemy was Soumaoro Kanté, the sorcerer-king of the Sosso. According to the epic, Soumaoro kept a secret chamber whose floor was carpeted with human skins, and on display in that room he kept the severed heads of nine kings. What were those nine heads?
answer: Kings Soumaoro had defeated
choices: Kings Soumaoro had defeated
Soumaoro's own ancestors
Gods the Sosso worshipped
Prophets who cursed him
context: The chamber of human skins and nine kings' heads marks Soumaoro as the terrifying villain Sundiata must overthrow. Told as legend. Source: https://www.enotes.com/topics/sundiata/part-summary/part-iv-summary-soumaoro-kante-sorcerer-king

question: At the Battle of Kirina around 1235, Sundiata Keita finally faced the sorcerer-king Soumaoro Kanté, whose magic had made him seem unbeatable. In the epic, Sundiata had learned the one thing that could break that magic, and he tipped an arrow with it to wound his enemy. What was Soumaoro's secret weakness?
answer: A white rooster's spur
choices: A white rooster's spur
A drop of his own blood
A buried iron mask
A stolen golden ring
context: Wounded by the cock's-spur arrow, Soumaoro's magic failed and he vanished into the Koulikoro mountains; Kirina (c. 1235) is treated as the founding moment of the Mali Empire, which ruled most of West Africa for two centuries. Told as legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kirina

question: After winning the empire, Sundiata Keita gathered the clan chiefs on a granite clearing around 1236 and proclaimed the Kouroukan Fouga, the Manden Charter — the constitution of Mali, never written down but passed mouth-to-mouth for centuries. Scholars praise it as one of the world's earliest declarations of what?
answer: Human rights
choices: Human rights
Trade tariffs
Royal bloodlines
Battle tactics
context: Its articles include 'To satisfy one's hunger is not robbery,' that women be associated with all governance, and a rule to check tree branches for fruit or flowers before clearing land by fire; UNESCO added it to its heritage list in 2009. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kouroukan_Fouga

question: When the Prophet Muhammad died in 632, the young Muslim community faced one urgent question that would split it for centuries. What were they arguing about?
answer: Who should lead the community after him
choices: Who should lead the community after him
Which city should become the capital
How many times a day to pray
Which language the Quran should use
context: The whole Sunni-Shia divide began as a succession dispute. At a meeting in the Saqifa (a roofed courtyard) of the Banu Sa'ida, the elder companion Abu Bakr was acclaimed as the first caliph. One faction insisted Muhammad had already chosen his cousin Ali. (World History Edu, 'Succession Following the Death of Muhammad'; detailedpedia.com 'Succession of Muhammad')

question: Ali ibn Abi Talib was raised in the Prophet Muhammad's own household after being orphaned, and some early sources say he was the first male to accept Islam at about age eleven. How was Ali related to Muhammad by blood?
answer: He was Muhammad's first cousin
choices: He was Muhammad's first cousin
He was Muhammad's older brother
He was Muhammad's uncle
He was Muhammad's grandfather
context: Ali was Muhammad's first cousin AND son-in-law, marrying the Prophet's daughter Fatima around 623-625. For Shia he is the first Imam; for Sunni he is the fourth of the 'Rightly-Guided' (Rashidun) caliphs. The faction that backed him became the 'shi'at Ali' -- the party of Ali, the Shia. (Wikipedia, 'Ali')

question: Ali ibn Abi Talib finally became caliph in 656, but in 661 a man struck him on the head with a sword inside the Great Mosque of Kufa. What had been done to that sword blade to make sure the wound would kill him?
answer: Its blade had been smeared with poison
choices: Its blade had been smeared with poison
Its edge had been notched like a saw
Its tip had been dipped in molten lead
Its handle had been wrapped in nettles
context: The assassin, the Kharijite Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam, poisoned the blade; Ali died of the wound about two days later, around age 62. He is believed to be buried at the Imam Ali Shrine in Najaf, Iraq -- a major Shia pilgrimage site. (Wikipedia, 'Assassination of Ali' and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam')

question: In 680 the Prophet's grandson Husayn, son of Ali, refused to swear allegiance to the Umayyad caliph Yazid. Near Karbala in Iraq an Umayyad army numbering in the thousands surrounded him. How large was the band of family and followers facing them with Husayn?
answer: Only about seventy to a hundred people
choices: Only about seventy to a hundred people
Around five thousand fighters
Nearly twenty thousand troops
A force evenly matched with the enemy
context: Husayn and his roughly 70-100 followers and family were overwhelmed on 10 October 680 (10 Muharram). His head was cut off and carried to the governor Ibn Ziyad and then to Yazid in Damascus; the surviving women and children were taken captive. This is the emotional core of Shia devotion. (World History Encyclopedia, 'Battle of Karbala'; Wikipedia 'Battle of Karbala')

question: At the Battle of Karbala in 680, a named officer led the cavalry that first blocked Husayn's road and trapped his tiny band against the army. The morning of the battle, moved by Husayn's speech, this officer, al-Hurr ibn Yazid, did something startling. What did he do?
answer: He rode over to Husayn's side and died fighting for him
choices: He rode over to Husayn's side and died fighting for him
He quietly slipped away from the battlefield at night
He sent a secret message begging Yazid for mercy
He ordered his men to lay down their weapons and watch
context: Al-Hurr ibn Yazid al-Tamimi defected to the man he had been sent to trap, and was killed fighting for Husayn -- one of the most retold moments of Karbala. (Wikipedia, 'Battle of Karbala')

question: Forty days after Ashura, Shia pilgrims walk on foot to Husayn's shrine in Karbala for Arba'in. With over 20 million people, how does this gathering compare to the Hajj pilgrimage to Mecca, which draws about 2-3 million?
answer: Arba'in is the largest annual gathering on earth
choices: Arba'in is the largest annual gathering on earth
The two draw almost exactly the same crowds
The Hajj is several times larger than Arba'in
Arba'in is a small, local event by comparison
context: Karbala is relived every year on Ashura (10 Muharram) with mourning processions and chest-beating (matam). The Arba'in walking pilgrimage forty days later is the largest annual gathering on earth -- many times the size of the Hajj. (Wikipedia, 'Battle of Karbala' and 'Arba'in pilgrimage'; Religion Media Centre)

question: Salvador Dali painted 'The Persistence of Memory' in 1931, with its famous soft watches drooping like they have gone limp in the heat. When the physicist Ilya Prigogine asked Dali if the melting watches came from Einstein's theory of relativity, Dali said no — they came from something he had watched go runny in the summer sun. What was it?
answer: A wheel of Camembert cheese
choices: A wheel of Camembert cheese
A candle on his windowsill
A block of butter on bread
A bar of soap in the bath
context: Dali called the soft watches a surrealist 'camembert of time,' inspired by watching a Camembert melt in the sun on a summer evening — not by Einstein. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Persistence_of_Memory; salvadordali.com/melting-clocks-persistence-of-memory/

question: In Salvador Dali's 'The Persistence of Memory,' three of the watches sag and droop like soft cheese — but down in the lower-left corner sits one orange pocket watch with its case shut tight, the only one that has NOT gone soft. Dali covered that closed watch with something he used again and again to stand for things rotting away. What is crawling all over it?
answer: A cluster of black ants
choices: A cluster of black ants
A trail of green moss
A patch of grey mold
A web of fine cracks
context: The closed pocket watch is swarmed by black ants — Dali's recurring symbol of decay. It is the one watch in the painting that stays hard instead of melting. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Persistence_of_Memory

question: The Thuggee were bands of stranglers who roamed the roads of India. They would join travellers for days, sharing food and friendly talk to win their trust, then turn on them without warning and strangle them. What did the Thugs call the strangling-cord they used?
answer: The rumal
choices: The rumal
The katar
The chela
The tabar
context: The rumal was a cloth handkerchief with a knot tied in one end to give the strangler a grip. The spade the Thugs used to dig their victims' secret graves was treated as a sacred pickaxe, consecrated to the goddess the cult worshipped. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thuggee; victorianweb.org/history/empire/india/thuggee.html)

question: In China, foot-binding shaped a girl's foot by curling the toes under until they broke and then snapping the arch, binding the foot smaller year after year as it re-broke. The most prized result was a foot only about three inches long. What was that ideal tiny foot called?
answer: The golden lotus
choices: The golden lotus
The jade blossom
The silver crane
The lily slipper
context: Larger feet were ranked lower as the 'silver' lotus (about four inches) or the 'iron' lotus (five inches or more). A small foot was treated as a daughter's ticket to a good marriage and a step up for her whole family. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foot_binding; smithsonianmag.com/history/why-footbinding-persisted-china-millennium-180953971)

question: For years the British governors of India left the Hindu custom of suttee untouched. A widow would be burned alive on her dead husband's funeral pyre, and the governors feared that banning it would set off a religious revolt. In 1829 a new Governor-General signed a regulation declaring widow-burning illegal and punishable by the courts. Who finally outlawed it?
answer: Lord William Bentinck
choices: Lord William Bentinck
Lord Charles Cornwallis
Lord Richard Wellesley
Lord Warren Hastings
context: Bentinck's regulation of 4 December 1829 declared that 'the practice of suttee, or of burning or burying alive the widows of Hindus, is hereby declared illegal.' The campaign behind it joined two unlikely allies: the Baptist missionary William Carey and the Hindu reformer Raja Ram Mohan Roy, who argued that suttee was not actually required by Hindu scripture. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal_Sati_Regulation,_1829)

question: William Carey, a Baptist missionary, also served as the British government's official Bengali translator. One Sunday morning in 1829 the freshly-signed order abolishing suttee reached his desk to be rendered into Bengali. What did Carey do the moment it arrived?
answer: He handed his sermon to another preacher and raced to finish the translation that same day.
choices: He handed his sermon to another preacher and raced to finish the translation that same day.
He set it aside to translate carefully over the following week.
He read the order from the pulpit and preached on it before translating it.
He refused, saying a missionary should not do the government's paperwork.
context: Carey believed that every hour of delay might cost some widow her life, so he passed his pulpit to another preacher and had the decree translated into Bengali by that evening before any more burnings could happen. He had earlier collected statistics on sati from his mission at Serampore. (Source: christianhistoryinstitute.org/magazine/article/ministry-in-killing-fields)

question: The Thuggee cult had murdered travellers for generations, burying the bodies in secret and guarding the gang's ways from every outsider. The British officer William Henry Sleeman, put in charge of breaking the cult in the 1830s, found his great weapon in a captured Thug who agreed to do what?
answer: Turn informer and lead the soldiers straight to his old gang.
choices: Turn informer and lead the soldiers straight to his old gang.
Recite from memory the cult's entire secret coded language.
Convert and travel the roads preaching against his former cult.
Train a company of soldiers to fight in the Thugs' own ambush style.
context: Such a turncoat was called an 'approver.' The most important was Feringheea, arrested in 1830; in January 1831 he led Sleeman to graves outside the village of Salohda where 25 men had been buried over ten years, and his testimony helped identify 283 of 289 Thugs seized near Jhansi. By 1839 Sleeman declared Thuggee 'effectively destroyed as an organisation.' (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feringheea; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Henry_Sleeman)

question: Earlier campaigners against Chinese foot-binding had argued from Christian faith, which won few converts among the Chinese. In 1895 Alicia Little founded the Natural Foot Society in Shanghai and toured the country with a cleverer approach aimed at people who were not Christian. What did Little show her audiences?
answer: X-ray photographs of crushed feet, beside quotations from Confucius.
choices: X-ray photographs of crushed feet, beside quotations from Confucius.
Pamphlets from European doctors warning of the health dangers.
Cash rewards offered to families who left their daughters' feet natural.
A printed decree from the Emperor commanding the custom to stop.
context: Little dropped religious arguments and persuaded people on health and tradition instead. Chinese reformers worked alongside the missionaries: the Belfast-born John MacGowan had gathered 60 to 70 Chinese Christian women in Xiamen in 1874, the first such society, and Kang Youwei's Anti-Footbinding Society near Canton grew to a claimed 300,000 members. The Republic of China formally banned foot-binding in 1912, though the last lotus-shoe factory, in Harbin, did not close until 1999. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alicia_Little; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foot_binding)

question: Hong Xiuquan, a Chinese village schoolteacher, failed the imperial civil-service exam four times and collapsed with a fever in which he dreamed a golden-bearded old man cut out his organs and handed him a sword to purify the earth of demons. Years later, after reading a Christian pamphlet, he decided the old man had been God and that this made him what?
answer: The younger brother of Jesus Christ
choices: The reincarnation of the first emperor of China
The younger brother of Jesus Christ
A prophet chosen to restore the old gods
The last true descendant of Confucius
context: Hong Xiuquan (1814-1864) read Liang Fa's pamphlet 'Good Words to Admonish the Age' and concluded the bearded old man in his dream was God his father and Jesus his elder brother -- making Hong the literal younger brother of Christ, sent to rid China of demons. He proclaimed himself 'Heavenly King' in 1851 and launched the Taiping Rebellion. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Xiuquan; newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Hong_Xiuquan.

question: The Taiping Rebellion tore through China from 1850 to 1864 as Hong Xiuquan's 'Heavenly Kingdom' fought the empire. Historians count it as the deadliest war of the entire 19th century. Roughly how many people did it kill?
answer: Between 20 and 30 million
choices: Around 200 thousand
Around 2 million
Between 20 and 30 million
Around 500 thousand
context: Estimates run 20 to 30 million dead -- many times the toll of the American Civil War being fought in the same years, and one of the bloodiest wars in all of human history. Source: britannica.com/event/Taiping-Rebellion; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiping_Rebellion.

question: The Taj Mahal in Agra is one of the most beautiful buildings on Earth, with its white marble dome and four tall towers. But Emperor Shah Jahan did not build it as a palace to live in, or a mosque to pray in. Why did he build it?
answer: As a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who had died
choices: As a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who had died
As a fortress to guard the river crossing into the city
As a treasury to lock away the gold of his empire
As a throne hall where he would receive foreign kings
context: Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631 giving birth to their FOURTEENTH child. The grief-stricken emperor put about 20,000 artisans to work for roughly 22 years (1632-1653) building her a tomb of white marble quarried at Makrana. The poet Rabindranath Tagore later called it 'a teardrop on the cheek of time.' Source: britannica.com/topic/Taj-Mahal; mapsofindia.com.

question: Shah Jahan designed the Taj Mahal to be flawlessly symmetrical: matching towers, mirrored halls, and his wife Mumtaz Mahal's marble tomb resting dead-center beneath the great dome. The whole monument is perfectly balanced except for ONE thing that breaks the symmetry. What is that single off-center flaw?
answer: Shah Jahan's own tomb, added later beside his wife's
choices: Shah Jahan's own tomb, added later beside his wife's
A garden fountain dug nearer to the eastern wall
A doorway cut wider on the building's southern face
A staircase built taller on the river-facing side
context: Shah Jahan spent two decades perfecting the balance, but when he died his son Aurangzeb buried him squeezed in beside Mumtaz, slightly off-axis to the west, breaking the symmetry forever. Aurangzeb had earlier seized the throne and imprisoned his father in nearby Agra Fort, where the old emperor spent his last years (1658-1666) gazing at the Taj Mahal across the river. Source: smithsonianmag.com (Eight Secrets of the Taj Mahal); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumtaz_Mahal.

question: The Tang built their capital, Chang'an, into the largest city on Earth, and laid it out as one vast, deliberate shape — a rigid checkerboard of walls and broad tree-lined avenues. In Tang belief, what did this perfect grid mirror?
answer: The order of the cosmos
choices: The order of the cosmos
The body of a sleeping dragon
The route of the Silk Road
The shape of the emperor's seal
context: The Tang saw their gridded capital as a model of heavenly order on earth, with drainage ditches between the blocks and roughly a million people inside the packed-earth walls (2-3 million counting the suburbs). Source: worldhistory.org/Chang'an and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chang%27an

question: Chang'an's checkerboard grid so impressed the Tang's neighbors that their envoys carried its blueprint home and rebuilt their own capitals to match its high walls and wide avenues. Which set of foreign capitals were modeled on Chang'an?
answer: Nara and Kyoto in Japan, Gyeongju in Korea
choices: Nara and Kyoto in Japan, Gyeongju in Korea
Baghdad and Basra in Iraq, Cairo in Egypt
Athens and Sparta in Greece, Rome in Italy
Delhi and Agra in India, Kabul in Afghanistan
context: Japanese envoys studied Chang'an and brought its plan back; the Japanese capitals of Nara and Heian-kyo (Kyoto) and the Korean capital Gyeongju all copied its segregated districts and wide avenues. Source: worldhistory.org/Chang'an

question: Chang'an was carved into 108 walled, gated neighborhoods, and every night drums hammered out a curfew that slammed the gates shut — a commoner caught outside his neighborhood after dark was punished. Surprisingly, what were these inner walls mainly for?
answer: To keep the residents penned in at night
choices: To keep the residents penned in at night
To hide the emperor's palace from view
To block sandstorms blowing off the desert
To divide rich families from poor ones
context: Closing was announced by about 800 drumbeats and opening by about 300; the ward walls existed less to keep enemies out than to keep residents in. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chang%27an

question: When the elder court poet He Zhizhang first read Li Bai's poem 'The Road to Shu,' he was so stunned that he crowned Li Bai with a nickname that stuck for all time. What did He Zhizhang call him?
answer: The Banished Immortal
choices: The Banished Immortal
The Drunken Sage
The River Dragon
The Mountain Hermit
context: He Zhizhang hailed Li Bai as the 'Banished Immortal' (zhexian) — an immortal exiled from heaven to earth. Li Bai, born in 701 in the Silk Road town of Suyab, was also nicknamed the 'Wine Immortal.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Bai

question: Li Bai's four-line poem describes a traveler who sees moonlight on the floor, mistakes it for frost, then lifts his head to the moon and bows it in homesickness. What distinction does 'Quiet Night Thoughts' still hold in China today?
answer: It is the first poem most Chinese children memorize
choices: It is the first poem most Chinese children memorize
It is carved over the Great Wall's main gate
It must be sung at every Chinese wedding
It was banned by emperors for a thousand years
context: 'Quiet Night Thoughts' is the first poem most Chinese children learn and is quoted by adults to this day. About 1,000 of Li Bai's poems survive. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Bai and 100tangpoems.wordpress.com

question: He Zhizhang, the poet who had hailed Li Bai as the Banished Immortal, loved wine so much that one day, with no money to pay, he handed the tavern-keeper a priceless badge of his high government office to settle the tab. What did He Zhizhang trade away for a drink?
answer: The golden-tortoise ornament of his office
choices: The golden-tortoise ornament of his office
A jade seal given by the emperor
His ceremonial court sword
A silk scroll of his own poems
context: He Zhizhang unfastened the golden-tortoise ornament that marked his high rank and traded it across the counter for wine. Source: daydaynews.cc 'He Zhizhang'; theworldofchinese.com 'Alcoholics in ancient times'

question: Li Bai met the younger poet Du Fu in the autumn of 744; the two giants of Tang verse shared a room, hunted together, and parted as friends. Yet the friendship was strangely one-sided. In what way?
answer: Du Fu wrote Li Bai a dozen poems; Li Bai sent back just one
choices: Du Fu wrote Li Bai a dozen poems; Li Bai sent back just one
Li Bai dazzled the emperor's court; Du Fu never won a post there
Du Fu outlived Li Bai by decades; Li Bai died first and young
Li Bai roamed the rivers freely; Du Fu stayed bound to the city
context: The younger Du Fu wrote about a dozen poems to or about Li Bai, who left only one in return. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Du_Fu and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Bai

question: A monk named Xuanzang slipped out of Chang'an in 629 and trekked overland all the way to India, studying for years before returning in 645 with 657 sacred Sanskrit texts. Xuanzang's incredible journey later inspired what?
answer: The classic novel 'Journey to the West'
choices: The classic novel 'Journey to the West'
The building of the Great Wall of China
The invention of the magnetic compass
The founding of the Shaolin Temple
context: Xuanzang studied at Nalanda in India and on his return led the building of the Big Wild Goose Pagoda to house the texts; his 16-17 year trek inspired the Ming novel 'Journey to the West.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xuanzang

question: Tang craftsmen were carving whole pages onto woodblocks and printing them with ink centuries before Europe had a printing press. The most famous survivor — a Buddhist scroll called the Diamond Sutra, found at Dunhuang and dated to the year 868 — holds what record?
answer: The world's oldest dated, complete printed book
choices: The world's oldest dated, complete printed book
The longest poem ever written in Chinese
The first map to chart the whole Silk Road
The oldest surviving portrait of an emperor
context: The Diamond Sutra of 868 is the earliest dated, full-length printed book known, complete with a woodcut illustration — Tang woodblock printing spread scripture centuries before Gutenberg. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_and_technology_of_the_Tang_dynasty

question: Li Bai died in 762, and historians admit the true cause is lost. But the public has always clung to one romantic legend about how the great drunken poet met his end. What does the legend say killed him?
answer: He drowned leaning from his boat to embrace the moon's reflection
choices: He drowned leaning from his boat to embrace the moon's reflection
He froze while crossing a high mountain pass in deep winter
He was poisoned by a rival's hand at a grand banquet
He fell from a cliff one night while gazing up at the stars
context: Legend says Li Bai, drunk, leaned from his boat to embrace the moon's reflection on the water and drowned. The public clings to the moon-drowning because the moon shines through so much of his poetry. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Bai; sothebys.com 'Reaching For the Moon'

question: Returning home in 755, the poet Du Fu wrote a couplet that still cuts: behind the red-lacquered gates of the rich, 'wine sours and meat rots,' while out on the road 'lie the bones of the frozen and starved.' What grief met Du Fu at his own door on that same trip?
answer: His own young son had died of hunger
