choices: His own young son had died of hunger
His house had burned to the ground
His wife had fled with the children
His life's poems had all been stolen
context: Having just witnessed the gulf between feasting nobles and the dying poor, Du Fu reached home to learn his own young son had starved to death. He is honored as the 'Poet-Sage' and 'Poet-Historian'; about 1,500 of his poems survive. Source: live2makan.com 'Du Fu'; choubb.com

question: The An Lushan rebellion that began in 755 was so catastrophic that the empire's own census tells the story by itself: in 754 the Tang counted about 53 million people. Ten years later, in 764, the count had collapsed to roughly what?
answer: About 17 million
choices: About 17 million
About 35 million
About 45 million
About 50 million
context: The 754 census recorded about 52.9 million; the 764 census recorded only about 16.9 million. Whether from death, displacement, or the collapse of the tax-census itself, it marks one of history's most lethal upheavals and the permanent end of the High Tang. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_rebellion

question: As Emperor Xuanzong fled the An Lushan rebels in 756, his own soldiers mutinied at Mawei Station and refused to march another step until he met one terrible demand. What did the troops force the heartbroken emperor to do?
answer: Order the death of his beloved consort Yang Guifei
choices: Order the death of his beloved consort Yang Guifei
Surrender his throne to his own eldest son
Burn the imperial treasury as they retreated
Hand his crown to the rebel general An Lushan
context: The mutinous guards blamed Yang Guifei's family for the disaster; the emperor gave in and had Gao Lishi take her to a Buddhist shrine and oversee her forced suicide by strangling. She was one of the 'Four Beauties of China.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yang_Guifei; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_rebellion

question: An Lushan, the rebel general who had declared himself emperor, grew obese, blind, and paranoid — until in 757 his own servant Li Zhu'er hacked him to death in his tent, in a plot his son had backed. What did the dying An Lushan reportedly scream?
answer: 'A thief of my own household!'
choices: 'A thief of my own household!'
'The Tang gods have cursed me!'
'My son, seize the throne!'
'I should have stayed in the north!'
context: An Lushan had seized Luoyang and declared himself emperor of the 'Great Yan' before his son An Qingxu backed the plot that killed him; he reportedly screamed that this was 'a thief of my own household.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_rebellion

question: The Mexica people wandered for years looking for a home. Their god Huitzilopochtli told them to build their city on the exact spot where they spotted a certain sign. They found it on a swampy island in Lake Texcoco around 1325 and built Tenochtitlan there. What was the sign?
answer: An eagle on a cactus, eating a snake
choices: An eagle on a cactus, eating a snake
A white deer drinking at a still spring
A jaguar sleeping atop a fallen cedar
A serpent coiled around a stone idol
context: The Mexica found exactly that scene on the island and settled there. The eagle-on-a-cactus-eating-a-snake is now the centerpiece of the Mexican flag and coat of arms. This founding sign is told as legend. Source: education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/tenochtitlan and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenochtitlan

question: The city's name, Tenochtitlan, was not just a sound — in the Nahuatl language it described the very thing the Mexica saw on their island when they founded it. What does the name actually mean?
answer: The cactus growing on a stone
choices: The cactus growing on a stone
The island between two waters
The home of the wandering people
The place the eagle came to rest
context: From Nahuatl tetl (rock/stone) + nochtli (prickly-pear cactus) + the locative -tlan: 'the place of the prickly-pear cactus growing on a stone' — the same image as the founding sign. Source: worldhistory.org/Tenochtitlan

question: When the Spanish soldiers under Cortes first saw the white city of Tenochtitlan rising out of the lake, with its towers and long causeways, the soldier Bernal Diaz del Castillo said it looked like the enchantments in a book of knightly tales. How did Diaz say the soldiers reacted to the sight?
answer: Some asked whether it was all a dream
choices: Some asked whether it was all a dream
Some fell to their knees and wept openly
Some turned their horses and refused to go on
Some swore the towers were made of solid gold
context: Bernal Diaz wrote that the city 'was like the enchantments in the book of Amadis... and some of our soldiers even asked whether the things that we saw were not a dream.' Source: worldhistory.org/Tenochtitlan

question: The Aztecs grew their food on garden plots in the lake that people nicknamed the 'floating gardens.' But these plots, called chinampas, did not start out as land at all. How did Aztec farmers create each plot in the open water?
answer: They piled up mud, plants, and reeds from the lake bed
choices: They piled up mud, plants, and reeds from the lake bed
They floated woven rafts of logs lashed together
They dumped quarried stone until an island rose
They dammed a channel and drained it to dry soil
context: Farmers built each chinampa up from the lake bottom in layers of mud, decaying plants, and reeds, raising it about 50 cm above the water before planting. Source: worldhistory.org/Chinampas

question: At its peak, Tenochtitlan held somewhere between 200,000 and 400,000 people packed onto a reclaimed island in the lake. Compared with the famous European cities of the same era — places like London and Paris — how big was Tenochtitlan?
answer: Larger than most cities in Europe
choices: Larger than most cities in Europe
About the size of a large European town
Smaller than London but larger than Paris
Roughly equal to the biggest European port
context: With 200,000-400,000 people on roughly 8-13.5 square km, Tenochtitlan was one of the largest cities in the world at the time, bigger than most contemporary European cities including London and Paris. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenochtitlan

question: In the great markets of the Aztec capital there were no coins of any kind. For small everyday buys, shoppers handed over cacao beans. But for a big, expensive purchase, the soldier Bernal Diaz del Castillo recorded that traders measured out something else entirely. What did they pay with?
answer: Goose quills packed with gold dust
choices: Goose quills packed with gold dust
Polished discs of green jade
Stamped bars of hammered copper
Strings of drilled seashell beads
context: Diaz wrote that 'the gold is placed in the quills of the geese of the country, white quills, so that the gold can be seen through, and according to the length and thickness of the quills they arrange their accounts.' Source: mexicolore.co.uk/aztecs/aztefacts/great-market-tlatelolco

question: Three great stone causeways linked Tenochtitlan to the mainland, but engineers left gaps in them spanned only by loose wooden beams that could be lifted right out. Beyond letting canoes slip through, those removable beams gave the city a hidden defense. What did pulling the beams out do?
answer: It turned each gap into a moat the enemy could not cross
choices: It turned each gap into a moat the enemy could not cross
It dropped attackers into pits dug beneath the planks
It signaled the city's warriors to gather at the wall
It released lake water to flood the lower streets
context: During the Noche Triste (Night of Sorrows, June 1520), the removed beams trapped Cortes's fleeing men in the canals; many drowned, some dragged down by the gold they had stuffed into their clothes. Source: mexicolore.co.uk/aztecs/ask-us/how-did-the-causeway-bridges-work and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenochtitlan

question: People called the Aztec lake plots 'floating gardens,' but the chinampas did not float — each one was held fast to the lake floor. The farmers fixed them in place using something living, planted around the edges of every plot. What anchored a chinampa to the bottom?
answer: The deep roots of willow trees
choices: The deep roots of willow trees
Heavy nets weighted with lake stones
Stakes of fire-hardened hardwood
Thick mats of woven reed rope
context: Ahuejote willows (Salix bonplandiana) were planted at the corners and edges, and their roots gripped the lake floor and held each plot firmly — which is why the 'floating' nickname is a myth. Source: worldhistory.org/Chinampas

question: The biggest market of the Aztec world was in Tlatelolco, the sister-city beside Tenochtitlan. Cortes told the King of Spain it drew more than sixty thousand people in a single day. According to Bernal Diaz del Castillo, how was that enormous crowd organized as it bought and sold?
answer: Every kind of good had its own fixed section
choices: Every kind of good had its own fixed section
Sellers shouted prices from raised stone platforms
Buyers lined up by rank before the noble stalls
Goods were traded only at a single central scale
context: Diaz said the crowd's buzz 'could be heard more than a league off,' and every type of goods had its own section — cloth, cacao, obsidian blades, jade, feathers, jaguar skins, dyes, and food of every kind. Judges sat in the market to settle disputes. Source: mexicolore.co.uk/aztecs/aztefacts/great-market-tlatelolco

question: Tenochtitlan sat in a salty lake, so fresh drinking water was piped from the springs of Chapultepec hill along an aqueduct. After a flood wrecked it, the poet-king Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco rebuilt it as TWO parallel terracotta channels running side by side instead of one. Why build a second channel?
answer: So one could be cleaned while the other kept flowing
choices: So one could be cleaned while the other kept flowing
So twice as much water reached the growing city
So a pipe on each side fed a different half of town
So one carried drinking water and one carried waste
context: Each channel ran over 4 km. By building two, Nezahualcoyotl made sure one pipe could be shut off for cleaning or repair while the other kept the city supplied — the aqueduct was begun in 1418 and rebuilt after a 1449 flood. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapultepec_aqueduct

question: Lake Texcoco was part fresh and part brackish, and floods threatened the city. So the Aztecs and Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco built a dike about 16 km long, finished around 1453, walling the lake in two. Besides holding back floods, what did this giant dike let the Aztecs control?
answer: How salty the water around the city stayed
choices: How salty the water around the city stayed
Which direction the canoe traffic could flow
How high the lake rose in the rainy season
Where the causeways met the open water
context: The Albarradon (Dike of Nezahualcoyotl) sealed off the brackish eastern part of Lake Texcoco from the fresh spring-fed water around Tenochtitlan, in effect controlling the lake's salinity so the city's side stayed fresh. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenochtitlan and mdpi.com/2073-445X/11/4/542

question: When Cortes laid siege to Tenochtitlan in 1521, he knew the island had no well or spring of its own — every drop of drinking water arrived from Chapultepec hill along the aqueduct. Cortes used that brilliant piece of Aztec engineering against the city. What did he do?
answer: He cut and destroyed the aqueduct to leave the city without water
choices: He cut and destroyed the aqueduct to leave the city without water
He poisoned the springs that fed the aqueduct uphill
He seized the aqueduct and rationed water to the defenders
He diverted the aqueduct to flood the lakeside streets
context: Because the island had no other source of drinking water, Cortes severed Tenochtitlan's fresh-water supply by destroying the Chapultepec aqueduct during the 1521 siege — turning the city's own engineering into a weakness. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapultepec_aqueduct

question: Around the 1400s the Aztecs came upon a vast city of empty stone pyramids, long abandoned, its real builders gone for centuries. Awed by the ruins, the Aztecs gave the place the grand Nahuatl name we still use today. What did that name mean?
answer: The City of the Gods
choices: The City of the Gods
The Valley of the Kings
The Field of Bones
The Harbor of the Sun
context: The Aztecs called it Teotihuacan, roughly 'the place where the gods were born' (or where men became gods). Nobody knows what the original builders called themselves or their city — the famous name is Aztec, slapped on a ruin they found empty. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teotihuacan; Britannica /place/Teotihuacan.

question: The grandest street in Teotihuacan is a boulevard about 40 meters wide and 4 kilometers long, lined with stepped temple platforms. The Aztecs, who found these platforms and mistook them for graves, gave the boulevard a grim name. What did they call it?
answer: The Avenue of the Dead
choices: The Avenue of the Dead
The Road of Kings
The Path of the Sun
The Way of Serpents
context: In Nahuatl, Miccaotli — the Avenue of the Dead. The Aztecs thought the platforms lining it were tombs; they were actually ceremonial buildings, not graves. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teotihuacan.

question: In 1971 workers near the Pyramid of the Sun stumbled on a hidden tunnel and followed it about 100 meters straight under the giant pyramid, ending in a sealed chamber. Many scholars think the whole pyramid was deliberately raised on top of it as a sacred 'place of emergence,' the earth's womb where the first people crawled into the world. What shape was that buried chamber?
answer: A four-leaf clover
choices: A four-leaf clover
A perfect circle
A tall narrow well
A long straight hall
context: The 1971 tunnel ran about 100 m under the Pyramid of the Sun and ended in a chamber shaped like a four-leaf clover, thought to be a 'place of emergence' — the womb of the earth from which the first humans came. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyramid_of_the_Sun; ancient-origins.net.

question: One temple at Teotihuacan is studded with about 260 carved stone heads jutting straight out of its walls — great fanged creatures, each open mouth wide enough to hold a marker, alternating with a blocky war-headdress figure. What creature are those 260 snarling heads?
answer: Feathered serpents
choices: Feathered serpents
Roaring jaguars
Screaming eagles
Horned bulls
context: It is the Temple of the Feathered Serpent — the god the Aztecs would later call Quetzalcoatl, here alternating with a second war-headdress figure. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_the_Feathered_Serpent,_Teotihuacan.

question: At its height around 400-500 CE, Teotihuacan held an estimated 125,000 people. Archaeologists rank it that way not just against the Americas but against every city alive in its day. Where did that put Teotihuacan in the whole world?
answer: Among the six biggest cities on Earth
choices: Among the six biggest cities on Earth
The single biggest city on Earth
Bigger than Rome at its peak
The largest city ever built in stone
context: With roughly 100,000-200,000 people, Teotihuacan was the largest city anywhere in the Americas before the 1400s and ranked among the six largest cities on the planet in its day. Archaeologist George Cowgill: 'the largest city anywhere in the Western Hemisphere before the 1400s.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teotihuacan; National Geographic.

question: Teotihuacan's wealth ran on a striking green volcanic glass it mined and shaped into blades and masks — and it held the only source of that green obsidian in all of Mesoamerica. Archaeologists later dug up that exact green glass buried at a distant Maya city more than 1,000 kilometers away. Which faraway city?
answer: Tikal
choices: Tikal
Palenque
Copán
Monte Albán
context: The green obsidian came from the Pachuca / Sierra de las Navajas mines and turned up at Tikal in Guatemala, roughly 1,000-1,280 km away — proof of Teotihuacan's enormous trade reach. Source: worldhistory.org/article/2060/obsidian-in-mesoamerica; Cambridge, 'Mexican Obsidian at Tikal.'

question: Teotihuacan's signature buildings stack the same two parts again and again: a sloping ramp-like wall topped by a flat rectangular panel framed like a picture, jutting out above it. This slope-and-panel look became such a recognizable fingerprint that spotting it lets archaeologists trace the city's influence in faraway places. What is this building style called?
answer: Talud-tablero
choices: Talud-tablero
Flying buttress
Corbel arch
Post-and-lintel
context: Talud (the sloping wall) plus tablero (the framed panel). The stacked style spread across Mesoamerica and marks where Teotihuacan's reach extended. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talud-tablero.

question: Teotihuacan was a city of immigrants, with whole neighborhoods set aside for foreigners — one barrio full of Zapotec people from Oaxaca with their own pottery and tombs, another packed with Gulf Coast merchants in round houses. How did scientists prove these residents had actually been born far from the city?
answer: By testing the chemistry of their bones
choices: By testing the chemistry of their bones
By matching their DNA to living relatives
By reading their tomb inscriptions
By tracing their family names
context: Bone-chemistry (isotope) tests showed large fractions of some neighborhoods were people born far away — the chemistry of bones and teeth records the water and food of one's childhood homeland. The Tlailotlacan barrio was Zapotec; the Barrio de los Comerciantes housed Gulf Coast merchants. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teotihuacan; CLACS Berkeley, 'Teotihuacan: A Multiethnic Metropolis.'

question: When archaeologists dug beneath the Temple of the Feathered Serpent in the 1980s, they uncovered the remains of more than 200 people buried with their hands tied behind their backs, dated to around 150-200 CE when the pyramid was dedicated. Many wore necklaces strung from one particular material. What were those necklaces strung from?
answer: Real human teeth and jawbones
choices: Real human teeth and jawbones
Polished river pebbles
Painted clay beads
Woven palm fiber
context: Over 200 sacrificed people (the count may reach 260), many warriors buried with obsidian-tipped weapons and necklaces strung from real human teeth and jawbones, marked the pyramid's dedication. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_the_Feathered_Serpent,_Teotihuacan; FAMSI Cowgill report.

question: In 2003 a sinkhole opened after heavy rain, and the archaeologist Sergio Gomez crawled into a sealed tunnel deep beneath the Temple of the Feathered Serpent, untouched for around 1,800 years. He called what he found 'one of the most important discoveries in the history of Mexico.' At the tunnel's end, what was lying on the floor?
answer: Pools of liquid mercury
choices: Pools of liquid mercury
Stacks of gold coins
A buried wooden ship
Rows of empty thrones
context: Gomez found pools of liquid mercury, with walls dusted in powdered pyrite and magnetite that glittered like stars — the builders had recreated the starry underworld underground. The tunnel also held tens of thousands of objects, including hundreds of mysterious pyrite-coated yellow spheres whose purpose is still unknown. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_the_Feathered_Serpent,_Teotihuacan; ancient-origins.net.

question: On January 16, 378 CE, a warlord marched into the distant Maya city of Tikal — and that very same day Tikal's king, Chak Tok Ich'aak ('Jaguar Paw'), died. Within a year a boy was crowned Tikal's new king, said to be the son of a Teotihuacan lord. Maya carvings give this warlord a fearsome name. What did his name, Siyaj K'ak', mean?
answer: Fire Is Born
choices: Fire Is Born
Smoking Frog
Stone Jaguar
Lightning Sky
context: Siyaj K'ak' — 'Fire Is Born' — arrived under the authority of a Teotihuacan lord called Spearthrower Owl; within a year a boy claimed as Spearthrower Owl's son took Tikal's throne. Many scholars call this the 'entrada,' Teotihuacan's reach into the Maya world. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siyaj_K%CA%BCak%CA%BC; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spearthrower_Owl.

question: Around 550 CE the heart of Teotihuacan was burned and smashed. Sifting the wreckage, archaeologists found the fire had not struck the city evenly at all — one kind of building bore almost all the destruction, while others were spared. Which buildings took the brunt of the burning?
answer: The rulers' palaces and temples
choices: The rulers' palaces and temples
Every home in the city equally
The outer city walls and gates
The foreign merchants' quarters
context: The systematic burning targeted mainly the palaces and temples of the ruling class, not ordinary homes — pointing many archaeologists to an internal uprising or revolt rather than a foreign army. Famine in the harsh '535-536 mystery cloud' years may have lit the fuse. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teotihuacan.

question: Egypt left god-kings in golden tombs; the Maya carved boastful portraits of their rulers in stone. Yet for all Teotihuacan's size, archaeologists have found no royal tomb, no king's portrait, and no inscription naming a single ruler. From this strange silence, what kind of government do many archaeologists now think the city had?
answer: A shared or collective rule by noble houses
choices: A shared or collective rule by noble houses
A single god-king on a golden throne
A line of warrior-pharaohs
A foreign Aztec overlord
context: Wikipedia notes 'evidence of a king or other authoritarian ruler is strikingly absent.' Many archaeologists now propose collective or shared government — perhaps competing noble houses — rather than one god-king, making Teotihuacan unlike Egypt or the Maya. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teotihuacan; National Geographic.

question: In March 1974, near the city of Xi'an in China, a farmer named Yang Zhifa and his brothers were digging a well during a drought when their shovels struck something about four meters down. They had broken into a buried pit holding thousands of what?
answer: Life-sized soldiers made of clay
choices: Life-sized soldiers made of clay
Chests of gold and jade coins
Stone tablets carved with laws
Bones from an ancient battle
context: The farmers first thought the clay head was a 'Pottery God.' They had stumbled onto the Terracotta Army — roughly 8,000 life-sized clay soldiers buried to guard the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, China's first emperor. Source: travelchinaguide.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army

question: About 8,000 life-sized clay soldiers stand in battle formation guarding the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, China's first emperor. When you walk down the rows and look from soldier to soldier, what is strange about them?
answer: Every single warrior has a different face
choices: Every single warrior has a different face
They all face away from the tomb
Each one is shorter than the last
None of them were given any weapons
context: Artisans built the heads from about ten basic molds, then hand-pressed extra clay onto each one to give every soldier unique features, hair, and expression. Rank was readable too — generals stand up to about 2 meters, taller than the footsoldiers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army; history.com

question: Every clay soldier in the Terracotta Army was originally painted in bright colors — pink skin, black hair, robes of red, green, blue, and purple — and the paint survived 2,200 years sealed underground. Then archaeologists dug the warriors out into the open air. What happened to the colors?
answer: They began flaking off within minutes of hitting the air
choices: They began flaking off within minutes of hitting the air
They glowed faintly for several nights
They slowly faded over the next ten years
They washed away in the first rainfall
context: The paint sat on a thin lacquer layer that dried and curled the instant it met dry air — colors started changing in about 15 seconds and flaked off within four minutes of being unearthed. That is why most of the warriors today look bare gray. Source: travelchinaguide.com; ecns.cn

question: In 9 AD the emperor Augustus learned that three whole Roman legions had been ambushed and wiped out in the forests of Germania. He tore his clothes, let his hair and beard grow ragged for months, and kept beating his head against the doorposts, crying out the name of the dead general. What did Augustus shout?
answer: "Quintilius Varus, give me back my legions!"
choices: "Quintilius Varus, give me back my legions!"
"Carthage must be destroyed at any cost!"
"You too, my child, have you betrayed me?"
"Let the dice be cast, the river is crossed!"
context: The Latin was 'Quintili Vare, legiones redde!' The commander Publius Quinctilius Varus had marched the 17th, 18th, and 19th legions to their destruction; Augustus kept the anniversary of the defeat as a personal day of mourning for the rest of his life. Source: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 23.

question: When three Roman legions were ambushed and annihilated in the forests of Germania in 9 AD, the man who sprang the trap, Arminius, was no stranger to the Roman commander Varus. So who exactly was Arminius to the Romans he slaughtered?
answer: A trusted officer in Varus's own army, Roman-trained and secretly plotting
choices: A trusted officer in Varus's own army, Roman-trained and secretly plotting
A foreign king who had openly declared war on Rome the year before
A runaway gladiator leading an army of escaped slaves
A rival Roman senator competing with Varus for command of the legions
context: Arminius was a Cherusci chieftain raised in Rome as a hostage, trained as a Roman officer, made a citizen and equestrian, and serving as a squadron leader under Varus while secretly arranging the ambush. The disaster stopped Rome's expansion cold and made the Rhine River its permanent frontier forever after. Source: worldhistory.org/article/1010; britannica.com/event/Battle-of-the-Teutoburg-Forest.

question: When the caliph al-Mansur founded a brand-new capital on the Tigris in 762, he laid the whole city out in one unusual shape about two kilometers across, said to copy the geometric order he had studied in Euclid. What shape was the city?
answer: A perfect circle
choices: A perfect circle
A perfect square
A five-pointed star
A crescent moon
context: It became known as the Round City of Baghdad. Al-Mansur reportedly studied Euclid and laid the streets out to display geometric order. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round_City_of_Baghdad

question: Al-Mansur's round capital on the Tigris is famous today as Baghdad, but that everyday name came from an older settlement on the site, not from him. What hopeful name did al-Mansur officially give his new round capital?
answer: Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace
choices: Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace
Dar al-Khilafa, the House of the Caliph
Madinat al-Nur, the City of Light
Bab al-Dhahab, the Gate of Gold
context: Madinat al-Salam means City of Peace. The everyday name Baghdad came from an older settlement on the site. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round_City_of_Baghdad

question: The Round City of Baghdad had exactly four great gates in its ringed walls. How were those four gates named?
answer: Each was named for the far-off city its road led toward
choices: Each was named for the far-off city its road led toward
Each was named after one of the four seasons
Each was named for a son of the caliph
Each was named after a planet in the sky
context: The four gates were Bab al-Kufa, Bab al-Basra, Bab al-Sham (toward Damascus), and Bab al-Khorasan, where the Great Khorasan Road to Central Asia began. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round_City_of_Baghdad

question: At the dead center of the Round City stood al-Mansur's own palace and main mosque, while everyone else's houses were pushed out to the rings. The palace was crowned with a single landmark that gave it its grand nickname. What topped the Palace of the Golden Gate?
answer: A great green dome
choices: A great green dome
A pair of bronze lions
A spire of pure silver
A garden of palm trees
context: The central plaza was kept almost empty around the caliph's palace and mosque. The green dome made the palace visible from far across the city. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round_City_of_Baghdad

question: The caliph Harun al-Rashid wanted to dazzle the distant Frankish emperor Charlemagne, so he sent an astonishing living gift the whole way from Baghdad to Aachen, arriving in July 802. What did Harun send?
answer: A live elephant
choices: A live elephant
A flock of peacocks
A giant tortoise
A team of camels
context: The Asian elephant was named Abul-Abbas and was escorted by the envoy Isaac the Jew across North Africa and over the Alps. It died in 810 of pneumonia near the Rhine. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abul-Abbas

question: Harun al-Rashid's elephant, Abul-Abbas, is named in two Frankish sources, the Royal Frankish Annals and Einhard's Life of Charlemagne. There is one strange gap in the record of this famous gift. What is missing?
answer: No surviving Abbasid record mentions the gift at all
choices: No surviving Abbasid record mentions the gift at all
No one ever wrote down the elephant's name
The Frankish texts never say where it arrived
Charlemagne's own letters deny receiving it
context: The gift is well documented on the Frankish side but absent from surviving Baghdad records, an odd one-sided memory of a famous exchange. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abul-Abbas

question: The Arabic word al-jabr appears in the title of a mathematics book written at Baghdad's House of Wisdom by the scholar al-Khwarizmi. That single word grew into a subject every schoolchild now studies. Which English word came from al-jabr?
answer: Algebra
choices: Algebra
Almanac
Alchemy
Alcohol
context: His book was Al-Kitab al-mukhtasar fi hisab al-jabr wal-muqabala. The Latin form of his own name, Algoritmi, separately gave us the word algorithm. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Khwarizmi

question: At Baghdad's House of Wisdom, scholars translated Greek, Persian, Sanskrit, and Syriac books into Arabic. Much of the hardest Greek-to-Arabic work was done by one group, a fact showing the Golden Age was the work of many faiths together. Who did much of that Greek translating?
answer: Syriac-speaking Nestorian Christian scholars
choices: Syriac-speaking Nestorian Christian scholars
Buddhist monks traveling from India
Norse traders settled in the city
Egyptian temple priests
context: Nestorian Christians already read Syriac and Greek, making them vital translators. The so-called Islamic Golden Age drew on Christians, Jews, Zoroastrians, and others. Source: https://www.middleeasteye.net/discover/iraq-baghdad-house-wisdom-uniting-east-west

question: Harun al-Rashid's glittering Baghdad court, with his vizier Jafar the Barmakid and the poet Abu Nuwas, was remembered for centuries in a beloved collection of tales in which Harun himself wanders the city in disguise. Which collection grew up around his court?
answer: The Thousand and One Nights
choices: The Thousand and One Nights
Aesop's Fables
The Canterbury Tales
The Tales of King Arthur
context: In the stories, Harun slips through Baghdad in disguise to see his city by night. The disguised-caliph adventures are legend, not court record. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Thousand_and_One_Nights

question: At its ninth-to-tenth-century peak Baghdad may have passed one million people, making it the largest city on Earth. To picture how huge that was, it stood shoulder to shoulder with the great capital at the other end of the trade roads. Which rival giant city did Baghdad match?
answer: Tang China's Chang'an
choices: Tang China's Chang'an
Aztec Tenochtitlan
Inca Cusco
Viking Hedeby
context: Baghdad and Chang'an were the twin giants of the medieval world, anchoring the western and eastern ends of the Silk Road. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baghdad

question: The caliph al-Ma'mun loved knowledge so much he funded teams to do something no ruler had organized before: he sent astronomers onto the flat plain of Sinjar around 830, one party walking due north and one due south, carefully pacing out a single degree along the ground. What were they measuring?
answer: The size of the whole Earth
choices: The size of the whole Earth
The distance to the Moon
The height of the tallest mountain
The speed of a galloping horse
context: By pacing out how far you walk to cover one degree of the planet's curve, you can calculate Earth's whole circumference. Al-Ma'mun's teams got remarkably close to the true value. Source: https://www.chalkefestival.com/history-hub/writing/power-and-curiosity-how-the-abbasid-caliph-al-mamun-pushed-the-boundaries-of-scientific-knowledge/

question: In February 1258 Hulagu Khan's Mongols stormed Baghdad and ended the five-hundred-year Abbasid line. The Mongols believed it taboo to spill royal blood on the ground, so they killed the last caliph, al-Musta'sim, in a strange bloodless way. How was he put to death?
answer: He was rolled inside a carpet and trampled by horses
choices: He was rolled inside a carpet and trampled by horses
He was thrown from the highest tower
He was beheaded before the city gate
He was drowned in the Tigris river
context: The carpet kept his royal blood from touching the earth. Some sources say instead he was starved, so the exact manner is disputed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Musta%27sim

question: Legend says the Mongols hurled so many books from Baghdad's libraries into the Tigris that the river ran black with ink. The historian Michal Biran dug into what really became of the city's learning and found this total-erasure tale was overstated. What did Biran show actually happened?
answer: Large libraries reopened for teaching within two years
choices: Large libraries reopened for teaching within two years
The books had all been moved to Maragha before the siege
Only the caliph's own palace collection was destroyed
Monasteries outside the city secretly kept every copy
context: The black-ink river is a dramatic legend; Baghdad's intellectual life was wounded but not erased, with teaching resuming within a couple of years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Baghdad

question: At the 1258 siege of Baghdad the last caliph still commanded twenty thousand cavalry, yet the Mongols beat that army before the real fight even began. Without charging the horsemen head-on, the Mongols turned the wet ground itself against them. What did the Mongols do to trap the riders?
answer: They broke the dikes and flooded the ground behind the army
choices: They broke the dikes and flooded the ground behind the army
They poisoned every well outside the walls
They set the whole grain harvest on fire
They built a wall to cut off the bridges
context: By breaking the dikes of the Tigris-side canals, the Mongols turned the ground behind the cavalry to mud and water, trapping and crushing them. Engineering, not just numbers, doomed Baghdad. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Baghdad

question: In November 1942, workers at Kaiser's Richmond, California shipyard wanted to prove America could build cargo ships faster than German U-boats could sink them. They fitted together about 250,000 parts to assemble one whole Liberty ship, the SS Robert E. Peary. How long did the whole ship take?
answer: About 4 days
choices: About 4 days
About 4 weeks
About 4 months
About 4 hours
context: The SS Robert E. Peary was assembled in 4 days, 15 hours, and 29 minutes -- roughly 14 million pounds of steel snapped together as a deliberate message to the U-boats. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Robert_E._Peary

question: When America entered World War II, the government began rationing food so soldiers and the war effort got enough. Every family got War Ration Book Number One, nicknamed for the very first item the country rationed, on April 27, 1942. What was the first thing rationed?
answer: Sugar
choices: Sugar
Beef
Bread
Eggs
context: Families got about one pound of sugar per person every two weeks; the booklet was even nicknamed the 'Sugar Book.' Coffee followed in November 1942 when German U-boats sank the ships bringing it from Brazil. Source: https://www.nps.gov/articles/rationing-in-wwii.htm

question: Norman Rockwell painted his muscular 'Rosie the Riveter' for the Saturday Evening Post cover, posing her like a prophet from Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel with a rivet gun across her lap. To show exactly who she was fighting, he painted her loafers crushing one particular book underfoot. What book?
answer: Hitler's Mein Kampf
choices: Hitler's Mein Kampf
A German dictionary
The factory rulebook
Her own diary
context: Rockwell stamped her lunch pail 'Rosie' and put her shoes squarely on a copy of Mein Kampf -- the cover ran on Memorial Day, May 29, 1943. Source: https://www.nrm.org/rosie-the-riveter/

question: Before any poster or magazine cover, the name 'Rosie the Riveter' came from a catchy 1942 song that an African-American vocal group, The Four Vagabonds, turned into a 1943 hit. In the song, why is Rosie working so hard on the assembly line?
answer: To protect her marine boyfriend Charlie by building the planes he'd fly
choices: To protect her marine boyfriend Charlie by building the planes he'd fly
To win a prize being offered at her factory that year
To earn enough money to buy a house of her own
To follow in the footsteps of her riveter father
context: The Redd Evans and John Jacob Loeb song described Rosie guarding her sweetheart Charlie 'over there' by riveting the planes he flew -- the name caught on long before any of the famous images. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosie_the_Riveter

question: At Ford's mile-long Willow Run plant, production boss Charles Sorensen made a brash boast about how fast the factory would turn out four-engine B-24 Liberator bombers. By April 1944, running two nine-hour shifts six days a week, the plant actually hit his target. What was the astonishing pace?
answer: A finished bomber every 63 minutes
choices: A finished bomber every 63 minutes
A finished bomber every single day
A finished bomber every working week
Ten finished bombers every single hour
context: Sorensen's boast was 'a bomber an hour,' and Willow Run rolled one out every 63 minutes. Charles Lindbergh, a Ford consultant and test pilot, called the giant factory 'the Grand Canyon of a mechanized world.' Source: https://interestingengineering.com/culture/how-fords-willow-run-factory-turned-car-assembly-lines-into-bombers-built-by-the-hour

question: The 'We Can Do It!' poster, with its bandana-wearing woman flexing her arm, was painted by J. Howard Miller in 1942 as a brief factory morale poster for Westinghouse -- shown to workers for only about two weeks before it vanished for decades. For years people thought a Michigan worker was the woman behind it, until Seton Hall professor James Kimble proved in 2016 it was really a California shipyard worker photographed in 1942. Who was she?
answer: Naomi Parker Fraley
choices: Naomi Parker Fraley
Geraldine Hoff Doyle
Mary Doyle Keefe
Rose Will Monroe
context: The 1942 photo of Naomi Parker Fraley at a lathe in Alameda, California carried a caption warning she 'might catch her nose in the turret lathe she is operating.' Fraley lived to 96 before Kimble set the record straight in 2016. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/naomi-parker-fraley-real-rosie-riveter-has-died-96-180967935/

question: In the ancient world almost everyone worshipped many gods. The Hebrews were different: their central daily declaration, the Shema, begins 'Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is...' What single word ends that line and sums up the whole tradition?
answer: one
choices: one
mighty
holy
near
context: The Shema (Hebrew for 'Hear,' from Deuteronomy 6:4) is the heartbeat of Hebrew faith: in a world of countless gods, they insisted there was only ONE. Source: https://pluralism.org/god-biblical-monotheism ; Deuteronomy 6:4.

question: On the night of the tenth plague in Egypt, each Hebrew family killed a lamb and, with a bunch of hyssop, smeared its blood on the doorposts and lintel of their home. When death came for Egypt's firstborn that night, what did it do at the blood-marked houses that gave the holiday its name?
answer: it passed over them
choices: it passed over them
it knelt before them
it wept outside them
it fled the whole land
context: Death 'passed over' the blood-marked homes (Exodus 12) — remembered every year ever since as Passover. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passover ; Exodus 12:7,13. (Told as the tradition tells it.)  (Legend.)

question: Moses came down from Mount Sinai carrying two stone tablets fresh from God — and found the Hebrews dancing around an idol they had melted down and built while he was gone. In a rage, Moses smashed the tablets. What was the idol they had made?
answer: a golden calf
choices: a golden calf
a bronze serpent
a silver throne
a stone eagle
context: The golden calf (Exodus 32): Moses shattered the first set of tablets and had to climb Sinai again for a second. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Ten-Commandments ; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Sinai-covenant ; Exodus 32. (Told as the tradition tells it.)  (Legend.)

question: At the burning bush, Moses asks God what name to give the Israelites. God answers with a name that is not a label at all but a statement about His own existence, and tells Moses to say that this is who sent him. What does God tell Moses to say His name is?
answer: I AM
choices: I AM
I WILL BE
I MADE ALL
I FORGET NONE
context: 'I AM WHO I AM' (Ehyeh asher Ehyeh, Exodus 3:14) — 'I AM has sent me to you.' Not a label for one deity among many, but the self-existent, eternal One. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Am_that_I_Am ; Exodus 3:14. (Told as the tradition tells it.)  (Legend.)

question: The Hebrews wrote God's personal name with four letters — YHWH, the 'Tetragrammaton' — but came to consider it so holy that they stopped speaking it aloud entirely, reading a different word in its place. That very ancient habit is why English Bibles still do what when they reach that name?
answer: print 'the LORD' in small capitals
choices: print 'the LORD' in small capitals
leave a blank space on the page
spell it out as four letters
translate it as 'the Nameless'
context: Because Jews said 'Adonai' rather than pronounce YHWH, translators mark the spot with small-capital LORD to this day. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Am_that_I_Am ; https://www.biblestudytools.com/bible-study/topical-studies/why-does-god-call-himself-i-am-that-i-am.html

question: The Hebrews told their whole history as one long covenant — a binding agreement between God and a people. It begins with a promise to a single man that his descendants would become a great nation loyal to the one God. Which figure, the start of that chain, is later called 'the father of monotheism'?
answer: Abraham
choices: Abraham
Noah
Solomon
Joshua
context: God's promise to Abraham underlies the later Sinai covenant; the Hebrew story is one continuous binding agreement. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Sinai-covenant ; https://www.chapelwithoutwalls.org/sermons/2020/7/26/monotheism-and-the-jews.html. (Told as the tradition tells it.)  (Legend.)

question: In July of 587/586 BCE the Babylonian army under King Nebuchadnezzar broke into Jerusalem and carried the Hebrews off into exile. Before they marched the people away, they burned down the great sanctuary that King Solomon had built generations earlier. Which building did the Babylonians destroy?
answer: Solomon's Temple
choices: Solomon's Temple
the king's palace
the city granaries
the eastern gate
context: The burning of Solomon's Temple is still mourned every year on the fast of Tisha B'Av. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/Babylonian-Captivity ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Jerusalem_(587_BC).

question: Rabbi David Wolpe calls a single Hebrew idea 'Judaism's greatest gift to the world' — the startling claim that every human being, slave or king, rich or poor, carries the same God-given dignity. According to that idea, every person is made in the image of what?
answer: God
choices: God
the king
the law
the stars
context: The imago Dei (Genesis 1:27): dignity is not earned by rank or wealth but given to all alike; historians credit it as a headwater of universal human rights. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image_of_God ; https://www.holypost.com/post/imago-dei-the-foundation-of-human-dignity ; Genesis 1:27.

question: The exile ended when Cyrus the Great of Persia conquered Babylon in 539 BCE and let the deported peoples go home. So grateful was the Hebrew Bible that it gave this foreign, non-Israelite king a sacred honorific it grants to no other outsider — calling him God's what (Isaiah 45:1)?
answer: his anointed one
choices: his anointed one
his chosen prophet
his second Moses
his true son
context: 'Anointed' translates to 'messiah' — and Cyrus is the only foreigner ever given the title. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/Babylonian-Captivity ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_to_Zion ; Isaiah 45:1.

question: The Hebrew prophet Amos raged at a society that cheated the poor — rigging its scales and 'selling the needy for a pair of sandals.' To Amos, mistreating the widow and the orphan was an offense against God Himself, and he demanded one thing in a single thundering line. Which words are his?
answer: Let justice roll down like waters
choices: Let justice roll down like waters
Blessed are the poor in spirit
Love your neighbor as yourself
Walk humbly with your God
context: '...and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream' (Amos 5:24). The prophets fused worship with justice. Source: https://www.ibelieve.com/christian-living/what-does-let-justice-roll-like-a-river-mean-amos.html ; Amos 5:24, Amos 2:6.

question: Far from their ruined city, deep in their conquerors' land, the exiled Hebrews wrote one of the most famous laments ever set down, vowing 'If I forget you, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill.' How does that psalm — Psalm 137 — open?
answer: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept
choices: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept
Out of the depths I have cried unto thee, O Lord
How long, O Lord, wilt thou forget me forever
The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want
context: '...when we remembered Zion.' The grief of the Babylonian exile, set to verse. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/Babylonian-Captivity ; Psalm 137.

question: In 1979, inside a burial cave at Ketef Hinnom near Jerusalem, archaeologists found the oldest words of the Hebrew Bible ever discovered — dated to around 600 BCE, four centuries older than the Dead Sea Scrolls. Worn as protective amulets, what physical objects carried the text?
answer: two tiny silver scrolls
choices: two tiny silver scrolls
a clay prayer tablet
a painted papyrus strip
a carved cedar box
context: The scrolls (about 2.5 cm) carry the Priestly Blessing of Numbers 6: 'The LORD bless you and keep you...' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ketef_Hinnom_scrolls ; https://biblearchaeology.org/research-articles/the-blessing-of-the-silver-scrolls/.

question: Winners at the ancient Olympic Games were the most celebrated men in Greece, yet the champion of each event was handed no gold and no money. What did an Olympic victor actually receive as his prize?
answer: A crown of wild olive leaves
choices: A crown of wild olive leaves
A purse of silver coins
A bronze statue of himself
A team of racing horses
context: The prize was the kotinos, a crown of wild olive cut with a golden sickle from one sacred tree at Olympia called the Kallistephanos ('tree of the beautiful crown'), said to have been planted by Hercules. The glory, not the goods, was the reward. Source: World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Olympic_Games/.

question: Greek athletes at Olympia followed one custom that startles people today, traced to about 720 BC and to a runner named Orsippos of Megara. How did the athletes compete in their events?
answer: Completely naked
choices: Completely naked
In matching white tunics
Wearing painted leather masks
Barefoot but cloaked in red
context: The story goes that Orsippos of Megara lost his loincloth during a race in 720 BC; afterward Greek athletes competed nude, the body itself displayed as a tribute to Zeus. Source: World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Olympic_Games/; GreekReporter, 'Why Did Athletes in the Ancient Olympic Games Compete in the Nude?'

question: The Greek city-states fought each other constantly, but before every Olympic Games heralds traveled out from Elis proclaiming the ekecheiria, the sacred truce. As long as it held, what did this truce demand of all Greece?
answer: All wars stopped and no army could enter Elis
choices: All wars stopped and no army could enter Elis
Every city sent a tribute of grain to Olympia
All slaves were freed for the month of the festival
Each city closed its temples until the Games ended
context: The ekecheiria halted fighting across Greece so athletes and as many as 40,000 spectators could travel to Olympia safely; no one could carry weapons into Elis. It was eventually extended to three months. Source: World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Olympic_Games/; International Olympic Truce Centre, olympictruce.org.

question: Milon of Kroton was the most famous champion of the ancient Games, winning the wrestling crown six times. Legend says he built his enormous strength with one strange daily routine. According to the story, what did Milon do every day to train?
answer: Carried a young calf until it grew into a bull
choices: Carried a young calf until it grew into a bull
Wrestled a different opponent at every dawn
Swam against the current of a mountain river
Lifted the bronze gates of his city at sunrise
context: The legend says Milon carried a calf daily until it became a full-grown bull, which he then carried around the stadium, killed, and ate in a single day. He won the boys' crown in 540 BC and then five straight men's titles, 532-516 BC. Told as legend. Source: Britannica, 'Milo of Croton'; World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Olympic_Games/.

question: Cheating at Olympia was rare partly because of a clever punishment: an athlete caught breaking the rules had to pay a heavy fine, and the officials spent that fine money in a way meant to shame him forever. What did the fines pay for?
answer: Bronze statues of Zeus that every athlete walked past
choices: Bronze statues of Zeus that every athlete walked past
A marble wall carved with the cheater's full name
A feast for the rivals the cheater had wronged
A new gate barring him from ever returning
context: The fines paid for bronze statues of Zeus called 'Zanes,' lined up along the path to the stadium so every competitor passed them on the way in. The stone bases of the Zanes are still visible at Olympia today. Source: World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Olympic_Games/; Working Classicists, 'Ancient Athletics Part Three: No Cheating!'

question: The Assyrians built history's first true army out of a single metal — cheap enough to mass-produce, so they could equip a standing professional force of up to 200,000 men, the largest the ancient Near East had ever seen. Which metal armed the Assyrian war machine?
answer: Iron
choices: Iron
Bronze
Copper
Tin
context: The Assyrians fielded history's first true iron army. Iron weapons were not only sharper than bronze but could be mass-produced, so they equipped a standing force of 150,000 to 200,000 men. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Neo-Assyrian_Empire/

question: King Ashurbanipal commanded the Assyrian war machine at its height, but he bragged about a skill that set him apart from every warrior-king before him — a skill so rare for a king that he was proud to have trained for it as a boy. What was Ashurbanipal's unusual skill?
answer: He could read and write
choices: He could read and write
He could tame wild lions
He could forge iron weapons
He could speak to the gods
context: Ashurbanipal trained as an apprentice scribe and mastered the wedge-shaped cuneiform script, even learning the ancient Sumerian language — then ordered cities across his empire to send copies of every text they had. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Ashurbanipal

question: To show off his glittering new capital at Kalhu in 879 BCE, King Ashurnasirpal II threw a feast that lasted ten days and fed nearly 70,000 guests. He had the whole menu carved in stone to brag about it — including 1,000 oxen and 10,000 fish. Which drink did he serve, 10,000 jars of it?
answer: Beer
choices: Beer
Wine
Mead
Milk
context: Ashurnasirpal II's Banquet Stele records 69,574 guests and a menu of 1,000 oxen, 14,000 sheep, 10,000 fish, 10,000 eggs, and 10,000 jars of beer. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Ashurnasirpal_II/

question: King Ashurbanipal gathered over 30,000 clay tablets at Nineveh — the first great library in the world. In 612 BCE his enemies stormed the city and set it ablaze. What did that fire do to the clay tablets?
answer: Baked them rock-hard
choices: Baked them rock-hard
Burned them to ashes
Melted them into glass
Crumbled them to dust
context: When Nineveh burned in 612 BCE, the fire baked the clay tablets hard instead of destroying them, accidentally preserving the first systematically gathered library in the world for us to read today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Ashurbanipal

question: Because the Assyrians' great library at Nineveh accidentally survived the city's burning, one ancient poem came down to us — the oldest great story humans ever wrote, telling of a hero who survives a world-drowning flood and sends out a dove from his ship. What is this oldest surviving epic?
answer: The Epic of Gilgamesh
choices: The Epic of Gilgamesh
The Epic of Atrahasis
The Epic of Creation
The Epic of Etana
context: Among the tablets Ashurbanipal's library preserved was the Epic of Gilgamesh — the oldest great story ever written, including a flood account with a man building a boat and sending out a dove. The brutal Assyrians are the reason humanity still has this poem at all. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Ashurbanipal

question: In 701 BCE King Sennacherib of Assyria surrounded Jerusalem and its king, Hezekiah. On a six-sided clay prism he bragged about the siege — yet his own words quietly admit he never actually captured the city. Sennacherib boasted that he had shut Hezekiah up like what, inside his royal city?
answer: A caged bird
choices: A caged bird
A cornered rat
A chained dog
A netted fish
context: Sennacherib's prism reads: 'As for Hezekiah... I shut him up like a caged bird in his royal city of Jerusalem.' Strikingly, the inscription never claims he captured the city — the Assyrian king's own brag admits Jerusalem held out. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sennacherib's_Annals

question: The Assyrians describe siege ramps all over their inscriptions, but archaeologists have ever dug up only ONE of them — at Lachish, a colossal mound of roughly three million stones. Buried inside it, astonishingly, they recovered the very iron object that once swung the one-ton battering ram. Which iron piece survived in the ramp?
answer: An iron chain
choices: An iron chain
An iron axle
An iron blade
An iron hook
context: At Lachish in 701 BCE the Assyrians built a siege ramp of about three million stones (roughly 20,000 tons) to haul battering rams up to the walls. It is the only Assyrian siege ramp ever found, and archaeologists even recovered the iron chain that swung the ram. Source: https://phys.org/news/2021-11-siege-ramps-breached-walls-ancient.html

question: When the holy city of Babylon rebelled against him, King Sennacherib decided to wipe it off the map so completely that no one would ever remember where it had stood. In his own inscription he describes exactly what he did to erase the city in 689 BCE. How did Sennacherib destroy Babylon?
answer: He flooded it with water
choices: He flooded it with water
He burned it with fire
He buried it in sand
He smashed it with rams
context: Sennacherib bragged: 'In order that the site of that city and its temples would never be remembered, I devastated it with water so that it became a mere meadow.' He dug canals and flooded the ruins flat. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/745/the-mutual-destruction-of-sennacherib--babylon/

question: The Assyrians invented a chilling new way to crush rebellion: rather than just defeat a people, they marched the whole population off to distant lands so they could never rise again. After Sargon II captured Samaria and deported its 27,290 people, those exiled Israelite tribes earned a famous name. What are the deported tribes of Israel called?
answer: The Ten Lost Tribes
choices: The Ten Lost Tribes
The Babylonian Exiles
The Wandering Tribes
The Forgotten Twelve
context: The Assyrians invented mass deportation as state policy to break rebellion. Sargon II recorded: 'I besieged and conquered Samaria, led away as booty 27,290 inhabitants of it.' The exiled northern tribes of Israel became known as the Ten Lost Tribes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assyrian_captivity

question: Most conquerors hid their cruelties, but King Ashurnasirpal II carved his into a royal inscription as a BOAST, meant to be read aloud so rival cities would surrender in terror. According to his own proud words, what did he do to the chiefs of a city that had rebelled against him?
answer: Flayed them and hung their skins on a pillar
choices: Flayed them and hung their skins on a pillar
Burned them alive inside their own temple
Hurled them down from the high city walls
Buried them alive beneath the city gate
context: Ashurnasirpal II boasted in his own inscription: 'I built a pillar over against the city gate and I flayed all the chiefs who had revolted and I covered the pillar with their skins.' The Assyrians recorded their terror as a point of pride, not shame — deliberate psychological warfare, written to be feared. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Ashurnasirpal_II/

question: Among the carvings from King Ashurbanipal's palace at Nineveh — praised as the supreme masterpieces of Assyrian art — one panel from about 645 BCE is singled out as one of the greatest artworks of the entire ancient world, prized for the raw realism of a single wounded creature pierced with arrows. What is this famous carving called?
answer: The Dying Lioness
choices: The Dying Lioness
The Dying Lion
The Wounded Lion
The Roaring Lion
context: The 'Dying Lioness' shows a wounded lioness roaring as she drags her paralyzed hind legs, pierced by arrows. Part of Ashurbanipal's Royal Lion Hunt reliefs (British Museum), it is praised as one of the greatest works of art from the entire ancient world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lion_Hunt_of_Ashurbanipal

question: In 1872 the self-taught scholar George Smith was quietly reading a clay tablet from Nineveh's ruined library in the British Museum when he suddenly realized its ancient words described a great flood and a ship landing on a mountain — a story echoing Noah's. He was so overwhelmed that, as the tale is told, he did what right there in the museum room?
answer: Tore off his clothes and ran about shouting
choices: Tore off his clothes and ran about shouting
Leapt onto a table and danced wildly
Kissed the tablet and burst into song
Fainted dead away onto the floor
context: Reading a Nineveh tablet, George Smith realized it described a great flood and a ship landing on a mountain; he reportedly began tearing off his clothes and ran around the room shouting. Weeks later he lectured on it before Prime Minister Gladstone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Smith_(Assyriologist)

question: King Sennacherib lined his palace at Nineveh with enormous stone carvings of his conquest of the city of Lachish, captioned as 'the booty of Lachish passed before him' while he watched from his throne. Long after his death, someone crept up to these carvings and deliberately destroyed one specific part of the king's own image. What part of Sennacherib did they chisel away?
answer: His face
choices: His face
His hands
His feet
His crown
context: The Lachish reliefs (now in the British Museum) show captives executed before the enthroned king, beneath the caption naming him 'king of the world, king of Assyria.' Sennacherib's own face was deliberately chiseled out in antiquity. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lachish_reliefs

question: For centuries the Assyrian Empire terrified the whole Near East, and its capital Nineveh seemed unstoppable — the Hebrew prophet Nahum had even written a whole short book promising this proud city would one day fall. Then in 612 BCE an army of Medes and Babylonians laid siege to Nineveh, broke through its walls, and burned it to the ground. After the empire had dominated for centuries, how long did the siege take to bring mighty Nineveh down?
answer: Three months
choices: Three months
Seven years
A single night
Twenty years
context: In 612 BCE a coalition of Medes and Babylonians besieged Nineveh, broke in after just three months, and burned it. The Hebrew prophet Nahum had foretold the city's fall in the biblical Book of Nahum; after dominating the Near East for centuries, Assyria was gone within a few years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Nineveh

question: On the stretch of West African coast that Europeans called the Slave Coast, traders did not buy captured people with gold or silver coins. They paid in small white seashells, fished thousands of miles away in the Maldive Islands and shipped to Africa by the ton as ballast. Between 1500 and 1875 at least 30 billion of them were unloaded at the Bight of Benin alone. What were these shells called?
answer: Cowrie shells
choices: Cowrie shells
Conch trumpets
Scallop tokens
Nautilus beads
context: Cowries were the working money of the Slave Coast: tiny shells gathered in the faraway Maldives, carried west as ship ballast, and counted out by the thousand to buy human beings. (projectmanifest.eu/cowries-the-currency-of-trading-en-fr; theconversation.com/small-seashells-tell-a-big-story-of-slavery-and-transoceanic-trade-500-years-ago-166363)

question: From the 1500s to the 1800s the enslaved Africans carried across the Atlantic did not all go to the same place. One single country, home to vast sugar and gold colonies in the New World, received almost half of all of them, far more than any other place in the Americas. Which country took in by far the most enslaved Africans?
answer: Brazil
choices: Brazil
Jamaica
Cuba
The United States
context: About 46 percent of all enslaved Africans who reached the New World were landed in Brazil, roughly 4.9 to 5.5 million people, to work the sugar and gold colonies of Portugal. Most people wrongly assume the United States was the main destination. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_slave_trade_to_Brazil)

question: Ask most Americans where the enslaved Africans were taken, and they will say the United States. In fact only about 388,000 captives were carried straight to mainland North America, while the rest were landed in Brazil and the Caribbean by the millions. Of every hundred Africans shipped across the Atlantic in the whole trade, how many came directly to what is now the United States?
answer: Fewer than four
choices: Fewer than four
About twenty-five
About fifty
About sixty-five
context: Only about 388,000 of the roughly 10.7 million survivors were carried directly to mainland North America, under 4 percent of the whole trade, a strikingly small share that surprises most people. (pbs.org/wnet/african-americans-many-rivers-to-cross/history/how-many-slaves-landed-in-the-us)

question: At European slave forts on the African coast, such as Cape Coast Castle and Elmina, captives were marched in chains through one final seaward doorway and straight down into the boats that rowed them out to the waiting ships. For the people forced through it, that doorway was the last they ever saw of their homeland. By what stark name is that doorway remembered today?
answer: The Door of No Return
choices: The Door of No Return
The Gate of Sorrows
The Iron Threshold
The Weeping Arch
context: Once a person stepped through the Door of No Return onto the boats, they never came back. Excavators at these castles later found dungeon waste compacted up to 30 cm deep, with iron shackles and cowrie shells still in it. (thinkglobalheritage.wordpress.com/2016/11/30/dark-heritage-the-door-of-no-return-at-elmina-castle-in-ghana)

question: The Atlantic trade ran in a great triangle. European ships carried guns and cloth to Africa and traded them for captives; the captives were shipped across the Middle Passage and sold in the Caribbean and Brazil for sugar and molasses; and the molasses was shipped north to New England. There the colonists boiled it down into one product, which was then carried back to Africa to buy still more captives. What did New England make from the molasses?
answer: Rum
choices: Rum
Beer
Wine
Gin
context: The loop closed on itself: molasses from slave-grown sugar was distilled into New England rum, and the rum was shipped back to Africa to purchase more captives. The same cycle paid for itself again and again. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangular_trade)

question: Here is a hard truth about the Atlantic slave trade, told straight: the Europeans who bought captives at the coast rarely marched inland to seize people themselves. The captives were brought to them at the shore, already in chains, by sellers who had taken them in raids and wars. Who were these sellers who supplied most of the captives the Europeans bought?
answer: Other African kingdoms
choices: Other African kingdoms
Arab caravan traders
European sea pirates
Portuguese soldiers inland
context: Both truths stand together, and neither excuses the other: strong coastal kingdoms such as Dahomey, the Oyo Empire and the Asante made war on their neighbors and sold the prisoners at the shore for guns, cloth and shells, and European buyers shipped them into bondage. Dahomey controlled the slave port of Ouidah and profited so heavily that Britain had to force it to stop selling captives only in 1852. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dahomey; britannica.com/place/western-Africa/The-southward-expansion-of-Oyo)

question: Elmina Castle in Ghana, built by Portugal in 1482, is the oldest European building south of the Sahara. Below it sat a stone dungeon where hundreds of enslaved men were chained in the dark, waiting to be shipped across the ocean. Right above their heads, on the floor over the dungeon, the Portuguese built one particular room for themselves. What did they build directly on top of the male slave dungeon?
answer: A Christian church
choices: A Christian church
A gunpowder store
A grand ballroom
A grain warehouse
context: Worship above, chained captives below: the Portuguese held church services on the floor directly over the men's slave dungeon. (ancient-origins.net/ancient-places-africa/elmina-castle-and-its-dark-history-enslavement-torture-and-death-003450; witnesstreeinstitute.org/blog-2023/confronting-the-heartbreaking-truth-at-elmina-castle)

question: Olaudah Equiano was kidnapped from his African village as a boy and dragged aboard a slave ship. Decades later, freed and living in Britain, he wrote a memoir about the crossing that helped fuel the campaign to abolish the trade. He recalled that when the white sailors first hauled him below deck, with their red faces and loose hair, he was gripped by one terrified belief about what they meant to do to him. What did the boy Equiano fear the sailors were about to do?
answer: Eat him
choices: Eat him
Drown him
Whip him
Brand him
context: In his own words, Equiano asked whether 'we were not to be eaten by those white men with horrible looks, red faces, and loose hair.' His 1789 Interesting Narrative described a stench below deck so foul it was dangerous to stay there, and two chained captives who jumped into the sea rather than go on. (worldhistory.org/article/2672/olaudah-equianos-account-of-the-middle-passage; Equiano, Interesting Narrative, 1789)

question: In 1788 British abolitionists printed a diagram of the slave ship Brookes showing 482 human beings packed in rows with no space between them, the most the law allowed it to carry. The image became the most famous picture of the whole anti-slavery movement. Yet ship records showed that on an earlier voyage the real Brookes had broken even that crowded legal limit. How many people had it actually carried on that voyage?
answer: As many as 740
choices: As many as 740
About 560
Around 900
Over 1,100
context: The Brookes poster showed 482 people, the legal maximum, yet the ship had once crammed in as many as 740. Over 7,000 copies were printed, and it became the abolition movement's most iconic image. (abolitionseminar.org/brooks; encyclopediavirginia.org/4303hpr-7e68246b9587078)

question: After William Wilberforce and his allies won the Slave Trade Act of 1807, Britain sent a Royal Navy fleet called the West Africa Squadron to hunt down slave ships at sea for the next fifty years, capturing around 1,600 of them. Each captured ship still held chained Africans below deck. Over that half-century, about how many captives did the squadron set free?
answer: About 150,000
choices: About 150,000
About 1,500
About 15,000
About 1.5 million
context: Between 1808 and 1860 the West Africa Squadron seized about 1,600 slave ships and freed around 150,000 Africans. The captured ex-slaver HMS Black Joke alone took eleven slavers in a single year. The Royal Navy's African Names Database later recorded about 67,000 of these freed people by name, restoring identities the trade had tried to erase. (historic-uk.com/HistoryUK/HistoryofBritain/West-Africa-Squadron; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Africa_Squadron)

question: Historians built a database from the actual logbooks and sale records of the slave ships themselves, so the scale of the Atlantic trade is measured, not guessed. Between about 1525 and 1866, captured Africans were forced aboard ships bound for the Americas. About how many human beings were loaded onto those ships across the whole trade?
answer: About 12.5 million
choices: About 12.5 million
About 1.2 million
About 4 million
About 50 million
context: About 12.5 million Africans were forced aboard the ships; roughly 10.7 million survived the Middle Passage to step ashore alive, meaning between about 1.2 and 2.4 million died during the crossing itself, with many more dying in the raids and forced marches to the coast. (pbs.org/wnet/african-americans-many-rivers-to-cross/history/how-many-slaves-landed-in-the-us; Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database, eds. Eltis & Richardson)

question: Hunting slave ships was deadly work, and not only for the captives. Across half a century chasing slavers off the African coast, the Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron lost more than 1,500 of its own sailors, most of them to tropical disease rather than enemy fire. Contemporaries summed up the human cost of the campaign with a single grim ratio, comparing sailors lost to Africans freed. What was that ratio?
answer: One sailor dead for every nine slaves freed
choices: One sailor dead for every nine slaves freed
One sailor dead for every slave freed
One sailor dead for every hundred slaves freed
One sailor dead for every thousand slaves freed
context: Suppression cost Britain dearly: over 1,500 sailors died, summed up at the time as about one sailor for every nine slaves freed, and at its height the campaign consumed roughly 2 percent of national GDP. (historic-uk.com/HistoryUK/HistoryofBritain/West-Africa-Squadron)

question: On December 2, 1942, under the empty football stands at the University of Chicago, Enrico Fermi's team stacked graphite bricks laced with uranium into a 20-foot pile and pulled out the control rods. At 3:22 p.m. they made history with the world's first what?
answer: Controlled nuclear chain reaction
choices: Controlled nuclear chain reaction
Launch of a guided rocket
Working electric battery
Long-distance radio broadcast
context: Chicago Pile-1 (CP-1), built in a converted squash court, achieved the first controlled, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction. Source: https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/history/chicago-pile-1/

question: Just before dawn on July 16, 1945, the United States set off the world's first atomic bomb in the New Mexico desert. The plutonium device sat atop a 100-foot steel tower at a test site codenamed Trinity. What did the blast do to that steel tower?
answer: Vaporized it completely
choices: Vaporized it completely
Knocked it flat to the east
Left it standing and scorched
Buried it under sand
context: The Trinity device, nicknamed 'the Gadget,' detonated at 5:29:45 a.m. and vaporized the 100-foot tower it was hoisted on. Oppenheimer named the site 'Jornada del Muerto' (Journey of the Dead Man). Source: https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/history/trinity-test-1945/

question: The Trinity atomic blast was so hot it melted the desert floor, fusing the sand into a strange new substance scattered across the crater. Scientists gave this radioactive green glass its own name. What was it called?
answer: Trinitite
choices: Trinitite
Obsidian
Quartzite
Tektite
context: General Thomas Farrell described the flash as 'a searing light with the intensity many times that of the midday sun.' The heat fused the sand into a radioactive green glass named trinitite. Source: https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/history/trinity-test-1945/

question: The moment Fermi's reactor in Chicago proved a chain reaction worked, Arthur Compton phoned James Conant in a made-up code so no spy could understand. He said, 'The Italian navigator has landed in the New World.' Who was the 'Italian navigator' he meant?
answer: Enrico Fermi
choices: Enrico Fermi
Arthur Compton
Eugene Wigner
Niels Bohr
context: Fermi, like Columbus, was Italian — hence the code. Conant asked, 'How were the natives?' and Compton answered, 'Very friendly.' Source: https://www.lanl.gov/media/publications/the-vault/0822-chicago-pile

question: After Fermi's pile in Chicago went critical, the scientists had no speeches ready. Physicist Eugene Wigner quietly produced something he had bought beforehand, and the team drank a silent toast from paper cups to mark what they had unleashed. What did Wigner pull out?
answer: A bottle of Chianti
choices: A bottle of Chianti
A box of cigars
A folded American flag
A pot of coffee
context: Wigner had secretly bought the Chianti in advance. There were no speeches — just a silent toast from paper cups. Source: https://www.archives.gov/chicago/highlights/chianti

question: Watching the Trinity fireball rise over the desert, J. Robert Oppenheimer later said a line from the Hindu scripture the Bhagavad Gita came into his mind. He repeated it himself in a filmed 1965 interview. What was the line?
answer: Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds
choices: Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds
The atom holds the fire of a thousand suns
Let there be light, and there was light
We have opened a door that cannot be shut
context: Oppenheimer recounted the Bhagavad Gita line in a 1965 filmed interview. Source: https://www.atomicarchive.com/media/videos/trinity.html

question: At the Trinity test, Enrico Fermi wanted a quick guess of the bomb's power. As the blast wave swept past, he tore up a sheet of paper and dropped the scraps from about six feet, then measured how far the wind shoved them. What did he use this scrap-paper trick to estimate?
answer: The bomb's explosive yield
choices: The bomb's explosive yield
The distance to the tower
The speed of the shock wave
The height of the mushroom cloud
context: The wind pushed the scraps about 2.5 meters; from that Fermi reckoned roughly ten thousand tons of TNT — within a factor of two of the real ~19-kiloton yield. Source: https://www.atomicarchive.com/resources/documents/trinity/fermi.html

question: The bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki used two different designs. Hiroshima's 'Little Boy' was a 'gun-type' weapon — it fired one piece of uranium down a barrel into another to start the reaction. Nagasaki's 'Fat Man' worked by a different method, the same one tested at Trinity. How did Fat Man set off its plutonium core?
answer: Crushing the core inward with high explosives
choices: Crushing the core inward with high explosives
Firing two plutonium pieces together
Heating the core with an electric spark
Spinning the core at high speed
context: Fat Man was an implosion bomb: a shell of high explosives crushed the plutonium core inward, the design proven at Trinity. The two bombs used different fuels (uranium vs. plutonium) and different triggers. Source: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/bombing-nagasaki-august-9-1945

question: In 1885 in Mannheim, Germany, Karl Benz finished a three-wheeled machine with a small gasoline engine bolted at the back — the first vehicle ever built to make its own power instead of being a horse-carriage with a motor strapped on. What did he name this first practical car?
answer: The Benz Patent-Motorwagen
choices: The Benz Patent-Motorwagen
The Mannheim Steam Runabout
The Benz Horseless Phaeton
The Rhineland Road Locomotive
context: Karl Benz's 1885 Patent-Motorwagen had a single-cylinder four-stroke engine of just 0.75 horsepower. On 29 January 1886 he received German patent No. 37435 for it — often called the birth certificate of the automobile, and today part of the UNESCO Memory of the World register. Source: https://group.mercedes-benz.com/company/tradition/company-history/1885-1886.html

question: In August 1888 Bertha Benz took her husband Karl's automobile without telling him and drove 66 miles from Mannheim to her mother's town with her two teenage sons — the first long-distance car trip in history. When the fuel line clogged on the road, she unclogged it then and there with an ordinary item off her own person. What did she use?
answer: Her hat pin
choices: Her hat pin
Her garter
Her hairpin
Her shoelace
context: On that same 1888 drive Bertha Benz insulated a frayed ignition wire with her garter, had a blacksmith mend the drive chain, and at a cobbler's shop had leather nailed onto the brakes — inventing the world's first brake linings. She refueled at the Stadt-Apotheke pharmacy in Wiesloch, making it the first filling station in the world. Her journey proved to a skeptical public that the car actually worked. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertha_Benz

question: When the wandering Mexica people went looking for the place their god Huitzilopochtli had promised them, they were told to settle where they saw a certain sign on a marshy island in the lake. They had searched roughly 175 years for it. In 1325 they finally spotted it and founded Tenochtitlan there. What was the promised sign?
answer: An eagle perched on a nopal cactus
choices: An eagle perched on a nopal cactus
A jaguar drinking at a spring
A serpent coiled around a stone
A heron standing on a reed
context: Later tradition added a snake in the eagle's beak. That eagle-on-a-cactus is still at the center of the Mexican flag today. (https://www.inside-mexico.com/the-legend-of-tenochtitlan/ ; https://mythopedia.com/topics/huitzilopochtli/)
