question: To explain how Charles Babbage's planned Analytical Engine could handle ideas and not just sums, Ada Lovelace reached for a vivid image from the textile mills of her day. She saw that the stiff cards full of punched holes that told a mill machine which pattern to make could also tell a machine how to handle symbols. Which textile machine did she compare the engine to?
answer: The Jacquard loom
choices: The Jacquard loom
The spinning jenny
The cotton gin
The water frame
context: Lovelace grasped that the Jacquard loom's punched cards could let a machine manipulate symbols, not just crunch numbers — a startling leap toward the modern idea of a programmable computer. The spinning jenny, water frame, and cotton gin were other famous textile machines of the era, but only the Jacquard loom was run by punched cards. Source: https://www.computerhistory.org/babbage/adalovelace

question: Skeptical Members of Parliament kept asking Charles Babbage whether his calculating machine, if fed wrong numbers, might somehow still produce right answers. Babbage said he could not even grasp the confusion of mind behind the question. His exasperated reply is now remembered as an early version of which enduring computing principle?
answer: 'Garbage in, garbage out'
choices: 'Garbage in, garbage out'
'Move fast and break things'
'The customer is always right'
'Measure twice, cut once'
context: From Babbage's 1864 memoir Passages from the Life of a Philosopher. A machine only ever does what it is told — feed it wrong figures and it faithfully produces wrong answers. Source: https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Babbage/quotations/

question: In 1843 Ada Lovelace published a step-by-step method, labeled 'Note G,' for Charles Babbage's never-built Analytical Engine to compute a sequence of values entirely on its own — now honored as the first computer program in history. What did this very first program calculate?
answer: The Bernoulli numbers
choices: The Bernoulli numbers
The phases of the moon
Compound bank interest
The digits of pi
context: Note G was the last of a series of notes (A through G) Lovelace appended to her translation of a lecture on the Analytical Engine. While working it out she even caught a bug in Babbage's own underlying math. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Note_G

question: At Britain's secret Bletchley Park codebreaking station during World War II, Alan Turing designed an electromechanical machine that whirred through millions of possible settings to break the Germans' main cipher. Cracking that cipher is credited with shortening the war. Which German cipher did Turing's machine attack?
answer: The Enigma cipher
choices: The Enigma cipher
The Caesar cipher
The Morse cipher
The Vigenère cipher
context: Turing's machine was called the Bombe; the first was installed on 18 March 1940. It improved on an earlier Polish machine, the bomba kryptologiczna, built by Marian Rejewski's team, who had first broken into Enigma before the war and shared their work with Britain. Source: https://www.iwm.org.uk/history/second-world-war/how-alan-turing-cracked-the-enigma-code

question: In a 1936 paper, 'On Computable Numbers,' Alan Turing imagined a stripped-down machine that simply reads and writes symbols along an endless paper tape by following a table of rules. His key proof was that a single one of these machines was enough to run any computation at all. What is this founding idea of the general-purpose computer now called?
answer: A universal Turing machine
choices: A universal Turing machine
A stored-program machine
A finite-state machine
A logical computing machine
context: John von Neumann said 'the central concept of the modern computer was due to Turing's paper.' One machine that can carry out any computation is exactly what every modern computer does when it runs different programs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Turing_machine

question: Ada Lovelace argued, a full century before electronic computers, that a calculating engine could never truly think: it 'has no pretensions whatever to ORIGINATE anything,' she wrote, and 'can do whatever we know how to order it to perform.' When Alan Turing later debated whether machines could be intelligent, he took this exact challenge seriously and answered it. What is the challenge called today?
answer: The Lovelace objection
choices: The Lovelace objection
The Babbage objection
The Byron objection
The von Neumann objection
context: Turing named the challenge after Ada Lovelace, who first raised it, and answered it when arguing that machines might one day count as intelligent — for instance in his 1950 'imitation game,' the test now called the Turing Test. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ada_Lovelace

question: The men who wrote the U.S. Constitution in 1787 had just fought a war to escape a king, and they were terrified of putting all the power in one person's hands again. So they split the federal government into three separate branches. What job did they give to Congress?
answer: Making the laws
choices: Making the laws
Judging the laws
Carrying out the laws
Vetoing the laws
context: Congress (Article I) makes the laws, the President (Article II) carries them out, and the courts (Article III) judge them — three branches so no single person holds all the power, and each can 'check' the others. Source: Cornell LII, Wex, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/separation_of_powers_0

question: Under the Constitution, the President can reject a bill Congress has passed — a move called a veto. But Congress is not helpless: it can turn that rejected bill into law anyway, without the President's signature. What must happen for Congress to override a veto?
answer: Two-thirds of both the House and the Senate vote for it again
choices: Two-thirds of both the House and the Senate vote for it again
The President changes his mind and signs it
The Supreme Court orders the President to sign
A simple majority of the House votes for it once more
context: A veto override requires a two-thirds majority in BOTH chambers — a very high bar, which is why overrides are rare. Source: Constitution Annotated, Art. I Sec. 7, https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/essay/artI-S7-C2-2/ALDE_00013645/

question: George Washington used the President's brand-new veto power for the very first time on April 5, 1792 — the first presidential veto in American history. What kind of bill did Washington kill with it?
answer: A bill dividing up House seats among the states
choices: A bill dividing up House seats among the states
A bill raising taxes on imported tea
A bill building a new national capital
A bill creating a standing army
context: Washington vetoed an apportionment bill, saying it broke the Constitution's own rule of no more than one representative per 30,000 people. He was sparing with the power — only TWO vetoes in eight years. Source: Avalon Project, Washington's Veto Message, April 5, 1792, https://avalon.law.yale.edu/18th_century/gwveto1.asp

question: Impeachment is built like a two-step machine, and the two chambers of Congress do different jobs. The House of Representatives 'impeaches' an official — meaning it formally accuses them of wrongdoing. What is the Senate's separate job in this machine?
answer: Holding the trial and voting whether to remove the official
choices: Holding the trial and voting whether to remove the official
Choosing which official gets accused
Signing the accusation into law
Picking the judge who will hear the case
context: The House accuses; the Senate judges. It takes a two-thirds Senate vote to convict and remove someone. Source: Constitution Annotated, Art. I Sec. 3, https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/essay/artI-S3-C6-5/ALDE_00000710/

question: In 1868 the U.S. Senate put President Andrew Johnson on trial to throw him out of office over his bitter fights with Congress about Reconstruction. It came down to one man: Kansas Senator Edmund Ross held the deciding vote. The count stood at 35 to convict and 19 to acquit — exactly one vote short of the two-thirds needed to remove Johnson — and the packed chamber fell silent as Ross rose to give his verdict. What did Ross say?
answer: "Not guilty"
choices: "Not guilty"
"Guilty"
"I abstain"
"Present"
context: Ross's vote left the count one short of the two-thirds (36) needed to convict, so Johnson stayed in office. The charge: Johnson had fired Secretary of War Edwin Stanton in defiance of the Tenure of Office Act. Source: U.S. Senate, https://www.senate.gov/about/powers-procedures/impeachment/impeachment-johnson.htm

question: Three U.S. presidents have been impeached by the House of Representatives — Andrew Johnson, Bill Clinton, and Donald Trump (twice). In every single one of those cases, the Senate trial ended the same way. What happened to all three at the end?
answer: None was convicted, so none was removed from office
choices: None was convicted, so none was removed from office
All three were convicted and forced to resign
Two were removed and one resigned first
All three were barred from ever holding office again
context: No U.S. president has ever been removed from office by impeachment — the two-thirds Senate bar has never been met for a president. Source: Britannica, https://www.britannica.com/topic/Which-US-Presidents-Have-Been-Impeached; History.house.gov, https://history.house.gov/Institution/Origins-Development/Impeachment/

question: The President can sign treaties with foreign nations, but a treaty only becomes binding if two-thirds of the Senate approves it — and in 1919 and 1920 the Senate used that power to stop President Woodrow Wilson cold. Which of Wilson's treaties did the Senate refuse to approve, twice?
answer: The Treaty of Versailles
choices: The Treaty of Versailles
The Louisiana Purchase treaty
The Treaty of Ghent
The Panama Canal treaty
context: By rejecting the Treaty of Versailles (38-53 in 1919, 49-35 in 1920), the Senate kept the United States out of the League of Nations entirely. The Senate's 'advice and consent' can override the President on foreign agreements. Source: U.S. Senate, https://www.senate.gov/about/powers-procedures/treaties/senate-rejects-treaty-of-versailles.htm

question: In the case of Marbury v. Madison, decided February 24, 1803, Chief Justice John Marshall did something no court had ever done: he struck down a law passed by Congress as unconstitutional. In doing so he invented a brand-new power for the courts that is still used today. What is that power called?
answer: Judicial review
choices: Judicial review
Habeas corpus
Executive privilege
Eminent domain
context: Marshall wrote, 'It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.' Judicial review lets the courts strike down laws that violate the Constitution. Source: National Archives, https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/marbury-v-madison

question: Congress holds several checks on the President, but one is nicknamed the 'power of the purse' — and many call it the strongest check of all. It is the power that controls something a President cannot get from anywhere else. Which of these powers is the 'power of the purse'?
answer: Cutting off the money for a war the President has ordered
choices: Cutting off the money for a war the President has ordered
Blocking the judges the President wants to appoint
Rejecting a treaty the President has signed
Overriding a bill the President has vetoed
context: The 'power of the purse' is Congress's control over spending: Article I forbids any money being drawn from the Treasury except by a law Congress passes. So even a war the President has ordered must be funded by Congress — one of the legislature's strongest checks on the executive. Blocking judges, rejecting treaties, and overriding vetoes are real Congressional checks too, but the 'purse' means the money. Source: Cornell LII, Constitution Annotated, https://www.law.cornell.edu/constitution-conan/article-1/section-1/separation-of-powers-and-checks-and-balances

question: James Madison explained why government needs branches that fight each other in Federalist No. 51, with a line famous enough that people still quote it. He argued that because human beings are flawed and grasping, each branch's hunger for power must be turned against the others. How did Madison sum up why government is necessary at all?
answer: "If men were angels, no government would be necessary"
choices: "If men were angels, no government would be necessary"
"All men are created equal"
"Power tends to corrupt"
"Government of the people, by the people"
context: Madison's fix: 'Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.' Because people are not angels, each branch's appetite for power is used to block the others. Source: Bill of Rights Institute, Federalist No. 51 by James Madison, https://billofrightsinstitute.org/primary-sources/federalist-no-51/

question: Everyone treats judicial review — the courts' power to strike down laws — as a basic part of American government, yet there is a surprising fact about it: those words appear nowhere in the text of the Constitution. So where did the Supreme Court get the power to overturn acts of Congress?
answer: The Court claimed it for itself in Marbury v. Madison
choices: The Court claimed it for itself in Marbury v. Madison
A 1789 act of Congress handed it to the Court
President Jefferson granted it by executive order
It was added later in an early amendment
context: After claiming the power in 1803, the Court was so cautious that it did not strike down another act of Congress for 54 years — not until the Dred Scott case in 1857. Source: National Archives, https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/marbury-v-madison

question: Most national constitutions are surprisingly fragile. A landmark study of every constitution written since 1789 found that the typical one gets thrown out and replaced after only about 19 years. The U.S. Constitution, by stunning contrast, has never once been replaced — it has run without a break since the day it took effect. Roughly how long has the U.S. Constitution lasted?
answer: More than 230 years
choices: More than 230 years
More than 60 years
More than 110 years
More than 160 years
context: America's constitution has lasted more than 230 years — over ten times the roughly 19-year median the study found — and has been amended only 27 times. Study: Elkins, Ginsburg & Melton, 'The Endurance of National Constitutions,' https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1536925

question: The Council of Trent met in the alpine city of Trent in northern Italy to plan the Catholic Church's response to the Protestant Reformation. The council wanted ONE official Bible that everyone would use. Which Bible did it name as the sole authentic scripture?
answer: The Latin Vulgate translated long before by Saint Jerome
choices: The Latin Vulgate translated long before by Saint Jerome
A fresh Italian translation made by the council itself
Martin Luther's recent German translation
The original Greek text owned only by the pope
context: Decreed in April 1546, Trent named the Latin Vulgate, translated centuries earlier by Saint Jerome, as the sole authentic scripture, and ruled that the Church alone could authorize new translations. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Council_of_Trent/

question: The Council of Trent's most genuine reform attacked a real rot in the Church: many priests were poorly trained, and some bishops collected the income of a diocese they had never even visited. To train priests properly, Trent ordered every diocese to build one specific kind of institution. What was it?
answer: A seminary to train its priests
choices: A seminary to train its priests
A printing house for Bibles
A hospital for the poor
A court to try heretics
context: Trent's biggest real reform ordered every diocese to build a seminary and required bishops to actually reside in their dioceses rather than collect income from afar. Source: https://www.saet.ac.uk/Christianity/CouncilofTrent

question: In 1547, partway through the Council of Trent, a typhus plague scare gave the pope's legates an excuse to vote to move the whole council out of Trent to Bologna, deep inside the Papal States and beyond the reach of Emperor Charles V. Charles, who wanted the council where he could influence it, reacted by doing what?
answer: Forbidding his own bishops to follow it to Bologna
choices: Forbidding his own bishops to follow it to Bologna
Sending his army to occupy the city of Bologna
Declaring himself the new head of the council
Quietly agreeing and moving his court to Bologna too
context: Furious at the move, Charles V forbade his bishops to follow; the Bologna sessions produced no decrees and the council stalled for years before resuming back at Trent. Source: https://christianhistoryinstitute.org/magazine/article/the-persistent-council

question: Martin Luther taught that a person is saved by faith alone (sola fide). The Council of Trent struck directly back at this, decreeing that justice is preserved and even increased through good works as well as faith. Trent's decrees drove the point home by ending, over and over, with one fearsome Latin word meaning 'let him be cursed and cut off.' What was that word?
answer: Anathema
choices: Anathema
Indulgentia
Purgatorium
Transubstantio
context: Trent decreed: 'If any one saith that the justice received is not preserved and also increased before God through good works... let him be anathema.' Anathema means cursed or cut off, and it closes decree after decree. Source: https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/9-things-you-should-know-about-the-council-of-trent/

question: Where Protestant reformers smashed religious images, the Counter-Reformation answered by commissioning the most dramatic, theatrical art yet seen, launching the Baroque. Its showpiece is a marble sculpture by Gian Lorenzo Bernini that freezes the exact moment Teresa of Avila described from her own vision: an angel thrusting a golden spear tipped with fire into her heart, a pain she called surpassingly sweet. What is this sculpture called?
answer: The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa
choices: The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa
The Anathema of Saint Teresa
The Coronation of Saint Teresa
The Martyrdom of Saint Teresa
context: Bernini's marble Ecstasy of Saint Teresa (1647-1652) sits in Santa Maria della Vittoria in Rome, where the Cornaro family watches from carved marble 'opera boxes' on the side walls. Teresa called the spear-vision the transverberation: 'so surpassing was the sweetness of this excessive pain, that I could not wish to be rid of it.' Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/The-Ecstasy-of-Saint-Teresa

question: To join the First Crusade, a fighter swore his vow and then had a badge cut from cloth and sewn onto his tunic and cloak as the public sign that he had taken the oath. What shape was the badge?
answer: a cross
choices: a cross
a sword
a crown
a lion
context: From the cross came the word itself: Latin 'crux' gave Old French 'croisade', and a fighter who 'took the cross' was a 'croise' — literally a cross-bearer. Source: https://www.etymonline.com/word/crusade ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crusades

question: In November 1095 Pope Urban II called for the First Crusade in a speech at the Council of Clermont. The chronicler Robert the Monk says that when he finished, the whole crowd roared the same three words back at him — and Urban told them to make it their battle-cry. What did they shout?
answer: God wills it!
choices: God wills it!
Death to the king!
Rome has fallen!
Take up the sword!
context: 'Deus vult! Deus vult!' Urban answered that the word had been given to them by God and should be their cry in battle. Source: https://sourcebooks.fordham.edu/source/urban2-5vers.asp ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Clermont

question: When the Fourth Crusade plundered Constantinople in 1204, the blind Doge Enrico Dandolo shipped one prize of ancient artwork home to Venice, where it has stood over the front of St Mark's Basilica ever since. What was this famous plunder?
answer: a team of bronze horses
choices: a team of bronze horses
a great temple bell
a marble lion statue
a jeweled gold throne
context: The four gilded-bronze Horses of Saint Mark were taken from Constantinople's Hippodrome; they have crowned St Mark's facade since the 13th century. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Crusade ; https://ertungaecir.com/blog/from-constantinople-to-venice/

question: After the First Crusade took Jerusalem in 1099, Godfrey of Bouillon was offered the crown and the title 'King of Jerusalem' — and he refused to be crowned king. By tradition, he said he would not wear a crown of gold in the one city where Christ had worn a crown of what?
answer: thorns
choices: thorns
iron
olive leaves
fire
context: Instead of king, Godfrey took the humbler title 'Advocatus Sancti Sepulchri' — Defender of the Holy Sepulchre — on July 22, 1099. The crown-of-thorns saying is a cherished tradition. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Godfrey_of_Bouillon ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Jerusalem_(1099)  (Legend.)

question: Around 1118, to protect Christian pilgrims on the dangerous roads to Jerusalem, Hugues de Payns and eight companions founded a brand-new kind of brotherhood: men who took monks' vows of poverty and chastity but also fought as armored knights. What was this famous warrior-monk order called?
answer: the Knights Templar
choices: the Knights Templar
the Black Friars
the Swiss Guard
the Round Table
context: They were headquartered on the Temple Mount — hence 'Templars.' In 1147 Pope Eugene III let them wear a red cross, said to recall the blood they shed defending the Holy Land. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knights_Templar

question: In 1212, by a half-legendary story, a French shepherd boy named Stephen of Cloyes led thousands of children south to the port of Marseille, certain that God would perform one specific miracle there so they could walk all the way to the Holy Land. What did they believe would happen at the shore?
answer: the sea would split open
choices: the sea would split open
an angel would carry them
ships would appear from heaven
the walls would fall flat
context: They expected the Mediterranean to part like the Red Sea. It never did; by tradition many were stranded and some were sold into slavery, though modern historians debate how much of the tale is true. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children%27s_Crusade  (Legend.)

question: When Pope Urban II called the First Crusade, the chronicler Fulcher of Chartres recorded the exact reward he promised every man who joined: that anyone who died on the journey or in battle against the enemy would immediately receive what?
answer: remission of all his sins
choices: remission of all his sins
a lordship in the Holy Land
a chest of Byzantine gold
a seat at the king's table
context: This spiritual promise was called an indulgence — the reward was forgiveness, not loot. Historians cite the real motives as protecting pilgrims, answering the Byzantine appeal for aid after the 1071 disaster at Manzikert, and the papal call itself. Source: https://sourcebooks.fordham.edu/source/urban2-5vers.asp ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Urban_II

question: On July 4, 1187, Saladin trapped the entire Crusader army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem on two parched hills called the Horns of Hattin, cut off from water in furnace heat. To break the exhausted, thirst-maddened knights completely, Saladin gave one cruel order. What did he do?
answer: set the hillside on fire
choices: set the hillside on fire
poisoned the wells below
burned their supply wagons
cut off their retreat
context: Saladin set the dry brush alight so the smoke would choke the trapped army, then crushed it — and captured the Crusaders' holiest relic, a fragment of the True Cross the bishop of Acre had carried into the battle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hattin ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Battle_of_Hattin/

question: When the First Crusade stormed Jerusalem on July 15, 1099, the killing was so total it became a byword for massacre. The eyewitness Raymond of Aguilers wrote that in the Temple of Solomon, horsemen rode through blood so deep it reached one shocking height. How high did Raymond say the blood ran?
answer: up to the horses' reins
choices: up to the horses' reins
up to the men's ankles
up to the altar steps
up to the courtyard walls
context: Raymond wrote that men rode in blood 'up to their knees and bridle reins.' Another eyewitness account, the Gesta Francorum, made the lower claim that the crusaders 'waded in blood up to their ankles.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Jerusalem_(1099) ; https://sourcebooks.fordham.edu/source/gesta-cde.asp

question: The Fourth Crusade set out in 1202 for the Holy Land, but the crusaders could not pay the Venetians the 85,000 silver marks they owed for the fleet. To work off the debt, the blind ninety-year-old Doge Enrico Dandolo first turned the entire crusading army against one city and sacked it. Which city did the crusaders sack to pay their debt?
answer: the Catholic city of Zara
choices: the Catholic city of Zara
the Muslim port of Acre
the Turkish city of Nicaea
the desert fortress of Damascus
context: Zara was a fellow Catholic Christian city — the first time a crusading army ever attacked other Catholics. Pope Innocent III briefly excommunicated the whole crusade for it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Crusade ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Fourth_Crusade/

question: In April 1204 the Fourth Crusade did the unthinkable: instead of fighting in the Holy Land, it stormed and sacked Constantinople, the greatest Christian city in the world. The Byzantine eyewitness Niketas Choniates described the desecration of the great church of Hagia Sophia, including a mockery the crusaders made of the patriarch's own throne. According to Choniates, what did they put on that sacred throne?
answer: a drunken dancing prostitute
choices: a drunken dancing prostitute
a fully armored war-horse
a chained Greek bishop
a bronze statue of the Doge
context: Choniates wrote that a drunken woman sat in the patriarch's throne 'singing an obscene song and dancing,' while crusaders led mules into the sanctuary to cart off its silver and smashed the altar to bits. Source: https://sourcebooks.fordham.edu/source/choniates1.asp ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Constantinople

question: When news reached Rome that the Fourth Crusade had sacked Constantinople, Pope Innocent III — the very man who had launched that crusade — wrote a furious letter to his legate in July 1204. He raged that these soldiers, who should have turned their swords against the enemies of the faith, had behaved so monstrously that the Greeks now, in his words, 'with reason' did what?
answer: detest the Latins more than dogs
choices: detest the Latins more than dogs
would never trust a Latin again
cursed the Pope who sent them
vowed to take back their city
context: Innocent wrote that the crusaders, 'dripping with Christian blood... have spared neither age nor sex' — so the Greeks 'with reason, detest the Latins more than dogs.' Even the Pope who began the crusade called the sack a scandal. Source: https://apholt.com/2016/10/28/pope-innocent-iii-reprimand-of-peter-a-papal-legate-for-the-sack-of-constantinople-july-1204/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Constantinople

question: In 1879 the excavator Hormuzd Rassam dug a small baked-clay object out of the foundations of Babylon's great temple. About 9 inches long and shaped like a barrel, it was covered with 45 lines of cuneiform pressed into the wet clay. What do we call this clay barrel that records the deeds of Cyrus the Great?
answer: The Cyrus Cylinder
choices: The Cyrus Cylinder
The Babylon Tablet
The Marduk Scroll
The Esagila Stone
context: The Cyrus Cylinder, dug up by Hormuzd Rassam in 1879 from the foundations of the Esagila (the temple of the god Marduk) in Babylon, is a baked clay barrel about 22.5 cm long carrying roughly 45 lines of cuneiform. Source: britishmuseum.org object W_1880-0617-1941; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrus_Cylinder.

question: On the Cyrus Cylinder, Cyrus the Great boasts of one striking deed after taking Babylon: he says he gathered captive peoples whom earlier kings had carried off, and he carried the seized statues of foreign gods back to their own cities. What did Cyrus claim to have done with these deported peoples and their gods?
answer: Returned them to their own homes and temples
choices: Returned them to their own homes and temples
Melted their statues into a victory monument
Kept them as hostages inside Babylon
Sold them to merchants across the empire
context: Line 32 of the cylinder has Cyrus declaring 'I gathered all their inhabitants and returned to them their dwellings,' restoring the carried-off divine statues to their temples. The Book of Ezra credits Cyrus with the same policy toward the exiled Jews, letting them return and rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem (for them it was the sacred Temple vessels, not god-statues, that were restored), though the cylinder itself never names Jerusalem or the Jews. Source: livius.org Cyrus Cylinder translation Line 32; biblicalarchaeology.org.

question: The Cyrus Cylinder is often sold as 'the first declaration of human rights' — a label Iran's Shah pushed in 1971, when he had a replica handed to the United Nations. British Museum Assyriologist Irving Finkel, an expert on the object, bluntly rejects that label. What does Finkel say the cylinder really is?
answer: Royal propaganda about restoring peace, not a rights charter
choices: Royal propaganda about restoring peace, not a rights charter
A forged copy made for the Shah's 1971 festival
A legal contract between Cyrus and the priests
An early census of every people in the empire
context: Finkel says 'There are no human rights in antiquity' and calls the cylinder royal propaganda whose 'only concern is with restoring peaceful circumstances.' Scholars like Amelie Kuhrt note the brief text contains no formal statement of rights, and Jacob Wright argues it paints Cyrus too virtuously and glosses over his bloody conquests — so historians treat it as a genuine early experiment in imperial tolerance, not a modern rights charter. Source: peabody.yale.edu/news/finkel_talk; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrus_Cylinder.

question: In May 1521 Emperor Charles V declared the monk Martin Luther an outlaw whom anyone could kill without penalty. As Luther rode home, his protector Frederick the Wise of Saxony staged a fake ambush to spirit him into hiding at Wartburg Castle. To pass unrecognized there, Luther grew a beard and lived under what new identity?
answer: A knight named Junker Jorg
choices: A knight named Junker Jorg
A wandering pilgrim from Rome
A traveling wine merchant
A village priest in exile
context: At Wartburg, disguised as Junker Jorg (Knight George), Luther translated the entire New Testament from Greek into German in about three months. Source: learn.ligonier.org/podcasts/5-minutes-in-church-history-with-stephen-nichols/junker-jorg; worldhistory.org/article/1900/luthers-speech-at-the-diet-of-worms/

question: Ordered to take back his books before Charles V at Worms in 1521, Martin Luther refused, saying his conscience was captive to the Word of God and that he could not go against conscience. The version of his speech every schoolbook quotes ends with the ringing words 'Here I stand. I can do no other. God help me. Amen.' What do historians say about that famous closing line?
answer: Those words were added later and are missing from the earliest records
choices: Those words were added later and are missing from the earliest records
He shouted it in German, then again in Latin
He wrote it as the title of his next book
He spoke it kneeling before the emperor
context: The conscience reply is documented, but the celebrated 'Here I stand' tag does not appear in the earliest accounts of what Luther actually said. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diet_of_Worms; worldhistory.org/article/1900/luthers-speech-at-the-diet-of-worms/  (Legend.)

question: In 1086 William the Conqueror sent officials across England to write down who owned every estate, field, and farm animal in the kingdom. The English gave the resulting book a grim nickname: just as on the Last Judgement no soul could appeal its verdict, no landholder could argue with this book. What grim nickname stuck to it?
answer: The Domesday Book
choices: The Domesday Book
The Conqueror's Roll
The Iron Ledger
The Winchester Writ
context: Around 1179 the royal treasurer Richard FitzNeal explained in the Dialogus de Scaccario that the survey was named for the Day of Judgement: 'from it, as from the Last Judgement, there is no further appeal.' Its word could not be denied or set aside without penalty. (Dialogus de Scaccario c.1179, via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domesday_Book)

question: When William the Conqueror's commissioners reached each district to record the Domesday survey, a sworn jury of local men had to confirm every answer under oath. William wanted a record neither side could quietly rig in its own favour, so he fixed exactly who sat on that jury. How was each jury deliberately made up?
answer: Half English and half Norman
choices: Half English and half Norman
Entirely the king's own clerks
Only the wealthiest local lords
Only sworn churchmen and bishops
context: Splitting each jury half English, half Norman meant neither the conquered nor the conquerors could fix the record alone — an early example of England's precocious centralized administration and rule-of-law instinct. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domesday_Book; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_Inquisition)

question: On the morning of April 14, 1935, the Oklahoma plains woke to a clear blue sky, so families went out for the day. That afternoon at 2:49 PM something rolled in from the north at 50 to 60 mph that made eyewitnesses think the world was ending. What came?
answer: A black wall of dust 500 to 600 feet high
choices: A black wall of dust 500 to 600 feet high
A line of tornadoes touching down
A flash flood off the river
A swarm of locusts blotting the sun
context: This was Black Sunday, the most famous dust storm of the Dust Bowl. The rolling black 'duster' swallowed farms so completely that people groped for the walls of their own homes. Source: NWS Norman OK (weather.gov/oun/events-19350414); Wikipedia, 'Black Sunday (storm)'.

question: Caught in the Black Sunday storm six miles north of Boise City, Oklahoma, on April 14, 1935, Associated Press reporter Robert Geiger filed a story the next day that gave the whole stricken region a nickname that stuck for good. What did he call it?
answer: the Dust Bowl
choices: the Dust Bowl
the Big Blow Country
the Dead Plains
the Brown Frontier
context: Geiger's April 15, 1935 wire story coined 'the dust bowl,' and the name became permanent. Source: Wikipedia, 'Black Sunday (storm)'; mentalfloss.com/black-sunday-dust-bowl-storm.

question: Before the plows came, the native buffalo grass of the Great Plains held the soil down with roots running as deep as 5 feet. Then a new machine let a single farmer tear up 50 acres of that sod in a day, instead of just 3 acres behind a horse. What machine ripped open the prairie and left the bare dirt for the wind to lift?
answer: the gasoline tractor with a disc plow
choices: the gasoline tractor with a disc plow
the steam-powered cotton gin
the horse-drawn seed drill
the windmill water pump
context: During the WWI wheat boom, gasoline tractors with disc plows let farmers turn under millions of acres of deep-rooted sod. With nothing to anchor it, the dried topsoil blew away. Source: encyclopedia.com (Dust Bowl); PBS Ken Burns, 'The Great Plow-Up'.

question: In March 1935, soil scientist Hugh Bennett was testifying to Congress to win funding to fight the dust storms. He timed his speech so that, as he spoke, a real dust cloud blown east from the plains darkened the Capitol windows on cue. A senator looked up and remarked, 'It does look like dust.' What did Congress do the very next day?
answer: passed the Soil Conservation Act, creating a permanent Soil Conservation Service
choices: passed the Soil Conservation Act, creating a permanent Soil Conservation Service
ordered the army to plant trees across Oklahoma
banned all tractor farming on the plains
declared a national day of prayer for rain
context: Bennett's perfectly timed testimony helped pass the Soil Conservation Act in 1935, founding the Soil Conservation Service, which eventually bought back over 10 million acres to return to grassland. Source: boundarystones.weta.org/2012/11/19/hugh-bennett-and-perfect-storm.

question: The Rock of Gibraltar, the famous crag guarding the gateway from Africa into Spain, is named after the Berber general whose army of about 7,000 men landed there around April 711. The English name 'Gibraltar' is worn down from the Arabic 'Jabal Tariq.' What does that Arabic name mean?
answer: The Mountain of Tariq
choices: The Mountain of Tariq
The Harbor of Tariq
The Victory of Tariq
The Gateway of Tariq
context: Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed the strait around April 711 with roughly 7,000 men; 'Jabal Tariq' (the Mountain of Tariq) was slurred over the centuries into 'Gibraltar.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tariq_ibn_Ziyad

question: The Arab general Khalid ibn al-Walid was remembered as never losing a battle in his whole life, and earned the title 'Sayf Allah' — the Sword of Allah. By legend the name was given after one furious fight at Mu'tah where he held the line so hard that something happened to his weapons. According to the legend, what did he do?
answer: He broke eight swords in his hands
choices: He broke eight swords in his hands
He fought on after losing both eyes
He held the bridge entirely alone
He slew the enemy king in single combat
context: The legend says Khalid ibn al-Walid shattered eight swords holding the line at the Battle of Mu'tah, earning 'Sayf Allah' (the Sword of Allah); he is remembered as undefeated. Told here as legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Yarmuk; studioarabiya.com/the-sword-of-allah

question: At the four-day Battle of al-Qadisiyyah in November 636, the Persian army fielded about 33 war elephants that trampled into the Arab lines. The Muslim soldiers worked out a way to turn the giant beasts against their own side. What did they do to the elephants?
answer: Blinded them and cut their trunks
choices: Blinded them and cut their trunks
Set their tower-howdahs on fire
Dug pits to topple them over
Fed them poisoned river water
context: The Muslims learned to blind the elephants and sever their trunks and girths; the panicked beasts stampeded back through the Persian ranks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_al-Qadisiyyah

question: After the Persians lost the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah in 636, the victorious Arabs seized the Sasanian empire's most sacred treasure — the Derafsh-e Kaveyan, the jewel-encrusted royal battle-banner that Persian kings had carried for centuries. What became of its great central jewel?
answer: It was cut up and the pieces sold in Medina
choices: It was cut up and the pieces sold in Medina
It was set into the new ruler's crown
It was hurled into the Tigris by the last shah
It was hidden in a desert tomb and lost
context: The captured Derafsh-e Kaveyan (Flag of Kaveh) had its great jewel cut up, and the pieces were sold off in Medina — the sacred banner of Persia dismantled and scattered. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_al-Qadisiyyah

question: In the very same year, 711, the early Muslim conquests reached two opposite ends of the known world at once: Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed into Spain in the far west. At the empire's other end, the young general Muhammad bin Qasim marched through Makran and conquered Sindh that same year. Where is Sindh?
answer: On the Indus River in India
choices: On the Indus River in India
On the Nile in Egypt
On the Danube in Europe
On the Volga in the steppe
context: Sindh sits on the Indus valley; so in one year, 711, the conquests touched both Spain and India — the Atlantic edge and the Indus edge of the known world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Muslim_conquests

question: Within roughly a century of Muhammad's death in 632, Arab armies overran the two great powers of the day, the Byzantine and Sasanian Persian empires. Historians point to one reason both giants fell so fast: what condition were the two empires in when the Arab armies struck?
answer: Exhausted from a long war against each other
choices: Exhausted from a long war against each other
Split by a sudden outbreak of plague
Leaderless after both emperors died young
Frozen in place by an unusually harsh winter
context: Byzantium and Sasanian Persia had bled each other white in the war of 602-628, so both were spent when the Arabs struck. The resulting empire stretched from the Atlantic in Spain to the Indus — about 13 million sq km, the largest the world had yet seen. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Muslim_conquests

question: In 1989 Boris Yeltsin, then a rising Soviet politician, made an unplanned stop at an ordinary Randall's supermarket in Houston, Texas, and wandered the aisles for twenty minutes past shelves crammed with roughly 30,000 everyday products. The abundance was so far beyond anything in the USSR that Yeltsin reacted with one suspicion. What did he suspect about the store?
answer: That it had been specially staged to fool him
choices: That it had been specially staged to fool him
That the goods were reserved only for officials
That the prices were secretly subsidized
That the food on the shelves was counterfeit
context: Yeltsin could not believe an ordinary American shop stocked that much for any shopper; on the flight afterward his aide Lev Sukhanov said 'the last vestige of Bolshevism collapsed inside him,' and Yeltsin asked aloud, 'What have they done to our people?' He warned that if Russians saw such stores 'there would be a revolution.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_visit_by_Boris_Yeltsin_to_the_United_States

question: The economist Ludwig von Mises argued in 1920 that a state owning all factories can never tell whether it is using resources wisely, because without buying and selling there are no market prices for capital. The Soviet planners proved his point at scale: their price agency was fixing about 24 million prices by hand, yet the central plan could only draw up balanced production targets for a tiny sliver of the goods the economy actually made. Roughly how many goods could the annual plan actually balance?
answer: Around 2,000 goods
choices: Around 2,000 goods
Around 2 million goods
Around 200 goods
Around 20 million goods
context: Gosplan's annual plan covered material balances for only about 2,000 goods (around 200,000 once every ministry was counted) out of roughly 24 million distinct items the economy produced — so almost the entire economy ran on guesswork. Friedrich Hayek added the deeper objection: the knowledge of millions of changing local needs can never be gathered into one office. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_calculation_problem ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet-type_economic_planning

question: A famous Soviet parable describes a nail factory whose output was set by the central plan rather than by what customers wanted. When the plant's quota was measured in total weight, the managers met it in a way that hit the target number perfectly while producing something completely useless. What did the factory make?
answer: One single gigantic nail
choices: One single gigantic nail
A pile of bent scrap nails
Thousands of identical hammers
A stack of empty crates
context: Told as a parable (a teaching story rather than a documented event), it shows the calculation problem in miniature: with no real prices, a tonnage target was met by forging one enormous useless nail — and when planners switched the quota to quantity, the factory churned out millions of tiny worthless pins instead. Khrushchev himself griped that tonnage targets produced chandeliers so heavy 'they pull the ceilings down on our heads.' Source: https://kyytpress.substack.com/p/the-parable-of-the-soviet-nail-factory  (Legend.)

question: Guy de Maupassant, the famous French writer, was one of about 300 Parisians who signed a manifesto attacking the new Eiffel Tower as a 'useless and monstrous' eyesore. Yet the story goes that after it was built he ate lunch in the tower's own restaurant nearly every single day. Why there, of all places?
answer: It was the one spot in Paris from which he could not see the tower he hated
choices: It was the one spot in Paris from which he could not see the tower he hated
It was the only restaurant in Paris that would still serve a man who had insulted it
It was the cheapest meal a struggling writer could find anywhere in the city
It was the only place high enough to escape the noise of the crowded streets
context: Maupassant had signed the 14 February 1887 protest in the newspaper Le Temps alongside Alexandre Dumas fils and Charles Garnier (architect of the Paris Opera). The lunch story is a beloved legend, told to mock how the tower took over the Paris skyline. Source: thevintagenews.com / toureiffel.paris.

question: The Eiffel Tower was never meant to last. Gustave Eiffel's permit ran out after 20 years, and on 1 January 1910 the City of Paris could have torn it down and sold it for scrap iron. Instead it still stands today. What use did Eiffel find for the tower that made it too valuable to scrap?
answer: He turned it into a giant radio antenna
choices: He turned it into a giant radio antenna
He turned it into a giant lightning rod
He turned it into a giant water tower
He turned it into a giant clock face
context: Wireless telegraphy experiments began on the tower in 1898, and by 1908 it transmitted signals up to 3,700 miles. In World War I its radio station even intercepted a coded German message about 'Operative H-21' that helped convict the spy Mata Hari. Source: history.com 'eiffel-tower-survival' / toureiffel.paris.

question: In June 1752, Benjamin Franklin flew a kite up into a thunderstorm to prove that lightning was a form of electricity. A metal key hung from the wet kite string. When Franklin slowly moved his knuckle close to that key, what happened?
answer: A spark jumped from the key to his hand
choices: A spark jumped from the key to his hand
The key melted into a small lump of metal
The whole kite burst into bright flames
The wet string turned to brittle glass
context: The spark proved the electricity in a storm cloud was the same thing as the spark from a lab. The key was borrowed from his neighbor Benjamin Loxley, and his son William was with him. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kite_experiment

question: Michael Faraday, born in 1791 to a poor blacksmith, had almost no schooling. At fourteen he was apprenticed to a London bookbinder. How did this penniless boy teach himself science?
answer: He read the very books he was binding
choices: He read the very books he was binding
He paid a private tutor with his wages
He snuck into a university's lectures at night
He memorized one borrowed encyclopedia
context: The books passing through his hands taught him everything, including the encyclopedia's article on electricity and Jane Marcet's 'Conversations on Chemistry.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Faraday

question: In the 'War of the Currents,' Thomas Edison backed direct current (DC) while Nikola Tesla and George Westinghouse backed alternating current (AC). AC won, and it powers the world's grid today for one big reason. What could AC do that DC could not?
answer: Travel long distances at high voltage
choices: Travel long distances at high voltage
Run completely silent, without any hum
Work without any copper wire at all
Be made far more cheaply from coal
context: AC can be stepped up to high voltage with transformers and sent for hundreds of miles; Edison's DC fizzled out after less than a single mile. That is why AC runs the whole planet's power grid. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/what-was-the-war-of-the-currents

question: In 1821 Michael Faraday built the very first machine that turned electricity into nonstop movement, the ancestor of every electric motor. In his little device, what spun round and round?
answer: A wire circling a magnet
choices: A wire circling a magnet
A glass globe full of sparks
A wheel hung with spinning keys
A copper coil dipped in acid
context: This homopolar motor, a wire endlessly spinning around a magnet, made Faraday the inventor of the electric motor, ten years before his even greater discovery. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Faraday

question: Benjamin Franklin gave us electrical words we still say every day. He threw out the clumsy old terms 'vitreous' and 'resinous' for the two kinds of charge and replaced them with which plain pair?
answer: Positive and negative
choices: Positive and negative
Hot and cold
Strong and weak
Open and closed
context: Franklin coined positive and negative (plus and minus), and the word 'battery' for stored charge, and invented the lightning rod to carry strikes safely into the ground. Source: https://physicstoday.aip.org/features/benjamin-franklin-and-lightning-rods

question: The secret of the AC motor, a rotating magnetic field, came to Nikola Tesla in a single flash of insight in 1882, as he walked through a Budapest park reciting poetry. Having no paper at that moment, how did he capture the design?
answer: He drew it in the dirt with a stick
choices: He drew it in the dirt with a stick
He scratched it onto his shirt cuff
He recited it aloud as a new verse
He carved it into a wooden park bench
context: The rotating magnetic field is what lets a motor spin on alternating current. Tesla said the whole design appeared to him complete in that instant in the park. Source: https://teslasciencecenter.org/pivotalmoments/alternating-current/

question: Young Michael Faraday, still only a bookbinder, was desperate for a science career. After attending the chemist Humphry Davy's public lectures, he used the one craft he had mastered to win Davy's attention. What did Faraday make and send to Davy?
answer: His own notes, bound into a handsome book
choices: His own notes, bound into a handsome book
A jar of chemicals he had mixed himself
A long letter begging for any position
A small model of one of Davy's experiments
context: Faraday took careful notes at the lectures and bound them into a beautiful 300-page volume. Davy hired him as a laboratory assistant at the Royal Institution in 1813. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Faraday

question: At his Colorado Springs laboratory in 1899, Nikola Tesla switched on a giant coil, chasing his dream of sending electricity through the air without wires. What did the coil hurl out, crackling up to 135 feet across the room?
answer: Bolts of man-made lightning
choices: Bolts of man-made lightning
A churning wall of white smoke
A blinding shower of sparks
Ribbons of blue flame up the walls
context: Tesla's artificial bolts reached up to 135 feet (41 m), and the crash was reportedly heard 15 miles away, all in the service of his dream of beaming power wirelessly. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesla_Experimental_Station

question: In 1831 Michael Faraday wound two separate coils of wire on opposite sides of an iron ring, never touching. He flicked the current in the first coil on and off, and each time, a pulse of electricity leapt up in the SECOND coil. What deep rule had he just uncovered, the rule behind every electric generator since?
answer: A changing magnetic field creates electric current
choices: A changing magnetic field creates electric current
Electricity always flows from hot metal to cold metal
Two magnets pushed together will store a charge
Coiled wire slowly leaks its electricity into the air
context: This is electromagnetic induction: a moving or changing magnetic field makes electric current flow. Every power station on Earth still works on the principle Faraday found that day. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Faraday

question: In 1895 the world's first great power plant at Niagara Falls proved that electricity could be MADE in one place and used far away. Tesla and Westinghouse's alternating current was generated by the falling water and sent 26 miles. To do what?
answer: Light up the city of Buffalo
choices: Light up the city of Buffalo
Run the streetcars of New York City
Power the docks of Chicago's harbor
Light the lamps of Toronto across the lake
context: Power made at a waterfall lit a city 26 miles away, the proof that electricity could travel. Two years earlier AC had also lit the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, after Westinghouse underbid General Electric. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/what-was-the-war-of-the-currents

question: On August 6, 1890, William Kemmler became the first person ever executed in an electric chair, and it went horribly wrong: a first jolt failed to kill him, and a second left smoke rising from his head. Hearing of the gruesome scene, George Westinghouse delivered a bitter verdict. What did he say?
answer: "They would have done better with an axe."
choices: "They would have done better with an axe."
"No machine should ever do this work."
"This is murder dressed up as science."
"Let the inventor sit in it himself."
context: The first jolt of about 700 volts ran 17 seconds and failed; a second of over 1,000 volts ran two minutes. Westinghouse, whose AC was used in the chair to smear his technology, was disgusted. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Kemmler

question: Michael Faraday, a humble and devout Christian, was offered a knighthood by his nation in honor of his discoveries. He turned it down, and later refused burial among the kings and great men of Westminster Abbey too. What did he say he wished to remain to the end?
answer: Plain Mr Faraday
choices: Plain Mr Faraday
A faithful servant of God
A simple London workman
The bookbinder's apprentice
context: Faraday belonged to a small Christian sect, the Sandemanians, and his faith shaped his humility; he wished to remain 'plain Mr Faraday to the end.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Faraday

question: Nikola Tesla's 1888 deal with George Westinghouse promised him $2.50 for every horsepower of AC power the world would ever generate, a deal that could have made him history's first billionaire. When Westinghouse's company nearly went broke, what did Tesla reportedly do with that contract?
answer: He tore it up to save the company
choices: He tore it up to save the company
He sold it to a rival for quick cash
He sued Westinghouse for every cent
He locked it away and bided his time
context: By reportedly tearing up the royalty contract, Tesla traded a future fortune for a lump sum so Westinghouse could survive, an act of loyalty that may have cost him a billionaire's wealth. Source: https://www.celebritynetworth.com/articles/entertainment-articles/in-1897-nikola-tesla-tore-up-a-contract-that-would-have-made-him-the-worlds-first-billionaire/

question: Thomas Edison had once opposed the death penalty, but to terrify the public away from his rival's alternating current, he staged gruesome public shows meant to prove how deadly AC could be. At these demonstrations, what did Edison electrocute before the crowds?
answer: Live animals
choices: Live animals
Convicted criminals
Wax dummies wired to coils
Iron statues packed with gunpowder
context: Edison publicly electrocuted animals and quietly helped develop the electric chair using an AC generator, so that execution could be nicknamed being 'Westinghoused', turning his rival's own technology into propaganda against it. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/what-was-the-war-of-the-currents

question: On January 1, 1863, Abraham Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation declared the enslaved people in the rebelling states free. One ringing phrase in it became the document's most-quoted line — the very words Lincoln chose to describe the new and permanent condition of the freed. What was that phrase?
answer: Thenceforward, and forever free
choices: Thenceforward, and forever free
Loosed from every earthly chain
Restored to their God-given liberty
Delivered out of the house of bondage
context: The exact phrase from the document is 'thenceforward, and forever free.' Lincoln chose words meant to sound permanent, not provisional. Source: Avalon Project, Yale Law School (full text), https://avalon.law.yale.edu/19th_century/emancipa.asp

question: On the night of December 31, 1862, enslaved and free Black Americans crowded into churches across the country — many of them meeting in secret — to pray and wait for the stroke of midnight, when the Emancipation Proclamation would take effect. People still gather on that same night every New Year's Eve. By what name is that vigil known?
answer: Watch Night
choices: Watch Night
Jubilee Eve
Morning Star service
The Midnight Cry
context: Watch Night, also called Freedom's Eve, traces back to the Moravians and the Methodist preacher John Wesley, but December 31, 1862, gave it new meaning as the wait for emancipation. The tradition is still kept. Source: NMAAHC, The Historical Legacy of Watch Night, https://nmaahc.si.edu/explore/stories/historical-legacy-watch-night

question: At Camp Saxton in Port Royal, South Carolina, the Proclamation was read aloud under the live-oak trees to the 1st South Carolina Volunteers — a regiment of formerly enslaved men. As a U.S. flag was handed to them, a cracked old man's voice and two women's voices rose unprompted from the crowd, and the rest joined in. What song did they begin to sing?
answer: 'My Country, 'Tis of Thee'
choices: 'My Country, 'Tis of Thee'
'Go Down, Moses'
'The Battle Hymn of the Republic'
'Roll, Jordan, Roll'
context: Colonel Thomas Wentworth Higginson, who commanded the regiment, wrote that the spontaneous singing 'seemed the choked voice of a race, at last unloosed.' Sources: NPS, Camp Saxton, https://www.nps.gov/places/camp-saxton.htm ; UChicago Press, Higginson's Civil War Journal, https://press.uchicago.edu/Misc/Chicago/333302.html

question: The Proclamation took effect in 1863, but in remote Texas the news did not arrive for two and a half years. When Union General Gordon Granger finally rode into Galveston and read General Order No. 3, announcing that 'all slaves are free,' the day of his arrival became the oldest celebration of the end of American slavery. What is it called?
answer: Juneteenth
choices: Juneteenth
Emancipation Day
Jubilee Day
Freedom Sunday
context: On June 19, 1865, Granger's order reached the last enslaved people in Texas; the holiday's name — Juneteenth — blends 'June' and 'nineteenth.' Sources: American Battlefield Trust, General Order No. 3, https://www.battlefields.org/learn/primary-sources/general-order-no-3 ; National Archives, https://www.archives.gov/news/articles/juneteenth-original-document

question: When Abraham Lincoln picked up the pen to sign the Emancipation Proclamation on New Year's Day, 1863, he spoke plainly about what the act meant to him. He said he had never in his life felt more certain he was doing right, and that if his name went into history, it would be for this. How did he finish that thought?
answer: My whole soul is in it
choices: My whole soul is in it
Let the nation be cleansed
The debt of two centuries is paid
Now the war has a meaning
context: Lincoln's full line: 'I never, in my life, felt more certain that I was doing right, than I do in signing this paper... and my whole soul is in it.' He signed, looked up, and said simply, 'That will do.' Sources: American Battlefield Trust, 10 Facts; NPS, https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/10-facts-emancipation-proclamation ; https://www.nps.gov/articles/the-emancipation-proclamation.htm

question: Lincoln had the Emancipation Proclamation ready months early, but Secretary of State William Seward warned that announcing it right after Union defeats would look like the war effort's 'last shriek of retreat.' So Lincoln held it back until the army won a major battle, then issued the preliminary version five days later, on September 22, 1862. Which battle gave him the victory he was waiting for?
answer: Antietam
choices: Antietam
Gettysburg
Bull Run
Shiloh
context: The Battle of Antietam (September 17, 1862) was the bloodiest single day in American history, but it was enough of a Union success to let Lincoln act from a position of strength rather than desperation. Sources: American Battlefield Trust, 10 Facts; NPS, https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/10-facts-emancipation-proclamation

question: The Emancipation Proclamation did more than declare people free on paper. It added a clause aimed at the war effort itself — one no earlier emancipation had ever included. What new path did that clause open to freed Black men?
answer: Enlisting as Union soldiers and sailors
choices: Enlisting as Union soldiers and sailors
Working Union supply depots for wages
Settling land seized from the plantations
Voting in Union-occupied Southern towns
context: The Proclamation declared that freed men 'will be received into the armed service of the United States to garrison forts... and to man vessels of all sorts.' Nearly 200,000 Black soldiers and sailors went on to fight for the Union. Sources: National Archives, https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/emancipation-proclamation ; NPS, https://www.nps.gov/articles/the-emancipation-proclamation.htm

question: Lincoln later told his cabinet that the timing of the Proclamation was not only strategy — he had made a private bargain with God. He said he had made a solemn vow that if one thing happened on the battlefield, he would answer it by declaring freedom for the enslaved. What did he vow to act on?
answer: If General Lee was driven back from Pennsylvania
choices: If General Lee was driven back from Pennsylvania
If the Mississippi River fell to the Union
If Richmond surrendered before the new year
If England refused to recognize the South
context: Lincoln's words, recalled by historian James M. McPherson: 'I made a solemn vow before God, that if General Lee was driven back from Pennsylvania, I would crown the result by the declaration of freedom to the slaves.' Source: NPS, The Emancipation Proclamation, https://www.nps.gov/articles/the-emancipation-proclamation.htm

question: In Boston on January 1, 1863, thousands packed Tremont Temple while messengers ran between the hall and the telegraph office, waiting for word that the Proclamation had taken effect. As midnight came and went with no news, Frederick Douglass said the suspense was becoming agony. How did Douglass describe the thing the crowd was waiting for?
answer: Like a bolt from the sky that would rend the fetters of four million slaves
choices: Like a bolt from the sky that would rend the fetters of four million slaves
Like a long-promised harvest finally ripe for the reaping
Like a single candle held against two centuries of darkness
Like a debt the whole nation had at last agreed to pay
context: Douglass wrote that they waited 'as for a bolt from the sky, which should rend the fetters of four millions of slaves... longing for the answer to the agonizing prayers of centuries.' When the news finally arrived, the hall erupted in song. Source: NPS / Frederick Douglass Papers Project, https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/douglass-emancipation-boston.htm

question: The original 1863 signed manuscript draft of the Emancipation Proclamation no longer exists. After the war it was donated to a charity fair raising money for wounded soldiers, and there a single catastrophe destroyed it for good. What claimed the original signed draft?
answer: The Great Chicago Fire of 1871
choices: The Great Chicago Fire of 1871
A flood that swept the Ohio River valley
A boiler explosion aboard a Mississippi steamer
A robbery at the charity fair
context: The fair was held in Chicago, and the signed draft burned in the Great Chicago Fire of October 1871. The neatly copied, Lincoln-signed engrossed version now held by the National Archives is what survives. Source: The Legal Genealogist (cross-checked against National Archives holdings), https://www.legalgenealogist.com/2012/10/08/up-in-flames/

question: Lincoln knew a president could not simply abolish slavery by decree — that would take an act of Congress he did not have. So in the document itself he justified it under his authority as Commander-in-Chief, labeling it with a term that tied emancipation to military necessity rather than to morality. What did he call it?
answer: A fit and necessary war measure
choices: A fit and necessary war measure
A solemn act of national justice
A proclamation of universal liberty
A sacred duty owed to the enslaved
context: By calling it 'a fit and necessary war measure for suppressing said rebellion,' Lincoln anchored emancipation in his war powers — the only legal hook that let him free anyone without Congress. Source: National Archives, https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/emancipation-proclamation

question: Because Lincoln's war powers reached only the rebelling Confederacy, the Proclamation freed no one in the loyal slave-holding border states like Kentucky and Maryland, where slavery stayed legal. It took a change to the Constitution itself, ratified December 6, 1865, to finally end slavery everywhere in the United States. What was that change?
answer: The 13th Amendment
choices: The 13th Amendment
The 14th Amendment
The Civil Rights Act
The Missouri Compromise
context: The Emancipation Proclamation reframed the war as a fight against slavery, but it could not reach the loyal border states. The 13th Amendment, ratified December 6, 1865, abolished slavery nationwide and finished what the Proclamation began. Source: Wikipedia, Emancipation Proclamation (border-state exclusions; 13th Amendment), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emancipation_Proclamation

question: At the Battle of Agincourt in 1415, Henry V's army was not built around mounted knights at all. For every man-at-arms in his ranks, how many of his soldiers were common longbowmen?
answer: About five archers to every man-at-arms
choices: About five archers to every man-at-arms
About one archer to every man-at-arms
About two crossbowmen to every archer
About three knights to every archer
context: Roughly 5,000 longbowmen stood beside only about 1,000 men-at-arms — five of every six men were archers. The common bowman, not the mounted noble, had become the heart of the English army. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Agincourt

question: The English war bow was a giant compared to a sporting bow. Stand an English longbow on its end beside the archer who drew it, and how big was it?
answer: About 6 feet — as tall as the man himself
choices: About 6 feet — as tall as the man himself
About 3 feet — up to his waist
About 4 feet — up to his chest
About 10 feet — twice his height
context: The longbow was cut from a single stave of yew and stood roughly six feet, as tall as or taller than the archer drawing it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_longbow

question: English war arrows were not made to slash flesh — they were made to punch straight through a knight's mail and plate armour. What was this short, narrow, square-pointed steel arrowhead called?
answer: A bodkin point
choices: A bodkin point
A broadhead point
A barbed point
A blunt point
context: The bodkin was a thin square-section steel spike designed to pierce armour. The arrows themselves ran about 30 inches long. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_longbow

question: At Agincourt the English archers planted a defence in the soil in front of their line so that charging French horses would impale themselves or shy away. What did each bowman drive into the ground before him?
answer: A sharpened wooden stake angled toward the enemy
choices: A sharpened wooden stake angled toward the enemy
A small iron caltrop with spikes
A deep hidden pit
A tall woven wicker screen
context: The angled stakes turned the archers' position into a hedge of spikes that broke the cavalry charge. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Agincourt

question: A single yew stave makes a better bow because the two halves of the wood do opposite jobs. The pale sapwood is kept on the back of the bow and the darker heartwood on the belly — so the wood behaves like one natural spring. What is the sapwood on the back especially good at resisting?
answer: Being stretched as the bow bends
choices: Being stretched as the bow bends
Being squashed as the bow bends
Rotting in the rain
Catching fire from a spark
context: Sapwood resists stretching (tension) on the back; heartwood resists squashing (compression) on the belly. One piece of wood works like a laminate spring. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_longbow

question: A modern Olympic recurve archer pulls a bow of about 40 to 50 pounds. The war bows raised from Henry VIII's sunken warship the Mary Rose were far heavier. Roughly how much force did an English war bow take to draw?
answer: About 150 pounds
choices: About 150 pounds
About 60 pounds
About 25 pounds
About 500 pounds
context: Mary Rose bows are estimated at about 150-160 pounds, some up to ~185 — three to four times the pull of a sporting bow today. The ship sank in 1545. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_longbow

question: At Agincourt the French knights had to attack across a narrow ploughed field that heavy rain had turned to deep mud, and men in full plate armour sank to their knees as they came. When a knight lost his footing and went down in the crush of bodies, what became of many of them?
answer: They suffocated or drowned in the mud before rising
choices: They suffocated or drowned in the mud before rising
Their squires dragged them back to safety
They cut themselves free and escaped on foot
They lay frozen where they fell until dawn
context: Armoured knights sank to their knees; when they fell in the press of bodies, many were trampled, suffocated, or effectively drowned in the mud before they could rise. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Agincourt

question: At Crécy in 1346 the French front line was about 6,000 hired Genoese crossbowmen. They were quickly outshot and broke — partly because the big shoulder-high shields they sheltered behind had been left in the baggage train. What were those shields called?
answer: Pavises
choices: Pavises
Bucklers
Targes
Mantlets
context: Without their pavise shields and spare bolts, the Genoese shot exposed and outranged, then fled — and French knights rode down their own retreating crossbowmen. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy

question: Legend says English archers at Agincourt taunted the beaten French by waving back the very fingers the French had vowed to hack off any bowman they captured. In the popular story, which fingers did the archers wave in defiance? (Legend — no medieval source records it.)
answer: The index and middle fingers
choices: The index and middle fingers
The thumb and index finger
The three middle fingers
The ring finger and little finger
context: Legend: archers waved the two bow-fingers (index and middle) in defiance. But it is unrecorded medievally — the chronicler Jean de Wavrin says the threat was to cut off THREE fingers, and the gesture story only appears from the 1970s. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V_sign

question: Because a war bow took years to master while a crossbowman could be trained in weeks, in 1363 King Edward III ordered every able-bodied Englishman to practise archery on holidays. To keep men at the practice-butts, his law also banned a popular idle pastime. Which one?
answer: Football
choices: Football
Chess
Singing in taverns
Horse-racing
context: The 1363 law required holiday archery practice and banned idle games like football that lured men away from the butts. A longbowman took a lifetime to make; a crossbowman, only weeks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_longbow

question: The blind, 50-year-old King John of Bohemia insisted on charging into the fight at Crécy, though he could not see. To grant his wish, his loyal knights did something so they could lead him into the press — and next morning all of them were found dead together. What had they done before the charge?
answer: Tied all their horses' reins together
choices: Tied all their horses' reins together
Carried him forward on a shield
Blindfolded themselves to match him
Sent him in alone on foot
context: His knights bound their horses' reins to his so he could ride in and strike one blow; at dawn they lay dead in a circle, their horses still tied together. Froissart has him beg his men to 'bring me so far forward that I may strike one stroke with my sword.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Bohemia

question: At Crécy the 16-year-old Black Prince was hard-pressed, and a messenger begged his father Edward III — watching from a windmill — to send help. The king refused, wanting his son to earn his own glory. What did Edward III famously say?
answer: 'Let the boy win his spurs'
choices: 'Let the boy win his spurs'
'Order the archers to fall back'
'Bring the prince to me at once'
'Sound the trumpets for retreat'
context: Froissart's fuller line: 'suffer him this day to win his spurs, for if God be pleased, I will this journey be his, and the honour thereof.' The prince held and won renown. Source: https://x.com/LandsknechtPike/status/1960608786416120295

question: Archaeologists who studied the skeletons of the Mary Rose longbowmen could tell at a glance which men were archers — a lifetime of drawing a 150-pound bow from boyhood had reshaped their bones. What was the tell-tale physical mark, found in about a fifth of the crew?
answer: A twisted, over-built left arm and shoulder
choices: A twisted, over-built left arm and shoulder
Thickened collarbones and a curved spine
A worn, flattened right shoulder socket
Spurred and curled finger bones
context: The bones show an over-built left arm, twisted spine, bone spurs, and a flat-socketed shoulder blade (os acromiale) in about 19% of the crew — the signature of drawing a war bow since childhood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_longbow

question: The Epic of Gilgamesh is the oldest written story known on Earth, older than the Iliad and older than the Bible. Long before paper existed, scribes in ancient Mesopotamia first recorded it. What did they write the story on, and how?
answer: Wedge-shaped marks pressed into wet clay tablets
choices: Wedge-shaped marks pressed into wet clay tablets
Black ink brushed onto long papyrus scrolls
Letters carved into tall standing stones
Words inked across stretched animal-skin parchment
context: The script is called cuneiform, made by pressing a cut reed into soft clay, which then hardened. The earliest Sumerian versions date to roughly 2100 BCE. Source: Britannica, Epic of Gilgamesh; Yale University Press.

question: In the Epic of Gilgamesh, the gods create a hairy giant named Enkidu to be the hero's equal. Before he ever sees a city, Enkidu lives far out in the wilderness. Who did Enkidu grow up among out there?
answer: The wild animals, eating grass beside the gazelles
choices: The wild animals, eating grass beside the gazelles
A roaming band of desert shepherds
A hidden village of mountain hermits
The soldiers of a forgotten frontier fort
context: Enkidu lived covered in hair, ate grass with the gazelles, and drank at the waterhole alongside the beasts -- a man raised by animals. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_of_Gilgamesh; SparkNotes Gilgamesh summary.

question: When the wild man Enkidu finally comes to the city of Uruk, he plants himself in a doorway and blocks the path of King Gilgamesh himself. The two giants crash together and wrestle. Gilgamesh wins the fight -- so what happens between the two of them next?
answer: They become inseparable best friends
choices: They become inseparable best friends
Gilgamesh throws Enkidu into the city dungeon
Enkidu flees back into the wilderness forever
Gilgamesh makes Enkidu his lowly servant
context: Enkidu's strength so impressed Gilgamesh that the two became inseparable -- their friendship is the heart of the whole story. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_of_Gilgamesh; worldhistory.org/gilgamesh.

question: At the very end of the Epic of Gilgamesh, the hero finally holds a prickly plant from the bottom of the sea that can make an old man young again. He sets it down to bathe in a cool pool. While his back is turned, a snake slips up and swallows the plant. Ancient storytellers said this explains a real thing snakes do -- what?
answer: Snakes shed their old skin
choices: Snakes shed their old skin
Snakes grow a whole new set of fangs
Snakes flick their tongues to taste the air
Snakes can swallow prey bigger than their heads
context: As the snake slid away it shed its skin -- which the storytellers said is why snakes renew themselves, while Gilgamesh went home empty-handed. Told as legend, the ancient explanation for a real animal trait. Source: worldhistory.org, The Eternal Life of Gilgamesh.

question: The Epic of Gilgamesh opens by boasting that its hero is the strongest of all kings and the builder of the mighty walls of Uruk -- a man who is part god and part human. Exactly how much of Gilgamesh does the poem say is divine?
answer: Two thirds
choices: Two thirds
One half
One quarter
Nine tenths
context: The poem calls him 'two thirds divine and one third mortal.' His mother was the goddess Ninsun and his father the priest-king Lugalbanda. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilgamesh; Wikiquote Epic of Gilgamesh (Andrew George 2000).

question: In the Epic of Gilgamesh, the goddess Ishtar demands that Gilgamesh marry her. He refuses and mocks her, so in a rage she unleashes the monstrous Bull of Heaven on the city. Enkidu grabs the bull by the tail while Gilgamesh drives an axe into its skull. Then Enkidu does one more thing as the ultimate insult to the watching goddess -- what?
answer: He tears off the bull's haunch and hurls it up at Ishtar
choices: He tears off the bull's haunch and hurls it up at Ishtar
He drinks a horn of wine in front of her
He carves her name into the dead bull's hide
He drags the carcass to the temple steps
context: Enkidu flung the bull's haunch up at Ishtar as she watched from the city walls. Ishtar had threatened to smash the gates of the underworld and let the dead devour the living if refused. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilgamesh; worldhistory.org.

question: Gilgamesh and Enkidu march to the Cedar Forest to fight its giant guardian, the monster Humbaba. The sun-god Shamash sends thirteen great winds that pin the monster down and blind him. Beaten, Humbaba begs the two heroes for mercy. What do they do to him?
answer: They cut off his head
choices: They cut off his head
They spare him and take his oath
They chain him and haul him to Uruk
They leave him blinded in the forest
context: Despite Humbaba's pleas, the two heroes beheaded the forest guardian. Source: worldhistory.org; k12.hillsdale.edu abridged Gilgamesh.

question: In 1872, a self-taught British Museum scholar named George Smith was piecing together a broken clay tablet from the ruins of Nineveh when he suddenly read an ancient flood story -- a boat resting on a mountain, a bird sent out to find dry land.
