According to the famous account, how did Smith react in that moment?
answer: He leaped up and ran round the room
choices: He leaped up and ran round the room
He bolted out to telegraph the news to a rival
He locked the tablet in a drawer that night
He smashed the case glass grabbing for it
context: Smith was so overcome he ran about the room and even began tearing at his clothes. He had found a Babylonian flood story older than the Bible's, and announced it on December 3, 1872, to an audience that included prime minister William Gladstone. Source: National Geographic, 'Discovering Gilgamesh'; Smithsonian Magazine 'Epic Hero'.

question: When his best friend Enkidu dies, Gilgamesh cannot accept it. He weeps over the body for six days and seven nights, refusing to let anyone bury his friend, as if his grief could bring him back. What finally forces Gilgamesh to give up the body -- and fills him with terror that he too must die?
answer: A maggot drops from Enkidu's nose
choices: A maggot drops from Enkidu's nose
The body begins to glow at dawn
A vulture circles down over the corpse
The gods send a dream commanding it
context: Seeing the maggot, Gilgamesh accepts that death is final -- and is struck with terror of his own death, which sends him searching for immortality. Source: SparkNotes Tablets 8 & 9; learner.org, 'Experts' View: Enkidu's Death.'

question: A flood survivor named Utnapishtim tells Gilgamesh how he found dry land after the great deluge. He released three birds from his stranded boat, one after another. A dove flew out and came back. A swallow flew out and came back. The third bird flew out and never returned, proving the waters had gone. Which bird was it?
answer: A raven
choices: A raven
An eagle
A falcon
A heron
context: The raven found the waters gone and never came back. Afterward Utnapishtim sacrificed, and the gods crowded around the sweet smell 'like flies.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilgamesh_flood_myth; Wikiquote Tablet XI (Andrew George 2000).

question: In the flood story Gilgamesh hears, the survivor Utnapishtim is warned by a god to tear down his house and build a great boat to ride out the coming deluge. The boat he builds is not shaped like a normal ship at all. What shape is Utnapishtim's ark?
answer: A giant cube with seven levels inside
choices: A giant cube with seven levels inside
A long, narrow war-galley
A round basket of woven reeds
A flat raft of lashed logs
context: Each side measured 120 cubits, its floor covered the area of a whole field, and it held seven levels divided into compartments. He loaded family, craftsmen, and animals before the waters came. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilgamesh_flood_myth; shmoop.com Tablet 11.

question: When George Smith read out the Babylonian flood tablet in 1872, Victorian London was stunned -- because the story sounded deeply familiar. In it, a god warns one righteous man to build a boat, he saves his family and the animals, the boat lands on a mountain, and he releases birds to test for dry land. Which famous story does the Gilgamesh flood closely match?
answer: Noah's Ark in the Book of Genesis
choices: Noah's Ark in the Book of Genesis
Deucalion's flood in Greek myth
Manu and the fish in Hindu myth
Atlantis sinking in Plato's tale
context: The two flood stories share the boat, the rescued animals, the mountain landing, and the released birds. The Gilgamesh version was written down centuries before the Hebrew one -- a fascinating resonance between two ancient peoples. Source: biblicalarchaeology.org; National Geographic.

question: Almost every story from the ancient world is a mystery in some way -- when it was made, how it was first recorded, or who actually composed it. The polished standard version of the Epic of Gilgamesh, shaped around 1200 BCE, is unusual among these ancient tales. What makes it stand out?
answer: Its author is one of the few from antiquity we can name
choices: Its author is one of the few from antiquity we can name
It was sung from memory and never written down
It was set down by a king, not by a scribe
It was pressed into gold tablets, not into clay
context: The scribe-priest Sin-leqi-unninni wove together the standard Babylonian version between roughly 1300 and 1000 BCE -- making him one of the earliest authors in all of history whose name we still know, when nearly every other ancient story comes down to us anonymous. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilgamesh; worldhistory.org/gilgamesh.

question: After Moses led the freed Hebrew slaves out of Egypt and into the trackless desert, the people had no roads or maps to follow. The story says God himself went out ahead of them to lead the way, and the sign of his presence looked one way by day and a different way by night. What guided the Israelites through the wilderness?
answer: A pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night
choices: A pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night
A great white star by day and a burning torch by night
A circling eagle by day and a golden lamp by night
A long trumpet blast by day and a steady drum by night
context: By day a pillar of cloud and by night a pillar of fire went before them so they could travel at any hour. Source: Exodus 13:21-22 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parting_of_the_Red_Sea).

question: Moses and his brother Aaron walked straight into the court of the most powerful king on earth, the Pharaoh of Egypt, carrying a single demand from the God of the Hebrew slaves. Thousands of years later that exact demand would become the rallying cry of people fighting slavery around the world. What did Moses and Aaron demand of Pharaoh?
answer: Let my people go
choices: Let my people go
Lower our daily quota
Give back our stolen land
Spare our newborn sons
context: The full demand was 'Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness.' Pharaoh sneered back, 'Who is the LORD, that I should obey him? I do not know the LORD.' Source: Exodus 5:1-2 (https://www.biblestudytools.com/bible-study/topical-studies/who-hardened-pharaohs-heart-in-exodus.html).

question: On the night of the last and most terrible plague, every Hebrew family was told to smear the blood of a lamb on the wooden frames of their doors as a sign. The story says that when the LORD swept through Egypt to strike down every firstborn son, he treated the blood-marked houses differently from all the rest. What did the LORD do at those marked doorways?
answer: He passed over them
choices: He passed over them
He sealed them shut
He set them aflame
He turned away from them
context: Because the LORD 'passed over' the blood-marked houses and spared everyone inside, the festival has ever since been called Passover. Source: Exodus 12:13 (https://www.bible.com/bible/296/EXO.12.13-28.GNBUK).

question: To prove their God's power, Aaron threw his shepherd's staff down on the floor of Pharaoh's court and it became a snake. Pharaoh's own court magicians scoffed and threw down their staffs, and those turned into snakes too. Then one thing happened that settled whose power was greater. What did Aaron's snake do?
answer: It swallowed up all of the magicians' snakes
choices: It swallowed up all of the magicians' snakes
It spat fire across the whole throne room
It coiled itself around Pharaoh's high throne
It grew as long as the great hall itself
context: Aaron's serpent devoured all the magicians' serpents. Later, when the magicians could not even copy the plague of gnats, they admitted to Pharaoh, 'This is the finger of God.' Source: Exodus 7:10-12 (https://biblehub.com/exodus/7-12.htm).

question: Trapped against the sea with Pharaoh's chariots thundering up behind them, the Israelites watched Moses stretch out his hand. A strong east wind blew the waters back all night, and the people crossed on the dry seabed between two standing walls of water. Then the whole Egyptian army charged in after them across the seabed. What happened to the Egyptians' war-chariots as they drove?
answer: Their wheels jammed and clogged
choices: Their wheels jammed and clogged
Their wheels snapped off
Their wheels sank into the sand
Their wheels caught fire
context: God 'clogged the chariot wheels' so the Egyptians drove with difficulty; then the wind dropped, the walls of water collapsed, and the sea returned over Pharaoh's army. Source: Exodus 14:21-28 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parting_of_the_Red_Sea).

question: Moses had been gone forty days up on Mount Sinai, and the restless people below gave up waiting for him. They talked Aaron into melting all their gold earrings into an idol shaped like a calf, and they bowed down to it. When Moses came back down and saw the idol, his fury was famous, but it is what he did to the golden calf itself that nobody ever forgets. What did Moses do to the idol?
answer: He ground it to powder and made the people drink it
choices: He ground it to powder and made the people drink it
He threw it into a fire and burned it to ash
He buried it in the sand and marked the spot
He smashed it apart and handed back the gold
context: Moses burned the calf, ground it to powder, scattered it on water, and made the Israelites drink it. The people had declared of the idol, 'This is your god, O Israel.' Source: Exodus 32 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_calf).

question: While herding sheep on the slopes of Mount Horeb, Moses came upon the strangest sight: a bush wrapped in flame that burned and burned but never turned to ash. A voice from the fire called him to go free the Hebrew slaves. Moses asked the voice what name he should give the people when they asked who had sent him. What name did the voice give itself?
answer: I AM WHO I AM
choices: I AM WHO I AM
I am the God of your fathers
I am the First and the Last
I am the Light of the World
context: In Hebrew the name is 'ehyeh asher ehyeh.' God told Moses, 'Say to the people: I AM has sent me to you.' Source: Exodus 3:2-14 (https://www.esv.org/Exodus+3/).

question: Starving in the desert, the Israelites woke to find the ground covered in thin white flakes like frost, food they believed God had rained down from heaven. They had never seen anything like it before, and the name they gave it preserves, word for word, what they first said when they saw the strange flakes. What does the word 'manna' actually mean?
answer: What is it?
choices: What is it?
Is it bread?
Where is it from?
Who sent it?
context: The name comes from the people's own startled question, 'man hu?', meaning 'What is it?' God also sent flocks of quail to them in the evenings. Source: Exodus 16 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massah_and_Meribah).

question: After leading the Israelites through forty long years of wandering in the wilderness, Moses climbed alone to the top of Mount Nebo, by then an old man of a hundred and twenty. Spread out below him in the distance lay the Promised Land, the whole goal of the entire journey. What happened to Moses there on Mount Nebo?
answer: He was allowed to see the land but never to enter it
choices: He was allowed to see the land but never to enter it
He led the people down into the land at last
He chose to turn back into the desert alone
He vanished from the mountaintop in a cloud
context: Moses died at 120 on Mount Nebo, permitted to see the Promised Land but not to set foot in it, after the people had been sentenced to wander forty years. Source: Deuteronomy 34:1-7 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses).

question: Every English Bible calls the water that Moses parted the 'Red Sea,' and generations of readers have pictured that exact body of water. But the original Hebrew name was Yam Suph. When ancient Greek translators first turned the Hebrew scriptures into Greek, they rendered Yam Suph as 'Red Sea,' a label that then stuck for two thousand years. What does the Hebrew name Yam Suph actually mean?
answer: Sea of Reeds
choices: Sea of Reeds
Sea of Blood
Sea of Storms
Sea of the End
context: Yam Suph literally means 'Sea of Reeds'; the familiar 'Red Sea' comes from the later Greek translation, not the Hebrew. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parting_of_the_Red_Sea.

question: Joseph, who had died in Egypt centuries before the Exodus, had made his family swear a solemn oath: they were to remember him when God finally led them out of Egypt. On the chaotic night the Israelites finally fled, while everyone else was loading up silver and gold, Moses kept that ancient promise. How did Moses keep Joseph's oath?
answer: He carried his bones out with him
choices: He carried his bones out with him
He buried an empty coffin in his honor
He built a tomb for him in Egypt
He spoke his name over the people
context: The Israelites left in such haste their bread had no time to rise, and they 'plundered the Egyptians' of silver and gold; even so, Moses carried out the bones of Joseph, just as Joseph had made them swear generations earlier. Source: Exodus 13:19; Joshua 24:32 (https://www.esv.org/Exodus+13:19;Joshua+24:32/).

question: In 1776 the brand-new United States needed an official Great Seal, and Benjamin Franklin had a bold idea: an image of Moses raising his hand over the Red Sea to drown Pharaoh and his chariots. Beneath the picture Franklin wanted a short, defiant motto. What motto did Franklin propose for the seal?
answer: Rebellion to Tyrants is Obedience to God
choices: Rebellion to Tyrants is Obedience to God
These are the times that try men's souls
Give me liberty, or give me death
We hold these truths to be self-evident
context: Franklin's proposed seal showed 'Moses... extending his hand over the sea,' casting the American rebels as the freed Israelites and King George as Pharaoh. Thomas Jefferson separately proposed the Israelites in the wilderness led by a cloud and a pillar of fire. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Seal_of_the_United_States.

question: The story of the Exodus became the story that enslaved African Americans told about themselves, singing spirituals about escaping their own bondage in Egypt. One real woman risked her life again and again guiding people north along the Underground Railroad, and those she helped gave her a nickname taken straight from the Exodus story. What was Harriet Tubman's nickname?
answer: Moses
choices: Moses
Miriam
Aaron
Joshua
context: Harriet Tubman was called 'Moses' for leading her people to freedom; enslaved African Americans sang the spiritual 'Go Down, Moses,' crying 'Let my people go.' The night before he was murdered, Martin Luther King Jr. preached, 'I've been to the mountaintop... and I've seen the Promised Land.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Go_Down_Moses.

question: James Hargreaves, a Lancashire weaver who could not read or write, built a new spinning machine around 1764. An ordinary spinning wheel could spin only one thread at a time. How many threads could Hargreaves' very first 'spinning jenny' spin at once?
answer: Eight threads at once
choices: Eight threads at once
Two threads at once
Four threads at once
Sixteen threads at once
context: One spinner could now do the work of eight. Hargreaves built his jenny at Stanhill, near Blackburn; the machine kicked off the mechanization of cotton spinning. (britannica.com/biography/James-Hargreaves; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinning_jenny)

question: James Hargreaves was a poor Lancashire weaver, and as legend tells it the idea for his spinning jenny came to him by accident inside his own cottage. What did he supposedly see that gave him the idea?
answer: A spinning wheel knocked over, its spindle still turning upright
choices: A spinning wheel knocked over, its spindle still turning upright
His wife spinning faster than any neighbour in the village
A broken loom that wove two cloths instead of one
A water mill wheel turning steadily out his window
context: The story says his daughter knocked the wheel over and Hargreaves noticed the spindle kept spinning while standing upright, which suggested several spindles could stand in a row and spin together. It is a charming legend, not a documented fact. (britannica.com/biography/James-Hargreaves)

question: In 1768 a mob broke into James Hargreaves' house near Blackburn and smashed his spinning jennies, terrified the machines would steal spinners' jobs. Yet the rioters reportedly did not destroy every machine. Which jennies did they choose to spare?
answer: Any jenny with twenty spindles or fewer
choices: Any jenny with twenty spindles or fewer
Any jenny owned by a poor widow
Any jenny that was still half-built
Any jenny made of oak rather than iron
context: The rioters judged only the bigger machines 'mischievous' enough to threaten their livelihoods, so they spared the smaller ones. Hargreaves fled south to Nottingham. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinning_jenny)

question: Richard Arkwright would later be celebrated as a pioneer of cotton-spinning machinery, but he did not begin life as an engineer or a mill owner. What was Arkwright's trade in Bolton before he turned to spinning machines?
answer: A barber and wig-maker
choices: A barber and wig-maker
A blacksmith
A weaver
A clockmaker
context: Arkwright shaved chins and made wigs before patenting the water frame in 1769. He worked out the machine with clockmaker John Kay (the third choice's near-miss). (scienceandindustrymuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/richard-arkwright)

question: Richard Arkwright built the world's first water-powered cotton spinning mill at Cromford in Derbyshire in 1771. From 1772 the mill ran on two thirteen-hour shifts. Put together, how long did the mill keep running each day?
answer: Around the clock, day and night
choices: Around the clock, day and night
Eighteen hours, then closed overnight
Two ten-hour shifts, twenty hours in all
Around the clock, but closed on Sundays
context: Two thirteen-hour shifts kept the machinery turning the full twenty-four hours. Sir Robert Peel testified the machines were often 'employed for the whole four-and-twenty hours.' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cromford_Mill)

question: At Richard Arkwright's Cromford mill the gates were shut at six in the morning and six at night, exactly on time. A worker who turned up even a little late after the gates closed faced a harsh penalty. What was it?
answer: He lost that day's pay and was fined a second day's wages
choices: He lost that day's pay and was fined a second day's wages
He was sent home with a warning the first time
He had one hour docked from his pay
He was locked out for the rest of the week
context: A latecomer lost a day's pay for the work he missed AND was fined another day's pay on top of it. Strict clock discipline like this was new to workers used to setting their own pace at home. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cromford_Mill)

question: Richard Arkwright staffed his Cromford mill with workers brought in from outside the area, and built them a cluster of cottages, plus shops, pubs, chapels and a school. What did this make Cromford?
answer: The first purpose-built factory village in the world
choices: The first purpose-built factory village in the world
The first English town with a public library
The first village in Britain lit by gas lamps
The first mill town served by its own railway
context: Arkwright built a whole village from scratch so his imported workforce would have somewhere to live next to the mill, the first factory housing development anywhere. His workforce was mostly women and children, the youngest only seven years old. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cromford_Mill)

question: Richard Arkwright rose from a barber to the owner of mills employing nearly a thousand people, and by the time he died in 1792 his cotton fortune had made him extraordinary. What was Arkwright said to be at his death?
answer: The wealthiest untitled man in Britain
choices: The wealthiest untitled man in Britain
The best-paid worker in all Lancashire
The largest landowner in Derbyshire
The richest man in the whole world
context: No lord or duke, just a former wig-maker, Arkwright died richer than any other commoner in the land. His factory model had spread across Britain. (scienceandindustrymuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/richard-arkwright)

question: Samuel Crompton, working in a tiny upstairs study he called his 'conjuring room' in a Bolton manor house, finished a new spinning machine around 1779. He named it the spinning 'mule.' Why that odd name?
answer: Because it crossed two earlier machines, the jenny and the water frame
choices: Because it crossed two earlier machines, the jenny and the water frame
Because it was as stubborn as a mule to keep running
Because a real mule turned the wheel that powered it
Because Crompton had bred mules before he built it
context: A mule is the cross of a horse and a donkey, so Crompton's machine, which brought together Hargreaves' jenny and Arkwright's water frame, got the same name. Its sliding carriage rolled back and forth 54 inches and spun thread fine enough for muslin. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Crompton)

question: Edmund Cartwright patented the first power loom in 1785, mechanizing the weaving of cloth just as spinning had been mechanized. The remarkable thing is that he had never built a machine in his life before a 1784 visit to Arkwright's mills inspired him. What had Cartwright been until then?
answer: A country clergyman
choices: A country clergyman
A retired sea captain
A Manchester cotton merchant
A blacksmith's apprentice
context: Cartwright was the rector of Goadby Marwood, a parish priest with no engineering training. His first loom barely worked, but by 1789 he had coupled an improved one to a Boulton and Watt steam engine. (britannica.com/biography/Edmund-Cartwright)

question: Britain banned exporting its textile machinery and even forbade skilled mill workers from emigrating. In 1789 Samuel Slater, just 21, slipped out of England disguised as a farm labourer to take Arkwright's machine designs to America. How did he carry the secret designs past the ban?
answer: Entirely in his memory, with no drawings at all
choices: Entirely in his memory, with no drawings at all
Sewn into the lining of his coat
Hidden inside a hollow walking stick
Locked in a false-bottomed trunk
context: Slater memorized the whole machine and carried not a single plan, so nothing could be found on him. In Rhode Island his water-powered mill began spinning on 20 December 1790; back home in Belper his old neighbours branded him 'Slater the Traitor,' while Andrew Jackson later called him the 'Father of the American Industrial Revolution.' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Slater)

question: The youngest children in the cotton mills had a job called 'scavenger.' David Rowland, who did it, told a parliamentary committee in 1832 that he was in danger of accidents constantly because the machinery never stopped moving. What was a scavenger's actual task?
answer: To crawl under the moving machinery and sweep up loose cotton
choices: To crawl under the moving machinery and sweep up loose cotton
To carry water to the thirsty spinners
To oil the gears high above the floor
To tie broken threads back together
context: Rowland testified: 'I frequently had to be under the wheels... I was very frequently obliged to lie flat, to avoid being run over or caught.' Some scavengers were only seven years old. (spartacus-educational.com/IRscavengers.htm)

question: Robert Blincoe, a London workhouse orphan, was sent at age seven in 1799 to scavenge in the cotton mills, ending up at the notorious Litton Mill. His 1828 'Memoir of Robert Blincoe' described the beatings and starvation he suffered. That memoir is widely argued to have inspired which Charles Dickens novel?
answer: Oliver Twist
choices: Oliver Twist
Hard Times
Great Expectations
David Copperfield
context: Blincoe's account of a beaten, half-starved workhouse orphan strongly echoes Dickens's most famous orphan, Oliver Twist. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Blincoe)

question: Michael Sadler's 1832 parliamentary committee questioned eighty-nine former child workers, who described twelve-to-sixteen-hour days in the textile mills. When the exhausted children began nodding off at the machines late at night, what did the committee hear the overseers did to keep them working?
answer: Beat them to keep them awake
choices: Beat them to keep them awake
Doused them with cold water
Pinched and shook them hard
Made them stand on one leg
context: Children too tired to stay upright were beaten awake so the machines kept running. This testimony drove the Factory Act of 1833, which limited children's hours and, for the first time, sent government inspectors into the mills. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sadler_report)

question: In February 1834 the owners of the cotton mills at Lowell, Massachusetts, cut the wages of their young mill girls by 12.5 percent. About 800 of the women walked out together in a 'turn-out,' or strike, and the strike set off a run on two of Lowell's banks. What did the mill girls do that triggered the run?
answer: Withdrew all their savings at once
choices: Withdrew all their savings at once
Refused to repay their store debts
Stopped depositing their weekly pay
Demanded their wages in gold coin
context: The mill girls lived in company boardinghouses on a strict bell schedule, with just thirty minutes each to rush home for breakfast and dinner. When 800 of them emptied their savings accounts at the same time, two banks faced a run. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowell_mill_girls)

question: On 4 September 476 the Western Roman Empire, after ruling the Mediterranean for some five centuries, ended not with a great battle but with a frightened boy. He was only about ten years old, a powerless puppet his soldiers had put on the throne months earlier. When the barbarian commander Odoacer marched on the capital, the child was forced to step down before the Senate. History would never forget his name. What was this last Western Roman emperor called?
answer: Romulus Augustulus
choices: Romulus Augustulus
Constantine I
Marcus Aurelius
Julius Caesar
context: The haunting part is the name itself. 'Romulus' was the legendary FOUNDER and first king of Rome; 'Augustus' was its first emperor. The empire that began with a Romulus and an Augustus ended with a single child who carried both names at once. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romulus_Augustulus

question: When the conqueror Odoacer deposed the ten-year-old emperor Romulus Augustulus in 476, the fallen boy was at his mercy. Other toppled rulers of the age were killed, blinded, or shut away in monasteries — but Romulus met a far gentler end. What became of the deposed child emperor?
answer: Spared, with a pension and a seaside villa near Naples
choices: Spared, with a pension and a seaside villa near Naples
Married off to a daughter of the eastern emperor
Tonsured a monk and sent to a Greek monastery
Kept as a hostage in chains at Odoacer's court
context: Odoacer granted Romulus 6,000 gold solidi a year and exiled him to the Castellum Lucullanum, a grand estate near Naples first built by the famous general Lucullus around the 60s BC. The last emperor of Rome simply retired into comfortable obscurity. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romulus_Augustulus

question: On the night of 24 August 410, Alaric's Visigoths broke through the walls and plundered the city of Rome itself — the first time a foreign enemy had taken the city in nearly 800 years. Word of it stunned the whole Roman world. Far away in Bethlehem, the scholar Jerome was so shaken he stopped his work and mourned in a letter. What did Jerome write?
answer: "The city which had taken the whole world was itself taken."
choices: "The city which had taken the whole world was itself taken."
"Rome has fallen; now let the heavens fall with her."
"The wolves have entered the eternal city."
"Our mother is dead, and we are left orphans."
context: The sack of 410 was a psychological earthquake — Rome had not fallen to an outside foe since the Gauls centuries before. Jerome's grief captured the disbelief of an age that thought the city eternal. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(410)

question: In June 455 the king Gaiseric and his men plundered Rome for two full weeks, so methodical that they stripped the gilded bronze roof tiles right off the Temple of Jupiter. Their thoroughness so impressed later generations that, during the French Revolution, people coined a brand-new word to mean wanton destruction. Which English word do we owe to Gaiseric's plunderers?
answer: Vandalism
choices: Vandalism
Sabotage
Pillage
Mayhem
context: Gaiseric's people were the Vandals; their two-week sack (2-16 June 455) became the byword for needless wreckage, and the term 'vandalism' was coined in 1794 by a French bishop describing revolutionary destruction. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(455)

question: Long before the final collapse, the Roman Empire had already been cut in two: an eastern half that grew rich and, ruled from its new capital Constantinople, would survive another thousand years, and a western half that fell apart in 476. Around 285-293 AD it was a single ambitious emperor who first carved the empire into these two pieces to make it easier to govern. Which emperor first split Rome in two?
answer: Diocletian
choices: Diocletian
Constantine the Great
Caesar Augustus
Theodosius the Great
context: Diocletian's division is why we speak of a Western Roman Empire that 'fell' while the Eastern (later Byzantine) Empire lived on until 1453. The two halves drifted apart in wealth, language, and fortune. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/8-reasons-why-rome-fell

question: The boy-emperor's full title sounded magnificent: Romulus AUGUSTULUS. But Augustulus was no honor — Romans threw it at the powerless child as an insult even while he reigned. What did the nickname 'Augustulus' actually mean?
answer: "Little Augustus" — a sneer at a powerless boy
choices: "Little Augustus" — a sneer at a powerless boy
"Second Augustus" — a hopeful new beginning
"Augustus reborn" — a sign from the gods
"Young Caesar" — an affectionate pet name
context: In Greek the mockery went further: he was called 'Momylus,' meaning 'little disgrace.' The grandest name in Rome had been turned into a playground taunt for a child who never truly ruled. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romulus_Augustulus

question: The real power behind the throne in 476 was not the boy emperor at all but his father Orestes, the army's supreme commander, who had placed his own son on the throne. Yet Orestes had once held a startling job earlier in his career — he had worked as the personal secretary to one of Rome's most feared enemies. Whom had Orestes served?
answer: Attila the Hun
choices: Attila the Hun
Constantine the Great
The Vandal king Gaiseric
The eastern emperor Zeno
context: Orestes had been notarius (personal secretary) to Attila himself before rising in Roman service. The man who installed the last Western emperor had once taken dictation for the 'Scourge of God.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romulus_Augustulus

question: Having conquered Italy and deposed the boy emperor in 476, Odoacer could have placed the imperial crown on his own head and declared himself Augustus of the West. He refused the crown — and then did something unexpected with the trappings of empire that came with it. What did Odoacer do with the western crown and imperial robes?
answer: Shipped them across the Adriatic to Constantinople
choices: Shipped them across the Adriatic to Constantinople
Burned them publicly in the Roman Forum
Locked them away in his private treasury
Wore them at his own grand coronation
context: Odoacer sent the imperial regalia east to Emperor Zeno, declaring the West needed no emperor of its own, and claimed for himself only the humbler title 'King of Italy.' He governed Italy without ever pretending to be a Roman emperor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deposition_of_Romulus_Augustus

question: Odoacer, the man who ended the Western Roman Empire, met a grisly end himself. In 493, after a long siege of Ravenna, the Ostrogoth king Theodoric invited him to a banquet to make peace — then drew his sword and, by tradition, split Odoacer from collarbone to thigh in a single stroke. According to the legend, what did Theodoric say as he looked at the body?
answer: "The wretch can't have had any bones in his body."
choices: "The wretch can't have had any bones in his body."
"Now Ravenna is mine, and all Italy with it."
"Let no man speak to me of mercy again."
"So perish every traitor who would be king."
context: The single-stroke killing and the boast are reported by tradition rather than proven fact, so they read as legend. Theodoric went on to rule Italy for over thirty years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodoric_the_Great

question: School textbooks treat 476 AD as THE date the Roman Empire fell — one of the most famous years in all of history. But to the people actually living through it, Odoacer's takeover looked like just another change at the top, and chroniclers barely remarked on it. The year only became a world-historical turning point centuries later, when one British historian fixed it in everyone's mind in his great 1700s work 'The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire.' Which historian made 476 'the Fall of Rome'?
answer: Edward Gibbon
choices: Edward Gibbon
Peter Brown
Bryan Ward-Perkins
Alexander Demandt
context: Fifth-century Romans saw Odoacer's coup as ordinary politics; almost no one thought an empire had ended. It was Edward Gibbon, writing in the 1700s, who turned 476 into the grand symbol of Rome's fall that schoolchildren learn today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Roman_Empire

question: Most people learn that Romulus Augustulus was the last Western Roman emperor. Yet many historians argue he doesn't really count — that the true last emperor was a rival whom Orestes had earlier overthrown, a man who kept the imperial title in exile in Dalmatia and was still recognized as the rightful emperor by the eastern court until his own guards murdered him in 480. Whom do these historians name as the real last Western emperor?
answer: Julius Nepos
choices: Julius Nepos
Flavius Glycerius
Flavius Majorian
Flavius Avitus
context: Julius Nepos was still treated as the legitimate Western emperor in Constantinople after 476; the counts Ovida and Viator killed him at his villa near Salona on 9 May 480. By this reckoning the empire 'ended' in 480, not 476 — proof that even Rome's final date is debated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Nepos

question: Ask why Rome fell and you will not get one clean answer — historians have never agreed. In 1984 the German scholar Alexander Demandt actually counted up every explanation ever proposed and reached 210 different reasons, ranging from barbarian invasions and a broken economy to causes that sound almost absurd. Which of these genuinely strange theories was on Demandt's list?
answer: Romans bathed too much
choices: Romans bathed too much
Romans ate too much bread
Romans slept too little
Romans sang the wrong hymns
context: Demandt's catalogue of 210 reasons really does include excessive bathing and over-deforestation alongside the serious theories. The sheer length of the list is the lesson: honest history admits that the 'fall of Rome' has no single tidy cause. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire

question: The ancient Greeks named this land Mesopotamia, after its two great rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates, which both pour down from the mountains of eastern Turkey toward the Persian Gulf. In Greek, the name describes exactly where all that farmland sat. What does the name 'Mesopotamia' literally mean?
answer: the land between the rivers
choices: the land between the rivers
the valley below the mountains
the plain beside the salt sea
the gift of the flooding river
context: 'Mesopotamia' is Greek for 'the land in the middle of rivers' (mesos, 'middle' + potamos, 'river'). The two rivers are the Tigris and the Euphrates; both rise in the mountains of eastern Turkey and run down to the Persian Gulf. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Mesopotamia

question: Southern Mesopotamia got almost no rain, yet its farmers grew enough food to feed entire cities. The secret was the yearly flood: when the Tigris and the Euphrates overflowed their banks and then drained away again, they left a fresh layer of one thing spread across the fields. What did the floodwater leave behind on the farmland?
answer: a layer of river mud
choices: a layer of river mud
a drift of fine sand
a scatter of broken shells
a mat of dead reeds
context: Each flood spread a fresh coat of silt (river mud) over the fields, working like free fertilizer left behind by the water. The Tigris and Euphrates carried several times more silt for the same amount of water than the Nile did. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/9/agriculture-in-the-fertile-crescent--mesopotamia/

question: In ancient Sumer, one grain became the king of the fields, because it could keep growing in salty, sun-baked soil where finer grains gave out. The Sumerians prized it so much that they used it as everyday money and baked it into their daily flatbread. Which grain was it?
answer: barley
choices: barley
wheat
millet
oats
context: Barley shrugged off the salty, sun-baked southern soil, so Sumerians treated it as everyday money and baked it into flatbread. Wheat and emmer were the fancier grains, saved for beer and luxury foods. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/9/agriculture-in-the-fertile-crescent--mesopotamia/

question: For thousands of years a plow did just one thing: drag a furrow through the soil. About 5,000 years ago, Sumerian farmers bolted a clever attachment onto their plows so that, in the very same pass that cut the furrow, the machine handled the next chore as well. What second job did the Sumerian seed plow do all on its own?
answer: it planted the seed in the furrow
choices: it planted the seed in the furrow
it watered the soil from a tank
it raked the furrow shut again
it spread manure over the row
context: A funnel attached to the plow dropped seed straight into the furrow as it was dug, doing both jobs in one pass. It took a crew of three to run: one to lead the ox, one to steer the plow, and one to pour grain down the funnel. Source: https://www.thecollector.com/mesopotamian-inventions-2/

question: Before farming, nearly every person had to spend the whole day just finding food, so almost no one had time for anything else. Then Mesopotamian irrigation changed everything: a handful of farmers could suddenly grow far more grain than their own families could eat. Historians say this extra food is the very thing that made the first cities possible. What did all that surplus grain let the rest of the people finally do?
answer: take up crafts and trades of their own
choices: take up crafts and trades of their own
march off to conquer distant neighbors
wander away to live as roaming herders
stop all work and live in ease
context: Once a few farmers could grow more than they ate, everyone else was freed up to become potters, weavers, priests, scribes, and rulers. That division of labor is what defines a civilization, and scholars often point to Eridu as the place it first happened. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/9/agriculture-in-the-fertile-crescent--mesopotamia/

question: In January 1942, fifteen senior Nazi officials gathered in a Berlin suburb to coordinate the murder of every Jew in Europe. The whole meeting was over fast. How long did it take?
answer: About 90 minutes
choices: About 90 minutes
About three days
About eight hours
About two weeks
context: Adolf Eichmann, who took the notes, later estimated the Wannsee Conference lasted 'between an hour and an hour and a half.' Fifteen men coordinated the murder of a continent's Jews in the time of a long lunch. Source: nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/wannsee-conference-1942

question: The Nazi officials who met in January 1942 to organize the murder of Europe's Jews gathered at a property the SS had bought in 1940 to use as a private retreat, in a southwest Berlin suburb on the shore of a lake. What kind of building was it?
answer: A lakeside villa
choices: A lakeside villa
A mountain fortress
An army barracks
A railway depot
context: The Wannsee Conference was held in a villa at Am Grossen Wannsee 56-58, on a lake in southwest Berlin. The setting was as ordinary and pleasant as the plan was monstrous. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wannsee_Conference

question: The fifteen men at the Wannsee table were not there to argue about whether to murder Europe's Jews. That decision had already been made at the very top. So what was the actual purpose of the meeting?
answer: To coordinate HOW to do it across every ministry
choices: To coordinate HOW to do it across every ministry
To draft the legal decree that would authorize it
To prepare a public announcement of the new policy
To choose which single official would run it alone
context: The extermination decision was already settled. Wannsee existed only to coordinate the machinery -- to get every government ministry pulling together on the logistics of genocide. Source: encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/wannsee-conference-and-the-final-solution

question: The man who chaired the Wannsee Conference was SS General Reinhard Heydrich, head of the Reich Security Main Office. Cold and feared even inside the SS, he carried a chilling nickname given to him by Hitler himself. What did Hitler call Heydrich?
answer: The man with the iron heart
choices: The man with the iron heart
The fox of the desert war
The wolf of the U-boat fleet
The eagle of the Luftwaffe
context: Hitler called Heydrich 'the man with the iron heart.' He ran the conference that turned the Final Solution into an administrative program. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinhard_Heydrich

question: It would be comforting to imagine the men who planned the Holocaust as a mob of ignorant thugs. The truth is colder. Of the fifteen officials at the Wannsee table, how many held academic doctorates?
answer: Eight of the fifteen
choices: Three of the fifteen
Eight of the fifteen
Eleven of the fifteen
All fifteen of them
context: Eight of the fifteen attendees held doctorates, and ten had a university education. Educated, lettered men administered genocide as paperwork. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wannsee_Conference

question: At Wannsee, Reinhard Heydrich put the target of the 'Final Solution' at about eleven million Jews. Strikingly, his count did not stop at the lands Germany occupied. How far did his list extend?
answer: Into neutral nations like Sweden, Switzerland, and Ireland
choices: Into neutral nations like Sweden, Switzerland, and Ireland
Into Soviet territory as far as the Ural Mountains
Into Jewish communities across the United States
Into every nation of North and South America
context: Heydrich's eleven-million figure counted Jews in Britain, Ireland, Switzerland, Sweden, Spain, Portugal, and Turkey -- nations beyond Nazi reach. The plan was the murder of every Jew on the continent, occupied or not. Source: encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/wannsee-conference-and-the-final-solution

question: Reinhard Heydrich never saw his plan completed. On May 27, 1942, two British-trained Czech and Slovak agents ambushed his open car in Prague. When the first agent's gun jammed, the second man, Jan Kubis, acted in an instant. What did Kubis do?
answer: Threw a grenade at the car
choices: Threw a grenade at the car
Drew a sword on Heydrich
Set the car on fire
Fired a hidden rifle
context: In Operation Anthropoid, Jan Kubis threw a grenade when the gun jammed. Heydrich died of his infected wounds on June 4, 1942. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Reinhard_Heydrich

question: After the Wannsee chairman Heydrich was assassinated in 1942, the SS honored their fallen golden boy by naming, in his memory, the secret operation that murdered roughly 1.7 million Jews at the Belzec, Sobibor, and Treblinka death camps. What was that killing operation called?
answer: Operation Reinhard
choices: Operation Reinhard
Operation Barbarossa
Operation Valkyrie
Operation Sea Lion
context: The murder operation at Belzec, Sobibor, and Treblinka was code-named Operation Reinhard (Aktion Reinhard), named in memory of the slain Wannsee chairman. Source: encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/operation-reinhard-einsatz-reinhard

question: Adolf Eichmann sat at Wannsee with a statistical table listing Europe's Jews country by country, like stock counted in a warehouse. Each line was a whole nation's Jewish population, marked for the Final Solution. The single largest entry was nearly three million people. Which country headed the list?
answer: Ukraine
choices: Ukraine
Poland
Hungary
France
context: Eichmann's table listed Ukraine's Jews at 2,994,684 -- almost three million human beings entered as a single bureaucratic figure in a spreadsheet of intended victims. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wannsee_Conference

question: The official Wannsee minutes never use the words 'murder' or 'kill.' Mass extermination was wrapped in mild office language. Jews worked to death building roads were described not as dying but in a phrase that sounded almost like accounting. What term did the protocol use?
answer: Dropping out through 'natural diminution'
choices: Dropping out through 'natural diminution'
Suffering 'an unavoidable accident'
Quietly 'lost to enemy action'
Becoming 'casualties of the campaign'
context: The protocol said able-bodied Jews on road-building would have 'a large number undoubtedly drop out through natural diminution.' Deportation itself was called 'evacuation to the East.' The euphemism was the point -- clean words for an unspeakable act. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wannsee_Conference

question: The Wannsee protocol even planned the fate of those who might survive forced labor. The toughest survivors, it argued, were the most dangerous of all and had to be 'treated accordingly.' What reason did the document give for murdering the survivors?
answer: Freed, they could become 'the seed of a new Jewish revival'
choices: Freed, they could become 'the seed of a new Jewish revival'
Freed, they would testify against the Reich before the world
Freed, they would demand all the back wages owed to them
Freed, they could not be fed during the wartime shortages
context: The protocol reasoned that any 'remnant' surviving the labor, if freed, could become 'the germ cell of a new Jewish revival' -- and so had to be destroyed too. The logic of total extermination, written plainly. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wannsee_Conference

question: The clean written protocol hid the meeting's real talk. At his 1961 trial, Adolf Eichmann recalled how, near the end at Wannsee, butlers passed around cognac and the officials grew blunt. According to Eichmann's testimony, what did they openly discuss once the polite language dropped?
answer: Methods of killing, liquidation, and extermination
choices: Methods of killing, liquidation, and extermination
How to divide up the murdered Jews' property
Which ministries were dragging their feet
How to deceive the foreign press about the deportations
context: Eichmann testified that over the cognac 'they minced no words at all... they spoke about methods of killing, about liquidation, about extermination.' The written minutes buried that plain truth under euphemism. Source: holocausthistoricalsociety.org.uk/contents/naziseasternempire/wannseeconference.html

question: About thirty numbered copies of the fifteen-page Wannsee protocol were made. As Germany collapsed in 1945, the SS tried to destroy every trace of the plan, and nearly all the copies were burned. Of those roughly thirty copies, how many survived the war?
answer: Just one
choices: Just one
About half of them
All thirty copies
None at all
context: Only a single copy survived -- copy No. 16, stamped 'Secret Reich Matter!' U.S. prosecutor Robert Kempner found it in 1947 in seized German Foreign Office files. That one document is the chief proof the conference ever happened. Source: encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/wannsee-protocol

question: In 1961, Israel put Adolf Eichmann on trial in Jerusalem. He was no snarling monster but a mild, fussy clerk who insisted he had merely followed orders and done his job. Watching him, the philosopher Hannah Arendt coined a famous phrase for the horror of ordinary functionaries running a death machine. What phrase did she create?
answer: The banality of evil
choices: The banality of evil
The triumph of the will
The cult of obedience
The machinery of hatred
context: Hannah Arendt called it 'the banality of evil' -- the chilling lesson that thoughtless, ordinary bureaucrats, not raving fanatics, administered genocide. It is the load-bearing warning of Wannsee: evil can wear an office suit. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eichmann_in_Jerusalem

question: At the Council of Clermont in 1095, Pope Urban II called on the knights of Europe to march east and free Jerusalem. The crowd reportedly roared back two Latin words, and Urban told them to make those very words their war-cry in battle. What did they shout?
answer: "Deus vult!" — "God wills it!"
choices: "Deus vult!" — "God wills it!"
"Memento mori!" — "Remember death!"
"Pax vobis!" — "Peace to you!"
"Veni, vidi!" — "I came, I saw!"
context: The cry became the rallying phrase of the whole crusading movement. Source: Fordham Medieval Sourcebook, Urban II at Clermont, Robert the Monk version (sourcebooks.web.fordham.edu/source/urban2a.asp).

question: When Pope Urban II's call for the First Crusade spread across Europe in 1095, those who vowed to go marked their own outer clothing in a way that gave the whole movement its very name. What did a crusader do to show he had taken the vow?
answer: He sewed a cloth cross onto his outer clothing
choices: He sewed a cloth cross onto his outer clothing
He shaved the crown of his head bald
He carried a sealed letter from the Pope
He wore an iron ring on his sword hand
context: The cloth went on the right shoulder or between the shoulders, so they were called 'crucesignati' — 'those signed with the cross' — and from this came the very word 'crusade.' Source: Wikipedia, Crusades (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crusades); Crusading movement.

question: After the First Crusade captured Jerusalem in 1099, the army offered Godfrey of Bouillon the crown and the title of king. He refused to be called king of Jerusalem, giving one famous reason. What did Godfrey say?
answer: That he would not wear a crown of gold where Christ had worn a crown of thorns
choices: That he would not wear a crown of gold where Christ had worn a crown of thorns
That only the Pope in Rome had the right to crown a king
That he had sworn never to rule a city he had not been born in
That a soldier should never become a lord while the war went on
context: Godfrey took instead the title 'Advocate (Defender) of the Holy Sepulchre.' Source: Wikipedia, Godfrey of Bouillon (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Godfrey_of_Bouillon); Siege of Jerusalem (1099).

question: During the brutal siege of Antioch in 1098 the crusaders were starving and losing hope. Then a peasant named Peter Bartholomew claimed Saint Andrew had appeared to him in visions, pointing to a sacred relic hidden in the floor of a church inside the city — and on 14 June 1098 they dug it up, electrifying the army. What relic did they find?
answer: The Holy Lance — the spear that pierced Christ's side
choices: The Holy Lance — the spear that pierced Christ's side
The Crown of Thorns from the crucifixion
A nail from the True Cross
The shroud that had wrapped Christ's body
context: The 'discovery' inside the Church of St Peter rallied the starving crusaders to break the siege. Source: Wikipedia, Peter Bartholomew (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Bartholomew); Britannica, Siege of Antioch 1097-1098.

question: When the crusaders reached Jerusalem in 1099 they had a problem: the defenders had cut down every tree for miles, so there was no wood to build siege towers to scale the walls. The Genoese commander Guglielmo Embriaco found a startling solution. What did Embriaco do to get his timber?
answer: He dismantled his own ships at the coast and hauled the wood inland
choices: He dismantled his own ships at the coast and hauled the wood inland
He sailed back to Italy to fetch a fresh supply of lumber
He bought planks from merchants in nearby Egyptian towns
He had his men dig up old timbers from abandoned ruins
context: Embriaco took his ships apart at Jaffa and carried the timber overland to build two huge siege towers. Source: Wikipedia, Guglielmo Embriaco (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guglielmo_Embriaco); Siege of Jerusalem (1099).

question: On 8 July 1099, a week before the final attack on Jerusalem, a priest told the crusaders that the dead bishop Adhemar had appeared to him in a vision with instructions. About 15,000 of them obeyed and did one thing together around the city while the defenders jeered from the battlements. What did the crusaders do?
answer: They walked barefoot in procession around the city walls
choices: They walked barefoot in procession around the city walls
They knelt and fasted in total silence for three days
They burned their siege engines as an offering
They sent their swords to be blessed at the river
context: The barefoot march ended on the Mount of Olives; the final assault came a week later. Source: Wikipedia, First Crusade (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Crusade); Warfare History Network, Battle for Jerusalem.

question: The final assault on Jerusalem came on 15 July 1099. A Flemish knight named Lethold of Tournai, fighting from the siege tower commanded by Godfrey of Bouillon, earned a single famous distinction in that attack — and when the defenders saw it, they began to flee inward. What did Lethold of Tournai do?
answer: He was the first crusader over the city wall
choices: He was the first crusader over the city wall
He cut down the commander of the garrison
He planted the crusader banner on the gate
He opened the main gate from the inside
context: Once Lethold was atop the wall, the defenders' line broke and the city fell. Source: Wikipedia, Ludolf of Tournai; Siege of Jerusalem (1099) (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Jerusalem_(1099)).

question: After the Holy Lance was dug up at Antioch, the papal legate Adhemar of Le Puy publicly called the peasant Peter Bartholomew a fraud. On 8 April 1099 Peter Bartholomew agreed to prove the relic was genuine by undergoing a terrifying ordeal. What did he do to prove it?
answer: He walked a path between two walls of fire
choices: He walked a path between two walls of fire
He drank from a cup said to hold poison
He let himself be sealed alive in a tomb
He fought a champion chosen by the legate
context: Peter Bartholomew was terribly burned and died of his injuries twelve days later, on 20 April 1099. Source: Wikipedia, Peter Bartholomew (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Bartholomew).

question: While besieging the town of Ma'arra in late 1098, the crusaders ran out of food and some did something so shocking that two separate chroniclers — Fulcher of Chartres and Ralph of Caen — recorded it with horror. According to those eyewitness writers, what did the starving crusaders do at Ma'arra?
answer: They cooked and ate the flesh of dead bodies
choices: They cooked and ate the flesh of dead bodies
They butchered and ate all of their warhorses
They poisoned the town's wells in revenge
They burned the survivors alive in the square
context: Fulcher of Chartres wrote that Christians ate the flesh of dead Muslims; Ralph of Caen described bodies cooked in cauldrons. Source: Wikipedia, Siege of Ma'arra (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Ma%27arra).

question: The sack of Jerusalem in 1099 was a horrific massacre of the city's Muslims and Jews. The eyewitness chronicler Raymond of Aguilers tried to convey the scale of the killing in the Temple area with one grisly image. How did Raymond of Aguilers describe it?
answer: That men rode in blood up to their knees and bridle reins
choices: That men rode in blood up to their knees and bridle reins
That the streets were piled head-high with the dead
That the fires burned for seven days and nights
That not one living soul was left in the whole city
context: His line — 'in the Temple and porch of Solomon, men rode in blood up to their knees and bridle reins' — became the most quoted account of the massacre. Source: Wikipedia, Massacre of Jerusalem (1099), quoting Raymond of Aguilers.

question: After capturing Jerusalem in 1099 the crusaders turned the city's great Muslim holy sites into churches, including the converted al-Aqsa Mosque. In 1141 one famous military order moved its headquarters into that converted al-Aqsa building — and took its own name from it. Which order was it?
answer: The Knights Templar
choices: The Knights Templar
The Knights Hospitaller
The Teutonic Knights
The Order of Saint Lazarus
context: The crusaders renamed al-Aqsa 'Templum Salomonis' (Solomon's Temple), and the order took its very name — 'Templars' — from that 'Temple of Solomon' headquarters. Source: Wikipedia, Siege of Jerusalem (1099) (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Jerusalem_(1099)).

question: Long before the trained armies of knights set out, a preacher named Peter the Hermit gathered a ragtag 'People's Crusade' — a mob of ordinary folk rather than soldiers — and marched it east in 1096, ahead of the real armies. What became of this first wave?
answer: It set out and was wiped out before the knights' armies even reached the Holy Land
choices: It set out and was wiped out before the knights' armies even reached the Holy Land
It was made up of seasoned knights sent ahead as the army's vanguard
It captured the town of Civetot and held it until the main army arrived
It turned back to Europe after Peter the Hermit lost his nerve
context: The Seljuk Turks ambushed and slaughtered them at Civetot on 21 October 1096, where the knight Walter Sans Avoir — 'Walter the Penniless' — was killed, long before the main army reached the Holy Land. Source: Wikipedia, People's Crusade (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Crusade); Battle of Civetot.

question: When the crusaders stormed Jerusalem on 15 July 1099, you might expect that scaling the walls of a fortified holy city against desperate defenders would cut the attackers to pieces. Yet by the reckoning historians find most plausible, the crusaders' own losses in taking the city were strikingly light. Roughly how many crusaders died?
answer: About 3,000
choices: About 3,000
About 1,000
About 12,000
About 40,000
context: Modern historians treat the medieval death tolls (Ibn al-Athir claimed 70,000 defenders killed in al-Aqsa alone) as large exaggerations; the scholar Conor Kostick puts crusader losses at roughly 3,000. Source: Wikipedia, Siege of Jerusalem (1099); Madden 2005, Kedar 2004 cited therein.

question: In December 1932, with no captured machine and no spy's stolen pages, Polish mathematician Marian Rejewski sat down to defeat the German army's Enigma cipher machine, whose scrambling rotors could be wired in countless hidden ways. Seven years before the war began, how did Rejewski work out the secret internal wiring of those rotors?
answer: He deduced the wiring by pure mathematics, using the algebra of permutations
choices: He deduced the wiring by pure mathematics, using the algebra of permutations
He bribed a German clerk to photograph the factory blueprints
He took apart a machine smuggled out of Berlin in a diplomat's trunk
He guessed the wiring by listening to thousands of intercepted messages
context: Working from intercepted message patterns alone, Rejewski applied permutation group theory to reconstruct Enigma's rotor wirings without ever seeing inside the machine. Bletchley Park's I. J. Good later called this 'the mathematical theorem that won World War II.' Sources: ams.org/publicoutreach/feature-column/fcarc-enigma; militaryhistorynow.com/2018/10/04/marian-rejewski-meet-the-polish-cryptographer-who-cracked-germanys-top-secret-enigma-code-seven-years-before-ww2/

question: On 1 August 1944 the Polish Home Army rose in Warsaw and fought the German occupiers for 63 days, while Stalin's Red Army halted just across the Vistula River and watched the city be destroyed. When Britain and America asked to fly supplies to the dying fighters, what did Stalin do?
answer: He refused to let the Allied supply planes even land at Soviet airfields
choices: He refused to let the Allied supply planes even land at Soviet airfields
He sent Red Army tanks across the river to break the German lines
He ordered his own air force to parachute weapons into the city
He demanded the Home Army surrender to his troops instead
context: With his army idle across the river, Stalin blocked British and American planes from landing at Soviet bases, writing that the USSR would not 'associate themselves... with the adventure in Warsaw.' The rising was crushed: about 150,000 civilians and 20,000 Home Army fighters were dead, and Himmler ordered the city razed so that 'no stone can remain standing.' Sources: nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/allied-responses-warsaw-uprising-1944; britannica.com/event/Warsaw-Uprising

question: In 1793, revolutionaries stripping Notre-Dame cathedral in Paris for their new 'Cult of Reason' looked up at 28 tall stone statues lined across the front of the church. Believing the figures were old kings of France, they pulled every one down and knocked off its head. But the carvers had never meant them to be French kings at all. Who were the 28 statues actually made to represent?
answer: Kings from the Old Testament of the Bible
choices: Kings from the Old Testament of the Bible
Saints of the early Christian church
Knights who had fought in the Crusades
Emperors of ancient Rome
context: The 28 figures on Notre-Dame's west front were Old Testament kings of Judah and Israel; the mob mistook them for kings of France and beheaded all 28. Statues of 'Liberty' were then set where the Virgin Mary and the saints had stood. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/notre-dame-fire-french-revolution

question: On 10 November 1793 the revolutionary government turned Notre-Dame cathedral in Paris into a 'Temple of Reason.' They tore out the Christian altar, built a fake mountain in the nave topped by a little Greek temple, and held a festival to worship 'Reason' itself in place of God. At the very center of the ceremony, on the spot where the altar had stood, what did they put?
answer: A living woman dressed as the Goddess of Reason
choices: A living woman dressed as the Goddess of Reason
A marble statue of the writer Voltaire
A burning torch on an empty golden throne
A great open book holding the new laws
context: An actress in Republican blue-white-red was enthroned as the living Goddess of Reason, lit by a single 'torch of Truth,' as the centerpiece of the atheistic Cult of Reason meant to replace Christianity. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_Reason and http://rodama1789.blogspot.com/2019/05/the-fete-de-la-raison-at-notre-dame.html

question: Madame Roland, a leader of the moderate Girondin faction, was carried to the guillotine in Paris on 8 November 1793. Tradition says that as the cart passed a tall statue of Liberty set up beside the scaffold, she turned to it and cried out a single line that has echoed ever since as the most famous thing anyone said about the whole Revolution. What did she reportedly cry out?
answer: 'O Liberty, what crimes are committed in thy name!'
choices: 'O Liberty, what crimes are committed in thy name!'
'Liberty, Equality, Fraternity, or else death!'
'Long live the Republic and death to all tyrants!'
'Show my head to the people; it is worth seeing.'
context: Legend: the line ('O Liberte, que de crimes on commet en ton nom!') is the traditional account of Madame Roland's last words, the most famous indictment of a revolution that killed in liberty's name. (The fourth option were the real last words of Georges Danton.) Sources: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Madame_Roland and https://www.thisdayinquotes.com/2023/11/o-liberty-what-crimes-are-committed-in-thy-name/

question: Maximilien Robespierre sat at the head of the Committee of Public Safety and was the driving force behind the Terror, signing off on thousands of executions across France. Then, on 28 July 1794, barely two months after he had stood at the very height of his power, the Revolution turned on its own master. What happened to Robespierre himself?
answer: He was beheaded on the guillotine, the machine of his own Terror
choices: He was beheaded on the guillotine, the machine of his own Terror
He escaped Paris and lived out his days in exile
He seized total power and made himself dictator of France
He was set free and faded quietly into private life
context: The night before, when soldiers stormed the Hotel de Ville, a pistol shot shattered Robespierre's jaw; at the scaffold the executioner tore off the bandage, ripping the jaw loose, and the crowd cheered. He was killed as a declared outlaw, with no trial. About 21 of his allies died with him, including Saint-Just (the 'Archangel of the Terror'), the paralyzed Georges Couthon, and his own brother Augustin. The machine its leaders built consumed the leaders too. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/2119/fall-of-maximilien-robespierre/

question: Maximilien Robespierre, defending the mass executions before the National Convention on 5 February 1794, made one of the most infamous arguments of the Revolution: that the Terror was not a betrayal of its ideals but flowed straight out of them. In his speech 'On Political Morality,' how did Robespierre define the word 'terror' itself?
answer: As justice itself, prompt and inflexible, an emanation of virtue
choices: As justice itself, prompt and inflexible, an emanation of virtue
As a hard medicine that heals the sick body of the nation
As the shield that guards the Republic from hidden enemies
As the price of freedom, paid now so that peace can follow
context: Robespierre's actual words: 'Terror is nothing but prompt, severe, inflexible justice; it is therefore an emanation of virtue.' He paired them: 'virtue, without which terror is fatal; terror, without which virtue is impotent' - turning mass execution into a moral duty. Source: https://revolution.chnm.org/d/413 (Robespierre, 'On Political Morality').

question: The famous victims of the guillotine were the king and queen, Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, and a long parade of proud aristocrats, so most people picture the Terror as a slaughter of the rich and titled. Yet when the historian Donald Greer counted the roughly 17,000 official death sentences carried out during the Terror, one group turned out to be the overwhelming majority. Which group was it, at about 85% of those executed?
answer: Ordinary commoners: day-labourers, servants, and peasants
choices: Ordinary commoners: day-labourers, servants, and peasants
Titled aristocrats: counts, dukes, and marquises
Catholic clergy: priests, monks, and bishops
Foreign enemies: spies, traitors, and captured soldiers
context: Greer's 1935 study counted 16,594 official executions (2,639 in Paris); about 85% were commoners of the Third Estate, only ~8.5% nobility and ~6.5% clergy. Tens of thousands more died in prison or without trial, putting total deaths near 35,000-45,000. The Revolution mostly devoured ordinary people. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reign_of_Terror and https://theconversation.com/the-french-revolution-executed-royals-and-nobles-yes-but-most-people-killed-were-commoners-200455

question: Edmund Burke, an Irish-born British statesman, published 'Reflections on the Revolution in France' in 1790, before the king was executed and before the Terror had even begun. Watching the Revolution's early contempt for old traditions, he predicted exactly how all the chaos would finally end. According to Burke, who or what would rise out of the disorder to take absolute power?
answer: A popular army general who would rule as a dictator
choices: A popular army general who would rule as a dictator
A council of foreign kings who would carve up France
A street mob that would govern with no leader at all
A line of small republics constantly at war with each other
context: Burke forecast that contempt for tradition would slide into bloodshed and finally a 'popular general' seizing absolute power - which Napoleon then did, making Burke look prophetic and earning him the title of founder of modern conservatism. It is the great contrast with America: the founders drew on Locke and Montesquieu (limited government, separation of powers, checks on the majority), while the radical French drew on Rousseau's 'general will' to justify unlimited power - same Enlightenment seedbed, one path to a constitution, the other to the guillotine. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Reflections-on-the-Revolution-in-France and https://oll.libertyfund.org/publications/reading-room/2023-03-21-donway-french-revolution-classic-conservatism-burke

question: At Gettysburg in 1863, Abraham Lincoln spent his last sentence defining what kind of government the dead had died to save. The three-part phrase he used became the most quoted definition of democracy in the English language. How did Lincoln describe that government?
answer: government of the people, by the people, for the people
choices: government of the people, by the people, for the people
a government by the consent and for the welfare of the governed
liberty, equality, and justice for all who are governed
a rule of the people, for the people, and crowned by the people
context: The Bliss copy reads '...that government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth.' It is the most quoted line of the 272-word address and is carved on the south wall of the Lincoln Memorial. Source: Bliss copy full text, AbrahamLincolnOnline.org/lincoln/speeches/gettysburg.htm.

question: Edward Everett, the most celebrated orator in America, delivered the main two-hour oration at Gettysburg before Lincoln rose and spoke for barely two minutes. The next morning Everett sent Lincoln a note comparing their two speeches. What did Everett write?
answer: that his long oration had not struck the heart of the day as Lincoln's few words did
choices: that his long oration had not struck the heart of the day as Lincoln's few words did
that the muted crowd proved the brief remarks had plainly failed
that the president ought to have spoken at far greater length
that he envied the louder cheers his own oration had drawn
context: Everett wrote: 'I should be glad, if I could flatter myself that I came as near to the central idea of the occasion, in two hours, as you did in two minutes.' Lincoln replied he was 'pleased to know that... the little that I did say was not entirely a failure.' Source: Massachusetts Historical Society / MassMoments, 'Edward Everett Gives Gettysburg Address,' massmoments.org.

question: Andrew Carnegie, who became one of the richest men in America, started work at age 13 as a 'bobbin boy' in a Pittsburgh cotton mill. A kind man named Colonel James Anderson let working boys borrow books from his private library on Saturdays. What did the young Carnegie vow to do if he ever got rich?
answer: Give other working boys the same chance to read
choices: Give other working boys the same chance to read
Build the tallest building in Pittsburgh
Buy the cotton mill where he had worked
Return to Scotland and live as a lord
context: Carnegie kept the vow, funding about 2,509 free public libraries across the English-speaking world. As a poor immigrant boy from Scotland he earned $1.20 a week for 12-hour days, six days a week. Source: Columbia University Libraries; Bill of Rights Institute.

question: Cornelius Vanderbilt earned a famous nickname long before he ever owned a railroad. At age 16 he started a one-boat ferry between Staten Island and New York and built it into the largest steamship operation on the Hudson River. What nickname did this earn him?
answer: the Commodore
choices: the Commodore
the Steel King
the Railroad Baron
the Oil Tycoon
context: 'Commodore' is a naval rank, fitting for a man who ruled the water before he ever touched the rails. He didn't switch to railroads until his late 60s. Source: Britannica.

question: The devout John D. Rockefeller, who built the Standard Oil empire, kept his pockets full of small change when he walked out in public, so he could press a little gift into the hands of children he met along with a word of advice. What did he famously hand them, and what did he tell them?
answer: Shiny dimes, urging them to work hard and save
choices: Shiny dimes, urging them to work hard and save
Bright new pennies, telling them to give to the church
Silver half-dollars, telling them to spend on themselves
Freshly minted nickels, telling them to invest in oil stock
context: He handed out shiny dimes and nickels, telling the children to work hard and save their money. Source: New World Encyclopedia; Digital History, University of Houston.

question: During the 1892 Homestead Strike against Carnegie's steelworks, plant manager Henry Clay Frick sealed off the entire mill with a barrier 3 miles long and 12 feet high, topped with barbed wire and pierced with peepholes for rifles. What did the workers nickname this wall?
answer: Fort Frick
choices: Fort Frick
the Iron Curtain
the Steel Cage
Carnegie's Wall
context: On July 6, 1892, hundreds of Pinkerton guards floated up the Monongahela River on barges to seize the mill; a 13-hour gun battle left roughly seven workers and three Pinkertons dead before the Pinkertons surrendered. Source: Zinn Education Project; Britannica.

question: In 1889 Andrew Carnegie wrote an essay called 'The Gospel of Wealth,' arguing that a rich man's surplus fortune is a trust fund he must administer for the good of the community while he is alive. He summed up his belief in one harsh, famous line about a man who hoards his wealth to the end. How did Carnegie say such a man dies?
answer: He 'dies disgraced'
choices: He 'dies disgraced'
He dies a stranger to his own children
He dies owing more than he kept
He dies remembered only as a thief
context: His exact line: 'the man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.' Carnegie lived by it, selling his steel empire and giving away the bulk of his fortune. Source: Wikipedia, citing Carnegie's 1889 essay.

question: At Gordium in Phrygia in 333 BC, an oracle promised that whoever untied the city's ancient knot would rule all of Asia. Alexander the Great studied the tangle, found no end to start from, and lost his patience. What did he do to the knot?
answer: Drew his sword and sliced it in half with one stroke
choices: Drew his sword and sliced it in half with one stroke
Ordered his soldiers to burn the cart it bound
Left it untouched and marched his army onward
Carried the whole cart back to Greece as a prize
context: Arrian's Anabasis Alexandri (2.3) records the famous sword-stroke: rather than untangle the knot the slow expected way, Alexander solved it with one bold cut. He went on to conquer the Persian Empire, fulfilling the oracle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordian_Knot (Arrian, Anabasis Alexandri 2.3).

question: An ancient oracle promised an enormous reward to whoever could loosen the impossible knot that bound the old wagon of King Gordius in Phrygia. For generations travellers tried and failed, until Alexander the Great strode up and slashed it open with his sword. What had the oracle promised the man who undid that knot?
answer: That he would rule over all of Asia
choices: That he would rule over all of Asia
That the gods would grant him a single immortal life
That he would never lose a battle as long as he lived
That the city's treasury would be opened to him
context: Phrygian legend (Arrian; Plutarch): the cart of Gordius was dedicated to Zeus and tied with a knot impossible to undo; an oracle foretold that whoever loosed it would rule all of Asia. Alexander cut it with his sword at Gordium in 333 BC, and 'cutting the Gordian knot' became a phrase for solving a hard problem with one bold stroke.

question: In 133 BC the tribune Tiberius Gracchus pushed a law to give public land to Rome's landless poor. When a fellow tribune, Marcus Octavius, used his veto to freeze the bill, Tiberius answered with a move no Roman had ever made against a sitting tribune. What did he do to Octavius?
answer: Had him stripped of his office and dragged out of the tribunate
choices: Had him stripped of his office and dragged out of the tribunate
Had him exiled to a frontier province for ten years
Had him fined his family's entire fortune in silver
Had him barred from speaking in the Forum for a year
context: A tribune's person was sacrosanct and his veto absolute, so deposing one mid-term broke a core norm of the Republic and turned the Senate against Tiberius. The land law itself (lex Sempronia agraria) revived an old limit of 500 iugera per citizen and handed ~30-iugera plots to poor families. Source: worldhistory.org/article/95 and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius_Gracchus.

question: By 121 BC the younger brother, Gaius Gracchus, and his supporters had armed themselves on the Aventine hill. To crush them, the Senate invented an emergency order it had never issued before, the senatus consultum ultimum, the 'ultimate decree,' handing the consul Lucius Opimius a power Rome had always denied its magistrates. What did the decree let the state do to its own citizens?
answer: Kill them with any force needed, with no trial
choices: Kill them with any force needed, with no trial
Strip them of citizenship and seize their children
Sell them into slavery to foreign buyers
Tax their estates at the full value each year
context: The senatus consultum ultimum let Opimius use lethal force against Gaius and his followers without due process; it became the emergency tool later turned on figures like Catiline. After the fighting, the bodies of Gaius, Fulvius Flaccus, and about 3,000 followers were thrown into the Tiber. Source: worldhistory.org/article/95 and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Opimius.

question: By 1933, at the very bottom of the Great Depression, nearly 13 million Americans were out of work, and breadlines of hungry families stretched down whole city blocks. The collapse was so total that about one in how many American households had no money coming in at all?
answer: One in four
choices: One in four
One in ten
One in twenty
One in fifty
context: At the depth of the Depression, 24.9% of the labor force — 12,830,000 people — had no job, and roughly one in four households had zero income. Even workers who kept their jobs were hammered: wage income fell 42.5% between 1929 and 1933. (FDR Presidential Library & Museum, Great Depression Facts, fdrlibrary.org/great-depression-facts)

question: As the Great Depression threw millions of Americans out of their homes, jobless families threw together shacks out of packing crates, scrap wood, and tarpaper. Whole shantytowns of them sprang up across the country — even in New York's Central Park and along Seattle's waterfront. What mocking nickname did Americans give these shabby camps?
answer: Hoovervilles
choices: Hoovervilles
Crashtowns
Slumpvilles
Bustburgs
context: They named the camps 'Hoovervilles' — a jab at President Herbert Hoover, whom they blamed for the misery. The other great image of the era was the breadline: long rows of once-middle-class families waiting for soup or bread handed out by churches and charities.
