(FDR Presidential Library, fdrlibrary.org/great-depression-facts; University of Washington Great Depression Project, depts.washington.edu/depress/hooverville_seattle.shtml)

question: Franklin Roosevelt was sworn in as president on March 4, 1933, at rock bottom of the Depression, with banks failing by the thousands and millions of Americans out of work. In his very first speech as president, he tried to steady a frightened nation with a single famous line. He declared that the only thing Americans had to be afraid of was what?
answer: Fear itself
choices: Fear itself
Defeat itself
Hunger itself
Despair itself
context: 'The only thing we have to fear is fear itself.' Two days later, on March 6, Roosevelt shut every bank in the country in a 'Bank Holiday' to stop the panic. (National Archives, FDR's Fireside Chat on the Recovery Program, archives.gov/education/lessons/fdr-fireside)

question: Between 1930 and 1933 more than 9,000 American banks failed. Whenever a rumor spread that a bank was shaky, its depositors would rush in to yank out all their cash at once — a 'bank run' that could drain a bank dry in a single day. Why did a bank run in 1932 wipe out ordinary families far more completely than a bank failure would today?
answer: Back then no government agency insured deposits, so once the bank's cash ran out, your savings were simply gone
choices: Back then no government agency insured deposits, so once the bank's cash ran out, your savings were simply gone
Back then the bank had quietly lent your deposit out to others and could not call the loans back in time
Back then a failed bank was allowed to repay you in its own now-worthless company stock instead of cash
Back then the law let a shaky bank freeze your account for up to ten years before it had to pay you
context: There was no deposit insurance yet. Congress created the FDIC in 1933 precisely so a bank failure could never again swallow a family's life savings. (HISTORY, How Bank Failures Contributed to the Great Depression, history.com/articles/bank-failures-great-depression-1929-crash)

question: On April 14, 1935, families across the drought-stricken Great Plains looked up to see a churning wall of dust 500 to 600 feet high rolling toward them at about 60 miles an hour, turning the middle of the day pitch black. In a single afternoon it tore 3 million tons of topsoil off the land. Survivors gave that one storm a grim two-word name. What did they call it?
answer: Black Sunday
choices: Black Sunday
Black Tuesday
Black Friday
Black Easter
context: They called it 'Black Sunday' — the worst single storm of the Dust Bowl. Years of drought and over-plowed land had left the topsoil loose, and the wind simply carried the Great Plains away. ('Black Tuesday' was something else entirely — the day of the 1929 stock-market crash.) (Dust Bowl, Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dust_Bowl; HISTORY, Dust Bowl, history.com/articles/dust-bowl)

question: When Franklin Roosevelt became president in March 1933, panicked Americans had pulled so much cash out of the banks that many were hiding their savings at home. On March 12, 1933, Roosevelt went on the radio for the very first of his 'fireside chats' to calm the country. What did Roosevelt tell Americans about their money in that first fireside chat?
answer: Their money was safer in a bank than under the mattress
choices: Their money was safer in a bank than under the mattress
Their money was safest buried somewhere out in the backyard
Their money should be traded for gold and locked away at home
Their money should be kept at home in a coffee can within reach
context: The reassurance worked spectacularly: when most banks reopened on March 15, 1933, the stock market had one of its best days ever — the Dow jumped about 15% in a single session as confidence came flooding back. (National Archives, FDR's Fireside Chat, archives.gov/education/lessons/fdr-fireside; janos.nyc, FDR's Bank Holiday, 1933)

question: The Dow Jones average is the main scoreboard of the U.S. stock market. On September 3, 1929, just before the Crash, it stood at a towering peak of 381. Then it slid for nearly three years, and on July 8, 1932 it hit the lowest point it would close at in the entire twentieth century. Down from 381, what number did the Dow bottom out at?
answer: About 41
choices: About 41
About 60
About 110
About 180
context: From 381 all the way down to about 41, the Dow lost almost nine-tenths of its value — a fall of about 89%, and the lowest it would close in the whole twentieth century. The collapse began on 'Black Tuesday,' October 29, 1929, when panicked investors dumped about 16 million shares in a single day and wiped out roughly $14 billion. (Federal Reserve History, Stock Market Crash of 1929, federalreservehistory.org; Britannica, Black Tuesday)

question: In June 1930, with the Depression already biting, Congress sent President Herbert Hoover the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, which jacked up taxes on more than 20,000 imported goods. Over a thousand economists signed a public petition begging Hoover to veto it, warning it would raise prices and provoke a trade war. The banker Thomas Lamont pleaded with Hoover face to face — he later said that to stop 'the asinine Hawley-Smoot tariff,' he almost did what?
answer: Got down on his knees to beg the president
choices: Got down on his knees to beg the president
Resigned from his bank in open protest
Offered the president his entire fortune
Camped out on the White House lawn
context: Lamont said he 'almost went down on my knees to beg Herbert Hoover to veto the asinine Hawley-Smoot tariff.' Henry Ford called the bill 'an economic stupidity' to Hoover's face. Hoover signed it anyway. The petition gathered over 1,250 signatures, organized by economists including Irving Fisher and Paul Douglas. (Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoot-Hawley_Tariff_Act)

question: After Herbert Hoover signed the Smoot-Hawley tariff in 1930, America's trading partners — Canada, France, Italy, Spain, and others — struck back with steep tariffs of their own, exactly as the economists had warned. As trade walls went up everywhere, what happened to world trade between 1929 and 1934?
answer: It collapsed by roughly two-thirds
choices: It collapsed by roughly two-thirds
It dipped by only about a tenth
It held roughly steady
It actually doubled
context: World trade shrank by about two-thirds, deepening the global slump. U.S. exports alone fell from about $5.4 billion in 1929 to $2.1 billion in 1933. A tariff meant to protect American workers helped strangle the world economy. (Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, Wikipedia; EFG International, When Protectionism Backfired, efginternational.com)

question: In the summer of 1932 about 17,000 World War I veterans — many jobless and hungry — camped with their families in Washington, demanding early payment of a bonus the government had promised them for their service. On July 28, President Hoover sent in the U.S. Army. General Douglas MacArthur led infantry with fixed bayonets, cavalry, and six tanks against the veterans, drove them off with tear gas, and burned their camp. Seeing newspaper photos of the blaze, Franklin Roosevelt — then running against Hoover — reportedly turned to an aide and said what?
answer: "This will elect me"
choices: "This will elect me"
"God help this country"
"Hoover has lost his mind"
"Send those men some food"
context: That November, Roosevelt beat Hoover by seven million votes. The veterans' camp was a Hooverville on the Anacostia Flats, and the 'Bonus Army' of about 43,000 people was led by a former sergeant named Walter W. Waters. (Bonus Army, Wikipedia; PBS American Experience, The Bonus March, pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/macarthur-bonus-march-may-july-1932)

question: The Great Depression was not only an American disaster — it crippled Germany too. As American banks called in the loans that had been propping up the German economy, German unemployment exploded to over 6 million by 1932. In the desperate election of July 1932, one extreme party's share of the vote leaped from just 2.6% four years earlier to become the largest party in Germany. Which party surged up out of the ruined German economy?
answer: The Nazi Party
choices: The Nazi Party
The Communist Party
The Social Democratic Party
The Catholic Centre Party
context: Adolf Hitler's Nazi Party went from 2.6% of the vote in 1928 to 37.4% in July 1932 — 230 of the 608 Reichstag seats, the biggest total any party won in Weimar Germany. The economic collapse that began on Wall Street helped carry Hitler toward power. (USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, encyclopedia.ushmm.org; July 1932 German federal election, Wikipedia)

question: Economists have argued for decades about what really caused the Great Depression. In his 1936 book 'The General Theory,' John Maynard Keynes pointed to the 'paradox of thrift': when frightened people all rush to save at once, businesses lose customers and the slump only gets deeper. To break that vicious cycle, what did Keynes say the government itself should do?
answer: Pay for public works and jobs to put money in people's hands
choices: Pay for public works and jobs to put money in people's hands
Order households to save much more until confidence slowly returned
Raise taxes steeply and cut spending to keep the budget balanced
Wait calmly for wages and prices to fall until the slump cured itself
context: Keynes's cure — government spending, public works, and deficits working through a 'multiplier' — became the most influential idea in 20th-century economics. But it is genuinely contested: monetarist and Austrian economists give very different accounts, each with serious defenders, and the debate is not settled. (Keynesian economics, Wikipedia; IMF Finance & Development, What Is Keynesian Economics?, imf.org)

question: Not everyone blamed too little spending for the Great Depression. In their 1963 book 'A Monetary History of the United States,' economists Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz argued the Federal Reserve had turned an ordinary recession into a catastrophe by standing by and letting one crucial thing shrink by about a third between 1929 and 1933 — a disaster they named the 'Great Contraction.' What did Friedman and Schwartz say the Fed let collapse?
answer: The nation's money supply
choices: The nation's money supply
The government's gold reserves
The number of open factories
The total wages paid to workers
context: Friedman and Schwartz argued the Fed could have stopped the banking panics and kept the money supply from collapsing — and that its failure to act was the real catastrophe. (A Monetary History of the United States, Wikipedia; University of Chicago Harris School, harris.uchicago.edu/files/monetaryhistory_1.pdf)

question: A third school blamed the boom, not the bust. In his 1963 book 'America's Great Depression,' the economist Murray Rothbard argued the Federal Reserve's easy, cheap credit during the 1920s had lured businesses into bad, wasteful investments — and that the painful bust was simply the necessary cure clearing them out. In Rothbard's view, what made the Depression drag on for years instead of ending quickly?
answer: Hoover propped up wages and prices instead of letting them drop
choices: Hoover propped up wages and prices instead of letting them drop
Hoover slashed federal spending far too deeply and far too fast
Hoover pulled the dollar off gold and let its value float freely
Hoover sat back and did nothing while the slump slowly healed on its own
context: Rothbard, in the Austrian tradition of Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek, argued that Hoover's interventions — propping up wages and prices, blocking the necessary liquidation — prevented the bust from clearing and so prolonged the depression. It is the mirror image of Keynes: where Keynes wanted MORE government action, Rothbard blamed government action for the delay. (America's Great Depression, Wikipedia; Mises Institute, The Great Depression, mises.org/library/book/great-depression)

question: Why did a slump that began on Wall Street spread to the whole world? In 1992 the economist Barry Eichengreen pinned much of the blame on the gold standard, in a book he pointedly titled 'Golden Fetters' — fetters meaning chains. To keep their money pegged to gold, central banks were trapped: they could not print money to rescue failing banks or revive their economies. Eichengreen pointed to a pair of early escapers that cut loose from gold back in 1931 and were among the first to recover. Which were they?
answer: Britain and Scandinavia
choices: Britain and Scandinavia
France and Italy
Germany and Austria
the United States and Canada
context: The gold standard was the channel that carried the American collapse around the globe — the longer a country clung to gold, the deeper its slump. Britain and the Scandinavian countries cut loose from gold early, in 1931, and were among the first to climb out. France, by contrast, clung to gold for years and stayed mired. (Barry Eichengreen, Golden Fetters, NBER, 1992, nber.org/books-and-chapters/golden-fetters; CEPR VoxEU, The End of the Gold Standard, cepr.org)

question: The builders of the Great Mosque of Cordoba salvaged old Roman and Visigothic columns for the prayer hall, but the columns were too short to hold up a high roof. Instead of throwing them out, the masons found a trick that let short pillars carry a tall ceiling. What did they build on top of each lower arch?
answer: A second arch stacked above the first
choices: A second arch stacked above the first
A thick band of solid stone
A row of wooden beams
A heavy clay dome
context: They set a horseshoe arch low to brace the short column, then a second semicircular arch above it to lift the ceiling and let in light - two arches doing the work of one tall pillar. The striped red-and-white look comes from alternating bands of red brick and pale stone, not paint, across roughly 856 columns. Source: european-traveler.com Mezquita; thenotsoinnocentsabroad.com Mezquita blog; en.wikipedia.org Mosque-Cathedral of Cordoba.

question: In the Alhambra palace in Granada, the Court of the Lions has a marble fountain held up by twelve stone lions that spout water from their mouths. Scholars think the original Nasrid builders set the twelve spouts at slightly different heights for a hidden reason: as the water rose, one lion after another began to spout, until at midday all twelve ran at once. What do scholars believe the fountain secretly worked as?
answer: A clock that marked the twelve hours
choices: A clock that marked the twelve hours
A pump to cool the whole palace
A tester for the water's purity
An instrument that played music
context: The Nasrid court was built 1362-1391; the staggered tube heights meant each lion 'turned on' at its own hour, so the lions together counted out the day. This reading is a scholarly reconstruction, not certain. Source: iflscience.com 'This Incredible Islamic Fountain From The 1300s Might Have Actually Been A Clock'; ijisrt.com IJISRT22JAN498.  (Legend.)

question: The Great Pyramid of Giza is the largest pyramid in Egypt, built around 2560 BC to be one man's tomb. Which Egyptian pharaoh was buried under all that stone — the king the Greeks later called Cheops?
answer: Khufu
choices: Khufu
Ramesses
Tutankhamun
Thutmose
context: Khufu was the second king of Egypt's 4th Dynasty; the Greeks called him Cheops. The Great Pyramid was raised as his tomb around 2560 BC. (britannica.com/place/Great-Pyramid-of-Giza; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza)

question: Ancient writers fixed a famous list of the Seven Wonders of the World: a giant statue, a river-terrace garden, a towering lighthouse, a great stone tomb, and more. Earthquakes, fires, and looters brought six of them down so completely that not one stone still stands where it stood. Of the seven, only one is still whole today, old enough that the others were already new beside it. Which Wonder is the lone survivor?
answer: The Great Pyramid of Giza
choices: The Great Pyramid of Giza
The Colossus of Rhodes
The Hanging Gardens of Babylon
The Lighthouse of Alexandria
context: The Great Pyramid of Giza is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and the only one still substantially intact; the other six were destroyed by earthquakes, fire, or dismantling. (Britannica, Seven Wonders of the Ancient World)

question: When Khufu's builders laid the last block of the Great Pyramid around 2560 BC, it rose about 481 feet — and no human being would ever build anything taller until an English cathedral spire finally beat it in the 1300s AD. For roughly how long did the Great Pyramid hold the record as the tallest structure on Earth?
answer: About 3,800 years
choices: About 3,800 years
About 500 years
About 1,200 years
About 100 years
context: The Great Pyramid held the title of tallest human-made structure on Earth for roughly 3,800 years — longer than any other building in history — out-topped only around 1311 AD by the spire of Lincoln Cathedral. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza; mused.com/items/503/khufu-pyramid-or-the-great-pyramid/)

question: The Egyptians didn't call Khufu's tomb 'the Great Pyramid' — they gave it a soaring name of its own: 'Akhet-Khufu.' Translated, that ancient name calls the pyramid Khufu's what?
answer: The Horizon of Khufu
choices: The Horizon of Khufu
The Mountain of Khufu
The Throne of Khufu
The Gate of Khufu
context: The Egyptians named the Great Pyramid 'Akhet-Khufu,' meaning 'the Horizon of Khufu.' The name appears in the world's oldest papyrus, the Diary of Merer. (nationalgeographic.com/premium/article/red-sea-scrolls-pyramids-egypt; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza)

question: The Great Pyramid looks rough and stepped today, but it didn't start that way: it was sheathed in about 144,000 polished white limestone stones so smooth and bright it flashed in the desert sun like a mirror. After a 1303 earthquake shook the casing loose, what did Sultan an-Nasir's men do with that gleaming white stone around 1356 AD?
answer: Hauled it away to build the city of Cairo
choices: Hauled it away to build the city of Cairo
Ground it into powder for medicine
Shipped it to Rome as a gift
Buried it in a pit beside the pyramid
context: Sultan an-Nasir's men stripped the loosened white Tura limestone casing around 1356 AD and carted it off to build Cairo — which is why the pyramid looks rough and stepped today instead of mirror-bright. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza; mused.com/items/503/khufu-pyramid-or-the-great-pyramid/)

question: In 2020 Elon Musk tweeted 'Aliens built the pyramids obv.' Egypt's minister Rania al-Mashat fired back with a public reply, inviting Musk to come to Giza and see one thing for himself. What did she point him to?
answer: The tombs of the pyramid builders
choices: The tombs of the pyramid builders
The workers' bakery and beer vats
The foremen's payroll records
A wall of crew-name graffiti
context: Rania al-Mashat invited Musk and SpaceX to visit the tombs of the pyramid builders — the real workers' graves at Giza — as her answer to the 'aliens built them' claim. (bbc.com/news/world-africa-53627888; thejakartapost.com)

question: For a long time people imagined whip-cracked slaves dragging stones to build the Great Pyramid. But archaeologists found the builders' own town and tombs at Giza, and the workers had scrawled their team names right on the stones. What did these work-gangs call their teams?
answer: 'Friends of Khufu' and 'Drunkards of Menkaure'
choices: 'Friends of Khufu' and 'Drunkards of Menkaure'
'Companions of Ra' and 'Champions of Sneferu'
'Falcons of Khafre' and 'Lions of Giza'
'Servants of the Sun' and 'Sons of the Nile'
context: Archaeologists Mark Lehner and Zahi Hawass found the builders' town and tombs at Giza; the workers' graffiti shows organized crews with names like 'Friends of Khufu' and 'Drunkards of Menkaure' — not slaves. (harvardmagazine.com/2003/07/who-built-the-pyramids-html; guardians.net/hawass/buildtomb.htm)

question: Khufu's builders aimed the four sides of the Great Pyramid at true north, south, east and west — and missed perfect alignment by less than one-fifteenth of a degree, an accuracy no modern building beats by eye. With no compass and no GPS, how does one leading theory say they found true north so precisely?
answer: By using the autumn equinox
choices: By using the autumn equinox
By following a sacred map from the temple
By copying an older pyramid's angle
By guessing and getting lucky
context: The four sides miss true north–south–east–west by only about 3 minutes 38 seconds of arc. A leading theory holds the builders used the autumn equinox to find true north. (livescience.com/61799-great-pyramid-near-perfect-alignment.html; smithsonianmag.com)

question: Deep inside the Great Pyramid sits the King's Chamber, and inside it rests Khufu's granite coffin box. Here's the puzzle: that stone coffer is wider than the doorway into the room, so it could never have been carried in. What does its size prove about how the chamber was built?
answer: The coffer was set in place first, and the room was built up around it
choices: The coffer was set in place first, and the room was built up around it
The coffer was carved from a block already inside
The doorway was later narrowed by robbers
The coffer was lowered through a hole in the ceiling
context: The granite sarcophagus is wider than the doorway — proof it was placed first and the King's Chamber built up around it. It was found completely empty, with no mummy ever inside. (ancientegyptonline.co.uk/kingschambergp/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza)

question: In 2013 Pierre Tallet dug at the Red Sea port of Wadi al-Jarf and found the oldest surviving papyrus in the whole world. It turned out to be the work logbook of an inspector named Merer, written in Khufu's 27th year. What everyday job does Merer's diary record him doing for the Great Pyramid?
answer: Shipping white limestone by boat to the pyramid
choices: Shipping white limestone by boat to the pyramid
Counting the gold buried in the king's tomb
Guarding prisoners chained at the work site
Drawing the secret plans for the burial chamber
context: The Diary of Merer — the world's oldest surviving papyrus — is the logbook of an inspector who led a 200-man crew shipping white Tura limestone by boat to 'Akhet-Khufu,' a roughly 3-day trip. One entry reads: 'Inspector Merer sets sail... laden with stone blocks, to Akhet-Khufu.' (nationalgeographic.com/premium/article/red-sea-scrolls-pyramids-egypt; history.com)

question: In 2017 physicists pulled off something amazing: they used cosmic-ray muons — tiny particles that rain down from space and pass right through solid stone — to X-ray the Great Pyramid without ever drilling into it. Published in the journal Nature, what did this particle-scan reveal hidden above the Grand Gallery?
answer: A mysterious empty 'Big Void' at least 100 feet long
choices: A mysterious empty 'Big Void' at least 100 feet long
A second royal coffin filled with gold
A network of flooded tunnels
A statue of Khufu sealed in stone
context: The 2017 muon scan, published in Nature, found a mysterious empty 'Big Void' at least 30 meters (100 ft) long above the Grand Gallery — the first major hidden space discovered inside the pyramid since the 1800s. (nature.com/articles/nature24647; sci.news)

question: One of the deepest mysteries of the Great Pyramid is simply HOW workers dragged 2-tonne stone blocks up to dizzying heights without machines. At the Hatnub quarry, archaeologists found a 4,500-year-old ramp from Khufu's reign with a row of wooden post-holes running up each side. How do these post-holes show the workers hauled the giant stones up steep slopes?
answer: They tied ropes to the posts to drag sledges up the ramp
choices: They tied ropes to the posts to drag sledges up the ramp
They rolled the stones over the posts like logs
They floated the stones up a water channel beside the posts
They balanced the stones on the posts as scaffolding
context: The 4,500-year-old Hatnub ramp is flanked by two staircases full of post-holes: workers tied ropes to the wooden posts and used them to help drag sledges loaded with stone up slopes as steep as 20%. (news.liverpool.ac.uk/2018/11/02; livescience.com/63978-great-pyramid-ramp-discovered.html)

question: On July 16, 1054, three envoys sent from Rome strode into the great church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople while the patriarch was in the middle of celebrating the church service. They were not there to pray. What did they place on the high altar?
answer: A written order excommunicating the patriarch
choices: A written order excommunicating the patriarch
A bag of gold coins for the church
The keys to the city of Rome
A signed treaty of friendship
context: The document was a 'bull' of excommunication, drawn up by Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida, laid right on the altar during the Divine Liturgy. This dramatic scene is the famous flashpoint of the East-West split between the Catholic and Orthodox churches. Source: christianhistoryinstitute.org/magazine/article/east-west-schism ; oca.org church-history eleventh-century the-great-schism.

question: One of the bitterest quarrels between the Christians of Rome and those of Constantinople was over the bread used in Communion. The Latin West used flat, unleavened bread with no yeast; the Greek East used risen, leavened bread. In 1053 the patriarch's chancellor Nicephorus broke into the Latin churches in the city and did what to their unleavened Communion bread?
answer: Trampled it underfoot
choices: Trampled it underfoot
Sold it in the market
Locked it in a golden box
Mailed it back to Rome
context: Nicephorus burst open the Latin tabernacles and trampled the consecrated bread because, being unleavened (azyme), the Greeks did not accept it as true Communion bread. Patriarch Michael Cerularius had ordered all the Latin churches in the city closed. Source: newadvent.org/cathen/10273a.htm ; courses.lumenlearning.com great-schism-of-1054.

question: On July 16, 1054, the Roman envoys finished laying their excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia and walked out. At the threshold they turned, shook the dust of the cathedral off their feet, and shouted a single Latin sentence. What did they shout?
answer: 'Videat Deus et judicet!' — 'May God see and judge!'
choices: 'Videat Deus et judicet!' — 'May God see and judge!'
'Roma locuta, causa finita!' — 'Rome has spoken!'
'Veni, vidi, vici!' — 'I came, I saw, I conquered!'
'Pax vobiscum!' — 'Peace be with you!'
context: Cardinal Humbert led the legation; shaking the dust off the feet echoes a gesture of final rejection. The three legates were Humbert of Silva Candida, Frederick of Lorraine (later Pope Stephen IX), and Peter, Archbishop of Amalfi. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humbert_of_Silva_Candida ; greekcitytimes.com On This Day Great Schism.

question: After the Roman legates dumped their excommunication on his altar, Patriarch Michael Cerularius struck back. On July 24, 1054, he gathered a synod of bishops in Hagia Sophia and proclaimed an anathema of his own — but he was careful about exactly whom he condemned. Whom did Cerularius's anathema actually excommunicate?
answer: Only the three legates, named one by one
choices: Only the three legates, named one by one
The entire Western Church and its pope
Every Latin living in Constantinople
The emperor who had welcomed the legates
context: Cerularius convened 21 metropolitans and bishops and excommunicated the three envoys by name, not the whole Latin Church — one reason historians say the 'total' break of 1054 is overstated. The bull was then publicly burned in Constantinople. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_I_Cerularius.

question: The excommunication the legates laid on the Hagia Sophia altar in 1054 carried a hidden flaw that ruined its legal force. Pope Leo IX had sent the legates — but what had happened to Pope Leo by the time they acted?
answer: He had died three months earlier
choices: He had died three months earlier
He had secretly recalled them to Rome
He had reconciled with the patriarch
He had been deposed by the emperor
context: Leo IX died on April 19, 1054; the excommunication came on July 16. With the pope who authorized them already dead, the legates technically had no authority to excommunicate anyone — Humbert is said to have 'taken advantage of the papal vacancy to retaliate.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_I_Cerularius ; oca.org the-great-schism.

question: Buried in the legates' bull was a list of eleven accusations against the Greeks. One charge was that the Greeks had 'omitted a clause from the Creed' — the so-called filioque, the phrase saying the Holy Spirit proceeds 'and from the Son.' Why do historians call this particular accusation backwards?
answer: The West had ADDED the clause; the East never accepted it
choices: The West had ADDED the clause; the East never accepted it
The Greeks had written the original Creed themselves
The clause had been removed by the emperor, not the church
Both sides had agreed to drop it centuries earlier
context: The filioque ('and the Son') was a Latin addition to the Nicene Creed; the East held the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone and rejected the addition as tampering. So the bull accused the Greeks of removing something the West had in fact inserted. Tellingly, the filioque was only the SEVENTH of the eleven charges — the dispute over leavened versus unleavened bread came first. Source: mgr.org/PapalBull1054.html ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East%E2%80%93West_Schism.

question: The mutual excommunications hurled across the altar of Hagia Sophia in 1054 were not quietly forgotten — they stood on the books for 911 years. In December 1965 Pope Paul VI and Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras I finally agreed to do what with them, in twin ceremonies held at the same hour in Rome and Istanbul?
answer: Commit them 'to oblivion' and lift them
choices: Commit them 'to oblivion' and lift them
Re-read them aloud as a warning
Carve them into the walls of both churches
Mail the original bull back to Rome
context: On December 7, 1965, the two leaders lifted the anathemas simultaneously, agreeing to 'commit these excommunications to oblivion' — 911 years after Humbert's legates first laid the bull on the altar. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic%E2%80%93Orthodox_Joint_Declaration_of_1965 ; vaticannews.va lifting-anathemas.

question: The Great Sphinx is a giant lion with a human face crouched on the Giza plateau in Egypt. Most enormous statues are stacked from cut blocks, but the Sphinx isn't built that way at all. How did its makers, around 2500 BC, actually shape it?
answer: They carved the whole beast in place from one ridge of natural limestone bedrock
choices: They carved the whole beast in place from one ridge of natural limestone bedrock
They stacked thousands of quarried limestone blocks into a lion shape
They cast it in a giant mold from melted desert sand
They assembled it from cedar timber hauled in from Lebanon
context: Sculptors cut the lion-body directly out of the living rock of the Giza plateau rather than building it up from blocks, which is why the Sphinx is the oldest known monumental sculpture in Egypt. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Sphinx_of_Giza

question: The Great Sphinx is missing its nose — a gap over three feet wide where chisel marks show someone deliberately pried it off. A popular tale says Napoleon's soldiers blasted it away with a cannon when France reached Egypt in 1798. What proves that story can't be true?
answer: A drawing by Frederic Louis Norden, made in 1737, already shows the nose gone
choices: A drawing by Frederic Louis Norden, made in 1737, already shows the nose gone
An ancient Egyptian inscription on the Sphinx blames a desert sandstorm
Napoleon's own diary records that the nose was already missing in Paris
Cannons of that era could not be aimed high enough to reach the face
context: Norden sketched the noseless Sphinx more than 60 years before Napoleon's troops ever reached Egypt, so they cannot have been the ones who broke it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Sphinx_of_Giza

question: The eastern end of the Great Wall of China runs all the way to the coast and plunges right into the sea, where the stonework juts out into the Bohai Gulf. Builders gave this spot a name because the long wall looks like a giant creature stretching down to drink from the water. What did they call it?
answer: Old Dragon's Head
choices: Old Dragon's Head
Tiger's Leap Gorge
The Sleeping Giant
Crane's Beak Point
context: Laolongtou, 'Old Dragon's Head,' sits near Shanhai Pass, the wall's eastern terminus on the Bohai Gulf. The pass itself was nicknamed 'the First Pass Under Heaven.' Source: chinahighlights.com; amusingplanet.com.

question: For years people repeated that the Great Wall of China is the one human-made thing you can pick out from the Moon with your naked eye. When China's first astronaut, Yang Liwei, orbited Earth in 2003, he was asked about the famous wall. What did Yang Liwei report?
answer: He could not pick out the structure with the naked eye
choices: He could not pick out the structure with the naked eye
He said it was the clearest human mark on the land
He said it stood out sharply along the old Silk Road
He said rivers and snowfields hid it from view
context: National Geographic helped spread the myth in 1923; Neil Armstrong said after Apollo 11 he saw no sign of it. Yang Liwei said from orbit he 'couldn't identify the structure with the naked eye.' It is only sometimes glimpsed from LOW orbit under slanting sunlight. Source: smithsonianmag.com.

question: Ask people what the Great Wall of China is and most will describe one long stone wall. Historians who study the actual brick and rammed earth tell a more surprising story about how it was really built. Which description matches what they found?
answer: Many separate walls built across many different dynasties
choices: Many separate walls built across many different dynasties
A single wall finished by one emperor in his own lifetime
Mostly natural mountain ridges with only short stretches of masonry
One short fortress wall that guarded the capital and nothing more
context: Historians and archaeologists: the 'Great Wall' is not one continuous structure but many walls and fortifications of stone, brick, and rammed earth, raised, abandoned, and rebuilt by successive dynasties over roughly two thousand years, the best-preserved sections being Ming-era.

question: Hundreds of thousands of forced laborers — peasants, soldiers, and convicts — died building the Great Wall of China in brutal cold, on steep terrain, with too little food. So many were lost that the wall earned a grim nickname. What was it called?
answer: The longest cemetery on Earth
choices: The longest cemetery on Earth
The wall of a thousand tears
The emperor's stone curse
The road of broken backs
context: One common estimate puts the death toll around 400,000. Bodies were buried in mass graves alongside the wall, earning it the nickname. Source: smithsonianmag.com; factretriever.com.

question: Ming-dynasty builders needed their wall to survive earthquakes and centuries of weather, so they stirred something unexpected into their lime mortar to make an early super-strong 'composite' glue. What did they mix in?
answer: Sticky rice
choices: Sticky rice
Beaten egg whites
Honey
Bean paste
context: The rice's amylopectin made an early composite mortar that helped walls resist earthquakes and weathering. Some old accounts add egg whites. Source: smithsonianmag.com; newworldencyclopedia.org.

question: In 1644 the mighty Great Wall of China was finally beaten — but not by an army smashing through the stones. A Ming general named Wu Sangui, who was supposed to guard it, made one fateful choice that sealed the fall of the Ming dynasty. What did Wu Sangui do?
answer: He swung open the gates of Shanhai Pass to the Manchu army
choices: He swung open the gates of Shanhai Pass to the Manchu army
He set fire to his own watchtowers and then fled west
He bribed the invaders to march around the wall instead
He tore down a wall section to build himself a fortress
context: Wu Sangui, a Ming general, opened the gates of Shanhai Pass to the Manchu army in 1644, ending the Ming dynasty. The wall was undone by a traitor, not a siege. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org.

question: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn was a decorated Red Army artillery captain fighting in East Prussia in February 1945, in the middle of a war he was helping to win, when his own side arrested him at the front. What was the offense that sent a decorated captain to eight years in the labor camps?
answer: Private letters mocking Stalin to a school friend
choices: Private letters mocking Stalin to a school friend
Deserting his artillery battery under enemy fire
Losing a key battle on the East Prussian front
Passing secret maps to the German army
context: He criticized Stalin in private wartime letters to his school friend Nikolai Vitkevich and was sentenced under Article 58, 'counter-revolutionary activity,' to eight years. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Aleksandr-Solzhenitsyn

question: Across Stalin's Russia, prisoners and guards alike used one word for the camp world: GULAG. But it names no single place on any map. The five letters G-U-L-A-G actually spell out the name of what?
answer: A government bureau running the whole camp system
choices: A government bureau running the whole camp system
The largest prison camp in all of Siberia
The frozen wasteland the camps were built on
The secret police force that made the arrests
context: GULAG is an acronym for the Russian 'Glavnoe Upravlenie Lagerei' — the Main Directorate of Camps, the office that ran the system. Solzhenitsyn's title compares the scattered camps to a hidden 'archipelago,' a chain of islands. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gulag_Archipelago

question: In 1962 the Soviet journal Novy Mir printed a short novel by Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn — the first honest account of Stalin's labor camps ever published openly inside the USSR, approved personally by Nikita Khrushchev over the objections of other Party bosses. How much of an ordinary prisoner's camp life does the whole book portray?
answer: A single ordinary day
choices: A single ordinary day
His entire eight-year sentence
His first month behind the wire
The morning of his release
context: The book is 'One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich,' following the prisoner Ivan Denisovich Shukhov through one unremarkable day. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Day_in_the_Life_of_Ivan_Denisovich

question: In the Kolyma region of far-northeastern Siberia, prisoners hacked a 2,000-kilometer highway inland from Magadan through ground frozen solid. So many died building it that the guards packed the dead bodies straight into the roadbed. What grim name did the highway earn?
answer: The Road of Bones
choices: The Road of Bones
The Iron Road
The Frozen Highway
The White Road
context: Kolyma's prisoners also mined gold in lethal cold — at its height the region produced about a third of the world's gold. Source: https://factsanddetails.com/russia/Places/sub9_9e/entry-7102.html

question: The very first camp of the entire Soviet system rose around 1923 on the frozen Solovetsky Islands in the White Sea, and Solzhenitsyn said every later camp took its cruel cues from it. But the buildings standing there had been raised long before, for the opposite purpose. What had stood on those islands first?
answer: An ancient Orthodox monastery
choices: An ancient Orthodox monastery
A tsar's summer palace
An abandoned naval fortress
A remote fishing village
context: Solovki was a place of prayer turned into a place of death — the model, Solzhenitsyn said, from which all later camps were copied. Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/literature-and-writing/gulag-archipelago-1918-1956-aleksandr-solzhenitsyn

question: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn walked out of the labor camps a free man in 1953, and by an extraordinary stroke his very first day of freedom fell on the exact day of what event?
answer: The day Stalin died
choices: The day Stalin died
The end of the Second World War
The launch of the first Sputnik
The outbreak of the Korean War
context: His first day free was March 5, 1953 — the day Stalin died. He was then sent to internal exile 'in perpetuity' in Kazakhstan, where he nearly died of cancer. Source: https://www.solzhenitsyncenter.org/timeline

question: Accepting the Nobel Prize for Literature, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn closed his lecture with an old Russian proverb that became the motto of his whole fight against the lie of the Soviet state. Which line did he end on?
answer: One word of truth shall outweigh the whole world
choices: One word of truth shall outweigh the whole world
A lie will travel the length of the earth
Truth is the patient daughter of time
The axe forgets, but the tree remembers
context: He won the Nobel in 1970 but did not dare travel to collect it, fearing he would not be let back into the USSR; he finally accepted it in person in Stockholm in 1974. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/literature/1970/solzhenitsyn/lecture/

question: In the camps Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn was forbidden pencil and paper, yet he still composed poetry in his head and had to hold thousands of lines without ever losing his place. How did he keep count of it all?
answer: He broke matchsticks into beads and told them like a rosary
choices: He broke matchsticks into beads and told them like a rosary
He scratched tally marks into the prison wall each night
He tied a row of small knots along a length of thread
He carved the finished lines into a hidden bar of soap
context: He laid the matchstick pieces in rows of tens and units on his cigarette case, running them through his fingers as he recited. By this method he carried roughly 12,000 lines of verse out of the Gulag in his memory. Source: https://nevalalee.wordpress.com/2016/07/11/solzhenitsyns-rosary/

question: As Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn secretly wrote 'The Gulag Archipelago,' the KGB hunted the manuscript, and a single police raid could have destroyed the entire book at a stroke. How did he make sure no one raid ever could?
answer: He never kept the whole book in one place, hiding fragments with scattered friends
choices: He never kept the whole book in one place, hiding fragments with scattered friends
He wrote the entire book in one hidden night and burned his notes
He mailed each finished chapter straight out of the country
He disguised every page to look like a routine Party report
context: He worked on only fragments at a time and stashed the pieces with trusted friends around Moscow and at a secret retreat in Estonia, so no single seizure could capture the whole. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gulag_Archipelago

question: The KGB interrogated Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn's typist, Elizaveta Voronyanskaya, for days in 1973 until she revealed where a copy of 'The Gulag Archipelago' was hidden; days after her release she was found hanged in her own stairwell. When Solzhenitsyn learned of her death, what did he do?
answer: He ordered the book published at once in the West
choices: He ordered the book published at once in the West
He burned every remaining copy he still held
He fled Moscow and went into deep hiding
He wrote an open letter naming the KGB officers
context: 'The Gulag Archipelago' appeared from YMCA-Press in Paris on December 28, 1973. Months later Solzhenitsyn was arrested for treason, stripped of his citizenship, and expelled to West Germany. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gulag_Archipelago

question: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn deliberately named his book 'The Gulag Archipelago 1918-1956,' reaching back to the Civil War years when Lenin held power and Stalin was still a minor figure. By starting the clock in 1918, what charge was he leveling at the Soviet system?
answer: That the camps were built into the state from its first year, not a Stalin aberration
choices: That the camps were built into the state from its first year, not a Stalin aberration
That the Civil War forced a brief cruelty the state later left behind
That the guilt rested only on Lenin's small inner circle
That the Western powers had goaded the Soviets into the camps
context: Solzhenitsyn's thesis aimed the accusation at the system itself rather than one tyrant: the camps, he argued, were a core feature of the Soviet state from 1918 onward. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gulag_Archipelago

question: In 'The Gulag Archipelago,' Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn wrote its most-quoted line about good and evil — and he refused the comfortable idea of simply drawing the line between good people and evil people. So where did he say the line between good and evil truly runs?
answer: Right through every human heart
choices: Right through every human heart
Between the rich and the poor
Between Russia and the West
Between the jailers and the jailed
context: The full line: the dividing line 'passes not through states, nor between classes, nor between political parties either — but right through every human heart.' He added that even in the worst heart 'one small bridgehead of good is retained.' Source: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/The_Gulag_Archipelago

question: After Alexander the Great's armies reached India, Greek-trained sculptors in Gandhara (today's Pakistan and Afghanistan) made the world's first statues of the Buddha as a man. Earlier Buddhists had refused to show his body at all, marking his presence only with an empty throne or a pair of footprints. How did these sculptors dress their brand-new Buddha?
answer: In a Greek himation, the toga-like robe with deep folds
choices: In a Greek himation, the toga-like robe with deep folds
In the silk court robes of a Persian emperor
In the saffron rags of a wandering beggar-monk
In the jeweled armor of an Indian warrior-prince
context: Greco-Buddhist art at Gandhara produced the first human images of the Buddha, draped like a Greek in a deeply folded himation. Before this, the Buddha was shown only through symbols such as an empty throne or footprints. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco-Buddhist_art

question: In the Buddhist carvings of Gandhara, the Buddha walks with a bodyguard named Vajrapani who protects him. But the sculptors there, trained in the Greek style, did not invent a new guardian — they borrowed a famous hero from Greek myth and made him the Buddha's protector. Which Greek figure became Vajrapani?
answer: Herakles, the muscular hero with his club
choices: Herakles, the muscular hero with his club
Zeus, the king of the gods with his thunderbolt
Hermes, the swift messenger with winged sandals
Achilles, the warrior dipped in the river Styx
context: In Gandharan art the Buddha's guardian Vajrapani is sculpted as Herakles (Hercules), a muscular strongman carrying his club — a Greek demigod reused as a Buddhist protector deity. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco-Buddhist_art

question: Alexander the Great's conquests carried a simplified, stripped-down form of Greek across the whole ancient world, from Egypt all the way to India, where merchants and scholars used it as their shared language. This 'common tongue,' called Koine, outlived Alexander's empire by centuries — and became the original language of one of history's most-read books. Which one?
answer: The New Testament
choices: The New Testament
The Iliad
The Odyssey
Aesop's Fables
context: Koine ('the common tongue') spread from Egypt to India as the language of trade and learning. Centuries later it was the language in which the New Testament and the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) were written. Homer's epics and Aesop's fables were composed in older forms of Greek. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koine_Greek

question: Around 240 BC the librarian Eratosthenes, working in Alexandria, set out to do something no one had managed before — using nothing but shadows. He knew that at noon on the summer solstice the Sun shone straight down a well at Syene but cast a 7-degree shadow far to the north at Alexandria. From that single gap between two shadows, what did Eratosthenes work out?
answer: The circumference of the whole Earth
choices: The circumference of the whole Earth
The distance from the Earth to the Sun
The exact length of one year
The height of the Great Pyramid
context: Using the 7-degree difference in shadow angle between Syene and Alexandria, Eratosthenes calculated the Earth's circumference around 240 BC — landing astonishingly close to the true figure of about 24,900 miles. Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/eratosthenes-measures-earths-circumference

question: King Ptolemy of Egypt wanted to starve his rival, the great Library of Pergamon, so he banned the export of Egyptian papyrus — the standard writing material — to choke off their supply of books. Instead of giving up, the people of Pergamon perfected writing on treated animal skins. What lasting thing came out of Ptolemy's ban?
answer: Parchment
choices: Parchment
Papyrus
Vellum
Velvet
context: When Ptolemy banned papyrus exports to cripple the Library of Pergamon, its people developed fine animal-skin writing material — 'parchment,' from pergamenum, 'from Pergamon.' Vellum (calfskin) is named from the Latin for calf, not from the city. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Library_of_Pergamon/

question: Alexander the Great founded so many cities and stamped his own name on them that ancient writers count roughly twenty to thirty 'Alexandrias' scattered across three continents. But one city he founded in India did not carry his name at all — he built it in honor of a beloved companion who had just died. Who or what did Alexander name that city for?
answer: His warhorse, Bucephalus
choices: His warhorse, Bucephalus
His mother, Olympias
His tutor, Aristotle
His friend, Hephaestion
context: Alexander founded roughly twenty to thirty cities named Alexandria across three continents. After his beloved horse Bucephalus died in India, he founded a city named for it: Bucephala. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_founded_by_Alexander_the_Great

question: The serene, idealized face that the Buddha wears in statues all across Asia did not begin in India — its calm features were copied from a Greek statue, the Belvedere Apollo of around 330 BC. From that Greek model, the Buddha permanently inherited one signature feature of his look. Which one?
answer: His wavy curls gathered into a topknot
choices: His wavy curls gathered into a topknot
His long, drooping earlobes
His half-closed, meditating eyes
His upraised, open right hand
context: The Buddha's iconic wavy, curly hair gathered in a topknot was copied from the curly Mediterranean hairstyle of the Belvedere Apollo (c. 330 BC); the idealized Greek face became the standard look of the Buddha across Asia. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco-Buddhist_art

question: At Ai-Khanoum, a fully Greek city out in Afghanistan — complete with a 5,000-seat theater and a gymnasium honoring Hermes and Heracles — a man named Klearchos set up a stone slab carved with wisdom sayings. They were the very same sayings that had stood for centuries at Apollo's most sacred temple back in Greece. What did Klearchos carve onto that stele, thousands of miles east near India?
answer: The Delphic Maxims
choices: The Delphic Maxims
The maxims of the Seven Sages
The oath of Hippocrates
The laws of Solon
context: Klearchos carved the Delphic Maxims — the wisdom sayings from Apollo's temple at Delphi — onto a stele at Ai-Khanoum in Afghanistan. It is the oldest surviving copy of the maxims; none remain at Delphi itself. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ai-Khanoum

question: Menander I, a Greek king the Indians called Milinda, ruled an Indo-Greek kingdom in India in the 100s BC. The geographer Strabo paid him an astonishing compliment about the sheer scale of what he had achieved. According to Strabo, Menander did what?
answer: Conquered more tribes than Alexander the Great
choices: Conquered more tribes than Alexander the Great
Lived longer than any other Greek king
Built a library larger than Alexandria's
Owned more war elephants than any rival
context: Menander I (Pali: Milinda) ruled an Indo-Greek kingdom in the 2nd century BC. Strabo wrote that Menander 'conquered more tribes than Alexander the Great.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menander_I

question: When the Greek king Menander I died around 130 BC, the writer Plutarch reported that the cities of his Indian kingdom quarreled over his ashes — exactly the way Buddhist tradition says cities once fought over the Buddha's own relics. By legend, how did Menander's cities finally settle the dispute over a Greek king's remains?
answer: They divided the ashes and raised stupas over them
choices: They divided the ashes and raised stupas over them
They scattered the ashes into the Ganges river
They sealed the ashes inside a single golden statue
They returned the ashes to his homeland in Greece
context: Plutarch recorded that Menander's cities divided his ashes among themselves and built monuments (stupas) over them — a Greek king honored exactly like the Buddha. This account is preserved as legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menander_I

question: Around 113 BC a Greek ambassador named Heliodorus was sent by an Indo-Greek king to an Indian royal court — and while he was there, he did something no one expected of a Greek diplomat. He took up an Indian religion and raised a stone pillar at Besnagar declaring himself a devotee. To which Indian god did Heliodorus dedicate himself?
answer: The Hindu god Vishnu, worshipped as Krishna
choices: The Hindu god Vishnu, worshipped as Krishna
The Buddha, the awakened teacher
Indra, the storm-god king of heaven
Agni, the god of sacred fire
context: Around 113 BC Heliodorus, a Greek ambassador, converted to the worship of Vishnu and erected a pillar at Besnagar topped by Garuda, calling himself a 'Bhagavata' (devotee of Vasudeva-Krishna) — one of the earliest recorded worshippers of Krishna. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heliodorus_pillar

question: Divers exploring an ancient shipwreck recovered a corroded lump of bronze gears, made around 150-100 BC, that turned out to be a hand-built machine of astonishing precision. By turning its gears, this Hellenistic device could track the Sun and Moon and even forecast eclipses years in advance — so far ahead of its time that no comparable gearwork appeared again for over a thousand years. What is this object called?
answer: The Antikythera mechanism
choices: The Antikythera mechanism
The Archimedes screw
The Rosetta Stone
The astrolabe of Hipparchus
context: The Antikythera mechanism, a bronze geared device from c. 150-100 BC found in a shipwreck, could predict the positions of the Sun and Moon and forecast eclipses decades ahead — a Hellenistic 'analog computer' unmatched for over a thousand years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antikythera_mechanism

question: By the legend recorded in the Letter of Aristeas, King Ptolemy II of Egypt gathered seventy-two Jewish scholars in Alexandria to translate the Hebrew Bible into Greek, creating the Septuagint. The writer Philo added an even more remarkable claim about how the scholars worked. According to Philo, what happened when the seventy-two translated in separate cells?
answer: They each produced word-for-word identical translations
choices: They each produced word-for-word identical translations
They finished the entire task in a single night
They refused to eat until the work was complete
They burned every draft that contained an error
context: By legend (the Letter of Aristeas), Ptolemy II had 72 Jewish scholars translate the Hebrew Bible into Greek, producing the Septuagint ('seventy'). Philo claimed the 72 worked in separate cells yet produced word-for-word identical translations. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Septuagint

question: The architect Sostratus built the towering Lighthouse of Alexandria, the Pharos, which stood over 100 meters tall and ranked among the Seven Wonders of the World. King Ptolemy expected his own royal name on the monument. Legend says Sostratus found a sly way to claim lasting credit anyway. According to the story, what did Sostratus do?
answer: He carved his own name in the stone beneath the king's plaster
choices: He carved his own name in the stone beneath the king's plaster
He hid a portrait of himself inside the lighthouse flame
He signed each block with a secret mason's mark
He built a smaller twin tower bearing only his name
context: The Pharos of Alexandria, built under Ptolemy II, towered over 100 meters (330+ feet). Legend says its architect Sostratus secretly carved his own name into the stone under a layer of plaster bearing the king's name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lighthouse_of_Alexandria

question: A copper relief at United Nations headquarters in New York reproduces an agreement carved on silver tablets around 1258 BC between Egypt's pharaoh Ramesses II and the Hittite king Hattusili III. The UN displays it because, of all such documents ever found, this one is the oldest surviving WHAT in the world?
answer: peace treaty
choices: peace treaty
marriage contract
trade agreement
law code
context: The Treaty of Kadesh, sealed about 1258 BC, is the oldest surviving peace treaty in the world. Turkey gifted a copper bas-relief replica to the UN; Secretary-General U Thant accepted it on September 24, 1970, and it hangs in the second-floor delegates' corridor near the Security Council Chamber. Source: https://www.un.org/ungifts/replica-peace-treaty-between-hattusilis-and-ramses-ii

question: Iron was so rare in the Hittites' day that a foreign ruler wrote to the Hittite king Hattusili III begging for 'good iron' -- and Hattusili could send back only a single dagger-blade. In his letter, what did the king himself confess about the iron in his own storehouse at Kizzuwatna?
answer: that he had none of it ready to give
choices: that he had none of it ready to give
that he had pledged all of it to his army
that he kept all of it locked from foreigners
that he had traded the last of it for gold
context: Hattusili III wrote: 'good iron is not at present available in my storehouse in Kizzuwatna... At present I am sending you an iron dagger-blade' -- even a king could not yet supply the iron requested. Anatolia has the earliest textual evidence of iron smelting (2nd millennium BC), but modern scholars reject the old idea that a Hittite 'state monopoly' on iron won them their wars (distractor C). Sources: https://periclespress.net/Hittites_iron.html ; https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-019-09129-6

question: In March 1933 the Welsh journalist Gareth Jones walked from village to village across Soviet Ukraine, and in every single one the starving peasants greeted him with the very same words, which he wrote down in his diary. What was the cry he heard everywhere he went?
answer: "There is no bread. We are dying."
choices: "There is no bread. We are dying."
"The harvest will save us next year."
"Take us with you to the West."
"The soldiers have left us nothing."
context: Jones made the line the heart of the press release that first told the West the truth, issued in Berlin on 29 March 1933 and printed in the Manchester Guardian the next day. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gareth_Jones_(journalist)

question: Foreigners were banned from the famine zone, so Gareth Jones found a way in that no permit could stop. He got off the train about forty miles early and crossed into Soviet Ukraine on foot, carrying a knapsack he slowly emptied as he walked. What did he give away to the starving people he met along the road?
answer: His bread and chocolate
choices: His bread and chocolate
His coat and boots
His train ticket and money
His camera and notebook
context: Jones had packed the knapsack with bread and chocolate specifically to hand out as he tramped from village to village gathering testimony. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gareth_Jones_(journalist)

question: Just weeks before he exposed Stalin's famine, Gareth Jones pulled off a different scoop: on 23 February 1933 he became one of the first foreign journalists ever to fly aboard an aircraft with a rising politician, the plane carrying the propagandist Goebbels toward Frankfurt. Whom was Jones flying with?
answer: Adolf Hitler
choices: Adolf Hitler
Hermann Goering
Gregor Strasser
Ernst Roehm
context: Jones wrote that if the plane had crashed, "the history of Europe would be changed." The aircraft was named the Richthofen, and Jones flew with the British reporter Sefton Delmer. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gareth_Jones_(journalist)

question: Two days after Gareth Jones reported the Ukrainian famine, the New York Times' Moscow correspondent Walter Duranty answered him in print, insisting there was no starvation. He dismissed the millions of deaths with a single callous saying that became infamous. What was Duranty's line?
answer: "You can't make an omelette without breaking eggs."
choices: "You can't make an omelette without breaking eggs."
"You can't bake bread without burning a few loaves."
"You can't harvest wheat without losing some grain."
"You can't fill a granary without spilling some seed."
context: Duranty also wrote that "any report of a famine in Russia is today an exaggeration or malignant propaganda." His denial ran under the headline "Russians Hungry, But Not Starving." Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor_denial

question: While Gareth Jones told the truth about the famine and was banned from the USSR for life, his rival Walter Duranty did the opposite and was richly rewarded for it. In 1932 Duranty won a major American journalism award for an eleven-part series praising Stalin's system. Which award did he win?
answer: The Pulitzer Prize
choices: The Pulitzer Prize
The Peabody Award
The Polk Award
The Hearst Medal
context: To this day the Pulitzer Board has refused to revoke Duranty's 1932 prize, despite his famine denial. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Duranty ; https://www.pulitzer.org/news/statement-walter-duranty

question: Soviet law turned hunger itself into a crime. Under a decree of 7 August 1932, a starving Ukrainian peasant caught picking up a few leftover stalks of grain from a collective field could be shot or sent to a camp for ten years. The peasants gave this decree a bitter nickname after the tiny scraps it punished people for taking. What was it called?
answer: The Law of Spikelets
choices: The Law of Spikelets
The Bread Decree
The Iron Harvest Act
The Hunger Statute
context: Its formal name was the Decree on the Protection of Socialist Property. Over 200,000 people were sentenced under it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor

question: When a Ukrainian village failed to hand over its grain quota, the regime added its name to a register that amounted to a collective death sentence: every store was closed, all trade and goods were cut off, and the whole place was sealed shut, children and teachers included. What was this register called?
answer: The black board
choices: The black board
The black book
The quota roll
The hunger register
context: In Ukrainian, chorni doshky. Hundreds of collective farms and dozens of districts were blacklisted, each one cut off to starve. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor

question: Gareth Jones, the reporter who first told the West the truth about Stalin's famine, did not live to see himself vindicated. On 12 August 1935, the day before his 30th birthday, he was shot three times and killed while travelling in Japanese-occupied Inner Mongolia. What about his travelling companion later deepened suspicion that the killing was revenge?
answer: The companion was a Soviet NKVD agent
choices: The companion was a Soviet NKVD agent
The companion vanished before the police arrived
The companion had warned Jones not to go
The companion inherited Jones's papers
context: His companion, Herbert Müller, was later revealed to be an agent of the Soviet secret police, fueling the belief that the NKVD engineered Jones's death. Foreign Commissar Maxim Litvinov had earlier told Jones he was banned from the USSR for life. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gareth_Jones_(journalist)

question: In public Walter Duranty assured New York Times readers that "there is no famine or actual starvation" in the USSR. But in September 1933 he told officials at the British embassy in Moscow a private death toll that flatly contradicted his own reporting. How many did Duranty privately admit may have died?
answer: As many as ten million
choices: As many as ten million
About half a million
A few thousand at most
Around one hundred thousand
context: Duranty had earlier told a U.S. embassy official that his dispatches, by arrangement with the Soviet authorities, "always reflect the official opinion of the Soviet government and not his own." Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Duranty ; https://holodomormuseum.org.ua/en/news/a-tale-of-two-journalists-walter-duranty-and-gareth-jones/

question: The famine was no accident of weather. After raising Ukraine's grain quota until it stripped the villages bare, Joseph Stalin and Vyacheslav Molotov signed a directive on 22 January 1933 aimed at the starving peasants themselves. What did this order do to them?
answer: It sealed the borders so they could not flee for food
choices: It sealed the borders so they could not flee for food
It drafted them into labor brigades
It forgave the unpaid grain quotas
It opened state granaries to feed them
context: Combined with the internal-passport system introduced in December 1932, peasants were legally forbidden to leave the famine zone in search of food, trapping them inside to die. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causes_of_the_Holodomor ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor

question: Even at the height of the dying in 1932-33, the Soviet state was shipping roughly 1.8 million tonnes of grain out of the country. The historian Michael Ellman calculated that this exported grain alone could have kept people alive for a year. About how many?
answer: Roughly five million people
choices: Roughly five million people
Roughly two million people
Roughly eight million people
Roughly one million people
context: The grain was sold abroad for hard currency while Ukrainian villages were blacklisted and sealed off to starve. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor

question: The Moscow press corps knew Gareth Jones had told the truth, yet they sided against him to protect their visas. One of them, Eugene Lyons, confessed the shame of it in his memoir Assignment in Utopia, quoting the very words for how the correspondents handled Jones. How did Lyons say they treated him?
answer: "Throw him down we did, unanimously"
choices: "Throw him down we did, unanimously"
We called his account Soviet-baiting
We branded his story a clever lie
We said the truth lay somewhere between
context: Lyons wrote that denouncing Jones "was as unpleasant a chore as fell to any of us, but throw him down we did, unanimously and in almost identical formulas of equivocation." After agreeing to brand Jones a liar at a meeting with the Soviet censor Constantine Umansky, the correspondents ordered vodka and celebrated with him into the early hours. Source: https://www.garethjones.org/soviet_articles/assignment_in_utopia.htm

question: Ukrainians gave the catastrophe of 1932-33 a single grim word of their own — a name that says plainly what it was, not the neutral term 'famine.' It was no crop failure but a man-made disaster the Soviet state engineered. What does the name 'Holodomor' mean?
answer: Death by hunger
choices: Death by hunger
The great hunger
The years of sorrow
The stolen harvest
context: Holodomor combines holod (hunger) and mor (death/plague) -- literally 'to kill by starvation.' The name itself insists it was deliberate, not an accident of weather. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor

question: In August 1932 the Soviets passed a decree that starving Ukrainian peasants nicknamed the 'Law of the Five Spikelets.' Under it, what could happen to a hungry person caught picking up a few stalks of grain left in a collective field?
answer: Shot, or at least ten years in prison
choices: Shot, or at least ten years in prison
Stripped of all land and exiled north
Worked to death in a labor camp
Flogged, then sent home a marked thief
context: The August 7, 1932 decree let officials execute a peasant for gleaning a handful of grain, or hand down 10+ years in prison with all property seized -- punished for taking the very crop they had grown. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_Spikelets

question: To deepen the Ukrainian famine of 1932-33, armed Soviet brigades went house to house through the villages, hauling off everything a family had that could feed them or be sold for food. Of these, what did the brigades carry away?
answer: The seed grain set aside for planting
choices: The seed grain set aside for planting
The last cured ham in the cellar
The silver icons off the wall
Every coin kept in the house
context: The brigades took not only the grain meant for eating but next year's planting seed, the animals, and a family's final potatoes -- even pets -- guaranteeing the starvation would continue. The seed was the cruelest loss: it was next year's whole crop. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/ukrainian-famine-stalin

question: In March 1933, while most Western reporters stayed in Moscow hotels repeating the official line, a young Welsh journalist named Gareth Jones got off a train near Kharkiv determined to see the famine himself. How did Jones investigate it?
answer: He walked on foot through about twenty villages, sleeping in peasants' huts
choices: He walked on foot through about twenty villages, sleeping in peasants' huts
He flew over the region in a military plane
He interviewed officials from his hotel by telephone
He read the harvest reports in the state archive
context: Jones trekked roughly 40 miles north of Kharkiv on foot through some 20 villages and a dozen collective farms, sleeping in the huts so he could witness the famine firsthand. Source: https://education.holodomor.ca/gareth-jones/

question: Ukraine was the breadbasket of the entire Soviet Union, the land that grew the empire's grain. Yet at the height of the famine in June 1933, the people of that very breadbasket were dying at a staggering rate. How fast were Ukrainians dying that month?
answer: About 28,000 every day
choices: About 28,000 every day
About 28,000 every year
About 280 every day
About 2.8 million in a single week
context: Roughly 28,000 deaths a day -- about 17 every minute -- in the country that fed the USSR. The breadbasket starved while its grain was shipped out. Source: https://holodomormuseum.org.ua/en/mass-mortality/

question: As Gareth Jones walked the famine villages in 1933, he scribbled what the peasants told him into his pocket notebook -- the same words again and again. Which phrase did Jones record over and over from the villagers?
answer: 'There is no bread; we are waiting for death'
choices: 'There is no bread; we are waiting for death'
'The black earth will not feed us now'
'They left us nothing but the snow'
'Our children no longer ask for food'
context: Jones wrote down 'There is no bread; we are dying' and 'We are waiting for death,' plus the Russian 'Vse pukhli' -- 'everyone is swollen.' He saw children with swollen stomachs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gareth_Jones_(journalist)

question: On March 29, 1933, after walking out of the famine zone, Gareth Jones called a press conference in Berlin to break the story to the world while nearly every other Western reporter helped hide it. What did the headline on Jones's story announce?
answer: 'Famine Grips Russia, Millions Dying'
choices: 'Famine Grips Russia, Millions Dying'
'Stalin's Grain War Empties the Villages'
'Ukraine Starves as the Seed Is Seized'
'Red Famine Creeps Toward the Volga'
context: Jones told the truth -- 'Famine Grips Russia, Millions Dying' -- at the exact moment the press corps in Moscow was burying it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gareth_Jones_(journalist)

question: By January 1933 so many starving Ukrainians were trying to flee in search of food that Stalin and Molotov signed a directive about the peasants on the move. What did this order actually do to them?
answer: It sealed the borders with army and NKVD units
choices: It sealed the borders with army and NKVD units
It shot anyone caught on a train without papers
It sent the fleeing peasants to camps in the east
It fined each village for every missing worker
context: The January 22, 1933 directive 'On preventing the mass flight of starving peasants' sent military and NKVD units to seal the borders. The hungry were trapped to die where they stood. Source: https://cla.umn.edu/chgs/holocaust-genocide-education/resource-guides/holodomor

question: Just two days after Gareth Jones broke the famine story, Walter Duranty, the New York Times' Moscow bureau chief, answered him in print under the headline 'Russians Hungry, But Not Starving.' Brushing Jones aside as a 'big scare story,' what did Duranty flatly tell readers?
answer: 'There is no famine or starvation'
choices: 'There is no famine or starvation'
'Conditions are no worse than in 1921'
'The shortages are local and will soon pass'
'The peasants are merely underfed, not dying'
context: On March 31, 1933 Duranty wrote 'there is no famine or starvation' and waved Jones away. It was a direct, public denial of mass death he would later privately admit was real. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Duranty

question: Walter Duranty became infamous for one chilling line he used to excuse Stalin's brutal collectivization, treating millions of starving human beings as a necessary cost. What was Duranty's notorious justification?
answer: 'You can't make an omelet without breaking eggs'
choices: 'You can't make an omelet without breaking eggs'
'History is written by the victors'
'The ends are clouded but the cause is pure'
'A hard road builds a strong people'
context: Duranty's signature line -- 'But, to put it brutally, you can't make an omelet without breaking eggs' -- recast millions of dead Ukrainians as 'broken eggs' on the way to Stalin's project. Source: https://education.holodomor.ca/teaching-materials/quotations/suggested-quotes-to-use-with-student-activities/

question: Gareth Jones never lived to see his famine reporting proven right. While traveling in Japanese-occupied Inner Mongolia he was kidnapped by bandits and shot dead on August 12, 1935 -- one day before his 30th birthday. Who do some historians suspect was really behind his killing?
answer: The Soviet secret police, the NKVD
choices: The Soviet secret police, the NKVD
The Japanese occupation forces
The local bandits, acting on their own
A rival Chinese warlord's troops
context: Jones was murdered on August 12, 1935, one day shy of turning 30. Some historians suspect the Soviet secret police, the NKVD, arranged it -- a suspicion, not proven fact -- as payback for exposing Stalin's famine. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gareth_Jones_(journalist)  (Legend.)

question: Walter Duranty publicly insisted to New York Times readers that no famine was happening. But around September 1933 he told a British diplomat, William Strang, a very different figure for how many had died of hunger in the past year -- a number he never printed. What did Duranty privately concede?
answer: That perhaps ten million may have died from lack of food
choices: That perhaps ten million may have died from lack of food
That a few thousand had died in isolated villages
That the deaths could not be counted at all
That the harvest had merely been delayed
context: Duranty privately told Strang 'as many as ten million people may have died directly or indirectly from lack of food' -- the truth he hid from his own readers. A 1931 embassy memo recorded him admitting his dispatches 'always reflect the official opinion of the Soviet government.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Duranty

question: The year before he denied the famine, Walter Duranty had already won a major prize for a glowing 1931 series on the Soviet Union -- the same whitewash reporting. In 2003 historian Mark von Hagen reviewed it and urged the prize be stripped, yet the board refused, citing 'no clear and convincing evidence of deliberate deception.' Which prize did Duranty keep?
answer: The Pulitzer Prize
choices: The Pulitzer Prize
The George Polk Award
The Overseas Press Club award
The National Press Club medal
context: Duranty's 1932 Pulitzer still stands. Von Hagen called the work 'unbalanced and uncritical' and said the honor should be revoked; the NYT later called it 'some of the worst reporting to appear in this newspaper,' but the Pulitzer Board has never taken it back. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Duranty

question: Because reporters like Duranty buried the Holodomor, the establishment death toll was soft-pedaled for decades to only about half a million -- a figure that itself shows how thoroughly the truth was hidden. What do serious historians' estimates of the Ukrainian dead actually run to?
answer: Roughly 3.5 to 7 million
choices: Roughly 3.5 to 7 million
Roughly 400 to 600 thousand
Roughly 30 to 60 thousand
Roughly 12 to 15 million
context: Estimates run from about 3.5 to 7 million Ukrainians, with some figures reaching 10 million for the wider Soviet famine. The 'soft' half-million number was the measure of the cover-up. Ukraine's parliament declared the Holodomor a genocide in 2006. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/Holodomor

question: When the Lakota of the Plains first laid eyes on a horse, they had no word for the strange new animal. So they named it after the only pack animal they had ever used to drag their loads. What did they call the horse?
answer: The sacred dog
choices: The sacred dog
The great elk
The swift deer
The thunder bird
context: The Lakota called the horse 'sunka wakan' — sunka meaning dog, wakan meaning sacred or mysterious. Before the horse arrived, dogs were the only animals Plains peoples used to haul loads, so they named the newcomer after them: the 'sacred dog' or 'mystery dog.' Source: blog.nativehope.org/native-american-relative-horse; nativesunnews.today (Shunka Wakan, the Sacred Dog).

question: On his second voyage in 1493, Christopher Columbus shipped two dozen horses across the ocean to the Americas — the first horses to set hoof there in about 10,000 years. Why did that gap exist, so that horses had been absent for so long?
answer: Horses had once lived in the Americas but had gone extinct there
choices: Horses had once lived in the Americas but had gone extinct there
Horses had been hunted to nothing by early Spanish sailors
Horses could not survive the long ocean crossing until 1493
Horses had been kept penned in Spain and never allowed to leave
context: The horse actually EVOLVED in North America over millions of years, then died out on the continent about 10,000 years ago at the end of the last ice age. So when the Spanish brought Andalusian horses across the ocean, the animal was returning to the very land it had originally come from.
