Source: history.com/articles/horses-plains-indians-native-americans.

question: The Abbasid caliph al-Mansur founded a brand-new capital city in the year 762 and filled its palace with a great library. What was so unusual about the SHAPE of his new city?
answer: It was built perfectly round
choices: It was built perfectly round
It floated on the river
It was carved underground
It was shaped like a star
context: Baghdad's round city, founded by al-Mansur in 762, held a palace library modeled on the old Persian imperial collection; that library grew into the Bayt al-Hikma, or House of Wisdom. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Wisdom

question: Hunayn ibn Ishaq was the greatest book-translator in Baghdad, turning lost Greek works into Arabic. A later writer reported that the caliph paid him for each finished book in a jaw-dropping way. How was Hunayn reportedly paid?
answer: The book's exact weight in gold
choices: The book's exact weight in gold
A fine herd of Arabian horses
A grand palace beside the river
A chest of rare silver coins
context: The 13th-century biographer Ibn Abi Usaybia wrote that Hunayn was paid the weight of each completed book in gold. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hunayn-ibn-Ishaq

question: Around 830, a mathematician in Baghdad wrote a book whose Arabic title began with a word meaning to RESTORE or set a broken bone back together. A whole branch of math took its name straight from that title word. Which branch?
answer: Algebra
choices: Algebra
Geometry
Arithmetic
Calculus
context: Al-Khwarizmi's 'Kitab al-Jabr wa'l-Muqabala' (The Compendious Book on Calculation by Restoration and Balancing) gave us the word ALGEBRA, taken from 'al-jabr,' meaning restoration. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Jabr

question: The Baghdad mathematician al-Khwarizmi grew so famous in Europe that the Latin form of his NAME turned into an everyday math-and-computer word that people use constantly today. Which word came straight from al-Khwarizmi's name?
answer: Algorithm
choices: Algorithm
Equation
Decimal
Diagram
context: ALGORITHM comes from the Latinized name of al-Khwarizmi, whose works also helped carry the Hindu-Arabic numerals westward. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Khwarizmi

question: Legend says Caliph al-Ma'mun's hunger for Greek learning began with a dream: a pale, blue-eyed man with a broad forehead sat on a throne and talked with him about 'what is good,' urging him to gather the wisdom of the ancients. Which long-dead Greek philosopher did al-Ma'mun say he saw?
answer: Aristotle
choices: Aristotle
Socrates
Pythagoras
Plato
context: The dream of Aristotle is one of the famous legends behind al-Ma'mun's translation movement. Told as tradition, not fact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Wisdom

question: After his armies defeated the Byzantines, Caliph al-Ma'mun is said to have made a strange demand of the emperor as the price of peace -- not gold or land, but one prized ancient Greek book. Which work did he want handed over?
answer: Ptolemy's Almagest
choices: Ptolemy's Almagest
Homer's Iliad
Euclid's Elements
Aristotle's Politics
context: The Almagest (about AD 150) was Ptolemy's great astronomy book; al-Ma'mun is said to have demanded Greek manuscripts, including it, from Emperor Theophilus. Source: https://www.middleeasteye.net/discover/iraq-baghdad-house-wisdom-uniting-east-west

question: Caliph al-Mutawakkil offered the translator and physician Hunayn ibn Ishaq lavish rewards to brew a poison for an enemy. Hunayn refused -- and was thrown in prison for a whole year. What reason did Hunayn give for saying no?
answer: His oath as a physician bound him to heal, never to harm
choices: His oath as a physician bound him to heal, never to harm
His faith forbade him to take any human life
He had sworn that same healer's oath to the enemy too
He held that poisoning dishonored the calling of a healer
context: Hunayn answered that the physician's oath bound him to help and not to harm; al-Mutawakkil jailed him for a year. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunayn_ibn_Ishaq

question: When Hulagu Khan's Mongol army sacked Baghdad in 1258, chroniclers said so many books were hurled from its libraries into the river Tigris that the water itself changed. What did those writers claim happened to the river?
answer: It ran black with ink
choices: It ran black with ink
It ran red with blood
It rose and overflowed its banks
Its current slowed to a crawl
context: The 'river ran black with ink' image is a famous chronicle claim that historian Michal Biran calls a likely exaggeration; the astronomer Nasir al-Din al-Tusi is said to have rescued a huge trove of manuscripts and taken them to the Maragha observatory. Told as legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Wisdom

question: Caliph al-Ma'mun sent two teams of astronomers out onto a flat desert plain. One group marched due north and the other due south, carefully counting every step and planting arrows to mark how far they had gone. What were the astronomers trying to measure?
answer: The size of the Earth
choices: The size of the Earth
The distance to the Sun
The height of the sky
The width of the desert
context: On the plain of Sinjar al-Ma'mun's astronomers measured one degree of latitude as about 56 2/3 Arabic miles, landing within a few hundred miles of the true circumference -- then crossed the desert again to double-check. Source: https://www.chalkefestival.com/history-hub/writing/power-and-curiosity-how-the-abbasid-caliph-al-mamun-pushed-the-boundaries-of-scientific-knowledge/

question: Around 850 in Baghdad, the philosopher al-Kindi wrote the first known book on cracking secret codes. His big idea: find the symbol that shows up most often in the coded message, then swap it for whatever appears most often in the ordinary language. In a coded message, what does al-Kindi tell you to match that most-common symbol to?
answer: The most common letter of the ordinary language
choices: The most common letter of the ordinary language
The first letter the writer wrote down
The rarest letter of the ordinary language
The letter that looks most like the symbol
context: Al-Kindi's 'Manuscript on Deciphering Cryptographic Messages' invented the method now called frequency analysis -- match the commonest cipher-letter to the commonest plain-letter. The text was lost for centuries and only rediscovered in an Istanbul archive in 1987, about 800 years ahead of European cryptanalysis. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Kindi

question: Hunayn ibn Ishaq translated 129 works of the Greek doctor Galen into Arabic. For many of those books the Greek that Galen first wrote has vanished from the world -- every Greek copy lost. So how can a scholar today still read those vanished works of Galen at all?
answer: Only in Hunayn's Arabic translation
choices: Only in Hunayn's Arabic translation
From carvings found inside Galen's tomb
From a single Greek copy kept in Rome
Only by guessing at the missing text
context: Many of Galen's works survive only in Hunayn's Arabic, the Greek originals having been lost -- a vivid example of Baghdad preserving Greek learning the West had largely lost. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunayn_ibn_Ishaq

question: Roughly a thousand years before a famous Victorian naturalist would shock the world, the Baghdad-era writer al-Jahiz of Basra filled his seven-volume Book of Animals with over 350 creatures and a startling claim: animals are locked in a 'struggle for existence,' and the environment decides which ones survive. Which later scientific theory does al-Jahiz seem to foreshadow?
answer: Natural selection
choices: Natural selection
Inheritance of acquired traits
Laws of heredity
Germ theory of disease
context: Al-Jahiz's 'Kitab al-Hayawan' described a struggle for existence and how environment shapes survival -- ideas that foreshadow natural selection, named in Charles Darwin's 1859 'On the Origin of Species.' The distractors point to Lamarck (acquired traits), Mendel (heredity), and Pasteur (germ theory). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Jahiz

question: In February 1915 the doctor Charles Myers wrote up three British soldiers who had each been blown off their feet by bursting artillery shells — one couldn't taste or smell anything afterward, another had been buried alive for 18 hours and couldn't remember. Myers gave their strange new battlefield injury a name that stuck. What did he call it?
answer: Shell shock
choices: Shell shock
Trench fever
Combat fatigue
Soldier's heart
context: Charles Samuel Myers, director of the Cambridge Psychological Laboratory, first used 'shell shock' in print in The Lancet on 13 February 1915, after noticing how alike the symptoms were in three men each blown up by shells. Source: https://www.psychol.cam.ac.uk/news/2015-02-13-shell-shock

question: Doctors in World War I struggled to describe what a shell-shocked soldier looked like — the ringing ears, the dizziness, the sleepwalking, and above all the violent uncontrollable trembling of a man's whole body. One vivid description of that trembling stuck. They said the shaking was rather like what?
answer: A jelly shaking
choices: A jelly shaking
A leaf in the wind
A plucked harp string
A drum being beaten
context: Period doctors described the shell-shocked soldier's trembling as 'rather like a jelly shaking,' alongside ringing ears, dizziness, sleepwalking, and dreams of France and 'dead Germans.' Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/the-shock-of-war-55376701/

question: At Craiglockhart War Hospital near Edinburgh in 1917, Dr. W.H.R. Rivers treated shell-shocked officers with a gentle 'talking cure' instead of harsh methods. Two of his patients there were the war poets Siegfried Sassoon and Wilfred Owen, who met as fellow patients. During his recovery at Craiglockhart, Owen wrote which famous poem mourning the soldiers dying at the front?
answer: Anthem for Doomed Youth
choices: Anthem for Doomed Youth
The Charge of the Light Brigade
In Flanders Fields
The Soldier
context: Owen wrote 'Anthem for Doomed Youth' during his recovery at Craiglockhart, where Rivers' talking cure had brought him together with Siegfried Sassoon. Source: https://livesofthefirstworldwar.iwm.org.uk/story/78958

question: Private Harry Farr was so badly shell-shocked he could not even hold a pen, yet a British army court condemned him to death for cowardice in 1916. Marched out before the firing squad, Farr did one defiant thing that his family told for generations afterward — and that helped win him a posthumous pardon in 2006. What did he do?
answer: He refused the blindfold and looked the firing squad in the eye
choices: He refused the blindfold and looked the firing squad in the eye
He sang a hymn until the volley silenced him
He handed his medals to the chaplain
He saluted the officer who gave the order
context: Harry Farr, hospitalized for shell shock so severe he 'could not hold a pen,' was executed for cowardice on 18 October 1916; he refused the blindfold and faced the firing squad. In 2006 his granddaughter's campaign won a pardon for him and 305 other executed men. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Farr

question: Some World War I doctors tried brutal 'cures' for shell shock. Dr. Lewis Yealland treated soldiers who had been struck mute by the trauma by telling one patient, 'You will not leave this room until you are talking as well as you ever did' — then he forced the man's mouth open with a tongue depressor and applied a treatment to the back of his throat until speech returned. What did Yealland apply to the soldier's throat?
answer: A strong electric current
choices: A strong electric current
A scalding hot iron
A bitter chemical paste
A jolt of pressurized air
context: Dr. Lewis Yealland applied a strong faradic (electric) current to the back of mute soldiers' throats and claimed a 100% success rate — a violent contrast to Rivers' gentle talking cure. Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3673538/

question: After the English crushed the French at Crecy in 1346, the 16-year-old Edward, the Black Prince, walked the field and took the crest and motto of a dead enemy who had charged in blind: King John of Bohemia. Every Prince of Wales has carried that badge ever since. What is it?
answer: Three ostrich feathers and the motto 'Ich dien' ('I serve')
choices: Three ostrich feathers and the motto 'Ich dien' ('I serve')
A red dragon and the motto 'Cymru am byth' ('Wales forever')
A golden lion and the motto 'Dieu et mon droit' ('God and my right')
A silver unicorn and the motto 'Nemo me impune' ('None provoke me')
context: At Crecy the blind King John of Bohemia had his knights tie their horses' reins to his so he could charge in; they were found dead together the next morning. The 16-year-old Black Prince took his crest of three ostrich feathers and motto 'Ich dien,' and every Prince of Wales has used the badge since. (englishmonarchs.co.uk/black_prince.htm; baldwin.co.uk/news/edward-the-black-prince)

question: It is called the 'Hundred Years' War,' but the fighting between England and France over the French crown ran far longer than its name suggests -- a boy could be born, grow old, and die without ever seeing a single year of peace. Counting from 1337 to 1453, how long did it actually last?
answer: 116 years
choices: 116 years
104 years
131 years
97 years
context: The war ran from 1337 to 1453 -- 116 years -- and outlasted five English kings and five French kings. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War)

question: At Crecy in 1346, the aging King John of Bohemia rode with the French even though he had gone completely blind and could not see the enemy in front of him. Determined to strike at least one blow, what did he do?
answer: He had his knights tie their horses' reins to his and charge with him into the fight
choices: He had his knights tie their horses' reins to his and charge with him into the fight
He stayed at the rear and shouted commands to his marshals by name
He surrendered his sword to the English rather than risk his knights
He climbed a hill to be carried in a litter above the battle line
context: The blind king's knights lashed their reins to his so he could ride into a battle he could not see; the whole group was found dead together the next morning. (britishbattles.com/one-hundred-years-war/battle-of-crecy; britainuntold.co.uk)

question: At Poitiers in 1356, Edward the Black Prince did something almost unheard of: his army captured the actual King of France, John II, alive on the battlefield. That evening, at the victory banquet, the prince treated his royal prisoner with startling honor. What did he do for King John II?
answer: He stood and personally served the captured king his food at the table
choices: He stood and personally served the captured king his food at the table
He returned the king's sword and crown before the meal began
He freed the king on the spot and asked for nothing in return
He seated the king on his own throne and knelt at his feet
context: John II had surrendered by handing his right glove to a knight, Sir Denis de Morbecque. At the banquet the Black Prince waited on the defeated king himself, as a sign of chivalric respect for a brave enemy. (worldhistory.org/article/1511/battle-of-poitiers-1356-ce)

question: The Hundred Years' War ended at Castillon in 1453, where Jean Bureau's massed French cannon -- possibly more than 200 guns -- tore the English attack to pieces and killed the great commander John Talbot when a cannonball brought down his horse and pinned him. The longbow had won the war's most famous battles, but the cannon won the war. Of its old empire in France, what did England keep?
answer: A single port, Calais
choices: A single port, Calais
The whole region of Normandy
The wine-rich land of Gascony
The crown of France itself
context: Castillon was the first major European battle decided by massed cannon. After 116 years of war over the French crown, England was left with only the port of Calais -- the longbow had won the famous battles, but artillery won the war. (britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Castillon; britishbattles.com/one-hundred-years-war/battle-of-castillon)

question: During the Byzantine fight over holy images, the monk John of Damascus gave the pro-icon side its sharpest answer to the charge that kissing a painting of Christ was idol-worship. Honoring an icon, he argued, is no more idolatry than honoring the man himself, because what you do to the image does what?
answer: Passes through to the real person the image depicts
choices: Passes through to the real person the image depicts
Cleanses the painter of the sin of vanity
Binds an angel to guard the wooden panel
Stores up holiness inside the paint and gold
context: John of Damascus (a Syrian monk writing under Muslim rule, safe from the emperor) taught that the honor paid to an image passes through to its prototype — you do not worship the wood and paint, you honor the person it shows, the way one might kiss a portrait of a loved one. The Second Council of Nicaea (787) made this official church teaching. Source: Britannica iconoclasm article; New World Encyclopedia, Second Council of Nicaea; World History Encyclopedia, Byzantine Icons.

question: At the Council of Hieria in 754, the emperor Constantine V argued that anyone painting Christ falls into a trap: paint only his humanity and you rip his human nature away from his divine one; try to paint his divinity and you smear the two natures together. So Constantine declared there was only ONE true image of Christ — and pointed at what?
answer: The bread and wine of the Eucharist
choices: The bread and wine of the Eucharist
The wooden cross of the crucifixion
The empty tomb outside Jerusalem
The written words of the four Gospels
context: Constantine V was so committed he personally wrote 13 treatises against icons. His Christological dilemma — painting Christ forces you into either the Nestorian error (splitting his natures) or the Monophysite error (blurring them) — let him conclude the Eucharist was the only faithful image of Christ. The Council of Hieria condemned all icons as idols and cursed everyone who venerated them; the Second Council of Nicaea overturned it in 787. Source: Wikipedia, Council of Hieria; encyclopedia.com Iconoclasm; thecollector.com/what-was-iconoclasm-in-byzantium.

question: Romans split each month around a midpoint day they called the 'Ides.' In March the Ides fell on the 15th — the day in 44 BC that Julius Caesar was stabbed to death. In the Roman calendar, what point in the month did the 'Ides' actually mark?
answer: The middle of the month
choices: The middle of the month
The first day of the month
The last day of the month
The day of the new moon
context: The Ides was simply the middle — the 15th in March, May, July, and October, the 13th in the rest. After Caesar's murder, 'the Ides of March' became shorthand for looming doom. Source: britannica.com/topic/Ides-of-March; worldhistory.org/article/803.

question: A seer named Spurinna had warned Julius Caesar that danger would strike him no later than the Ides of March. On the morning of the 15th, walking to the Senate, Caesar grinned at Spurinna and said, 'The Ides of March are come.' What did Spurinna shoot back?
answer: 'Yes — but they are not gone.'
choices: 'Yes — but they are not gone.'
'Then the gods have spared you.'
'The omens have all passed.'
'Your fortune holds, Caesar.'
context: 'Yes, they are come, but they are not gone.' Hours later Caesar was dead. Spurinna was a haruspex — a priest who read omens. Source: worldhistory.org/article/803; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spurinna.

question: Everyone 'knows' that Julius Caesar was warned, 'Beware the Ides of March.' But that exact line appears in no ancient record at all — the real warning came from the seer Spurinna. Where does the famous phrasing actually come from?
answer: A play William Shakespeare wrote in 1599
choices: A play William Shakespeare wrote in 1599
A letter Caesar's wife sent that morning
A Roman law carved over the Senate door
A prophecy kept in the Temple of Vesta
context: Shakespeare invented the exact wording for his play 'Julius Caesar' (1599). Ancient writers Suetonius and Plutarch record only Spurinna's blunt warning, not that catchy line. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Et_tu,_Brute; britannica.com/topic/Ides-of-March.

question: As the attack began, the senator Tillius Cimber stepped up to Julius Caesar as if begging a favor — then grabbed Caesar's toga with both hands and yanked it down off his neck, the signal for the others to draw their daggers. What did Caesar shout as the cloak was hauled from his shoulders?
answer: 'Why, this is violence!'
choices: 'Why, this is violence!'
'Stand back, all of you!'
'Guards, to me at once!'
'Have you all gone mad?'
context: The toga-grab was the prearranged signal. Cimber pretended to plead for his exiled brother to get close enough to seize Caesar. Source: lexundria.com/plut_caes/66/prr (Plutarch); worldhistory.org/article/803.

question: The night before he died, Julius Caesar's wife Calpurnia woke from a terrible dream and begged him not to go out the next morning. He nearly agreed to stay home. What had Calpurnia seen in her dream? (Roman writers report this as a legend.)
answer: Caesar stabbed to death in her arms
choices: Caesar stabbed to death in her arms
A wolf loose inside the Senate house
Their children weeping over an empty bed
A fire sweeping through all of Rome
context: Suetonius reports Calpurnia dreamed the gable of their house collapsed and that Caesar was killed in her arms — told as an omen-legend. The conspirator Decimus Brutus arrived and coaxed Caesar into going anyway. Source: livius.org (Suetonius); worldhistory.org/article/803.

question: On his way into the Senate, Julius Caesar was handed a written note by a man named Artemidorus — a note that named the conspirators and laid out the whole plot. Caesar took the scroll in his hand. What happened to that warning?
answer: He never read it before he died
choices: He never read it before he died
He passed it straight to a guard
He read it and laughed it off
He dropped it in the crowd
context: Caesar tucked the note among his other papers in his left hand, meaning to read it later — and never did. The unread scroll could have saved his life. Source: livius.org (Suetonius); worldhistory.org/article/803.

question: Brutus minted a silver coin to take open credit for killing Julius Caesar — one of the most astonishing objects in ancient history. One side carries his own face; the other carries two daggers, a freed-slave's cap, and the words EID MAR ('Ides of March'). What makes this coin so jaw-dropping?
answer: A politician advertising a murder on money
choices: A politician advertising a murder on money
The first coin to ever show a living man
A coin secretly buried with Caesar's body
The only coin Rome made of solid gold
context: The two daggers flank a 'pileus,' the cap a freed slave wore — Brutus was bragging that the killing set Rome free. Only about 100 EID MAR denarii survive; they are among the most prized of all ancient coins. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ides_of_March_coin.

question: The very first dagger-blow against Julius Caesar — from the senator Servilius Casca, aimed at his neck from behind — was shallow and failed to kill him. Caesar did not go down quietly. With the only thing in his hand, he stabbed Casca right back. What did Caesar fight back with?
answer: His iron writing-stylus
choices: His iron writing-stylus
A dagger he tore loose
A bronze inkpot
A bench leg
context: Caesar seized Casca's arm and drove his stylus — a pointed metal pen — through it, shouting in Latin, 'Casca, you villain, what are you doing?' Source: livius.org (Suetonius); lexundria.com/plut_caes/66/prr (Plutarch).

question: At least sixty Roman senators joined the plot against Julius Caesar, and they did not see themselves as murderers. They even gave themselves a proud name and Brutus prepared a speech for the Senate afterward. In their own minds, what were these men doing by killing Caesar?
answer: Saving the Republic from a dictator
choices: Saving the Republic from a dictator
Avenging a personal family insult
Seizing his fortune for themselves
Obeying a secret order from the gods
context: They called themselves the 'Liberatores' (Liberators) and believed they were rescuing the Roman Republic from the man who had made himself dictator-for-life. The night was meant to restore liberty, not to be a crime. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Julius_Caesar; worldhistory.org/Marcus_Junius_Brutus.

question: As the daggers rained down, the conspirators were packed so tightly around Julius Caesar — every man pushing in to strike the same target — that, Plutarch records, the attackers did damage to each other. In the frenzy of the stabbing, who else ended up wounded?
answer: Several of the conspirators themselves
choices: Several of the conspirators themselves
Two senators who tried to help Caesar
A pair of guards at the doorway
Caesar's slaves waiting outside
context: Plutarch writes that 'the conspirators themselves were many of them wounded by each other, while they all aimed their blows at the same man.' Every plotter was meant to strike so that all shared the guilt. Source: lexundria.com/plut_caes/66/prr (Plutarch).

question: There is a bitter irony in exactly where Julius Caesar fell. The Senate was meeting that day in the great hall built by Pompey — the rival Caesar had crushed in civil war. At the foot of what did the bleeding Caesar finally collapse and die?
answer: A towering statue of Pompey
choices: A towering statue of Pompey
The Senate's bronze doors
An altar to the war-god Mars
The empty chair of the consul
context: Caesar fell at the base of a statue of Pompey the Great, his defeated enemy; Plutarch says the pedestal was 'drenched with his blood.' Just before striking, Cassius prayed to that same statue, as if calling on Pompey's ghost. Source: lexundria.com/plut_caes/66/prr (Plutarch).

question: After Julius Caesar's body was carried home, a physician named Antistius did something never recorded before — he examined the corpse to learn how Caesar died, then reported his finding aloud in the Forum. Of the 23 dagger-wounds in the body, what did Antistius conclude?
answer: Only one wound had truly been fatal
choices: Only one wound had truly been fatal
All 23 had struck at once
None alone could have killed him
The first blow was the deadly one
context: Antistius judged that only the second wound, in the chest, had actually killed Caesar — often called history's first recorded forensic autopsy. He announced it publicly in the Forum; the word 'forensic' itself comes from 'forum.' Source: livius.org (Suetonius); simplyforensic.com.

question: The senators who killed Julius Caesar believed his death would bring back the old Roman Republic. Within only a few years, Brutus and Cassius were both dead and Caesar's adopted heir Octavian ruled alone. So what did the assassination actually accomplish in the end?
answer: It ended the Republic for good
choices: It ended the Republic for good
It restored the Senate's full power
It split Rome into two republics
It returned Rome to electing kings
context: The murder triggered fresh civil wars and destroyed the very Republic it was meant to save; Octavian became Augustus, Rome's first emperor. The act meant to save liberty ended it forever. Source: history.com/articles/julius-caesar-assassination-fall-roman-republic.

question: The Inca built their capital city of Cusco high in the Andes and believed it sat at the exact center of everything — the one point where the four parts of their empire all came together. In their Quechua language, what does the name 'Cusco' (Qosqo) mean?
answer: The navel of the world
choices: The navel of the world
The roof of the sky
The gate of the sun
The heart of the mountain
context: Qosqo is a Quechua word meaning 'navel' or 'center.' The Inca saw their capital as the navel of the world — the point where the empire's four quarters joined. Source: https://www.britannica.com/place/Cuzco

question: The Inca did not call their realm 'the Inca Empire' — that is our name for it. Their own name for it was Tawantinsuyu, and it described how the whole empire was split into great quarters that all met at Cusco. What does Tawantinsuyu mean?
answer: The Realm of the Four Parts
choices: The Realm of the Four Parts
The Children of the Sun
The Throne of the Andes
The People of the High Snows
context: Tawantinsuyu means 'the Realm (or Land) of the Four Parts.' Four quarters (suyu) radiated out from the capital, so the name itself was a map of how the empire was organized. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_Empire

question: An Inca founding legend tells how the sun god Inti sent the first Inca, Manco Cápac, and his sister Mama Ocllo out of Lake Titicaca carrying a golden staff. Inti told them to wander until the staff did one particular thing, and there they must build their city. What were they told to watch for?
answer: The golden staff sinking into the earth
choices: The golden staff sinking into the earth
A condor circling above a peak
The staff turning warm in their hands
A spring of water bursting from the rock
context: In the legend, Inti said to settle wherever the golden staff sank into the ground — and it sank at Cusco. This is a founding legend, told as sacred story, not as recorded history. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_mythology

question: The ninth Inca ruler, Pachacuti, is said to have rebuilt Cusco in the shape of a single animal whose body became the city's plan — the great fortress of Sacsayhuamán formed its head, the main plaza its belly, and two rivers met to make its tail. According to the legend, what animal was Cusco built to resemble?
answer: A crouching puma
choices: A crouching puma
A coiled serpent
A soaring condor
A charging llama
context: Legend says Pachacuti laid out Cusco as a crouching puma — the symbol of Inca might — with Sacsayhuamán as the head and the plaza as the belly. This is a traditional account of the city's design. Source: https://smarthistory.org/city-of-cusco/

question: Inca stonemasons cut and fitted enormous boulders together so perfectly that the walls have outlasted the Spanish buildings later piled on top of them, surviving earthquakes that toppled everything else. People still marvel at how tightly the giant stones lock together. Which of these is the famous true description of those joints?
answer: You cannot slip a sheet of paper or a knife blade into them
choices: You cannot slip a sheet of paper or a knife blade into them
The stones were ground to fit using only sand and water
A thin clay bead you cannot see fills each hidden seam
The blocks rocked a little but somehow never fell down
context: The Inca fitted massive stones with no mortar so precisely that you cannot slide a sheet of paper or a knife point into the seams — which is part of why the walls still stand after centuries of earthquakes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coricancha

question: The Inca ran a vast empire but never invented writing — no letters, no books. To take the census, count tribute, and track the llama herds and storehouses, their record-keepers used a tool made of dyed strings tied with knots at different heights to stand for ones, tens, and hundreds. What was this knotted record-keeping device called?
answer: The quipu
choices: The quipu
The codex
The abacus
The cuneiform
context: The quipu (khipu) was a bundle of knotted, colored strings; clusters of knots at different heights recorded numbers in a decimal system. Specialist keepers called quipucamayocs read them. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Quipu/

question: With no horses and no wheel, the Inca still moved news across thousands of miles of mountains astonishingly fast. They posted trained relay runners, the chasquis, in huts every few kilometres, each sprinting his stretch and handing off to the next. Running this way around the clock, what could the chasquis deliver to the emperor in Cusco?
answer: Fresh ocean fish, still good to eat
choices: Fresh ocean fish, still good to eat
Sealed clay tablets of new laws
Live messenger pigeons from the coast
Barrels of fresh mountain snow
context: Running in relay day and night, chasquis could cover up to about 150 miles in a day — fast enough to bring fresh sea fish up to the emperor in the mountains, or send a message from Quito to Cusco in roughly five days. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/757/the-inca-road-system/

question: High in the freezing Andes, the Inca invented a way to make potatoes last for up to ten years in storage. They left the potatoes out in the bitter night cold, let them thaw by day, and then trampled the water out of them with their bare feet, leaving a rock-hard preserved food called chuño. What technique were they using, thousands of years before modern food science gave it a name?
answer: Freeze-drying
choices: Freeze-drying
Pickling
Smoking
Salting
context: Making chuño is essentially freeze-drying: freeze by night, thaw by day, stomp out the water by foot. The hard result kept for up to ten years in stone warehouses — a hedge against famine. Source: https://machupicchu-tours.com/blog/inca/agriculture-of-the-incas/

question: Because the Inca had no iron and no wheel, they could not build the metal bridges we know — so they wove their bridges out of twisted grass and slung them across deep river gorges. One of these, Q'eswachaka, still hangs over the Apurímac River canyon today. How do the local communities keep this grass bridge from falling apart after five hundred years?
answer: They tear it down and reweave it from fresh grass every year
choices: They tear it down and reweave it from fresh grass every year
They coat the old ropes in animal fat each spring
They have replaced the worn strands with steel cable
They let no one cross it except once a year
context: Every June the local communities take down Q'eswachaka — about 118 feet of grass rope over the Apurímac gorge — and reweave it entirely from new grass, exactly as their ancestors have for five centuries. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/travel/article/inca-grass-rope-bridge-qeswachaka-unesco

question: Before he was emperor, the prince later called Pachacuti led the defense of Cusco against the rival Chanca army and crushed them at the battle of Yahuar Pampa, then turned that single city into a vast empire. He took the throne-name Pachacuti for himself. What does the name Pachacuti mean?
answer: Earth-Shaker, Reverser of the World
choices: Earth-Shaker, Reverser of the World
Lord of the Golden Sun, Child of Inti
Father of the Four Quarters, Son of the Andes
Master of the High Snows, Keeper of the Sun
context: Pachacuti (Quechua pacha kutiy) means 'Earth-Shaker' or 'Reverser/Turner-Over of the World.' He took the name after defeating the Chanca and transforming Cusco from a city into an empire. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Pachacuti_Inca_Yupanqui/

question: Cusco's holiest temple, the Qorikancha or 'Golden Enclosure,' had walls lined with hundreds of sheets of solid gold and a garden of life-size gold and silver corn and llamas. The Spanish stripped the gold, melted it into bars, and raised the Church of Santo Domingo on the temple's foundations. Centuries later, when earthquakes in 1650 and 1950 wrecked the Spanish church, what happened to the Inca stonework beneath it?
answer: The Inca walls stood firm and survived
choices: The Inca walls stood firm and survived
The Inca walls crumbled to dust first
The Inca walls were swallowed by a sinkhole
The Inca walls were found to be hollow inside
context: The Spanish melted down the Qorikancha's roughly 700 gold sheets and built Santo Domingo on top — but the mortarless Inca foundations outlasted the colonial church, surviving the earthquakes that wrecked it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coricancha

question: In 1532 the Spanish captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa and held him for ransom. To buy his freedom he made a staggering offer: he would fill the room he was held in once with gold and twice over with silver, up to a line he could reach on the wall. The Inca delivered tons of treasure, the Spanish melted it all down — and then what did they do to Atahualpa?
answer: They executed him anyway
choices: They executed him anyway
They let him go free as promised
They crowned him a Spanish vassal king
They shipped him across the sea to Spain
context: Atahualpa filled the Ransom Room with roughly 13,000 lb of gold and 26,000 lb of silver. The Spanish melted it into bars and then strangled him on August 29, 1533, breaking the bargain. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ransom_Room

question: The Inca built the largest empire in the ancient Americas without a single horse, ox, or any large work animal — except one. They had just one kind of pack animal to carry their loads up and down the mountains. Which animal was it?
answer: The llama
choices: The llama
The horse
The ox
The camel
context: The llama was the Inca's only beast of burden, and even it could carry only about 40 kg. With no horses, oxen, or wheels, almost everything else was moved by human muscle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_Empire.

question: High above the city of Cusco, the Inca stacked the fortress walls of Sacsayhuaman out of gigantic stones — some heavier than 100 tons — fitted together with NO mortar to glue them. The stones were cut to lock together so perfectly that, famously, you cannot do one thing. What can you NOT do?
answer: Slip a sheet of paper between two blocks
choices: Slip a sheet of paper between two blocks
Find any two blocks the same size
Climb the wall without a ladder
See the wall from inside Cusco
context: This is called polygonal masonry: huge blocks shaped with many faces that interlock in three dimensions. The joints are so tight you cannot push a knife blade or even a sheet of paper into them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacsayhuaman.

question: The Inca ran a vast empire even though they never invented writing. To keep their records — censuses, harvests, taxes — they used something completely different from books or letters. What did an Inca record actually look like?
answer: Knots tied in colored strings
choices: Knots tied in colored strings
Symbols carved into clay tablets
Pictures painted on deer hide
Marks pressed into soft wax
context: This knotted-string device was the quipu (khipu). The color, the fiber, and the type of knot all carried meaning — a record kept entirely in cords instead of words. Source: worldhistory.org/Quipu.

question: The Inca laced their mountain empire together with two great highways — one along the coast, one through the peaks — that they used to move armies and messages across the whole Andes. They named this royal road the Qhapaq Nan. What does that name mean?
answer: Road of the Lord
choices: Road of the Lord
Path of the Sun
Way of the Mountains
Trail of the Four Winds
context: The Qhapaq Nan ('Road of the Lord') ran for over 40,000 km (25,000 miles) through what is now Peru, Ecuador, Chile, Bolivia, and Argentina — all built with no wheel and no iron. Source: worldhistory.org/article/757/the-inca-road-system.

question: Perched on a high ridge about 80 km from Cusco, the stone city of Machu Picchu was built around 1450 of granite blocks fitted without mortar. It was not a fortress and not a temple-city. What was Machu Picchu actually built to be?
answer: A mountain estate for the emperor Pachacuti
choices: A mountain estate for the emperor Pachacuti
A fortress guarding the road to Cusco
A prison for captured enemy kings
A market town for coca traders
context: Machu Picchu was a royal estate for the emperor Pachacuti, sitting at 2,430 m (7,970 ft) — a private mountain retreat for the ruler, not a city for ordinary people. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machu_Picchu.

question: At the very top of Machu Picchu the Inca carved a single block of stone, lining it up with the sun on the shortest day of the year so their priests could track the seasons and time the great festivals. They gave this sun-stone a striking name. What was it called?
answer: The Hitching Post of the Sun
choices: The Hitching Post of the Sun
The Mirror of the Moon
The Gate of the Condor
The Throne of the Stars
context: The Intihuatana, the carved 'Hitching Post of the Sun,' is aligned to the winter solstice. The Inca used it like a calendar in stone, watching the sun to know when the festivals should begin. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machu_Picchu.

question: To carry news across the Inca empire, fast relay runners called chasqui were posted every few kilometers along the royal roads, each one sprinting his stretch and handing off to the next. Running day and night, they could even rush one surprising luxury all the way up to the emperor in Cusco. What did they deliver?
answer: Fresh fish from the Pacific coast
choices: Fresh fish from the Pacific coast
Snow packed from the high peaks
Letters sealed with the royal stamp
Gold dug from the southern mines
context: By handing off to a fresh runner each leg, the chasqui could cover up to 240 km in a single day — fast enough to bring the mountain capital fresh seafood from the ocean. ('Letters' is a trick: the Inca had no writing.) Source: worldhistory.org/article/757/the-inca-road-system.

question: To survive years when the harvest failed, the Inca invented the world's first freeze-dried food. They left potatoes out to freeze in the icy Andean nights, then stomped them underfoot by day to crush out the water, over and over, until they turned rock-hard and would keep for YEARS. What was this storable food called?
answer: Chuno
choices: Chuno
Quinoa
Charqui
Maize
context: Chuno (freeze-dried potato) could be stored for years and fed the empire when crops failed. The other three were all real Andean foods too — but chuno was the freeze-dried one. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuno.

question: Where the royal roads crossed deep canyons, the Inca wove suspension bridges out of braided grass rope. One of these grass bridges, the Q'eswachaka over the Apurimac River, still survives after five centuries — and the local Quechua communities do something astonishing to keep it standing. What do they do?
answer: They reweave it from fresh grass each year
choices: They reweave it from fresh grass each year
They reinforce it with hidden steel cables
They rebuild the cracked spans in stone
They coat its ropes in tar each spring
context: Every June the communities tear the old bridge down and rebuild it from scratch: women twist ichu grass into thin rope, the strands are braided into heavy cables, and the whole bridge is finished in just three days of work, prayer, and festival. Source: nationalgeographic.com/travel/article/inca-grass-rope-bridge-qeswachaka-unesco.

question: On a quipu, the Inca wrote numbers using knots in a base-10 system — a figure-eight knot stood for one, and longer knots stood for the bigger digits, stacked in rows for tens, hundreds, and thousands. So when a number had a zero in one of its columns, how did the quipu-maker show it?
answer: They left a gap with no knot
choices: They left a gap with no knot
They tied a special black knot
They added a bright red string
They doubled the figure-eight knot
context: A missing knot meant zero — the Inca recorded 'nothing' simply by leaving an empty space on the cord, a true place-value system with no writing at all. Source: worldhistory.org/Quipu.

question: In 1532 the Spaniard Francisco Pizarro marched into the Inca empire with only 168 men. At Cajamarca he came face to face with the emperor Atahualpa, who was surrounded by thousands of his own warriors. What did Pizarro's tiny force actually do?
answer: Ambushed the crowd and seized the emperor
choices: Ambushed the crowd and seized the emperor
Retreated into the mountains by night
Challenged the emperor to single combat
Offered to fight as his hired soldiers
context: On 16 November 1532, Pizarro's hidden cavalry charged the gathering and grabbed Atahualpa in the middle of his own army — capturing the ruler of millions with fewer than 170 men. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ransom_Room.

question: After Spanish soldiers captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa, he made a staggering offer to buy his freedom: he would fill his prison cell once with gold and twice with silver, as high as he could reach. Over four months, llama trains delivered tons of treasure. Once the ransom was fully paid, what did the Spanish do?
answer: They executed him anyway
choices: They executed him anyway
They set him free as promised
They crowned him a Spanish lord
They shipped him home to Spain
context: The ransom came to roughly 6,100 kg of gold and 11,820 kg of silver — and the Spanish strangled Atahualpa to death in 1533 regardless. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ransom_Room.

question: The Inca empire had no coins and no money of any kind, yet every community still owed a 'tax' to the emperor each year, a duty they called the mit'a. Since they could not pay in cash, how did an ordinary family pay this tax?
answer: By giving the state a turn of labor
choices: By giving the state a turn of labor
By handing over their firstborn child
By surrendering half of their herd
By paying a yearly tax in gold
context: The mit'a was a tax paid in WORK: each community owed the state a turn of labor — building roads, terraces, and bridges, or farming state land. The yearly rebuilding of the Q'eswachaka grass bridge began as exactly this kind of mit'a duty. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queshuachaka.

question: In 1438 a single Inca war-leader began the conquests that, in just three generations, would stretch his realm across the entire length of the Andes. When he took the throne he chose the name Pachacuti. What does that name mean?
answer: The Overturner of the World
choices: The Overturner of the World
The Child of the Sun
The Breaker of Mountains
The Lord of the Sky
context: Pachacuti means 'cataclysm' or 'the turning-over of the world' — a fitting name for the ruler who exploded one mountain valley into the largest empire the Americas had ever seen. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_Empire.

question: High in the Peruvian Andes, four Quechua communities gather every June to rebuild the Q'eswachaka, the last Inca rope bridge left in the world, anchoring it to the same carved stone their ancestors used centuries ago. What is the whole bridge made from?
answer: Braided grass
choices: Braided grass
Animal hide
Wooden planks
Woven vines
context: The Q'eswachaka, spanning a gorge of the Apurimac River, is woven entirely from grass — q'oya, a cousin of the tough Andean ichu grass. Over 1,000 people from four communities (Huinchiri, Chaupibanda, Choccayhua, and Ccollana) rebuild it by hand in about three days, twisting straw into six great cables as thick as a person's thigh, then dropping the old bridge into the river. UNESCO named the annual renewal an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2013. Sources: ich.unesco.org/en/RL/...q-eswachaka-00594 ; nationalgeographic.com/travel/article/inca-grass-rope-bridge-qeswachaka-unesco

question: The Inca Empire had no horses, yet its chasqui — relay runners posted in pairs along the royal roads — carried messages and cargo across the Andes faster than any other power of their day. They moved one load so quickly that it could reach the emperor in his capital of Cusco, over 3,000 metres up and days inland, still good to eat. What did the runners famously deliver to him?
answer: Fresh fish from the sea
choices: Fresh fish from the sea
Fruit from the warm lowlands
Snow from the mountain peaks
Honey from the forest hives
context: A fresh runner sprinted alongside each arriving one to take the message without stopping, so the relay could move news up to about 240 km (150 miles) a day — fast enough that fish caught in the Pacific reached the emperor's table in Cusco in roughly two days, still fresh. The Spanish chronicler Pedro de Cieza de Leon judged the system unbeatable, writing that 'news could not have been transmitted by greater speed than with the swiftest horses' — and the Inca had none. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chasqui ; thecollector.com/chasquis-famed-inca-couriers/

question: Measured in today's money, the average person earned only about $2 a day in the time of Christ. Income then barely moved for a thousand years and more. By the time William the Conqueror set sail to invade England in 1066, where did that daily income stand?
answer: Still about $2 a day
choices: Still about $2 a day
Up to about $5 a day
Up to about $10 a day
Up to about $20 a day
context: For roughly 1,800 years the world's income line was essentially flat: about $2 a day (in 2011 dollars) at the time of Christ, still about $2 a day in 1066, and only crept to $2.80 a day by 1800. That long flat stretch is the 'shaft' of the hockey stick — then the line bent sharply upward around 1800. Source: Human Progress, 'The Great Miracle of Industrialization,' citing the Maddison Project's per-person-per-day figures.

question: The smoky factory age of the early 1800s — the 'dark satanic mills' — is usually blamed for child labor and choking smoke. Yet during that same grim era, one shocking trend quietly reversed for the first time in human history. Which surprising thing actually began during it?
answer: The death of young children began its long collapse
choices: The death of young children began its long collapse
Family sizes began shrinking sharply
Children's reading and writing began falling
Village famines began striking more often
context: Around 1800 more than one-third of all children died before their fifth birthday — in some places every second child — and a typical mother of five to seven children expected to bury two or three. Losing children was, as historians put it, 'not a rare occurrence but the norm.' The industrial era is exactly when that began its long fall; the global rate today is around 4%. The escape from death and poverty, not the misery of the mills, is the real headline of the age. Source: Our World in Data, 'How child mortality has declined in the last two centuries.'

question: The Royal Navy's fastest slave-hunter on the West Africa patrol, HMS Black Joke, was famous for catching slave ships at sea — eleven of them in a single year. What was surprising about the Black Joke's own past?
answer: She had been a captured slave ship herself.
choices: She had been a captured slave ship herself.
She had been a pirate ship the Navy hunted down.
She had been a royal yacht handed to the Navy.
She had been built in Britain as a warship.
context: Black Joke was the Baltimore-built Brazilian slaver Henriquetta, seized in 1827 and renamed after an English song. The Navy turned a slave ship into the slavers' nightmare — in one year she ran down eleven of them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Black_Joke_(1827)

question: The most powerful slave-and-ivory trader in East Africa was a Zanzibar man named Hamad bin Muhammad, who led caravans of thousands of armed men deep into the Congo. He was far better known by a nickname — 'Tippu Tip.' Where did that name come from?
answer: From the tip-tip sound of his men's guns.
choices: From the tip-tip sound of his men's guns.
From the tip of the spear he always carried.
From a mountain peak where he was born.
From the tipping scales he used to weigh ivory.
context: Tippu Tip (born about 1832) ran the East African trade long after the Atlantic trade was dying. By 1895 he owned seven clove plantations and around 10,000 slaves; in 1887 the Belgian-run Congo Free State even made the slaver its district governor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tippu_Tip

question: The Kingdom of Dahomey raided its neighbors and marched the captives to the slave-ship port of Ouidah. According to tradition, before they were sold, the captives were forced to circle one particular tree a set number of times — a ritual said to do what to them?
answer: Wipe away the memory of their homes and families.
choices: Wipe away the memory of their homes and families.
Bind their spirits to serve the king forever.
Protect the slave ships from storms at sea.
Bring a good price from the waiting traders.
context: Tradition calls it the 'Tree of Forgetfulness,' meant to erase a captive's memory of homeland and kin before the ocean crossing. The detail is legend rather than documented fact, but it captures what the trade tried to do to a person. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dahomey

question: When the explorer David Livingstone — who had spent his last years exposing the East African slave trade — died deep in Africa in 1873, his African companions buried his heart under a tree there. To send the rest of him home to Westminster Abbey, what did they do?
answer: Dried it in the sun and carried it 930 miles overland to the coast.
choices: Dried it in the sun and carried it 930 miles overland to the coast.
Floated it down the river by canoe to the coast.
Loaded it onto a trade caravan heading for the coast.
Packed it in salt and sent it by ox-wagon to the coast.
context: Livingstone's companions dried his body and carried it on foot 930 miles to be shipped to Westminster Abbey. His last written plea, now on his Abbey memorial, begs heaven to bless anyone 'who will help to heal this open sore of the world.' Source: https://www.westminster-abbey.org/abbey-commemorations/commemorations/david-livingstone

question: On 1 February 1829 the two-gun HMS Black Joke beat a Spanish slaver carrying fourteen guns and freed the 466 enslaved people crammed in her hold. A naval surgeon wrote that this one little ship had done more to end the slave trade than what?
answer: Than all the other ships of the station put together.
choices: Than all the other ships of the station put together.
Than every treaty Britain had signed with Spain.
Than all the speeches ever given in Parliament.
Than the entire blockade of the African coast.
context: Black Joke had chased the slaver El Almirante for 31 hours — even rowing with oars when the wind died — then won in 80 minutes. The West Africa Squadron freed about 150,000 people at sea between 1808 and the 1860s. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Black_Joke_(1827)

question: In 1873 Britain forced the Sultan of Zanzibar to shut down the largest slave market in East Africa. On the very ground where the market had stood, builders raised an Anglican cathedral, and they set one part of the church deliberately over the spot of the old whipping post. Which part did they place there?
answer: The altar.
choices: The altar.
The bell tower.
The main doorway.
The baptismal font.
context: Britain closed the Zanzibar market under the 1873 Frere Treaty. The cathedral's altar was set deliberately over the site of the slave-market whipping post — turning the cruelest spot in the market into its holiest. Source: https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2017/01/05/zanzibar-cathedral-restoration-shows-past-can-unite-rather-than-divide-us

question: When British envoys pressed King Ghezo of Dahomey in the 1840s to stop selling captives to the slave ships, he flatly refused, calling the trade the ruling principle of his people. In his own words, the slave trade was the source of his people's what?
answer: Their glory and wealth.
choices: Their glory and wealth.
Their peace and safety.
Their faith and law.
Their freedom and pride.
context: Ghezo's refusal is part of the honest record the usual story leaves out: the trade had a large internal-African supply side, and powerful African kings defended it. It took a Royal Navy blockade in 1851 to force Dahomey into a treaty the next year. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dahomey

question: HMS Black Joke was the fastest slave-hunter in the Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron — yet the Navy had not built her. Where did this swift ship come from?
answer: A captured slaver — turned against the trade
choices: A captured slaver — turned against the trade
A captured pirate sloop — pressed into service
A Baltimore-built privateer — the Navy bought her
A French warship — taken as a prize of war
context: HMS Black Joke was the former Henriquetta, a fast Baltimore-built slaver seized by the Royal Navy and pressed into the West Africa Squadron to hunt other slave ships. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Black_Joke

question: The Kingdom of Dahomey's most feared raiders captured people from neighboring states to sell into the Atlantic slave trade — and European visitors were astonished by who actually served in this elite regiment. Who made up the force?
answer: Women — about 6,000 in an all-female regiment
choices: Women — about 6,000 in an all-female regiment
Boys — taken from conquered villages and raised to fight
Foreigners — mercenaries hired with European guns
Priests — who fought between the kingdom's festivals
context: The Agojie — nicknamed the 'Dahomey Amazons' by Europeans — numbered about 6,000 at their 1840s peak and were Dahomey's raiders, taking captives to sell or to be sacrificed at the kingdom's Annual Customs. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dahomey_Amazons

question: Hamad bin Muhammad al-Murjabi grew from fewer than 100 armed men out of Zanzibar into one of the richest slave traders who ever lived. He is remembered by the nickname 'Tippu Tip,' which he said came from a sound he made famous in Central Africa. What sound was it?
answer: The 'tip-tip' of his guns firing
choices: The 'tip-tip' of his guns firing
The 'tip-tip' of rain on his tent
The tapping of his cane as he walked
The clink of the coins he counted
context: Tippu Tip said his nickname came from the 'tip-tip' sound of his guns; by 1895 he controlled seven plantations and 10,000 enslaved people. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tippu_Tip

question: In the 1700s the Asante Empire of the Gold Coast became the most powerful state on the coast through a self-feeding cycle with British and Dutch slave traders. Asante handed over war captives, and in return took the one thing that let them conquer more peoples and seize still more captives. What did they take in trade?
answer: Firearms
choices: Firearms
Salt
Horses
Sailing ships
context: Asante sold war captives to European traders for guns, which let them conquer more peoples and capture more slaves — a cycle that made Asante the dominant coastal power by the mid-1700s. https://blackpast.org/global-african-history/ashanti-empire-asante-kingdom-18th-late-19th-century/

question: Slavery existed inside Asante society long before Europeans came to buy. But historians point to one feature of Akan slavery that was the biggest difference from the chattel slavery Europeans practiced across the Atlantic. What could happen to an enslaved person in Akan society that almost never happened under European slavery?
answer: They could rise to become an influential figure in the community
choices: They could rise to become an influential figure in the community
They were always freed after exactly seven years
They could never be bought or sold, only inherited
They were paid wages for the work they did
context: In Akan society an enslaved person could rise to real standing in the community — historians cite this as the biggest difference from European chattel slavery, which fixed a person's status for life. https://blackpast.org/global-african-history/ashanti-empire-asante-kingdom-18th-late-19th-century/

question: On 15 July 1871 the explorer David Livingstone was standing in the crowded riverside market at Nyangwe, on the Lualaba River, when the slave trader Dugumbe's men suddenly turned their guns on the shoppers. Some 400 to 500 people were killed in the panic. What did that single day become for Livingstone?
answer: The emotional center of his campaign to end the East African slave trade
choices: The emotional center of his campaign to end the East African slave trade
The reason he finally turned back and sailed home to Britain
The day he was taken prisoner by the slavers
The moment he abandoned exploring to become a missionary
context: Livingstone witnessed Arab/Swahili slavers under Dugumbe open fire on the Nyangwe market crowd, killing 400-500; the horror became the heart of his crusade against the East African trade. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyangwe

question: Deep in the Congo in 1871, David Livingstone had run out of paper and ink but was determined to record what the slavers were doing. He brewed makeshift ink from clothing dye — and to find a writing surface for his field diary, he used the only printed pages he had. What did he write his diary on?
answer: In the margins of an old newspaper
choices: In the margins of an old newspaper
On strips of bark peeled from trees
On the blank backs of his maps
On the inside covers of his Bible
context: Out of supplies, Livingstone wrote his 1871 field diary — including his account of the Nyangwe massacre — in the margins of an old copy of The Standard, in ink brewed from clothing dye. https://livingstoneonline.org/spectral-imaging/livingstones-1871-field-diary

question: David Livingstone, a year to the day before his death, wrote a prayer about the East African slave trade so powerful it was later carved onto his tomb in Westminster Abbey. What did he call the trade?
answer: This open sore of the world
choices: This open sore of the world
This chain that girdles the earth
The great wound of Africa
The shame of all the nations
context: Livingstone wrote the prayer on 1 May 1872, a year to the day before his death, praying for 'every one, American, English, or Turk, who will help to heal this open sore of the world'; the line is engraved on his tomb in Westminster Abbey. https://blog.library.si.edu/blog/2013/10/23/david-livingstone-and-the-other-slave-trade-part-iii-the-slaver-and-the-abolitionist/

question: After Britain banned the slave trade in 1807, it sent the Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron to hunt slave ships along thousands of kilometers of African coast. Over roughly fifty years of patrols, what did the Squadron actually achieve against the trade?
answer: About 1,600 slave ships seized and about 150,000 Africans freed
choices: About 1,600 slave ships seized and about 150,000 Africans freed
About 600 slave ships seized and about 40,000 Africans freed
About 3,000 slave ships seized but fewer than 10,000 Africans freed
About 250 slave ships seized and about 75,000 Africans freed
context: From about 1808 to 1860 the West Africa Squadron patrolled 5,000+ km of coast, seizing roughly 1,600 slave ships and freeing around 150,000 Africans. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Africa_Squadron

question: The West Africa Squadron's patrol off the slave coast was so deadly that the region earned a grim nickname among British sailors. Between 1830 and 1865 about 1,600 Royal Navy sailors died on the duty — almost all of them not in battle, but from one cause. What killed nearly all of them?
answer: Tropical disease
choices: Tropical disease
Slaver cannon fire
Storms and shipwreck
Starvation at sea
context: Roughly 1,600 West Africa Squadron sailors died between 1830 and 1865, almost all from tropical disease — the patrol was so lethal the coast was nicknamed 'the white man's grave.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Africa_Squadron

question: The scholars Robert Pape and Chaim Kaufmann put a price tag on Britain's sixty-year campaign to suppress the Atlantic slave trade. They found it consumed about 1.8% of the nation's income — and they gave the campaign a striking superlative. How did Pape and Kaufmann sum up what Britain had done?
answer: The most expensive case of costly international moral action in modern history
choices: The most expensive case of costly international moral action in modern history
The costliest overseas military campaign Britain waged in the whole 19th century
A vast expense that Parliament deliberately hid from the British public
A moral burden that later judges said outweighed any good it achieved
context: Pape and Kaufmann calculated the campaign cost about 1.8% of national income, calling it 'the most expensive example of costly international moral action recorded in modern history.' https://library.fes.de/libalt/journals/swetsfulltext/7064300.pdf

question: In June 1873 Britain forced Sultan Barghash of Zanzibar to shut the largest slave market in East Africa, which had passed as many as 50,000 captives a year. To mark the victory, Christ Church Cathedral was built directly on the closed market — and one detail inside makes the triumph unmistakable. What stands where the market's whipping-post once stood?
answer: The cathedral's altar
choices: The cathedral's altar
The bell tower
The main doorway
The baptismal font
context: Under the 1873 Frere Treaty Barghash closed Zanzibar's slave market; Christ Church Cathedral was built on the site with its altar placed where the whipping-post had stood. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_Church,_Zanzibar

question: King Agaja of Dahomey built his power on a self-feeding loop: his armies raided neighboring peoples and seized thousands of captives, and Dahomey sold those captives to European traders waiting at the coast. Historian Robert Harms explains why the kingdom could never stop — the trade bought the one thing the armies needed to keep raiding for more captives. What did Dahomey receive from the Europeans in exchange for captives?
answer: Firearms and gunpowder
choices: Firearms and gunpowder
Cloth and cowrie shells
Horses and iron bars
Rum and tobacco
context: This is the 'gun-slave cycle': coastal kingdoms sold captives mainly for guns, then used those guns to make war and take more captives to sell for more guns. Robert Harms notes that once King Agaja (reigned 1718-1740) re-armed his soldiers from bows to muskets, the only way to keep getting gunpowder was the slave trade itself — so the wars and the selling fed each other. The European ships were the buyers; the capturing and selling ran through African coastal kingdoms. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agaja (Robert W. Harms); MPRA gun-slave-cycle papers.

question: People sometimes assume European traders introduced slavery to West Africa in the 1400s. But the Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta crossed the wealthy Mali Empire in the 1300s — long before any European slave ship reached the coast — and recorded how its people showed off their rank. What did Ibn Battuta say the people of Mali competed over?
answer: How many slaves and servants they had
choices: How many slaves and servants they had
How much gold dust they could wear
How many horses they could field
How large their household compounds were
context: Ibn Battuta in the 14th century described Mali's people 'competing in the number of slaves and servants they had.' Slavery existed in West Africa for centuries before 1492 — Ghanaian historian Akosua Perbi dates indigenous slavery in the Ghana region to the 1st century AD. The Atlantic trade did not invent the system; European demand massively expanded an older internal one. (Stated as historians' record, holding the fact without minimizing the European demand that later fueled the Atlantic trade.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_Africa (Akosua Perbi; Ibn Battuta's 14th-c. account of Mali).

question: On October 29, 1969, UCLA programmer Charley Kline tried to type the word 'LOGIN' to a Stanford computer over ARPANET, the network that grew into the Internet. The Stanford machine crashed after just two letters. So what was the first word ever sent across the network that became the Internet?
answer: LO
choices: LO
HI
GO
OK
context: The crash meant only 'L' and 'O' got through. Leonard Kleinrock, whose UCLA lab sent it, loved that the accident spelled 'LO, as in lo and behold!' About an hour later, after Stanford fixed the bug, the full 'LOGIN' finally went through. Source: lk.cs.ucla.edu/internet_first_words.html (Leonard Kleinrock, UCLA).

question: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN, building the pages and links the whole world now reads through browsers. He could have patented it and charged for every use, becoming one of the richest men alive. On April 30, 1993, CERN instead did what with the Web's source code?
answer: Released it into the public domain for anyone to use free, forever
choices: Released it into the public domain for anyone to use free, forever
Sold the patent rights to a group of American telephone companies
Licensed it to universities for a yearly subscription fee
Kept it secret inside CERN to protect Europe's lead in computing
context: Berners-Lee refused to patent the Web or charge a cent. He explained: 'You can't propose that something be a universal space and at the same time keep control of it.' That royalty-free gift is why the Web belongs to everyone. (Note: he invented the WEB, which runs on top of the older INTERNET — they are different things people often confuse.) Source: home.cern/science/computing/birth-web/short-history-web.

question: In March 1946, at a tiny college gymnasium in Fulton, Missouri, Winston Churchill — voted out as Prime Minister but still the West's loudest voice — warned that a line now split free Europe from the half Moscow controlled, running from Stettin on the Baltic down to Trieste on the Adriatic. What did he say had 'descended across the Continent' along that line?
answer: An iron curtain
choices: An iron curtain
A shadow of night
A wall of silence
A chain of fear
context: Churchill: 'From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent.' The official title was 'The Sinews of Peace.' He did not coin the phrase — he had even used it privately in a 1945 telegram to Truman — but this speech made 'iron curtain' the name for the Cold War's dividing line. https://www.nationalchurchillmuseum.org/sinews-of-peace-iron-curtain-speech.html

question: By 1948 Czechoslovakia was the last democracy left in Eastern Europe — Churchill's one bright exception. After the communists seized total power in February 1948, foreign minister Jan Masaryk, son of the country's founding president, met a death that shocked the world. How was Jan Masaryk found?
answer: Dead on the pavement beneath his bathroom window
choices: Dead on the pavement beneath his bathroom window
Poisoned at his own dinner table
Shot in a locked prison cell
Drowned in the river below the castle
context: On March 10, 1948, Jan Masaryk was found dead below his bathroom window — a 'defenestration.' It was officially ruled suicide but long suspected to be murder; a 2021 Czech investigation could not rule murder out. With his death the last democracy in Eastern Europe was gone. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1948_Czechoslovak_coup_d'%C3%A9tat

question: Hungary's communist boss Matyas Rakosi bragged about how he had destroyed every rival party — not by banning them all at once, but by demanding a little more each day until each was cut away. He compared it to slicing an expensive sausage thin slice after thin slice. What did Rakosi call this method?
answer: Salami tactics
choices: Salami tactics
The silent harvest
The creeping siege
The paper purge
context: Matyas Rakosi coined 'salami tactics' for taking power thin slice after thin slice. It became the textbook name for how Soviet-backed parties dismantled their opposition piece by piece across Eastern Europe after 1945. https://time.com/archive/6794585/hungary-salami-tactics/

question: The Peacemaker, Deganawida, brought the five warring nations together to end their endless fighting. To seal the peace, he uprooted a great white pine, and asked each nation to do one thing with their weapons of war before he set the tree back in place. What did the nations do with their weapons?
answer: Buried them in the hole beneath the tree's roots
choices: Buried them in the hole beneath the tree's roots
Burned them all in a great ceremonial fire
Threw them into the river that ran past the council
Snapped each blade across a warrior's knee
context: Deganawida replanted the white pine over the buried weapons as the Tree of Peace — and this is the literal origin of the English phrase 'burying the hatchet.' Legend recorded in Haudenosaunee tradition. Sources: onondaganation.org/culture/wampum/hiawatha-belt/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree_of_Peace

question: The Grand Council of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy seats 50 sachems — chiefs in fixed numbers from each nation. But the men who held these chief titles did not choose themselves, and they could be stripped of the title if they failed their people. In Haudenosaunee government, who chose the chiefs and held the power to remove them?
answer: The clan mothers, the senior women of each clan
choices: The clan mothers, the senior women of each clan
The eldest sachem of the Onondaga firekeepers
A vote of all the warriors of the nation
The Peacemaker's appointed line of successors
context: The clan mothers — the senior women of each clan — both selected the sachems and could depose them. This is one reason historians like Jack Rakove and Elisabeth Tooker caution against the claim that the Great Law shaped the U.S. Constitution: the Constitution gave women no such power. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Law_of_Peace; onondaganation.org Hiawatha Belt

question: Europeans named the great flowering of art and learning that began in Italy the 'Renaissance,' borrowing the word straight from French. What does that French word mean?
answer: Rebirth
choices: Rebirth
Golden light
Awakening
New dawn
context: 'Renaissance' is French for 'rebirth' — the era when Italians revived the art and learning of ancient Greece and Rome. The art historian Giorgio Vasari first used the Italian word rinascita ('rebirth') in 1550 to describe artists returning to the ancient manner. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance

question: Florence's enormous cathedral carries the name Santa Maria del Fiore. In English that title honors Saint Mary — and adds what?
answer: Of the Flower
choices: Of the Flower
Of the Sea
Of the Tower
Of the Mountain
context: Santa Maria del Fiore means 'Saint Mary of the Flower.' Work on it began in 1296, but for over a century it stood with a gaping hole where its dome should be — nobody knew how to roof a span that wide without it collapsing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Cathedral

question: Florence minted a gold coin so dependable that merchants and kings all across Europe trusted it as the standard money of the age. What was this coin called?
answer: The florin
choices: The florin
The ducat
The crown
The guilder
context: Florence's gold florin was trusted as the standard currency across Europe — at a time when a skilled craftsman earned only 30 to 50 florins in a whole YEAR. The wealth behind it came largely from the Medici bank. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medici_Bank

question: Donatello cast a bronze statue of the young hero David for the Medici, who proudly stood it on a column in the courtyard of their palace. This statue was the first of its kind made anywhere in over a thousand years. What made it so groundbreaking?
answer: It was a free-standing nude figure
choices: It was a free-standing nude figure
It was plated in solid gold
It stood taller than a grown man
It was the heaviest bronze in Italy
context: Donatello's bronze 'David' (probably 1440s) was the first free-standing nude statue cast since ancient Rome — over a thousand years earlier. It stood in the courtyard of the Medici palace. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_(Donatello,_bronze)

question: Sandro Botticelli's painting 'The Birth of Venus' shows the goddess Venus arriving full-grown at the seashore, carried to land while standing on a single object. What is she standing on?
answer: A giant scallop shell
choices: A giant scallop shell
A great golden raft
A leaping dolphin's back
A swell of sea-foam
context: In Botticelli's 'The Birth of Venus' (mid-1480s), the goddess floats ashore on a giant scallop shell, blown by the wind-god Zephyr. It was among the first large paintings since antiquity to make a pagan goddess its central figure, and it hangs today in the Uffizi Gallery in Florence. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Birth_of_Venus

question: Florence's cathedral had stood for over a century with a gaping hole where its dome belonged — the span was simply too wide to roof without the whole thing caving in. Filippo Brunelleschi finally solved it by laying more than four million bricks in a self-locking pattern that let the dome hold up its own weight as it rose. What is that brick-laying pattern called?
answer: Herringbone
choices: Herringbone
Basketweave
Honeycomb
Pinwheel
context: Brunelleschi's dome (1420–1436) used a herringbone pattern the Italians call spinapesce ('fish-spine') — the first octagonal dome ever raised WITHOUT a wooden support frame underneath. At about 25,000 tons and 44 meters (144 feet) across, it is still the largest brick-and-masonry dome in the world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Cathedral

question: Legend says that when Filippo Brunelleschi was competing for the job of building the cathedral dome, he challenged his rivals to a contest: stand an egg upright on a slab of smooth marble. Every one of them failed. How did Brunelleschi then make the egg stand?
answer: He cracked its bottom flat on the marble
choices: He cracked its bottom flat on the marble
He spun it fast like a spinning top
He balanced it inside a ring of salt
He propped it up against a gold coin
context: Vasari told this tale in 1550: Brunelleschi cracked one end of the egg so it stood, then said his rivals could have built the dome too — if only they knew how. Historians doubt it really happened, so it is told as legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egg_of_Columbus

question: A colossal slab of Carrara marble nicknamed 'the Giant' sat abandoned in Florence's cathedral yard for some forty years — two sculptors had already hacked at it and quit, leaving it scarred and half-ruined. In 1501 one daring 26-year-old took on the spoiled block and carved a towering 'David' from it. Who was he?
answer: Michelangelo
choices: Michelangelo
Donatello
Raphael
Ghiberti
context: Michelangelo carved his 'David' — a 5.17-meter (17-foot) colossus — from a block two earlier sculptors had given up on. It was installed in 1504 outside Florence's town hall. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_(Michelangelo)

question: Petrarch, the scholar later honored as the 'Father of Humanism,' did something in 1336 that struck people of his day as strange: he hiked all the way up Mont Ventoux purely to stand at the summit and take in the view. Centuries later this habit earned Petrarch a playful nickname. What was it?
answer: The first tourist
choices: The first tourist
The first mountaineer
The first explorer
The first naturalist
context: Petrarch is nicknamed 'the first tourist' for climbing Mont Ventoux in 1336 just to enjoy the view. He also rediscovered a lost cache of Cicero's personal letters in a Verona cathedral library in 1345 — a find often credited with helping spark the whole Renaissance. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petrarch

question: Cosimo de' Medici ran Florence for thirty years without ever wearing a crown or taking a royal title — a banker quietly pulling the city's strings. A pope said of him, 'he is king in all but name.' When Cosimo died in 1464, the grateful city carved a single Latin title onto his tomb. What did it call him?
answer: Father of the Fatherland
choices: Father of the Fatherland
First of the Romans
Saviour of the Republic
