Prince of all Florence
context: Florence carved 'Pater Patriae' — 'Father of the Fatherland' — on Cosimo's tomb. Pope Pius II said political questions were settled in Cosimo's house and that he was 'king in all but name,' though he never held a royal title. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosimo_de'_Medici

question: On 26 April 1478 the rival Pazzi family launched a plot to murder both ruling Medici brothers as they worshipped inside Florence Cathedral. The assassins agreed to wait for one signal before drawing their daggers — the most sacred instant of the Mass. Which moment did they choose to strike?
answer: When the priest raised the Host
choices: When the priest raised the Host
When the choir began to sing
When the bishop blessed the crowd
When the bells rang for noon
context: The Pazzi struck as the Host was raised. Giuliano de' Medici was stabbed 19 times and killed, but Lorenzo escaped with a neck wound. Furious Florentines hunted the plotters down, and about 80 people were executed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pazzi_conspiracy

question: In 1417 the tireless book-hunter Poggio Bracciolini was searching the dusty shelves of a remote German monastery when he pulled down a forgotten manuscript — the last surviving copy of a great Roman poem the world had very nearly lost forever. Which ancient poem did Poggio rescue from oblivion?
answer: On the Nature of Things
choices: On the Nature of Things
The Songs of Fallen Troy
On the Glory of Old Rome
The Book of the Seven Stars
context: Poggio recognized the name of Lucretius's poem 'On the Nature of Things' from a Cicero quotation, then put the rescued text back into circulation. Hunters like him saved many ancient works — Poggio also recovered Vitruvius's architecture manual, which later inspired Leonardo da Vinci's 'Vitruvian Man.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poggio_Bracciolini

question: On June 28, 1914, an earlier bomb thrown at Archduke Franz Ferdinand's motorcade in Sarajevo had bounced off and missed, and the open car had sped away. Later that day the driver took a wrong turn, then braked and stalled while reversing — coming to a dead halt just steps from where Gavrilo Princip was standing. In front of which Sarajevo spot did the car stop?
answer: Moritz Schiller's delicatessen
choices: Moritz Schiller's delicatessen
The Latin Bridge over the Miljacka
Sarajevo's town hall steps
The Austrian garrison barracks
context: The car came to a dead stop in front of Moritz Schiller's delicatessen, the exact spot where Princip happened to be (the building is now the Museum of Sarajevo 1878–1918); the Latin Bridge is across the road but, contrary to common belief, is not where the shooting occurred. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/gavrilo-princips-sandwich-79480741/

question: On July 5, 1914, Kaiser Wilhelm II of Germany met with Austria-Hungary, which wanted to punish Serbia but feared Russia would defend the Serbs. The Kaiser promised Austria it could rely on Germany's full support no matter what it chose to do against Serbia. Historians gave that open-ended promise a nickname. What did they call it?
answer: Germany's blank cheque
choices: Germany's blank cheque
The iron handshake
The Berlin guarantee
The Kaiser's open door
context: Vienna was promised backing for whatever it decided, before anyone knew what that would be — like signing a cheque and leaving the amount blank. The promise emboldened Austria to take a hard line with Serbia. Source: https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/july-5/germany-gives-austria-hungary-blank-check-assurance

question: In the last days of July 1914, Kaiser Wilhelm II of Germany and Tsar Nicholas II of Russia — first cousins both descended from Tsar Paul I — tried to stop the slide to war by firing off frantic personal telegrams to each other. They signed them informally as 'Willy' and 'Nicky.' What surprising thing did these two emperors do in those telegrams?
answer: They wrote to each other in English
choices: They wrote to each other in English
They wrote entirely in rhyming verse
They wrote in a secret cipher only they knew
They wrote in ancient Latin
context: The German Kaiser and the Russian Tsar were cousins and wrote in English, the family's common tongue. Nicholas even begged Wilhelm to hand the whole dispute to the international peace court at The Hague. The telegrams failed, and the cousins' empires went to war anyway. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willy%E2%80%93Nicky_correspondence

question: On August 4, 1914, German troops invaded neutral Belgium, breaking a 1839 treaty in which Germany itself had promised to respect Belgian neutrality. Britain went to war to honor that same treaty. German Chancellor Theobald von Bethmann-Hollweg, stunned, complained to the British ambassador that Britain would fight only for the old treaty document. What dismissive phrase did he use for it?
answer: A scrap of paper
choices: A scrap of paper
A dusty relic
A broken promise
A foreign quarrel
context: Bethmann-Hollweg's 'scrap of paper' jab at the 1839 treaty was meant to mock Britain for fighting over an old document — but it backfired. British propaganda seized on the phrase to show Germany held its sworn word worthless. Source: https://www.firstworldwar.com/source/scrapofpaper2.htm

question: On the evening of August 3, 1914, with Britain about to declare war on Germany, British Foreign Secretary Sir Edward Grey stood at his office window watching the street lamplighters at dusk and spoke a line he would publish in his 1925 memoirs — words that became one of the most haunting images of the coming war. What did Grey say he was watching?
answer: The lamps going out all over Europe
choices: The lamps going out all over Europe
The clocks striking the final hour
The crowds cheering for a war they'd regret
The last summer the world would know
context: Grey's full line: 'The lamps are going out all over Europe; we shall not see them lit again in our lifetime.' Britain declared war on Germany the next day, August 4, 1914. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_lamps_are_going_out

question: By July 31, 1914, Tsar Nicholas II of Russia wanted to mobilize only against Austria, to avoid threatening Germany — but his generals said it could not be done. Russia's war plans had been built for FULL mobilization only, so a partial call-up would have tangled the railway timetables and left Russia defenseless. The Tsar wired Wilhelm that stopping the military machine was now what?
answer: Technically impossible
choices: Technically impossible
A betrayal of Serbia
Against the constitution
Too costly to attempt
context: The Tsar's exact wire said it was 'technically impossible to stop our military preparations.' The general staffs had drawn up only one plan — total mobilization — so once it began, no one could safely halt it. As one phrasing goes, machinery, not malice, made the crisis unstoppable. Source: https://alphahistory.com/worldwar1/nicky-and-willy-telegrams-1914/

question: Twice the Mongols sailed against Japan, and twice — in 1274 and 1281 — a sudden typhoon rose up and shattered Kublai Khan's invasion fleet at sea before it could conquer the islands. The Japanese were certain the gods themselves had sunk the ships, and they gave these storms a name that has echoed ever since. What did they call the typhoons?
answer: The kamikaze, the divine wind
choices: The kamikaze, the divine wind
The shogun's tide, the great surge
The thunder of Hachiman, the war drum
The black rain, the drowning sky
context: 'Kamikaze' means 'divine wind.' The Japanese believed the storms of 1274 and 1281 were the gods' answer to their prayers, sent to wreck the fleets of the largest empire on earth. The name would be revived centuries later. https://www.britannica.com/event/kamikaze-of-1274-and-1281

question: When Kublai Khan's second fleet — some 4,400 ships — reached Japan in 1281, the Mongols feared night raids by samurai swimming out in small boats. So they roped and chained their ships together hull-to-hull for safety. Then the typhoon struck. What did the Japanese gain from a fleet that had bound itself together?
answer: The chained ships smashed each other to pieces against the rocks
choices: The chained ships smashed each other to pieces against the rocks
The chained ships rode out the storm and landed the army safely
The chains held the fleet together long enough to flee to China
The chained ships formed a bridge the Mongols marched ashore on
context: Lashed together, the ships could not ride the waves independently — the storm hurled them against one another and the rocks. Between half and two-thirds of the roughly 100,000-man army died, and stranded survivors were executed. https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1415/the-mongol-invasions-of-japan-1274--1281-ce/

question: For centuries the wrecking of Kublai Khan's fleets lived as a national legend — divine storms no one could prove had happened. Then in 2014 the geologist Jon Woodruff drilled cores from the mud of lakes near Hakata Bay, where the Mongols had landed. What did the sediment hold?
answer: Storm layers dated to the late 1200s, matching 1274 and 1281
choices: Storm layers dated to the late 1200s, matching 1274 and 1281
Mongol coins minted in the reign of Kublai Khan
Bones of the drowned soldiers preserved in the silt
Timbers from the lashed-together invasion ships
context: Woodruff found distinctive typhoon-deposit layers in the lake mud dated to exactly the right years — physical proof that the legendary kamikaze were real storms. https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/141104-kamikaze-kublai-khan-winds-typhoon-japan-invasion

question: Vasily Blokhin, the NKVD's chief executioner, shot thousands of Polish prisoners over 28 nights in the spring of 1940 — but he brought a briefcase of German-made Walther pistols to do it, instead of Soviet revolvers. He had a cold reason for choosing foreign guns. What was it?
answer: The bullets would point at Germany if the graves were ever found
choices: The bullets would point at Germany if the graves were ever found
The foreign pistols fired far quieter than Soviet revolvers
The briefcase hid the guns from the other prison guards
The German rounds were cheaper to stockpile in bulk
context: Blokhin used .25 Walther pistols partly because the Soviet revolvers recoiled too hard for hour after hour of shooting, and partly for 'plausible deniability' — so that if the graves were ever found, the bullets would point at the Germans, not the Soviets. The cover-up was built into the murder weapon itself. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katyn_massacre

question: In April 1943 the Germans announced they had found mass graves holding thousands of Polish officers, and they accused the Soviets of the killing. Britain's own officials privately judged Soviet guilt a near certainty. Yet in a secret message to Stalin, Prime Minister Winston Churchill made a promise about any Red Cross inquiry into the graves. What did he promise?
answer: That Britain would vigorously oppose any such investigation
choices: That Britain would vigorously oppose any such investigation
That Britain would demand a full international inquiry
That Britain would stay neutral and let the Red Cross decide
That Britain would publicly name the Soviets as the killers
context: On 24 April 1943 Churchill assured Stalin: 'We shall certainly oppose vigorously any "investigation" by the International Red Cross or any other body in any territory under German authority' — even though his own officials privately judged Soviet guilt a 'near certainty.' Western leaders knew, and chose silence to keep the wartime alliance intact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katyn_massacre

question: When the communist Khmer Rouge seized Cambodia's capital, Phnom Penh, on April 17, 1975, they declared that history itself was starting over. They abolished money, schools, markets, and religion, and renamed that year to mark a fresh beginning with no past. What did they call it?
answer: Year Zero
choices: Year Zero
The Great Leap
The First Dawn
The New Order
context: 'Year Zero' was the Khmer Rouge's attempt to erase Cambodia's past and rebuild it from scratch as a classless peasant society. (factsanddetails.com Khmer Rouge Year Zero; jpost.com/history/article-852264)

question: On April 17, 1975, Khmer Rouge soldiers needed to empty all two million people out of Phnom Penh. Rather than admit the truth, they shouted a single lie over loudspeakers to send the whole city fleeing on foot in under three days. What lie did they shout?
answer: The Americans are about to bomb the city
choices: The Americans are about to bomb the city
A great flood is coming down the river
A plague has broken out in the markets
The king has ordered everyone to the fields
context: It was a deception. Almost no one was ever allowed back. In under 72 hours the entire city was driven out at gunpoint. (cambodgemag.com April 17 1975 evacuation; ushmm.org Experiencing Forced Displacement: Cambodia)

question: The Khmer Rouge emptied Phnom Penh so completely that they cleared out the hospitals too, forcing about 20,000 sick and wounded patients out into the streets. Some patients were too weak to walk. How were they moved out of the city?
answer: Still lying in their hospital beds, wheeled away
choices: Still lying in their hospital beds, wheeled away
Carried on the backs of their own doctors
Loaded onto trucks bound for the coast
Left where they lay until they could stand
context: Patients were pushed out into the streets still in their beds, with IV bottles. The Khmer Rouge spared no one. (cambodgemag.com 17 April 1975; factsanddetails.com Emptying of Phnom Penh)

question: Under the Khmer Rouge, simply being educated could get you killed. Guards sorted villagers using crude physical clues to spot the hated city-bred 'new people' — soft hands, knowing a foreign language, and one ordinary everyday object. What object marked a person for execution?
answer: Eyeglasses
choices: Eyeglasses
A wristwatch
Leather shoes
A wedding ring
context: Eyeglasses, soft hands, and a foreign tongue were read as marks of the educated class the regime wanted to destroy. (cla.umn.edu/chgs Cambodia resource guide; thevintagenews.com academics 1970s Cambodia)

question: In Phnom Penh the Khmer Rouge ran their most infamous prison, code-named S-21, where some 16,000 people were tortured and only about a dozen came out alive. The chilling thing was what the building had been before. What was S-21 originally?
answer: A high school
choices: A high school
A Buddhist temple
A hospital ward
A railway station
context: S-21 was the former Tuol Svay Prey high school; the Khmer Rouge turned its classrooms into torture and interrogation cells. Today it is the Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum. (tuolsleng.gov.kh/en/museum/building; DC-Cam 'Fact Sheet on S-21')

question: At the S-21 prison, every new arrival was photographed and forced to write out their whole life story, then tortured until they 'confessed' to secretly working for a foreign enemy. Once they signed the confession, they were marked for death. Which foreign powers were prisoners forced to name as their secret masters?
answer: The CIA, the KGB, or Vietnam
choices: The CIA, the KGB, or Vietnam
The French, the Thai, or Japan
The British, the Chinese, or Taiwan
The Indians, the Japanese, or Laos
context: The forced confessions named the CIA, KGB, or Vietnam as the prisoner's supposed masters — pure fiction, extracted by torture, used to justify the killing. (DC-Cam S-21 Fact Sheet; Nate Thayer FEER interview 1997)

question: One painter, Vann Nath, walked out of the S-21 prison alive when nearly everyone else was murdered. The prison chief Duch spared him for one specific skill the regime wanted put to use. Why was Vann Nath kept alive?
answer: To paint flattering portraits of Pol Pot
choices: To paint flattering portraits of Pol Pot
To forge documents for the guards
To repair the prison's broken radios
To teach the guards to read and write
context: After the regime fell, Vann Nath painted the tortures he had witnessed; his paintings became key evidence, and his memoir is the only written account by an S-21 survivor. (en.gariwo.net Vann Nath; aljazeera.com Killing Fields painter dies 2011)

question: Prisoners from S-21 were trucked to a field called Choeung Ek and murdered beside pits many had been forced to dig themselves. To save their precious bullets, the Khmer Rouge killed people another way entirely. How did they carry out most of the killings?
answer: Beating victims to death with hoes, hammers, and axes
choices: Beating victims to death with hoes, hammers, and axes
Drowning them in the flooded rice paddies
Locking them in sheds without food or water
Burying them alive under the dug pits
context: To conserve ammunition, the Khmer Rouge bludgeoned victims with farm tools, hammers, axes, and bamboo. The Choeung Ek site holds 129 mass graves. (DC-Cam S-21 Fact Sheet; agatetravel.com Choeung Ek)

question: At the Choeung Ek killing field stands a tree the Khmer Rouge used to murder babies and small children, swinging them against its trunk. Their reasoning was deliberate and cold. Why did they kill the youngest children?
answer: So they could never grow up to avenge their parents
choices: So they could never grow up to avenge their parents
So no records of the families would remain
So the guards would not have to feed them
So the parents would confess more quickly
context: The Chankiri 'Killing Tree' is now hung with colored bracelets left by visitors. A nearby memorial stupa holds nearly 9,000 skulls. (Chankiri Killing Tree, tripzilla.com; agatetravel.com 8,985 skulls)

question: For years ordinary Cambodians did not even know the name of the man ruling them. He hid behind a faceless title meaning 'the Organization,' and was called 'Brother Number One.' He gave no interview for 18 years, until 1997. By what mysterious name did the regime make people obey him?
answer: Angkar
choices: Angkar
The Marshal
The Red Sun
Comrade Zero
context: 'Angkar' ('the Organization') was Pol Pot — real name Saloth Sar. Journalist Nate Thayer finally reached his jungle hideout at Anlong Veng in 1997. (Far Eastern Economic Review, Nate Thayer interview Oct 30 1997)

question: In 1997, dying in a jungle hut, Pol Pot gave his first interview in 18 years. The journalist Nate Thayer asked whether he felt remorse for the roughly two million Cambodians who had died under his rule. What was the heart of Pol Pot's answer?
answer: 'My conscience is clear'
choices: 'My conscience is clear'
'The people demanded it'
'History will judge me'
'I gave the orders, yes'
context: He said, 'I came to carry out the struggle, not to kill people... am I a savage person? My conscience is clear.' Asked directly if he wished to apologize, he answered simply, 'No.' (Far Eastern Economic Review, Nate Thayer, Oct 30 1997, verbatim)

question: To justify working the educated city classes to death, the Khmer Rouge taught a brutal slogan that survivor Teeda Butt Mam remembered being told. How did the slogan go?
answer: 'To keep you is no benefit; to destroy you is no loss'
choices: 'To keep you is no benefit; to destroy you is no loss'
'The nail that stands up must be hammered down'
'Bend with the wind, or the wind will break you'
'Better a dead enemy than a living doubter'
context: This official Khmer Rouge slogan reduced a person's life to a cost-benefit calculation that always came out the same. (Quote attributed to Khmer Rouge, goodreads.com/quotes/720775; iwmf.org 'To Keep You Is No Benefit')

question: The Khmer Rouge turned its paranoia on itself, purging its own leaders until, of the 22 men on the original ruling central committee, only six were left alive. In 1997 Pol Pot ordered his old defense minister Son Sen executed — and went further still, killing along with him what?
answer: Fourteen of Son Sen's family, including grandchildren
choices: Fourteen of Son Sen's family, including grandchildren
Eleven of his personal bodyguards and drivers
Nine other generals on the central committee
Twenty officers from his old command
context: Wiping out Son Sen's family, grandchildren and all, finally turned Pol Pot's own men against him and triggered his downfall. (Far Eastern Economic Review, Nate Thayer 1997)

question: The Khmer Rouge nightmare finally ended not from within but when neighboring Vietnam invaded and took Phnom Penh on January 7, 1979. The Khmer Rouge leaders fled into the jungle. What did the soldiers find waiting in the captured capital?
answer: A ghost city of barely 70 inhabitants
choices: A ghost city of barely 70 inhabitants
Warehouses stacked with looted gold
The leaders' abandoned battle plans
Crowds cheering them through the gates
context: Four years after two million people were marched out, the once-teeming capital held about 70 living souls. (history.com Pol Pot overthrown Jan 7 1979; cambodgemag.com January 7 1979)

question: Years before the Khmer Rouge took power, the United States secretly carpet-bombed Cambodia from 1969 to 1973, dropping over half a million tons of ordnance in raids with grimly casual code-names: Breakfast, Lunch, and Dinner. Historians argue this devastation did what to the Khmer Rouge?
answer: Helped them recruit and seize power
choices: Helped them recruit and seize power
Drove peasants into the cities for safety
Turned many villagers against the communists
Had little effect on their rise
context: The chaos of 'Operation Menu' helped the Khmer Rouge recruit. When US support for the region collapsed, Phnom Penh fell weeks before Saigon — a consequence of the American withdrawal from Indochina. (theconversation.com Kissinger bombing campaign Cambodia; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Menu)

question: The League of Nations was the first attempt to build a world body to stop wars, and its loudest champion was a sitting president who even won the 1919 Nobel Peace Prize for the idea. Yet the very country whose president founded it never joined. Which nation stayed out of the League it had proposed?
answer: The United States
choices: The United States
Great Britain
France
Italy
context: President Woodrow Wilson championed the League and won the 1919 Nobel Peace Prize, but the U.S. Senate refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles, so America never joined the world body it had proposed. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Henry-Cabot-Lodge-United-States-senator-1850-1924 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_and_the_League_of_Nations

question: The League of Nations met in Geneva, Switzerland, and from 1936 it gathered in a grand new headquarters built just for it. What was this purpose-built home for the world's nations called?
answer: The Palace of Nations
choices: The Palace of Nations
The Hall of Treaties
The Tower of Peace
The House of Assembly
context: The League moved into the specially built Palace of Nations in Geneva in 1936 (it had earlier used the Palais Wilson). Its two official languages were French and English. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/League_of_Nations

question: On 18 September 1931, a Japanese officer set off a small charge of dynamite beside Japan's own South Manchuria Railway near Mukden. The blast was so weak that trains kept running over the spot — yet Japan blamed China for it. Why did Japan stage this fake attack on its own railway?
answer: To create a pretext to seize all of Manchuria
choices: To create a pretext to seize all of Manchuria
To force China to pay for the damaged track
To test a new kind of military explosive
To provoke the League into sending troops
context: Lt. Kawamoto Suemori set off the charge in what became the Mukden Incident; Japan used the false-flag blast as its excuse to overrun Manchuria and install the puppet state Manchukuo. Source: https://history.state.gov/milestones/1921-1936/mukden-incident ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mukden_incident

question: The League's Lytton Commission investigated Japan's conquest of Manchuria and rejected Japan's claim that the puppet state Manchukuo was truly independent. When the Assembly adopted that report on 24 February 1933 by a vote of 42 to 1 — Japan the lone 'no' — how did Japan's delegation respond?
answer: It walked out of the Assembly and quit the League
choices: It walked out of the Assembly and quit the League
It demanded the report be put to a second vote
It agreed to pull its troops out of Manchuria
It asked Germany and Italy to walk out with it
context: Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka led the Japanese delegation out of the Assembly, reportedly saying 'We are not coming back'; Japan formally withdrew on 27 March 1933. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lytton_Report ; https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/japan-withdraws-league-nations

question: When Mussolini's Italy invaded Abyssinia in 1935, Britain's Foreign Secretary Samuel Hoare and France's Pierre Laval publicly backed the League's condemnation — but secretly drew up a deal that December to hand Mussolini roughly two-thirds of Abyssinia. A French newspaper leaked it, and the public outrage was so fierce it cost both men their jobs. What is this secret deal called?
answer: The Hoare-Laval Pact
choices: The Hoare-Laval Pact
The Geneva Protocol
The Stresa Agreement
The Rome Accord
context: The Hoare-Laval Pact was leaked by a French paper on 13 December 1935; the backlash forced both Samuel Hoare and Pierre Laval to resign, exposing the gap between the League's words and its great powers' deals. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoare%E2%80%93Laval_Pact ; https://www.britannica.com/event/Hoare-Laval-Pact

question: The League's Council was built so that any single member could veto action, and it had no army of its own — it could only ask member states to supply force, which they rarely did. When Haile Selassie, the exiled emperor of conquered Abyssinia, stood before the Assembly in Geneva on 30 June 1936 as Italian journalists jeered him, what warning did he give the great powers?
answer: 'It is us today. It will be you tomorrow.'
choices: 'It is us today. It will be you tomorrow.'
'A treaty without swords is a treaty of paper.'
'You have chosen peace and you will have war.'
'History will remember who stood silent here.'
context: Haile Selassie warned the Assembly that the aggression unanswered against his country would come for them next; World War II broke out just over three years later. The League's fatal design — a unanimity rule that let any member veto enforcement, and no army of its own — meant collective security existed only on paper. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Selassie%27s_speech_to_the_League_of_Nations_(1936) ; https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Haile_Selassie

question: Alexandria's rulers were obsessed with gathering every book in the world for their great Library. So they ordered the harbor officials to search every ship that docked for any scrolls aboard. When a scroll was found, what did the scribes do with the original?
answer: Copied it, then kept the original and handed the owner the copy
choices: Copied it, then kept the original and handed the owner the copy
Burned it once a second copy had been safely made
Returned it untouched after paying the owner in silver
Sold it to a rival library across the Mediterranean
context: The Library kept the originals and gave the travelers the fresh copies. These confiscated books were catalogued under the label 'books from the ships.' Source: worldhistory.org/Library_of_Alexandria; Galen via Britannica.

question: The Pharos lighthouse of Alexandria towered over 100 meters high, the tallest building of its age after the Great Pyramid. At its summit, sailors far out at sea could see its warning by day and by night. What sat at the top that threw the light so far across the Mediterranean?
answer: A polished bronze mirror that caught the sun and reflected a fire
choices: A polished bronze mirror that caught the sun and reflected a fire
A ring of torches carried up the stairs each evening
A cluster of crystal lenses ground by Alexandrian scholars
A beacon of burning oil floated on a pool of seawater
context: By day the mirror flashed sunlight; by night it reflected a great fire, throwing the warning far out to sea. The Pharos stood roughly 1,600 years before earthquakes toppled it. Source: worldhistory.org/Lighthouse_of_Alexandria; memphistours.com.

question: When the first Star Wars movie (1977) needed the secret Rebel base on the jungle moon Yavin 4, the filmmakers found a real ancient city whose stone temples rise above the rainforest. A Rebel watches the Millennium Falcon arrive from the top of one towering temple. Which real ruins played Yavin 4?
answer: Tikal, in Guatemala
choices: Tikal, in Guatemala
Angkor Wat, in Cambodia
Machu Picchu, in Peru
Petra, in Jordan
context: Tikal is a Classic Maya city deep in Guatemala's Peten jungle. The Yavin 4 shot was filmed from the top of Tikal's Temple IV, looking east across the canopy to other temples poking through the trees. Sources: tikalnationalpark.org/tikal-and-star-wars; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yavin_4.

question: Chichen Itza's great stepped pyramid, El Castillo, was built for the feathered-serpent god Kukulkan -- and the Maya hid their calendar inside it. It has four staircases of 91 steps each, plus one shared platform at the very top. Counted all together, what does the pyramid secretly equal?
answer: 365 steps -- one for each day of the year
choices: 365 steps -- one for each day of the year
52 steps -- one for each week of the year
12 steps -- one for each month of the year
7 steps -- one for each day of the week
context: Four staircases of 91 steps make 364, and the shared top platform makes 365 -- the length of the Maya solar year, with the calendar literally built into the stone. Sources: chichenitza.com/chichen-itza-pyramid; Britannica, 'What's Inside the Pyramid at Chichen Itza.'

question: The Maya wrote numbers with only a few marks: a single dot meant one, and a bar meant five. For zero -- the powerful idea of 'nothing' holding a place -- they drew a picture of one everyday thing. They were among the very first people on Earth to write zero at all. What did the Maya draw for zero?
answer: a shell
choices: a shell
a feather
a pebble
an open eye
context: In Maya numerals a dot = 1, a bar = 5, and a shell shape = 0. The Maya were among the first civilizations anywhere to use a symbol for zero as a placeholder. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_numerals; penn.museum, 'Maya Long Count Numbers.'

question: Twice a year, on the spring and fall equinox, crowds pack the plaza at Chichen Itza in the late afternoon to watch El Castillo. As the low sun strikes the pyramid's stepped corner, a row of light-and-shadow triangles ripples straight down the edge of the north staircase. For a few minutes the shape crawling down the steps makes the whole crowd gasp. What does it look like?
answer: a giant serpent gliding down the steps
choices: a giant serpent gliding down the steps
a river of fire pouring up the pyramid
the whole temple splitting in two
a golden doorway opening in the stone
context: The zig-zag of triangles meets a carved stone serpent head at the base, so it looks like Kukulkan, the feathered serpent, is slithering down the pyramid. Sources: kidsdiscover.com (serpent shadow of Chichen Itza); chichenitza.com/equinox.

question: The Great Ball Court at Chichen Itza is the biggest ball court in all the ancient Americas -- a stone alley longer than a football field, walled in on both sides. The Maya built one astonishing trick into this court that still works today, and visitors test it every time they come. What can the Great Ball Court do?
answer: carry a whisper from one end clear to the other
choices: carry a whisper from one end clear to the other
stay icy cold even in the noon sun
glow faintly in the dark
make a thrown ball curve in midair
context: A person whispering at one end temple can be heard clearly at the far temple about 460 feet (140 m) away, and a single clap echoes back several times. Many scholars think the Maya designed these sound effects on purpose. Sources: worldhistory.org/image/751 (Great Ball Court); ResearchGate, 'Acoustics of the Great Ball Court at Chichen Itza.'

question: Along the walls of the Great Ball Court at Chichen Itza, carved stone panels show exactly what the high-stakes ballgame could cost the players. One panel shows a kneeling player who has just lost his head -- and from the stump of his neck, instead of blood, something startling pours out. What sprouts from the player's neck?
answer: a tangle of serpents
choices: a tangle of serpents
a fountain of gold
a swarm of bats
a burst of flame
context: The carving shows serpents (and a plant) rising from the neck stump in place of blood -- evidence the ballgame could end in human sacrifice. Sources: worldhistory.org/image/751 (Great Ball Court).

question: At the edge of Chichen Itza yawns the Sacred Cenote, a huge natural sinkhole pool. The Maya gave gifts to the rain-god Chaac by throwing them into its deep water -- gold, jade, copper, and incense. Divers who later dredged the cenote pulled up those treasures, and something startling lay mixed in with them at the bottom. What else did they find down there?
answer: the skeletons of about 200 people
choices: the skeletons of about 200 people
a hoard of about 200 gold masks
the timbers of about 200 sunken canoes
a heap of about 200 carved stone skulls
context: The Maya threw people as well as offerings into the cenote for Chaac. Dredging recovered the bones of roughly 200 victims, many of them children -- told straight, this was real human sacrifice. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacred_Cenote; yucatanmagazine.com/sacred-cenote-chichen-itza.

question: In the Maya city of Palenque, a boy named Pakal was crowned king at just 12 years old. He went on to rule for so long that no monarch anywhere in the world would beat his record for over a thousand years afterward. About how long did King Pakal reign?
answer: about 68 years
choices: about 68 years
about 45 years
about 58 years
about 80 years
context: Pakal took the throne on July 27, 615 CE at age 12 and ruled until his death around 683 CE -- roughly 68 years, one of the longest verified reigns of any monarch in world history. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K'inich_Janaab_Pakal.

question: Tunneling deep inside Tikal's Temple I, archaeologists broke into a sealed royal tomb -- the burial of King Jasaw Chan K'awiil I. He lay on jaguar skins, surrounded by pearls and stingray spines, wearing the tomb's most dazzling treasure. What was it?
answer: a jade necklace of 114 huge beads
choices: a jade necklace of 114 huge beads
a gold collar of 96 small rings
a coral belt of 72 round disks
a bone crown of 58 carved spikes
context: The jade necklace of 114 beads weighed about 8.6 lb (3.9 kg). The tomb (Burial 116) also held 37 carved bones inscribed with Maya glyphs. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal_Temple_I; kids.kiddle.co/Tikal_Temple_I.

question: The Maya carved thousands of tiny picture-signs into their temples and monuments -- more than 800 different signs in all, enough to spell out any word in their language. For centuries no one alive could read a single line of it. When scholars finally cracked the Maya code, experts ranked the achievement right beside one other famous decipherment. Which code did breaking the Maya script get compared to?
answer: reading Egyptian hieroglyphs
choices: reading Egyptian hieroglyphs
cracking the Roman alphabet
translating Chinese characters
decoding Viking runes
context: The Maya built the only fully developed writing system in the ancient Americas -- a logo-syllabic script of 800-plus signs. Cracking it is ranked alongside deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs as one of history's great code-breaking feats. Sources: mayan.org/civilization/writing; britannica.com/topic/Maya-hieroglyphic-writing.

question: In 1952, archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier pried up a stone slab in the floor of Palenque's Temple of the Inscriptions and found a hidden stairway choked with rubble. He dug downward for years until, about 80 feet down, he broke into a sealed chamber no one had entered in roughly 1,300 years. What did Ruz prove that no one had known before?
answer: that a Maya pyramid could hide a king's tomb deep inside
choices: that a Maya pyramid could hide a king's tomb deep inside
that the Maya had crossed the ocean from Africa
that Palenque was older than the Egyptian pyramids
that the temples had been raised by ancient giants
context: Ruz reached Pakal's burial chamber about 25 m down -- the first proof that a Maya pyramid could be a royal tomb, not just a temple platform. He was the first person to see the king's burial in roughly 1,300 years. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_the_Inscriptions; artsq.org/blog/pakal-tomb-sarcophagus.

question: When Alberto Ruz finally reached the crypt under Palenque's Temple of the Inscriptions, he found King Pakal in a stone coffin sealed by a single carved limestone lid weighing about 7 tons. The carving on that lid is one of the most famous images in all Maya art: it shows Pakal at the very instant of his death. What is happening to him in the picture?
answer: he tips backward into the underworld's jaws as a great tree grows out of his body
choices: he tips backward into the underworld's jaws as a great tree grows out of his body
he climbs a golden rope toward the sun god as eagles circle his head
he sails off in a canoe rowed by snarling jaguars across a dark sea
he stands atop a mountain gripping a bolt of lightning in each raised hand
context: On the lid Pakal falls into the open jaws of Xibalba, the underworld, while the great World Tree rises from his body with the Celestial Bird perched on top -- a whole Maya cosmos carved on one stone. Sources: mayan.org/mysteries/pakal-tomb-lid-decipherment; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_the_Inscriptions.

question: The Maya invented a written sign for ZERO centuries before Europe used one — one of only a handful of peoples on Earth to think it up on their own. In their carvings, what everyday object did they draw to mean zero?
answer: A shell
choices: A shell
A flower
A feather
A stone
context: The Maya zero was a stylized shell glyph. A true zero is hard to invent — most civilizations never did. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_numerals

question: The Maya could write any number using just THREE simple marks. A dot stood for one and a shell stood for zero. What did a single horizontal bar stand for?
answer: Five
choices: Five
Ten
Twenty
Two
context: Dot = 1, bar = 5, shell = 0. So three dots over two bars is 13. A whole counting system from three signs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_numerals

question: Our counting goes in tens because we have ten fingers. Maya counting went in TWENTIES instead. What did the Maya use to reach twenty that we leave out when we count?
answer: Their toes
choices: Their toes
Their knuckles
Their elbows
Their teeth
context: Maya math was base-20 (vigesimal) — fingers AND toes. Numbers stacked vertically, each level worth twenty times the one below. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_numerals

question: Archaeologists found the Maya word kakaw painted on tomb pots, and a Hershey chemist later tested the residue inside and confirmed it. The Maya buried their dead with jars of a drink so prized it marked your status. What was the drink?
answer: Chocolate
choices: Chocolate
Honey wine
Spiced beer
Fruit cider
context: The glyph kakaw was deciphered in the 1980s; the chemist found theobromine, chocolate's chemical fingerprint, in elite Maya pots. Source: https://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/mayan-chocolate

question: The Maya solar calendar had 18 months of 20 days, which left 5 extra days at the end of the year with no month to belong to. The Maya called these the Wayebʼ, and they were so feared that people stayed home and avoided strangers. What did the Maya believe happened during those 5 days?
answer: The doors to the Underworld swung open
choices: The doors to the Underworld swung open
The sun stopped moving across the sky
The gods abandoned the world entirely
The rivers ran backward toward the sea
context: The 5 'nameless days' were considered dangerous and unlucky. Per Maya belief, the barrier between the living world and the Underworld opened. (Legend.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_calendar

question: The Maya were never one empire — they were rival city-states, and the two biggest, Tikal and Calakmul, fought a war so long and bitter that archaeologists gave their feud a striking nickname. What do scholars call the Tikal-versus-Calakmul rivalry?
answer: The Star Wars
choices: The Star Wars
The Hundred Years
The War of the Twins
The Jaguar Wars
context: In 562 CE Calakmul's king Sky Witness crushed Tikal, beginning Tikal's 130-year 'hiatus' of decline. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal%E2%80%93Calakmul_wars

question: For 130 years the city of Tikal had been beaten down by its rival Calakmul. In 695 CE the Tikal king Jasaw Chan Kʼawiil I finally won the war — and to break Calakmul's power for good, he carried off something no ordinary loot. What did he capture?
answer: Calakmul's patron god
choices: Calakmul's patron god
Calakmul's royal library
Calakmul's water supply
Calakmul's tallest temple
context: Seizing a city's patron god ended its supremacy and restored Tikal as the dominant power of the Maya lowlands. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal%E2%80%93Calakmul_wars

question: In 1952, after clearing rubble for four years, archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier reached the hidden tomb of King Pakal deep inside Palenque's Temple of the Inscriptions. The king's face was covered by something that has dazzled visitors ever since. What was the mask made of?
answer: Jade
choices: Jade
Gold
Bone
Obsidian
context: Pakal wore a jade mosaic mask. His carved sarcophagus lid was so strange that fringe theorists nicknamed it the 'Palenque Astronaut.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakal_the_Great

question: Many people heard that the Maya Long Count calendar 'ended' on December 21, 2012, and feared the world would too. But that date, written 13.0.0.0.0, was never a doomsday to the Maya. According to scholars, what did the Maya actually expect to happen?
answer: The cycles would roll over and keep going
choices: The cycles would roll over and keep going
A new sun god would be born
The calendar would have to be rewritten
The kings would all step down at once
context: The Long Count counted days from a mythic creation date of August 11, 3114 BCE. One inscription even projects a date out to 4772 CE. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoamerican_Long_Count_calendar

question: In 1562 in the town of Maní, the Spanish friar Diego de Landa decided the Maya's painted books were 'superstition and lies of the devil' and threw them onto a single bonfire. The loss was so total that only three pre-Columbian Maya books survive in the whole world today. How many did de Landa burn that day?
answer: Twenty-seven
choices: Twenty-seven
Forty
Sixty
Ninety
context: De Landa wrote that the Maya 'regretted to an amazing degree' the loss. The three survivors plus a fragment of a fourth are nearly all the Maya literature left. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_de_Landa

question: For generations no one could read Maya writing. In 1952 the Russian scholar Yuri Knorozov solved it with one key idea: the mysterious marks scribes used were not an alphabet of letters at all. What did Knorozov realize the signs actually stood for?
answer: Syllables of speech
choices: Syllables of speech
Whole sentences
Numbers and dates
Names of gods
context: Knorozov showed the dismissed 'de Landa alphabet' was really syllable signs, the breakthrough that unlocked the script. About 80% of Maya writing can now be read. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_script

question: One of the three surviving Maya books, the Dresden Codex, is essentially a manual of astronomy, and it includes a table for tracking the planet Venus. Tested against the real 584-day Venus cycle across a span of 500 years, how far off does the Maya table drift?
answer: Less than a couple of hours
choices: Less than a couple of hours
About three weeks
Nearly a full year
Almost a decade
context: The Maya value (584 days) is off the true 583.92 days by under two hours, and the table holds that accuracy across centuries — naked-eye astronomy of the first rank. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Caracol,_Chichen_Itza

question: In Florence around 1436, Cosimo de' Medici put his banking fortune behind an eccentric, often broke architect named Filippo Brunelleschi to finish a project no one knew how to complete. What did Brunelleschi build that still stands as the largest masonry dome in the world?
answer: The great dome of Florence Cathedral
choices: The great dome of Florence Cathedral
The bell tower of the Florence Cathedral
The bronze baptistery doors of Florence
The grand staircase of the Medici palace
context: Brunelleschi crowned Santa Maria del Fiore in 1436 with a dome still unmatched in masonry size. Cosimo de' Medici bankrolled the difficult, debt-ridden genius to pull it off. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosimo_de'_Medici

question: During High Mass in Florence's cathedral on Easter Sunday 1478, assassins stabbed Lorenzo de' Medici in the neck. Bleeding, Lorenzo ran for the sacristy. What saved his life once he was inside?
answer: Heavy bronze doors were slammed shut behind him
choices: Heavy bronze doors were slammed shut behind him
A loyal guard carried him out a side gate
A crowd of worshippers surrounded and hid him
A priest disguised him in clerical robes
context: Wounded but alive, Lorenzo fled into the sacristy and his friends slammed its heavy bronze doors against the attackers. His younger brother Giuliano was not so lucky. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pazzi_conspiracy

question: The Pazzi family plotted to murder the Medici brothers inside Florence's Duomo during Easter Mass in 1478, and they needed a single moment when everyone would be looking forward and the brothers would be exposed. What did the conspirators choose as their signal to strike?
answer: The priest raising the consecrated Host at the altar
choices: The priest raising the consecrated Host at the altar
The first peal of the cathedral's largest bell
The choir beginning the closing hymn
The archbishop stepping up to the pulpit
context: They timed the murder to the elevation of the Host, the holiest instant of the Mass. Giuliano de' Medici was stabbed 19 times on the cathedral floor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pazzi_conspiracy

question: After the failed Pazzi plot of 1478, a conspirator who had fled all the way to Constantinople was captured, dragged back to Florence, and hanged from a window of the city's government palace. A young artist studied the dangling corpse and drew it in careful detail. Which future master made that sketch?
answer: Leonardo da Vinci
choices: Leonardo da Vinci
Sandro Botticelli
Donatello
Michelozzo di Bartolomeo
context: In 1479 Leonardo da Vinci sketched the hanged body of Bernardo Bandini dei Baroncelli, even noting the colors of his clothes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pazzi_conspiracy

question: The Pazzi conspirators meant to cut down Lorenzo de' Medici during Easter Mass, but the professional soldier they hired refused to commit murder inside a church. Who stepped in to take the killer's place as Lorenzo's would-be assassins?
answer: Two priests
choices: Two priests
A pair of bankers
Two foreign mercenaries
A group of city guards
context: With the hired soldier unwilling to spill blood in church, the priests Stefano da Bagnone and Antonio Maffei da Volterra took up the attack on Lorenzo. Both missed killing him. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pazzi_conspiracy

question: Two sons of the Medici line rose to become popes. One of them, Pope Clement VII, faced a furious King Henry VIII of England who demanded the church end his marriage to Catherine of Aragon. What did Clement VII do about Henry's demand?
answer: He refused to grant the annulment
choices: He refused to grant the annulment
He quietly approved the annulment
He crowned Henry head of England's church
He excommunicated Catherine of Aragon
context: Clement VII would not annul Henry VIII's marriage to Catherine of Aragon, a refusal that helped push England to break from Rome. The other Medici pope was Leo X, son of Lorenzo the Magnificent. Source: https://www.thecollector.com/medici-popes/

question: A medieval peasant owed the Church a 'tithe' — one-tenth of everything he grew or raised, every single year. For most peasants, how was this tenth actually handed over to the Church?
answer: In goods — wheat, barley, animals, and fish
choices: In goods — wheat, barley, animals, and fish
In silver and copper coins, counted by hand
In long days of unpaid labor on Church land
In wax candles and prayers said at the altar
context: The word 'tithe' comes from the Old English 'teotha,' meaning 'tenth.' Most peasants had little coin, so they paid 'in kind' — actual sheaves of grain, livestock, and fish handed straight to the Church. Source: https://aprilmunday.wordpress.com/2022/02/13/medieval-tithes/ ; https://historyrise.com/how-local-governments-in-medieval-europe-collected-tithes/

question: Every English parish built a huge locked barn just to gather in the Church's share of the grain — and many of these 'tithe barns' still stand today. As the harvest poured in, what single danger were the builders most determined to keep away from that stored crop?
answer: Fire
choices: Fire
Thieves
Damp and rot
Rats and mice
context: These 'tithe barns' were built of solid stone precisely because fire was the great enemy of a stored harvest. As the crop came in, peasants had to deliver their tithe sheaves to the barn before they were allowed to store their own share. Source: https://ruralhistoria.com/2023/02/20/tithe-barns/ ; https://archaeology.org/news/2013/08/06/130806-england-medieval-tithe-barn/

question: In the Church's most solemn curse — 'bell, book, and candle' — a bishop and twelve priests tolled a bell, shut the holy book, then dashed a lit candle to the ground and snuffed it out. What did snuffing that candle stand for?
answer: The sinner's soul, cast out from God's light
choices: The sinner's soul, cast out from God's light
The sinner's good deeds, now counted as nothing
The sinner's years still owed in purgatory
The sinner's old self, dying to be reborn
context: This was the rite of anathema, the gravest form of excommunication, cutting a person off from the sacraments and from all Christian society. As they snuffed the candle, the priests cried 'Fiat, fiat, fiat' — 'So be it.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell,_book,_and_candle ; https://www.britannica.com/topic/bell-book-and-candle-Roman-Catholicism

question: After Pope Clement IV died in 1268, the cardinals gathered to elect a new pope — and argued for almost three years without agreeing. The furious townsmen of Viterbo locked them in the palace and cut their meals to bread and water. When that failed, what drastic thing did the townsmen do to the building?
answer: Tore the roof clean off over the cardinals' heads
choices: Tore the roof clean off over the cardinals' heads
Set fire to the great doors at the front
Bricked up every window to seal them inside
Knocked a hole through the outer wall
context: That election lasted 1,006 days — the longest in history. The newly chosen Pope Gregory X then made the rule that cardinals must be locked in until they decide, which is why a papal election is called a 'conclave' — from the Latin 'cum clave,' 'with a key.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1268%E2%80%931271_papal_election ; https://www.vaticannews.va/en/vatican-city/news/2025-05/how-locking-cardinals-in-a-room-became-known-as-a-conclave.html

question: To shelter the poor, the sick, and weary pilgrims, the medieval Church founded the Hotel-Dieu — the 'hostel of God' — beside Notre-Dame in Paris. What is remarkable about it today?
answer: It still treats patients as a hospital
choices: It still treats patients as a hospital
It was rebuilt as the Louvre museum
It became a royal palace for kings
It now lies in ruins under the city
context: The medieval Church effectively invented the hospital as an institution — Emperor Charlemagne ordered one built beside every cathedral and monastery. The Paris Hotel-Dieu is still in operation, making it one of the oldest working hospitals on earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals ; https://www.medievalists.net/2022/06/the-early-medieval-hospital/

question: When King John of England rejected the Pope's choice for Archbishop of Canterbury, Pope Innocent III shut down the whole of England in 1208 — no Mass, no weddings, the dead left unburied — for over six years. Across the land one familiar sound that also rang out the hours and sounded the alarm fell silent. What was it?
answer: The pealing of the church bells
choices: The pealing of the church bells
The cry of the night watchman
The horn blown from the city gate
The beat of the town war-drum
context: This kingdom-wide punishment was called an interdict — excommunication aimed at a whole nation. Town bells rang the hours and sounded warnings, so their loss was a daily, eerie reminder of the Church's power over all of England. The interdict lasted until 1214. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papal_Interdict_of_1208 ; https://www.rte.ie/brainstorm/2021/0129/1193824-pope-innocent-iii-papal-interdict-church-lockdown/

question: In 1077 the Pope, Gregory VII, excommunicated the Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV. Desperate to be forgiven, Henry crossed the Alps in the dead of winter and came to the castle of Canossa, where the Pope was staying. To prove his penitence, what did the emperor do?
answer: Stood barefoot outside the gate for three days
choices: Stood barefoot outside the gate for three days
Knelt in chains before the high altar
Crawled the final mile on his bare knees
Fasted alone in a cold cell for a week
context: Henry wore only a rough wool penitent's garment. Gregory finally relented and absolved him, and that evening the pope, the emperor, and Countess Matilda of Tuscany — the castle's owner — shared communion together. 'To go to Canossa' still means to humble yourself and eat humble pie. Source: https://christianhistoryinstitute.org/magazine/article/humiliation-of-king-henry ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_to_Canossa

question: In the Book of Acts, a sorcerer named Simon offered the apostles money to buy the power of giving people the Holy Spirit. The apostle Peter's blistering reply became so famous that the Church named the whole sin of buying holy office 'simony,' after him. What did Peter say to Simon?
answer: 'May your silver perish with you'
choices: 'May your silver perish with you'
'Get behind me, Satan'
'Your faith has made you well'
'Sell all you own and follow me'
context: Peter's full rebuke was 'May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money.' Stamping out simony — the buying and selling of church offices — was a central goal of the 11th-century Gregorian reformers. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simony ; https://www.britannica.com/topic/simony

question: By the early 1500s the Church was selling 'indulgences' — pardons that were said to cut a soul's time in purgatory — to raise money to rebuild St. Peter's Basilica in Rome. The friar Johann Tetzel grew infamous for a catchy sales rhyme. How did his jingle go?
answer: 'As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs'
choices: 'As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs'
'Lay a gold piece on the holy shrine, and lift a soul from purgatory's line'
'Drop a silver in the begging bowl, and purgatory frees a waiting soul'
'Give the friar a coin to ring, and from the fire a soul takes wing'
context: Tetzel's sales tactics provoked Martin Luther's 95 Theses in 1517. Scholars note the exact wording of the jingle may be a paraphrase, but two of Tetzel's contemporaries attribute it to him. Source: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Johann_Tetzel ; https://www.ncronline.org/news/guest-voices/peddling-purgatory-relief-johann-tetzel

question: The medieval Church guided a Christian's whole life through its holy rites — from Baptism at birth to the last rites at death, with the Eucharist, confession, and marriage in between. The Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 confirmed their number. What were these seven rites called together?
answer: The seven sacraments
choices: The seven sacraments
The seven holy orders
The seven mysteries
The seven virtues
context: The seven were Baptism, Confirmation, the Eucharist, Penance (confession), Extreme Unction (last rites), Holy Orders, and Marriage. The theologian Peter Lombard was first to fix the list at seven, around 1150. Source: https://christianhistoryinstitute.org/magazine/article/what-did-sacrament-mean-and-how-many-were-there ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacraments_of_the_Catholic_Church

question: People often picture 'indulgences' — pardons for sin — as nothing but a money racket. But the very first one had nothing to do with cash. In 1095 Pope Urban II promised this pardon to anyone who did one thing out of pure devotion. What act earned that first indulgence?
answer: Marching on Crusade to free Jerusalem
choices: Marching on Crusade to free Jerusalem
Walking the long pilgrimage to Canterbury
Fasting in a monastery for forty days
Freeing a Christian captive from his chains
context: At the Council of Clermont in 1095, Urban II declared that anyone who marched to free Jerusalem out of devotion — not for honor or wealth — would have that journey 'reckoned in place of all penance.' This first plenary indulgence remitted the penance owed by someone who had already confessed; only centuries later did indulgences become a sales racket. Source: https://www.historyofinformation.com/detail.php?id=223 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crusade_indulgence

question: The friar Thomas Aquinas, who fused the philosophy of Aristotle with Christian faith in his vast 'Summa Theologiae,' taught that a human rule only counts as true law if it agrees with the moral law that reason itself can know. How did Aquinas describe a rule that breaks with that higher moral law?
answer: 'An unjust law is no law at all'
choices: 'An unjust law is no law at all'
'An unjust law still binds the conscience'
'A law is just because the king commands it'
'Any written decree is a true and binding law'
context: Aquinas (c. 1225-1274) held that a law out of step with the moral law is not truly law but a perversion of law. This natural-law idea — that there is a higher moral law against which human laws can be measured — still echoes in Western political philosophy. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treatise_on_Law ; https://www.nlnrac.org/classical/aquinas.html

question: Pope Innocent III, who ruled from 1198 to 1216 and was the first pope to regularly call himself the 'Vicar of Christ,' claimed his authority stood above every earthly king's. He drove the point home with one striking comparison. How did Innocent picture the pope beside kings?
answer: The pope is the sun; kings are the moon that shines by his light
choices: The pope is the sun; kings are the moon that shines by his light
The pope is the shepherd; kings are the dogs that guard his sheep
The pope is the head; kings are the hands that do his will
The pope is the rock; kings are the towers that rest on him
context: Innocent III was perhaps the most powerful man in Europe. In his own words, 'just as the moon derives its light from the sun... so too the royal power derives the splendour of its dignity from the pontifical authority.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Innocent_III ; https://www.britannica.com/biography/Innocent-III-pope

question: In 1868 a teenaged emperor, Mutsuhito, took power back from the Tokugawa shogun who had ruled in his place, and chose a brand-new name for his reign and his whole era. What did the name he picked, 'Meiji,' mean?
answer: Enlightened Rule
choices: Enlightened Rule
Heavenly Peace
Eternal Spring
Bright Harmony
context: Mutsuhito was only about 15. 'Meiji' means 'Enlightened Rule,' and the era it named (1868 on) became Japan's great leap into the modern world. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Meiji ; britannica.com/event/Meiji-Restoration

question: Japan's Conscription Law of 1873 forced every able-bodied man into the army, not just the samurai. Officials nicknamed military service the 'blood tax,' and across the countryside ordinary peasants rose up in the 'blood tax riots' because they took that nickname literally. What did they actually believe the government meant to do?
answer: Drain the blood from their bodies
choices: Drain the blood from their bodies
Send only firstborn sons forever
Seize their family's rice fields
Forbid them from ever marrying
context: The Japanese term was ketsu-eki, 'blood tax.' Frightened villagers thought it meant their blood would literally be taken, and rioted to dodge the draft. The law ended the samurai's centuries-old monopoly on bearing arms. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_tax_riots ; courses.lumenlearning.com/suny-worldhistory/chapter/27-2-7-japanese-militarization/

question: To learn from the West firsthand, Japan's leaders toured Europe and America on the Iwakura Mission, and they also sent five Japanese girls along to be educated in the United States, some staying about ten years. The very youngest, Tsuda Umeko, who came home and later founded a women's college, set sail at an astonishing age. How old was she?
answer: Six
choices: Six
Nine
Thirteen
Sixteen
context: Tsuda Umeko was just six when she left for America in 1871, stayed about a decade, and later founded the school that became today's Tsuda University. Sources: nippon.com/en/japan-topics/b07228/ ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iwakura_Mission

question: By the final battle of the Satsuma Rebellion in 1877, Saigo Takamori's samurai had been ground down to a few hundred men and had run clean out of ammunition. To keep firing at the imperial army, what did they melt down and cast into bullets?
answer: Metal Buddhist statues
choices: Metal Buddhist statues
Their iron cooking pots
Brass temple bells
Bronze treasury coins
context: At the Battle of Shiroyama, Saigo's roughly 500 survivors faced some 30,000 imperial conscripts under General Yamagata Aritomo. Civilians smuggled in metal Buddhist statues, which the rebels melted down and cast into bullets. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Shiroyama

question: At dawn on the last day of the Satsuma Rebellion, Saigo Takamori was shot through the thigh and could go no farther. His loyal retainer Beppu Shinsuke carried him down the hill so he could die with dignity, then did one more thing to stop the imperial troops from claiming a trophy. What did Beppu do?
answer: Cut off Saigo's head and hid it
choices: Cut off Saigo's head and hid it
Burned Saigo's body where it lay
Buried Saigo beneath the battlefield
Threw Saigo's sword into the river
context: Beppu Shinsuke beheaded the dying Saigo and concealed the head so the enemy could not claim it. The last samurai then drew their swords and charged the guns: about 500 rebels died versus roughly 30 imperial troops. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Shiroyama

question: Saigo Takamori died in 1877 a branded traitor, killed leading the samurai's last revolt against the Meiji government. Twelve years later, in 1889, that same government reversed his standing entirely, on the very day it proclaimed Japan's first modern constitution. What did the state do about Saigo that day?
answer: Pardoned him and restored his court rank
choices: Pardoned him and restored his court rank
Tore down every shrine in his name
Stripped his family of their lands
Renamed the rebellion after his enemy
context: On February 22, 1889, Saigo received a posthumous pardon and his court rank back, the same day the new constitution was proclaimed. The rebel who died fighting the new Japan was rehabilitated as a national hero, later honored by the famous Ueno Park statue showing him in a plain kimono walking his hunting dog, Tsun. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saig%C5%8D_Takamori

question: In the Aztec ball game ollamaliztli, players kept a heavy solid-rubber ball in play by striking it back and forth -- but they were forbidden to use their hands or their feet. What body part did they hit the ball with instead?
answer: Their hips
choices: Their hips
Their heads
Their shoulders
Their knees
context: Players bounced the ball mainly off their hips and upper thighs, never the hands or feet, until one team failed to return it. The Aztecs called the game ollamaliztli and the stone court tlachtli. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoamerican_ballgame

question: The Mesoamerican ball game was played with a solid rubber ball about a foot across and weighing up to 8 or 9 pounds. The oldest such rubber balls ever found, pulled from a sacrificial bog at El Manati in Veracruz, are dated to about 1700-1600 BC. Set against the very first Greek Olympic Games, how old does that make this contest?
answer: Older than the first Olympics by over a thousand years
choices: Older than the first Olympics by over a thousand years
Older than the first Olympics by about fifty years
Younger than the first Olympics by a few centuries
Played at the very same time as the first Olympics
context: The El Manati balls predate the first Greek Olympic Games by more than a millennium, making this arguably the oldest known team sport on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoamerican_ballgame ; https://mayan.org/civilization/ball-game/

question: To make their ball bounce, Aztec craftsmen mixed latex from the Castilla elastica tree with sap from the white morning-glory vine, hardening the soft rubber into a springy, durable ball. An American named Charles Goodyear is famous for 'inventing' this same hardening process, called vulcanization. What does the Aztec ball reveal about that claim?
answer: The Aztecs were vulcanizing rubber centuries before Goodyear
choices: The Aztecs were vulcanizing rubber centuries before Goodyear
Goodyear learned the technique directly from Aztec survivors
The Aztec method made rubber too brittle to bounce
Vulcanized rubber was first created in Goodyear's own lifetime
context: By blending Castilla elastica latex with Ipomoea alba (morning-glory) sap, Mesoamericans vulcanized rubber centuries before Charles Goodyear is credited with the discovery. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoamerican_ballgame

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was a Dutch cloth merchant in Delft, not a trained scientist, who ground his own tiny glass lenses for fun. One day he scraped the white gunk from between his own teeth, smeared it under a lens, and became the first human ever to see a thing no one knew existed. What did he see swimming in the scrapings from his teeth?
answer: Tiny living creatures he called 'animalcules'
choices: Tiny living creatures he called 'animalcules'
Tiny grains of colored sand
Tiny threads of woven cloth
Tiny flakes of dried blood
context: In 1683 Leeuwenhoek wrote the Royal Society that he saw 'very little animalcules, very prettily a-moving' in the scrapings of his teeth — the first sight of living bacteria in human history. The self-taught draper became known as the Father of Microbiology. Source: https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rstl/article/17/197/646/109982/IV-An-extract-of-a-letter-from-Mr-Anth-Van-Leuwenhoek-concerning

question: In his 1665 book Micrographia, Robert Hooke sliced a thin piece of cork and looked at it under his microscope. He saw it was full of tiny empty boxes, like a honeycomb. The little boxes reminded him of the bare rooms monks slept in at a monastery, so he borrowed that word to name them. What did Hooke call these tiny boxes — a word biology still uses today?
answer: Cells
choices: Cells
Pores
Grains
Combs
context: Hooke wrote that the cork was 'all perforated and porous, much like a Honey-comb,' and named the boxes 'cells' after the small rooms (cells) that monks live in at a monastery. The word stuck and is now basic to all of biology. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micrographia

question: When Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a cloth merchant with no university training, wrote the Royal Society in 1676 that a single drop of pond water and pepper-water was swarming with thousands of invisible 'little animals,' the learned members flatly refused to believe an untrained amateur. Rather than simply print or reject his claim, what did the Royal Society do to settle it in 1677?
answer: Sent their own observers to verify the swarming creatures
choices: Sent their own observers to verify the swarming creatures
Awarded him a medal for the marvelous discovery
Banned him from sending any further letters
Bought his secret lens-grinding method outright
context: The Royal Society did not believe Leeuwenhoek, so they dispatched observers to check — and his claim was confirmed in 1677. His best single-bead lenses could magnify roughly 270 times, far beyond any rival's, and he guarded the grinding method as a secret. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonie_van_Leeuwenhoek

question: The Atlantic slave trade ran in three legs, like a triangle drawn on the ocean. The middle leg, the 'Middle Passage,' was the crossing where ships carried captured Africans in chains from Africa to the Americas. Over the centuries of the trade, how many people were forced aboard those ships?
answer: More than 12 million
choices: More than 12 million
More than 3 million
More than 8 million
More than 30 million
context: Roughly 12.5 million Africans were forced aboard slave ships across the whole history of the trade. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Passage

question: Aboard the slave ships, despair drove captives to throw themselves over the rail, and the crews rigged netting around the sides of the deck to stop them. Many of the enslaved jumped anyway, not out of mere hopelessness, but because they believed that in death they would go somewhere. Where did they believe drowning would carry them?
answer: Home to their family and village
choices: Home to their family and village
Down to a kingdom beneath the sea
Into the body of a great fish
Onto a passing ship sailing back
context: Many believed death would return them across the water to their homeland, so they leapt despite the nets. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Passage

question: Slave-ship crews wanted their captives to look healthy and sell for a good price at the end of the voyage, so they forced the chained Africans up onto the deck to move their bodies for the buyers' sake. Anyone who refused was flogged. What grim name did the crews give this forced exercise?
answer: Dancing the slaves
choices: Dancing the slaves
Working the deck
Trotting the line
Airing the cargo
context: The chained captives were made to jump and move on deck to stay fit for sale; those who would not 'dance' were whipped. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Passage

question: Olaudah Equiano survived the Middle Passage as a boy, later bought his freedom, and in 1789 wrote his own account of the crossing. The very first time the crew hauled him up onto the deck, the pale sailors with their red faces and loose hair so terrified him that he asked his fellow captives one specific, horrifying question about what these strangers meant to do to him. What did he fear?
answer: That they were going to eat him
choices: That they were going to eat him
That they were sea-demons in disguise
That they would drown him at once
That they would sell him to giants
context: Equiano wrote that the crew's strange faces and hair convinced him he would be eaten. His book was 'The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano.' https://www.worldhistory.org/article/2672/olaudah-equianos-account-of-the-middle-passage/

question: Some captives refused to eat, choosing starvation over a life in chains. To force food down them, slave-ship crews used a metal screw-and-divider tool that had originally been invented for doctors to pry open the locked jaws of patients with lockjaw. Cranked into a captive's mouth, what was this device called?
answer: The speculum oris
choices: The speculum oris
The iron muzzle
The branks
The jaw-vice
context: The speculum oris, a mouth-opener made for lockjaw patients, was used to force-feed captives who tried to starve themselves. https://digital.librarycompany.org/islandora/object/Islandora:2746

question: Olaudah Equiano remembered the worst of it happening below deck, where chained captives lay packed in the dark for weeks. In his account he wrote that two sounds together made the place a scene of horror almost beyond imagining. What two sounds did he name?
answer: The shrieks of the women and the groans of the dying
choices: The shrieks of the women and the groans of the dying
The rattle of chains and the crack of the whip
The roar of the sea and the shouts of the crew
The weeping of children and the prayers of the old
context: Equiano wrote that 'the shrieks of the women, and the groans of the dying, rendered the whole a scene of horror almost inconceivable.' https://www.americanyawp.com/reader/british-north-america/olaudah-equiano-describes-the-middle-passage-1789/

question: In 1788 a small abolition society in Plymouth, England, printed its diagram of the slave ship Brookes, laying out row upon row of human figures in the hold with each man allotted a strip of floor only six feet long and sixteen inches wide. The picture was meant to show how many bodies a trader would cram below to chase a profit. A slaver later admitted the Brookes had once sailed with how many people aboard on a single voyage?
answer: 609 people
choices: 609 people
215 people
330 people
780 people
context: The 1788 Brookes stowage diagram, engraved by Sir William Elford and published in Plymouth, allotted each man six feet by sixteen inches; a trader admitted the ship had once carried as many as 609 people. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooks_(1781_ship)

question: In November 1781, the British slave ship Zong sailed for Jamaica with its captain claiming the ship was running short of drinking water. Over several days the crew began doing something to the enslaved Africans aboard that even hardened slavers were rarely accused of so openly. What did the Zong's crew do?
answer: Threw living captives into the sea
choices: Threw living captives into the sea
Sold the captives to a passing pirate
Abandoned the ship and rowed away
Locked the captives below to starve
context: Over several days from 29 November 1781 the crew threw enslaved Africans alive overboard; roughly 130 were killed, and about ten more jumped to their deaths in defiance. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zong_massacre

question: When the Zong reached Jamaica after its captain had drowned scores of captives at sea, the ship's owners, a Liverpool slave-trading firm, did not face a murder trial. Instead they demanded about thirty pounds for each drowned African as a simple loss of property. The court therefore treated the killings not as murder but as what?
answer: An insurance claim
choices: An insurance claim
A smuggling charge
A mutiny trial
A debt lawsuit
context: The Gregson syndicate had insured the captives at about £30 a head and filed an insurance claim for the 'lost cargo' rather than answering for murder. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zong_massacre

question: The Zong's crew swore they had thrown the captives overboard because the ship was running out of drinking water. But the excuse did not hold: heavy rain had fallen during the very days of the killings, and when the ship finally docked in Jamaica the casks were checked. About how much drinking water was still aboard the Zong when it reached port?
answer: About 420 gallons
choices: About 420 gallons
About 200 gallons
About 50 gallons
About 600 gallons
context: The Zong arrived with 420 gallons still aboard and rain had refilled casks on 1 December, leading historians to suspect the killings were planned insurance fraud. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zong_massacre

question: When the Zong killings came before an English court in 1783 as the insurance case Gregson v Gilbert, the judges did not treat the drowned Africans as murdered people at all. Lord Chief Justice Mansfield reported that the jury saw the deaths as nothing more than a loss of property, comparing the people to what kind of cargo thrown overboard?
answer: Horses
choices: Horses
Barrels
Timber
Grain
context: Mansfield reported the jury's view that 'the Case of Slaves was the same as if Horses had been thrown over board' — the law saw a property loss, not a crime. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zong_massacre

question: Olaudah Equiano carried the news of the Zong massacre to the leading English abolitionist Granville Sharp in March 1783, and Sharp pressed hard to have the crew tried for murder. What came of the case against the men who had drowned the captives?
answer: No one was ever prosecuted
choices: No one was ever prosecuted
The owners collected their insurance payout
The captain alone was hanged
The whole crew was jailed
context: Equiano alerted Granville Sharp, who pressed for murder charges, but no member of the Zong's crew was ever prosecuted; the outrage instead helped fuel the abolition movement. https://blackpast.org/global-african-history/zong-massacre-1781/

question: In February 1987 a band of grave-robbers tunneled into a mud-brick pyramid at Sipan on Peru's north coast and hauled out armloads of Moche gold. The rest of the royal tomb survived unlooted only because of one thing that happened next among the robbers themselves. What was it?
answer: They quarreled over the loot, and one of them tipped off the police
choices: They quarreled over the loot, and one of them tipped off the police
They struck a deeper chamber too heavy to carry out by hand
They feared a curse and refused to disturb the burial further
They ran out of nights before the rainy season flooded the tunnel
context: The looter Ernil Bernal led the huaqueros; a fight over the spoils sent word to the police, who tipped off archaeologist Walter Alva. Alva then excavated the first unlooted tomb of a Moche royal ever found, packed with 451 objects of gold, silver, copper, turquoise and spondylus shell around the warrior-priest now called the Lord of Sipan. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_of_Sipan; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huaca_Rajada

question: The Lord of Sipan was not buried alone: laid in the tomb around the Moche ruler were three young women, two warrior men, a child of about nine, a dog and two llamas. One of the guard's bodies had been deliberately altered before burial in a way meant to bind him to his post forever. What had been done to that guardian?
answer: His feet had been amputated
choices: His feet had been amputated
His eyes had been covered in gold
His hands had been bound in copper
His mouth had been packed with shell
context: One of the warrior-guardians buried with the Lord of Sipan had his feet cut off, as if to guarantee he could never walk away from his duty watching over the dead lord. The ruler himself stood about 1.63m and died aged roughly 35 to 45. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_of_Sipan; world-archaeology.com/features/tombs-of-the-lords-of-sipan
