Mtepe Sawahil
Qasr al-Bahr
context: Husuni Kubwa also had a stepped courtyard that doubled as a warehouse-and-rest-stop where merchants stored goods and reloaded them onto ships. Source: panafrocore.com/2024/03/13/husuni-kubwa-palace-a-brief-history ; nationalgeographic.com/history/history-magazine/article/abandoned-east-african-city-kilwa

question: The Kilwa Chronicle tells how the Persian prince Ali ibn al-Hasan bought the island of Kilwa from its local Bantu king. The price the king named sounds simple, but it took an astonishing amount of one trade good to pay it. According to the chronicle, Ali paid in enough colored cloth to do what?
answer: Stretch all the way around the island's edge
choices: Stretch all the way around the island's edge
Fill the king's largest warehouse to the roof
Drape every house in the king's own town
Load the holds of a hundred trading dhows
context: Legend, per the Kilwa Chronicle. When the king later regretted the deal and tried to take Kilwa back, he found the Persians had dug away the narrow land bridge, so Kilwa was now a true island, cut off and no longer his. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_ibn_al-Hassan_Shirazi ; pieterderideaux.jimdofree.com/.../kilwa-chronicle/

question: In 1414 envoys from the Swahili city of Malindi brought a strange long-necked animal as a gift to the Ming court of China, where it was handed to the admiral Zheng He's fleet. The Chinese had never seen such a creature, and they decided it was a famous mythical beast whose appearance was said to mean a wise and good ruler sat on the throne. What did the Chinese believe the giraffe was?
answer: The qilin, a unicorn-like omen-beast
choices: The qilin, a unicorn-like omen-beast
A young dragon of the eastern sea
The phoenix returned in the flesh
A guardian lion sent from heaven
context: By ancient tradition the qilin appeared only when a wise and virtuous ruler held the throne, so the giraffe became powerful propaganda for the emperor. Source: face2faceafrica.com/article/how-a-giraffe-cemented-east-africas-trade-relations-with-china-in-1414 ; smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/peculiar-story-giraffes-medieval-china

question: Kilwa minted its own copper coins around 1150-1330. In 1944 an Australian soldier, Morry Isenberg, picked some odd old coins off a beach in the Wessel Islands off northern Australia and dropped them in a tin, where they sat for 35 years. When experts finally identified them in 1979, what made the find a real mystery?
answer: They were medieval Kilwa coins, the oldest foreign object found in Australia
choices: They were medieval Kilwa coins, the oldest foreign object found in Australia
They were forged copies stamped centuries after Kilwa fell
They matched no mint and could not be dated at all
They were Portuguese coins lost in a later shipwreck
context: Nobody knows how copper coins from a medieval African city crossed the entire Indian Ocean to a beach in northern Australia. Source: australiangeographic.com.au/history-culture/2014/08/mystery-of-ancient-african-coins-found-in-australia/ ; thehistoryblog.com/archives/26800

question: The whole Indian Ocean trade ran on the monsoon winds, which for three or four months blew toward the East African coast, then reversed and blew back toward Arabia and India. Because of this rhythm, a merchant who sailed in on one wind often could not leave for months. Historians point to that forced wait as the very thing that created the Swahili. How did the stranded waiting build a blended people?
answer: Marooned traders married into local families
choices: Marooned traders married into local families
Idle crews built the coral-stone palaces
Waiting merchants taught the locals Arabic
Stuck sailors drew the first coast maps
context: With the wind against them, traders waited out the season ashore, married into Bantu families, and over generations the African and Arab worlds fused into the Swahili. Source: courses.lumenlearning.com/suny-hccc-worldcivilization/chapter/the-swahili-culture/

question: Kilwa's golden age ended with the Portuguese. In 1505 Francisco de Almeida landed about 500 troops, fought through the narrow streets, and plundered and burned the city. To hold the harbor for Portugal's ships bound for India, Almeida left a permanent mark on the conquered town. What did the Portuguese build at Kilwa?
answer: A stone fort, the Gereza, to control the harbor
choices: A stone fort, the Gereza, to control the harbor
A new cathedral over the Great Mosque
A treaty-house for the captured sultan
A shipyard to repair their war fleet
context: Three years earlier Vasco da Gama had already forced Kilwa's ruler to promise yearly tribute in gold and pearls. After taking Kilwa, the same Portuguese fleet sailed north and sacked and burned Mombasa on 13 August 1505, the second great Swahili port to fall in one voyage. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Kilwa ; zum.de/whkmla/military/16cen/kilwa1505.html

question: On May 24, 1844, Samuel Morse sat in a room of the U.S. Capitol and tapped out the first long-distance telegraph message down a wire to Baltimore. What four words did he send?
answer: "What hath God wrought"
choices: "What hath God wrought"
"Come at once, Vail"
"The line is open"
"Glory to the Union"
context: The line ran from the Old Supreme Court Chamber in the Capitol to Morse's partner Alfred Vail in Baltimore. The four words are a Bible verse, Numbers 23:23, and 17-year-old Annie Ellsworth picked them — Morse had promised her the first dispatch because she rushed him the news that his funding bill had passed Congress. Sources: history.house.gov; Smithsonian National Museum of American History nmah_713485; loc.gov.

question: Three weeks before Samuel Morse's famous official message, his half-finished telegraph line was already being tested. On May 1, 1844, word that the Whigs had nominated Henry Clay for president was wired from Baltimore to Washington — and a train was also steaming toward Washington carrying the very same news. What happened that made this moment historic?
answer: The wired news arrived about an hour before the train carrying it
choices: The wired news arrived about an hour before the train carrying it
The train's passengers cheered when they saw the message posted
Clay telegraphed his own thanks back down the line
Morse rode the train to confirm the wire had worked
context: The telegraphed report beat the train into Washington by roughly 64 minutes — the first time information traveled faster than the person carrying it. Distance had been annihilated: news could now outrun the messenger. Source: Boundary Stones (WETA), 'What Hath God Wrought: The Long Road to Washington's First Telegraph.'

question: When the law was given at Mount Sinai, the whole mountain was wrapped in smoke 'like the smoke of a kiln' and quaked while thunder rolled and lightning flashed. One more thing pierced the chaos and kept growing louder and louder until the people trembled. What was it?
answer: The blast of a trumpet, a ram's-horn shofar
choices: The blast of a trumpet, a ram's-horn shofar
The roar of a great waterfall below
The drumming of an unseen army
The howling of wind through the rocks
context: Exodus 19:16-19 describes the shofar (ram's-horn trumpet) sounding 'long and growing louder' as the mountain smoked and quaked. The shofar became Israel's instrument for sacred, awe-filled moments. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Sinai_(Bible); bible.usccb.org/bible/exodus/19.

question: The book of Exodus says God himself produced the writing on the first two stone tablets given at Sinai — the only time the Bible describes something as inscribed personally by God. The phrase it uses for HOW they were written is famous. What is that striking phrase?
answer: Written 'by the finger of God'
choices: Written 'by the finger of God'
Carved 'with a tongue of flame'
Burned 'by the breath of heaven'
Cut 'with the sword of the word'
context: Exodus 31:18 says the tablets were 'written with the finger of God.' Nothing else in the Bible is described as inscribed directly by God. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tablets_of_Stone (citing Exodus 31:18).

question: Moses came down Mount Sinai carrying the stone tablets and found the people had built a golden calf and were dancing around it. His anger 'burned.' In that fury, what did Moses do with the tablets right there at the foot of the mountain?
answer: Smashed them to pieces on the ground
choices: Smashed them to pieces on the ground
Hid them inside his cloak
Held them up to silence the crowd
Buried them beneath the altar
context: Exodus 32:19 — seeing the golden calf and the dancing, Moses 'threw the tablets out of his hands, breaking them at the foot of the mountain.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tablets_of_Stone; biblehub.com/exodus/32-20.htm.

question: After confronting the golden calf at Sinai, Moses burned it, then ground the gold down to fine powder and scattered it over water. He then forced the Israelites to do one humiliating thing with that water. What did he make them do?
answer: Drink it down
choices: Drink it down
Wash their faces in it
Carry it back up the mountain
Pour it over the altar
context: Exodus 32:20 — Moses 'strewed it upon the water, and made the children of Israel drink of it,' forcing them to swallow their own false god. Source: biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/32-20.htm (KJV Exodus 32:20).

question: Aaron was the one who had actually made the golden calf out of the people's gold. When Moses demanded an explanation, Aaron dodged the blame in a famously feeble way. How did Aaron say the calf came to be?
answer: He threw the gold in the fire and 'out came this calf'
choices: He threw the gold in the fire and 'out came this calf'
A stranger had cast it while he slept
The people had forced his hand with threats
He had shaped it only as a harmless toy
context: Exodus 32:24 — Aaron claims he threw the gold into the fire 'and out came this calf,' blaming the fire rather than his own hands. Source: bibleproject.com/bible/nlt/exodus/32/; enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-32/.

question: The Code of Hammurabi survives carved on a black basalt stele over seven feet tall, topped by a carved scene of King Hammurabi standing before a seated god who hands him a ring and a rod as symbols of law-giving power. Which god is shown granting Hammurabi that authority?
answer: Shamash, the sun god
choices: Shamash, the sun god
Marduk, the chief god of Babylon
Enlil, the king of the gods
Ea, the god of the deep
context: The relief atop the Louvre's Hammurabi stele shows Shamash, the sun god and patron of justice, handing the king a ring and rod. Hammurabi's law thus claims a god-given mandate to a single ruler. Source: louvre.fr/en/the-code-of-hammurabi; smarthistory.org/hammurabi-2/.

question: At Sinai the people were so terrified by the fire, smoke, and the voice from the mountain that they stood far off and begged Moses to be their go-between. What did the people plead with Moses in Exodus 20:19?
answer: 'You speak to us, but do not let God speak to us, lest we die'
choices: 'You speak to us, but do not let God speak to us, lest we die'
'Lead us away from this mountain at once'
'Tell us the words later, when the fire has passed'
'Let the elders alone come near to listen'
context: Exodus 20:18-19 — the people 'stood at a distance' and begged Moses to receive the words so they would not have to hear the voice directly and die. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Sinai_(Bible) (citing Exodus 20:18-19).

question: After the first tablets lay shattered, God provided a second set — but the renewed covenant was made by a striking split of labor between God and Moses. Exodus 34:1 describes who did what. How were the second tablets produced?
answer: Moses carved the blank stones, then God re-wrote the words on them
choices: Moses carved the blank stones, then God re-wrote the words on them
God produced both the stones and the writing again
Moses both carved the stones and copied the words himself
An angel cut the stones and Moses inscribed them
context: Exodus 34:1 — God tells Moses to cut two new tablets himself, and God will write the words on them. The renewed covenant is thus cut by human hands but inscribed by God. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tablets_of_Stone (Exodus 34:1).

question: The Sabbath commandment ordered a day of rest, and it reached people no other ancient law protected. In Exodus 20:10, alongside sons and daughters, which group is explicitly guaranteed that same day of rest?
answer: Slaves, work animals, and the foreigner within the gates
choices: Slaves, work animals, and the foreigner within the gates
The king, the priests, and the temple guards
Travelers and merchants passing through the land
The firstborn son of every household
context: Exodus 20:10 / Deut 5:14 extend rest to son, daughter, male and female slave, the ox and donkey, and 'the foreigner within your gates' — a guaranteed day off for slaves and animals alike, unheard of in the ancient world. Source: biblehub.com/exodus/20-10.htm; biblehub.com/deuteronomy/5-14.htm.

question: We call them the Ten Commandments, but the Hebrew Bible never uses the word 'commandments' for them at all. It calls them 'Aseret ha-Devarim.' What does that Hebrew name literally mean?
answer: The Ten Words
choices: The Ten Words
The Ten Laws
The Ten Judgments
The Ten Decrees
context: 'Aseret ha-Devarim' means the Ten Words (or Ten Utterances). The Greek Septuagint rendered this 'deka logoi,' the source of our word 'Decalogue.' Source: jewishvirtuallibrary.org/decalogue; thetorah.com/article/the-decalogue-ten-commandments-or-ten-statements (Deut 4:13, 10:4).

question: The Ten Words are written as flat, absolute commands — 'You shall not steal,' full stop. Every other ancient Near Eastern law code, including Hammurabi's, was written in a completely different grammar. What form did those other codes take?
answer: Case law: 'If a man does X, then Y follows'
choices: Case law: 'If a man does X, then Y follows'
Blessings and curses: 'Do this and live; do that and be cut off'
Prayers asking the gods to punish wrongdoers
Lists of rewards for the obedient
context: Scholars call the Ten Words 'apodictic' (flat command, no penalty) versus the 'casuistic' case-law of Hammurabi and other codes, framed as 'if a man does X, then Y.' Source: jewishvirtuallibrary.org/decalogue; openmedia.yale.edu Yale RLST 145 transcript 10.

question: Hammurabi's famous rule 'an eye for an eye' (Law 196) sounds like equal justice, but it did not apply equally. A noble who blinded another noble lost his own eye — but if the victim was a slave, the offender simply paid silver. How much silver was a slave's eye reckoned to be worth?
answer: Half the slave's purchase price
choices: Half the slave's purchase price
A fixed fine of sixty shekels
One-third of the slave's purchase price
Twice the slave's purchase price
context: Hammurabi's Law 196-199 graded penalties by class: destroying a noble's eye cost your own, but a slave's eye was paid off in silver, valued at half the slave's price. The Decalogue, by contrast, bound everyone equally. Source: courses.lumenlearning.com (Law 196-199); encyclopedia.com 'Class and Society in Ancient Near Eastern Law.'

question: Hammurabi's laws were handed down by a god-king and applied differently depending on a person's rank. The Ten Words were delivered very differently at Sinai. According to Exodus, how did the people first receive them?
answer: Proclaimed aloud to the whole assembled people at once
choices: Proclaimed aloud to the whole assembled people at once
Written privately and given only to the priests
Revealed in a dream to Moses alone, who recited them later
Posted on a stone pillar for scribes to copy
context: Unlike a king's decree handed to elites, the Decalogue was spoken directly to the whole assembled nation at Sinai, making the entire people — not just rulers — party to the covenant. Source: britannica.com/topic/Sinai-covenant; crosstocrown.org Tablets of Stone ch.6.

question: At the ruined Toltec city of Tula in central Mexico, four nearly identical giant figures still stand on top of Pyramid B, each carved from basalt, about 15 feet tall, and built from four stacked stone drums. What does each of these towering carved figures depict?
answer: A warrior dressed for battle
choices: A warrior dressed for battle
A seated and robed priest
A coiled feathered serpent
A kneeling captive bound with rope
context: Nicknamed the 'Atlanteans,' the four warriors each wear a tall feathered drum-headdress and a butterfly-shaped chest plate, carry an atlatl (spear-thrower), and wear a round solar-disk back-plate. They likely once stood as columns holding up the temple roof. The four are so alike that Toltec stone workshops must have mass-produced huge sculptures to a standard pattern. Source: World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Toltec_Civilization/; EBSCO Research Starters 'Toltecs Build Tula.'

question: Long after Tula fell, the Aztecs looked back on the Toltecs as a lost golden-age people, the masters of every craft. The Aztecs took the very name of that people and turned it into an everyday word in their Nahuatl language. When an Aztec called a person a 'Toltecatl,' what did the word mean?
answer: A skilled artist or craftsman
choices: A skilled artist or craftsman
A foreign tribute-payer
A wandering desert nomad
A priest of the feathered serpent
context: 'Toltecatl' came to mean artist, craftsman, or wise man, and 'toltecayotl' (Toltec-ness) meant art, culture, and civilization itself — the opposite of 'chichimecayotl,' the savage nomadic state. To say someone had a 'Toltec heart' meant they excelled at their craft. Source: Wikipedia 'Toltecayotl'; World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Toltec_Civilization/.

question: On May 10, 1869, two crews finally met at Promontory Summit, Utah: the Central Pacific Railroad, which had been building east from Sacramento, and the Union Pacific, which had been building west from Omaha. To celebrate joining their tracks into the first railroad across America, the bosses tapped in one last ceremonial spike made of a very precious material. What was that famous last spike made of?
answer: Gold
choices: Gold
Iron
Copper
Bronze
context: The golden spike was 17.6-carat gold engraved to honor the railroad's completion. It was never left in the track — it was pulled out after the ceremony and given to Stanford University, where it is still on display. (Three other ceremonial spikes were also tapped that day: a second gold one, a silver spike from Nevada, and a blended iron-silver-gold spike from Arizona, all into a polished laurelwood tie.) Source: Union Pacific official history, up.com/about-us/history/golden-spike.

question: At Promontory Summit on the day the transcontinental railroad was finished, two steam locomotives rolled up until they stood nose-to-nose: the Central Pacific's 'Jupiter' and the Union Pacific's 'No. 119.' A photographer captured the rival crews leaning out to shake hands in the narrow gap between the engines. By what nickname is that famous photo known?
answer: The Wedding of the Rails
choices: The Wedding of the Rails
The Meeting of the Engines
The Last Spike
The Golden Junction
context: The journey from coast to coast dropped from four-plus months to about one week once the rails were joined. The two engines facing each other — Jupiter pointing east, No. 119 pointing west — made the photo an instant icon. Source: NPS 'Everlasting Steam: The Story of Jupiter and No. 119,' nps.gov/gosp.

question: The golden spike was wired to the telegraph so the whole nation could 'hear' each blow land. Leland Stanford, president of the Central Pacific, lifted the heavy silver maul, took aim at the spike, and swung in front of the watching crowd. What happened on that first swing?
answer: He swung and missed the spike completely
choices: He swung and missed the spike completely
He drove the spike in with one clean blow
He shattered the soft gold spike in half
He stopped and handed the maul to a worker
context: Then Union Pacific's Thomas Durant — nursing a headache from too much partying — swung and missed too, and the construction bosses had to finish the job. After the misses, the telegraph operator simply tapped out the message himself: a single word flashed across America — 'DONE.' Cannons fired in San Francisco and the Liberty Bell was rung in Philadelphia. Source: Salt Lake Magazine, saltlakemagazine.com/golden-spike.

question: On April 28, 1869, the Central Pacific raced to lay an unheard-of amount of track in a single day, finishing with 10 miles and 56 feet of rail set down by hand — a record no hand crew has ever beaten. The very last rails were carried by a team of eight Irishmen, each man estimated to have lifted about 125 tons of iron that day. When lunch came and fresh workers were offered to relieve the eight, what did they do?
answer: They turned down the relief and carried the rails the rest of the day
choices: They turned down the relief and carried the rails the rest of the day
They handed off to the fresh crew and finally rested
They quit early, too exhausted to keep lifting iron
They refused to work again until they were paid more
context: The eight rail handlers were named in the record: Michael Shay, Thomas Daley, George Elliott, Michael Sullivan, Edward Killeen, Patrick Joyce, Michael Kennedy, and Fred McNamara. Reporters timed cars of rail being emptied in 75-80 seconds each across the roughly 12-hour day. Source: Irish America, irishamerica.com 'April 28, 1869'; CPRR Museum 'Ten Mile Day.'

question: To carry the Central Pacific over the Sierra Nevada at Donner Pass, thousands of Chinese workers — about eight in ten of the railroad's whole western crew — had to keep blasting rock tunnels straight through the winter of 1866-67, when forty-four storms buried the summit under more than forty feet of snow. To reach the granite and keep drilling, where did these crews live and work for months on end?
answer: In snow tunnels they dug, living underground by lantern light
choices: In snow tunnels they dug, living underground by lantern light
In heated railcars hauled up to the summit each night
In timber bunkhouses built above the level of the snow
In caves they blasted out of the granite cliffs nearby
context: They carved snow tunnels 50 to 500 feet long with air shafts bored through the walls, almost never seeing the sky. Leland Stanford himself testified of the Chinese workers, 'Without them it would be impossible to complete the western portion of this great national enterprise.' Source: PBS American Experience 'Tunneling in the Sierra Nevada'; Stanford Chinese Railroad Workers Project FAQ, web.stanford.edu/group/chineserailroad.

question: In summer 1958 Jack Kilby was so new at Texas Instruments that he had no vacation time, so while nearly the whole company went on its mass summer break he worked alone in an empty lab. There he had the idea that became the first integrated circuit. On September 12, 1958, he showed it to TI executives, flipped a switch, and got proof it worked when something appeared on an oscilloscope screen. What did they see?
answer: A green wavy line rolling across the screen
choices: A green wavy line rolling across the screen
A row of numbers counting upward
A bright flash that then went dark
A steady straight line holding flat
context: Kilby's first chip was a rough patchwork of germanium holding a transistor, a capacitor, and resistors joined by fine gold 'flying-wires' on one piece of semiconductor. The green wavy line was a working oscillator. Kilby and Robert Noyce are both credited as inventors of the integrated circuit; Kilby won the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics. Source: Computer History Museum, Silicon Engine; TI.com 'From idea to invention'.

question: By the 1950s engineers building complex machines hit what they called the 'tyranny of numbers': a single machine needed so many separate transistors, resistors, and capacitors that nobody could reliably wire them all together by hand. What was the breakthrough that solved this — letting a whole circuit live on one block of semiconductor?
answer: The integrated circuit
choices: The integrated circuit
The vacuum tube
The copper wiring harness
The magnetic tape reel
context: Instead of soldering thousands of separate parts, the integrated circuit put the transistors, resistors, and capacitors all onto one chip. Jack Kilby built the first one in 1958; Robert Noyce at Fairchild devised a version in 1959 using the 'planar process' that printed the connecting wires right onto the chip, making mass production practical. Source: Computer History Museum, Silicon Engine: 'All Semiconductor Solid Circuit is Demonstrated'.

question: In 1971 the Intel 4004 became the first microprocessor — an entire computer's central processor squeezed onto a single chip, packing 2,300 transistors into a die about 12 square millimeters. Its designer, Federico Faggin, was so proud of the chip that he left a personal mark on it. What did he do?
answer: Etched his initials 'F.F.' onto the chip itself
choices: Etched his initials 'F.F.' onto the chip itself
Mailed the first chip to his old professor
Named the chip after his daughter
Kept the first chip locked in a safe
context: The Intel 4004 shrank a whole CPU onto one chip — the leap that led toward personal computers. Faggin's initials are etched right into the silicon. The path ran from the 1947 Bell Labs transistor, to Kilby and Noyce's integrated circuit, to the microprocessor that built the modern world. Source: Computer History Museum, Silicon Engine: 'Microprocessor Integrates CPU Function onto a Single Chip'; IEEE Spectrum 'Chip Hall of Fame: Intel 4004'.

question: After ten years of war, the Greek army still could not break through the walls of Troy. So they built one enormous thing, left it standing outside the gates, and pretended to sail home in defeat. What was it -- and what was its secret?
answer: A giant hollow wooden horse with Greek warriors hidden inside it
choices: A giant hollow wooden horse with Greek warriors hidden inside it
A towering bronze statue of the goddess Athena holding a spear
A huge wooden tower on wheels packed with barrels of fire
An immense heap of treasure and weapons piled before the gates
context: The Trojans dragged it inside themselves; that night the hidden men climbed out and opened the gates. This is where the phrase 'Trojan horse' comes from -- any gift or offer with an attack hidden inside (in computing, a 'Trojan' is malware disguised as something harmless). Legend, from Homer and Virgil. Source: Britannica, 'Trojan horse'; Wikipedia, 'Trojan Horse'.

question: Laocoon, a priest of Troy, saw the danger in the wooden horse and hurled his spear into its side, warning his people: 'I fear the Greeks, even those bearing gifts.' Then a sudden horror fell on him that the Trojans read as a sign from the gods to bring the horse in instead. What struck Laocoon down?
answer: Two giant serpents rose from the sea and crushed him and both his sons
choices: Two giant serpents rose from the sea and crushed him and both his sons
A bolt of lightning split the sky and struck him and his sons dead
A sudden plague swept the temple and killed him and his household
The earth cracked open beneath the altar and swallowed him whole
context: So the warning that should have saved Troy is exactly what doomed it -- the Trojans took the serpents as proof the gods wanted the horse inside. The Latin line 'Timeo Danaos et dona ferentes' comes from Virgil's Aeneid; the marble statue of Laocoon and his sons in the serpents' coils was dug up in Rome in 1506 and now stands in the Vatican Museums. Legend. Source: Virgil, Aeneid Book 2 (via World History Encyclopedia, 'Laocoon').

question: Before Rome wrote down its laws around 450 BC, only a small circle of upper-class priests called the pontifices knew what the law actually said. They alone interpreted the old customs, all of it kept in their memory. Then the Romans carved the laws onto bronze tablets and did the one thing that ended the priests' secret hold on the law. What did they do with the tablets?
answer: They bolted the tablets up in the Forum, where every citizen could read the same law
choices: They bolted the tablets up in the Forum, where every citizen could read the same law
They handed the tablets to an assembly of plebeians to guard in secret
They made the priests swear a public oath to interpret the tablets honestly
They burned the old memorized customs so only the new tablets remained
context: The Twelve Tables (c. 451-450 BC) were posted in the Forum, the open square every Roman crossed, so a plebeian and a patrician could read the very same law with their own eyes. That broke the pontifices' monopoly: no one could now claim the law said something secret. Historians count it a distant ancestor of the Western ideal that the law is written down, public, and the same for everyone. Sources: worldhistory.org/Twelve_Tables; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve_Tables

question: Table III of the Twelve Tables dealt with Romans who could not pay their debts. An unpaid debtor was bound in chains weighing at least fifteen pounds, and if no one paid for his release by the third market day, the law allowed his creditors to do something shocking. What could they legally do to him?
answer: Cut his body into pieces, and divide the parts among themselves
choices: Cut his body into pieces, and divide the parts among themselves
Brand his forehead with a hot iron and then set him free
Sell him across the Tiber into slavery in a foreign land
Throw him from the Tarpeian Rock onto the stones below
context: The Latin reads 'partis secanto' — let them cut the parts. The clause even added that if the creditors cut more or less than their share, it was no crime. It is the most notorious line in the Twelve Tables, a glimpse of how harsh early Roman debt law could be. Sources: thelatinlibrary.com/law/12tables.html; thecollector.com/twelve-tables-rome

question: The Rock of Gibraltar guards the strait between Spain and Africa, and its name is a worn-down version of the Arabic 'Jabal Tariq.' In 711 the Berber general Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed there to invade Spain and the great rock was named in his honor. What does 'Jabal Tariq' mean?
answer: The Mountain of Tariq
choices: The Mountain of Tariq
The Gateway of Tariq
The Harbor of Tariq
The Sword of Tariq
context: Tariq ibn Ziyad led the Umayyad invasion of Spain in 711. The landing rock became 'Jabal Tariq' ('Mountain of Tariq'), which English later mangled into 'Gibraltar' — so the famous rock still carries his name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_Caliphate

question: In 750 the Abbasid revolution crushed the Umayyad dynasty at the Battle of the Zab and hunted down the ruling family. One young prince, Abd al-Rahman I, escaped the slaughter of his relatives and fled west across the whole length of North Africa. Where did he finally rebuild a new Umayyad state?
answer: Cordoba, in Spain
choices: Cordoba, in Spain
Cairo, in Egypt
Kairouan, in Tunisia
Tangier, in Morocco
context: Abd al-Rahman I was the sole prince to survive the Abbasid massacre. After fleeing across North Africa he founded an Umayyad state at Cordoba in Spain that became a famed center of learning. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_Caliphate

question: In 1550 the Spanish emperor Charles V did something almost no empire has ever done: he ordered all new conquests in the Americas to STOP, and summoned a panel of judges to Valladolid to settle a single question in public, under his own crown. What was the question they were ordered to settle?
answer: Whether it was just to wage war on the native peoples of the Americas
choices: Whether it was just to wage war on the native peoples of the Americas
Whether to share captured gold among the conquering soldiers
Whether to build a new cathedral in the conquered cities
Whether to send more ships across the Atlantic that year
context: Charles V halted new conquests and convened the Valladolid debate (1550-51) to ask whether the conquest of the Indigenous peoples was just. It is one of the only times an empire paused its own expansion to argue, openly and under its own crown, whether what it was doing was right. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valladolid_debate

question: At Valladolid, the scholar Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda built his case for war on the native peoples atop Aristotle's idea of the 'natural slave' — a class of people he claimed were born to be ruled by their betters. To rank the native peoples beneath the Spanish, what startling comparison did Sepúlveda's argument reach for?
answer: They stood to Spaniards as children to adults, as women to men, even as apes to men
choices: They stood to Spaniards as children to adults, as women to men, even as apes to men
They were a lost tribe of Israel scattered after a forgotten war
They were descended from sailors blown off course centuries earlier
They were a people cursed to wander after defying their own gods
context: Sepúlveda argued the native peoples were as inferior to Spaniards 'as children to adults, as women to men,' and even fell 'between apes and men' — so, he claimed, it was natural and right for Spain to rule them. It was a serious, learned argument of its day, not a cartoon; the point of Valladolid is that the West argued such claims out in the open. Bartolomé de las Casas answered that the native peoples had real laws, agriculture, and religion and were 'fully capable of reason.' Source: https://www.columbia.edu/acis/ets/CCREAD/sepulved.htm

question: The Thirty Years' War began in 1618 when angry Protestants in Prague threw two Catholic officials and their secretary out a castle window about 70 feet up. Astonishingly, all three men survived the fall. What had they landed in that broke their fall?
answer: A pile of dung
choices: A pile of dung
A flowing moat
A stack of timber
A market awning
context: The 23 May 1618 Defenestration of Prague: Bohemian Protestants hurled two Catholic imperial regents and their secretary from a Prague Castle window roughly 70 feet up, and all three landed on a dung heap and lived. Catholics called the survival a miracle; Protestants said it was just the manure. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defenestration ; private-prague-guide.com 'The Second Defenestration of Prague')

question: The French Wars of Religion began on 1 March 1562 when the Duke Francois de Guise and his men killed about a hundred Huguenots in the town of Wassy. The victims were not soldiers but ordinary people, caught while they were worshipping. Where had they gathered to worship?
answer: In a barn
choices: In a barn
In a cathedral
In a town hall
In a vineyard
context: The Massacre of Vassy (Wassy), 1 March 1562: the Duke Francois de Guise and his men killed roughly a hundred Huguenots who were worshipping in a barn, lighting the fuse for thirty-six years of civil war. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_of_Vassy ; Musee protestant, 'The eight wars of religion 1562-1598')

question: During the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre of 24 August 1572, Catholics in Paris hunted Huguenots house by house through the streets. To keep from killing one another in the chaos, the attackers all wore the same mark on their sleeves. What did they wear so they could tell friend from foe?
answer: White scarves
choices: White scarves
Red crosses
Black ribbons
Iron badges
context: The St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre began in the dark hours of 24 August 1572, set off by church bells tolling for matins near the Louvre. Catholic attackers wore white scarves or armbands on their sleeves to distinguish friend from foe as they hunted Huguenots house by house. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Bartholomew's_Day_massacre)

question: On St. Bartholomew's Day in 1572, men of the Duke of Guise dragged the Huguenot leader Admiral Gaspard de Coligny from his bed and killed him. A killer reportedly said he never saw anyone die more steadfastly. What did the men then do with Coligny's body?
answer: Threw it from the window
choices: Threw it from the window
Burned it in the courtyard
Sank it in the Seine
Buried it in secret
context: Gaspard de Coligny was dragged from his bed, killed by the Duke of Guise's men, and his body was thrown out the window into the street. The historian Jacques-Auguste de Thou recorded a killer saying Coligny 'never saw anyone less afraid in so great a peril, nor die more steadfastly.' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Bartholomew's_Day_massacre, quoting Jacques-Auguste de Thou)

question: In 1598 King Henry IV ended the French Wars of Religion with the Edict of Nantes. Beyond letting Huguenots worship and hold public office, the edict gave them a guarantee that no mere promise of tolerance could match: it let them keep more than a hundred of one specific thing across France. What did it let them keep?
answer: Fortified towns they could garrison
choices: Fortified towns they could garrison
Seats on the royal council
Their own printing presses
Tax-free trading harbors
context: The Edict of Nantes, promulgated at Nantes on 13 April 1598, let Huguenots worship in many parts of the kingdom (not Paris), opened universities and office to them, and let them keep over a hundred fortified 'places of safety' they could garrison, including La Rochelle, Montauban, Montpellier, and Saumur. Catholicism stayed the state religion. (britannica.com/event/Edict-of-Nantes ; worldhistory.org)

question: The 1555 Peace of Augsburg tried to end Germany's religious war by letting each prince pick Catholicism or Lutheranism for his own land -- 'whose realm, his religion.' But it had a fatal flaw: it recognized only those two faiths and refused to include one fast-growing Protestant group, which helped set up the far bloodier Thirty Years' War. Which group did the peace leave out?
answer: The Calvinists
choices: The Calvinists
The Anabaptists
The Jesuits
The Orthodox
context: The Peace of Augsburg (1555) enshrined cuius regio, eius religio -- 'whose realm, his religion' -- but recognized only Catholics and Lutherans, leaving out the Calvinists. That omission helped set the stage for the much deadlier Thirty Years' War (1618-1648). (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuius_regio,_eius_religio ; encyclopedia.com 'Augsburg, Religious Peace of 1555')

question: When news of the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre reached Rome, Pope Gregory XIII did not mourn -- he celebrated, ordering a Te Deum of thanksgiving sung and striking a commemorative medal. The blunt Latin words stamped on that medal named the killing for exactly what it was. What did the medal's inscription call the event?
answer: The Slaughter of the Huguenots
choices: The Slaughter of the Huguenots
The Triumph of True Faith
The Peace of Christendom
The Deliverance of Paris
context: Pope Gregory XIII greeted the massacre with a Te Deum and a commemorative medal reading 'VGONOTTORVM STRAGES 1572' -- 'Slaughter of the Huguenots, 1572' -- its reverse showing an angel with cross and drawn sword striking down the fallen Protestants. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Bartholomew's_Day_massacre ; Carleton, 'Medal in Commemoration of the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre')

question: In 1878, long before they built anything that could fly, the Wright brothers' father came home with a small toy that he tossed into the air. It buzzed up to the ceiling, fluttered, and sank to the floor, and the two boys never forgot it. What was this toy that first set them dreaming of flight?
answer: A little helicopter of paper, bamboo and cork
choices: A little helicopter of paper, bamboo and cork
A wooden glider carved like a bird
A brass model of a hot-air balloon
A kite shaped like an eagle
context: Orville and Wilbur Wright recalled watching it 'fly across the room till it struck the ceiling, where it fluttered awhile, and finally sank to the floor.' Their father, Milton Wright, brought it home in 1878. Source: AOPA, 'What you never knew about the Wright brothers' (aopa.org).

question: The men who built the first airplane were not professors, scientists, or trained engineers. Neither Orville nor Wilbur Wright ever earned a high school diploma, and they taught themselves by reading. What was their actual day job back home in Dayton, Ohio?
answer: They built and sold bicycles in their own shop
choices: They built and sold bicycles in their own shop
They were professors at a university
They worked as railroad engineers
They ran a newspaper printing press
context: The Wright Cycle Company sold bikes the brothers built themselves, including their 'Van Cleve' and 'St. Clair' models. The mechanical skill they learned fixing and building bicycles is what let them build a flying machine. Source: Wikipedia, 'Wright Cycle Company'; AOPA (aopa.org).

question: On the morning of December 17, 1903, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville Wright lay flat on the lower wing and flew the first powered, controlled airplane in history while Wilbur ran alongside the wingtip. This single flight changed the world. How long did it actually last?
answer: About 12 seconds
choices: About 12 seconds
About 8 minutes
About half an hour
About two hours
context: Twelve seconds, covering 120 feet, at 10:35 a.m. into a 27-mph wind. A tiny hop, but it was the first time a powered, heavier-than-air machine carried a person under control. Source: NPS, 'First Flight' (nps.gov); Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum (airandspace.si.edu).

question: In 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first human to walk on the Moon. To honor how far flight had come in just 66 years, he carried a small relic of the very first airplane all the way to the lunar surface. What did Armstrong take with him to the Moon?
answer: A piece of wood from the 1903 Flyer's propeller and a swatch of its wing cloth
choices: A piece of wood from the 1903 Flyer's propeller and a swatch of its wing cloth
A photograph of Orville and Wilbur Wright
A bolt from the 1903 Flyer's engine
Wilbur Wright's pocket watch
context: Armstrong carried wood from the propeller and a piece of unbleached muslin from the wing, linking the first 12-second flight at Kitty Hawk to the first Moon landing. Source: AOPA (aopa.org).

question: Other inventors could build wings and engines, but their machines kept crashing because the pilot could not keep them level. The Wright brothers' great breakthrough was a way to tip the plane and turn it by physically twisting the very tips of the wings in opposite directions. What was this control method called?
answer: Wing-warping
choices: Wing-warping
Tail-dragging
Air-braking
Skid-steering
context: Wing-warping let the Wrights control roll, the third piece of true three-axis control (pitch, roll, and yaw). Wilbur reportedly got the idea while idly twisting an empty long cardboard bicycle inner-tube box in the shop and noticing it could twist while staying rigid. Source: Wikipedia, 'Wing warping'; wright-brothers.org.

question: The Wright brothers needed a gasoline engine light enough to fly, but no company could build one. So a machinist in their bicycle shop built one from scratch in about six weeks, working from rough sketches with no formal plans. Who built the engine that powered the first flight?
answer: Charlie Taylor, the brothers' shop machinist
choices: Charlie Taylor, the brothers' shop machinist
Henry Ford, the automobile maker
Thomas Edison, the inventor
Glenn Curtiss, a rival airplane builder
context: Charlie Taylor's engine was a 4-cylinder of about 12 horsepower. To save weight he cast its engine block from aluminum, the first time aluminum was ever used in an aircraft engine. Source: NPS, 'Wright Flyer' (nps.gov); macsmotorcitygarage.com.

question: Orville and Wilbur Wright flipped a coin to decide who would get to fly first. Wilbur won the toss and made the first attempt on December 14, 1903, but he pulled the nose up too sharply, stalled, and dove into the sand after only about three seconds. Because of that, what happened on December 17?
answer: Orville took the controls and made the famous successful flight
choices: Orville took the controls and made the famous successful flight
Wilbur flew first again and finally succeeded
They called off all flying until the spring
They flipped the coin a second time
context: Wilbur's December 14 try ended in a harmless nose-dive into the soft sand. Three days later it was Orville's turn at the controls for the first true flight. Source: Wikipedia, 'Wright brothers'; NPS, 'First Flight' (nps.gov).

question: Within minutes of making history at Kitty Hawk on December 17, 1903, the Wright brothers nearly lost their machine entirely. A sudden gust of wind tumbled the parked Flyer over and over across the sand and even caught one of the helpers, rolling him along inside it. What became of the 1903 Flyer after that gust?
answer: It was damaged badly and never flew again
choices: It was damaged badly and never flew again
They repaired it and flew it for years
They flew it home to Dayton the next week
They sold it to the Smithsonian intact
context: The gust caught lifesaver John T. Daniels and rolled him in the machine; he was shaken but unhurt. The Flyer was wrecked beyond simple repair and never flew again. Source: NPS, 'First Flight' (nps.gov); Wikipedia, 'Wright brothers'.

question: The Wright brothers made four flights on December 17, 1903, each one longer than the last. The first was just a 120-foot hop. Wilbur flew the fourth and best one of the day, going far enough that the era of brief hops was clearly over. How far did that fourth flight go?
answer: 852 feet in 59 seconds
choices: 852 feet in 59 seconds
410 feet in 28 seconds
1,340 feet in 95 seconds
2,100 feet in 140 seconds
context: Orville's telegram home read 'Success four flights Thursday morning... longest 57 seconds inform Press home Christmas' - the telegraph operator garbled the 59 as 57 and even misspelled Orville's name. Source: Library of Congress original telegram (loc.gov); Wright State University Libraries.

question: When the Wright brothers needed propellers, they found there was no real science of how a propeller should be shaped, so they had to invent it. Their key insight was that a propeller is not really a kind of screw at all. So what did they realize a propeller actually is?
answer: A wing turned sideways, spinning in a vertical circle
choices: A wing turned sideways, spinning in a vertical circle
A simple paddle that pushes air backward
A screw that bites into the air like wood
A fan that only cools the engine
context: Treating the propeller as 'a wing rotating in the vertical plane,' the Wrights designed theirs from their own wind-tunnel airfoil data and computed the thrust to within about 1% of what the propellers actually delivered. Source: Wikipedia, 'Wright brothers'; Hartzell Propeller (hartzellprop.com).

question: In 1901 the Wright brothers built a wooden wind tunnel in their shop and tested tiny model wings inside it. The results shocked them: the published wing data from the world's most famous glider pioneer, the German Otto Lilienthal, simply did not match what the brothers measured. How wrong did Lilienthal's lift numbers turn out to be?
answer: Their wing made only about a third of the lift his tables predicted
choices: Their wing made only about a third of the lift his tables predicted
His numbers matched their wing almost exactly
His numbers were too small by about half
His numbers only failed in very light winds
context: The brothers threw out the accepted numbers and built their own corrected lift-and-drag tables from scratch, testing between 100 and 200 miniature wing shapes. Trusting their own data over the famous expert's is what let them succeed. Source: NASA Glenn Research Center (grc.nasa.gov).

question: While building the airplane, the Wright brothers checked a number called the Smeaton coefficient, a constant that everyone calculating lift and air pressure had trusted for more than a century. When they measured it themselves in their wind tunnel, they found the long-accepted value was badly off. By how much was this century-old constant wrong?
answer: Off by nearly a factor of two
choices: Off by nearly a factor of two
Off by less than one percent
Off by exactly ten times
Off by a factor of a thousand
context: The accepted Smeaton value was about 0.0054; the Wrights' tests showed the true figure was closer to 0.0033. A number engineers had relied on for over a hundred years was nearly off by half, and the bicycle mechanics were the ones who caught it. Source: NASA Glenn Research Center (grc.nasa.gov); Wikipedia, 'Wright brothers'.

question: At the pass of Thermopylae in 480 BC, the Persian king Xerxes sent King Leonidas of Sparta a written demand: hand over your weapons. With just a few thousand Greeks against a vast army, Leonidas sent back a two-word reply that became the most famous battle cry in history. What did he write?
answer: "Come and take them."
choices: "Come and take them."
"We will never kneel."
"Sparta does not yield."
"Take them by force."
context: In Greek, 'Molon labe.' The line is recorded by Plutarch in his 'Sayings of Spartans,' not by the eyewitness historian Herodotus, so it is a celebrated later tradition rather than a verified quote. Source: https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/e/roman/texts/plutarch/moralia/sayings_of_spartans*/main.html  (Legend.)

question: Before the battle of Thermopylae a Greek warned the Spartan soldier Dieneces that the Persian archers were so many their arrows would blot out the sun. Far from afraid, Dieneces answered with a joke that Herodotus says made him the bravest man there. What did Dieneces say?
answer: "Then we shall fight in the shade."
choices: "Then we shall fight in the shade."
"Then we shall die in glory."
"Then the gods will guide my spear."
"Then their arrows will find Spartan shields."
context: Herodotus singled out Dieneces as the bravest of all the Greeks at Thermopylae for this calm retort. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dienekes

question: The narrow coastal pass where Leonidas and the Greeks made their stand was named for the sulfur springs that steamed up out of the rocks there. In Greek that name, Thermopylae, means what?
answer: the Hot Gates
choices: the Hot Gates
the Iron Pass
the Burning Road
the Smoking Cliffs
context: The steaming sulfur springs gave the defile its name; the cliffs and sea squeezed the road so tight that a small force could hold off a huge one. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/history-magazine/article/betrayal-crushed-spartas-last-stand-at-the-battle-of-thermopylae

question: The Greeks held the pass until a local man named Ephialtes of Trachis showed Xerxes a hidden mountain trail for a reward, letting the Persians slip behind them. The Greeks never forgave him: his name lived on in their language as the word for what?
answer: a nightmare
choices: a nightmare
a coward
a stranger
a debt
context: 'Ephialtes' became the ordinary Greek word for nightmare and, by extension, traitor. The hidden route he revealed was the Anopaea path over the mountains. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ephialtes_of_Trachis

question: To take the secret mountain trail, Xerxes sent his elite bodyguard corps, ten thousand picked soldiers the Greeks called the Immortals. The name came from a rule about how the unit was kept. What kept the Immortals always exactly ten thousand strong?
answer: Every man who fell was instantly replaced.
choices: Every man who fell was instantly replaced.
They were sworn never to retreat in battle.
They alone wore armor no arrow could pierce.
They were the king's own blood relatives.
context: The moment a soldier was killed, wounded, or sick, a waiting replacement stepped into his place, so the corps never dropped below 10,000 and seemed never to die. Xerxes sent them by night under his commander Hydarnes. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/history-magazine/article/betrayal-crushed-spartas-last-stand-at-the-battle-of-thermopylae

question: Long after the battle, a stone was raised over the Spartan dead at Thermopylae carved with a line by the poet Simonides — perhaps the most famous war epitaph ever written. Which words did it carry?
answer: "Stranger, go tell the Spartans that here we lie, obedient to their laws."
choices: "Stranger, go tell the Spartans that here we lie, obedient to their laws."
"Here sleep the sons of Sparta, who chose death over chains."
"Weep not for these, who gave their lives that Greece might live."
"Remember the three hundred who feared no king of Persia."
context: Simonides's epitaph speaks in the voice of the fallen, asking any passing traveler to carry word home that they died doing exactly what Spartan law demanded. Source: https://www.attalus.org/poetry/simonides.html

question: As the Persian army gathered, a scout Xerxes sent ahead came back baffled: the Spartans outside the pass were calmly doing something instead of preparing for war. The exiled Spartan king Demaratus explained it was their custom whenever they were about to risk their lives. What were the Spartans doing?
answer: combing and dressing their long hair
choices: combing and dressing their long hair
sharpening their spears in silence
singing hymns to their war-god
feasting on their last provisions
context: Demaratus told Xerxes that grooming their hair was how Spartans prepared to die well. The sight of warriors calmly tending their hair before a hopeless fight unnerved the Persians. Source: https://www.livius.org/sources/content/herodotus/herodotus-on-thermopylae/

question: A thousand Phocian Greeks were posted up on the mountain to guard the secret trail. When the Immortals climbed it by night, the Phocians did not see or hear soldiers at first — they noticed one small thing in the dark that told them the enemy was upon them. What gave the Persians away?
answer: the rustling of oak leaves under their feet
choices: the rustling of oak leaves under their feet
the glint of moonlight on their spears
the smell of smoke from their torches
the distant call of a Persian horn
context: In the still night the thick carpet of fallen oak leaves crackled under the climbing Persians, and the Phocians realized too late they had been outflanked. Source: https://www.livius.org/sources/content/herodotus/herodotus-on-thermopylae/

question: On the last day at Thermopylae the surrounded Greeks fought until their spears snapped, then drew their swords and fought until those broke too. Herodotus says that even then they did not stop, but kept fighting the Persians with what?
answer: their hands and teeth
choices: their hands and teeth
stones torn from the ground
the broken shafts of their spears
the shields of the fallen
context: Herodotus writes that weaponless, the Greeks fought on 'with their hands and teeth' until the Persians overwhelmed them with arrows. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Thermopylae

question: Greeks of that age held it sacred to return an enemy's body for honorable burial. When the battle ended, Xerxes — furious that so few had defied him for so long — broke that custom and ordered something done to the corpse of King Leonidas. What did Xerxes order?
answer: that the head be cut off and set on a stake
choices: that the head be cut off and set on a stake
that the body be burned to leave no grave
that the bones be carried back to Persia
that the body be thrown into the sea
context: Beheading a fallen foe and displaying the head violated every Greek convention of honoring the dead; Herodotus presents it as a measure of Xerxes's rage at how dearly the pass had cost him. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/history-magazine/article/betrayal-crushed-spartas-last-stand-at-the-battle-of-thermopylae

question: Two of the 300 Spartans had bad eye-disease and were excused before the final fight. One, Eurytus, had a slave lead him blind into the battle and died there. The other, Aristodemus, went home to Sparta alive — and was punished by his whole city in a way that marked him as a coward. How did Sparta treat Aristodemus?
answer: No Spartan would speak to him or give him fire.
choices: No Spartan would speak to him or give him fire.
He was stripped of his land and exiled for life.
He was made to serve the families of the dead.
He was forbidden ever to carry arms again.
context: Aristodemus was shunned as 'the Trembler' — denied conversation and even a light for his hearth. A year later he erased the shame by fighting with reckless courage at the Battle of Plataea. Source: https://www.livius.org/sources/content/herodotus/herodotus-on-thermopylae/

question: The exiled Spartan king Demaratus tried to warn Xerxes that the Spartans would stand and fight no matter how badly they were outnumbered. According to Herodotus, what did Demaratus say held the Spartans in place and made them fight to the death?
answer: a Law they feared more than the Persians feared the king
choices: a Law they feared more than the Persians feared the king
an oath they had sworn to the gods of Greece
the shame of facing their wives if they fled
the promise of glory and reward after victory
context: Demaratus told Xerxes the Spartans' true master was the Law, which forbade them to flee and commanded them to conquer or die — and they feared it far more than Xerxes's own soldiers feared him. Source: https://classics.mit.edu/Herodotus/history.7.vii.html

question: Thomas Aquinas grew up huge, heavy, and so quiet in class that his fellow students mocked him with a cruel animal nickname. What did they call the boy who would become one of history's greatest thinkers?
answer: the Dumb Ox
choices: the Dumb Ox
the Sleeping Bear
the Mud Toad
the Quiet Crow
context: His teacher Albertus Magnus shut the mockers down: 'You call him the dumb ox, but in his teaching he will one day produce such a bellowing that it will be heard throughout the world.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Aquinas ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Thomas_Aquinas/

question: Thomas Aquinas was the youngest son of a noble Italian family, and by custom the youngest boy was given to the Church to rise one day as a rich and powerful abbot. How young was Thomas when his family handed him over to be raised by the monks of Monte Cassino?
answer: five years old
choices: five years old
nine years old
twelve years old
sixteen years old
context: He was sent at about age five to the great Benedictine monastery of Monte Cassino, where his family hoped he would grow up to become its wealthy abbot. Source: https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/14663b.htm ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Aquinas

question: At nineteen, Thomas Aquinas shocked his family by choosing to join the Dominicans — friars who lived by begging — instead of becoming a rich abbot. His family was enraged. Who ambushed him on the road and locked him in the family castle for nearly a year to break his will?
answer: his own brothers
choices: his own brothers
the monks of Monte Cassino
a band of hired soldiers
the local bishop's men
context: His brothers held him captive for almost a year trying to force him to abandon the begging order. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Aquinas ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Thomas_Aquinas/

question: Thomas Aquinas's family could not break his will even after holding him prisoner in their castle for nearly a year. In the end, how did he finally get free to go and study in Paris?
answer: his mother had him lowered through a window at night
choices: his mother had him lowered through a window at night
the Pope ordered his noble family to release him
he overpowered the guards and fled on a stolen horse
the Dominicans paid his family a ransom in gold
context: His mother, Theodora, gave up the fight and arranged for him to be let down through a window after dark; he then went to Paris to study under Albertus Magnus. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Aquinas

question: As a boy, Thomas Aquinas was mocked as 'the Dumb Ox.' Centuries later the Church reversed that verdict entirely, naming him the patron saint of all Catholic schools and universities and giving him a new, glowing nickname. What is he called now?
answer: the Angelic Doctor
choices: the Angelic Doctor
the Golden Preacher
the Seraphic Father
the Universal Bishop
context: He was canonized in 1323 by Pope John XXII, declared a Doctor of the Church in 1567, and in 1880 made patron saint of all Catholic schools and universities — his nickname now the 'Angelic Doctor.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Aquinas

question: While Thomas Aquinas was held prisoner in his family's castle, his brothers sent a woman into his locked room to seduce him out of his vow of celibacy. According to the records gathered for his sainthood, what did Thomas do?
answer: snatched a burning log from the fire and drove her out
choices: snatched a burning log from the fire and drove her out
knelt in the corner and prayed until she left
bribed the guards to carry her away by morning
recited Aristotle aloud until she fell asleep
context: Legend, from the canonization records: after driving her out, he is said to have used the firebrand to scorch the sign of the cross onto the wall. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Aquinas ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Thomas_Aquinas/

question: Legend holds that after Thomas Aquinas finished writing about the Eucharist, a voice spoke to him from the crucifix: 'You have written well of me, Thomas. What reward would you have?' How did Thomas answer?
answer: "Nothing but you, Lord."
choices: "Nothing but you, Lord."
"Only to finish my work, Lord."
"A place in heaven, Lord."
"Wisdom above all men, Lord."
context: In the Latin of the legend: 'Non nisi te, Domine.' The abbey's sacristan was said to have witnessed the exchange. Source: https://melbournecatholic.org/news/nothing-but-you-lord-the-heart-of-st-thomas-aquinas ; https://www.regnumchristi.com/en/st-thomas-aquinas/

question: When Thomas Aquinas died at the abbey of Fossanova, the monks there were terrified that rival friars would come and steal the body of a man already rumored to be a saint. To make sure they could keep him, what did the Fossanova monks do to his corpse?
answer: cut off his head and boiled the flesh from his bones
choices: cut off his head and boiled the flesh from his bones
sealed it inside the abbey's thickest stone wall
buried it secretly beneath the high altar at night
dressed it in armor and posted guards around it
context: In 1369 about 50 of his bones were finally handed to the Dominicans of Toulouse, where his tomb stands today — and two rival skulls are still each claimed as his. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonization_of_Thomas_Aquinas ; https://live.christian.expert/skull-aquinas

question: The Summa Theologica, Thomas Aquinas's masterwork, is a monster of a book — roughly 3,000 pages holding about 512 great 'Questions' split into thousands of short 'Articles.' Who did Aquinas say he wrote this enormous work for?
answer: beginners in Christian doctrine
choices: beginners in Christian doctrine
the Pope and his cardinals
the masters of the University of Paris
monks preparing to become priests
context: He genuinely framed his 3,000-page colossus as a textbook to instruct beginners in the faith. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summa_Theologica ; https://christianhistoryinstitute.org/magazine/article/summa-and-its-parts

question: Thomas Aquinas's grand project was to wed the logic of a long-dead pagan Greek to Christian faith, arguing that faith and reason can never truly contradict. He admired this Greek thinker so much that he usually didn't bother writing the name, using one reverent title instead. What did Aquinas simply call Aristotle?
answer: "the Philosopher"
choices: "the Philosopher"
"the Teacher"
"the Sage"
"the Master"
context: Aquinas leaned on Aristotle's ideas of motion, cause, potentiality, and final ends as the scaffolding for his own arguments — and referred to him throughout simply as 'the Philosopher.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Ways_(Aquinas) ; https://www.philosophynotebook.com/intro/aquinas.shtml

question: On 6 December 1273, while saying Mass, Thomas Aquinas had a shattering mystical experience — and from that day he refused to write another word, leaving the Summa unfinished. When his secretary Reginald begged him to keep working, what did Aquinas say about everything he had written?
answer: it seemed like straw to him
choices: it seemed like straw to him
it was the best work of his life
it must all be burned after his death
it would be finished by another hand
context: His exact reported words: 'I cannot, because all that I have written seems like straw to me.' He died about three months later. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Aquinas ; https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/14663b.htm

question: Thomas Aquinas built every section of the Summa the same combative way: he posed a 'Whether...' question, and then — before giving his own view — he did something most arguers refuse to do even today. What did he set down first, at the very start of each section?
answer: the strongest arguments against his own position
choices: the strongest arguments against his own position
a prayer asking God for the right answer
a quotation from Scripture to open the topic
a list of the questions he would tackle
context: Each Article states the Objections (the best arguments against him) fairly and first, then a 'Sed contra' ('On the contrary...'), then his own answer 'Respondeo' ('I answer that...'), then a point-by-point reply to every objection. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summa_Theologica ; https://christianhistoryinstitute.org/magazine/article/summa-and-its-parts

question: Near the start of the Summa, Thomas Aquinas lays out five separate arguments that he believed each prove God exists — one from motion, one from cause, one from a necessary being, one from degrees of perfection, and one from the design of nature. By what famous name are these five arguments known?
answer: the Five Ways
choices: the Five Ways
the Five Pillars
the Five Proofs
the Five Mysteries
context: The 'Five Ways' (Quinque viae) appear in Part I, Question 2, Article 3 — and each one closes with the same line: 'and this everyone understands to be God.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Ways_(Aquinas) ; https://www.britannica.com/topic/the-Five-Ways

question: In the Summa's section on law, Thomas Aquinas argued that above all human laws stands a 'natural law' that every person can grasp by reason, beginning 'good is to be done, and evil avoided.' Centuries later, passing through the philosopher John Locke, this very idea shaped one of the most famous documents in history. Which document's founding truths grew from Aquinas's natural law?
answer: the American Declaration of Independence
choices: the American Declaration of Independence
the United States Bill of Rights
England's Magna Carta
France's Napoleonic Code
context: Aquinas's ladder of law (eternal, natural, human, divine) and his reason-grasped natural law are the seed that grows, through Locke, into the 'self-evident' natural rights the American Founders wrote into the Declaration. Source: https://www.nlnrac.org/classical/aquinas.html ; https://firstamendment.mtsu.edu/article/natural-rights/

question: King Henry II had spent years feuding with Thomas Becket, the Archbishop of Canterbury, over the power of the Church. According to the famous story, the king flew into a rage at his court and shouted a complaint about Becket that four of his knights took as an order to kill -- then rode off to Canterbury and cut the archbishop down. What is Henry said to have shouted?
answer: "Will no one rid me of this turbulent priest?"
choices: "Will no one rid me of this turbulent priest?"
"Bring me the head of this rebel archbishop!"
"Let the man be banished from my kingdom forever!"
"I shall ride to Canterbury and judge him myself!"
context: The line is the most famous royal outburst in English history, but it appears in no contemporary account and is almost certainly apocryphal -- chroniclers report Henry cursing the 'low-born clerks' he had raised who let one man shame him. The four knights -- Reginald FitzUrse, Hugh de Morville, William de Tracy, and Richard le Breton -- murdered Becket inside Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170. Source: historic-uk.com/HistoryUK/HistoryofEngland/Thomas-Becket/  (Legend.)

question: After King Henry II's knights murdered Thomas Becket in Canterbury Cathedral in 1170, the monks stripped the archbishop's body to prepare it for burial. Beneath his fine robes they uncovered a hidden secret -- something he had worn against his bare skin every day -- that convinced people more than the murder itself that he had been a true saint. What did the monks find under his robes?
answer: A coarse goat-hair shirt crawling with lice and vermin
choices: A coarse goat-hair shirt crawling with lice and vermin
A jeweled silver cross worth a small fortune
A letter naming the four knights who hunted him
A wound from an old assassination attempt
context: The lice-ridden goat-hair shirt was a hidden penance; the monks were stunned that their archbishop had secretly mortified his own flesh. Reported miracle cures soon poured in at his tomb, and Pope Alexander III canonised Becket in 1173 -- barely three years after his death. Sources: learning.canterbury-cathedral.org/a-walk-through-time/becket/ and Cambridge, 'Dirty Laundry: Thomas Becket's Hair Shirt and the Making of a Saint'

question: Thomas Edison invented so many things at his New Jersey laboratory that by 1878 his fame had spread worldwide and people gave him a single magical nickname. What did they call Thomas Edison?
answer: The Wizard of Menlo Park
choices: The Wizard of Menlo Park
The Sorcerer of Manhattan
The Genius of New York
The Magician of Detroit
context: Edison's New Jersey lab turned out invention after invention, and the world was calling him 'The Wizard of Menlo Park' by 1878. Source: Thomas Edison Center at Menlo Park, https://www.menloparkmuseum.org/history

question: In 1877 Thomas Edison built a hand-cranked machine wrapped in tinfoil that could record a voice and play it right back — the first device ever to do so. The very first words he shouted into it, then heard repeated back to him, came from a nursery rhyme. Which words were they?
answer: "Mary had a little lamb"
choices: "Mary had a little lamb"
"Twinkle, twinkle, little star"
"Hark, the herald angels sing"
"Hickory dickory dock"
context: Edison's first phonograph (1877) was a tinfoil cylinder with one needle to scratch the grooves and another to play them back; even Edison was startled it worked on the first try with 'Mary had a little lamb.' Source: ASME, https://www.asme.org/about-asme/engineering-history/landmarks/68-edison-experimental-recording-phonograph

question: When Thomas Edison's first bulb finally glowed for over thirteen hours straight in 1879, the thread burning inside it wasn't anything rare or costly. It was an everyday household item, baked black into carbon and sealed inside a vacuum. What was that first filament made from?
answer: A loop of cotton sewing thread
choices: A loop of cotton sewing thread
A strand of fine silk thread
A length of braided horsehair
A strip of folded writing paper
context: The filament in the first successful 1879 lamp (which burned about thirteen and a half hours) was a loop of ordinary carbonized cotton sewing thread. Sources: U.S. Dept. of Energy, https://www.energy.gov/articles/history-light-bulb ; IEEE, https://ethw.org/Edison's_Incandescent_Lamp

question: On New Year's Eve in 1879, Thomas Edison strung rows of glowing electric lamps around his Menlo Park grounds and turned night into day. The Pennsylvania Railroad ran special trains and crowds poured in to gawk at the spectacle. What did some of those visitors do to the bulbs?
answer: They stole eight of them as souvenirs
choices: They stole eight of them as souvenirs
They smashed several in a panic
They painted them different colors
They unscrewed them to keep warm
context: Edison explained the lamps 'in plain language and a homespun manner,' but eight of the bulbs walked off as souvenirs that night. Source: History.com, https://www.history.com/articles/when-edison-turned-night-into-day

question: Thomas Edison was almost completely deaf, yet he still wanted to enjoy music. A famous story says that to 'hear' a piano he would lean in and bite down on its wooden case, so the vibrations traveled up through his jaw into his skull. How did Edison describe doing this?
answer: "I hear through my teeth"
choices: "I hear through my teeth"
"I listen with my bones"
"The music lives in the wood"
"My jaw became my ear"
context: Edison was deaf in his left ear and roughly 80% deaf in the right; the bite-the-piano story ('I hear through my teeth') is told as legend, and a surviving Steinway grand bears bite marks believed to be his. Source: Mental Floss, https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/641725/thomas-edison-facts ; VOA, https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/piano-belonging-to-thomas-edison-shows-unusual-marks/6815113.html

question: Hunting for a bulb filament that would last, Thomas Edison sent scouts across the world and carbonized thousands of plant fibers. The winner — burning some 1,200 hours and serving as his standard filament for nearly a decade — was a fiber a scout shipped home from a grove beside a far-off shrine. What plant gave Edison that long-lasting filament?
answer: Japanese bamboo
choices: Japanese bamboo
Brazilian palm
Egyptian papyrus
Himalayan cotton
context: In 1880 Edison's scout William H. Moore sent samples from a bamboo grove by the Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine near Kyoto (Phyllostachys bambusoides); carbonized, it burned about 1,200 hours. Sources: Amusing Planet, https://www.amusingplanet.com/2019/05/how-japanese-bamboo-helped-edison-make.html ; Government of Japan, https://www.gov-online.go.jp/eng/publicity/book/hlj/html/202208/202208_08_en.html

question: In 1882 Thomas Edison opened the Pearl Street Station in lower Manhattan, America's first central power plant, run by giant 27-ton generators. He nicknamed those huge machines after the most famous animal of the day — P.T. Barnum's enormous circus elephant. What were Edison's generators called?
answer: Jumbo
choices: Jumbo
Goliath
Mammoth
Titan
context: On September 4, 1882, at 3 o'clock Edison flipped the switch at Pearl Street Station; its 27-ton 'Jumbo' dynamos were named after Barnum's celebrated elephant. Source: IEEE, https://ethw.org/Pearl_Street_Station ; https://ethw.org/Milestones:Pearl_Street_Station,_1882

question: Thomas Edison tried thousands of materials before finding a bulb filament that worked, failing over and over. Asked about all those failures, he gave a famously stubborn answer that refused to call them failures at all. What did Edison reportedly say?
answer: "I have not failed — I've found 10,000 ways that won't work"
choices: "I have not failed — I've found 10,000 ways that won't work"
"I have not lost — I've ruled out a thousand wrong roads"
"I have not quit — I've crossed off 5,000 dead ends"
"I have not stumbled — I've mapped the road around each miss"
context: The legendary '10,000 ways that won't work' line is the famous version; the earliest documented form (Dyer & Martin, 1910) is gentler: 'I have gotten a lot of results! I know several thousand things that won't work.' Source: Quote Investigator, https://quoteinvestigator.com/2012/07/31/edison-lot-results/

question: Thomas Edison's laboratory at Menlo Park was something the world had never seen: a place built on purpose to produce one new device after another, with teams of workers and equipment all under one roof. Edison coined a nickname for this first-of-its-kind operation. What did he call it?
answer: The Invention Factory
choices: The Invention Factory
The Idea Mill
The Thinking Shop
The Genius Works
context: Menlo Park was the world's first industrial research-and-development laboratory; Edison called it the 'Invention Factory,' and while based there he applied for about 400 patents. Source: Thomas Edison Center at Menlo Park, https://www.menloparkmuseum.org/history

question: Thomas Edison knew a light bulb was useless with nothing to power it, so he built an entire electrical system: generating plants, wires running into homes, sockets, and switches. He also invented one more device so the new electric company could fairly charge each customer. What was it?
answer: An electric meter that measured each home's use
choices: An electric meter that measured each home's use
A coin slot built into every lamp
A bell that rang when a bill came due
A clock that shut the power off at night
context: Edison invented the whole system around the bulb — central power plant, distribution wires, sockets and switches — plus the first electric meter to measure each customer's use and bill them. Source: U.S. Dept. of Energy, https://www.energy.gov/articles/history-light-bulb ; IEEE, https://ethw.org/Edison's_Electric_Light_and_Power_System

question: A common story credits Thomas Edison with inventing the light bulb. But Britain's Joseph Swan had already demonstrated his own carbon-filament bulb and held a British patent in 1878, before Edison's. When Swan and Edison clashed over the invention in British courts, how did the case end?
answer: Edison lost the case and took Swan in as a partner
choices: Edison lost the case and took Swan in as a partner
Edison won the case and Swan paid him royalties
Edison and Swan both quit the light-bulb business
The British court banned both men from selling bulbs
context: Edison didn't invent the bulb — he made it practical. He lost a British patent-infringement case to Swan and had to take him in as a partner, forming the Edison & Swan United Electric Light Company in 1883. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edison_and_Swan_Electric_Light_Company ; IEEE, https://ethw.org/Edison's_Incandescent_Lamp

question: Rival inventors built bulbs with thick filaments that gulped huge currents. Thomas Edison's key breakthrough was the opposite: a hair-thin filament with high resistance, which needed only a small current. Why did that thin, high-resistance filament matter so much for lighting a whole city?
answer: It let thin, cheap copper wires feed many bulbs at once
choices: It let thin, cheap copper wires feed many bulbs at once
It made each bulb glow ten times brighter than rivals'
It let the bulbs run with no power plant at all
It allowed bulbs to work underwater without sealing
context: High resistance and a small current meant power could travel through thin, cheap copper wires to many bulbs at once — which is what made a citywide lighting system affordable. Source: IEEE, https://ethw.org/Edison's_Incandescent_Lamp ; U.S. Dept. of Energy, https://www.energy.gov/articles/history-light-bulb

question: Thomas Hobbes argued that without any government to keep order, human life would collapse into fear and violence. In his book Leviathan (1651), he summed up what life would be like in four grim words. According to Hobbes, life with no government is solitary, poor, nasty, and what?
answer: Brutish and short
choices: Brutish and short
Cruel and bitter
Savage and cold
Wretched and dark
context: The full line: in the state of nature, with no government to keep order, the life of man is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' (Leviathan, Book I, Ch. 13, 1651). It is Hobbes' single most famous sentence. Source: https://1000wordphilosophy.com/2021/07/14/hobbes-on-the-state-of-nature/
