question: Thomas Hobbes titled his great book about government after a monster from the Bible's Book of Job — a creature so terrifying it was called 'king over all the children of pride.' Hobbes wanted his all-powerful ruler to overawe everyone the way this monster did. What creature did he name the book after?
answer: The Leviathan, a sea serpent
choices: The Leviathan, a sea serpent
The Behemoth, a land beast
The Phoenix, a fire bird
The Basilisk, a serpent king
context: Hobbes named his book Leviathan after the monstrous sea serpent of the Book of Job. The sovereign, like the serpent, is a fearsome creature that must overawe everyone to keep the peace. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leviathan_(Hobbes_book)

question: Thomas Hobbes was born early on April 5, 1588, when his mother heard the Spanish Armada was sailing to attack England and the terror sent her into labor. In his autobiography he joked about the fear that surrounded his birth with a famous line. What did Hobbes say was born alongside him?
answer: His twin, Fear
choices: His twin, Fear
His enemy, War
His shadow, Doubt
His friend, Reason
context: Hobbes wrote that 'fear and I were born twins together' — his mother went into early labor on hearing the Armada was coming. Fear of violent death is the engine of his whole philosophy. Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/thomas-hobbes

question: Thomas Hobbes wrote Leviathan in exile in Paris while England tore itself apart in civil war and King Charles I was beheaded. To Hobbes, the only escape from such chaos was for every person to make a single deal: each gives up the right to govern himself, but only if everyone else does the same, and all hand that power to one ruler. In exchange for what does Hobbes say people surrender their freedom to the sovereign?
answer: Protection
choices: Protection
Wealth
Glory
Wisdom
context: Hobbes' social contract: each says 'I authorise and give up my right of governing myself to this man... on this condition, that thou give up thy right to him,' trading liberty to one sovereign — an 'artificial man' — for protection. Hobbes reasons from the same state of nature as Locke but lands on absolute rule, not limited government. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leviathan_(Hobbes_book)

question: The 1651 frontispiece of Leviathan, engraved by Abraham Bosse, shows a crowned giant towering over the land, gripping a sword in one hand and a bishop's crosier in the other. Look closely and the giant's body is not solid — it is built entirely out of something. What makes up the giant's body?
answer: More than 300 tiny people
choices: More than 300 tiny people
Coins stamped with crowns
Stone blocks of a fortress
Coils of an iron chain
context: The giant's body is built from more than 300 tiny human figures — the people themselves make up the sovereign. The sword stands for worldly power, the crosier for church power. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leviathan_(Hobbes_book)

question: Thomas Hobbes lived to age 91 and died at the Cavendish family's Chatsworth House on December 4, 1679. According to a long-told story, this philosopher who built his whole life's work on the fear of death faced his own end with a single calm, witty remark. What were Hobbes' reported last words?
answer: A great leap in the dark
choices: A great leap in the dark
A long sleep, well earned
The final war is won
No more fear for me
context: Hobbes' reported last words were 'a great leap in the dark.' This is traditional testimony rather than documented fact — told as legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hobbes

question: In June 1776 Congress picked five men — Thomas Jefferson, John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Robert Livingston, and Roger Sherman — to write a declaration of independence. The committee handed the actual writing to Jefferson, the youngest at 33. Why did John Adams insist Jefferson take the pen instead of doing it himself?
answer: Adams thought Jefferson could write better than he could
choices: Adams thought Jefferson could write better than he could
Adams was too busy arguing with the other delegates
Adams was not yet a member of the Continental Congress
Adams could not write because his hand was injured
context: Adams later recalled telling Jefferson he had a far better pen — and a reputation to match. The five-man 'Committee of Five' was appointed in June 1776; the 33-year-old Jefferson was its youngest member. Source: Committee of Five — Wikipedia; Monticello / jeffersonpapers.princeton.edu drafting page.

question: In 1803 Thomas Jefferson, as president, bought the vast Louisiana Territory from Napoleon for about $15 million — roughly three cents an acre. What did this single purchase do to the United States?
answer: It doubled the size of the United States overnight
choices: It doubled the size of the United States overnight
It gave the United States its first ocean port
It ended a war between the United States and France
It paid off the young country's entire national debt
context: The roughly 830,000 square miles would eventually become all or part of 15 states. Jefferson got it for about three cents an acre. Source: Constitution Center — 'The Louisiana Purchase, Jefferson's Constitutional Gamble'; Louisiana Purchase — Wikipedia.

question: Thomas Jefferson loved books so much he once wrote, 'I cannot live without books.' In 1814, after the British burned Washington and destroyed the Library of Congress, what did Jefferson do?
answer: He sold his own library of nearly 6,500 books to rebuild it
choices: He sold his own library of nearly 6,500 books to rebuild it
He sailed to London to buy replacement books himself
He ordered the British ambassador to pay for new books
He wrote new books from memory to refill the shelves
context: Jefferson sold the government his personal collection — nearly 6,500 volumes — for $23,950, and it became the new core of the Library of Congress. Source: Library of Congress; Wikipedia (Thomas Jefferson).

question: After the Louisiana Purchase, Thomas Jefferson wanted to know what was actually out in the new western land. He launched the Corps of Discovery, which traveled nearly 8,000 miles up the Missouri River all the way to the Pacific Ocean and back. Who led this expedition for him?
answer: Meriwether Lewis and William Clark
choices: Meriwether Lewis and William Clark
Daniel Boone and Davy Crockett
Robert Livingston and Roger Sherman
John Adams and Benjamin Franklin
context: Lewis had been Jefferson's own personal secretary. The Corps set out up the Missouri in May 1804 and reached the Pacific. Source: National Archives — Lewis & Clark lesson; Lewis and Clark Expedition — Wikipedia.

question: Thomas Jefferson handed Congress his draft of the Declaration of Independence — then had to watch the delegates spend two days arguing over it and cutting roughly a quarter of his words before they adopted it on July 4, 1776. How did Jefferson reportedly behave during the editing?
answer: He sat in unhappy silence while they cut his words
choices: He sat in unhappy silence while they cut his words
He stood up and read the whole draft aloud again
He stormed out and refused to sign the final text
He cheerfully helped the delegates rewrite each line
context: Congress slashed about a quarter of his text before adopting it on the afternoon of July 4, 1776. Jefferson, by accounts, sat in pained silence as delegates trimmed his prose. Source: National Archives; History.com — writing of the Declaration of Independence.

question: Thomas Jefferson designed his own tombstone and wrote his own epitaph, listing just three accomplishments he most wanted to be remembered for: author of the Declaration of Independence, author of Virginia's statute for religious freedom, and father of the University of Virginia. What did he pointedly leave OFF the stone?
answer: That he had been President of the United States
choices: That he had been President of the United States
That he had drafted the Declaration of Independence
That he had founded the University of Virginia
That he had written Notes on the State of Virginia
context: He served two terms as the third president — and deliberately omitted it, choosing instead the things he had created. Source: Library of Congress — Jefferson exhibit; Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom — Wikipedia.

question: Thomas Jefferson called architecture his delight and filled his mountaintop home Monticello with his own gadgets — a dumbwaiter, a polygraph copying machine. He also built a Great Clock in the entrance hall. What unusual weights kept that clock running?
answer: Revolutionary-War cannonballs
choices: Revolutionary-War cannonballs
A pair of brass church bells
Buckets of Virginia river water
Iron horseshoes from his stable
context: Jefferson tinkered with Monticello for decades, calling 'putting up, and pulling down' a favorite amusement; his Great Clock was driven by cannonball weights. Source: Monticello encyclopedia; American Scientist — 'Jefferson's Old Bones.'

question: In the Declaration of Independence Thomas Jefferson wrote that 'all men are created equal' — the founding creed of human equality. Yet across his own life, the man who wrote those words personally did something that flatly contradicted them. What was it?
answer: He enslaved more than 600 people
choices: He enslaved more than 600 people
He enslaved more than 50 people
He enslaved more than 200 people
He enslaved more than 1,000 people
context: Jefferson enslaved over 600 human beings across his lifetime, about 130 at the time he died — the founding's sharpest contradiction: the man who penned the creed of equality owned the people who served his dinner. Source: Wikipedia (Thomas Jefferson); The Henry Ford; Monticello.

question: John Adams and Thomas Jefferson — friends, then bitter political rivals, then friends again by letter — both died on the very same day: July 4, 1826, exactly 50 years after the Declaration. Adams died a few hours after Jefferson but never knew it. What were Adams's reported last words?
answer: 'Thomas Jefferson survives'
choices: 'Thomas Jefferson survives'
'Independence forever, and amen'
'I have done my duty to the end'
'Let the trumpets sound for liberty'
context: Adams died believing his old rival had outlived him — but Jefferson had died hours earlier. Jefferson's own last conscious words were 'Is it the Fourth?' Source: Library of Congress blog (Headlines & Heroes, 2022); Monticello encyclopedia (John Adams); Constitution Center.

question: Thomas Jefferson's original draft of the Declaration of Independence included a fierce 168-word passage attacking King George for the slave trade — calling it a 'cruel war against human nature itself.' That passage was struck out, so the final Declaration says nothing against slavery. Who forced Jefferson's anti-slavery passage to be removed?
answer: Delegates from South Carolina and Georgia
choices: Delegates from South Carolina and Georgia
Delegates from Massachusetts and Connecticut
Delegates from Pennsylvania and New York
Delegates from New Hampshire and Rhode Island
context: South Carolina and Georgia, deeply tied to the slave trade, demanded the passage be cut, and Congress complied. Jefferson's draft had blamed the King for violating the 'most sacred rights of life & liberty in the persons of a distant people.' Source: The Henry Ford — deleted slavery passage; History.com.

question: The French naturalist Buffon claimed that animals in America were smaller and weaker than those of Europe. Thomas Jefferson, who took this as an insult to his country, collected huge mastodon ('mammoth') bones to prove him wrong — and went further with a bold claim about the giant beasts. What did Jefferson argue about them?
answer: That they might still be alive, roaming the unexplored West
choices: That they might still be alive, roaming the unexplored West
That their bones proved a great flood had once drowned America
That they were the ancestors of America's modern bears
That European hunters had killed off all the largest ones
context: Jefferson's only published book, Notes on the State of Virginia, was partly a catalog of American nature meant to refute Buffon. He genuinely hoped the mammoths still walked the West. Source: American Scientist — 'Jefferson's Old Bones'; Notes on the State of Virginia — Wikipedia.

question: Thomas Jefferson seized the chance to buy Louisiana from Napoleon in 1803 and doubled the nation — but the purchase troubled his own conscience. He wrote that he was acting 'beyond the Constitution' and would have to rely on the nation to forgive it. What exactly did Jefferson privately doubt about the deal he had just made?
answer: Whether the Constitution gave him any power to buy foreign land
choices: Whether the Constitution gave him any power to buy foreign land
Whether Napoleon would actually hand over the territory
Whether the $15 million price was far too high to pay
Whether the Senate would ever agree to approve it
context: Jefferson believed the federal government 'has not given it power of holding foreign territory' and thought an amendment was needed — yet told John Dickinson they must 'ratify and pay our money... and rely on the nation to sanction an act done for its great good.' Source: Constitution Center — 'Jefferson's Constitutional Gamble.'

question: Thomas Jefferson, who designed his own epitaph around religious freedom, also wrote a famous 1802 letter to a group of worried Baptists in Danbury, Connecticut, explaining what the First Amendment did to the relationship between government and religion. What phrase did Jefferson coin in that letter — words the Supreme Court would later quote?
answer: A wall of separation between Church and State
choices: A wall of separation between Church and State
A common altar for every American faith
A shield of conscience over every believer
A bridge of tolerance among all the churches
context: Jefferson's 'wall of separation' became the Court's authoritative reading of the religion clauses. His 1786 Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom — which barred forcing anyone to support or attend worship — had been the direct model for those clauses. Source: Library of Congress — Danbury letter; Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom — Wikipedia.

question: A popular myth says the Constitution's three-fifths clause was the framers declaring an enslaved person to be 'three-fifths of a human being.' The real fight at the 1787 Convention was the reverse: a battle over who got to COUNT enslaved people toward a state's seats in Congress. Which side pushed hardest to count them?
answer: The slave states, who wanted more seats in Congress
choices: The slave states, who wanted more seats in Congress
The antislavery states, who wanted to honor the enslaved
The small states, who feared being outvoted
The frontier territories, who wanted faster statehood
context: The counterintuitive truth: slaveholding states fought to count the very people they held as property, because more counted heads meant more seats in the House and more votes for president. Antislavery delegates resisted exactly this. Three-fifths was a grim bargain to hold the union together, not a measure of a person's humanity. (Britannica, 'Three-fifths compromise'; Constitutional Accountability Center, theusconstitution.org)

question: Frederick Douglass, who had escaped slavery himself, refused to call the Constitution a slaveholders' document. He pointed out that the three-fifths clause counted a FREED person as a whole person, not three-fifths — so every enslaved person a state set free made that state GAIN seats in Congress. What did Douglass argue this hidden arithmetic handed the South?
answer: A built-in reward for freeing its slaves
choices: A built-in reward for freeing its slaves
A permanent veto over all Northern laws
A secret right to expand slavery westward
A guaranteed standing majority in the Senate
context: Douglass called the clause 'a standing rebuke' to the South — a built-in bribe to free the enslaved, since each freed person became a whole person in the count and won the state more representation. Against William Lloyd Garrison, who burned the Constitution as a pro-slavery pact, Douglass insisted it was an antislavery document and 'not a word' of it needed changing to abolish slavery. (Cato Institute, 'Frederick Douglass: The US Constitution Is an Anti-Slavery Document'; Douglass, 1860 Glasgow speech)

question: Corn grew from a wild Mexican grass called teosinte, which native farmers bred into maize over thousands of years. But teosinte barely resembles corn: instead of a fat cob, its tiny ear holds only about two rows of a handful of kernels, and each kernel is sealed inside something a corncob never has. What encased each teosinte kernel?
answer: A rock-hard shell, like a little acorn
choices: A rock-hard shell, like a little acorn
A papery husk you peeled away
A coat of fine silk threads
A ring of sharp green spines
context: Wild teosinte kernels were locked inside a stony 'fruitcase' shell, two rows of only 5 to 12 of them per tiny ear, nothing like the naked kernels of a modern cob. Native farmers in Mexico turned this scrawny branching grass into corn. Source: evolution.earthathome.org maize-domestication; Native Seeds Search teosinte page.

question: Wild teosinte kept its seeds locked inside stony shells, useless to eat without cracking each one open. Corn's kernels sit naked and ready to eat. Geneticists found that flipping one single gene, called teosinte glume architecture1 (tga1), made that exact change happen. What did that one gene's change do to the kernels?
answer: It popped them out of their hard cases
choices: It popped them out of their hard cases
It doubled how many rows the ear grew
It turned them from blue to golden yellow
It made the whole ear grow twice as long
context: A single mutation in tga1 freed the kernels from their armored 'fruitcases', turning teosinte's locked seeds into corn's naked, eat-anytime kernels. A second gene, tb1, collapsed the bushy grass into one upright stalk. Source: evolution.earthathome.org maize-domestication.

question: On the morning of June 5, 1989, the day after soldiers crushed the Tiananmen Square protests in Beijing, a lone man in a white shirt walked into the middle of a wide avenue and planted himself directly in front of a column of advancing army tanks. What was he holding in his hands as he stood there?
answer: two shopping bags
choices: two shopping bags
a protest banner
a bicycle
a bullhorn
context: The man, known only as 'Tank Man,' stepped into Beijing's Chang'an Avenue carrying two ordinary shopping bags. When the lead tank tried to steer around him he sidestepped to block it again, and even climbed onto the hull to speak to the crew before resuming his stand. To this day nobody knows his name or what became of him. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tank_Man

question: The most famous photo from Tiananmen — a lone man in a white shirt blocking a column of tanks — almost never reached the outside world. Police were seizing journalists' film across Beijing, so an American exchange student named Kirk Martsen volunteered to slip the exposed roll past them to the Associated Press office. Where did Martsen hide the film on his body?
answer: inside his underwear
choices: inside his underwear
taped against his chest
hidden in his shoe
sewn into his hat
context: AP photographer Jeff Widener shot the Tank Man picture from a sixth-floor hotel balcony half a mile away — while sick with flu and nursing a concussion from a rock that had hit his head the day before. To get the film past police, Martsen hid the roll in his underwear. (Newsweek's Charlie Cole, facing a room raid, hid his own roll in a hotel toilet tank.) Source: https://www.wral.com/story/the-man-in-front-of-the-tank-how-journalists-smuggled-out-the-iconic-tiananmen-square-photo/21465861/

question: In 1352 the great Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta crossed the deep Sahara to Taghaza, a salt-mining village so soaked in salt that the people cut blocks of it straight from the ground and stacked them into the walls of their houses — and even their mosque. With no wood or stone for miles, what did they lay across the top of those salt-block buildings to roof them?
answer: Camel skins
choices: Camel skins
Palm fronds
Clay tiles
Woven reeds
context: Ibn Battuta found Taghaza's houses and mosque built of salt slabs and roofed with camel skins — there was no timber in that bleak place. Salt was literally the building material because the ground was made of it. (Ibn Battuta, Travels in Asia and Africa, 1352 account; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taghaza)

question: When the traveler Leo Africanus visited Timbuktu around 1510, the desert city was a famous market for gold, salt, and captives hauled across the Sahara. Yet Leo wrote that one trade good there earned merchants higher profits than any of those. Which good brought the greatest return in Timbuktu?
answer: Books
choices: Books
Gold
Salt
Captives
context: Leo Africanus wrote that in Timbuktu 'more profit is to be made there from the sale of books than from any other branch of trade' — handwritten manuscripts out-earned even gold and salt. The city's libraries held hundreds of thousands of volumes on astronomy, medicine, law, and poetry. (Leo Africanus, The Description of Africa, 1526; brians.wsu.edu)

question: Timbuktu grew rich because it sat where the Sahara desert meets the Niger River: camel caravans brought slabs of salt down from the desert, and boats brought gold up from the forests of the south. At the Timbuktu market, traders swapped salt for gold at a rate that stuns people today. About how much salt did it take to buy a pound of gold?
answer: about one pound of salt
choices: about one pound of salt
about ten pounds of salt
about a hundred pounds of salt
about a thousand pounds of salt
context: Salt was so precious in the heat of West Africa -- the body needs it to survive -- that at Timbuktu it traded against gold almost weight for weight. (World History Encyclopedia, 'The Salt Trade of Ancient West Africa', worldhistory.org/article/1342)

question: Far out in the Sahara, many days from anywhere, stood a lonely mining town called Taghaza. When the traveler Ibn Battuta reached Taghaza in 1352, he found no wood and no stone there to build with -- yet he was amazed to see that the townspeople had built their houses, and even their mosque, out of slabs of what?
answer: slabs of salt
choices: slabs of salt
slabs of dried mud
slabs of baked clay
slabs of packed sand
context: Taghaza sat on top of the salt, so the miners simply cut building blocks from it. Ibn Battuta wrote that nothing grew there but sand and salt, and the roofs were covered with camel skins. (Wikipedia, 'Taghaza', citing Ibn Battuta's Rihla)

question: Timbuktu's Great Mosque, the Djinguereber, has stood for almost 700 years -- yet it is built entirely of mud, straw, and wood, with no stone at all. Every single year the people of Timbuktu gather and do one thing to the whole mosque so the desert rains can never melt it away. What do they do to the Djinguereber every year?
answer: replaster it by hand from top to bottom
choices: replaster it by hand from top to bottom
raise wooden roofs over its open courts
dig new channels to carry the rain off
hang woven mats along its outer walls
context: Built around 1327, the Djinguereber is made of earth, mud, straw and wood. Each year the whole town turns out to replaster it by hand, sealing the cracks before the rains so the mosque does not wash away. (Wikipedia, 'Djinguereber Mosque')

question: In 1324 Mansa Musa, the emperor of Mali, set out across the desert on a pilgrimage so magnificent that stories about it spread all the way to Europe. Walking ahead of him, the tales say, marched 500 servants -- and every one of the 500 carried the very same costly object. According to the legend, what did each of Mansa Musa's 500 servants carry?
answer: a staff of solid gold
choices: a staff of solid gold
a chest of silver coins
a bottle of fine perfume
a roll of patterned silk
context: By legend each of the 500 attendants carried a gold staff weighing about 6 pounds. Mansa Musa's pilgrimage became the talk of the medieval world. (World History Encyclopedia, 'Mansa Musa I')

question: In 1324 the Mali emperor Mansa Musa, on his pilgrimage to Mecca, stopped in the great city of Cairo and gave away gold everywhere he went -- to officials, to the poor, to shopkeepers -- so freely that he upended the city's whole economy. The damage took Cairo roughly twelve years to repair. What did Mansa Musa's spending do to Cairo?
answer: it sent the price of gold crashing down
choices: it sent the price of gold crashing down
it drove the price of bread sky-high
it emptied every market of its goods
it threw thousands of traders out of work
context: So much gold flooded Cairo that its value dropped about 20%, and the price took roughly twelve years to recover. (World History Encyclopedia, 'Mansa Musa I')

question: Around 1375 a European mapmaker drew Mansa Musa of Mali on the famous Catalan Atlas, enthroned as the richest ruler of the south. The artist put a royal scepter in one of his hands. In his other hand, for all of Europe to see, Mansa Musa holds up a single object made of gold. What does he hold?
answer: a great raw nugget of gold
choices: a great raw nugget of gold
a golden crown of his own
a golden drinking goblet
a small golden statue
context: On the 1375 Catalan Atlas, Mansa Musa sits enthroned holding a gold scepter and a great gold nugget -- this was how medieval Europe pictured the king of Timbuktu's land. (World History Encyclopedia, 'Mansa Musa I')

question: Around 1526 the traveler Leo Africanus visited Timbuktu and listed the goods sold in its markets: salt from the desert, gold from the south, cloth, and hand-written books carried in by caravan. One of these, he wrote, brought the merchants more profit than everything else combined. Which trade did Leo Africanus say made the most money in Timbuktu?
answer: the trade in hand-written books
choices: the trade in hand-written books
the trade in desert salt
the trade in southern gold
the trade in fine cloth
context: Leo Africanus wrote that hand-written books imported from Barbary sold for 'more profit... than from all other merchandise' -- in the city of gold and salt, books were the best business of all. (Leo Africanus, 'The Description of Africa', 1526)

question: Ahmad Baba was the most famous scholar in Timbuktu's history. In 1591 a Moroccan army invaded the city, looted his library, and dragged him in chains to Morocco. Standing before the Moroccan sultan, Ahmad Baba protested the theft of his books -- and then stunned the court by adding that his collection had been one of the SMALLEST among his relatives. How many books did Ahmad Baba say had been stolen from him?
answer: more than 1,600 books
choices: more than 1,600 books
more than 16 books
more than 160 books
more than 16,000 books
context: Ahmad Baba (1556-1627) told the sultan, 'I have the smallest library among my kin, and you have stolen from me more than 1,600 books' -- proof that learned Timbuktu families owned books by the thousand. (Kentake Page, 'Ahmed Baba'; Tombouctou Manuscripts Project)

question: People sometimes imagine Timbuktu's tens of thousands of manuscripts are all about religion -- but open them up and you find astronomy, mathematics, medicine, law, poetry, and history. One astronomy book even contains a careful diagram of the turning night sky, drawn to teach students two things: the motions of the planets, and how to do what by reading the stars?
answer: find the direction to Mecca
choices: find the direction to Mecca
predict the coming year's floods
tell a person's fortune at birth
guide caravans across the dunes
context: Timbuktu's manuscripts span astronomy, math, medicine, botany, law, poetry, history and ethics. One astronomy diagram of the rotating heavens taught students the planets' motions and how to find the direction of Mecca by the stars. (Google Arts & Culture / SAVAMA-DCI; Wikipedia, 'Timbuktu Manuscripts')

question: In 2012 armed fighters seized Timbuktu and threatened to burn its ancient libraries. A quiet librarian named Abdel Kader Haidara set out to smuggle the manuscripts away and hide them -- but first he needed thousands of containers to pack them in, fast and in secret. What did Haidara do to get enough containers?
answer: bought every metal trunk in the markets, then beat old oil drums into more trunks
choices: bought every metal trunk in the markets, then beat old oil drums into more trunks
sealed the books in clay jars, then buried them out in the desert sand
wrapped each book in oiled cloth, then walled them up in hidden cellars
packed the books into grain sacks, then floated them away on fishing boats
context: Haidara bought up every metal trunk in Timbuktu's markets, and when those ran out had old oil drums hammered into trunks -- then hid and smuggled the manuscripts to safety. (National Geographic, 'The Brave Sage of Timbuktu: Abdel Kader Haidara')

question: When Timbuktu was retaken in 2013, people feared the worst for its libraries -- the city had held nearly 400,000 ancient manuscripts, and the fighters had sworn to burn them, so the world braced for a catastrophe. When the books were finally counted, how many of the nearly 400,000 had the attackers actually managed to destroy?
answer: about 4,000
choices: about 4,000
about 40,000
about 200,000
about 400,000
context: Of nearly 400,000 manuscripts, only about 4,000 were lost. Volunteers had spirited roughly 350,000 of them out of Timbuktu by donkey, road and river, past armed checkpoints, working by flashlight after the power was cut. (National Geographic, 'The Brave Sage of Timbuktu'; Wikipedia, 'Timbuktu Manuscripts')

question: Most of what the world knows about the medieval empires of Mali and Songhai comes from two history books written in Timbuktu, the Tarikh al-Sudan and the Tarikh al-Fattash. Historians treasure these two chronicles for a reason that was rare in the medieval world. Who wrote them?
answer: they were written by West Africans telling their own history
choices: they were written by West Africans telling their own history
they were written by Arab traders passing through the city
they were written by a European mapmaker who visited Mali
they were written by Moroccan soldiers after the invasion
context: The Tarikh al-Sudan and Tarikh al-Fattash are among the oldest histories of West Africa written by West Africans themselves -- the chronicles scholars still use to reconstruct the empires of Mali and Songhai. (Tombouctou Manuscripts Project, 'Timbuktu's History')

question: The scribes of Timbuktu copied their books in glossy black ink and brilliant colors that they brewed themselves from plants -- their green ink, for instance, came from boiling mango leaves. To get a deep RED ink, a Timbuktu scribe would grind up and boil which plant?
answer: the stalks of the sorghum plant
choices: the stalks of the sorghum plant
the bark of the acacia tree
the roots of the indigo bush
the petals of the desert rose
context: Timbuktu's copyists made their own inks -- red from sorghum, green from mango leaves -- and kept their lines of script perfectly straight with a little tool of stretched threads, writing with reed pens. (Google Arts & Culture / SAVAMA-DCI, 'What's Special About the Timbuktu Manuscripts?')

question: Timur the Lame, the conqueror who turned Samarkand into a blue-tiled jewel, crushed the city of Isfahan after it rebelled against him in 1387. To terrify every other city into obedience, what did Timur have his soldiers build from the bodies of the slain?
answer: Towering pyramids built of human heads
choices: Towering pyramids built of human heads
A long wall sealing the city gates shut
A great pyre that burned for seven days
A bridge of stones across the city moat
context: Eyewitnesses described more than 28 towers, each piled from roughly 1,500 heads. Timur used the same horror at Delhi in 1398, stacking skulls into towers as a warning. The man who built these also raised the Registan and the Bibi-Khanym Mosque in Samarkand. Source: medievalists.net, 'Timur the Lame's Pyramids of Skulls' (2025); Wikipedia, 'Timur'.

question: Timur the Lame was carried home to Samarkand and buried under the blue ribbed dome of the Gur-e-Amir. His grandson Ulugh Beg later hauled a single enormous treasure all the way from Mongolia to lay over the grave. What covers Timur's tomb?
answer: The world's largest block of dark-green jade
choices: The world's largest block of dark-green jade
A solid slab of beaten Silk Road gold
A carved screen of white Indian marble
A great disc of polished Persian bronze
context: The slab is the largest single block of dark-green nephrite jade in the world. The Persian conqueror Nadir Shah later tried to carry it off, and it cracked in two when it was dropped crossing a river. Source: advantour.com, 'Amir Timur's Gravestone'; Britannica, 'Gur-e-Amir'.

question: Trajan's Column still stands in Rome today, dedicated in 113 AD. A single carved band winds all the way up the tall marble shaft, spiraling around it 23 times from bottom to top. What does that one long, unbroken carving show?
answer: The whole story of Trajan's Dacian Wars, scene after scene
choices: The whole story of Trajan's Dacian Wars, scene after scene
A portrait of every god worshipped across the Roman Empire
The faces of all the emperors who had ruled before Trajan
The name of every legion that ever marched for Rome
context: The spiral relief is like a stone documentary film in marble: unwound, the carved band would stretch about 190 metres (620 feet), packed with thousands of figures telling the war from start to finish. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trajan's_Column

question: A bronze statue of the emperor Trajan once stood on the very top of Trajan's Column, but it vanished sometime in the Middle Ages. In 1587 Pope Sixtus V had a brand-new bronze statue hoisted up to crown the column, and it still stands up there today. Whose statue is on top of Trajan's Column now?
answer: Saint Peter
choices: Saint Peter
The Virgin Mary
The emperor Augustus
The angel Gabriel
context: Pope Sixtus V replaced the lost statue of the pagan emperor with the apostle Saint Peter on 4 December 1587 — a Christian saint left standing atop a monument to a Roman conqueror. Inside, a hidden spiral staircase of 185 steps climbs the hollow shaft to the top. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trajan's_Column

question: In 106 AD the Dacian king Decebalus was chased into the mountains by Roman cavalry, who were closing in to take him alive and march him through Rome as a prize. Rather than be captured, what did Decebalus do — a moment carved right onto Trajan's Column?
answer: Cut his own throat with a curved Dacian sword
choices: Cut his own throat with a curved Dacian sword
Set fire to his fortress with himself inside
Drank a cup of poison handed to him by a priest
Hurled himself off the cliff onto the riders below
context: The curved sword was a falx. The carving on the Column shows the exact instant — the king kneeling under a tree, blade to his neck, Roman riders bearing down. He chose death over being paraded as a trophy. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trajan's_Dacian_Wars

question: Under Trajan the Roman Empire swelled to the largest it would EVER be. By 117 AD it stretched from the rainy hills of northern Britain in the west all the way to one far eastern shore that Roman soldiers reached for the first and only time in their whole history. What body of water did Rome's frontier finally touch at that farthest point?
answer: The Persian Gulf
choices: The Persian Gulf
The Caspian Sea
The Indian Ocean
The Red Sea
context: At its peak Rome ruled about 5 million square kilometres and roughly 60 million people, after Trajan took Dacia, Armenia, Mesopotamia, and even the Parthian capital Ctesiphon in modern Iraq. His successor Hadrian gave up much of the eastern conquest within months. Source: https://www.visualcapitalist.com/map-roman-empire-maximum-extent-in-117-ad/

question: Tiberius Claudius Maximus was the Roman cavalryman who reached the dying king Decebalus first, cut off his head, and carried it back to Trajan. He was so proud of that deed that he had it recorded in one lasting place, where archaeologists later found it spelled out in writing. Where did Tiberius Claudius Maximus have his capture of Decebalus recorded?
answer: On his own tombstone
choices: On his own tombstone
In a letter to the Roman Senate
On a silver coin struck in his honor
In a marching song of his legion
context: His gravestone, found at Philippi in Greece, brags that he was promoted 'because he had captured Decebalus and bore his head to him in Ranisstorum' — the camp where he delivered it to Trajan. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius_Claudius_Maximus

question: Trajan was born in Spain, the first Roman emperor to come from the provinces rather than Italy, and he ruled so well that the Senate gave him the title 'Optimus' — 'the best.' Romans held him up as the model emperor for centuries, so at the crowning of every NEW emperor afterward the Senate called out one set wish, measuring the newcomer against the two greatest names in Roman memory. What did that Senate wish say?
answer: That he be luckier than Augustus and better than Trajan
choices: That he be luckier than Augustus and better than Trajan
That he be braver than Caesar and richer than Crassus
That he be wiser than Hadrian and stronger than Nero
That he rule longer than Tiberius and fall less than Pompey
context: The Latin was 'felicior Augusto, melior Traiano.' For generations, every new emperor was wished good fortune beyond Augustus and goodness beyond Trajan — Trajan had become the gold standard a ruler was measured against. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felicior_Augusto,_melior_Traiano

question: At Taghaza, a salt-mining town in the middle of the Sahara, the ground held so much salt that the miners cut it into blocks and used it for building. When the traveler Ibn Battuta stayed there in 1352, what did he find the houses and even the mosque were built out of?
answer: Blocks of solid salt, roofed with camel skins
choices: Blocks of solid salt, roofed with camel skins
Mud bricks baked hard in the desert sun
Stones hauled in by the camel caravans
Palm-wood beams from the southern oases
context: Ibn Battuta called Taghaza 'an unattractive village' whose houses and mosques 'are built of blocks of salt, roofed with camel skins.' Nothing grew there — the only thing the place had in plenty was salt. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'The Salt Trade of Ancient West Africa' (worldhistory.org/article/1342); Ibn Battuta's Rihla (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taghaza).

question: To cross the Sahara, traders relied on one animal so suited to the desert it was nicknamed 'the ship of the desert.' It had padded feet that kept it from sinking in soft sand and could go many days without drinking. Which animal carried the caravans across the sand?
answer: The camel
choices: The camel
The horse
The donkey
The ox
context: A camel could haul about 240 kg (a horse or donkey managed only ~60 kg), travel roughly 48 km a day, live up to 50 years, and go many days without drinking before gulping prodigiously at an oasis. Without it the crossing was simply impossible. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'The Camel Caravans of the Ancient Sahara' (worldhistory.org/article/1344).

question: In the tropical south of West Africa there was no rock salt in the ground, yet bodies needed salt to survive the heat — so salt became staggeringly precious. At the trading city of Timbuktu, how valuable was a block of salt said to be?
answer: Worth almost its own weight in gold
choices: Worth almost its own weight in gold
Worth a handful of copper coins
Worth a sack of millet grain
Worth a day's wage for a porter
context: At Timbuktu salt traded 'almost weight for weight with gold.' A 90-kilo block carried on south to Djenne could double to roughly 450 grams of gold. The south had gold but no salt; the north had salt but craved gold — and the caravans bridged the two. Source: World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/article/1342); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans-Saharan_trade.

question: An Arab traveler in the 900s recorded an odd ritual at the edge of the goldfields, where two groups of traders did business without ever meeting or sharing a language. One group laid out their goods, beat a drum, and withdrew; the gold-bearing Wangarans crept up and set down gold beside the goods. How did the first group then complete the deal?
answer: If they judged the gold fair, they returned and took it; if not, they withdrew and waited for more
choices: If they judged the gold fair, they returned and took it; if not, they withdrew and waited for more
They rang a second drum to summon the Wangarans back to bargain in person
They left a written tally scratched in the sand for the other side to read
They sent a child runner to carry the gold back and forth until both agreed
context: This was the 'silent trade.' Neither side saw the other's face. The Wangarans guarded the secret of WHERE their gold came from — the upper Niger and Senegal river country — so fiercely that for centuries no Arab or Berber merchant ever learned the location of the goldfields. The silence hid the source as much as it bridged the language gap. Source: World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/article/1342); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent_trade.

question: The everyday money of West Africa was not a coin at all but a small glossy seashell, near-impossible to forge and easy to count, that came from the Maldives in the distant Indian Ocean and was carried a handful at a time across the desert by the caravans. What was this shell used as money?
answer: The cowrie shell
choices: The cowrie shell
The conch trumpet
The pearl oyster
The nautilus shell
context: Cowrie shells reached the Sahel by at least the 7th century, ferried across the desert by the same camel caravans that hauled salt and gold. Lightweight, near-impossible to counterfeit, and easy to count, billions eventually circulated as West Africa's everyday currency. Source: The Collector, 'How Underwater Shells Became the First Global Money'; Cultures of West Africa, 'The Cowrie Shell'.

question: In 1324 Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire, crossed the Sahara on pilgrimage to Mecca with a caravan carrying tons of gold. Passing through Cairo, he handed out and spent so much of it that he did lasting damage to Egypt's economy. What happened to the price of gold in Egypt?
answer: It crashed, staying low for about twelve years afterward
choices: It crashed, staying low for about twelve years afterward
It soared as merchants hoarded every nugget they could find
It held steady because Cairo's market was too large to move
It was fixed by the sultan to stop the foreign gold spreading
context: Mansa Musa traveled with around 60,000 people, including attendants in Persian silk, servants each carrying a roughly 3-kg gold staff, and 100 camels each loaded with about 135 kg of gold. He gave away and spent so much that he flooded Cairo's market and pushed the price of gold down for roughly twelve years — one traveler's generosity wrecking a whole economy's currency. Source: Britannica, 'Musa I of Mali'; Al-Umari's account; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansa_Musa.

question: The 1783 Treaty of Paris, which ended the Revolutionary War, did more than make Britain admit the United States was free — it roughly DOUBLED the new country's size compared to the original thirteen colonies hugging the Atlantic coast. To do that, the treaty pushed the young nation's western boundary clear across the wilderness to one great natural landmark. What was the new western edge of the United States?
answer: The Mississippi River
choices: The Mississippi River
The Appalachian Mountains
The Ohio River
The Great Lakes
context: The treaty's borders ran: the Atlantic to the east, British Canada and the Great Lakes to the north, Spanish Florida to the south, and the Mississippi to the west — a continent's worth of future land. Source: americanrevolution.org/treaty-of-paris ; courses.lumenlearning.com/wm-ushistory1/chapter/the-treaty-of-paris.

question: Henry Laurens, one of the Americans sent to negotiate the 1783 Treaty of Paris, has a grim distinction: captured at sea off Newfoundland, he became the only American ever locked inside the Tower of London. He sat there fifteen months before Britain finally swapped him on the last day of 1781. The British general he was traded for had, just weeks earlier, surrendered an entire army at Yorktown. For which defeated British general was Laurens exchanged?
answer: Lord Cornwallis
choices: Lord Cornwallis
General Burgoyne
General Howe
General Clinton
context: Cornwallis surrendered at Yorktown in October 1781; Laurens was exchanged for him on December 31, 1781. Source: twonerdyhistorygirls.blogspot.com/2011/09/henry-laurens-only-american-imprisoned ; britannica.com/biography/Henry-Laurens.

question: Benjamin West set out to paint the signing of the 1783 Treaty of Paris, lining up the five proud American negotiators on the left of his canvas. But his famous painting was never completed — and the reason is right there on the canvas for anyone to see. The British delegation flatly refused to sit for it, since, as it was put, 'Britain had no desire to commemorate its defeat.' What does West's unfinished painting look like as a result?
answer: The right side is a blank patch of bare canvas
choices: The right side is a blank patch of bare canvas
The British figures are turned away from the viewer
The room is left dark and shadowed on one side
The signatures on the document are smudged out
context: British negotiator Richard Oswald (reportedly ugly and blind in one eye) and his secretary Caleb Whitefoord refused to pose, so West left their half of the canvas blank. Only the five Americans were ever painted. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Paris_(painting).

question: In 1494 Spain and Portugal signed the Treaty of Tordesillas and drew a single line from pole to pole down the whole globe, set 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands: everything east went to Portugal, everything west to Spain. When the South American coast was mapped, its easternmost bulge poked across onto Portugal's side of the line. Which land did that hand to Portugal -- the reason it speaks a different language from the Spanish-speaking continent around it?
answer: Brazil
choices: Brazil
Mexico
Peru
Cuba
context: The Tordesillas line fell at roughly 46 30' West, and Brazil's coast 'juts out from the continent in such a way as to cross the line,' landing on Portugal's side -- which is why Brazil became Portuguese-speaking while the rest of Latin America became Spanish. Sources: https://www.worldhistory.org/Treaty_of_Tordesillas/ ; https://www.britannica.com/event/Treaty-of-Tordesillas

question: The Tordesillas line was almost unmeasurable -- in 1494 no one could fix longitude at sea, so the boundary was a theoretical line nobody could locate on the ocean. Pedro Alvares Cabral made it real: on 22 April 1500 his fleet of 13 ships reached an unknown coast near Porto Seguro, where his men celebrated mass and planted a wooden cross. Why did Cabral claim this new land for Portugal?
answer: It lay on Portugal's side of the Tordesillas line
choices: It lay on Portugal's side of the Tordesillas line
It was closer to Lisbon than to Spain
Its people offered him gold and spices
A storm had blown his fleet off course
context: Cabral's fleet reached the Brazilian coast on 22 April 1500, celebrated mass, planted a wooden cross, and claimed the land for Portugal because it fell on the Portuguese side of the Tordesillas line. The voyage turned a theoretical meridian into Portugal's claim on Brazil. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Pedro-Alvares-Cabral ; https://www.historytoday.com/archive/months-past/cabral-discovers-brazil

question: The Allies did not pick the signing date by accident. They forced Germany to sign the Treaty of Versailles on 28 June 1919 — exactly five years to the day after the event that lit the fuse of the First World War. What anniversary was it?
answer: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
choices: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
The sinking of the passenger liner Lusitania
The German army's invasion of neutral Belgium
The United States declaring war on Germany
context: On 28 June 1914 a Serbian student, Gavrilo Princip, shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo, setting off the chain of events that became WWI. The Allies chose the same calendar day five years later on purpose. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Versailles

question: The French chose the signing room as deliberate payback. In that exact room — the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles — back in 1871, fresh from beating France, the Germans had done what?
answer: Proclaimed their new empire and crowned Wilhelm I
choices: Proclaimed their new empire and crowned Wilhelm I
Signed France's surrender to the Kingdom of Prussia
Crowned Napoleon as the Emperor of the French
Held the funeral of the last king of France
context: Germany was 'born' in that hall in 1871 after defeating France. Clemenceau deliberately dismantled Germany in the very room where it had been created, reversing France's old humiliation. Source: chateauversailles.fr/discover/history/key-dates/treaty-versailles-1919

question: The treaty was a monster: 440 articles across 15 parts. Its very first part created the body that was President Woodrow Wilson's dream and his number-one priority for the whole peace. What was that first creation?
answer: The League of Nations
choices: The League of Nations
The International Red Cross
A permanent world court at The Hague
The Geneva Conventions on war
context: Part I of the Treaty of Versailles was the Covenant of the League of Nations. Wilson cared about it more than any other clause and fought to put it first. Source: legion.org/information-center/news/honor/2019/june/10-facts-about-the-treaty-of-versailles

question: The instant the Germans put their names to the treaty inside the Hall of Mirrors, the celebration erupted outside. How did Versailles and Paris mark the moment?
answer: The fountains were turned on and cannons thundered a salute
choices: The fountains were turned on and cannons thundered a salute
A victory parade marched the length of the Champs-Elysees
Church bells fell silent and the city lights were dimmed
Crowds filled the streets and a national holiday began
context: The great fountains of Versailles were switched on for the first time since the war began in 1914. Eyewitness Harold Nicolson wrote: 'Suddenly from outside comes the crash of guns thundering a salute. It announces to Paris that the Treaty of Versailles has been signed.' Source: military-history.org/behind-the-image

question: Georges Clemenceau wanted every delegate to feel the war's cost the moment they arrived. He positioned something right in the entryway where each one had to walk past it on the way in — a sight that reportedly brought even Clemenceau himself to tears. What did he place there?
answer: Five French soldiers whose faces had been wrecked by shrapnel
choices: Five French soldiers whose faces had been wrecked by shrapnel
Five battlefield nurses blinded by German poison gas
Ten war widows standing silently dressed in black
A long line of empty wheelchairs and broken crutches
context: These men were the 'gueules cassees' — French for 'broken faces' — veterans whose features had been destroyed by shrapnel. Clemenceau made every delegate confront them. Source: Union des Blesses de la Face; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gueules_cassees

question: Marshal Ferdinand Foch was disgusted by the treaty — not because it was too harsh, but because he thought it was too SOFT on Germany. He refused to celebrate and made a grim prediction that turned out to be chillingly accurate. What did he say?
answer: 'This is not peace. It is an armistice for twenty years.'
choices: 'This is not peace. It is an armistice for twenty years.'
'Germany will be back in arms within ten short years.'
'We have won the war, but we have lost the peace.'
'No treaty written in anger has ever kept the peace.'
context: Foch reportedly said this in 1919. WWII began on 1 September 1939 — twenty years and about two months later, eerily close to his prediction. Reported as a famous saying; treat as testimony rather than a recording. Source: history.com/articles/ferdinand-foch  (Legend.)

question: Most people assume Germany's First World War debt was paid off generations ago. In fact Germany kept making payments on those 1920s bonds for an astonishingly long time. When did Germany finally make its very last reparations payment?
context: Germany made the final $94 million installment on 3 October 2010 — over 90 years after the war ended. By chance it landed on the 20th anniversary of German reunification. Source: history.com/articles/germany-world-war-i-debt-treaty-versailles

question: Germany lost about 13% of its land, but one territorial change was hated above all the rest: the 'Polish Corridor,' a strip handed to Poland so it could reach the Baltic Sea. What did carving out that corridor do to German territory?
answer: It cut East Prussia off from the rest of Germany
choices: It cut East Prussia off from the rest of Germany
It handed the capital city of Berlin over to Poland
It gave France permanent control of the Rhineland
It split the kingdom of Bavaria away from the north
context: The corridor gave Poland access to the sea but sliced East Prussia off from the main body of Germany entirely, leaving it stranded. Germany lost roughly 6-7 million people along with the territory. Source: encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/map/german-territorial-losses-treaty-of-versailles-1919

question: Article 231 became infamous as the 'war-guilt clause.' Germans read it as branding them the sole villains of the war and never forgave it. But legal historians point out a strange fact about how the clause was actually written. What is it?
answer: The word 'guilt' never actually appears in it
choices: The word 'guilt' never actually appears in it
Germany's own lawyers had quietly helped write it
It legally applied to Austria but never to Germany
It was secretly deleted from the final signed copy
context: Article 231 said Germany must accept responsibility 'for causing all the loss and damage' of the war. It was written as a legal hook for reparations — but the word 'guilt' is nowhere in the text. Germans still read it as a moral death sentence. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Article_231_of_the_Treaty_of_Versailles

question: British economist John Maynard Keynes quit the conference in disgust at how Germany was being treated. The book he then wrote attacking the treaty was translated into 12 languages within six months and became a bible for resentful Germans. What was the book called?
answer: The Economic Consequences of the Peace
choices: The Economic Consequences of the Peace
The Decline of the West
The Great Illusion
The Twenty Years' Crisis
context: Keynes called the settlement a 'Carthaginian peace' — a peace so crushing it would wreck the loser and all of Europe. His December 1919 book made that argument famous and shaped how a generation viewed Versailles. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Economic_Consequences_of_the_Peace

question: A young kitchen helper at a Paris hotel slipped into the edges of the conference carrying a petition that begged the Great Powers for Vietnamese rights and self-rule. They ignored him completely. Years later the world knew him by a new name. What was it?
answer: Ho Chi Minh
choices: Ho Chi Minh
Chiang Kai-shek
Kim Il-sung
Mao Zedong
context: The kitchen helper was Nguyen Tat Thanh. Brushed off at Paris, he later took the name Ho Chi Minh and led the fight for Vietnamese independence. Source: theworldwar.org/learn/educator-resource/letter-ho-chi-minh-secretary-state-robert-lansing

question: Germany never forgave the humiliation of Versailles, and in June 1940, after conquering France, Adolf Hitler staged his revenge with theatrical precision. He forced the French to surrender in the same railway carriage where, in 1918, Germany had signed its armistice ending WWI. Where did Hitler stage the French surrender?
answer: In the same railway carriage near Compiegne
choices: In the same railway carriage near Compiegne
Inside the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles
Inside the Reichstag building in Berlin
On the steps of Notre-Dame in Paris
context: Hitler deliberately dragged the 1918 armistice carriage out of its museum so France would surrender on the exact spot of Germany's earlier humiliation — turning the grudge full circle. Source: history.co.uk/article/the-compiegne-wagon-one-train-carriage-two-peace-treaties

question: The headline reparations bill was a staggering 132 billion gold marks, roughly $33 billion. But economists studying the fine print found a catch that most people miss about that famous figure. What was true of the 132-billion-mark number?
answer: A huge chunk was a fake figure Germany would never really pay
choices: A huge chunk was a fake figure Germany would never really pay
The entire sum was legally due within a single year
It was to be paid off completely in coal and steel
It was quietly cancelled outright by the Allies in 1921
context: The bill was split into A, B and C bonds. The 82-billion-mark 'C bonds' were deliberately a paper number for angry voters; Germany was privately told it would never truly have to pay them. The real bill (A+B bonds) was about 50 billion marks. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I_reparations

question: The popular story is that crushing reparations ruined Germany and helped cause WWII. Historian Sally Marks studied the numbers and reached a very different conclusion that challenges that whole picture. What does Marks argue?
answer: Germany could have paid but defaulted on purpose to kill the treaty
choices: Germany could have paid but defaulted on purpose to kill the treaty
The reparations were impossible and doomed Germany from day one
The reparations were secretly forgiven by France in the 1920s
The reparations money was never actually collected at all
context: Marks argues Germany could have easily paid the real 50-billion-mark bill through taxes, but defaulted repeatedly as a political strategy to overturn the whole treaty — making 'crushing reparations' partly propaganda. Presented as her contested historical argument, not a settled verdict. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I_reparations

question: In the trenches of World War One, the ordinary British foot soldier had a nickname that came from the sample name a soldier saw printed in his army pay book, showing him how to fill out the form. What was that everyman nickname for a British soldier?
answer: Tommy
choices: Tommy
Digger
Doughboy
Jock
context: The 1815 War Office pay/record book used the specimen name 'Thomas Atkins' to show a soldier how to fill it in — so the whole British infantry ended up named after a blank form's example. Source: historic-uk.com (The British Tommy / Tommy Atkins); Wikipedia 'Tommy Atkins'.

question: In a World War One trench, an officer's whistle would shriek, and the British soldiers had to climb a ladder up out of the trench and run across the open ground toward enemy machine guns. What three-word phrase for launching that attack came from this climb up and out?
answer: Over the top
choices: Over the top
Into the breach
Up and at
Through the wire
context: At the whistle, men went 'over the top' — up the ladder, over the parapet, and across no man's land, often straight into machine-gun fire. The phrase came to mean any all-out attack. Source: theworldwar.org (Trench Warfare); historyonthenet.com.

question: Between the two enemy front-line trenches of the Western Front lay a cratered strip of ground, clogged with barbed wire, shell holes, and unburied bodies, that in places was only about 50 yards wide. What grim name did the soldiers give this killing ground?
answer: No Man's Land
choices: No Man's Land
The Dead Zone
The Killing Fields
The Devil's Acre
context: No man's land — the gap between the front-line trenches — could be as narrow as about 50 yards (165 feet), strung with barbed wire and littered with the dead. Source: worldhistory.org (Trench Warfare on WWI's Western Front); theworldwar.org.

question: The floor of a World War One trench was a soup of freezing mud that could swallow a man's boot. To give the soldiers something solid to walk on, slatted wooden planks were laid down the length of the trench. What were these wooden walkway boards called — a word coined in the trenches that we still use today?
answer: Duckboards
choices: Duckboards
Stepboards
Trenchboards
Mudplanks
context: Duckboards — slatted wooden planks — were laid along the muddy trench floor so men could walk without sinking; the word itself was coined for the boards used in WWI trenches and camps. Source: worldhistory.org (Trench Warfare on WWI's Western Front); fdotstokes.com.

question: Inside a World War One trench, a soldier needed to bring his rifle over the sandbagged front wall without exposing his whole body. So the front wall had a ledge built about two or three feet up that a man climbed up to use, to see and aim over the parapet. What was this firing ledge called?
answer: The firestep
choices: The firestep
The parados
The banquette
The sap-head
context: The firestep was a ledge 2-3 feet up the trench's front wall; a soldier stood on it to see and shoot over the parapet (the sandbagged front wall). The rear wall was the parados. Source: spartacus-educational.com (FWW trench system); worldhistory.org.

question: In the freezing winter of 1914-15, more than 20,000 British soldiers were pulled out of the trenches with a single affliction caused by standing for days in icy, waterlogged mud. Their feet went numb, swelled to two or three times normal size, and if gangrene set in, had to be amputated. What was this condition called?
answer: Trench foot
choices: Trench foot
Frostbite
Gangrene rot
Mud sickness
context: Trench foot rotted men's feet after days in freezing waterlogged trenches — the foot went numb, turned red or blue, and swelled two or three times its size; gangrenous cases meant amputation. Over 20,000 British soldiers were treated for it in the winter of 1914-15 alone. Source: spartacus-educational.com (FWW foot).

question: To stop their feet rotting in the wet trenches, British soldiers were ordered to change their socks several times a day and to rub a thick, smelly oil into their feet — so much that one battalion at the front could get through about ten gallons of it a day. What grease were they ordered to coat their feet with?
answer: Whale oil
choices: Whale oil
Goose fat
Axle grease
Pig lard
context: Soldiers greased their feet with whale oil and changed socks several times a day to fight trench foot; a single battalion at the front could use about ten gallons of whale oil per day. Source: spartacus-educational.com (FWW foot).

question: World War One veterans like Harry Patch were haunted for life by the vermin that swarmed the trenches and grew fat feeding on the bodies in no man's land. Officer Major Walter Vignoles wrote that some were 'nearly as big as cats.' What animal was he describing?
answer: Rats
choices: Rats
Crows
Feral dogs
Flies
context: Veteran Harry Patch and Major Walter Vignoles both described trench rats grown 'as big as cats,' fattened on the dead. Rats gnawing the corpses in no man's land — eating the eyes first — was a memory many veterans never shook. Source: spartacus-educational.com (FWW rats); firstworldwar.com.

question: World War One soldiers, lousy with body lice, spent idle hours running a candle flame or a thumbnail down the seams of their shirts to crack the lice and their eggs. This shared, grumbling pastime gave us an everyday English word for casual idle talk. Which word likely came from it?
answer: Chatting
choices: Chatting
Nattering
Yarning
Griping
context: Men passed idle hours 'chatting' — running a flame or thumbnail down the shirt seams to kill lice (called 'chats'); lice in the seams is likely the origin of 'chatting' meaning idle talk. Source: iwm.org.uk (Voices of the First World War – Trench Life); historyhit.com.

question: German heavy artillery sent over big shells that burst with a cloud of thick black smoke, and the British troops named them after the first African-American world heavyweight boxing champion of the day, a man nicknamed 'The Big Smoke' whose name matched the black cloud. What did the soldiers call these black-smoke shells?
answer: Jack Johnsons
choices: Jack Johnsons
Coal Boxes
Black Marias
Woolly Bears
context: The big German 15 cm 'five-nine' shells were nicknamed 'Jack Johnsons' for their black smoke, after the heavyweight champion 'The Big Smoke.' Robert Graves: 'five-nines [were] called Jack Johnsons because of their black smoke.' Source: wordsinwartime.wordpress.com; brightonmuseums.org.uk.

question: Raising your head over the trench parapet could get you shot by a sniper, so in May 1915 a British Lance Corporal named William Beech rigged up a device using mirrors that let a soldier aim and fire over the sandbags while his own head stayed a foot below the top. What was this mirror-aimed weapon called?
answer: The periscope rifle
choices: The periscope rifle
The trench mortar
The sniper scope
The hyposcope sight
context: Men watched no man's land through trench periscopes; in May 1915 Lance Corporal William Beech invented the 'periscope rifle' — mirrors let a soldier aim and fire over the sandbags with his head a foot below the parapet. Source: americanrifleman.org; awm.gov.au (Gallipoli – periscope rifle).

question: A World War One trench was never dug as one long straight ditch. Instead it ran in a zigzag — short straight 'fire-bays' broken every few yards by mounds of earth called 'traverses.' Soldier John Raws explained the deadly reason for this design. What did the zigzag prevent an enemy from doing if he captured a stretch of the line?
answer: Firing straight down the trench's whole length
choices: Firing straight down the trench's whole length
Climbing out into no man's land
Tunneling beneath the front wall
Spotting the dugouts from the air
context: The zigzag of fire-bays and earth traverses meant a shell-burst was contained and a captured stretch couldn't be raked end-to-end. John Raws: '...to localise the explosion of shells or prevent an enemy... being able to pour fire right down the length of a trench.' Source: spartacus-educational.com (FWW trench system).

question: During the unofficial Christmas Truce of 1914, men climbed out into no man's land to swap food and bury their dead, and by legend a kickabout broke out on the frozen mud. A letter in The Times and German Lieutenant Johannes Niemann both reported the same playful score for this match between the two sides. According to that story, who won, and by what score?
answer: The Germans, 3-2
choices: The Germans, 3-2
The British, 2-1
A scoreless draw
The British, 4-3
context: Told as legend: a letter in The Times said a regiment 'actually had a football match with the Saxons, who beat them 3-2,' and Lt. Johannes Niemann recalled goals marked with caps on the frozen mud — 'the Fritzes beat the Tommies 3-2.' Source: iwm.org.uk (The Real Story of the Christmas Truce); christmastruce.co.uk.

question: In March 1947 President Harry Truman asked Congress for $400 million in emergency aid to rescue two countries from communist takeover -- the request remembered ever since as the Truman Doctrine. Which two countries was the aid for?
answer: Greece and Turkey
choices: Greece and Turkey
Poland and Hungary
Italy and France
Korea and Japan
context: Greece was fighting communist rebels, and neighboring Turkey was under Soviet pressure to give up control of its straits. Truman's $400 million for the two became the opening move of the policy that defined the next 40 years. Source: https://history.state.gov/milestones/1945-1952/truman-doctrine

question: On March 12, 1947, President Harry Truman stood before Congress and described Greece's suffering in shocking numbers to win their votes. To convey how dire things had become for the country's children, what did Truman tell the room?
answer: Eighty-five percent of the children were tubercular
choices: Eighty-five percent of the children were tubercular
Sixty percent of the children had been orphaned
Forty percent of the children could no longer read
Ninety percent of the children had fled their villages
context: In the same speech Truman said more than a thousand Greek villages had been burned and that Greece was 'without funds to finance the importation of those goods which are essential to bare subsistence.' The grim picture was meant to move a reluctant Congress. Source: https://millercenter.org/the-presidency/presidential-speeches/march-12-1947-truman-doctrine

question: Saving Greece suddenly became America's problem in 1947 for a simple reason: the great power that had been keeping Greece afloat sent word it was bankrupt and would pull all its support by March 31. Which broke world power dumped Greece in America's lap?
answer: Great Britain
choices: Great Britain
France
The Netherlands
Italy
context: Exhausted and nearly bankrupt after World War II, Britain told Washington on February 21, 1947 -- just three weeks before Truman's speech -- that it could no longer prop up Greece. The crumbling British Empire was handing the job of resisting communism to the United States. Source: https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/truman-doctrine

question: In a closed-door 1947 briefing to win over skeptical senators, Undersecretary of State Dean Acheson reached for a vivid image to explain how one communist country could doom its neighbors -- the idea later nicknamed the 'domino theory.' What did Acheson compare a single communist state to?
answer: One rotten apple that spoils the whole barrel
choices: One rotten apple that spoils the whole barrel
A single spark that sets a dry field ablaze
A crack in a dam that floods the valley below
A loose thread that unravels an entire coat
context: Acheson warned that if Greece fell, the rot would spread to Turkey, then the Middle East, then Western Europe -- one bad apple after another. The picture frightened the senators into backing the aid. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truman_Doctrine

question: The whole Truman Doctrine boils down to a single sentence Truman spoke in 1947 -- a promise so open-ended it committed America to fight communism almost anywhere on earth for the next 40 years. What did that sentence pledge?
answer: To support free peoples resisting armed minorities or outside pressures
choices: To support free peoples resisting armed minorities or outside pressures
To station American combat troops in every major European capital
To rebuild the shattered economy of every war-torn European nation
To place all American atomic weapons under United Nations control
context: Truman's exact words: 'It must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures.' That open-ended promise became the spine of American Cold War strategy. Source: https://history.state.gov/milestones/1945-1952/truman-doctrine

question: Harry Truman didn't only want to fight communism with guns -- in his 1947 speech he offered a theory of WHY it spreads. He said the 'seeds of totalitarian regimes' sprout in one particular kind of 'soil,' and that draining that soil was the real cure. What 'soil' did Truman say grows tyranny?
answer: The evil soil of poverty and strife
choices: The evil soil of poverty and strife
The frozen soil of fear and silence
The barren soil of ignorance and sloth
The poisoned soil of envy and pride
context: Truman's full line: 'The seeds of totalitarian regimes are nurtured by misery and want. They spread and grow in the evil soil of poverty and strife. They reach their full growth when the hope of a people for a better life has died.' His remedy was to give desperate people hope before the communists could. Source: https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/truman-doctrine

question: Truman nearly lacked the votes for his 1947 aid bill until Republican Senator Arthur Vandenberg gave him blunt advice on how to win over Congress. According to Vandenberg, the only way to get the bill passed was for Truman to do what?
answer: Make a speech and scare the hell out of the country
choices: Make a speech and scare the hell out of the country
Quietly promise each senator a pet project back home
Hand the whole problem over to the United Nations
Cut the dollar figure in half and ask again later
context: Truman took the advice, framed the world as a stark choice between two ways of life, and the bill passed Congress by huge margins in May 1947. Critics later said the scare tactics oversold a smaller threat. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truman_Doctrine

question: In February 1946 a U.S. diplomat in Moscow named George Kennan was asked a narrow question -- why the Soviets opposed the new World Bank -- and instead fired back a sweeping cable of roughly 5,000 words diagnosing the entire Soviet mind. By what nickname is that famous cable known?
answer: The Long Telegram
choices: The Long Telegram
The Moscow Memorandum
The Iron Curtain Cable
The Kremlin Dispatch
context: The word 'containment' was effectively born in this cable. Historian John Lewis Gaddis called it 'the basis for United States strategy toward the Soviet Union throughout the rest of the Cold War.' Source: https://www.cfr.org/articles/george-kennan-and-the-long-telegram

question: In July 1947 George Kennan published 'The Sources of Soviet Conduct' in the journal Foreign Affairs -- the essay that carried containment's defining line to the public -- but because he still worked for the State Department, he couldn't sign his own name. What single letter did he sign the article with instead?
answer: X
choices: X
K
Z
Y
context: Kennan's line defined the strategy: U.S. policy 'must be that of a long-term, patient but firm and vigilant containment of Russian expansive tendencies.' The anonymous byline lasted barely a week before a columnist outed him. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X_Article

question: In his famous 1947 essay in the journal Foreign Affairs, George Kennan forecast that patient containment would one day force the Soviet system to break apart or 'mellow' -- and decades later the Soviet Union's collapse proved him right. Counting from his 1947 prediction, how long did the world wait for it to come true?
answer: Forty-four years
choices: Forty-four years
Sixteen years
Sixty-eight years
Ninety-two years
context: Kennan predicted in 1947 that containment would 'promote tendencies which must eventually find their outlet in either the break-up or the gradual mellowing of Soviet power.' The Soviet Union broke up in 1991 -- 44 years later, almost exactly as he forecast. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X_Article

question: George Kennan became famous as the 'father of containment' -- yet he spent the rest of his life insisting everyone got it wrong. He complained the idea had been twisted by 'the people who understood it,' who pursued it as the one thing he never meant it to be. What did Kennan say containment was wrongly turned into?
answer: A mainly military concept
choices: A mainly military concept
A purely economic aid program
A short-term emergency measure
A United Nations peacekeeping mission
context: Kennan meant political and economic pressure, not a global arms race or a war like Vietnam, which he testified against in 1966. In a 1996 interview he said his idea had been 'distorted by the people who understood it and pursued it exclusively as a military concept.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_F._Kennan

question: Containment's fiercest critic was the columnist Walter Lippmann, who blasted Kennan's open-ended commitment as a 'strategic monstrosity' across fourteen newspaper columns. The title of his 1947 book attacking the policy ended up giving the entire 40-year era its lasting name. What did Lippmann's book title call it?
answer: The Cold War
choices: The Cold War
The Long Twilight
The Iron Peace
The Great Standoff
context: Lippmann argued the open-ended promise handed the initiative to Moscow and chained America to weak, unreliable client states. His attack failed to stop the policy, but his book's title named the era that followed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X_Article

question: At a 1944 meeting in Moscow, Winston Churchill scribbled on a half-sheet of paper how Eastern Europe should be split between Britain and the Soviets -- marking Greece 90% British -- and slid it across the table to Stalin. Churchill gave that scrap of paper a now-famous nickname. What did Churchill call it?
answer: His naughty document
choices: His naughty document
His midnight bargain
His gentleman's ledger
His Moscow napkin
context: Here is the buried irony: while Truman rallied America to save Greece from Moscow, Stalin had already written the Greek rebels off, honoring this deal that made Greece 90% British. When Tito sealed the Yugoslav border in July 1949, the abandoned rebels collapsed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percentages_agreement

question: The Tuskegee Airmen were the first Black pilots in U.S. military history, trained at a segregated airfield in Tuskegee, Alabama. By 1944 their 332nd Fighter Group flew P-51 Mustangs with their tails painted bright red. What did white bomber crews -- who normally refused to fly alongside Black pilots -- do about these red-tailed escorts?
answer: specifically requested them by name as escorts
choices: specifically requested them by name as escorts
filed complaints to have them grounded
demanded white pilots replace them
refused to take off until they left
context: Bomber crews started calling the 332nd the 'Red Tails.' White bomber crews who normally despised flying with Black pilots specifically requested the Red Tails as their escorts, because they were so good at protecting the bombers. Sources: https://news.va.gov/130142/the-tuskegee-airmen-332nd-fighter-groups-red-tails/ ; https://www.sfomuseum.org/exhibitions/red-tails-ramitelli

question: On March 24, 1945, Benjamin O. Davis Jr. led the Red Tails on a 1,600-mile round trip to Berlin, the longest escort mission of the war. Over the target his pilots ran into a German weapon the Allies had never faced before -- and shot three of them down. What were those revolutionary aircraft?
answer: ME-262 jet fighters
choices: ME-262 jet fighters
Zeppelin airships
Fokker triplanes
autogyro scouts
context: The Messerschmitt ME-262 was the world's first operational jet fighter, far faster than any propeller plane. The Red Tails downed three of them on the Berlin mission and won a Distinguished Unit (Presidential Unit) Citation. Sources: https://news.va.gov/130142/the-tuskegee-airmen-332nd-fighter-groups-red-tails/ ; https://www.nationalww2museum.org/articles

question: Years before he commanded the Tuskegee Airmen, Benjamin O. Davis Jr. was the only Black cadet at West Point, and the other cadets agreed to 'silence' him for all four years to drive him out: no roommate, no one speaking to him outside of duty, eating alone.
