How did Davis answer that treatment?
answer: he graduated near the top of his class
choices: he graduated near the top of his class
he resigned to join the Navy instead
he transferred to a segregated academy
he washed out in his final year
context: The cadets meant to break him; instead Davis graduated in 1936, ranked 35th of 276. He went on to command the Tuskegee Airmen and became the first Black general in the U.S. Air Force, as his father had been the Army's first Black general. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_O._Davis_Jr. ; https://www.military.com/history/gen-benjamin-o-davis-jr.html

question: On 26 November 1922, after years of digging in Egypt's Valley of the Kings, Howard Carter chiselled a hole in a sealed door, pushed a candle through, and looked in. His backer Lord Carnarvon asked, 'Can you see anything?' What did Carter answer?
answer: 'Yes — wonderful things.'
choices: 'Yes — wonderful things.'
'No — only darkness.'
'Yes — a heap of rubble.'
'Wait — the air is foul.'
context: Carter saw gold glinting everywhere — statues, dismantled chariots, shrines and furniture. His own dig diary records the plainer 'Yes, it is wonderful'; 'wonderful things' is the famous polished version. Source: National Geographic, 'Unmasking Howard Carter'; Historic UK.

question: When Howard Carter finally reached the mummy of the pharaoh Tutankhamun, a portrait covered the boy-king's face: eyes of quartz with obsidian pupils, eyebrows of deep-blue lapis lazuli, weighing over 22 pounds. What was this famous object made of?
answer: Solid gold
choices: Solid gold
Painted clay
Carved cedar
Polished bronze
context: The death mask is about 10.23 kg (22.6 lb) of nearly pure gold, hammered from two sheets. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mask of Tutankhamun'; Smarthistory.

question: In his own time Tutankhamun was a minor pharaoh, a boy-king who ruled barely nine years and was so unimportant that later Egyptians almost erased his name. Yet today he is the most famous pharaoh of all. What turned this forgotten boy-king into a worldwide sensation in 1922?
answer: His tomb was found still sealed and packed with untouched treasure
choices: His tomb was found still sealed and packed with untouched treasure
His mummy was the tallest and best-preserved ever uncovered in Egypt
A long inscription named him the builder of the Great Pyramid
His war diaries described the largest battle of the ancient world
context: Howard Carter opened Tutankhamun's tomb in the Valley of the Kings in November 1922 with its seals largely intact after more than 3,000 years; almost uniquely among royal tombs it had escaped major looting, and its dense treasures, crowned by the solid-gold death mask, made the obscure short-reigned king world-famous.

question: Before Howard Carter ever saw gold, the very first sign of Tutankhamun's hidden tomb appeared on 4 November 1922. As the story goes, a young Egyptian water boy clearing the ground uncovered something half-buried in the rubble. What had he found?
answer: A single stone step
choices: A single stone step
A scrap of gold leaf
A painted clay pot
A worker's old sandal
context: The step turned out to be the top of a staircase leading down to a sealed door. The water-boy detail is the beloved popular version of the story. Source: HISTORY, 'Entrance to King Tut's tomb discovered'; National Geographic.  (Legend.)

question: The back of Tutankhamun's golden throne shows a tender scene: his young queen Ankhesenamun leans in to anoint him with perfumed oil, the sun's rays ending in tiny hands offering the sign of life. The artist added one homely touch showing how close the royal couple was. What do they share in the picture?
answer: A single pair of sandals
choices: A single pair of sandals
A long royal cloak
A golden drinking cup
A small pet monkey
context: Tut wears one sandal, Ankhesenamun the other — an intimate detail on a king's throne. Source: Egypt Museum, 'Golden Throne of Tutankhamun'.

question: Inside Tutankhamun's tomb the king's body lay nested in three coffins, one inside the next like Russian dolls. The outer two were gilded wood. The innermost coffin, the one cradling the mummy itself, was made of a single astonishing material. What was it?
answer: Solid gold
choices: Solid gold
Carved black ebony
Beaten silver sheet
Pale carved alabaster
context: The innermost coffin is solid gold weighing about 110 kg (around 243 lb). Source: Egypt Museum, 'Innermost Coffin of Tutankhamun'.

question: Most royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings were robbed bare long ago, yet Tutankhamun's survived nearly full. The reason was an accident next door: when workers later built the tomb of Ramesses VI, what they left behind ended up over Tut's hidden entrance and sealed it for good. What had piled over the door?
answer: A pile of workmen's stone huts
choices: A pile of workmen's stone huts
A wall of mud-brick storerooms
A row of timber tool sheds
A stack of empty grain bins
context: Rubble and the workmen's stone huts hid the door so well that later diggers camped on top of it without knowing. Source: Egypt Ministry of Tourism & Antiquities; National Geographic.

question: Among Tutankhamun's treasures Carter found a dagger whose blade puzzled scientists: it is iron carrying about 11% nickel, made roughly 600 years before Egyptians could smelt iron at all. Tests revealed where that strange metal came from. Where was the iron in the dagger from?
answer: A fallen meteorite from the sky
choices: A fallen meteorite from the sky
Bog ore dug in the Nile delta
Bars smelted by Hittite traders
An old weapon melted down again
context: The 11% nickel and 0.6% cobalt are the fingerprint of an octahedrite meteorite — sky-metal, more precious than gold. Source: HeritageDaily, 'The mystery of Tutankhamun's meteoric iron dagger'.

question: The boy-king was not born 'Tutankhamun.' He started life as 'Tutankhaten' under his father Akhenaten, who had banned Egypt's old gods to worship only the sun-disc Aten. When Tut took the throne he chose a new name that announced a reversal. What did the name 'Tutankhamun' proclaim?
answer: He had restored the old gods
choices: He had restored the old gods
He served the sun-disc alone
He was now Amun's high priest
He had merged two gods in one
context: 'Tutankhaten' meant 'living image of the Aten'; 'Tutankhamun' means 'living image of Amun' — one of the old gods he brought back. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tutankhamun'.

question: Tutankhamun's tomb is often called untouched, but that is not quite true: robbers broke in twice within a few years of the burial. So why did so much treasure still survive for Carter to find?
answer: Officials caught the thieves and resealed the tomb
choices: Officials caught the thieves and resealed the tomb
The thieves grabbed only the loose jewelry and left
A second gang buried part of the loot to fetch later
Guards walled off the burial chamber before the raids
context: Necropolis officials caught the robbers, hastily repacked the treasures, and resealed the tomb both times; one gang had about eight hours inside. In their panic the thieves even dropped a linen scarf knotted around eight solid-gold rings, which the guards stuffed back in a box — Carter found it still tied 3,000 years later. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tomb of Tutankhamun'; Ancient Origins.

question: When Lord Carnarvon, who had funded the dig, died on 5 April 1923 from an infected mosquito bite he reopened while shaving, newspapers cried 'the curse of the pharaohs.' Howard Carter was the man who actually opened the tomb and unwrapped the mummy. What became of Carter in the years after the discovery?
answer: He lived on for about seventeen more years
choices: He lived on for about seventeen more years
He died within weeks of Carnarvon
He fell deathly ill inside the tomb
He fled Egypt and was never seen again
context: Carter died of natural causes in 1939 — the 'curse' conveniently skipped its most obvious target. Even Sherlock Holmes author Arthur Conan Doyle had blamed Carnarvon's death on the curse. The curse was a press legend, not fact. Source: Britannica, 'Howard Carter'; Live Science.

question: Tutankhamun was long imagined as a healthy golden boy, but a 2010 DNA and CT-scan study published in JAMA painted a harsher picture of his short life. Besides a club foot that forced him to walk with a cane, what did the scans suggest finally killed him?
answer: A broken leg that turned deadly with malaria
choices: A broken leg that turned deadly with malaria
A poisoned cup at a feast that stopped his heart
A chariot crash that shattered his royal skull
A festering wound from a fall while hunting
context: The study found Tut suffered from malaria and likely died after a broken leg turned deadly when malaria struck; the same tests showed his parents were brother and sister. Source: National Geographic, 'King Tut Was Disabled, Malarial, and Inbred, DNA Shows'; JAMA study.

question: The Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe lost the bridge of his nose in a sword duel fought in the dark on a December night in 1566, after he and his own cousin quarreled at a party over which of them was the better mathematician. For the rest of his life he wore a metal false nose. Legend insisted it was silver and gold, but when scientists dug up his body and tested a bone sample in 2010, what cheap everyday metal was the prosthesis actually made of?
answer: Brass
choices: Brass
Silver
Gold
Iron
context: The 2012 analysis of Tycho Brahe's exhumed remains showed his everyday false nose was brass, not the fabled silver and gold (he may have owned fancier ones for special occasions). The duel was against his third cousin Manderup Parsberg. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tycho_Brahe

question: Tycho Brahe spent twenty years measuring the planets with giant instruments and no telescope, recording positions accurate to within 1 to 2 arcminutes — the sharpest naked-eye observations ever made. After Tycho died, his assistant Johannes Kepler found that a perfect circle fit Tycho's records of Mars almost exactly, except for one stubborn gap of 8 arcminutes. Trusting that Tycho's data were too precise to be wrong, Kepler chased those 8 minutes and overturned 2,000 years of astronomy by proving that orbits are not circles but what shape?
answer: Ellipses
choices: Ellipses
Spirals
Squares
Triangles
context: Kepler wrote that 'these eight minutes alone will lead us along a path to the reform of the whole of Astronomy.' Because Tycho Brahe's Mars data were trustworthy to 1–2 arcminutes, the 8-arcminute discrepancy could not be fudged away, and following it forced Kepler to abandon perfect circles for elliptical orbits. Source: https://www.astronomy.ohio-state.edu/pogge.1/Ast161/Au06/Unit3/watershed.html

question: The Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe lost a chunk of his nose in a sword duel at age twenty and wore a metal replacement for the rest of his life. For centuries everyone assumed the false nose was gold and silver to match his noble rank. When his body was dug up in 2010, the green stains on his nasal bones gave away what his everyday nose was really made of. What was it?
answer: Brass
choices: Brass
Solid gold
Pure silver
Carved ivory
context: The stains were equal parts copper and zinc — the recipe for brass, a cheap workhorse metal, not the precious alloy of legend. He likely kept a fancier gold-and-silver nose for special occasions and wore the brass one day to day. Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) lost the nose in 1566 dueling fellow student Manderup Parsberg over which of them was the better mathematician. Source: Aarhus University tycho-brahe project (projekter.au.dk); phys.org 2012.

question: On November 11, 1572, Tycho Brahe watched a brilliant new star blaze up in Cassiopeia, brighter than Venus and visible in daylight. Ancient teaching held the heavens were perfect and never changed — so any new light had to be something close by, below the Moon, in the changeable air. Tycho measured the star's position night after night and found it never shifted against the surrounding stars, the way a nearby object would. What did that absence of shift prove about the new star?
answer: It lay far beyond the Moon, out among the fixed stars
choices: It lay far beyond the Moon, out among the fixed stars
It was a flame burning in Earth's upper air
It was a comet swinging close past the Moon
It was a reflection thrown off the planet Venus
context: A nearby object shifts against the background when you view it from different angles (parallax); a truly distant one does not. The new star showed no shift, so it sat out among the fixed stars — meaning the supposedly perfect, unchanging heavens had changed. Tycho's book De nova stella (1573) helped give us the word 'nova.' Source: Britannica, De nova stella; NCAR High Altitude Observatory.

question: In 1854 a savage cholera outbreak hit London's Soho neighborhood, killing roughly 500 people in just ten days. Dr. John Snow had mapped every death and noticed they clustered around one source of drinking water on Broad Street. To end the outbreak, what did he convince the parish to do to that water pump?
answer: Take the handle off so no one could draw water from it
choices: Take the handle off so no one could draw water from it
Burn incense and herbs around it to purify the air
Post a constable to guard it day and night
Pour lime and ash down its well to sweeten the water
context: On 7 September 1854 the parish removed the Broad Street pump handle; once people could no longer drink from it, the outbreak died away. Mapping deaths to a single pump and acting on it is celebrated as the founding moment of epidemiology. Source: https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/collections/london-stories/john-snow-cholera-broad-street-pump/

question: As cholera tore through Soho in 1854, John Snow noticed one strange pocket of safety: the workers at the Lion Brewery on Broad Street almost never caught the disease, even as it killed their neighbors. What were those brewery workers doing that kept them safe from the contaminated pump?
answer: Drinking their daily ration of free beer instead of pump water
choices: Drinking their daily ration of free beer instead of pump water
Boiling all their drinking water over the brewery fires
Living and sleeping inside the sealed brewery vaults
Washing constantly with the brewery's strong soap
context: The brewers' free daily beer ration meant they never touched the Broad Street pump's contaminated water, so the disease passed them by. The brewery's survival was a vivid clue pointing Snow straight at the water. Source: https://historycollection.com/john-snow-stopped-cholera-london-help-500-beer-drinkers/

question: In the hot summer of 1858 the human and industrial sewage dumped into London's River Thames baked in the heat until the smell became unbearable. This 'Great Stink' grew so overpowering that it finally forced action from one group of people in particular. Who got driven out by the stench, pushing them to fund a proper sewer system?
answer: The lawmakers in the riverside Houses of Parliament
choices: The lawmakers in the riverside Houses of Parliament
The merchants trading at the London docks
The patients in the city's largest hospital
The brewers working along the riverbank
context: The stench from the Thames drove the lawmakers out of the Houses of Parliament, sitting right on the river. The disgust finally pushed Parliament to fund a proper sewer network for London. Source: https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/collections/london-stories/great-stink-of-1858/

question: When John Snow blamed Soho's 1854 cholera on dirty water, a local clergyman, Reverend Henry Whitehead, set out to prove him wrong and show the outbreak was instead an act of God. Whitehead went door to door interviewing survivors. What did his own investigation end up doing to Snow's water theory?
answer: It confirmed the theory and traced the source to a leaking cesspool
choices: It confirmed the theory and traced the source to a leaking cesspool
It disproved the theory and showed bad air was to blame
It proved the disease had spread person to person, not by water
It revealed the pump water had actually been perfectly clean
context: Whitehead's interviews ended up confirming Snow's water theory. He helped trace the source to a sick baby at 40 Broad Street whose mother rinsed the infected nappies into a cesspool that leaked into the pump well. Source: https://www.choleraandthethames.co.uk/cholera-in-london/cholera-in-soho/

question: Engineer Joseph Bazalgette designed London's huge new sewer network in the 1860s. Legend says that after he calculated exactly how wide the pipes needed to be for the city's population, he made one bold decision about every pipe diameter, reasoning the city would only be dug up for this once. According to the story, what did he do with his calculated sizes?
answer: He doubled every pipe diameter to leave room for future growth
choices: He doubled every pipe diameter to leave room for future growth
He shrank every pipe to save on the cost of bricks
He built two parallel pipes everywhere instead of one
He left the pipes at exactly the size his math required
context: As the story goes, Bazalgette doubled every diameter, reasoning the city would only be dug up once. That extra capacity is why his 1860s sewers still cope with a London many times larger. (Told as a celebrated engineering legend.) Source: https://blog.nationalarchives.gov.uk/saviour-of-the-sewers

question: On V-E Day, May 8, 1945, the 19-year-old Princess Elizabeth — the future Queen Elizabeth II — slipped out of Buckingham Palace and into the celebrating London crowd in disguise, pulling her uniform cap down over her eyes so no one would recognize her. What did she and her sister Margaret do that night, which Elizabeth later called one of the most memorable of her life?
answer: Danced the hokey-cokey and conga'd through the Ritz hotel
choices: Danced the hokey-cokey and conga'd through the Ritz hotel
Climbed onto the palace gates to wave at the crowd below
Rode in an open car down the length of Whitehall
Lit the first bonfire in Trafalgar Square at midnight
context: Princess Elizabeth, then a teenager, and her 14-year-old sister Princess Margaret danced the hokey-cokey and the Lambeth Walk and conga'd right through the Ritz hotel, anonymous in the V-E Day crowd. She later called it 'one of the most memorable nights of my life.' Source: https://www.itv.com/news/2020-04-29/princess-elizabeth-celebrated-unnoticed-among-the-crowds-on-ve-day

question: When General Douglas MacArthur signed Japan's surrender aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay on September 2, 1945, he used six pens — and handed two of them to Lt. General Jonathan Wainwright and Lt. General Arthur Percival, who had stood beside him for the signing. Why those two men?
answer: They had been forced to surrender to Japan early in the war and survived as prisoners
choices: They had been forced to surrender to Japan early in the war and survived as prisoners
They had drafted the terms of the Instrument of Surrender
They commanded the warships staged in Tokyo Bay that day
They were the longest-serving generals in MacArthur's command
context: Wainwright surrendered the Philippines and Percival surrendered Singapore in the war's dark early days; both endured years as Japanese prisoners of war. MacArthur, presiding over the 23-minute ceremony, gave them the pens that ended the war they had once lost — closing the circle. Source: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/topics/v-j-day-surrender-japan

question: About 2,000 of George Washington's soldiers died during the six-month Valley Forge encampment of 1777-78 -- roughly one in six men. People picture them freezing in the snow, but that frozen image hides the real killer. What killed the most men in the camp?
answer: Sickness sweeping the crowded camp
choices: Sickness sweeping the crowded camp
Freezing solid in the deep snow
Starving once the food ran out
British soldiers raiding the huts
context: Influenza, typhus, typhoid, and dysentery spread through the packed log-hut camp and killed far more men than the cold. The encampment held about 12,000 soldiers in 1,500-2,000 huts -- briefly one of the largest 'cities' in America. Source: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/10-facts-valley-forge

question: At Valley Forge in 1778, the Prussian officer Baron Friedrich von Steuben drilled Washington's ragged, half-starved army into a real fighting force -- and to do it, he sat up at night by candlelight scribbling the next day's lesson in French for his aides to translate. What was von Steuben writing in those candlelit nights?
answer: The army's first drill manual
choices: The army's first drill manual
A surrender note to the British
Washington's wartime diary
A new flag for the army
context: Von Steuben's manual was published as the 'Regulations for the Order and Discipline of the Troops of the United States' -- the 'Blue Book' -- and stayed the U.S. Army's official guide until 1812. Its diagrams were drawn by Pierre L'Enfant, the future designer of Washington, D.C. Source: https://www.americanrevolutioninstitute.org/steubens-blue-book-manual/

question: Vincent van Gogh painted his swirling masterpiece The Starry Night in June 1889. Where was he living when he painted it?
answer: in a room in a mental asylum, looking out a barred window
choices: in a room in a mental asylum, looking out a barred window
in a seaside cottage he shared with other painters
in a Paris apartment above his brother's art shop
in a farmhouse he rented out near the wheatfields
context: Van Gogh had voluntarily committed himself to the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum in Saint-Remy, France, and painted The Starry Night from a barred second-floor window. The year he spent there was the most productive of his life — over 150 works, including his Irises. Source: MoMA, moma.org/collection/works/79802.

question: In December 1888 in Arles, after a bitter quarrel with the painter Paul Gauguin, Vincent van Gogh took a razor and cut off part of his own ear. What did he then do with the severed ear?
answer: wrapped it up and gave it to a young woman, telling her to keep it carefully
choices: wrapped it up and gave it to a young woman, telling her to keep it carefully
mailed it in a small box to his brother Theo up in Paris
buried it in the garden behind the Yellow House
left it nailed to the door of Gauguin's room
context: The woman fainted. Newspapers called her 'Rachel'; researchers later identified her as Gabrielle Berlatier, a teenage farm girl working as a maid. Source: The Art Newspaper, theartnewspaper.com/2016/07/20/name-of-mystery-woman-who-received-van-goghs-ear-revealed-for-first-time; Artnet, news.artnet.com/art-world/van-gogh-ear-gabrielle-berlatier-566720.

question: While living at the asylum, Vincent van Gogh became obsessed with painting tall, dark cypress trees. In a letter to his brother Theo, he said a cypress was as beautiful in its lines and proportions as what?
answer: an Egyptian obelisk
choices: an Egyptian obelisk
a Gothic cathedral
a ship's mast
a burning candle
context: From letter 783 to Theo, 25 June 1889: a cypress is 'beautiful as regards lines and proportions, like an Egyptian obelisk.' Cypresses tower over The Starry Night. Source: Van Gogh letters, vangoghletters.org/vg/letters/let783/letter.html.

question: Over about ten years Vincent van Gogh made roughly 900 paintings — about one every four days. Yet during his whole life he is known to have sold only ONE of them. Which painting was it?
answer: The Red Vineyard
choices: The Red Vineyard
The Starry Night
Sunflowers
The Potato Eaters
context: The Red Vineyard was bought by Belgian painter Anna Boch for 400 francs at the 1890 Les XX exhibition in Brussels. Almost unknown and poor in his own time, Van Gogh is now among the most famous painters ever — his works sell for over 100 million dollars. Source: My Modern Met, mymodernmet.com/vincent-van-gogh-only-painting-sold-lifetime.

question: Most people assume Vincent van Gogh painted The Starry Night outdoors at night. In fact he painted it during the day, from memory. What he had really seen was one dawn: he wrote to his brother Theo that before sunrise he saw a single, very big bright point in the sky. That 'morning star' was actually which object?
answer: the planet Venus
choices: the planet Venus
the planet Mars
the star Polaris
a passing comet
context: Letter 777 to Theo: 'This morning I saw the countryside from my window a long time before sunrise with nothing but the morning star, which looked very big.' The 'morning star' is the planet Venus. The church steeple in the painting wasn't even visible from his window. Source: vangoghletters.org/vg/letters/let777/letter.html; Artnet, news.artnet.com/art-world/3-things-about-vincent-van-goghs-starry-night-2020713.

question: On 27 July 1890 Vincent van Gogh shot himself in a wheatfield near Auvers-sur-Oise, then walked back wounded to his room at the Auberge Ravoux inn, where he died a day and a half later with his brother Theo beside him. Theo reported that among Van Gogh's last words was which line?
answer: "The sadness will last forever."
choices: "The sadness will last forever."
"I have done my life's work."
"Tell them I tried my best."
"Now I can finally rest."
context: As reported by Theo, the French was 'La tristesse durera toujours.' Questioned by police about blame, the wounded Van Gogh reportedly said, 'Do not accuse anybody, it is I that wished to commit suicide.' Both lines are remembered testimony (reported by family), not court record. Source: Death of Vincent van Gogh, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_of_Vincent_van_Gogh.  (Legend.)

question: Vasco da Gama reached the East African port of Malindi in 1498 needing to cross the wide-open Indian Ocean to India, with no coast to follow. A local pilot showed him a seasonal wind that blows steadily from the southwest for part of the year and could carry a ship straight across the open water. What wind did da Gama ride across the ocean to India?
answer: The summer monsoon
choices: The summer monsoon
The Atlantic trade winds
The cold polar easterlies
The dry desert sirocco
context: At Malindi da Gama took aboard a skilled local pilot (often said to be the famous Arab navigator Ahmad ibn Majid — that identification is legend) who knew the southwest monsoon. Riding it, the fleet crossed the open Indian Ocean and anchored off the spice port of Calicut on 20 May 1498 — the first ship ever to sail all the way from Europe to India. Source: Britannica (britannica.com/biography/Vasco-da-Gama); EBSCO Research Starters.

question: Before Vasco da Gama, the pepper and spices of India reached Europe only after a long overland and Red Sea journey through Arab merchants and the merchants of Venice, who marked the goods up at every step. When da Gama's ships carried spices straight from India to Lisbon by sea in 1499, whose long-held grip on the spice trade did the new ocean route break?
answer: The Venetian and Arab middlemen's monopoly
choices: The Venetian and Arab middlemen's monopoly
The Spanish crown's royal treasury
The Ottoman Sultan's personal navy
The Chinese emperor's tribute fleet
context: The sea route broke the centuries-old Venetian and Arab overland/Red Sea hold on the spice trade, letting Portugal ship pepper straight to Europe — a single cargo could sell for many times its purchase cost, reorienting world trade toward the Atlantic. The Berrio was first home, reaching Lisbon on 10 July 1499, almost exactly two years after the fleet set out. Source: World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/article/2025/the-portuguese-conquest-of-india); Britannica.

question: In July 1497 Vasco da Gama sailed out of Lisbon with four ships, aiming to be the first European to sail all the way around Africa to India. After almost a year at sea he finally dropped anchor at a spice port on India's southwest coast in May 1498. Which Indian city did da Gama reach?
answer: Calicut
choices: Calicut
Lisbon
Malindi
Mecca
context: Da Gama reached Calicut on 20 May 1498 after leaving Lisbon on 8 July 1497 with four ships built specially for the voyage — the flagship Sao Gabriel, the Sao Rafael under his brother Paulo da Gama, the caravel Berrio under Nicolau Coelho, and a storeship. He was the first European to sail from Europe all the way to India. (Source: Roteiro, the eyewitness journal of the voyage, via Internet Modern History Sourcebook; Mariner's Museum Ages of Exploration.)

question: To mark the coasts he claimed for Portugal, Vasco da Gama left behind a string of tall carved stone pillars, each one topped with a Christian cross, planted at his landing spots along the African and Indian shores. What did the Portuguese call these stone marker-pillars?
answer: padrao
choices: padrao
caravels
Berrio
Sao Gabriel
context: Da Gama's expedition set up about six padrao — tall carved stone pillars crowned with a cross — to claim the coasts for Portugal. (Source: World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Vasco_da_Gama.)

question: When the first of Vasco da Gama's men stepped ashore near Calicut in 1498, two Tunisian Moors who happened to speak Spanish snapped at him: 'May the Devil take thee! What brought you hither?' Asked what he had crossed half the world to find, the Portuguese sailor gave a famous two-word answer — what was he after?
answer: Christians and spices
choices: Christians and spices
Gold and silver
Slaves and silk
Land and glory
context: The eyewitness answered that they came 'in search of Christians and of spices' — the twin goals of the voyage. (Source: Roteiro eyewitness journal, via Internet Modern History Sourcebook.)

question: Vasco da Gama could not actually have crossed the open Indian Ocean on his own — Portuguese ships had never made that run before. At the East African port of Malindi he solved the problem by taking a particular expert aboard, after which his fleet ran straight across the ocean and sighted India's mountains in about 23 days. What did da Gama take on at Malindi?
answer: a local pilot who knew the route to India
choices: a local pilot who knew the route to India
a fresh cargo of gold and coral
a hundred armed guards
a chest of Portuguese trade goods
context: At Malindi (in modern Kenya) da Gama took aboard a local pilot who already knew the route, and the fleet crossed to sight the Ghat mountains in about 23 days. The old tale that the pilot was the famous Arab navigator Ahmad Ibn Majid has been disproved by scholars. (Source: World History Encyclopedia; Mariner's Museum Ages of Exploration.)

question: Vasco da Gama laid out his presents for the Zamorin, the king of Calicut: twelve pieces of striped cloth, four scarlet hoods, six hats, some strings of coral, and casks of sugar, oil, and honey. The king's officials burst out laughing and refused to even pass the gifts along. What insult did they throw at the great explorer's offering?
answer: the poorest merchant from Mecca gave more
choices: the poorest merchant from Mecca gave more
such trinkets were fit only for slaves
Portugal must be a land of beggars
they would feed it to the king's dogs
context: The officials laughed that it was no gift for a king — even 'the poorest merchant from Mecca gave more' — and said a real present should be in gold. Beside the Zamorin sat a golden cup-spittoon holding about 8 pints and a gold basin a man could barely encircle with his arms; da Gama's cheap goods looked shabby by comparison. (Source: Roteiro eyewitness journal, via Internet Modern History Sourcebook.)

question: Vasco da Gama's second voyage to India in 1502 was sent for vengeance, not trade. Off the Indian coast he stopped a ship called the Miri carrying Muslim pilgrims home from Mecca — and committed an atrocity that has stained his name ever since. What did da Gama do to the Miri and the people aboard her?
answer: seized its cargo and burned it with hundreds of passengers aboard
choices: seized its cargo and burned it with hundreds of passengers aboard
ransomed every passenger back to the Zamorin for gold
sank it in a sea battle after the pilgrims resisted
let it pass and seized the port of Calicut instead
context: Da Gama seized the Miri's cargo and set the ship on fire, burning hundreds of pilgrims including women and children, then bombarded the unfortified port of Calicut for two days, nearly destroying it. (Source: World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/article/2025/the-portuguese-conquest-of-india.)

question: On 25 September 1513, Vasco Nunez de Balboa and his men hacked across the jungles of Panama chasing a rumor of a sea no European had ever seen. Near the top of the last hill, Balboa did something so he alone would be the first European to lay eyes on it. What did he do?
answer: Climbed the final hill alone, ahead of all his men
choices: Climbed the final hill alone, ahead of all his men
Fired his cannon to announce the discovery first
Sent his fastest scout sprinting to the summit
Knelt and waited for a sign before climbing
context: Balboa ordered his party to halt and went up the last slope by himself, so that he would be the first European to see the ocean; only then did he call the rest of the men up to look. He named it the South Sea (Mar del Sur) because his march had gone south across the isthmus. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_N%C3%BA%C3%B1ez_de_Balboa

question: Days after first sighting the new ocean, Vasco Nunez de Balboa reached its shore at the Gulf of San Miguel. In full armor, sword in one hand and a banner of the Virgin Mary in the other, he claimed the whole ocean and all its shores for the kings of Spain. The name he gave that ocean came from one plain fact about his journey. What was it?
answer: He had marched south to reach it, so he called it the South Sea
choices: He had marched south to reach it, so he called it the South Sea
He claimed it on a feast day, so he called it the Holy Sea
Its water was warm, so he called it the Summer Sea
He saw it at dawn, so he called it the Morning Sea
context: Balboa waded knee-deep into the surf to take possession and named the ocean Mar del Sur, the South Sea, simply because his expedition had crossed Panama heading south. It kept that name until Ferdinand Magellan rechristened it the Pacific in 1520. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_N%C3%BA%C3%B1ez_de_Balboa

question: In Diego Velazquez's huge 1656 painting Las Meninas, the little Spanish princess and her maids fill the room, and Velazquez even paints himself at his easel. But King Philip IV and Queen Mariana, who ought to be the painting's subject, are nowhere among the figures. So where in the painting do you finally spot the king and queen of Spain?
answer: As a small, dim reflection in a mirror on the back wall
choices: As a small, dim reflection in a mirror on the back wall
Seated together on twin thrones along the left edge
Painted in miniature on the easel's hidden canvas
Standing in the bright doorway at the very back
context: The royal couple show up only as a faint reflection in a mirror on the rear wall — which means they must be standing right where WE, the viewers, stand, looking into the room. That puzzle of who is looking at whom is what makes the painting famous. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Meninas

question: On Velazquez's chest in Las Meninas glows the red cross of the knightly Order of Santiago — yet the painter signed the work in 1656 and was not made a knight until 1659, three years later. By tradition, who added that red cross to the painting after Velazquez had died?
answer: King Philip IV, the painter's own royal master
choices: King Philip IV, the painter's own royal master
The Order of Santiago, finally relenting
A rival court painter, mocking his ambition
His widow, Juana, completing his last wish
context: Legend holds that King Philip IV himself painted the Santiago cross onto Velazquez's chest after the painter's death — the king's way of honoring (and avenging) a painter the snobbish Order had refused to accept as a true nobleman. This is tradition rather than documented fact. Source: https://mymodernmet.com/diego-velazquez-las-meninas/

question: Johannes Vermeer, the Dutch painter behind the luminous 'Girl with a Pearl Earring,' worked his whole life and is now ranked among the greatest masters of the Golden Age. Yet for all that fame, only a startlingly small number of his paintings still survive from his entire career. About how many?
answer: Around 34 paintings
choices: Around 34 paintings
Around 340 paintings
Around 900 paintings
Around 3,400 paintings
context: Only about 34 paintings survive from Vermeer's whole career (a 35th is disputed) — a tiny output that makes each one precious. 'Girl with a Pearl Earring' is small too, about 44.5 by 39 cm, signed 'IVMeer' in the top-left corner but never dated; scholars place it around 1665. Source: https://www.essentialvermeer.com/catalogue/girl_with_a_pearl_earring.html

question: The shining pearl in Vermeer's 'Girl with a Pearl Earring' looks round, heavy, and perfectly real — but up close, restorers found there is no hook, no chain, and almost no detail at all. Vermeer conjured the whole glowing jewel out of just one trick. What did he actually paint?
answer: Two brushstrokes of white — a bright highlight on top and a soft reflection below
choices: Two brushstrokes of white — a bright highlight on top and a soft reflection below
A web of fine silver threads to catch the eye
Dozens of tiny dots layered into a sphere
A real pearl pressed into the wet paint
context: Vermeer painted the famous pearl with essentially two strokes: one bright white highlight at top left catching the window light, and a softer reflection at the bottom catching light bouncing up off her white collar. There is no painted hook holding it on. The 'pearl' may not even be a pearl — experts think it is a drop of glass varnished to look matte, or simply invented; astrophysicist Vincent Icke argued it looks more like polished tin. Source: https://www.essentialvermeer.com/catalogue/girl_with_a_pearl_earring.html

question: As a young student at Louvain, Andreas Vesalius wanted a real human skeleton to study but had no legal way to get one. What did he do to obtain a complete set of human bones?
answer: Stole a hanged criminal's body from a roadside gallows and carried the bones home to reassemble
choices: Stole a hanged criminal's body from a roadside gallows and carried the bones home to reassemble
Bought a preserved skeleton from a traveling merchant who sold curiosities
Copied the bone drawings out of an ancient Greek anatomy manual
Talked a city official into letting him keep an executed prisoner's body
context: Vesalius climbed up to a gibbet outside the city walls, cut down a hanged criminal's body, and carried the bones home in pieces to reassemble - risking imprisonment to get a real human skeleton. Source: Stanford history13 Vesalius reading; Citizendium 'Vesalius'.

question: Andreas Vesalius revered the ancient authority Galen, whose anatomy had been trusted for over 1,300 years. But cutting human bodies apart with his own hands in the 1540s, Vesalius discovered why Galen had gotten the human body wrong more than two hundred times. What was Galen's mistake?
answer: Galen had dissected apes, dogs, and pigs, never an actual human body
choices: Galen had dissected apes, dogs, and pigs, never an actual human body
Galen had relied on injured soldiers who could not be cut open fully
Galen had copied his anatomy from even older Egyptian writings
Galen had studied only the bones and never the soft inner organs
context: In his preface to De Humani Corporis Fabrica (1543), Vesalius wrote that Galen 'deviated more than two hundred times from the correct description' of the human body - because Galen had dissected animals and assumed humans matched. Source: Stanford history13 Vesalius reading; PubMed 11625189.

question: Galen taught that blood crossed from one side of the heart to the other by seeping through tiny invisible holes in the thick wall between the chambers. When Andreas Vesalius examined that wall in real human hearts, what did he report finding?
answer: No holes at all - the wall was thick and solid
choices: No holes at all - the wall was thick and solid
A single large opening Galen had described too small
Holes only in the hearts of the very old
Channels that ran the wrong direction from Galen's account
context: Vesalius looked for Galen's holes in the interventricular septum and could not find them. This crack in Galen's blood theory helped open the path toward later discovering the circulation of the blood. Source: Biology Insights 'Andreas Vesalius's Discoveries'; Springer 'Circulation of Blood in Renaissance Medicine'.

question: On June 11, 1963, a 73-year-old Buddhist monk named Thich Quang Duc sat down in the lotus position at a busy Saigon intersection to protest his government's persecution of Buddhists, let fellow monks pour gasoline over him, and lit a match. What stunned the watching crowd as the flames rose?
answer: He sat perfectly still and never moved or cried out as he burned to death.
choices: He sat perfectly still and never moved or cried out as he burned to death.
He stood up and walked several steps through the fire before he collapsed.
He chanted a prayer aloud until the flames finally silenced him.
He raised one hand in a blessing toward the watching police lines.
context: AP photographer Malcolm Browne captured the moment, and the picture went around the world. President Kennedy said, 'No news picture in history has generated so much emotion around the world as that one.' Source: https://time.com/3791176/malcolm-browne-the-story-behind-the-burning-monk/

question: On June 8, 1972, AP photographer Nick Ut took one of the war's most famous photographs outside Trang Bang: 9-year-old Phan Thi Kim Phuc running down a road, naked and screaming, her skin burning after a South Vietnamese plane mistakenly dropped napalm on her own village. After he snapped the shot, what did Nick Ut do?
answer: He put down his camera, gave her water, and rushed her to the nearest hospital.
choices: He put down his camera, gave her water, and rushed her to the nearest hospital.
He kept shooting a full roll of film and then drove back to his bureau.
He wrapped her in his jacket and waited beside her for an ambulance.
He carried her to a nearby temple where the monks tended her burns.
context: Ut's act saved her life. The photo, titled 'The Terror of War,' won the 1973 Pulitzer Prize. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Terror_of_War

question: By April 29, 1975, North Vietnamese tanks were closing on Saigon and the US launched the largest helicopter evacuation in history. The secret signal telling Americans to head for the pickup points was a fake weather report -- 'The temperature in Saigon is 105 degrees and rising' -- followed on Armed Forces Radio by which song?
answer: 'White Christmas' by Bing Crosby
choices: 'White Christmas' by Bing Crosby
'We Gotta Get Out of This Place' by The Animals
'Fortunate Son' by Creedence Clearwater Revival
'Leaving on a Jet Plane' by Peter, Paul and Mary
context: In Operation Frequent Wind, 1,373 Americans and 5,595 Vietnamese were lifted out. So many South Vietnamese pilots landed their own helicopters on US Navy ships that the crews shoved aircraft overboard to make room. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Frequent_Wind

question: Desperate to fight, Dan Bullock walked into a Marine recruiting station and altered his birth certificate so he could pass for the required age of 18. He was killed by an enemy satchel charge thrown into his bunker at the An Hoa base on June 7, 1969 -- the youngest American to die in Vietnam, barely a month after he shipped out. How old was he really when he was killed?
context: Bullock had altered his certificate and joined up at just 14. He had been in the country less than a month when he died. Source: https://www.vvmf.org/stories/Dan-Bullock/

question: In May 1969 the 101st Airborne fought ten days up the steep, muddy slopes of Hill 937 in the A Shau Valley -- a meat-grinder battle the men nicknamed 'Hamburger Hill' -- and finally took the summit. Just over two weeks later the Army simply abandoned it. A soldier nailed a piece of cardboard to a tree reading 'Hamburger Hill,' and another GI scrawled three more words beneath it. What did they say?
answer: Was it worth it?
choices: Was it worth it?
For sale, cheap.
We gave it back.
Home of the brave.
context: The general who had ordered the hill's capture later admitted it had 'no military value whatsoever.' Weeks afterward, Life magazine printed the faces of 242 Americans killed in a single week in Vietnam, a moment that helped turn the public against the war. Source: https://time.com/archive/6634203/world-the-battle-for-hamburger-hill/

question: On March 16, 1968, helicopter pilot Hugh Thompson flew over the village of My Lai and saw American soldiers of Charlie Company gunning down hundreds of unarmed women, children, and old men. Thompson set his small helicopter down on the ground between the soldiers and a group of fleeing villagers. What order did he give his two crewmen?
answer: To open fire on the American soldiers if they kept shooting the villagers.
choices: To open fire on the American soldiers if they kept shooting the villagers.
To radio headquarters at once and report the officers by name.
To load as many wounded children aboard as the aircraft would hold.
To fire warning shots over the soldiers' heads to scatter them off.
context: Thompson then flew survivors to safety. Between 347 and 504 villagers were murdered at My Lai. Lieutenant William Calley was the only man ever convicted for the massacre. Source: https://armyhistory.org/my-lai/

question: Shot down over Hanoi, Navy pilot John McCain was held in the prison that American POWs bitterly nicknamed the 'Hanoi Hilton,' where they tapped coded messages to one another through the walls. When his captors learned his father was a famous admiral, they offered McCain an early release ahead of the other prisoners. What did he tell them?
answer: He refused, insisting the men be freed in the order they were captured.
choices: He refused, insisting the men be freed in the order they were captured.
He accepted only if his whole squadron was released along with him.
He demanded to be allowed to meet the International Red Cross first.
He agreed, but secretly passed the offer up to the senior officer.
context: The prison's real name, Hoa Lo, means 'fiery furnace.' Prisoners kept morale up with a WWII-era tap code on the pipes and concrete. McCain stayed more than five years. Source: https://allthatsinteresting.com/hanoi-hilton

question: The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, which handed President Johnson a blank check to wage war in Vietnam, rested partly on a reported attack by North Vietnamese boats on the destroyer USS Maddox on August 4, 1964. Years later, investigators reached a startling conclusion about that second attack. What was it?
answer: No North Vietnamese boats were even there that night -- the attack was never real.
choices: No North Vietnamese boats were even there that night -- the attack was never real.
The boats had fired first, but every torpedo missed the Maddox in the dark.
A single torpedo struck the Maddox that night but failed to explode on impact.
The Maddox had sunk two North Vietnamese patrol boats during the brief clash.
context: A real attack on the Maddox had happened two days earlier, on August 2 -- but the August 4 attack never occurred, and the NSA was later found to have skewed the intelligence to make it look as though it had. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/Gulf-of-Tonkin-incident

question: The Tet Offensive of January 1968 was actually a military disaster for the communists -- they lost far more fighters than the Americans and held no captured ground for long. Yet it broke American confidence in the war almost overnight, because of one scene that made a mockery of official promises that the war was nearly won. What did stunned Americans see on the evening news?
answer: Viet Cong fighters who had blasted their way inside the US embassy grounds in Saigon.
choices: Viet Cong fighters who had blasted their way inside the US embassy grounds in Saigon.
Marines setting fire to a village's huts with cigarette lighters on camera.
A South Vietnamese officer shooting a bound prisoner dead in the street.
Tanks crushing the US ambassador's parked car outside the embassy gates.
context: General Westmoreland had just been promising 'light at the end of the tunnel.' The communists timed the offensive for the Vietnamese New Year, Tet, launching it on January 30, 1968. Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/analysis-we-are-mired-stalemate

question: On February 27, 1968, just after the Tet Offensive, the most trusted newsman in America -- CBS anchor Walter Cronkite -- broke his lifelong rule against giving his own opinion and told viewers the war could not be won. President Johnson reportedly said that losing Cronkite meant he had lost middle America. How did Cronkite sum up the war?
answer: He said America was 'mired in stalemate.'
choices: He said America was 'mired in stalemate.'
He said the war was 'a quagmire with no bottom.'
He said victory was 'a year, perhaps two, away.'
He said the fighting was 'a tragedy without purpose.'
context: Cronkite's exact words: 'To say that we are mired in stalemate seems the only realistic, if unsatisfactory, conclusion.' Source: https://learninglink.oup.com/access/content/schaller-3e-dashboard-resources/document-walter-cronkite-we-are-mired-in-stalemate-cbs-evening-news-broadcast-february-27-1968

question: After Saigon fell to the communists on April 30, 1975, more than a million Vietnamese over the next twenty years fled their own country by sea in tiny, overcrowded boats -- the 'boat people.' An estimated 200,000 to 250,000 of them never reached safety. Besides drowning in storms and starving, what was a major cause of their deaths?
answer: They were murdered by Thai pirates who hunted the refugee boats.
choices: They were murdered by Thai pirates who hunted the refugee boats.
They were sunk by the communist navy as they tried to leave.
They were turned away and died in camps on foreign shores.
They were swamped by passing freighters that refused to stop.
context: Within two weeks of Saigon's fall, about 132,000 people had already fled. In 1981 alone, 349 of the 452 boats that reached Thailand had been attacked by pirates, who abducted hundreds of women. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnamese_boat_people

question: When North Vietnamese troops captured the old imperial capital of Hue during the Tet Offensive, they held it for weeks. After allied forces retook the city, they began digging up shallow mass graves holding thousands of bound civilians -- some shot, some buried alive. Investigators then found proof that the killings had been planned well in advance. What was the proof?
answer: The troops had arrived carrying prepared lists naming people to be killed as enemies of the revolution.
choices: The troops had arrived carrying prepared lists naming people to be killed as enemies of the revolution.
The graves themselves had been dug by forced labor in the weeks before the city ever fell.
Radio orders had been broadcast in advance naming each neighborhood that was to be purged.
The wire used to bind the victims' hands had been shipped into the city by the truckload.
context: An estimated 2,800 to 6,000 civilians and prisoners were found in the graves around Hue, many bound together with wire and bamboo. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_at_Hu%E1%BA%BF

question: When America pulled out of Southeast Asia, neighboring Cambodia fell to the communist Khmer Rouge, who set out to murder everyone they branded an enemy. In the capital they turned a former high school into a secret prison, S-21, where more than 18,000 prisoners were photographed, tortured into confessing, and then executed -- almost none came out alive. What were prisoners tortured into 'confessing'?
answer: That they were secret spies for the American CIA or the Soviet KGB.
choices: That they were secret spies for the American CIA or the Soviet KGB.
That they had hidden gold and foreign money away from the state.
That they were plotting in secret to bring back the old king.
That they had deliberately sabotaged the country's rice harvest.
context: S-21 had been an ordinary Phnom Penh high school; only a handful of its 18,000-plus prisoners survived. The Cambodian genocide -- which killed roughly a fifth of the country -- ended only when communist Vietnam invaded in January 1979. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/Cambodian-genocide

question: Vikings got their name from the Old Norse word 'vik', and raiders launched their longships from exactly such spots along the coast. What did 'vik' originally mean?
answer: A bay or inlet
choices: A bay or inlet
A river mouth
A rocky headland
A fishing harbour
context: Old Norse 'vik' meant a bay or inlet — the sheltered spot a crew launched from. A 'vikingr' was the person; 'viking' (going 'a-viking') was the activity of raiding. The modern English word 'Viking' was actually revived only in the 1800s. (Source: The Conversation, 'What does the word Viking really mean?'; Britannica, 'Viking people'.)

question: Leif Erikson, son of Erik the Red who founded Greenland's first colony, sailed his crew to the coast of North America around the year 1000. Christopher Columbus would not cross the Atlantic until 1492. Roughly how far ahead of Columbus did Leif Erikson reach the New World?
answer: About 500 years
choices: About 500 years
About 50 years
About 150 years
About 1,000 years
context: Leif Erikson reached North America around the year 1000, roughly 500 years before Columbus. He named three lands along the coast: Helluland ('Stone-slab Land'), Markland ('Forest Land'), and Vinland. (Source: Wikipedia, Leif Erikson; World History Encyclopedia, 'Vinland'.)

question: Leif Erikson named three new lands he found in North America. According to the Saga of the Greenlanders, a crewman named Tyrker came running back to the ship excited, saying the land was good for making wine. So Leif named that land what?
answer: Vinland
choices: Vinland
Helluland
Markland
Greenland
context: Vinland means 'Wine Land' — Tyrker reported the land 'was full of vines and grapes.' (Helluland was 'Stone-slab Land,' Markland was 'Forest Land.') Leif himself was nicknamed 'Leif the Lucky' after he rescued shipwrecked sailors on a voyage home. This is preserved in saga tradition. (Source: Wikipedia, Leif Erikson; Saga of the Greenlanders.)  (Legend.)

question: The most feared Norse warriors were the 'berserkers', who threw themselves into battle in a wild, screaming frenzy. Their name in Old Norse, 'berserkr', is thought to mean which of these?
answer: Bear-shirt
choices: Bear-shirt
Wolf-skin
Iron-coat
Hide-cloak
context: 'Berserkr' is thought to mean 'bear-shirt' — warriors said to fight in a frenzy wearing animal pelts. Their wolf-skinned counterparts were the 'ulfhednar,' meaning 'wolf-coats.' These warriors are known from saga tradition. (Source: Study.com, 'Viking Berserker'; vikingr.org, 'Berserkers and Ulfhednar'.)  (Legend.)

question: On 8 June 793, raiders from across the sea beached at Lindisfarne, a tiny monastery island off Northumbria full of unarmed monks. They killed the older monks who could not flee, but they did not kill the young men. According to the records, what did the raiders do with the young monks?
answer: Carried them off as slaves
choices: Carried them off as slaves
Forced them to row the ships
Left them to guard the island
Made them swear loyalty to a Norse king
context: The raiders killed the older monks and carried the young off as slaves, then stripped the church of all its furnishings and treasure. This 793 raid traditionally marks the start of the Viking Age. (Source: Britannica, 'Lindisfarne Raid'; EBSCO Research Starters.)

question: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says that before the Viking raiders struck Northumbria in 793, terrible omens warned the people first: immense sheets of light rushed through the air, and whirlwinds tore the land. The Chronicle then records one more sign seen flying across the sky. What was it?
answer: Fiery dragons
choices: Fiery dragons
A blood-red moon
A rain of stones
A two-tailed comet
context: The Old English reads 'fyrenne dracan waeron gesewene on tham lifte fleogende' — 'fiery dragons were seen flying in the sky.' A great famine followed, and then the heathen raiders. (Source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, entry for 793.)

question: Norse longships had a very shallow bottom, so they sat high in the water and needed no harbour. This let a crew sail up rivers and strike far inland where no one expected ships. When a longship reached its target, it could do one thing a deep-keeled ship never could. What was it?
answer: Run straight up onto a beach
choices: Run straight up onto a beach
Carry far more cargo than a deep ship
Outrun any ship on the open sea
Sail for weeks with no resupply
context: The shallow draft let raiders run a longship right onto a beach — no harbour needed — which is exactly why an island monastery like Lindisfarne was so exposed. The ships were 'clinker-built' from overlapping oak planks riveted with iron, light and flexible enough to flex with the waves. (Source: Life in Norway, 'Vikings Longships'; Warfare History Network.)

question: Decades after the first hit-and-run raids, the Norse came to conquer and settle, not just to loot. In 865 the 'Great Heathen Army' landed in England, led by the sons of the legendary Ragnar Lothbrok. Which of these was one of those sons leading the army?
answer: Ivar the Boneless
choices: Ivar the Boneless
Leif the Lucky
Guthrum the Old
Erik the Red
context: The Great Heathen Army of 865 was led by sons of Ragnar Lothbrok, including Ivar the Boneless and Halfdan. Unlike earlier raiders, they came to stay, conquering Northumbria, East Anglia, and Mercia. (Source: Wikipedia, Great Heathen Army; History Skills.)

question: King Alfred of Wessex finally beat the Viking leader Guthrum in battle at Edington in 878. Instead of simply killing his beaten enemy, Alfred set a remarkable condition in the peace treaty. What did the treaty require Guthrum to do?
answer: Accept Christian baptism
choices: Accept Christian baptism
Hand over his longships
Pay a yearly tribute in silver
Sail back to Denmark forever
context: By the treaty after Edington, Guthrum accepted baptism and a border was drawn across England. The north and east, left under Norse law, became the 'Danelaw' — where town names ending in '-by' and '-thorpe' survive today. (Source: Wikipedia, Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum / Danelaw; Historic UK.)

question: Vikings crossed the open North Atlantic centuries before the magnetic compass reached Europe. By tradition, when fog or cloud hid the sky, a navigator could hold up a special crystal to find the way. What was this navigation crystal called?
answer: A sunstone
choices: A sunstone
A lodestone
A sea-glass
A star-shard
context: By tradition the Norse used a 'sunstone' — a crystal of Iceland spar — to locate the sun through fog. They also navigated by 'latitude sailing' using a wooden sun-compass; a fragment of one was dug up at Uunartoq, Greenland. The magnetic compass did not reach Europe until the 12th century. (Source: Scientific American, 'Did Vikings navigate by polarized light?'; The Archaeologist, 'The Viking Sun Compass'.)  (Legend.)

question: At L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, archaeologists found a Norse camp and used a giant 993 solar storm spiking the tree rings to prove the Norse cut wood there in the year 1021 -- five centuries before Columbus. Among the Norse rubbish they also found something that does not grow anywhere in Newfoundland, proving these Vikings had voyaged even farther south on the continent. What was it?
answer: Butternuts, which only grow far to the south
choices: Butternuts, which only grow far to the south
Grapevines carried home from a warmer coast
Cotton bolls traded from a distant people
Olive pits brought across the ocean from home
context: At L'Anse aux Meadows, butternuts and a metal-cut butternut burl -- a tree absent from Newfoundland -- showed the Norse ranged south toward the Gulf of St. Lawrence/New Brunswick; the 993 cosmic-ray (carbon-14) spike in cut wood fixed the felling year at 1021. Sources: Smithsonian Magazine (2021); National Geographic; Nature study.

question: Lindisfarne's monks held out for generations, but in 875, with Danish armies closing in, they finally abandoned their island. They fled carrying their two greatest treasures: the jewel-bright Lindisfarne Gospels, and one other precious thing. What was the second treasure they carried out?
answer: The body of St Cuthbert in his coffin
choices: The body of St Cuthbert in his coffin
A splinter of the True Cross
The silver shrine of St Aidan
A hoard of Northumbrian gold
context: St Cuthbert was the holy ex-bishop whose shrine had made Lindisfarne sacred. The monks carried his coffin and the Gospels and wandered for seven years before settling, eventually reaching Durham. (Source: Historic UK, 'The Lindisfarne Gospels'; Durham World Heritage Site, 'Cuthbert's Body'.)

question: A Northumbrian scholar named Alcuin of York, writing from Charlemagne's court, was horrified by the 793 raid on Lindisfarne. In his famous letter to Bishop Higbald he said the heathens had trampled the bodies of the saints in God's temple like one shocking thing in the street. Like what?
answer: Animal dung
choices: Animal dung
Fallen leaves
Broken pottery
Common mud
context: Alcuin wrote that the raiders 'trampled the bodies of saints in God's temple like animal dung in the street,' and 'poured the blood of saints within the compass of the altar.' He also asked the wounded question of the age: 'What security is there for the churches of Britain if St Cuthbert... will not defend his own?' (Source: Alcuin's letter to Bishop Higbald, 793.)

question: Rome's great national epic about Aeneas, the Trojan prince who escapes burning Troy to found the Roman bloodline, announces its two subjects in its very first three Latin words — warfare and the wandering hero. Which famous line opens it?
answer: Arma virumque cano — 'I sing of arms and the man'
choices: Arma virumque cano — 'I sing of arms and the man'
Veni, vidi, vici — 'I came, I saw, I conquered'
Carthago delenda est — 'Carthage must be destroyed'
Alea iacta est — 'The die is cast'
context: Virgil's Aeneid opens 'Arma virumque cano' — arma (warfare, echoing Homer's Iliad) and virum (the wandering hero, echoing the Odyssey). The 'man' is Aeneas, ancestor of the Roman line. Source: https://www.albert.io/blog/aeneid-book-1-opening-epic-begins-ap-latin-review/

question: The poet Virgil labored about eleven years on the Aeneid and died in 19 BC with his final revision unfinished. His dying wish was that the poem be BURNED. Instead of honoring it, what did the emperor Augustus do?
answer: He overruled the wish and ordered the poem published
choices: He overruled the wish and ordered the poem published
He honored the wish and had the poem burned at once
He locked the only copy away in his private library
He had Virgil's executors rewrite the unfinished ending
context: Augustus overruled Virgil's deathbed request and ordered the executors Varius and Tucca to publish the Aeneid with as few changes as possible. The epic became a pillar of the Western canon — over 1,300 years later Dante chose Virgil himself as his guide through Hell and Purgatory. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Virgil

question: The French writer born Francois-Marie Arouet in 1694 became one of the most famous voices for tolerance in history — but he is almost never called by his birth name. Across his life he scribbled under more than a hundred names to dodge the king's censors. Which pen name did he make world-famous?
answer: Voltaire
choices: Voltaire
Moliere
Rousseau
Beaumarchais
context: Francois-Marie Arouet adopted 'Voltaire' in 1718 — most likely an anagram of the Latinized 'Arouet le jeune' (AROVET LI). He used well over a hundred other pen names across his life to slip past the censors. Source: britannica.com/biography/Voltaire ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voltaire

question: In 1726 Voltaire mocked a nobleman, the Chevalier de Rohan-Chabot, who answered by having his servants beat the writer with clubs. When Voltaire demanded a proper duel to settle the insult, the powerful Rohan family pulled strings — and instead of facing the duel, Voltaire found himself sent where?
answer: into the Bastille prison
choices: into the Bastille prison
to the royal court
onto a Spanish galley
into a monastery
context: The Rohan family had Voltaire thrown into the Bastille, then released only on the condition that he leave France. He went into exile in England for nearly three years (1726-1729). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy_Auguste_de_Rohan-Chabot ; biography.com/authors-writers/voltaire

question: In Toulouse in 1762, the 64-year-old Protestant merchant Jean Calas was accused — on no real evidence — of murdering his own son. The court condemned him to a death so brutal Voltaire spent years trying to undo it: Calas was tied to a cross and, one by one, his limbs were shattered with an iron bar before he was strangled. What was this method of execution called?
answer: broken on the wheel
choices: broken on the wheel
drawn and quartered
the iron maiden
burning at the stake
context: On March 10, 1762, Jean Calas was 'broken on the wheel' — each limb broken twice with an iron bar, then strangled and his body burned. He proclaimed his innocence to the end and never confessed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Calas ; theparisreview.org/blog/2015/03/13/broken-on-the-wheel/

question: Voltaire is endlessly quoted as saying, 'I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it.' The line captures his spirit perfectly — yet historians say Voltaire never actually wrote it. So where did this famous sentence really come from?
answer: his biographer Evelyn Beatrice Hall coined it
choices: his biographer Evelyn Beatrice Hall coined it
Voltaire wrote it in a private letter
a French revolutionary carved it on a wall
it was a line in one of his plays
context: Voltaire's English biographer Evelyn Beatrice Hall (writing as S. G. Tallentyre) coined the line in her 1906 book 'The Friends of Voltaire' to SUMMARIZE his attitude after the government burned a book by Helvetius. It is her paraphrase, not his words. Source: quoteinvestigator.com/2015/06/01/defend-say/ ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evelyn_Beatrice_Hall

question: After fighting for nearly three years — writing letters across Europe and publishing his 'Treatise on Tolerance' — to clear the name of Jean Calas, the Protestant wrongly executed in Toulouse, Voltaire actually won. King Louis XV annulled the verdict and judges exonerated the dead man. Because of this victory, historians often call Voltaire's Calas effort the first of what?
answer: modern human-rights campaign
choices: modern human-rights campaign
national newspaper
public lottery
royal pardon law
context: Louis XV annulled the verdict, and in 1765 a panel of judges posthumously exonerated Jean Calas; the king paid the ruined family 36,000 livres. Voltaire's 'Treatise on Tolerance' (1763) grew directly out of the injustice, and historians have called the campaign the first modern human-rights campaign. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treatise_on_Tolerance ; museeprotestant.org/en/notice/the-calas-affair/

question: When the New York stock market collapsed in October 1929, the most famous headline came not from a money newspaper but from Variety, the show-business weekly. Using stage slang for a flop, what four words did Variety run on October 30, 1929?
answer: "WALL ST. LAYS AN EGG"
choices: "WALL ST. LAYS AN EGG"
"BANKS SHUT THEIR DOORS"
"FORTUNES VANISH IN HOURS"
"THE BUBBLE FINALLY BURSTS"
context: In theater slang, to 'lay an egg' meant to fail badly on stage. Variety, the entertainment trade paper, captured the crash better than the financial press. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street_Lays_an_Egg

question: The Wall Street crash of 1929 had several panic days that history gave grim color-names. The very worst was October 29, 1929, when a record number of shares were dumped on the New York Stock Exchange. By what name is that single worst day remembered?
answer: Black Tuesday
choices: Black Tuesday
Black Thursday
Black Monday
Black Friday
context: The panic ran across named days: Black Thursday (Oct 24) was the first day of panic, then Black Monday (Oct 28), then Black Tuesday (Oct 29) was the worst. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street_crash_of_1929

question: The Dow Jones Industrial Average peaked at 381 points on September 3, 1929, then the crash wiped it out. An investor who bought at that high and held on had to wait just to get back to 381 and break even. Counting from that 1929 peak, how long did it take the Dow to climb back to 381?
answer: Twenty-five years
choices: Twenty-five years
Five years
Ten years
Sixteen years
context: The Dow did not return to its September 3, 1929 peak of 381.17 until November 23, 1954 — twenty-five years later. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street_crash_of_1929

question: On Black Tuesday, October 29, 1929, so many shares were traded on the New York Stock Exchange — a record 16.4 million — that one crucial machine simply could not keep up and ran for hours behind the actual trading. Which machine was buried by the flood of trades?
answer: The ticker tape machine
choices: The ticker tape machine
The telephone switchboard linking the brokers
The elevator carrying clerks up to the floor
The bell that opened and closed each trading day
context: The ticker printed stock prices onto a ribbon of paper tape. On Black Tuesday it ran so far behind that it did not finish printing the day's prices until about 7:45 p.m. — hours after the 3 p.m. close — so for hours nobody on the floor knew the true prices. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street_crash_of_1929

question: At noon on Black Thursday, October 24, 1929, with the market collapsing, the bankers trying to stop the panic sent Richard Whitney, the Exchange's vice-president, striding across the trading floor in plain view. What did Whitney do that briefly halted the slide?
answer: He bid for 25,000 shares of U.S. Steel above the going price
choices: He bid for 25,000 shares of U.S. Steel above the going price
He begged the traders on the floor to please stop selling
He rang the closing bell early to end the trading day
He announced the Exchange would shut its doors for a week
context: In a loud voice Whitney bid $205 for U.S. Steel — above the market — then placed showy buy orders for other blue-chip stocks. The bluff briefly steadied the market. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street_crash_of_1929

question: Just nine days before the crash, on October 15, 1929, the famous Yale economist Irving Fisher reassured a dinner of business buyers that stocks were safe. His confident sentence became the most mocked prediction in economic history. What did Fisher say stock prices had reached?
answer: "A permanently high plateau"
choices: "A permanently high plateau"
"The dawn of a new century"
"A foundation built on rock"
"The first rung of a ladder"
context: Fisher was himself heavily borrowed against Remington Rand stock; the crash destroyed both his reputation and most of his fortune. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irving_Fisher

question: In some stocks the 1929 collapse was almost total. White Sewing Machine had traded near $48 a few months earlier and closed at $11 the night before Black Tuesday. As the panic raged the next day, how low did a buyer reportedly manage to catch a share of it?
answer: $1 a share
choices: $1 a share
$2 a share
$4 a share
$7 a share
context: At least one buyer caught a bid at $1 a share during the Black Tuesday chaos — a stunning fall from $48. Source: https://novelinvestor.com/notes/the-great-crash-1929-by-john-kenneth-galbraith/

question: Through the 1920s, ordinary Americans bought stock 'on margin' — putting down as little as a tenth of the price and borrowing the rest. By August 1929 brokers had lent out over $8.5 billion this way. The size of those loans was staggering: what did that borrowed sum actually exceed?
answer: All the paper money then in circulation in the U.S.
choices: All the paper money then in circulation in the U.S.
All the gold then stored in the U.S. Treasury
All the wages paid in America that year
All the farmland then owned in the U.S.
context: The $8.5 billion in margin loans was greater than all the currency then circulating in the country. When prices fell, lenders made 'margin calls,' forcing panic selling. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street_crash_of_1929

question: Everyone pictures ruined brokers leaping from windows after the 1929 crash, but New York's chief medical examiner Charles Norris actually checked the city's records and publicly knocked the story down. Compared with the same four weeks of 1928, what did the real suicide count for the month after the crash turn out to be?
answer: Lower than the year before
choices: Lower than the year before
Exactly the same as before
More than double the year before
The highest ever recorded
context: Norris found 44 suicides in Manhattan in the four weeks after the crash — fewer than the 53 over the same weeks in 1928. The leaping-broker image is mostly a myth. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/stock-market-crash-suicides-wall-street-1929-great-depression

question: Winston Churchill happened to be visiting New York during the 1929 crash — and, having lost money himself, watched the chaos from the visitors' gallery of the Stock Exchange. In a piece he wrote for London's Daily Telegraph, what did Churchill claim he had witnessed right beneath his window?
answer: A man hurling himself down fifteen storeys
choices: A man hurling himself down fifteen storeys
A crowd setting fire to a banker's car
A broker giving away fistfuls of cash
A line of ruined men selling their coats
context: Churchill wrote (Daily Telegraph, Dec. 9, 1929) that 'under my very window a gentleman cast himself down fifteen storeys and was dashed to pieces.' This is his personal testimony, written up dramatically, rather than a verified event. Source: https://winstonchurchill.org/churchill-central/image/wall-street-crash-image/  (Legend.)

question: Historians still argue over what really caused the 1929 crash. The Austrian economists Ludwig von Mises and F.A. Hayek offered a striking answer: they said the cheap credit pumped out by the Federal Reserve in the 1920s had blown up an artificial bubble. In their view, what was the true disease — and what was the crash itself?
answer: The boom was the disease; the crash was the cure
choices: The boom was the disease; the crash was the cure
The crash was the disease; the boom was the cure
Greed was the disease; the Fed was the cure
Trade was the disease; the tariff was the cure
context: Mises and Hayek argued the speculative boom itself was the sickness and the bust merely the correction; Hayek published articles in early 1929 warning the American boom would collapse. This is one serious account among several — others, like John Kenneth Galbraith, blamed runaway speculation rather than Fed policy. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian_business_cycle_theory

question: At a secret 1927 meeting of central bankers on Long Island, Benjamin Strong of the New York Fed agreed to cut interest rates — and reportedly described the move with a memorable metaphor. Austrian economists later pointed to that easy-money decision as fuel on the speculative fire. How did Strong reportedly describe the rate cut?
answer: A little shot of whiskey for the stock exchange
choices: A little shot of whiskey for the stock exchange
A nightcap to send the market off to sleep
A strong cup of coffee to wake the market up
A stiff drink to steady the market's nerves
context: Strong reportedly called it 'un petit coup de whisky for the stock exchange.' Austrians cite this as pouring fuel on the speculative fire, though other historians dispute how important it was. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Strong_Jr.

question: On August 24, 1814, during the War of 1812, British troops marched into Washington and set fire to the U.S. Capitol and the President's house. What grim distinction does that day hold in American history?
answer: It is the only time a foreign power has captured and burned the American capital
choices: It is the only time a foreign power has captured and burned the American capital
It was the bloodiest single battle ever fought on American soil
It was the last time British and American armies ever clashed
It was the first time the American flag was raised over a fort
context: August 24, 1814. To this day it remains the only time a foreign enemy has seized and burned Washington, D.C. The war was nicknamed the 'second war of independence.' Source: history.com, 'British troops set fire to the White House.'

question: As British soldiers closed in on Washington in 1814, First Lady Dolley Madison refused to flee the White House until one thing was saved. It was bolted to the wall, so she ordered the frame smashed and the canvas cut out. What did she rescue?
answer: The full-length Gilbert Stuart portrait of George Washington
choices: The full-length Gilbert Stuart portrait of George Washington
The original signed copy of the Declaration of Independence
The crystal chandelier from the State Dining Room
The silver tea service used by Martha Washington
context: The famous Gilbert Stuart portrait of George Washington was screwed to the wall; Dolley Madison had the frame broken and the canvas carried out before the British arrived. Source: history.com, 'Dolley Madison saves portrait from British.'

question: When British officers walked into the abandoned White House in 1814, they found a dinner First Lady Dolley Madison had ordered still set out on the table. Before they torched the house, what did the officers do at that table?
answer: They ate the meal and drank a mocking toast to 'Jemmy's health'
choices: They ate the meal and drank a mocking toast to 'Jemmy's health'
They smashed every plate and overturned the entire table
They wrote a polite apology and left it beside the food
They carried the whole dinner outside to feed their horses
context: The officers sat down, ate the dinner, and raised a sarcastic toast to 'Jemmy's health' — mocking President James Madison ('Jemmy') — before setting the house ablaze. Source: janehamptoncook.substack.com, 'White House Inferno.'

question: The Washington newspaper the National Intelligencer had insulted British Admiral George Cockburn, calling him a 'Ruffian.' When Cockburn reached its office in 1814, he took a peculiar revenge — he ordered his men to destroy every block of one particular letter from the printing type. Which letter, and why?
answer: The letter 'C', so the paper could no longer print his name
choices: The letter 'C', so the paper could no longer print his name
The letter 'R', the first letter of the insult 'Ruffian'
The letter 'A', the most common letter in English
The letter 'X', to mark the paper as condemned
