context: Cockburn ordered all the 'C' type destroyed 'so that the rascals can have no further means of abusing my name' — Cockburn begins with C. Source: Wikipedia, 'Burning of Washington.'

question: The British occupation of Washington in 1814 ended after barely 26 hours — not because American troops drove them out, but because of something that struck the city the very next day, August 25. What forced the British to flee?
answer: A violent storm and tornado that tore off roofs and put out the fires
choices: A violent storm and tornado that tore off roofs and put out the fires
A sudden outbreak of fever that swept through the British ranks
A massive American counterattack led by President Madison himself
A naval blockade that cut off the soldiers from their ships
context: On August 25, 1814 a tornado ripped roofs off houses, lifted and dropped cannons, killed about thirty British soldiers, and doused the fires. The British retreated after only about 26 hours. Source: prologue.blogs.archives.gov, 'Tornado Saves Capital, Scares British.'

question: Three weeks after Washington burned, the British bombarded Baltimore's Fort McHenry through the night of September 13-14, 1814. An American named Francis Scott Key watched, and at dawn the sight of the huge flag still flying over the fort moved him to write a poem. What did that poem become?
answer: 'The Star-Spangled Banner'
choices: 'The Star-Spangled Banner'
'America the Beautiful'
'Yankee Doodle'
'My Country, 'Tis of Thee'
context: Key's poem 'Defence of Fort M'Henry' was set to music and became 'The Star-Spangled Banner.' The flag he saw was a 30-by-42-foot garrison flag with 15 stars and 15 stripes, sewn by Mary Pickersgill; it now hangs in the Smithsonian. Source: gilderlehrman.org.

question: General Andrew Jackson won a crushing, lopsided victory at the Battle of New Orleans on January 8, 1815, and became a national hero. Yet there was a strange twist about that battle. What was it?
answer: The peace treaty had already been signed, but the news had not yet crossed the Atlantic
choices: The peace treaty had already been signed, but the news had not yet crossed the Atlantic
Jackson fought it without ever firing a single cannon
The British and American commanders were secretly cousins
Jackson had been ordered not to fight and disobeyed
context: The Treaty of Ghent had been signed December 24, 1814, ending the war — but word hadn't reached America, so Jackson's January 8, 1815 victory was fought after peace was made. The treaty restored the prewar status quo, ending the war essentially in a draw. Source: ebsco.com, 'Treaty of Ghent.'

question: Paul Jennings, a 15-year-old enslaved man in the White House, helped prepare the very dinner the British later ate. In his 1865 memoir, he pushed back on the popular story that Dolley Madison personally took down the Washington portrait. According to Jennings, who actually took it down?
answer: The doorkeeper John Susé and the gardener Magraw
choices: The doorkeeper John Susé and the gardener Magraw
Dolley Madison and President James Madison together
A pair of British officers who later regretted it
The portrait's painter, Gilbert Stuart, in person
context: Paul Jennings, in 'A Colored Man's Reminiscences of James Madison' (1865), credited doorkeeper John Susé and gardener Magraw with actually removing the canvas — a working man's eyewitness correction to the celebrated legend. Source: nps.gov, 'Paul Jennings.'

question: By Christmas 1776 George Washington's army was melting away — most of his soldiers' enlistments would run out on January 1, and another defeat could end the Revolution for good. For his desperate night attack across the Delaware, he wrote one secret password on paper for his officers: a sentry would call out the first word as a challenge, and the correct answer was the second. What grim two-word watchword did Washington choose?
answer: Victory or Death
choices: Victory or Death
Liberty or Chains
Freedom or Ruin
Glory or Defeat
context: Washington's parole and countersign for the entire operation was 'Victory or Death' — the challenge was 'Victory,' the reply was 'Death.' It captured a gamble where failure could finish the Revolution. Source: https://emergingrevolutionarywar.org/2018/12/26/victory-or-death/ ; corroborated https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/ten-crucial-days-path-trenton

question: On the storming night of December 25–26, 1776, George Washington had to push about 2,400 soldiers — plus horses and heavy cannon — across the ice-choked Delaware River in big flat-bottomed Durham boats. Chunks of floating ice slammed the hulls and one soldier said it 'blew a hurricane.' Whose men did the brutal work of rowing and poling that whole army across the freezing river?
answer: Colonel John Glover's Marblehead mariners
choices: Colonel John Glover's Marblehead mariners
Colonel Henry Knox's artillery crews
General Nathanael Greene's Virginia riflemen
Colonel John Cadwalader's Pennsylvania militia
context: The men who rowed and poled the army through the ice were Colonel John Glover's Marblehead mariners — experienced seamen and fishermen from Marblehead, Massachusetts. Source: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/revolutionary-war/battles/trenton ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington's_crossing_of_the_Delaware_River

question: George Washington spent Christmas of 1776 not at home with his family but on a desperate, freezing gamble that swung the whole Revolutionary War in the Americans' favor. Eight years later he would finally make it home for Christmas as a private citizen — but on that famous night in 1776, what was he doing?
answer: Leading his army across the Delaware River to surprise the Hessians at Trenton
choices: Leading his army across the Delaware River to surprise the Hessians at Trenton
Storming the British works at Yorktown to force the redcoats to surrender
Marching his troops away from the Hudson River to escape the British in New York
Wintering with his ragged, starving army in the deep snow at Valley Forge
context: On the night of December 25, 1776, Washington ferried his men across the ice-choked Delaware and struck the Hessian garrison at Trenton — a stunning win that revived a collapsing cause. He would not spend a Christmas at home again until December 24, 1783, days after resigning his command, his first Christmas at Mount Vernon in eight years. Source: emergingrevolutionarywar.org/2021/12/24/george-washingtons-christmas-eve-homecoming/

question: The American painter Benjamin West was at the court of King George III when he told the king something astonishing: George Washington, having won the war, meant to hand back all his power and simply go home to his farm. According to the story, the king replied that if Washington truly did that, it would make him what?
answer: The greatest man in the world
choices: The greatest man in the world
A fool for throwing away a crown
The most dangerous man in America
The rightful king of the colonies
context: The anecdote was recorded years later in the diary of the artist Joseph Farington (December 1799), so it is famous testimony rather than a verified quote — a legend, but a beloved one. The king who had spent eight years trying to crush Washington reportedly judged that voluntarily surrendering power, not winning the war, was the truly great act. Source: loc.gov/exhibitions/two-georges/access-text/washington-resigns-and-george-iii-ponders-abdication/

question: In March 1783 at Newburgh, Washington's own officers were on the brink of mutiny — furious over unpaid wages and ready to march on Congress. Washington walked in to face them and broke the revolt in a single moment, with one small human gesture and one quiet line. What did he do?
answer: He drew out a pair of spectacles and said he had grown gray, and nearly blind, in their service
choices: He drew out a pair of spectacles and said he had grown gray, and nearly blind, in their service
He drew his sword and swore he would cut down the first man who dared to march
He read aloud the names of the war's dead and begged them to honor that sacrifice
He tore up his own unpaid pay warrant and flung the pieces down at their feet
context: Few of the men had ever seen Washington wear glasses. As he fumbled them on he said, 'Gentlemen, you must pardon me. I have grown gray in your service and now find myself growing blind.' Officers who had been ready to revolt began to weep, and the Newburgh conspiracy collapsed on the spot. Source: gilderlehrman.org/history-resources/spotlight-primary-source/george-washington-and-newburgh-conspiracy-1783

question: When Washington resigned his commission at the Maryland State House in Annapolis in December 1783, the whole ceremony was staged to make one thing unmistakable: the army answered to the civilian Congress, not the other way around. The printed rules told the President and members of Congress exactly how to receive Washington when he rose and bowed to them. What did the rules require of them?
answer: To stay seated with their hats on, and answer his bow only by lifting their hats — never bowing back
choices: To stay seated with their hats on, and answer his bow only by lifting their hats — never bowing back
To rise to their feet and bow low in return, honoring him as the victorious general
To kneel as he entered and present him a ceremonial sword to seal the new peace
To stand bareheaded in respectful silence until he had taken a seat among them
context: The published protocol specified that Congress remain 'seated and covered' (hats on); when Washington bowed, they responded only 'by uncovering without bowing.' The deliberate one-sidedness dramatized civilian supremacy — the soldier bows to the people's government, and the government does not bow back. Source: msa.maryland.gov/msa/mdstatehouse/html/grand_staircase_washington_resigning.html

question: In 1796 George Washington decided not to seek a third term and wanted his farewell to reach ordinary Americans directly, not just the crowds who could hear a speech. So instead of standing up and delivering it as an address, how did Washington first send his Farewell to the country?
answer: He had it printed in a Philadelphia newspaper for people to read
choices: He had it printed in a Philadelphia newspaper for people to read
He read it aloud to a joint session of Congress
He had it carved onto a monument in the capital
He mailed a handwritten copy to each state governor
context: Despite its name, the Farewell Address was never spoken as a speech. Washington had it printed in Claypoole's American Daily Advertiser on September 19, 1796, so ordinary citizens could read it for themselves. Source: https://www.mountvernon.org/george-washington/the-first-president/the-farewell-address

question: In his 1796 Farewell, George Washington said he was warning the nation 'in the most solemn manner' about one danger above all -- something he feared could be sharpened by revenge until it hardened into 'a frightful despotism' and became a free people's 'worst enemy.' What was this danger Washington warned against most solemnly?
answer: The spirit of party and political faction
choices: The spirit of party and political faction
The growth of cities and the loss of farms
The size of the army during peacetime
The spread of newspapers and printed rumor
context: Washington warned 'against the baneful effects of the spirit of party,' arguing that faction driven by revenge could curdle into 'a frightful despotism' and was a free people's 'worst enemy.' Source: https://www.americanyawp.com/reader/a-new-nation/george-washington-farewell-address-1796/

question: In 1953, at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, James Watson and Francis Crick worked out the shape of the DNA molecule, the molecule that carries the instructions for life. Their discovery is now so famous it appears on logos and postage stamps. People most often say DNA is shaped like which everyday object?
answer: A spiral staircase
choices: A spiral staircase
A coiled garden hose
A woven basket
A folded paper fan
context: DNA is a 'double helix': two long strands wound around each other, exactly like the two railings of a spiral staircase, with rungs joining them in the middle. Watson and Crick figured this out in 1953 at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, England. Source: https://www.sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/francis-crick-rosalind-franklin-james-watson-and-maurice-wilkins/

question: On the morning of 28 February 1953, Francis Crick burst into the Eagle, a pub in Cambridge where the laboratory scientists ate their lunch. According to James Watson, Crick announced to the whole crowded room that he and Watson had just discovered something enormous. What did Crick declare they had found?
answer: The secret of life
choices: The secret of life
The cure for cancer
The fountain of youth
The lost city of gold
context: Watson tells this story; Crick himself later said he had no memory of saying it, so it is repeated as Watson's account rather than proven fact. The Eagle pub has been serving since 1667 and was the regular lunch spot for the Cavendish scientists. Source: https://www.thedrinksbusiness.com/2017/02/on-this-day-1953-discovering-dna/  (Legend.)

question: The most famous photograph of James Watson and Francis Crick shows the two men standing proudly beside a tall object at the Cavendish Laboratory, the very thing that finally let them show the world the shape of DNA. What were they standing next to?
answer: A metal model of the DNA molecule
choices: A metal model of the DNA molecule
A brass telescope on a stand
A blackboard full of equations
A glass tank of chemicals
context: Rather than rely on equations alone, Watson and Crick built a real, tabletop sculpture of the molecule out of metal plates and rods, and adjusted it until the pieces fit together. The famous photo of the two men beside this wire-and-metal model is one of the most recognisable images in science. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953_in_science

question: James Watson later wrote that the moment that cracked the whole mystery came when he was first shown a certain blurry X-ray photograph of DNA. In his memoir, he described how his body reacted in that instant: 'The instant I saw the picture my mouth fell open and ___.' How did Watson finish that sentence?
answer: my pulse began to race
choices: my pulse began to race
my hands started to shake
the room went silent
I knew that we had lost
context: Watson wrote this in his memoir 'The Double Helix.' The photograph that set his pulse racing was the X-ray image of DNA's 'B form' that revealed it must be a helix. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photo_51

question: The single most important clue to DNA's shape was a fuzzy X-ray photograph, now famous as 'Photo 51.' To a scientist who could read it, the blurry X-shaped pattern in the middle was an instant giveaway, a kind of fingerprint. What did that X-pattern prove about the shape of DNA?
answer: That it twists like a helix
choices: That it twists like a helix
That it is a flat ribbon
That it forms a hollow ring
That it folds like a sheet
context: An X-shaped pattern in an X-ray photograph is the tell-tale fingerprint of a helix, a spiral. Photo 51 captured this clearly, which is why it was the key piece of evidence for DNA's double-helix structure. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photo_51

question: Inside the DNA ladder, the two strands are joined by rungs, and each rung is a pair of chemicals called 'bases.' There are four bases, written A, T, G, and C, but they are picky: each one will only ever link up with a single specific partner. Which base does A always pair with?
answer: A always pairs with T
choices: A always pairs with T
A always pairs with G
A always pairs with C
T always pairs with G
context: This is called complementary base-pairing: A (adenine) always pairs with T (thymine), and G (guanine) always pairs with C (cytosine), fitting together like puzzle pieces. Because the pairing is so strict, the two strands always match each other exactly. Source: https://www.pearson.com/channels/microbiology/learn/jason/ch-15-dna-replication/chargaff-s-rules-Bio-1

question: Photo 51 was not a quick snapshot. To capture a clear image of DNA, Raymond Gosling, a PhD student working under Rosalind Franklin at King's College London, had to bombard a single thread of DNA with X-rays without stopping. For roughly how long did the X-rays blast the sample to produce that one photograph?
answer: About 62 hours
choices: About 62 hours
About 6 hours
About 6 minutes
About 6 seconds
context: Gosling took Photo 51 on 2 May 1952, exposing the DNA fibre to X-rays for about 62 hours to capture the 'B form' of the molecule. That long exposure is what made the helix fingerprint so sharp. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/rosalind-franklin-photo-51-dna

question: Rosalind Franklin's careful X-ray work had produced Photo 51, the picture that held the secret of DNA's shape, but Franklin had not yet finished her own analysis and had not published it. Her colleague Maurice Wilkins then took her photograph and did something with it that Franklin did not know about. What did Wilkins do?
answer: He showed it to James Watson without her permission
choices: He showed it to James Watson without her permission
He locked it away in a safe for years
He mailed it back to Franklin unopened
He published it under his own name
context: Wilkins showed Franklin's Photo 51 to Watson without her knowledge or consent, and that image became the evidence that let Watson and Crick crack the structure. Source: https://www.kcl.ac.uk/photo-51-and-the-discovery-of-dna

question: Watson and Crick were not the only ones racing to solve DNA. Linus Pauling, the most famous chemist in the world, published his own DNA model in early 1953 and got it badly wrong: his version had three strands instead of two, turned inside-out so that nothing held it together. A copy of Pauling's flawed paper reached Watson early through a surprising connection. Who passed it to Watson?
answer: Pauling's son, Peter Pauling
choices: Pauling's son, Peter Pauling
Pauling's rival, Francis Crick
Pauling's assistant, Maurice Wilkins
Pauling's colleague, Rosalind Franklin
context: Peter Pauling, Linus Pauling's own son, was a student at Cambridge and passed his father's paper to Watson. Seeing that even the great Pauling had failed told Watson and Crick the race was still open. Source: https://scarc.library.oregonstate.edu/coll/pauling/dna/narrative/page24.html

question: In 1962, the Nobel Prize in Medicine was awarded for working out the structure of DNA, the molecule of life itself. The prize can be shared by at most three people. Three men split it that year; the woman whose Photo 51 had been the crucial evidence was not among them. Which three shared the 1962 Nobel for DNA?
answer: Watson, Crick, and Wilkins
choices: Watson, Crick, and Wilkins
Watson, Crick, and Gosling
Watson, Crick, and Pauling
Crick, Wilkins, and Pauling
context: James Watson, Francis Crick, and Maurice Wilkins shared the 1962 prize. Rosalind Franklin, whose X-ray work was central, was not included: she had died in 1958, and a Nobel Prize cannot be awarded after death. Source: https://www.kcl.ac.uk/photo-51-and-the-discovery-of-dna

question: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray skill had produced the single most important clue to DNA's structure, yet she likely never learned that Watson and Crick had used her Photo 51 and her unpublished notes without asking. Before her death in 1958, Franklin threw herself into a brand-new line of X-ray research, publishing 17 papers in five years and helping create an entire field of science. Which new field did Franklin help found?
answer: The study of virus structures
choices: The study of virus structures
The study of ocean currents
The study of earthquakes
The study of comets
context: At Birkbeck College, Franklin used X-ray crystallography to map the tobacco mosaic virus and helped found structural virology, the study of the shapes of viruses. She died of ovarian cancer on 16 April 1958, aged only 37; after her death, Crick said her contribution to the DNA discovery had been critical. Source: https://www.sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/francis-crick-rosalind-franklin-james-watson-and-maurice-wilkins/

question: Watson and Crick realised something huge: because each base only ever pairs with one partner, every strand of DNA is a perfect mould for the other. Instead of trumpeting what this made possible, they buried it in one famously modest sentence ending their paper: 'It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible ___ for the genetic material.' How did that sentence end?
answer: copying mechanism
choices: copying mechanism
energy source
defence shield
growth signal
context: Because A always matches T and G always matches C, each strand carries all the information needed to rebuild the other, so DNA can unzip and copy itself. This single sentence, often called the greatest understatement in science, hinted at exactly how life passes on its instructions. Source: https://annex.exploratorium.edu/origins/coldspring/ideas/note-escaped.html

question: In Germany in November 1923, money lost value so fast that paper marks became worth less than the things they could be used for. Families stuffed bundles of banknotes into their stoves and burned them. Why did they burn the money instead of spending it?
answer: The banknotes were cheaper than buying firewood
choices: The banknotes were cheaper than buying firewood
The government had ordered all old money destroyed
Burning money was a traditional autumn festival
The ink on the notes was poisonous to touch
context: By late 1923 a bundle of marks cost less than the equivalent firewood, so Germans burned banknotes for heat and even pasted them on walls as wallpaper, since a one-mark note cost less than real wallpaper. Source: https://rarehistoricalphotos.com/banknotes-german-hyperinflation-1923/

question: During Germany's hyperinflation in 1923, a famous photograph shows two children standing beside a tall tower they had stacked and played with, like a pile of building blocks. What was the tower built from?
answer: Bundles of paper banknotes worth about one dollar
choices: Bundles of paper banknotes worth about one dollar
Loaves of stale bread the bakery threw away
Empty tin cans collected from the streets
Bricks taken from a bombed-out building
context: Children played with bricks and kites made of bundled banknotes; one famous photo shows kids beside a tower of 100,000 marks, worth roughly one U.S. dollar. Source: https://rarehistoricalphotos.com/banknotes-german-hyperinflation-1923/

question: By November 1923, prices in Germany rose so insanely that a single U.S. dollar could buy an almost unimaginable mountain of German marks. In 1914 the mark had traded at about 4 to the dollar. At the peak of the crisis, how many marks did one dollar buy?
answer: About 4.2 trillion marks
choices: About 4.2 trillion marks
About 4.2 million marks
About 42,000 marks
About 4,200 marks
context: At the peak in November 1923 one dollar was worth 4,210,500,000,000 marks, after the mark had traded around 4 to 5 to the dollar in 1914. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperinflation_in_the_Weimar_Republic

question: A German student in 1923 sat down at a cafe and ordered a cup of coffee for 5,000 marks. He drank it slowly, then ordered a second cup. By the time the waiter brought the second cup, its price had changed. What had happened to the price in the time it took to finish one cup?
answer: It had risen to 7,000 marks
choices: It had risen to 7,000 marks
It had stayed exactly the same
It had been cut in half as a discount
It had become free because the cafe ran out of change
context: Prices could double within hours; the student's second cup of coffee had jumped from 5,000 to 7,000 marks in the time it took to drink the first. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/hyperinflation-in-the-Weimar-Republic

question: As the German mark collapsed in 1923, people stopped trusting it and quietly began using a different everyday item as real money, because it was divisible, portable, and held its value. Workers traded it for goods when no one would take paper marks. What became the trusted money in the mark's place?
answer: Cigarettes
choices: Cigarettes
Postage stamps
Glass marbles
Train tickets
context: Cigarettes replaced the mark as everyday money, a real-life case of Gresham's law in reverse: cigarettes became the 'good money' people hoarded and used while the worthless mark became 'bad money.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperinflation_in_the_Weimar_Republic

question: By November 1923 the printed mark was hopeless, so Germany introduced a brand-new currency to stop the spiral. Its supply was strictly capped, and the new Reichsbank president Hjalmar Schacht refused every demand to print more. Within days prices stabilized. What was this rescue currency called?
answer: The Rentenmark
choices: The Rentenmark
The Goldmark
The Reichsthaler
The Federal mark
context: The Rentenmark, capped at 3.2 billion units and exchanged at 1 to 1 trillion old marks, ended the crisis; Schacht (Reichsbank president from Dec 22, 1923) refused to print more and prices stabilized within days. Source: https://www.britannica.com/place/Weimar-Republic/Toward-stabilization

question: When the U.S. Army searched the Little Bighorn battlefield two days after George Custer's command was wiped out in 1876, they found a single survivor of the fight, wounded with seven bullet wounds but still alive. What did the soldiers find?
answer: A cavalry horse
choices: A cavalry horse
A scout's dog
A young bugler
An army mule
context: The horse was Comanche, the mount of Captain Myles Keogh. In 1878 the regiment issued General Orders No. 7 naming him 'the only living representative of the bloody tragedy' and ruling that 'he will not be ridden by any person whatsoever, under any circumstances' — instead paraded saddled and draped in black. His preserved body still stands at the University of Kansas museum. (Wikipedia, 'Comanche (horse)'; University of Kansas Natural History Museum)

question: As the Ghost Dance spread among the Lakota in 1890, believers sewed special painted shirts and wore them in the face of the soldiers, trusting in one power they were sure the shirts held. What did the Lakota believe their Ghost Shirts could do?
answer: Turn aside bullets
choices: Turn aside bullets
Turn the wearer invisible
Heal any wound overnight
Call the buffalo back
context: The Ghost Dance began with a vision: on January 1, 1889, during a solar eclipse, the Paiute prophet Wovoka (Jack Wilson) fell into a trance and was told that if the people danced, the dead would rise, the buffalo would return, and the settlers would vanish. Fear of this peaceful dance is what brought the soldiers to Wounded Knee. (Britannica, 'Wovoka'; NPS, 'Wounded Knee and the Ghost Dance')

question: At a Sun Dance on Rosebud Creek in June 1876, the Lakota holy man Sitting Bull had a hundred small pieces of flesh cut from his arms and danced until he fainted from the blood loss. In the trance that followed he saw a sign his people read as a promise of victory. What did Sitting Bull see in his vision?
answer: Soldiers falling upside-down into the camp like grasshoppers
choices: Soldiers falling upside-down into the camp like grasshoppers
Fire sweeping the white men's forts off the plains
Buffalo returning in herds that hid the whole prairie
An eagle carrying off the soldiers' war banners
context: In the vision a voice said, 'I give you these because they have no ears' — meaning the soldiers would not listen. Weeks later at the Little Bighorn, Custer's soldiers did fall. (Intermountain Histories, 'Sitting Bull and the Sun Dance of 1876'; History.com, 'How Sitting Bull's Spirituality Fueled the Lakota Resistance')

question: Crazy Horse was the most feared war leader of the Lakota — the tactician who lured Captain Fetterman's whole command into a fatal ambush in 1866 and who flanked Custer from the north and west at the Little Bighorn. For all his fame, he held to one lifelong refusal that set him apart from other men. What did Crazy Horse refuse to do his entire life?
answer: Let anyone make a photograph of him
choices: Let anyone make a photograph of him
Speak the name of a dead warrior
Ride any horse but a white one
Take a single scalp in battle
context: He also refused to sign any document, and was famous for his humility. No verified photograph of Crazy Horse is known to exist. (Britannica, 'Crazy Horse'; Akta Lakota Museum, 'Crazy Horse')

question: In 1868 the United States signed the Fort Laramie Treaty, promising the Lakota that the Black Hills would be theirs 'as long as the grass should grow and the rivers flow.' Six years later an Army expedition under George Custer rode into those hills and found something there. Word of the discovery brought a flood of newcomers, the U.S. went back on its promise and demanded the Black Hills, and when the Lakota refused to sell, the Great Sioux War broke out. What did Custer's 1874 expedition find in the Black Hills?
answer: Gold
choices: Gold
Coal
Silver
Oil
context: An estimated 15,000 or more miners flooded the Black Hills after the 1874 find. The Lakota would not sell the land they had been promised forever, the U.S. broke the treaty, and the war began in 1876. (Smithsonian Magazine, '1868: Two Nations Made a Treaty. The U.S. Broke It'; National Archives, 'Sioux Treaty of 1868'; World History Encyclopedia, 'Great Sioux War')

question: On December 29, 1890, the 7th Cavalry surrounded a Lakota camp of about 350 people at Wounded Knee Creek, led by an ailing chief named Spotted Elk, and set four rapid-fire guns on the hill above. A shot rang out during a struggle over one warrior's rifle, and the soldiers opened fire. Between 250 and 300 Lakota died — and most of the dead belonged to one group. Who made up most of those killed at Wounded Knee?
answer: Unarmed women and children
choices: Unarmed women and children
The camp's mounted warriors
Aged chiefs and medicine men
Armed Ghost Dance fighters
context: Spotted Elk (Big Foot) was so sick with pneumonia he had to be carried on a wagon. A three-day blizzard then froze the bodies where they fell; days later a burial party laid about 150 frozen Lakota into one mass grave. The holy man Black Elk said, 'A people's dream died there.' Wounded Knee is remembered as the end of the Plains Indian Wars. (World History Encyclopedia, 'Wounded Knee Massacre'; History.com, 'What Happened at the Wounded Knee Massacre?')

question: In 1794 thousands of Pennsylvania farmers took up arms rather than pay the new federal tax on the whiskey they distilled. President George Washington gathered roughly 13,000 militiamen to march west and crush the revolt. What did Washington do that no sitting U.S. president has ever done before or since?
answer: He rode out at the head of the army to lead the troops himself
choices: He rode out at the head of the army to lead the troops himself
He declared the rebel counties to be outside the United States
He resigned the presidency to take up his old general's commission
He ordered the rebel towns burned to the ground as a warning
context: Washington personally rode west and reviewed the gathering militia at Bedford, Pennsylvania — the first and only time a sitting president has led troops in the field. He then handed command to Virginia Governor Henry 'Light-Horse Harry' Lee and returned to Philadelphia, while Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton stayed with the army. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whiskey_Rebellion

question: As George Washington's 13,000 troops marched west to put down the Whiskey Rebellion, they ran badly short of supplies and kept raiding farms along the way, stealing produce to feed themselves. Mocking their pillaging, locals pinned a ridiculous nickname on the army. What did people call Washington's soldiers?
answer: the Watermelon Army
choices: the Watermelon Army
the Whiskey Boys
the Liberty Pole Men
the Tom the Tinker Gang
context: Short on provisions, the troops raided farms for produce on the march, earning the mocking name the 'Watermelon Army.' (The rebels themselves were the 'Whiskey Boys.') By the time the army reached western Pennsylvania the rebels had melted away — there was no battle, and the show of force ended the rebellion without a fight. Source: https://paheritage.wpengine.com/article/whiskey-boys-versus-watermelon-army/

question: The white specks scattered through ancient Roman concrete were long shrugged off by scientists as proof of careless, sloppy mixing. Then a 2023 MIT study cracked the real reason the concrete lasts 2,000 years: what do these white specks actually do?
answer: They dissolve in rainwater and regrow as crystals that seal cracks back up
choices: They dissolve in rainwater and regrow as crystals that seal cracks back up
They trap tiny air bubbles and keep the heavy domes from caving in
They reflect sunlight and hold the whole structure cooler in the summer
They glue the volcanic ash together while the wet mix is still setting
context: The white specks are millimeter-scale 'lime clasts.' When a crack reaches one and rainwater seeps in, the lime dissolves and recrystallizes as calcium carbonate, sealing the gap 'almost like glue.' MIT proved it head-on: a Roman-recipe sample and a modern-style control were both cracked and flushed with water; within two weeks the Roman crack had healed shut and water could no longer flow, while the control never healed. The trick was 'hot mixing' with caustic quicklime, which Prof. Admir Masic says 'allows chemistries that are not possible if you only used slaked lime.' Source: MIT News, news.mit.edu/2023/roman-concrete-durability-lime-casts-0106, and Science Advances, Jan 2023. The sampled wall is the 2,000-year-old masonry at Privernum, Italy.

question: Modern engineers deliberately pick crushed rock that will NOT react with cement, because any chemical reaction could swell into a gel and crack the concrete. Geologist Marie Jackson found the Romans did the exact opposite in their seawater harbor walls, packing them with reactive volcanic ash on purpose. What did that endless reaction do to the walls over 2,000 years?
answer: It made them grow stronger as new crystals slowly knit the rock together
choices: It made them grow stronger as new crystals slowly knit the rock together
It made them dissolve away until only loose volcanic ash was left behind
It made them glow faintly from the minerals soaked up out of the seawater
It made them grow lighter and lighter until pieces floated free at high tide
context: Seawater filtering through the walls dissolves the volcanic ash and grows rare interlocking crystals (aluminous tobermorite and phillipsite) that bind the concrete tighter over the centuries. Around 79 CE the Roman writer Pliny the Elder had already described sea piers that become 'a single stone mass, impregnable to the waves and every day stronger' — confirmed by science almost 2,000 years later. Jackson contrasted modern building, which relies on steel rebar that rusts: at 120 years 'it would be a mass of corroding steel.' The proof came from four named ancient harbors — Portus Cosanus, Baianus Sinus in the Bay of Pozzuoli, Portus Neronis at Anzio, and Portus Traianus at Ostia. Source: Sci.News / EurekAlert, Marie Jackson (University of Utah), American Mineralogist 2017.

question: William Harvey wanted to disprove the 1,400-year teaching that the liver makes blood fresh from food which the organs then use up forever. So he did the arithmetic: the heart throws out about two ounces a beat, and at roughly 72 beats a minute that is over 500 pounds of blood pushed out every hour -- far more than a whole body holds or any liver could brew. What did that runaway number force Harvey to conclude?
answer: The same blood must travel in a circle and return to the heart
choices: The same blood must travel in a circle and return to the heart
The heart secretly makes the blood it pumps each hour
The lungs replace the blood faster than the liver can
Blood is far lighter inside the body than once weighed
context: Harvey published this in De Motu Cordis (1628): the blood moves 'as it were, in a circle.' His proof was not a new instrument but a calculation -- the heart moves more blood in an hour than the body could possibly hold, so it must recirculate. Discovery by counting. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exercitatio_Anatomica_de_Motu_Cordis_et_Sanguinis_in_Animalibus

question: William Harvey spent his life proving the blood is not used up but travels round and round the body in a closed loop. In 1657, at age 79, a brain hemorrhage struck him speechless on his deathbed. Unable to talk, he made signs asking his attendants for one thing -- the standard treatment of his day -- and died that same evening. What did the discoverer of circulation gesture to have done to him?
answer: To be bled, the old bloodletting cure of his era
choices: To be bled, the old bloodletting cure of his era
To be carried outside into the cold night air
To be given the king's own physician at once
To be read his own book on the heart aloud
context: Bloodletting was the routine remedy of the 1600s. The man who had revealed how blood truly moves through the body could not speak to refuse the era's blood-draining cure, and died that evening. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Harvey

question: Legend says that at the Battle of Edgehill in 1642, King Charles I handed his two young sons -- Prince Charles and the Duke of York -- to his physician William Harvey for safekeeping. As cannon fire boomed across the field, the calm Harvey pulled the boys behind a hedge and did something startling for the middle of a battle, until a cannon shot struck the ground nearby and made him move. What did Harvey calmly do behind that hedge?
answer: Took a book from his pocket and read to the boys
choices: Took a book from his pocket and read to the boys
Drew a sword and stood guard over the boys
Dug a shallow trench to shield the boys
Mounted a horse to gallop the boys away
context: This often-told story has Harvey, ever the scholar, settling the princes behind a hedge and reading to them mid-battle until a cannonball landed close enough to force him to a safer spot. Told as a beloved anecdote of his unflappable temperament. Source: https://history.rcp.ac.uk/blog/war-william-harvey-battle-edgehill  (Legend.)

question: On 13 May 1940, just three days into the job, Winston Churchill stood before the House of Commons to ask Britain to follow him into the war. He warned he could promise them no easy victory, only hardship and struggle. Which four-word promise of hardship did he offer?
answer: Blood, toil, tears and sweat
choices: Blood, toil, tears and sweat
Peace, order and good government
Liberty, equality and fraternity
Faith, hope and charity
context: Churchill's first speech as Prime Minister, 13 May 1940. Asked what the policy and aim were, he answered: 'Victory. Victory at all costs... for without victory there is no survival.' Source: International Churchill Society, 'Blood, Toil, Tears and Sweat.'

question: Winston Churchill ran much of the war from his bed and bath, but when the air-raid sirens wailed he needed clothes he could throw on in seconds. So he had a tailor make him a one-piece zip-up garment he nicknamed his 'siren suit.' What everyday object was this wartime outfit?
answer: A one-piece zip-up jumpsuit
choices: A one-piece zip-up jumpsuit
A long woollen naval greatcoat
A buttoned tweed hunting jacket
A flowing silk dressing gown
context: His staff just called it his 'rompers.' He owned several, including a bottle-green velvet one and a black velvet version for dinner; one survives at his London tailor, Turnbull & Asser. Source: International Churchill Society, 'The siren suit.'

question: After the small ships pulled over 338,000 trapped soldiers off the beaches at Dunkirk in 1940, Britons were tempted to celebrate. Winston Churchill cautioned the Commons that 'wars are not won by evacuations,' then promised to fight on every beach, field, and street, ending on three words that became Britain's vow. What were they?
answer: We shall never surrender
choices: We shall never surrender
We shall sue for honourable terms
We shall hold the Channel ports
We shall regroup in Canada
context: The 'We Shall Fight on the Beaches' speech, 4 June 1940. The rescue had wildly beaten the 45,000 first hoped for, but Churchill refused to call a retreat a triumph. Source: International Churchill Society, 'We Shall Fight on the Beaches.'

question: Speaking to Canada's Parliament on 30 December 1941, Winston Churchill reminded them that France's generals had sneered that within three weeks 'England will have her neck wrung like a chicken.' He paused, then fired back a two-part jab that brought the whole chamber down laughing. What did he say?
answer: Some chicken! Some neck!
choices: Some chicken! Some neck!
We are not dead yet!
England never surrenders!
Try it if you dare!
context: Britain had stood alone and unconquered for over a year, making the French prediction look foolish. Source: Wikipedia, 'Winston Churchill's address to the Canadian Parliament (1941)'; America's National Churchill Museum.

question: On 18 June 1940, France had fallen and Britain stood completely alone against Hitler. Winston Churchill told the Commons that if they failed, the whole world would 'sink into the abyss of a new Dark Age.' Yet in the same breath he gave that desperate moment a name people would remember for a thousand years. What did he call it?
answer: This was their finest hour
choices: This was their finest hour
This was Britain standing alone
This was the Empire at its peak
This was their darkest hour
context: 'Their Finest Hour' speech: 'if the British Empire and its Commonwealth last for a thousand years, men will still say, This was their finest hour.' He opened it noting 'the Battle of France is over... the Battle of Britain is about to begin.' Source: International Churchill Society, 'Their Finest Hour.'

question: On 16 August 1940, Winston Churchill watched from an underground bunker as every RAF fighter squadron was flung into the sky at once to defend Britain. Climbing into his car afterward, he told his general, 'Don't speak to me; I have never been so moved' — then spoke a single sentence honouring the handful of pilots. Which tribute was it?
answer: So much owed by so many to so few
choices: So much owed by so many to so few
A debt the nation could never repay
The bravest airmen the world had seen
Britain owed its life to its pilots
context: 'Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few.' First spoken in the car to General Hastings Ismay, repeated to the Commons four days later on 20 August 1940. Source: Wikipedia, 'Never was so much owed by so many to so few.'

question: Winston Churchill loved to greet crowds with two raised fingers in a 'V for Victory.' But early on, his own staff had to quietly take him aside and beg him to stop — he was about to cause a national scandal with the gesture. What was the problem with how Churchill was making the V sign?
answer: He was flashing it the rude way, palm inward
choices: He was flashing it the rude way, palm inward
He had borrowed it from the German enemy
He was holding up the wrong number of fingers
He had stolen it from a rival politician
context: Palm-inward, the two-finger V is the British working-class equivalent of flipping someone off. The V-for-Victory idea came from exiled Belgian politician Victor de Laveleye on the BBC in January 1941. Churchill switched to palm-out for the rest of his life. Source: Wikipedia, 'V sign.'

question: On 10 May 1940 — the very morning German armies came smashing across Western Europe — the King sent for the 65-year-old Winston Churchill to lead Britain. That night Churchill wrote that he felt strangely calm, sure his whole life had pointed to this one trial. In his own words, how did he describe that feeling?
answer: Walking with destiny
choices: Walking with destiny
Born for this trial
Chosen by the King
A man of his hour
context: 'I felt as though I was walking with destiny, and that all my past life had been but a preparation for this hour and for this trial.' He became Prime Minister the same day Germany launched its blitzkrieg in the West. Source: International Churchill Society, 'Walking with Destiny.'

question: All through the 1930s Winston Churchill was shut out of power, standing in a near-empty Commons reciting Germany's growing tanks and warplanes to colleagues who refused to listen and warning against making deals with Hitler. He later named the first volume of his war memoirs after this slowly approaching danger. What did he title it?
answer: The Gathering Storm
choices: The Gathering Storm
The Wilderness Years
The Locust Years
The Coming Reckoning
context: Only after the 1938 Munich deal and Hitler's seizure of Czechoslovakia did opinion shift to 'Churchill was right.' These were his 'wilderness years.' Source: International Churchill Society, Wilderness Years; America's National Churchill Museum, 'The Gathering Storm.'

question: The war's true turning point happened in private. On 28 May 1940, Foreign Secretary Lord Halifax pressed the cabinet to ask Mussolini to broker a peace deal with Hitler. Winston Churchill answered that nations that go down fighting rise again, while those that surrender tamely are finished — then told his ministers exactly how he would rather see Britain's long story end. How did he say it should end, if it must?
answer: With each of us choking in his own blood upon the ground
choices: With each of us choking in his own blood upon the ground
With the whole island buried under the rubble of London
With the last of the army driven into the sea at Dunkirk
With the people starved into surrender by the U-boats
context: 'If this long island story of ours is to end at last, let it end only when each one of us lies choking in his own blood upon the ground.' Minister Hugh Dalton recorded 'not even the faintest flicker of dissent'; ministers ran up to pat Churchill on the back. The peace idea was dead. Source: Wikipedia, 'War cabinet crisis, May 1940'; Hugh Dalton's diary.

question: Almost everyone thinks they have heard the live wartime broadcast of Winston Churchill growling 'we shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight in the fields.' In truth the public never heard him deliver it — he spoke it only to Parliament, which was not on the radio. So where did the famous recording everyone knows actually come from?
answer: He recorded it himself for a gramophone in 1949
choices: He recorded it himself for a gramophone in 1949
An actor secretly read it for him on the radio
He whispered it low so the enemy would not hear
The BBC lost the only wartime tape that existed
context: Churchill was persuaded to record his great speeches for posterity years after the war. The persistent 1972 story that actor Norman Shelley impersonated him on the wireless is a debunked myth. Source: International Churchill Society Myths, 'An actor read Churchill's wartime speeches'; Smithsonian Magazine.

question: In 1953 Winston Churchill — privately hoping to win the Nobel Peace Prize — instead won the Nobel Prize for Literature, partly for the speeches that had rallied a nation. The American broadcaster Edward R. Murrow captured what those speeches had done with one unforgettable image. According to Murrow, what had Churchill done with the English language?
answer: He mobilized the English language and sent it into battle
choices: He mobilized the English language and sent it into battle
He turned the BBC wireless into a weapon as deadly as any gun
He handed a frightened, beaten nation its lost courage back
He wrote the cleanest and finest English prose of his whole age
context: The 1953 Nobel honoured 'his mastery of historical and biographical description as well as for brilliant oratory in defending exalted human values.' Churchill, who wanted the Peace Prize, was a little deflated it was for Literature. Source: Nobel Prize, Literature 1953; Wikipedia, '1953 Nobel Prize in Literature.'

question: On January 8, 1918, with World War I still raging, President Woodrow Wilson stood before Congress and announced a numbered blueprint to end the war and remake the world. How many points did his plan have?
answer: Fourteen points
choices: Fourteen points
Seven points
Twenty-one points
Forty points
context: Wilson laid out fourteen numbered points before a joint session of Congress on January 8, 1918, as his blueprint for peace. Source: National WWI Museum, https://www.theworldwar.org/learn/peace/fourteen-points

question: President Woodrow Wilson's fourteenth and final point called for 'a general association of nations' to guarantee the independence of great and small nations alike. What world body grew out of that idea?
answer: The League of Nations
choices: The League of Nations
The United Nations
The Holy Alliance
The Hague Court
context: Point 14 sought 'mutual guarantees of political independence and territorial integrity to great and small nations alike' — the seed of the League of Nations. Source: National WWI Museum, https://www.theworldwar.org/learn/peace/fourteen-points

question: President Woodrow Wilson's very first point demanded an end to the secret deals struck behind closed doors that he blamed for the war. He summed up the new rule in a famous five-word phrase. What did he call for?
answer: 'Open covenants of peace, openly arrived at'
choices: 'Open covenants of peace, openly arrived at'
'Peace without victory, justice for all'
'The world made safe for democracy'
'A war to end all wars forever'
context: Point 1 demanded 'open covenants of peace, openly arrived at' — no more secret treaties. Point 2 was 'freedom of the seas.' Source: National WWI Museum; American Presidency Project full text, https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/address-joint-session-congress-the-conditions-peace-the-fourteen-points

question: President Woodrow Wilson did not write the Fourteen Points alone. His friend Colonel Edward M. House had secretly assembled a team of about 150 geographers, historians, and political scientists to guide the peace. What was this brain-trust called?
answer: The Inquiry
choices: The Inquiry
The Brain Trust
The Black Chamber
The House Committee
context: Colonel House's secret team of ~150 scholars, called 'The Inquiry,' produced roughly 2,000 reports and over 1,200 maps. Source: US State Dept Office of the Historian, https://history.state.gov/milestones/1914-1920/fourteen-points

question: France's Prime Minister Georges Clemenceau, who fought President Woodrow Wilson across the Paris peace table, mocked the American's lofty idealism with one cutting line history still remembers. What did Clemenceau say?
answer: 'God Himself was content with ten commandments. Wilson gives us fourteen.'
choices: 'God Himself was content with ten commandments. Wilson gives us fourteen.'
'Wilson speaks like Jesus Christ but acts like Lloyd George.'
'America is the only nation to pass from barbarism to decadence with no civilization between.'
'I have a list of fourteen points; Wilson has not even ten fingers.'
context: Clemenceau's quip was recorded in Lord Esher's diary on October 14, 1918. He resented Wilson's 'academic idealism' and his assumed 'monopoly of international morality.' Source: roadstothegreatwar-ww1.blogspot.com (citing Lord Esher diary and Robert Hanks).

question: The threading idea of the Fourteen Points was self-determination — letting each people govern itself. But President Woodrow Wilson's own Secretary of State, Robert Lansing, privately dreaded it, warning it would raise hopes that could never be met. What three-word verdict did Lansing give the phrase?
answer: 'Simply loaded with dynamite'
choices: 'Simply loaded with dynamite'
'A noble experiment'
'Built upon sand'
'The dream of fools'
context: Lansing feared self-determination 'will raise hopes which can never be realized,' cost thousands of lives, and be discredited as an idealist's dream. Source: 1914-1918-Online WWI Encyclopedia, https://encyclopedia.1914-1918-online.net/article/lansing-robert/

question: Robert Lansing warned that President Woodrow Wilson's principle of self-determination — meant to free oppressed peoples — was 'loaded with dynamite.' In the 1930s a dictator seized that very principle to justify annexing German-speaking lands, proving Lansing grimly right. Who did so?
answer: Adolf Hitler
choices: Adolf Hitler
Benito Mussolini
Joseph Stalin
Francisco Franco
context: Hitler made self-determination a central tenet of Nazi Party policy in the 1930s to justify annexing German-speaking territory. Source: 1914-1918-Online WWI Encyclopedia, https://encyclopedia.1914-1918-online.net/article/lansing-robert/

question: At the 1919 Paris Peace Conference the Allies wanted to punish Germany, not chase President Woodrow Wilson's ideals, so most of the Fourteen Points were watered down or dropped. Which single piece survived into the Treaty of Versailles?
answer: The League of Nations
choices: The League of Nations
Freedom of the seas
Open covenants of peace
Free trade between nations
context: The Allies sought punishment over idealism; the League of Nations was the one major point that survived into the Treaty of Versailles. Source: HISTORY, https://www.history.com/articles/14-point-plan-woodrow-wilson-world-war-i

question: President Woodrow Wilson won his League of Nations at Paris but lost it at home. In March 1920 the U.S. Senate, led by Henry Cabot Lodge, rejected the Treaty 49–35 over fears it could drag America into foreign wars. What was the result for the United States?
answer: It never joined the League it had invented
choices: It never joined the League it had invented
It joined the League only as an observer
It built a rival American alliance instead
It joined but withdrew within a year
context: Lodge objected that Article X could commit America to war without Congress's consent. The Treaty failed 49–35, and the U.S. never joined the League. Source: US State Dept Office of the Historian, https://history.state.gov/milestones/1914-1920/league

question: Desperate to rally Americans behind his League, the 62-year-old President Woodrow Wilson drove himself across 8,000 miles in 22 days of speeches despite pounding headaches. Days after his last speech in Pueblo, Colorado, on September 25, 1919, what struck him down?
answer: A massive stroke that left him paralyzed on his left side
choices: A massive stroke that left him paralyzed on his left side
A heart attack during a final rally
A collapse from exhaustion and pneumonia
A fall from the speaker's platform
context: Wilson's last speech came at Pueblo on Sept 25, 1919; on Oct 2 he suffered a massive stroke that paralyzed his left side. Source: HISTORY, https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/october-2/woodrow-wilson-suffers-a-stroke; Pueblo speech, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pueblo_speech

question: After President Woodrow Wilson's stroke left him unable to govern for months, one person controlled who could even see him, turning away the Vice President and Secretary of State alike — what historians call a 'shadow presidency.' Who held that power?
answer: First Lady Edith Bolling Galt Wilson
choices: First Lady Edith Bolling Galt Wilson
Vice President Thomas Marshall
Colonel Edward M. House
Secretary of State Robert Lansing
context: Edith Wilson and the president's physician controlled all access to him, fending off even the Vice President and Secretary of State — a 'shadow presidency.' Source: University of Arizona Libraries, https://lib.arizona.edu/hsl/materials/collections/secret-illness/wilson

question: In May 1915 a Canadian army doctor, John McCrae, looked out from a dressing station at the wild red flowers blooming among the fresh graves and wrote 'In Flanders Fields' — 'the poppies blow / Between the crosses, row on row.' That blood-red flower he named in the poem became the worldwide symbol people wear every year to remember the war dead. Which flower is it?
answer: The poppy
choices: The poppy
The rose
The lily
The daisy
context: The poppies were real: their seeds sprout in churned-up, disturbed earth, so they bloomed blood-red across battlefield soil torn by shelling. McCrae wrote the poem on 3 May 1915 at Essex Farm during the Second Battle of Ypres, the day after his friend Lieutenant Alexis Helmer was killed by a shell. Sources: britannica.com/topic/In-Flanders-Fields; greatwar.nl/frames/default-poppies.html

question: The poet Wilfred Owen wrote 'Dulce et Decorum Est,' a poem about a soldier 'guttering, choking, drowning' in a poison-gas attack. On 4 November 1918 Owen himself was cut down by German machine-gun fire while leading his men across the Sambre-Oise Canal — just one week before the war ended. The telegram telling his parents he was dead reached their home in Shrewsbury at a cruelly perfect moment. What was happening as it arrived?
answer: The church bells were ringing to celebrate the Armistice
choices: The church bells were ringing to celebrate the Armistice
A victory parade was marching through the town
A memorial service was being held for the fallen
A newspaper was printing the casualty lists
context: The telegram arrived on Armistice Day, 11 November 1918, as the bells rang to celebrate the war's end. Owen died at Ors, France. Sources: writersinspire.org/content/4-11-november-1918-wilfred-owen-armistice-day-memory-history; history.com/this-day-in-history/november-4/poet-wilfred-owen-killed-in-action

question: Wilfred Owen's poem 'Dulce et Decorum Est' takes its title from a Latin line written about 2,000 years earlier by the Roman poet Horace — 'It is sweet and proper to die for one's country,' the proudest boast of classical war-glory. After describing a soldier drowning in poison gas, Owen turns on that ancient line and brands it with three blunt words. What does he call it?
answer: The old Lie
choices: The old Lie
A noble dream
The soldier's hope
A sacred duty
context: Owen ends the poem by calling 'Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori' 'The old Lie' — taking the proudest line of Roman war-glory (Horace, Odes Book III, poem 2) and turning it into an accusation. Sources: poetryfoundation.org/poems/46560/dulce-et-decorum-est; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulce_et_decorum_est_pro_patria_mori

question: In 490 BC, about 10,000 Athenians and 1,000 Plataeans faced a far larger Persian army on the plain of Marathon. Their general Miltiades gave an order almost no Greek army had ever dared against the Persians. What did the heavily outnumbered Greeks do as they crossed the long open ground toward the enemy?
answer: They charged the whole way at a dead run.
choices: They charged the whole way at a dead run.
They formed a tight circle and waited to be surrounded.
They sent their cavalry ahead to scatter the enemy first.
They fell back into the hills to wait for nightfall.
context: Herodotus records a wildly lopsided result: 192 Athenians dead against 6,400 Persians. The running charge let the Greeks close the deadly arrow-zone fast and hit hard. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Marathon (Herodotus 6.117).

question: Before Marathon, Athens sent a long-distance runner named Pheidippides racing roughly 140 miles over the mountains to beg Sparta for help, a run he finished the day after he set out. Herodotus reports one strange thing that happened to Pheidippides on the lonely mountain road. What was it?
answer: The god Pan met him and asked why Athens neglected his worship.
choices: The god Pan met him and asked why Athens neglected his worship.
A Persian scout chased him for a full day and night.
He lost the road in thick fog and wandered for three days.
A Spartan patrol seized him at the border as a spy.
context: The familiar story of a runner who raced to Athens and dropped dead, giving us the word 'marathon,' is a LATER invention, first told by Plutarch some 500 years afterward. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pheidippides (Herodotus 6.105-106).

question: Xerxes, the Persian king, needed to march a vast army out of Asia and into Europe across the Hellespont, the sea-strait that divides the two continents. There was no way to ferry everyone across fast enough. How did Xerxes get his whole army over the water?
answer: He lashed hundreds of boats side by side into a floating road.
choices: He lashed hundreds of boats side by side into a floating road.
He waited for winter and marched across the frozen strait.
He dug a canal so the troops could walk the dry bed.
He built tall stone towers and strung rope walkways between them.
context: Herodotus counts about 674 boats, anchored and bound with giant cables of white flax and papyrus, then planked over and covered with brushwood and earth so the army could march across the sea. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xerxes'_pontoon_bridges (Herodotus 7.36).

question: When a storm smashed apart the first bridge Xerxes had thrown across the Hellespont, the king did not simply rebuild it. He decided the SEA itself had defied him and must be punished. As his heralds shouted that Xerxes would cross 'whether you wish it or not,' what did he order done to the water?
answer: Given three hundred lashes of the whip and shackled with iron fetters.
choices: Given three hundred lashes of the whip and shackled with iron fetters.
Boiled with fire-ships until the waves lay calm.
Cursed aloud by every priest in the army for a day and a night.
Pumped back with great engines to lay bare the seabed.
context: Heralds cried, 'You hateful water... Xerxes the king will pass over you, whether you wish it or not.' He also had the engineers who built the failed bridge beheaded. Source: brians.wsu.edu/2016/11/10 (Herodotus 7.34-35).

question: At Abydos, Xerxes sat above his enormous army and fleet, the shore packed with men as far as he could see, and at the very height of his power he suddenly burst into tears. When his uncle Artabanus asked why, what did the king say had come over him?
answer: Pity, that not one of this whole host would be alive in a hundred years.
choices: Pity, that not one of this whole host would be alive in a hundred years.
Fear, that the gods of the Greeks were stronger than his own.
Shame, that so many would die only to make him famous.
Doubt, that his own generals were secretly plotting against him.
context: Herodotus gives the words: 'There came upon me a sudden pity, when I thought of the shortness of man's life... not one will be alive when a hundred years are gone by.' Source: Herodotus 7.45-46 (wikisource, Godley translation).

question: Xerxes' best soldiers formed an elite corps that always stood exactly ten thousand strong. The instant any one of them was killed, wounded, or fell sick, another man stepped into his place, so the unit never showed a single gap, though of course its men died like any others. By what name did the Greeks know this corps?
answer: the Immortals
choices: the Immortals
the Companions
the Spearmen
the Shieldbearers
context: They never truly were deathless, that was the point of the nickname. Herodotus may even have confused the Old Persian 'anushiya' (companions) with 'anausa' (immortal). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immortals_(Achaemenid_Empire) (Herodotus 7.83).

question: At the pass of Thermopylae, a Spartan named Dienekes was warned that the Persian archers were so many their arrows would blot out the sun. Far from being frightened, Dienekes gave a reply that Herodotus calls the finest of all the Spartan one-liners spoken that day. What did Dienekes say?
answer: Good, then we shall fight in the shade.
choices: Good, then we shall fight in the shade.
Good, then our spears will fly twice as far.
Good, then the gods are watching us closely.
Good, then their quivers will soon be empty.
context: Herodotus singles this out (7.226) as the best of many Spartan retorts that day. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dienekes (Herodotus 7.226).

question: For three days the Greeks held the narrow pass at Thermopylae and the huge Persian army could not break through. Then a local man named Ephialtes came secretly to Xerxes, hoping for a reward, and what he handed over doomed the defenders. What did Ephialtes give the Persians?
answer: A hidden mountain trail that ran around behind the Greeks.
choices: A hidden mountain trail that ran around behind the Greeks.
The secret password the Greek sentries used at night.
A poison to foul the only spring in the Greek camp.
The hour the Greek king meant to slip away by sea.
context: Persian troops used the Anopaia path to come up behind the defenders. Ephialtes never got his Persian reward, the Greeks put a bounty on his head, and his name became the Greek word for 'traitor.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ephialtes_of_Trachis (Herodotus 7.213-218).

question: With the Persians closing in, Athens asked the oracle at Delphi how to survive and was told that only a 'wooden wall' would save the city. Some Athenians wanted to barricade the Acropolis with timber. The leader Themistocles insisted the oracle meant something else entirely. What did Themistocles argue the 'wooden wall' really was?
answer: The city's fleet of warships.
choices: The city's fleet of warships.
The sacred grove of Athena.
The hill-fort's ancient palisade.
The shields locked tight in the phalanx.
context: Themistocles also read the line about 'divine Salamis' to mean Greece's ENEMIES, not Athens, would die there. He staked the city's survival on its ships. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_oracular_statements_from_Delphi (Herodotus 7.140-143).

question: Themistocles wanted to fight the huge Persian navy inside the cramped strait of Salamis, where its great size would only get in its way, but the Persians would never sail in willingly. So he secretly sent his servant Sicinnus across to Xerxes with a lie. What lie did Sicinnus tell to spring the trap?
answer: That the Greeks were about to flee, so Xerxes should block the exits.
choices: That the Greeks were about to flee, so Xerxes should block the exits.
That the Greek crews had mutinied and would switch sides.
That a great storm was coming that would wreck the Greek fleet.
That Athens had already surrendered to the king in secret.
context: Xerxes obediently sealed the exits, trapping his own oversized fleet in waters too cramped to maneuver. About 370 Greek triremes wrecked a fleet of 600-plus; Herodotus says roughly 300 Persian ships were lost to about 40 Greek. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Salamis (Herodotus 8.75-76).

question: One of Xerxes' own naval captains was a woman, Queen Artemisia of Caria. Cornered in the chaos of Salamis with a Greek ship chasing her down, she rammed and sank a ship on her OWN side to look like a Greek and slip away. Xerxes, who thought she had sunk an enemy, watched in astonishment and said something about her. What did Xerxes say?
answer: My men have become women, and my women men.
choices: My men have become women, and my women men.
Even my enemies cannot match one woman of Caria.
Bring me a hundred more captains like the queen.
The sea itself has chosen her over all my admirals.
context: Xerxes never realized the rammed ship was on his own side. Artemisia I of Caria was one of the war's most remarkable commanders. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemisia_I_of_Caria (Herodotus 8.87-88).

question: A year after Salamis, the Greeks and Persians met for the final land battle at Plataea, where Greece fielded the largest army of armored hoplites it ever gathered. The fighting hung in the balance until one event shattered the Persian side completely and ended the whole invasion. What turned the battle?
answer: The Persian general Mardonius was killed, and his leaderless army fled.
choices: The Persian general Mardonius was killed, and his leaderless army fled.
A sudden eclipse panicked the Persian ranks into retreat.
The Persian cavalry bogged down crossing a flooded river.
The Greeks set fire to the Persian supply camp before dawn.
context: About 5,000 full Spartiates and 8,000 Athenians, among tens of thousands, fought under the Spartan regent Pausanias. When Mardonius fell fighting the Spartans, his army broke. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Plataea (Herodotus 9.61-65).

question: According to a story first told by Plutarch some five hundred years later, so it is cherished tradition more than recorded history, Xerxes sent word to King Leonidas at Thermopylae offering peace if the Spartans would simply lay down their weapons. Tradition says Leonidas sent back a defiant two-word answer. What were the two words?
answer: Come and take them.
choices: Come and take them.
We never surrender.
Try your luck.
Over our bodies.
context: The Greek phrase is 'Molon labe.' It does NOT appear in Herodotus and is first recorded by Plutarch about 500 years afterward, so it is best treated as cherished tradition rather than reported fact. Source: badancient.com/claims/molon-labe (Plutarch, Moralia 225c).  (Legend.)

question: On October 19, 1781, after Lord Cornwallis's siege collapsed, the beaten British army marched out of Yorktown to lay down its weapons before the American colonists it had spent years calling rebels. Legend says the British band played a tune whose very title mocked the moment. Which tune does the legend name?
answer: "The World Turned Upside Down"
choices: "The World Turned Upside Down"
"The British Grenadiers"
"The Rogue's March"
"Over the Hills and Far Away"
context: Per the legend, a British army surrendering to its own rebellious colonists was exactly the upside-down world the tune named. Often retold, though the documentary evidence is thin — so historians treat the band's choice of song as legend, not certain fact. Source: History.com 'Victory at Yorktown'; American Battlefield Trust.

question: Lord Cornwallis dug his army in on the Yorktown peninsula in 1781, certain a British rescue fleet would sail down from New York to carry him to safety. Instead he was trapped with no way out, and surrendered. What sealed his fate before any rescue could reach him?
answer: The French fleet beat the British navy and blockaded the bay
choices: The French fleet beat the British navy and blockaded the bay
Washington's men stormed the British forts in a night bayonet charge
Lafayette's troops captured the narrow neck of the peninsula
A storm scattered the British rescue ships off the Virginia coast
context: Admiral de Grasse's French fleet defeated the British navy at the Battle of the Chesapeake on September 5, 1781, then sealed the bay — so Cornwallis had no escape by water and no rescue by sea. It was the French alliance's payoff in full. The hoped-for fleet under Admiral Thomas Graves never came. Source: Wikipedia 'Battle of the Chesapeake'; Britannica.

question: On 12 April 1961 the 27-year-old Soviet pilot Yuri Gagarin sat atop the Vostok 1 rocket, about to become the first human in space. As the engines lit and the rocket climbed, he keyed his radio and shouted a single word that became the most famous cry of the whole Space Race. What did Gagarin shout?
answer: "Poyekhali!" — "Let's go!"
choices: "Poyekhali!" — "Let's go!"
"Vpered!" — "Forward!"
"Slava!" — "Glory!"
"Davai!" — "Come on!"
context: "Poyekhali!" (Russian for "Let's go!", also rendered "Off we go!") rang out as Vostok 1 lifted off, and it became the signature exclamation of the Space Race. Gagarin circled the entire Earth once in a single orbit lasting about 108 minutes — the first human ever to see the whole planet turn beneath him. Source: https://www.planetary.org/space-missions/vostok-1

question: Yuri Gagarin rode Vostok 1 once around the whole Earth and survived re-entry, but he never actually rode the capsule all the way to the ground. About 7 km up, over the Saratov region near the town of Engels, what did Gagarin do to finish the trip?
answer: He ejected from the capsule and parachuted down on his own
choices: He ejected from the capsule and parachuted down on his own
He rode the capsule down under its own braking parachute
He steered the capsule to a gentle splashdown at sea
He fired retro-rockets to set the capsule down upright
context: Gagarin ejected about 7 km up and floated down by parachute separately from Vostok 1, touching down near Engels in the Saratov region. The Federation Aeronautique Internationale's record rules required a pilot to land inside the craft, so Soviet officials hid the ejection at first — and once it came out, the FAI revised its rules and certified Gagarin's records anyway. Source: https://www.esa.int/About_Us/50_years_of_ESA/50_years_of_humans_in_space/The_flight_of_Vostok_1

question: In 1414 the Chinese admiral Zheng He sailed his treasure fleet home from the Indian Ocean carrying a live animal China had never seen: a giraffe, brought all the way from the coast of Africa. The emperor's court was astonished and hailed the strange beast as an auspicious creature of legend, said to appear only when a wise and virtuous ruler sat on the throne. Which mythical beast did the court declare the giraffe to be?
answer: A qilin
choices: A qilin
A dragon
A phoenix
A tiger spirit
context: Courtiers declared the giraffe a qilin, the mythical beast said to appear only under a sage ruler, treating it as heaven's blessing on the throne-usurping Yongle Emperor. The court painter Shen Du painted it with a poem calling it a qilin; that silk scroll survives today in the Philadelphia Museum of Art. Source: smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/peculiar-story-giraffes-medieval-china-180963737/

question: When Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492, he sailed with three small ships and about 90 men. Yet decades earlier, in 1405, the Chinese admiral Zheng He set out on his very first voyage with a fleet so enormous it is hard to picture: dozens of giant 'treasure ships' leading hundreds of vessels in all. Roughly how many men sailed in Zheng He's first fleet?
answer: About 28,000
choices: About 3,000
About 10,000
About 28,000
About 60,000
context: Zheng He's first fleet of 1405 carried roughly 27,800 men aboard about 62 giant treasure ships leading hundreds of vessels — almost ninety years before Columbus crossed with three ships and around 90 men. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ming_treasure_voyages ; worldhistory.org/article/1334/the-seven-voyages-of-zheng-he/

question: By the time the Chinese admiral Zheng He died around 1433, his treasure fleets had reached the coast of East Africa — generations before any European ship sailed so far. But after his death the Ming court forbade further voyages and let its great shipyards fall silent. To make sure no future emperor could ever send out the treasure fleets again, court officials took action against Zheng He's voyage logs and sea charts. What did these officials do to the records?
answer: Burned the records
choices: Burned the records
Locked the records in a vault
Hid the records in a temple
Buried the records at sea
context: After Zheng He's death the Ming court turned inward, halting the voyages and restricting sea travel; officials (associated with the minister Liu Daxia) suppressed or destroyed the voyage records so no emperor could sail again — helping hand the oceans, and the coming age of exploration, to Europe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zheng_He ; mingdynastyhistory.com/why-china-stop-zheng-he-voyages/

question: The best-preserved ziggurat is the Great Ziggurat of Ur, a brick mountain in southern Iraq raised around 2100 BCE by King Ur-Nammu. A shrine once crowned its summit, the earthly home of the city's patron god. Which heavenly body was that god, Nanna?
answer: The moon
choices: The moon
The sun
The morning star
The north wind
context: Nanna (also called Sin) was the moon god and patron deity of Ur. The temple to him stood at the very top of the ziggurat, but it has not survived. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ziggurat_of_Ur

question: Babylon's giant ziggurat was named Etemenanki, 'House of the Foundation of Heaven and Earth,' and rebuilt to its towering form by Nebuchadnezzar II. Scholars identify this real brick tower as the building behind which famous story?
answer: The Tower of Babel
choices: The Tower of Babel
The Walls of Jericho
Noah's Ark
The Temple of Solomon
context: Etemenanki was dedicated to Marduk, king of the Babylonian gods. Most scholars think Babylon's tiered ziggurat is the real structure behind the Bible's Tower of Babel. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etemenanki
